10625-a-concise-dictionary-of-middle-eng:
A. L. Mayhew of Wadham College, Oxford, and Walter W. Skeat, professor of Anglo-Saxon at Cambridge, compiled this Concise Dictionary of Middle English, published by the Clarendon Press in 1888. It covers English words used from about 1150 to 1580, the age of Chaucer, Langland, and the early Tudors. Skeat's preface explains how to use its entries and marks.

Students of medieval texts use it to unlock spelling, sense, and grammar that modern English has left behind. The dictionary is compact but scholarly, built for readers working through old poems and prose. Anyone reading Chaucer or Malory in the original will find it an essential companion.
23258-journal-of-jasper-danckaerts-1679-:
The Journal of Jasper Danckaerts records a Dutch journey across America in 1679 and 1680, in an edition issued in 1913. Its editors explain their text with care. The translation is substantially Mr. Murphy's, as printed in his edition of 1867, and Murphy was an excellent Dutch scholar.

Careful checks were made between that translation and the original manuscript. The Long Island Historical Society, which owns the manuscript, allowed the editors to examine it. Readers get both a first-hand early colonial travel record and a model of how such records are edited, checked, and brought back into print.
28079-the-honest-american-voter-s-little:
Blythe Harding published The Honest American Voter's Little Catechism for 1880 in New York with John Polhemus in 1880. The preface explains that Harding, invited to stenograph a discussion on the election, heard one disputant pump his antagonist dry by the method, and decided to give the dialogue to the public.

The catechism asks what a republic is, how the people exercise power through elected senators, who the president is, and whether electors are bound to follow the majority of their states. Harding's pamphlet is a lively civics primer for the election year, teaching the machinery of American government through questions.
31756-screw-thread-cutting-by-the-master:
Edwin A. Battison's Smithsonian paper, number 37 in United States National Museum Bulletin 240, published in Washington in 1966, studies screw-thread cutting by the master screw method since 1480. It is part of the museum's Contributions from the Museum of History and Technology, a series on science and technology. It includes the bulletin front matter and index entries with the single paper.

Its subject is a workshop technique with a long history: how threads were cut true by guiding a lathe with a master screw, and how that method developed over centuries. Readers get a specialist history of technology, precise about tools and practice, that explains a humble process behind modern machinery.
32510-the-life-of-william-ewart-gladston:
John Morley's Life of William Ewart Gladstone appears here in volume two of three, covering 1859 to 1880 and published in Toronto in 1903. Book Five, 1859 to 1868, follows the Italian revolution, the great budget, the battle for economy, and the spirit of Gladstonian finance. It also covers the American Civil War, Garibaldi and Denmark, defeat at Oxford, the death of Lord Palmerston, parliamentary leadership, and reform, including household suffrage and the opening of the Irish campaign.

Book Six, 1869 to 1874, treats religious equality, agrarian revolution, education, the Franco-German War, neutrality, the Black Sea, and a day's work of a giant, with Gladstone's autumn decline in popularity. Morley, a statesman and biographer, writes with close knowledge of Victorian politics. The volume suits readers who want Gladstone's middle career in full, detailed narrative.
37370-the-relations-of-science-and-relig:
Henry Calderwood weighs two great fields in The Relations of Science and Religion, the Morse Lecture of 1880. It was given for the Union Theological Seminary of New York. Calderwood taught moral philosophy at the University of Edinburgh. He had writ Relations of Mind and Brain.

Plates of nerve cells and nerve fibres front the argument, a sign of its method. The book stands in a Morse run with Dawson on nature and the Bible and McCosh on the Christian faith and positivism. Calderwood, a student of mind and brain, treats the claims of science and faith in one frame. Young readers whose faith may be in peril are the named hope of the house ads at the front.
38342-citt-and-bumpkin-1680:
Roger L'Estrange wrote Citt and Bumpkin in 1680, a dialogue. The Augustan Reprint Society reprinted it at Los Angeles in 1965. It stands number 117 in the society's list. Rahn wrote the introduction to this reprint edition. The Clark memorial library at the university issued the series.

A coffee dialogue between Tom and Dick parodies it. That parody was issued also as Crack-fart and Tony, the notes say. Knave and fool are its second title's plain terms there. Having appropriated the format, the parody follows its arguments too. Two speakers meet in a coffee house in that imitation piece. One agrees to speak and invent as Citt had done before. Matters of religion and government fill such dialogues of the time. The introduction traces how the original shaped its imitator. L'Estrange gives Restoration talk its citizen and its clown.
43806-sarah-dillard-s-ride-a-story-of-th:
James Otis sets his story of the Carolinas in 1780 near Gilbert Town, North Carolina, where two lads have halted in the woods on a September day. The Burt Company copyrighted the book in 1898.

Nathan Shelby, sixteen, is nephew to Isaac Shelby; Evan McDowells, a year younger, is a colonel's son. Both are sorely needed at home, or they would be enrolled with the Mountain Men. An opening note quotes Lossing on the backwoods soldiers who fought on potatoes, pumpkins, and venison. Chapters lead through a desperate venture and a prisoner to King's Mountain and success. Watson Davis drew the six page illustrations.
44980-colonel-thomas-blood-crown-stealer:
Abbott, professor of history at Yale's Sheffield Scientific School, told the life of Colonel Thomas Blood in the Rochester Reprints of 1910. Blood stole the crown jewels from the Tower, and Abbott begins by assuring the cautious reader that the story is true. Its material, he says, comes from the dullest and most sedate of sources: parliamentary reports, ministers' memoranda, warrants to gaolers, and newsletters two centuries stale.

Yet the career will not be dulled. Blood was the most famous and successful of English lawbreakers, a man on whom the law's provisions had borne hard, and a type of the irreconcilable Puritan in a critical age. The narrative crosses the Atlantic as his world did: Vane, once governor of Massachusetts, and the fugitive regicides Goffe, Whalley, and Dixwell in New England all enter it. A shilling shocker's life, documented like a state paper, is Abbott's method here.
4832-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
This thirtieth volume of The Rise of the Dutch Republic covers 1579 to 1580. Its file header numbers it as the thirty-second Gutenberg volume. Chapter two opens with Parma's feint upon Antwerp, as he invests Maestricht, while deputations and letters pass from the states-general, from Brussels, and from Parma to the Walloon provinces. Active negotiations by Orange and by Farnese run beside the siege.

Walloon envoys in Parma's camp before Maestricht, festivities, and the Treaty of Reconciliation follow, with rejoicings of the royalist party and a comedy enacted at Paris theatres. Religious tumults in Antwerp and Utrecht close the sampled scope, as reconciliation with Spain splits the provinces along lines of faith and loyalty. Parma's siege craft and Orange's diplomacy contend for the same towns, and the Walloon provinces choose. Readers get Motley's account of Maestricht, reconciliation, and religious tumult.
51175-source-book-of-london-history-from:
A Source Book of London History, edited by P. Meadows, came out at London in 1914. It gathers first hand records of the city from the earliest times to the year 1800. Each piece is set under its date, so the book reads as a chain of charters, laws, and tales across eight hundred years.

Early pages give the Conqueror's charter, Domesday notes on the city's edge, and a Norman picture of London. Later items cover Wat Tyler, Jack Cade, Evil May Day, and a lease held by Geoffrey Chaucer. Students get the city's own records, in short pieces, rather than one man's retelling of its past.
54636-the-american-missionary-volume-34-:
The American Missionary for February 1880 is one monthly number of a mission journal. The American Missionary Association published it in New York. This is the second number of volume thirty-four. The price was fifty cents a year. The motto declares that the gospel is preached to the poor.

Departments divide the field reports. Editorial paragraphs open the number. A freedmen section reports on schools across the South. A Georgia conference and an Atlanta report appear. Letters come from Florida, Louisiana, and Tennessee. One Tennessee letter describes labour among convicts. An Indians section tells of boys sent to Hampton. A Chinese section calls its report the romance of missions. Receipts and the association's constitution close the issue. Its officers fill two pages of front matter.
54688-the-american-missionary-volume-34-:
The American Missionary, volume thirty four, number four, is the April eighteen eighty issue of a mission journal. The American Missionary Association published it monthly from its rooms in New York. Its motto reads, To the poor the Gospel is preached, at the head. The price was fifty cents a year, paid in advance by subscribers.

Reports fill the issue from the association's fields among freedmen, Indians, and Chinese. Southern schools and churches in Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia send their news. Tougaloo in Mississippi and Fisk University in Tennessee report revivals and teaching work. Louisiana items cover a church dedication and a theological department of study. A children's page carries a voyage to Africa told for a small boy. Receipts, the constitution, and statistics of aid close the number.
54689-the-american-missionary-volume-34-:
The American Missionary for June 1880 is Volume Thirty-Four, Number Six, of the American Missionary Association's monthly. The Association published it at 56 Reade Street, New York, for fifty cents a year. Its motto runs: to the poor the Gospel is preached.

The contents show the Association's wide field fifteen years after the Civil War. A tour of the conferences reports on work among the freedmen, with items from North Carolina, Georgia, and Selma, Alabama. Other pieces weigh the status and exodus of the Negro, and the conditions of Indian civilization. A letter from Professor Chase reports from Africa, and a note treats the Chinese question. The children's page prints letters from Indian boys. Receipts, the constitution, and the Association's aims close the number.
54850-the-american-missionary-volume-34-:
The September 1880 number of a mission monthly came out at New York for fifty cents a year. It speaks for a society that ran schools and churches among freed folk, Indians, and Chinese in America. The contents open with notes on the yearly meeting and signs of the times.

Pieces treat help without money, the two parties and the Chinese, and Indians, reserves and rail roads. Reports from the field cover freedmen's schools in the District of Columbia, Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee. More news comes from the Mendi mission in Africa and the La Pointe agency. A children's page tells of a trip up the Yangtse river in China.
54981-american-missionary-vol-xxxiv-no-5:
American Missionary, volume thirty four, number five, is a monthly magazine for May 1880. Its motto on the cover reads, To the Poor the Gospel is Preached. Contents open with editorial paragraphs and General Grant's reception at Straight University. Old Nails Well Clinched gives the case in a nutshell after it. Southern Negroes in New York City stands among the early items.

Eastern North Carolina, Le Moyne Institute, and a Turkish slave trade pact follow. Stanley on the Congo and treasury gradations fill the middle pages. Items from the field and freedmen reports from the District come next. Wilmington and Raleigh revivals, an Alabama conference, and Kentucky follow in turn. Africa letters, Indian boys at Hampton, and Chinese items close it.
55008-the-american-missionary-volume-34-:
The American Missionary for November 1880, volume thirty four number eleven, is the monthly paper of the American Missionary Association of New York. The number reports the association's annual meeting, with the treasurer's summary, finance debates, and calls to enlarge the work. Its motto runs: to the poor the gospel is preached.

Reports then survey the fields one by one: schools for the freedmen of the South, the Mendi mission in Africa, work among the Indians, and missions to the Chinese. Speakers include Lyman Abbott and a letter from General Fisk. The issue is a full window on post Civil War mission work.
55016-the-american-missionary-volume-34-:
The American Missionary for December 1880 is the monthly magazine of the American Missionary Association, sold at fifty cents a year. The issue opens with comment, a sermon summary and a call for the work to grow. A review and outlook surveys the association's whole field.

Reports then come in by group: schools and churches for the freedmen, Indian schooling in the East, and work among the Chinese. Items name Atlanta University, Athens in Alabama, Tougaloo and Fisk University. A children's page tells a slave-girl's faith. Receipts, the constitution and lists of wants close the number, showing how the cause raised and spent its money.
55069-the-american-missionary-volume-34-:
The American Missionary for October 1880 is volume thirty-four, number ten of the monthly magazine of the American Missionary Association. The association published it from its rooms at 56 Reade Street, New York, at fifty cents a year. Its motto stands on the cover: to the poor the gospel is preached.

The contents divide by field. Editorial pages take up the annual meeting, the Jubilee Singers, Atlanta's colored people, and the association's schools. Reports from the freedmen follow, from McLeansville and Greenwood to Tougaloo University and Atlanta University. The Indians section carries the S'Kokomish Agency report by the Reverend Myron Eells and a Sisseton Agency letter. A sermon by Jee Gam represents the Chinese work, and a children's page closes the number.
55094-the-american-missionary-volume-34-:
The American Missionary, volume 34, number one, for January 1880, opens a new year of the American Missionary Association's magazine. It was published in New York at fifty cents a year, under the motto: to the poor the gospel is preached. A long roster of the association's officers fills the front pages, headed by its president, Tobey of Boston.

The contents divide by field. Editorials offer salutations and report an enlarged work, a professor in Africa, and Indian boys at Hampton. The freedmen section carries vacation reports and accounts from Georgia and Alabama, including the Emerson Institute's years from 1865 to 1879 and a revival at the Shelby Iron Works. An agency report from the S'kokomish covers Indian homes and schools, and a Santa Barbara mission letter covers work among the Chinese.
55224-the-american-missionary-volume-34-:
Volume 34, number 7 of The American Missionary appeared in July 1880 from the American Missionary Association in New York. The monthly journal reported on church mission work among Black schools in the South, Native peoples, Chinese workers, and fields in Africa. Its motto was 'To the Poor the Gospel is Preached.'

Inside, reports cover Fisk, Straight, Tougaloo, and Howard schools, the Hampton meeting, and work at S'Kokomish in Washington Territory. Short field notes, a children's page, receipts, and the group's charter and aims fill out the issue. Readers get a close look at how one large mission group raised money, staffed schools, and told its story in 1880.
55384-the-american-missionary-volume-34-:
The American Missionary, the monthly of the American Missionary Association, reached its thirty-fourth volume with the number for March 1880. Its motto is its program: to the poor the gospel is preached. The contents open with editorial paragraphs and an essay on zeal for study.

Tropical Africa and the Negro in America and Africa lead the articles. Blyden, the Liberian scholar, is quoted on the association itself. Then the field reports proceed by department. For the freedmen: Talladega, the McLeansville school, Charleston church and school work, the cause of the exodus, Atlanta University, Tougaloo, and Memphis. An Indian boy's letter represents the Indian work. The Chinese anniversary at Sacramento follows, and a children's page closes the number. The association ran schools across the Reconstruction South, and its magazine is the monthly ledger of that enterprise, five years after Reconstruction's fall.
55433-the-american-missionary-volume-34-:
The American Missionary for August 1880, volume thirty four, number eight, is a monthly magazine of the American Missionary Association of New York. The price was fifty cents a year. Its motto runs: to the poor the gospel is preached. Reports from schools and missions across the South and West fill the number.

An editorial treats the wrongs of the Poncas. Reports from the freedmen cover Atlanta University, Talladega College, Berea College, and Tougaloo University. A piece asks, teacher or missionary, which. Another reports the Negro on the Indian, and Black missionaries for Africa. Mission work among the Chinese miners of the West gets a report of its own. Receipts, the constitution, and the aims and wants of the association close the number.
58210-the-canadian-entomologist-vol-xii-:
Canadian Entomologist, volume twelve number two, dated February eighteen eighty at London, Ontario, is an issue of a journal of insect study. Its lead paper treats certain species of Satyrus, a genus of butterflies. The author is W H Edwards of Coalburgh, West Virginia.

Edwards begins with a species called Nephele, described by Kirby in eighteen thirty seven. He gives the markings of the wings above and below, with their eye spots. He then argues that the male form shades by degrees into a second form called Alope. Where each form is centred in North America is set out in detail. Quotations from other writers on Alope and its range in New England fill the later part shown.
62462-mineral-survey-procedures-guide-19:
The Mineral Survey Procedures Guide of 1980 serves Bureau of Land Management work. The Interior Department stands behind the guide. That department guards the nation's mineral and land wealth. The guide does not override the Bureau Manual, it warns. Federal and state mining law still rule in clash. The survey manual holds final word, it says.

Mining Laws fill Chapter One in full. Mining districts and federal law lead it. An abstract of state laws runs long there. Discovery and location fill Chapter Two. Lode claims and placer claims divide it. Mill sites and tunnel sites join the list. Mineral surveyors fill Chapter Three in turn. Their duties, contracts, and limits stand set out. A working guide for claim surveyors kept old mining law's paper road straight in a modern bureau.
8428-the-afghan-wars-1839-42-and-1878-80:
Archibald Forbes, war correspondent and historian, wrote this history of Britain's two Afghan wars, with portraits and plans. Part one covers the first war: the march to Cabul, the years of occupation, the road to ruin, the catastrophe of the retreat, the siege of Jellalabad, and retribution and rescue. The second war, 1878 to 1880, follows in the same detailed style.

Forbes wrote for readers who wanted campaigns explained by a man who knew war reporting. His account stresses marches, sieges, and the politics that sent armies into Afghanistan. Readers of military history get a Victorian classic, clear on battles and unsparing about blunders, and still useful for the long shadow those wars cast.
9180-life-of-johnson-volume-3-1776-1780:
This third volume of Boswell's Life of Johnson, in the Hill edition, covers March 1776 to October 1780. Boswell and Johnson change horses at Derby and enjoy talk with Dr. Butter, a Scots physician indignant over a militia bill. The volume adds notes on George Psalmanazar, Johnson's travels, and the inmates of his house.

Readers meet Johnson in late middle age, still fierce in talk and generous in friendship. Boswell's letters on a Royal Academy post close the volume. For lovers of the Life, this stretch keeps its famous mix of wit, learning, and daily life.
a-concise-dictionary-of-middle-english-f: Anthony Lawson Mayhew compiles a concise dictionary of Middle English from 1150 to 1580. Published at the Clarendon Press, it gathers ancient words for readers of old English texts. Mayhew draws on earlier scholarship and sets his entries out for practical use. The dictionary remains a handy guide to the language of Chaucer's age and beyond.
acosta-natural-moral-history-markham-vol:
José de Acosta, a Spanish Jesuit who spent years in Peru, published his Historia natural y moral de las Indias in 1590. Volume one here is Clements R Markham's Hakluyt Society edition of 1880, built on Edward Grimston's English translation of 1604. Acosta set out to describe the New World whole: its skies, lands, plants, and peoples.

His natural history reasons about winds, climates, and species with a scholar's care and a traveler's eyes. His moral history turns to the customs and beliefs of the native peoples. Acosta even framed an early theory of how humans first reached the Americas. The work became the first broad natural history and ethnography of the New World.

Volume two completes Markham's 1880 edition of José de Acosta's Natural and Moral History of the Indies. The Spanish work of 1590, in Grimston's English of 1604, joined two surveys in one: the nature of the Americas and the life of their peoples. Acosta wrote from long residence in Peru and wide reading of reports.

The second volume carries his account of native religion, government, and custom to its close. He treats the peoples of Mexico and Peru as nations with laws, rites, and histories of their own. That respect, rare in his century, gives the book lasting worth. With volume one, it forms the first systematic survey of the New World.
arxiv-2412-00080: Peter Seokhee Seong (2024) gives a new proof of a formula in knot theory. The classical Torres formula links the Alexander polynomial of a link to those of its sublinks. Morifuji had already extended the formula to the twisted setting. Seong reaches the same result through twisted Reidemeister torsion instead. The new route stays closer in shape to Torres' original argument. The paper is a short proof note for specialists in low-dimensional topology.
arxiv-2412-00180:
Thong Nguyen, Isabelle John, Tim Linden, and Tim Tait set strong limits on how fast dark matter can decay, using two space instruments, in a paper from 2024. The dark matter types in focus are dark photons and scalar particles, both of which could slowly break down into normal matter and light. Any such glow would show up in sky data.

Data from a gamma ray telescope and a cosmic ray detector on the space station were used to bound the decay rate. The search covered a huge mass span, from a millionth of a proton scale unit up to two thousand times it. Allowed lifetimes came out extremely long, far beyond the age of the universe for most masses. Such bounds cut into the space of workable dark matter models.
arxiv-2412-00980:
Dimitar Chakarov, Nikita Tsoy, Kristian Minchev, and Nikola Konstantinov study how to keep partners honest in federated learning, where many clients train one model without sharing raw data. A client can gain by sending doctored updates that steer the shared model its way. Uneven data across clients makes that temptation stronger.

The team first shows settings where cheating pays and the shared model suffers. They then design a payment rule for a standard protocol that provably makes honesty the best move. Bounds on the payments and on the model's convergence are derived. The work joins game theory with machine learning practice. Without such guards, pooled learning can be gamed by its own members. Their rule is a step toward trustable pooling.
arxiv-2412-01280:
Houhao Wang and co-authors hunt for crystals whose sound vibrations form linked rings in momentum space, a pattern called a Hopf link. Their paper appeared in 2024. Such interlocked nodal loops are exotic and rare. The team first listed 141 symmetry groups that can host the pattern. Then they screened a phonon database of 10,034 materials. Nearly all had plain loops or chains, but only 113 could host the full Hopf link in their vibration spectra.

Eight clean examples are showcased, from lithium gallium sulfide to a rubidium thorium fluoride. Surface vibration states tied to the loops are displayed for one of them. The authors offer the 113 materials as a shopping list for experimenters who want to probe linked-loop physics in real crystals.
arxiv-2412-01580: Thomas Chaffey, Andrey Kharitenko, Fulvio Forni, and Rodolphe Sepulchre prove a homotopy theorem for incremental stability, a strong form of steadiness for feedback systems. Their 2024 paper shows that a system's stability can be certified by walking it, step by step, from a system already known to be stable. One corollary recasts the check with scaled relative graphs and corrects two assumptions in an earlier theorem. A second gives an incremental form of the classic IQC stability test.
arxiv-2412-01680:
Ray Garner and co-authors used a galaxy survey to probe a link between two traits of star-forming clouds, in a 2024 paper. The clouds, called H II regions, glow where young stars light up gas. Their oxygen levels and their ionization state shape the light we see, and whether the two traits move together has long been debated.

Working with data on the galaxy NGC 628, the team fit models to more than 1,500 such clouds across its disk. The two traits did move against each other, as expected, but with wide scatter. Dust and the local pace of star birth may explain much of the scatter. The authors also warn that modeling choices color such findings.
arxiv-2412-01880:
Tao Zhou and co-authors project how well a planned particle experiment can spot a dark sector particle. Their 2024 paper studies SHiP, a new facility that will dump a proton beam and watch for rare decays, and focuses on long-lived dark vectors made inside electromagnetic cascades.

When beam photons breed showers of particles, those showers can spawn dark vectors far more often than the primary beam can. Simulations show event rates rising by three to four orders of magnitude over primary production alone. The gain is largest for light, long-lived vectors, where a low-energy annihilation channel dominates. The authors set out improved reach curves for dark photons and kin, and they urge close study of backgrounds for these faint signals.
arxiv-2412-02080: Peng Gao proves lower bounds in number theory in work from 2024. The paper deals with negative moments of Dirichlet L-functions, which are key tools for studying prime patterns. It fixes a prime modulus and covers all real powers below zero. The result rests on the assumption that the central values of these functions do not vanish.
arxiv-2412-02180:
Zhao and co-authors measure optical losses in the Virgo filter cavity in this 2024 paper. The cavity, 285 meters long, sharpens squeezed light that lowers quantum noise in gravitational wave detectors. Losses eat that gain, since the beam bounces many times inside. The team built an automatic system to map losses as the beam spot moves across the mirrors.

On the input mirror, losses swung clearly with spot position, from 42 to 87 parts per million. On the end mirror, they stayed far more even, from 53 to 61. The lowest values sat close to estimates made from single mirror tests before installation. The authors read that match as evidence no major loss source was missed. High loss spots likely trace to contamination. Their mapping also found a beam position with losses among the lowest ever measured, a guide for future detectors.
arxiv-2412-02380:
Lorna Wheaton and Sylwia Bujkiewicz review how stand-in measures are used in English cancer drug rulings in a 2024 paper. A stand-in, or surrogate, endpoint is an early sign, like tumor shrink, used to guess a final gain like longer life. Health boards lean on them more, and fresh rules urge care in proving the guess.

The pair read cancer appraisals by the board NICE from early 2022 to mid 2023. Of 47 cases, eighteen leaned on stand-ins, thirty-seven of them in all. The proof behind each link swung widely, from trial-grade to thin. The review maps that spread.
arxiv-2412-02480:
Yuzhi Che and co-authors show the strong force's grip can be read from B meson decays in two thousand twenty-four. That grip, the coupling alpha-s, is a core constant of particle physics. Their route uses the total rate of semileptonic B decays, where a bottom quark sheds a lepton pair.

The rate is written through the coupling, quark masses, and a mixing term, then fit to world averages for charged and neutral B mesons. The fit lands near the value from the Z boson scale after scaling, with the main error from the mixing term and theory sums. Future B and Z factories could sharpen the method to rival the best current measures, those from tau decays.
arxiv-2412-02780:
Rajat Shinde and co-authors release WxC-Bench, a ready-made dataset collection for training AI on weather and climate problems. Model builders have plenty of algorithms but few clean, prepared datasets, and each weather task eats data at a different scale. Their collection bundles tasks spanning neighborhood storms to continent-wide patterns: turbulence for aviation, hurricane strength and track, finding past weather twins, gravity wave modelling, and writing weather reports in words.

The dataset is public, with code to prepare it, and the paper documents its structure and runs baseline checks. The authors pitch it as shared ground where general weather AI can be trained and compared fairly.
arxiv-2412-02980:
Alex Havrilla and a large team of co-authors present a 2024 survey on synthetic data made by large language models. Fake training data can extend learning to many tasks, but methods for making it differ widely and are rarely compared head to head. The team judges each method by three traits of its output: quality, diversity, and complexity.

They find quality matters most for tasks like the training data, while diversity drives success on new kinds of tasks. Complexity helps both. The traits trade off against each other, so pushing one can hurt another. Many current models are tuned only for quality, which shrinks diversity and limits self-improvement. The authors sort existing methods by the parts they use and the trait mix they produce. They argue future training methods should balance all three traits.
arxiv-2412-03080:
Yunhi Cho and Hyounggyu Choi revisit the question of where the center of mass sits in curved geometries, and prove the answer is the only possible one. In flat space the balance point is obvious; on spheres and in hyperbolic space it needs axioms. Galperin built such an axiom system and proved uniqueness, but his argument was heavy.

The authors give a far simpler uniqueness proof and extend the system from finite point sets to general manifolds. As a payoff, they derive a sweeping generalization of Pappus's centroid theorem for volumes, covering flat, spherical, and hyperbolic geometry in all dimensions with unified proofs. One clean framework replaces three separate traditions.
arxiv-2412-03480:
Joachim Dahl Thomsen and co-authors study titanium films on graphene in a 2024 paper. Titanium is the standard sticky contact metal used across nanoelectronics research. Films grown on graphene turn out oddly sensitive to growth conditions, though.

Microscopy and spectroscopy mapped the films almost atom by atom. Quantum calculations backed the experimental picture of the buried interface. Layer count, support type, and deposition temperature drive the differences seen. Single-layer graphene grows rough, island-like films full of defects. Thicker graphene yields smoother, calmer films suited to real devices. Readers learn why a routine contact step can quietly fail.
arxiv-2412-03880:
Mingyuan Zhou, Xudong Jian, Ye Xia, and Zhilu Lai tackle bad data in the sensor records used to watch the health of bridges and other large structures. Faulty readings are common in those records and can mislead checks. Deep learning can spot them, but it needs many labeled examples, and labeling is slow and costly for huge data sets.

The team uses self-taught pre-training, where a model first learns from unlabeled data and is then tuned with a few labeled cases. That way, the model can learn useful patterns before it ever sees a label. Tests show the approach can spot faulty readings well while using far fewer labels. The method suits real monitoring work, where labeled data is scarce.
arxiv-2412-03980:
Vakada Naveen, Arvind Krishna Sridhar, Yinyi Guo, and Erik Visser built a chatbot that answers questions about sound. Their twenty twenty-four paper links many expert models in one system. A query may ask what was said, who spoke, what song played, or for new audio to be made.

A classifier first reads the intent of the query and sends it to the right expert. A context module pulls events and times from the audio, and a language model of modest size blends all outputs into one reply. On custom tests of time-based questions, the system beat large audio models. It also did well on a known sound bench, which makes it a good fit for use on a device.
arxiv-2412-04080:
Yi-Bao Zhang and co-authors test polymer drag cutting in swirling flow between two cylinders in 2024. Long chain additives are famous for easing flow friction. This setup hosts a strong steady vortex that hauls most of the flow. Two polymer weights were tried across a wide speed range. Drag cuts grew with dose toward a known ceiling.

At that ceiling, the total cut was only about twenty percent. Pipe flows reach far higher at like speeds. Shear stress did not vanish, unlike classic cases. The team shows polymers calm the choppy flow but barely touch the big vortex. That split explains the weak total cut. Wall layers also steadied under the additives.
arxiv-2412-04680:
Jaihyun Lew and eight co-authors rethink how vision models chop up images in a 2024 paper. Vision transformers split a photo into a grid of square patches. Each patch becomes a token the model can weigh against others. A square patch can mix two objects into one token, though.

Their method cuts the image into superpixels instead. Each superpixel hugs one visual region, so its token holds a single idea. Odd shapes and sizes make that swap hard to wire in. A two step pipeline first extracts, then merges features with care. Tests show gains in accuracy and toughness across tasks. The approach plugs into existing vision frameworks without deep changes.
arxiv-2412-04780:
Senaratne, Christen, Omran, and Williams present tools for finding and classifying anomalies in knowledge graphs in a 2024 paper. Graphs built by hand or by extraction collect redundant, clashing, and missing values. Cleaning them raises their quality.

Their system, SEKA, hunts abnormal triples and entities without labels. It adapts a path ranking algorithm to reward corroborated paths, flagging facts that lack support. A companion taxonomy, TAXO, sorts the anomaly types a graph can suffer. Tests on four real-world graphs, including Wikidata, beat the baselines. The authors argue detection plus classification beats detection alone. Better graphs serve search and question answering downstream. Coverage is kept while correctness improves.
arxiv-2412-04880:
Pawel Tomasz Pieta and co-authors release MozzaVID, a 3D image data set of mozzarella cheese, in a 2024 paper. Volumetric deep learning lacks shared benchmark data, so new 3D models are hard to compare fairly. The team scanned cheese samples with X-ray tomography to fill that gap.

The set covers twenty-five cheese types across 149 samples, offered at three resolutions with image counts from a few hundred to nearly thirty-eight thousand. Food structure is messy and disordered, which makes the choice of scan method and scale a real research question in itself. Beyond benchmarking 3D classifiers, the data let scientists probe how mozzarella's inner structure varies. The authors hope a clean public set will push volumetric methods forward.
arxiv-2412-05080: Ekaterina Amerik and Mikhail Lozhkin contribute a new example to a question about rational points on a special geometric space, in a 2024 mathematics paper. They study the third punctual Hilbert scheme of a K3 surface, a space that parametrizes clusters of three points on the surface. Their example shows potential density of rational points on that space, meaning rational points become dense after a finite extension of the number field.
arxiv-2412-05180:
Chaitat Utintu and co-authors edit video colors without any training in a 2024 paper. Recoloring video usually means frame-by-frame labor or fake-looking output. Temporal artifacts plague automated attempts at the task. Creators need precise control with professional polish.

Their framework splits the spatial and temporal problems apart. Users click to pick colors on key frames first. Automatic segmentation gives precise spatial control there. Color then propagates both directions through time. Natural motion patterns guide that spread. Motion-aware blending smooths transitions across complex movement. Extensive tests covered diverse editing scenarios. Quality matched or beat trained state-of-the-art methods. No specialized hardware is required to run it. The interface mirrors how editors already think. Keyframe artistry plus automatic follow-through is the formula. Content creation tools gain a practical addition.
arxiv-2412-05480:
Zongfeng Li and three co-authors store telecom light signals in a solid-state quantum memory. Their 2024 paper uses erbium ions in a crystal, a natural fit for telecom wavelengths. Such memories are needed to link future quantum networks. Past versions demanded extreme cold and huge magnetic fields.

The team stored qubits coded in three ways: polarization, frequency, and time slots. A new setup routine for the atomic frequency comb boosted storage efficiency over tenfold. It did so under practical working conditions. Full process checks confirmed the memory's quality, with fidelity above ninety-two percent. The result brings network-ready quantum memory closer to daily lab use.
arxiv-2412-05680:
Rory Conlin and co-authors compute free-boundary plasma equilibria at high order in the DESC code. The task asks what shape a hot plasma takes when its edge is not fixed by a wall. Such shapes matter for fusion devices that confine plasma with magnets. Boundary rules split into fixed and free cases, with a sheet current allowed at the edge in some.

The team reviews when that sheet current can exist at the plasma-vacuum seam. A fast, exact method scores how well a trial shape meets the rules. DESC then finds equilibria in vacuum and at set plasma pressure. Runs cover cases with and without the sheet current. The work backs design studies for stellarator fusion devices.
arxiv-2412-05980:
Yiren Song and co-authors shield personal photos from misuse by reference based image generators, in a paper from 2024. Such tools can clone a face or style from one photo to make fake news or harmful fakes.

Their method, Anti-Reference, adds noise too faint to see that still breaks the cloning step. One loss design hits fine tuned, instant, and human drive methods at once. A noise coder can guess the shield fast, or the noise can be tuned head on. Tests showed the shield moves across models and even fools some paid services.
arxiv-2412-06580:
Jürgen Reuter lists the hard road for mock-clash tools in a 2024 paper. Such tools feign the crash of grains so labs can read what a true clash would say, and fresh crash rigs will ask more of them than the great ring in use.

A lepton rig, most like a straight one, brings its own woes. The beam must be feigned in fine grain, with its twist held true. Spark laws need sums past the first rung, with soft spark sums re-added neat. The paper tours both the grand all-use tools and the slim craft codes. It lays out what each lacks for the rigs to come. Reuter writes for the span till such a rig first takes data, a span in which the tools must grow or fail.
arxiv-2412-06680:
Samuel Taylor, Cody Covington, and Kálmán Varga simulate molecules blown apart by intense light, in this 2024 paper. In a Coulomb explosion, charges strip away and the ions fly apart. The team compared three styles of simulation: fully classical, partly quantum, and a quantum method that follows electron density over time.

The quantum runs gave ions lower energies than the classical runs predicted. They also spread the ions over wider angles with more varied paths, matching what experiments see. Stronger light, and the extra ionization it causes, made the quantum effects bigger. The work helps explain how electron behavior shapes breakup patterns.
arxiv-2412-06780:
Yanbo Xu and co-authors present a method that makes image and 3D generation more varied, in work from 2024. A common tool guides 3D building with scores from a 2D image model trained to produce pictures from text. That tool tends to give near-identical results, even though the image model itself can produce varied pictures.

The new method borrows from how the image model samples pictures step by step. It guides building along paths set by random starting seeds, which spreads the results out. The team adjusts the idea for cases where the building steps cannot follow those paths exactly, such as 3D shapes whose views change together. Tests on 2D tasks, text-based 3D building, and rebuilding a scene from one photo show more varied results with quality kept.
arxiv-2412-06980:
Suchinthaka Wanninayaka and five co-authors enhance diffusion models for goal-oriented communications in a 2024 paper. As edge devices and the Internet of Things grow, the need to move data grows too, while spectrum stays tight. Goal-oriented systems send what the task at the far end needs most, not each bit in full.

Their framework, called Diff-GO, uses a noise-restricted forward diffusion step. That step speeds training and cuts the compute load for a diffusion-based sender. The aim is to trim the bandwidth a message needs while the media at the receiver stays at good quality.
arxiv-2412-07480:
Alexandra Müller, Tobias Schesny, Ben Steinfurth, and Julien Weiss use reinforcement learning to tune pulsed air jets that keep flow attached in a diffuser in this 2024 paper. Flow separation wastes energy in such widening ducts. Their wind tunnel setup reads wall shear stress to sense the flow state.

A policy algorithm adjusted the blowing signal step by step, guided by rewards for shrinking reversed flow per action. That reward proved the most sample-efficient of those tried. Under one hundred episodes sufficed to find the strongest settings at fixed air use. The winner used short pulses with long gaps, matching earlier studies. The authors promote reinforcement learning for tuning tasks on turbulent experimental data.
arxiv-2412-07680:
In string theory, certain particle-like states, called BPS states, form and split as conditions change. Le Floch, Pioline, and Raj map that behavior for a specific geometric setting: a non-compact space built over two projective lines. The map, called a scattering diagram, lays out walls in the space of conditions where states of a given charge can exist. Where walls cross, consistency rules fix the counts of all states.

The team first builds the diagram in two simple limits, near a special symmetric point and where both lines are large. They then merge those lessons into the diagram for the physical slice of conditions, which carries a rich symmetry group. Along the way they sketch a proof of the split attractor flow tree conjecture for this example, within a range of phases. An extra mass parameter makes this case harder than their earlier work.
arxiv-2412-07780:
Risto Uuk and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper that sorts the systemic risks of general purpose AI into a taxonomy. Systemic risks are harms that can hit whole societies or economies at once. The team started from a pool of more than seventeen hundred papers and read eighty-six in depth.

They find thirteen risk classes and fifty sources that feed them. The classes run from environmental harm and built-in discrimination to governance failure and loss of control. Sources cluster around knowledge gaps, trouble spotting harm, and the wild path of AI growth. The authors offer the map to help leaders rank risks and write rules with clearer eyes.
arxiv-2412-07980:
Mingxi Lei and five co-authors tackled a 2024 problem in machine learning: models often fail when new data drifts from their training data. One fix adapts the model while it answers, using nearby stored examples as guides. Those neighbor methods are simple, though, and their gains often fade fast.

Looking at the problem through geometry, the team found that neighbor methods rest on a classic shape model that splits space into cells. Their new frame uses that model to steer the adapting model more firmly. The result is a method that holds up better when data shifts, built on a clear picture of why the older methods work at all.
arxiv-2412-08280:
Liempi and co-authors published a 2024 astronomy paper on how giant black holes may have been born. Most large galaxies hold a dense cluster of stars at their center, and many also hold a black hole millions of times heavier than the sun. The two seem to trade places: in smaller galaxies the cluster dominates, in larger ones the black hole does. That pattern hints at a shared origin.

The team added two ideas to a computer model of galaxy growth. In the model, the central cluster forms in place as gas gathers and makes stars. Inside such a crowded cluster, stars can collide and merge, planting the seed of a black hole. Tight, compact clusters proved best at making seeds. Seeds of many sizes grew, some reaching the huge masses seen in real galaxies. The model's black hole counts matched what telescopes observe at the heavy end.
arxiv-2412-08680:
Scam and fraud are cousins, not twins, and telling them apart matters to the chatbots people now ask for help. Isha Chadalavada, Tianhui Huang, and Jessica Staddon build a labeling machine for that distinction in a 2024 paper. Their raw material is the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's complaint database, rich but unlabeled for this purpose.

An ensemble of large language models votes on each complaint, scam or fraud, creating the separation the corpus lacked. The authors report first findings on where the models shine and where they stumble in scam defense. Since users increasingly bring scam questions to LLM-enabled chatbots, knowing the models' blind spots is practical, not academic. The paper frames the ensemble as a tool for evaluating and improving those front-line answers.
arxiv-2412-08780:
Andrii Dzhoha, Alexey Kurennoy, Vladimir Vlasov, and Marjan Celikik argue that fixing position bias in rankings pays off through fairness, not just clicks, in work from 2024. Items shown higher get more clicks regardless of quality, which loops back into popularity. Most debiasing work chases short-term ranking gains.

Their large shopping platform ran offline and live tests. Removing position bias spread views and buys more evenly across the catalog. Engagement and revenue held steady while assortment use rose. A simple model of the popularity spread explains the squeeze and its release. Fairer rankings also court more sellers and content partners, the authors note, which compounds over time.
arxiv-2412-08980:
Márton Marits asks how many simple graphs it takes to cover a complicated one in this 2024 mathematics paper. The cover number counts the fewest graphs from a chosen family whose edges together make the target graph. The idea echoes a classic paper on graph covers.

For families defined by a rule linking colors needed to cliques present, he finds an exact formula that works for any non-decreasing rule. He then lines up five families in a chain, from the strictest equality of color and clique counts through perfect graphs and two split-like families to plain bipartite graphs. At every step of the chain the gap between cover numbers can be made as large as one likes. Finally he shows the cover number by unipolar graphs escapes any formula in the two classic counts. The results map where covering stays tame and where it runs wild.
arxiv-2412-09180:
Agustín Muñoz González and co-authors model shared liquidity pools as a game among many traders, in this 2024 paper. The pools sit inside automated market makers, the engines behind much decentralized finance trading. In such a pool, price is set by the pool's own reserves through a curved rule, not by a list of buy and sell orders. That twist sets this setting apart from classic market models.

The authors adapt mean field games, a framework for crowds where each player reacts to the whole. They use a probability-based weak form of the theory suited to the pool's rules. They prove that solutions to the game exist, a base step before any use in design. The work extends a well-worn use of the theory, price impact in order books, to pool-based markets.
arxiv-2412-09980:
Lingyun Wang and co-authors build a two-step fall detector for older people that runs on a phone. Falls are a growing threat as populations age, and a detector must be both sure and light on battery. Their 2024 system first lets the phone's motion sensors flag a possible fall with cheap checks.

A second check then reads WiFi signal patterns, which shift when a body falls, to confirm the event. It also judges whether the person can move afterward. If a fall is confirmed and the user stays still, the app sends an emergency alert. The WiFi model hit ninety-nine percent accuracy in tests, beating motion-only models, the authors report, while sparing the battery by waking only when needed.
arxiv-2412-10080:
Oleg Smirnov and co-authors present a workflow framework for radio astronomy in a 2024 paper. Telescope data reduction chains many tools in sequence. Stimela2 writes those chains as short readable recipes in YAML format. Each task is defined by its own schema of inputs and outputs.

Recipes can nest inside other recipes for modular design. Settings stay separate from the recipe logic. Tasks run natively or inside containers for reproducibility. A companion package maintains the open container images. The framework talks to the Slurm scheduler and the Kubernetes cloud system. That lets the same workflow scale from a laptop to a cluster. It is the fourth paper in the Africanus series on astronomy software.
arxiv-2412-10180:
Jakob Thumm, Julian Balletshofer, Leonardo Maglanoc, Luis Muschal, and Matthias Althoff gave a safety framework for robot arms near people in two thousand twenty-four. Robots could take on repetitive and hazardous work, but safe contact with humans must be guaranteed. Older methods are either too cautious for natural teamwork or assume a fixed path.

Their shield, called SARA, uses reachability analysis to sort possible contacts by type in a formally sound way. Loose contacts allow higher force than clamping contacts, where a body part is trapped. For each type they verify the robot's kinetic energy stays below pain and injury limits. Tests showed safe contact with much better speed than prior methods.
arxiv-2412-10380:
Gagan Bansal and seven co-authors catalog what makes talking with AI agents harder than talking with software. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Modern agents observe, use tools, and message other agents. Users still meet them through plain natural language. The agents' complexity hides many failure modes. Communication grounding, how partners build shared understanding, frames the analysis.

Twelve key challenges emerge from the study. Some block information flowing from agent to user. Others block the user's side of the channel. A third set spans every exchange. The authors ground each challenge in prior research. Designers of agent systems gain a checklist of conversational risks. Human-AI interaction research gets a shared agenda.
arxiv-2412-10580:
Belén Costanza, Claudia G. Scóccola, and Matías Zaldarriaga teach a neural network to clean maps of the faint glow left from the early universe. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Sharp maps of this cosmic microwave background help pin down how the universe began. A classic filter does the cleaning well but slowly.

Their network, DeepWiener, first learned the trick for heat maps and now handles polarised light too. It takes in the raw map, a noise map, and a mask of the blocked sky. A step-by-step loop splits the signal into its two modes and fixes leaks caused by the mask. The cleaned maps match the classic method but come far faster. Their error bars also beat a common shortcut method. Messy masks, the team notes, still make one mode hard to recover.
arxiv-2412-10780:
Cars that can tell who is driving, from the driver's habits alone, could block theft and tailor the ride. Mattia Fanan and co-authors test whether continual learning suits that task in a 2024 study.

Unlike a fixed model, a continual learner picks up new drivers and slow changes in style without forgetting old ones, and with modest computing cost. The team tried several such methods on a known driving data set across three scenarios of rising difficulty. The best older method lost only about a tenth of its accuracy versus a fixed setup. Two new smoothing methods from the team cut that loss to about two percent. The work supports in-car learning that keeps pace with real life.
arxiv-2412-10980:
Erman Isik works in Iwasawa theory, a branch of number theory that studies how number systems grow in tall towers of fields, in this 2024 paper. The focus is a family of symmetric objects called Hecke characters, tied both to special elliptic curves with extra symmetry and to Hilbert modular forms. The primes in play are ordinary, the well behaved case for this machinery.

Isik states and proves a main conjecture for the anticyclotomic setting, which links an algebraic object built from the tower to an analytic one built from special values. Such conjectures are the core predictions of the theory, tying arithmetic data to analysis. A second result bears on the rank of the rational points of the related abelian varieties, a basic measure of their arithmetic richness.
arxiv-2412-11080:
Wengang Guo and Wei Ye published a research paper in 2024 on a deep learning version of spectral clustering, a method that groups data by mapping it into an embedding space. The classic pipeline builds the embedding and then clusters it in two separate steps, so neither can correct the other. High-dimensional data also strain the similarity graph it needs.

Their design learns the embedding with a neural network and refines the clustering greedily, always fixing the worst-formed cluster direction next. The two parts train together end to end. On seven real data sets the joint method reached top clustering performance, showing the payoff of letting embedding and grouping teach each other.
arxiv-2412-11380:
Yingping Liang and Ying Fu work on teaching a new model from an old one without any of the old training data, in a 2024 paper. The method rebuilds fake data from the trained model itself. Past work chased variety across all data but missed variety within each class and overlap between classes, so the fake data came out too uniform.

Their approach works in two phases with an adversarial push and pull. First it spreads same class samples apart and draws unlike classes close; then training does the reverse for the student. A weighted sampling rule keeps the two goals from clashing. Tests across tasks showed gains in accuracy and data savings.
arxiv-2412-11480:
Young-Jae Park and co-authors build, in a 2024 paper, a rain call model that reads sky shots from orbit in place of ground radar. Radar is dear to run and set in place, so poor lands lean on coarse world models. Their model, NPM, reads three sky paths: heat glow at 10.5 microns, and water vapor high and low. Place codes tell it the time of year and day, since rain shifts with both. It calls rain for six hours out, with a fresh call each hour. The maps it draws have a 2-kilometer grain, near live.

Tests back the calls against ground truth. Code and data are shared in the open, the team notes. The aim is flood and slide warns where radar is thin.
arxiv-2412-11880:
Heinz Bauschke, Walaa Moursi, and Shambhavi Singh revisit a duality framework for optimization that was proposed twenty-five years ago by Eckstein, Ferris, Pennanen, and Robinson. The core problem is finding zeros of the sum of two maximally monotone operators linked by a linear map, a setup behind many splitting methods. The question is when primal and dual solutions mirror each other exactly.

The authors identify paramonotonicity as a broad condition that guarantees saddle points fill exactly the rectangle formed by the primal and dual solution sets. In the subdifferential setting they characterize when duality holds in total, with no gap anywhere. They also derive projection formulas for sets that arise when analyzing the Chambolle-Pock algorithm, using a recent framework by Bredies and co-authors. The paper tightens the theory beneath a widely used family of solvers.
arxiv-2412-11980:
Medina-Dozal, Urzúa, and Récamier-Angelini solved this quantum optics problem in twenty twenty-four. An optomechanical system couples light in a cavity to a moving mirror-like part. The coupling can be linear or quadratic in the light field, and an outside force may drive the system. Tracking its exact change over time is a hard algebra problem.

The authors use Lie algebra methods to build the time evolution operator in closed form. For the undriven case the result is exact. For the driven case they give a close approximation. Computer simulations matched the formulas well in both cases. The work gives theorists a clean tool for a widely used quantum device model.
arxiv-2412-12080: Kollár and Li present a 2024 number theory paper settling a conjecture of Mordell and Schinzel. The question concerns cubic Diophantine equations of the shape xyz = G(x, y), where G is a polynomial. Building on work by Mordell from 1952 and Schinzel from 2015, the authors prove such equations have infinitely many integer solutions. The head text is a one-sentence abstract, so the argument itself is not summarized there.
arxiv-2412-12380:
Clinical trial teams now write down exactly what effect they want to estimate before a study starts, using a guide called the estimands framework. Statisticians working in causal inference also define an estimand, and the overlap confuses both camps. Thomas Drury, Jonathan Bartlett, David Wright, and Oliver Keene compare the two approaches in 2024 with worked examples. They show how each one defines a summary effect for a stated group of patients.

The trial framework, they argue, is structured and plain enough for non-mathematicians, which helps teams talk clearly about goals. The causal approach states its quantity with full mathematical care and draws its assumptions as graphs. The authors urge both sides to treat the tools as partners, not rivals.
arxiv-2412-12480:
Alex Mallen and co-authors test whether language models can scheme against safety controls in this 2024 paper. A control protocol is a plan to use an AI system while blocking it from causing an unacceptable outcome. The test asks if a model, with no shared memory between its calls, can still plan and act to subvert such a plan.

Their test suite holds eight settings and six sets of extra tools that isolate single skills. Models from two makers were tested, including versions trained to be only helpful. None showed strong skill at this kind of plotting on their own. Giving models a way to share a plan between calls raised their scores a lot.
arxiv-2412-12580:
Tao Wang and three co-authors solve electron structure equations adaptively in a 2024 paper. The Kohn-Sham equation governs electrons in molecules and materials. Its solutions are smooth except right at atomic nuclei. A solver should spend effort near nuclei and relax elsewhere.

Their method builds on smooth spline basis functions of high order. A hierarchy of splines allows local refinement where the error indicator demands it. The resulting eigenvalue problem is solved with a preconditioned block method. Convergence of that solver did not depend on the spline order. A methane molecule test reached target accuracy with about six thousand degrees of freedom. That economy shows the adaptive scheme's competitiveness. All electron accuracy is kept without a uniform fine grid.
arxiv-2412-12980:
Fusion plasmas can shed runaway electrons, fast particles that threaten the vessel wall, and tracking their density over time is costly with standard solvers. McDevitt, Arnaud, and Tang use a physics-informed neural network to solve the adjoint form of the problem once, in a way that covers many plasma settings at once. From that single learned solution, the electron density can be projected forward for any starting spread of the particles.

Their forecasts matched a standard relativistic solver across starting states and physics settings, including how a runaway group fades below threshold. Once trained, the network produces these histories almost instantly. The authors offer it as a fast tool for reactor studies.
arxiv-2412-13280:
Morgan Wack, Kayla Duskin, and Damian Hodel measure how well fact-checking actually keeps up with election falsehoods, in a 2024 paper. Fact-checks are sold as a front-line weapon against political misinformation. The team compared the spread of false narratives around the 2022 United States midterm elections with the fact-checks answering them.

Fewer than half of prominent false narratives were ever fact-checked. Where checks existed, the median one arrived four days after the narrative first appeared. Network analysis showed fact-checks made up under 1.2 percent of the conversation around a narrative. When shared, they circulated almost entirely inside one partisan camp rather than across the divide. The data also contradicted the assumption that moderation leans against the political right. The authors conclude that limits in coverage, speed, and reach blunt fact-checking as the main defense.
arxiv-2412-13380:
Jonathan Shaki, Yonatan Aumann, and Sarit Kraus model how parties spend to make their best issues loom large in voters' minds, in a 2024 paper. Voters weigh issues by salience — how top-of-mind each issue feels — and campaigns can shift that ranking with money. This steering is called priming.

The team study priming contests with many issues and many parties. In parliamentary races, where parties chase vote share, a stable spending balance always exists and can be computed fast. With two parties, each side in balance pours everything into a single issue. In most winner-take-all presidential settings, by contrast, no stable balance exists at all. The results map when campaign spending wars settle and when they spiral.
arxiv-2412-13480:
Yvonne Alama Bronsard, Xi Chen, and Matthieu Dolbeault design computer schemes for three hard wave equations that are exact in time and highly accurate in space. The Benjamin-Ono, Calogero-Sutherland, and cubic Szegő equations are nonlinear and nonlocal, yet integrable, with rare exact solution formulas. The authors build fully discrete methods on those formulas. Each step costs the same no matter how far ahead the simulation runs.

They prove sharp convergence rates for the first two equations, with error growing only linearly in time rather than exploding. Tests at short and long times confirm the strength of the approach. Because cost ignores the final time, the schemes suit the study of long-term behavior. The authors present them as a new tool for integrable systems, where long horizons usually defeat standard methods.
arxiv-2412-13780: Beirão da Cruz e Silva and co-authors test silicon timing sensors after heavy proton exposure in a 2024 paper. The sensors, called LGADs, may time fast protons at colliders, but they must sit very close to the beam and take uneven doses of radiation. They report the first measures of current and voltage behavior after such uneven exposure, at very high total doses.
arxiv-2412-13880:
Shalini Saini, Anitha Chennamaneni, and Babatunde Sawyerr review how attackers and defenders duel around learning based network intrusion detectors, in work from twenty twenty-four. Deep learning guards scan huge traffic flows for odd patterns. Attackers can also bend those same tools against the guards.

The review covers poisoned training data, test time evasion, and reverse engineering of detectors. It traces how each attack works and what counters exist. The authors note the field is still young and oddly split: defenses lag attacks in real traffic settings. Gaps include scarce real attack data and weak testing of AI defenses. They frame the work as groundwork for sturdier network defense.
arxiv-2412-14280:
Andrea Legramandi and co-authors test how quantum chaos survives when a model's reach shrinks. The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, a benchmark of quantum chaos and holography, links every particle to every other. Real devices cannot do that, so the team studies a quadratic version whose interactions fade with distance by a power law.

Their diagnostic is the spectral form factor, a fingerprint of a system's energy levels over time. Surprisingly, its chaotic shape holds under a large cut in interaction range, thanks to cancellations in the math. Push further and new regimes appear, with a higher dip and a second plateau. The work maps where idealized chaos ends and laboratory reality begins.
arxiv-2412-14380:
Victor Farias and co-authors pick winners under several competing goals without leaking private data, in a 2024 paper. Differentially private selection usually serves one objective, yet real choices, from decision trees to influential users in a network, juggle many. Their two mechanisms take different routes.

PrivPareto scores candidates by closeness to the Pareto frontier, the set of unbeaten trade-offs. PrivAgg instead merges objectives by weighted aggregation, privately. Both handle global and local sensitivity bookkeeping, with guidance on composing the privacy cost of many utility functions. In experiments on cost-sensitive trees and network influence, local-sensitivity versions won clearly and stayed accurate at typical privacy budgets. The authors offer the pair as building blocks for private multi-goal analysis.
arxiv-2412-14480:
Saumya Saxena and co-authors present a 2024 system that lets a robot explore a new space and answer questions about it, called GraphEQA. The robot must build its own grasp of a place it has never seen, then answer a question tied to that place with care. Weak scene records and slow search make the task hard.

The system keeps a live 3D map labeled with what each part is, plus photos tied to the task, as its memory. A language-vision model reads that memory to answer. Planning runs in layers that mirror the map's own layers, and the labels in the map steer where the robot looks next. On two test sets the system beat leading rivals, answering more tasks right with fewer planning steps. Trials in real homes and offices backed the design.
arxiv-2412-14580:
Yiren Song, Xiaokang Liu, and Mike Zheng Shou present a way to judge how similar two images look, using a diffusion model, in a paper from 2024. Standard scores compare pixels and textures but miss layout, pose, and meaning. Other learned scores squeeze images so hard that fine appearance detail is lost.

Their method reads features inside the attention layers of a pretrained diffusion model. It scores both appearance and style likeness, and it matched human taste better than prior scores. The team also built two new benchmarks, one for style match and one for instance match. Across many tests, their method reached top performance, which they offer as a tool for judging custom image generation.
arxiv-2412-14980: Golo Wolff counts how often a family of cubic equations can be solved in every local number system, in a 2024 paper. The family takes the form a x-cubed plus b y-cubed minus z-cubed, with whole-number coefficients a and b. Local solubility asks for a nonzero solution in the p-adic numbers for every prime. Wolff derives an asymptotic formula for the number of coefficient pairs, within growing bounds and mild side conditions, whose forms pass that everywhere-local test.
arxiv-2412-15080:
Nico Guth and co-authors model a small effect that could matter a lot for fusion power. Pellets of frozen fuel fired into a hot, magnetically held plasma do not just slow down and dissolve. The plasma heats the pellet's vapor cloud unevenly, and the lopsided pressure pushes back like a tiny rocket, speeding the pellet up as it flies.

Their model starts from a round, even picture of the dissolving pellet and adds a small uneven correction. It predicts speed-ups near one hundred thousand meters per second squared in today's tokamaks, matching lab estimates. For the ITER reactor's high-performance runs, the push could reach ten times that, cutting how deep pellets fly. The authors warn this could weaken a key tool for calming dangerous plasma disruptions.
arxiv-2412-15180:
A black hole that dries up seems to shred facts, yet a famed curve says its links with the rays it sheds must rise, then fall. Talal Ahmed Chowdhury and co-authors run that tale on a real quantum chip in a 2024 study. Their toy model shuttles bits as a hole would shed them.

Scramble runs were built from chance gate sets. Two test plans then read the link load of the shed bits. Noise fixes kept the reads true on IBM gear. The Rényi link load came out right for the toy hole, Page curve and all. The work shows such chips can probe deep facts of holes and links.
arxiv-2412-15380:
Meghana Karri and co-authors put forth a frame in 2024 that outlines organs in medical scans when few scans are labeled. Hand labels are dear, so a good tool must learn from the unlabeled mass as well. Their frame trains twin networks that teach each other, with a cross-attention link that lets them swap what each sees best. A doubt gauge steers where the pair must agree, and a sharpness-aware step keeps the fit from brittle peaks.

On prostate and heart scans from many centers, the frame beat past half-labeled tools. With just a tenth of scans labeled, it drew near the scores of fully labeled runs. That reach counts where expert labels are scarce. Code is free in public.
arxiv-2412-15580:
Kazuya Iwata and Keiichi Maeda map the cell pattern of a helium blast on a white dwarf in a 2024 paper. Double detonation models of type Ia supernovae hinge on a helium shell blast that lights the core. Earthly blast science leans on cell size, the mesh of the blast front, to judge lighting, spread, and death of a wave. Star blast work had mostly skipped that lens.

Their two dimensional runs show a clear cell mesh across all densities and mixes tried. Core ash mixed into the shell shrinks cells fast, sped by alpha capture burns. Nickel output may lag in ash rich shells. The tiny cells strain full star sims that cannot resolve them. The authors urge built in cell models for trust in star blast outcomes.
arxiv-2412-15680:
Naoki Shioji, Satoshi Tanaka, and Kohtaro Watanabe count positive radial solutions of a nonlinear equation on ring-shaped domains of a sphere, in a 2024 paper. The Brezis-Nirenberg problem is a benchmark in the study of such equations, and here the domain is the band on the three-dimensional unit sphere between two distances from a pole. A radial solution depends only on that distance.

The authors work across a range of the equation main parameter, up to the first eigenvalue boundary, and vary the power of the nonlinear term. They show that the number of positive radial solutions changes with both the power and the parameter, for thin bands that nearly cover the sphere. The results separate ranges where the solution is unique from ranges where several exist. The paper adds a map of solution counts for a problem where existence does not tell the whole story.
arxiv-2412-15880:
Xiang Li, Yong Luo, and Jun Sun proved results in 2024 about a flow that moves surfaces to lower their area. The flow is mean curvature flow, studied here for a special class of surfaces called Lagrangian surfaces. The work deals with the worst kind of pinch point in the flow, where change speeds up without bound. At such a point, a blown-up view of the surface is used to read its shape.

The authors prove strict rules for those blown-up views when the surface has a zero Maslov class. They give the same kind of rules for flows that stay close to a set angle. One key case is a surface that moves by sliding alone. Past work had shown such rules in two dimensions, and this paper lifts them to any number of dimensions.
arxiv-2412-15980:
Huanqi Yang and co-authors build radar-like gesture signals out of motion data from wearable sensors, in a paper from 2024. Radar gesture sensing suits hands-free control, but large, clean radar data sets are hard to gather. Motion sensors in watches and bands, by contrast, are everywhere.

Their system, iRadar, first pulls key gesture features from both signal types. A diffusion model then translates motion data into the radar signal the same gesture would make. A transformer reads the result for recognition. Tests covered 18 gestures and 30 people in three settings, using five wearable devices. Top-3 accuracy hit 99.82 percent across settings, which the authors offer as a way to grow radar data cheaply.
arxiv-2412-16180:
Control engineers often replace a complex system with a finite, simpler copy they can verify, and Abdalla Swikir builds such copies for networks of impulsive systems. These are systems whose state jumps at certain moments while flowing smoothly between them, wired together into networks. His compositional method checks each subsystem against a finite abstraction using alternating simulation functions.

Dissipativity conditions, expressed through supply rates and storage functions, guarantee the pieces still fit together at network scale. Incremental passivity and forward completeness do the rest of the work. The result is a route to finite abstractions of large jumpy networks without analyzing the whole web at once.
arxiv-2412-16680:
Reza Kord Valeshabadi and Saman Rezaie release a C++ software library for the parton distribution functions that particle physicists use to price collision outcomes. Their 2024 paper covers two kinds of these functions, which describe how a proton's momentum is shared among its parts. Two older libraries supply them, but both restrict what users can change.

The new library handles both standard and transverse-momentum-dependent functions in one flexible frame. It also evaluates the strong coupling within the same toolkit and tracks uncertainties at the distribution level, features the authors say were missing. Plugged into the PYTHIA event generator, it reproduced known results for a standard process. Comparisons against the older libraries matched, backing its reliability.
arxiv-2412-16880:
Shenghai Yuan and co-authors present a method to calibrate ultra wideband anchors and locate objects at large scale. Ultra wideband gives exact indoor positions, as in consumer trackers, but warehouses and seaports pose hard problems. Blocked line of sight makes standard calibration slow, costly, and unreliable in such sites.

The method fuses ultra wideband ranges with lidar based motion tracks and uses Gaussian processes to infer anchor positions. One sampling pass calibrates an area as large as 600 by 450 square meters. For location, a range filter narrows the search for lidar loop closure and boosts both speed and accuracy. The approach offers a cheaper path to reliable tracking in large logistics sites.
arxiv-2412-16980:
Rousseeuw builds a chart to make straight line forecasts easy to explain in twenty twenty-four. Such forecasts are a basic tool, yet it is hard to see which inputs drive a given forecast up or down. His chart shows each input's push on the forecast for the case at hand. It works whether the formula was fit by hand or by machine.

The chart handles number inputs, group inputs, and inputs that act jointly. A second chart shows how the pushes link to each other across cases. Both charts are plain to read and pack a lot of facts into one view. The aim is to help users trust and explain a forecast as it stands.
arxiv-2412-17080:
Schooltink and Zennaro aligned two styles of causal abstraction in this paper from twenty twenty-four. Causal models can be zoomed out to simpler levels, but the levels must agree on cause and effect. Graphical methods zoom by clustering the diagram. Functional methods zoom by mapping variables and their values.

The authors prove the two styles match under set conditions. Cluster diagrams correspond to functional abstractions whose value maps are reversible, and to a third, constructive style. They then widen the graphical side with partial cluster diagrams. Those allow some clusters to stay unmerged. The results let theorems travel between the two frameworks, which had grown up apart.
arxiv-2412-17580:
Vignesh Anantharamakrishnan and Márcio Taddei tune quantum circuits with evolution search, in work from 2024. Variational quantum circuits need tuned dials before they can forecast time series well. Gradient steps rule that tuning, yet they can stick fast in poor local dips.

An evolution strategy instead breeds dial sets and keeps the best forecast scorers. Across real data sets, gradient runs stuck in dips that evolution routes dodged fully. Forecast error fell as much as six fold with evolution tuning in the best case. A mixed route keeps speed from gradients and escape power from evolution search. Accuracy sensitive tasks gain most from the swap in tuning style.
arxiv-2412-17980:
Dazhi Zhou and co-authors measure the cold gas in a young galaxy cluster in a paper from 2024. The cluster, SPT2349-56, sits at redshift 4.3, when the universe was young. It hosts at least a dozen dusty, star-forming galaxies packed close together.

A thirty-hour stare with a compact radio array in Chile targeted carbon monoxide gas. The array saw seventy-five percent more gas glow than sharper images of single galaxies added up. That excess means much gas lies spread between the galaxies. Blurring the sharp data to the same view gave the same result. A shared gas reservoir may feed the cluster's furious star birth.
arxiv-2412-18280:
Heavy quarks barely notice their own spin, a near-symmetry that shapes how particles containing a charm quark interact.
