Six authors work out the interaction rules for D mesons meeting nucleons and charmed baryons, building the full set of allowed terms, twelve in all. With the symmetry enforced, only certain pairings survive: one class of D meson couples to nucleons and one baryon type, while the other class couples to the remaining baryons.

Allowing the symmetry to break restores the full menu of interactions. The team then computes scattering rates for antiproton-proton collisions that create pairs of charmed baryons, the kind of reaction a planned facility in Germany will study. Their aim is precise production forecasts that experiments can test, showing exactly where the broken symmetry leaves its fingerprint on the rates.
arxiv-2412-18580:
Decentralized finance uses automated market makers that let traders swap tokens within set price ranges, a design called concentrated liquidity. Shen-Ning Tung and Tai-Ho Wang build a strict mathematical framework for these systems in continuous time, in a 2024 paper. They model how the full liquidity profile shifts as trading goes on, and study traders who exploit price gaps.

They solve for the best gap-trading strategy under three outlooks: greedy, fixed-horizon, and endless play. One striking result is that trading fees rule out whole classes of price paths, since wiggly prices would mint endless fees. The authors say this shapes how such markets should be designed.
arxiv-2412-18680:
Alicja Wierzcholska and Stefan Wagner track wild X-ray flares from a blazar in a 2024 arXiv paper. A blazar is a galaxy core that fires a jet of fast matter near the speed of light, pointed near Earth. This one, BL Lacertae, is odd in that its X-ray band can catch either end of its light output, and at times both ends at once.

Using space telescopes' data from 2020 to 2023, the pair chart strong flaring with color shifts in both branches. The two ends of the particle spread seem to vary on like timescales. A hard X-ray scope caught a curved dip in the spectrum that can climb to high energies. The source can pose as any of three blazar types, they note, depending on when you look.
arxiv-2412-18780:
The authors wrote a 2024 paper on how to spot human actions from skeleton data while still heeding joints that sit far apart. The work tracks joint spots over time. Most past work links just the joints that touch, so it misses how far-off joints move as one, as hands and feet do in a throw. It also finds it hard to score types of motion when the data have many parts.

Two fixes are put forth. A dependency refinement module explicitly models how each pair of joints relates, no matter the distance. A second part sorts actions with the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, sidestepping density estimation in high-dimensional space. The team derives learning objectives that guarantee precise recognition. On the three standard skeleton datasets, scores set a state-of-the-art mark. The work suits surveillance, sports analysis, and human-computer interaction.
arxiv-2412-18980:
Reza Jalayer and co-authors compare deep learning systems that diagnose faults in rotating machines while reporting their own uncertainty, in a paper from 2024. A diagnosis is safer when the model can say it is unsure. Doubt comes in two kinds: from unseen fault types and from plain noise in the data.

The team benchmarked the leading design families, including dropout sampling, Bayesian networks, and deep ensembles. Two cutoff rules decided when a reading counted as out of place. Against unseen faults, all models caught a large share of the odd data. Ensembles did best under either cutoff rule. Under noise, the picture was more mixed. The findings guide engineers who must field fault systems they can trust.
arxiv-2412-19280:
Clara Galimberti, Luca Furieri, and Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate tackle in this 2024 paper a core problem in control design: how to tune a controller for top performance without ever breaking stability. Their setting is output-feedback control of nonlinear discrete-time systems that must stay stable under outside disturbances. Using operator theory and neural networks, they parametrize every closed-loop behavior a stabilizing controller can reach.

That map turns design into free optimization over safe controllers only, merging older frames such as nonlinear Youla parametrization and internal model control. They add conditions for robustness when the model is off, and show stronger stability is possible when disturbances arrive with a step's delay. Tests on cooperating robots show the range.
arxiv-2412-19580:
Philipp Blumer and co-authors review the physics of muonium in this 2024 paper. Muonium is an atom-like system made of a muon and an electron. The paper focuses on one small energy gap in the system, known as its fine structure, and on what precise measures of that gap can test.

The authors give an updated value for the energy gap based on the latest theory work. They also show how the same measure could test whether the laws of physics stay the same in all directions and frames. Computer simulations suggest a sharp measure is within reach. A new high-intensity muon beam in Switzerland should supply the needed data.
arxiv-2412-19680:
Sanjay Pant and Himanshu Parihar compute how mixed-state entanglement fades in a heated, deformed quantum theory in a 2024 paper. Their arena is a field theory bent by a T-bar-T deformation, a controlled way to move a theory's cutoff inward. Its holographic mirror is a black brane spacetime sliced off at a finite radius.

Two probes of mixed-state entanglement get computed for strip-shaped regions: the entanglement wedge cross section, tied to entanglement of purification, and holographic entanglement negativity. Both respond to heat and deformation in the same direction, a notable rhyme. Turning either knob up shrinks the entanglement shared between the regions. The study maps that decline across regimes of temperature and deformation strength, giving the young field of mixed-state holography a concrete pair of curves to test ideas against.
arxiv-2412-20080: Azizul Hoque and Srinivas Kotyada construct families of quadratic fields whose class groups have n-rank at least 2 in a 2024 paper. The class group measures how far a number field's arithmetic strays from unique factorization, and its rank over the rationals' extensions is a basic structural invariant. The authors give parameterized families, both imaginary and real, where that rank is guaranteed to reach two.
arxiv-2501-00080:
Luis Crespo, Bret Stanford, and Natalia Alexandrov present a data-driven approach to risk-aware robust design in a 2025 paper. A robust design meets its needs across a set of scenes: set runs of a system under changed inputs or states. Those scenes can come from tests or from a model.

Two forms are set out, one that shuns risk and one that is neutral to it. To guard against overfitting the data, the scenes are also nudged in small ways. A slack step trades a bit of best score for a lot more trust. Set outliers can be dropped to strike that balance.
arxiv-2501-00180:
Tiny defects in diamond, called nitrogen-vacancy centers, can sense magnetic fields, but the shallowest ones lose their quantum memory quickly near the surface. Anton Pershin and co-authors used first-principles simulations to protect centers sitting just one nanometer deep, as the head of the paper reports in 2024. Surface charge noise can now be removed, yet magnetic noise from surface atoms still limits how long the spin state lasts.

The team shows that surface strain, paired with a small steady magnetic field, can stretch that coherence time close to the room-temperature limit set by lattice vibrations. The trick uses carbon-12 enriched diamond for the shallowest centers. It also helps centers about ten nanometers deep in natural diamond. There, the field direction changes the coherence, which enables tiny vector magnetometers.
arxiv-2501-00280:
Sharing quantum keys over long distances is limited by loss in ground fiber, so Yichen Gao, Guanqun Song, and Ting Zhu look to the sky. They study how fleets of satellites should be arranged to pass quantum signals between far-apart ground stations. Their plan adds relay satellites in Molniya orbits, the tall, stretched orbits that linger long over one hemisphere.

Those relays stretch the time a satellite can serve a target region, widening coverage and cutting delay in the quantum link. The team lays out a strategy for placing the fleet and its relays. Their aim is a sturdy world-wide quantum network that beats the reach of fiber alone.
arxiv-2501-00680:
Mauro Goncalves, Monica Graf, Marek Pasciak, and Jiri Hlinka wrote this materials paper, issued in two thousand twenty-four, on tiny crystals of bismuth ferrite. This compound is ferroelectric, and at nanoparticle size its inner electric pattern depends heavily on how the surface ends.

Using atomistic simulations grounded in first-principles data, the team varied the particles' surface endings and charge patterns. Many multi-domain layouts emerged, each with its own way for the order to bend near the surface. For neutral surfaces, an unusual phase appeared: not the bulk's rhombohedral form, but a stripe-like arrangement of polarization. The authors track polarization, oxygen cage tilts, and volume change across every layout found. The work shows how much a nanoparticle's skin can rewrite its core behavior.
arxiv-2501-01080:
Ferreira and Papavassiliou review how gluons, the carriers of the strong force, can gain a mass scale even though the basic theory says they are massless. The proposed route is the Schwinger mechanism, in which new massless scalar particles appear inside the theory's interaction points. Those poles stabilize the gluon's behavior at low energy and shift its governing identities in a characteristic way.

The article gathers the central ideas and methods behind this picture of dynamical mass. Special weight falls on newer results: the exact scaling of the mass, the nonlinear equation the poles must satisfy, and a classic theorem that decides when solutions exist. The overview serves researchers entering the field.
arxiv-2501-01680:
Prihadi, Dwiputra, Khairunnisa, and Zen wrote in twenty twenty-five about chaos inside charged black holes with scalar hair. Hair here means an extra field around the hole beyond mass and charge. They send charged shock waves in from the outer edge. Then they track special correlators that reveal how fast a small disturbance scrambles. Near the inner singularity, the space takes a Kasner form, with uneven stretching in different directions.

As the deformation grew, one chaos measure fell relative to surface gravity. At large deformation it could still beat a standard charged case. Deformation also cut the delay before scrambling began. A coupling in their model strongly shaped that delay. The results show how outer changes can reshape inner chaos.
arxiv-2501-01780:
Frank Calegari and Qiankang Chen determine over which number fields hyperbolic triangle groups can be defined. A compact hyperbolic triangle group has a canonical discrete representation into the real projective special linear group, unique up to conjugation. Its trace field is built from cosines of the triangle's angles, and the question is when the group can be realized over its own trace field, or over any totally real field.

The authors prove that exactly eleven such groups are conjugate to subgroups over their trace fields. They further prove no additional compact hyperbolic triangle groups work over any totally real field whatsoever. The result answers a question first raised by Waterman and Maclachlan. It also settles, positively, five interrelated recent conjectures of McMullen. The paper closes a classification problem at the meeting point of hyperbolic geometry and number theory.
arxiv-2501-01880:
Xinze Li, Yixin Cao, Yubo Ma, and Aixin Sun revisit a design choice for language models in a paper published in 2024. When a task needs long outside text, builders can either stretch the model's reading window or bolt on a retriever that fetches only the useful parts.

The authors first re-read earlier comparisons and found clashing claims, then ran a cleaner test of their own. They dropped questions a model could answer cold, sorted retrieval styles, and widened the data. Long windows won most question tests, above all on encyclopedia-style questions. A summary-based retriever nearly matched them, while chunk retrieval lagged. Retrievers did better on chat-style and general questions, so the choice depends on the job.
arxiv-2501-02080:
Seven authors led by Voncarlos Araujo teach a camera system to spot cows in messy farm scenes in a 2025 paper. Good cow spotting helps farms watch health and welfare with less hand labour. Real barns and fields fight the camera with poor light, blocked views, odd poses, and clutter. Past models trained in one place often fail when the scene changes.

The team built a data set from six farm settings, both indoors and out. Their model pairs a fast detector with an attention block that helps it weigh the right image parts. It beat three known models on the shared tests. Scores rose by 2.3 points over the base model, with high marks for both hit rate and box fit. The team frames the gain as a step toward round-the-clock welfare checks.
arxiv-2501-02180:
Ren Hu and Pan Lian worked in 2025 on rebuilding color images when part of the signal is lost. Their method uses quaternion math, which keeps the links between color channels intact. The lost-part task is known as phase retrieval. Solving it well matters for sharp image repair.

The authors build a main algorithm and three faster variants. A second algorithm is added that settles in a steady, straight-line pace. Tests on made-up data and on real photos showed gains in both repair quality and speed over prior methods. The work may help tools that rebuild images from partial scans.
arxiv-2501-02280:
Steven Gray and Erik Verriest study symmetry in systems that turn inputs into outputs in a 2025 paper. Symmetry ideas help judge when a system can run in reverse and bear on control and stability tasks. For a class of systems described by power series, an early form of symmetry lets the output be written as a simple function of the input integrals.

The authors define two new kinds of symmetry for these systems and show how each relates to that early form. They then study in depth a class whose series grow at the fastest rate that still converges. Those systems prove to need an endless state description, with set traits for their response lag and hidden dynamics.
arxiv-2501-02380:
Dave Dice and Alex Kogan design a new lock for shared-memory programs in a 2025 paper. A lock lets one thread at a time hold a shared part, so data stay sound. Their lock, Reciprocating Locks, aims for speed and fair turns at once. Entry and exit steps run in set time. Each thread needs just one wait slot, no matter how many locks it holds.

Waiters spin on local data, which spares the shared bus. The lock skips strict first-come order but caps how often a thread can be passed. That cap gives strong guards against starvation. Tests show high throughput when threads clash and low wait when they do not. The lock fits real homes such as the Linux kernel and thread kits. Its small size is a planned plus.
arxiv-2501-02680:
Li and a large team reviewed in twenty twenty-five how spread models, a kind of smart art tool, can help design proteins. Design of proteins with set traits has been hard for years. Spread models have strong math roots and have done well at such tasks.

The review lays out two main kinds of spread model and how each works. It then maps their use in protein design, short chain builds, drug hunts, and drug-protein binds. A key need is to keep the model true to three-view turns and flips of space. The team ends with paths to self-run protein design.
arxiv-2501-02980:
Georg Anagnostopoulos and Nikolas Geroliminis show that mixed city traffic acts like water through sand, in a study from 2025. Cities now mix cars with bikes, scooters, and other small rides. The mix looks messy, with data that spread far and wide, and old smooth-flow tools fit it poorly.

Based on vast field data and a fresh model, the pair place mixed traffic in a known class of far-from-calm systems: directed percolation in one space span. In that class, flow flips from stuck to free as a heat-like dial crosses a point, with a shared power law at the flip. Their model reads lane flow as the host and lane-free flow as a guest layer that stirs it. The stir gives the wide spread seen in real counts.
arxiv-2501-03080:
Junjie Wang and four co-authors present a 2025 paper on securing drone communications against eavesdroppers and jammers at once. Drone links are exposed: signals travel line-of-sight and many adversaries can listen or interfere. Their scheme embeds a fingerprint tag into each message for authentication. Cleverly, the same tag doubles as the key for encoding the message, buying secrecy at low extra cost.

The tag is generated symmetrically from a feature of the plaintext and a secret key, so a legitimate receiver can rebuild it from the ciphertext and verify the sender. An eavesdropper receives only a fuzzy tag that cannot unlock the message. Added artificial noise further degrades interception. The authors solve the power allocation for both secrecy and authentication goals. Simulations show the scheme beating an earlier noise-aided design on both fronts.
arxiv-2501-03180:
Christelle Hanoun and a large team show how to build cheaper recorders for terahertz pulses in a 2025 paper. Their method stretches a pulse in time so it can be recorded in a single shot, at up to millions of shots per second. It serves accelerator physics and tabletop spectroscopy alike. The catch has been cost: the readout needed very fast, pricey electronics, and cost grew with each added sample.

The team show that probes at a common telecom wavelength change the math. Their design uses only standard parts and a standard commercial probe laser, with no extra pulse broadening. At a synchrotron facility it recorded coherent terahertz pulses over an unmatched number of samples. The readout electronics needed only modest bandwidth. The authors present the design as a route to wider use of the technique.
arxiv-2501-03280:
Tong Liu and co-authors measure how the radio beams of twenty-five pulsars in globular clusters twist as they travel. Polarization profiles reveal a pulsar's magnetic geometry and emission habits, and clusters host dense, old pulsar populations worth surveying. The team used China's FAST telescope, the world's largest single dish, to record profiles for all twenty-five.

Fifteen of the profiles are firsts. One pulsar in M53 showed the strongest linear polarization of the set, at fifty-seven percent, while an M15 pulsar led in circular polarization. Cluster pulsars overall run less polarized than field pulsars measured elsewhere. Rotation measures, which gauge magnetism along the line of sight, varied by cluster, growing larger for clusters near the galactic plane, matching the galaxy's own magnetic haze.
arxiv-2501-03380:
Ignacio Garrón and Andrey Ramos present a 2025 paper on nowcasting carbon dioxide emissions for US states. Official emissions data arrive yearly and late, which slows climate policy. The authors build a panel framework that estimates current emissions growth at higher frequency.

Their model predicts per-capita energy use growth from quarterly income, monthly electricity use, and a weekly economic index, mixing data of different frequencies. A bridge equation, fitted with quantile regression, converts energy nowcasts into the full distribution of emissions growth. In a dress rehearsal over 2009 to 2018 that mimicked real release dates, the nowcasts beat a historical benchmark. The method gives policymakers an earlier, sharper read on state emissions.
arxiv-2501-03480:
Chan-Gyung Park and Bharat Ratra ask, in a 2025 paper, whether a quirk in space telescope data has been faking signs of restless dark energy. Some analyses of other data sets hint that dark energy changes over time, against the constant picture. The pair test six models where dark energy's push varies, using Planck satellite maps of the early universe plus a large set of other sky measures, from supernovae to galaxy spacing.

With a lensing setting held fixed, the shifting models look favored over a constant by a fair margin. Let that setting float, and the edge shrinks a lot. Data away from the satellite favor a gentler, quintessence-like energy at late times, while the satellite maps favor the wilder kind early on. The authors conclude that excess smoothing in the Planck data likely drives part of the case for change.
arxiv-2501-03680:
Maksymilian Wojnar and co-authors teach Wi-Fi access points to share airtime by reinforcement learning in a 2025 paper. The coming Wi-Fi 8 standard lets neighboring access points coordinate who transmits at once, a feature called coordinated spatial reuse. Picking good transmission groups in dense, shifting networks is the hard part. The team frames the choice as a hierarchical multi-armed bandit problem, the classic learn-by-trying setup.

Several bandit algorithms were tried across network shapes. The upper confidence bound method won out, converging fast, adapting when conditions changed, and holding its performance afterward. The authors present the result as early evidence that learning agents can run the coordination layer of next-generation Wi-Fi better than fixed rules.
arxiv-2501-04080:
Mónica Taormina and a large team of colleagues measure precise physical properties of three detached eclipsing binary systems in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Such systems anchor the extragalactic distance scale. The team modeled light and radial velocity curves, analyzed period changes, and ran detailed spectroscopic analysis for the system with O-type stars.

Component masses run from about twelve to twenty-two solar masses, with temperatures between 22,500 and 36,000 kelvin. One system appears to be at least triple; another shows a significant period decrease of unclear origin. For one system, mass and radius precision improved about sixfold over earlier work. The team also provides a new mass-luminosity relation for O and B stars in the Cloud.
arxiv-2501-04380:
The famous Stern-Gerlach experiment sorts atoms by spin using a magnet; a 2025 paper by Jiang-Lin Zhou and co-authors achieves the same sort with an electric barrier. In the classic setup, silver atoms bend in a lopsided magnetic field, revealing spin. The electric version treats the particle beam as a matter wave obeying the Dirac equation.

Solving that equation at a potential barrier, the team derives the incoming, reflected, and transmitted waves in closed form. Both outgoing waves shift sideways by amounts that depend on spin direction and arrival angle. Those shifts could separate particles by spin or read an unknown spin. The paper also discusses how spin and electric fields interact more broadly.
arxiv-2501-04580:
Marina Moore and Alex Zenla present Edera, a 2025 system for running cloud programs in strong isolation without losing speed. Cloud hosts run many users on one machine. Light containers share one core system, which keeps costs low but leaves a large attack surface if a program breaks out. Full virtual machines isolate better, yet they have been slower and harder to use.

Edera is a tuned top level virtual machine host that uses shortcuts to cut that cost. It can serve as the runtime under a common container manager, so users keep their usual tools. It can also isolate device drivers, including for graphics chips, so a flawed driver cannot harm the host or other programs.
arxiv-2501-04780:
Shubhayan Sarkar sets out the use of quantum far links to sync clocks in a safe way. He also uses them to back up facts of fast moves with no trust in the gear used. Plain clock sync can be hit with ease. A foe who holds a sign back by a bit can cause large flaws down the line. Those flaws hit tools from GPS to work split on more than one screen.

His fix uses a stamp of truth that needs no trust in gear and rests on quantum far links. Clocks can then be synced with no trust in any gear in the set. He then grows the plan to watch time stretch from fast moves in the same no trust way. The text is a plan in rules that links base quantum work to a real time task.
arxiv-2501-04980:
Isaac Chen and Oriol Solé-Pi introduce a finer way to describe crossings in graph drawings in a 2025 mathematics paper. Draw the complete graph with straight edges and many edges cross. Past work counted edges with no crossings or with exactly one. The full picture, how many edges suffer each number of crossings, was unexamined as a whole.

Their crossing profile is the full sequence of those counts. It fingerprints a drawing far more sharply than a single crossing total. The authors study what profiles can occur for rectilinear drawings of complete graphs. Such fingerprints may separate drawing styles that totals cannot, and they feed the old quest to minimize crossings in network layouts and circuit boards.
arxiv-2501-05280:
Oskar Vågerö and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a hands-on way to plan energy systems with the public in the loop. Involving stakeholders can make energy transitions more legitimate and more likely to happen. Standard modeling, though, forces preset scenarios on participants.

Their method starts from the full spread of near-optimal system designs. An interactive display lets stakeholders mix components freely, as long as the system still works. Information about each technology's trade-offs rides alongside the choices. People explore consequences instead of voting on someone else's shortlist. The framework aims for engagement that is both broad and honest about options. Planners gain input they can actually trace back to preferences.
arxiv-2501-06480:
Zhendong Zhang speeds up the attention step inside the Swin Transformer, a vision model that works on images window by window. Confining attention to small windows is already efficient, but Zhang wanted the extra gains that flash attention brought to language models. A straight swap fails, because flash attention is built for very long sequences, while window attention juggles many short ones at once.

His answer, Flash Window Attention, is reshaped around that many-small-windows pattern. In his tests it made the attention computation itself up to three times faster, and cut the whole model's running time by up to 30 percent. The code is published online. The report is a short technical note, aimed at practitioners who train or deploy Swin-style vision models at high resolution.
arxiv-2501-06580:
Jeong-Myeong Bae, Hammam Raihan Mohammad, Ewan Stewart, and Heeseung Zoe wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It calculates the ripples in the early universe's density that were seeded by heat jitter during a phase called thermal inflation.

In thermal inflation, the universe's temperature sets how long a burst of expansion lasts. Tiny thermal wiggles therefore stretch into lasting differences in density. Using plain thermodynamics, the authors work out the small-scale heat fluctuations and follow them as expansion carries them to large scales. They convert the resulting temperature differences into curvature ripples with a standard bookkeeping method. The paper ends with a closed formula for the ripple strength across scales. Such predictions let future sky surveys test whether a thermal inflation phase really happened.
arxiv-2501-06680:
Haoxiang Gao, Yu Zhao, and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on using vision language models to read pedestrian behaviour for self driving cars. Big models grasp scenes richly but are too heavy to run in a car. Their fix teaches a small vision network from the big model's knowledge, a distillation step.

The small network then predicts how people on foot will move and tags scene features in open vocabulary form. Extra pretrained models and voting schemes lift scores further. After distillation, the light model improved clearly on both perception and path tasks. The authors argue this path can raise end to end driving skill without car sized computers.
arxiv-2501-06780:
Jihoon Park, Jeongin Choe, Dohyun Kim, and Jae-Joon Kim present COMPASS in a 2025 paper, a compiler for in memory AI chips. Crossbar arrays compute inside memory at high speed and low energy, but chips hold only so many weights. As networks outgrow the chip, weights must swap in from outside memory.

Past tools assume all weights sit on chip, which no longer holds for big models. COMPASS splits layers into parts that each fit the array in turn. Its split plan weighs layer links, core use, and write counts to cut delay and traffic. Simulations show far larger networks fit a tiny footprint with this scheme. Throughput rose 1.78 times and energy delay fell as well against base splits.
arxiv-2501-06980:
Two researchers explore how language models can steer health programs that adapt to each user in a 2025 paper. Learning systems already adjust such programs over time, but they adapt slowly. A user's stated likes, limits, or health status could guide choices right away if the system could read them.

The hybrid method lets a language model filter the actions a learning system proposes. Text from the user enters the prompt, so preferences shape each choice on the fly. The team tests several prompt styles and ways to merge the two decisions. A simulated setting checks whether the mix speeds up personal fit while respecting user limits.
arxiv-2501-07980:
Ivan Nikolić and co-authors wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on finding bubbles of ionized gas in the early cosmos. The Webb space telescope now finds many galaxies from the era when the first stars lit up space. Groups of these galaxies with strong hydrogen glow likely sit inside large ionized bubbles that let the glow escape.

The team built a forward model that reads the spectra of a galaxy group and infers where its bubble is and how big it is. The model weighs the share of neutral gas, the shape of the era, and noise from the Webb tools. Tests on simulated data show the method can place a bubble within a small margin. A modest survey of a few dozen galaxies could supply the needed sample.
arxiv-2501-08280:
A classic model shows how mild personal tastes can sort a whole town into like-with-like blocks. Aleix Nicolás Olivé, Luce Prignano, Dimitri Marinelli, and Emanuele Cozzo turned that model into a board game study in 2025. Players move pieces under a rule drawn from the Schelling model of segregation. Their twin aims were less sorting and more happiness for the pieces.

A single dial balanced the two aims in the move rule. Game data were then matched to the model with a method that works backward from outcomes to causes. The fit showed how player plans lined up with group results. The authors argue games can help the public grasp hard social patterns. The setup also feeds lay choices back into formal models.
arxiv-2501-08680:
Junling Li, Cheng-Xiang Wang, and Chen Huang lay out a framework for live digital twins of wireless channels, in a paper from 2025. A channel model describes how radio signals change as they travel. Offline models cannot follow fast real changes, while a digital twin senses and updates in real time.

The article traces how the idea evolved, then gives design steps and building blocks for such twins. It shows uses in future 6G networks and presents a working platform tested in real scenes. The twin can display and predict channel changes as they happen, which keeps simulated and real network behavior in step. Open problems and future paths close the paper.
arxiv-2501-09080:
Jacob Adamczyk and co-authors present a new learning algorithm for long running tasks in a 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning trains agents by reward. One form judges an agent by its average reward over time, which suits endless tasks and avoids discounting the future. A second form adds a bonus for varied action, which helps in the discounted setting.

No deep method had yet joined those two ideas for the average reward goal. The authors fill that gap with an average reward soft actor-critic algorithm. It pairs an actor that picks actions with a critic that scores them, under the entropy guided average reward aim. Tests on standard benchmarks showed stronger results than past average reward methods. The work opens a new path for agents in ongoing tasks.
arxiv-2501-09780:
Celedón, Tappert, Schmidtobreick and Selman map in 2025 the shell left by the nova V1425 Aql using the MUSE instrument. The shell has two parts: a round inner shell and a faster, lopsided outer one. Spectra differ sharply between them. The inner shell shows both allowed and forbidden emission lines, while the outer shows only forbidden ones.

Their three-dimensional reconstruction shows the outer shell is an arc that partly wraps the inner sphere. Clumps appear inside as well. Why the ejecta took this shape is still unclear. The authors suggest continued monitoring may reveal the mechanism.
arxiv-2501-09880: Svetlik wrote a solo math study in twenty twenty-five that proves a stronger form of a known rule for smooth wave-like functions. The rule, Harnack's rule, bounds how much such a function can vary on a round disc when it stays above zero. His stronger form holds for the same class of functions on the unit disc. The proof of that stronger bound is the full content of the study.
arxiv-2501-10180:
A one-atom sheet of antimony does not lie as flat as its drawings suggest. The authors, a six-name team writing in 2025, compute the sheet's true shape from first rules. Left alone, the sheet's pucker wavers in a slight wave, and that wave steadies the whole. The wave also flattens the sheet's electron bands near the center, making it a true semiconductor.

Pull the sheet by about a tenth along one edge and a pair of cones opens in its band map, split by a hairline gap. Lay the sheet on gold and the tale sours: gold grips hard, warps the sheet, and mixes its own bands in. The cone pair spoils in the mix. The team warn that dreams of tuning the sheet by strain must face what a real base does to it.
arxiv-2501-10280:
Panigrahy Sandhyarani and ten colleagues watch gas stream into a forming massive star cluster in Cepheus A, in a 2025 paper. How gravity, magnetism, and turbulence share control of cluster birth is still unsettled. The team combined dust polarization maps with molecular line data at fine resolution.

Their maps show the gravity, magnetic, and velocity fields pointing the same way. Energy ranking put gravity first, magnetism second, and motion third. Gravity drives the inflow and drags the field lines along with it. Magnetic tension then calms the turbulence, letting the flow stay orderly toward the cluster. The measured inflow rate is substantial for a young cluster. The field direction holds steady from cloud scale down to disk scale. The picture flips the usual story: fields here help gravity rather than resist it.
arxiv-2501-10480:
Roy Burson wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025. It looks at the famous P versus NP problem through two lenses: the sliding tile puzzle and finding roots of polynomials. The focus is how the shape of the solution space drives how hard a problem feels.

The core contrast is between finding a solution and checking one. Checking is often far quicker. The paper argues the gap depends on how the set of possible states is laid out, and how fast it can be crossed. By counting configurations of the tile puzzle and relating them to search time, the author shows that navigating the space well matters as much as raw solving power. The study adds to the debate on why some problems resist efficient solution, tying algorithm design to the geometry of where answers live.
arxiv-2501-10780:
George Montagnon and Elizabeth Winstanley compute the electric current of a quantum field around a charged black hole, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The field is a light, charged scalar field, and the black hole can amplify waves that carry charge away. Three standard quantum states for the field are compared.

A mode-sum method with practical shortcuts yields the cleaned-up current for each state. The team traces how the current shifts with the charges of the hole and of the field. They also work out how the current feeds back on the surrounding electric field. The study sharpens tools for quantum fields in curved space.
arxiv-2501-10880:
Marcin Baranek proves that a deep neural network can, in principle, solve a hard class of equations without collapsing under high dimensions. The equations mix diffusion, memory terms, and jumps, and appear in finance and physics. Grid methods die exponentially as dimensions grow, the famous curse.

His route rewrites the solution through a classic theorem as an average over random paths. Properties of well-known estimators for those paths do the rest. The result shows a network of manageable size can reach any set accuracy. No computer runs are offered yet; the paper is pure theory. Existence proofs tell builders the search is not hopeless. Practice still has to catch up.
arxiv-2501-11080:
Iver H Brevik, Moshe M Chaichian, and Anca Tureanu ask what very strong magnetic fields do to light itself, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Past a huge threshold field, space can spark pairs of electrons and their mirror twins. Such fields live only near magnetars, dead stars with crushing magnetism. The trio ask whether weaker fields, below that line, still leave marks worth seeing.

Working from a classic theory of the quantum vacuum, they show the vacuum then acts much like a material medium. Light slows a touch, and a kind of wake radiation can appear. Their rough sums give a delay of hours for gamma-ray bursts that cross deep space in strong fields. They also weigh delays near magnetars and touch on claims that light's rules might bend.
arxiv-2501-11280:
Tsukasa Yoshida and Kazuho Watanabe present a 2025 statistics paper on why some sparse regression methods switch off irrelevant variables on their own. Lasso-style penalties shrink weak effects to zero, a behavior called automatic relevance determination. The empirical Bayes route estimates the penalty strength from the data itself. The authors derive these estimators for group lasso models with few parameters and find the exact condition under which the estimator blows up.

That blow-up is exactly the switch-off mechanism. They then prove the same effect arises in general penalized regression and map the conditions for ridge, lasso, and group lasso versions. The paper is mathematical, aimed at making clear behavior practitioners rely on but rarely see proved. It turns a folk habit of sparse modeling into stated theorems.
arxiv-2501-11580:
Thomas F Bloom extends a landmark structure theorem to polynomial worlds in a 2025 paper. In additive combinatorics, a set that barely grows when added to itself must have hidden order, roughly a generalized arithmetic progression. The recent polynomial-strength proof of that principle covered sets of numbers in finite fields.

Bloom carries it to sets of polynomials over a finite field. If adding a scaled copy of the set stays small, the set is covered by few shifts of a low-rank progression of controlled size. He also applies the result to prove a sharp lower bound for the growth of a set under a transcendental scaling. Inverse theorems like this power results across number theory.
arxiv-2501-11880:
He Yu and Jing Liu propose CTWalks in 2025, a method for learning from graphs that change over time. Such graphs model things like message networks where links appear by the minute. Older methods often lose either time detail or community structure.

CTWalks samples walks through the graph using community labels, with no tunable parameters in the sampler. It anonymizes the walks while keeping community tags, then encodes time flow with ordinary differential equations. The design captures both within-group and between-group interactions. Theory connects the method to matrix factorization and shows it avoids locality bias. On benchmark datasets it beat established methods at predicting future links.
arxiv-2501-12380:
Yilun Zhao and co-authors benchmark video understanding across expert fields in a 2025 paper. Their test holds three thousand expert-written questions in total. Twenty-seven subjects span science, health, humanities, and engineering fields together.

Ordinary video tests mostly check basic visual perception skills of models. These questions demand real domain knowledge plus careful reasoning instead. Answers require watching specialized footage with an expert's eye for detail. Model scores reveal how far video AI still is from expertise. The benchmark was annotated and checked by subject specialists throughout. Readers see a harder yardstick for machines that claim to understand video.
arxiv-2501-12680:
Negar Hashemi and co-authors hunt order-dependent flaky tests in JavaScript projects. Their twenty twenty-five paper studies tests that pass or fail by luck of run order. Such flaky tests erode trust in the whole test suite.

The team built a tool that shuffles tests at three levels: single tests, suites, and describe blocks. Each project got ten orders, each run ten times over. Any flip in outcome was logged, then read by hand to find the cause. The focus is Jest, the most used JavaScript test frame. Results show how often shared state between tests is to blame and how teams can expose it before release.
arxiv-2501-12780:
Zhiyu Zhang, Yongjian Zhu, and Liang Dai teach neural networks to recognize and to generate knotted molecules. Knots appear in real molecules and are engineered for special properties, but telling one knot from another mathematically is slow, and designing a chain that ties a chosen knot was unsolved.

A transformer network classifies the knot type of a given chain shape with accuracy above ninety-nine percent. It handles many chain lengths in one model and runs about forty-five hundred times faster than the standard polynomial method. A second, diffusion-based network then dreams up new chains that tie a requested knot. Machine learning turns knot theory into a practical design tool.
arxiv-2501-13080:
Melissa Kazemi Rad and five co-authors improve input guardrails that use a language model as judge, in a paper from 2025. Chat products need fast screening for malicious inputs before harm is done. A judge model that explains its verdict can serve as that shield, if tuned well.

They fine-tune judge models to reason step by step on a small training set, then align them for guardrail verdicts. Tests span varied attack and abuse types to check generalization. Even with limited data, tuned judges caught harmful inputs far better and held up across attack styles. The authors offer the recipe as a practical path to safer chat systems.
arxiv-2501-13180:
Maxime Van de Moortel (2025) reviews the strong cosmic censorship conjecture, an old claim about how gravity must behave. Roger Penrose proposed it in the wake of the relativity breakthroughs of the 1960s. The claim says, roughly, that singularities inside black holes must never leave the future open to arbitrary influence. If it failed, Einstein's theory would lose its power to predict what happens next. The question has driven deep work in mathematics ever since.

The review gathers recent progress made with modern methods for partial differential equations. Those tools let researchers test the conjecture in the setting where it was born: gravitational collapse. Van de Moortel traces how results on black hole interiors have sharpened both the claim and its possible exceptions. The paper is a map of where the conjecture now stands. It shows a physics idea still generating hard, fruitful mathematics sixty years on.
arxiv-2501-13580: Changjiang Du builds a bridge in p-adic number theory in a twenty twenty-five paper. He starts with a field K that is an unramified extension of the p-adic numbers. To each suitable representation of the Galois group of K, he attaches a module of a special multivariable kind. He then proves that this assignment is fully faithful and exact, so it keeps the structure of the representations intact. The construction is a p-adic analogue of recent work by Breuil and co-authors.
arxiv-2501-13780:
Trung-Khang Tran and Thach Bui tackle group testing when part of the test plan itself is lost, in a 2025 paper. Group testing finds a few defective items in a crowd by testing pools: a pool is positive if it holds at least one bad item. The plan is a matrix of who sits in which pool, usually fixed and known.

Their twist: some matrix entries go missing, so recovery must first rebuild the plan from sample outcomes. The problem blends Boolean matrix factorization with matrix completion, and the authors derive bounds on when rebuilding is possible and test them in simulation. Lost or corrupted plans occur in real screening programs, from labs to manufacturing, making the theory practical insurance.
arxiv-2501-13880:
Gustavo Kuratomi and co-authors build a campus assistant in a 2025 paper. Language models write well but stumble when answers live in set documents. Retrieval aided generation fixes that by fetching text chunks into the prompt. Their assistant serves the University of São Paulo, with a retriever and a generator as its two parts.

The team tried several models for each part and tuned chunk size and fetch count. The best retriever pairing anchors the final design. Students and staff ask institutions the same factual questions daily, so a grounded assistant can lift a real load. Careful tuning matters more than model size for such grounded tasks, the results suggest.
arxiv-2501-14480:
Andrea Cristofoli and Sonja Klisch recompute the gravitational wave left by a particle crossing a plane wave of gravity itself, in a 2025 paper. Past runs of this sum slighted how the incoming and outgoing states are framed at the edges. That framing is where gravitational memory lives: the lasting shift a passing wave stamps on space. They work with on-shell amplitudes, building the wave from real scattering pieces.

Their result is the first tree-level waveform that keeps every memory effect. It is written through a classic geometric helper, Synge's world function. The tail terms that trailing waves add are spelled out, and the weak-memory limit runs smooth. They also sort the frame choice for such waves. What flat space calls a soft dressing of the start state becomes, on a plane wave, a supertranslation of the wave. A phase shift in the background's own shape rides along.
arxiv-2501-14580:
Mark Shiliaev studied a number puzzle in a 2025 math paper. Take a number between zero and one, and try to stay just below it using the sum of two unit fractions. The allowed bottom numbers come from Fibonacci-type lists, where each term builds on the ones before it, like the famous Fibonacci list itself.

A greedy method picks the largest allowed fraction first, then the best second one. Shiliaev finds exactly which target numbers make that greedy pair the best possible pair of all. He then gives a neat, simple form for that set when the list is the Fibonacci list or the Lucas list. The work settles a clean question in approximation.
arxiv-2501-14680:
Jisi Zhang and three co-authors present a 2025 paper on generating music from text with diffusion models. Most such models guide generation using text features from one source only. The team conditions their model on two views at once: detailed local features from a language model and a global summary from an audio-language model. The global view steers the whole piece while the local view tracks detail.

They also show the global view can be squeezed out of the language model itself by pooling tricks, dropping the second encoder and saving parameters. Adding the audio-language summary improved how well the music matched its prompt. The pooled version gave the best raw audio quality with slightly weaker prompt match. The authors present both routes as efficient options. The trade-off between quality and text fit is mapped for builders of music generators.
arxiv-2501-14880:
José Calderón-Infante and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on how low-energy theories of gravity gain small corrections. They use string theory as a test case for quantum gravity. Their claim is that such theories show not one but two layered expansions at once.

One layer is the usual field theory growth, set by the mass of the lightest new particles. The other layer is tied to gravity itself and is cut off by a quantum gravity scale. In far regions of the theory space, that cutoff can be named as the species scale. The picture helps sort which corrections matter most. It also marks where a plain gravity account stops working.
arxiv-2501-15280:
Robin Young argues for a simple twist on cleaning the data used to train language models in a 2025 paper. Filtering harmful text from training sets is known to make models safer at no cost to skill. Young proposes doing it twice: let a model trained on filtered data filter the corpus again, then train on the cleaner set.

His analysis shows the loop settles at a point where the model approves of its own training data. Even if each pass is only as good as the last, harmful content decays round by round. A side benefit is a large set of preference labels over documents, which humans can audit even though model internals stay opaque. He calls for labs to test the loop.
arxiv-2501-15380:
Labani Mallick and colleagues published an astrophysics paper in 2025 on glowing black holes called active galactic nuclei. Gas spirals into these black holes through a hot disk. A surrounding corona shines in X-rays. Open questions include how power moves between disk and corona, and how fast the black holes spin.

The team fitted X-ray spectra from eleven nearby examples. Their data came from two space telescopes working together. A dense disk reflection model explained three sources fully. The rest still needed an extra warm gas component. That supports a mixed origin for a puzzling soft X-ray glow. The study also gives early estimates of disk-to-corona power sharing.
arxiv-2501-15480:
Tom Yaacov, Gera Weiss, Adiel Ashrov, Guy Katz, and Jules Zisser explore how a programming style pairs with AI and proof tools, in this 2025 paper. The style, behavioral programming, builds systems from small scenario threads. Its Python form is called BPpy. The team asked whether outside tools could stretch what BPpy can model and check.

They linked BPpy with logic solvers, symbolic and probabilistic model checkers, and deep reinforcement learning. Each link added reach: solvers pruned bad paths, checkers verified traits, and learning agents filled hard spots. The paper gives both numbers and case reports showing one task can draw on several tools at once. The authors present BPpy as a hub that lets developers mix AI and formal methods in a single workflow.
arxiv-2501-15580:
Niclas Gotting and co-authors tie light soak to memory in quantum reservoir computers in a 2025 paper. Such computers leave their inner weights fixed and train just the read out. They need a fading memory, which loss in real stuff gives for free.

The team vary qubit decay to tune that fade with care. At a sweet spot of loss strength, short term memory peaks in their tests. Light absorption, a plain lab gauge, tracks that peak in step. The link lets builders set memory by a bench test, not by blind trials. Loss turns from flaw to dial.
arxiv-2501-15680:
Jongwook Kim and his co-author relate two ways to handle non-stationary randomness in a 2025 paper. Many random processes drift over time, so plain stationarity fails. Two broader ideas cover such cases: processes whose increments are stationary, and intrinsic random functions defined through those increments. The two notions look alike but were used in separate literatures.

Working on the real line, the authors lay out exactly how the concepts connect. Under stated conditions, they prove the two classes coincide. That equivalence lets results proved for one framework transfer to the other. The paper serves statisticians who model trends, fields, and other drifting random data.
arxiv-2501-16380:
Zhiwei Chen and Hao Tang design a generative model that draws quantum circuits, borrowing a hybrid layout from image synthesis, in a paper from 2025. Quantum programs are built from gates on wires, and generating good ones automatically is hard. Diffusion models based on the older U-Net design have been tried, but they struggle with cost and with seeing the whole circuit at once.

Their architecture keeps the U shape's multi scale view while swapping in transformer blocks that track global context. On two tasks, creating entanglement and compiling target operations, the system beat previous methods. It also supports masking and editing circuits toward requested physical traits. The paper pitches the design as a step for both quantum tooling and generative modeling generally.
arxiv-2501-16680:
Sarvar Patel, Giuseppe Persiano, Joon Young Seo, and Kevin Yeo studied private ways to represent sets in 2025. The problem is to store a small set drawn from a huge universe while hiding whether any one item is present. Such privacy is called differential privacy.

Their first method builds a private form with low error and compact space, and it decodes fast. A second method gives a stronger form of privacy with like space but slow decoding. The authors also prove lower bounds that match their methods up to small factors. Their trick is to embed sets into random linear systems, a shift from older work that added noise to a plain answer.
arxiv-2501-17480:
Koray Koksal, Fatma Tambag, Jamal Berakdar, and Mohamed Babiker turn a classic magnetic light effect into a polarization sculptor. In a magnetic material, left and right circular waves travel at slightly different speeds. The lag rotates the polarization by an amount set by the field along the path. Their 2025 study feeds in Laguerre-Gaussian beams with radial or azimuthal polarization. Those structured inputs let the rotation paint a designed polarization map across the beam.

Choice of material and shape tunes the output pattern. A tight beam waist adds a twist of its own: the field gains a lengthwise part, no longer purely sideways. That extra component reshapes the texturing further. The work casts magneto-optics as a vectorial shaping tool for structured light.
arxiv-2501-17580:
Stolbov, Stepanov, and Raikher study a magnetic rubber strip lying on a table that, under a vertical field, either lifts its free end or folds into an arc. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The strip is soft magnetic: it magnetizes only while the field is on. As a bending element it mimics a single cilium.

Experiments show both shapes occurring, with a wide zone where either can persist. Cycling the field produces hysteresis between the modes. Theory finds the transition resembles a first-order jump, with a twist. The flat state never loses stability, even under huge fields. So the exact field at which bending starts is in principle unpredictable. That contrasts with in-plane fields, where bending is smooth and reversible. As a cilium the strip also behaves backwards from earlier designs. The work guides soft magnetic actuators.
arxiv-2501-18080:
Xinyi Gu, Mohammad Rowshan, and Jinhong Yuan study in 2025 how to make polar codes, a family of error-correcting codes, fail less often. Polar codes checked with a CRC code and decoded with a list decoder already perform well, and the authors look for gains in the lightest codewords, which dominate errors.

Borrowing an idea from a cousin code family, they shift the rate profile used before a convolutional precoding step. The change reshapes the weight distribution of the code and improves error performance by up to half a decibel for short codes. Small gains like this matter in tight power budgets for wireless links.
arxiv-2501-18280:
Haoyu Liang, Youran Sun, Yunfeng Cai, Jun Zhu, and Bo Zhang report a security flaw in AI safeguards, in a paper published in 2025. Many chatbots are screened by embedding models, which turn text into number codes and flag matches with banned content. The team found these codes are strongly skewed in one direction, a bias an attacker can exploit.

They built short 'magic words' that, added to any text, shove its code toward the bias and fool the screen. In tests, the trick weakened safeguards on a public benchmark, made real chatbots produce harmful output, and worked across languages and models. The authors also propose a fix that corrects the code bias without retraining, and it improved downstream results. They frame the work as a warning plus a remedy.
arxiv-2501-18380:
Hu and Kamada wrote in twenty twenty-five about gravitational waves from fading cosmic strings in the early universe. Cosmic strings are thin, dense threads predicted by some theories of cosmic history. Pulsar timing groups recently found hints of a faint nanohertz wave background. Metastable strings could explain that signal, but standard formation routes face problems. Their spectrum clashes with non-detections at higher frequencies for strong strings. A delayed scaling scenario, where strings start radiating later, eases both issues.

Dilution during inflation also thins out unwanted monopoles before strings form. The authors clarify the expected spectrum under that scenario. It fits pulsar hints while respecting higher-frequency limits. They explore signals future detectors could catch across many frequency bands. Links to inflation theory and grand unified theories are discussed. The work keeps cosmic strings a live explanation for the background.
arxiv-2501-18580:
Alessandro Barro applies graph neural networks to the Rubik's Cube, treating the puzzle as a vast graph of states. His 2025 study recasts the task of guessing how far a scrambled cube sits from solved as a node classification problem. Each node is a cube state, and its class is its distance from the goal.

After training on a random slice of the graph, Barro used the network's guesses to guide an A-star search for solutions. He then compared that guidance with the well-known DeepCubeA system. The paper walks through the graph setup and the distance goal before the search tests. It offers a fresh route into machine-guided puzzle solving.
arxiv-2501-18780:
Nojan Sheybani and co-authors put proof-friendly hash functions on fast hardware in this 2025 paper. Hash functions lock data against tampering, and zero-knowledge proofs lean on them heavily. Classic hashes make huge circuits inside proofs, while hashes designed for proofs crawl on normal processors because they use costly math.

Their collection, HashEmAll, builds three proof-friendly hashes into FPGA chips, each in a space-saving and a speed-first version. The speed versions ran at least ten times faster than processor versions, with the best at twenty-three times, while drawing less power. The parallel design scales well to big jobs such as sealing large data trees. The authors say the same recipe can move to other hashes and field sizes.
arxiv-2501-18980:
Kai Yi and Peter Richtárik give popular model-pruning tricks a theory, then use it to prune better, in this 2025 paper. Pruning shrinks large language models by deleting weights, and two methods, Wanda and RIA, work strikingly well without any retraining. One leans on activation sizes, the other on relative weight importance, but nobody had explained why they succeed. The authors rethink the objective pruning should minimize.

The new theory both explains the incumbents and suggests strategies that weigh activations and weights together. Experiments back the combined approach. Principled pruning matters because the field now shrinks nearly every big model before deployment. Rules of thumb got the field far; this paper tries to replace luck with understanding.
arxiv-2501-19080:
Reinforcement learning agents learn by trial and error, often on data about real people, so their training can leak private facts. Alexandre Rio, Merwan Barlier, and Igor Colin build a policy gradient method that carries a formal privacy promise. Their key move reframes the privacy noise as a question of trust regions, the limits on how far each update may move the policy.

Balancing noise against region size yields an agent that stays both private and capable, without giving up the theory behind the non-private method. On standard benchmarks the results improve clearly on earlier private algorithms for online learning, a step toward deploying learning agents where data is sensitive.
arxiv-2501-19380:
Karina Kohl and co-authors study how blind and low-vision software workers solve problems in creative ways, in a 2025 paper. Software work needs both technical skill and fresh thinking. Blind and low-vision professionals face tools they cannot use and hurdles in working with sighted colleagues.

The team held semi-structured interviews with thirty such professionals and analysed the talks for themes. Participants described building their own workarounds for blocked tools and leaning on supportive communities that share fixes. For them, creative problem-solving is not a bonus but a daily need for getting work done at all. Sighted peers, by contrast, tend to create for optimisation. The authors say workplaces should value this forced inventiveness and the communities that sustain it, rather than leave workers to cope alone.
arxiv-2502-00080:
Postnov, Porayko, and Pshirkov review pulsar timing and polarimetry, with results and perspectives for fundamental physics. Timing the arrival of pulses measures delays from many physical processes along the signal path. Arrays of pulsars together can hunt space time ripples, including gravitational waves.

Recent detection of a stochastic nanohertz gravitational wave background by several regional collaborations, now joining in an international array, anchors the review. Timing and polarimetry also constrain scalar ultralight matter, the pseudoscalar bosons sometimes proposed as dark matter. The authors survey current limits and the prospects of these tools for other problems in fundamental physics and cosmology. Few methods probe such faint effects with clocklike precision.
arxiv-2502-00180:
Roi Benita, Michael Elad, and Joseph Keshet analyze diffusion models in 2025 through the lens of frequency. These models start from pure noise and clean it step by step into images or sound. Some design choices, like how fast noise fades at each step, still rest on habit rather than theory.

Assuming the noise behaves in a standard way, the team derives a closed-form description of how each frequency in the signal evolves during generation. The formula turns schedule design into a matching problem: shape the noise path to the data's own frequency mix. The view explains why some schedules practitioners favor actually work.
arxiv-2502-00380:
Meziani and co-authors present a framework, published in 2025, that lets ordinary clustering methods handle data far too big for them. Clustering huge, high-dimensional datasets breaks standard tools on memory and time. Their method never changes the base tool's own logic. Instead it runs the tool many times on small random views of the data. The runs must then agree; consensus merges their answers into one.

Step by step the dataset shrinks, as groups are replaced by representatives. The hierarchy repeats until the problem fits the tool comfortably. Experiments span synthetic and real data and four families of clustering method. The framework also stays interpretable, since each merge is visible. Big-data clustering usually demands bespoke algorithms; this wrapper offers a shortcut. It treats agreement across views as the signal worth keeping.
arxiv-2502-00580:
Stuart Armstrong and co-authors defend language models against jailbreaks that hide in plain sight. Their 2025 paper studies Best-of-N attacks, where harmless-looking tweaks to spelling and punctuation are retried until a model slips and answers a banned request. The attack had beaten every major model in earlier work.

Their defense runs each incoming prompt past a judge model again and again. It hunts not just for harmful asks but for the shape of a jailbreak itself, until a stable safety rating emerges. It blocked every successful attack from the original study and nearly every one in the team's own rerun. Small judge models guarded almost as well as large ones. The authors argue the same sensitivity that makes models fragile also makes them sharp-eyed guards.
arxiv-2502-00680:
Klaus Meer and Adrian Wurm answer structural questions about a complexity class that lives between NP and PSPACE. The class captures deciding the existential theory of the real numbers, and a recent compendium collected open problems about its shape. This paper settles several.

Oracle worlds are built both ways: some where NP and the class separate, some where they coincide, echoing the classic Baker-Gill-Solovay result for P and NP. A Ladner-style theorem follows: if the classes differ, problems exist inside the bigger class that are neither in NP nor complete for it. A descriptive complexity characterization rounds out the structural portrait. The authors write for complexity theorists tracking how real-number computation reshapes the classical landscape.
arxiv-2502-00780:
Diogen Babuc laid out the base claims of a framework he calls the Theory of Proportions and Symbolic Allusions in twenty twenty-five. The framework joins math, language study, psychology, and game theory. Its core claim is that assigning numbers to symbols, dates, and words reveals patterns that repeat across scales and reflect deep rules of the world.

Babuc applies the scheme most fully in therapy. A patient might assign numbers to fingers, dates, or words and find links between private events and shared symbols, which can loosen rigid thinking. He suggests a similar reframing may help people with obsessive-compulsive disorder treat their fixations as codes to read rather than walls. Uses in teaching, ciphers, and language software are also proposed. The paper states the theory's aims and terms.
arxiv-2502-00980:
So-Yoon Cho, Sungchul Lee, and Hyun-Gyoon Kim wrote a 2025 finance paper forecasting the VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, with a new kind of neural network. Standard neural nets predict well but hide their reasoning, a problem in regulated finance. Kolmogorov-Arnold networks replace fixed activation rules with learnable curves that can be read back as formulas.

Their compact model's forecast comes out as a closed form equation in the input variables. That openness lets the authors check known VIX behavior inside the model, including its pull back toward average levels and its tendency to spike when stocks fall. Across several datasets and periods, the network matched standard models' accuracy while using far fewer parameters. The authors pitch it as interpretable forecasting for financial time series.
arxiv-2502-01280:
Zheng Xing and Weibing Zhao proposed in 2025 a way to reconstruct vehicle routes through city streets from wireless signal strength readings alone. Signal data are noisy and sparse, so raw readings misplace cars easily. Their method treats the route as a hidden sequence and infers it with a statistical model that respects both signal behavior and road layout.

A rough first estimate, capped by plausible speeds, guides the search toward good answers quickly. Alternating optimization then refines the trajectory while enforcing mobility rules and road-network compliance. The design leans on patterns linking measurements across space and time. The authors aim at traffic applications where satellite positioning is weak or unavailable, such as dense urban canyons.
arxiv-2502-01680:
Forecasting how many trips people will make guides roads and budgets, and Kamal Acharya and co-authors blend two styles of machine intelligence to do it in a 2025 paper. Decision trees first write plain if-then rules from travel data; those rules then join the raw data as extra inputs to a neural network.

The hybrid beat either ingredient alone across several accuracy measures, including how well predicted commuter flows matched real ones. Rules drawn with finer cuts captured subtler patterns and helped most. The authors argue the blend keeps the neural model's power while letting planners read its reasons, a pairing built for public decisions.
arxiv-2502-02080:
Brian Tapia-Contreras and co-authors study why the metal content of galaxies varies from centre to edge in unlike patterns, in a 2025 paper. Star-forming regions store a record of a galaxy enrichment history. Simple inside-out growth predicts a steady fall in metals outward, yet real profiles often break into drops and rises.

The team analyse simulated galaxies from a cosmology project, across a wide mass range, at the present day. A new fitting tool allows several slopes in one profile. Shapes found include inner and outer drops and rises, and some double breaks, with slope values that match observations. Case studies tie inner rises to fresh gas inflow and star formation, inner drops to gas blown out by supernova feedback, and outer rises to re-accreted gas and mixing with the halo. Outer drops at early times link to inflows of metal-poor gas.
arxiv-2502-02180:
Felix Hofstätter and five co-authors test how well safety checks can draw hidden skills out of AI models, in this 2025 paper. A model may hold a skill that early tests miss, and later users may unlock it. To judge the drawing-out methods fairly, the team built models with secret skills locked behind a password.

They also built a tougher model type, using a circuit-breaking method that resists unlocking better than plain password locks. On a test of multiple-choice questions, prompts alone unlocked the true skill in both model types, while steering the model's inner signals failed. On a coding task, only fine-tuning unlocked the hidden skill. Mixing methods helped, but the authors say fine-tuning should be the first choice when teams need checks they can trust.
arxiv-2502-02380:
Shiri Alouf-Heffetz and co-authors study the cost of liquid democracy in a 2025 paper. In liquid democracy, a voter may vote directly or hand the vote to a trusted delegate, who may pass it on again. The authors use an approval-based model where voting and delegating both carry costs, and a budget caps the total. A central planner must pick the casting voters so every voter is represented.

The team studies the problem through computational complexity. They ask how hard it is to keep total cost low, delegation paths short, and voting power from piling up in few hands. They also ask a control question: can an outsider tweak parts of the election to shift some voters' power? The results map where liquid democracy stays manageable and where it turns intractable.
arxiv-2502-02480:
Fabian Roth and co-authors teach neural networks physics rules so their forecasts stay stable, in a 2025 paper. Networks that learn motion from data alone often drift into impossible behavior. They can also fail when asked to predict beyond the data they saw. The team's design builds in energy saving and energy loss from the start.

The design rests on a classic physics frame that tracks how energy moves through a system. A built-in proof keeps the learned motion stable over time. In tests with sparse data, the model stayed sound and beat plain data-driven rivals. It also handled rich simulation data from coupled physics problems. The authors see it as a safer base for stand-in models.
arxiv-2502-02780:
Songlin Xu and five co-authors built simulated students for online education in twenty twenty-five. Teachers could rehearse and refine lessons against virtual learners, but past simulators ignored how course materials shape behavior, and the long texts involved strain language models. The team first ran a six-week workshop with sixty students on a custom platform that logged fine-grained learning behavior.

On that data they built a transferable iterative reflection module that strengthens both prompted and fine-tuned language models. The enhanced models simulated student learning more accurately than classical deep learning baselines, even with few demonstrations. They captured both the grain of individual progress and correlations across a class. The authors frame the result as a step toward a digital twin of the online classroom.
arxiv-2502-03080:
Aïssatou Diallo and four colleagues make language models show their knowledge trail with a structured prompting scheme, in a 2025 paper. Chain-of-thought prompting exposes reasoning steps, but which facts the model used, and where it might have gone wrong, stay hidden. Their method, IAO prompting, attacks that opacity.

Every step of the solution must name its Input knowledge, the Action performed, and the Output produced. The explicit flow lets users trace how stored knowledge moves through a problem. Factual consistency becomes checkable, and gaps or misapplied facts stand out. Experiments across varied reasoning tasks showed better zero-shot performance than standard prompting. Human judges confirmed the traces were easier to verify, and better at exposing hallucinations and reasoning slips. The authors pitch the template as both a performance trick and an audit tool for high-stakes model use.
arxiv-2502-03280:
Wouter Groeneveld argues that creativity is a practical tool for software engineers, in this 2025 paper. Modern software problems demand more than technical skill alone. Past studies name creativity as a prime factor in clearing hard hurdles. Programming itself is a deeply creative act, Groeneveld notes.

The paper carries findings from creativity research in cognitive psychology into software work. Seven linked themes for creative problem solving are laid out one by one. Each theme comes with practical views shaped for working developers. Groeneveld holds that creativity, like a coding language, can be learned and sharpened with practice. Teams gain a shared language for tackling problems that pure technique cannot crack.
arxiv-2502-03480:
Diana Koldasbayeva and Alexey Zaytsev lay a 2025 foundation for fair cross-validation of spatio-temporal models in species distribution modeling. Such models guess where a species lives, and cross-validation is the standard test of how well they will do on new ground.

When data points sit close in space, a random split can make scores look too good, since near twins land on both sides. The pair benchmark four machine learning methods on two real data sets, a plant and a fish. They try random, spatial, temporal, and forward splits, plus two ways to use training folds.
arxiv-2502-03780:
Javid Naikoo, Ravindra Chhajlany, and Adam Miranowicz report a sensitivity boost for quantum sensors in this two thousand twenty-five physics paper. Sensors can gain extreme sensitivity near singular points where a system's eigenvalues merge. Exceptional points and diabolic points are two different kinds of such degeneracies. The authors study a four-mode bosonic system at hybrid points that are both at once, doubly degenerate exceptional-diabolic singularities.

Near these hybrid points the response to a small linear perturbation is singular, and the pole order of that response sets how the estimation error scales. The hybrid points deliver a twofold improvement in error scaling over non-hybrid singular points. Quantum Fisher information gives the ultimate bound on the error, and the authors identify heterodyne detection as the measurement that achieves the optimal scaling. The result suggests a design principle for sensors targeting extremely weak signals.
arxiv-2502-03880:
Starovoitov and Kruglikov prove results on nonlinear Hermite-Chebyshev approximations in twenty twenty-five. Approximation theory swaps in simpler rational forms for hard functions. Hermite type forms match a function and its derivatives at once. The team studies systems of functions given by Fourier series.

They find sufficient conditions for such forms to exist at all. The results cover trigonometric versions named for Hermite and Jacobi. They also cover Chebyshev polynomial versions of the first and second kind. When they hold, explicit formulas follow from the proofs. Those formulas give the numerators and denominators of the forms. The work extends rational approximation theory for function systems.
arxiv-2502-03980:
Jiangtao Shi and co-authors prove a solvability result in finite group theory in a 2025 paper. An outside group acts on the main group without shared prime factors. Certain maximal invariant subgroups are assumed non-nilpotent with prime-power index. A normal subgroup inside a product-type maximal subgroup sets the stage.

Under those conditions, and barring one small exceptional factor, the group must be solvable. The proof sorts which structures the assumptions allow. Solvability matters because solvable groups decompose into simple steps. The result tightens a web of classification-style theorems about group actions.
arxiv-2502-04280:
Ankan Ganguly, Konstantinos Spiliopoulos, and Daniel Sussman work out what becomes of opinion-and-friendship models as the crowd grows without bound, in a 2025 paper. Their models hold many agents whose hidden opinions evolve as random processes, while the network among them rewires in response. Three realistic wrinkles are built in: opinions and links push on each other, today's network remembers yesterday's, and agents see only their neighbors.

The team characterizes the limit law of a random agent's opinion process and the joint behavior of opinions and links, plus the limit shape of the network itself. A general propagation-of-chaos result for conditional systems carries the proofs and may serve others. Numbers from simulations illustrate the theory. The results tell social modelers which features of huge co-evolving networks survive the passage to a tractable limit.
arxiv-2502-04580:
Taejong Joo and Diego Klabjan wrote this 2025 paper on how well large neural networks learn from examples placed in the prompt. Such networks can pick up a new task from a few shown cases, with no retraining. Some hoped this skill could beat models built for one task.

The authors set up a test world where each prompt defines a fresh fitting task. The hidden rule behind each task must be guessed at two levels. They compared the network's learning speed with the best possible method and with other sound methods. Early on, the network matched the best method's pace. The paper's title hints that this pace fades as prompts grow long.
arxiv-2502-05180:
Anas Mifrani published this mathematics note in 2025. It settles a conjecture by Richard Soland about decisions with several competing goals. In such problems, some solutions are efficient: no other option improves one goal without harming another. One might hope every efficient solution can be justified by a single scoring rule. Soland conjectured that a smooth scoring function, rising and bending the right way, could peak exactly at any chosen efficient solution's scores.

Mifrani proves that this need not hold. His argument shows that for a given efficient solution, such a well-behaved function may fail to exist.
