The result matters for multicriteria decision making, where analysts often justify choices by fitting a single utility function after the fact. If no suitable function exists, that justification route closes. Decision methods must then rest on the trade-offs themselves rather than on a hidden score.
arxiv-2502-05280:
Yackolley Amoussou-Guenou and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper that frames a shared model for agreements run by self-executing code on blockchains. Many blockchain problems are old distributed computing problems in new dress. The model must capture both the kinship and the difference. The focus is agreements where groups of parties act through trusted code that sits on the ledgers of more than one chain.

Such agreements can do broad work, but their main use is to track who owns coins and valuable data. So the model differs from the older ones in set ways. Some parties may behave falsely, so tasks are framed by what each side can gain. The parties name the desired moves, but the code, not the parties, makes the moves real. That reversal, since code alone controls ownership, is the core of the model.
arxiv-2502-05380:
Sarah Lotspeich and co-authors tackle, in 2025, the messy data problem in computing a whole-person health index from electronic health records. The index blends ten components, but records have gaps and errors. Checking charts by hand gives better data, yet only a small share of patients can be checked.

From a thousand patients, one hundred were validated with a new protocol that also recovered missing values from chart notes. Records proved accurate, and validation raised the average number of known components per patient. Simulations then compared ways to choose whom to validate, favoring a residual-based sampling plan. The methods aim at efficient, robust studies in learning health systems.
arxiv-2502-05780:
Danny Wang and co-authors present a way to spot out-of-place nodes in graph data without real odd examples, in this 2025 paper. Detectors learn best when shown odd cases, yet odd graph data is hard to gather. Image methods lean on giant pre-trained generators that graphs lack.

Their framework trains two parts in turns. A latent generator learns to mimic normal node codes from a shifting encoder. The encoder and detector learn to sort normal data while pushing their energy apart from the fake codes. The fakes thus act as stand-in odd cases. Tests on five benchmarks beat rivals that use no real odd data.
arxiv-2502-05880:
Taban Baghfalaki, Mojtaba Ganjali, and Rui Martins present a statistical model that follows two health outcomes at once in this 2025 paper. Many studies track a repeated measure, such as a blood marker over time, alongside the time until an event such as death. When patients also cluster by place, standard joint models can miss the spatial pattern.

Their model links the two outcomes in one Bayesian framework. A spatial term lets nearby regions share information, while a flexible curve captures how the repeated measure bends over time. Fast approximate methods keep the computing practical. Simulations showed the method recovers the truth well. The team then applied it to HIV and AIDS data from Brazilian states. The work gives health researchers a tool for map-aware studies where both a marker's path and survival matter.
arxiv-2502-06080:
Cold snaps and droughts struck early modern Europe together at times, and food prices felt the double blow. Emile Esmaili, Michael Puma, Francis Ludlow, and Eva Jobbova measure that compounding in a 2025 study. Price series span fourteen cities from 1565 to 1785.

Cold tracked dearer food across the long run. Drought's link ran positive but patchier. The famine decades of the 1590s and 1690s fit the cold pattern. Droughts from 1634 to 1636, amid a great war, spiked price swings. Years with both cold and drought shook prices most. Climate shocks, they show, multiply social ones.
arxiv-2502-06180:
Naome A Etori and Maria L Gini published a study in 2025 on reading mood and feeling in Kenyan social media posts. Kenyan users mix English, Swahili, and slang in a single message, and tools trained on plain English handle such code-switching poorly. Few labeled data sets exist for this style of writing, so the authors built one from ride-hailing posts.

They tested four large pre-trained language models in both fully guided and partly guided modes. One model led on sentiment with about sixty-nine percent accuracy, while another led on the harder emotion task. All models leaned toward neutral guesses. The paper also records the hard parts of gathering and labeling such data, a guide for other low-resource languages.
arxiv-2502-06280:
Li and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about graph neural networks that must learn from skewed class labels. In many graphs, a few classes hold most labeled nodes. Unlabeled nodes are plentiful but often ignored by past fixes. Their framework, IceBerg, trains the model partly on its own predictions for unlabeled nodes. Two problems dog that approach: bias toward big classes and shifted label patterns. A double balancing module tackles both with only a few lines of code.

They also split message passing from feature change to spread weak signals farther. Tests on standard benchmarks beat prior imbalance methods clearly. The framework also led the field when labels were extremely scarce. The authors argue unlabeled data are the bulk of the iceberg. Small, careful changes can unlock large gains, they conclude.
arxiv-2502-06380:
Yiru Jiao and co-authors teach neural networks on spatial time series without scrambling the map inside in a 2025 paper. Traffic flows, sensor webs, and weather grids all produce series tied to places. Contrastive learning builds representations by pulling similar examples together, but careless pulling can tear the very similarity structure, who is near whom, in space and time, that makes the data meaningful.

Two regularizers guard the geometry: one preserves the topology of similarities among instances, the other the graph shape of similarities across space and time. A dynamic weighting scheme balances the guards against the main objective so training stays stable. Tests ranged from general time-series classification to traffic prediction at two scales. Across them, the method kept latent neighborhoods truer to the original ones and improved on leading task scores. The authors offer it as a plug-in for any backbone facing geographic data.
arxiv-2502-06580:
Shirantha Welikala, Hai Lin, and Panos Antsaklis align inventories across supply chains in 2025. Recent shocks exposed how fragile supply networks are when each chain runs alone. Syncing stock levels across parallel chains could add coordination and strength.

Their method designs the sync controllers and the talk network together, using an energy-based theory of system parts. Only each chain's own behavior data is needed, and the design solves as a set of convex problems. That keeps the method scalable and cheap to compute. Numeric tests compare the approach against standard control styles, with gains against both bullwhip and ripple effects.
arxiv-2502-06780:
A quantum switch attack that breaks quantum key sharing is shown by Sumit Nandi and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Key sharing by quantum links was thought safe from spies. A quantum switch lets events run in no fixed order. A spy with such a switch can bend the shared channel in new ways, the team argues.

Three gauges, spy gain, shared signal, and Bell breach, all show the break. The switch lifts the spy's take past safe bounds. Past proofs missed this tool in spy hands. Guards must now plan for order-free attacks as well.
arxiv-2502-06980:
Chongjun Ouyang and co-authors study radio channels for a new kind of antenna array in work from 2025. In their system, the antenna is one smooth surface rather than many small parts. Such a surface changes how signals fade as they travel.

The authors work out the math for signal strength under spread-out scattering. They show that key values of the channel rise and fall in a step-like pattern. From that pattern they derive formulas for the chance of each signal level and for mean data capacity. Computer checks support the formulas. The results help engineers predict how these large surfaces will perform before building them.
arxiv-2502-07080:
Shadkhah and nine co-authors present MPF-Bench, a 2025 large data set for machine learning on multiphase flows, the physics of droplets and bubbles. Such flows drive industrial processes but resist fast simulation, thanks to instabilities, waves, and breakup. The team generated 11,000 simulations with a validated Lattice Boltzmann solver, capturing one million time snapshots of droplet and bubble dynamics.

Neural operators and foundation models were then trained with sequence-to-sequence methods on the data. The models captured transient dynamics and intricate fluid interactions well. The authors argue the benchmark can speed up scientific machine learning for multiphase problems. Cheaper learned solvers could aid design in energy, chemical, and manufacturing settings where these flows rule.
arxiv-2502-07780:
Shengkun Tang and four co-authors shrink large language models by an evolution-style hunt for the best cut set. Cutting whole parts, called structured pruning, speeds a model on any gear, unlike cuts that need posh chips. Parts of a model bear cuts with uneven grace, so a flat cut wastes skill. Their method breeds child models by small cuts, races them, and keeps the best for the next round.

Each child gets a short training burst as part of its race, with bursts that grow as weaklings drop out. That race thus scores not just the cut but how well the cut model can re-learn. Tests on three known large models beat past cut methods in their runs. One win used five times less re-train data than a famed rival. Code is shared in full.
arxiv-2502-07880:
Sandra Kvedaraitė, Tom Steudtner, and Max Uetrecht revisit a quantum field theory, in a paper published in 2025. The theory couples a field to itself six times over, in three dimensions, with many identical copies of the field. Earlier methods had drawn a line of special points, called tricritical, and the team check whether that line survives when the copy count grows without bound.

Working in the large-copy limit, they argue the line appears only as a strict limit trick and is not a real feature. They compute the energy landscape to the next order of precision and test its stability. A known oddity, where scale symmetry breaks on its own, also fades at that order. A fixed point found long ago does persist. The work cleans up the map of this theory.
arxiv-2502-08080:
Neha Srikanth and Rachel Rudinger break reasoning problems into atomic claims in a 2025 paper. Language models judge whether a sentence follows from another, but their verdicts can hide shaky logic. Splitting each claim into tiny factual pieces exposes exactly where reasoning wobbles.

The study builds atomic sub-problems for standard inference tasks and for a defeasible variant, where new facts can overturn old conclusions. Models then answer each small piece separately. Large models still showed logical inconsistency on these small steps. The team also finds which atomic pieces decide the overall label in defeasible cases. A new consistency score measures whether a model judges the same fact the same way across contexts. The method gives benchmark designers a finer lens on dataset variety.
arxiv-2502-08280:
Michael Neumann and Anne Leucht tackle trend estimation for time series whose noise has heavy, polynomial tails, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Data points arrive at uneven times, and rare large errors can wreck simple trend fits. The authors assume only that the trend varies in a bounded way and that the errors meet mild moment conditions.

They build an estimator from wavelets of the simple Haar type, reshaped to fit sample sizes that are not powers of two. A threshold rule, first worked out in a general sparse-signal setting with heavy-tailed noise, decides which parts of the signal to keep. The result is a trend fit designed to stay reliable when wild values appear now and then.
arxiv-2502-08480:
Martina Nicoletti and co-authors read a heart flaw in its field in place of its spark in a 2025 paper. The flaw is a split beat: near flesh rests long, far flesh rests short, and the seam can seed a wild beat.

Bench lore reads that split by the spark's own marks. The team ran a one-line heart thread in sums and read the field the thread throws out. The field's map drew the split plain, nodes and all. Its call-back curve ran on a new line, tied to the beat's rise in place of its rest. Heat shifts in the beat showed in the field as well. The authors cast the field as a touch-free gauge of risk.
arxiv-2502-08680:
Safal Shrestha, Minwu Kim, and Keith Ross probed math errors in large language models in a 2025 paper. Most math tests use small numbers, so a model can look sharp while still failing at real-world scales. Scores against a final answer also hide where the reasoning went wrong.

Their tool, GSM-Ranges, rewrites a known grade-school math set with numbers stretched across wide ranges. A new grading style then splits slips into logic errors and mere arithmetic slips. That split shows whether a model thinks wrong or just counts wrong. Builders can aim fixes at the true weak spot.
arxiv-2502-09080:
Qiwei Wang, Shaoxun Wu, and Yujiao Shi wrote a 2025 computer vision paper on BevSplat, a method for locating a ground camera against a satellite image. Cross view localization matters for navigation where GPS fails. The hard part is height: a ground photo and a flat satellite view disagree about how tall things are, and depth cues are missing.

BevSplat represents each ground image pixel as a 3D Gaussian blob carrying meaning and position features. These blobs are splatted into a bird's eye view feature map, from which the camera pose is read. A supervision trick based on a sphere mesh handles wide panoramic queries. The method was validated on two standard datasets covering both narrow and panoramic cameras. It avoids assuming flat ground.
arxiv-2502-09380:
Kalyan Banerjee proved a case in twenty twenty-five of Beilinson's conjecture for some K3 surfaces. It links special values of L-functions to regulators. Those values code the arithmetic of a surface. The regulators are built from its algebraic cycles. K3 surfaces are a rich test class for it. The claim is known in just a few scattered cases.

Banerjee treats K3 surfaces over the algebraic closure of the rationals. Each one has an involution, a symmetry of order two. The key condition on shape is this. If you quotient by that symmetry, you get the projective plane. It branches along a sextic curve. For those cases the note verifies the claim in full. Each new family makes the claim look more sound. It sharpens the tools at hand for the general case too.
arxiv-2502-09480:
Borkovits and a large team revisit triple star systems first found by the Kepler space telescope in twenty twenty-five. In a triple, a close pair of stars is orbited by a third, farther star. Shifts in the pair's eclipse times can betray the third star's pull. The team added eclipse times from a newer telescope, TESS, and from ground follow ups.

The longer record confirmed most old finds and sharpened their orbits. It also turned up fifty new triples with long outer periods. Some old candidates could not be solved anew, as eclipses had faded or data failed. In total, two hundred forty-three triple candidates now stand in the Kepler field. Tight triples show rich dance like effects worth close study.
arxiv-2502-09580:
José Reina-Valero and co-authors cross-correlate signals from several cavities to hunt axion dark matter with direction sense. Axion searches so far ignore how the detector's motion through the field should modulate the catch. Correlating signals across cavities grows the signal-to-noise faster than summing power. Three array layouts are simulated on paper.

Sets place cavities at scattered sites, at one site with mixed aim, or six at one site in varied directions. Phase gaps above two degrees appear for the longest cavities in two layouts. The six-cavity design shows a daily swing in the correlation's imaginary part. That swing could reveal the axion wind's speed spread.
arxiv-2502-09680:
Albina Klepach and a large team teach robots from raw video in a 2025 paper. The web holds vast video of acts, but none of it comes with the action labels a robot needs to learn. A past method guessed stand-in labels from the video itself, yet stray motion in the scene threw it off.

Their fix centers on objects, not raw pixels. A self-taught step splits the agent's moves from the shifting backdrop before labels are guessed. With the noise stripped, the learner locks onto true task acts. Tests show steadier learning when scenes hold strong decoys.
arxiv-2502-09780:
Tong Yang and co-authors drive scout play in shared games with no bonus goods, by tilt of the world guess. The work dates to 2025. Bands of agents learn in a shared dark world, a core case for group learn tech. Set cease marks, from lone-best to group-tied, frame the aims.

Their plan tilts the guess of the world's rules toward forms where the band's best joint move runs high. That tilt spurs the band off its rest point to scout more. All hands can shift at once with no pact. Proof sets the waste near the best known for both aim kinds, in line-form worlds.
arxiv-2502-10280:
Pengyu Zhang and co-authors propose, in 2025, a probabilistic method that sharpens low-resolution simulations of physical systems while honestly reporting uncertainty. Deep learning sharpeners usually need large labeled sets and give no error bars. Their framework blends a statistical finite element idea with an energy-based generative model.

The method predicts high-resolution fields with built-in uncertainty and avoids heavy labeled training data. On a two-dimensional test problem it beat simple interpolation baselines while running far faster than a full high-resolution solver. Reliable error bars matter when simulation results feed engineering choices, and this approach supplies them by construction.
arxiv-2502-10480:
Deep Parikh, David van Wijk, and Manoranjan Majji wrote a 2025 paper on safe satellite servicing by a swarm of small agents. The agents fly from a mothership to a tumbling space object and settle on it at once. Their poses are uncertain, read from range and motion sensors fused together.

Safety rules are coded as control barrier functions, which keep each agent clear of the others. A shape based check steers agents away from the tumbling body itself. The frame handles pose doubt inside the safety math, not as an afterthought. The goal is a servicing crew that can relocate on a spinning target without a single collision.
arxiv-2502-10580:
Yan Chen and co-authors speed up quantitative MRI, a scan style that maps tissue traits by taking many contrast images. Full 3-D sets take far too long to collect. Learning-based shortcuts exist, but they hunger for memory, compute, and training data on big volumes.

Their method, SS-MUSE, rebuilds the volume inside a low-dimensional subspace. It regularizes the spatial maps of all contrasts jointly with an energy-based prior learned at many scales. Because the energy is written out plainly, a splitting solver can do the rebuild with modest compute. The goal is crisp 3-D tissue maps from far fewer raw measures.
arxiv-2502-10880:
Maciej Kruk and co-authors review thirty years of work on atom number fluctuations in Bose-Einstein condensates in a 2025 paper. A condensate forms when a gas of bosons crowds into a single quantum state. Its average atom count is the same under any statistical lens, yet the spread around that average is not.

Microcanonical, canonical, and grand canonical ensembles give sharply different spreads, a sign that the usual equivalence of ensembles fails here. The review gathers the main attack routes: exact results for one-dimensional gases, recurrence methods, large-number approximations, laser theory tricks, and stochastic sampling schemes like the team's hybrid method. Fresh lab control over total atom counts has revived interest, and the weakly interacting case still holds open questions the authors map out.
arxiv-2502-11080: Chih-Wei Chang and Yen-An Chen study limits on geometric structures called toric foliations in a 2025 maths paper. The brief report names two themes. One asks when such structures form a bounded family, a key finiteness trait. The other asks how their special loci, where they misbehave or split, link together. The authors also show that a set of threshold values obeys a falling chain rule, so no endless shrinking run occurs.
arxiv-2502-11680:
Lerner, Burgun, and Bach learn link graphs from ward time series with rough time stamps in this twenty twenty-five paper. Ward series are tracked in many sick folks with gaps and odd gaps in time. Past graph tools need neat, even time steps to read such links well.

Inside, their frame casts all series as one shared wave law with the same links. A graph is drawn as a set of one-way links with no loops in the chain. A bent-note tool then solves a chain of smooth fits to get that graph back. Mock runs got most true links back at high catch and fair truth grades. The path of shrink weights proved key to name the true graph in tests.
arxiv-2502-12380:
Five researchers present a new chip design for unruly workloads in a 2025 paper. Reconfigurable chips suit tight edge devices, yet they handle neat, regular tasks far better than messy ones. Sparse math and graph work are messy, with access patterns that jump around and are hard to foresee.

Their design, the Nexus Machine, spreads sparse data across the chip fabric. Live messages carry instructions that can change shape as control flow shifts at run time. Idle units can take up work as it passes by, which evens out the load. Tests show large gains in speed and in how much of the chip stays busy, at the same power and size.
arxiv-2502-12680:
Mark Colley, Jonathan Westhauser, Jonas Andersson, Alexander Mirnig, and Enrico Rukzio compare ways to remote-control driverless cars at road works, in this 2025 study. Cars that drive themselves still stall at odd spots, and a human far away must step in. The team built three control styles: drawing the path, guiding the trajectory, and dropping waypoints, then let twenty-three users juggle up to four waiting cars at once.

Path drawing won a clear preference and the top usability score, though satisfaction lagged. Trajectory guidance cleared the fewest requests. Each style traded speed, control feel, and workload differently. The authors offer the comparison as groundwork for the control rooms that fleets will need.
arxiv-2502-13680:
Some metal mixes may turn waste heat into power at high heat with rare yield. Mohd Zeeshan, Indranil Mal, and Mani chart four such mixes by pure computing, in work from twenty twenty-five. The mixes pair light alkali metals with silver and one of two heavy partners. First-principles math gives their heat and charge flow traits.

Heat flow through the crystal ran very low, which rivals the best known heat-power stuff. The team traces the low flow to shaky bonds, slow sound waves, and short wave lives. In the potassium mixes, flat wave modes slow sound further. Yield scores at high heat topped the two mark for the best mix. The set may seed a fresh class of heat harvesters.
arxiv-2502-13780:
Beatrice Savoldi, Alan Ramponi, Matteo Negri, and Luisa Bentivogli argue, in a position paper published in 2025, that machine translation research must center ordinary users. Translation tools now serve the general public, and chatbots add translation to their skills. Yet most users know little about the languages or the technology, and their needs are barely studied.

The authors trace how the user base changed from experts to laypeople. They name three forces that shape lay use: usability, trust, and literacy about the tool. A system can be accurate and still fail users who cannot tell when it errs. The paper draws on work across fields to set out what user-centered translation should measure and fix. It calls on builders to test with real lay users, not just with benchmark scores.
arxiv-2502-13980:
A large collaboration presents results in two thousand twenty-five on how momentum is shared inside two light particles, the pion and the kaon. Inside each particle, quarks and gluons each carry part of the total momentum. Measuring the split tests our picture of the strong force.

Using lattice simulations with realistic quark masses, the team computed both shares and, for the first time, extrapolated cleanly to the continuum for the physical pion. Quarks carry a bit over half the pion's momentum and about two-thirds of the kaon's. The shares add up to the required total, checking the method.
arxiv-2502-14280:
Subhajit Chaudhury and co-authors give language models a memory for long texts in 2025. Models struggle to use very long contexts well, even when the text fits in memory. Their method stores the context in an episodic memory module that attends to relevant chunks as a whole.

The memory output then reweights the model's own attention to its stored context. That happens both in training and while generating replies. Across recall and question tasks from sixteen thousand to a quarter million tokens, the method beat plain models. It also beat popular retrieval-based frames on robustness across lengths.
arxiv-2502-14480:
Group theory sorts finite groups by their internal structure, and one family is picked out by counting certain kinds of subgroups. Maria Loukaki, writing alone in a 2025 note, settles a conjecture about that family. The family holds groups with exactly five classes of nontrivial subgroups that fail to normalize themselves.

Earlier authors who defined the family guessed that every group in it is solvable, with a derived length of at most three. Loukaki verifies that guess. Solvable groups can be built up from simple pieces in a controlled way, so the result pins down the shape of the family. Short notes like this one close gaps that larger classification projects leave behind.
arxiv-2502-14580:
Three researchers set out a quantum computing plan for a hard learning problem in a paper from 2025. The problem comes from learning probability patterns on curved spaces, a method used with complex data. At its heart sits an operator named after Fokker and Planck, whose solutions are out of reach for normal computers. The team reshapes that problem so a quantum machine could handle it.

They turn the main equation into a form like the one used for electrons. A hard part is a curved energy term, which they replace with a simpler polynomial fit. They then map each term onto quantum bits with set formulas. The paper is a blueprint, not a run on real hardware.
arxiv-2502-15180:
Junliang Chen and co-authors speed up occupancy forecasting for self-driving cars in this 2025 paper. Such forecasting predicts which space around a car will be filled moments ahead, from camera history alone. Heavy compute has kept the method off small on-board systems.

Their frame, OccProphet, splits the job among three light parts: an observer, a forecaster, and a refiner. A triple-attention trick squeezes features from stacked frames at low cost. Across three driving data sets the frame cut compute by well over half and ran more than twice as fast. Accuracy also rose above the best prior system, the authors report.
arxiv-2502-15280:
Hojoon Lee and co-authors present SimbaV2, a reinforcement learning design that scales up without the usual training wobble, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Bigger models help in supervised learning but often overfit or shake in reward learning on shifting data. Two guards anchor the design.

Weights and features are pinned to a sphere so their size cannot run away. Value reads come as spreads with reward scaling to keep gradients steady. Built on a soft actor-critic base, the system topped fifty-seven control tasks across four domains. Code is shared openly. Readers who scale reward learning get a stability recipe that holds at size.
arxiv-2502-15680:
Jaydeep Borkar and co-authors study how private data, such as names and addresses, can leak from language models in surprising ways. Owners of such data may ask for it to be added to or removed from training sets, and builders often assume each item stands or falls on its own. The team shows that memory of data is in fact a shifting trait.

Three ripple effects stand out. A like item seen later in training can wake up memory of an earlier one. Adding some private items can raise how much a model memorizes of others, by up to about sevenfold. Removing items can also push the model to memorize what remains. Builders must weigh these second-order risks, they warn.
arxiv-2502-15880:
Ashley Francis, Liliya Williams, and Jens Hjorth test a first-principles account of how dark matter halos settle, by their energy spread. Halos in simulations settle into nearly one shape for all, yet why was not known. A maximum-entropy account, DARKexp, gives the settled shape from the energy spread of the parts. Their 2025 work fits that account to large halos of a known world simulation, IllustrisTNG. Then it tracks their entropy from young space to now.

The account fits the energy spread of the settled halos to a fine grade. Their entropy climbs as time runs, in the main. Halos thus grow toward their maximum-entropy rest, and DARKexp names that rest right. A law-first root for the one-shape rest gains ground.
arxiv-2502-15980:
Tian and a team including Li present SQLsynth in twenty twenty-five, a tool for building text to SQL data. Such models turn plain language questions into database queries. They drop in accuracy when moved to new, specialized database schemas. The main cause is a lack of domain specific training data.

Getting high quality data for each new schema is very costly by hand. SQLsynth pairs humans with language models in a structured workflow. That pairing streamlines the creation of accurate training sets. A user study compared it with manual annotation and with a chat model alone. SQLsynth sped up annotation and lowered mental load. Its data sets were also more accurate, natural, and diverse.
arxiv-2502-16780:
Henri Berestycki, Cole Graham, and Juncheng Wei study how domain shape controls solution counts for a class of elliptic equations. Their 2025 paper works on unbounded domains shaped as epigraphs, the region above a graph. The equations are of bistable, field type.

A sharp split appears. Epigraphs bounded below hold at most one positive bounded solution. Those that contain a wide cone hold endlessly many. Yet every epigraph holds at most one strictly stable solution. The uniqueness proof sharpens a classic moving-plane method with a split domain trick. The many-solution proof borrows from the geometry of Delaunay surfaces. Results extend to outer domains and other wide-cone shapes.
arxiv-2502-16980:
Theodoros Katsoulas and Kyriakos Tamvakis widen a variant of gravity and follow its early-universe story, in a 2025 paper. Their frame is Einstein-Cartan gravity, where space can twist as well as bend. The action keeps terms up to the square of two curvature measures, one the classic Ricci scalar, one the Holst invariant. A scalar field rides along, tied to curvature even through its own motion.

Rewritten as a plain metric theory, the frame grows a second living field, a pseudoscalar born of the Holst term. On an expanding background the two fields rush into lockstep, acting as one inflation driver. That single-field play matches the latest sky data across a wide span of settings. The match sets caps on how hard the field's motion may grip curvature. The authors present the caps as the paper's hard yield.
arxiv-2502-17180:
Mark Voit explains why counting the energy needed to free gas from cosmic structures requires a better map of the universe than the usual halo model gives. He proposes dividing the cosmos into bound domains: the gravitationally bound islands that will drift far apart as expansion continues. Thinking in these units changes the answer to how deeply gas is held.

A bound domain's gravity well, he shows, was already about as deep a billion years after the Big Bang as it is today. That stability reframes questions about where ordinary matter sits in and around galaxy groups and clusters. The tutorial lays out how future work can exploit the bound-domain view.
arxiv-2502-17380:
Qiuming Zhao and co-authors present a 2025 paper on merging speech models trained for different languages into one system. Speech-to-text tools must serve many languages, for both recognition and translation. Training one giant model for all of them is costly, tangles the languages, and is hard to extend.

Their method, called LoRS-Merging, blends separate models by keeping each weight change in a compressed low-rank and sparse form. Only the essential structure of each specialist model is retained, which cuts computing cost while guarding skill in each language. The authors present merging as a cheaper path to broad multilingual coverage than joint training from scratch.
arxiv-2502-17580:
Scott J Kenyon and Benjamin C Bromley present a 2025 arXiv paper, the fifth in a series, on the small moons of Pluto and Charon. Using 275 fresh orbital simulations stacked on earlier work, they cap the total mass of the four small satellites. For the volumes New Horizons measured, that cap pins the density of Nix and Hydra near or below Charon's.

Systems under a slightly lower mass stayed stable for the Sun's whole age, with Nix and Hydra clearly lighter than Charon. New telescope state vectors sharpened the orbits of Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra. Styx came out more eccentric and flatter, which leaves it more exposed to tugs from Nix.
arxiv-2502-17980:
A superconducting nanowire switch can flip in a billionth of a second, and Zoltán Scherübl and co-authors found a second, faster way back, in work from twenty twenty-five. Gate pulses drive the aluminum wire while a microwave probe watches its state. The usual leak-driven flip to normal took one to two nanoseconds.

Return by leak lagged at ten to twenty. A quirk of the gate's charge storage offers a shortcut: the displacement surge drives the flip both ways. Return then took four to six nanoseconds. Fast, low-power superconducting logic gains a new trick, with thermal design the next lever.
arxiv-2502-18080:
Wenkai Yang, Shuming Ma, Yankai Lin, and Furu Wei ask how long a language model should think in a 2025 paper. Longer chains of thought often boost hard reasoning scores. Yet the team suspected that too much thinking could also hurt.

Tests on math reasoning showed that very long chains did lower accuracy in some domains. Each domain had its own best range of response length. Their strategy first teaches a model varied effort levels using a small seed set. The model then picks its shortest correct answer among tries at different effort levels. This thinking-optimal scaling aims for strong results without wasted computation. It reframes test-time effort as a choice, not a race.
arxiv-2502-18280:
Ishan Koralege and five co-authors improve wireless networks that use smart reflecting surfaces in this two thousand twenty-five paper. These surfaces, called RIS, are panels that bounce radio waves in controlled directions. They are seen as a key part of future 6G networks. Setting their many phase shifts well needs accurate knowledge of the radio channel. Getting that knowledge is costly and often stale.

The team proposes to predict the channel instead of measuring it each time. A transformer model, the same family used in language AI, forecasts channel states. Their method unfolds a classic optimization into a learning system. The predicted channel then drives the phase settings. The work aims at stronger signals and wider coverage with less overhead.
arxiv-2502-18380:
Haodong Zhang, Fei Wang, and Britta Nestler rethink slip and friction where a fluid meets a solid, through the idea of an adsorption layer. Classic flow models assume no slip at the wall or set a slip length by fiat, neither with firm ground. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The layer is a thin zone at the wall where fluid and solid pulls govern both clinging and slip. From an energy low point rule, the authors derive balance laws that link wall friction, thick flow stress, and clinging shifts. The frame joins this zone to the bulk fluid in a self matched way. It explains why water slips more in tight carbon tubes, matching lab and model data where classic models fail.
arxiv-2502-18780:
Qian Cui and co-authors count blue straggler stars in far-off open clusters in a 2025 paper. Blue stragglers are stars that look younger and bluer than their cluster mates, likely after gaining mass. Using data from the Gaia mission, the team searched fifty-three clusters, most in the outer disk of the Milky Way.

They confirmed more than a hundred blue stragglers and flagged hundreds more as possible cases. The new finds grow the known sample for the outer disk by nearly half. The team also studied how much extra mass the most extreme stragglers carry. That peak rose with cluster mass, which fits the idea that heavier clusters make mergers more likely. Age alone showed little link to the peak.
arxiv-2502-19180:
Melanie Schaller and four co-authors use automated machine learning to fight sensor drift in industrial systems, in a 2025 paper. Sensors age, and their slow drift quietly poisons the models that read them. The team first show that the usual way of validating models, cross-validation, flatters them here: shuffling data lets future drift leak into training, hiding the problem. They propose a validation scheme that respects time and drift.

On top of that, their AutoML system searches over balancing, ensembles, features, and tuning to build drift-resistant classifiers. It also adapts as drift severity changes. The combined approach markedly improved classification under drift in their tests. The authors present the work as a practical kit for factories whose sensors cannot be recalibrated often, keeping monitoring honest as instruments age.
arxiv-2502-19280:
Akash Dhasade and co-authors route questions to the right databases in retrieval-augmented generation, in a 2025 paper. Language models hallucinate less when they fetch documents first. Yet in hospitals, firms, and agencies, the useful documents sit scattered across owners who will not centralize them, and asking every source wastes bandwidth.

Their system, RAGRoute, trains a small neural classifier to pick which sources a query should visit. Selective routing cut communication volume by over eighty percent and latency by about half across three benchmarks. Accuracy matched the query-everything baseline. The work shows federated search can stay private and cheap at once, a practical shape for real-world retrieval systems.
arxiv-2502-19680:
Kai Hu and co-authors teach a smart tool to pick the frames that count in a 2025 paper. A film tool fed each frame of a long clip chokes on bulk, so most shops feed it a blind, even pick.

A blind pick can skip the one stretch that bears the ask. Their pick is a light tool that reads the ask and keeps the frames that fit. It learned from two calls: a sight call that scores lone frames, and a time call that weighs runs by their word dress. The picked frames then feed a froze grand tool for the last call. On four test sets of film asks, mid and long, the pick lifted scores clear. The authors cast frame pick as a craft of its own.
arxiv-2502-19880:
Yongjun Yun and Jungjai Lee reconstructed a holographic dark energy model with torsion in 2025, without letting dark energy and dark matter interact. Holographic models tie dark energy to a length cutoff, here the Hubble radius. Torsion, a twist in spacetime sourced by the spin of matter, enters the gravity side of their Friedmann cosmology.

In the regime they study, a time-varying torsion term dominates. Even very weak torsion then drives cosmic acceleration, in their result. The present-day equation of state dips within a range they compute as a free parameter varies, and near one end it behaves a little differently from a pure cosmological constant. Readers get a route where the Hubble radius works as a cutoff on its own, because torsion does part of the job interaction used to do.
arxiv-2502-20080:
Djardiel Gomes and five co-authors run computer studies of a very thin carbon ribbon, twelve atoms wide, in both solid and hole-punched forms. Their 2025 paper follows a lab success in making these graphene nanoribbons. Holes spaced along the ribbon let scientists tune how it handles electrons, light, and heat.

Quantum calculations showed the holes widen the energy gap for electrons and create trapped states. Light checks found strong effects from bound electron pairs and shifts in what colors the ribbon absorbs. Heat flowed far less well through the holed form, since the holes scatter vibrations. The ribbons grew softer and weaker yet stayed stable. The authors see hole design as a dial for future tiny devices.
arxiv-2502-20380:
Arnav Kumar Jain and co-authors addressed multi-step coding help in 2025, where a program is fixed over several rounds of test feedback. Past tools either ignore feedback or use complex training schemes. Their system learns from a reward given at each single step instead.

The key claim is that correct code can be reached in one step from any flawed draft. So the system trains both a writer that uses past feedback and a checker that scores new code. Tests showed clear gains over strong prior tools. Study of the reward and checker choices showed why feedback helps, and the code was shared in public. In short, a simple reward proved enough for a multi-step task.
arxiv-2502-20480:
Chaoyu Li, Sid Padmanabhuni, Maryam Cheema, Hasti Seifi, and Pooyan Fazli present a method and data set for describing videos so blind and low-vision viewers can follow them, in a 2025 paper. Auto-generated descriptions often disappoint because the human examples used for training are weak. Their approach pairs large multimodal models with established accessibility guidelines.

With it, they built a set of forty thousand described videos, the largest of its kind. In trials with hundreds of sighted viewers, forty blind or low-vision participants, and seven professional describers, the new descriptions beat novice human work. They matched trained human descriptions on clarity, accuracy, and satisfaction. Models fine-tuned on the set also produced strong accessible descriptions, and both code and data are public.
arxiv-2502-20580:
Maher Hanut and Jonathan Kadmon show that large neural networks can train on low dimensional error signals in this 2025 paper. Standard training ships high dimensional error back through every layer, a costly process with little sign the brain does the same. Most tasks, though, have small outputs. The authors build a local learning rule on feedback alignment that sends back a slim error instead. The backward pass is split from the forward pass, so the error's size can be set freely.

Theory for linear networks grounds the method. It then extends to nonlinear, convolutional, and transformer models. Even an error as small as the task's own output size matched full backpropagation scores. Convolutional networks, long resistant to feedback alignment, trained well with minimal error. The authors argue that gradient signals need not be rich to teach big systems.
arxiv-2502-21180:
Anca Preda, Goran Senjanović, and Michael Zantedeschi revisit a minimal SO(10) grand unified theory in two thousand twenty-five. The theory joins forces in one frame based on the SO(10) group. Three Higgs sets drive breaks at the top, middle, and weak scales. The model can be renormalized, a trait the title stresses.

Tests of the joining rules allow the left right scale to sit near LHC reach. The quark lepton scale can drop near its lowest allowed bound. Neutron to anti-neutron shifts could show at current reach in both cases. Light new scalars could also drive a rare double decay. A fine tuning worry for the light Higgs is weighed.
arxiv-2502-21280:
Sherlon Almeida da Silva, Davi Geiger, Luiz Velho, and Moacir Ponti blend geometry and learning for stereo depth from two views, in a paper from 2025. Their system builds explicit three-dimensional surface models as seen by a single cyclopean eye. Such models handle depth jumps and blocked regions in a principled way.

Learned stereo features supply matching strength, while the surface model enforces coherent shape. A prior single-eye surface model fills gaps where matching fails, such as blocked or texture-free areas. Results already match top purely learned methods on scores and look much better to the eye. The authors argue geometry still has much to give vision research.
arxiv-2503-01080:
Chen Tong and Peter Reinhard Hansen wrote a 2025 paper on a new model for how asset returns move together. Stock returns in the same trade group often swing in linked ways. Their link also shifts over time and can spike in wild markets.

The new dynamic factor correlation model tracks these links through a few shared factors. A fresh setup for the factor weights keeps the model clean and free of clashes. It handles many assets at once and allows fat-tailed shocks. The team tests it on 12 asset returns for close checks, then on 323 returns to show scale. Banks and funds use such models to gauge joint risk.
arxiv-2503-01180:
Deciding whether two groups are secretly the same, under a renaming of their elements, is the group isomorphism problem, a classic hard nut in computer science. Saveliy Skresanov proves that this problem reduces, in polynomial time, to the group automorphism problem: telling whether a single group has hidden symmetries. The result mirrors a famous fact for graphs, where isomorphism and automorphism are known to be polynomial-time equivalent. His reduction places the two group problems on the same footing.

Skresanov also gives reductions to related tasks, including counting automorphisms. Reductions of this kind matter because they let algorithms and hardness results travel between problems: a fast method for one becomes a fast method for the other. The author presents the work as closing an analogy that graph theory had long enjoyed and group theory had not.
arxiv-2503-01580:
Hanmo Liu and five co-authors address learning on changing networks in a 2025 paper. Networks like social graphs gain new kinds of nodes over time, so a classifier must learn new classes without forgetting old ones. Retraining on everything is costly, but training only on the new makes the model forget.

Older fixes keep a small set of old examples, yet they ignore how old classes themselves evolve over time. The team's framework keeps small, well-chosen subsets of old data and aims them at the future shape of each class. They derive a bound on the error this swapping causes and turn it into rules for picking and using the subsets. Tests on three real data sets show the method holds accuracy for old classes while adding new ones. The work names and tackles a problem real graph systems face daily.
arxiv-2503-01680:
Thibaut Delcroix and Simon Jubert built new numerical tests for special geometric metrics in a 2025 paper. On certain complex shapes, called Fano varieties, prized metrics with constant scalar curvature may or may not exist, and stability invariants predict the answer in the unweighted case. The authors work in a weighted setting, where a chosen weight function reshapes both the metrics and the solitons that generalize them.

They define a weighted delta invariant, plus a reduced version, that characterize when weighted solitons exist, and prove a sufficient condition for weighted constant-curvature metrics. Links to the best lower bound on weighted Ricci curvature are spelled out, with a general cap from moment images. Fibration examples show how to estimate the bound from base and fiber.
arxiv-2503-02380:
Michael Good and Eric Linder argue that a universe born from a vacuum blip must speed up late in its life, in a paper from 2025. Most accounts start the cosmos in a hot, dense Big Bang state. Their account starts it as a chance flicker of empty space instead. From that start, they derive a sum rule for how expansion must unfold.

The rule rests on a form of the expansion equations tied to a special math function. It forces the growth of space to cross into speeding up at late times. They note links to symmetry maps used in geometry. They also check the rule against current data on the cosmos. The data fit a past crossing of the key quantity through zero. In the standard model, that crossing would not have happened yet.
arxiv-2503-02480:
Marcel Reginatto, Andrés Bermúdez Manjarres, and Sebastian Ulbricht rebuilt classical mechanics in 2025 inside Hilbert space, the quantum formalism's home; the catalog creator field carries affiliation numbers. Their route follows van Hove's unitary picture of contact transformations, not the older Koopman and von Neumann theory.

In this picture, classical observables are operators that both describe quantities and generate motion, so no hidden helper operators are needed. A fixed phase condition on the wavefunction keeps the theory consistent with classical behaviour. The frame extends to mixed systems with classical and quantum parts together. As a test, the authors treat a classical device measuring a quantum two-level system.
arxiv-2503-02780:
How much abuse can a computer network take and still do its job? Xavier Cadet and co-authors give that quality, cyber resilience, a number in a 2025 paper. Their formula weighs several defender goals at once, along with how critical each network resource is to daily operations, and stays readable for human operators.

The team tests the measure inside CybORG, a training ground for automatic defense agents. They show how to roll the score across changing attack patterns and across different network layouts. Then they train reinforcement learning defenders guided by the metric and compare them with rule-based rivals. Two habits proved decisive: hardening the network before attacks land, and restoring compromised machines quickly. The paper argues resilience can be managed once it can be measured.
arxiv-2503-03280:
Truong Cong and co-authors present BEVMOSNet, a system that spots moving objects from above for self-driving cars, in a 2025 paper. Cameras alone miss objects at night or in rain. Radar and laser scans hold up in bad weather, and radar also reports speed. The new system blends all three feeds into one map view.

The team also tested how best to mix the feeds, using a flexible attention step to share facts across sensors. On a large public driving set, the blend beat a camera-only system by a wide margin on overlap score. It also edged past an older three-sensor system. The authors call it the first end-to-end blend of its kind for this task.
arxiv-2503-04280:
Niccolò Turcato and five co-authors let a robot arm learn by trial with AI-set rewards in a 2025 paper. Trial learning can teach fine hand skills, but it feeds on reward marks, and hand-made marks for real tasks are slow to craft and easy to get wrong. Sparse marks leave the arm blind for long runs.

Their chain, called ARCHIE, asks a top language model to write reward code from the task's plain account. The arm then trains on those marks with no man in the loop. Real-world tests show the chain reaching sound skill. AI-set marks may cut the craft cost of robot learning.
arxiv-2503-04880:
Cem Eroncel and co-authors proposed a new birth channel for dark matter in two thousand twenty-five. The QCD axion is a leading dark matter candidate. A fast-rolling field in the early universe is the setting. Ripples in space curvature mix with that rolling field. Their product seeds fluctuations that become axions. Those axions could supply all the dark matter seen today.

The channel opens a wide range of axion masses. The QCD axion range is a special focus. Upcoming experiments target exactly that range. The authors review limits the mechanism must respect. Passing gravitational waves could carry a signature as well. The idea links inflation physics to lab searches. It gives hunters fresh motivation for wide scans.
arxiv-2503-05280:
Governments censor social media posts, but the rules behind each removal are rarely visible from outside. Neemesh Yadav and co-authors use language technology to reverse-engineer those rules across countries. They train classifiers on collections of posts sampled from the old Twitter stream and study which posts each country blocked.

The team explains the classifiers' calls with importance scores and with plain-language explanations drafted by language models. Human judges then rated how good those explanations were across three different models. Patterns emerged in what gets censored, both between countries and across time. The authors close with the limits and ethics of peering into state censorship this way. Their code and data are public for others to build on.
arxiv-2503-05380:
Bálint Hartmann and co-authors compare three ways to strengthen a power grid in a 2025 study, using two models of the Hungarian high-voltage network built from the operator's own data. Grids need spare paths so one failed line does not cascade into wide blackouts.

One plan doubles the links between grid zones, one adds bypasses near weakly synced nodes, and one shores up lines whose loss sparks the largest cascades. Doubling the zone links gave the best gains on all measures. The team also checked for the odd case where added capacity makes the grid less stable. Line-cut tests showed cascade sizes with heavy tails at mid strength. Grid planners get a ranked, tested menu of upgrades.
arxiv-2503-05680:
Paul Hacking and Ailsa Keating prove a mirror symmetry conjecture for K3 surfaces in this 2025 math paper. Homological mirror symmetry, proposed by Kontsevich, predicts that two very different mathematical structures built from a space and its mirror should match exactly.

The authors prove it for projective K3 surfaces. The Fukaya category of such a surface equals the derived category of coherent sheaves on its mirror, itself a K3 surface of high Picard rank over a field of formal series. The result extends earlier work by Seidel on the quartic surface and by several other groups. K3 surfaces are a central test case for the conjecture.
arxiv-2503-05980:
Samir Abdaljalil and co-authors build SINdex, a score for catching made-up answers from large language models. Their 2025 paper tackles hallucination, where a model states falsehoods with confidence. Their method needs no outside data and works with standard models, which makes it easy to adopt.

The system embeds a model's sampled answers as points of meaning, then groups them with hierarchical clustering. SINdex measures how inconsistent those groups are, since shaky answers scatter more. Clusters came out cleaner than with older measures, and detection scores rose by up to about nine percent on standard question sets. Careful knock-out tests confirmed each part of the pipeline earns its place.
arxiv-2503-06380:
Khang Vo, Tho Quan, and co-authors join text and image maps with an energy based train plan, in a 2025 paper. Text and sight speak in unlike codes, so fused tools oft miss fine cross links. Their plan scores pairs by a shared energy that sinks for true mates.

Loose self taught steps let the plan bend to rich cross links with no hand marks. Tests on mood from mixed posts beat past train plans by a clear edge. The team sees gains for mixed ask tools as well. Energy frames may thus lift fused sense in broad smart work.
arxiv-2503-06580:
Yuxiang Zhang and co-authors build agent models that carry their action plans inside their reasoning, in a 2025 paper. Most AI agents today follow scripts pasted in from outside prompts, which tell them when to call tools. That harness limits how freely they can plan.

Their framework, AutoCoA, trains the model to grow its own chain of actions as it thinks. It learns when to fire a step-level action, how to polish whole action chains, and it keeps an inner world model to cut costly trials in the real setting. Training mixes guided examples with reward-based learning. On open question tasks, the agent models beat prompt-driven rivals by a clear margin, above all on long, multi-step jobs. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2503-06880:
Tianyi Zhou surveys ways to tell when a math space has a key bounce-back trait in a 2025 paper. The spaces, called Banach spaces, are full sets where length and limits behave well. A reflexive space is one that matches its own double mirror, a trait that helps prove many deep results.

The survey gathers known tests for the trait from many angles. Some rest on means of sums, some on tight sets, and some on flat sets in the space or its mirror. A test for two bad guest spaces also gets full play, since their presence can rule the trait out. Links past the trait, to stronger shape traits, close the survey.
arxiv-2503-07080:
Lázaro Costa, Susana Barbosa and Jácome Cunha present SciRep, a framework that packages computational experiments so anyone can rerun them and get the same result. Reproducibility fails when code, data, languages and libraries drift apart. SciRep records all of them up front, then seals the whole experiment into a capsule that runs on any machine.

The team tested the tool against three rivals on eighteen published experiments from fields from medicine to computing. SciRep reran sixteen, eighty-nine percent, and every rerun matched the published result. The rivals managed at most sixty-one percent. The authors offer the capsule idea as a cure for a wide trust problem.
arxiv-2503-07180:
Marcin Wachowiak and co-authors redesign a switched antenna array for OFDM signals in a 2025 paper. Time-modulated arrays steer beams by switching antennas in timed patterns, a cheap trick with two flaws. Switching must run very fast, and the pattern sprays unwanted harmonic copies of the signal.

Their fix shapes the transmitted blocks so the harmonic copies fold back onto the signal itself and add up usefully. Switching can then run slower by a chosen factor, at the cost of the same factor in data capacity. Sideband radiation drops as well. The trade suits sensing and low-rate links where hardware simplicity beats raw speed.
arxiv-2503-07380:
One calcium line in the Sun's skin scatters light with the strongest slant signal at the limb, a tracer of the air's hidden grain. Harsh Mathur, Anusha, and Devang Agnihotri read that signal in 2025 against a full three-axis model of the solar air, built by fluid-and-magnet maths. Past reads leaned on flat, hand-tuned air models.

Light is then flown through the model column by column to forge the slant profiles. A grouping pass sorts the profiles into families. The hunt is for what bends them: the heat map, the density map, or both. The line forms high, in the chromosphere, where the Sun's weather turns wild. A tracer that reads that layer cleanly serves all solar watching.
arxiv-2503-07480:
Prabhash Kumar, Anu Nath, Mahesh Panchagnula, and Anubhab Roy study how small heavy particles move in a Taylor-Green vortex flow, in a two thousand twenty-five fluid mechanics paper. A classic result says particles below a critical Stokes number get trapped by the flow's separatrices.

Earlier work treated particles as points with density effects only. Here the authors add two neglected forces: added mass and the Boussinesq-Basset history force. Linear stability analysis near stagnation points maps trapping conditions in the Stokes number and density plane. Added mass creates extra stagnation points and shifts behavior between trapped, diffusive, and ballistic regimes. With both forces included, all particles turn ballistic.
arxiv-2503-07580:
Zijun Liao, Jinbiao Chen, Debing Wang, Zizhen Zhang, and Jiahai Wang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It trains neural nets to solve hard routing and scheduling tasks, where reward signals are sparse and good tries often go to waste.

Their method, BOPO, learns from pairs of tries ranked by their true scores. Each pair is anchored on the best try found, and the loss scales with how far apart the pair's scores are, so no reward model or fixed guide policy is needed. Tests on job-shop scheduling, the traveling salesman problem, and a flexible job-shop variant beat top neural rivals and close much of the gap to the best known answers. BOPO can plug into most net shapes already in use.
arxiv-2503-07680:
Yongqiang Yao and co-authors speed up in this 2025 paper the fine-tuning of language models on very long texts. Mixing long and short training samples unbalances the work across machines: attention costs skew and chatter between chips goes to waste. Their method, Hierarchical Balance Packing, sorts samples into layers, each with its own packing length and machine settings.

Each sample lands in the layer that fits it best, with parallelism and memory tricks set per layer. A matching training pipeline adds staged difficulty, flexible parallelism, and steady loss. Across data sets and open models, training time fell sharply; on the largest test model, a 236-billion-parameter system, speed rose about 2.4-fold with quality held.
arxiv-2503-07880:
A large team reviews what fifteen years of a solar imaging instrument have revealed about the Sun's interior, in a paper from 2025. The catalog creator field garbles the names with doubled initials, but the head gives a clean long byline. The instrument watches sound waves rippling through the Sun from a space observatory.

Those waves give a three dimensional view of structure and flows beneath the surface. Findings cover deep circulation, the roots of sunspots, and how magnetic fields rise and twist. The authors compare the results with theory and simulations of the solar interior. They frame the program as a benchmark for understanding other stars as well.
arxiv-2503-08280:
Zhenxiong Tan and co-authors present OminiControl2, a faster way to steer image generation models with image conditions, in a 2025 paper. Fine control of these transformer-based models matters for real use. Prior methods handle many control signals, but long conditional inputs make them slow and costly.

The new frame adds two ideas. A dynamic compression step keeps only the most meaningful tokens from the condition during generation. A reuse step computes condition features once and shares them across all denoising steps. Together they cut the computing load while keeping the prior frame's low parameter cost and range of uses. The work aims at practical, controllable image generation.
arxiv-2503-08380: Fujita proved in twenty twenty-five a guessed rule for a class of sym-met-ric mul-tiple zeta val-ues, sums built from ones and threes in turn. Past work by Hirose, Murahara, and Saito showed some such val-ues can be writ-ten as sums of plain zeta val-ues. Their proof had left this case, start-ing with one and end-ing with three, as a con-jec-ture. Fujita's proof settles that case in full.
arxiv-2503-08480:
Soumyajyoti Biswas and co-authors present a 2025 study of unequal rewards in science. They track how citations split among the papers of single researchers. Data come from a large scholar index for 2012 to 2024. Fields include physics, chemistry, medicine, and economics. Nobel laureates are compared with other researchers.

Citation counts turn out to be very unequal, and more so for laureates. Two index scores of inequality help tell laureates apart from others. The authors link high inequality to a system near a tipping point. Laureates also show lower scores on two spread measures, which points to a tighter shape. The team finds a like pattern in Olympic medal counts by country. Readers in science policy get a fresh lens on fame and reward. Top success, in their data, goes with sharp peaks rather than even spread.
arxiv-2503-08680:
The hot gas that fills a galaxy cluster should cool and rain down over time. Yet in some clusters it stays smooth and calm, with little star birth to show for the cooling. Muzi Li and co-authors read the gas's ripples in a 2025 paper, using X-ray images of five such clusters. Small flickers in brightness mark where the gas thickens or thins.

Four clusters showed ripple sizes near the norm for cluster cores, while one ran quieter. Turning ripples into speeds gave slow drifts, on par with the one direct speed reading taken by a past X-ray mission. The heat those motions stir in matches the heat the gas loses by glowing. Sloshing and gentle turbulence, the authors argue, may help hold cooling at bay.
arxiv-2503-08780:
Biplob Bhattacherjee and co-authors study how a future electron-positron collider could spot long-lived particles linked to the Higgs boson. Their 2025 paper focuses on the proposed FCC-ee machine and its IDEA detector. Such particles travel some distance before breaking apart, which makes them hard to catch with standard searches.

The team modeled particles born in B-meson and Higgs decays and worked through the messy background from ordinary long-lived particles. They also tested extra detectors placed around the main one in varied shapes and spots. A design called DELIGHT B caught the most signal particles. Ring-shaped add-on detectors around IDEA would also boost the odds of seeing decays that happen far out.
arxiv-2503-08880:
Shuoxue Li, Chenghan Li, Huanchen Zhai, and Garnet Chan stretch an embedding method from still states to moving spectra in tied lattices, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The method nails ground-state values cheaply, but motion reads stayed open. A single-mode kick ansatz supplies the bridge.

Embedding tools fill the matrix parts that the kick form needs. On the one-dimensional Hubbard model, results track gold-standard answers closely. Neutral kicks, single-particle spectra, and charge and spin waves all come out. The team frames the route as a cheap path to dynamics in hard lattices. Readers get motion from a still-state workhorse.
arxiv-2503-09180:
Alberto Sciaccaluga and five co-authors model the polarization of synchrotron light from a recollimated blazar jet, in work from 2025. New X-ray polarimetry lets astronomers track jet polarization across many bands. The team starts from relativistic fluid simulations of a jet that is squeezed back into shape, then follows nonthermal particles with a macroparticle code to get their light.

Shocks from recollimation are mostly superluminal, which limits particle acceleration in smooth flow. With small-scale turbulence, though, acceleration can proceed, and the model then matches the observed rise of polarization with frequency. Polarization angle stays stable between optical and X-ray bands. The result supports an energy-stratified shock account of the satellite data.
arxiv-2503-09680:
Sánchez-Alarcón and a large team complete a landmark infrared census of nearby galaxies, in a 2025 paper. The original Spitzer survey imaged over twenty-eight hundred galaxies within forty megaparsecs, deep and uniform. Its velocity-based selection, however, had silently missed over four hundred galaxies that optical data say belong.

The team gathered archival images and new observations for the missing set, calling it the Disc Galaxy extension. The complete survey now holds 3,239 galaxies with consistent imaging, brightness profiles, and freshly revised shapes. Masses, sizes, and concentrations were re-measured the same way for everyone, old and new. The sample captures at least 99.94 percent of the intended nearby population. Scaling relations in the infrared are showcased as a taste of the science enabled. The authors offer the catalog as the reference set for galaxy structure studies.
arxiv-2503-09780:
Arman Zharmagambetov and co-authors present AgentDAM, a benchmark that tests whether web agents keep private data private, in a research paper from 2025. Autonomous web agents can carry out long, multi-step tasks for users, which often means handling personal details. The rule they should follow is data minimization: use a private fact only when the task truly needs it.

AgentDAM stages realistic web tasks end to end and fits any current web agent. Agents built on GPT-4, Llama-3, and Claude all leaked, using sensitive facts they did not need. A prompting defense cut the leakage in the team's tests. The authors argue that end-to-end trials give a truer read on privacy than asking models abstract questions.
arxiv-2503-10180:
Li and a team of colleagues dissected a gravitational lens nicknamed the blue eye in twenty twenty-five. An Einstein ring forms when a massive galaxy bends light from a background source into a near-perfect circle. Spectroscopy confirmed this Kilo-Degree Survey find: an early-type lens galaxy and a background emitter at much greater distance.

Lens modeling on sharp telescope images gave an Einstein radius of about ten and a half kiloparsecs. The total density slope matched that of lower-redshift galaxies, suggesting growth through dry mergers plus mild accretion. Stellar population analysis put the lens's stellar mass near four times ten to the eleventh suns, leaving a dark matter fraction around thirty percent inside the effective radius. Fitting the dark matter halo's own slope required either halo contraction or a heavier-than-usual initial mass function.
arxiv-2503-10280:
Ali Elkeshawy, Haifa Fares, and Amor Nafkha tackle a wireless puzzle: spotting which small devices are awake in a web of spread-out antennas. Huge antenna arrays can serve vast numbers of machine devices, but first the net must learn who is sending. Their 2025 work sets that task in a cell-free layout, where many access points share the work.

Awake devices send known signals at once, and access points pass what they hear to one central unit. The team's learning method reads that mix and picks out the awake set. They also stress-test the method with noise and flaws in the input. A check on cheap fixed-point math shows how the method holds up on lean hardware.
arxiv-2503-10580:
Ishaq Aden-Ali bounds the size of sums of random tensors in this 2025 paper. The injective norm measures a tensor's largest stretch along unit directions. Adding random, well-behaved tensors raises hard questions about how large the sum can grow. His proof is strikingly short and avoids the usual geometric machinery.

The argument leans on the PAC-Bayesian lemma, a tool from learning theory used to tame certain random processes. The resulting bound improves a very recent result by another team. In the flat, Euclidean case it sharpens a classic bound by Latała. That classic bound anchored estimates of Gaussian chaos moments, and the new route gives a simple proof of that core result.
arxiv-2503-11280:
Big multilingual models are often said to build a shared inner space where languages meet, but the evidence is mixed. The four authors test 31 languages that vary in resources, family, and region, and they find that cross-lingual alignment inside these models is inconsistent. They propose a framework that separates the shared semantic subspace from fragmented parts left over by representational limits.

They also introduce the Interlingual Local Overlap score, which compares the local neighborhood shapes of high-dimensional representations to grade alignment. Using it, they show that fine-tuning on one language alone disturbs alignment in the early layers. Freezing those layers keeps the shared space intact and improves cross-lingual generalization. The authors argue that interlingual alignment is a load-bearing part of scalable multilingual learning, and they offer their metric as a way to check it.
arxiv-2503-11380:
A research team simulates a tiny twisting jet on the Sun to test how such eruptions ignite, in a 2025 paper. Spiral jets shoot plasma upward with a visible rotation, and their trigger was unsettled. The team anchored their model in real magnetic measurements from the Solar Orbiter probe, targeting a jet seen in March 2022.

The simulation starts from the measured surface field, extrapolated upward, with an unstable magnetic rope inserted into a fan-spine field layout. The magnetic null point collapses into a curved current sheet where reconnection fires. The rope surges up, links to the open spine field, and hands over its twist and cool material, producing the observed spiral jet. The same recipe matches larger jets, the authors note. Scale, they conclude, does not change the mechanism: one eruption script runs from miniature to grand.
arxiv-2503-11480:
Christian Groß and co-authors match two simulation styles for a gauge theory in this 2025 physics paper. Lagrangian and Hamiltonian methods give slightly different results at finite lattice spacing. As the time spacing shrinks to zero, the first method should reproduce the second.

The team ran Monte Carlo simulations on lattices stretched in the time direction. For each run they used the static quark potential to set the scale ratio. Then they extrapolated to zero time spacing. Their values matched Hamiltonian results at small volumes within two standard deviations. The match lets future work translate between the two formalisms with more trust.
arxiv-2503-11680:
Romulo Damaselin Chaves dos Santos and Jorge Henrique de Oliveira Sales set out new math in a 2025 paper on neural operators, models that learn to solve hard equations. Their work adds kernels that adapt and a way to weigh noise across scales.

The authors prove four main results. One splits bias from spread for a class of spread-out operators. One shows the models stay stable under heavy-tailed noise. One beats the growth of cost as the number of inputs grows. One gives a faster search method drawn from quantum ideas. As a test case, they apply the tools to plasma swirls in fusion work and report a large gain over the best prior models.
arxiv-2503-11880:
Jieming Bian and colleagues personalized federated fine-tuning of language models in a 2025 paper called FedALT. Devices can adapt a shared model on private local data, but averaging all local versions blurs each user's gains when data differ a lot. Standard averaging-based tuning suffers exactly that cross-client interference, trading personal fit for shared knowledge.

FedALT keeps each client's own adapter training locally instead of restarting from the average. A second adapter carries knowledge from the rest of the world, and a learned mixer blends the two afresh for each input, borrowing the mixture-of-experts idea. Tests on language benchmarks beat leading personalized methods on local fit. Privacy stays intact, since raw data never leaves the device.
arxiv-2503-12280:
Future wireless arrays will be huge and work close to their users, where beams have a depth as well as a direction. Panagiotis Gavriilidis and George C Alexandropoulos ask how losses inside one antenna type blur that depth, in a 2025 paper. The antennas steer waves through strips that feed many small elements. Those strips waste energy as signals travel, unlike an ideal surface.

The team derives formulas for beam gain when the focus point and the user sit apart in space. Depth limits are worked out from no loss up to extreme loss. The math shows how wasted energy reshapes near-field beams. Network designers can use the bounds to judge real hardware. The work fills a gap in near-field theory.
arxiv-2503-12680:
Steven Brill, Britton Olson and Guillaume Bokman extended in 2025 a numerical method for flows where two fluids meet and barely mix. The localized artificial diffusivity method steadies simulations of several materials, but it struggled when densities differed hugely or when fluids must stay unmixed. The authors traced the flaws to how the smoothing flux was built. Their fix aims the smoothing at volume fraction edges instead of mass fraction.

An added bulk diffusion term keeps pressure and temperature in balance across the boundary. A further term holds the interface at a finite thickness, as immiscible flows need. The design works for any number of materials at once. Tests on standard cases and on microbubble collapse in water matched measured data. The authors present the method as a robust tool for hard multi-fluid problems.
arxiv-2503-13080:
Hubert Szolc and co-authors describe in 2025 a drone system that counts fruit on its own for smart farming. A camera and a depth sensor feed a vision method that finds the fruit as the drone flies a planned route.

The system also plans flight paths that keep time and distance low. In test flights run in a simulator, the method scored well across five hundred missions. The team then flew it at a drone contest in 2024, where it placed sixth of twenty three teams and reached the finals. A reader sees a full loop from flight plan to fruit count.
arxiv-2503-13180:
Jungwon Seo and co-authors improve federated learning, the method that trains one model across many private data owners. Their 2025 paper tackles client drift: when each owner's data differs sharply and only some join each round, local training pulls the shared model apart.

Older fixes lean on past snapshots as reference points, which falter when participation is partial. Their method, GC-Fed, instead uses a fixed hyperplane as a timeless reference and centralizes gradients both during local training and at the server. Feature layers get the local treatment and classifier layers the global one. In tests on standard tasks the method curbed drift and lifted accuracy by up to twenty percent under patchy participation.
arxiv-2503-13580:
Sijia Gu, Noor Nashid, and Ali Mesbah present Panta, a 2025 technique that helps language models write better unit tests for tangled code. Models can draft tests quickly but miss deep branches because they cannot follow complex control flow on their own.

Panta mimics a human tester: it reads the code's static flow map, runs drafts to see which paths stay untested, and feeds that back to the model for another round. On the most complex classes from open-source projects, the loop gained twenty-six percent more line coverage and twenty-three percent more branch coverage than the best prior method. Iteration, not bigger prompts, did the work.
arxiv-2503-13680:
Özer and Aytül Filiz study edge symmetries of a two dimensional gravity model with a larger symmetry group in 2025. The model pairs gravity with a scalar field called the dilaton. The team builds the full algebra of symmetries at the far edge of the space. They ask how the scalar field trims those symmetries.

In the larger group case, the scalar keeps only part of a richer symmetry set. The kept part matches the base group itself. The result clarifies how scalar dynamics break symmetry at the boundary. It also bears on dual descriptions of such spaces. The authors see a path to wider gauge groups in flatland gravity. Heat and shape of these spaces are tied in.
arxiv-2503-13980:
Haolin Wang and co-authors teach language models to play decision games in a 2025 paper. Models shine at many tasks yet stumble on games that demand layered reasoning and planning. Games thus make ideal sandboxes for testing and training those skills.

The team built algorithmic pipelines that synthesize large offline data sets from two classic games, a card game and Go.
