Training recipes folded that data into two agents that play each game competitively. Adding game data also improved some general reasoning measures. The authors draw lessons for how synthetic decision data should be gathered and used in model training.
arxiv-2503-14380:
Sara Cabo and co-authors rethink how to shield light sensors in huge particle detectors from Earth magnetism, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The sensors lose skill when a sideways field crosses them, and past designs judged shields by how many sensors saw a high field. Coil sets cancel much of the field around the detector.

The team argues the mean leftover sideways field tracks lost skill better than the old count rule. A coil design tuned to that mean gives good results at fair cost. As detectors grow, the cheaper and truer gauge matters more. Readers who build large detectors get both a new yardstick and a workable shield plan.
arxiv-2503-14680: Zijie Zhou studies averages of derivatives of L-functions, the central objects of analytic number theory, after they are twisted by quadratic characters. Two distinct modular L-functions are twisted at once, and the paper computes an asymptotic formula for the resulting moment. Ian Petrow had reached a similar result earlier, but only by assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis. Zhou's proof removes that assumption, making the asymptotic unconditional.
arxiv-2503-15080:
Suemin Lee and co-authors propose a method to predict phase changes in a 2025 paper. Phase changes, like freezing or protein folding, are hard to watch directly. Often data exist only far from the change point and under one set of conditions.

Their method, called expTM, blends physics with generative AI. It maps sparse data onto a simple tilted bell curve whose center and spread link to heat, pressure, and chemical drive. From that map it can sample other phases under new conditions. Tests show the samples stay true to the physics. The tool may help labs plan where to look next.
arxiv-2503-15380:
Bruno França, Denis Kolegov, and Igor Konnov lead a team presenting the consensus protocol that orders transactions inside the ZKsync rollup. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Blockchains need agreement among machines that may lie or fail. This protocol blends ideas from three earlier fault-tolerant designs.

It works by committee with a single round of voting per decision. Slots finalize one at a time with modest communication growth. The tolerance threshold demands more honest nodes than classic setups, a deliberate trade. Simplicity, low latency, and reduced complexity were the design goals. Formal methods were used to analyze and test the protocol before this write-up. The audience is the ZKsync community and anyone auditing its safety. The paper is as much assurance document as research. It shows its work for a system holding real value.
arxiv-2503-15880:
Yunan Wang and co-authors blend on- and off-policy data for preference tuning in a 2025 paper. Direct preference optimization aligns models with human choices. Samples from the model itself stay on-distribution but cap quality. External data can be better yet shifts the distribution.

Their method synthesizes preference pairs from both sources. Dynamic adjustment balances shift against quality continuously. The optimal trade-off is found during training. Limitations of each source alone are overcome. Two public alignment benchmarks evaluated the approach. It beat both pure on-policy and pure off-policy training. A top win rate on the hard benchmark was reported. The base method remained ordinary preference optimization. Data synthesis, not a new loss, drives the gain. Alignment teams can reuse existing external corpora safely. Quality ceilings imposed by weak generators loosen.
arxiv-2503-15980:
Giuseppe Galante and co-authors propose a software platform to support the financial health of supply chains, in work from 2025. A chain can fail when money flows between its many firms go wrong. Watching those flows is hard because records are split and some data are private.

The platform gathers transactions and firm data to build a knowledge base and a digital twin of the chain. That twin can be viewed and tested to spot risks early. The design joins tools such as AI, blockchain, and knowledge graphs. The aim is to pick the right finance tools to cut risk.
arxiv-2503-16180:
Rasmus Nielsen and co-authors report in 2025 that a crystal called BaZrS3 glows far more brightly than earlier work suggested. The material is a chalcogenide perovskite, prized for solar and light uses because it is stable and made of common elements. Past samples gave only weak, muddy glow, which raised doubts about its quality. The team grew clean single crystals and measured them closely.

Their crystals showed strong glow at room temperature, though the glow faded fast. Sound-wave tests found all twenty-three expected vibration modes. The fast fade seems tied to how electrons couple with those vibrations. The paper sets a reference for the material and points to tweaks that could extend the glow.
arxiv-2503-16280:
Rafael Frongillo, Ian Kash, and Mary Monroe study peer prediction when people see more than they can report, in a 2025 paper. These mechanisms reward honest answers by comparing one person's report with another's, but theory usually assumes the signal and the report have the same shape. In practice, agents observe rich detail and must compress it into a coarse report.

The team models real-valued signals squeezed into binary reports through a threshold rule. Several classic mechanisms lose most of their equilibria under this richer model, and dynamics show some surviving thresholds are unstable. The authors then design a mechanism with many more stable thresholds, giving designers more freedom in practice.
arxiv-2503-16380:
Quantum mechanics forbids broadcasting an unknown quantum state to many receivers, a cousin of the no-cloning rule. Yunlong Xiao, Xiangjing Liu, and Zhenhuan Liu asked in 2025 whether virtual tricks, which simulate impossible operations statistically, can make broadcasting practical.

They set a practical bar: a scheme must beat the naive plan of just preparing fresh copies. Under that bar, no linear process can keep sample efficiency while respecting symmetry and classical consistency at once. They pin down the unique virtual map meeting the other demands and cost it exactly. A link to quantum spacetime descriptions holds only in the smallest case, hinting at a deep space-time asymmetry.
arxiv-2503-16480:
Yara Kyrychenko and four co-authors studied in 2025 what makes people prefer one AI chat answer over another in hard conversations. Their data holds over seven thousand five hundred chats from people in seventy-four countries, talking with twenty-one models. The team coded answers for traits tied to constructive talk, such as reasoning and nuance.

Users favored well-reasoned, nuanced replies and rejected answers heavy on personal storytelling. Users who wanted AI to mirror their own values cared less about reasoning and more about curiosity. Models also mirrored the tone of the user, even its toxicity, a warning for alignment work.
arxiv-2503-16580:
Kevine Meugang Toukam introduced a new distance between distributions in a 2025 maths paper. The Procrustes Wasserstein metric modifies a classic flow-based approach so the distance stays unchanged under rigid motions such as rotations. The problem then reduces to studying orthogonal transformations.

The distance is defined by penalising action while allowing free movement that keeps a particle's direction and speed. For Gaussian distributions, it comes down to the plain distance between their ordered lists of eigenvalues. The author also shows a direct use: recovering hidden Gaussian distributions from observed data. The work links optimal transport with shape matching ideas.
arxiv-2503-16680:
Shuang Liang and co-authors, with the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration, tackle a quiet flaw in deep sky surveys: pairs of galaxies merged into single detections. Such unrecognized blends are expected in fifteen to thirty percent of ground-based detections and can bias cosmology. The team asks whether plain catalog data — colors, brightness, and size — can flag them. They train four machine learning methods on the COSMOS catalog, using sharper space-based images as truth.

About seventeen percent of the ground catalog's objects proved to be blends. The methods caught between thirty and eighty percent of them, at the cost of discarding ten to fifty percent of all detections. Results held when only optical bands were used. Color-outlier hunters also removed redshift errors better than blend hunters did. The authors offer the approach as a purity filter for the coming LSST survey.
arxiv-2503-16780:
Uihyun Cho and Namhun Kim give in 2025 a routed clean up frame for low dose body scans. One clean tool strains to span all body zones, since each zone's tone spread and form shifts. Their frame fields three zone apt clean tools under one chat agent chief.

The chief reads sense cues from a med clip tool and routes each scan to the apt hand. Split work guards past false fit by spread of load. No hand steps are owed in the run. On a known scan set, the frame beats a lone clean tool on all three score marks.
arxiv-2503-16880:
Zhiyu Zhao and co-authors time test crystals for a future collider eye in a 2025 paper. A fine crystal calorimeter is planned for the Circular Electron Positron Collider, and sharp timing helps sort its events. The team paired three crystals, BGO, PWO, and BSO, with silicon light sensors.

Beam tests at CERN and DESY set the units under pions and electrons alike. An exponential fit with a set fraction rule gave the best time marks. Of like sized crystals, PWO timed best on its fast rise, with BGO and BSO close behind. Long BGO bars held even timing along their span, sharp under heavy showers.
arxiv-2503-17180:
M. Orte-García and co-authors measured chlorine in the glowing gas clouds where stars are born, in a 2025 study of the local universe. Amount ratios such as chlorine to oxygen trace how generations of stars have enriched their galaxies, but chlorine is rarely measured well. The authors mined a large data store of ionized region spectra, selecting over two hundred spectra of galactic and extragalactic star-forming regions where the doubly ionized chlorine amount could be determined.

All actual conditions and part amounts were recomputed uniformly for the sample, a deliberate choice for comparability. A central methodological contribution is a scheme for choosing which electron heat level indicator best shows the zone where the chlorine ions live, boosting the amount determination. The team then weighed results under two ionization correction schemes and set the nebular chlorine-to-oxygen pattern against what stars themselves show.
arxiv-2503-17280:
Stanislav Alexeyev and co-authors model the shadows of rotating black holes in theories that extend general relativity. Each rival theory bends the shadow in its own way, so sharp images can test them. Their 2025 paper builds rotating solutions for six such theories, from Horndeski gravity to loop quantum gravity, using an improved Newman-Janis method.

With those metrics in hand, the team computes the shadow each theory predicts. For some models, a critical spin value appears beyond which the picture changes character. Rotation can amplify or cancel a theory's own corrections, in either direction. The authors argue shadow images can join gravitational wave tests as a real check on gravity. Astrophysicists get templates for the next, sharper black hole photos.
arxiv-2503-17780:
Junpeng Hu and co-authors give in 2025 a quantum steep est fall plan to tune curve fit models that carry doubt marks. Those fits are prized in learn work, yet their core math cubes in cost as data grows. Tune of their dials stacks that cost more.

Late quantum line math lets their plan read the tune grades at a vast speed gain. The whole fall run sits in one quantum ring. Run time and fault bound reads back the gain. Large data fits that once cost too much come in reach.
arxiv-2503-17880:
Almasi, Moradpouri, and Shahbazi test a claim about quantum black holes: that certain measures of their curvature shrink in a perfectly smooth, one-way fashion. Their 2025 paper studies a clean family of such holes, still and round, set by mass alone. In the classical limit the family melts back into the standard Schwarzschild hole.

The authors marshal evidence that small quantum fixes, computed step by step, could never break the smooth pattern, so the trait looks deep rather than accidental. They also show these holes cannot be built from stepwise corrections to Einstein's equations at all. On the heat side, the holes cap their temperature at a ceiling set by the Planck length. Their entropy always beats the classic area-over-four bound. A critical mass makes the temperature vanish.
arxiv-2503-18080:
Learning by worked examples can wake up passive software classes, but how well it works needs mapping. Tiago Bonetti, Williamson Silva, and Thelma Colanzi map the evidence in a 2025 review. They gather thirty studies on example-based learning in software engineering courses.

The method helped students grasp and apply concepts, and it raised drive and confidence. It also made class talk livelier. Costs fell on teachers, who spent more effort and time building good examples. Some diagrams even carried errors that confused learners. Support tools for teachers lag behind the method's promise. The map shows where course designers should invest next.
arxiv-2503-18280:
Mykhaylo Khoma gives a new way to compute the tone values of a broad wave rule. The work dates to 2025. The rule covers both real and mixed inputs. His trick is to use the exact slopes of the tone values as he solves, which trims loss of care.

The slopes come as three-step chains inside a chain-frac method tied to the wave rule. Sharp results hold across a wide span of inputs. As a show case, he computes cell energies for three small charged pairs. Runs reach to vast split spans for one pair's high states. He also runs the mixed input case and weighs his reads next to past work.
arxiv-2503-18380:
Gulnara Suliyeva and nine co-authors published a 2025 study of the Fan-Wang spacetime, a model of a black hole that stays regular at its centre. The model comes from a theory where electric and magnetic fields behave in a nonlinear way. The team compared its geometry with how particles actually move in it.

They worked out how light and matter bend around the object, how much it can capture, and how its gravity shifts light toward red. A magnetic charge in the model adds a small correction to the classic black hole solution. That correction changes even local predictions of Einstein’s theory. The authors argue that future instruments could test whether such an object exists.
arxiv-2503-18480:
Elisabeth Sola and a large team of co-authors catalog the faint tidal structures that wrap many galaxies. When galaxies merge, they leave dim streams and shells of stars that record the event. Their 2025 study uses deep images from a Canada-France-Hawaii telescope survey, with the faint features marked by hand. It then asks how the count and look of these structures depend on the host galaxy's traits and on its surroundings, such as group or field settings.

Such links test the standard story that mergers build galaxies over time. Faint features are hard to count the same way twice, so a hand-marked set has lasting value. The authors aim to give modelers a clean yardstick. The work also guides future deep surveys hunting the same ghostly traces.
arxiv-2503-18580:
Talal Ahmed Chowdhury, Kwangmin Yu, and Raza Sabbir Sufian measure entanglement growth in a model of quantum chaos on real quantum computers, in two thousand twenty-five. The model is a standard test bed for chaos, many-body physics, and ideas linking gravity and quantum theory. Today's machines are noisy, so checking known results on them matters.

The team tailored two measurement protocols to a commercial superconducting machine with limited links between qubits. They ran circuits in parallel to improve one protocol's results. With error reduction steps added, the machine's readings matched theory well. The authors take that as a sign that current hardware can probe chaotic quantum dynamics.
arxiv-2503-18880:
A person scanning a room hears a voice and a clatter at once and knows where each came from; machines usually handle speech and other sounds in separate passes. Hyeonggon Ryu, Seongyu Kim, Joon Son Chung, and Arda Senocak built one model in 2025 that grounds both in the same visual scene, even when the sounds are mixed together.

Their mix-and-separate training feeds the model blended audio and teaches it to pull the strands apart into distinct embeddings, each tied to its source in the image. A new dataset tests exactly that mixed case, and the model beat prior methods on it. It also matched or beat specialists on standard segmentation and retrieval tasks.
arxiv-2503-18980:
Yexin Li and co-authors published this paper in 2025. It addresses exploration, the stubborn problem of reinforcement learning: an agent that only exploits what it knows never discovers better moves. Their method, CAE, turns the critic, the network that already judges actions, into the explorer.

Borrowing tricks from the multi-armed bandit literature, CAE nudges the agent toward uncertain, promising actions, scaled in a way that carries proof of sublinear regret. The change needs about ten lines of code and adds no new parameters. For tasks where the judge itself is hard to train, an extension adds a tiny helper network, under one percent more parameters. Tests on robot control, game, and navigation benchmarks showed stable, strong exploration. The authors pitch the method as a rare mix of theory, simplicity, and results that practitioners can adopt quickly.
arxiv-2503-19280:
Amogh Inamdar and co-authors published this education technology paper in 2025. Propositional logic proofs are a core skill in computer science degrees, but students need guided practice to master them. Tutoring on demand is rarely available, and many students fear judgment when asking for help. The team lists what a good practice tool should do. They built LogicLearner, a web application for step-by-step proof practice.

Students work through proofs in the interface and can request guidance whenever they stall. An automatic solver generates solutions on the fly, powering that guidance. The team piloted the tool across two semesters of a discrete mathematics course. Student surveys praised its usability and teaching value. The authors say LogicLearner is, to their knowledge, the only tool offering a complete practice environment for logic proofs. Its feedback is immediate and judgment-free, which they argue is what beginners need.
arxiv-2503-19780:
Martin Bauer, Stephen Preston, and Justin Valletta wrote a 2025 math paper on when smooth solutions of the EPDiff equation break down. This equation models flows where the velocity field is built from a momentum field through a smoothing operator. It appears in shape analysis and fluid mechanics.

The authors study the case where the smoothing uses a whole number power of the Laplacian. For radial starting data with a sign condition on momentum, they prove the solution's slope blows up in finite time across a wide range of powers. Their method recasts the equation as an ordinary differential equation in Lagrangian coordinates and compares it with a classic equation. The result is a step toward a full conjecture on which powers give solutions that last for all time.
arxiv-2503-19880:
The HALHF Collaboration lays out in 2025 a hybrid linear Higgs factory that mixes plasma and radio frequency acceleration. Electrons ride plasma wakefields to high energy, while positrons use standard cavity technology. Colliding cheap low energy positrons with costly high energy electrons gives the best value design.

The plan yields luminosity much like that of the baseline International Linear Collider design at far shorter length. The collision frame carries a set boost toward the electron side. Named for its asymmetric layout, the concept is a full facility proposal with named parts. It targets Higgs production for precise particle physics at lower cost than all radio frequency designs.
arxiv-2503-19980:
Basabendu Barman, Nicolás Bernal, and Javier Rubio wrote a guide to the reheating of the young universe for particle physicists. Their review, from twenty twenty-five, deals with the shift from inflation to a hot thermal cosmos. This phase is key yet oft misread. The plain Boltzmann path, they argue, misses the wild first steps of energy hand off. Those steps are non perturbative and nonlinear by nature.

Burst like particle making, inflaton break up, turbulence, and the settle to heat all sit in that gap. The team maps the tool box, from Boltzmann math to lattice sims, and says when each fits. Readers get a clear on ramp to a phase that sets the stage for all later cosmos.
arxiv-2503-20180:
Hiroyuki Uchida and a very large team of co-authors wrote this 2025 report on the first in-orbit performance of Xtend, the soft X-ray imaging telescope aboard the XRISM observatory of Japan. Xtend stares at a wide patch of sky, 38.5 arcminutes square, catching the full field of its partner spectrometer in a single frame. Ground calibration only goes so far; the report grades the instrument in space.

Data come from first-light targets, onboard calibration sources, and a cross-calibration campaign with other flying X-ray observatories. The team check image sharpness, spectral response, background levels, and timing against pre-launch expectations. Such reports are the reference card every later user of the data from the telescope will consult. The verdict certifies Xtend as ready for its survey of hot gas across the universe.
arxiv-2503-20880:
Amaya Gallagher-Syed and co-authors build BioX-CPath, a pathology AI that shows its reasoning in biological terms. Tissue slides stained in several colors hold rich clues, yet most models treat them as plain pictures. Doctors also distrust scores they cannot inspect.

The system turns each slide into a graph and reasons across stains jointly. A new pooling part, stain-aware attention, builds a patient summary that weights each stain by its worth. Scores top prior work on rheumatoid arthritis and Sjogren's disease slide sets. The readouts go further: attention per stain, spread gauges, and stain interplay scores show what swayed the call. Those views can be checked against known disease pathways. Code and guides are public for clinics and labs to test.
arxiv-2503-21080:
Yunbo Long and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on an AI debt collector that learns to handle emotional tactics without being thrown off. As language model agents start dealing with each other, debt talks are a risky test bed: fake distress can derail a collector trained on human chat. The team built a simulation bench of debt recovery talks to study the problem.

Their agent, EmoDebt, treats its own emotional tone as a choice to tune. A Bayesian learning engine adjusts that tone policy online against each debtor's tricks. On the bench, EmoDebt beat fixed and emotion-blind rivals on success rate and speed. Code is public. The work frames a base for agents that must stay steady under pressure.
arxiv-2503-21480:
John Murzaku and Owen Rambow test whether big multimodal AI models can read feelings in speech without training. Their study, OmniVox, is the first broad check of such models on this task. They ran four models on two known test sets of acted and TV dialogue. The models took in sound alone, text alone, or both.

With no task training at all, the models matched or beat audio models that had been tuned for the job. The pair also tried a prompt style that asks the model to weigh tone traits first. Adding talk context around each clip helped scores, mostly on the acted set. A close look at errors shows where the models still misread mood.
arxiv-2503-21580:
Fabian Bäuerlein, Leah Kurki Schätzler, and Samuele Riccò prove regularity results for a class of energy functionals with two growth regimes, in a 2025 paper. Such double-phase energies model materials that switch behavior depending on local conditions.

The setting is a domain whose outside region is thick enough near every boundary point, in a capacity sense the authors define for this energy. Under that condition, solutions gain better integrability across the whole domain. A Hardy inequality, bounding functions by their gradients near edges, follows. Fatness of the outside region turns out equivalent to several other boundary inequalities. A counterexample shows one hoped-for step on the path does not hold in general.
arxiv-2503-21680:
Malik works through the symmetry rules of a field model in a 2025 paper. The model joins two kinds of gauge fields in four dimensions, the normal count for space and time. Malik uses a known scheme that adds extra symmetry rules to keep the math in line.

He shows two sets of rules at work: some that square to zero and some that do not. A pair of mirror rules also appears and swaps parts of the model. Malik maps how all these rules combine and finds the pattern matches one from geometry. He also notes the model needs no odd fields with the wrong sign, a point he stresses.
arxiv-2503-21880:
Inflation-era correlations between cosmic fields get corrections from loops, and those corrections carry telling singularities. Supritha Bhowmick and co-authors study that singular structure in a systematic way. They compute several loop diagrams directly, spot a pattern, and turn it into rules anyone can apply.

With their rules, the poles and branch cuts of any two-site one-loop diagram follow from the energies running through parts of the graph. No hard integrals are needed. They also trace a strange off-shell energy branch point that shows up under two different cutoff schemes. Renormalized results, they show in 2025, repackage the cuts into tidy ratios of scales.
arxiv-2503-21980:
Simon Preston and co-authors build a statistics model in 2025 for random curves that live on curved surfaces. Think of rolling a ball along a flat drawing without slipping: the ball traces a matching curve on its surface. That rolling trick extends to many curved spaces, and the team uses it to move a well-known random curve model from flat space onto surfaces.

The rolled model can generate new curves and can be fitted to real curve data. The team gives conditions under which the rolled center matches the natural average of the process. They also propose simple estimators and prove how fast the estimates sharpen. Examples cover a sphere, matrix spaces, and robot arm orientations.
arxiv-2503-22280:
Rrubaa Panchendrarajan, Rubén Míguez, and Arkaitz Zubiaga introduce a data set paper from 2025 about fact-checking. Fact-checkers often see the same claim repeated across sites and in many tongues, and grouping those claims can speed up their work. The team built MultiClaimNet, a set of three linked collections of fact-checked claims sorted into clusters that share the same core fact.

The claims cover eighty-six languages and many topics. The two smaller sets came from older claim-matching data, while the large one holds more than eighty-five thousand claims in seventy-eight languages. To build it, the team paired likely matches and used large language models to judge how alike the pairs were. They also ran tests with several grouping methods to set baseline scores for later work.
arxiv-2503-22380:
Murauer, Krishnakumar, Tornow, and Geierhos tested in twenty twenty-five a quantum tool that learns from a stream of data with loops fed back. Old quantum pool tools must restart the loop at each step, which wastes time. Pure stream tools are fast but lack the back-links that boost scores.

Their plan adds back-links that work while the quantum bits still hold their state. On a small test case it kept a trace of past inputs, as a short-term memory score showed. That score was not zero, which means the links work mid-stream. The plan may give stream tools the gains of restart tools at less cost.
arxiv-2503-22680:
Jack Edward Tisdell, Rustum Choksi, and Xin Yang Lu count flaws in optimal point patterns on a torus in a 2025 mathematics paper. Quantization scatters n points over a surface to represent it faithfully; the best local pattern is hexagonal, and every non-hexagonal cell is a defect. On closed surfaces defects cannot vanish entirely, so the question is how fast they must grow. The authors build a proof strategy from error bounds and special integers tied to hexagonal lattice constructions.

On the hexagonal torus they prove defects grow no faster than the fourth root of n, fewer than on surfaces with edges. They conjecture the true rate is merely logarithmic. Pattern flaws on curved worlds echo through materials and graphics alike.
arxiv-2503-22880:
Matias Valdenegro-Toro and co-authors release data sets of sonar images of underwater trash, in this 2025 paper. Sonar is the main sense for robots working below the surface, where cameras fail. AI tools for sonar lag behind, in part because public training data are scarce. Their sets aim to close that gap for the task of finding marine debris.

Images were gathered in three settings of rising realism: a water tank, a turntable setup, and a flooded quarry. The sets support several tasks, from naming objects to outlining them pixel by pixel. The paper describes the data, gives first test results, and links a public archive. Robots that can spot trash are a step toward cleaning harbors and coasts.
arxiv-2503-23180:
Maroussia Slavtchova-Bojkova and Penka Mayster push a branching crowd through a wild rain of new blood, in a study from 2025. Branch math tracks lines that birth and die by lot. Here the new blood comes in bursts from a stable law with no mean, a rain whose sums grow by leaps.

The breed law, too, has no cap on spread. The pair seek the shape of the count law for the whole crowd, writ as its code form. From that form, the odds the line dies out can be read. Wild in, wild breed: the long fate of such a line is the ask, and the form gives a grip where means give none. Rare-event fields, from germs to claims, share the shape.
arxiv-2503-24080:
Marco Gallo and a co-author study a class of wave equations in a 2025 math paper on normalized solutions. The work treats a fractional Schrödinger equation, where the spread of the wave is not the usual local kind. The team seeks solutions with a fixed total mass, a value set in advance. The force term can grow very slowly, as with a log term, which breaks many standard tools.

To get past those breaks, the team builds near solutions first, then passes to a limit with a fresh method based on a classic identity for such waves. They find a true solution when the mass is large, and for each mass in the slow-growth case. Some of the results are new even for the standard, local form of the equation.
arxiv-2503-24280:
Annabella Meech and co-authors read the air of a hot Jupiter in this 2025 paper. The planet, TrES-4b, circles its star in step with the star's spin, and the team watched starlight filter through its atmosphere with the Webb telescope.

Water vapor showed up clearly, with hints of carbon monoxide and a trace of carbon dioxide. The carbon to oxygen ratio landed between 0.30 and 0.42, and the air's metal content measured only about half the Sun's, below its star. Those lean values strain standard formation stories. The authors suggest the planet drank oxygen rich gas, or mixed poor gas with carbon poor solids. The work feeds a program comparing aligned and tilted hot Jupiters.
arxiv-2504-00080:
Julián Barragán Amado, Tiago Fernandes, and David Lopes compute ringing modes of a massive vector field around a five-dimensional black hole in this 2025 paper. Such quasinormal modes describe how the hole settles after a disturbance. The field's parts split by how they behave on the surrounding three-sphere.

Two parts stay coupled through the mass term until a field change splits them, at the price of a complex parameter with two allowed values. Those values name two polarizations of the sector. The radial equations become classic Fuchsian equations with four or five singular points. Using the isomonodromy method, the authors recast the problem through a famous tau function and expand it in series. Their small-horizon modes match numerical integration well, validating the method.
arxiv-2504-00180:
Vignesh Gokul, Srikanth Tenneti, and Alwarappan Nakkiran test whether large language models can spot contradictions inside documents retrieved for them, in a 2025 paper. Retrieval-augmented systems fetch fresh documents to ground their answers, but the fetches can disagree, above all in fast-moving news. Contradictions then leak into answers as errors or wobble.

The team built a generator that simulates several kinds of contradiction, then graded models acting as context checkers. Even the best current models found the task hard, and skill varied sharply by contradiction type. Bigger models did better overall, while step-by-step prompting helped some models and hurt others. The authors urge sturdier checking before such systems are trusted.
arxiv-2504-00280:
Gunbir Baveja tested a diffusion-based policy for robot learning in worlds that will not sit still, in a solo paper published in 2025. Tasks in real factories and driving work shift their rules and aims over time. The policy builds actions by slowly removing noise from a rough guess, which gives smooth, fitting action chains. Vision feeds the policy in the tests.

On game-like worlds and a maze task, the policy beat two standard learners on mean and top scores. Its scores also varied less from run to run. The cost was more computing per action. The author flags sharp, fast world shifts as the weak spot that remains. The findings support diffusion policies for work where the ground rules drift, from assembly line robots to self-driving.
arxiv-2504-00380:
Yang Hai and colleagues sped up video frame interpolation in 2025 by teaching a diffusion model to imagine motion rather than pictures. Frame interpolation invents the in-between frames that make video smoother. Diffusion-based versions had lagged older methods in both accuracy and speed, partly because they denoise in a large image-like space. The new method models optical flow from both directions explicitly, in a hierarchy, which shrinks the search space.

A flow-guided synthesizer then builds the final frame from the predicted motion. The two parts train together end to end. The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy while running more than ten times faster than other diffusion-based interpolators. That combination matters for practical video work, from slow-motion generation to streaming, where earlier diffusion methods were simply too slow to use.
arxiv-2504-00880:
Galaxies grow by swallowing smaller ones, often in groups led by a big companion. Thomas Callingham and Amina Helmi trace those group falls in a 2025 study. They use simulated Milky Way twins to follow the debris.

Big-event debris lands on tightly bound orbits deep inside. Companion stars spread looser, with the first-lost bits staying closest in feel. Early builders' companions likely sprinkle the Sun's own neighborhood. The last big merger's companions reach both near and far halo zones. Recent or small groups keep tighter shared motion. Group falls, they conclude, sculpted our halo.
arxiv-2504-00980:
Mitch Hamidi, Lara Ismert, and Brent Nelson study when a quantum graph algebra is simple, meaning it has no hidden two-sided parts, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Quantum graphs extend the graph idea into the quantum setting. The work links traits of the graph to traits of its algebra.

They give conditions on the graph that ensure the algebra is simple. They also build a map from one form of the algebra onto a related form. Joined, the results yield the first case where two named forms of the algebra truly differ. Set cases, such as complete and trivial quantum graphs, are settled as well.
arxiv-2504-01380:
Zhe Jiang, Sam Ainsworth, and Timothy Jones build a guard chip in a 2025 paper. Fast chips run steps out of turn to gain speed, which makes fine checks on each step hard to bolt on. Past guards were tried in toy sims that hide the true snags.

Their build is the first such guard on a real fast chip core. They set out the snags, from race paths to wire fights, and solve them in the full stack: chip, board, code rules, and user model. Tests show fine step checks can run with small cost. Chip teams gain a real base for guards once trapped in sims.
arxiv-2504-01580:
Alexandre Wagemakers assembles a zoo of systems that can settle into several different fates, in a 2025 paper. Such multistable systems appear everywhere: ecosystems flip between states, circuits latch, and lasers choose modes. Which fate occurs depends on the starting point, and the map of starting points leading to each fate is called a basin of attraction.

The paper catalogs notable examples across scientific fields, classified for easy browsing. Companion code lets readers reproduce every basin picture themselves, turning the survey into a working tool. For researchers meeting a new multistable system, the zoo offers analogies at a glance: someone has likely mapped a cousin of your problem. It also serves teaching, since basins make abstract dynamics visible at once.
arxiv-2504-01680:
Adam Stokes and Ahsan Nazir build a general framework for quantising light-matter systems whose constraints change with time in 2025. In quantum theory, the choice of gauge is usually a matter of taste, but when time dependence is added at the Hamiltonian level, different gauges can give genuinely different theories.

The authors define an irrotational gauge as one that stays correct whether the time dependence is introduced early or late. Their framework unifies scattered examples of such gauges in the literature. A notable consequence is that the popular Coulomb gauge is not generally irrotational for time-dependent interactions, so it enjoys no special status despite its fame.
arxiv-2504-01880:
Sriram Shastry, writing alone, finds a shortcut to special zeros of quantum systems in a 2025 paper. The zeros belong to the partition function, a master quantity in statistical physics, read in the Yang-Lee picture. Locating them for lattice fermions, like the Hubbard model, is normally heavy going. Shastry proves a theorem about the single-electron self-energy in the imaginary-time formulation.

The theorem maps each zero to a virtual energy labeled by wavevector and spin. Those energies solve equations built from the self-energy at matching labels. What was a global hunt becomes a set of local solves. Shastry shows the method at work in simplified cases. The author presents the link as a new handle on phase behavior, since Yang-Lee zeros mark where phases change. The proof's core is the self-energy's hidden bookkeeping of the zeros.
arxiv-2504-02180:
Pei-Chi Chen and six co-authors generate camouflaged images with better foreground care in a 2025 paper. Fake training images can ease data scarcity for systems that spot hidden objects. The leading method builds scenes from foreground objects alone, but two flaws persist.

Background knowledge often clashes with the foreground, breaking color harmony. Small foreground objects also warp during generation, losing their true shape. The new model adds a module that blends foreground features with background knowledge more tightly. A custom loss term supervises foreground rebuilding during the noise removal steps. Tests on several data sets beat the prior approach. Cleaner synthetic scenes should train sharper camouflage detectors for wildlife and search tasks.
arxiv-2504-02980:
Michael Taylor, Jonathan Soderquist, and Pengfei Huo reframe how light modes count inside big optical cavities, in a study from 2025. A Fabry-Pérot cavity traps light between two mirrors. In strong coupling, light and matter wed, but the crowd of light modes in a big cavity blurs the math.

Their frame rolls the crowd into a few stand-in modes. Those modes give back the true spread of speeds the cavity shows. The trick find: a stand-in mode's size does not grow with the mirrors' face. It tracks how hard light grips matter, which the mirror shine and gaps set. That frees the math from the cavity's bulk: a vast hall and a small chip can share one form if their grip is the same.
arxiv-2504-03380:
Sanghwan Bae and five co-authors study how to pick training tasks when teaching language models to reason, in this 2025 paper. The catalog creator carries stray affiliation text, but the head gives the clean byline. In this training style, models earn rewards only for answers that can be checked, so rewards are sparse and task choice matters a lot.

The team proves that expected learning gains are bounded below by how much success rates vary across tasks. Tasks of middle difficulty, where the model sometimes wins, teach the most. A balanced filter that keeps such tasks therefore lifts the bound. Tests on math reasoning benchmarks matched the math: balanced filtering sped training and raised final scores by up to twelve percent, in under half the usual steps. The authors offer the result as a base for future curricula.
arxiv-2504-03480:
Dafne Zorzetto and co-authors build a Bayesian model to estimate how wildfire smoke changes the chemical mix of fine air particles, in a paper from 2025. Smoke worsens air quality through a blend of many species at once. Past work mostly tracked total particle mass, not the recipe inside it.

Their model joins causal inference for many outcomes at once with a factor model of the hidden structure among species. A flexible prior lets the factor scores differ by treatment state. Focusing on the scores also solves the missing outcome problem that haunts causal work. Simulations checked the model's accuracy. Applied to US data, it estimates smoke's effect on 27 chemical species in fine particles.
arxiv-2504-03980:
Roberta Mota, Ehud Sharlin, and Usman Alim build a virtual lens for volume views in a 2025 arXiv paper. Volume rendering shows 3D data as glowing clouds, but fixed color rules can hide mixed traits. Their lens lets users mark target traits right in the view with bendy quadric shapes. Stacked lenses can hug traits with odd forms that stiff shapes miss.

Two-hand virtual input steers the lenses, which cuts head and body strain. A pilot test with an expert used an asteroid strike data set. The trial showed gains and snags of bendy lenses and points to next steps for the tool.
arxiv-2504-04080:
Pavel Exner and David Spitzkopf wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five about rows of potential wells and what happens when a few of them shift. A potential well traps a quantum particle in a small region. An even row of wells spreads allowed energies into bands, with gaps where no extended state can live.

The authors study an array of separate wells laid along a straight line in two or more dimensions. They shift a finite number of wells along the line, keeping them apart. Under a stated limit on the shape of each well's support, they prove the shift creates bound states in the gap below the lowest band. Such localized states are the mathematical sign that a small local change can trap a particle.
arxiv-2504-04280:
Runlong Yu and co-authors survey large pre-trained models built for environmental science, in a 2025 paper. Field models of ecosystems guide resource care and planning, but older data methods struggle with tangled processes and sparse records. Large models trained on vast mixed data may capture change over space and time more fully.

The survey maps uses such as forecasting, filling data gaps, blending records into models, sharpening coarse maps, and aiding choices. It also walks through how such models are built, from data gathering to design, training, tuning, and testing. The authors discuss open problems and future paths. They call for closer teamwork between computing and field experts to speed progress on hard environmental problems.
arxiv-2504-04480:
Braghadeesh Lakshminarayanan, Margarita Guerrero, and Cristian Rojas improve estimators that learn from simulators, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Factories now run digital twins of real systems, but the twin's settings must be tuned to match reality. One route generates fake data at sampled settings and trains a model to read settings back from data.

Trouble comes when the true settings sit outside the sampled range. Predictions then skew, a flaw known as out-of-distribution error. The authors add a fine-tuning stage to a known two-stage estimator that corrects for this drift. Simulations confirm the fix sharpens accuracy. The work targets engineers who must calibrate twins that start far from the truth.
arxiv-2504-04780:
Chenxi Zhao, Daochang Wang, Siqian Zhang, and Gangyao Kuang built a radar target recognizer that reads scattering cues in a 2025 paper. Radar images from a moving platform can spot vehicles and other targets, but deep models often treat them like photos. That leaves the physics of how waves scatter off a target unused, and results can be brittle.

Their network starts from the scattering itself. A first part draws out local scattering traits in place of a standard photo backbone. A second part picks out scattering pieces of the target without labels, giving a fine account of it. Those pieces are then pooled into a full description. Tests on two data sets checked the gain, with the authors stressing clearer reasoning as well as accuracy.
arxiv-2504-04880:
Ju-Jun Xie and Cheng Chen use clash data to probe the inner charge shape of heavy particles called baryons. When electrons and their anti-partners collide, they can form a baryon and its mirror twin. The rates of those events reveal how charge and magnetism spread inside the particles. Their 2025 study fits a model to those rates.

The model matches the known data well, and gives estimates for charge size that agree with lab values. The team also check a claimed wave-like pattern in one particle type and do not confirm it. For a heavier charmed particle, wiggles in the data are explained by excited states of a related particle family. Sharper data could pin those states down.
arxiv-2504-05380:
Ewan McCulloch and co-authors argue that quantum chaos forgets more slowly than expected in a 2025 paper. Chaotic quantum systems are supposed to act as their own heat baths, erasing local superpositions fast. Conservation laws, the authors argue, quietly sabotage that erasure in one dimension.

All local correlations then decay as stretched exponentials or slower, not the brisk exponential decay once assumed. The effect is purely quantum and vanishes if outside noise dephases the system. Its culprit is persistent inert regions the authors call voids. Energy conservation guarantees such regions exist. Textbooks on thermalization may need a footnote with teeth.
arxiv-2504-05580:
Peter Todd Williams presents a computer model for detonation in hard to set off explosives, in a paper from 2025. The model, called Salinas, describes how a reaction wave moves through the material. Such models help engineers predict how a charge behaves when the blast has to turn a corner inside a device.

Salinas builds on a known family of flow models but draws on others that handle corner turning well. The paper reports how the model handles those turns, including cases where the reaction fails and dead zones form where nothing burns. The model runs fast and uses few free values to tune. Those traits make it handy for design work where many test runs are needed in a short time.
arxiv-2504-06080:
Paul Kühler and Dominik Stöckinger tackle a hard step in theory work on weak force models. They ask how to treat a special matrix, gamma five, in a scheme that changes the number of space dims. The catalog creator field adds school address text, but the head byline names just the two authors.

The pair give the first full two-loop result for a chiral SU(2) gauge theory in this scheme. They list all the extra finite terms needed to restore a key symmetry that the scheme breaks. With one new term, the list has the same shape as the known one-loop list.
arxiv-2504-06780:
Yong Bai and co-authors present CHIME in a 2025 paper on modeling what users like as a whole. Recommender systems gain from full interest models, but cost soars and mixed data types are hard to fuse. Search based methods that pick a slice of past behavior can drop key signals.

CHIME adapts large language models to encode a user's full behavior with mixed inputs. A learning aim at two grain sizes catches both lasting tastes and brief whims. A coding step then packs those codes into compact vectors for fast use. Tests across diverse data sets show top ranking scores for the method. The authors pitch CHIME as a robust, scalable fix for interest modeling at platform scale.
arxiv-2504-06980:
Sujoy Bhore, Ameet Gadekar, and Tanmay Inamdar give fast approximation schemes for clustering with side constraints, in a 2025 theoretical computer science paper. Clustering points into k groups gets harder when rules are added, such as capacity limits, fairness, or backup centers. Their unified framework works on metric spaces with bounded scatter dimension, a family that includes Euclidean space, planar maps, and many graph metrics.

Earlier methods in this setting only handled objectives where each point joins its nearest center. The new schemes cover the constrained variants in full, giving the first such guarantees for capacitated and fair median and means problems beyond Euclidean space. They also speed up the plain versions. The result answers an open question posed by the scatter dimension framework's founders.
arxiv-2504-07380:
Liyu Zhong, Sheng Mao, and Yang Jiao link hidden order in messy materials to their working traits in a 2025 physics paper. Disordered hyperuniform materials mix local chaos with long-range order. That blend grants them unusual physical properties. Here the local property varies as a smooth random field.

A spectral curve describes the microstructure in compact form. Its small-scale exponent sorts materials into three classes. A fast generator builds samples across that whole spectrum. Perturbation math ties property wiggles to field wiggles. Strongly hyperuniform cases pass their order to the fields. Push the contrast higher and the order breaks down. Conductivity is mapped end to end from the spectrum.
arxiv-2504-07480:
Marios Papachristou and Jon Kleinberg build tools to measure and shrink the gap in where public debate lands for different social groups. Their 2025 paper calls that gap consensus disparity. It sits inside a classic model of opinion dynamics, where people hold some private conviction against the pull of their neighbors.

The team first settles how hard the measure is to compute when group membership is unsure. A structural result shows disparity can dwarf plain polarization even in well-connected networks that carry a clear group split. For the fix, they give robust methods that reweigh recommendations or seed opinions to cut the worst-case gap, with proven guarantees. Real social networks served as the test bed.
arxiv-2504-07780:
Tao-Lin Tan and Yi-Ping Huang proposed a new kind of quantum scar in two thousand twenty-five. Scar states stay orderly while their neighbors turn chaotic. They hold finite energy yet refuse to thermalize. The new scars arise from exact destructive interference. Wave paths cancel on a graph of possible states. That cancellation cages the state onto a few graph corners.

A link ties interference zeros to graph symmetry. Vertices are classed by the graph's local topology. Robustness comes from that topology, not conserved quantities. A graph search algorithm hunts the caged states. It found them in a spin chain model and beyond. The framework widens the known routes to non-thermal states. Quantum simulators could test the cages directly.
arxiv-2504-07880:
Fabien Casse and co-authors simulate the years before two black holes merge, when one still owns a private disk of gas. Mergers are now heard through gravitational waves, and much work studies the shared disk of the final act. The earlier configuration, a secondary black hole orbiting outside the primary's accretion disk, was largely unexplored. Their 2025 paper runs two-dimensional fluid simulations of that arrangement, with both holes' gravity fully counted.

Three effects stand out. The disk's outer edge is cut back hard, and how far it reaches, relative to the pair's separation, depends only on the two holes' mass ratio. Two spiral arms wind through the disk's gas. And the trimmed edge takes an elliptical shape set mainly by that same mass ratio. The authors give observers a set of fingerprints: a disk shaped this way betrays the companion waiting outside it.
arxiv-2504-08580:
Kripko and a large collaboration measure how spinning protons respond when struck by electrons and shedding kaons, in a 2025 paper. The experiment ran at Jefferson Lab with the CLAS12 spectrometer, using electron beams of about ten gigaelectronvolts. Positively charged kaons produced off protons were tracked across a wide span of energies and angles. The team extracted beam single spin asymmetries, subtle left-right imbalances tied to the beam's polarization.

The result is the first finely binned measurement of its kind for kaons in the valence quark region. Such asymmetries probe a twist-three structure function sensitive to quark-gluon correlations inside the proton. Model comparisons explore how the reaction mechanism shifts across the measured range. The data tighten the picture of the proton's inner dynamics.
arxiv-2504-08680:
Di Palma and co-authors compute kaon decay rates with lattice simulations at true quark masses in a 2025 paper. Kaons are short-lived particles whose decays test the weak force with fine care. The decays studied shed a photon as the kaon breaks down.

The team ran large grid simulations that now count effects past work skipped, with boxes of varied size and three grid spacings. Error bars on key shape factors shrank by near half. Results sit uneasily beside one major experiment yet agree with another. In the muon channel, tension with two data sets persists, keeping the puzzle alive.
arxiv-2504-08780:
Light-touch tuning teaches search models to rank passages, and Atharva Nijasure, Tanya Chowdhury, and James Allan peek inside to see how the relevance sense forms, in work from twenty twenty-five. Three base models were tuned on a big query set under many tuning shapes. Rank size, checkpoint age, and part choice were all varied.

Peeling back parts showed which layers and paths carry the ranking skill. Some parts matter far more than others, and the pattern shifts as tuning deepens. All tuned models were shared for reuse. The study gives later probing work a map of where relevance lives inside a tuned model, and which knobs shaped it.
arxiv-2504-08880:
Josiek and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper on joining atmosphere models to life-story models of very massive stars. Such stars flood young clusters with light and wind. Their growth models, though, treat the outer layers crudely. The team bolted detailed atmosphere calculations onto structure models of a star 150 times the Sun's mass.

Sixteen snapshots span the star's main life phase. At each, two atmosphere versions attach at different depths, one reaching below a hot iron layer that helps drive the wind. Spectra and structure from both versions are compared in detail. A general fix for surface temperature readings follows. The work aims at honest wind loss rates for the biggest stars.
arxiv-2504-09180:
Akatoki Noboriguchi and seventeen co-authors give dust-choked galaxies an X-ray census in a 2025 paper. These galaxies hide furiously growing black holes behind veils of dust and gas. Their X-ray glow would betray the veil's thickness and the feeding state, but the galaxies are rare and past sky surveys too patchy.

A new all-sky instrument's deep field changed that. In one well-mapped patch, the team catalogued over five thousand infrared-bright dusty galaxies and caught sixty-five in X-rays. The X-ray group spans even lightly veiled systems. Their findings open a statistical window on how black holes grow inside their dust cocoons.
arxiv-2504-09480:
Vision-language models can find objects described in words, even categories they never trained on, but how they fare at ordinary detection work was untested. Yongchao Feng and co-authors supply the test in a 2025 review and evaluation. They treat these models as foundation models and grade them across sixteen scenario families.

Eight detection settings, from crowded scenes to new domains, and eight segmentation settings, from few-shot to small objects, expose where each architecture shines and where it limps. Detection was graded under three tuning styles: no tuning, visual tuning, and prompt tuning. The analysis ties performance to task traits, architecture, and training choices. The authors aim the findings at anyone choosing a model for a real vision job.
arxiv-2504-09880:
Chung-Ru Lee offers a 2025 theory paper on superconductors, materials that carry current with no loss below a key temperature. The paper links that temperature to two gaps in the energy of the material.

In the model, fermions pair up into a single bound state as the material cools. From that picture Lee derives a short formula for the key temperature in terms of the main gap and the pseudogap. With no pseudogap, the formula gives the classic ratio known from older theory. With one, it explains why the ratio grows in odd materials. Data from copper based and iron based materials fit the claim.
arxiv-2504-10380:
Andrea Mondino and Clemens Sämann build a way to say when spacetimes converge, in a 2025 paper. Their setting is Lorentzian geometry, the math of relativity. A famous result for ordinary metric spaces links convergence with a compactness test. No full twin of that result existed for spacetime-like spaces. Their method uses nets of causal diamond regions.

Only the time separation function is needed to define the convergence. It applies to both smooth spacetimes and rougher synthetic ones. The authors prove a compactness theorem where covers by balls become covers by diamonds. Classes of well-behaved spacetimes pass the test under stated controls. Applications include known approximation schemes and stability of curvature bounds. They also introduce tangent spaces at a point for this setting and note links to causal set theory.
arxiv-2504-10580:
Jacopo Gliozzi and co-authors challenge a known wall in a 2025 paper on one-way quantum stuff. In such stuff, states pile at the edge, a trait called the skin effect. Dirt in the stuff can pin those states back into the bulk, a shift long framed by a classic claim.

The team stretches that claim to sets that keep not just charge but its lean and higher kin. Edge pile then gives way to a pinned phase as dirt grows, with a sharp shift in how links spread. With no edge, the pile turns into a one-way flow phase. When lean is kept, the wall bends in fresh ways.
arxiv-2504-10980:
Mohammad Shafiei and Milorad Milošević explain how a planar Hall effect switches on in ultrathin topological insulator films in a 2025 paper. The effect, a sideways voltage under an in-plane magnetic field, was linked to exotic semimetals. In flat topological insulators it should vanish, since their Berry curvature points the wrong way to steer carriers.

Real films are quasi-two-dimensional, and tunneling between the two surfaces changes everything. Paired with in-plane magnetization, that coupling bends electronic behavior enough to allow a finite effect. Strong in-plane fields can even stabilize a quantum anomalous Hall state usually tied to out-of-plane magnetization. Magnetic topological devices gain design room.
arxiv-2504-11380:
Mark Edison Jim and co-authors design an augmented reality coach for public speaking, called SpeakAR, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Fear of speaking is wide, yet live practice chances are few. Virtual audience members react as the user speaks, giving a safe stage.

Five users with mixed fear levels each ran six speaking tasks. Users said the tool helped practice and lifted confidence. Lively faces and small idle moves in the virtual crowd were flagged as key for realism. The work draws on past virtual training and feedback studies. Readers who build learning tools get design cues for calm, real-feeling rehearsal.
arxiv-2504-11480:
Andrea Lucchini wrote a 2025 paper on a graph built from the subgroups of a finite group. In this graph, each subgroup is a point, and joined points mark a set relation between them. A graph is regular when every point has the same number of links.

Lucchini proves a crisp rule for when this subgroup graph is regular. It happens only when the group is cyclic, meaning one element generates the whole group. The group's order must also be square-free, with no prime factor repeated. Both traits are needed, and together they are enough. Short proofs of sharp rules are prized in group theory, and this one closes the question fully.
arxiv-2504-11680:
Bo Gong and co-authors offer a new way to compute resonances of the Schrödinger operator, in this 2025 paper. Resonances mark states that linger for a while before fading, a key idea in quantum physics. Theory has mapped where they sit and how they spread out. Yet computing them past one dimension stays rare, since the problem is nonlinear and the space runs on without bound.

Their method joins three tools: finite elements, a boundary map, and a spectral indicator scheme. The boundary map is set on a cut-off edge of the working region to mimic open space. Finite elements handle tricky potential shapes with ease. Together the parts pick out the complex values that mark each resonance.
arxiv-2504-11980:
Nicholas Fazio and nine co-authors report a new way to measure errors in a quantum computer, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their test case is a key two-qubit operation used in logic built to resist errors. The work ran on a sixteen-qubit register in a trapped-ion machine.

Their method rebuilds the error pattern of a full cycle of operations. It can spot errors that depend on context, so those errors can be eased. It also shows how single gates behave inside larger logical operations. The team says the method can predict how well error correction will work, and can tell fixable errors from those that cannot be fixed.
arxiv-2504-12480:
Srinivasan, Plenz, and Girvan improve in twenty twenty-five a lean form of neural computing that borrows ideas from the brain. Their system keeps a fixed random network, called a reservoir, and trains only the output layer. That design is cheap, but it is fussy about its settings and ignores a key brain trait: the balance between go and stop signals.

They show the system works best when stop signals match or slightly outweigh go signals. They then add a self-tuning rule that adjusts each unit's balance to hit a target firing rate. Gains were large on memory and forecast tasks. Varied targets across units cut the need for fine tuning even more, across simple and hard tasks alike.
arxiv-2504-12680:
Baining Zhao and co-authors introduce Embodied-R in 2025, a framework meant to give foundation models stronger spatial reasoning from video. People can watch a stream of views from their own eyes and judge how places and objects relate. Models often lack that skill, and the team splits the job between a large vision-language model that perceives and a small language model that reasons.

Training used reinforcement learning with rewards that check whether the thinking and the final answer agree in logic. After training on only five thousand video samples, their small reasoning model matched leading large models on spatial tasks, both familiar and new. The paper also probes answer length, reward design, and how fine-tuning and reinforcement learning differ.
arxiv-2504-12780:
Beam halls use hollow metal drums to push charged bits, and the push can leak side kicks that bend the beam. Wroe, Wuensch, and Apsimon grow a drum design trick in a 2025 study. The trick cuts the drum wall in a wave round its rim, so the field inside holds just the kick parts the user wants.

The team works out the field sums for such drums with beam pipes, and the push change for bits that fly through near light speed. A 3D sim of one drum, built for three kick parts, matched the sums well. Two uses are shown: a clean drum with no side kicks, and a drum that flattens a beam's spread. Beam runs back the sums.
arxiv-2504-12980:
Jiangnan Biguo and Xiaoquan Yu chart how dark solitons move inside trapped superfluids that carry spin, in a 2025 paper. A ferrodark soliton is a traveling dip in the fluid's density with a magnetic twist. The authors split the force on such a soliton into a buoyancy part and spin corrections. The corrections come from the hollow core and from the coupling between the soliton's motion and its spin mixing.

In a bowl-shaped trap, the math maps the soliton's path onto a marble rolling in a quartic valley. Near the center it swings to one side only, like a marble caught in one dip of a double well. Starting farther out brings three regimes of swing before that one-sided motion. In a hard-walled trap with a slope, the motion turns into a plain harmonic swing.
arxiv-2504-13080:
Abhishek Ghadai, Pradip Kumar Bera, and Sayantan Majumdar present a 2025 study of a rod dragged through a soap-like fluid of worm-shaped micelles. Past a speed line, the rod's path turns wild and stress swings wide. The team built a rig on a shop rheometer to log the stress on the rod live. Flow cameras mapped the speed field around it at the same time.

Past the line, stress climbed slowly, then dropped in a snap, the sign of stored stretch let go. The stretch zone's size matched the build time times the rod speed. Shear and stretch gauges at the flip shared one threshold number. At higher drives the rod churned in mixed stick-slip bursts. Such fluids fill foods, gels, and oil work.
arxiv-2504-13480:
Minsu Koh, Beom-Chul Park, Heejo Kong, and Seong-Whan Lee improve machine learning for physics equations in a 2025 paper. Many science and engineering problems are stated as partial differential equations, and learned solvers can be much faster than classic ones. Grid-based solvers struggle on odd shapes, while attention-based solvers often miss fine local detail.

Their model, LA2Former, groups nearby points into patches that adapt to the shape at hand. It mixes a fast attention that reads the whole field with a close-range attention that reads local structure. Across six test data sets, accuracy rose by more than half over existing methods. The design keeps computing cost in check while handling complex shapes and fine detail together.
arxiv-2504-13580:
Yuchen Rao and co-authors show that machine-made labels can teach 3D scene models better than hand-drawn ones. Their 2025 paper starts from a pipeline that matches objects in scanned rooms to catalog CAD models and records their full poses. That pipeline had annotated an older dataset; here it is run on the newer ScanNet++ scans, which lacked such labels.

Models trained on the automatic labels beat models trained on manual labels at two tasks. One task fills in missing parts of point clouds. The other finds and aligns the right CAD model from a single view. The authors read this as proof that automatic annotation can raise quality while cutting cost at the same time. They release the new annotations, called SCANnotate++, with their trained models.
arxiv-2504-14280:
Jindong Li and co-authors survey how a joint image-text model helps learning systems cope with new domains, in a 2025 paper. Models often fail when data shift to new settings. The surveyed model, trained on vast image-text pairs, can often work in fresh domains with no new labels.

The survey first sets clear terms for study setups, covering data access, number of sources, and how labels relate across domains. It then sorts methods that tune prompts, methods that use the model as a feature backbone, and methods that adapt with or without source data. Trend analysis draws out shared principles. Open problems include real-world deployment, forgetting, and fusing data types. The authors aim to guide sturdy systems for messy settings.
arxiv-2504-14480:
Margarida Ferreira, Victor Nicolet, Joey Dodds and Daniel Kroening present a method to synthesise programs from partial traces of their runs. The traces record only the calls that have side effects, yet the built program must mix those calls with pure functions and control flow. Uses include rebuilding an API script from call logs, with only positive examples given.

Their method generalises from the traces and uses cost measures to stop over-general fits, so no negative examples are needed. It joins optimising rewrites with syntax-guided synthesis, and the result is correct by construction: it can always replay the input traces. Tests on real-world benchmarks weighed how metric choice shapes program quality and speed.
arxiv-2504-14580:
Viet Hung Pham, Malte Wagenfeld, and Regina Bernhaupt study how virtual reality can help judge and improve walkability in city planning, in a paper from 2025. Classic planning tools, such as flat maps and fixed renders, miss how a street actually feels to walk. Fast urban growth and green goals make that gap costly.

Virtual reality lets residents and planners step inside a design, spot walking problems, and suggest fixes on the spot. Early interviews with residents of Eindhoven in the Netherlands surfaced what pedestrians value and where they struggle. Next, the team plans prototypes that fuse the virtual scenes with a live digital twin of the city. A design generator would then propose options. The goal is a decision tool that folds public views into design.
arxiv-2504-14980:
Xin-yi Lin, Zhengxiang Li, and Jian-dong Zhang ask whether lensed gravitational waves can tell bare primordial black holes from dressed ones, in a 2025 paper. If particle dark matter exists beside such black holes, each hole wears a dark matter coat. At high frequencies, coated and bare holes bend waves almost alike. Future detectors will listen exactly in that band.

Bayesian model comparison is their tool for telling the two apart. Two planned third-generation detectors serve as test cases. Across a broad frequency range, the detectors separate the models well. A heavier black hole inside the coat sharpens the distinction further. Lens masses from a tenth to a hundred suns are in play. The work supports using lensing as a dark matter probe. Coexistence of both dark matter forms becomes testable, they argue.
arxiv-2504-15280:
Seeing a scene from several angles and stitching the views together is easy for people and hard for AI. Chun-Hsiao Yeh and co-authors measure that gap in this 2025 paper with All-Angles Bench, over 2,100 hand-checked questions across 90 real scenes. Six tasks probe counting, traits, distance, direction, object moves, and camera pose across views.

Twenty-seven leading vision-language models, including famous commercial systems, fell far short of human scores. Two weak spots stood out: matching objects across partly blocked views, and pinning down rough camera positions. The authors argue models need built-in multi-view awareness, not just bigger training. Robots and embodied agents, which must act in 3D space, have the most at stake.
arxiv-2504-15480:
Antonin Brun, Gale Lucas, and Burçin Becerik-Gerber study stress at work through the eyes of office staff. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, is based on long talks with eight workers. Stress harms health and output, yet most aids treat people as if they were all alike. The team asks what sets off stress and how workers cope day to day.

Patterns show stress is shaped by place, timing, and the person. Workers named clear triggers and their own coping tricks. They also said stress is not all bad and can sometimes push good work. The authors draw design lessons for aids that fit the moment. Help should arrive at the right time and in the right form.
arxiv-2504-15680:
Bikash Chandra Roy, Aroonkumar Beesham, and Bikash Chandra Paul built a model of the late universe in a new gravity frame. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses f(Q) gravity, where a nonmetricity term drives the action. They built models for a few forms of that function. Each model tracks how the young fast phase gave way to the late speed up of cosmic growth.

They set the model with a fixed jerk value and fit its parts to real data. The data came from Hubble rate facts and a supernova set. They traced how the slow down term, energy density, and the state term shift with time. Readers in cosmology get a test of whether this gravity frame fits the late universe.
arxiv-2504-15880: Alvaro Otero Sanchez breaks a key exchange protocol in a 2025 paper on cryptography. The protocol builds shared secrets from a two sided multiplication action over a digital semiring. Sanchez finds the top solution of a linear system over that semiring. Matrix traits of a special circulant form then expose the flaw. The attack rebuilds the shared secret from public data for any case, in polynomial time, so the protocol falls in practice.
arxiv-2504-16080:
Le Zhuo and co-authors teach image generators to look at their own work, admit the flaws, and repaint. Their 2025 paper introduces ReflectionFlow, which scales effort at inference time along three axes. It searches for better starting noise and sharper prompts. Most notably, it adds explicit reflection, where the model assesses its last image and states what to fix.

Reflection needs training data, so the team built GenRef: a million triplets of a critique, a flawed image, and its improved version. A leading diffusion model was then reflection-tuned on it. The full system clearly beat naive noise scaling on hard generation tasks. Language models gained reasoning power by critiquing themselves at runtime; this paper ports the trick to pixels. Compute spent reflecting, it turns out, buys quality that compute spent sampling does not.
arxiv-2504-16180:
Md Saeed Siddik, Hao Li, and Cor-Paul Bezemer wrote this review in two thousand twenty-five. It maps software engineering research on Jupyter Notebook, the tool that blends code, text, and output in one page.

The team picked well over a hundred papers from a large bibliography, through the end of two thousand twenty-four, and sorted them by topic. Top venues for this work sit in human-computer interaction, not classic software venues. Hot topics run from code reuse to readability to run settings. Yet few studies could be reused from their links, and most code packs lack lasting homes. Testing, refactoring, and group documentation stay thin, the authors say.
arxiv-2504-16380:
When data must be squeezed with help available at the decoder, rates below the limit fail fast and hard. Shun Watanabe proves how fast, in a 2025 paper on lossy source coding with side information. That setup is known as the Wyner-Ziv problem. Past work had a lower bound on the failure rate, but not the exact value.

Watanabe finds the tight exponent, the exact rate at which success odds fall to zero. The same result covers the related task of computing a function across split sites. The proof uses a change-of-measure method and a soft constraint from earlier work. A matching upper proof uses a new pairing method. An example shows why the soft constraint cannot be dropped.
arxiv-2504-16580:
Ignacio Peis and co-authors introduce hyper-transforming latent diffusion models in a 2025 paper on generating functions, not just images. Their frame joins implicit neural representations, which encode shapes as functions, with transformer hypernetworks.

Older hypernetworks use plain multilayer nets that scale poorly. A transformer decoder here generates the function parameters from latent codes, lifting both capacity and speed. A trick called hyper-transforming tunes only the decoder while freezing a pretrained latent space. That adapts strong models to function outputs without full retraining. Tests across media show better scale, expressiveness, and generalization than past function generators. The work unifies function learning under one flexible frame.
arxiv-2504-16880:
Hudson Leone, Peter S. Turner, and Simon Devitt write a 2025 study on how to mimic an optical device, called an interferometer, on a quantum computer. Their work was spurred by new quantum proof-of-work ideas. In their plan, the registers of the machine stand for the paths that light can take.

They break the math of the device into small two-by-two blocks, turn each block into circuit steps, and join the steps. They also built a software tool, named Aquinas, that does this work. As a test, it built a circuit for a five-path device with two photons, using ten qubits and a deep stack of steps.
arxiv-2504-16980:
Safety tuning after training can fail, since a model may learn unsafe habits deep in its first pass over the web. Pratyush Maini and co-authors build safety into that first pass in a 2025 paper. Their plan sorts web text by safety, rewrites unsafe text into safer tales, and adds refusal lessons.

A marked token also flags unsafe text during training, so the model can be steered at use time. Attack success on standard safety tests fell from 38.8 percent to 8.4 percent. Scores on general tasks did not drop. The team frames the work as a root-level fix, not a patch. Data, not just rules, carries the safety lesson.
arxiv-2504-17480:
Xin Yi and co-authors show how to wash a watermark out of a language model, or forge one, by copying it. Watermarks tag machine text so owners can spot misuse, and they leak into student models trained on a teacher's output, a quirk called radioactivity. That leak lets owners detect unauthorized copying, but it may also invite attack.

Their method decodes with contrast, pitting the student against weakly marked reference text to extract spoiled or boosted watermark samples. Fresh students trained on those samples learn either to scrub marks or to fake them, while keeping general skill intact. The authors warn that future marks must be both hard to remove and hard to counterfeit.
arxiv-2504-17580:
Debanjit Mondal studies global controllability of nonlinear dispersive equations in a 2025 mathematics paper. The equations are of KdV type, in third and fifth order forms, posed on a torus. The question is whether a fixed, small control can steer solutions approximately between states.

Instead of standard saturation machinery, Mondal uses a linear test strategy. Control design rests on a simpler Burgers equation linearized around a carefully built return trajectory. The resulting control depends continuously on the start and target states, and splits into a bounded linear part plus a fixed remainder. The linear part is independent of the dispersion order.
arxiv-2504-17780:
