Sneh Pillai studies how language models can keep old skills while learning from a live data stream in a 2025 paper. Models tend to forget earlier facts when new data arrives, a flaw called catastrophic forgetting. Real uses, from clinics to law, need steady learning on tight budgets.

Pillai pairs a light tuning method with a tiny replay store of past items. Tests ran across three fields: medical questions, genetics, and law. Scores tracked how well the model learned, forgot, and recovered over time. Forgetting did occur on its own. Even a small replay set steadied the model and restored much lost ground. The work offers a cheap recipe for models that must adapt on the fly.
arxiv-2504-17880:
Alexander Becoy, Kseniia Khomenko, Luka Peternel, and Raj Thilak Rajan send a four-legged robot to scan a room on its own. Room scans need full sweep paths, and bent, blocked rooms break plain grid methods. Their 2025 plan takes the skeleton line of a prior map, the thin core line of free space, and beads points of interest along it. The beads are then strung in a best order from the spot of the robot.

A state switch flips the robot from trek mode to scan mode at each bead. Map reading took 2.52 milliseconds per dot and planning took 1.7 on test maps. In five runs on a bent, clear room, the robot hit 86.5 percent of its beads. Drift in the built map is the known flaw, they note.
arxiv-2504-17980:
Anna Shelton and co-authors perfect a recipe for poling thin films of lithium tantalate, a crystal workhorse for mixing light. Periodic poling flips the crystal's domains in a striped pattern, which lets one color of light double into another. Their process holds up across acoustic and optical grade films, electrode metals, and oxide layers alike.

One short high-voltage pulse, ten milliseconds at peak with a slow ninety-second ramp down, sets neat rectangular domains that stay put. Second-harmonic microscopy confirms the stripes. Ridge waveguides built by poling after etching converted telecom light at 1550 nanometers to 775 with an efficiency close to theory. The result widens the platform's reach in quantum photonics, sensing, and spectroscopy.
arxiv-2504-18180:
Þórir Hrafn Harðarson, Hrafn Loftsson, and Stefán Ólafsson test whether preference-based training makes language models better at summarizing Icelandic legal texts, in a 2025 paper. Legal writing's terminology and formal style strain general models, and Icelandic adds the challenge of a smaller language. The team compared models fine-tuned the conventional way with models trained by reinforcement learning from human feedback and by direct preference optimization.

Preference training improved the legal accuracy of the summaries over standard fine-tuning. It did not, however, significantly improve the general quality of the Icelandic itself. Automated scores and human judgments also disagreed at points, which the authors flag as a warning. The paper argues that in specialized domains and smaller languages, qualitative human assessment remains essential, since metrics alone would have told a cleaner story than the texts deserved.
arxiv-2504-18380:
Steven Hasler and Philipp Ackermann present a framework that lets extended reality apps reason about three-dimensional scenes. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Headsets already track objects and merge sensor data. What apps lack is a way to state facts such as one object being on, behind, or near another, and to draw conclusions from them.

Their system wraps each object in an oriented box and computes a rich set of spatial links. Those links form a knowledge graph of the scene. A pipeline then answers queries and applies rules as the scene changes. Both on-device and server versions were built and tested. The design stays independent of any one headset or engine. It can plug into learning systems and language tools as well.
arxiv-2504-18480:
Li-Wei He and three co-authors probe, in a 2025 paper, a plateau in the magnetization of a frustrated magnet. The magnet sits on a kagome lattice, a weave of corner-sharing triangles that blocks spins from settling at once. In a magnetic field, its spin climbs, stalls at one third of full, then climbs again. New tests on a copper-based crystal made its cause a live question.

The team ran two computer methods, variational Monte Carlo and exact diagonalization, on the Heisenberg model of this lattice. They find three degenerate valence-bond-solid states with a David-star pattern of spin values. In them, spins take two fractional values, and the states swap into each other by shifts. Their spin links stay short-ranged, like a quantum spin liquid. Yet a measure shows no topological order. The authors tie the plateau to these states.
arxiv-2504-18580:
Shi Jie Yu and Sehyun Choi propose a smarter way to merge saved snapshots of a language model into one better model when only small adapter modules were trained. Merging checkpoints can save training time, but simply averaging them treats good and bad snapshots alike. Their method weights each snapshot by its performance, using training loss or step count, with one penalty knob to shape the weighting.

Across math reasoning, preference alignment, and instruction tuning tasks, the weighted merges beat plain averaging. Weighting by loss worked best, lifting accuracy by up to five percent over the uniform merge. It even beat the final checkpoint alone. The method adds almost no computing cost.
arxiv-2504-18680:
Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes from deep space, and one was caught in 2020 from a magnetar inside our own galaxy. The Galactic Radio Explorer, GReX, is an all-sky monitor built to catch such exceptionally bright events from the Milky Way and its satellite galaxies. Kiran Shila and co-authors describe the instrument in 2025: low-cost stations spread around the globe, watching the whole sky with time resolution down to 32 microseconds.

The paper covers the hardware and software design, sensitivity tests, and checks using the hydrogen line. It then asks what the silence since 2020 means. No new burst has appeared in the years since that first galactic event, and the team's updated rate says such brilliant bursts are even rarer than the single detection first suggested. The design shows how a worldwide network of modest instruments can patrol the sky for rare radio flashes.
arxiv-2504-19080:
Zhenkai Qin, Jiaquan Liang, and Qiao Fang present an attention method that treats channel and space together, in a paper from 2025. Attention helps deep networks focus on the most telling parts of an input. Most methods score channel importance on its own and spatial saliency on its own. That misses how the two act on each other.

Their method, MIA-Mind, fuses both in one cross-attentive step, built on the MindSpore framework. The design stays light and modular, while recalibrating features in fine detail. Tests ran on three data sets: image sorting, a cell image task, and network intrusion data. On the first, accuracy reached eighty-two point nine percent. On the second, accuracy reached seventy-eight point seven percent. On the third, accuracy reached ninety-one point nine percent. The authors plan tests on larger data sets and adaptive fusion next.
arxiv-2504-19280:
Xiaorong Zou solves stubborn differential equations by fitting their curvature with waves. The target is a second-order nonlinear equation whose solution must meet mixed conditions at its ends. Instead of attacking the solution directly, Zou represents its second derivative as a trigonometric polynomial. Integration then rebuilds the solution and its slope.

An optimization loop bends the polynomial until the rebuilt curves satisfy the equation itself. Fast Fourier transforms carry the gradient work, keeping the method quick. Adding grid points raises accuracy sharply. When several solutions exist, the search can be steered toward a desired one, such as a positive solution. Tests under varied boundary conditions behaved as hoped. Zou notes the scheme extends to higher-order equations, at the price of heavier implementation.
arxiv-2504-19780:
Pedro G Massey and co-authors prove commutation principles for optimization problems in Euclidean Jordan algebras, published in 2025. The problems involve spectral functions that are strictly Schur-convex, a strong form of symmetry and convexity. The question is when an optimizer must commute, in the operator sense, with a shift term in the problem.

Under set conditions, the authors show that a local optimizer and the shift do indeed commute. They make no extra smoothness assumption on the function. Instead they use the smooth structure of the algebra's symmetry group and tools from majorization of eigenvalues. The principles let them treat several known problems at once, including one about minimizing the condition number in this setting.
arxiv-2504-19980:
Manuel Parra-Diaz and Carlos Castro-Iragorri present a 2025 paper on portfolio design with deep learning. Risk budgeting spreads risk across assets by set shares rather than by money shares. End-to-end learning can tune such portfolios directly from data. Past versions were fragile: random starting weights swung results wildly. Their framework cuts that start sensitivity while keeping the learning end to end.

Stability arrives without a performance cost in their tests. The method consistently beats the classic risk parity benchmark, as the authors report. Investors get a learning-based allocator they can rerun without lottery-like swings. Reproducibility is not a luxury in finance; audits demand it. A robust declarative frame also lets rules be stated cleanly inside the model. The paper speaks to quant teams who want deep learning gains with benchmark-grade trust.
arxiv-2504-20580:
Amirhossein Azarbahram and four co-authors design a sense then charge protocol for wireless power transfer to devices that cannot reply. The devices have unknown locations, so a multi antenna system must find them before it can beam power efficiently. No channel state data are available at the start.

Each transmission block splits into a sensing phase and a charging phase. Echoes from sensing signals yield location estimates through signal classification and least squares fits. Those estimates predict channels and steer the power beam. Simulations show a best split between sensing and charging that depends on setup. With enough antennas and power, the protocol nears optimal performance and beats channel free rivals, but it struggles as device counts grow under tight resources.
arxiv-2504-20680:
Networks of coupled oscillators can compute in parallel while sipping energy. Bram Haverkort and Aida Todri-Sanial study digital versions of these oscillatory neural networks. The standard design links every oscillator to every other. That full wiring makes the coupling hardware grow with the square of the network size. Their hybrid design mixes serial and parallel coupling to tame the growth. Hardware then scales almost linearly, at about 1.2 times per added oscillator.

On a common FPGA board the design fit 506 fully connected oscillators. That is a tenfold jump over the recurrent baseline at the same precision. The authors call it the largest such digital network built so far.
arxiv-2504-20780:
Aaron Bernstein, Sayan Bhattacharya, Peter Kiss, and Thatchaphol Saranurak give a fast deterministic algorithm for keeping a maximal matching in a graph that keeps changing, in a paper from 2025. A maximal matching pairs up vertices so no free edge remains. Updating it after each change used to cost time linear in the graph size on dense graphs, a barrier that stood for years.

Their method updates in well under linear time on average. The key tool, an edge-degree constrained subgraph, is used in a new way: it keeps high-degree vertices matched cheaply, leaving the easy low-degree ones for direct handling. Random walks on expander graphs and a classic dynamic tree structure fill out the toolkit. A randomized variant runs faster still, even against an adaptive adversary.
arxiv-2504-21080:
Kelsey Glazer and co-authors stack spectra of early galaxies to read the gas between their stars, in work from 2025. Using the James Webb Space Telescope, they gathered 64 galaxies seen as they were within the universe's first billion years or so.

Averaging the spectra exposed faint absorption lines from cool gas, transmitted hydrogen emission, and glowing nebular lines. Compared with later galaxies, these early ones show weaker absorption, small gas outflow speeds, and strongly suppressed hydrogen emission, hinting that more of their ionizing light escapes into space. The subset shining in hydrogen emission shows strong oxygen-related lines and signs of intense ionizing output. Stacking proves a powerful way to study faint early galaxies.
arxiv-2504-21180:
Algebra studies abstract systems of numbers and operations, and one way to understand an algebra is to map how it can be stretched, averaged, and folded onto itself. Ahmed Zahari Abdou works through these maps for five-dimensional nilpotent algebras over the complex numbers in this 2025 paper.

The paper first lists the known classes of such algebras in dimensions below five. It then works out, class by class, their derivations, which act like rates of change inside the algebra, their centroids, and their inner derivations. The result is a reference table for researchers who use these small algebras in wider theory.
arxiv-2504-21380:
Diffusion image makers are heavy to train, and Inês Oliveira, Decebal Mocanu, and Luis Leiva train them sparse from the first step, in work from twenty twenty-five. Three sparse training styles were tried on two model kinds across six data sets. Most weights stay zero through the whole run.

The sparse models matched their dense twins, and often beat them, while using far fewer weights and far less math. Safe sparsity levels are named for builders. The work moves thrift from the serving side to the training side, where the big bills sit. Labs with small clusters gain the most.
arxiv-2505-00780:
The Milky Way's thick disc is an old, puffed-up layer of stars whose true size is still argued over. Roman Tkachenko and co-authors measure it with RR Lyrae stars, reliable distance markers. They combine three major surveys of these pulsating stars. Bayesian sampling methods then fit the disc's shape under two different vertical profiles.

Both profiles agree on a scale length of just over two kiloparsecs. The scale height differs by model: well under one kiloparsec for the exponential form, about one for the alternative. The inner halo follows a power law with a flattened shape. Ratios between halo and disc density are also pinned down. Such numbers anchor models of how the galaxy assembled its oldest stellar populations.
arxiv-2505-01080:
Salvatore Mancuso wrote a 2025 paper on sharpening solar storm forecasts with a radio trick called Faraday rotation. As radio waves from distant galaxies cross the sun's corona, their twist records the gas density and magnetic field along the path. Those measures can tune the big computer models used for forecasts.

He revisits a 2012 eruption seen from three spacecraft at once. Shape, speed, and shock stand-off were drawn from the images. Rare twist data, taken hours before the blast, then checked the model's field and density. With two scale fixes, model and data agreed closely on shock strength. The work offers a way to fine tune storm models before eruptions.
arxiv-2505-01180:
Dimitrios Tsitsigkos, Achilleas Michalopoulos, Nikos Mamoulis, and Manolis Terrovitis present a faster in-memory index for data, in a research paper from 2025. The index is based on the B-tree, a classic balanced tree used in databases. Node sizes are set to blocks that modern chips can scan in parallel.

Their design leaves gaps inside each node by copying some key values. Those gaps let searches and updates run without branching or shifting keys around. A compression trick also shrinks the memory used. In tests with mixed queries and updates, the index beat both classic in-memory indexes and newer learned ones, in single and multi-threaded runs.
arxiv-2505-01280:
Musa Furkan Keskin and co-authors test in 2025 whether the data a radio link carries can itself sharpen the link's sensing of its surroundings. Future networks aim to communicate and sense with the same hardware. In their setup, separate sites send and receive, and the sensing side knows only the pilot tones by default.

Their receiver loops: it senses, decodes data, then uses the decoded data as extra known signal to sense again. Each round refines both the channel estimate and the data. In simulations, this data aided scheme beat pilot only sensing by a wide margin, above all with several targets. It came close to a genie system that knows the data in advance. Better sensing from the same signals serves cars, drones, and smart factories.
arxiv-2505-01480:
Gunnar Brinkmann describes a program for drawing maps on curved surfaces in a 2025 paper. Mathematicians study maps drawn on surfaces like spheres and doughnuts, and good pictures are hard to make by hand. Flat maps have several drawing tools; surfaces with holes had few.

His program, planar_draw, outputs files in a popular typesetting format that users can tweak freely. It draws maps of any genus inside a fundamental polygon, or shows the wrap-around cycles as separate rings to be glued mentally. Options can force chosen edges to stay inside the polygon, for example. Paired with an embedding program, the tool also handles graphs that arrive without a surface layout. Brinkmann presents it as a practical aid for geometers.
arxiv-2505-01680:
Tamim Ahmed and Thanassis Rikakis automate the scoring of a standard arm test used after stroke, in a 2025 paper. Clinicians score the Action Research Arm Test by hand, which takes time and varies between raters. Their system watches videos of patients performing tasks from three camera angles. Several video models read body keypoints and object positions, and their outputs are fused across views. Statistical models then infer movement quality parts, keeping the scoring explainable.

Five clinicians reviewed five hundred system-generated ratings and judged accuracy and ease of use. The fused system reached eighty-nine percent accuracy against reference scores. Its quality estimates also tracked manual assessments closely. A dashboard shows task scores, times, and quality notes for each session. The authors pitch the tool as a scalable aid that supports, rather than replaces, therapist judgment.
arxiv-2505-02380:
Arnab Sanyal and co-authors introduced EntroLLM in this 2025 paper on running large language models on small devices. Big models need lots of storage and memory, which phones and other edge devices lack. The team built a way to shrink model weights without retraining the model.

EntroLLM mixes two forms of number rounding with an entropy coding step that packs the weights more tightly. Tests on three small models cut storage by up to 30 percent over one common format and 65 percent over another. Inference also ran faster on a small NVIDIA board built for edge use. The method fits into existing compression pipelines, so teams can adopt it with little fuss.
arxiv-2505-02580:
Barta and co-authors rebuild heat and pressure fields in turbulent convection from particle motion data alone. In Rayleigh-Benard convection, warm fluid rises and cool fluid sinks in loops. Measuring speed, heat, and pressure together is hard in practice.

Their method trains a physics-informed neural network on tracer paths. One data set came from direct simulation with many tracer particles. The other came from a water tank experiment with tracked particles. The network rebuilt realistic heat and pressure fields in both cases. The simulated case matched the true fields closely. Success on lab data shows the method works beyond theory. It offers labs a way to see hidden fields cheaply.
arxiv-2505-03080:
Sea ice that stretches, flows, and cracks is modeled by a standard system mixing elastic, viscous, and plastic behavior. Proving that system always has one sane solution has lagged behind its daily use in climate work. Daniel Boutros and co-authors supply that proof in a 2025 paper, for a smoothed version of the model. The smoothing acts on the stress equation that tracks the ice's inner forces.

With the smoothing in place, they show solutions exist for all time and are the only ones, even without the artificial caps on viscosity that older workarounds needed. The model shares bones with a known class of gooey fluid models, which guided the proof. A firm math base matters because forecasters lean on this ice model hard.
arxiv-2505-03480:
Music fans drift across genres over time, and Lilian Marey and co-authors model those drifts as paths that can be learned, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their frame borrows from dictionary learning: whole paths are built from short shared chunks, which they call pathlets. Each fan's path becomes a mix of those chunks.

Tests used two thousand fan histories from a streaming firm, tagged by genre over more than a year. The learned chunks matched clear listening habits that could be read and counted. The frame makes taste change legible, chunk by chunk, rather than a blur of single plays. The authors see gains for studies of fan acts and for song picks that keep taste broad, and they share the data and code.
arxiv-2505-03980:
Aroon Sankoh and Victor Wickerhauser compare classic statistics against deep learning for fitting stochastic equations in a 2025 paper. Processes like the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model describe prices and temperatures that wander with a pull back to center. Knowing their parameters makes forecasts and risk estimates possible.

Maximum likelihood, the old workhorse, is pitted against a recurrent neural network across a series of experiments. Both accuracy and computing cost are scored. The contest asks whether the neural approach's flexibility beats the estimator's theory-backed efficiency on this classic problem. The setup frames a fair head-to-head for a workhorse model of continuous-time randomness.
arxiv-2505-04080:
Shengya Huang and co-authors introduce MojoFrame, a 2025 dataframe library for the Mojo programming language. Mojo offers Python-like syntax with hardware tuning for modern chips, and it performs well on tensor math. Work with tables, such as filtering, joining, and grouping, had not been explored in Mojo.

No dataframe library existed in the Mojo system before this work. The authors present the first one and test it on common data science tasks. For data teams, the library opens the door to Mojo's speed on everyday table work, not just on raw number crunching.
arxiv-2505-04280:
Madan Mahana, Sanket Das, and Tarak Dey study photon blockade in a cavity with parametric amplification in this 2025 physics paper. A blockade device lets one photon in and bars the next, a route to single photon sources. The unconventional route uses quantum interference rather than brute strong coupling. Their system holds one two level atom in a cavity, plus an amplifier stage that squeezes the light field. Calculations found the best amplifier gain and phase for the strongest effect.

Simulations at those settings showed strong antibunching, the statistical signature of one at a time photons. Driving the atom beat driving the cavity. A twist appeared: some atom cavity coupling hurt the effect when the cavity was driven, yet helped when the atom was driven. That asymmetry gives experimenters a design rule. The authors present the scheme as a practical recipe for a strongly antibunched source.
arxiv-2505-04580:
Ron Ofir and three co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on better yardsticks for how fast distributed systems reach consensus. Consensus, where many agents settle on one value, underlies distributed sensing and control. Proving how fast it happens, with bounds that are easy to compute, is still hard.

The authors revisit a family of seminorms proposed for this job. They correct an error in the original claim: one seminorm was said to equal a famous ergodicity coefficient, and it does not. They then widen the family and show contraction in any of them forces exponential convergence for matrix products whose rows sum to one. That generalizes classic results beyond stochastic matrices. Finally, they show these yardsticks cannot bound anything beyond the known class of scrambling matrices.
arxiv-2505-05280:
Hwasoo Shin, Marco Ferreira, and Allison Tegge wrote this statistics paper in 2025. Many data sets need two things at once: fewer dimensions to grasp, and groups to sort cases. Their frame, Bayesian clustering factor models, does both in one model. Shared factors sum up each case, and the factors themselves are drawn from a blend of bell curves, which forms the groups.

A Gibbs sampler explores the model's odds, so doubt is measured, not hidden. A set information rule picks how many groups and factors to use, and it beat a past rival rule in tests. Fake-data trials showed sound recovery of the truth. The team then sort people recovering from opioid addiction, where sound groups could shape care fitted to each person.
arxiv-2505-05380:
Chenghong Zhu, Xian Wu, Hao-Kai Zhang, Sixuan Wu, Guangxi Li, and Xin Wang wrote a 2025 paper on searching for good quantum circuit designs. Variational quantum computing needs circuits that are both expressive and easy to train. Finding that balance by hand is slow, so automated search methods design circuits for each problem.

Their framework judges circuits without training them. It reads how the cost landscape rises and falls, a signal that predicts how learnable a circuit will be. A two level search then homes in on strong, large circuits with fewer gates. The method used far less classical computing than prior work. It also held up on a demanding simulation with fifty qubits, a sign it can scale to harder problems.
arxiv-2505-05480:
Ryan Williams asks what natural selection can and cannot shape about conscious experience. Qualia, the felt qualities of experience such as the redness of red, may or may not march in step with the physical structures that carry them. His 2025 paper builds information measures for how tightly structure and quality determine each other, a fidelity between the two domains.

Those fidelity measures are then fed into the Price equation, the bookkeeping identity of evolutionary change. The result is a set of formal bounds: conditions under which selection acting on structure can reliably move qualities, and limits on that transmission. Williams also examines how higher-order structures pass between the domains. A companion paper places the results in wider philosophical context. The work gives consciousness theories a set of hard constraints to answer to, rather than another verbal position.
arxiv-2505-05780:
Satoshi Yano surveys the science case for a new particle collider in this 2025 paper. The Electron-Ion Collider is being built at Brookhaven National Laboratory. It will smash electrons into protons and ions, with the spin of each beam under close control.

The machine aims to give sharp views of the strong force, named QCD. It should map the inner parts of protons in three dimensions and show how gluons supply their mass and spin. It will also probe dense gluon states and how nuclei change the force. A new detector, ePIC, is being built to catch the results.
arxiv-2505-05880:
Bettina Fazzinga and co-authors combine two tools in a 2025 paper for reading streams of low-level process events. Firms track each step of their work as events, but the raw events often do not match the named steps of the business process. Someone must translate each event into the step it belongs to, and that mapping can be unsure.

One known approach frames the task as argumentation, weighing which readings of an event hold up against prior knowledge of the process. That route can be slow and can leave too many readings open when doubt is high. The authors add machine learning to the mix to guide the choice. The blend aims for faster, sharper readings of live event streams, with reasons kept for the cases that clash with what is known.
arxiv-2505-05980:
Björklund and Hartnick extend the Radon transform to transverse dynamical systems in a 2025 mathematics paper. The classic transform is defined for pairs of homogeneous spaces of a group. Their version replaces one space with a dynamical system and a suitable cross section.

The framework covers known examples from the geometry of numbers, translation surfaces, and time-frequency analysis. The main results give conditions for the transforms to be bounded and integrable. They also show how the transforms embed group representations into function spaces. Uses include hulls of approximate lattices and cut-and-project sets. For the Heisenberg group, the authors give explicit formulas and isometric embeddings.
arxiv-2505-06580:
Dongyoon Yang, Jihu Lee, and Yongdai Kim introduce a 2025 method called TAROT for training models that must work across new settings and still resist attacks. Models often fail when the data shifts or when small, crafted changes trick them. The authors seek a way to keep accuracy steady across domains while also holding up under attack.

They first derive a new bound on risk for the target setting, using a fresh measure of the gap between domains. They then build TAROT to learn features that stay the same across domains. In tests, the method beat prior work on accuracy and on strength under attack. It did well on the hard DomainNet set, which spans many kinds of images.
arxiv-2505-06680:
Linxuan Huang and co-authors survey how data-taught models call a driver's lane change, in a survey from 2025. Lane change is a small act with big wake: safety and flow both ride it. Old hand-built rules call it in stiff forms that miss how folk split and mix on real roads.

Taught models read rich road banks and learn the hid marks of a choice. The survey walks the whole build: banks and their clean-up, in and out marks, aims, frames, and grade ways. It ends with the gaps: crash-safe calls, doubt kept in hand, and one frame that fits smart and self-drive fleets. The field, they say, has the data; it owes the care.
arxiv-2505-06880:
Longtian Wang and five co-authors probe a weakness in how code-writing language models are graded, in a 2025 paper. Standard benchmarks give each programming problem one fixed prompt, but real users phrase the same problem many ways, typos included. A model's score can swing with the wording, so a single prompt may misstate its skill.

The team designed ten mutation strategies that perturb prompts in realistic ways and three new metrics to measure the fallout. They generated 12,834 prompt variants and tested five popular code models. Scores on the mutated prompts differed significantly from the clean benchmark results. The authors argue that future benchmarks need this kind of robustness testing built in.
arxiv-2505-06980:
Lei Wan and co-authors present a cooperative sensing system for self-driving cars that pools views across vehicles and road posts, in work from 2025. Single cars see too little: range is short, views get blocked, and one bad sensor can blind the system. Weather and dim light make it worse.

Their rig fuses laser, radar, color, and heat cameras on both cars and roadside poles. Heat cameras help spot people at night or in glare. Roadside views fill the gaps that block a car's own sight. A health monitor watches each sensor and flags faults early. The team built the system and tested it on a real-world track, reporting gains in reach and robustness.
arxiv-2505-07180:
Ruichu Cai and co-authors fill gaps in time series with care for how the gaps came to be. The work dates to 2025. Gaps can come by chance tied to seen facts, or by chance tied to the lost facts. Past fill tools oft use one model for all gap kinds, which can skew reads.

The team first maps the birth path of the data for each gap kind. Hid states and gap-cause terms sit in that map. A flow-based net then learns the hid terms' spread. Proofs show the hid terms can be set apart in their frame. Tests across sets with split gap kinds beat past fill tools.
arxiv-2505-07880:
Jared Hand and a large team from the Nearby Supernova Factory wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on Type Ia supernovae. These exploding stars are used as yardsticks for cosmic distances. To use them well, scientists need a model of how their light rises and fades over time and across colors.

The team built a fresh model from their own survey data, with few set views about what shape it should take. Their model uses three patterns of color change, one tied to the burst's phase and two that stay steady. The fit shows the bursts vary in color in ways dust alone cannot explain. That finding matters for fine measures of the expanding universe.
arxiv-2505-08080:
Dong Shu and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on finding the inner features of a language model that truly drive its output. Sparse autoencoders unpack model activity into readable features, but most checks only watch which features switch on. The authors argue that switched on features do not pull equal weight.

Their method adds output side gradient data to rank features by real causal pull. Only high pull features, they hold, can steer a model well. The approach is simple and, by their tests, effective. It moves interpretation from what lights up to what actually matters, a shift with stakes for control and safety work.
arxiv-2505-08180:
Mihai Cucuringu, Kang Li, and Chao Zhang forecast how much of a stock will trade, hour by hour, with machine learning, in a 2025 paper. Intraday volume steers how big traders slice their orders, and a standard benchmark, the volume-weighted average price, grades their craft. Flexible forecast tools for this curve have been scarce. The team feeds a suite of learning models a rich set of fast market signals.

The volume curve proved highly predictable, the more so when the models learned the tide that lifts all stocks at once. Sharp forecasts then paid in cash terms: trading plans built on them beat the benchmark by clear margins in tests. The authors frame volume foresight as an edge hiding in plain sight. For high-frequency desks, they argue, the intraday tide is a forecastable thing, not noise to ride blind.
arxiv-2505-08280:
Emmanuel Humbert, Romain Petrides, and Bruno Premoselli ask which shapes extremize the eigenvalues of a family of geometric operators in a 2025 paper. On a curved space, one can deform the metric within its conformal class. Then one can watch the GJMS operator's values move. Their extreme values are geometric invariants, but the best metrics, when they exist, need not be smooth.

The authors build a framework for such values for singular conformal metrics, with renormalized values, continuity results, and equations that local extremals must satisfy. With mild assumptions, they prove new results on when such best forms do and do not exist. These include a maximization for negative values and a look at the round sphere. Optimizers connect strongly with solutions of prescribed curvature equations. The theory allows operators of any order, even with a kernel.
arxiv-2505-08380:
Chitradeep Saha, Sanghita Chandra, and Dibyendu Nandy asked how much magnetic flux the Sun needs to climb out of a grand minimum. A grand minimum is one of the decades-long lulls when sunspots nearly vanish, like the Maunder minimum. During such lulls the Sun's polar fields fade and stop reversing. Using dynamo simulations spanning thousands of years with random forcing, the team measured the polar flux at which reversals resume.

A clear threshold emerged: once enough polar flux accumulates, regular cycles restart. How long a minimum lasts did not depend on how fast it began, and recovery speed was steady. The threshold gives forecasters a target for judging when a future minimum might end. Predicting when one will start, the authors admit, remains unsolved.
arxiv-2505-08980:
Adem Limani proved summable versions of a classical theorem in a 2025 mathematics paper. The Ivashev-Musatov theorem concerns objects that behave pathologically on parts of their domain. Limani moves the question into sequence spaces: weighted versions of the space of absolutely summable sequences, and Orlicz spaces, which generalize that scale. There, the paper constructs elements whose support and range are critically strange.

The pathology is twofold: topological, in how the sets sit inside the space, and measure-theoretic, in their size. Such elements mark the threshold where good behavior breaks down. The results complement earlier work by Kahane, Katznelson, and Körner on related borderline phenomena. Threshold effects of this kind map the exact edge of a theorem's reach.
arxiv-2505-09080: Marcello Lanfranchi and Jean-Simon Pacaud Lemay sort all the slope-like structures, of a named kind, that the world of affine schemes can bear. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five, in the math of categories. That world is a tangent world, whose slope bundle comes from a known form of calculus. The team asks how rare that is. They coin a tool, the tangentoid, for objects that breed such a structure by pairing. They prove such objects, for rings, match a class of solid rings.
arxiv-2505-09380:
Qinghui Liu and seven co-authors report a three-month hospital trial of a platform for running medical AI, in a 2025 paper. Hospitals struggle to deploy and improve AI tools safely in daily radiology work. The platform, NeoMedSys, combines a web image viewer, a labeling system, and links to hospital records. On it ran VIOLA-AI, a model that detects bleeding inside the skull on scans. Cases came from a large emergency setting.

Clinicians could inspect the model's calls, correct them, and feed improvements back. The study judged whether the setup worked in real practice and whether the model got better with use. Interactive refinement of this kind may be the route by which hospital AI earns trust, one corrected case at a time.
arxiv-2505-09480:
Weikai Qi, Shreya Tiwary, and Richard Bowles simulate how tiny glassy particles slow down as they cool, in a 2025 paper. Supercooled liquids stiffen toward glass without freezing into crystals. In nanoparticle form, the change happens at lower temperatures. The team asked how structure and motion stay coupled at that scale.

Computer dynamics tracked a two-component particle across sizes. Its glass point fell as size shrank, following a set power law. Relaxation times were read from scattering measures. Favored local structures gathered into physical clusters as cooling deepened. A droplet model from glass theory described the coupling well, though its exponents shifted with particle size. The results guide design of glassy nanomaterials.
arxiv-2505-09580:
Kristina Rannu studies, in a 2025 physics paper, how magnetic fields reshape the phase behavior of a holographic model for heavy quarks. The model pictures strongly interacting matter through a five-dimensional gravity setup. A special term in the setup tunes how the matter responds.

Rannu examines cases of direct and inverse magnetic catalysis, two opposite ways a field can shift matter's phases. She presents a phase diagram built from a first-order transition and time-like Wilson loops. The diagram fits the stable direct catalysis scenario. String tension behavior in the field is also discussed. Holographic models like this give theorists a laboratory for matter too hot or dense for direct study.
arxiv-2505-09780:
Royina Karegoudra Jayanth and co-authors improve inertial tracking by feeding neural priors with Lie events instead of raw sensor data. Inertial odometry drifts over time without outside fixes. Neural displacement priors can curb that drift and report uncertainty.

Priors trained on raw data fail when sampling rates change. They also falter on new motion profiles in the field. Lie events fire only when integrated motion crosses a threshold. That trigger makes them robust to rate changes. Signed strengths within the algebra replace simple on-off marks. Training on these events cut trajectory error sharply. Gains came with only minor extra preprocessing. The method suits drones and wearable trackers alike.
arxiv-2505-10280:
Sboychakov studies how a material packed with hollow magnetic balls responds to fast-changing magnetic fields, in a 2025 paper. Each ball is a thin magnetic shell around an empty core, set in a non-magnetic base. Inside each shell the magnetism twists into a vortex pattern, held in place by one of two kinds of directional preference.

Working in the case where the balls do not affect each other, the author tracks how the response changes as the shell grows from thin to nearly solid. Thick shells behaved much the same under both preferences, while thin shells under one preference mimicked a flat film. The results can guide designs for high-frequency magnetic materials.
arxiv-2505-10380:
Naoko Nakagawa and Shin-ichi Sasa propose a variational principle in twenty twenty-five. Consider a liquid-gas system where gravity favors one stacking and heat flow favors another. Predicting the stable arrangement is a fundamental problem. Standard equilibrium thermodynamics cannot settle it, since the state is a non-equilibrium steady one.

Their principle rests on an extended framework called global thermodynamics. Within it, gravity and heat flow merge into one parameter, effective gravity. The sign of that parameter decides the outcome. Positive effective gravity puts liquid at the bottom. Negative values let liquid float above the gas. The result is a quantitative tool for configuration prediction under competing drives. Readers get a single dial where two forces used to fight.
arxiv-2505-10480:
Ilani Axelrod-Freed and co-authors study the geometry of spaces built from alternating sign matrices, in a 2025 paper. Alternating sign matrices are grids of zeros, ones, and minus ones with row and column rules, long loved by combinatorialists. Intersecting classical matrix Schubert varieties produces a newer family, ASM varieties, whose basic properties are far harder to pin down than their parents'.

The paper focuses on two questions: how large these varieties are, and when they enjoy the Cohen-Macaulay property that makes their algebra well behaved. The key tool is studying how a pair of matrices and their direct sum relate. The authors also reinterpret ASM pattern avoidance geometrically. Their results narrow the gap between the tidy Schubert theory and these wilder intersections.
arxiv-2505-10780:
Trisha Das, Afrah Shafquat, Beigi Mandis, Jacob Aptekar, and Jimeng Sun wrote a 2025 paper on finding past clinical trials that resemble a new one. Trial designers learn from history: similar trials reveal pitfalls in dosing, recruiting, and safety. But trial documents are long and varied, so finding true matches by hand is slow.

Their system, called SECRET, sums up each trial protocol and searches by meaning. It learns from partly labeled data, since full labeling is costly. The authors report it beats all rival methods they tested. Better matching at the design stage could cut failed trials, which waste years and large sums and delay new treatments for patients.
arxiv-2505-11180:
Chuan Xu, Qiaosheng Chen, Yutong Feng, and Gong Cheng introduce a benchmark for testing retrieval-augmented generation systems in this 2025 paper. Such systems fetch documents to help a language model answer, but most tests only check plain text and grade the final answer as a whole. Their benchmark, mmRAG, widens the evidence to text, tables, and knowledge graphs.

The authors gathered questions from six question-answering data sets and converted all the source material into documents that can be retrieved in one uniform way. They labeled which documents are relevant to each question, following standard retrieval practice. That labeling lets evaluators grade the parts of a system, such as retrieval accuracy and query routing, rather than only the finished text. A wide range of existing systems was run through the benchmark to set baseline scores for future work.
arxiv-2505-11280:
Horacio Thompson and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on spotting online risk early. The task is to flag users who may face health or social harm, post by post. A good system must be both right and fast, since a late flag can miss the chance to help.

The authors propose a new way to train transformer models that builds time into the training itself. The method reads a full post history and judges the model with scores that count both right calls and delay. Tests used Spanish posts tied to low mood and eating disorders. The method matched the best systems from a 2023 shared task on those topics.
arxiv-2505-11380:
Alejandro Moreo, writing alone in 2025, proves that three seemingly separate problems in machine learning are secretly the same problem. The setting is dataset shift, where test data drifts from training data. The three tasks are calibrating a classifier's scores, estimating the share of positives in new data, and predicting the classifier's accuracy on that new data.

Moreo shows each task can be reduced to the others: an oracle for any one solves all three. That equivalence lets methods cross borders. Adapting a strong calibration method yields a quantification method, and so on. In tests, the borrowed methods often matched or beat the dedicated ones. The paper urges the three research communities to build unified tools.
arxiv-2505-11480:
Anjiang Wei and six co-authors turn language models into assembly code superoptimizers, in work from 2025. Superoptimization rewrites a program into the fastest version with the same behaviour, a job compilers only partly solve. Their benchmark holds over eight thousand real assembly programs, far larger than the toy sets used before, and twenty-three models were tried on it.

The best off-the-shelf model passed about half the tests with a solid average speedup over the top compiler setting. Fine-tuning a seven-billion model with reinforcement learning on a reward mixing correctness and speed produced SuperCoder, which passed ninety-five percent of tests and ran faster still. Sampling and refinement added more gains.
arxiv-2505-11580:
Andrew Liu and six co-authors present Flash Invariant Point Attention in two thousand twenty five. Invariant Point Attention drives geometry aware protein and RNA models. Its quadratic cost caps the sequence lengths it can handle in practice. FlashIPA refactors the method around FlashAttention instead.

Memory and time now scale linearly with sequence length. Performance matches or beats standard IPA in their tests. Training reaches lengths that were out of reach before. Generative models retrained without length caps make thousand residue structures. The code is public for structural biology teams worldwide.
arxiv-2505-11680:
Yunus Seker, Shobhit Aggarwal, and Oliver Kroemer present a 2025 robot method that transfers a skill to a new object with no extra training. The first author's middle initial appears in the byline. Moving skills between objects is a core problem in open world robot work. Objects differ in shape at a high level, yet the low level contact control stays much the same. Their method splits a skill into a ranked list of controllers. Each controller acts along one axis.

Each controller is anchored to key points and axes on the object, such as a screw head and its shaft. A vision foundation model then finds matching points on a new object by meaning, which grounds the same skill there. Real robot tests covered screwing, pouring, and scraping with a spatula. The authors report robust, flexible transfer across all three tasks.
arxiv-2505-11780:
Zeinab Shiralizadeh reviews a parallel algorithm that learns decision trees from endless data streams, in this 2025 paper. Streams from sensors and services never stop, so models must update on the fly. The algorithm under review, pdsCART, splits the work across many machines.

Three traits define the method. It builds trees step by step as data arrive, rather than in one batch. It processes high-volume streams in parallel for scale. And it plugs into the MapReduce framework that powers distributed computing. Shiralizadeh lays out the design and weighs reported results on speed and growth, judging where the method fits big-data practice.
arxiv-2505-11880:
Digital locks for small connected devices must be fast and frugal, and the AES cipher is the standard lock. Six authors present AES-RV, a hardware accelerator built on the open RISC-V processor design. It adds custom low-latency AES instructions, wide internal buffers that keep data flowing, and a pipelined layout with a ping-pong memory scheme that overlaps loading and computing.

Built on a Xilinx FPGA board, the design ran up to about 256 times faster than the baselines it was compared against. It also used energy up to about 453 times more efficiently. Against other published AES accelerators, it showed stronger throughput for its area. The authors present AES-RV as covering all AES modes and key sizes in real time, making it a strong candidate for secure embedded and Internet-of-Things systems.
arxiv-2505-12480:
Maxim Kontsevich and Alexander Odesskii compute, in exact formulas, where deformed operators live in arithmetic terms. Their work came out in 2025. The start is a product operator built from simple scaling pieces. Rational shifts mark each factor in that product. A formal deformation then perturbs the operator term by term. The question is the arithmetic support of the whole series that results. It is a hard question, and exact answers of this kind are rare.

For large enough primes, monodromy data in characteristic zero decides the answer. The monodromy tracks how solutions wind around singularities as they move. A twin result covers q-difference operators, which replace derivatives with scaled shifts. The work ties arithmetic to analytic winding in a concrete way.
arxiv-2505-12580:
Priyank Pathak and Yogesh Rawat teach surveillance models to re-identify people who have changed clothes, even in poor video. Their 2025 paper tackles a hard corner of person re-identification: real footage is pixelated, blurred, and shaky, unlike the clean images most systems train on. Low quality corrupts both visible traits and the model's internal features, so wrong people start to cluster together.

Their framework alternates two fixes. Coarse attribute prediction feeds the model rough external cues that survive noise. Task-agnostic distillation then pulls the features of blurry images toward those of clean ones, using an outside dataset for the lesson. On three real-world benchmarks the method gained several points of top-one accuracy over rivals. The authors argue robustness to bad footage, not benchmark polish, is what deployment actually needs.
arxiv-2505-12780:
Soohwan Lee, Seoyeong Hwang, and Kyungho Lee argue that design for artificial intelligence needs a new unit of analysis: the group, in this 2025 paper. User experience research studies one person at a time, yet people increasingly meet AI in teams, classrooms, and families, where feelings and judgments emerge between members, not inside one head. They name that collective layer Group Experience, or GX.

From GX they propose Group-centered AI, systems designed to mediate group dynamics, amplify quieter voices, and support fair collective decisions rather than merely serving each user separately. The framework borrows from social psychology and organizational behavior, and it calls for new metrics that capture collaboration itself. The provocation is deliberately unfinished: it asks the design community to build methods for the space between individual experience and society-wide impact.
arxiv-2505-12880:
Angle-keeping maps matter in physics and vision, and a neural network that respects them could learn faster. Maksim Zhdanov and co-authors build such a network in a 2025 paper. Their trick lifts flat data into a curved space called anti-de Sitter space. In that space, angle-keeping changes of the flat data act as distance-keeping moves, which are easier to build into a network.

Layers pass messages based on true distances in the curved space, keeping the cost of computing low. Tests came from vision tasks and from statistical physics setups. The network performed strongly and generalized well to new cases. It could even read off key scaling numbers learned from data. The authors frame it as a bridge between geometry and learning.
arxiv-2505-13180:
Matteo Merler and colleagues present ViPlan, a benchmark for visual planning with symbolic predicates. Their 2025 arXiv paper compares two ways to plan with vision-language models. One route uses the model to ground symbols for a classic planner. The other lets the model plan directly from images. No open benchmark had compared them on equal terms before.

Tasks grow harder across two visual domains. One is a visual form of the classic Blocksworld problem. The other is a simulated household robotics setting. Grounded symbolic planning won clearly in Blocksworld tasks. It solved far more tasks than direct planning there. Household tasks proved harder for both approaches. The benchmark is open source for matched future comparisons.
arxiv-2505-13280:
Elias Collaert and co-authors present FlowPure, a defense that washes adversarial attacks out of images before classification. Their 2025 paper addresses a known weakness: tiny crafted changes to an image can fool a trained model while looking harmless to people. Leading defenses use diffusion models that add noise, then denoise, which can also blur the true content.

FlowPure instead trains continuous normalizing flows to map attacked images directly back to clean ones. One version uses knowledge of the attack; a general version trains on Gaussian noise for unknown threats. On standard image benchmarks it beat rival purification defenses and kept accuracy on clean images in blind settings. It also spotted attacked samples with near-perfect accuracy, hinting at a second career as a detector.
arxiv-2505-13480:
As people in crisis increasingly confide in chatbots, Avinash Patil and co-authors test whether language models can grade suicide risk responsibly. They used the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale, a seven-level clinical ladder, to score posts in zero-shot fashion. Six models, including Claude, GPT, Mistral, and LLaMA variants, were compared against human annotations. Claude and GPT tracked human judgments most closely, while Mistral made the smallest ranking errors.

Most mistakes landed on neighboring severity levels, suggesting the models sense gradations of risk. The authors stress human oversight, transparency, and cautious deployment before any clinical use, and they share their code openly.
arxiv-2505-13580:
Hanzhao Wang and three co-authors build OMGPT, a transformer for operations decisions. Their 2025 paper frames pricing, stocking, allocation, and queue control as one sequence problem. In that frame, the best next action is predicted from the full history. Classic methods instead assume a tidy model for each task.

A GPT-style network, trained from scratch, learns the mapping from history to actions. It can draw on large pre-training data without assuming a task's structure. A Bayesian view ties its skill to the variety of pre-training tasks and their distance from the test task. Early numbers support the approach across the named tasks. The work marks a shift toward one general decision engine.
arxiv-2505-13680:
Siddharth Prasad, Maria-Florina Balcan, and Tuomas Sandholm design a new family of auctions for selling bundles of items, where bidders value combinations. Their paper came out in 2025. Good auctions in this space pin prices so no group of bidders, together with the seller, would rather renegotiate the deal.

Their twist is to use what the designer already knows about bidders before bidding starts, expressed as limits on plausible valuations. That information, they show, can break a known impossibility result about honest bidding in such auctions. Their new designs minimize bidders' total incentive to bid dishonestly. Computing the prices needs new constraint methods built on quadratic programming. Experiments favored the new auctions on honesty, revenue, fairness, and speed against designs used in real high-stakes sales.
arxiv-2505-13780:
Hanlun Lei and Evgeni Grishin build a sharper model for three-body orbits in a 2025 arXiv paper. Triple systems with weak hierarchy are common, from high lunar satellites to binaries near a black hole. Standard averaged models miss strong nonlinear effects in such systems.

Their extended Brown Hamiltonian adds quadrupole terms from both the inner and outer bodies. The formulas for the energy and for element conversion stay in elegant closed form. Tests on Jupiter's irregular satellites match direct simulations well over long spans. The model targets von Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai oscillations, the slow swings of tilt and stretch in triple systems.
arxiv-2505-13880:
A model that listens should handle speech, everyday sounds, and music in one head, yet most audio models specialize. Ziqian Wang and co-authors build a unified listener in a 2025 paper, wiring three specialist encoders, one per sound kind, into a large language model. A mixture-of-experts bridge routes and blends what each encoder hears.

A second module hunts redundant sound features and corrects their meaning under language guidance, tightening the match between sound and words. Across benchmarks the system beat both specialist models and earlier audio language models. It also handled tasks it was never trained on, hinting at broad generalization.
arxiv-2505-13980:
In control engineering, one key score for a system is its L-infinity norm, a measure of worst case gain tied to stability and robustness. Grace Younes and two co-authors survey in 2025 how exact symbolic methods can compute that score where number crunching methods hit limits. They review three tools from computer algebra and how each fits the task.

The survey weighs symbolic results against standard numerical ones across test cases. Exact methods shine when the system carries unknown parameters, since they return formulas rather than single numbers. They can also be slow or heavy on memory. The authors close with the open problems in merging the two styles for control work.
arxiv-2505-14080:
Language models carry gender stereotypes, and a 2025 audit by Franziska Sofia Hafner, Ana Valdivia, and Luc Rocher argues the problem runs deeper than word links. Fixing which jobs get tied to which gender leaves untouched a deeper harm: models that treat gender as fixed biology can erase trans and diverse identities.

Guided by gender performativity theory, the team turned ideas about how language builds gender into testable checks. They then ran those checks on sixteen language models of varied designs, training data, and sizes. The audit shows how the models encode gender itself, not just pairs of words. The authors call on fairness research to widen its meaning of gender bias, since downstream harms range from misgendering users to wrong medical guesses.
arxiv-2505-14280:
German debate on Twitter, now called X, looks split into two hostile camps, and Armin Pournaki and two co-authors ask who builds that split. Their 2025 study reads trending topics and reposts from March 2021 to July 2023, sorting users by the views their posts signal. Two camps stood out, one mostly left leaning and one mostly right leaning.

Views on separate issues lined up far more tightly than surveys would suggest. The authors trace that tight fit to two kinds of heavy users: influencers who post charged content, and multipliers who spread it. Multipliers act as filters, passing on only what matches their side. The authors say the pair together shape how divided the platform feels.
arxiv-2505-14480:
Studying cause and effect in human lives often means working with a single precious dataset, where peeking at the data can bias the verdict. Samrat Roy and co-authors propose a discipline for that bind in this 2025 paper, called two team cross-screening. They apply it to the long-term effects of unwanted pregnancies carried to term, using a Wisconsin study that followed mothers for decades.

The researchers split into two teams, and the data split along a meaningful trait. Each team explored its own half freely, then wrote the analysis plan for the other half. Only ideas that looked promising got forwarded, which trims false leads. Outcomes covered mental and physical health, money, and life satisfaction in later years.
arxiv-2505-14680:
Sunhao Dai and co-authors argue that AI search needs a rebuilt feedback system in this 2025 conference paper. Generative search answers questions directly, sparing users the work of browsing pages. That ease comes at a hidden cost to how search improves.

Classic web search learned from clicks and reading time on each page. AI search runs a longer chain, from splitting the query to drafting the answer. User signals blur across that chain, so models learn less from each visit. NExT-Search proposes a new ecosystem for gathering useful feedback. It aims to restore the loop that made web search steadily better. Search firms face this design problem right now.
arxiv-2505-14880:
Chris Sypherd, Sergei Petrov, Sonny George, and Vaishak Belle argued in 2025 that prompting strategies for language models should be judged on token cost as well as accuracy. A clever prompt can win on score while burning many more tokens, which costs money and time. The usual score-only ranking hides that trade-off.

The team proposes a theory frame that describes how token use grows with each strategy, in the style of big-O notation, plus a hands-on measure of tokens spent per unit of performance. Applied to several common strategies, both tools show that extra tokens bring steeply shrinking gains. Readers get a practical correction to prompt engineering culture: count the tokens, not just the wins, before calling a strategy better.
arxiv-2505-14980:
More and more cameras record the world only for other machines: traffic counters, robots, and self-driving cars that never show the footage to a human. Ivan Bajić asks how small such footage can be squeezed while staying accurate for its machine viewer, in this 2025 paper. The field calls this coding for machines, and it prizes task accuracy over pretty reconstruction.

Borrowing math from classic lossy coding of simple sources, Bajić derives bounds: the lowest bitrate any method could reach at a set accuracy, for several standard vision tasks. Today's best methods sit at least ten times above those bounds, and sometimes a hundred or a thousand times above. The gap, he argues, is the headline: coding for machines has far more room to improve than its current pace suggests.
arxiv-2505-15280:
Arkadiusz Kobus and co-authors design a multi-setting test that can spot Bell correlations in high-spin atomic clouds. Their 2025 protocol targets squeezed states in Bose-Einstein condensates, where atoms pair into linked subsystems. Proving such quantum links normally needs many measurement setups.

The test uses several settings at once to catch two-body Bell correlations. Lab data from the spin-one case back the design. Computer simulations using a standard phase-space method extend the proof to spin two and three. The authors say the scheme widens the reach of Bell tests in ultracold atom labs. It also paves a path toward quantum information work on high-spin platforms.
arxiv-2505-15580:
Van Roestel and co-authors present a 2025 paper reporting seven pairs of white dwarf stars that eclipse each other. A sky survey that watches for changing brightness offered a way to find such tight pairs systematically. Their orbits take from forty-five minutes to three hours, so the stars circle each other at a furious pace.

Fast light curves, older data across wavelengths, and spectra pinned down each pair's properties. Six pairs hold two helium-core white dwarfs of low mass; the seventh pairs a carbon-oxygen dwarf with a helium one. All are spiraling inward as they shed energy in gravitational waves, set to merge within tens of millions to a billion years. The tightest pair should show a measurable timing drift within a decade.
arxiv-2505-15680:
Rivero-Acosta and four co-authors work out light-shed rates for rare heavy baryons in this twenty twenty-five paper. These short-lived bits hold one heavy bottom quark and sit in a small kin class. Light-shed paths can prove a state is real when strong paths are shut.

Inside, a quark build frame sets the rates from high shell states down to ground and bent states. The work gives first rates for a class of wave states and mixed states not yet charted. Both test error and model error are folded into each rate as a range. Such rates also help split states that share mass and width, the team notes. The set gives hunters a map for ring lab checks.
arxiv-2505-15780: Debraj Chakrabarti and Prachi Mahajan describe a method to define a Hermitian metric on hyperbolic complex manifolds. Their short paper from 2025 deals with Kobayashi hyperbolic spaces, a core topic in complex geometry. The metric they build shrinks distances under holomorphic maps, up to a fixed factor. The method differs from the classic construction by Wu. The authors expect their metric to have better smoothness traits than the classic one, which would make it easier to use in later proofs and estimates on such manifolds.
arxiv-2505-15980:
Konstantinos Boutivas, Dimitrios Katsinis, Ioannis Papadimitriou, Georgios Pastras, and Nikolaos Tetradis studied entanglement in a curved space in 2025. Their setting is anti-de Sitter space, a model space with constant negative curve, in three space dimensions plus time. The field is a free scalar field with mass, held in its ground state.

They look at round regions centered at the origin and ask how much the entropy of entanglement grows without bound. Such growth splits into terms that depend on the cutoff scale. The team found the form of those terms and computed the numbers in front of each. They also confirm that the number on the log term matches a known trait of the field theory, the conformal anomaly.
arxiv-2505-16180:
Dahal, Ghimire, Murad, and Rahimi proposed this scoring framework in twenty twenty-five for judging image captions. Captions written by AI need fair grades, yet older metrics often miss meaning or reward awkward wording. Bad scores can mislead builders about real progress. The team's Redemption Score grades a caption on both what the image shows and how the words read.

The score blends three signals into one number. One checks how well the caption's meaning lines up with the image. One rebuilds an image from the caption and compares it with the original. One compares the caption's wording with human-written references. On a standard photo test set, the score matched human rankings better than most older metrics, with no special training needed.
arxiv-2505-16480:
Akriti Garg and Ayan Chatterjee study collapsing matter in an expanding universe in a 2025 paper. Their setting is de Sitter space, a universe driven by a steady expansion like our own late-time cosmos. They follow round clouds of matter as gravity pulls them inward, for many kinds of matter, from simple dust to fluids with pressure and viscosity.

Mixing exact math with computer work, they track how trapped surfaces form and grow during the collapse. These surfaces are the seeds of horizons. The authors show that black hole horizons and the universe's own cosmological horizon can both be read as the time history of such surfaces. The framework gives a unified way to follow horizon birth in an expanding cosmos.
arxiv-2505-16680:
Filip Thor and Carl Nettelblad learn genome structure from short DNA fragments in a 2025 paper. Sequencing yields floods of short reads that must be reassembled, a costly step. Their contrastive method trains an encoder so fragments from the same region land near each other in an embedding space.

Region order survives as paths through that space, giving one representation for many read tasks. Trained on the Escherichia coli genome, the model maps simulated ancient DNA reads and flags structural variants. It also sorts species in mixed samples. Small prediction heads matched the standard mapping tool on speed and accuracy for short genomes. Training can run self supervised on raw reads, skipping assembly entirely.
arxiv-2505-16780:
Zhi-Xuan Meng, Shuai-Xia Xu, and Yu-Qiu Zhao present a study from twenty twenty-five on a one dimensional gas of bosons that cannot share a spot. Links between points in space and time are the key gauge. That gauge can be written with a determinant of a sine based kernel and with answers to a set of split wave equations.

The team works out how the gauge grows at large time and span. Two zones of the space time plane get unlike forms: a space like zone and a time like zone. A phase shift marks the line between them. That shift is told by a set answer to the Painlevé IV equation, a known special equation.
arxiv-2505-16880:
Saša Ceci, Hedim Osmanović, and Branimir Zauner resolve a puzzle about a famous particle resonance in a 2025 physics paper. The resonance, called Δ(1232), is a short-lived excited state of nuclear matter. Its traits are usually read from a pole in the scattering math: the pole's place gives mass and total width, and the size of its residue gives the partial width.

That reading fails here, because it makes one part of the decay wider than the whole. The team builds a simple model that predicts residue phases for several well-known particles, light mesons among them. With those phases the anomaly dissolves. Their moral is sharp: a pole residue is not a basic trait of a resonance.
arxiv-2505-17280:
Text-to-image models carry biases — about age, ethnicity, gender, and more — and fixing one can quietly bend another. Pushkar Shukla and co-authors build a tool, BiasConnect, that maps these interactions. It intervenes on one bias axis at a time and estimates how mitigation there will ripple to the others. Those estimates correlated strongly with the outcomes actually observed after mitigation.

On top of the map they build InterMit, a mitigation method steered by the user's target distributions and priorities across axes. It reached lower bias than traditional techniques while taking fewer mitigation steps and producing better images. The implementation needs no retraining and can wrap around many existing debiasing methods. The work argues that fairness in image generation must be handled as one connected system, not as a row of separate dials.
arxiv-2505-18280:
Tsai Hor Chan, Dora Yan Zhang, Guosheng Yin, and Lequan Yu improve how Bayesian neural networks handle noisy features, in a research paper from 2025. These networks treat their weights as ranges rather than fixed values, which helps them report uncertainty. A poor prior choice can bloat that uncertainty or crush real signals.

Their design applies a prior that shrinks useless weights toward zero while sparing key features. A new inference method mixes sampling steps with gradient updates for steadier estimates. The authors back the method with theory on how fast the posterior settles. Tests on natural and medical images show good accuracy and uncertainty scores.
arxiv-2505-18380:
Praphul Singh, Charlotte Dzialo, and five colleagues build RedactOR, a system that scrubs private details from medical records on its own, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Health data must stay private, yet hospitals and researchers still need records that read coherently for analysis.

Older scrubbing tools miss items, fail on new kinds of records, or cost too much to run. RedactOR handles structured files, free-text notes, and even clinical audio. It mixes cheap rule-based passes with language model passes, routing each piece of data to the cheaper method that can handle it. Audio is cleaned in two steps. When a private name is swapped out, a retrieval step keeps the replacement consistent across the whole record. The design aims to protect patients without gutting the data's usefulness for AI-driven care and research.
arxiv-2505-18680:
Yuanhe Zhang and co-authors built a defense in 2025 for language model services against attacks that waste computer power. Such attacks can slow a server or crash it by forcing very long replies. Past work had few fixes for this threat, the authors say.

Their pluggable frame acts on both input and output. On input, an index of resource use guides how requests are polled and scheduled under heavy load. On output, a rule ends runaway replies from attackers early. Tests across six models showed user access rising as much as fivefold under attack load. The work is framed as a step toward sturdier, resource-aware service.
arxiv-2505-18880:
Turning a long documentary into a short teaser takes more than cutting: the short must tell a story and still quote real clips. Weihan Xu led a team that built REGen, a system for that job. First, a fine-tuned language model drafts the teaser's script, leaving placeholders where a quote belongs. Then a retrieval model picks, for each placeholder, the clip from the source film that best fits the story.

Tests on documentary teasers showed the method weaves clips in while keeping the tale coherent. In a viewer survey it beat both cut-only and write-only rivals on coherence, fit, and realism. The team frames the work as editing by writing first and quoting second.
arxiv-2505-18980:
Ibuki Kuroyanagi and colleagues improve anomalous sound detection when machine data are scarce. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles a factory monitoring problem. Detectors falter when similar machine sounds or state labels are missing. The team built a pipeline from three linked components. Each part extends earlier work into the unlabeled setting.

First, a selector curates outside audio that resembles the target machine. Triplet learning then assigns pseudo-labels to unlabeled clips. Those labels allow finer sorting of working sounds and faint anomalies. Iterative training refines both selection and labeling over rounds. Tests on standard challenge datasets showed clear accuracy gains. Unlabeled settings gained the most on average. The method helps monitor machines with little labeled history.
arxiv-2505-19180:
Lukas Exl and Sebastian Schaffer upgrade a fast method for computing the stray field a magnetized body casts around itself. That field is a core cost in micromagnetic simulation. Their tensor grid approach works on rectangular domains. It dodges the singular kernel convolution by using a super-potential formulation. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the extension represents magnetization and field in higher-order spline bases. That buys accuracy and smoothness. The field is stored as a compressed functional Tucker tensor built from separable pieces. A multilinear version of extreme learning machine training fits the representation.

Because the scheme is mesh-free, the field can be evaluated continuously anywhere, not just at grid points. Numerical tests confirmed high accuracy. The energy error fell exponentially as the expansion grew, and cost rose only linearly in the tensor rank. The method targets large, high-fidelity micromagnetics.
arxiv-2505-19380:
Peter Renkel proposes in 2025 an experiment to test whether quantum measurement truly collapses the wave function. The rival views are collapse models and purely unitary evolution. His setup uses an unconscious observer: a device that measures a system and sets another system's state from the result. An experimenter then probes that second system with weak measurements.

The key question is how distinguishable the observer's resulting states are. Interference patterns in the setup should reveal whether a collapse happened. Renkel argues the design can separate the two families of interpretations in practice. It turns a long-standing philosophy debate into a lab test.
arxiv-2505-19580:
Murooka and six co-authors enabled whole-body contact motion for humanoid robots in twenty twenty-five. To work in tight spaces, humanoids must lean and brace with knees, elbows, and forearms, not just hands and feet. Sensing those mid-limb contacts is the challenge.

Flexible sheet sensors spread over the limbs measure contact force without changing the robot's shape much. The team extended an existing multi-contact controller, built for hands and feet, to use these mid-limb signals. Feedback from the sheet sensors steadied the motion. Simulations showed better stability against pushes and errors in the environment model. A life-sized humanoid, RHP Kaleido, then demonstrated the skills: stepping while bracing on a forearm, and balancing seated with thigh contact.
arxiv-2505-19680:
Xinrui Wang and co-authors help image models keep learning from endless streams without forgetting. Their setting is harsh: each photo can carry many labels, some labels go missing, and classes arrive lopsided. Older methods fight forgetting and imbalance but skip a basic trick from multi-label learning, finding the exact region each label owns.

The team first checks that pretrained models can indeed locate label regions on their own. Their method, CUTER, then sharpens those regions, cuts them out, and replays them as compact memories. The cutouts give fine-grained lessons that fight forgetting, patch missing labels, and balance rare classes at once. The trick also plugs into rival methods without friction, and tests on several benchmarks put it ahead.
arxiv-2505-19780:
Amrita Dey studies the topology of convergence in measure on a ring of measurable functions, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The setting is a probability measure space with its real-valued measurable functions. Equality between functions is understood in the almost everywhere sense. On that basis the space turns out to be completely metrizable.

Dey introduces the notion of a measure being bounded away from zero. Such a measure is exactly one that is purely atomic with at most finitely many disjoint atoms. Several topological properties hinge on this condition, including being a P-space and extremal disconnectedness. The space is shown never to be Lindelöf, hence never separable or compact. Connectedness holds exactly when the measure is non-atomic. Dey also computes the component of a point in full generality.
arxiv-2505-20080: Yulin Ye studies whether helicity stays conserved for weak solutions of the compressible Euler equations. Helicity gauges how swirled a fluid flow is. The flow sits inside a bounded box that may include vacuum regions. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Ye derives a sufficient condition for conservation. It joins inner regularity of a Besov type with vanishing mean oscillation. It also needs velocity and vorticity to stay smooth near the boundary. Extra regularity demands on the density near vacuum are added. The pressure law is left general.
arxiv-2505-20180:
Sylvain Fichet, Rodrigo Fresneda, Lucas de Souza, and Dmitri Vassilevich test a shortcut for counting how much fractional fermion charge a vortex carries. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Fermion number on a swirling field background is famously hard to compute directly. A recent proposal ties it to a heat-flow coefficient and to states at the region's edge.
