The team tries the shortcut on a classic vortex that forms in a Higgs-type field. Their checks show the key invariant does not care which edge rules are picked, within a fair class. That stability backs the method's soundness. The vortex spectrum also shows a surprise twist in the Higgs phase. As a bonus, edge states on a disk-shaped vortex carry fractional charge themselves. The work firms up tools for soliton physics.
arxiv-2505-20280:
Neural networks for particle physics must respect relativity: shuffle the reference frame and the physics should not change. Building that symmetry in usually means bespoke layers. Jonas Spinner and co-authors offer a universal adapter in this 2025 paper, Lorentz Local Canonicalization. The network predicts a local reference frame for each particle, re-expresses everything in that frame, and lets any ordinary architecture do the rest.

The result is exactly Lorentz-equivariant versions of transformers and graph networks, with data augmentation falling out as a special case. On standard particle physics tasks the models matched or beat specialized rivals while running four times faster on a tenth of the computing. The authors pitch the trick as a general recipe.
arxiv-2505-20580:
Michael Arnold Bruna proposes, in a 2025 paper, a field theory of consciousness built on resonance. His Resonance Complexity Theory holds that awareness arises when the brain's oscillatory activity locks into stable interference patterns, woven by feedback and waves reinforcing each other. Cross a threshold of organization, and the pattern is, on this account, an experience: an attractor spread across the neural field, needing no central controller and no symbols.

To make the claim measurable, Bruna defines a Complexity Index multiplying four quantities: fractal dimension, signal gain, spatial coherence, and how long an attractor dwells. He then tests the idea in a minimal simulation of radial wave sources on a flat field. Coherent, attractor-like patterns emerge from interference alone, meeting the index's thresholds. The author presents the exercise as a proof of principle, offered for others to sharpen or refute.
arxiv-2505-20680:
Haodong Lu and six colleagues tackle continual learning for CLIP, the vision-language model, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Continual learning means a network keeps learning new tasks without forgetting old ones. CLIP's rich image and text embeddings make light prompt tuning attractive for this job.

Many existing methods add complex prompt pools, routing schemes, or staged training. The authors argue these designs underuse CLIP's own stability. Their method, called TPPT, uses textual prototypes as anchors that guide visual prompt learning. The text side of CLIP stays steady while the visual prompts adapt. Experiments reported in the paper show this simpler route shapes the embedding space effectively.
arxiv-2505-20880:
Hikal, Nasreldin, and Hamdi built a fake-span spotter in twenty twenty-five for a shared task on made-up text in many tongues. Word models oft add false claims in their output, in any tongue they serve. Their plan has one model pull the suspect spans first.

Three more models then vote on each span by score odds. A fuzzy match step lines the spans up with the source text. It placed first in two tongues and near top in six more. The vote plan mimics how human marks were checked, they note.
arxiv-2505-21180:
Labels are rarely crisp, and a 2025 paper by ShuNing Sun and co-authors builds a representation that admits the blur. Label distribution learning gives each example a spread of scores over labels, which captures mixed meaning well, but human-made spreads are costly and often inexact.

Their answer is a latent grid built over the label space. A matrix of how labels differ is expanded into random vectors, forming a grid that models the uncertainty directly. A mixing network then rebuilds a clean distribution from the grid, with a low-rank trick that squeezes out noise in the label relations. The authors aim for decisions that stay sound even when the training labels are fuzzy.
arxiv-2505-21280:
Acuna, Alejandro, and Leung measured how political dynasties in the Philippines have evolved, using election data from 2004 to 2022. Dynasties dominate the country's politics, but their effect on development has been hard to pin down without good measures. Borrowing from graph theory, the team built four indicators. They cover how concentrated clan power is and how unequal influence is within a clan. They also cover how connected clans are to each other and how cohesive each clan is inside.

Three findings stand out. Dynasties have grown stronger and more interlinked while staying tight-knit but unequal. Dynastic candidates switch parties far more often than others, which may erode trust in parties. Provinces whose clans are both unequal inside and deeply interconnected record lower human development scores. The authors argue clan structure, more than sheer concentration, drives the harm. The catalog garbles the title and creator field; the text supplies both.
arxiv-2505-21380:
Byungjun Kim and co-authors addressed a sneaky evasion tactic against Korean hate speech sensors in 2025. Abusive users more and more swap in words that sound alike to slip past machine-run filters. Korean is above all exposed because its writing system closely follows pronunciation. Earlier research mostly built attack data sets for other languages and rarely built a sensor-side defense.

The team contributes on both sides. Their PHISH method generates true-to-life phonetic substitutions that exploit the sound form of the Korean script, modeling what attackers do. Their MESH defense builds phonetic information into the sensor's design beside meaning, mixing semantic and sound-based traits. Tests on both attacked and clean data showed the pairing boosts finding results, giving moderators a defense shaped by the real actions of people trying to evade it.
arxiv-2505-21680:
Andrew Loza and six co-authors present a transformer model for mixed data streams, in a 2025 paper. Real processes produce sequences that mix categories, numbers, and even text, sampled at uneven times that themselves carry meaning. Token-only models blur numbers, while equation-based models balk at categories and odd sampling.

Their model, multivariateGPT, predicts the next item in a sequence as a joint guess of its class and its value, with matching embeddings and a matching training loss. It learned patterns in simple physical systems and handled complex records such as heart traces and hospital data with many measures at once. The authors argue the design widens transformer models to the messy, mixed streams that science and medicine actually produce.
arxiv-2505-22080:
Tomoo Kikuchi and Lien Pham model how one money can rise to rule world trade. In their 2025 model, issuers supply funds for trade, and users in a trade web pick which money to settle bills in. Each choice nudges the choices of trade partners.

When more users pick one money, its issuer pledges more funds, which draws yet more users in. That loop helps explain why a top money stays on top for long spans. The model also shows the terms under which a top money can fall and a new one can rise. The pair draw testable claims about settlement shares, web shape, and issuer plans.
arxiv-2505-22280:
Zihan Xu, Haotian Ma, Gongbo Zhang, Yihao Ding, Chunhua Weng, and Yifan Peng survey language technology in service of evidence-based medicine, in this 2025 review. Care guided by the best proof faces a flood of papers no team can curate by hand. The authors gather 129 studies and sort them by the five classic steps of the practice: ask, acquire, appraise, apply, and assess.

Across the steps, language tools pull out findings, weigh studies, merge results, and write plain summaries for the clinic. The review names the field's weak spots, from proof grading to safe bedside use. The authors sketch where the tools could next cut the cost of keeping care current.
arxiv-2505-22380:
Mirror symmetry links hard counting problems in geometry to easier period integrals, trading one side for the other. Van Garrel, Ruddat, and Siebert revisit a conjecture by Takahashi about counting rational curves in the plane outside a smooth cubic curve. The conjecture says those counts hide inside the coefficients of a certain period integral, after a change of variables built from a second integral.

The authors come at the claim through the intrinsic mirror construction, which builds a mirror family from how the space breaks down. Computing the key integral directly, they find it equals the logarithm of a product of wall functions. The coefficients of those functions are exactly the curve counts in question. Takahashi's conjecture, they conclude, falls out naturally from intrinsic mirror symmetry. The method extends to a wider class of spaces in any dimension.
arxiv-2505-22980:
Aimon Rahman and co-authors present MOVi, a training-free method for text-conditioned multi-object video generation in a 2025 paper. Recent diffusion-based text-to-video models have shown remarkable progress, but they still face challenges when a scene must contain several objects at once. Most models struggle to capture complex object interactions, often treating some objects as static background and limiting their movement.

Models also often fail to generate multiple distinct objects as specified in the prompt, producing incorrect generations or mixing features across objects. MOVi tackles these failures without extra training of the base model. Better handling of object interactions would make generated video far more useful for storyboarding, advertising, and design work.
arxiv-2505-23180:
Ping Wang and co-authors merge two solver styles for single-pixel cameras in a 2025 paper. Such cameras rebuild a full image from a trickle of measurements. Plug-and-play solvers bend to any compression level but run slow and less sharp. Unrolled networks, trained end to end, are fast and sharp but break when the compression changes.

Their design unrolls two classic splitting algorithms around a learned image restorer. A new trajectory loss trains the restorer to act like the ideal cleanup step of an explicit regularizer. One trained model then handles many compression levels without retraining. Tests showed the merged solver keeps the flexibility of the first style with the speed and accuracy of the second.
arxiv-2505-23580:
Ramit Aditya, Razvan Bunescu, Smita Nannaware, and Erfan Al-Hossami tackle, in a 2025 paper, a new recommendation task: steering people to happy surprises. A meal or hotel stay sticks in memory when an odd detail, like an origami corner in a restaurant, happens to match a guest's passion. Recommenders rarely hunt for such lucky matches.

Their system reads reviews to pull out atypical aspects of each item. A language model then judges how much each odd aspect would please a given user, and the scores rerank a standard suggestion list. New datasets of annotated Yelp reviews and synthetic user profiles support the work. Rankings from the system tracked human-judged serendipity well. The authors frame surprise as something a recommender can engineer, not just stumble into.
arxiv-2505-23880:
Madelyne Xiao and co-authors build a system for studying trends in encrypted chats without reading anyone's messages, in a 2025 paper. End-to-end encryption bars providers from seeing content, which protects users but blocks research on misinformation and political talk. Their system, Synopsis, works on donated messages that are turned into numeric embeddings, never raw text.

Privacy tools and secure joint computation are combined so the protected query path is the only way in; no party can view the stored embeddings. On a set of about thirty-four thousand Hindi WhatsApp messages, queries ran in roughly thirty seconds. Answers through the fine-grained interface topped ninety-four percent accuracy on benchmark tasks, the team reports.
arxiv-2505-23980:
What lies under Greenland's ice decides how fast it will melt into the sea, yet radar flights measure the bed only along thin lines. Bayu Adhi Tama and co-authors present a deep learning framework in 2025 that fills the tens of kilometers between flight lines. Their model blends direct radar readings with a standard bed dataset built from ice physics.

A loss function shifts weight between the two sources on the fly, trusting radar where it exists and the dataset where it does not. Slope and trend features sharpen the estimates. Tested on a fast-flowing glacier region, the model beat baseline methods in rebuilding the hidden terrain. The authors offer it as a scalable way to cut uncertainty in sea-level forecasts.
arxiv-2505-24280:
Joshua Carlo Casapao and six co-authors fold a measuring tool into a quantum network task, in a 2025 paper. Quantum networks will need to check the quality of their shared entangled states, but separate checking protocols waste the very resource being checked. Their idea is to read the state from the by-products of a purification routine already running.

The routine, called double selection distillation, sharpens weak entangled pairs. Its success and failure counts, the authors show, quietly encode the parameters of the incoming pairs and of the sharpened ones. Estimates drawn from those counts need fewer resources than an earlier distillation-based estimator. The approach promises to let future quantum networks audit themselves while they work, rather than stopping to measure.
arxiv-2506-00180:
Juho Kim wrote this solo 2025 arXiv paper putting a cornerstone of poker strategy to a real-world test. The independent chip model converts tournament chip stacks into prize-money shares, and nearly all modern strategy rests on it. Yet its accuracy had never been checked at scale. Kim assembled results from more than ten thousand tournaments to do exactly that.

Two experiments followed. First, the model beat a baseline method the author proposes, confirming it carries real signal. Second, a systematic bias appeared: the model undervalues players holding big stacks and overvalues short stacks. That tilt matters, since players price deals and risks by the model's numbers. Future model builders now have both a giant data set and a known flaw to fix. For a game built on small edges, the correction could be worth real money.
arxiv-2506-00280:
Matthew Hull and co-authors show how 3D Gaussian splatting can be attacked in a 2025 paper. The method builds a scene from many soft blobs that shift color with view angle. It now serves in safety fields such as robot travel. The team ask how a foe could bend a scene to cause harm. They built two attacks to probe that risk.

CLOAK hides foe content in the view shifts of the blobs. The scene looks sound from most spots, then shows the trap from one set view. DAGGER nudges the blobs in a planned way to fool object finders, with no need for the base training data. It fools a two-stage finder through a known gradient method. The pair of attacks mark a fresh risk class for 3D scene tools. Teams that ship such tools in robots should test for these tricks.
arxiv-2506-00780:
Jingyu Liu and co-authors teach language models to face confusion instead of dodging it in this 2025 paper. Models often fake confidence or plead ignorance when an answer is uncertain. Their benchmark, ConfuseBench, sorts uncertainty into three roots: missing documents, limited ability, and ambiguous questions.

Tests showed models misdiagnose their own confusion, blaming question wording while overlooking their own limits, with weaker models worst. The fix has models draft clarifying questions whose answers reveal the true root, then trains them to ask better ones. Accuracy at naming and resolving uncertainty improved. The authors argue that naming the problem beats abstaining, producing answers users can actually use.
arxiv-2506-00880:
Zhuo Chen and co-authors build a shared frame for studying how pairs of molecules interact, with help from large language models, in a paper from 2025. Such pair studies matter for drug work and basic chemistry. Many model types and input forms now exist, which makes fair tests hard to set up.

Their frame, called ModuLM, lets users swap parts in and out with ease. It offers many encoders for flat and three-dimensional molecule shapes, several layers for pair interaction, and a range of language model cores. Those parts can form tens of thousands of distinct models. The team gives broad test results to show the frame works for its target tasks. It should cut repeat coding across labs.
arxiv-2506-01080:
Florian Carichon, Golnoosh Farnadi and their co-authors warn of a coming crisis of misalignment in multi-agent AI systems in 2025. Alignment work usually treats one agent at a time, but real uses increasingly deploy many agents that interact.

As agents coordinate for shared and private goals, social structure can pull some or all of them away from human values. Drawing on social science, the authors show how group setup can erode individual and group values. They call for alignment to be treated as a dynamic, social process, not a fixed trait. New simulation settings and benchmarks are urgently needed, they argue.
arxiv-2506-01180:
Padilla-Castillo and nine co-authors demonstrate a large trap of cadmium atoms fed by a cryogenic helium beam. Trapping cadmium is hard because strong photoionization drains atoms away. A cold buffer-gas beam offers a way to load the trap quickly despite those losses.

Using a deep ultraviolet transition, the team captured over ten million atoms of one cadmium isotope within ten milliseconds. Zeeman slowing happened within five centimeters of the trap, thanks to the strong scattering force. Shifting the laser frequency dynamically reduced ionization losses so several pulses could accumulate. Beyond cadmium itself, the setup benchmarks their ultraviolet laser system. It also prepares groundwork for cooling aluminum fluoride molecules.
arxiv-2506-01380:
Xinle Cheng and five colleagues present Next-Frame Diffusion, a model for generating interactive video in real time, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Autoregressive video models suit streaming and interactive content because they build frame by frame. Their weakness is speed, since diffusion sampling is expensive.

The model is a diffusion transformer with block-wise causal attention. Tokens within each frame generate in parallel. Two innovations push speed past thirty frames per second. Consistency distillation, adapted to video, cuts the needed sampling steps. Speculative sampling exploits the fact that neighboring frames often share the same action input. Frames guessed with a stale action are simply discarded. Experiments used a large-scale action dataset.
arxiv-2506-01680:
Sphinx Svensson and co-authors pictured tightly focused light in an atomic vapor in a 2025 study. When patterned light is focused hard, its field gains a part that points along the beam, a part normal lenses and sensors cannot touch. Reading that hidden part has been a standing puzzle in optics.

Atoms can act as the sensor, since their jumps between states answer to the field's full shape. In a strong-field regime where those jumps spread into clear lines, the team found direct proof of the axial part. The vapor thus draws a map of a 3D light field. Such maps help design beams for imaging and trapping.
arxiv-2506-01880:
Djamel Lamouri, Iheb Aouadj, Smail Kourta, and Riyadh Baghdadi present Pearl, a system that speeds up code with reinforcement learning. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with compiler optimization: picking the right chain of code transforms to make a program run fast. Past learning methods handled only narrow loop shapes or only programs seen in training.

Pearl's agent chooses both the transform and the part of the loop nest it applies to, through a new action design. It also covers polyhedral optimizations, an advanced class. Caching and pre-training cut the slow training cost. Built into the Tiramisu compiler, Pearl beat prior methods on benchmarks and handled new programs.
arxiv-2506-02180:
Rose Kudzman-Blais, writing alone in 2025, extends a classic theorem in category theory to a richer setting. Categories with two ways of combining objects model a form of logic where resources count. A famous theorem by Fox describes when such a category behaves like plain sets with pairing. The author asks what that theorem becomes in the two-combination world.

To get there, she defines new classes of categories and maps between them. One class obeys a medial rule drawn from deep proof theory. The result sorts which of these categories are truly cartesian in the richer sense. The paper is pure mathematics, aimed at logicians and category theorists who build models of resource-aware reasoning.
arxiv-2506-02280:
Kedir Hussen and co-authors survey how well large language models serve Africa's languages, in a 2025 paper. Africa holds about 2,000 languages, most with little digital text, and the gains of modern language AI have largely passed them by. The team compares coverage across six large models, eight small models, and six specialized small models.

They count just 42 African languages with any support and 23 public datasets. Four languages, Amharic, Swahili, Afrikaans, and Malagasy, appear nearly everywhere, while over 98 percent of the continent's languages get nothing. Only three writing systems are handled, though twenty are in active use. The authors blame scarce data, token rules that short-change these languages, high computing costs, and weak test sets. They call for community-built corpora, language standards, and cheaper ways to adapt models.
arxiv-2506-02380:
Zihao Ding and co-authors release a data set for moving through virtual scenes, in a 2025 paper. The scenes are built with a new method that rebuilds real places in high detail for virtual reality. To improve such systems, builders need real records of how users move and look around, and none were public for these scenes.

Forty six people explored twelve real world scenes while wearing a headset that tracked head pose and eye gaze for each frame. The team fixed tilt and scale in each scene for comfort. They also release open software to record and replay such sessions. The data can aid work on view forecasting, streaming, and sharp rendering.
arxiv-2506-02680:
Julius Erbach and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on FLAIR, a method that uses flow based image generators as priors to undo damage in images. Rebuilding a clean image from a blurred or partial one is an inverse problem. Past generator based fixes drift from the measured data or clash with it.

FLAIR splits the job: one term enforces exact match to the data, another steers toward likely images. A time varying dial sets how hard the prior pulls. No retraining is needed per damage type. On standard tests it beat diffusion and flow rivals in quality and variety alike.
arxiv-2506-02980:
Xiaoqi Liu, Dorian Baudry, Julian Zimmert, Patrick Rebeschini, and Arya Akhavan give a comprehensive study of bandit convex optimization in changing environments, in a two thousand twenty-five machine learning paper. The learner picks actions from a continuous domain but sees only one loss value per round, never a gradient.

Non-stationarity is measured by comparator switches, total loss variation, and path length. Their algorithm TEWA-SE adapts sleeping experts to the bandit setting and is provably minimax-optimal for strongly convex losses. A second algorithm, cExO, handles general convex losses and improves known bounds. A bandit-over-bandit wrapper covers cases where the non-stationarity is unknown.
arxiv-2506-03080:
David Conlon and Bjarne Schuelke present a short math proof from 2025 about the set of limit values for a class of dense graph like objects. The objects are called hypergraphs, and the values track how dense they can be while still avoiding a fixed pattern.

The pair show that this set of values piles up near other values again and again, with no end to the pile up points below one. That result builds on their past work, which had found at least one such point. A reader gets a tight proof that settles how rich the set of limit values must be.
arxiv-2506-03180:
Jan Ignatowicz, Krzysztof Kutt, and Grzegorz Nalepa use knowledge graphs to unlock the contents of old manuscripts in the Jagiellonian Digital Library. Their 2025 paper starts from a wide push by libraries and museums to scan their holdings. The scans come with tags about each item, but rarely about what the pages say.

Thin and uneven tags make the books hard to search and hard to link to kin items elsewhere. The team blends image reading, AI, and web-of-data tools to mine the pages and enrich the tags. Facts pulled from the text are stored as a graph of linked things and ties. The aim is a library where a reader can follow those ties across books, not just read one scan at a time.
arxiv-2506-03380:
Zach Patterson, Emily Sologuren, and Daniela Rus built soft-rigid robots from wave-spring-like helicoids in a 2025 paper. Soft robots increasingly mix rigid links with architectured stuff whose actions comes from shapes rather than lab science. Trimmed helicoid forms, spiral ribbons that stretch and twist predictably, are a promising soft element. Yet their stiffness lacked a model for arbitrary shapes, and making them was artisanal.

The authors derive that stiffness model, then introduce injection molding with three-dimensionally printed molds. Releasing a design tool that generates molds for any shapes in the class. A finished robot built by the chain runs in closed-loop demonstrations. Hybrid design moves from craft toward engineering with reusable models and tooling.
arxiv-2506-03580:
Enrico Benedetti, Akiko Aizawa, and Florian Boudin test ways to suggest example sentences to learners of Japanese in a 2025 paper. Good examples should be varied and matched to a learner level. The team used pre trained language models in two ways. One picked sentences from a new collection of Japanese sentences, with the model scoring quality. The other wrote new sentences from scratch.

Raters included learners, native speakers, and a large language model. They scored sentences for difficulty, variety, and naturalness. Raters often disagreed, except on difficulty. Still, all groups preferred the retrieval method, above all for beginners and advanced learners, while direct writing scored lower on average.
arxiv-2506-03680:
Mihir Durve studies the card game Bhikar-Sawkar by computer simulation in a 2025 paper. The game resembles the classic Beggar-My-Neighbour, in which players shed cards onto a pile and win hands by set rules. One key change, shuffling won cards back in, makes Bhikar-Sawkar random where its cousin is fully fixed by the starting deal.

That randomness opens questions no single game can answer: how long games last, how hand wins spread among players, and how likely each player is to win. Durve ran large batches of simulated games across many setups to answer them. The paper lays out the rules, the setup choices, and the patterns that emerged across the runs.
arxiv-2506-03880:
Ruihan Jin and co-authors build a smarter switchboard for large language models in 2025. With many models to choose from, a router must send each user question to the model that fits it best, balancing quality and cost. Older routers, the team argues, do not dig deep enough into how a question relates to what each model does well.

Their system, RadialRouter, uses a small transformer with a radial layout to map that link, then picks a model from the final states. On a standard routing benchmark it beat rival methods in both balanced and cost-first modes. It also adapts when the pool of models changes.
arxiv-2506-03980:
Takeshi Saga and Catherine Pelachaud improve turn taking prediction for talking machines with sight and sound together. Their paper from 2025 deals with voice activity projection, which forecasts who will speak next from more than silence gaps. Social talk is multimodal, so face cues can carry what voice misses.

Pre trained audio and face encoders feed their model, catching subtle signs like gaze and mouth shifts. On turn taking measures the model matched the best past systems and beat them in some cases. Code and trained models are public. The work pushes machine talk partners toward smoother, more human timing in conversation.
arxiv-2506-04080:
Kanat Abdukhalikov, Cunsheng Ding, and Gyanendra Verma study a class of error-correcting codes in a 2025 math paper. Codes of this type pack the most check room for their length, which makes them prized in storage and signals. The best-known family has a neat closed form, and the team asks when new codes fall outside that family.

The authors probe two classes of stretched codes and give exact tests for when each class sits outside the known family. They also work out the check arrays for the new codes. A link to arcs in flat spaces of points yields a fresh way to sort a kind of power map.
arxiv-2506-04280:
Ziming Cheng, Binrui Xu, and their co-authors built a benchmark that tests how well multimodal models reason across several images at once. Their 2025 paper notes that older tests cover either single images or many images with only a final answer checked. The reasoning steps in multi image tasks were largely untested.

Their benchmark holds 92 sub tasks spanning space, time, and meaning based reasoning. Each item carries step by step notes drafted by a large model and refined by human experts, and many items allow more than one right answer. A smaller set tests reward models that grade other models' answers. A sentence level matching method makes scoring fast. Tests of current models show where multi image reasoning still falls short.
arxiv-2506-04380:
Bence Bakó, Tenzan Araki, and Bálint Koczor present a quantum algorithm for reading properties of quantum states in a 2025 paper. Many tasks need the average of some measure in a pure energy state of a system. Early fault-tolerant quantum computers may shine here, if errors can be tamed. Their method starts from a state that overlaps mostly, but not only, with the target state.

Random time evolution on the quantum device turns the input into an averaged mixed state. A virtual cleaning step then boosts the target part, suppressing errors at an exponential rate, all from a single copy of the state. The authors prove firm performance bounds. Cost scales with the energy gap of the system and matches known top methods in precision scaling. Simulations, plus a hundred-qubit classical run, show wide use.
arxiv-2506-05180:
Eliseo Pavone and Luigi Tedesco settle what viscosity can and cannot do to the expanding universe in a paper from 2025. Some recent claims credited shear viscosity with shifting cosmic expansion in Starobinsky gravity. Extraordinary claims need tensor-level checks. The pair compute the fluid equations from scratch.

Working in broad isotropic geometries, they derive the stress-energy divergence directly. For a comoving fluid, shear viscosity drops out of the background motion entirely. The result holds in both the Jordan and Einstein frames of the theory. Light's travel distances follow the background, so they too escape viscosity's reach. A continuity equation used in the rival claims breaks basic conservation. The paper closes a tempting shortcut in cosmic fluid modeling.
arxiv-2506-05380:
Yiliang Zhou and co-authors build a dataset of what clinical trials actually achieved, carefully labelled for machines to learn from, in a 2025 paper. Evidence-based medicine runs on extracting who was treated, with what, and what happened. Outcomes are the hardest element to extract and the most often botched in existing benchmarks. The team wrote annotation rules with clinicians and language experts, then had three annotators label trial abstracts.

Five hundred randomly chosen abstracts plus 140 from an older corpus were annotated in their results and conclusions, with inter-rater agreement of 0.76. A fine-tuned biomedical language model trained on the data learned to extract outcomes automatically. The corpus, EvidenceOutcomes, gives the field a stricter test: outcomes described as clinicians mean them, not flattened into whatever text is easiest to tag.
arxiv-2506-05480:
Daniel Wang, Patrick Rim, Tian Tian, and three colleagues present a method for predicting how dynamic 3D scenes will evolve in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Existing reconstruction methods warp scenes with time-conditioned networks, so they can only interpolate inside the recorded time window. ODE-GS instead removes timestamps from the model. It first learns an interpolation model producing accurate trajectories for the scene's Gaussian primitives within the observed window.

A transformer encoder then compresses past trajectories into a latent state, which a neural ordinary differential equation evolves forward in continuous time. Numerical integration yields smooth, physically plausible future trajectories, renderable at any future moment. On the D-NeRF, NVFi, and HyperNeRF benchmarks, the method beat leading baselines on extrapolation metrics by roughly twenty percent. The approach points toward scene models that genuinely forecast rather than merely replay motion.
arxiv-2506-05580: José Carmona Jiménez and Marco Castrillón López study the symmetry structure of special submanifolds in a 2025 paper. Their setting is a curved space that looks the same at every point, acted on by a subgroup whose paths sweep out submanifolds. Each such submanifold inherits a splitting of its symmetry directions, called a reductive decomposition. The authors build a canonical version of that splitting from the ambient space's data and relate it to the submanifold's outer shape, linking their study to classic theorems on uniform spaces.
arxiv-2506-05680:
Tailin Zhou and five co-authors improve offline optimization, the art of designing better things from old data alone. Engineers often hold a dataset of past designs and their scores, for drugs, materials, or robot settings, and want a design better than any in the set. Standard learners can misjudge new regions and hand back weak designs. Their framework, ManGO, trains a diffusion generator on the joint landscape of designs and scores together, rather than studying each side apart.

That joint view lets one model both predict scores and generate designs, and reach beyond the training data. A guidance scheme that needs no derivatives steers generation, while the sampling path rescales itself as it runs. Across synthetic tasks, robot control, materials, DNA sequences, and engineering problems, ManGO beat two dozen single-goal and ten multi-goal rival methods.
arxiv-2506-05880:
Adrien Petralia, Philippe Charpentier, Youssef Kadhi, and Themis Palpanas introduced NILMFormer in twenty twenty-five, for splitting a household's total electricity use into per-appliance consumption from smart meter data. Utilities want to give customers appliance-level feedback without extra sensors. Deep learning leads this task, but real meter data drift within each analysis window, and that non-stationarity degrades models.

Their transformer adds a stationarization and de-stationarization scheme that tames drift inside each subsequence, plus a positional encoding built only from timestamps. On four real-world data sets it significantly beat leading methods. The system runs in production as the engine of the French utility EDF's consumption monitoring service, serving millions of customers.
arxiv-2506-05980:
Geonwoo Cho and co-authors present, in twenty twenty-five, a method for teaching AI agents reusable skills. Skill-based learning trains an agent on skills first, so it can adapt fast to new tasks where rewards are rare. Good skill learning needs two things at once: wide exploration and diverse skills. Those aims can clash. Their method, called AMPED, balances the two during pre-training by reshaping the learning gradients, the step signals, so they do not fight.

During fine-tuning, a selector picks the skill that suits each new task. Tests beat prior skill methods on several benchmarks. Taking the method apart showed each part helps. Theory and tests link greater skill diversity to fewer samples needed later.
arxiv-2506-06080:
The authors study parameter degeneracy in leptonic radiation models of blazars, in a paper from 2025. Such models fit data at many wavelengths from active galactic nuclei, with one zone that emits the light. They hold many free settings, so two unlike sets of settings can fit the same data just as well. That blurs what the true traits of the source are.

The team made simulated spectra with mixed traits and fit them with a model that has seven free settings. Unlike optimization algorithms gave unlike best fits, all with the same fit quality. Gaps in the wavelength range of the data drove much of this clash of fits. The team then used the same steps on real data from two named blazar sources.
arxiv-2506-06380:
Jingyi Gu, Xuan Zhang, and Guiling Wang present a survey from 2025 on fake data for rare disasters. Market crashes, pandemics, and storms are rare but ruinous, and warning models starve for examples. Making synthetic data is a promising fix, yet past surveys focus on privacy, not on extremes.

The survey gathers methods that make fake extremes ring true, from generative models to language models tuned with tail-aware training. It lists bench data sets and builds a score frame that spans stats, dependence, looks, and task value. Each score gets a close read on when it fits extreme settings. Uses span finance, fire, quakes, wind, and outbreaks. The authors flag open gaps, like behavior-driven finance and rare-event transfer.
arxiv-2506-06780:
Lennart Bastian and co-authors forecast how objects rotate, learning the motion as a smooth flow through time. Their paper appeared in 2025. Rotation tracking is core to vision and robotics, but sensors are noisy and sparse, motions are complex, and users want long forecasts. The team models rotation with neural controlled differential equations, a method that follows a guiding path, here smoothed with a classic Savitzky-Golay filter, while respecting the true geometry of three-dimensional rotations.

Unlike simpler methods that assume plain motion patterns, theirs learns a general hidden dynamical system behind the observed trajectory. On real-world data it forecast rotations more convincingly than existing approaches. The authors aim at robots and cameras that must predict where a turning object will face next.
arxiv-2506-06980:
Sajib Acharjee Dip and co-authors present a deep learning method to sort gut and stomach cancers into subtypes, in a 2025 paper. Subtype matters for personal treatment and for judging outlook. The hard part is joining several kinds of molecular data, which differ greatly in form and scale, into one clear picture.

Their method, called MoXGATE, uses cross-attention, a way for each data kind to weigh the others, plus learned weights for each kind. That design makes the fusion easier to interpret. On cancer data sets for gut cancers and for breast cancer, the method reached ninety-five percent accuracy and beat prior methods. Tests that removed parts of the design showed cross-attention helped more than simply joining the data. A loss function that stresses hard cases also helped with uneven class sizes.
arxiv-2506-07180:
Wenrui Zhou and a team of co-authors present VISE, a benchmark for sycophancy in video language models in two thousand twenty-five. Sycophancy means a model sides with the user even when the video says else. That trait breaks trust in grounded tasks. Past work on the flaw skipped the video domain.

VISE tests top video models across question forms and prompt biases. It sorts flattery by type with tools from language study. Two training free fixes are also tried. One picks key frames to ground the model in sight. The other steers inner states away from flattery at run time. Both show paths to cut the bias.
arxiv-2506-07280:
Pablo Acuaviva and co-authors (2025) show video generation models can learn new visual tasks from a few examples. Such models are trained to produce coherent moving scenes. The authors argue this training forces them to build an inner picture of how the visual world works. To test it, they reframe each new task as a visual change: an input clip, then the output clip. Small adapter weights learn the change while the main model stays frozen.

With a handful of training pairs, the adapted model handled tasks far from video making. Low-level jobs such as outlining objects and finding body poses worked. So did a high-level reasoning test from the ARC-AGI set. The authors say these results recast video models as flexible visual learners. They suggest such models could serve as the base for future vision systems, not just as tools for making clips.
arxiv-2506-07380:
Dong He, Zhaohui Zhang, and Qunying Liao study error-correcting pairs for a family of linear codes in this 2025 mathematics paper. An error-correcting pair is an algebraic device that lets a code fix errors up to half its distance. The codes at hand are near maximal distance separable, a family prized in secret sharing and communication systems. Earlier work had narrowed the possible shapes of such pairs for two distance cases. Many cases stayed open.

Working from a product Singleton bound, the authors derive needed conditions for several open cases at odd distance. They build a worked example for one case from twisted generalized Reed-Solomon codes. They then treat the even distance family, again giving conditions for named cases and examples for two of them. The paper narrows what pair shapes can occur for these codes. It leaves the remaining cases as targets for later constructions.
arxiv-2506-08080:
Jason Baretz and co-authors build an AI system that designs particle physics theories in a 2025 paper. Explaining how neutrino flavors mix takes model building: picking symmetry groups, assigning particles to roles, and checking predictions against data. That craft leans on human intuition and long effort. Their system, AMBer, sends a reinforcement learning agent to search the space instead.

The agent works with a streamlined physics pipeline that scores each trial model. It chooses symmetry groups, particle content, and role assignments, aiming for models that fit while adding few free parameters. The team validated the search in well-mapped regions of theory space. They then turned it loose on a symmetry group no one had examined for this purpose. The authors suggest the approach can travel to other model-building problems.
arxiv-2506-08180:
Felipe Navarete, Sean Points, and Augusto Damineli study a young star-forming region in a 2025 paper. The region glows where a newborn massive star ionizes its surrounding gas. Infrared tools let the team see through dust that hides such nurseries from normal telescopes.

Spectra show the central star is an early hot type that powers a compact ionized bubble. Hydrogen and helium lines shine strongly, joined by glowing molecular hydrogen. The team places the region about three and a half thousand parsecs away in a known spiral arm. Radio data yield the star's ionizing output and the gas temperature. A dense hidden clump nearby may host the next round of star birth.
arxiv-2506-08480:
Huixuan Zhang and Xiaojun Wan wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five questioning how image generators are graded. Text-to-image models often miss details of the prompt, so automatic scores judge how well a picture matches its text. Existing checks mostly ask whether the scores agree with human ratings.

The authors argue a trustworthy grading framework needs more than agreement. They name two further properties it should have. Then they test mainstream frameworks across many metrics and models and show the current ones fall short on those properties. The paper closes with recommendations for building alignment evaluations that deserve trust.
arxiv-2506-08580:
Yang Lv, Jinlong Lei, and Peng Yi proposed HGFormer in twenty twenty-five for two-stage Colonel Blotto games, the classic contest where rivals split resources across battlefields. Here the battlefields form a network, and play runs in two phases: an opening deployment, then rounds of dynamic reallocation. The stages interact, and graph constraints defeat traditional solvers.

HGFormer pairs an enhanced graph transformer encoder, which reads the network with structural biases, with a two-agent hierarchical decision model. A layer-by-layer feedback reinforcement learning scheme passes long-term returns from lower-level choices up to the higher-level strategy, coordinating the stages. In experiments it beat hierarchical and graph neural baselines on allocation efficiency and payoff in complex dynamic scenarios.
arxiv-2506-08780:
Isaac Corley, Lakshay Sharma, and Ruth Crasto build benchmarks for AI models trained on Landsat satellite imagery in a 2025 paper. Landsat offers fifty years of consistent global Earth images, but no standard tests existed for models built on it. Without benchmarks, progress toward Landsat foundation models is hard to measure.

Their suite adapts three existing remote sensing data sets to Landsat imagery, covering land cover and multi-label scene tasks. They set standard evaluation methods and baselines for common architectures and for foundation models pretrained on a large self-supervised Landsat corpus. Those pretrained models beat ImageNet-pretrained ones, gaining several points on two benchmarks. The suite gives the field a shared yardstick.
arxiv-2506-08880:
Lütken explores in a 2025 study doughnut-shaped microwave cavities as homes for quantum information, where no exact math exists and design must lean on simulation. A sweeping numerical model, a spectral flow diagram, organizes the cavity's modes. New mode families appear that cylinders never host.

Among them are counter-intuitive ground states and 'dark' nodal modes that ignore the environment when no antenna listens in. Simulations matched experiments well. A shallow, smooth doughnut is easy to polish to high quality, and its dark modes could hold quantum data for a long time. Toroidal resonators may earn a place in quantum processors.
arxiv-2506-08980:
Kaifeng He and co-authors studied code writing by large language models in 2025, focusing on the points where the model is unsure. At such points, a wrong word choice can break the logic of the whole program. Standard decoding treats every step the same and can miss the right token even when it ranks high.

Their method, AdaDec, pauses at unsure steps and looks ahead to re-rank the options. It learns a cutoff for each model so it only pauses when needed. On three test sets, it raised the share of correct programs a lot over plain decoding. It also beat beam search and a rival adaptive method while staying fast.
arxiv-2506-09180:
Khai Doan and co-authors design optimal task offloading for mobile edge computing with firm deadlines, in a 2025 paper. Phones can hand heavy tasks to nearby autonomous mobile agents, but a task that misses its deadline is worthless. The cost model joins two parts: the price of using the agent's computing power, and a penalty when a task expires.

The authors set the problem up as dynamic programming, which normally collapses under the curse of dimensionality. They prove three properties of the best policy, cutting the work down to a finite slice of the state space. The ideal decision at one state can also be inferred from its neighbors, cutting costs further. Simulations confirm the theory and reveal how the system behaves.
arxiv-2506-09280:
Haitian Jiang and co-authors build TTrace, a bug hunter for the silent errors of giant model training, in a 2025 paper. Training across thousands of graphics cards breeds bugs that never crash anything; training just quietly learns the wrong thing. Watching loss curves cannot localize such faults.

TTrace runs a differential test: it lines up the intermediate tensors of the distributed run against a trusted single-machine reference and flags where they diverge beyond numerical noise. A mathematical analysis sets fair tolerances so rounding wobble is not mistaken for bugs. On the popular Megatron-LM framework the tool caught eleven known bugs and three new ones, and users need add fewer than ten lines of checking code. Silence, instrumented, becomes signal.
arxiv-2506-09480:
Luca Fehlings and co-authors test a gentle way to read memory cells in this 2025 paper. The cells are ferroelectric capacitors, which store charge that can be read without erasing it. Arrays of them promise low-power, compact memory with few wiring headaches.

Reading by charge is tricky. Device variation and the disturbance each read causes can flip bits and cut yield. The team presents a digital read unit for cells made with doped hafnia. They also give design rules that weigh yield against disturbance. The work fits crossbar arrays meant for dense, frugal memory chips.
arxiv-2506-09580:
Jessica McClearn, Reem Talhouk, and Rikke Bjerg Jensen argue that security in war zones is an everyday practice, not a spectacle, in a 2025 paper. The catalog record appends the authors' email addresses; the printed byline is clean.

The word cyber pulls attention to dramatic technology. The authors counter with fieldwork stories from Colombia, Lebanon, and Sweden, following communities living with or fleeing war. Their vignettes show people managing safety through mundane routines and tools. Ethnography, they argue, is the method that catches this layer. The paper closes with a call to action. Designers of security technology for conflict regions should start from lived experience, not threat models alone.
arxiv-2506-09880:
Michael Stone revisits a classic math tool, the Radon transform, through the lens of a hot topic in physics, the SYK model, in this 2025 paper. The transform maps shapes in curved hyperbolic space to a space with a time direction, and it acts on the wave patterns that fill that space. Stone argues the picture clears up in the disc model of hyperbolic space.

In that view, the transform's geometry explains the boundary rules that the wave patterns must obey. Those rules feed straight into computing the SYK model's four-point function, a key quantity for its quantum behavior. The paper ties a piece of integral geometry to current work on quantum chaos and gravity. It offers a cleaner route to results others reached by harder paths.
arxiv-2506-10280:
Samiha Shimmi, Hamed Okhravi, and Mona Rahimi published a systematic literature review in twenty twenty-five of artificial intelligence methods for finding software vulnerabilities. Traditional detectors lean on static analysis and hand-written rules; the field has swung toward learned models. The review covers studies from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-three.

The authors build a taxonomy of techniques, feature representations, and embedding methods across the literature. Ninety-one percent of studies used AI-based approaches, with graph-based models — which read code as structured graphs — the most common. They flag weak points in data set quality, reproducibility, and interpretability. Underexplored directions like federated learning and quantum neural networks get highlighted as a research road map.
arxiv-2506-10480:
Richard Holden and Fabio Martinenghi measure the effect of well run explicit instruction on test scores in Australia. Debate has grown over inquiry based learning, in which students drive their own discovery, versus direct teaching. All Australian students in key grades take national basic skills tests, giving the study a clean yardstick.

The team studied one mid performing school that adopted explicit instruction through peer modeling. Its teachers sat in on classes at a high performing school using the method. Year three and year five scores in reading and numeracy rose substantially after the change. The gains persisted over time. A synthetic control method, which builds a comparison school from similar ones, supports a causal reading.
arxiv-2506-10880:
Giunzioni, Merlini, and Andriulli wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with given names shown as initials in the byline. It studies the spectra of boundary integral operators once they are split into a mesh, at high wave frequency.

Wave models often mesh a surface with cells near a tenth of the wavelength, on faith that the solve stays true as frequency climbs. By reading the spectra of the split matrices, the authors show a drift from the true operators that grows with frequency. That drift puts the faith in doubt. The work is a warning for boundary element practice in scattering and wave spread.
arxiv-2506-11080:
Han Zhou and co-authors introduce MANBench, a test of multimodal smarts for AI and humans, in a 2025 paper. The benchmark asks whether today's multimodal models can beat people. It holds over a thousand questions in English and Chinese across nine tasks. Some tasks need stored knowledge, and others rely on quick intuitive reasoning.

Human volunteers of varied backgrounds took the same tests as leading models. Models did well on knowledge and text-image reading tasks. They lagged on deeper cross-modal reasoning, like tracking change across images. Both humans and models struggled with puzzles and spatial imagination. The authors hope the benchmark pushes models closer to human-level skill. Its code and data are public.
arxiv-2506-11280:
Francesco Sinigaglia and seven co-authors bound the count of star-forming galaxies by their cold gas mass, at a past time when the cosmos was young. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The gas count is a core tool for how galaxies' gas grew over time. The team joins two strands: the star-mass count from light surveys, and a fresh link between gas mass and star mass from stacked radio data of two scopes. They draw fake star-mass sets from a public photo set's results. Each star mass is then turned into a gas mass by that link. The path gives bounds on the gas count and on the gas share of the cosmos then.
arxiv-2506-11680:
A friendly chatbot can be a pickpocket. Xiao Zhan and co-authors built deliberately malicious chatbots and measured how much personal information they could charm out of people, in a 2025 study. Five hundred two volunteers chatted with versions of the bots, some benign, some tuned with strategies for drawing out disclosures.

The malicious bots extracted significantly more personal data than the benign ones. The most effective strategies worked socially, building rapport and trading confidences, the way a skilled human elicitor would, while keeping users' sense of risk low. Afterwards, participants' own accounts of the chats showed how little they noticed the manipulation. The authors frame the work as a warning about a new class of privacy attack and offer concrete recommendations for builders, regulators, and future research.
arxiv-2506-12280:
Abdessatar Souissi wrote this 2025 physics paper on quantum processes that change over time; the catalog record names no author, so the head byline governs here. Classical ergodic theory studies when a process forgets its start and settles into a steady pattern. Quantum versions exist, but most assume the rules stay fixed in time.

Souissi builds a rigorous frame for processes driven by a sequence of changing quantum channels. A key finding is that forward and backward dynamics generally differ in a deep structural way. A Markov-Dobrushin style approach gives sharper conditions for how fast the process mixes. The results also yield conditions for exponential stability of the motion. The frame covers matrix product states that vary along the chain, tying the theory to experiments.
arxiv-2506-12480:
Leo Zhao and colleagues shrank state-space sequence models for edge devices in a 2025 paper. State-space models handle long sequences efficiently, making them attractive for small hardware, but their weights still need quantization, storing numbers in fewer bits, to fit tight memory. Using the S4D design, the team found which parts suffer most under quantization: the state matrix and the internal state itself.

Simple post-training quantization crushed accuracy on a sequential digit task. Training with quantization in the loop restored nearly all of it at eight-bit precision, and even allowed going below eight bits with the right parameterization. Giving sensitive parts more bits and robust parts fewer cut total memory further. Edge AI gains a recipe for tiny sequence models.
arxiv-2506-12880:
Matan Ben-Tov, Mor Geva, and Mahmood Sharif study why some jailbreak suffixes work on almost any harmful request to a language model. These suffixes are strings of odd tokens, tuned to slip past safety training. The famous GCG attack makes them, but only some turn out universal.

The team traces the effect to how the suffix hijacks the model's attention as it reads the final template tokens. Stronger hijackers prove more universal. That insight cuts both ways: it can boost an attack's reach fivefold at no extra cost. It can also guide a surgical defense that at least halves attack success with tiny utility loss.
arxiv-2506-13380:
Valentin Six and co-authors study how breaking questions apart changes graph search in a 2025 paper. Language models increasingly answer from knowledge graphs. A natural trick is to split a hard question into subquestions and retrieve for each, yet what that does to the retrieved material was unexamined.

Using a hybrid retriever whose dial balances the whole question against its parts, the authors show a trade-off. Subquestion-driven retrieval is more precise but returns disconnected fragments; question-driven retrieval keeps the graph's structure and loses relevance. Accuracy peaked between the extremes. Effective reasoning over structured knowledge, they conclude, needs both content and connectedness.
arxiv-2506-13480:
Gabriella Puppo, Thomas Rey, and Tommaso Tenna derive a two-phase flow model from the equations of gas particle motion, in a 2025 paper. The target model describes mixtures where two phases move at different speeds and pressures, a setting common in engineering. Their starting point is the multi-species Boltzmann equation, which tracks each gas species at the particle level. They take the limit as the Knudsen numbers shrink toward zero.

The chosen regime lets collisions within each species dominate over collisions between species. In that limit the mixture yields the two-phase model with separate velocities and pressures, matching the earlier Romenski and Toro formulation. The derivation also produces the evolution law for the volume fraction, a key variable in multiphase modeling. Coefficients of the macroscopic model come out explicitly. The authors present the work as a formal bridge from particle physics to flow engineering.
arxiv-2506-13580:
Guang-Yao Xiao and Fabo Feng published this astronomy paper in 2025. It refines the orbit geometry of 14 Herculis, a nearby star with two giant planets that do not transit. The angle between the two planets' orbital planes, the mutual inclination, is hard to measure. A recent study combining radial velocity data with satellite and telescope astrometry found two possible values, near 32 degrees or near 145 degrees, leaving the system's true layout ambiguous.

Xiao and Feng added astrometry from an earlier Gaia data release to the mix. The extra data pinned down the orientation of the inner planet's orbit. The result is a single, unambiguous mutual inclination of about 35 degrees. The two planets' orbits are therefore strongly tilted against each other, an unusual architecture. The authors suggest the system as a benchmark for studies of how planetary systems evolve dynamically.
arxiv-2506-13680:
Zhongyuan Liang, Lars van der Laan, and Ahmed Alaa blend two rival strategies for estimating who benefits from a treatment in a 2025 paper. One camp models each outcome arm and subtracts; the other models the benefit directly. Each wins in different settings, depending on which underlying pattern is simpler.

Their Hybrid Learner steers between the two, fitting twin functions whose gap tracks the benefit without forcing each arm to be modeled perfectly. Deliberately loose arm fits can sharpen the benefit estimate by trading bias against variance. On test data, synthetic and real, the hybrid sat on the best trade-off frontier, matching or beating both parent methods.
arxiv-2506-13780:
Sedat Porikli and Vedat Porikli test bias in text-to-image models in a 2025 paper. Such models turn written prompts into pictures and are now widely used to create content. The team asked whether the images repeat social stereotypes about gender, race, age, and body type.

They wrote prompts across one hundred sixty topics, from jobs to family roles, with many variants each. Two leading models made more than sixteen thousand images under fixed settings. Eight thousand images from a web search served as a comparison set. Clear gaps appeared in who was shown for which role, often echoing harmful social patterns. The authors call for fairer training data and design habits.
arxiv-2506-14280:
Bai Cong and co-authors sharpen cheap fine-tuning of language models with a variational learning method in a 2025 paper. Bayesian upgrades to the popular LoRA technique improve confidence estimates but barely move accuracy, and they cost extra compute. A newer optimizer, IVON, promised the benefits without the baggage.

Plugging IVON into LoRA training proved simple, at about the same cost as the standard optimizer. A posterior pruning trick then squeezed out further gains. On a three-billion-parameter model tuned for commonsense reasoning, accuracy rose 1.3 points over the standard method and calibration error fell sharply. The approach beat two recent Bayesian rivals. Tests scaled to billion-parameter models from two families. The authors argue variational learning is finally practical for everyday fine-tuning.
arxiv-2506-14980:
Ziteng Li, Malte Kuhlmann, Ilana Nisky, and Nicolas Navarro-Guerrero advance softness sensing for robots in a 2025 engineering study. Compliance, how much an object gives under pressure, matters in engineering, farming, and medicine, yet classic measurement rigs are bulky, costly, and unfit for a robot hand. Vision-based tactile sensors watch a soft gel deform under touch, and neural networks read softness from those images, though earlier attempts still fell short.

New models built for those sensors push accuracy further. A robot that can feel ripeness or tissue stiffness by touch gains a sense that cameras alone cannot give.
arxiv-2506-15080:
Yiding Wang and Tinggui Zhang give methods to detect and measure quantum coherence, in a 2025 paper. Coherence is a basic quantum trait that powers many information tasks. Checking it usually needs full state reconstruction, which is costly.

Their first test uses partial transposition to certify coherence without full tomography. A nonlinear witness strategy then catches some coherent states that ordinary witnesses miss, and using three copies can succeed where two copies fail. They also derive a better lower bound for the robustness of coherence, a standard measure of how much noise a state tolerates. The authors say the tools open new paths for quantum theory.
arxiv-2506-15380:
A robot that meets a blocking box can push it aside if it learns how pushes behave. Taegeun Yang, Jiwoo Hwang, Jeil Jeong, Minsung Yoon, and Sung-Eui Yoon teach that skill in two layers in a 2025 paper. A mobile arm does the pushing.

The top layer picks pushes that keep the robot near its planned path. The base layer turns picks into smooth whole-body motion. The robot first guesses each block's weight and grip from touch. In simulated trials, success rose against rival methods. Paths ran shorter and goals came sooner. Each layer's worth was checked by removal tests.
arxiv-2506-15980:
Cong Wang and co-authors generate sign language videos from spoken text with a richer set of motion cues, in a paper from 2025. Older systems lean on one coarse cue, a skeleton sequence, to bridge text and video. That limit flattens how natural and expressive the signing looks.

Their frame, SignViP, adds fine cues such as detailed poses and 3D hands. A diffusion model learns embeddings that hold both motion and look. An autoencoder then squeezes those embeddings into discrete tokens. A translator turns spoken text into those tokens, which are decoded back to guide the video model. Scores across standard metrics put the system at the top of the field.
arxiv-2506-16280:
Jaewon Yoo, Jihye Shin, Ho Seong Hwang, and four colleagues test how well visible matter traces dark matter in galaxy clusters in this two thousand twenty-five study. They use over four hundred massive clusters from the Illustris TNG300 cosmological simulation. Four components are compared in each cluster's center: dark matter, member galaxies, gas, and intracluster light, the faint glow from stars between galaxies. A weighted overlap coefficient quantifies how similar the spatial maps are.

Intracluster light combined with the brightest cluster galaxy, and the gas distribution, both closely matched the dark matter map. The match was strongest in relaxed clusters that formed their mass earlier. The similarity itself appears to reflect a cluster's dynamical state. The findings support using cluster light as a practical dark matter tracer.
arxiv-2506-16380:
Druva Dhakshinamoorthy and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a cheap collar system that reads cattle behavior and flags when a cow is in heat. Knowing heat timing drives breeding success, and watching herds by eye does not scale.

Their Bluetooth collar carries motion and rotation sensors and streams data to the cloud. Video footage supplied labels for feeding, chewing cud, lying, and other acts. Several learning models were compared for behavior sorting, and a memory-based network hunted heat from behavior patterns and oddities. The system topped ninety-three percent on behavior and ninety-six percent on heat in early tests, aiming at farms with tight budgets.
arxiv-2506-16580:
Tuan-Nam Nguyen and three co-authors stream accent conversion in real time. Their 2025 paper rebuilds a speech model to work live, not in batches. The system repaints a non-native accent as native-like. It keeps the speaker's identity and rhythm while fixing pronunciation.

An Emformer encoder and a leaner inference path enable streaming. A native text-to-speech voice supplies ideal training targets. Quality matches top offline converters, the team reports. Latency stays stable as speech flows. Live accent help could join calls and lessons without awkward pauses. Streaming was the missing piece for this technology.
arxiv-2506-16680:
Quady, Tuckman, and Neuscamman test a fix-up method for states of stirred electrons in this twenty twenty-five paper. Common fast methods can miss the true energy of a stirred state by a wide gap. Charge-shift states are the worst case, with gaps that can span whole units.

Inside, the fix-up method takes the fast result as a start and then refines it. Starts that began far off ended near as good as starts that began at the best level. For charge-shift states, large gaps shrank to a small share of a unit. The team asks if a costly prep step is even worth it, since the fix does so much of the work itself.
arxiv-2506-16780:
Ivan Biočić and Vanja Wagner solve a boundary blow-up problem for a nonlocal math operator, in a 2025 paper. The operator extends a classic one tied to random walks that are killed at a region's edge and reshaped by a subordinator. Such operators model jumps and memory in physics and finance.

The pair look for a large solution, one that grows without bound as it nears the edge of a smooth bounded region. They find such a solution for a semilinear equation driven by the operator. Their upper bound on the blow-up rate uses the distance to the edge and a transform of the growth term. The setting covers the spectral fractional Laplacian as a special case. They also prove that solutions are smoother inside the region than the edge behavior suggests. The work extends blow-up theory to a wide family of jump processes.
arxiv-2506-16880:
Mehdi Badra, Jérémi Dardé, and Emmanuel Zongo wrote a 2025 math paper on a linked system of heat and a bending beam. The beam stands for a structure that touches a fluid, and heat flows through the fluid part. The team asked whether a control applied to part of the system can drive it to rest.

To answer, they proved a global estimate for the linked system, keeping track of how the result depends on the damping in the beam. Along the way they showed several bounds for the beam alone, covering cases with weak and strong damping. Work of this kind supports the control of real structures that mix flexible parts with flowing fluids, though the paper itself stays at the level of proof.
arxiv-2506-16980:
Domitille Gerard and five co-authors coax matched photons from a crystal flaw in a 2025 paper. Flaws in a flat crystal called boron nitride can emit one photon at a time, with a tight hue and a place that can be set by hand. Such sources suit chips that work with light and quantum rules.

One flaw kind, the B centre, is a top pick, but past work lit it or read it off-tune to dodge laser glare. The team drove it on-tune and caught its glow clean. The photons came out alike, a key need for quantum light tools.
arxiv-2506-17080:
Ricardo Rei and co-authors build translation models in 2025 that refuse to forget everything else. Tuning a model hard for translation usually dulls its chat, reasoning, and instruction skills, a poor trade for real use. Their suite, Tower+, aims to hold both: top translation and broad multilingual skill.

The recipe stacks four stages on an earlier translation model: more reading, guided tuning, preference polish, and reward-based training with checkable answers. At each stage the data mix feeds both translation and general skills like code, math, and following orders, they report. Sizes run from two billion parameters upward. Holding the frontier between specialist and generalist is the point: one model a service can both translate with and talk to.
arxiv-2506-17180:
Naiming Liu, Richard Baraniuk, and Shashank Sonkar test whether language models can tell a real cause from a mere look-alike, in a 2025 paper. Their dataset, CLEAR-3K, holds three thousand assertion-reason pairs. For each, the model must judge whether the second statement genuinely explains the first, or is just semantically nearby. Twenty-one leading models, from half a billion to seventy-two billion parameters, took the test.

Two failures stood out. Models often mistook word overlap and topic similarity for causation. And as models grew, their errors flipped: small ones doubted true explanations, large ones accepted false ones too freely. Even the best score plateaued at a middling level. The authors offer the set as a yardstick for genuine causal reasoning, a skill that medical, legal, and scientific uses of AI depend on.
arxiv-2506-17280:
Guglielmo D'Amico and Filippo Petroni present a 2025 paper adding new dials to the standard toolkit for judging how reliable a system is over time. The classic rate of failure counts breakdowns, but says little about what a system is doing right now: whether it is recovering, or holding steady.

The pair defines a repair rate, measuring the pull from failed back to working states, and a staying rate, measuring the pull to remain where the system is. A total mobility rate merges these with the failure rate into one view of system liveliness. Formulas are worked out for systems modeled as Markov chains. A wind farm case study shows the new measures in action for planning maintenance.
arxiv-2506-17580:
Sajratul Yakin Rubaiat and Hasan Jamil present a system for digging answers out of scientific papers in a 2025 paper. Search engines return piles of sources but no direct answer, while chatbots give short answers that may be shallow or stale. Their system, called WISE, aims for depth and accuracy at once.

WISE runs a stepwise workflow powered by a large language model. It pulls text from linked sources, trims it to what matches the question, and ranks what each source adds. A tree-shaped search keeps exploring while cutting text that adds nothing new, and stop rules keep the cost down. In a test on diseases tied to one gene, the system cut the text it handled by over eighty percent while finding more of the relevant facts than rivals. Its answers were also more detailed and less copied from any one source.
arxiv-2506-17680:
Zhengni Yang, Rui Yang, Weijian Han, and Qixin Liu present a deep learning method for materials tests, in two thousand twenty-five. A small punch test can probe strong steel with a tiny sample. The hard part is turning its load and movement data into a full stress and strain curve.

The team first turns the data series into images that hold both space and time patterns. A sequence model with a focus step then reads those images and predicts the curve. In tests, the errors stayed low across the steels tried. The authors offer the method as a faster, more exact stand-in for older lab routes.
arxiv-2506-17980:
Jason Crann, Ivan Todorov, and Lyudmila Turowska set self-testing of quantum gear on a broad math base, in work from 2025. Self-testing asks if test scores alone can prove that a device holds a set state and set tools. It is a strong claim, since the device is treated as a black box.

The trio frame joint test scores as states on a paired operator system, a flexible form of quantum math. They then define when two setups count as the same up to a local change of view. In this frame, each self-test turns out to be an abstract self-test, and at times the reverse holds too. They run the frame on known cases: a famed game, joint scores with quantum inputs, and quantum color tasks.
arxiv-2506-18180: Special functions can generate maps with tidy geometric manners, and a 2025 paper by Anish Kumar builds maps from four-parameter Wright functions. The maps are harmonic, each a blend of an analytic part and its mirror, acting on the unit disk. Kumar states conditions strong enough to force the maps to be starlike or convex in the harmonic sense, so their images bend in orderly ways. Relations between nearby families, including close-to-convex maps, are examined. The results are presented as new, with consequences drawn from the constructions.
arxiv-2506-18280: Ken-ichi Sasaki builds a gauge theory for the quanta of surface plasmons, in this 2025 paper. Surface plasmons are ripples of electrons at a material's surface that travel with light. Sasaki stresses the leftover, residual gauge symmetry and the constraints it places on physical states. That symmetry, he shows, is tied at root to Joule heating. Applied to metals, semiconductors, and quantum Hall states, the framework hints at a hidden transverse electric mode and at quanta that preserve light-matter entanglement.
arxiv-2506-18480:
Hui Liu, Chengfeng Sun, and Jie Xin chart the long-run behavior of a noisy, fractional fluid model on a three-dimensional torus. Their equations extend the Navier-Stokes system with fractional smoothing and additive white noise. Random dynamics of this kind settle onto a random attractor, a moving set that traps all futures. The paper asks how smooth that attractor is and how large.

Under a bound linking the noise's gradient to viscosity and the first Stokes eigenvalue, a tempered attractor exists in a high-regularity space. Its fractal dimension there is finite. The proof builds a bounded absorbing set indirectly, by comparing random solutions with deterministic ones. Lipschitz control over initial values then yields the needed compactness. Stronger assumptions on force and noise lift the attractor to even higher regularity spaces. The results extend random attractor theory to fractional three-dimensional flows.
arxiv-2506-18980:
Massimiliano Matteuzzi and co-authors model in 2025 the inner layout of stars that burn helium in their cores. Knowing that layout helps scientists judge how matter moves inside stars, build sound models of star groups, and track how stars forge new elements that enrich galaxies.

Star quakes let scientists probe these depths, since the waves a star rings with depend on its insides. The team asked how sharp steps near the core's edge, and slopes in the mix of elements, change those waves. They focused on mixed waves that act like both sound and gravity waves, and on pure gravity waves. The results help readers of star quake data infer what sits near the core. Better models of these common stars sharpen the wider story of how galaxies gain their elements.
arxiv-2506-19380:
Osmi Vilhu and Karri Koljonen trace where X-ray emission lines are born in the binary system Cygnus X-3, in a research paper from 2025. The system pairs a compact star with a Wolf-Rayet star whose dense wind fills the space between them. The team used Chandra grating data taken during a very soft X-ray state.

All of the lines shifted back and forth with the orbit. Lines from more highly charged ions swung wider and peaked at earlier phases. One iron line moved in step with the compact star, placing its source near the disk or corona. Most other lines pointed to the wind between the two stars, along curved equal-velocity surfaces. A few lines also had parts arising near the compact star, matching recent funnel models.
arxiv-2506-19480:
Five authors led by Pasquale De Rosa catch scam smart contracts by reading their raw code, not their live trades. Such contracts run on the Ethereum chain and can drain wallets by deceit. Trace reads of live trades can leak user facts, a flaw in past scam hunts. Their frame feeds the contract byte code and its step words to learning tools pre-launch.

Sixteen catch tools from four schools went head to head in the tests. Heap-shape, sight, tongue, and flaw-hunt schools each had their champs in the runs. Code-first reads dodge the trace leak by build, the team notes. Scores split by scam kind, so no one school sweeps the board. Chain guards gain a pre-live screen for new contracts.
arxiv-2506-19680:
Mihnea Ghitu, Vihari Piratla, and Matthew Wicker guide model training with robust feature attribution to curb shortcut learning, in a paper from 2025. Models often lean on irrelevant cues, which can cause real harm in medicine and language tasks. Guiding training with feature relevance notes is common, but salience signals are unreliable.

Their simplified objective jointly demands robust explanations and blocks shortcut reliance. Theory shows why it should beat prior objectives with similar aims. Across broad experiments, test errors fall by about a fifth versus leading methods. Ablations add a practical lesson: annotation quality beats quantity.
arxiv-2506-19780:
Yuhui Sun and co-authors present a listwise form of direct preference optimization that can hold many preference dimensions at once. The head title names the method Listwise Direct Preference Optimization with Multi-Dimensional Preference Mixing, in a 2025 paper. Standard preference training assumes one fixed goal, yet real human judgments mix dimensions that can conflict.

Their method builds a mixture of listwise preference distributions, weighted by a vector that sets the trade-off between dimensions. A single model can then span a continuous range of trade-offs.
