A scheduler samples the weights based on measured performance, guarding against bad fixed choices. Tests across model families and six benchmarks showed steady gains over baselines.
arxiv-2506-19880:
Stefanos Achlatis, Efstratios Gavves, and Jan-Jakob Sonke present physics-guided deep learning for radiotherapy treatment planning in a 2025 paper. In volumetric modulated arc therapy, a beam machine swings around the patient while its leaves and dose rate shift on the fly. Plans must be reworked often as the body changes, and that rework is slow by hand.

Their pipeline runs in two stages. First, a network learns to output the machine settings themselves, the leaf positions and monitor units. Then a second signal, drawn from the dose map the settings would give, steers the training. Physics thus guides the learning, toward plans that are fast to make and sound to give.
arxiv-2506-19980:
Václav Cenker, Ivan Chajda, and Helmut Länger study the symmetric difference operation beyond Boolean lattices, in a 2025 paper. In Boolean settings the operation has two classic definitions that agree. In any bounded lattice with complements, both definitions still make sense, but they can part ways. The authors examine the class of lattices where the two forms coincide and name some notable subclasses.

Using a result of Berman, they estimate the sizes of free algebras in those subclasses. The headline theorem is sharp: the symmetric difference is associative exactly when the lattice is Boolean. A single two-variable identity also captures Booleanness on its own. They further characterize lattices carrying an operation that obeys the De Morgan laws. The paper sorts out where Boolean behavior truly comes from.
arxiv-2506-20380:
Zhengpeng Feng and co-authors build a base model that turns satellite time series into compact Earth codes. Their 2025 paper tackles ragged data: orbits and clouds leave gaps, and stacking frames to fill them erases crop timing cues. Their model, TESSERA, reads light and radar series pixel by pixel and learns codes that hold across gaps.

Training tricks force the codes to stay steady when valid views are few or shuffled. Across mapping, splitting, and regression tasks the codes lead the field while needing few labels. The team releases world maps of the codes at ten-meter grain, plus open weights and light task heads. Planetary-scale land study gets cheaper as a result.
arxiv-2506-20680:
Oscar Custance and co-authors image water on a flawed cerium oxide surface in a 2025 paper. The oxide helps split water and drive redox chemistry in industry. Missing oxygen atoms below the surface may steer how water lands. A microscope with oxygen tipped probes pictured single water molecules there.

Water showed as lopsided boomerang shapes, not the neat triangles once assumed. Those shapes clustered near hidden defects under the surface. Math modeling pointed to altered cerium sites beside the gaps as the favored spots. Force measures told the two cerium states apart by their touch signatures.
arxiv-2506-20880:
Sheth and four co-authors study how plasma speeds up through a bent field that first narrows then widens, in a paper from 2025. Such a setup, called a magnetic nozzle, can push plasma past the speed of sound.

An exact math solution said the fast flow should follow one set path fixed by the field shape. The team checked that claim with full two dimensional models. Near the core the match was good, and the flow settled to the set path through a sharp jump in speed and push. Even when the start field differed, the field reshaped itself to fit the path.
arxiv-2506-21080:
Chowdhury and co-authors build EgoAdapt, a system that makes first person perception models cheaper to run without losing much skill. Models for video from a wearer's view, mixing sight and sound, are heavy, and heavy models strain small devices. Their 2025 framework learns when to lean on a big teacher model and when a light path will do, guided by a policy module.

The policy adapts to each task's choices, so one framework serves action recognition, active speaker spotting, and behavior prediction. Across three datasets, the method cut compute by up to about eighty nine percent and parameters by up to about eighty two percent. Energy use fell as much as 9.6 fold. Accuracy stayed level with, and often beat, the best prior models.
arxiv-2506-21280:
Akash Halder and co-authors solve a quantum problem with a moving wall in a paper from 2025. A particle sits in a pseudo-harmonic trap whose boundary shifts over time. Such setups model molecules squeezed in tight spaces, where the walls shape their behavior.

The team found an exact solution of the Schrödinger equation for any angular momentum state. A key quantity is the ratio of distances between nuclei, tied to a classic equation named for Ermakov. They derive the average energy in closed form, plus force and pressure. Tests on six small molecules, from hydrogen to carbon monoxide, show how survival odds and lifetimes shift over time.
arxiv-2506-21380:
Olivier Benoist answers a question about sums of squares in certain abstract fields, in a 2025 paper. The Pythagoras number of a field is the smallest count such that every sum of squares in that field can be written using no more than that many squares. For fields built from rational functions in one variable over the rational numbers, earlier work left the exact value open.

Benoist proves that five squares always suffice for such fields, settling a question raised by Pop and Pfister. The key step is a representation theorem about quadratic forms in the function field of a curve over a number field. Forms of rank at least five, with coefficients in the base field, represent what they need to. The result ties a concrete number to deep structure in quadratic form theory.
arxiv-2506-21780:
Anya Osborne and five co-authors study meetings in social virtual reality in a twenty twenty-five paper. After the pandemic, many teams meet by video call, and social VR offers a more shared feel. The team asks which avatar styles and which virtual rooms help groups do creative work.

Two studies build on each other, both on the Mozilla Hubs platform. The first asked eighty-seven people what avatar and room traits they prefer for varied meeting types. The second put forty people in pairs, as avatars in headsets, to do creative tasks in distinct settings. The results guide how avatar looks and room design shape teamwork.
arxiv-2506-22180:
Önder Gürcan, writing alone, compares two ways of running smart contracts and finds one clearly safer. This 2025 simulation study starts from the stakes: contracts are permanent once deployed, so their execution architecture matters. The two designs differ in order. One executes a transaction and then orders it into the ledger; the other executes, orders, and then validates before committing.

Gürcan built an evaluation model for the security of contract execution, then a realistic case study of an internet-of-things energy system run by contracts. Simulations exercised the known vulnerability classes from the literature against both architectures. The execute-order-validate design came out ahead on reliability and security. The paper offers the comparison as guidance for industry builders who must choose a platform for autonomous systems and cannot patch their way out later.
arxiv-2506-22580:
Vasilis Siomos, Jonathan Passerat-Palmbach, and Giacomo Tarroni present a 2025 method for training medical image models across sites. In this shared training style, each site keeps its own data but helps build one joint model. Scans differ by device and by patient mix, which can weaken the joint model.

Their method, called FedCLAM, gives each site a push term based on how fast its own training loss fell. A damping factor, set per site, curbs overfitting to local scans. A further step matches the brightness of the target area across sites. The aim is steadier training for tasks such as marking organs or lesions in scans.
arxiv-2506-22780:
Dibyajyoti Chakraborty and co-authors use generative models to sharpen weather data from sparse readings, in work from 2025. The method learns the score, a kind of slope map, of full weather fields. Reversing a noise process with that map can then rebuild detailed fields that fit live readings.

Their test rebuilds a standard global weather record from a blurred version and from scattered balloon readings. The same sampling trick also yields spread estimates, which tell users how sure each rebuilt value is. The authors frame the approach as a new route for fusing model output with real observations. It suits data streams that arrive mixed in kind and timing.
arxiv-2506-22880:
Jisheng Dang and co-authors split the marks a video cutter reads, so text sense and image flow stop fouling each other. Stock cutters fuse features in one pot, which blurs both. Their 2025 scheme first pre-trains with text marks turned to point prompts and text masks, honed by a mixed loss. Then a linear split pulls the hidden states of the big model in two: a text field and a visual field.

A live fusion joins the split fields at the end, watched by three marks: predicted text mask, predicted visual mask, and true mask. Top grades land across image cutting, image grounding, video cutting, and video grounding sets. Code sits free. Split first, fuse last is the craft.
arxiv-2506-22980:
Hui Zhang wrote a 2025 math paper on blocks that stop points from existing on shapes over number fields. Classic descent theory says two sets built in unlike ways match for points on a smooth shape. Zhang asks if the match holds for zero cycles, which are formal sums of points with weights.

Using a cohomology theory built for this setting, he defines a new descent block set for zero cycles. He proves that set equals the Brauer-Manin set, the standard block in the field. He also shows the new set is the closure of a known descent set when the shape is of two special kinds. The result extends a core tool for testing whether shapes carry points at all.
arxiv-2506-23080:
Fang, Tao, and Li sketch a five-stage tale of how AI has grown in this twenty twenty-five paper. They say its path mirrors the long path of human thought tools, from early marks to strict logic frames. Each stage turns on a fresh way to store and work with ideas.

Inside, the frame runs from marks and script through rules of tongue and math to formal logic. Past AI shifts, from rule-based tools to the current big nets, are mapped onto those stages. The authors say AI now nears a self-aware stage marked by step-by-step thought prompts. They close with a path to AI that can check its own work and with tips for firms that build it.
arxiv-2506-23280:
Chaoqun Du and co-authors learn the best call rule for sight kinds in plain form, to beat the skew of rare kind data, in a paper from 2025. Stock nets learn the rule in hid form through a loss slope, which skew data warps. Their path writes the best rule terms out and solves them point by point.

A shift trick then bends the learnt rule to any test mix at no more cost. Gains stack with past rare kind tricks, since those work the hid path while this works the plain one. Four long tail sets, from toy to vast wild kinds, show wide gains for stock nets.
arxiv-2506-23480:
Tang, Zhou, Tan, and Grauer present a neural method to reconstruct fluid structure interaction in twenty twenty-five. Such interaction covers cases where a flow moves a solid and the solid reshapes the flow. Measurements near a moving boundary are often sparse or missing. The team aims to infer both the flow and the motion from sparse data.

Their method combines a modal model of the surface with neural fields for the fluid and solid. Physics equations and interface conditions constrain the learning. It needs only particle tracks away from the body and a moving wall condition. Tests cover a flapping plate, a flexible pipe, and flow around a swimming fish. Reconstructions stayed accurate even with very sparse data near the interface.
arxiv-2506-23780:
Mike Hewitt and Giovanni Pantuso studied in 2025 how a firm should plan production when both demand and output are uncertain. The firm must choose how much finished stock to source from several plants with limited capacity, to make the most profit from sales. Output at each plant varies, and that variation itself depends on which plant is used and how much it makes.

They model the choice as a two-stage problem under uncertainty and give an exact algorithm to solve it. They prove the method is correct and show in large computer tests that it beats known rivals. The work also shows the value of modeling both kinds of uncertainty rather than demand alone.
arxiv-2506-23880:
Matthew Cellot builds higher-dimensional path machinery for tracking how connections transport along routes, surfaces, and volumes. Holonomy classically assigns a group element to each loop, measuring a connection's twist. Building on ideas of Kohno, the framework uses formal power series connections as the transported objects. Higher holonomy functors then arise naturally.

Functors are constructed from the path groupoid, the path two-groupoid, and the path three-groupoid of a manifold, each layer remembering homotopies of the one below. The showcase application is a Gray functor on the path three-groupoid of a configuration space: the space of several distinct points moving in at least four dimensions. Such configuration spaces underlie braid-like phenomena in higher dimensions. The work extends a classical bridge between geometry and algebra into the categorical heights where modern mathematical physics increasingly lives.
arxiv-2507-00480:
Design problems often hide their rules: a candidate can be scored only by running a costly test, and many candidates break hidden constraints. Kiyoung Om, Kyuil Sim, Taeyoung Yun, Hyeongyu Kang, and Jinkyoo Park recast that search as a reasoning problem in this 2025 paper. Instead of hunting in the raw design space, they hunt inside the compact code space of a generative model.

First, flow-based models learn what past candidates look like, and helper models predict each candidate's score and rule breaks. Then candidate choice becomes drawing from a probability distribution that favors high scores and clean records. A borrowed diffusion model does the drawing, which avoids a common failure where all samples collapse to one point. On test problems, both made-up and real, the method beat its rivals.
arxiv-2507-00880:
Ruihan Xu and co-authors present NN-Former in a 2025 paper on predicting how a neural network will perform before it is trained. Designers rely on such predictors to judge accuracy and speed cheaply. Graph-based predictors miss rich features, while transformer-style ones falter as networks grow deeper, so the team rethought how a network's structure is encoded.

Their key insight is that sibling nodes, layers fed by the same parent, matter more than past work assumed. NN-Former blends a graph network with a transformer and adds a mixer that pays attention to siblings. A second new part passes messages both ways along the graph. Across tests, the predictor led rivals on both accuracy and speed estimates. The authors share their code openly.
arxiv-2507-01080:
Edouard Lansiaux and co-authors compare three AI models for predicting emergency department triage levels in a French hospital. Triage errors persist amid crowding and staff shortages. Wrong sorting can delay care for the sickest patients.

Seven months of adult triage records fed the study. Models used language processing, a large language model, and JEPA. They were judged against the French scale and nurse practice. The language model system won on accuracy overall. It also best predicted who would be hospitalized. It handled both structured fields and raw transcripts well. The authors see safety gains from such support tools. Adoption still needs workflow care and oversight.
arxiv-2507-01280:
Kazue Matsuyama and Jeff Greensite present a 2025 physics paper on BCS states and d-wave condensates in the 2D Hubbard model, a standard model of electrons in a square lattice. The head title gives that framing. They start near a Hartree-Fock ground state and relax BCS-form states to nearby energy minima.

As in the older method, a vast number of minima appear, near equal in energy. What is new is a region where the minima clearly take the form of d-wave condensates, in the underdoped regime. Hints of a second d-wave form show in the overdoped region, at least in this approximation. Condensates also span ranges of settings on triangular lattices. The map may guide work on high-temperature superconductors.
arxiv-2507-01380:
Seokcheon Lee, in a solo paper from 2025, rechecks what the newest sky survey data say about rival models of the universe. The data measure baryon acoustic oscillations, a frozen sound pattern from the early universe that works as a cosmic ruler.

Lee compares three models that differ in how dark energy behaves over time. Using the ruler data alone, all three models fit well. Fancy model scores give at most a weak edge to the simplest model. Lee then fixes the ruler's true length using early universe data, instead of using the full sky microwave analysis. Under that anchor, there is no significant sign that dark energy changes over time. The choice of anchor, he argues, is what drives claims of change.
arxiv-2507-01480:
Qingfeng Cao and Ying Zhang present a 2025 frame for the mass patterns of the basic matter particles. Why quarks and leptons span such wide mass ranges is a deep open puzzle, tied to how they mix. The authors build a factorized mass form straight from the seen rank order of masses.

A family symmetry with two fold turns helps explain why the light quark pairs sit near each other in mass. Small fixes from the lightest members enter at second order. The team then fits all mass patterns at once, for both quark mixing and lepton mixing data. Light neutrinos of the standard kind extend the lepton side. The fits hold, which the authors read as a fresh window on the coupling at play.
arxiv-2507-01580:
Kostadinka Koleva and co-authors examine two eruptions of cool gas ropes from the Sun that veered off the straight outward path, in a 2025 paper. Such eruptions can fling vast plasma clouds into space, and their direction decides whether they head toward Earth. Both events took place in the Sun's southern half, in 2017 and 2021.

Images from several space observatories tracked the ropes and their clouds across many wavelengths. Both clouds drifted sideways by a clear margin from the line above their source. The team blames nearby coronal holes, dark patches of open magnetic field at low latitudes. Knowing what bends these clouds helps forecasters judge which ones may reach Earth.
arxiv-2507-01780:
Eric Vin, Kyle Miller, and Daniel Fremont present a library in 2025 that unifies ways of reasoning about time based rules inside a proof tool. Such rules state what must hold as a system runs, step by step, over a finite or an endless trace. Their library works inside Lean, a system where proofs are checked by computer.

Users can mix the classic rule syntax with any Lean terms, which makes it easy to state rules about numbers and other data. The team proves that the standard flavors of these logics all fit inside their frame. The library also has automation that works with Lean's proof tactics. Example cases show it in use on systems from real applications. A shared frame could end the need to rebuild the same logic in each new tool.
arxiv-2507-01880:
Stefano Schuppli and co-authors present a 2025 report on reshaping a supercomputer center's services for machine learning work. Their Alps machine fields over ten thousand GPUs for Swiss research. Classic supercomputer services, built for batch physics runs, fit AI training poorly. Since early access in 2023, the team logged the friction points. They propose a user space that trades some raw speed for ease, plus a quick speed-screen tool for code in growth.

Watch tools and data feeds for live training runs join the list. A node health check, a service plane for support and serving jobs, and storage shaped for AI data round out the plan. Centers worldwide face the same graft of AI onto classic frames.
arxiv-2507-01980:
Linh Nguyen, Marcel Boersma, and Erman Acar detect fraud in financial networks with a learning method that also explains its flags, in a research paper from 2025. Fraud costs the industry billions yearly, but labeled cases are scarce and regulators demand reasons for alerts. Their method learns from mostly unlabeled transaction graphs.

A graph neural network flags suspect items using weak labels. Each flag is then explained by pointing to related items that drive it, using a causality test borrowed from time-series analysis. On a real financial dataset, the method performed well without assuming the network's shape ahead of time. Explainable alerts could ease compliance review.
arxiv-2507-02480:
Ali Banjafar and Guido Falk von Rudorff wrote a 2025 paper on how many true dimensions hide inside molecular properties. Chemical space is vast, and its raw size grows with each atom. Yet learning models do well, hinting that most properties depend on far fewer free knobs.

Allowing a tiny error cuts the needed knobs sharply. That holds for total energy and key orbital energies across many neutral molecules up to twenty atoms. Their method bounds the true count for a chosen accuracy. The count is steady across molecules, so it belongs to the property, not the sample. They argue standard molecule encodings can be squeezed further.
arxiv-2507-02880:
Edwina F Yeo and co-authors set a theoretical limit on how fast bacteria can stick to a surface in flowing fluid, published in 2025. Controlling that sticking, and the biofilms that follow, matters for safety in medical and industrial systems. The team isolates how swimming and fluid flow interact near a surface.

Using the gap between fluid speed and typical swimming speed, they derive how bacteria spread near surfaces. That spread depends on swim speed, how fast cells turn, and cell shape. They then bound the adhesion rate by assuming cells stick for good on first contact. The theory predicts peak adhesion at middle flow rates. Gentle flow brings more cells in, while faster flow turns cells away by shear.
arxiv-2507-03080:
Forés-Toribio and co-authors report, in a 2025 astronomy paper, a star that faded deeply for eight months and then recovered. The star, cataloged as ASASSN-24fw, had sat quiet for over a decade in survey records. It dropped by about 4.1 magnitudes starting in September 2024.

Light patterns before the event fit a young or slightly evolved F-type star with warm dust. During the fade, the light color barely changed, yet blue light dipped a bit more, and the light came out polarized by up to four percent. Signs point to a small companion star and a wide disk around the pair, tilting on a long cycle. Big grains of carbon or ice in the disk best explain the even fade. The event may repeat on a cycle near 43.8 years.
arxiv-2507-03380:
Shailesh Kumar, Tieguang Zi, and Arpan Bhattacharyya present a 2025 physics paper on small objects spiraling into black holes. In these extreme mass-ratio inspirals, a compact body slowly winds around a much larger black hole and emits gravitational waves. Such signals could test whether space has extra dimensions.

The authors study orbits around a black hole from a braneworld model, where extra dimensions leave a mark called a tidal charge. They use an improved equation framework that handles the curved space more exactly than an older approximation. Both methods gave nearly the same bound on the tidal charge. The gap between them grows as orbits get more stretched. Future space detectors could use such signals to probe new physics.
arxiv-2507-03680:
Yue Chen and Robert Shrock work Jones counts for a knot and link clan in 2025. The clan holds swap-form knots with end-less cross counts in the chain. Graph counts for the clan graphs feed the Jones counts by set swaps of marks. Past paths blow up in cost as cross counts grow.

Their path skips that blow-up and gives counts for all cross spans in the clan. Zero spots of the counts are tracked as cross counts run to end-less. Heap marks of those zeros form the tail read of the work. The heap set may name the clan in the end-less case.
arxiv-2507-03980:
Xi He and co-authors present a functional design for generators that list combinations, in a 2025 paper. Programs that solve hard search problems often begin by generating every candidate answer, then filter the list down. When few candidates get filtered out, the speed of the whole program rests on the generator itself.

The team argues that generator design should respect the hardware it runs on, not just formal correctness. Their design, built on convolution, aims for two things at once: smooth use of the memory cache, and parallel runs that need no chatter between processors. The paper develops the method within a program-transformation approach, where proofs and code grow together. It speaks to builders of optimization software who need raw generation speed on modern machines, graphics chips included.
arxiv-2507-04180:
Nazerian, Asllani, Tyloo, Ku, and Sorrentino study the frequency response of networks treated as open systems, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Real networks exchange signals with their surroundings through chosen nodes. Whether structure passes or blocks signals is the core question. The H-two norm quantifies amplification for any input-output choice.

Many natural networks prove organized to enhance signal passing. Food webs, signaling pathways, and gene circuits show this pattern. Power grids, by contrast, seem built to suppress propagation. The contrast separates evolved from engineered design logics. Input and output node choice matters as much as wiring.
arxiv-2507-04280:
Akihito Katsumata and Tomohiro Harada wrote this relativity paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on orbits around a stretched black hole. The Zipoy-Voorhees spacetime describes a static, axisymmetric mass that can be deformed by one parameter; at a set value it reduces to the round Schwarzschild case.

The pair derive a fresh formula for periapsis shift, the slow swing of an orbit's closest point, using a post-Newtonian expansion. The hole's quadrupole shape turns out to enter the shift at an early order. They test the formula on S2, a star that loops around the Milky Way's central giant. The data bound the deformation from below, which means the central object cannot be very prolate, or cigar-shaped. A new series form of the solution also converges fast in both weak and strong fields.
arxiv-2507-04380:
Yuya Yoshikawa and three colleagues give plain prediction models the power to explain their image decisions, without retraining, in a 2025 paper. Some models already explain themselves, highlighting the regions behind each call, but owners of ordinary models face costly relabeling and retraining to gain that skill.

The transfer uses task arithmetic: the difference between a self-explaining model and its plain twin becomes a portable explanation skill. Because their self-explaining design extends a standard vision transformer, the skill fits many trained models as-is. Across image data sets, transfers worked except between unrelated domains, and explanation quality rose while accuracy barely moved. The method targets users who cannot rebuild models from scratch.
arxiv-2507-04680:
Wenhao Li and co-authors teach vision-language models to purge their own made-up details, in a 2025 paper. Such models can describe images fluently yet invent objects that are not there, which hurts trust. Fixes that lean on outside tools or repeated checks slow every answer down.

Their method, SEED, works in three steps: find the false content inside the model, isolate and purge it, then distill the cleaned knowledge back in. A mode-seeking twist keeps training from scattering into empty output zones. A small adapter learns the cleaned habits and corrects the base model. On standard tests with two known models, the fix cut hallucinations by a wide margin without slow per-answer checks.
arxiv-2507-04780:
Kamal Dingle and co-authors tackle guessing the past of a chaotic system in a 2025 paper. Given the final value of a sequence and the rule that steps it forward, they ask which starting value most likely produced it.

Chaos makes this hard, since one final value can have hugely many possible starts. Two ideas come from the theory of information and complexity. One picks the simplest candidate start. The other picks a start from the thinnest region of the candidate set. Tested on four classic chaotic maps, the methods ranked the true start well in some settings and beat rival methods that failed to beat chance. Cost and noise sensitivity remain open problems.
arxiv-2507-04980:
Francesco Zerman builds a Kolyvagin system for families of modular forms over quaternion algebras in two thousand twenty-five. Kolyvagin systems are rigs of cohomology classes that bound the size of Selmer groups, a core task in number theory. The starting stock here is an Euler system of big Heegner points on towers of Shimura curves.

The new system adapts that stock to a quaternionic setting and drops a classic side condition on the family's tame conductor. The route extends prior work by Buyukboduk to the wider frame. As a by-product, one side of the anticyclotomic Iwasawa main conjecture is proved for Hida families. The result links curve points to deep claims about L-values.
arxiv-2507-05280:
Andras Ferenczy, a solo author, assesses Hungary's artificial intelligence strategy in a two thousand twenty-five paper, and compares it with the strategy in Singapore. The work draws on strategy texts, public funding records, and talks with Hungarian AI leaders. Twenty-two goals from the Hungary strategy are scored on design, governance, timing, and funding.

Public spending on AI in Hungary was put at several billion euros. Yet funding data were public for just half the goals, and three projects made up nearly all the funding on record. The plan's rollout was split up after ministry reshuffles, and planned two year reviews have not taken place since two thousand twenty. The advice for the next plan is to adapt to large language models. It also urges the use of the car industry as an East West test ground for AI in cars.
arxiv-2507-05380:
Charlotte Ward and co-authors count feeding black holes whose gas disks sign their light with twin peaks, in a 2025 paper. Some active galactic nuclei show broad lines split in two, the mark of a rotating disk seen at a tilt. From a hard X-ray picked sample, the team read spectra of 343 broad-line nuclei close to home. They fit each line set for disk shape and tilt.

Seventy-one double-peaked emitters turned up, about a fifth of the sample, in line with past counts. Their black holes ran heavier and fed more slowly than the single-peaked rest, and they favored oval hosts and hotter X-ray glow. In other lights, from radio to mid-infrared, the two crowds looked alike, with no split in flare habits. The authors warn that hidden disk glow in the rest can bias the mass counts drawn from broad lines.
arxiv-2507-05680:
Nine authors, led by Patrick Müller, report in 2025 a precise laser measure of the size of the carbon-13 nucleus. Nuclear size is a basic trait, yet measures from electrons, lasers, and muon atoms do not always agree, as a famed proton puzzle showed. Light nuclei with firm data from all routes are rare, and carbon is a prized exception.

The team read a fine split in the light from carbon ions against a frequency comb ruler. Their size value sharpened the electron based result sixfold. It also clashed, beyond error bars, with the muon atom value of like precision. First principles nuclear models were run for comparison.
arxiv-2507-05880:
Zeyuan Meng, Zixuan Yi, and Iadh Ounis revisit, in 2025, a language-model system that ranks recommendations for users. The original system sampled users by clustering, built a first ranking with a standard model, then fine-tuned a language model to refine it. Which parts drove its strong results was unclear.

The team rebuilt the whole pipeline and tested each piece. Two of its three ranking methods matched the original scores. The third looked suspiciously strong because true answers had leaked into its prompts. They offer a flexible test framework covering five design choices, and check results on several datasets, noting one dataset could not be fairly tested.
arxiv-2507-05980:
Chua, Tan, Ge, and Lee build a safety test set for low-resource languages in a 2025 paper. Language models often guard English well but slip in local tongues and mixed speech. Their set, RabakBench, covers Singlish, Chinese, Malay, and Tamil as used in Singapore. Real unsafe web text was widened by model red-teaming, tagged by model votes, then translated with care to keep its bite.

Over five thousand examples span six harm types, with human checks holding agreement high. Thirteen top guard systems lost clear ground on the set. The authors offer the three-stage build as a repeatable recipe for other underserved speech communities.
arxiv-2507-06080:
Joaquim Comas and five co-authors put out CAST-Phys, a data set to know moods with no touch of the one felt. Touch tools worn as moods are called up can warp the moods that staff gauge. Their base in its place backs fetch of body signs from far. It pairs high grade face film with no squeeze with base signs for truth.

The tapes hold light pulse signs from skin, sweat gland acts, and breath. They sit next to the face film from which such signs might be read. Reads show body cues count in real scenes where faces sole are not clear. Tests of sole signs and of signs joined show the hope of far mood reads in more than one mode. The set aims at mood screen staff who need truth on the ground for no touch ways.
arxiv-2507-06280:
Thibault Chassereau and co-authors find plain proof that growth tips of a thread fungus steer by the threads they near. The work dates to 2025. The web grows from one spore in straight, fast spokes with oft branch splits. Pure push with no talk back could waste space and food reach.

The team rebuilt all tip paths past each split in one growth set. A drift form with pull terms fit the paths. Lone tips and near-thread tips were set side by side. Near tips showed a sharp slow and turn mark that lone tips lacked. The mark makes the case for live steer in the web.
arxiv-2507-06480:
Sengupta and co-authors show in 2025 a neat link between wave shapes and a hidden trait of strong magnetic fields in plasma. That trait lets a three dimensional field hold charged bits of matter well. Finding such fields is hard, since the core math is tangled and over set.

From a large set of tuned field designs, the team finds the field strength on one surface is set by just three or four flux values. Those values tie to a classic wave form known from soliton theory. The claim holds across the full surface, not just near the core line of the field.
arxiv-2507-06780:
George Papadopoulos and George Vouros ask how a machine can copy an expert and still obey safety limits. Their 2025 paper works in imitation learning, where a policy learns from sample runs made by an expert. The goal is a policy with high entropy that stays inside the limits the expert runs show.

The pair ties the task to probabilistic inference, which gives their aim a firm base. Their method trains with dual gradient descent, a two-sided update they find steady and sound. Tests show the learned policies respect limits of more than one kind and still act well on new cases. Robot and control readers get a principled route to safe copied behavior.
arxiv-2507-06880:
Orlando Oliveira wrote a 2025 physics paper on the meeting point of a photon and a fermion in quantum electrodynamics. That meeting point, called the vertex, obeys a self referential equation known as a Dyson-Schwinger equation. Oliveira works in four dimensions and in a family of standard gauge choices. The lengthwise part of the vertex is written in a classic basis, and the crosswise part in a more recent one.

Joining a key identity with the vertex equation yields an exact set of integral equations for the crosswise part. Those equations hold for any gauge in the family and must be solved as a consistent whole. Oliveira discusses approximations that extend past one loop results. Several special momentum setups are examined as well. The paper also computes the step by step perturbative solution for all crosswise factors, with their behavior at extremes.
arxiv-2507-06980:
Binquan Zhang and six co-authors grade the reasoning steps that language models produce before writing code in 2025. These chains of thought act like design notes, so their quality should drive the code's quality. The team dissected over a thousand failed solutions from two standard benchmarks.

Outside factors, unclear demands and missing context, caused over half the bad reasoning; the rest came from the models misreading prompts. Even with sound reasoning, nearly a fifth of the code still failed from poor instruction following, while some correct code rode on flawed reasoning. Feeding detailed problem statements let models repair weak chains, sketching a path to more trustworthy code generation.
arxiv-2507-07180:
Innes Bigaran, Stephen Parke, and Pedro Pasquini settle a debate about telling Dirac from Majorana neutrinos in a two thousand twenty-five particle physics paper. The Dirac-Majorana confusion theorem says any telling-apart vanishes as neutrino mass goes to zero.

Recent claims hinted multi-neutrino events might evade the theorem. Using spinor-helicity methods spread to massive fermions, the authors compute every helicity amplitude for a light scalar decaying into two neutrinos and two oppositely charged leptons. The calculation exposes exactly where earlier thinking could go wrong. With correct antisymmetrization and all contributions summed, the decay obeys the confusion theorem, backing a foundational result about neutrino identity.
arxiv-2507-07280:
Mariah Bradford, Nikhil Krishnaswamy, and Nathaniel Blanchard study how classroom background chatter affects the detection of interruptions. Interruptions shape how small groups learn together, and teachers could use AI help to follow them. Most detection research, though, assumes one clean conversation at a time, nothing like a busy classroom.

Their 2025 paper compares detection in single conversations and in multi-group recordings full of overlapping speech. They then build a method that stays accurate when other groups talk over the target group. The analysis also surfaces how interruptions sound and read in group work, in both tone and wording. The findings guide builders of classroom listening tools toward the noise they will really face.
arxiv-2507-07380:
Jacob Wise and co-authors present one of the brightest cosmic explosions ever recorded in this 2025 paper. The event, AT2019cmw, blazed at the center of an early type galaxy and then faded with a smooth, featureless spectrum at every check.

Its peak output reached a level few thermal transients attain. Over about three hundred days it cooled from roughly thirty thousand degrees to ten thousand, a cooling path unusual enough to reshape how future surveys pick candidates. No X-rays or radio waves appeared, ruling out a jet aimed at Earth. Light curve modeling points to a star of tens of solar masses torn apart by a supermassive black hole. The sleepy host galaxy hints at a pocket of hidden star birth near its core.
arxiv-2507-07480: Tobias Kappé surveys when two programs count as the same if one ignores what their steps mean. His short paper, from twenty twenty-five, covers propositional equivalence. Swapping the branches of an if-test and flipping its guard gives the same program, whatever the parts are. He frames new results through a logic of guarded tests and loops, known as GKAT, and notes where the theory stands.
arxiv-2507-07680:
Atsushi Ono, writing alone, revisits a physics question in a 2025 paper on crystals that hold an electric charge pattern. When a low pulse of electric field hits such a crystal, the charge shifts and the light it doubles in frequency changes too. Many workers assumed the two shifts move in step.

Ono uses response theory to write out both shifts over time. The math shows the rate of change of the field also matters, not just the field itself. Even when that term is tiny, the light shift can run against the pulse. Tests on a model crystal support the math. The result warns against reading charge shifts straight from light shifts.
arxiv-2507-07780:
Mélanie Roschewitz, Raghav Mehta, Fabio de Sousa Ribeiro, and Ben Glocker run a wide work on how true chance calls stay when art sort tools face real world data shift. They weigh ways to set calls right past train and ways in train like smooth of marks. That work spans eight sort tasks and more than one art field. Base model tunes are in the set next to models trained from scratch.

A join of a push to spread picks with smooth of marks gave the best raw set right scores in shift. Tools set right past train that saw a bit of off task data proved most firm. New ways built for shift scarce beat plain past train fixes. Gains in shift scores often made in set scores worse. Groups of models lent aid, most when set right came first and models sprang from base weights.
arxiv-2507-08080:
Benjamin Sappler, Masataka Kawano, Michael P Zaletel, and Frank Pollmann introduce a new form for tensor network states in two dimensions. Their 2025 paper deals with ways to write down complex quantum states on large grids. A one-dimensional form exists, but extending it to flat grids has been hard.

Their form adds helper tensors to mark the surface where states stay properly normalized. They run a standard time-step method on this form and test it on a classic magnet model. Ground states and short-time motion came out accurately, even at the critical point, on grids of more than a thousand sites. The form also fits other grid shapes, such as honeycomb layouts. The work gives simulators a cleaner tool for flat quantum systems.
arxiv-2507-08280:
Jihye Lee, Minseo Kang, and Dongha Kim address a common data problem in twenty twenty-five. Tables used for prediction often have missing values. Those gaps reflect how data was collected, and the pattern of gaps can shift across time or place. The facts under the gaps may stay the same while the gap pattern changes. That shift can badly hurt a model at test time.

Their method, MIRRAMS, is built for the hard case where test data is unseen. They set conditions based on mutual information to steer the model toward label-relevant facts. Simple loss terms enforce those conditions during training. Readers get a way to keep tabular models steady when missingness shifts.
arxiv-2507-08480:
Youngjoon Jang and co-authors study how the language mix of training data shapes Korean-English cross-lingual retrieval. Search systems that cross languages are vital in a multilingual web, yet builders rarely test what the training blend does. The team built parallel Korean-English datasets and trained retrievers on varied combinations.

A clean trade-off appeared: blends that lift cross-lingual search tend to drag same-language search down, and the two are tightly linked. Model merging, averaging trained models, eased the trade-off and delivered strong results on both sides. The data-centric lesson is practical: curate the language recipe, then merge to keep the best of each training run.
arxiv-2507-08980:
Blur to sharp tools learn to make shots from noise, and a guide that aims their mid marks at a taught eye's marks makes them learn fast and well. Chenyu Wang and co-authors set that guide's rules in a 2025 study. Their frame splits the tool's sum in ways that fix when and how the guide's marks join the run.

Two new plays come from the split. One pairs each shot with marks of its own or of a twin kind, and learns the pair as one. The twin sets the school pace twixt mark learn and shot learn. On shot, ware chain, and drug form tasks, the guide both lifts the ware and speeds the school, by a wide span on the head test.
arxiv-2507-09080:
Ecology runs on scattered data sets, each with its own model, and little of it transfers between regions or species. Athanasios Trantas and six co-authors build a shared foundation model for European biodiversity in 2025, trained on species records woven together with satellite, climate, and land data. Light fine tuning then aims the one model at many jobs.

Trials covered joint maps of five hundred plant species and monthly climate probing, where it gave a strong starting point for both living and weather tasks. It can simulate a year ahead at monthly steps. The team open sources the weights and training code. They present it as shared infrastructure for conservation planning.
arxiv-2507-09480:
Guoyou Wang, Yihua Tan, and Shiqi Liu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a fresh way to read off derivatives from sampled points, and to rebuild a smooth function near them, based on Taylor's classic formula.

Taylor's form frays in high dimensions, and errors grow as derivatives are chained from discrete data. The new operator uses a Vandermonde matrix from the cut Taylor series. It gets all low-order derivatives in one pass, which curbs error growth. Even spacing gives high-order accuracy and softens the dimension curse. Tight error bounds are proved for both tasks. In tests it beats finite differences at slopes, and splines at rebuilds, and it extends to two dimensions.
arxiv-2507-09780:
Feilong Qiaoyuan and co-authors present BitParticle in a 2025 paper on faster hardware for deep neural networks. These networks use many multiply and add steps, and much of the data is sparse, meaning many bits are zero. Old bit-serial chips waste one of the two sparse factors, and uneven sparsity leaves parts of the chip idle.

The design splits both factors into small parts so both kinds of sparsity can be used at once. Simple control logic stops the number of part products from growing too large. A near-sync scheme adds slack at the cycle level, so the array stays busy and uses less energy.
arxiv-2507-09880:
Virtual worlds need software that can label the parts of a moving human body, from hands to feet, in video over time. Keito Suzuki and co-authors present OpenHuman4D in a 2025 paper, a system built for that task. Older systems worked from a fixed list of body parts and ran slowly.

Their system tracks masks across frames instead of labeling each frame from scratch, which saves time. Extra modules catch new targets and repair tracking slips, and a fusion step blends evidence across the whole clip. The system also accepts new part names in plain words, not just a fixed list. Tests showed sound labeling at up to 93 percent less run time than the prior best method.
arxiv-2507-09980:
Zhipeng Xue and co-authors build a method for judging how much to trust AI decisions made from several kinds of data at once. Images, text, and other views of the same case often arrive incomplete or noisy. Models that merge these views can be accurate yet unsure, and standard ways of measuring that doubt ignore the gaps between data types.

Their network, KPHD-Net, scores each view's evidence and combines it using a theory built for weighing uncertain proof. It replaces the usual distance measure with one based on Hölder divergence, which the authors show tracks real gaps between distributions better. In wide tests, the method beat leading rivals in accuracy, toughness against noise, and honesty about its own doubt.
arxiv-2507-10180:
Mutsumi Sugizaki, Tatehiro Mihara, Kohei Kobayashi, and six colleagues report observations of a violent X-ray transient in this two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. The source, MAXI J0709-159, was discovered in January two thousand twenty-two during a fast outburst. Its luminosity swung enormously within hours, and its position matches the Be star LY CMa, also identified as a B supergiant. The team analyzed data from the NICER telescope taken from three hours to six days after discovery.

Activity continued for about seven hours as sparse flares, each under one hundred seconds, with luminosity briefly reaching extreme levels. Light curve and spectral features fit accretion of a clumpy stellar wind onto a magnetized neutron star. During the brightest flare the variability spectrum showed a broad peak near one hertz, resembling a quasi-periodic oscillation. If that peak marks the Keplerian orbital frequency, it constrains where the accreting gas orbits.
arxiv-2507-10280:
Haomiaomiao Wang, Conor Fennell, Swati Poojary, and Mingming Liu build a digital twin of road traffic with the SUMO simulator, in work from 2025. The twin copies mixed traffic of fuel and electric cars on a major motorway stretch. Data came from road loops, GPS probes, and toll records.

The model was checked with full and with partial data. It matched mean speed and trip length closely in both cases. Output for carbon output was only a bit high, and electric power use was a bit low. The results suggest the twin stays sound even when car type data are incomplete.
arxiv-2507-10380:
Tasa-Chaveli and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper tracing isotope ratios in the cold cores where stars are born. Starless cores are dense gas clouds not yet forming stars. Their chemical fingerprints, especially isotope ratios, hint at the origin of material that later built the Solar System.

Using the IRAM 30-meter telescope, the team measured deuterium and nitrogen isotope ratios in three molecules across 23 cores in varied environments. Deuterated forms appeared in every core. Their fractions scattered widely and correlated only weakly with temperature, pointing to core age as another driver. A chemical model matched the data with ages of a few hundred thousand years, differing by region. Nitrogen ratios differed between the two carrier molecules. The results chart chemical evolution before star birth.
arxiv-2507-10680:
Luca Vecchi, a solo author, revisits a puzzle about why the strong nuclear force barely breaks a key symmetry, in a 2025 paper. Theories that impose that symmetry force a certain angle in the theory to one of two values: zero or pi. Only zero fits the world we see, so symmetry alone cannot settle the puzzle.

Vecchi shows that zero is picked naturally when the symmetry is combined with embedding the Standard Model in a suitable larger gauge group. Without that extra step, a hidden quality problem lurks in symmetry-based solutions. Rival solutions use a hypothetical particle, the axion. The paper clarifies what symmetry-based models must add to truly solve the strong CP problem, rather than merely restating it.
arxiv-2507-10780:
Thomas Wright sharpens, in a 2025 number theory paper, what can be said about primes in arithmetic progressions when a rare Siegel zero is assumed to exist. A Siegel zero is a near-miss zero of an L-function that warps how primes spread among residue classes. Under a strong form of that assumption, he tracks Chebyshev's counting function for primes in one class.

For moduli up to nearly x to the two-thirds, his formula matches the expected main term, corrected by a character term, for almost all classes at once. A swapped version fixes the class and lets almost all moduli vary. Earlier results under the same assumption reached far smaller exponents. The gain matters because exceptional zeros, if real, would bend prime races in ways these formulas now describe tightly.
arxiv-2507-10880:
Large firms must assign the right tax code to thousands of products and services, and a wrong code can bring penalties. Souvik Nath, Sumit Wadhwa, and Luis Perez built a small language model for that job in 2025. Tax codes are hierarchical, built level by level, so the team chose a model that generates the code as a sequence, capturing how each level depends on the last.

Trained to adapt to the tax domain, the model beat flat classifiers on the Harmonized System codes. It also beat models that only encode or only decode text. The authors say the same approach can extend to other official code systems used in Brazil and by the United Nations.
arxiv-2507-10980:
Shawn Ong and Dexter Kozen give an algorithm that decides whether two programs of this kind mean the same thing. Their 2025 paper works in a Kleene algebra enriched with chance and a friendly form of nondeterminism, where choices are tracked as multisets rather than sets. A companion paper had shown that automata and regular expressions in this setting express exactly the same behaviors.

Equivalence is the harder question, and the authors answer it with polynomial algebra. Their procedure translates the problem into ideal membership, tested with Gröbner basis methods, the workhorse machinery of computational algebra. If the difference of two descriptions lands in the ideal, the two are equivalent. The paper is a compact theoretical result: a decidable semantics for a formalism meant to reason about such computation, with the decision method resting on classical algebra.
arxiv-2507-11180:
Jian Li and a team of co-authors report a way to prepare and check quantum states in real time, in two thousand twenty-five. Good state preparation is central to quantum work. Full checks of a state take huge effort as systems grow, yet quick checks often rest on guesswork.

The team turn a checking method into a guide for preparation itself. The checks state which measures to take and give a clear score for quality. In a test with a three-part state, nine settings were enough to guide the work. The result matched full checks that need far more data. The plan could later feed into fast, closed-loop control.
arxiv-2507-11280:
Gábor Kovács, R. Szabó, and J. Nuspl open a new line of work on pulsing stars in this 2025 paper. The stars are RR Lyrae variables, whose outer layers churn with hot rising gas. Old one-layer models handled that churning well for years, but sharper modern data expose their limits. The team builds multi-dimensional models to compare against the old ones.

They ran a code called SPHERLS on still envelope models with varied widths and grid fineness. Using statistics and wave analysis, they measured the size of the churning eddies and mapped energy flow. Models narrower than nine degrees gave a distorted picture of the churning zone. The zone itself holds two loose, unstable regions rather than one. The work sets a baseline for fair tests between old and new star models.
arxiv-2507-11380:
Pérez-Ràfols and co-authors give the final list of quasars picked from a sky survey that reads light through many narrow color bands. Their 2025 paper is the fifth in a series on the miniJPAS survey. Quasar lists feed many uses, from picking targets for deep spectra to weighing black holes and mapping the cosmos.

The team blends the calls of eight learning methods into one sorter, tuned to pick quasars well. They weigh which sorters matter most. Three distance gauges then give sharper guesses of how far each quasar lies. The list is checked against both fake skies, where the truth is known, and real spectra. The result is a vetted catalog for the survey's data release.
arxiv-2507-12080:
Mrityunjoy Charan, Jaban Meher, and Siddhi Pathak settle a conjecture in analytic number theory in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Ramanujan polynomials, studied earlier by Murty, Smyth, and Wang, are a notable family of reciprocal polynomials. Maji and Sarkar proposed a two-parameter generalization and conjectured a precise statement about where its zeros lie. The zeros' location matters because it governs the polynomials' analytic behavior and their connections to related number-theoretic quantities.

The authors prove the conjecture in full. For positive integer parameters, all zeros of the generalized polynomials lie on the unit circle, with exactly two exceptions, both real. Unit-circle results of this kind echo famous phenomena like the Lee-Yang circle theorem and often signal hidden structure. The paper thus closes an open question and confirms that the two-parameter family keeps the striking zero geometry of the original Ramanujan polynomials.
arxiv-2507-12180:
Luc Pirio studies webs, families of curves that cross a surface in set directions, on a special class of surfaces and on a tenfold space tied to spinors. A prior paper showed one such web shares many rare traits with a classic example called Bol's web. His 2025 paper traces where those shared traits come from.

By direct, explicit sums, Pirio shows the likeness extends to a second web built as a quotient of the spinor space web. That web acts as a rank five version of Bol's web. It carries a special relation that widens a famous five term identity for the dilogarithm. From that relation, a weight three identity for any quartic del Pezzo surface can be recovered.
arxiv-2507-12380:
Maximilian Krahn and Vikas Garg present a 2025 paper on topological neural networks. Such networks extend graph learning to higher-order structures. Their message passing is powerful but costly. The team builds a Laplacian operator on combinatorial complexes, a broad shape frame. Heat kernels from that operator serve as node descriptors. The descriptors carry multiscale shape facts at low cost.

Theory says the method is as expressive as possible: it can tell apart any unlike complexes. Tests show big speed gains over past topological methods. Scores on standard molecule data sets stay competitive with the best descriptors. Harder shape tests favor the new method as well. ML researchers get topology tools that fit transformer-style models without heavy cost. That opens higher-order learning to larger data than past methods could handle.
arxiv-2507-12580:
Josephine Borre and co-authors probe age and language bias in speech emotion AI in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Most such systems train on adult, English, unplanned speech. How they read acted emotion from teens or older adults, or in other tongues, is little tested.

Twelve teens and twelve adults over fifty-five acted four target emotions in Danish and English, steering toward points on a mood grid. A live system scored their voices at once. Against expectations, age and language groups barely differed, though high-arousal feelings were read poorly. The authors urge a shift from raw accuracy toward models built around users, and warn of gaps between human intent and machine reads.
arxiv-2507-12680:
Eduardo Serrano-Ensástiga, Olivier Giraud, and John Martin wrote this 2025 physics paper on how quantum links are shared among several qubits. A rule called monogamy limits how strongly one qubit can be tied to two others at once. These limits shape what quantum networks and codes can do.

The authors measure shared correlation through sector lengths, averages of correlation terms of each size. They derive a fresh set of inequalities that complete an older family known as shadow inequalities. For systems of up to five qubits in a pure state, the allowed values now form a fully known shape, a convex polytope. Key quantities can then be optimized by checking the corners of that shape. For six or more qubits, the picture grows much harder, and the authors mark that frontier.
arxiv-2507-12980:
Kyosuke Maeda and Ken-ichi Yoshida classify special ideals on a family of singular surfaces. Their paper appeared in 2025. The surfaces are rational triple points, a standard class of two-dimensional singularities. The ideals in question, called Ulrich ideals, are tightly tied to the shape of the singularity. The authors first show that one canonical ideal, the trace of the dualizing module, is always Ulrich for these surfaces.

From that anchor they list every Ulrich ideal on a rational triple point. They also prove that for quotient singularities with multiplicity at least four, the maximal ideal is the only Ulrich ideal. Together the results complete the classification for both families. Such lists help algebraists read a singularity's structure from its ideals.
arxiv-2507-13180:
Umair Javed and co-authors study pores in a two-dimensional material in a 2025 paper. Hexagonal boron nitride grows triangular holes under an electron beam, a fact known for near twenty years. The shape was blamed on boron atoms being easier to knock out than nitrogen atoms.

In ultra-clean vacuum, the team instead got round pores from the same beams. Even a trace of oxygen in the chamber pushed growing pores back into triangles with nitrogen-lined edges. The pattern held across sample brands, beam energies, and beam styles. The authors say stray gas chemistry, not atom thresholds alone, sets the shape. That gives a firm way to carve exact pores in the material.
arxiv-2507-13780:
Frederik Broucke published a mathematics paper in 2025 linking zero-free regions of zeta functions to the error term in the prime number theorem. Where a zeta function provably has no zeros controls how sharply primes can be counted. For a wide class of such regions, the author derives an improved upper bound on the counting error. The method covers not just the classic zeta function but generalized Beurling versions.

Broucke also builds Beurling zeta functions with endlessly many zeros on a chosen curve and none beyond it. The matching oscillation result for the error term shows the new bound is nearly best possible. The paper tightens a classic bridge between zeros and primes.
arxiv-2507-13880:
Marten Kreis and Benjamin Kiefer fuse live ship video with chart marks to sharpen sea vision, in a paper from 2025. Crews must match buoys they see to buoys on the chart, a task that sags in glare, spray, and chop. The system lays chart marks on the video once each buoy in view is paired with its chart twin.

A block net scans the frame and calls out buoy boxes with a trust score for each call, which lets the pair step run end to end. The team sets it next to a ray cast guess and a tuned spot net with a range add on. On real sea scenes the new pair step wins on both spot truth and match truth by a clear edge, even in hard light.
arxiv-2507-14080:
Derek Leung, Nickolai Zeldovich, and Frans Kaashoek present Shipwright in a 2025 paper, a framework for proving that a distributed system keeps making progress even when some of its members act maliciously. Systems like PBFT, which let many machines agree on a shared log, have no single operator who can restart them, so a hidden stall bug can freeze them for good. Until now, no one had verified both correctness and this forward-progress property, called liveness, for a runnable version.

Shipwright adds three techniques. One supports reasoning about dishonest participants. Another splits systems and proofs into matching modular parts. A third handles digital signatures inside messages in a sound way. The team used it to build and verify a starter version of single-entry agreement in PBFT. They turned it into a working Go program and showed it running through normal operation and failure cases.
arxiv-2507-14680:
Xinheng Lyu and co-authors present a team of software agents for analyzing whole slide tissue images in a 2025 paper. Such slides hold gigapixel views used across many pathology tasks. Large multimodal models can handle many tasks in plain language, but often trail models built for one task. Their system splits work among specialist agents to keep both range and accuracy.

One module assigns each task to an expert agent drawn from a model library. A checking step tests consistency inside the system and against pathology knowledge and specialist models. A summary module then merges results with visual maps. Tests on multi modal benchmarks beat current slide models and medical agent systems across tasks. Readers see teamwork as a design for medical image tools.
arxiv-2507-14780:
Phillip Isaac and Mitchell Ryan analyzed the Dirac oscillator through unusual symmetry algebras in 2025. The Dirac oscillator is a relativistic model where a particle feels a spring-like pull written in Dirac's equation. Its raising and lowering operators, which step between energy levels, turn out to generate graded Lie superalgebras with a double grading, one family in each spatial dimension from one to three.

Those algebras connect to parastatistics, a generalized rule for how identical particles may share states, and to the state spaces built from them. Isaac and Ryan show the algebras organize the oscillator's energy levels neatly, with the richest payoff in full three-dimensional space. Algebra becomes a lens for the model's spectrum.
arxiv-2507-14980:
Tianle Li and co-authors work on federated learning when the training data follow a long tail. Federated learning trains one model across many sites without moving private data. When some classes are rare, momentum-based training can drift, favor common classes, and fail to settle.

Their 2025 paper first probes this failure with tests that include a layer-by-layer look at network behavior. They then propose FedWCM, which adjusts momentum on the fly using global and per-round data. The change corrects the directional bias that long-tailed data create. In broad tests, FedWCM fixed the failure to converge and beat prior methods, even when clients held very unlike data.
arxiv-2507-15280:
Privacy rules increasingly demand that a model forget specific data, but deletion requests rarely arrive all at once. Shaofei Shen and co-authors handle that stream of requests in this 2025 paper. Standard unlearning wipes a whole batch of data in one go. When requests trickle in, batch methods waste effort and can lose accuracy.

The authors recast streaming unlearning as a shift in the data distribution. They estimate the new distribution after each removal and update the model toward it. Their method needs no access to the original training data, a common legal limit. Theory in the paper backs the approach. Tests weigh how well the model keeps its skill while forgetting on the fly. Streaming forgetting fits real products, where takedown requests never stop.
arxiv-2507-15480:
Liang Chen and four co-authors improve how vision-language models are fine-tuned in a paper from 2025. Models like CLIP join image and text features, and the final merged table of scores drives each prediction. Most tuning methods adjust the image or text side alone and ignore that merged table, where the decision is actually made.

Their method, RAda, adds one light attention layer at the very end of the model. It learns a mask that reweights each entry of the merged table during tuning. Tests across settings, including tuning on unlabeled test data, matched or beat current methods with minimal code change.
arxiv-2507-15780:
Christian Kassel and Christophe Reutenauer study two intertwined sets of whole number sequences that come from counting ideals in a ring of polynomials in two variables. In past work they found a count that forms a symmetric polynomial with a neat factor.

From that factor they build a new polynomial for each count. They show its values sit close to a sum of scaled Chebyshev polynomials, a classic family in math. They give an exact formula that mixes those sums, with the mix set by the odd divisors of the count. The two forms match in full exactly when the count is a power of two.
arxiv-2507-16080:
Riki Shimizu, Richard J. Antonello, Chandan Singh, and Nima Mesgarani ask what speech models actually learn about the brain in this 2025 paper. Large speech foundation models predict brain responses to speech well, but their inner workings are hard to read. The authors test whether plain, clear-cut speech features can explain that success.

They built brain encoding models from six feature families, from sound spectra to word meaning, plus three large speech models. Recordings from sensors placed on the brain surface showed how much of the response each family explained. Most of the large models' match with the brain came from simple features they had picked up. Yet the large models also held real word-meaning signals that simple features missed, and that part grew with model size. Mixing clear features into the models made them more accurate and easier to interpret.
arxiv-2507-16580:
Olmo and four co-authors draw how black holes with free-form traits would look through their disk glow in this twenty twenty-five paper. The holes are set by long lists of free values, with no tie to one gravity frame. Two known free-form sets are used, each trimmed by sun-system and far-field checks.

Inside, disk-lit views are made for holes whose dark core is blown up or shrunk. Ring size and ring glow traits are weighed in depth for each view. The team says next-wave long-base scopes could tell such holes from the plain round case. Views of bare cores with no dark zone are also drawn and weighed in the mix.
arxiv-2507-16780:
Smearing a black hole's point-like heart into a soft Gaussian lump was meant to tame its singular core. Gokhan Alkac and co-authors check whether the famous smeared solution truly obeys Einstein's equations. Their target is the noncommutative geometry inspired Reissner-Nordstrom black hole. The metric and its headline properties survive the audit. But some components of the field equations quietly fail.

The authors build an improved energy-momentum tensor that satisfies every component. The fix changes a physical prediction: where the strong energy condition breaks down. For some parameter choices, the violation now sits outside the inner horizon. That region could, in principle, leave observable signatures. The paper is a reminder that an elegant solution sketch still has to pass every line of the equations.
arxiv-2507-17280:
Shubham Kala and Jaswinder Singh study, in a 2025 physics paper, how light bends around a black hole of a modified gravity theory. They also examine the shadow it casts, when hot gas plasma surrounds it. The black hole follows Horndeski theory with a non minimal coupling, a leading alternative to Einstein's gravity. The plasma is cold, magnetized, and without pressure.

They derive a formula for the bending angle and trace how plasma traits and the theory's coupling constant shift it. The ring of light orbits that edges the shadow is analyzed for even and uneven plasma spread. Shadow sizes are then set against real telescope measurements of the black holes in our galaxy and in M87. Those comparisons bound the model's parameters. They also model shadow images lit by gas falling inward, with brightness profiles to match.
arxiv-2507-17580:
Amandeep Singh Bhatia and Sabre Kais propose improving quantum federated learning with Fisher information. In federated learning, clients train a shared model without handing over sensitive data. The quantum version adds parameterized circuits, with promise for fields like health care and finance, but communication costs and uneven client data remain obstacles.

Fisher information measures how much a quantum state reveals about its parameters, capturing geometric and statistical structure. The authors use it, computed on each client's local model, to spot the parameters that matter most for performance. Those critical parameters are then protected during the shared training process. The goal is faster, safer learning across unevenly split datasets.
arxiv-2507-17880:
Adithya L J and co-authors study how stable continuous time quantum walks stay on complex networks when noise creeps in. A quantum walk spreads a walker over a graph with quantum rules, and stability here means keeping its quantum traits. Six network shapes are tested, from rings and stars to scale free webs.

Three noise types are applied: energy based self decoherence, node based noise, and edge based noise. Five yardsticks track the damage, among them coherence and fidelity. Self decoherence kept coherence longest, while edge noise killed it fast. Dense and hub based webs stood firm under node noise but broke fast under edge noise when started at a hub.
arxiv-2507-18080:
Makoto Nakashima studies the critical two-dimensional stochastic heat flow in a two thousand twenty-five mathematics paper. This random object arises as a scaling limit of directed polymers in random environments. It also appears as a limit of solutions to a smoothed stochastic heat equation.

Nakashima focuses on the mass the flow assigns to pairs of balls in the plane. He establishes an upper bound on the lower tail of that mass. Small values, in other words, cannot be too likely. Two consequences follow from the bound. The logarithm of the mass is integrable, and the mass itself is strictly positive. These results partly answer open questions about the flow's local behavior.
arxiv-2507-18180:
Weak-value amplification is a quantum trick that makes tiny parameters readable by letting a measurement pointer shift more than it should. An auto-correlative variant improves on the standard scheme, but it needs real-time multiplication and integration hardware to shine. Jing-Hui Huang, Guang-Jun Wang, and Xiang-Yun Hu built that hardware in 2025 as an analog circuit, using a commercial multiplier chip and an operational amplifier as the integrator.

Tested with Gaussian pointers, the circuit stayed sensitive across signals from 200 hertz to 20 kilohertz. Head to head with the standard method, the auto-correlative version was more accurate and far tougher against noise in a low signal-to-noise band. The authors note the same circuit can serve other detection schemes built on correlated signals, not just quantum metrology.
arxiv-2507-18380:
Tianyu Xie, Yicong Mao, and Cheng Zhang presented ARTreeFormer in 2025, a faster model for phylogenetic inference. Reconstructing family trees of species means modelling a huge space of possible tree shapes. A prior deep model could cover the whole space but wasted time on repeated tree walks and local message passing.

ARTreeFormer replaces that computation with a fixed-point iteration that computes node embeddings in a vectorised way, fast on graphics hardware. An attention-based global message scheme adds speed while keeping approximation quality strong. Benchmarks on hard real data sets for family tree inference showed the method is both effective and efficient, aiding work on larger data.
arxiv-2507-18480:
David Nunez, Francesc Wilhelmi, Lorenzo Galati-Giordano, Giovanni Geraci, and Boris Bellalta study coordinated spatial reuse as a way to cut latency in Wi-Fi 8. Their 2025 paper is set against apps such as cloud gaming and extended reality, which need high throughput and low delay.

Coordinated spatial reuse can let access points transmit at the same time, raising spectral efficiency in dense settings. The authors propose an implementation aligned with ongoing Wi-Fi 8 standardization. They evaluate it in a Wi-Fi simulator across relevant scenarios. Results in a wireless local area network show how the mechanism behaves under load. Better reuse could raise overall network performance without new spectrum.
arxiv-2507-18580:
Jiahao Wang, Ramen Liu, Longhui Zhang, and Jing Li report a system for fine-grained detection of hate speech in Chinese text. Their report is from two thousand twenty-five. The task is hard because hate can hide in coded words and group labels. A good system must pull out who is targeted, with what words, and in what way.

Their design first simplifies the task from four linked parts to three. It then searches the training set for similar examples and feeds them in as context. Last, it runs the model several times and takes a vote across rounds, which steadies the output. On the test data, their system beat a top commercial model by a wide margin. It also edged out the same base model trained in the standard way.
arxiv-2507-18680:
Oscar Fernandez Vicente studies machine learned trading in a 2025 thesis on market making. Market makers quote buy and sell prices all day, keeping markets liquid. They face real hazards: stock piles up on one side, rivals undercut them, and markets shift without warning.

Reinforcement learning trains an agent by trial and reward inside a simulated market. The thesis builds such agents for lone and multi agent settings. Stock risk is handled two ways, through reward design and through hedging rules. The work asks whether learned agents can adapt their quoting to stay profitable as conditions move, rather than follow fixed rules set by hand.
arxiv-2507-18880:
Luca-Maxim Meinhardt and Enrico Rukzio rethink accessible prototyping methods for blind and visually impaired passengers in highly automated vehicles. Such cars could improve how this group gets around. The hard part is to make tools that do not use sight, yet keep riders aware of the drive at each point in time.

Two participatory design workshops looked at what facts riders need and what a tool of this kind might look like. In the first, riders built their own low fidelity prototypes. In the second, they tried and talked through the test models the team had made for them. What they said in both rounds shaped the last systems, built to keep riders aware on the road. The authors lay out each set up and share what they learned on how these methods could be made better for this group.
arxiv-2507-19480:
Bešlić and a large team of co-authors mapped the ionization fraction across the Orion B molecular cloud in twenty twenty-five. The ionization fraction is the share of gas particles that carry an electric charge. It shapes how clouds form stars, but it is hard to measure outside dense cores, where only a few faint lines can be seen.

The team used fresh chemical models that pick out line ratios able to trace the fraction in thin and thick gas alike. They observed many molecular lines in the three-to-four millimeter band across Orion B. The fraction ran far higher in thin, lit gas than in dense gas. In dense regions lit by ultraviolet light, it fell as density rose. The map gives star formation studies a firmer base across a whole cloud.
arxiv-2507-19680: Niclas Göring and five co-authors question how well current theory explains learning in neural networks, in a research paper from 2025. Networks can beat older methods by a wide margin because they learn useful features from data. The team proposes a measure called feature quality and tests show that current theories mostly gauge how strongly a network learns features, not how good those features are. They conclude these theories alone cannot explain why networks generalize well to new data.
arxiv-2507-19780:
Zhiming Liu, Paul Hill, and Nantheera Anantrasirichai present a compact framework that both clears air turbulence from images and finds targets in them, in a paper from 2025. Turbulence warps video with ripples, blur, and flicker. That hurts both image quality and detection. Doing the two jobs in sequence wastes effort and loses accuracy.

Their framework, JDATT, joins a strong clearing model and a detector, then shrinks both by joint distillation. A large model's skill is passed to a small one at two levels: inner features and final outputs. Tests on synthetic and real turbulence data showed better restored images and detection scores. Model size and running time fell sharply, suiting live use on light gear such as remote cameras.
arxiv-2507-19880:
