Croce and South show how a fake tool server can trick an AI aid into theft in this twenty twenty-five paper. A shared tongue now lets aids call out to tools from far firms with ease. That trust opens a door that had not been probed in depth till now.

Inside, a fake sky tool hides a hunt for a linked bank tool in its code. Once called, it steers the aid to pull a user's bank sums out. The whole chain needs just base code skill and free web tools to run. No costly rig or deep hack craft is part of the chain at all. The pair urges quick shields now and tongue rules that curb cross-tool trust.
arxiv-2507-20280:
Keyan Ding and co-authors build SciToolAgent in a 2025 paper, a language model agent that runs many science tools for the user. Modern research leans on expert software, yet picking and chaining tools takes deep skill.

At its core sits a knowledge graph of tools that guides smart choice and step order through graph-based search. A safety check module guards against unsafe or unethical tool use. Tests on a curated benchmark show the agent beats prior methods by a clear margin. Case studies span protein design, reaction prediction, synthesis, and screening of porous materials. The agent aims to open expert tools to non-experts too.
arxiv-2507-20380:
Yu-Kuo Hsiao, Yan-Li Wang, and Wen-Juan Wei hunt for the elusive kappa meson in semileptonic D decays, in a two thousand twenty-five particle physics paper. The kappa, also called K0 star 700, is the least settled of the light scalar resonances.

A partial-wave analysis of the decay D plus to K minus, pi plus, positron, and neutrino extracts a clear kappa signal. Its branching fraction, formerly assumed negligible, actually dominates the observed s-wave rate, meaning the evidence sat mislabeled as background. The extracted form factor is far below the quark-antiquark prediction and close to the tetraquark expectation. The authors read this as support for a compact tetraquark nature of the kappa.
arxiv-2507-20480:
Shiyang Liu and five co-authors present a way to merge 3D scene maps without human help. Their 2025 paper works with 3D Gaussian Splatting, a method that builds scenes from many soft blobs for fast rendering. Most work builds one map at a time. Joining several sub-maps into one scene usually needs manual steps and blunt filtering.

The team first pulls out the skeleton shape of each scene to line the sub-maps up. A special filter reads the blobs' traits to make the match robust. For merging, a multi-factor plan replaces hard cut-offs that used to drop scene detail. On test scenes, alignment error fell by about forty-two percent on hard cases. Render quality after merging rose sharply, keeping fine structure intact.
arxiv-2507-20680:
Deepak Joshi and Mayukha Pal teach a light transformer to paint solar panel faults in drone heat images. Hotspots and snail trails sap a module's output and can worsen unseen. Their 2025 study starts from 277 aerial thermal images shot by a drone-mounted infrared camera. Contrast boosting, denoising, and normalization prep each frame. A trimmed SegFormer model then segments faults pixel by pixel, trained on hand-labeled regions.

Four rival networks face the same data and prep. The light model wins on accuracy and efficiency, especially for small, ragged defects. Scores span Dice, F1, kappa, overlap, and pixel accuracy. Its small footprint suits edge devices on the drone itself. Farm-scale automatic inspection is the target use.
arxiv-2507-20780:
Churazov leads a team explaining how fast electrons can cross galaxy clusters without losing their energy in a 2025 paper. Radio-bright electrons should fade within short travel distances under normal conditions. Yet glowing filaments stretch for hundreds of thousands of light years.

The authors argue that filaments with ordered magnetic fields and non-thermal pressure change the rules. Inside them, the limiting wave speed is far higher than in the surrounding hot gas. Electrons can stream along such filaments without the usual expansion losses. The model predicts how the radio spectrum should bend with local gas pressure. It also predicts strongly polarized emission. Some filaments may hide as diffuse glow while still channeling electrons. No reheating shock is needed.
arxiv-2507-20880:
Renhang Liu and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on JAM, a compact flow-based model that turns lyrics into songs. Recent song generators sound decent but give musicians little control at the word level. JAM claims the first word-level timing and duration control in this class, letting users place each sung word in time.

A preference tuning method polishes quality using a synthetic feedback set, with no hand labels needed. The team also released a public test set, JAME, to standardize how lyrics-to-song models are judged. On the authors' measures, JAM beat current rivals on music-specific traits while staying small.
arxiv-2507-21380:
Dylan Jow, Anna Tsai, and Ue-Li Pen ask how sharp a gravitational wave sky map can be in a 2025 paper. Pulsar timing arrays have found evidence for a background hum of very long waves. The usual test compares correlation curves but gives no direction and ignores wave polarization.

The authors build a simple estimator that maps wave power across the sky. Their map also tracks polarization state, which doubles the space the map must cover. They then ask how many independent pixels such a map can truly hold. That count sets the real resolution limit for this young field. Knowing the limit guides how future data should be read and displayed.
arxiv-2507-21980:
Finding what microbes live in a soil or water sample usually takes lab work, but the sample's paperwork alone may betray the answer. Hyunwoo Yoo and Gail Rosen test in 2025 whether large language models can read environmental metadata and name the habitat class, even flagging the risk of contamination by a common gut bacterium. They try four leading models with no training examples and with a few.

Across several real data sets the language models beat random forests at sorting samples into ontology classes. They also predicted contamination risk well, carrying across sites with different paperwork styles. The authors present metadata only reading as a real option where samples are few and labels messy. Biosurveillance is among the uses they name.
arxiv-2507-22080:
Sun and co-authors grow in 2025 training data for code writing models by letting two agents argue their way to better examples. Hand made instruction code pairs are costly, and machine made ones often rest on rigid recipes that flatten the logic. Their Coder writes solutions while a Reviewer steers the whole path.

The Reviewer drafts a schema that plans difficulty and structure before code appears. Compiler verdicts plus semantic checks verify each pair in the loop. The resulting hundred thousand pairs carry stepped difficulty. Models tuned on them beat baselines across coding benchmarks, the team report.
arxiv-2507-22380:
Yifei Chen and four co-authors help robots that learn by copying experts stop being fooled by side details in what they see. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Copy-based training can latch onto clues that do not drive the expert's acts. When the scene shifts a little, those false clues break the robot.

Their fix learns which parts of the view truly cause the expert's moves. It does so by stepping in and changing the policy's inputs, then watching what shifts. The team shows the heavy feature-splitting step used before is not in fact needed. Their light framework plugs into modern copy-based systems. Tests with a two-armed robot in simulation show far better carry-over to new scenes. The method could make trained robots less brittle on factory and lab floors.
arxiv-2507-22780:
Ocampo and co-authors forecast consistency tests of the standard cosmology model with the Euclid mission in a 2025 paper, written for the Euclid Consortium. The model, called Lambda CDM, ties cosmic expansion to structure growth. Growth rate data can check whether the two sides still agree as precision improves.

The team simulates what Euclid's growth measurements will allow scholars to conclude. Tensions, if real, would show as failed consistency checks between expansion and growth. The forecasts help the mission plan analyses that squeeze the most from its data. Cosmology's standard model faces its sharpest audit in the coming decade.
arxiv-2507-23380:
Shane Cooper and Ilia Kamotski study how a mixed material with tiny repeated fibers behaves at large scale. Their 2025 paper treats a material made of stiff directional fibers set in a plain base, with fiber spacing shrinking toward zero. In some directions the material loses its grip as the pattern shrinks, which breaks standard tools.

Past work showed the bulk response settles to a limit as spacing shrinks. Here the authors give a full near-limit account and prove error bounds of the first order in spacing. A thin layer near each fiber needs its own care, since the loss of grip acts unevenly by direction. Such bounds matter for design of fiber composites in planes and machines.
arxiv-2507-23580:
Bradley Keister, Saeed Najafi, Joan-Emma Shea, and Krastan Blagoev study why droplets in living cells do not merge and grow the way simple physics predicts, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In a still system, big droplets tend to swallow small ones in a process called Ostwald ripening. Cells stay out of balance, though, and their droplets seem protected from that fate.

The authors ran computer models of particles that pull on each other, then pushed the system out of balance in two ways. In one, particles randomly flipped between two states; in the other, their speeds were randomly reset. In every driven case, ripening stopped, while calm systems ripened as expected. The team suggests this effect may be what keeps cell droplets stable.
arxiv-2507-23680:
Alexis Béjar-López, Rafael Granero-Belinchón, Carlos Pulido, and Juan Soler analyze a model of cell crowds pushed by their own pressure, in work from 2025. Density and occupied area feed back on each other: crowding raises pressure, and pressure spreads or squeezes the tissue. Such loops shape growth and motion.

Their system pairs porous-medium spreading with cross terms that tie area change to density change, plus a term that works against spreading. They prove short-term solutions exist and stay non-negative for smooth starts. Sameness of solutions needs a mild extra condition. Some starts blow up in finite time, hinting at sharp fronts. The crowd's footprint stays fixed in shape under their rules.
arxiv-2507-23780:
In ordinary flat materials, even slight disorder traps electrons and kills metallic behavior. Alexander Tyner and co-authors show that a special kind of two-dimensional system escapes that fate. They build it by projecting a 3D crystal down: starting from a three-dimensional lattice, they mathematically integrate out some degrees of freedom, leaving a 2D projected brane that remembers its parent.

Large computer calculations show these branes keep stable metal and semimetal phases, just like the 3D originals. The critical exponents at their phase transitions, where metal turns to insulator or semimetal to metal, land close to the 3D values. The authors call the branes holographic images of the parent crystals. They point to photonic lattices, where disorder can be dialed in through the refractive index, as a realistic place to build and test them.
arxiv-2508-00180:
Averaging model weights during fine-tuning smooths wild swings, but the average lags behind fresh learning. Adam Block and Cyril Zhang fix that lag in work from twenty twenty-five. Small batch sizes in fine-tuning make the swings worse, so the smoothing trick is widely used despite its cost.

Their fix, a bias-corrected average, keeps the calm of averaging while wiping out the lag bias. A simple math model proves the fix can beat both plain training and the old average. Broad tests on language models backed the claim: faster settling and better final scores on standard checks. The change is small and cheap to add, which the authors pitch as its main charm for busy training teams.
arxiv-2508-00580:
Raul Castilla-Arquillo and four colleagues build a perception system, in a 2025 preprint, to help planetary rovers judge the ground ahead. A rover must sort sand, bedrock, and packed soil to travel safely. No single sensor sees all of that well. Color, depth, and heat images each carry part of the story. Heat images in particular reveal soil type through how fast ground warms and cools. The team fuses all three in one network.

Their network, OmniUnet, is built on transformer blocks. To train it, they mounted a custom sensor box on a test rover and drove it in a Spanish semi-desert that mimics Mars. Part of that data was labeled by hand. The network reached pixel accuracy above eighty percent on tests. It answered in well under a second on a small onboard computer. The team released the code and labeled data for others to use.
arxiv-2508-01480:
Dimitra Panou and co-authors pool many language models to answer biomedical questions in a 2025 paper. Biomedical literature grows fast, which makes text mining and question answering both vital and demanding. Their entry to a long running biomedical challenge uses open source large models as retrieval augmented generators for two question tasks.

Thirteen top open models were evaluated, and all combinations were explored to build tailored pipelines per question type. Majority voting settles yes or no questions, while list and factoid answers merge the union of model outputs. In the 2025 challenge rounds their system placed first for ideal answers in one task round, among other top placings.
arxiv-2508-01780:
Guozhao Mo and co-authors benchmark AI agents on using a vast ocean of software tools, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A common protocol now links language models to over ten thousand tool servers. Past tests used one server and fed tools straight to the model, skipping the hard parts.

Their bench holds ninety-five real daily tasks and a suite of seventy servers with hundreds of tools. An automated judge checks true task outcomes. Twelve top models were graded: the best passed near four in five tasks, while most passed only a third to a half. Retrieval slips caused near half of all failures.
arxiv-2508-01880:
Duo Zhang and co-authors give volatility forecasts a moving sense of the market's mood. Their 2025 paper notes a trade-off in finance models: full multivariate models are too heavy for real portfolios, while factor models freeze the links between assets just when those links matter most.

Their framework answers with factors whose loadings drift over time, pulled cheaply from realized volatility data. The same dynamic factors plug into both classic statistical models and AI forecasters, so each asset's own rhythm and the market's shared swings are modeled together. Across big tech stocks and major cryptocurrencies, at one-day and one-week horizons, forecasts sharpened. A pairs-trading strategy built on them earned stronger risk-adjusted returns, especially in rough markets.
arxiv-2508-01980:
Xiaoyu Zhang and co-authors thin out point clouds in a 2025 paper while keeping the points that matter for self driving cars. Point clouds from car sensors are huge, which strains storage, bandwidth, and processing budgets.

Their method works in two steps. First it detects which objects are present, using either an unsupervised density method or a simple trained classifier, to suit the scene. Then it splits the sampling budget so object points are kept at a high rate while background points are cut hard. Tests on two major driving data sets beat top baselines at many sampling rates. The method is model agnostic and can sit in front of many downstream tools.
arxiv-2508-02280:
Databases in memory need short strings squeezed hard yet readable one at a time, and a 2025 arXiv paper by Francesco Gargiulo and Rossano Venturini offers a compressor built for that niche. Their method, OnPair, grows a dictionary by merging the most common neighbor pairs in one pass over a sample.

A capped variant keeps entries at sixteen bytes, which speeds up matching. Because each string is compressed on its own, any single value can be read without unpacking a block. On real datasets the pair matched the squeeze of the standard learned method while running faster and using less memory. The authors aim it at in memory stores.
arxiv-2508-02680:
Pragya Singh and co-authors published a study in 2025 on a framework for collecting emotion data in daily life for AI training. Emotion AI needs quality labeled data from real settings, not just labs. The team gathered views from the public, professionals, and experts through surveys, interviews, and group talks. Over one hundred stakeholders informed the design.

Their framework, AnnoSense, supports gathering body-signal emotion data with sound labels in everyday contexts. Two dozen emotion AI experts judged it clear, useful, and adaptable. The paper closes with next steps and what the framework means for future work on real-world emotion data.
arxiv-2508-02880:
Pengwei Sun and four co-authors evaluate fake-but-plausible brain scans in twenty twenty-five. Counterfactual generation simulates how a scan would look under a hypothetical change. It could help explain disease and create realistic training data. For 3D brain MRI, the task is hard: data is scarce, anatomy is complex, and no standard evaluation exists.

The team converted six generative models into counterfactual ones. Each was guided by a causal graph in which regional brain volumes act as direct inputs. They judged the models on composition, reversibility, realism, effectiveness, and minimality. Scans came from a major Alzheimer's disease imaging initiative. They also tested how well each model carried to other data. Readers get a benchmark for a fast-growing medical imaging idea.
arxiv-2508-03280:
Fact graphs can hold more than plain links: a fact may carry side notes, such as a time or a place. Yubo Wang and co-authors ask in 2025 if the extra notes drive the wins of graph learn tools, or if the base tool does. They turn rich graphs into plain ones in three ways and test old tools on them.

Some old tools matched the rich tools, which blurs the claim. The turns, though, warp the graph's shape and lose some facts. Rich tools, in turn, oft lose long range links or squeeze side notes too thin. The team then builds a tool that keeps the graph whole, reads far links, and joins side notes with care. It beat the rich pack.
arxiv-2508-03380:
Sreenath Manikandan and Frank Wilczek estimate a quantum twist in gravitational waves in a 2025 paper. When black holes merge, the final hole rings down with fading tones called quasinormal modes. Nonlinear gravity in that ringdown can spawn higher tones at set amplitude ratios.

Those ratios let the authors estimate how much squeezing the waves carry. Squeezing is a quantum trait where noise drops below the usual floor in one measure. For a non-spinning black hole, the estimate lands near one percent. The effect is small but, in principle, stamped on real signals. Future detectors with finer ears could hunt for this faint quantum mark.
arxiv-2508-03780:
Katharina Hoedt, Arthur Flexer, and Gerhard Widmer ask in a 2025 paper whether music emotion models that stay easy to read are also harder to fool. Models that guess mood from songs can flip their answer after tiny input changes that people would not notice. The team compared a readable model with a black box model when both faced crafted tricky inputs. They also added a model trained to resist such tricks.

The readable model held up better than the black box one under attack. Its strength was close to that of the attack trained model, but at lower computing cost. Readers learn that building a model around clear, meaningful features may buy safety as well as clarity, at least in this music task.
arxiv-2508-04080:
Jinfan Tang, Kunming Wu, and co-authors build in a 2025 paper a framework that sharpens language model guesses about places. Standard prompting treats each place apart, ignoring how near places sway each other. Even strong models drift from spatial sense and favor crowded regions in their answers.

Their framework refines guesses step by step over a graph built on the fly. One operator lays the graph so near nodes respect a spatial Markov rule. A second enriches nodes with task fit facts drawn from text sources. A third passes plain language messages between nodes to shrink spatial mismatch. Tests on physical and social economic tasks beat plain prompting by wide margins. Geographic bias shrank as a side gain of the refinement loop.
arxiv-2508-04280:
George Bredis, Stanislav Dereka, Viacheslav Sinii, and co-authors train vision-language models in cheap virtual worlds so the skills carry to real tasks. Models that see and read still struggle to turn what they see into a sound chain of actions. Prior training in simulators seldom proved that the skill would transfer.

Their method updates action words with a standard policy method while learning value only at the level of whole steps. Training in one simple simulator at a time led to gains on game control, spatial planning, and web tasks with real images. General image understanding stayed intact, which supports training in synthetic worlds.
arxiv-2508-04380:
Tuan Hoang, Chuyen Nguyen, and Thanh Pham blend two access schemes for light-based wireless networks in a 2025 paper. Their users share LED light links, served in time slots. Inside each slot, up to two users can share one channel at once by power splitting, if their signal strengths differ enough for clean separation.

The pairing choice is the crux. For any pair, the authors compute the range of channel-strength ratios where sharing beats taking turns, solving two optimization problems with an approximation method. Simulations across user counts and LED powers show their adaptive scheme beats the fixed hybrid baseline on total data rate. The design aims to keep the added complexity low.
arxiv-2508-04580:
Yi and four colleagues probe how electrons localize in a near periodic lattice with mixed disorder in twenty twenty-five. In the clean case, waves spread, then pass through a middle phase, then trap as the pattern strengthens. Adding staggered or sequence based patterns changes the story. One kind merely shifts the trapping point.

Two sequence patterns trap waves at once, and the team ties that to pattern complexity. A typical fidelity measure scales cleanly at the transition, giving firm exponents. One pattern family shows fresh exponent values distinct from known models. Two unlike patterns share one exponent, though. The work unifies trapping rules across pattern types.
arxiv-2508-04780:
Lin Jiang, Dahai Yu, Rongchao Xu, Tian Tang, and Guang Wang design fairer power repair after disasters in a 2025 paper. Storms knock out power more often, and crews must choose where to work first. Firms often follow request counts, but poorer areas send fewer requests. That leaves them waiting longer, the authors show.

Their frame first predicts repair times with a method that states its own uncertainty in an equity-aware way. A learning agent then plans repairs while adapting to that uncertainty across areas. Tests cut average outage time by a few percent and cut inequity between communities by a larger share, they report.
arxiv-2508-05280:
James M Cline writes a comment on a claimed unified field theory, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The theory, set out in a recent post, says it joins gravity with the Standard Model. It claims to be finite and unitary, and to predict all values of the model from just two inputs.

Cline points to a missed result: the photon gains mass at one loop in that model. The cause is a lack of gauge invariance in its non-local interaction points. He also clears up a point about Wick rotation that had clouded the debate. He spells out more of the gauge troubles, and he flags a domain wall problem in the model as well.
arxiv-2508-05680:
Urchs and co-authors test whether search and retrieval systems treat academic men and women even handedly. Algorithms shape who gets seen in science, yet are often assumed neutral. Their 2025 study defines fairness as outputs that mirror real gender shares without widening them, then audits a mixed dataset of German academic profiles.

No outright discrimination appeared. Still, male professors drew more search results and tidier publication records, while women's online visibility swung more widely. The authors trace the pattern to a blend of platform ranking, institutional curation, and personal self presentation. They argue fairness checks must weigh both technical accuracy and fair representation, since quiet imbalances can shape careers.
arxiv-2508-05780:
Paulo Carvalho-Neto and co-authors widen an energy bound for fractional time equations in a 2025 paper. Energy estimates steer the study of how systems evolve, but with fractional time derivatives the classic identity needs a smoothness trait that is hard to check. The team recasts the bound for square integrable functions on open domains.

Their proof asks only that the solution stays essentially bounded in time. The needed smoothness then shows up inside the argument on its own. That wider reach backs the Faedo Galerkin method for such problems. As a payoff, they prove firm results for the fractional heat equation.
arxiv-2508-05880:
Bhattacharyya and co-authors compare how large language models and humans sort feelings into categories. Their study, titled Too Categorical to be Human, asks whether models hold emotion ideas in a human-like way. Feelings shape how models behave in high-stakes chats, so their inner grasp of emotion matters for safety and for apps that face users.

Direct checks of a model's inner workings cannot be matched against the human brain, where emotion is spread widely. So the team uses an outside test: how each side judges emotional scenes along clear scales, such as whether a scene feels good or bad, expected or surprising. Those judgment patterns act as fingerprints of the underlying ideas. Comparing the fingerprints shows where models match people and where they differ.
arxiv-2508-05980:
Yun Gao proves rigidity results for holomorphic maps between Shilov boundaries of type-I bounded symmetric domains, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The work starts by defining an orthogonal structure on complex Grassmannians, and from it a class of orthogonal mappings that generalizes the holomorphic maps in question.

Analyzing the geometry of these mappings yields rigidity: the maps are forced into simple forms. For maps from a rank-one boundary, meaning unit spheres, into a higher-rank boundary, Gao shows they must be constant in one parameter range. In a middle range they reduce, after normalization by automorphisms, to standard linear embeddings. The bounds are optimal and extend known results for maps between rank-one cases.
arxiv-2508-06080:
Bin Xia and co-authors build DreamVE, one model that edits both images and video from plain text instructions. Editing by instruction is easy for users, but video editors have been held back by scarce training data. Their 2025 paper trains in two stages: images first, then video, so the model learns from plentiful image data before the harder task.

The team also built data pipelines that make training pairs at scale. One route pastes objects and backgrounds into collages for tasks like object swaps and text changes. Another uses generative models to build pairs. Vision readers get a unified editor design plus a recipe for the data such models need.
arxiv-2508-06180:
Ten Kate, Ohnmacht, and eleven colleagues listen to the bound states inside germanium Josephson junctions with microwave spectroscopy, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Germanium quantum wells, paired with superconductors, are a fresh platform for Andreev bound states, thanks to strong spin-orbit coupling and clean transport.

The team built junctions in proximitized germanium wells and read their spectra with microwaves. A short junction, three hundred fifty nanometers long, showed signs of several bound states, matched by a model with finite-length effects. A longer junction, one point two micrometers, needed a model with three bound states in two channels plus Coulomb interaction between charges. Interactions, often ignored, clearly shape the spectra. The results form a base for controlling these states in future devices. Germanium is attractive because it fits the silicon technology world.
arxiv-2508-06280:
Gokul Adethya and Jaya Nirmala test continual learning for Indian speech recognition in a 2025 paper. India tongues arrive one by one in real data, and a model that retrains on all at once breaks privacy and scale. Continual learning adds new languages while guarding old ones.

A Conformer model tuned first on Hindi then learned eight more languages in line. Three guard methods, elastic weight consolidation, memory aware synapses, and learning without forgetting, faced plain fine tuning. Word error and backward transfer scores on clean and noisy speech showed the guards curb forgetting. Epoch counts per task were varied as well.
arxiv-2508-06480:
Yaoxuan Zeng and Malte Jansen study heat flow in the oceans of icy moons in a 2025 paper. How heat moves under the ice shapes the thickness of the ice shell, which spacecraft can observe. Global models cannot resolve the small scale churning that carries much of that heat.

The pair run fine scale simulations of slantwise convection, where churning follows the spin axis rather than straight up and down. They isolate that process from other sources of motion. Total heat flow followed a known scaling law, with a latitude effect added. Upward flow grew toward the poles, and sideways flow ran poleward too. The pattern would thin ice near the poles, matching what is seen on Enceladus.
arxiv-2508-06580:
Three authors led by Achraf Zinihi price germ insurance on a live epidemic model, not on still death tables. Old life cover maths miss how a germ wave bends death odds month by month. Their SEIARD frame tracks the well, the bare, the sick with and sans signs, the healed, and the dead. Rent, payout, and pure price sums are built on those flows.

A hold-back fund path is traced through the wave in the same frame. Germ push, death push, and leave push each get a sway read on life odds. Odd-step sims run the sums across cover kinds and wave grades. Insurers gain a wave-true price kit for the next outbreak.
arxiv-2508-06680:
Douglas Ulmer and Jose Felipe Voloch study rare meets on curved surfaces in a 2025 math paper. Their stage is a surface swept by elliptic curves, with a marked path that runs without end. Past work by Ulmer and a partner counted how often that path just grazes a twist-fixed path, a rare meet by any count.

Such counts were first done with tools that fail where the base field has prime cycles. The pair extend the counts to those fields, and add a fresh route for the classic case. Their new meets tie to a famed map of Manin, a deep bridge in the field.
arxiv-2508-06780:
Nizamudheen V, Riyasudheen T K, Noufal Asharaf, and Shefeeq T solve a fractional option pricing equation numerically in a 2025 study. The time-fractional Black-Scholes equation prices European options when prices move with long memory, as if through a fractal market process. Fractional derivatives look backward over history, which makes accurate solutions hard to compute.

Their algorithm combines a standard fractional time step with a spatial method based on modified cubic splines. Differential quadrature turns the spatial part into algebra a computer can solve efficiently. The hybrid scheme aims for accuracy without heavy cost. Better solvers help test whether fractional models describe real option markets.
arxiv-2508-07180:
Zhe Zhang and co-authors build a new way to test code-writing models in a 2025 paper. Static test sets get leaked into training data, and weak tests let wrong code pass. Their answer scales two things at once: fresh problems drawn from live code bases, and tough auto-built tests that must cover every branch.

The first suite holds tasks in Python and Java drawn from real projects. Testing ten top models showed they handle simple API use well but falter at writing fresh algorithms. Language ecosystem shaped scores strongly. Strict testing exposed an illusion of correctness in easier benchmarks. Readers get a harder, fairer yardstick for coding models.
arxiv-2508-07380:
Taegeun Song and Nojoon Myoung published a paper in 2025 on electron interferometers built inside graphene, where split electron waves recombine and betray their phases. In strong magnetic fields, junctions between oppositely doped regions form the beam splitters, and the interference is unusually robust. The authors study what happens when the two junctions are gated unequally.

Unequal gates resize the loop the electrons enclose, and at higher filling factors extra paths appear, tangling the signal into beat patterns. A machine-learning-assisted Fourier analysis untangles those beats more cleanly than standard processing. Visibility, the contrast of the interference fringes, peaks when the gates are symmetric. The work reads as a tuning manual for graphene quantum optics, where asymmetry is a knob, not just a flaw.
arxiv-2508-07680:
Zhiying Li and eleven co-authors improve virtual try-on software, which shows shoppers how clothes look on their photos. A common hard case is swapping a long-sleeved top for a short-sleeved one. Current tools often fail there because the photo hides the arm, and the software fills in skin poorly. The team traces the flaw to a habit of these models: they copy the majority pattern of the input, which buries the bare arm.

Their framework virtually removes the top to reveal the torso, then dresses it in the new garment, splitting one hard step into two easier ones. It needs no training and wraps around existing try-on tools. Added steps sharpen detail and keep quality steady during generation. The team built a test set for this sleeve swap task. Across tests, their method beat the best tools on detail and image quality.
arxiv-2508-07780:
Georg Kyhn, Eric Lindstrom, and Larisa Beilina rebuild the electric traits of skin cancer in three dimensions from waves bounced off a true shape model, in a paper from 2025. Those traits set how the tumor takes fields, which counts for scan and heat care plans. The team fits traits that make a sim bounce match the bounce felt at the skin of the model.

A split solve that pairs two grid maths runs the fit, with slope led hunts for the best trait maps. Tests at a high wave band give trait maps that match the true model in form and in size to a fair grade. The authors frame the work as a step to trait maps that can steer care for this cancer.
arxiv-2508-08080:
Cas Oude Hoekstra and Floris den Hengst extend an interpretable modeling method from averages to the whole shape of an outcome's distribution, in a 2025 paper. Symbolic regression builds small, readable formulas that predict a target's mean. But decisions in safety-critical fields need more: the median, or a worst-case extreme. Their method, symbolic quantile regression, fits readable formulas to any chosen quantile of the outcome.

In an extensive evaluation, the method beat other transparent models and matched a strong black-box baseline, all without giving up readability. A case study on airline fuel use shows the explanatory payoff: separate formulas for extreme and central outcomes reveal how a factor's influence changes across the distribution. The authors conclude the approach is fit for predicting conditional quantiles where the reasoning must be inspectable. They frame it as a step toward white-box models that describe distributions, not just averages.
arxiv-2508-08380:
Rohan Bali, Trevor Bailey, Michael Bullock, and Boulat Bash published this communications paper in 2025. Covert communication hides the very existence of a message, not just its content. Theory sets a strict limit, the square root law: over a channel used n times, only about the square root of n bits can pass undetected. Turning that math into hardware is hard, because ordinary link upkeep operations would give the game away. Only two prior experiments existed, both on optical channels.

The team demonstrates provably covert radio communication using software-defined radios. Their setup sends messages that a watcher cannot reliably distinguish from noise, within the proven limits. The authors say the experiment validates the theory on a radio channel for the first time. It also opens practical questions about building real covert systems and about what adversaries would need to detect them.
arxiv-2508-08480:
Camerlo, Marcone, and Motto Ros settle a question Krasner posed in the nineteen fifties about symmetry groups of ultrametric spaces. Their 2025 paper characterizes the isometry groups of Polish ultrametric spaces, which are separable and complete. The answer uses generalized wreath products of full permutation groups.

The work also closes a 2003 problem of Gao and Kechris, since the solution lives in the finer world of topological groups. Natural subclasses of these spaces match exactly to wreath product variants proposed by Hall, Holland, and Malicki. Ultrametric spaces appear across number theory and computer science, so a full symmetry catalogue has wide reach. The authors present the match as exact, not approximate, on both sides of the correspondence.
arxiv-2508-08680:
Armel Zebaze, Benoît Sagot, and Rachel Bawden generate topic-diverse training text for low-resource translation in a 2025 paper. Language models translate well into big languages but stumble into small ones, and the parallel data that could teach them is scarce and narrow. Back-translation helps only when good target texts exist.

TopXGen flips the flow: the model writes fresh, varied target-language texts itself, exploiting its strength in big languages and its multilingual reach. Those texts are then translated back into a rich source language, yielding diverse parallel pairs. Used for fine-tuning and in-context examples, the synthetic data lifted translation quality into low-resource languages. Code and outputs are public.
arxiv-2508-08880:
Marcin Sendera, Amin Sorkhei, and Tomasz Kusmierczyk study how to give Bayesian neural networks function-space priors by learning their activation functions, in a 2025 paper. A prior in function space states beliefs about the model's outputs directly. That is a more natural way to encode what a user expects, and it helps with uncertainty and risk-aware choices. The hard part is forcing a network to match a rich target prior.

Their approach trains the activation functions themselves. They try flexible forms, such as rational functions and piecewise linear functions. They also discuss the learning snags that arise, such as identifiability and symmetries in the loss. Even a network with one wide hidden layer could match complex target priors in their tests. That opens a simpler path to priors.
arxiv-2508-09180:
Huifa Li and co-authors cluster single cells by learned graphs in a 2025 paper, presenting scAGC. Naming cell types from single-cell RNA data is a key analysis step, but the data are vast, sparse, and full of zeros. Graph methods that freeze cell links in advance suffer from noise and lopsided neighborhoods.

ScAGC learns the cell graph and the cell features together, end to end. A sampling trick lets the graph rewire itself during training toward balance. A loss built for zero-heavy count data keeps reconstruction honest, and a contrastive term steadies the graph. On nine real data sets it beat rival methods on standard scores.
arxiv-2508-09380:
Pete Rigas studies what happens when multiplayer quantum games are repeated in parallel, published in 2025. In such games, several players answer questions without communicating, and quantum strategies can beat classical ones. Parallel repetition asks how fast the winning chance falls when many copies of a game are played at once.

Rigas works with an anchored form of the game, a variant used to make the analysis tractable. He shows that the optimal winning value of the anchored game decays exponentially under parallel repetition. The proof leans on several probability calculations: expected values under the anchoring change, measurement operators tied to those quantities, and relative entropy measures. Generalized error bounds from his earlier work on multiplayer games also play a role.
arxiv-2508-09680:
Autistic workers bring prized strengths to software work, from sharp focus to care for detail, yet hiring and office habits built for the majority shut many out. Orvila Sarker, Mona Jamshaid, and Ali Babar gather what is known about fixing that in a 2025 review. They screen thirty studies and sort the success factors for a full career path.

Eighteen factors fall into four groups: schooling, career training, the work setting, and assistive tools. Gaps named in the studies span stiff hiring, noisy open rooms, and thin support from workmates. The review turns those findings into plain advice for schools, employers, and tool makers. Clear roles, structured rooms, and meeting habits that share the floor all make the list, along with tailored adjustments for each worker.
arxiv-2508-09880:
Noureldin Bayoumi and co-authors compare ways to combine rival speech recognition systems in a 2025 paper. Different model designs explore the search space in different ways, so their errors differ too. Merging their strengths can yield a better final transcript than any single system gives.

Their method works in two passes. Each model first drafts its own candidate transcripts, then the drafts are pooled, rescored by both models, and merged with a weighted score to pick the winner. This keeps comparisons fair across designs, unlike merging during the first pass where decoding styles clash. They test pairs across four model families with varied label units on a standard nine-hundred-sixty-hour English task.
arxiv-2508-10080:
Jiaqiang Yan and co-authors report a change of crystal form in a lead-lanthanum oxide that may compete with superconductivity, in a paper from 2025. The compound cools through a transition point at 225 kelvin. Below that point, pairs of atoms shift along one axis and the crystal takes a new symmetry. Electric and heat measures show kinks at the change.

Under pressure, the change fades away. In its place, signs of superconductivity appear, peaking at a transition near ten kelvin. Computer models show the electron states barely shift at the change point. That hints the shift is driven by chemical bonding, not by the electron sea. The compound offers a clean stage for studying how weak structural shifts and superconductivity interact.
arxiv-2508-10480:
Grontas, Terpin, Balta, D'Andrea, and Lygeros present a paper from twenty twenty-five on neural networks that always respect hard constraints. Their added output layer projects network answers onto the allowed set. Splitting methods make those projections fast and reliable. Backpropagation runs through an implicit function result. The layer acts as a stand-in solver for families of optimization problems. Single problems solve faster than classic solvers at modest accuracy. Batches of problems solve dramatically faster still.

Training time and solution quality beat prior learning methods by wide margins. Multi-vehicle path planning tests the non-convex side. A graphics-ready package in JAX is released. Feasibility by design is the core promise.
arxiv-2508-10680:
Busra Bulut and a large team sharpen brain scans of unborn babies in a 2025 paper. A measure called T2 mapping can describe the growing brain, above all on gentler mid-strength scanners where the signal fades more slowly. Fetal scans, though, come as stacks of thick slices spoiled by the baby’s motion, and mapping needs repeats at several echo settings.

Their method rebuilds all echo settings jointly into one crisp 3D volume. A neural field stands in for the volume, and a physics-based penalty keeps the signal decay honest across settings. Joint rebuilding cuts scan time and resists motion better than stacking separate runs. Clearer maps could help doctors read brain growth before birth with more confidence.
arxiv-2508-10780:
Alessandro Adami and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on teaching robots to stack tasks in the right order on their own. Robots with spare joints must rank jobs like safety, aim, and speed. Hand built stacks take long to tune. Their frame learns the whole stack from a cost score that states the user's likes.

Genetic search with simulation tests both the rank order of tasks and their gains. A dual arm mobile robot served as the test bed. Learned stacks dropped moot tasks on their own and looked like expert work. All stacks moved from simulation to the real robot with no more tuning. They dodged blocks and tracked paths well, even near people.
arxiv-2508-11180:
Yiyang Shen and Weiran Wang build a learning model for data that arrives in several views, with some views missing and most labels absent. Their 2025 paper, titled No Data Wasted, extends a line of probabilistic models that merge present views by a product of experts and squeeze them through an information bottleneck. That frame, though, is fully supervised, so unlabeled rows sit idle.

The new generative model trains on both kinds of rows: likelihood on the unlabeled, bottleneck on the labeled, one shared latent space for both. View specific detail is kept in the likelihood terms, and a cross view agreement term pulls shared signal out. On complex datasets with missing views and few labels, prediction and generation both improved.
arxiv-2508-11280:
Six authors evaluate language models on tourism without labeled data in this 2025 paper. Domain benchmarks are costly to annotate, and models also hallucinate, so the team built a judge from expert reasoning structures instead of answer keys.

Their framework refines a tree of thought built by experts, checked against general quality dimensions and expert feedback, and it beat baselines by clear margins. Applied to models from thirty-two to six hundred seventy-one billion parameters, it found that scale still helps in this domain, with the largest model on top. Smaller models with explicit reasoning closed much of the gap, and for mid sized models they were more accurate and concise.
arxiv-2508-11380:
Dolev Mutzari and co-authors model city defense against drone attacks in a 2025 paper. Defenders place their own drones across a city to stop an attack and limit harm. The contest is framed as a game where the defender commits to a plan first and the attacker then picks the best reply.

The team built a method, called S2D2, that outputs a defense plan in mixed steps. Tests on data from 80 real cities showed the method beat simpler greedy rules drawn from past work. Under stated city shape rules, the authors also prove how close the plan sits to the best plan a defender could choose.
arxiv-2508-11480:
Vyacheslav Shatokhin and co-authors report light signals from a warm cloud of atoms in a 2025 physics paper. The cloud is dilute potassium vapor at room temperature. When lit, the atoms glow, and the glow carries patterned signals that point in set directions rather than spreading evenly.

The team show, by both lab work and theory, that a delayed pull between atoms explains the pattern. Light takes time to travel between atoms, and that lag shapes how they act in step. Once that lagged effect is included in full geometric detail, the theory matches all the main features of the measured spectra. The result shows that even in a thin, warm gas, atoms do not act alone.
arxiv-2508-11680:
Aditya Akella and Jonathan Farah test whether a pretrained forecasting model can predict how the United States population will change. Planners need good demographic forecasts for housing, health care, and budgets, yet classic tools demand heavy tuning for each series. The authors took population data from the Census Bureau and a federal economic database. They pitted the foundation model TimesFM against three standard baselines across six varied states.

TimesFM posted the lowest squared error in nearly 87 percent of the test cases. It did especially well for minority populations, where history is sparse and older methods wobble. Because the model arrives pretrained, it needed little task-specific adjustment. The authors say such models could help governments act earlier on demographic change. Note that the catalog creator field mixes email addresses into the author names.
arxiv-2508-11780:
An X-ray shows several shapes at once, heart, lungs, ribs, and their arrangement carries the diagnosis. Issam-Ali Moindjié and co-authors build a way to analyze that arrangement in a 2025 paper, treating all the outlines in an image as one joint object rather than separate contours.

Their method aligns the joint shapes, measures how far apart two shapes are, computes average shapes, and flattens each shape into coordinates that ordinary classifiers can use. Keeping the contours together preserves relative position, size, and tilt, the between-part information a one-by-one analysis throws away. In tests the method recovered shape changes accurately as noise grew. On segmented chest X-rays it spotted an enlarged heart more accurately than single-contour and naive rivals, and it shrugged off misalignment that hurt the others.
arxiv-2508-12280:
Bing-Sui Lu studied in a 2025 paper how random frozen charges inside a nearby slab tug on an atom's energy levels. The charges sit scattered through the slab's bulk or on its faces, fixed in place like static. Against them works the well-known Casimir-Polder pull, which draws atoms toward surfaces.

With the charges spread in a bell-shaped random pattern around zero, Lu finds the disorder always pushes levels down, an attraction. Far enough from the slab, that pull can beat the standard force. The effect fades with distance at a rate set by whether the charges hide in the bulk or on the face. Between two slabs, the resting point where the pulls cancel sits nearer the cleaner slab. The results matter for precision atom experiments near chips.
arxiv-2508-12580:
Kuan-Cheng Chien and Ming-Hsuan Kang classify special point sets on spheres in a 2025 paper. A spherical design spreads points so evenly that averages over them match the whole sphere. One way to build such sets is to orbit a point under a finite symmetry group. The pair ask exactly which group orbits meet the second moment test.

Their answer ties these orbits to orbits of compact groups inside the regular representation. The classification runs through how the space splits into symmetry blocks. Moment conditions then pick out which blocks can appear. Geometry and representation theory end up describing the same objects from two sides.
arxiv-2508-12680:
Vision-language models reason well on math puzzles but stumble across wider everyday domains, mostly for want of training data. Yuheng Zha and co-authors build that data at scale in a 2025 paper. Their set draws from forty-six sources across eight fields, from charts and screens to medicine and spatial scenes. An influence score picks the most useful samples, and a difficulty filter trims the rest.

Their model, Vision-G1, trains in rounds on the picked data with a rising curriculum. It topped similar-sized rivals on visual reasoning tests, the team reports. Even some big closed models were beaten. Data, code, and the model were released in public.
arxiv-2508-13080:
Alon Gurman and four co-authors ask whether the gas around young galaxies holds molecular hydrogen, in a 2025 astronomy paper. At great distances, clouds of neutral hydrogen block quasar light and appear as damped Lyman-alpha absorbers. Simulations suggest much of that gas may sit around galaxies rather than inside them. Its density rivals gas inside galaxies, where molecules form readily, so molecules may be present in the halo gas too.

The team builds an analytic model to estimate how much molecular hydrogen such clouds should hold. They also study whether the molecules could be detected through far-ultraviolet absorption lines. A positive detection would reshape views of how early galaxies were fed and how their surrounding gas cooled and formed stars.
arxiv-2508-13380:
Seohyeon Cha, Kevin Chan, Gustavo de Veciana, and Haris Vikalo schedule AI models across phones, edge servers, and the cloud in a 2025 study. Real services run many tasks at once, such as detection, segmentation, and depth estimation for driving or augmented reality, while older frameworks assumed one task and one model. Loading a model onto a tier costs time, and batching requests changes the math again.

Their framework decides jointly which models to load or unload at each level, with batching built into the accounting. Smart placement keeps weak devices responsive without wasting cloud capacity.
arxiv-2508-13480:
Mithra Karamchedu and Lucas Bang list a graph's spanning trees and count twin copies as one. For series-parallel graphs, they solve the task in full. Plain lists drown in twin copies from the graph's own shape flips. The paper scans the task for graphs at large, then builds tools for the two-end set.

Where each end is marked on its own, list time tracks list size. In the half-marked case, ends are a marked pair with no set roles, and the same tools bend to fit. The case with no marks at all is left to notes and open asks. One sharp point: the tools never work out the flip group as such. The loop shape of the twins' traits tracks the loop shape of the trees.
arxiv-2508-13580:
Oriana Presacan and co-authors show that how a medical chatbot picks its next words can matter as much as the model itself. Decoding is the rule that turns word odds into text. Their 2025 study tests eleven decoding rules on five open medical tasks, from translation to image captioning. Both medical and general models of several sizes took part. Speed and quality were scored side by side.

Steady rules beat random ones. Beam search, which weighs whole phrases, scored highest. Two sampling styles trailed the field. Slower rules tended to write better text. Bigger models scored more but were not tougher against bad decoding. Medical models won only two of five tasks and swung more with the rule. Careful rule choice is a cheap quality lever, the team argues.
arxiv-2508-13680:
The authors introduce a Vietnamese benchmark for vision-language models in a paper from 2025. The head of the record titles it VMMU, a multitask multimodal benchmark. It holds about two and a half thousand exam-style questions in Vietnamese across seven tasks, from science problems to rule-based visual puzzles, all needing true joint use of image and text.

Top commercial and open models were tested on the full set. Despite strong scores at reading Vietnamese text in images, the best models averaged only about sixty-six percent correct. Failures came mostly from weak grounding and reasoning over the two inputs, not from misread text. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2508-13780:
Christian Johansen and co-authors present a 2025 theory paper on false vacuum decay. A false vacuum is a state that looks stable but can give way to a lower state. Bubbles of the true state form and grow inside it. The team studies this process in a chain of quantum spins. Such chains can be built and watched in labs, unlike the early universe.

Their many-body theory tracks how bubbles form and move together. The math stays workable and matches heavy computer runs in all tested ranges, up to mid times. The team maps distinct regimes and the physics behind each. They also spell out how the lab case matches and differs from the cosmos picture. Each claim is tied to values a lab can measure. Quantum researchers get a clear frame for a classic problem, plus testable signs to hunt in spin chain trials.
arxiv-2508-13880:
Valentina Corbetta and five co-authors introduced LCRReg in twenty twenty-five, a training method that keeps medical image models honest. Deep networks often ace familiar data but fail when conditions shift, leaning on spurious cues like scanner marks instead of real anatomy. LCRReg steers a network toward features clinicians actually care about.

The method needs no concept labels in the main training set. A small side data set yields clean examples of chosen concepts, from which latent concept directions are extracted. A penalty then nudges the network to work inside those directions. On a toy task it resisted planted spurious cues, and on diabetic retinopathy screening it improved accuracy under both faked shifts and true out-of-distribution tests. It beat multitask and post-hoc rivals while staying light and architecture-free.
arxiv-2508-13980:
Almat Akhmetali studies how the setting of a star cluster shapes its form, in a 2025 paper. Open clusters, loose swarms of young stars, live alone, in pairs, or in groups. The author measured mass, age, size, tightness, and fractality for 1,876 of them, split across the three settings. Fractality marks how clumpy and self-similar a swarm's spread looks, scored by two gauges.

Group clusters came out younger, lighter, a touch larger, and looser at the core than pairs or singles. Clumpiness grew with company: about 44 percent of group clusters showed fractal bones, against about a third of singles. Both fractal gauges rose step by step from singles to pairs to groups. Heavy clusters tend to settle into smooth, round, tight forms, while light ones keep their clumps longer. The lesson is plain: no cluster ages alone, and its neighbors steer its shape.
arxiv-2508-14080:
Guanghao Jin and co-authors build a 2025 test for vision models that must find objects named in text. The task, called referring expression work, asks a model to locate the right item in one image. Older tests lean on clues inside the image alone. They thus fail to probe knowledge of the wider world.

Their benchmark, KnowDR-REC, needs fine reasoning across text and image with real-world facts. Tricky near-miss cases were built by small edits to the referring phrases. Those cases test strength against false but plausible answers. Three new scores trace how a model reasons, not just what it picks. Sixteen top models were tried on the set. All still struggled with knowledge-driven grounding. Many leaned on memorized shortcuts instead of true joint reasoning. The authors hope the test spurs more robust and clear systems.
arxiv-2508-14180:
Gaurav Bhatt and four co-authors present RewardRank, a new way to train search ranking systems, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Old rankers learn from stand-in goals that treat users in a simple way. They miss real habits, such as favoring items near the top of a list. As a result, rankers that score well in tests often fail to lift clicks or sales in live trials.

RewardRank first learns a reward model that scores any ranking from past user clicks. It then trains the ranker to make that score as high as it can. The team also built two test suites for fair checks. One uses an open click model as a stand-in judge on a public data set. The work aims to close the gap between test scores and real gains.
arxiv-2508-14380:
Nicole Fronda and co-authors propose a flight planner for city air taxis in a 2025 paper. Urban air mobility would let crew free aircraft carry people and goods over cities. The aircraft belong to rival operators with clashing goals, yet all must share the same airspace safely.

Their planner, Fair-CoPlan, works in three steps with a central service provider. The provider first limits take off and landing choices based on space at the ports. Operators then plan their own paths under those limits. Last, the provider resolves clashes and spreads the cost of detours fairly across operators. Tests in simulation gave fairer results than a planner that ignored fairness, with only minor delays as the trade off.
arxiv-2508-14480:
Filip Najman and Ivan Novak determined the quadratic points on a family of modular curves in twenty twenty-five. Modular curves, written X0(N), are curves whose points encode extra structure on elliptic curves. Quadratic points are those defined by square-root extensions of the rational numbers, and listing them all is a classic hard task in number theory.

The authors settle every level up to one hundred that was still open, eleven levels in all. Their tool is an improved going-down method. It uses the fact that all quadratic points are known for some smaller level dividing the target level, then lifts that knowledge upward. The result completes a case-by-case map that other researchers had built over many years.
arxiv-2508-14680:
Ethan Levien, Yair Hein, and Farshid Jafarpour present a 2025 math biology paper on cell groups that grow at uneven rates. In their model, each cell grows based on a changing inner trait, such as gene activity. Earlier models had shown that this trait can sometimes act apart from cell size.

The authors give general rules for when that split holds, in both single cell lines and whole groups. They link the rules to the Feynman-Kac formula, a known tool for such growth problems. When the split holds, size growth can be recast as a simpler, even process, which makes key values easier to compute.
arxiv-2508-14980:
Balykin and five co-authors built this face security method in twenty twenty-five. Face recognition can be fooled in two ways: by physical fakes, such as photos or masks, and by digital forgeries. Separate detectors for each kind add cost and leave gaps. The team trained one model to catch both.

Their method pairs each real selfie with a matched attack version during training. Contrasting the pairs teaches the model signs of liveness that work across attack types. On a major challenge benchmark, the method posted a low average error of about two percent. It beat earlier solutions while staying light and quick to train. The team released code and trained models for others to use.
arxiv-2508-15180:
Kai Xiong and co-authors build a factory for logic puzzles with checkable answers, in a paper published in 2025. Language models need large sets of math and logic problems to learn reasoning, but model-written sets are often flawed, narrow, or hard to scale. Their framework, PuzzleClone, writes puzzles from formal specs instead of free text.

Seed puzzles are first encoded in a small domain language. The system then varies numbers and rules to spawn new versions, and a solver checks each one for validity. The result was a set of over eighty-three thousand verified puzzles across many formats and difficulty levels. Training on the set raised model scores sharply on its own test and on seven outside benchmarks. The authors release code and data for reuse.
arxiv-2508-15280:
Yuanchen Zhao, Li Rao, and Dong E. Liu wrote a 2025 physics paper on weak measurements in quantum systems. Weak measurements nudge a system gently instead of forcing it into one state. The authors study what happens when two kinds of weak measurement compete and do not commute, meaning the order in which they act changes the result.

Using theory and computer simulations, the team maps out the phases the system can enter. The outcome depends heavily on whether the measurement results are read out fully, partly, or not at all. Full readout can build long-range entanglement, while no readout leads to a different kind of order. The work gives experimenters a clearer guide for building stable entangled states.
arxiv-2508-15380:
Vishwa Prakash, Ruta Mehta, and Prajakta Nimbhorkar present a 2025 paper on splitting indivisible goods fairly when people come in few types. Fairness here means approximate envy-freeness up to any single good: nobody should envy another's bundle once one item is ignored. Earlier results guaranteed such allocations for at most three distinct valuation types, or weaker fairness for up to seven agents. The authors extend the guarantee.

With at most four distinct valuations, a two-thirds-strength version of the fairness property always exists, for any number of agents. They also study a relaxed version where some goods go to charity, unallocated, and nobody envies the charity pile either. There, near-perfect fairness needs a charity pile that shrinks as the number of types shrinks. The paper is theoretical computer science about fair division.
arxiv-2508-15980:
Memory hardware is a bottleneck for data-hungry programs like language models and key-value stores. Yiwei Yang and co-authors use CXL memory, a newer link whose channels carry reads and writes at once, unlike the half-duplex design of standard memory. That two-way design should shine under mixed traffic, yet today's software ignores it. Their measurements confirm the prize: CXL beat flat DDR5 bandwidth by over half at balanced read-write mixes.

Their framework, CXLAimPod, closes the gap inside the Linux kernel using eBPF programs. It mixes scheduling strategies and takes hints from process groups about what each program needs, balancing speed, delay, and overhead. Tests showed gains of about seven percent on average for Redis, with far larger jumps on some patterns, and over seventy percent for language model text generation. The work shows that two-way-aware scheduling pays off.
arxiv-2508-16080:
When a curved equation's solution blows up at a point, the mass it piles there often comes in fixed units. Xia Huang and three co-authors prove that unit rule in 2025 for a hard case: an equation set in a space whose yardstick bends with direction. Their result stretches a classic one from the flat case of the nineties.

Two past steps had each moved part way, one for a bent-yardstick form in the plane, and one for a higher-power form in more axes. The new work joins both lines at once. Such unit rules are load-bearing in the study of curved equations, since they pin what a blow-up can look like. The proof gives analysts a firmer grip on a whole class of such problems.
arxiv-2508-16480:
Linda Hirsch, James Fey, and Katherine Isbister turn local flood actions into cards for a table game, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Work ran with a community-led learning center through field watch, expert groups, and a survey. The aim is bottom-up flood strength, not top-down drills.

Twenty-seven acts that lift or keep flood strength were found. Twenty became playing cards in a bigger interactive table game still in build. The team argues cards can teach non-experts through play. Local fit came from the joint design path itself. Readers in game design get a method for grounding serious play in place.
arxiv-2508-16580:
Weiyu Ma and co-authors present Adaptive Command, a system that lets players steer a StarCraft II army by talking. The 2025 framework joins a large language model with behavior trees, a classic tool for game control. A player speaks or types strategy in plain words, and the system turns it into orders the game units can carry out at once.

The language model acts as a strategic advisor that reads the state of play. The behavior tree then runs the chosen plan step by step. In user studies, the setup sharpened players' decisions and helped them adapt as battles shifted. Novice players and players with disabilities gained the most. The authors see lessons for other fast, complex team settings beyond games.
arxiv-2508-16780:
Sanchita Pal and co-authors untangle the pile-up of solar eruptions behind the great geomagnetic storm of May 2024 in this 2025 paper. That storm was the strongest in two decades. Five eruptions from the Sun merged into one tangled structure on the way to Earth, and the team asked why two neighboring parts of it hit so differently.

Using readings from two spacecraft at different spots, plus images of the eruptions leaving the Sun, they mapped each part's magnetic content. One part, born from eruptions of shared origin twisted the right way to merge, carried far more magnetic energy and twist than the other. Its neighbor held a left-handed eruption whose twist fought the merging. Same storm cloud, different weapons. The authors warn that early sightings alone cannot tell forecasters which part of such a pile-up will strike hardest.
arxiv-2508-16980:
Luis Mathias and co-authors keep a smart radio mirror aimed at moving users by predicting where they will be, in this 2025 paper. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces bounce signals toward devices, but slow position updates let the beam go stale. A phone can move far between two location fixes.

Their controller watches the sparse position reports and infers speed and acceleration. A predictor then rolls that motion forward at a high rate, letting the surface retune ahead of time. The physics-based design needs little computing and works across many movement patterns. Simulations show timely adjustments even for fast-moving users. The authors present it as a practical fix for real deployments.
arxiv-2508-17180:
Pande, Yerramilli, Tamarapalli, and Grover built this benchmark in twenty twenty-five to test AI vision on math. Multimodal models describe images well but may not truly reason over them. Surface plots, the graphs of math functions, strip away everyday meaning and leave pure shape. That makes them a clean test of spatial and math reasoning.

The benchmark, MaRVL-QA, holds two task types. One asks models to count features such as peaks on a plotted surface. The other asks which geometric change was applied to a shape. The plots come from a curated function library with checks against ambiguity. Even top models scored poorly and leaned on shortcuts. The authors offer the set as a yardstick for deeper reasoning.
arxiv-2508-17480:
Brian Chao and co-authors present, in 2025, a wave-optics method for making holograms from three-dimensional scenes built of translucent pieces. Holographic near-eye displays are compact, but standard methods use smooth phases, which blur focus poorly and waste the display's capacity. Their method gives each piece a random phase instead.

A new compositing step blends millions of pieces with correct color and blocking, using time-multiplexed frames as an exact blending mechanism rather than a speckle trick. The results improve use of the display bandwidth, enlarge the viewing zone, and render focus blur and parallax more faithfully. Modern scene formats, from blobs to triangles, are supported.
arxiv-2508-17580:
Fan Nie and co-authors present a benchmark built from questions no one has solved in this 2025 paper. Good tests for AI should be both hard and realistic. Exam-style tests can be made hard in artificial ways, while tests from real user chats tend to skew easy. Unsolved questions offer a way out of that tension.

Their testbed, called UQ, holds 500 hard and varied questions drawn from a public question site. Topics run from computer theory and math to science fiction and history. Questions are gathered with rule filters, model judges, and human review. Candidate answers are pre-screened by checker tools, then verified by the community over time. The platform stays open for experts to add and judge work.
arxiv-2508-17780:
Lee, Ma, and Zhao build a sound way to draw facts about a new group from a model trained on an old one in twenty twenty-five. Labels are costly to gather for the new group, so only unlabeled data exist there. When the mix of labels shifts between groups, naive reuse misleads. Their method models how outcome density changes between the groups.

The estimate grows in three stages: a rough guess, then a steady estimate, then a sharp one. Each stage feeds the next, a self improving path that is new in this field. They prove the math traits of the final estimate. Tests on fake and real data beat past methods, they report.
arxiv-2508-17880:
Aditi Bhalla and three co-authors release a dataset on trust in self-driving cars in a 2025 paper. Trust and comfort decide whether people accept such vehicles, yet past work studied them separately with thin data. Their dataset records drivers in a simulator running fully self-driving trips. Participants voted their trust in real time and rated comfort continuously throughout each drive.

Body signals such as heart rate, gaze, and emotion were captured alongside car and traffic data. Questionnaires before and after trips added context. Learning models trained on the body data predicted trust and comfort well, with tree-based methods on top. The authors aim at cars that adapt to their riders.
arxiv-2508-18080: Three large collaborations, LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA, issued version 4.0 of their gravitational-wave transient catalog in 2025, and the head of the record introduces that release. The catalog gathers the groups' detected wave events from their observatory networks. The author list spans the full membership of the three teams, reflecting the scale of the joint effort behind the catalog.
arxiv-2508-18380:
Hung-Tien Huang, Dzung Dinh, and Junier B. Oliva propose a new way to decide which data features to buy before making a prediction, in a 2025 paper. In active feature acquisition, a system gathers features one at a time, paying a cost for each, and stops when it knows enough. Older methods either train hard-to-optimize policies or pick features greedily, one by one.

Their framework learns a small library of templates, sets of features that are informative together, and lets those templates guide what to gather next. Working from templates shrinks the choices the policy must weigh and avoids modeling the full data distribution. On synthetic and real datasets, the method beat leading rivals at lower cost.
arxiv-2508-18880:
Eljas Linna and Tuula Linna examine what generative AI would need to reason about law the way courts do. Language models are entering legal work, yet their limits in this high-stakes field are poorly mapped. Writing in 2025, the authors break legal reasoning into its hard parts.

A sound legal answer must pick the right framework across legal systems, argue from accepted sources of law, and separate a ruling's binding core from its side remarks. It must also handle vague clauses like reasonableness, clashing rules, and the burden of proof. The authors match each challenge against current AI boosters, such as retrieval systems, multi-agent setups, and hybrid symbolic tools. These help on narrow points but fail where judgment and open justification are required. The paper proposes sorting legal demands into four kinds that can be turned into testable design duties.
arxiv-2508-19280:
Partha Ghose proposes rebuilding the unification of forces on random processes in a 2025 paper. Earlier work showed that core quantum equations and the Born rule can emerge from classical stochastic motion with finite speeds and random reversals. A built in fundamental length keeps the math finite where field theories usually blow up.

Within this frame, electrodynamics and linearized gravity can be quantized, and the key vector formalism extends to non abelian fields without leaning on gauge symmetry. Coupling those fields to spin networks, which chop space into a discrete web, yields a single picture of matter and geometry. At large scales the model returns standard quantum field behavior while staying background independent underneath.
arxiv-2508-19580:
Omkar Gurjar, Agam Goyal, and Eshwar Chandrasekharan build a new benchmark for argument summarization in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Pulling key points from debates is a core summarization task. The standard data set, though, poorly matches real human conversation.

Their new set, ArgCMV, holds about twelve thousand arguments from real online debates across more than three thousand topics. Its arguments run longer, refer back to each other, and carry more subjective material than the old set. Existing extraction methods adapt badly to it. The authors benchmark classic baselines and fresh open models to show the gap. They pitch ArgCMV as the proving ground for the next wave of language model summarizers.
arxiv-2508-19780:
Machine learning usually chases accuracy, but sometimes the more interesting model is the one that surprises. Ryoma Sato argued in 2025 for classifiers built to be interesting first, choosing features for novelty rather than raw predictive power.

His framework, EUREKA, asks a language model to rank features by how interesting they seem, then builds transparent classifiers from those picks alone. Predicting room occupancy from humidity rather than carbon dioxide loses some accuracy but tells a richer story. In a set of academic papers, the method found that titles containing a colon predict future citations. Sato presents such models as tools for discovery and communication.
arxiv-2508-19980:
Dylan Sam and co-authors tested in 2025 whether language models can reason about confidential information. As models act as agents in high-stakes settings, they must follow user-set access rules. The team built a benchmark where a model must judge if a request is authorised by a correct password.

Current open and closed models struggled with this seemingly simple task. Stronger reasoning did not generally help, and reasoning traces often leaked the secret itself, raising doubts about exposing them. Tests grew harder with jailbreak pressure and longer multi-turn chats. The authors conclude that frontier models are not yet suited to guarding confidential information.
arxiv-2508-20080:
Changha Shin, Woong Oh Cho, and Seon Joo Kim present a method for clean, seamless full-circle views from imperfect camera shots. Their 2025 paper works with dual-fisheye cameras, the common consumer gear for 360-degree images. Two lenses never line up fully, so stitched panoramas show seams and warps. Their method folds a model of the dual camera into a modern scene-building method based on soft three-dimensional blobs.

Camera traits such as lens gaps and angle warps are tuned jointly with the scene itself. The system thus learns from flawed inputs and still renders flawless new views. Tests on real-world sets beat rival 360-degree renderers. The gain matters for virtual reality, robots, and self-driving systems that rely on full-circle sight. Cleaner views from cheap cameras widen access to all three fields.
arxiv-2508-20480:
Tingbin Cao and Jiahu Peng wrote a 2025 math paper that builds a tropical version of Nevanlinna theory for several variables. Nevanlinna theory measures how often a function takes set values. Tropical math swaps normal sums for max-based rules, which changes the tools. The authors set up the basic measures for this case.

They define the counting, proximity and growth functions for tropical maps. They prove a first main theorem and versions of a key lemma on log derivatives. Then they prove a second main theorem for maps that meet a set of surfaces. Growth limits and degree terms shape the final bound.
arxiv-2508-20980:
Siyao Li and co-authors study how much secret data a beam-based radio link can carry safely. Their 2025 paper uses a simple model for the narrow beams used in fast new radio bands. A base station sends to one true user while a silent listener tries to hear in. Both face random beam angles that stay fixed for a block of sends, then change.
