Their domain decomposition splits the problem into sub-problems. Schur complements couple the pieces at their interfaces. That coupling breaks the matrix form FFT inversion needs.

Their fix is an FFT-based preconditioner for the GMRES iteration on the interface system. The preconditioner inverts the block operator without the Schur part, which FFT handles fast. Each step keeps optimal complexity. On a cross-shaped domain, accuracy matched the scheme's second order. Speed beat a classic sparse solver by over forty times.
arxiv-2509-23280:
Balancing assets against liabilities over time is a control problem with money at stake. Yilie Huang casts asset-liability management as continuous-time reinforcement learning. The setup uses a linear-quadratic form with interim and terminal goals. A model-free soft actor-critic learns the strategy by policy gradient. The actor explores in an adaptive way, and the critic explores on a set schedule, which limits hand tuning.

Two hundred randomized market scenarios frame the tests. Rivals include enhanced classic strategies, a model-based RL method, and three modern RL algorithms. Huang's method earned higher average rewards than all of them. Gains came fast and held. The edge came from learning the strategy directly, not from bigger networks.
arxiv-2509-23780:
A supersonic jet plowing through quark-gluon plasma leaves a Mach cone, and behind it a depleted wake. Zhong Yang and Xin-Nian Wang review that diffusion wake in a research perspective. The wake shows up as a shortage of soft hadrons flying opposite to the jet. Coupled transport and hydrodynamic simulations predict a valley in the two-dimensional correlation between jets and hadrons, cut into the ridge from many parton interactions.

That valley, seen with photon-tagged jets, would be a clear signal. In two-jet events with a rapidity gap, an asymmetry in the correlation offers a second, background-free signal, usable for both event types. Measuring either would teach us about the plasma's properties.
arxiv-2509-23880:
Self-driving stacks that learn from unlabeled data live or die by the quality of their pseudo-labels. Taehun Kong and Tae-Kyun Kim build a semi-supervised 3D detection framework whose pseudo-label picker is learned, not hand-set. Teacher-student setups usually filter teacher guesses with manual confidence thresholds, ignoring distance, class, and learning state. Two added networks at the teacher's output fuse scores and set context-adaptive thresholds, supervised by how pseudo-labels align with true boxes.

A soft supervision strategy helps the student favor clean labels over noisy ones. On KITTI and Waymo, the method picked high-precision labels with wider coverage and recall, and detection improved clearly over rivals.
arxiv-2509-23980:
Upscaling a video with a diffusion model wastes effort re-imagining content the blurry input already contains. Jinpei Guo and 10 co-authors cut that redundancy with OASIS, a one-step diffusion model for real-world video super-resolution. An attention specialization routing assigns attention heads to distinct patterns by their behavior. That routing trims redundant work while preserving what the pretrained model knows.

A progressive training plan starts with temporally consistent degradations, then moves to inconsistent ones, easing the model into hard cases. OASIS topped synthetic and real-world benchmarks in their tests. It also ran more than six times faster than a leading one-step baseline.
arxiv-2509-24180:
Boger fluids stay nearly steady in thickness while stretching like elastic, which makes them ideal for flow tests. Jonghyun Hwang and Howard A Stone tackle a stubborn prep problem: making a set of such fluids with chosen elastic traits. Adjusting one trait without moving the others has been hard to do by trial and error.

The pair exploit quirks of polyisobutylene fluids to build a design equation. It takes the wanted shear modulus, relaxation time, and normal-stress coefficient as inputs. It returns the polymer content, molecular weight, and solvent thickness to mix. Fluids made this way carry their elastic traits by design, known before the first flow test runs.
arxiv-2509-24280:
Marko Lela proves a sharp split between entropy and degree for low-degree tests in the Sum-of-Squares hierarchy. The setting pairs a target distribution with a product-like proxy on a calibrated window, after a gadget layer. The core quantity is the best edge a low-degree polynomial test can gain in telling the two apart.

Lela ties that edge to the low-degree moments of the pair, using an orthonormal basis and a moment-matching fact. A windowed form of a classic inequality then gives strong tail bounds. The upshot: a test edge above a set size forces any refutation to use degree that grows with the window. Constants stay explicit throughout.
arxiv-2509-24380:
Services computing built mature rules for reusable software functions, from web services to serverless platforms. Shuiguang Deng and 8 co-authors argue that language-model agents now form a new kind of service. Value comes not just from calling fixed functions but from delegating goals to autonomous entities that grasp context, use tools, work with peers, and act in open settings.

They name this shift Agentic Services Computing and set out a research roadmap for it. A lifecycle view links service objects, system structures, infrastructure, metrics, application evidence, and open challenges. The aim is a base where agents can be described, composed, delivered, watched, audited, and evolved as first-class services.
arxiv-2509-24480:
Deciding whether a group element lies inside a given submonoid sounds basic, yet it can be undecidable. Islam Foniqi and Robert D Gray prove a batch of decidability and undecidability results for that membership problem in one-relator, surface, and hyperbolic groups. The work is driven by the word problem for one-relator inverse monoids.

A general theorem gives conditions where membership in submonoids of certain one-relator groups is decidable, which settles many families inside surface groups. Graded submonoids get distortion results, and the prefix monoid of a surface group proves to have linear distortion. The Magnus submonoid problem is decidable in several families. A new construction shows the related positivity problem can be undecidable, settling a question from 2006.
arxiv-2509-24580:
Diffusion models can restore damaged images by sampling from a posterior, but the balance between prior and likelihood is set by a hand-tuned fixed scale. Lingyu Wang and Xiangming Meng argue that static balance is the weak point: the ideal scale shifts across timesteps and across tasks. Their module, SAIP, refines that scale adaptively at each timestep, with no retraining and no change to the diffusion backbone.

SAIP plugs into existing samplers built on common likelihood estimators. Across diverse restoration tasks, including hard cases, it consistently improved reconstruction quality. A small plug-and-play part thus buys broader generalization for a whole family of solvers.
arxiv-2509-24680:
Keisuke Harigaya and co-authors wrote this 2025 physics paper on a parity-based fix for a puzzle in the strong force. Their model adds a mirror copy of the weak force and tightly shapes how particles gain mass. In that setup, the small mass of neutrinos comes out naturally, while lepton number can be broken strongly at reachable energies.

The paper works out what a future muon collider, called μTRISTAN, could see. When two positive muons collide, they could make new heavy partner particles of the W boson. A machine at ten trillion electron volts could probe such particles up to about the same mass. Off-shell effects could stretch the reach higher still. Checks from double beta decay data also bound the model.
arxiv-2509-24780:
Forecasters who predict the euro area's output right now, before official numbers land, often model the whole bloc at once. Andrii Babii, Luca Barbaglia, Eric Ghysels, and Jonas Striaukas ask whether that shortcut throws away useful news from the bloc's small countries. They build forecasts country by country for nineteen members, using standard data releases plus daily news, then add the pieces up.

The bottom-up route wins, above all across the pandemic years, when small and mid-sized countries carried signals the big four missed. News data helped most while official statistics lagged. The team also proves the edge on paper: pooling data across countries lowers the error in each forecast, so the summed result beats a direct guess at the total.
arxiv-2509-24980:
Diffusion models trained to generate images quietly learn rich features of bodies and scenes, and Shuang Liang and co-authors borrow those features for human pose estimation in a 2025 paper. Their system, SDPose, targets the hard case: poses in domains unlike the training data, under noise, weather, and blur.

A systematic sweep of the layers of the diffusion network found which levels carry the most robust features for the job. Those features are fused by a small aggregation module, and training pairs keypoint supervision with a reconstruction loss that protects the borrowed prior. The authors built a new out-of-domain benchmark from a standard data set, with style-shifted and corrupted splits. Light fine-tuning on it delivered strong cross-domain results.
arxiv-2509-25080:
Bogdan Raonic, Siddhartha Mishra, and Samuel Lanthaler propose a task aware way to flag out of distribution data for scientific AI, as a step toward a certificate of trust. Data driven models now serve in weather and fluid work, where off range inputs can break them. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Flagging such breaks in regression tasks is still an open problem. The method gauges joint likelihood with a score based diffusion model, weighing both the input and the model's own forecast. That gives a trust score tied to the task. Across science sets, from physics equations to brain tumor cuts, the score tracked forecast error closely, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-25280:
Moinak Bhattacharya, Gagandeep Singh, and Prateek Prasanna build a digital twin that grows a tumor together with the tissue around it. Most models of disease progression track the tumor alone, yet real tumors evolve unevenly, shaped by treatment and by the tissues they push against. A twin that ignores surrounding anatomy misses half the clinical story.

Their framework, Anatomy-DT, couples physics-based equations with trainable deep learning. Anatomy is encoded as a field of class probabilities and evolved by a cross-diffusion system that enforces competition between tissue types, keeping each region purely one type. A topology penalty keeps centerlines intact and punishes overlaps between regions. On synthetic benchmarks the method reached top accuracy while preserving anatomy, and it also led on a clinical dataset. The authors present the system as a principled route to realistic simulation of whole anatomy that stays consistent.
arxiv-2509-25380:
Shane Bergsma, Nolan Dey, and Joel Hestness study when training data should appear during language model training, in a 2025 paper. Order matters, yet rules for placing data were guesswork. Their tool, the training re-evaluation curve, grades each past batch with the finished model's weights, showing how well data met at each stage is retained.

Across models from small to near four billion parameters, putting top data at the curve's low points lifted scores. Better still, the curve can be forecast before training from traits of the optimizer, so menus can be planned in advance. The team used it to explain past recipes and to improve a huge continual training run.
arxiv-2509-25780:
Jih-Hsin Cheng, Hung-Lin Chiu, Paul Yang, and Yongbing Zhang study special surfaces in a curved three-dimensional space. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The surfaces are tied to an energy that stays the same under a group of symmetry moves. Setting that energy's key term to zero gives an equation for the surface.

The authors show the equation is of hyperbolic type, like the wave equation. They prove that, near a starting curve, at most one surface fits the stated data. They then sort all such surfaces that are symmetric under rotation. One famous surface, the Clifford torus, is tested as a candidate for least energy. A second-variation check shows it is not a local minimum after all.
arxiv-2509-25880:
Luke Bayzid, Alexandre Madeira, and Manuel Martins present a 2025 logic paper on a single framework for many kinds of representations. Scientists model ideas in many ways, and each way has its own strengths. Comparing results across frameworks can be hard because each uses its own setup. The authors build a general structure from basic set theory that can hold many logical and semantic systems at once.

They show the framework's range by rebuilding modal logic inside it. Modal logic deals with claims about what is possible or necessary. In their result, every modal logic can be represented within the one structure. A shared home like this could make it easier to move results between fields. The paper is a work of theory, aimed at logicians who juggle several formal systems.
arxiv-2509-25980:
Mykola Bordyuh, Djork-Arne Clevert, and Marco Bertolini solve a quantum version of the bridge problem exactly in a 2025 study. The classical bridge asks for the most likely stochastic path between two distributions; the quantum version lets the dynamics follow the Schrödinger equation instead of a real wave equation. The problem was known to mathematicians, but the authors recast it from a Lagrangian angle aimed at generative modeling.

Their derivation shows the evolution equation takes a tractable form with exact solutions in the cases they treat. Exact bridges could give quantum-inspired generative models the same firm footing diffusion bridges gave classical ones.
arxiv-2509-26080:
Madden weighs what social scientists may, and may not, claim when they use large language models as stand-in people in a 2025 paper. Models now fill in survey answers and populate multi-agent simulations, inviting researchers to treat their outputs like human data. The paper argues that is a category error.

The safer framing treats models as high-capacity pattern matchers that interpolate quasi-predictions inside explicit scope conditions, not as substitutes for statistical inference about people. Practical guardrails follow: draw independent samples, preregister human baselines, validate with reliability in mind, and calibrate by subgroup. With those in place, the author allows prototyping and forecasting uses. Without them, synthetic agents risk dressing up model habits as social facts.
arxiv-2509-26180:
Shoham Letzter, Abhishek Methuku, and Benny Sudakov prove that dense regular graphs can be almost perfectly packed with copies of any fixed bipartite graph. A packing lays down disjoint copies of a small pattern graph across a big host. Kühn and Osthus posed the packing question in two thousand five, with tightness doubts on every side.

Their 2025 paper shows any proportionally regular host admits a packing that leaves only a constant number of vertices bare, however large the host grows. The claim collapses without regularity and density, and non-bipartite patterns can fail entirely. A companion result tiles hosts with subdivisions of complete graphs, settling a second old problem. Robust expanders and the regularity and blow-up lemmas carry the proof.
arxiv-2509-26480:
Kunhao Zhong and Bhuvnesh Jain test whether dark energy really changes over time, in work from 2025. Recent survey results favor a dark energy that evolves, but the claim rests on combining several kinds of data.

The authors isolate the pure geometry in weak lensing data from the Dark Sky survey's third year, setting aside growth effects with an extra parameter. Combined with distance measures and early-universe data, the evolving model wins at about three standard deviations. Adding supernova data makes the answer fragile: leaving out the nearest supernovae, or using only distant ones, drops the support below two. Future lensing surveys should match today's supernova power.
arxiv-2509-26580:
Luca Lanzendorfer, Constantin Pinkl, and Florian Grotschla teach machines to split blended voices in a cappella song. Their 2025 paper faces a shifting cast: the number of active singers changes from mix to mix, and training sets of many-singer stems are small. A power-set trick answers the data gap, recombining stems into far more training mixes.

Their model adapts a top speaker-splitting design with wave-shaped activations and a loss that still learns when a stem sits silent. On a known Japanese a cappella set, the method set new best scores for full casts and for subsets alike. It beat spectrum-based rivals and held up on mixes with varied singer counts.
arxiv-2510-00080:
Hanze Guo, Yijun Ma, and Xiao Zhou published this 2025 paper on SoREX, a recommendation system that can explain itself. Social recommenders suggest items by using a person's friends and past clicks, which helps when data is thin. Graph neural networks made these systems more accurate, but their picks come with no clear reasons. SoREX was built to give reasons a user can inspect.

SoREX models friendships and item clicks in two linked towers, plus a helper task that sharpens the friend signals. For each suggested item it pulls out short paths through the user's social circle. Those paths become plain comparisons between candidate items, showing why one ranked above another. Tests on four standard datasets confirmed strong accuracy for the system. Separate checks, both numeric and by reading examples, confirmed that the explanations hold up well.
arxiv-2510-00180:
Amit Milstein, Nir Shlezinger, and Boaz Rafaely at Ben-Gurion University published this 2025 paper on upgrading spatial audio. Ambisonics stores a full three-dimensional sound field in a set of channels. First-order recordings are cheap to capture but sound spatially coarse. Raising them to third order by pure signal processing is underdetermined, so the team turns to diffusion models instead.

Their method, DiffAU, learns the distribution of rich sound fields and samples plausible upgrades. It works in a cascaded fashion, stepping up the order in stages. Tests used several speakers at once in an echo-free room setting. By objective measures the upgraded audio beat the standard baseline clearly. Listeners in perceptual tests could not distinguish the result from true third-order recordings. The work points toward cheaper capture rigs that still deliver immersive playback.
arxiv-2510-00280:
Ruochen Li and four colleagues published this 2025 paper questioning how AI-written radiology reports get graded. Automatic metrics often award high scores to reports that clinicians refuse to trust. The authors argue the metrics themselves misread clinical meaning. They propose a meta-evaluation framework that judges the judges against real clinical standards.

Their team built a dataset of true reports paired with rewritten versions carrying labeled errors. Each error carries a clinical significance tag and a written explanation. Testing popular metrics on it exposed systematic blind spots. Metrics failed to separate dangerous errors from harmless wording changes. They also over-penalized innocent variation and ranked error severity inconsistently. The framework spells out what a trustworthy metric must do: discriminate, stay robust, and worsen steadily as errors grow worse.
arxiv-2510-00480:
Kenjiro Ide and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on teaching AI agents to read soccer tactics like analysts do. Twenty-two players interacting on one field create a huge, tightly coupled state space. The authors propose Expandable Decision-Making States, a representation that enriches raw positions and speeds. Relational variables score space, passing options, and scoring chances for each player.

An action-masking scheme gives ball carriers and off-ball players their own legal decision sets. Learned values then map onto concepts a coach recognizes, like marking pressure and open passing lanes. Against a physics-only baseline, the new states with masking cut both action-prediction loss and value error. Visualizations of the learned values spotlighted fast counterattacks and defensive breakthroughs as prized patterns. The team folded the method into an open-source library that accepts several data providers. Reproducible tactical analysis across datasets is the stated goal.
arxiv-2510-00680:
Cui and six co-authors present TShape in this 2025 arXiv paper on time series anomaly detection for IT operations. The hardest failures hide as shapelet anomalies, stretches whose shape looks wrong to a human expert while simple statistics stay normal. Many detectors miss them because they compare values point by point instead of reading the shape of a window. TShape reads each series patch by patch, at several scales at once.

A patch-wise dual attention mechanism balances fine local shape detail against long-range context from distant, similar patches. Multi-scale convolution captures the sub-sequence patterns at different resolutions, and learnable gating blends the two views. Across five diverse benchmarks, TShape beat the leading existing methods by about ten percent in average F1 score, the authors report. Attention visualizations confirmed the model focuses on the truly anomalous segments.
arxiv-2510-00780:
Razzaque and Ghosh model the afterglow of the short gamma-ray burst GRB 160821B across wavelengths in this 2025 arXiv paper on high-energy astrophysics. The burst, at redshift 0.161, remains the only short GRB detected at very high energies above one hundred gigaelectronvolts. MAGIC telescopes caught it about four hours after the trigger. Earlier studies fitted its broadband spectrum by eye and favoured an external Compton explanation for the energetic emission.

The authors combine synchrotron, synchrotron self-Compton, and external Compton components and fit them properly with Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling. The external Compton contribution came out negligible, and the self-Compton model explained the data well for a wind-like surrounding medium. The burst emerges as the least energetic very-high-energy GRB known, sitting in an unusually dense wind for a short burst. It also lies outside the three-sigma correlation region that other energetic bursts follow.
arxiv-2510-00880:
Bergeron, Buhnila, François, and State present HalluGuard in this 2025 arXiv paper on trustworthy language models. Retrieval-augmented generation feeds documents to a model so its answers stay grounded, yet models still invent claims the documents never made. HalluGuard is a small reasoning model, with four billion parameters, built to catch exactly that failure. It labels each document-claim pair as grounded or hallucinated and explains its verdict.

The team trained it on a synthetic dataset built from FineWeb text, with both grounded and fabricated claims. Preference-based fine-tuning then distilled large-model reasoning into the small backbone. On the RAGTruth benchmark subset, HalluGuard reached a balanced accuracy score matching a rival model twice its size. Across the full benchmark it scored about level with GPT-4o, a far larger general-purpose system.
arxiv-2510-01280:
Barros and co-authors ask whether adding sideways motion can protect a quantum detector from the noise of acceleration. An accelerated detector perceives a thermal bath where empty space should be, an effect that erodes quantum information. The team gives the detector constant transverse velocity on top of its acceleration.

Three test systems, a single qubit and two interferometric circuits, received exact analytical treatment at modest speeds. Coherence, visibility, and distinguishability all degraded slightly less with the motion added. At ultra-relativistic speeds the effect vanishes entirely because the detector stops responding. The protection is real but very small, a composite of velocity and acceleration. Finite interaction time keeps the setup honest to real experiments. Complementarity relations bind the coherence and path measures together. Perturbation theory supplies the non-relativistic formulas. Tiny protections matter where acceleration is unavoidable in practice.
arxiv-2510-01480:
Podplutova and co-authors generate new drug candidates guided by pharmacophores, the spatial feature patterns that make molecules bind, instead of expensive docking scores. Docking as a reward costs heavily and misleads often during generative training. Their framework balances likeness to proven actives against structural novelty.

Users supply custom reference sets, from approved drugs to clinical candidates. The case study targets the estrogen receptor pathway in breast cancer. Generated compounds kept high feature fidelity while differing sharply in structure. Standard drug-likeness checks confirmed the molecules remain plausible as drugs and open to patents. Hit-to-lead work is the stage the framework speeds up. Novelty matters because patents require structures nobody has claimed. Fidelity matters because activity lives in the pharmacophore. Breast cancer supplies the concrete medical test case. Drug-like property panels grade the outputs beyond likeness. Custom inputs make the tool work across diseases.
arxiv-2510-01680:
Kobayashi and three co-authors address the strong CP problem in this 2025 particle theory paper. Quantum chromodynamics allows a vacuum angle that should cause large CP violation, yet experiments find it tiny. The authors work inside a grand unified model inspired by the SU(5) group. They impose a non-invertible symmetry on the mass patterns of quarks and leptons.

That symmetry forces the determinants of the quark mass matrices to stay real numbers. Real determinants make a zero vacuum angle natural rather than finely tuned. The team builds a three-zero texture model under a doubled non-invertible symmetry. Quantum corrections break the texture only slightly, at a level too small to spoil the solution. The same framework also speaks to the CP-violating phase seen in neutrino behavior, which links two open puzzles in particle physics.
arxiv-2510-01980:
Görlach and Sevenheck work out the dual side of tautological differential systems in this 2025 mathematics paper. Tautological systems encode equations attached to group actions on algebraic varieties. They appear in mirror symmetry and the theory of linear free divisors. Duality inside mixed Hodge modules makes their holonomic duals a central object to understand.

The authors study that dual for general tautological systems, generalizing classic GKZ theory. Their main tool is a Chevalley-Eilenberg type complex that extends Euler-Koszul machinery beyond the torus case. They prove the complex is equivariant and holonomic. A striking consequence limits when the dual is again a tautological system from the same data. That clean self-duality holds essentially only when the group's dimension equals the variety's dimension. The result explains why the torus case felt deceptively simple. Applications to linear free divisors and homogeneous spaces motivate the whole analysis.
arxiv-2510-02080:
Hu, Ait Oufroukh, Bonardi, and Ghandour build a dense mapping system for a single uncalibrated camera in this 2025 robotics paper. Monocular dense SLAM usually demands heavy computation, large GPU memory, and known camera calibration. Their system, EC3R-SLAM, drops the calibration requirement entirely. A tracking module maintains a sparse feature map for localization.

A mapping module, built on a feed-forward three-dimensional reconstruction model, estimates the camera's own intrinsics on the fly. Local and global loop closures keep the map consistent over short and long horizons. Multi-view consistency from those closures lifts both accuracy and robustness. Across benchmarks, the system matched state-of-the-art accuracy while running faster. It also consumed far less GPU memory than rival dense methods. It even runs effectively on modest hardware. The combination suits robots and phones that cannot carry laboratory cameras or servers.
arxiv-2510-02180:
Sapora and four co-authors recover reward functions as readable code in this 2025 machine learning paper. Inverse reinforcement learning infers what an expert is optimizing from demonstrations. Classic methods return black-box reward networks that nobody can inspect or debug. Their framework, GRACE, uses a language model inside an evolutionary search instead.

Candidate rewards are written as executable code, then mutated and selected against the expert trajectories. The winning reward function can be read, verified, and edited by a human. Tests on the BabyAI and AndroidWorld benchmarks learned accurate rewards efficiently, even in multi-task settings. Policies trained on those rewards matched strong imitation and online reinforcement learning baselines that used true rewards. The framework also assembles complex reward APIs across tasks. Explainable rewards close the loop between learning from people and trusting the result. Debugging a reward becomes editing a program, not probing a network.
arxiv-2510-02280:
Biasse and Song give full proofs for a fast quantum algorithm in number theory. Their 2025 paper revisits a result first announced in 2016. The algorithm computes S-unit groups inside number fields. Number fields extend the rationals with algebraic roots. Their unit groups encode deep arithmetic structure. Classical methods for these groups run far too slowly. The quantum method finishes in polynomial time. Several classic problems fall out as direct corollaries.

Class groups and unit groups become computable at quantum speed. The principal ideal problem also falls to the method. So do certain norm equations over number fields. Other teams built on the principal ideal result. Their work finds short generators of principal ideals. Related methods find mildly short vectors in ideal lattices. Those lattice results matter for cryptography design. The proofs here supply the missing detailed foundation.
arxiv-2510-02480:
Wynn and co-authors guard in-context learning against poisoned examples with formal risk control. Their 2025 machine learning paper starts from a flexibility problem. Language models learn tasks from a few shown examples. An attacker can slip wrong or harmful examples into that set. The team defines a safe baseline for behavior. Zero-shot performance, with no examples, sets the floor. Distribution-free risk control then bounds how far examples may drag performance. The trick uses early exit predictions inside the model. Later attention heads that focus on unsafe inputs get ignored.

The framework also gains speed from those early exits. Helpful examples still improve results beyond the floor. Harmful ones lose their power to degrade the model. Guarantees hold without assumptions about input distribution. Mixed quality demonstrations are the realistic setting here. Support tools and chatbots ingest untrusted examples daily. Built-in risk control beats hoping examples stay clean.
arxiv-2510-02580:
The CMS Collaboration measures collective flow in oxygen and neon nucleus collisions at the LHC. Their 2025 nuclear physics paper uses data from the CMS detector. Smashing light nuclei tests how fluid-like behavior emerges. The collisions ran at five point three six tera electron volts per pair. Oxygen runs delivered far more data than neon runs. The team measured correlations between produced particles. Patterns spanned nearly five units of rapidity. Both systems showed elliptic and triangular flow signals. Ratios between the neon and oxygen results carried information.

Those ratios sense quadrupole shapes inside the nuclear wave functions. Hydro models with first principles structure inputs matched the trends. One framework tracked the measured ratios more closely than another. Triangular flow ratios still defied all three models tried. Small collision systems now constrain nuclear structure. Deformed neon geometry shows up in the flow data. Initial state modeling for tiny systems needs improvement.
arxiv-2510-02780:
Movva probes how vision-language models reason through rebus puzzles, exposing sharp cognitive limits. Her 2025 paper builds a benchmark of two hundred twenty one puzzles. Rebus puzzles mix pictures, letters, and wordplay. Models ace many multimodal tasks yet stumble here. Solving rates alone hide why they fail. The dataset sorts puzzles into six thinking categories. Each item carries careful notes for analysis. Three prompt styles drew out different reasoning styles. Scoring separated reasoning quality from final answer correctness. Visual composition emerged as a relative strength.

Absence reading failed in a fundamental way. Cultural symbols also blocked the models. Failure modes included surface fixation and phonetic drift. Negation inside puzzles was often simply neglected. Prompt choice reshaped the reasoning process substantially. Lateral thinking stresses machinery that benchmarks usually miss. Explainable scoring turns wrong answers into diagnoses.
arxiv-2510-02880:
Ma and co-authors bring reward-based training to discrete diffusion models. Such models build text or images by refining many tokens at once. They do not write one token at a time like chat models do. That parallel style breaks the usual math of policy training. Importance sampling, a core tool, becomes hard to compute. Their method, MaskGRPO, is the first workable fix for this setting.

The team first clarified the theory under the models. They built an estimator that tracks which token changes matter. Updates then focus on those valuable swings. For images, they tailored the rollout step to yield varied samples. Gradients from those samples proved steady and useful. Tests spanned math reasoning, coding, and image generation. Updates were more stable than with prior attempts. Reasoning scores and image quality both improved. The study opens reward training to a whole model family.
arxiv-2510-03080:
Pang and co-authors propose a new rule for joining field theories at network nodes. Network conformal field theory places a theory on each edge of a graph. The edges must meet cleanly at the shared nodes. The usual rule keeps the field itself continuous there. Their rule instead keeps its normal derivative continuous. They check that the rule respects the action principle. Energy conservation holds under it as well.

A tabletop system of thin rigid rods realizes the rule in practice. The team then studies the Casimir effect on polyhedral networks. That effect is a force from quantum vacuum fluctuations. Both joining rules were applied to the same shapes. The new rule generally gave a smaller Casimir force. With one edge, the rules match the two classic boundary types. The derivative rule thus looks as natural as the old one.
arxiv-2510-03280:
Ni and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on how to train large diffusion language models at the best size and cost. Their guide, called Quokka, is the first scaling law for these models. It covers cases where computing power is the limit and cases where training data runs short. The team draws on labs in Singapore and China, and they compare their rules with the Chinchilla rules for older models.

The study finds that diffusion models need far more data than word by word models at the same cost. In their tests, the data need ran two to five times higher, which favors smaller models fed with larger text sets. Masked diffusion beat the uniform kind at scale. A noise schedule worked best and stayed stable. Training settings from older models also carried over well. Builders can use these rules to spend computing budgets with far less guesswork.
arxiv-2510-03580:
Burnham-Schmidt and González present a 2025 arXiv paper in combinatorics on pinnacle sets for complex reflection groups. A pinnacle set collects the values that sit at peaks, where a value towers over both neighbors. Earlier work settled which pinnacle sets can occur for permutations and for signed ones. This paper extends the answer to the family of groups written G(m,p,n), which includes generalized symmetric groups. The authors characterize and count the admissible pinnacle sets for these nonexceptional groups.

As a payoff, they prove a conjecture about pinnacles of signed permutations. The proof closes a gap left by the signed case study that inspired the conjecture. Peak style statistics link combinatorics with geometry and representation theory, so a census matters beyond its charm. Enumerative formulas now exist for a wider range of symmetry types. Future work can build generating functions and random generation methods on this ground.
arxiv-2510-03680:
Kim and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper diagnosing why instruction tuned diffusion language models stop generating too early when given longer output budgets. These models write text by denoising. The failure, named eos overflow, appears as budgets grow: answers shrink or dissolve into end of sequence tokens. The cause is that one token doubles as both the stop signal and the padding filler. Probability mass piles onto it at later positions and the pull propagates backward, triggering premature stops.

Their fix, Rainbow Padding, fills padding slots with a repeating cycle of tokens instead. Spreading the mass breaks the stop token's dominance. As few as seven padding tokens prevented early termination in their experiments. A single epoch of fine tuning on data installed the fix in existing models. Output quality and length robustness improved. Diffusion based generators are an alternative to autoregressive ones, and this removes a flaw cheaply.
arxiv-2510-03980:
Bestvina, Bromberg, and Rasmussen wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in geometric group theory, on the curve graph of a surface. The curve graph records how loops on a surface relate, and it is a central tool for studying the mapping class group. Hamenstädt earlier built a sequence of graphs that starts at the curve graph and ends near a tree. The authors prove several properties she had conjectured about that sequence.

Each graph in the sequence is hyperbolic, a strong form of negative curvature. The fibers of the maps between consecutive graphs are quasi-trees, which are graphs that behave coarsely like trees. These facts bound the asymptotic dimension of every graph in the chain. They classify the boundary of each graph and how individual mapping classes act on it. The results tighten the coarse geometry picture of a fundamental object.
arxiv-2510-04180:
Eisenberg and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on image classifiers that explain themselves through visible concepts in specific regions. Concept bottleneck models reason through human-interpretable concepts, but they need costly concept annotations and cannot say where a concept appears. Models can also cheat by exploiting background correlations, like water behind waterbirds. The authors ground concepts spatially by segmenting the image first.

Their framework, SEG-MIL-CBM, treats each segmented region as an instance in an attention-based multiple-instance learning setup. Attention aggregates evidence across regions while exposing which regions support which concepts. No concept or group annotations are required at all. Experiments showed substantially better worst-group accuracy on spurious-correlation benchmarks. It stayed competitive on large-scale recognition and proved more robust to input corruptions. Spatially grounded explanations address both the trust problem and the shortcut problem in safety-critical vision.
arxiv-2510-04280:
Serra-Gómez and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper unifying several model-based reinforcement learning methods that plan with a learned policy as a proposal distribution. In Model Predictive Path Integral control, a planner samples trajectories and scores them with a learned value function. Trouble arises when the policy supplying samples drifts away from the planner's actual behavior. The value function is then trained on unlikely actions, producing unreliable estimates and poor learning.

The authors introduce Policy Optimization-Model Predictive Control, a family that treats the planner's action distribution as an prior. A KL term controls how far policy optimization can move toward raw return maximization and away from that prior. Earlier methods emerge as special parameter choices, while previously unexplored configurations become available. Experiments found that several extended configurations learn faster and more stably than established baselines, advancing MPPI-based continuous control.
arxiv-2510-04480:
Yunuo Cen and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on solving constraint satisfaction problems with continuous math. Such problems ask for values that satisfy a set of constraints, and they sit at the base of many fields. Clause learning solvers rule Boolean problems, but continuous local search has recently rivaled them on some classes. The team extended that continuous approach beyond Boolean variables. Their framework is called FourierCSP.

FourierCSP turns varied constraints into compact polynomials using a generalized Fourier transform. The trick avoids extra helper variables and the bulky encodings they require. An objective built from circuit output probabilities can be evaluated and differentiated with ease. A projected gradient method then searches for solutions, with theory backing its behavior. On benchmark suites, the solver proved scalable and competitive with established tools. The work widens the range of problems that continuous search can attack.
arxiv-2510-04580:
Tomoyuki Kaneko and Shuhei Yamashita wrote this 2025 paper on fully solving a smaller variant of the game 2048. In 2048, a player slides numbered tiles on a grid and merges equal tiles for points. A strong solution gives the best move in each reachable state, not just good play on average. The pair solved the variant played on a board with four columns and three rows.

Their key device is the age of a state, the sum of all tile values on the board. Age never changes between a move and the position it creates, and it rises by a fixed step after each tile drop. Sorting states by age lets them list every state one layer at a time. Values then follow by working down from high ages. The count came to more than a trillion states. Under best play, the expected score for the opening is about fifty thousand points.
arxiv-2510-04880:
Zhuoran Bao and Daniel James wrote this 2025 physics paper asking whether a qubit must be a two level system. Textbooks define a qubit as two quantum states or their mixtures. Real atomic levels come in degenerate families with sub states at one energy. The authors ask whether two such families could serve as a qubit. They study an atom of the kind used in several quantum computing platforms.

Selection rules from angular momentum pick out the transition between families. Under a driving field, the atom still performs Rabi oscillations between the levels. Those oscillations are what qubit gates are built from. The authors compute the gate fidelity for a degenerate atom. They work out what interaction two such atoms would need for a controlled Z gate. If the scheme holds, qubits could hide inside atomic structure than textbooks assume. That freedom might ease addressing and readout problems in large machines.
arxiv-2510-04980:
Fangzhou Liang and four co-authors test whether AI agents can read each other's minds in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their testbed is Hanabi, a cooperative card game. Players can see everyone else's cards but never their own. Winning depends on guessing what partners intend from the hints they give.

The team built an automated benchmark that scores both game results and mind-reading skill. Across many models, stronger theory-of-mind scores went with stronger play. First-order skill, reading a partner's intent, mattered far more than second-order skill. Large reasoning models beat standard models on both measures. The authors say future team agents should train basic intent reading first.
arxiv-2510-05280:
Elvar Atlason and Simon Guest build shapes that bend without stretching in this 2025 arXiv paper. A paper polyhedron normally cannot flex at all, because its faces lock together. Rare symmetric exceptions have been known since Bricard's flexible octahedra of 1897. Truly embedded examples without self-intersection are scarcer still.

The authors generalize Bricard's method through a construction they call twinning. Twinning produces an infinite family of flexible polyhedra with self-intersections. Removing one edge from such a model creates a crinkle building block. Assembling crinkles then yields flexible polyhedra with no self-intersection at all. One worked example flexes through a large range of motion. The family opens many new topologies for deployable structures.
arxiv-2510-05580:
Li and colleagues make robot vision-language-action models cheaper to adapt. Such models link images, instructions, and motor actions for embodied tasks. In practice they still need costly fine-tuning for each new job. Their 2025 framework, MetaVLA, folds many tasks into one training stage.

MetaVLA adds auxiliary tasks beside the target tasks during co-training. A light meta-learning mechanism, drawn from attentive neural processes, speeds adaptation. On the LIBERO benchmark, it beat OpenVLA by up to eight percent on long-horizon tasks. Training steps fell from 240 thousand to 75 thousand. GPU time dropped by about seventy-six percent as well. The framework stays agnostic about the underlying model backbone. One unified model handled all four task suites, unlike per-task rivals. The authors aim next at larger data and real-robot deployment. That path points toward general-purpose embodied agents at low cost.
arxiv-2510-05680:
Nalpantidi and Karlis build a joint model for two ordinal time series. Ordinal series take ordered categories, like credit ratings or pollution levels. Each series needs its own memory, and the pair needs cross-dependence too. Their 2025 BDAR model extends the classic discrete autoregression to two series.

Each current value either copies its predecessor or draws an innovation. Bernoulli switches make that choice inside each series. Copulas tie the switches and the innovations across the two series. The construction captures serial correlation and cross-correlation in one frame. Pegram's operator supplies the mixing mechanics behind the model. Simulations show efficient estimates even at moderate sample sizes. Ordinal data appear in health, sports, environment, and economics alike. Flexible copula choices cover many dependence shapes between series. A real application models unemployment states in two countries jointly.
arxiv-2510-05880:
Klasen reviews the nCTEQ program of nuclear parton distribution fits. Nuclear PDFs describe quark and gluon momentum inside bound protons and neutrons. They also set initial conditions for quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ion collisions. The 2025 review consolidates analyses since 2020 and previews a new global fit.

The new analysis builds on a modern proton baseline without nuclear data. It merges Jefferson Lab scattering, neutrino scattering with dimuons, and LHC data. Collider inputs include W and Z bosons, single hadrons, and heavy quarks. Relaxed kinematic cuts plus corrections described the precise Jefferson Lab data well. Proton-lead collisions opened a wide new kinematic regime for the fits. Uncertainties at large momentum fraction shrank, especially for up and down quarks. Preliminary results agree fully with the earlier data-driven approach. The forthcoming nCTEQ25 fit adds fully perturbative heavy-quark calculations.
arxiv-2510-06080:
Nguyen and co-authors build a sharper way to read mosquito release experiments in a 2025 modeling paper. Programs that release sterile males need honest estimates of how far the insects spread and how long they live. Simple summaries of trap returns can bias both numbers.

The framework starts from individual mosquitoes wandering as a two-dimensional diffusion with random death and capture. Its large-scale limit becomes a reaction–diffusion system fitted to daily trap counts through a Poisson observation model. A parametric bootstrap supplies uncertainty ranges, and simulations first confirm the parameters can be identified. The team then analyzed four weekly releases of sterile Aedes aegypti males in El Cano, Havana. The best model gives a post-release life expectancy near five days and a typical displacement near 180 meters. Such grounded estimates help planners design and judge sterile-insect campaigns in cities.
arxiv-2510-06280:
Siddiqui and five co-authors audit vision–language models for demographic bias in healthcare roles in a 2025 computing and society study. Models like CLIP absorb stereotypical profession–demographic links from web-scale data. In healthcare, such bias can leak into hiring tools and workforce analytics.

The team built a three-part evaluation protocol. A taxonomy spans clinician and allied roles like surgeon, cardiologist, dentist, nurse, pharmacist, and technician. A profession-aware prompt suite probes how models associate roles with faces. A balanced face corpus benchmarks the demographic skew. Across roles and vision models, the audits found consistent demographic biases. As the title notes, surgeons skew toward Indian males and speech therapists toward white females. The authors stress operational risk for compliance and patient trust. Their protocol gives healthcare AI buyers a concrete pre-deployment test.
arxiv-2510-06380:
Arun and Thahir ask whether the cosmological constant leaves a fingerprint in hadron physics in a 2025 particle phenomenology paper. Einstein gravity with a cosmological constant rewrites as a scalar theory whose coupling tracks Newton's constant times that constant. Quantum triviality would drive the coupling to zero unless matter couplings intervene.

The authors study hadron spectra holographically in an AdS5 geometry with an induced cosmological constant on its hypersurface. Measured rho and a1 meson spectra, excitations, and decay constants favor a non-vanishing induced constant. The preference appears in both hard-wall and soft-wall models, more sharply in the hard-wall case. The Gell-Mann–Oakes–Renner correction also depends inversely on the induced constant. That underscores its role in holographic low-energy QCD. A parameter usually reserved for cosmology thus earns a place in models of strongly interacting matter.
arxiv-2510-06580:
Sajad Dabiri and Reza Asgari build theory for how exotic materials respond to light. Their 2025 paper studies pseudo-Hermitian systems, a class used for media with balanced gain and loss. They want formulas for nonlinear optical conductivity when such a system reaches a steady state. Two standard ways of computing, called gauges, should agree if the theory is sound.

The authors derive compact formulas for the first- and second-order responses in both gauges. They prove the two gauges give exactly the same answers. The proof uses generalized sum rules and identities about Berry connections. Applied to a simple parity-time symmetric system, the theory predicts effects with no ordinary counterpart. These include extra conductivity terms, a direct photocurrent, and sharper resonance structures. The results matter for photonics built on engineered loss. They also guide work on quantum devices that use dissipation as a design tool.
arxiv-2510-06780:
Luca Giordano and Simon Razniewski ask how much of a language model's stored knowledge can be pulled out as structured facts. Their 2025 paper studies knowledge materialization, where a model is prompted to build a knowledge base. A method called GPTKB does this by recursive extraction. Three questions were open.

Does the extraction ever stop, do repeated runs agree, and do small changes break the output? The team ran domain crawls in history, entertainment, and finance to find out. They varied the seed entities, the language, the randomness, and the model. Termination rates were high but depended on the model. Reproducibility came out mixed across their measures. Runs agreed well on how much was extracted, less on wording. Robustness stayed high for new seeds and temperature changes. It dropped when the language or the model changed. The results suggest the method surfaces a model's knowledge dependably, with caveats.
arxiv-2510-06880:
Zhiyu Wang, Sonia Koszut, Pietro Liò, and Francesco Ceccarelli help computers merge the many data layers measured from single cells. Their 2025 paper works on multi-omics integration, where one cell yields gene, protein, and accessibility data at once. Each layer is huge and noisy, and the links between layers are tangled. Fixed diagrams of those links limit what models can learn.

Their system, MoRE-GNN, builds the relationship graph directly from the data instead. It is a graph autoencoder that mixes convolution with attention over typed edges. On six datasets, it captured biologically meaningful relationships better than rival methods. The advantage grew when the layers correlated strongly with each other. Learned cell descriptions predicted one data layer from another accurately. On one bone marrow dataset, protein predictions tracked measured values with a correlation near zero point nine five. Performance dipped on the noisiest datasets, which the authors report openly.
arxiv-2510-07480:
Huber, Clackdoyle, and Desbat characterize which data pairs a two-view tomography system could possibly produce. Their 2025 paper models each view as a line-integral operator along families of curves. Two projections together form a projection pair operator. Real measurements must lie in its range, and describing that range yields consistency conditions on the data. Such conditions power practical tasks like scanner calibration, motion detection, and parameter identification.

Their main theorem pins those conditions down and proves a strong uniqueness: all range conditions for a given pair operator are equivalent to each other. A supporting result shows the annihilating distributions of the range form at most a one-dimensional space. Together these results mean researchers no longer need to catalog competing consistency conditions for two-view systems.
arxiv-2510-07680:
Cristofaro-Gardiner wrote these 2025 lecture notes on low-dimensional topology and symplectic dynamics. The notes accompany his talks at the 2024 Current Developments in Mathematics conference at Harvard and MIT. They survey recent progress on dynamical systems in two and three dimensions. Tools from the topology of three-dimensional spaces drive much of that progress. Symplectic versions of Weyl's law, which counts oscillations, play a key role throughout.

The heart of the notes treats two longstanding problems in depth. One is the Simplicity Conjecture, and the other is the two-or-infinity conjecture of Hofer, Wysocki, and Zehnder. He sketches the key ideas and many steps of their proofs. Shorter sections cover symplectic Weyl laws and related results on periodic orbits. A final application concerns geodesics under Finsler metrics, which generalize distance. The notes aim at a mathematical audience and point to what remains unknown in higher dimensions.
arxiv-2510-08080:
Ibrahim and four coauthors wrote this 2025 survey of research on ultra-reliable low-latency communication for sixth-generation networks serving Industry 5.0. The new industrial vision stresses human-centric, resilient production. It demands sub-millisecond delays and near-perfect reliability that earlier generations cannot promise. The authors build a taxonomy spanning application domains, technical enablers, design challenges, and performance enhancements. Enablers include terahertz links, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, edge computing, and AI-driven cross-layer optimization.

They map these tools onto scenarios like smart manufacturing, connected healthcare, and autonomous mobility. Trade-offs among latency, reliability, scalability, and energy use are analyzed across representative studies. Digital twins and predictive resource orchestration receive detailed treatment. Open problems remain, including security without slack and channel estimation for smart surfaces. The survey gives engineers a structured map of a fast-moving field. It also frames the research agenda for making industrial wireless truly deterministic.
arxiv-2510-08280:
Lorenzo Peerani, Saburo Howard, and Ravit Helled ask how inner structure changes what we infer about giant planets, in a 2025 arXiv paper. A planet's bulk metallicity, its share of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium, hints at how it formed. But the same planet can yield different values under different structure guesses. The team tested three guesses on forty-four giant exoplanets.

The three structures were a core plus envelope, a dilute spread-out core, and a fully mixed interior. For each planet they ran evolution models with the CEPAM code and retrieved metallicity. Across all structures, heavier planets held more heavy elements in total, yet lower metallicity shares. Dilute core models gave values close to core-plus-envelope ones. Non-adiabatic dilute cores raised retrieved metallicity by up to thirty-five percent in some cases.
arxiv-2510-08380:
S. Abbaslu and the DUNE collaboration report a kaon selection in the ProtoDUNE-SP detector in a 2025 arXiv paper. DUNE, the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment, will hunt for proton decay, a process never yet observed. Some decay channels end with charged kaons, rare particles that signal the event. ProtoDUNE-SP was a 0.77 kiloton prototype that ran at CERN from 2018 to 2020.

The team picked low-energy kaons from particles made in test-beam reactions at six and seven GeV momenta. Their selection kept a sample purity of ninety-two percent, at an efficiency of one percent. The chosen kaons' energies cover the range expected from proton decay in DUNE, below about two hundred MeV. The work also shows the detector separates kaons from protons and muons well. Measured energy loss in liquid argon matched simulations closely.
arxiv-2510-08580:
Benjamin Shiue-Hal Chou and co-authors catch music practice mistakes with a multimodal transformer in a 2025 arXiv paper. Students benefit when tools flag wrong, missed, or extra notes against the score. Older systems compare audio to scores with heuristics, or fuse the streams only at the end. Late fusion weakens alignment between what is heard and what is written.

Their model, LadderSym, interleaves the streams instead of merging them late. A two-stream encoder whose alignment modules link the streams compares audio and symbolic score continuously. Symbolic scores also prompt the decoder directly, cutting ambiguity when many notes sound at once. On the MAESTRO-E data set, missed-note detection F1 more than doubled, rising from 26.8 percent to 56.3 percent with the new design. Extra-note detection gained 14.4 points, reaching 86.4 percent in the same tests.
arxiv-2510-08780:
Hu and co-authors propose a reusable starting point for neural networks that approximate functions, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such networks help solve science and engineering problems, but each new target function usually means training from scratch. Results also swing with design choices, and models often fail outside the range they trained on. The team's answer is to pretrain small networks on families of simple curves called polynomials.

Those pretrained networks cover one standard reference range, and their learned settings seed networks for harder targets. A mapping step reshapes any new input range to fit the reference range, keeping the seed useful. Tests in one and two dimensions showed clear gains in training speed. The seeded models also generalized better beyond their training range and transferred more readily between tasks, which supports modular reuse.
arxiv-2510-08980:
Ozkan and co-authors teach self-driving cars to save fuel by worrying about traffic jams they cannot yet see, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Eco-driving controllers plan a car's speed over a short horizon using route previews and messages from other vehicles. Trouble lurks beyond that horizon: an upstream jam will soon force braking that a short-sighted plan never priced in. The result is wasted energy when the jam arrives.

Their method folds the distant traffic into the plan through the terminal cost, the charge a controller assigns to whatever state it ends in. A neural network learns that charge while explicitly accounting for upstream traffic dynamics. The traffic-aware plans produced smoother, more energy-efficient speed profiles than traffic-blind rivals, with barely any cost in travel time. The framework runs in real time and is built to stay robust when traffic conditions swing unexpectedly.
arxiv-2510-09080:
Liu, Parreira, and Ju teach machines to read a person's face and voice to know when a robot has failed yet again, in this 2025 arXiv paper. People telegraph robot errors unasked: confusion first, then visible frustration, with raised eyebrows, tight lips, and impatient tones. Earlier work showed reactions can flag a single failure. This study asks whether the progression of reactions can reveal which failure in a sequence just happened.

The data comes from twenty-six people chatting with a robot programmed to fail repeatedly. The team extracted facial, gaze, posture, audio, and text features from the recordings. Models trained on one person at a time detected errors with about ninety-four percent accuracy on average. Classifying which successive error had occurred reached about eighty-four percent. Training across people probed whether the readings generalize to strangers.
arxiv-2510-09280:
Cirant and Continelli prove that a game played by a huge crowd of identical agents has exactly one equilibrium when the players are impatient enough, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Mean field games model crowds, traffic, or markets where each agent reacts to the population's overall distribution. Their equations couple one agent's optimal value with the crowd's motion, and solutions need not be unique. Uniqueness is usually bought with monotonicity assumptions on the costs, which many models fail.

The authors find a different regime. When the discount factor, measuring how sharply future rewards are devalued, is large enough, and the control cost is proportionally small enough, solutions are unique. Impatience shrinks each agent's horizon until feedback loops can no longer sustain multiple equilibria. The regime is asymptotic, appearing as the discount grows, and falls outside the classical monotonicity territory.
arxiv-2510-09380:
Reza Sedghi, Anand Subramoney, and David Kappel look for wasted computation in a vision transformer in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their target is DETR, a pretrained model that detects objects in images. Inside its feed-forward layers, many neurons stay inactive for a given image, and that natural sparsity could save work if the model could skip those neurons without retraining.

Their first method guesses inactive neurons from fixed activation patterns, but the gains stay small because sparsity changes with each input. The second method adds a tiny gating layer that predicts, for each input, which neurons to skip. It reached activation sparsity between eighty-five and ninety-five percent. On the COCO image benchmark, the gated model kept or even improved detection quality while cutting computation sharply, offering a practical route to cheaper deployment.
arxiv-2510-09480:
Noé Brucy and four co-authors ask how much gravity drives the growth of star-forming clouds, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Molecular clouds are the cold, dense regions where stars are born, and how they gather their mass remains unsettled. The role of gravity between the scale of a galactic disc and tiny prestellar cores is still debated.

The team studies one giant molecular cloud complex inside a numerical simulation of the interstellar medium, with ionising light and supernova blasts driving the gas. Tracer particles follow the gas and record the forces acting on it as clouds assemble. Up to twenty percent of the gas at the hundred-parsec scale was gravity-driven, and the share rose to forty-five percent inside dense molecular gas. Even so, most cloud-building motion came from supernova-driven turbulence pushing flows together, and gravity barely affected the gas linewidth at large scales.
arxiv-2510-09580:
Margarita Belova, Jiaxin Xiao, Shikhar Tuli, and Niraj Jha introduce GraphMERT in a 2025 arXiv paper, a small model that builds knowledge graphs from raw text. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked entities and relations, giving artificial intelligence a symbolic form it can check. Deriving reliable graphs automatically from text corpora has stayed an open problem, and large language models prompted for the job prove unreliable.

GraphMERT is a tiny graphical encoder that distils a graph from unstructured text and from its own internal representations. Paired with its graph, it forms a neurosymbolic stack: neural learning below, symbolic reasoning above. The authors target domain graphs that are factual, with provenance for each fact, and valid, with relations that respect the domain's ontology. They report state-of-the-art benchmark accuracy with symbolic representations superior to the baselines, including graphs generated by a large model such as Qwen3-32B.
arxiv-2510-09780:
ChengAo Shen and six co-authors build a tiny forecasting model that borrows the habits of giant vision models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Large pretrained models forecast time series well but cost heavily in energy, hardware, and inference. For a specific task, a small specialised model may serve users such as small businesses far better.

The authors first identify the key inductive biases that make large vision model forecasters good at long-term forecasting, treating them as a kind of physics of the big models. SVTime encodes those biases in a compact model of crafted linear layers and constraint functions. Against twenty-one baselines, from lightweight models to large pretrained ones, across eight benchmark datasets, SVTime beat the leading lightweight models. It rivalled the large models while using about a thousand times fewer parameters than the vision forecasters, and it trains and runs efficiently in low-resource settings.
arxiv-2510-09880:
Kim, Changwoon Choi, and Young Min Kim propose geometry-aware scene layouts in this 2025 arXiv paper on novel view synthesis. The task is to render new views of indoor scenes from partial observations, so a user can move through a space that was never fully captured. Indoor scenes mix several rooms with clutter, blocked views, and flat walls.

The authors allocate the model's limited capacity in a scene-adaptive way, spending more where geometry is complex and less where it is plain. Geometric priors, structural hints left over from earlier processing steps, guide that spending. The approach aims to make fuller use of a fixed budget. The result targets immersive indoor experiences that stay sharp despite incomplete input.
arxiv-2510-10080:
Kim constructs multiset spaces with metric topologies in this 2025 arXiv paper in topology. A multiset is a collection where elements may repeat, like a bag of values. The paper builds a space of multisets over a metric space, a space where distances are defined.

Kim equips that multiset space with a natural matching metric, which measures how well two multisets can be paired off. The result is a metrizable abelian topological monoid, a space where multisets can be combined continuously and distances still make sense. The construction also admits a group completion, extending the bag-like structure to one with inverses. The work gives multisets a rigorous geometric home for use in data analysis.
arxiv-2510-10680:
Nassim Athmouni analyzes fractional discrete Laplacians living on a half lattice, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These operators are discrete cousins of fractional diffusion, and the half lattice is a grid cut off at an edge, possibly with a different fractional order along each axis. Athmouni writes the half lattice case as the full lattice operator restricted to the boundary, plus a bounded, relatively compact correction.

From that split, both share the same essential spectrum and threshold structure. For potentials that decay at infinity, an operator method gives a strict Mourre estimate on energy windows inside the continuous spectrum, away from thresholds. As a consequence, a localized limiting absorption principle holds: there is no singular continuous spectrum, eigenvalues are finite in number, and weighted transport bounds hold. The approach also extends to negative orders.
arxiv-2510-10780:
Maxwell Fogler studies how a good or bad harvest changes whether Rwandan children stay in school, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Farming households face a trade off between immediate production needs and long term investment in education. Rwanda relies heavily on rain fed agriculture. Fogler uses a district level panel dataset from 2010 to 2021. Rainfall variation serves as an instrument for satellite measured vegetation health, letting him read the effects causally.

The pattern splits by school level. For primary school, where costs are low, enrollment is countercyclical: good shocks lower enrollment, as children are pulled into farm work. Boys' primary enrollment responds significantly more than girls'. For secondary school, which costs real money, enrollment is strongly procyclical: good shocks raise it. A sustained positive shock, though, is followed by a decline in female secondary enrollment. The results challenge the regional claim that girls act as a buffer that absorbs shocks.
arxiv-2510-10880:
Zhaofang Qian and eleven co-authors test whether vision language models can figure out where a photo was taken, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Geolocation from a single image is hard and useful, yet open world skill here was not comprehensively measured. Their benchmark, EarthWhere, holds 810 globally distributed images at two scales. One part asks for the country, with 500 multiple choice questions over panoramas. The other demands street level identification in 310 tasks needing multi step reasoning.

They score final answers by distance and also grade the reasoning chains against human verified visual clues. Thirteen leading models were benchmarked with web search tools. Gemini-2.5-Pro did best, averaging 56.32 percent accuracy, while the strongest open weight model reached 34.71 percent in the reported results. Search and reasoning did not guarantee gains when visual clues were scarce. Models also showed regional bias, scoring up to 42.7 percent higher in some regions than others.
arxiv-2510-11480:
Vanadium dioxide flips between a metallic phase and an insulating phase near room temperature, and squeezing the crystal with strain can move that transition. Peter Mlkvik, Lena Geistlich, Nicola A. Spaldin, and Claude Ederer compute how strain shifts the balance in this 2025 arXiv materials paper. Using density-functional theory, they compare the metallic rutile phase and the insulating monoclinic M1 phase under strain conditions like those in grown films.

Their calculations confirm that strain along the c axis, the direction of the vanadium-vanadium dimer chains in the insulating phase, dominates the relative stability of the two phases. The analysis suggests the effect comes mainly from a weakening of the lattice stiffness under that strain, with changes in electron hopping along the axis playing only a minor role. Even when the basal plane is deformed, the induced c-axis strain still dominates the phase stability.
arxiv-2510-11780:
Rodrigo Córdova Rosado and six colleagues ask whether hidden and visible quasars live in the same neighborhoods. Quasars are brilliant galactic centers powered by growing black holes. Type I quasars show themselves directly, while Type II quasars hide behind dust. The team's 2025 arXiv paper cross-matches about twenty-eight thousand five hundred machine-learning-selected active galaxies against one and a half million luminous red galaxies from the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey.

Using halo occupation modeling, which links clustering to host dark matter halos, the team finds sharp differences. Type I quasars sit in halos roughly three times more massive than those of Type II quasars, a gap significant at over five sigma. Type I quasars also almost never live in satellite galaxies, while Type II quasars show ordinary satellite rates. Together, these results challenge the idea that the two types differ only by viewing angle.
arxiv-2510-11880:
David Fabre questions a textbook story about when wakes turn unsteady. Behind a slender body, flows are said to destabilize through a pocket of absolute instability near the body. Fabre's 2025 arXiv paper examines a thin plate facing the flow squarely. Global stability analysis finds many unstable modes there, even though no absolutely unstable pocket exists.

The modes form a pattern he calls an arc-branch, and it shifts suspiciously with the size of the simulation box. Fabre traces them to a numerical artefact: the no-stress outlet condition creates a stray pressure disturbance that travels back upstream and triggers vortex shedding at the plate's edge. For a NACA0012 wing at small angles, both this fake feedback and the genuine local mechanism operate. Enlarging the box does not help. Filters that damp spatial growth do. With them, he maps the critical Reynolds and Strouhal numbers for incidences up to five degrees.
arxiv-2510-11980:
Andrew Pendleton counts a new species of number square in this 2025 arXiv paper. An equi-n-square is a grid where symbols repeat with perfect evenness, a relative of the Latin square. Pendleton's consecutive variant demands that at least one row or column run in consecutive, or reverse-consecutive, order. Unlike stricter cousins, not every symbol must appear in every line.

He derives exact counting formulas for small cases and asymptotic formulas for large ones. The headline estimate shows the consecutive squares form a vanishing slice of all equi-n-squares: their proportion races toward zero as the size grows. He also analyzes how the squares distribute under uniform random sampling. An algebraic lens recasts the squares as Cayley tables, the multiplication charts of algebraic structures, connecting the counting to group-like symmetries. Monte Carlo simulations for small sizes confirm the formulas.
arxiv-2510-12480:
Janson defines two new variants of U-statistics for data arranged in cycles or with alternating signs, in a 2025 arXiv statistics paper. U-statistics are averages of a function over tuples of observations, a workhorse of nonparametric statistics. The variants here use only order two, meaning pairs of observations, and are inspired by special cases that arose in the study of random permutations.

Cyclic U-statistics assume the variables come with a cyclic order, like positions around a circle. Alternating U-statistics sum their terms with alternating signs, in three distinct ways. Janson proves limit theorems analogous to the classical results for standard U-statistics, describing the distribution of the statistic for large samples. The versions differ in their limits: some give nondegenerate normal limits, while others give degenerate, non normal limits. The paper carefully separates which variant falls in which camp, extending permutation motivated examples into a general theory.
arxiv-2510-12580:
Dizenhaus, De Simone, and Patterson show that a single hidden leader can rhythmically steer a swarm of simple robots, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The steering is strongest at an intermediate noise level. Their experiments use Kilobots, small robots that move and sense neighbors, plus matching numerical simulations. One leader alternates between clockwise and counterclockwise motion on a fixed schedule, while followers use a stochastic majority rule.

The leader does not change the swarm's global order. Yet correlations between the leader's motion and the collective response peak at intermediate perturbation levels. The pattern resembles stochastic resonance, where noise amplifies a weak signal. Simulations confirm the resonance occurs when the leader's reversal period matches the average time the unperturbed system spends in one state. The results add to understanding decision making in active matter, systems of self driven units. They also suggest principles for steering robotic swarms under minimal leadership input.
arxiv-2510-12680:
Wang and colleagues test whether language models that switch between thinking aloud and answering directly keep the two modes separate, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Hybrid thinking promises efficiency: reason when needed, answer at once when not. Their experiments reveal only partial separation, with reasoning behavior leaking into the no think mode, wasting tokens.

Analyzing what governs controllability, they identify four factors that matter most. These are larger training data scale, and think and no think answers drawn from different questions. Also key are a moderate increase in no think data, and a two phase recipe that trains reasoning first, then hybrid switching. Their practical recipe maintained accuracy in both modes while sharply cutting no think output length on a math benchmark. Markers of leaked reasoning, such as a characteristic hesitation word, fell more than tenfold. They offer the recipe as a fix for leaky mode switching.
arxiv-2510-12780:
Aggazzotti and co-authors tackle privacy in long recordings in this 2025 arXiv paper. Voice anonymization can hide who is speaking in short clips, but interviews, calls, and meetings contain many utterances from one person. An attacker could then identify the speaker from word choices, sentence habits, and turns of phrase even if the voice itself is fully disguised.

The team built content anonymization methods that rewrite automatic transcripts inside a speech pipeline, changing speaker-specific style while keeping the meaning intact, before speech is regenerated. On long telephone conversations they first showed that content-based attacks work against voice-only anonymization. Their rewriting then reduced that risk while keeping the speech useful, and they recommend paraphrasing as a standard defense step.
arxiv-2510-12880:
Raja and Ganesh merge two famous exactly solvable models in this 2025 arXiv paper. The AKLT model describes a chain of spin-1 particles, while Kitaev models use direction-dependent couplings between spins. Both are prized because their ground states, the lowest-energy configurations, can be written down exactly through fractionalization, splitting spins into simpler fictitious particles.

The authors build a chain with both two-spin and four-spin interactions of Kitaev type. At a special point, the energy operator becomes a sum of projection operators. Theirs, though, project along bond directions rather than total spin. The model then has exponentially many ground states, each written compactly as a matrix product state. Varying the interaction balance yields a phase diagram, and the exact states give approximate pictures for the ground state and lowest excitations of the spin-1 Kitaev chain.
arxiv-2510-13080:
