Because the defense sits outside the model, it can protect different systems the same way. Tests aim to keep helpful answers flowing while blocking manipulation. Safer deployment is the practical goal.
arxiv-2511-07680:
Sajad Salami bounds the arithmetic complexity of a family of algebraic curves. For curves shaped by a simple power equation, their Jacobian varieties carry a Mordell-Weil group whose rank counts independent rational points. Whether ranks stay bounded as the curve varies within the family was open.

Assuming a strong form of Lang conjecture on rational points, Salami proves uniform rank bounds across the family. The proof builds a parameter space for curves with chosen point patterns, extending Yamagishi geometric approach. Uniform bounds are prized in number theory because they promise whole families behave tamely, not just single examples checked one by one.
arxiv-2511-08080:
Ziyu Fan and co-authors propose HSPAG, a data efficient method for generating and editing molecules under property limits. Drug discovery needs molecules that meet several property goals at once, but structure property links are tangled and annotations are sparse. Note the arXiv title differs from the older evidence title for this record.

HSPAG aligns molecule structure and properties at atom, substructure, and whole molecule levels, treating SMILES strings and properties as paired views. Scaffold clustering picks representative training samples, while a variational model finds hard cases, cutting data needs. Masking based on property relevance and varied perturbations improve generation, and two real cases test editing.
arxiv-2511-08180:
Guido Masarotto presents a full algorithm for fitting generative models whose likelihoods and moments cannot be computed directly. Many realistic models can only be simulated, leaving standard inference tools unusable. His method needs only limited prior information about the parameters, aiming at a general solution rather than a model specific trick.

A global search first locates the promising region of parameter space. A local search then imitates a trust region form of Fisher scoring to produce a quasi likelihood estimate. Comparisons with rival methods show strong performance across cases. An R package on CRAN implements the algorithm for direct use by practitioners.
arxiv-2511-08380:
Bao-Jun Cai, Bao-An Li, and Yu-Gang Ma revisit whether a sharp first order phase transition can occur inside cold neutron stars, the densest visible matter in the universe. A hadron to quark transition would appear as a flat plateau in the equation of state, pressure against energy density. Many numerical studies accept such models because their mass radius curves look reasonable against observations.

The authors argue the plateau is intrinsically incompatible with regularity conditions required by the Tolman Oppenheimer Volkoff equations that govern star structure. Seemingly fine numerical integrations can hide that inconsistency. The result adds a structural consistency test for dense matter equations of state, complementing observational constraints on neutron star interiors.
arxiv-2511-08780:
Mohammadali Aligholi, Laurenţiu Maxim, and Jörg Schürmann survey recent progress on a class version of the Hodge index theorem for singular algebraic varieties. Brasselet, Schürmann, and Yokura proposed that the homology L-classes of Goresky and MacPherson can be computed from Hodge-theoretic L-classes, even when the variety has singular points.

Along the way the authors clarify how several rival notions of L-classes in the record relate to one another. They also add many new families where the conjecture now holds: all compact toric varieties, matroid Schubert varieties, Richardson and intersection varieties, and projective simply connected spherical varieties. Compact complex algebraic surfaces and threefolds are covered as well. The paper serves as both a map of the area and a research result.
arxiv-2511-08880:
Chayapatr Archiwaranguprok and four co-authors build a testing ground for the psychological harms chatbots might cause or worsen, from addiction and eating disorders to psychosis and suicide. Rather than waiting for more real cases, they simulate risky conversations at scale, seeded by documented incidents where AI interactions contributed to severe outcomes.

Eighteen real cases supply the harmful interaction patterns, which are expanded into two thousand one hundred sixty simulated scenarios judged with clinical staging models. Four major language models play through more than one hundred fifty-seven thousand conversation turns. The analysis finds gaps in spotting distress, answering vulnerable users well, and stopping escalation. Performance varies by persona, worse for elderly users and better for lower-income ones. Fifteen failure patterns cluster into four categories of AI-enabled harm.
arxiv-2511-09580:
Sudip Kumar Kar and Valeriya Mykhaylova extend a quantum kinetic account of spinning particles to obey Fermi-Dirac statistics. The Wigner function is the phase-space stand-in for a quantum state. A recent version described massive spin-half particles in local equilibrium under Boltzmann rules. Real fermions, though, must respect the exclusion principle.

The new formula keeps the mean polarization vector correctly normalized. It also reproduces the thermodynamic relations with spin found in earlier work. The authors show the large-scale currents follow from differentiating one generating function with respect to temperature, flow, and chemical potentials. That generating function reveals the approach belongs to the divergence-type family of theories, a well-structured class in relativistic fluid dynamics.
arxiv-2511-09680:
Shunyuan Shang and two co-authors model an underwater optical link. It delivers data and power through the same beam of light. Underwater sensors are hard to recharge, so a photovoltaic panel receiver that decodes signals while harvesting energy is attractive. Their system uses simultaneous lightwave information and power transfer across two phases.

The authors build a composite channel model covering distance-dependent absorption, turbulence-induced fading, and beam misalignment from pointing errors. From it they derive closed-form expressions for outage probability, average bit error rate, capacity, and harvested power, using advanced special functions. The framework is meant as practical design guidance for self-powered underwater sensor networks. It clarifies how ocean conditions trade against communication reliability and energy income.
arxiv-2511-09780:
Nikolay Blagoev, Oğuzhan Ersoy, and Lydia Yiyu Chen examine security in decentralised training of large language models with GRPO, a reinforcement learning method. Because nodes exchange only short text completions, training can be split across many machines, which also opens a door: a malicious node can share poisoned completions. The paper presents the first adversarial attacks built for this setting.

Across math and coding tasks, the attacks drove success rates as high as 100 percent within as few as fifty training rounds. The authors then test two defenses, one checking completion probabilities and one using a language model as judge. Both stopped every attack except a denial-of-service variant that forces overly long but correct answers, and the code is public.
arxiv-2511-09980:
Bo Li and five co-authors improve dynamic retrieval-augmented generation, where a model fetches outside knowledge mid-answer. Timing is the hard part: waiting for low token confidence can mean retrieving only after an error has already spread. Their method, Entropy-Trend Constraint, watches how the model's uncertainty evolves rather than its level at one instant.

Using first and second differences of the token entropy sequence, the method detects a rising uncertainty trend early and triggers retrieval then. It needs no training and plugs into existing decoding pipelines for any model. On six question-answering benchmarks with three model backbones, it beat strong baselines while retrieving less often, with especially robust results in domain-specific settings. Ablations supported the trend-aware design.
arxiv-2511-10080:
Yasuyuki Kawahigashi, writing alone, connects two languages for describing two-dimensional topological order: the tensor networks used by condensed matter researchers and the subfactor theory of operator algebras. Physicists' four-tensors in these networks were expected to match bi-unitary connections in Jones' theory. Kawahigashi makes that identification precise, including the exact normalization constants.

He then proves that two-tensors satisfying the zipper condition from physics are exactly the flat fields of strings in that theory, which correspond to elements of the higher relative commutants. Notably, the proof needs neither flatness nor finite depth of the connection, and it generalizes the tensors so all four index sets may differ. The bridge lets results travel between physics and algebra.
arxiv-2511-10280:
Dogan Akpinar, writing alone, computes how a graviton scatters off a massive spinning compact object, working to second order in Newton's constant and through quartic order in the object's spin. This classical one-loop gravitational Compton amplitude is a building block for modeling binary systems with gravitational waves. The calculation includes spin-induced finite-size effects up to hexadecapolar order, extending earlier minimal-coupling results that stopped at quadratic spin.

From the amplitude, Akpinar extracts the scattering phase in momentum space, valid in both eikonal and wave regimes. In the eikonal limit, the spin-independent part is isolated and tied explicitly to a massless scalar probe moving in a Kerr background. The paper claims the first complete description at this order for generic spinning objects.
arxiv-2511-10680:
Jean-Philippe Lignier presents LAD-BNet, a neural network built to forecast energy use in real time on small edge devices, the kind of hardware smart grids and intelligent buildings can actually deploy. The design goal is accuracy at short horizons without the memory and speed costs of cloud-scale models.

The architecture has two branches. One exploits time lags in the consumption signal directly. A temporal convolutional branch with dilated convolutions captures short- and long-term patterns together. On real consumption data sampled every ten minutes, the model reached a mean absolute percentage error under 15 percent at the one-hour horizon. It answered in 18 milliseconds on a Coral Edge TPU, and beat both LSTM and pure convolutional baselines while fitting in 180 megabytes.
arxiv-2511-10880:
Momchil E. Molnar and six co-authors report early observations of waves in the Sun's corona from Cryo-NIRSP, a newly commissioned infrared spectropolarimeter at the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope in Hawaii. Coronal waves are candidates for delivering the energy that heats the corona and drives the solar wind, but their high-frequency behavior has been hard to catch.

Pointed off the solar limb at closed structures in an active region, the instrument recorded two forbidden iron lines with spatial resolution of a few arcseconds and cadence faster than a second. Wave power stays enhanced up to one hundred millihertz. The data also show a significant anti-correlation between the main line's peak intensity and its width, a possible signature of compressive magnetohydrodynamic wave modes. The authors say the results show DKIST's promise for coronal wave studies.
arxiv-2511-10980:
The Belle II Collaboration reports the first search for a rare decay in which a B meson turns into a strange particle system plus a pair of neutrinos. Neutrinos leave no trace in the detector, so the decay is hard to spot. Data came from the Belle II detector at the SuperKEKB collider in Japan, with a large sample taken at a known resonance.

One B meson of each pair was fully rebuilt from a known decay, which let the team infer the other side. Thirty decay routes were combined to catch the rare signal across three mass ranges. No clear signal was seen, so the team set upper limits on how often it can occur.
arxiv-2511-11580:
Andrei Gyarmathy and Georgy Lukyanov modeled how costly peace signals between hostile groups can both prevent wars and, once fighting starts, lock in stalemates. Their overlapping-generations setup has older members privately signaling younger ones, with group types that persist and memories of past encounters that stay noisy.

Within that model, reassurance signals lowered the chance of conflict starting, while publicity around signals could lengthen conflicts already under way. The authors later withdrew the submission after finding errors in the equilibrium characterization and the comparative-statics results, and a substantially rebuilt model was reported as in preparation. The record is kept here with that withdrawal stated plainly.
arxiv-2511-11780:
Hossein Mohebbi and four co-authors present Image-POSER. It creates and edits images by directing a team of specialist models. One generator is not trusted alone. Long, complex creative prompts defeat single models, since each has blind spots.

A registry of pretrained text-to-image and image-editing experts is run step by step. Prompts are split into tasks. Each step is checked by a vision-language critic. The pipeline adapts based on that feedback. The setup is framed as a Markov decision process. It learns non-obvious ways to combine experts. Reported results beat baselines, including frontier models, on industry-style tasks.
arxiv-2511-11880:
David Montero and eight co-authors compare two deep learning families on a carbon task. The task is to estimate gross primary production in forests. That is the carbon plants absorb through photosynthesis. Flux towers measure it well, but only at scattered points. Models must stretch those readings across whole landscapes with remote sensing.

Single-sensor indices and plain statistical models miss the time dynamics of vegetation. Transformer and recurrent networks are tested on fused, multi-source data. Which design tracks seasonal and weather-driven swings best is the core question. The answer matters for carbon accounting. Forest uptake estimates feed climate policy and carbon market choices far beyond the tower sites.
arxiv-2511-12180:
Ge Cheng, Shuo Wang and Yun Zhang seek a clearer theory for InfoNCE, the main loss used in contrastive learning across vision, language and graph tasks. Contrastive learning trains models by pulling matched views together and pushing others apart, yet why InfoNCE works has stayed partly unclear.

The authors model augmented views in a feature space and use a transition matrix to capture how augmentation moves between them. They show InfoNCE drives matched views toward a target set by that matrix, which naturally forms clusters. Building on that, they propose a scaled version with a tunable target. Tests on image, graph and text benchmarks show strong results.
arxiv-2511-12580:
Hajime Kobayashi and four co-authors analyze how a non-rotating black hole responds to tidal forces. That response shapes the gravitational waves from merging pairs. It can also reveal the theory of gravity at work. They work in the low-frequency regime for static, spherically symmetric black holes in general relativity.

The analysis matches two tools: an analytic method for black hole perturbations and a worldline effective theory that computes binary dynamics efficiently. They show the renormalized tidal response carries unavoidable ambiguities. These come from the choice of scheme and from the starting conditions for its flow. Once those are fixed, dynamical tidal Love numbers tied to the scheme follow. Extensions to neutron stars and to theories beyond general relativity are discussed.
arxiv-2511-12680:
Martin Ridout surveys the tredoku tilings of Donald Preece, a combinatorial design theorist who died in 2014. Shortly before his death, Preece gave two talks on these tilings, which grew out of a puzzle of the same name, and offered a conjecture about when such tilings exist. That conjecture has since been proved by Simon Blackburn. Ridout's paper is both a memorial overview and a research contribution in its own right.

Alongside Preece's work, the paper covers his generalization called quadridoku tilings. Ridout gives new proofs of parts of the existence theorem and reports a computer enumeration of the distinct tredoku tilings with up to sixteen tiles. A short section introduces tilings with holes. Readers get a guided tour of a small, self-contained corner of tiling theory, written by a close follower of the originator's work.
arxiv-2511-12780:
Thomas Sales and Iain Smears prove existence results for fully nonlinear mean field games with Hamiltonians that are not differentiable. Mean field games model crowds of agents optimizing against the group's distribution, as a coupled equation system. With a nondifferentiable Hamiltonian, the transport side becomes a partial differential inclusion driven by a set-valued subdifferential, which standard methods cannot handle directly.

The authors recast that inclusion as a nonstandard variational inequality, a reformulation that makes limit arguments flexible. Under uniform ellipticity and a Cordes condition on diffusion, they prove solutions exist for stationary systems with general couplings and nonnegative source terms on bounded convex domains. They also prove uniqueness for strictly monotone couplings and show the rough system arises as a limit of smooth ones. The paper is foundational analysis for crowd models with kinked cost structures.
arxiv-2511-12980:
Hidetsugu Sakaguchi and Boris A. Malomed repair a textbook theorem for quantum fluids trapped in a box. The Ehrenfest theorem normally ties the motion of a wave packet's center of mass to a classical equation of motion. Inside a potential box with hard walls, that form fails, because the walls themselves push back. An earlier fix added an effective force from the box edges for a single particle. The authors extend the corrected theorem to the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, which governs Bose-Einstein condensates with interactions, and to a two-dimensional square box.

In their amended equations, the nonlinear interaction term contributes nothing directly, yet it acts through the edge force, and can make the center-of-mass motion irregular. Numerical simulations confirm the amended law in both dimensions, speaking directly to experiments with condensates in box traps.
arxiv-2511-13080:
Steven Landers and Benjamin Marsh analyze extractable value in blockchains where several proposers build blocks at once. In normal chains a single block order is fixed before execution, but in multiple concurrent proposer designs, several blocks become available before anyone knows their final order. That concurrency opens new extraction channels: duplicate transactions racing in the same tick, auctions between proposers, and timing games. The authors model delay and inclusion with a hazard-normalized model and solve for equilibria of the resulting games.

They show that deterministic priority scheduling on a directed acyclic graph, combined with payouts that account for duplicates, can neutralize the same-tick extraction while keeping throughput. The setups they recommend need no central block builder. The paper speaks to protocol designers weighing concurrency for speed: parallel blocks multiply the ways value can be siphoned, unless the rules price those moves away in advance.
arxiv-2511-13780:
Nihal Mehta offers a unified reading of the transformer design through distributional semantics. Self-attention, he argues, arises from mapping corpus-level word co-occurrence statistics into the context of a single sequence. Starting from the same matrix behind GloVe embeddings, that mapping naturally yields contextual influence between tokens.

The query, key, and value mechanism then appears as the natural asymmetric extension for directional relations. Position marks and multi-head designs follow as structured refinements of the same idea. On this account, the transformer's basic shape is not an arbitrary invention but a consequence of those principles, a viewpoint that may guide how future architectures are derived rather than guessed.
arxiv-2511-13880:
Saleh Momeni, Changnan Xiao, and Bing Liu work on teaching AI models new classes over time without forgetting old ones. This class-incremental learning problem often uses a frozen pretrained model plus a formula-based classifier, which works well but never adapts the underlying features. Their method, AnaCP, aims to keep the efficiency while letting features improve.

AnaCP adapts features step by step through analytic contrastive projection, with no gradient-based training at all. Removing gradient updates removes the main source of catastrophic forgetting in this setup. In experiments the method beats existing baselines and reaches the accuracy of joint training, where all classes are learned together, long treated as the ceiling for this task.
arxiv-2511-14080:
Chao Zhang and Tao Zhu study periodic orbits around a deformed black hole and the gravitational waves those orbits emit. The spacetime is the gamma-metric, a static vacuum solution with a mass and a deformation parameter. When the deformation equals one it reduces to the familiar Schwarzschild case, so any difference traces the loss of spherical symmetry.

Periodic orbits are sorted by three topological numbers that capture their zoom-whirl character. The authors show deformation shifts orbit radii and angular momentum, reshaping that taxonomy, and they compute example waveforms. Deformed orbits show phase shifts and amplitude changes tied to the zoom-whirl structure, suggesting extreme-mass-ratio inspiral signals could measure such deformations.
arxiv-2511-14280:
Daniele Martinelli, Andrea Martin, Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate, and one co-author define a new yardstick for distributed controllers. Large systems, from power grids to process plants, use controllers wired along the same graph that couples their parts. The authors introduce spatial regret: the worst-case gap between such a controller and an oracle allowed extra sensors on an enlarged information graph.

Minimizing spatial regret produces controllers that mimic the oracle's response to typical large-network disturbances, such as localized shocks. The authors give a convex reformulation, a finite approximation, and an efficiently minimizable upper bound for big networks. On power-system models the resulting controllers handled localized disturbances better than classically designed ones.
arxiv-2511-14580:
Yiming Zhu studies quasi-Albanese morphisms for log canonical Calabi-Yau pairs in algebraic geometry. These pairs are singular spaces with controlled boundary structure. The quasi-Albanese map is a universal map toward a semi-abelian variety. Understanding it reveals global structure of the pair.

Zhu proves several structural results about these maps in the log canonical setting. As a direct application, he gives a characterization of toric pairs. Toric pairs are a concrete class built from combinatorial data. A clean criterion for recognizing them is valuable. Though short and technical, the note links abstract Albanese theory to a concrete classification result that other geometers can apply.
arxiv-2511-14680:
Shijun Liang, Ismail Alkhouri, Qing Qu, Rongrong Wang, and Saiprasad Ravishankar extend diffusion-based image reconstruction from flat pictures to 3D CT scans. Diffusion solvers for inverse imaging have grown strong by casting sampling as a fitting step that enforces consistency with the measurements and with the diffusion process itself. Those methods, though, were built for 2D tasks and do not carry over directly to volumetric scans, where slices must agree with each other.

Their method, NERD, adds a penalty term that encourages continuity across neighbouring slices, cutting inter-slice artefacts and promoting coherent volumes. Two fast methods solve the resulting problem. For medical imaging, coherent 3D reconstructions from limited data are the difference between a scan a radiologist can trust and one full of seams.
arxiv-2511-15180:
Geng Chen, Faris A. El-Katri, and two co-authors prove that certain smooth flows of a compressible gas must break down in finite time. The setting is the Euler equations with radial symmetry, for an ideal gas that heats strongly under compression. The flow in question is a supersonic wave rushing inward toward the center.

The proof follows the flow along its natural paths, the method of characteristics. An invariant domain idea fences in the solution along the way. Together they show a singularity forms for a class of such starting waves. The result covers gases with a heat ratio at or above a stated threshold. Finite-time breakdown results mark the exact limits of smooth models for imploding gas flows.
arxiv-2511-15280:
Sam Adriaensen, Jan De Beule, and two co-authors connect two classification stories in algebraic graph theory and finite geometry, while openly flagging a problem with their own chain of reasoning. A 1999 result by Weng nearly classified classical distance-regular graphs of negative type with diameter at least four. Recent work removed the last leftover family for diameter three, which completes the classification for larger diameters as well.

Through a result of Vanhove, that completion would prove that certain hemisystems in Hermitian polar spaces cannot exist. The authors warn plainly that an error in the literature means these conclusions cannot yet be trusted. The note's purpose is to record the interesting link and the caveat together, so others can repair the argument.
arxiv-2511-16280:
Shota Komatsu and Pronobesh Maity present a worldsheet action, the surface a moving string sweeps out in string theory. Their action reproduces a family of dual resonance amplitudes that build on the famous Veneziano amplitude for open strings. Their proposal builds on a recently introduced chiral composite linear dilaton.

Working from that action, the authors compute extensions to higher-point amplitudes, where more particles take part. They also compute closed-string analogs of the same formulas. Those extensions show partial crossing symmetry, a consistency property linking different scattering channels. The result gives a concrete worldsheet origin for amplitudes that had earlier been discussed mainly as formulas, tying them back to an underlying string picture.
arxiv-2511-16380:
Kibok Jeong and Soochang Lee give a field theory realization of the non-unitary WRT topological quantum field theory built from the Lie algebra sl(2,C). At the principal root of unity this theory is unitary and comes from SU(2) Chern-Simons theory. At other roots it is non-unitary and had no known field theory home.

The proposal is that the non-unitary theory arises from the topological twist of a three-dimensional supersymmetric rank-zero theory, assembled by joining several T[SU(2)] theories. The authors construct the modular matrices of their theory and match them with those of the WRT theory, pinning down the relation between the parameters up to a separate unitary factor. The match gives the non-unitary invariant a concrete gauge theory origin.
arxiv-2511-16580:
El-Mehdi Mehiri introduces block-separated overpartitions, a new family in partition theory. Overpartitions allow the first occurrence of each part size to be overlined. The block-separated version adds a local rule that no two consecutive distinct part-blocks may both be overlined, interpolating between ordinary partitions and full overpartitions.

Once the set of distinct part sizes is fixed, the allowed overlining patterns are counted by Fibonacci numbers, which drives the whole theory. Mehiri expands the generating function in symmetric functions, gives a two-state transfer-matrix form, and extracts an Euler product form. From it flow normalized and second-order recurrences, determinantal formulas, and a continued-fraction form for finite truncations. The counting function grows on the same exponential scale as ordinary partitions, with a different constant below that scale.
arxiv-2511-16780:
Robert J. S Airey and six co-authors recover the spin state of Ajisai, a spherical Japanese satellite covered in mirrors, from streaked telescope images, as a rehearsal for active debris removal. Knowing how a debris target tumbles is essential for safe capture, yet rotation must usually be inferred from unresolved imaging alone.

Four SuperWASP observations from August 2019 provided high-cadence photometry extracted from the streaks. A Markov chain Monte Carlo method compares the alignment between modeled mirror positions and a derived map of surface reflectivity to pin down the spin axis and period. The solutions agree with empirical expectations and align the reflectivity map with the mirrors well. The demonstration shows modest ground instruments can characterize fast spinners, a scalable skill for the growing debris population.
arxiv-2511-17080:
Arnau Mir, Alejandro Mus, and Juan Vicente Riera work on discrete fuzzy numbers, a way to encode words like low, medium, or high as mathematical objects on a finite scale. Ranking such numbers with a total order lets engineers build logical connectives for fuzzy systems, but finding each number's exact position in the ranking was costly. The authors revisit that positioning problem with fresh algorithms.

Their methods exploit the combinatorial structure of admissible orders to compute a number's position, and to invert the computation, exactly. The cost grows only modestly with the size of the scale and the number of membership levels, with the level count as the dominant factor. Lower costs make operations like aggregation and implication practical for larger fuzzy systems. The framework supports linguistic computing that stays exact rather than approximate.
arxiv-2511-17280:
Xavier Bardina and three co-authors extend a family of approximations that build Brownian motion from renewal processes, random event streams with independent gaps. In earlier work, Bardina and Rovira built such processes converging strongly to Brownian motion. Here the team shows some of those processes can approximate richer Gaussian processes, including fractional Brownian motion, which has long-range memory, and multiple Stratonovich integrals.

The paper gives sufficient conditions on the underlying renewal process for the convergence to hold. Fractional Brownian motion with any Hurst parameter serves as the illustrative example, covering both rougher and smoother behavior than ordinary Brownian motion. Approximations of this kind matter because Gaussian processes are usually defined abstractly, while the renewal constructions are concrete paths one can simulate and manipulate. The results tie a simple random mechanism to a broad class of Gaussian limits.
arxiv-2511-17380:
Zheng Wang and four co-authors propose a more honest way to measure how robust a neural network is to small input perturbations. Probabilistic robustness asks how likely a model is to stay correct under random noise, but existing versions assume the noise distribution is known in advance, which real deployments cannot promise. Their non-parametric version instead learns the perturbation distribution from data, optimized to give a conservative estimate under distributional uncertainty.

An estimator built on Gaussian mixture models covers cases where the noise does or does not depend on the input. The authors work out how their measure relates to both classic probabilistic and adversarial robustness. Experiments on three image datasets across several network architectures consistently gave lower, more cautious robustness estimates than methods assuming standard noise distributions. They offer the metric as the practical choice when the true perturbations are unknown.
arxiv-2511-17480:
V. Nagpal and six co-authors characterize a frustrated magnet built on a triangular lattice of iron ions. In RbFe(HPO3)2, each iron carries spin five halves, and the triangular arrangement frustrates antiferromagnetic order, since not all neighbors can oppose each other at once. Using X-ray diffraction, magnetization, heat capacity, and phosphorus nuclear magnetic resonance on a polycrystalline sample, the team maps the compound's structure and magnetic phases in detail.

Long-range order sets in near 7.8 kelvin, with a second, field-induced ordering at lower temperature in stronger fields. The frustration ratio, about seven, signals moderate frustration. Resonance data reveal two inequivalent phosphorus sites coupling differently to the iron moments, and susceptibility fits a spin five-halves triangular model with a modest exchange coupling. Below the ordering temperature, relaxation follows a cubic temperature law, pointing to two-magnon scattering, and the field-temperature phase diagram shows three clear regimes.
arxiv-2511-17980:
Anubhab Chowdhury and Erik Larsson study a wireless system that senses targets and sends data at the same time, helped by a repeater that almost instantly retransmits signals with a gain. In a bi static setup with separate transmitter and receiver, the repeater strengthens target echoes and fills coverage holes.

The repeater also adds noise and interference on both the sensing and data sides. Their framework accounts for those tradeoffs and designs the transmitter signal carefully. Placing repeaters near target hot spots lets the system reach a higher chance of detection while tolerating much weaker target reflections, a clear practical gain.
arxiv-2511-18480:
Zhijia Zhang and nine co-authors build ultra clean nanochannels between flat crystals in hours, not days. Such channels, a few atoms tall, let labs probe water and ion flow at the smallest scale. Old builds leave polymer grime on the walls and take long craft, which spoils flow and blocks scale up.

Their Mask and Stack method cuts a hard stencil mask, then dry stacks the crystal layers with no polymer touch. Surface probes and light spectra confirm clean walls. Devices show steady, repeatable ion flow over long runs. The flow works with many flat materials, so scale up looks near. Clean fast builds aid work from quantum flow to energy gear.
arxiv-2511-18680:
Xiang Gao and ten co-authors tackle inverse rendering for surfaces with many holes, shapes whose topology defeats standard reconstruction. Meshes are the preferred form for graphics work because they support geometry theory and modern pipelines. But methods that deform a mesh to match photos often collapse on high-genus surfaces, losing the holes that define them, and oversmooth simpler surfaces. The team traces the failure to the optimiser, whose gradients can vanish or explode.

Their fix pairs a cycle of coarsening and refining the mesh as it deforms with a reworked optimiser that keeps gradients in check. The mesh periodically rebuilds itself at several resolutions, gaining awareness of both global topology and fine detail. Tests on multi-view images are presented as evidence the method holds together where earlier ones tore.
arxiv-2511-19080:
Fan Nie and five co-authors work on spotting deepfakes that fake both sound and picture together. Fake media can mislead viewers, and clues often hide in mismatches between what is heard and what is seen. Their method, called FoVB, learns that audio-visual link as a hidden Gaussian variable using variational Bayes, a way of estimating probability models.

Special filters first pull out local and global forgery traces from each stream. The hidden variable is then split into parts tied to one stream and parts shared across both, kept apart by a constraint. Building on pretrained backbones, the design aims at detectors that still work on new kinds of fakes.
arxiv-2511-19280:
Jinyuan Wu and three co-authors work out what a trion, a bound state of three charged particles in a semiconductor, would look like in time and angle resolved photoemission. That technique kicks electrons out and records their energies and angles. Excitons, two particle states, have been seen this way, but trions have only been probed optically.

Simulations for a monolayer material show that left behind particles shift trion signals by energies comparable to the exciton binding energy. Positive trions give distinctive asymmetric features, while negative trions mirror the exciton band structure, including dark states. The results offer a direct momentum resolved probe of both.
arxiv-2511-19380:
Maroun Ayli, Youssef Bakouny, Tushar Sharma, Nader Jalloul, Hani Seifeddine, and Rima Kilany build a search engine for enterprise software screens. Large firms keep thousands of interface screens across products and versions, and finding patterns, enforcing consistency, or checking compliance means searching that mass. Visual similarity and text search miss the structure that defines an interface: which elements contain which, and how they are arranged. The team converts each screenshot into an attributed graph capturing that hierarchy and layout.

A contrastive graph autoencoder then learns embeddings that preserve similarity at visual, structural, and semantic levels at once. Their analysis finds these structural embeddings discriminate better than leading vision encoders. The representation should transfer to other structured images, such as documents and architectural diagrams, the authors note.
arxiv-2511-19480:
Pinaki Prasad Guha Neogi, Ahmad Mohammadshirazi, Dheeraj Kulshrestha, and Rajiv Ramnath study a misuse risk unique to mixture-of-experts language models. Such models route each input to a subset of expert subnetworks, which makes them efficient, and also modular enough that an adversary could prune away most experts. Cheaply fine-tune the rest for one task, and so obtain a working model while bypassing licensing or security limits. The team calls this unauthorised compression.

They first build a method to identify which experts matter most for a given task, then measure what pruning and realigning those experts costs. Keeping task accuracy is possible for isolated experts, but broad knowledge degrades badly without targeted retraining. Based on that trade-off, they propose defences for model owners who release expert-based systems.
arxiv-2511-19680:
Ying Bao and Jessie Liu model how even neutral content moderation can polarize what people create online. Users both write and read posts, differ in ideology, and dislike content from the other side. Moderation in their model targets only toxicity, never viewpoint, which is the usual fairness aim.

Removing toxic posts gives clean posts more exposure, a benefit majority creators partly enjoy. Yet the same shift raises out-group hostility toward minority creators, who do not share in the benefit. Creation from the minority then dries up, echoing the spiral of silence. The result shows a fair-seeming rule can leave minority users facing a more one-sided feed.
arxiv-2511-19780:
Ioannis Tzachristas and Aifen Sui help phone agents understand requests that carry several intents at once. A mobile agent must turn natural language into executable actions under tight speed and privacy limits, and simply enlarging the language model is wasteful. Their layer, NOEM3A, adds an intent ontology to compact models.

For each query, the system pulls a small neighborhood of the ontology, feeds candidate action labels into the prompt, and biases decoding toward valid labels. A hierarchy-aware score judges near misses by meaning, not spelling. On MultiWOZ dialogues, the ontology boost improves small Llama models on exact match and slot scores alike.
arxiv-2511-20280:
Liu, Zhao, Wen, Dai, and Huang coach video generators to respect real physics. Their 2025 paper refines generated videos through guided self-correction. Modern video models produce gorgeous but physically wrong clips. Objects float, collide wrongly, or melt through each other. Prompt quality strongly steers what models can do.

Their framework loops a vision-language critic over drafts. The critic spots physical inconsistencies in each attempt. A multimodal chain-of-thought turns complaints into better prompts. Regeneration then fixes the flagged errors progressively. No training is needed for the generator itself. The loop plugs into many video models as-is. Tests ran on the PhyIQ physics benchmark. Scores rose from 56.31 to 62.38 overall. That is a gain of about six points. Language models supply the physics-aware guidance throughout. Prompt design emerges as a capability trigger. World-model ambitions need exactly this grounding. The authors frame it as early exploration.
arxiv-2511-20380:
Ibnyahya and Reiss redesign the filters that shape artificial room echo. Their 2025 paper makes attenuation filters for feedback delay networks trainable. Such networks fake the late reflections of real spaces. Each delay line needs a filter taming its decay. Different pitches should fade at different rates.

Graphic equalizer designs stack many filters per line. The new design uses parametric equalizer sections instead. Each section is a second-order filter block. Frequency, gain, and quality factor are its knobs. Those knobs are shared across all delay lines. Only gain adjusts to each line's length. Parameter counts drop sharply as a result. The whole design stays differentiable end to end. Gradient-based training can fit target decay curves directly. Fitting uses supervised learning on smooth targets. Accuracy matches the state of the art reported. Computing cost falls significantly at the same time.
arxiv-2511-21080:
Yeswanth Ravichandran, Duoduo Liao, and Charan Teja Kurakula automate in 2025 the hunt for hidden damage inside concrete bridge decks. The context is stark: about 7.5 percent of America's 617,000 bridges are structurally deficient, with a repair backlog near 125 billion dollars. Their framework uses impact-echo testing, tapping the deck and listening to resonances. Fourier analysis extracts each point's dominant peak frequency, and the values are interpolated into spatial maps of the deck.

Unsupervised k-means clustering flags low-frequency, defect-prone zones, checked against ground-truth masks from laboratory slabs with seeded defects. Ordered peak-frequency sequences from validated zones then feed a stacked LSTM network. It classifies four defect types, shallow and deep delamination, voids, and honeycombing, at 73 percent overall accuracy. Field tests on an in-service deck showed laboratory-trained models generalising despite coupling and noise differences, a step toward network-scale, repeatable bridge monitoring.
arxiv-2511-21180:
Computer scientist Shuhan Xia and five coauthors present CAHS-Attack in 2025, a method for breaking the safeguards of Stable Diffusion, a popular program that turns text prompts into images. Earlier attacks needed the model's internal gradients, meaning its built-in correction signals, or relied on hand-written trick prompts. CAHS-Attack instead works from outside, as a black-box attack, judging tries only by the images that come back.

The search pairs Monte Carlo tree search, a method that explores options through many trial simulations, with a genetic algorithm that breeds the most promising starting prompts. A CLIP-aware score, based on the model's own text encoder, keeps the most disruptive result at each step. In tests on short and long prompts, it beat rival attacks including QF-Attack and PGD. The authors trace the weakness to the CLIP text encoder itself, a risk shared by many image generators.
arxiv-2511-21880:
Bahini and colleagues dissect the fine structure of a giant vibration of the magnesium-24 nucleus, a strongly deformed nucleus. The vibration, the isoscalar giant monopole resonance, is a collective breathing mode whose details reveal how stiff nuclear matter is. In deformed nuclei it mixes with a quadrupole vibration, producing extra structure at lower energies. The team used alpha-particle scattering data from iThemba LABS in South Africa, covering excitation energies from 9 to 25 MeV.

They analysed the data with wavelet transforms, which pick out characteristic energy spacings, against QRPA theory with two Skyrme models. The model with low nuclear incompressibility, 202 MeV, matched the data best across the full range studied. Instead of isolated spacings, they found a continuous range of scales from 200 to 1,000 keV, confirming Landau damping, the spreading into simpler motions, as the main decay route.
arxiv-2511-22280:
Kong, Wang, Tian, and colleagues find the dial that controls super-Heisenberg quantum sensing. Quantum metrology beats classical precision limits, and tricks like indefinite causal order reportedly push error scaling beyond the Heisenberg limit. Why they help was murky. The team introduces the nilpotency index, a number measuring how deeply the encoding operators fail to commute, nested commutator by nested commutator, and proves it governs the achievable scaling directly.

With a finite index K, measurement error scales as the number of resources to the power minus one-plus-K, already beating Heisenberg scaling without any indefinite causal order. Indefinite causal order becomes necessary only when the deepest commutator degenerates to a constant. In the infinite-index limit the scaling turns exponential, error falling like e to the minus N over N. The authors back the theory with experimentally feasible protocols, recasting exotic causal-order effects as ordinary, engineerable non-commutativity.
arxiv-2511-22380:
Alpturer and colleagues study how computers can reach one shared decision at the same moment even when some crash. Reaching simultaneous agreement is tied to common knowledge, where everyone knows a fact, knows everyone knows it, and so on. Earlier optimal protocols shared everything agents knew, making messages huge. The team instead asks what is achievable when agents exchange only limited information.

For each of several limited exchanges, the authors find the earliest round at which common knowledge can arise. They derive protocols deciding exactly then. The exchanges include the classic FloodSet method and versions where agents count failures or tag values with owners. They also introduce SendWaste, a new exchange where agents share their known values plus an estimate of wasted messages. SendWaste decides at most one round later than the best full-information protocol of Dwork and Moses, while using less computation, memory, and message size.
arxiv-2511-22480:
Sheleg and colleagues demonstrate a hallmark quantum effect using ordinary radio waves at room temperature. Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, where two identical photons entering a beam splitter always leave together, is a standard test of quantumness. At 120 megahertz no practical single-photon sources or detectors exist, and microwave versions need deep cooling. Their workaround builds an approximation of a single-photon state conditionally, from classical phase-averaged coherent states.

By choosing the mixture carefully, the team reproduced the interference signature: the normalised second-order correlation dipped below 0.5, the classical limit, just as a true single-photon experiment would show. The construction's fidelity can be tuned to suppress noise, at the cost of longer measurement time. Quantum interference experiments can thus run where genuine quantum hardware is unavailable, and the authors suggest the same trick could enable Bell inequality tests with radio waves.
arxiv-2511-22880:
Jaiswal and a team from Microsoft and universities fix a serving problem LoRA's success created. Low-Rank Adaptation fine-tunes language models cheaply, so production platforms host hundreds of adapters of varying rank sharing one base model. Existing serving systems batch these adapters, causing performance skew and forcing operators to add GPUs to meet service-level objectives, while optimisations ignore rank diversity.

LoRAServe treats placement as a workload-aware decision: it dynamically rebalances adapters across GPUs by rank and demand, and uses GPU Direct RDMA to reach stored adapters. On production traces from an anonymised company, LoRAServe delivered up to twice the throughput and nine times lower time-to-first-token than state-of-the-art systems. It used up to 50 percent fewer GPUs under the constraints and cut adapter storage by up to sixteen times in the evaluations. The lesson generalises: in multi-tenant inference, heterogeneity is the workload.
arxiv-2511-22980:
Ren and colleagues study four layers of graphene stacked in an ABCB pattern, a sheet material whose layers carry a built-in electric polarization, meaning a permanent separation of charge. They ask what ground states emerge when electrons in this stack interact strongly and also feel spin-orbit coupling, the link between an electron's spin and its motion through the sheet.

They use a standard band model with self-consistent Hartree-Fock calculations, a method that lets each electron feel the average field of the others. They find that at strong interaction strength the stack becomes a Chern insulator with Chern number 3, a quantum anomalous Hall state, with no external electric field applied. At a weaker interaction strength a small field is still needed. And the calculations also predict quarter-filled and three-quarter-filled metallic phases, making the stack a tunable test bed for topological states.
arxiv-2511-23080:
Voisin asks whether a boundedness pattern known for del Pezzo surfaces extends to higher-dimensional Fano manifolds, shapes whose geometry is governed by polynomial equations. For surfaces, the pattern is sharp: a degree-2 del Pezzo surface that has a point of odd degree has a point of degree 1, 3, or 7. A cubic surface with a suitable cycle has a point of degree 1 or 4.

The answer in higher dimensions is no, in two senses, shown through the group of zero-cycles, combinations of points that algebra uses to probe a shape's arithmetic. For quartic threefolds that possess a point of odd degree, there is no Coray-type ceiling on the odd degree of a point. For Fano hypersurfaces the zero-cycle group can be unbounded in Mumford's infinite-dimensionality sense, meaning no threshold degree above which every cycle is guaranteed to come from points.
arxiv-2511-23380:
Awasthi and colleagues show that the chemistry of a surface steers how living cells move collectively around a topological defect. A vortex-like singularity in the cells' alignment pattern. Working with fibroblast monolayers confined by a ring-shaped topographical pattern that imposes an integer-charge defect. They vary how strongly cells stick by coating the surface with poly-D-lysine, fibronectin, or covalently bonded fibronectin, measuring adhesion with atomic force microscopy in the experiments.

Weakly adhered cells on the poly-D-lysine coating stream strongly inward, while strongly attached cells on fibronectin move tangentially around the ring. And the spindle-shaped cells on the adhesive coatings align better and spawn two half-integer defects inside the monolayer. Comparing coatings, the authors conclude that surface chemistry itself, rather than the absolute adhesion force, governs the collective behavior, a design lever for directing organization in engineered tissues and scaffolds.
arxiv-2512-00080:
The MARWIN robot checks radiation levels inside the long tunnels of the European XFEL accelerator. André Dehne, Juri Zach, and Peer Stelldinger evaluate whether deep visual stereo odometry could guide it, in a 2025 study. The tunnels are long and look nearly the same everywhere, so standard ways of tracking position struggle there.

MARWIN now finds its place with lidar edge detection and wheel and lidar odometry. It also uses periodic QR code checks and fuzzy control of its distance to the wall. The authors weigh a camera-based depth method against that setup. Their work speaks to anyone building robots that must navigate plain, repetitive spaces where landmarks are rare.
arxiv-2512-00480:
Fetching a record from a public database can reveal exactly what you were looking for. Liang Feng Zhang presents a unified framework for information-theoretic private information retrieval in 2025. These protocols let a user retrieve any entry without revealing which entry it was.

Private retrieval protects readers of sensitive material, from medical guidance to legal records, against profiling by servers. A unified construction aims to organize many known protocols under one design logic. Such frameworks help engineers choose protocols with proven privacy rather than ad hoc promises, as these tools move from theory into real services. Information-theoretic privacy means security that holds even against unlimited computing power.
arxiv-2512-00880:
Haijian Shao, Wei Liu, Xing Deng, Qi Liu, and Yingtao Jiang propose a quantum-inspired method for neural operators in a 2025 paper. Multimodal AI on home-grade hardware faces tight limits: mixed data types, real-time demands, and repeated operator blocks that waste capacity. Neural operators are the building blocks that transform data inside such models.

Their framework describes each operator by its singular value spectrum, a fingerprint of how it stretches data, placed on a geometric sphere. That view lets them test when two operators are equivalent and prune ones that repeat work. Leaner models could run better on modest devices.
arxiv-2512-01080:
Benhour Amirian, Ashley Dale, Sergei Kalinin, and Jason Hattrick-Simpers set out what trustworthy AI for materials discovery should mean in a 2025 paper. Artificial intelligence and machine learning now speed up the hunt for new materials, including in autonomous laboratories that run experiments themselves. Speed is worth little if scientists cannot trust the models.

The authors define a framework with named criteria, including whether methods are generalizable, interpretable, fair, transparent, explainable, robust, and stable. They tie evaluation to simple summary scores. A shared trust framework could help labs decide which machine learning claims to build on.
arxiv-2512-01680:
Mihai Prunescu builds arithmetic closed forms for famed prime families. Mersenne primes, Fermat primes, and twin-prime pairs each have long open tales. Sophie Germain primes join the set here. Closed forms that list them are rare objects in number theory.

Prunescu gives forms that generate each family, with repeats allowed. He also gives forms that count each family up to a bound. Counting forms turn existence hunts into sums that can be studied. The work is a formal build, not a proof of how many such primes exist in total. Counting forms double as membership tests, since a prime family count that jumps at a point marks that point as a family member.
arxiv-2512-01880:
Chess engines are built to find the best move, but people rarely play the best move. A 2025 paper by Daren Zhong, Dingcheng Huang, and Clayton Greenberg takes the human side instead, trying to predict which move a person will actually choose, given their skill level.

Their tool is a family of n-gram language models, one trained for each skill group, that learn the patterns in how players at that level continue a game. Because beginners and experts make different kinds of choices, separate models capture habits a single model would blur. The work offers a window into human decision-making, not just machine strength.
arxiv-2512-01980:
Shrinking a neural network by low-rank approximation is like surgery: cutting the model down costs accuracy, and fine-tuning afterward is the rehab that wins it back. Haoran Qin and four co-authors propose in 2025 flipping the order, preparing the network before compression so the cut does less damage.

Methods based on singular value decomposition, including Fisher-weighted and activation-aware variants, have become standard compression tools. The authors' preparation step, nicknamed Prehab, shapes the network in advance so its important structure survives decomposition. If preparation pays off, smaller models could keep more of their skill, easing deployment on limited hardware.
arxiv-2512-02280:
Modern AI perceives, speaks, and reasons impressively, yet it cannot reliably watch itself, catch its own errors, or govern its behavior as conditions change. Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz, Sindhuja Penchala, and Shahram Rahimi survey in 2025 the gap between today's systems and cognitive autonomy, and what bridging it would take.

Self-monitoring, self-correction, and self-regulation in dynamic settings are the missing capacities the authors emphasize. Perception and language advances alone do not supply them. The paper frames the research agenda for autonomous systems that could be trusted in open environments, where no human can pre-script every response.
arxiv-2512-02680:
Keiichi Maeda and co-authors study an unusual stellar explosion, the supernova called SN Ic 2022esa. Some stripped star explosions show late narrow lines from oxygen rich material around the star. Those lines suggest the blast wave is hitting nearby gas shed before the explosion.

The team reads 2022esa as the death of a massive Wolf-Rayet star in a binary system. Its companion may later explode as well, leaving a pair of black holes. Odd supernovae like this one help trace how massive pairs live, die, and seed the black hole mergers that gravitational wave detectors hear. Each odd burst of this class adds a clue to how pairs of big stars live out their last years.
arxiv-2512-02880:
R. Grau and A. Moralejo mine old MAGIC telescope data to bound the faint glow filling the universe. The extragalactic background light is all light emitted across cosmic history, from ultraviolet to infrared. Stars and dust in galaxies should be its main source.

Gamma rays from distant objects fade as they cross that glow, leaving a measurable imprint. Archival MAGIC observations turn that fading into constraints on the background level. Tighter bounds test models of star formation history and help correct gamma ray spectra for other studies. Old data is free data. A fresh read of it can fence in the glow of all past stars with no new scope time spent.
arxiv-2512-02980:
Elise Bailly-Rioufreyt and a large team generate entangled light from pairs of semiconductor nanowires. Quantum entanglement powers secure communication and enhanced sensing. For decades, polarization entangled photons came mainly from bulk crystals using down conversion, a method that blocks scaling and chip integration.

Orthogonal gallium arsenide nanowires offer a compact alternative source. Their near infrared photon pairs are tunable, the title notes. Chip scale entangled sources would let quantum networks shrink from optical tables into devices, a step toward practical quantum links in cities. Small sources that pair up clean can be set in rows on a chip. Rows of them are what a real net needs to span a town with links.
arxiv-2512-03080:
Language models need a good way to read molecules. Mingxu Zhang, Dazhong Shen, and Ying Sun present a new atom-level tokenizer in this 2025 work. A tokenizer cuts input into small pieces the model can handle, here one atom at a time.

Their tool, AtomDisc, uses molecule graphs that show how atoms connect. Those links shape how atoms act and what a molecule does. The authors say the tool lifts model results and reveals links between structure and traits. Better molecule reading could speed drug and materials research done with AI help. Chemists may value how atom-level pieces keep local bonds clear to the model.
arxiv-2512-03880:
Spongy trabecular bone gets its strength from a delicate internal lattice, and doctors would like to predict that strength from scans. John Rick Manzanares, Richard Leslie Abel, and Paweł Dłotko test a topological approach in a 2025 quantitative biology preprint. Their concern is that such summaries of bone structure should not depend on an arbitrary choice of sideways coordinate frame.

The team built a frame-invariant method. They compared its strength predictions with signed distance persistent homology and conventional shape measurements. The test set held two dozen human bone cores. Prediction errors from those models ran close to or below standard morphometry, though intervals overlapped. Equal-removal experiments found localised removal weakened cores more, despite a smaller change of that kind. Frame invariance, the authors conclude, cleans up the approach, and the component-based scores deserve testing on larger external datasets.
arxiv-2512-04180:
Chains of Majorana fermions, particles that are their own antiparticles, host phase transitions theorists prize as laboratories. Hekai Zhao and Philip W. Phillips analyse a family of interacting Majorana chains in a 2025 preprint. Each shows a tricritical point between an Ising critical phase and a supersymmetric gapped phase. The chains split into even and odd personalities depending on the interaction's range.

Even-range chains develop competing order and resist numerical treatment, while odd-range chains possess a solvable point where entanglement vanishes. The authors introduce a swirling twist. It rewraps each chain into a two-dimensional model of half the width. A helical boundary condition stitches the end of one row to the start of the next. In that picture, the one-dimensional transition becomes a finite-size transition of the two-dimensional system. Finite-size scaling predicts how the critical coupling moves with range.
arxiv-2512-04580:
Huifeng Zhu, Shijie Li, Qinfeng Li, and co-authors introduce CryptoTensors, a file format that keeps large language models secret while they travel and deploy. Firms now tune models on private data from health, law, and finance. Those tuned weights count as personal assets or trade secrets. Yet standard model formats ship weights in the open, with no access control built in. Their 2025 arXiv paper fills that gap with a lightweight secure format.

CryptoTensors wraps model weights with protection designed for sharing and deployment. It avoids the heavy cost of full encryption schemes and the lock-in of private servers. The design also fits trusted hardware, so models can run inside guarded enclaves. Owners gain control over who can load a model and where. As tuned models grow more valuable, such formats help hospitals, banks, and law firms share tools without leaking the crown jewels inside them.
arxiv-2512-04780:
Apurva Seth works out when tensor products of one algebra family keep a stability trait no matter what they pair with. The family is the diagonal AH-algebras, built as limits of matrix-like blocks joined by diagonal maps. They sit at the heart of work sorting C-star algebras. K-stability asks whether an algebra's K-theory behaves well under stabilization. His 2025 arXiv paper studies products of such an algebra with arbitrary partners.

The main result is a clean test: the product stays K-stable for every partner exactly when the block sizes in the building system grow without bound. Uses follow at once. Villadsen algebras of the first kind that lack Z-stability still pass the test when paired with anything. Any simple, unital, endless diagonal AH-algebra meets the growth rule alone. Such results tell which K-theory counts survive pairing, a daily question in the field.
arxiv-2512-05080:
Ian Dunn, Liv Toft, Tyler Katz, and four co-authors present OMTRA, a single generative model for structure-based drug design. Designing a drug molecule that fits a chosen pocket on a protein involves many related jobs. They include inventing new candidates, docking them into the pocket, and searching by shape. Each job usually gets its own tool. The authors argue these jobs share one structure, so one model should be able to perform them all.

OMTRA is built on flow matching, a generative technique, and moves flexibly between the tasks, including some with no counterpart in standard workflows. To train it, the team assembled a vast dataset of molecular shapes alongside protein-ligand data. The system reaches top performance on inventing pocket-fitting molecules and on docking, though the authors note the benefits of huge pretraining and multi-task training are modest. Code, models, and data are released openly.
arxiv-2512-05180:
Zijian Zhang and a very large team of co-authors report two gravitationally lensed Little Red Dots, the puzzling compact objects the Webb telescope has been finding in the early universe. Most vary little over days to years, keeping their nature, probably feeding black holes, unsettled. These two sit behind a galaxy cluster, and one of them, RX1, is imaged four times, with the light paths differing by well over a century.

Comparing the four images is like watching one object at four epochs at once. RX1 changes in colour and brightness between them by a large margin, in a pattern matching temperature swings of a glowing surface. That suggests long-term pulsation, like a Cepheid star's, but from a vastly larger, more massive envelope. The authors propose Little Red Dots are a distinct class of active nucleus wrapped in such an envelope.
arxiv-2512-05280:
Laura Estridge and Joel Franklin introduce the CUBE, a virtual reality immersion built to make electromagnetic fields visible. Fields are abstract and hard to picture. The radiation fields covered in upper-level physics courses are the least familiar of all: students meet them as equations long before they can imagine them. The CUBE puts the student inside the field instead, letting them stand within the patterns that textbooks can only draw.

The note explains the pedagogical thinking behind the software's features: why particular views and interactions were chosen, and what each is meant to make intuitive. It then gives a brief overview of the CUBE in use. As a short introduction rather than a manual, the paper's purpose is to put the tool on record for other instructors. It is a worked example of virtual reality aimed at a specific, stubborn visualization problem in physics teaching.
arxiv-2512-05380:
Xinyue Yin and Sibo Zheng ask whether a future CERN experiment could catch the mediator of a two-step dark matter origin story. In sequential freeze-in, dark matter is produced so feebly that it normally leaves no trace in detectors. Adding a second field changes the picture: a dark photon mediator, produced out of equilibrium, feeds the dark matter, and the mediator might be visible at the proposed SHiP experiment.

Requiring the dark photon to stay out of equilibrium while the final dark matter abundance matches observation pins the model's parameters into a narrow corridor. The authors then compute what SHiP's proton beam would produce through bremsstrahlung over years of running. The projected sensitivity excludes most of the surviving corridor at high confidence, leaving only a sliver, where the mixing is weakest, for other experiments. A nearly invisible scenario becomes, on paper, almost fully testable.
arxiv-2512-05580:
Aurprita Mahmood and five co-authors test whether branching reasoning beats linear reasoning for mathematics in Bengali, a low-resource language. Math word problems demand language understanding and multi-step calculation together; chain-of-thought prompting helps, but its line of reasoning propagates early errors. The authors run a comparison on a set of problems from the SOMADHAN dataset. They evaluate several large language models under plain prompting, chain-of-thought, and tree-of-thoughts, which explores several reasoning branches before committing.

Chain-of-thought lifts accuracy over plain prompting, and tree-of-thoughts adds a gain, reaching the best result with the largest model. The advantage concentrates in medium and large models; small ones benefit less from the branching. The study establishes tree-of-thoughts as a strategy for problem solving in Bengali and, more broadly, evidence that structured reasoning transfers to languages where training resources are thin.
arxiv-2512-05680:
Alexander Mattick and four co-authors address how phones keep a fast wireless link while moving through 5G and 6G networks. Modern antenna arrays form narrow beams, each aimed a different way from a fixed codebook. Picking the best beam, again and again, is tricky when reflections and blockages keep changing the picture. Their 2025 paper frames the search differently, as a game played under partial information.

The codebook itself becomes the world of the game. At each step the method holds a belief about where the unseen best beam is, probes a candidate, and updates the belief. A meta-learning layer of multi-armed bandits learns how to search well across many such games. Because nothing is memorized about fixed paths, the method copes with new routes and changed surroundings. In tests it beat earlier approaches by orders of magnitude, a large margin.
arxiv-2512-05880:
Simon Guiroy, Mats Richter, Sarath Chandar, and Christopher Pal tackle a quiet decision that shapes many applied AI projects. Which checkpoint of a big pretrained vision model should you fine tune for a new task? When target data is scarce and unlabeled, validation collapses. Their selection method needs only a few unlabeled examples from the target task itself. It rests on a new measure called Neural Coherence.

Coherence profiles a model's activation statistics on source and target data. Rankings by coherence pick starting points that go on to generalize better. In experiments with ImageNet pretrained models aimed at food photographs, plant images, and wildlife data, the method improved results over established baselines across the board. The team further shows coherence can select training data, not just models. A model's internal orderliness, read cheaply, predicts its future on unfamiliar ground.
arxiv-2512-05980:
A large international team from the COSINUS collaboration and Duke University reports careful calibration work behind one of dark matter's longest running arguments. Sodium iodide crystals doped with thallium are the detectors of DAMA/LIBRA, the experiment that claims an annually modulating dark matter signal no one else sees. Reading them hinges on the quenching factor: a recoiling nucleus makes less light than an electron of the same energy. The team measured that factor for sodium recoils, varying both recoil energy and the crystal's thallium concentration.

Five ultrapure crystals were exposed to a neutron beam in North Carolina. A dependence on thallium content appeared under one calibration scheme, using an americium source, but vanished under another, using a low energy barium line. Calibration is where discovery claims stand or fall. If the light to energy translation shifts, so does the claim's meaning. Such measurements corner the truth slowly.
arxiv-2512-06080:
Tzofi Klinghoffer and seven co-authors teach lidar to see around corners by listening to light that bounced twice. Ordinary lidar times light reflecting straight back. Two bounce light secretly encodes occluded geometry and mirrors. Earlier work lit one point at a time. This team tackles the practical case: many laser spots lit at once, their bounced contributions tangled together with shadows and specular reflections.

So the method is learned. About one hundred thousand simulated transients trained a light transport prior. From one measurement the system then reconstructs hidden and mirrored geometry. Code and data are public. Robots gain safety by sensing what occlusion hides.
arxiv-2512-06380:
Xiao Zhan, Guangzhi Sun, Jose Such, and Phil Woodland raise a privacy risk in voice assistants: they hear everyone in the room, not just the person talking to them. A bystander's words can be picked up, stored, and later revealed, yet past tests never measured whether a model can listen to one speaker and refuse to spill what another said nearby.

The team builds SH-Bench, a test set of mixed speaker audio, both real and made up, with tens of thousands of questions. A new score weighs both grasp of the main speaker and guarding of the bystander. Top models, open and closed alike, leaked bystander detail freely; strong hearing did not mean safe hearing. The authors then fine tune models to refuse bystander questions, and that training lifted privacy sharply while keeping the main speaker clear. The work sets a bar for voice tools used in shared spaces.
arxiv-2512-06680:
Quentin Ehret opens the study of a hybrid algebraic structure in the trickiest arithmetic setting, where two plus two can equal zero. Poisson superalgebras blend a commutative product with a Lie bracket, graded by a parity that adds signs, and they encode the algebra behind classical and quantum mechanics. In characteristic two, where the sign rules collapse, much of the usual theory must be rebuilt from scratch.

Ehret works through the basics in this setting: how such algebras act on spaces, how two can be joined into a semidirect product, and the cohomology that classifies their deformations. He defines their universal enveloping algebras, the associative homes where they can be computed with. A companion structure, Lie Rinehart superalgebras, turns out to share the same enveloping algebra, a tidy bridge between the two. Worked examples and a first look at pre Poisson superalgebras round out the foundations.
arxiv-2512-06980:
J Allagan, G Morgan, and D Sinclair count ways to split graphs into groups, extending two classic counting sequences into the world of networks. Bell numbers count the ways a set can be divided into blocks, and Stirling numbers refine that count by block number. The authors work out exact formulas for several families: complete multipartite graphs, complete bipartite graphs with a perfect matching removed, and Mycielskian graphs built from trees.

For multipartite graphs they give a simpler proof that the count factors into a product over the parts. Star graphs under the Mycielski construction yield neat closed forms at key values. Computer checks tie these graph counts to known sequences in the standard online encyclopedia of integer sequences, several of them newly identified. The formulas extend from stars to arbitrary trees, giving counters a ready toolkit for these network families.
arxiv-2512-07080:
Madison D Griffin and co-authors read the life stories of Chesapeake Bay oysters out of two decades of shell measurements. Virginia's reefs look age-truncated, with old oysters scarce, a pattern blamed on overfishing, disease outbreaks, habitat decline, and climate change. Yet hints of resilience exist, and a huge state archive of shell lengths, gathered across hundreds of reefs from the early two thousands onward, had never been mined for lifespans.

The team fits mixture models to each reef's yearly shell lengths, teasing apart the overlapping size bands of different age groups. A linking algorithm then follows each band through time, forbidding the impossible step of shells shrinking, to form true cohorts. Only a subset of reefs had data thick enough for the treatment.
arxiv-2512-07180:
Nawshad Ahmed Evan and Md Raihan Uddin deploy decoys inside a working production network and report what happens. A honeypot is a fake resource, built to look valuable, that lures attackers away from real systems; a honeynet strings several decoys into a believable environment. With company services increasingly dependent on the internet, such traps both divert intruders and record their methods for study.

The authors describe setting the honeynet into live network infrastructure, where the decoy must pass as a genuine production resource. Attackers who take the bait can be observed safely while their tools and habits are analyzed, rather than merely blocked at the wall. The demonstration covers how the trap is presented, how intruders are misled inside the simulated environment, and what their behavior reveals.
arxiv-2512-07280:
Hendrik Reiter and a large consortium of co-authors move process mining out of the data center and into the machines where work actually happens. Process mining reconstructs how an organization really operates from event logs, but it traditionally gathers those logs centrally. Industrial internet-of-things systems instead sprawl across edge devices and clouds, with tight limits on energy, bandwidth, and privacy. Their framework, ContinuumConductor, decides step by step where each mining task belongs.

For every stage of the pipeline, from preprocessing through correlation to discovery. The authors weigh decentralizing against centralizing and propose explicit decision criteria, aiming at mining that is private, responsive, and light on resources. The framework is demonstrated on a live use case, optimizing processes in inland ports, where machinery, vehicles, and control systems all generate events at the edge.
arxiv-2512-07680:
P. A. Wigner and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 robotics paper on a crawler for tree canopies. Studying or sampling high branches is hard for people and drones alike. Their machine, AMBER, is built to be dropped in by air and then climb.

The crawler grips branches with tracks lined in compliant microspines. A rotary gripper with two tracks and an elastic tail helps it hold on. Branches of varied curve and tilt are its home terrain. In experiments it keeps its grip through steep rolls and climbs. It moves along horizontal branches at a steady pace. Its tracks can also yaw slightly, adding steering on rough bark. Power use is strikingly low next to a hovering drone's appetite. That thrift suits long sensing and sampling missions in the canopy. Full integration with a delivery drone remains future work. The deployment itself is shown at a feasibility level for now.
arxiv-2512-07780:
Jenny Gonzalez-Jara and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on the faint outskirts of galaxies. A stellar halo is the sparse cloud of old stars around a galaxy's bright body. Its mass and metal content follow a relation astronomers call the MZhR.

The team asks when that relation appears and when each halo settles onto it. They use the CIELO simulations, following central galaxies across most of cosmic time. Halos are traced in an outer shell. A new tool, the halo cardiogram, charts each halo's assembly history. From it they define a stability time for the halo's metal content. Simulated halos already trace the relation in the young universe. The slope matches today's surprisingly early. At fixed halo mass, metals grow steadily as satellites accrete and enrich the halo. One dominant contributor can lock the metal content once it fully disrupts.
arxiv-2512-07980:
Xiaoyang Huang, Zohar Komargodski, Andrew Lucas, and two co-authors wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper. Order usually melts as temperature climbs without limit. Entropy, the champion of disorder, can paradoxically favor order instead.

In some systems, generic high-energy states are the ordered ones. Symmetry then breaks spontaneously at arbitrarily high temperatures. The authors present minimal models where that entropic order appears. Their leading example replaces ordinary Ising spins with non-negative integers. An arithmetic Ising model, plus its quantum analogue, carries the argument. A large-flavor expansion and numerical simulations do the heavy lifting. Both classical and quantum versions order in their hot phase. Classical gas models join the menagerie with the same trick. Their interactions drive the gas into a crystal when heated.
