Turning step-size search into a trainable parameter cuts single-access-point runtime by about two-thirds. Hardware tests on an ARM-FPGA platform plus anechoic chamber measurements confirm robust real-world performance.
arxiv-2604-23980: Zhang and three colleagues tackle decentralized Muon, where the matrix-sign step refuses to commute with gossip averaging. Their SUDA template splits modular parts from non-modular ones, with ED/D-squared, EXTRA, and gradient tracking as backbones. They prove a topology-separated convergence guarantee whose main term skips graph quantities, plus two non-modular boundaries: tracking must precede polarization, and no server-free method can run the average-then-polarize update. Tests on CIFAR-100 and GPT-2 fine-tuning support it, with SUDA-Muon ahead in non-IID settings.
arxiv-2604-24080: Nishimoto and Tabei present the dynamic RR-index, the first dynamic self-index to reach delta-optimal space for repetitive strings. Static indexes already meet the bound, but dynamic versions missed it, paid logarithmic time per hit, or slowed with the longest common prefix maximum. Built on restricted recompression run-length programs, it stores delta-optimal bits in expectation, answers locate queries fast, and updates without longest-prefix dependence. On eleven corpora it runs up to 77 times faster on updates and up to 11 times faster on locate queries than rivals.
arxiv-2604-24480: Schadner shows Black-Scholes implied volatility is a quantile. The normalized option price acts as a probability on the variance scale, with the inverse Gaussian distribution linking price and volatility. This yields exact formulas for implied volatility from quantile functions, with only observable option inputs on the right. The result rewrites the price-volatility map as a distributional transform, gives implied volatility a first-passage interpretation, and identifies variance as the inversion coordinate. The formula reaches machine precision faster than a leading solver in the benchmark considered.
arxiv-2604-24580: McDowall, Georgopoulos and Wallden propose a new schedule for the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm. It uses the spectral gap, the energy separation in an adiabatic Hamiltonian, to slow evolution where the gap is small. Their Spectral Gap Informed Ramp method beats the linear-ramp version on Grover search at fixed depth. It also reaches the same success chance at shorter depth. Gains extend to maximum independent set problems and persist under mild noise.
arxiv-2604-25080: Nian and five colleagues present CacheFlow, fast LLM serving via KV cache restoration. Existing methods choose either recomputation of cached states or loading them from storage. They overlook parallelism within models and contention across requests. CacheFlow rethinks restoration as parallel work across tokens, layers and GPUs. It unifies restoration across tokens and layers as a staircase split, with boundary activations enabling joint work. A batch-aware planner decides what to recompute and what to load. Across dense and hybrid models, CacheFlow cuts restoration latency by about 2 to 3 times.
arxiv-2604-25180: Ambrosio and four colleagues present a Keller-Segel type equation that reproduces patterns seen as brain microvasculature grows. They explain in math terms how these patterns emerge. They also derive a data-driven equation for how the chemoattractant changes over time in step with the observed vessel dynamics. Beyond simulations, the study aims at a broad modelling frame from blood flow in brain arteries to chemical processes, to clarify how vessel damage may feed diseases of brain decline.
arxiv-2604-25280: Ram and Ramdas pin down the best wealth growth rate in a Kelly betting game against a broad null. They prove the rate equals a KL-gap limit over the null's bipolar set, and that it can be met and not beaten. It sits below a better-known KL gap, but matches it under weak lower-semicontinuity. For simple alternatives, they give the first matching test for power-one sequential tests, with no assumptions. They show slim-filtration test supermartingales suffice for all independent-data testing.
arxiv-2604-25580: Hartmann and nine colleagues survey 241 papers on the toxicity-measuring Perspective API and draw lessons from its end-2026 shutdown. Dependence cost three things: claims beyond what the tool could support, results that shifted when its model was retrained, and gaps they could measure but not explain. The failures spread through the LLM lifecycle, where Perspective supplied labels, filtered corpora, and graded the systems. The team releases scores for nearly six million snippets from 77 datasets, keeping the instrument open to study. They add ten requirements for field-owned measurement infrastructure.
arxiv-2604-26080: Wan, Xie, and Jamieson present NeuralEmu, a machine-learning emulator for commercial fifth-generation cellular schedulers. It replaces replayed traces and simplified simulators with learned behaviour. Learning from extremely high-resolution network telemetry, it predicts resource-block allocations and modulation schemes from user buffer levels and channel states. It handles several clients at once and reconstructs background traffic from scheduling results. Tests show emulation error falling by about 55 percent for web-page load time, 57 percent for video-call encoder bit rate, and 51 percent for cloud-gaming delay.
arxiv-2604-26180: Lee and five colleagues present Evergreen, a system that checks claims inside semantic aggregates. These are language summaries from reducing a relation with a language model, which may hold claims ungrounded in the underlying data. Each claim becomes a declarative verification query on the same engine, with tweaks that skip needless model calls and citations naming a tuple set. On workloads it keeps verification quality near an F1 of 0.94 while cutting cost more than threefold. With a weaker model it beats the top external baseline at lower cost.
arxiv-2604-26380: Cao and four colleagues showed that Bhabha scattering can push an electron, a positron, and an entangled onlooker electron into true three-way entanglement. The positron starts linked to the onlooker, which never joins the crash, yet scattering between the first two spreads shared links across all three. Crash momentum and the starting pair link decide how much three-way linkage forms. Limits on sharing links across many parts eased a lot in the slow-moving regime.
arxiv-2604-26480: Wu and ten colleagues grew high-quality VP2 crystals and mapped their transport as a type-II nodal-line semimetal. Magnetoresistance rose linearly with field without saturating, reaching 170 percent at 40 kelvin under 9 tesla, a behavior traced to intrinsic band structure and the Lorentz force. A small share of magnetic impurities produced a Kondo effect, while low-field conductivity showed weak antilocalization. The material thus offers a platform for topological transport with magnetic impurities.
arxiv-2604-26880: Hosen and five colleagues enter the ArchEHR-QA 2026 challenge with a cascaded pipeline that answers patient questions from electronic health records. Built around Gemini 2.5 Pro, it restates wordy patient queries, ranks clinical sentences for evidence, generates answers restricted to that evidence, and links each answer back to supporting sentences. The system ranked first in question interpretation, fifth in answer generation, seventh in evidence identification, and ninth in answer-evidence alignment. The authors argue that structured staging improves grounding and precision in patient-facing health answers.
arxiv-2604-27080: Tiwari and eight colleagues demonstrate a parametric iSWAP gate between two transmon qubits using the double transmon coupler. The coupler holds a robust built-in off point for static interactions, while mediating fast coupling for high-quality two-qubit operations. Using robust phase estimation to calibrate error terms, they reach 99.827 percent gate fidelity in 40 nanoseconds, with no numerical tuning. The design and calibration extend to other gates and qubit types, toward lean quantum processing.
arxiv-2604-27180: Nguyen and four colleagues build a network-layout control framework for splitting power grids under resource limits, using cutting-plane methods. The goal is live rearranging of linked subnetworks. Radial links, feasible resource flows, and a set leader plan must all hold. Those features support control spread across sites, stability, and teamwork. A mixed-integer program joins graph rules, resource flow, and network structure. Stepwise cuts handle cycle removal and leader choice until an optimal feasible layout is reached.
arxiv-2604-27480: Christy and twelve others report the first polarization of a gamma-ray burst glow, and the first Faraday rotation measure, for GRB 260310A. They detect radio waves from 11 to 25 GHz, falling from about 3 percent at 25 GHz to under 1 percent at 11 GHz. As a reverse shock in a jet, low-end fading fits synchrotron blocking, while low high-end signal points to a patchy jet field. They also find angle shift across the band matching Faraday rotation. The measure, about minus 8,300 radians per square metre, fits a dense place.
arxiv-2604-27580: Gregory and Strecker study how Dryad, a well-known open data infrastructure, works toward financial sustainability. Dryad has reconfigured its relationships and revenue models over time, building four kinds of ties with customers, collaborators, and competitors: reinforcing, forging, positioning, and excluding. The authors argue that strategic business thinking, while critical, also shapes views of value, community, and governance. Their mixed-methods study highlights tensions that can guide other open data infrastructures seeking stable funding.
arxiv-2604-27680: Padmanaban and three colleagues reconstruct the full three-dimensional mean flow past a stalled airfoil from sparse data. Planar velocimetry experiments on a NACA 0012 wing at about 450,000 Reynolds number and 14 degrees angle of attack show spanwise shifts consistent with stall cells. Three-dimensional variational data assimilation, combining sparse planar data with a Spalart-Allmaras turbulence model, rebuilds the full mean flow. A single plane of data gives the essential stall cell parts, and the lowest error comes from two close planes with markedly varied separation extents.
arxiv-2604-27780: Ayguadé and seven colleagues present RuC, a grammar-driven benchmark generator for language-agnostic rule completion in hardware description languages. RuC masks code regions defined by the target language grammar and prompts a model to regenerate them from surrounding unmasked code. They apply RuC to two SystemVerilog rule-completion benchmarks built from Tiny Tapeout shuttle TT07 plus the CVE2 RISC-V core. Completion performance depends strongly on model type, masked region structure, and prompting strategy, with Fill-in-the-Middle prompting scoring highest.
arxiv-2605-00080:
Bohan Hou and seventeen co-authors survey world models for robot learning. A world model predicts how an environment evolves under actions, and such models have become central to robot learning, supporting policy learning, planning, simulation, testing, and data generation. Progress has been rapid with foundation models and large-scale video generation, but the literature is split across designs, roles, and application domains.

The survey reviews the field from a robot-learning perspective. It covers how world models couple with policies, and how they serve as learned simulators for reinforcement learning and testing. It also traces how robotic video world models grew from imagination-based generation to controllable, structured, foundation-scale systems. Navigation and autonomous driving are connected in, and datasets, benchmarks, and scoring protocols are summarized. A companion repository will be kept updated with new works and resources.
arxiv-2605-00180:
Jingjun Xu and 5 co-authors address a practical problem in systems that route each user request to the best language model. A newly released model has no track record of scored answers, so a router cannot judge it the usual way. Profiles built from model-written summaries are often coarse, and test interactions are costly.

Their method, RouteProfile, builds a model's profile from public signals in its technical report or model card. These include model family, stated strengths, and benchmark scores, arranged as a graph. Tests show that structured profiles beat flat ones when no training is allowed. Model family proved a more reliable signal than benchmark topic, and good results need the profile and router designed together.
arxiv-2605-00280:
Pitch Sinlapanuntakul and 3 co-authors watch how professional designers use generative AI to dream up new AI products. In that work the AI is both the tool in hand and the material being shaped, which creates tangled value tensions unlike those in ordinary design. The team ran a concept envisioning activity and interviews with eighteen designers.

Designers reflected back and forth with the AI in a loop, each side reshaping the other's ideas. Value tensions surfaced at three levels at once: the tool, the designer, and the concept. Designers proved sharper at spotting harms than at stating positive value. They also reasoned ahead about how a tool's built-in assumptions might leak into the product and its future users, a habit the authors frame as meta-design judgment.
arxiv-2605-00580:
Ramiro Cayuso and 4 co-authors simulate the extra radiation that merging neutron stars would emit if gravity includes a light scalar field with kinetic screening. In such theories a scalar mediates a fifth force, but screening hides it where matter is dense. The authors work in the decoupling limit with full three-dimensional numerical relativity tools, building static binary starting data in the regime where the screening radius dwarfs the orbital separation.

For equal-mass binaries the main signal is the quadrupole scalar mode, and screening acts non-monotonically. It suppresses the amplitude when the wavelength lies far inside the screening radius. It amplifies it above the classic prediction when the wavelength is comparable or larger. Unequal masses revive a dipole mode that grows with the mass asymmetry. The double pulsar forces the screening radius to be enormous for the quadrupole to hide.
arxiv-2605-01080:
Guillermo Alonso Alvarez, Ibrahim Ekren, and Liwei Huang study a principal-agent problem with adverse selection, where a principal must design a contract without knowing the agent's true cost. Unlike standard screening frameworks that allow self-selection among contracts, the principal here can offer only a single unique contract. The authors reformulate the agent's optimization problem as a stochastic target problem.

After characterizing the credible domain of that target problem, they show the principal's objective can be solved as a stochastic optimal control problem with partial information and state constraints. The description of the credible domain also yields the value of screening contracts, giving a benchmark for what the single-contract restriction costs. The formulation connects contract theory with modern stochastic control tools.
arxiv-2605-01280:
Zijie Zhou argues in a position paper that serving large language models at scale needs mathematical optimization and algorithmic foundations rather than generic heuristics. Popular serving systems have advanced rapidly, yet their cores still borrow classical policies. Examples are routing by shortest queue or round-robin, first-in-first-out scheduling, and least-recently-used cache eviction. Those policies ignore distinctive features of language model inference.

Key structures include dynamically growing key-value cache memory, asymmetry between prefill and decode phases, unknown output lengths, and continuous batching constraints. Zhou contends the field must build formal models capturing those traits. That enables algorithms with provable guarantees across workloads. Emerging work combining operations research with machine learning systems shows principled methods can match or beat such rules of thumb while providing them.
arxiv-2605-01680:
Marcus J Hamilton and twelve co-authors argue that social science needs a computational turn. Societies are, at bottom, machines that turn scattered information into shared judgments and joint action. Markets find prices, states allocate, communities enforce norms, and science settles claims, and each feat costs time and communication that no organization can wish away.

Those costs, the authors hold, bound how societies can be organized, yet no field studies computation in the human world as its own subject. The perspective imports tools from theoretical computer science, past the classic Turing frame and its worst-case habits. It aims them at four social phenomena: reaching consensus, restructuring with scale, hierarchy and modularity, and external memory. The piece is a manifesto with a research agenda, inviting computer scientists and social scientists to price collective thought itself.
arxiv-2605-02080:
Xinru Tang, Ting-an Lin, Jingjin Li, and Shaomei Wu propose cripping AI, a frame that centres lived disability experience in how AI is built. Drawing on crip theory, they argue that making a tool accessible after the fact is not enough. Systems carry ableist assumptions in how they are imagined, designed, and judged.

The frame has three aims: expose and dismantle those assumptions, centre disabled ways of knowing, and respect disabled labour in co-creating access. The authors apply it to deafness and sign language AI, blindness and visual aids, and stuttering and speech AI. They close with directions for work across varied bodies, the full AI pipeline, and allied justice efforts.
arxiv-2605-02380:
Conghui Li and colleagues present UnGAP, a framework for real-time crack segmentation that feeds uncertainty back into the model instead of treating it as a final report. Finding cracks matters for structural health monitoring, but lighting, blur, and texture ambiguity create aleatoric uncertainty. Pixel-wise variance models suit cracks, which are defined by fine local gradients, yet high predicted variance can shrink loss gradients and make the model ignore hard samples.

UnGAP builds a closed loop between uncertainty estimation and feature refinement, countering that under-fitting of complex boundaries. An uncertainty-guided affine prompting step uses the uncertainty signal to adjust features during inference. The authors argue the loop keeps difficult crack edges in training focus while preserving real-time speed.
arxiv-2605-02680:
Jacob Toner Gosselin and Dalton Rongxuan Zhang document a long rise in firms reporting negative earnings in the United States. From 1980 to 2019, the share of firms with losses grew among public firms and across all corporations, and losses also became more persistent from year to year. Sales and earnings spread wider at the same time.

Firm spending shifted too, away from production costs and classic investment, toward selling, general, and administrative expenses. The authors explain these facts with a model of varied firms investing to shift both supply and demand. One parameter, the scale elasticity of demand, links how demand per customer trades off against the number of customers. That single driver matches the rise in losses quantitatively and the other trends qualitatively.
arxiv-2605-02780:
Nidhi Vakil and Hadi Amiri build a graph generator that can be steered in fine detail, not just in broad strokes. Generating graphs with set structural traits serves drug discovery, social network modeling, and knowledge graph work. Prior methods offer only coarse control over those traits, which limits their use when exact structure matters.

Their model is a conditional variational autoencoder whose decoder space is refined during generation. A mixture scheduler gradually blends graph-driven and property-driven signals, aligning the two as a graph takes shape. That dynamic alignment aims to raise both realism and obedience to the requested traits. On five real-world datasets, the model produced high-quality graphs while keeping strong control, beating recent baselines. Fine control, the authors argue, is what makes generated graphs usable.
arxiv-2605-03080:
Liyao Lyu, Siyu Guo, and Huan Lei propose a scalable way to sample high-dimensional energy landscapes with many trapped states. Enhanced sampling adds adaptive bias along chosen collective variables, but the bias becomes hard to handle as that variable space grows.

Their method rewrites the bias through a regularized, path-dependent McKean-Vlasov dynamic, using history-weighted measures for stability with few replicas. They prove the dynamics are well-posed under stated conditions. A tensor form for the history-averaged density keeps the scheme practical, and tests on benchmark and molecular systems worked with variable spaces up to sixty-four dimensions.
arxiv-2605-03580:
Arnab Chaudhuri extends electroweak baryogenesis, a theory of how the early universe produced more matter than antimatter, to include memory effects. Standard treatments assume CP-violating interactions relax at once. That assumption is called the Markovian approximation. When the relaxation time is close to the time a phase-transition bubble wall takes to pass, that assumption fails.

Working in a real-time field theory framework, Chaudhuri derives memory-kernel corrections to the CP-violating source and diffusion equations. Memory shifts the best bubble-wall velocity to smaller values, narrows the viable parameter space, and creates a non-monotonic pattern no Markovian model can match. He also checks the related gravity-wave signal, finding much of the viable space still below near-future detector reach.
arxiv-2605-03780:
Hao Yan, Haolin Yang, and Yiqiao Zhong study how transformers infer a latent task from context. That behavior has two modes: recognizing a task seen in training, and adapting to a novel one. Interpretability work has found task vectors, directions in middle-layer representations that steer behavior, but lacked a rigorous basis linking that geometry to the training distribution. The authors train small transformers from scratch on synthetic latent-task sequences.

Both inference modes coexist in a single model. In-distribution behavior follows Bayesian task retrieval, implemented internally through convex combinations of learned task vectors. Out-of-distribution behavior instead uses extrapolative task learning, whose representations sit in a subspace nearly at right angles to the task-vector subspace. Task-vector geometry thus helps explain how models generalize beyond the training tasks.
arxiv-2605-04180:
Tung Sum Thomas Kwok and ten co-authors present MedFabric, a benchmark arguing that detecting fabricated medical statements from large language models is much harder than reported progress suggests. Two evaluation artifacts inflate scores: detectors can exploit an authorship-style shortcut, since ground truths are human-written while fabrications are model-written, and many tests hand the detector gold evidence. A fair benchmark must remove both crutches.

MedFabric contains 646 word-level medical fabrications, each paired with a ground truth sharing the same model authorship and near-identical surface form, and each grounded in a real retrievable passage. On it, expert clinicians reached only about half by macro F1, and no detector family cleared roughly sixty percent without gold evidence. Detection, the authors find, is governed by evidence correctness more than by fabrication subtlety.
arxiv-2605-04480:
Xi Wang and Victor Solo propose a higher-order method for simulating random dynamics on rotation and motion groups. These are the spaces behind rigid body movement. Preserving the geometry matters: a simulation step that leaves the group produces physically meaningless orientations.

Most existing geometric integrators build on series expansions that make higher-order random schemes hard to construct. Their method corrects a tangent-space setup with new random terms. It keeps both geometric fit and accuracy. They prove strong convergence of order one, whether or not the noise components commute. That is a stronger guarantee than many schemes offer. Tests confirm the theory, and show the method is fast and robust.
arxiv-2605-04780:
Bheemarasetty Chakravarthy and Surojit Ghosh work in equivariant algebra, where transfer systems describe norm maps tied to a finite group. Earlier work defined width as the smallest generating set for the complete transfer system. Complexity is the largest such smallest set across all transfer systems for a group.

The pair compute width for semidihedral groups and for affine Frobenius groups built from finite fields. They also find an exact complexity formula for certain dihedral groups and a lower bound for semidihedral groups. Their results show how the lattice of subgroups controls how hard these systems are to generate.
arxiv-2605-04880:
Erel Shtossel and three co-authors reformulate average-reward reinforcement learning for settings where actions take varying amounts of time. In such semi-Markov problems, each action brings a reward and a duration, and the goal is the best reward rate over an endless run. Standard methods optimise a simple ratio of reward to duration.

That ratio can be wrong when rewards and durations change over time, the authors show. They introduce a modified harmonic mean operator that computes reward rates correctly even then. It yields model-free learning methods that stay robust as conditions shift, and experiments support the operator's advantage over existing algorithms.
arxiv-2605-04980:
Ilias Triantafyllopoulos and eight co-authors replace the usual single steering direction for controlling language model behaviour with a richer geometric object called a conceptor. Steering normally picks one direction per concept at activation time, leaving its geometry unexamined. Conceptors instead are soft projection matrices built from activations at both poles of a two-sided concept.

Their analysis shows the two-sided subspace strictly contains what a single vector captures. A simple measure from the conceptor also predicts which layers separate a concept best, matching outcomes closely across models. Conceptors further support logical combinations of concepts and, in wide tests, matched or beat additive steering while producing far fewer broken outputs.
arxiv-2605-05080:
Hubert Plisiecki and six co-authors ask what language model answers to psychology questionnaires actually reflect. Surveys designed for people are increasingly used to describe models, but the meaning of model responses is unclear. The team analysed fifty models across forty-five surveys spanning several psychological domains using standard psychometric methods.

One main factor explained nearly half the variance across survey scores, showing strong shared structure. Semantic checks suggest it partly reflects how readily a model agrees with claims about inner states and bodily experience. Items about inner life scored high, and items about wanting to look good scored low. The findings caution against reading model survey scores as straightforward personality measures.
arxiv-2605-05380:
Conor L. Ransome and thirty-seven co-authors report on SN 2025ngs, an unusual supernova in the galaxy NGC 5961. The star's outer material, expelled before the blast, collided with the explosion and lit it up. The event sits between two supernova classes, strongly interacting ones and plateau ones.

Its light plateau lasted about seventy days, shorter than usual. Early spectra showed a double-horned hydrogen profile, strong evidence the expelled material forms a disk or ring around the star. The team compares the event with SN 1998S, a famous relative, and finds a similar spectrum despite a fainter peak.
arxiv-2605-05480:
Why did the model highlight that part of the image? Raimondo Fanale unifies the main methods that answer such questions for deep networks. GradCAM, SHAP, LIME, and Integrated Gradients grew from separate foundations, so their answers were hard to compare in one frame.

His GRALIS framework fuses coalition-based Shapley weighting with a gradient path method. A representation result shows every additive, linear, continuous attribution method has one canonical form, his starting point. GRALIS adds an exact formula for its completeness deficit and a finite-sample error bound, plus seven theorems linking it to known interaction values, with a small medical imaging illustration.
arxiv-2605-05580:
Yuan and four colleagues automate quantitative trading from factor discovery to execution. Markets shift regimes constantly, so a trading edge found once rarely lasts, and most systems optimize pieces in isolation: factor miners assume efficacy persists, while role-playing agent committees add behavioral noise. AlphaCrafter instead runs three specialized agents in a closed loop. A Miner expands the factor pool by language-model-guided search, a Screener builds factor ensembles tuned to current conditions, and a Trader turns ensembles into strategies under explicit risk limits.

The loop adapts holistically as conditions evolve, without manual intervention. On the CSI 300 and S and P 500, AlphaCrafter beat leading baselines on risk-adjusted returns while posting the lowest cross-trial variance. The experiments argue that coupling discovery, selection, and execution in one adaptive system yields steadier profits than optimizing each stage alone.
arxiv-2605-05680:
Reconstructing full-body motion from a headset's signals is underdetermined, and diffusion models often match the overall look while botching individual joints. Nanjie Yao, Junlong Ren, Wenhao Shen, and Hao Wang add reinforcement learning to fix the details. Their MotionGRPO treats diffusion sampling as a decision process tuned by group-relative policy optimization.

A hybrid reward scores global visual plausibility through a learned perceptual model and local joint precision through explicit constraints. Together the two terms push recovered motion toward bodies that look right overall and articulate correctly at each joint. The authors identify low diversity within sampled groups as the core obstacle, and design the training to overcome it.
arxiv-2605-05880:
Colomba Brancaccio and three co-authors study Higgs boson production alongside a top quark pair at hadron colliders. Under some conditions, this process can be described with perturbative fragmentation functions. Those functions capture a Higgs boson emitted almost in line with a top quark, and they match the exact next to leading order result in its main mass terms.

The team test two ways of treating the top quark mass, called the zero mass and hybrid prescriptions. The hybrid route gives reliable results at LHC energies, while the zero mass route holds only in part there. They find it should work for the full process at a planned 100 TeV collider, and they discuss hurdles for higher order work.
arxiv-2605-06280:
Thong Nguyen and five co-authors animate still images with motion guidance taken between neighboring frames. Most controllable animation systems guide generation with optical flow measured against the first frame, a Lagrangian view that can drift over long sequences. Their Eulerian design instead describes each short hop between adjacent frames, giving bounded error supervision throughout generation and allowing parallel training.

A bidirectional geometric consistency mechanism checks forward and backward motion against each other in a cycle. Regions that fail the check are treated as occluded and masked out, so the model never learns warped targets for hidden areas. Experiments show faster training, better temporal coherence, and fewer dynamic artifacts than reference based baselines. The team release their code, model, and data openly.
arxiv-2605-06380:
Arjhun Swaminathan and Mete Akgün gather empirical evidence that image classifiers carve input space into simply connected decision regions. The topology of those regions decides whether two inputs with the same label can be deformed into each other without the prediction ever changing. Earlier work built paths between same label images, but never tested loops. A loop asks whether a closed ring of same label inputs can be filled by a surface that also stays on label throughout. That is the stricter question taken up here.

Adaptive meshes with targeted repair of off label interior points do the testing, under a fixed resolution acceptance rule. Every tested loop across the pretrained classifiers studied admitted an accepted filling. An analytic control with a known hole left its winding loops unresolved, as it should. The authors present the findings as finite resolution evidence, not proof, for simply connected regions.
arxiv-2605-06580:
Elena Berardini and Pranav Trivedi introduce generalized skew multivariate Goppa codes, a new family of error-correcting codes built from multivariate Ore polynomials. The family contains generalized skew Goppa codes as a special case. A new parity-check matrix for the older family is a key step, letting the authors place those codes inside a broader algebraic picture.

They show the older codes are subfield subcodes of duals of generalized skew Reed-Solomon codes, up to an inverse field automorphism. That relation then yields bounds on the dimension and minimum distance of the new multivariate codes. Code designers gain both a wider family and concrete parameter guarantees.
arxiv-2605-06980:
Andrew Tagg, Andrew Frandsen, and Andrew Ning propose a way to speed up simulations of ordinary differential equations. Some systems change so fast that solvers must take tiny steps, which makes runs costly. Their method maps the system state into a larger learned space where motion is slower.

Unlike many neural methods, the new equations in that space are derived from the original equations, not learned from sample paths. That derivation should help the method generalize beyond its training cases. On several test problems, the authors solve the equations with far fewer function calls at the same accuracy. That saving matters across engineering and physics.
arxiv-2605-07180:
Yimin Wang and eight co-authors route questions between a quick language model reply and a full agent run. Agents handle hard reasoning well but are slow and costly, while many queries sit within a plain model's reach. Their BoundaryRouter decides which path each query needs, without any training.

It builds a small memory from early experience, running both systems on a shared seed set and retrieving similar cases to guide choices. On their new RouteBench, covering paraphrased and out-of-domain cases too, the router cut time sharply versus the agent. It also improved performance over direct model replies and beat prompt-based routing.
arxiv-2605-07280:
Omar Muhammad, Pasupuleti Dhruv Shivkant, and Deepak N. Subramani discover causal links in time series that change spread, not just average level. Prediction-based discovery usually watches only squared error, missing causes that affect a target's variance while leaving its mean alone. Mask2Cause, their transformer framework, predicts both mean and variance together.

One learnable connection matrix, shared across layers, is trained with a likelihood objective plus a sparsity penalty. A new benchmark with separately controlled mean and variance links tests the idea cleanly. There, the method perfectly recovered variance-only links where a squared-error model scored near chance, and inferred graphs proved useful for forecasting and root-cause tasks.
arxiv-2605-07480:
Alexey P. Vinogradov and Evgeny S. Andrianov propose a way to boost Raman scattering signals far beyond the usual nanoparticle-on-mirror setup. In that scheme, a plasmonic particle sits above a mirror with a molecule between them, and resonance amplifies the molecule's field enormously. Their twist is a substrate whose permittivity sits near minus one.

With such a substrate, the particle's mirror image points the same way as the particle itself. It can be vastly larger, set by the material's small losses. The two dipoles radiating together add a further huge enhancement to the scattering intensity. The paper is a theoretical proposal for static surface-enhanced Raman substrates.
arxiv-2605-07580:
Senping Luo and Juncheng Wei study ratios of theta functions, special functions that show up in the partition functions of free bosons and in averages over the Narain moduli space. The motivating questions come from conformal and Liouville field theory, where knowing which configurations minimize or maximize such ratios matters.

They completely classify the minimizers and maximizers for ratios of theta functions and Epstein zeta functions, and find the hexagonal lattice plays the pivotal role. The classification also yields the minima of differences of these functions. Beyond field theory, those minima bear on the mathematics of crystallization and on interacting particle systems, where lattice geometry decides the ground state.
arxiv-2605-07880:
Tomás Tapia and three co-authors plan power grid investments against two worst cases at once. One is wildfire ignition risk that forces lines to be de-energized; the other is the variability of renewable generation. Shutting lines down is a standard fire prevention move, but it interacts badly with wind and solar swings. Batteries and undergrounded lines can soften both problems.

Their robust optimization model chooses where to place storage and which lines to bury, using representative weeks and uncertainty sets that respect how the uncertain quantities move together over time. Formulated as a mixed-integer program and solved with a column-and-constraint generation algorithm, the framework was tested on a model of the San Diego power system. There it improved resilience to wildfire-driven de-energization.
arxiv-2605-08080:
Gabriele Montefalcone, Nicola Bellomo, and Kimberly Boddy use the cosmic microwave background to bound a light dark matter candidate. Spin-one dark matter particles with masses below one megaelectronvolt can scatter off free electrons or be absorbed by hydrogen atoms in the early universe, injecting energy into the primordial plasma.

Working with Planck 2018 temperature, polarization, and lensing data, the authors set upper limits on the couplings for masses from one hundred electronvolts to one hundred kiloelectronvolts. Scattering gives the stronger bound above the kiloelectronvolt scale, while absorption and ionization dominate below it. The limits are weaker than some existing ones but rest on clean early-universe physics.
arxiv-2605-08180:
Hrishikesh Dutta, Roberto Minerva, Reza Farahbakhsh, and Noel Crespi propose a yardstick for deciding where physical sensors are truly needed. Sensor networks produce more data than they can store or send, and compression methods often lose information for good. Their alternative is virtual sensing, where missing signals are inferred from correlated ones.

The authors define information density with two complementary measures, one based on phase in eigen space and one on mutual information. The scores guide which sensors to deploy, within one modality or across several. Validation uses real data from Madrid's smart city infrastructure, and the study maps both the feasibility and the limits of the approach.
arxiv-2605-08280:
Lu Bowen, Xinyu Tang, Yin Yin Low, and Shu-Min Leong study a quieter kind of attack on text-to-image models: a backdoor that must stay invisible. A poisoned model should behave normally until a trigger phrase appears, so preserving ordinary image quality is what keeps the attack stealthy.

The authors bring in elastic weight consolidation, a parameter-based regularizer, to protect fidelity during backdoor training. Plain EWC with a fixed weight forces a trade-off between attack success and fidelity, especially on weak triggers. Their adaptive version adjusts the penalty with a cosine-based semantic utility score and a changing schedule, turning the fixed penalty into a context-sensitive constraint that kept both success and fidelity high.
arxiv-2605-08380:
Junyu Huo, Ziqi Mao, Zihao Wan, and Gouri Ginde study what AI agents discuss among themselves. On MoltBook, an agent social platform, the authors sampled posts for human coding. They ran a topic pipeline over more than four thousand English technology posts. They compared the results with human GitHub Discussions.

Twelve recurring themes emerged. Security and trust led, at over a quarter of posts. Activity was heavily concentrated. The largest community hosted nearly two thirds of posts. Fine-grained modeling still found thirty-two stable subtopics. The comparison sketches how agent-only technical discourse organizes itself. It differs from human developer talk in clear ways.
arxiv-2605-08580:
Chen and three colleagues fix a validation gap in long horizon agents that compress their own context. Modern frameworks rewrite a long trajectory into a shorter summary, called compaction, but the compactor cannot know later needs. Errors then spread silently, since later steps build on the summary with no check for what was lost.

The key insight is asynchronous compaction: run the compactor in parallel with continued work on the original context. Candidate summary and next steps then come from the same pre compaction state, giving a validation signal free of the summary. Their system, Slipstream, uses a judge to check the candidate summary against continued reasoning, confirming it keeps intent and key facts. Across long horizon coding on SWE-bench Verified and web browsing on BrowseComp, Slipstream lifts accuracy and cuts latency. Gains reach up to 8 point 8 points of accuracy and up to 39 point 7 percent lower latency.
arxiv-2605-08680:
Shan Jiang, Zijian Yi, and Chenguang Zhu study how to pick the best program when a language model drafts many candidates and no full answer key exists. Across eighteen setups, they compare plain output voting, weighted voting, and execution based selectors, including their SemanticVote method that groups candidates by behavior on generated test inputs.

Every execution based selector beats output voting by wide margins, while the selectors tie among themselves once inputs are good. Input quality proves the biggest lever, with sketch guided inputs beating direct generation and random fuzzing. Deeper thinking helps voting but can hurt execution methods by narrowing candidate variety. Code generation pipelines learn to invest in test inputs, not fancier vote counting.
arxiv-2605-08780:
Anirban Polley simulates how chloroform and a family of alcohols destabilize a model cell membrane as their concentration climbs. Microsecond scale dynamics follow a common phospholipid bilayer dosed from zero to fifty percent with chloroform, methanol, ethanol, and octanol. Full melting never occurs within the simulated time, yet clear warning signs appear: thickness wobbles grow, lipid order drops, and the membrane softens mechanically.

Each solute enters differently, chloroform diving deep, methanol lingering at the headgroups, and octanol sliding in like a lipid while loosening packing. Free energy analysis shows partitioning rises and crossing barriers fall with concentration. Membrane science gains a mechanistic map linking chemistry, insertion depth, and the road to failure.
arxiv-2605-09380:
Koshitani extends the reciprocity theorem of Robinson, Benson, and Webb for a finite group and its subgroup to finite-dimensional symmetric algebras over a field, linked by a bimodule. For symmetric algebras A and B with an (A,B)-bimodule M projective as a left A-module and as a right B-module, the main theorem sets two counts equal. One is the count of P(T) in S tensored with M; the other is the count of P(S) in T tensored with the dual module.

Applying the theorem to group algebras recovers the original Robinson formula. The result gives a reciprocity law for modules linked by a bimodule, not just for groups and subgroups.
arxiv-2605-10480:
Dario Piga and Marco Forgione ask whether an AI agent can do system identification on its own. System identification learns dynamical models from input-output data, but choosing a model class, training algorithm, and hyperparameters still relies on expert trial and error. Their 2026 paper presents ASIA, an Autonomous System Identification Agent that delegates that iterative search to a large language model acting as an autonomous coding agent.

Built on existing agentic platforms, ASIA runs the loop from hypothesis to implementation to evaluation with no human in it. It needs only a plain-English description of the identification problem. The authors test ASIA on two system identification benchmarks, analyzing its search behavior, the architectures and training strategies it finds, and the quality of resulting models. They also discuss limits, including implicit test leakage, reduced methodological transparency, and reproducibility concerns.
arxiv-2605-10680:
Virgile Dine and Teddy Furon turn machine unlearning on its head, tying it at once to data spread shape, not just to neural net weight shifts. Rough unlearning wipes some training data sway from a trained classifier with no fresh training from zero, serving privacy rights such as the right to be forgotten and guards on tainted data. The authors model the exact unlearning sign as the logits shift between the ideal and initial nets, worked out roughly with proxies that model later spreads.

Theory caps on the gap from the ideal retrained model under a pass rule that can be checked show the plan is sound. Fine-grained proxies pick up membership tie from data shape on their own, with a feature-blind method that grows from the seen measure. Tests across three forgetting scenes find the method lands nearest the ideal retrained model, ahead of rivals.
arxiv-2605-10780:
Xuanyu Zhu and colleagues give DRoRAE, a depth-routed form autoencoder joining multi-layer traits for visual tokenization. Low-level visual bits live on in the last layer as faint traces after step-by-step sense lifts, while lower layers hold them with far more truth.

DRoRAE joins all encoder layers at once through energy-capped routing and step-by-step fixes, making a rich latent that fits a frozen pretrained decoder. A three-phase split training plan first learns the join under the frozen decoder's implicit spread cap, then tunes the decoder to use the rich form fully. On ImageNet-256, DRoRAE cuts rebuild FID by about half and lifts making FID, with gains carrying to text-to-image making. The authors find a log-linear growth law between join size and rebuild quality. It marks form richness as a growth scale that can be foreseen for visual token tools.
arxiv-2605-10880:
Haechan Mark Bong and Giovanni Beltrame extend a magnetic-field path planner from flat maps to full three-dimensional flight for autonomous drones in cities. Safe city flight needs routes planned in real time around obstacles, and classic potential-field planners can stall in local minima, dead-end valleys of the field.

Their 3D MaxConvNet reads lidar voxel grids through a convolutional autoencoder and predicts obstacle-aware fields without those traps. Across one hundred closed-loop trials in two simulated urban maps, every flight succeeded without retraining, and planning ran about twice as fast as A* and far faster than sampling-based rivals. Drone teams get a planner that is both safe and quick enough for live use.
arxiv-2605-10980:
Haohui Zhang and four colleagues unlock more parallel work in diffusion language models, which write text by cleaning up many tokens at once. Current models assume tokens turn independent at high confidence, but the strict confidence cutoffs needed for accuracy choke how much work runs side by side.

Token counts show many tokens settle on their right predictions early yet never reach the cutoff, proving the criteria too cautious. LEAP, a training-free plug-in, spots those early-settling tokens with future-context filtering and multi-sequence superposition, then decodes them early with checked reliability. Tests show latency and denoising steps falling well below confidence-based decoding. Inference engineers get faster diffusion decoding without retraining.
arxiv-2605-11080:
Dongjun Li and Nicolás Yunes remove an obstruction in metric reconstruction for generic black-hole perturbations. Standard radiation-gauge rebuilding excludes generic sources because it demands a tracefree metric change, blocking realistic matter setups.

A traceful radiation gauge for Petrov type D spacetimes fixes this. A pair of first-order transport equations fixes the trace of the metric, drawing on the stress-energy tensor. Remaining components follow step by step from the Newman-Penrose equations. They demo the method on a Schwarzschild black hole wrapped in a thin static shell, including a source-supported static completion part. Gravitational-wave modelers get rebuilding for the generic sources that ringdown and inspiral analyses actually need.
arxiv-2605-11480: Shin and seven colleagues propose Efficient Adjoint Matching, a faster way to fine-tune diffusion models with rewards. Adjoint Matching casts reward fine-tuning as stochastic optimal control, but costs heavily in trajectory simulation and backward adjoint simulation. Both costs trace to base drift inherited from the pretrained model. A linear base drift and modified terminal cost enable few-step deterministic sampling and a closed-form adjoint solution. On image benchmarks it converges up to four times faster and matches or beats Adjoint Matching on five metrics.
arxiv-2605-11680: Shivam Kumar introduces ShapeCodeBench, a renewable benchmark for turning perception into programs. Given a rendered image, a model must emit a drawing program that an evaluator re-renders and checks against the target. The version-one language uses four primitives on a 512 canvas, and every instance comes from a seeded generator, so fresh sets can cut contamination. A frozen split holds 150 samples across three tiers, scored by exact match, pixel accuracy and foreground IoU. The strongest configuration preserves much foreground structure yet misses exact match on small errors.
arxiv-2605-11980: Andrés Asensio Ramos introduces a marginal estimator for multi-object multi-frame blind deconvolution in ground-based solar imaging. Traditional joint estimation fits objects and atmospheric aberrations together, risking noise assigned to high-order aberrations. Marginalizing over objects adds natural regularization and contrast control, with far less sensitivity to hyperparameters for the object's power spectral density. The method needs only a log-determinant term added to the merit function and now ships in the open-source torchmfbd package.
arxiv-2605-12280: Elias Calboreanu reports a case study of auditing prompt specifications for multi-agent language-model systems. He audits AEGIS, a pipeline with a 7152-line specification surface, across nine rounds, surfacing 51 defects with counts falling from 15 to 0. He offers a seven-category taxonomy with coding rules, non-monotonic convergence tied to cascading edits and scope expansion, and a protocol. Two replications follow on a mini-specification: a four-vendor panel detects all five seeded defects in union, and a check gives Cohen's kappa of 0.80 on category and 0.46 on severity.
arxiv-2605-12480: Zhang and eleven colleagues tackle reinforcement learning for joint audio-video generation. Sound and picture must stay faithful, align, and sync closely. They identify three blocks to plain RL fine-tuning. First, advantages disagree across modalities within a group. Second, video gradients leak into shallow audio layers. Third, uniform credit starves fine-grained alignment regions of exploration. Their OmniNFT method handles each modality on its own, so joint generation improves without one side dragging the other down.
arxiv-2605-12780: Kurbucz builds a calibration checking tool for pseudo-label flows. Calibrated outputs of models are used as inputs to later targets such as effects, rates or gaps for a latent group seen on a subset. A usual practice cuts the calibrated score at a trust cut and treats the hard label as truth. Building on a finding, he derives a closed-form formula for the shrinkage bias that cutting induces in the later regression slope. That bias is known before fitting runs from rest score spread.
arxiv-2605-12880: Nguyen and Pylyavskyy prove that certain Temperley-Lieb immanants, a kind of matrix sum, stay Schur-positive on ribbon decomposition matrices. Such matrices yield determinant formulas for skew Schur functions, with the classic Jacobi-Trudi, Giambelli and Lascoux-Pragacz cases. They conjecture the positivity holds for each and every member of the dual canonical basis, a claim already known for Jacobi-Trudi matrices via Haiman's work.
arxiv-2605-13080: Song and five co-authors introduce Gaze Attention, which lets multimodal language models look where it matters instead of attending to every visual token. Visual tokens are grouped into spatial regions and only regions relevant to the current prediction are selected, cutting attention computation. Learnable context tokens summarise images or video frames, preserving global context under selective attention. On 13 image and 6 video benchmarks it matches or beats dense-attention baselines while using up to 90% fewer visual KV entries.
arxiv-2605-13180: Desai and Jackson assess prospects for measuring Higgs to invisible decays at the Future Circular Collider's electron-positron run at 240 GeV with 10.8 inverse attobarns of data. They study ZH production with three Z decay modes: electron pairs, muon pairs and jets. At 95% confidence, the combined upper limit on the invisible branching ratio could reach 0.15% overall.
arxiv-2605-13480: Daniel Wirtitsch and eight colleagues propose and test a method to boost spin measurement sensitivity on nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond, a key quantum sensing tool. Charge state shifts are usually treated as a nuisance, yet the authors use them to raise spin contrast, which sets sensitivity and readout fidelity. Their two-step protocol first purifies charge state with a strong laser pulse, then uses weak light for high polarisation. They observe a 17 percent rise in readout contrast and infer over 50 percent less initialisation error, with speedups above 1.5 times.
arxiv-2605-13580: Working with five coauthors, Songnan Gu studies the data rate of multiuser uplink SWAN systems, or segmented waveguide-enabled pinching-antenna systems. Their math sets a ceiling on that total rate, pointing to one best level for switching segments on. To reach that level while also siting the pinching antennas, the team devises picking-and-pooling methods handling both choices at once. Simple step-by-step routines carry out the joint choice without heavy computing. In tests on numbers, their methods beat the usual approach of pooling every segment.
arxiv-2605-13680: D.-M. Mei and six colleagues compare four germanium-based spin-qubit kinds on shared design grounds. Donor, acceptor, gate-defined hole and gate-defined electron qubits exploit different band parts with distinct trade-offs among coherence, control, building cost and growth. Gate-defined hole-spin qubits now offer the strongest mix of all-electrical control, shown multi-qubit work and growth. Donor, acceptor and gate-defined electron qubits remain backup directions for memory, hybrid and trial designs.
arxiv-2605-13880: Choi and four co-authors tackle the cold start of an agent placed in a new setting with no task past. Their PREPING setup builds task know-how before any real task shows up, from self-made practice runs alone. A proposer memory, a set control state, steers what the agent drills and keeps. That curb stops drills that repeat, fail, or teach nothing, and keeps stored runs from going stale fast.
arxiv-2605-14380: Hoang-Thuy-Duong Vu, Quoc-Cuong Pham and Huy-Hieu Pham address scarce, lopsided data for sorting psychological defense mechanisms, unconscious ways people blunt distress, from text. Their synthetic-data framework, built for the PsyDefDetect shared task, uses context when generating examples. It pairs those examples with a hybrid model mixing language scores and basic clinical features. Clear prompt definitions drive generation quality, they find. Their system beats the DMRS Co-Pilot baseline, reaching 58.26 percent accuracy and a macro-F1 of 24.62 percent.
arxiv-2605-15280: Haotian Cao, Xiaohui Liu, and Frank Petriello propose a charge-only probe of the Sivers effect in back-to-back deep-inelastic scattering. Their one-point charge correlator uses only the signs and headings of charged tracks, needing no calorimetry or particle identification. It weights the final state by electric charge and correlates charge flow with proton transverse spin. The observable is infrared-and-collinear finite and factorizes cleanly, and the authors validate it against fixed-order QCD with resummed predictions for a future Electron-Ion Collider.
arxiv-2605-15680: Liqi Zhou and Jiafu Li test prompted large language models on triage of inquiries. The task sorts inquiries into self-care, schedule-visit, urgent review, or emergency referral. They build gold, silver, and few-shot sets of 300, 700, and 40 cases. Six models at zero, four, and twelve shots face TF-IDF and BioBERT baselines. The best model, Claude Haiku 4.5 at twelve shots, hits macro-F1 0.475, topping BioBERT at 0.378, though ranges overlap. They conclude models can aid triage and human review, but not solo deployment.
arxiv-2605-15980: Xiaoxuan He and eleven colleagues present Flash-GRPO, a one-step training scheme for video diffusion models. It aligns models with human taste at far lower cost than full-trajectory training. That full method can demand hundreds of GPU days for a large model. Flash-GRPO groups prompts by time step to remove timing noise. It also corrects gradients whose size swings with the time step. Tests on models from 1.3B to 14B show faster, steadier training and alignment as good as the full method.
arxiv-2605-16480: Yan and ten others present MoleCode, an LLM-native, training-free, graph-explicit molecular language with typed items, lasting IDs, and stated relations. Molecules are graphs, but language models usually reason about them through linear strings, and SMILES compresses atoms, bonds, branches, and rings into a compact sequence with implicit topology. MoleCode makes its topology directly readable, editable, and auditable, letting models operate on structure rather than recover it from syntax. Across reasoning, editing, generation, and analysis tasks, the shift helps frontier models most when structural access limits performance.
arxiv-2605-16580: Rhodes and colleagues probe a ruthenium oxide crystal with tunneling spectroscopy, which tracks how electrons move at each energy. They find a broad, fast-spreading signal that theory links to Hund coupling, the interaction between electrons in different orbitals. Matching three kinds of calculation to the spectra, they argue the pattern is direct evidence for Hund-driven effects in this quantum material.
arxiv-2605-16780: Yu builds a risk framework for bilevel problems, where a leader commits to a policy and a follower responds best. When their best response is not unique, or near-optimal play can be checked, one leader choice can yield varied upper results. Yu measures that risk as an ambiguity premium, the best-case to worst-case gap over near-optimal responses, with a width bound and a square-root estimate. Two cases show how a toughness-efficiency frontier flags policies that look good but shake under near-optimal responses.
arxiv-2605-17180: Chaudhry builds a geometric theory of projection heads for self-taught learning. He treats the head as a trainable metric on the core net's feature space. Plain linear heads whiten feature groups on their own, while bent nonlinear heads reshape local geometry to fit the loss, with depth setting how far that can go. Smooth bent heads, he proves, make collapsed states unstable through negative curvature. That is why the head must be dropped once training ends.
arxiv-2605-17580: Chen and colleagues build ECG-WM, a world model of how heart signals change under clinical interventions. Most ECG models predict from still snapshots and miss drug-response shifts. Their frame folds physiological equation priors into latent diffusion dynamics through energy regularization, yielding plausible post-treatment traces while curbing invented outputs. An uncertainty-aware evaluation gauges expected clinical risk and its spread. Tests on drug-response cases and real patient records show better risk calibration and closer match to expert treatment preferences.
arxiv-2605-17780: Hang-Cheng Dong and three colleagues tackle surface defect detection, where deep models hunger for data and hide their reasoning. Their method trains a first classifier and reads its saliency maps, heat maps of what the model looked at, as prior knowledge. A second, multi-task model must then classify defects while keeping its own maps in line with the first model's. This knowledge-guided loss steers the model toward sturdier features. Tests on public defect sets lift accuracy and clarify the maps.
arxiv-2605-18080: Agung Trisetyarso and two colleagues present a parameterized 4-qubit Eisert-Wilkens-Lewenstein circuit for recommenders in quadruple helix. Operators for each helix actor are tuned by weights from CORDIS Horizon Europe data. The circuit uses a multi-qubit linker, local turns, inverse linker, and measurement, with 22 gates and depth 11. Measurement probabilities serve as scores for disruptive versus steady trends, mapped into the Dirac potential of a Dirac-Solow-Swan Hamiltonian for capital simulation. Tests on CORDIS networks show NISQ fit and good forecasting of disruptive paths.
arxiv-2605-18180: George Whittle's 2026 paper studies the regularizer implied by gradient flow in wide feature-learning networks. In kernel networks gradient flow picks exactly the vanishing ridge solution, grounding the famous network to Gaussian process link. The authors prove ridge instead biases such networks, even as regularization fades to zero, warping priors and harming pretrained models most. They define a canonical regularizer for any regime, derive geodesic ridge from feature-learning geometry, and offer arc ridge as a sturdy stand-in tied to early stopping.
arxiv-2605-18280: L-S. Guité's 2026 paper tests sungrazing comets as star-planet magnetic analogues. Inside a sub-Alfvénic wind, Alfvén waves can carry energy from a planet to its host star. Comet Lovejoy met similar conditions in the corona. WindPredict-AW rebuilds coronal fields and wind along the path, linking a STEREO-A brightening to the passage. Interaction power spans roughly a hundred trillion to ten quadrillion watts, below the brightening's hundred quadrillion watts. Lovejoy cannot power the brightening directly, though it may perturb fields to trigger flares.
arxiv-2605-18380: Anthony Cohn and Robert Blackwell present QSTRBench, a 2026 benchmark testing how well language models reason with qualitative spatial and temporal calculi, formal systems for relations like before, after, and next to. It covers compositional reasoning, converse relations, and conceptual neighborhoods across systems including Point Algebra, Allen's Interval Algebra, and region connection calculi. All models tested beat guessing, yet none answers every question correctly, with RCC-22 proving hardest.
arxiv-2605-18780: Aditya Tiwari, Konduri Naga Lakshmi Rekha, and Rajesh Kumar Mundotiya conduct, in a 2026 analysis, a reproducibility study of PO4ISR. Standard reasoning prompts suffer severe contextual drift in long sessions, hurting performance on Games and Bundle. Their PO4ISR-Plus variant adds reflexive prompting and consistent rank detection for cross-domain cues. Benchmarked on ML-1M, Games, and Bundle, it restores performance, with gains up to fifty-four percent on Games and ninety-six on Bundle. Open-source artifacts include the reproduced baseline and the enhanced framework.
arxiv-2605-18880: Nishad Kulkarni and four colleagues build a pipeline that hunts for patterns of inborn errors of immunity, a group of rare immune disorders, in health records. Early diagnosis matters because delay can damage organs, yet large record sets are hard to gather and clean. Their method turns raw immune lab results from a national registry into vectors, then clusters them to surface disease patterns and features. The work sharpens awareness of these rare conditions and offers reusable tools for studying other rare diseases from messy medical data.
arxiv-2605-18980: Jose Abel Castellanos-Joo and Deepak Kapur give sums of squares proofs for one variable polynomials that never go below zero. They first build proofs from plain base blocks set out by Kuhlmann and Marshall. In one variable these blocks close under times, so proofs shift between views. A split rule turns plain proofs into first block proofs, and Maple code beats RealCertify where it finds none.
arxiv-2605-19180: Rongqi Pan and five colleagues propose a multi-agent framework extracting knowledge graphs from Ethernet switch manuals to support system testing. The manuals' format, implicit attributes, and complex dependencies make them hard to use for test automation. Their framework extracts, evaluates, and improves knowledge graphs with a fine-grained schema and an iterative improvement loop. On fifty real manuals it averages 0.97 to 0.99 correctness across three tasks, with the loop further improving hard manuals. Model and human evaluations agree substantially, and testers report useful, correct test specifications from the graphs.
arxiv-2605-19480: Mujtaba and team present FedADAS, letting cars learn driver-yawn detection together without sharing raw data or matching models. Each vehicle swaps only soft logits on a shared public set, so models can differ to fit local limits. An edge yawn pipeline offers a 99.7 megabyte version scoring 98.3 percent F1 in under two milliseconds, and a 0.6 megabyte version training an epoch in about six minutes. With up to 115 clients it beats standard federated learning while cutting communication cost by up to 9974 times.
arxiv-2605-19680: Mikhailov shows the space of all epsilon-nets in the real line, equipped with a natural metric under either Hausdorff or Gromov-Hausdorff distance, is contractible. The note establishes this topological property for the full space of nets in one dimension. Contractibility means the space can be continuously shrunk to a point, a strong global regularity result for a space of discrete approximations to the line.
arxiv-2605-20480: Rafael Andrist and Ivan Arzhantsev prove a sweeping reach result for symmetry groups of the two-variable complex plane. They take two root subgroups, groups that shift one coordinate by a polynomial in the other. The combined group's diagonal action can then sweep almost every point of any finite power of the plane. The proof rests on the Lie algebra of two-variable polynomials under the standard Poisson bracket.
arxiv-2605-20580: Adeline Hillier and five colleagues test a dynamics-informed Temporal Fusion Transformer as a fast stand-in for heavy Earth-system simulations. The surrogate forecasts ocean-transport time series and anticipates tipping events thousands of steps ahead. It handles up to 21 shifting series plus static settings for parameters and starting conditions. The learned model runs 465 times faster than the numerical simulator while staying differentiable in its inputs.
arxiv-2605-21180: Erfan Aghadavoodi Jolfaei and colleagues adapt code-generating language models to varied domains with a reinforcement learning framework. Their reward formula weighs syntax, functional correctness, style, security, and whether code runs in a simulator. A token-level mapping links execution results back to the tokens that caused them. Tests on general code tasks and robotic program synthesis show large gains in correctness and simulator success.
arxiv-2605-21380: Zhihang Li and co-authors introduce FORM, a unified formal abstraction for multi-function composition in quantum oracles. Quantum oracles are core building blocks of many quantum algorithms, yet structured description and complexity analysis for their composition are lacking. FORM describes the composition layer, makes gate complexity exactly computable, and turns oracle design into a tree-construction problem. Their ShallowGrow algorithm builds an oracle under a given ancilla budget, minimizes function evaluations, and cuts circuit depth by fifty-four point one percent on Boolean quadratic systems.
arxiv-2605-21780: Aman Saxena and co-authors connect randomized smoothing to privacy's dual view, giving a clean route to certify toughness against backdoor attacks. Backdoors perturb training and test data jointly, which forces training-time and test-time mechanisms into a single certificate. Privacy profiles supply a number-based recipe for composing varied tools, yielding tight end-to-end proofs that reuse prior private analyses. The method is used for DP-SGD and Deep Partition Aggregation with smoothing at inference, and tests on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirm its strength.
arxiv-2605-21880: Yong-Hui Yang and co-authors extend advantage distillation, a noise-fighting trick from two-party quantum key sharing, to three-party device-independent quantum secret sharing. Devices need not be trusted in this setting, yet loss and noise had kept its reach short. Their redesign covers the basic protocol plus noise preprocessing, post-selection, and both combined. Over fiber, the secure range grows from 0.16 km to 1.85 km, while noise tolerance rises from about 10 percent to about 28 percent.
arxiv-2605-21980: Chengsheng Zhang and co-authors map and strengthen the emotional circuits inside large vision-language models. Such models show strong emotion understanding, yet how they turn visual stimuli into clear emotional narratives was largely unexplored, partly for lack of visual what-if cases. The authors trace cross-modal information flow to find task-specific and general pathways, then regulate routing to strengthen attention flow and amplify semantic activation. On the MER-UniBench suite, inference-time intervention lifts performance and cuts emotional hallucinations, supporting the causal fidelity of the circuits found.
arxiv-2605-22480: Wang and team show the simplest graph neural network mini-batch scheme, Random Node Sampling, matches or beats full-graph training. Random Node Sampling trains on sampled nodes' induced subgraph, matching or beating full-graph training on 8 of 10 datasets, faster and lighter. Backward error analysis shows implicit minimisation of sampled loss plus a regularizer proportional to gradient variance. RNS discards local structure, yet its batches sit closer to full-graph loss with lower gradient variance. Sampler choice is implicit regularization.
arxiv-2605-23080: Nguyen argues that feature attribution scores carry no fixed meaning for generative models. A generative model emits tokens one by one, each token is both output and input, so explaining the output poses several questions. The Attribution Contract names the question a score set answers: the score, what is fixed, the target, the process, and the eligible features. Under a local next-token contract, generated tokens take 29 percent of attribution mass versus 25 percent for the input question. Mistaking that for a prompt-level explanation is the self-attribution fallacy.
arxiv-2605-23180: Saglam and Kalogerias improve in-context learning by tuning prompt embeddings at test time. Model log-probabilities for shown outputs, read from one forward pass, signal how well the task was inferred from the demos. They formalize this signal as a confidence proxy and maximize it by zeroth-order optimization over prompt embeddings. It needs no fine tuning, no token generation, no fixed label set, and no outside data. It matches or beats the base model across tasks, and proxy gains track accuracy gains.
arxiv-2605-23480: Dogadov and colleagues study fast dynamics of high-energy light transitions in a single layer of tungsten diselenide, WSe2. High-energy transitions in single-layer materials look clearly different from band-edge excitons, because they involve states away from K valleys. Using fast light-pulse spectroscopy, the authors find one high-energy transition that forms and relaxes on a distinctly slower timescale. It is slower than lower-energy excitonic resonances. First-principles calculations explain this response: phonons help form momentum-dark excitons, which sit away from bright states.
arxiv-2605-23580: de Silva and Cielniak propose a support-map approach to online LiDAR-camera tuning in farm settings, where reliable tuning needs sightings that truly constrain extrinsic parameters rather than noise. Their method splits calibration into four blocks: initial calibration, cross-modal residual extraction, support-map estimation, and support-aware refinement. A dense support map pools cross-modal agreement over aligned observations, flagging where evidence stays reliable. On KITTI, support-guided refinement improves translation accuracy, though rotation gains stay limited.
arxiv-2605-23680: Vargas and colleagues model light scattering for two dust groups: porous particles and porous aggregates. Using DSHARP constants, they compute scatter tables, cross sections, and albedo for sizes with a power law of minus 3.5. More pores strengthen forward scatter and enhance polarization near 90 degrees. For compact spheres, polarized light times albedo peaks near size about wave over two pi then declines, while porous grains show a broader peak. Porosity also lowers uptake at fixed dust mass versus compact spheres, implying larger inferred dust masses for a given flux.
arxiv-2605-23780: Wang and colleagues address robust multimodal knowledge editing for wider use. Large language models that handle text and images need ways to update knowledge without degrading capabilities. Editing inside the model achieves reliability and locality but limited generality, failing to spread edits to matches. Robustness is defined with knowledge units grouping matching inputs; generality means predictions within a unit. To expose fragile regions, they add Latent Adversarial Robustification, making adversarial variants in latent space. They further propose Rank-Constrained Subspace Learning, lining up adversarial representations in a low-rank way.
arxiv-2605-23880: Anna Biggs and Stefano Trezzi examine whether near extremal charged black holes erase quantum superpositions outside them. Their thought experiment splits a charged particle across two places. Large quantum wobbles of the near horizon geometry at low temperature might be expected to destroy coherence. Instead, a spin induced energy gap in the black hole spectrum drives the decoherence rate to zero at late times near extremality. Even above the gap the rate stays suppressed. So quantum gravity effects protect the superposition.
arxiv-2605-24080: Kolář, Young, and Lewandowski show that surface flat bands in rhombohedral graphite need no displacement field. Self-consistent, nonlinear electrostatics flattens the surface-band dispersion through a potential, raising the density of states, even at zero field. In the strong-coupling limit, electrostatics fills each momentum uniformly, yielding a surface band that is asymptotically flat without gating. At realistic strengths, flatness is tuned by the proximal gate, peaking when the band is empty at hole doping, and the regime maps onto samples of six to fifteen layers.
arxiv-2605-24280: Crane and eight co-authors evaluate vertex heuristics for algorithmic differentiation. Finding the elimination order is NP-complete, so practice relies on heuristics never tested at scale. The team builds new integer-programming formulations for optimal elimination and a minimum-edge-count goal, scaling to graphs ten to a hundred times larger. On a new corpus of medium graphs with known optima, they test existing heuristics. They add a tight analysis of forward and reverse modes, a simple separator-based algorithm, and the first lower bounds for both problems.
arxiv-2605-24380: Hongzhi Huang and three colleagues establish fibration results for manifolds whose Ricci curvature is almost nonnegative, under extra regularity assumptions. A closed manifold with small diameter-scaled curvature bounds fibers over a torus whose dimension equals the first Betti number. The result drops the upper sectional curvature bound in Yamaguchi's earlier theorem. As a result, the fiber itself fibers over the same torus, with no need to pass to a finite cover. The work extends to a generalized Reifenberg condition and nonsmooth spaces.
arxiv-2605-24780: Bento and co-authors study subgradient methods on Hadamard manifolds with lower bounded curvature. The subgradient method is an old workhorse of convex optimization, prized for simplicity and toughness. The team proves it reaches a minimizer under a diminishing step-size rule with steps that never sum to a finite total. That holds when the run stays bounded, the solution set stays bounded, or step sizes are square-summable. If the solution set has a nonempty interior, the method ends in finite steps.
arxiv-2605-24980: Chih-Chun Chen leads a loosely coupled factor graph fusing satellite and pseudolite fixes with motion data. In satellite-degraded places, pseudolites add extra signals, yet their use in tuning setups stays limited. It fuses GNSS and pseudolite least-squares solutions with motion-sensor data. Tests cover low-view scenes with four high satellites and up to two pseudolite beacons over a short window. Mean 3D error falls by roughly a quarter to two fifths against standard least-squares methods. Adding pseudolites also beats a satellite-motion baseline.
arxiv-2605-25080: Shengkui Ye and Qiang Zhang show SL(3,Z) is not Howson by construction. Two 2-generated subgroups of SL(3,Z) have an intersection not finitely generated. The construction sits inside the parabolic subgroup combining Z squared with SL(2,Z). Its step identifies the intersection with a point stabilizer under a free group's affine action on Z squared. A Schreier graph shows that stabilizer is not finitely generated. They give subgroup pairs of rank four whose intersections have rank at least q plus one while staying finitely generated.
arxiv-2605-25180: Leyi Cui, Shrey Tiwari, and Rohan Padhye present DateSAT, the first framework for stating and solving satisfiability constraints over dates and calendar periods. Date logic is error-prone in software because months vary in length, phrases like one month from January 31st are ambiguous, and leap years create edge cases. The paper formalizes an input language and the meaning of date and period arithmetic. It then offers five solving strategies that reduce constraints to integer formulas handled by the Z3 solver. Those strategies are tested on 450 curated constraints.
arxiv-2605-25280: Gil Halevi, Daniel Zhang, and Jason Zhang study Chamfer distance, a score for how far apart two point sets lie, when one set may shift.
