Across two benchmarks, two base models, and twelve languages, the recipe reaches the best balance of accuracy, language fidelity, and token use. Gains are strongest on lower-resource, out-of-domain languages.
arxiv-2606-15180:
Zheng and coauthors propose a spectroscopy scheme to pin down five thorium-229 nuclear parameters at once, in a 2026 physics paper. Thorium-229 has an unusually low-energy excited nuclear state, ideal for a nuclear optical clock. Building that clock needs precise values for several nuclear quantities, now known only loosely. The scheme uses two highly charged thorium ions whose electrons sit far above the nuclear transition. That arrangement mixes the nuclear states with the electronic ground state.

Precision measurements on both ions feed one unified analysis. The analysis extracts both magnetic dipole moments, the bare transition energy, and the charge-radius difference. It also yields the transition matrix element governing the isomer's lifetime. No outside nuclear inputs are needed, removing a major error source. Estimated uncertainties shrink about threefold for the transition energy and twofold for the radius difference. The scheme could benchmark nuclear theory and advance the nuclear clock.
arxiv-2606-15480:
Diemert and coauthor model how much work it takes to apply quantitative confidence methods to assurance cases, in a 2026 safety engineering paper. An assurance case is a structured argument, backed by evidence, that a critical system meets its goals. Confidence methods attach numbers to how strongly the argument should be believed, but practitioners cite the extra effort as a barrier. The authors define decision complexity, the count of judgments a user must supply, and how it scales with argument size.

The model compares three methods: a Bayesian belief network approach, a Dempster-Shafer approach, and the mixed method Certus. Certus carries the highest worst-case decision count, thanks to its flexible belief propagation, yet in the average case its effort falls below the Bayesian method and to roughly half the Dempster-Shafer method. Designers can now quote scalability up front instead of leaving adopters to discover the cost.
arxiv-2606-15780:
Das and Sarkar solve coefficient problems in 2026 for the apple-like convex subclass of univalent functions. The class is defined by a subordination condition involving e to the z times the square root of one plus z. Coefficient bounds describe how large the Taylor coefficients of such functions and their inverses can be. Sharp bounds are the exact extremes, attained by specific extremal functions.

They find sharp bounds for the first three inverse logarithmic coefficients and for the difference of the second and first moduli. They bound the second-order inverse logarithmic Hankel determinant from above, characterise the generalised Fekete-Szegő functional for all real parameters, and compute sharp bounds for the third-order Hermitian-Toeplitz determinant. Every bound is proved sharp by exhibiting its extremal function, using Carathéodory functions and parametric optimisation. Such exact constants complete the picture of how inverse mappings distort this apple-shaped class.
arxiv-2606-15880:
Lin and colleagues tackle AI-generated image detection in 2026, asking whether multimodal language models can perceive low-level generator artifacts without losing semantic knowledge. Their analysis shows semantic information forms in early-to-middle layers, and fine-tuning directly for artifacts disrupts it. The conflict explains why naively trained detectors forget semantics and generalise poorly to new generators.

Their model, Deep Visual Residual MLLM, keeps early layers frozen and injects artifact signals as a residual into an intermediate layer. Fused with the semantic tokens, they propagate through later layers, which learn to combine both. The model adapts which level of forensic signal it leans on to the input. Across benchmarks including GenImage and the WildRF set, it reaches state-of-the-art detection on most, and stays robust under compression and resizing. The design offers a template for adding low-level perception to models trained for meaning.
arxiv-2606-16180:
Singh and colleagues study machine unlearning for 3D medical image segmentation in a 2026 paper driven by privacy law. Rules such as the GDPR let people demand their data be erased, including from trained models. Retraining from scratch is costly, so approximate unlearning strategies try to scrub one subject's influence.

A 3D ResNet-50 model, pretrained with Med3D, segments the MRBrainS18 dataset. Strategies based on four unlearning mechanics are judged by Dice score and error on retained versus forgotten subjects, at 20 and 50 epochs. The Noisy Label strategy gives the best overall trade-off in the reported results. After 50 epochs it cuts forget-set performance by 93 percent while keeping 84 percent accuracy on retained subjects. Other strategies forget too aggressively at higher epochs, damaging retained performance. Feature-space interventions also prove unstable at standard learning rates.
arxiv-2606-16680:
Osano revisits the origin of cosmic magnetic fields in a 2026 cosmology paper. Galaxies and clusters are threaded by magnetic fields, yet the early universe should have started with none. Some seed field must have formed first, later stretched and amplified by galactic motion. Osano compares three proposed seed mechanisms inside one kinetic theory framework.

Starting from the coupled Maxwell-Boltzmann equations, the full derivation runs through the collision terms to a generalized Ohm's law and a second-order induction equation. One mechanism uses Thomson scattering, which pushes electrons far more than protons and so drives a current. Osano isolates a new source term coupling photon density contrast with the electron-photon velocity gap, missed as a separate term before. Numerical evaluation near recombination shows it nearly doubles the scattering contribution in total effect. A rival bulk-flow mechanism can dominate only above flow limits already set by Planck data.
arxiv-2606-16780:
Sausar Karaf and colleagues present DIFF-IPPO in a 2026 robotics paper on path planning. A searching robot should not wander evenly: it should spend its sensors where the target is most likely to be. Belief maps from open-vocabulary perception, where users name targets in plain words, are messy and multi-peaked, unlike the smooth maps older planners assume.

Their pipeline pairs an open-vocabulary belief map generator with a diffusion-based planner, a generative model that drafts whole trajectories at once. Planned paths concentrate coverage over high-belief regions, earning strong normalized detection scores across several dataset scenarios. In a simulated search-and-rescue test, five drones search a square kilometre of buildings for a burning one. Batched, belief-guided trajectory generation finds the fire quickly, with first detections in a few minutes. The work shows generative planning can handle the irregular belief maps that modern semantic perception produces.
arxiv-2606-17080: Abbas Mammadov and colleagues solve linear inverse problems, recovering a sharp image from blurry measurements, by estimating the exact posterior score. The score tells a diffusion model which direction points toward likely solutions. Their exact estimation removes a common source of error, sharpening reconstructions in medical imaging and astronomy.
arxiv-2606-17180:
Luna and colleagues build a fast graph neural surrogate for underground carbon storage in a 2026 geoscience paper. Simulating how injected carbon dioxide migrates through rock is essential for safe storage, but full reservoir simulators are slow. A learned surrogate could scan scenarios quickly, if it respects the flow physics.

The benchmark is SPE11A, an industry test with sharp gas-water interfaces, strong directional transport and density-driven fingering. The formation becomes a graph: cells are nodes, edges carry flow strength plus shape attributes. Message passing is anisotropic, with geometry-based edge weights biasing flow along real transport directions. Time evolution runs in latent space through a graph-convolution LSTM with residual steps. Forecasts of gas saturation and liquid density stay competitive over long horizons, in injection and post-injection phases, and generalize to unseen layouts. Direction-aware passing, the authors argue, is what graph simulators for subsurface flow lacked.
arxiv-2606-17580:
Capozziello and Meluccio present a 2026 arXiv paper on the pre-geometric roots of the geometric trinity of gravity, the fact that general relativity can be told three ways. Curvature, torsion, and non-metricity each serve as gravity's source in one telling, with identical dynamics across all three. Pre-geometric gravity starts earlier, before any metric exists, and the authors ask whether that starting point can honestly give birth to all three tellings at once.

In the pre-geometric picture, a Yang-Mills style gauge theory with a Higgs-like field breaks its symmetry and an effective metric emerges. The authors derive the needed action forms and gauge-fixing choices in the unbroken phase for each trinity member. Emergent gravity in the broken phase then matches all three formulations, in actions and in connection gauge choices alike. The trinity gains a single common ancestor.
arxiv-2606-17680:
Wang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on EnvRL, a way to train language model agents that learns from the environment's behaviour, not just from final success or failure. Standard reinforcement learning for long tasks pays out only at the end, wasting the rich feedback inside each interaction trace. The authors argue those traces quietly teach how the world changes from step to step. An agent holding a better inner model of those changes should choose better actions throughout a task.

EnvRL adds two helper tasks beside the main reward: predicting the next state, and inferring which action caused a change. Trained jointly, these push the policy to internalise the environment's dynamics from its own rollouts. On two long-horizon benchmarks, success rates jumped markedly for the same base model over reward-only training. Gains appeared with more than one underlying learning algorithm in the tests.
arxiv-2606-17780:
Vo and Wang analyze how identical oscillators in a network can fall out of step with each other, in a 2026 paper on symmetry breaking. The system pairs two slow and fast oscillators with strong nonlinear mutual inhibition, so each one suppresses the other. Intuition says the pair should stay mirror symmetric, yet the authors show the break starts right on the symmetry axis itself.

Using geometric singular perturbation theory and a blow-up method, they trace the cause to canard dynamics at a folded node sitting on that axis. They show the fold curve meets the axis at a right angle there, that only one main maximal canard exists, and that it lies on the axis. The number of rotations around it proves to be the local feature that decides whether the rhythm stays symmetric or splits.
arxiv-2606-17980:
Wong and colleagues report the first X-ray polarization measurements of the Kes 75 supernova remnant, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Inside the remnant sits a pulsar blowing a wind nebula, and the team observed the pair twice with the IXPE telescope, in late 2024 and again in spring 2025. Polarization reveals the shape of the magnetic field that lights the nebula.

The second visit detected clear polarization of about ten percent, with an angle matching a toroidal field wrapped around the nebula's symmetry axis. The first visit gave only an upper limit, and its pulsar light curve looked changed, with an extra pulsed component halfway through the rotation that matches a two-pulse profile. Phase-resolved analysis supports a rotating vector pattern, which may explain why the averaged signal washed out in the first epoch.
arxiv-2606-18080:
Marion builds a pocket model of gradient descent in its most unruly regime, in a 2026 paper. Deep learning often trains at the edge of stability, where the sharpness of the loss hovers right at the threshold set by the learning rate. There the usual smooth-flow picture breaks down, and training oscillates while still making progress, defying classical analysis.

Edge Flow captures that behavior with just three coupled ordinary differential equations. One tracks a center that follows a modified gradient flow on a symmetrized loss. One follows the top curvature direction. The third tracks the size of the oscillation, which grows or shrinks as sharpness crosses the threshold. Stability emerges from a self-correcting feedback loop inside the system. Simulating it needs only two gradient evaluations and one curvature product per step, and experiments show it shadows real gradient descent faithfully.
arxiv-2606-18180:
Guo and colleagues turn professional Counter-Strike matches into a training ground for world models, in a 2026 dataset paper from City University of Hong Kong. Interactive world models need data where video, actions, and language align in time. Such data is scarce. Web video lacks executable actions, robot logs are costly and narrow, and simulators rarely hold real human play at scale.

Their EgoCS-400K dataset mines public professional match demos from Counter-Strike and its sequel, which preserve full human trajectories. From each demo they extract player states, view directions, movement, and key and button inputs. They also record weapon use and game events, then re-render clean first-person video from the same timelines. The result spans over four hundred thousand aligned segments for studying navigation, active perception, and action-conditioned prediction in a rich, fast, human-driven world.
arxiv-2606-18280:
Jalilian tackles a quiet flaw in spatial statistics: the map units you choose can change the answer, in a 2026 methods paper. Fixed units such as administrative borders or one-size hexagonal grids ignore where the information actually is, so dense, fine-scale phenomena get averaged away inside coarse cells. His method, IOAH3, builds the partition from the data instead, on Uber's hierarchical H3 grid.

Three stages do the work. Principal component analysis scores each cell's importance from road, point-of-interest, and building density plus terrain roughness, with population and flood hazard as auxiliary signals. A Markov random field graph cut then selects cells, rewarding importance while keeping the selection spatially coherent. Finally, high-importance regions are refined to finer H3 resolutions. The result concentrates detail where it matters over a complete coarse background, fully automated and reproducible.
arxiv-2606-18380:
Delgado, Eberhardt, and Tomašević ask why spacetime in type II string theory must admit a spin structure, a requirement usually stated as a background assumption, in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. Their answer derives the condition from the consistency of the string worldsheet itself rather than imposing it from outside.

The obstruction, they show, is a mixed global anomaly between a worldsheet symmetry and the target space background data, detected through a spin bordism group that they compute. For smooth target spaces, demanding that the anomaly vanish is exactly the condition that spacetime be spin. For orbifold spaces, the requirement becomes an equivariant spin structure instead. The authors also classify all possible theta angles of the worldsheet theory and show they match the continuous and discrete background fields a target space theory can show in string perturbation theory. A familiar rule thus becomes a derived consistency check.
arxiv-2606-18680:
Han and the team present a four-degree-of-freedom parallel leg mechanism for insect-scale robots, in a 2026 microrobotics paper. Small legged robots promise access to tight, risky spaces, for search and rescue or scouting. But tiny actuators are weak. Most small robots give up leg degrees of freedom to stay light, and with them mobility and posture control. Serial legs with joint-mounted actuators swing heavy limbs.

Inspired by insect locomotion, the design pairs two spherical five-bar linkages inside a parallel four-bar architecture. A concentric layout simplifies the kinematic solution, and all actuators mount on the body, so moving parts stay light. The full system weighs under nineteen grams. It delivers about half a newton at the foot, and reaches a workspace over twenty-two thousand cubic millimeters. Experiments showed strong motion flexibility, supporting parallel micro-legs as a route to agile microrobots.
arxiv-2606-18880:
Roy and colleagues study Engel word maps on two-by-two matrix groups over local rings in 2026. A word map plugs group elements into a fixed word, here built from repeated commutators. The question is surjectivity, whether every group element arises as an output. Work of this kind is well developed for finite simple groups, but far less so for groups over local rings.

Under mild conditions on the residue field size, the authors show all lifts of non-scalar elements lie in the image of the Engel map on the special linear group. For large enough fields, that image is thus very broad. They also prove all Engel maps are surjective on the projective group over a length-two ring. The results extend word-map theory from finite fields to richer local settings used in number theory.
arxiv-2606-19080:
Peivand and colleagues propose a Byzantine-resilient federated learning framework for interconnected microgrids in 2026. As distribution networks go digital, linked microgrid clusters face stealthy false data injection attacks. Such attacks slip past bad-data detectors and spread through tie lines and shared learning channels. Each microgrid runs a local actor-critic agent. Its policy splits into a shared federated encoder and a private action head, so no site reveals its device layout or capacities.

Actions perturb line reactances, redirect battery output, reshape exchanges between grids, and can trigger islanding to cut a grid loose. A two-stage aggregation rule uses trimmed-mean filtering plus reward-weighted updates to resist Byzantine clients. A detection-quality score also penalizes clients that raise false alarms. Simulations on four linked microgrids built from standard test systems show the method mitigates coordinated attacks well. It contains cascading disruption through adaptive isolation.
arxiv-2606-19180:
Joshi and colleagues track quantum magic through a wormhole-inspired teleportation protocol in 2026. Magic, formally non-stabilizerness, is the resource that lifts quantum circuits beyond classically simulable stabilizer behavior. The protocol runs in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model through scrambling, message insertion, left-right coupling, and extraction stages. The team measures magic with a Rényi entropy score at each stage and compares it with teleportation fidelity.

In the low-temperature gravitational regime, fidelity rises together with magic from early times. In the high-temperature peaked-size regime, magic saturates near the Haar-typical value before teleportation begins. A chaotic model that makes near-maximal magic yet fails to teleport, and a magic-free Clifford scrambler that also fails, give sharp contrasts. Structured redistribution of magic, not its amount, underlies successful traversal. The coupling first suppresses magic, then channels it toward the signal. Magic also dips at the fidelity peak.
arxiv-2606-19480:
Zheng Zhang releases sft-wick in 2026, an open Python package for stochastic field theory, the study of fields driven by random noise. Cast as a path integral, the theory expands into Feynman diagrams whose count grows factorially. Fields may have many components, tensor couplings, and noise with arbitrary correlation patterns.

Given an action and a target quantity, sft-wick lists each distinct diagram shape once. It works out multiplicities, coupling sums, signs, and causal limits for every entry in the table. Spatial shapes are listed before component indices are routed, avoiding a slow pairing-by-pairing expansion. Rules such as the Itô prescription and the ban on causal response loops are enforced during the search. Integrals are then computed numerically from user-supplied response and noise functions. Checks against direct Langevin simulation agree within the noise of the simulation itself.
arxiv-2606-19680:
Hao Wang and seven colleagues predict eye disease courses from irregular follow-up scans in 2026. Eye prognosis work tracks how a disease will unfold over visits. Follow-up sequences arrive sparse, unevenly spaced, and incomplete.

Neural controlled equations model such data in smooth time, but two flaws persist. Smooth latent dynamics miss abrupt shifts from treatment, recurrence, or long gaps. Long integrations also pile up error, blurring class boundaries. Their framework, ImProNCDE, adds Residual Impulse Calibration at each visit. Corrections fire when observations stray from smooth predictions, resetting the latent state. A Prototype-guided Trajectory Stabilizer pulls latent paths toward learnable class prototypes. Tests on private and public datasets totalling over 1,206 samples beat leading sequence models. Steadier long-range forecasts could guide visit timing and care choices, since each scan a patient skips or takes too late can hide a turn for the worse.
arxiv-2606-19780:
Jeonghwan Ahn, Seoung-Hun Kang, and Jaron Krogel track how arsenic layers bond as stacks thicken, in a 2026 study. Arsenene is a layered form of arsenic with buckled honeycomb sheets. Layer coupling is often assumed to carry from two layers to the bulk, an assumption that can fail.

Diffusion quantum Monte Carlo and density functional theory combine to test that assumption. Bulk gray arsenic packs compactly, the Monte Carlo runs show. Few-layer stacks keep far wider layer gaps despite sharing the same stacking registry. Thickness and coordination, not registry alone, set the bonding regime. One functional, SCAN plus rVV10, best matches the Monte Carlo spacings and stacking energies. Benchmarked calculations then predict a stacking shift as layers grow. The shift coincides with a band-gap collapse driven by stronger coupling between arsenic orbitals across layers.
arxiv-2606-19880:
Guillaume Delord gives a fresh proof of the Rapid Decay property for free groups in 2026. Rapid Decay bounds how fast convolution operators can grow with word length. Haagerup's inequality is its classic form for free groups.

Delord bounds operators tied to the quasi-regular representation on the group's Gromov boundary. The bounds hold across Lp spaces for a range of exponents. At exponent two they recover Haagerup's inequality exactly. Riesz-Thorin interpolation then carries the endpoint bounds across the scale. The free group's Rapid Decay follows as a corollary of that interpolation route. A property once proven by direct estimation gains a cleaner functional-analytic proof. New proofs of old landmarks often unlock generalisations the first route hid.
arxiv-2606-19980:
Wenli Xiao and sixteen colleagues present ENPIRE in 2026, a harness that lets coding agents improve real robot policies on their own. Dexterous manipulation research normally leans on constant human supervision and hand engineering. ENPIRE closes a physical loop instead: reset the scene, run the policy, verify the outcome, then refine. Four modules handle environment reset and checking, policy improvement, rollouts on one or many robots, and evolution of code and infrastructure by the agents.

Frontier coding agents using the loop reach ninety-nine percent success on hard tasks such as PushT, sorting pins into a box, and cutting a zip tie. New efficiency metrics track robot and token use across a fleet. Heuristic, cloning, and reinforcement regimes all plug into the same loop. Autonomous robotics research gains a working template.
arxiv-2606-20080:
Pai Peng and twelve colleagues study how a layered material called an InSb/CdTe heterostructure can shift terahertz waves to higher frequencies. Their 2026 paper reports the first strong second-harmonic generation in this material under an in-plane magnetic field. It also reports third-harmonic output rivaling Dirac materials such as graphene. Small, efficient terahertz sources are wanted for future wireless links, imaging, and sensing, so new routes to frequency conversion draw wide interest.

Measurements and theory show the second harmonic comes mainly from an orbital-Zeeman correction, a magnetic tweak to how electrons drift. The third harmonic follows Drude-like behavior tied to free carriers. Because the effect rests on high carrier mobility rather than one exotic compound, the same approach should work in other fast materials. The work gives device designers a general recipe for compact terahertz multipliers.
arxiv-2606-20480:
Sergios Agapiou, Ismaël Castillo, and Paul Egels show how heavier prior tails buy adaptation in Bayesian nonparametric inference. Their 2026 paper studies posterior contraction when function coefficients over a basis or dictionary carry p-exponential priors, from Laplace tails to heavier ones.

Contraction rates improve as p decreases, and full adaptation to smoothness, up to logarithmic factors, arrives in an appropriate small-p regime. Applications cover series priors in white noise regression and shallow ReLU networks in random design regression. Overparametrized shallow ReLU networks adapt to any regularity between 0 and 2. A simulation study supports the theory.
arxiv-2606-20680:
Ajan Ahmed and Masudul Imtiaz argue in 2026 that biometric verification is often reported with the wrong summary score. Deployed systems work under a strict false match budget. Only a narrow low-error slice of scores is ever used. A standard asks for error rates at stated operating points, tradeoff curves, and uncertainty intervals. In practice, many papers report one summary score.

Ahmed and Imtiaz show why that habit misleads. A full curve average weights score ranges where the system never operates. Low false-match behavior can stay hidden. Even the ranking of two systems can reverse. They revisit the guideline and test it against seven pretrained matchers across four modalities, such as face and fingerprint data. Reporting at the real operating point would give a clearer view of risk.
arxiv-2606-20780:
Takumi Araki and nineteen colleagues present a white paper in 2026 for a deep-ocean neutrino experiment designed to measure Earth's mantle. The detector would sense geoneutrinos from uranium and thorium decay inside Earth. Those signals constrain how much heat Earth produces from radioactivity. They also reveal chemical makeup. No active or planned experiment mirrors this mobile deep-ocean design, according to the authors.

Ocean placement should cut crustal background by fifty to one hundred times, compared with similar land detectors. Direct mantle measurements then become possible. Mobility also allows views from several positions, mapping how heat-producing elements vary in space. The paper covers concept, prototype design, projected costs, and science goals. Recent hardware prototyping is reported. If built, the experiment could join physics and geoscience data to give a clearer picture of Earth's deep interior and heat budget.
arxiv-2606-20980:
Adrian Cespedes and five colleagues benchmark humans and vision-language models in 2026 for autonomous driving judgments in Lima and New York City. Self-driving systems are expanding into new countries. Their vision models act as a cognitive backbone for action. Generalization to edge cases in new geographies is an open question. Both cities are hard driving settings where no self-driving company operates.

Dashcam footage from both cities is shown to local and foreign human drivers and to models. Questions span factual, rating, counterfactual, and reasoning categories. Humans answer similarly regardless of home city. Humans and models diverge in their responses. Divergence is modulated by question type. To their surprise, no strong geography effect appears for humans. Benchmarks rooted in real local footage can reveal where model judgment departs from broadly shared human judgment about risky road scenes.
arxiv-2606-21180:
Taiki Kawamuro and five colleagues report the first XRISM observation in 2026 of the low-mass active galaxy NGC 4395, with time-resolved iron line spectroscopy. The galaxy hosts a black hole of only tens of thousands of solar masses, in a nearby dwarf galaxy. A simultaneous NuSTAR observation complements the XRISM data. The continuum is fit jointly while excluding the iron band, setting a clean baseline.

Against that baseline, the average spectrum shows a narrow neutral iron core with a redward wing. A relativistically broadened iron component reproduces the wing. Time-resolved spectra over the long observation vary significantly. Changes in the inner radius of the emitting region can explain the evolution. A possible periodic modulation hints at precession of a tilted inner flow. Watching an inner disk change in real time tests accretion physics at the smallest supermassive black hole scales.
arxiv-2606-21280:
Simon Goodwin, Lewis Topley, and Matthew Westaway study minimal modules in 2026, the smallest representations of reduced enveloping algebras attached to Lie algebras in positive characteristic. These algebras govern representation theory for reductive algebraic groups, and their minimal modules have the least dimension the theory allows. The authors use modular finite W-algebras, a tool built for exactly this terrain, to ask where minimal modules come from.

For p-characters lying in a unique sheet, they show a clean pattern. In classical types and most exceptional types, every minimal module is parabolically induced, built up from a Levi subalgebra and a rigid p-character. They prove the same for minimal modules fixed under twisting by the component group. The results tie the smallest representations to rigid building blocks, sharpening the structure theory of modular representations.
arxiv-2606-21580:
Rodrigo Dourado and four colleagues show in 2026 that quantum capacitance measurements can grade Majorana devices, not just read them out. Majorana bound states are the building blocks of proposed topological qubits, prized because information stored in their shared fermion parity resists local noise. Quantum capacitance, probed with an auxiliary quantum dot sensor, was already known to read out that parity.

The authors show the same measurements also reveal two quality figures at once: the ground-state energy splitting and the overlap between the Majorana states. Positions and heights of capacitance peaks in the even and odd parity sectors give both numbers through analytic formulas from a low-energy model. A microscopic model of dot-based Kitaev chains confirms the formulas, establishing capacitance as an optimization tool that leaves parity untouched.
arxiv-2606-21680:
Martin G. Zizler, Malte Prieß, and Christoph P. Neumann examine what it really takes to run one workload across AWS and Alibaba Cloud in 2026. Multi-cloud strategies promise agility, resilience, and freedom from vendor lock-in, but the global market leader and China's top provider differ in architecture, services, and policy in ways that complicate migration.

Using provider-native and open-source infrastructure-as-code tools, they run an exploratory case study migrating Internet of Things workloads between the two clouds. The comparison surfaces concrete technical trade-offs, feature gaps in managed services, and the replatforming workarounds they demand. Their best practices for secure multi-cloud deployment target multinational firms that must bridge Western and Chinese cloud ecosystems, a pairing the existing literature barely covers.
arxiv-2606-21780:
Chacón and Sellers prove new congruences in 2026 for overcubic partition tuples, counting functions from number theory that enumerate special ways of splitting integers into parts. Earlier authors had established divisibility patterns for small tuple sizes, case by case. This paper revisits those results with generating functions, the algebraic tools that package counting sequences into power series, and looks for the pattern behind them.

The generating function approach reproves several known results and yields multiple infinite families of congruences that had not appeared in print. A new viewpoint explains why these counting functions are so often divisible by powers of two. Other families involve odd moduli: for instance, one family shows the counts at a certain arithmetic progression of weights are always divisible by eleven. Another family, indexed by two free parameters, gives divisibility by three. The work turns scattered small cases into general theorems.
arxiv-2606-22080:
Kim and colleagues optimize, in 2026, the pump conditions of parametric amplifiers used to read out superconducting qubits. These low-noise amplifiers form the first stage of most readout chains, and their performance depends sensitively on how the pump is set. In multiplexed readout, several qubits share one chain, so the right target is not average performance but the total time the whole measurement takes.

Their strategy chooses the pump to maximize the signal-to-noise improvement at the readout frequency of the limiting qubit, the one needing the longest readout to hit its target signal quality. Minimizing that bottleneck minimizes the total multiplexed readout time. The team demonstrated the calibration experimentally on a five-qubit multiplexed chain with a traveling-wave amplifier. Against a strategy optimizing average improvement across all qubits, their choice cut total readout time by 320 nanoseconds, with no qubit's target signal quality degraded.
arxiv-2606-22380:
Zhenjie Li reports an eight-loop computation in planar N=4 super-Yang-Mills theory in this 2026 paper, written as a conference talk. The theory is a highly symmetric quantum field theory used as a testing ground for scattering amplitude methods. Its simplest nontrivial process, six-gluon scattering, is already known to eight loops through a duality with a three-point form factor, a related quantity.

Li describes the parallel eight-loop computation for a different operator built from three scalar fields. The result lives in the same restricted space of polylogarithms as the earlier form factor. The paper also reports patterns that hold at every loop order in sequences of coefficients inside the symbols of these results. It further treats the leading discontinuity, a specific singular part, of the new form factor. Such patterns help check results at loop orders beyond direct calculation.
arxiv-2606-22680:
F. Blaschke, T. Romanczukiewicz, K. Slawinska, and A. Wereszczynski offer a unified view of oscillons in this 2026 paper. Oscillons are long-lived, localized lumps of a field that oscillate in place instead of dispersing. Where they come from, in the zoo of a theory's modes, was not cleanly understood.

The authors show that an oscillon can be understood as a localized discrete resonant mode, a mode that is not normalizable in the usual sense. In the vacuum, the oscillon arises from the threshold mode at the edge of the continuous spectrum, which the nonlinearity traps into a lump. Following the same idea, they find wobblerons, excitations of kinks that bind an oscillon to a kink. They also show an oscillon can come from an antibound mode, a discrete positive-energy mode likewise not normalizable. One mechanism thus explains oscillons in several settings.
arxiv-2606-22780:
Ahnaf Atef Choudhury and three colleagues predict mental health problems among people who use drugs, in this 2026 paper. Early detection is hard in many regions. Past studies often handled rare outcome classes poorly, tuned their models weakly, and gave predictions that clinicians could not inspect or trust.

Feature selection mixes principal component analysis with information gain, shrinking many categorical fields. A generative adversarial network then creates extra examples of rare classes, so the training set is less lopsided. The classifier is XGBoost, tuned by the dragonfly algorithm, a swarm-based search method. It reached about ninety-four percent accuracy, with a weighted F1 score nearly as high, beating the baselines tried. Sleep quality, physical health, and emotional control were the strongest signals, while demographic factors mattered little. SHAP values explain each prediction in plain terms.
arxiv-2606-23180:
Jan Dreier and Szymon Toruńczyk prove a rank-preserving locality theorem in a 2026 logic paper. Locality theorems say that a statement in first-order logic depends only on small neighborhoods around the points it mentions. Rank-preserving versions keep the logical complexity of the statement unchanged during that reduction. Gaifman proved the classic locality result, and later authors added a rank-preserving one. This paper proves the theorem for a variant of first-order logic, syntactic in form, built around distance. The variant admits a weak form of scatter sentences, statements about many far-apart witnesses.

Dreier and Toruńczyk show those weak scatter sentences can be evaluated faster than the usual ones. That speed matters for their target application. The theorem feeds into the study of graphs of bounded merge-width, a recent measure of graph complexity. Efficient evaluation there depends on exactly this kind of locality control.
arxiv-2606-23380:
Carolin Ifländer and colleagues argue that AI safety is missing the emotional dimension in a 2026 paper. Safety research has focused on knowledge harms like misinformation and bias, plus physical reliability. Harms arising from how systems engage human emotional life stayed fragmented and undertheorized. The authors propose affective safety as one unified class of concerns. It rests on the simple fact that humans are affective beings. Their taxonomy sorts the harms into recurring types. These include self-alienation, fairness and bias harms, and relational harms.

Ifländer and colleagues show the same harm types recur across very different system types. That recurrence, they argue, reflects structural traits of how AI engages emotion, not isolated product flaws. Their survey finds current frameworks handle affective safety narrowly or not at all. They close with the technical and regulatory challenges tied to cumulative, relational effects.
arxiv-2606-23480:
Jay Kueny and colleagues image the debris disk around the star HR 4796A in visible light in a 2026 astronomy paper. Debris disks are rings of dust left around mature stars. The team used MagAO-X, an extreme adaptive optics instrument on the Magellan telescopes, across observing runs from 2023 to 2025. They detected the disk with high signal-to-noise in four optical bands. A star-hopping technique captured the whole disk, including the dramatic forward-scattering brightening along its minor axis. The images then went through a battery of modeling techniques to pin down the disk's geometry and photometry.

Kueny and colleagues modeled the scattering phase function, how dust brightness varies with scattering angle, using Legendre polynomial basis functions. To fight self-subtraction artifacts from angular differential imaging, they built a forward-modeling pipeline that generates pixel-level disk models for direct comparison with the data.
arxiv-2606-23580:
Yamanaka reviews how flavor-diagonal CP violation at the hadron level feeds into precision experiments hunting new physics, in a 2026 particle physics contribution. CP violation means matter and antimatter behaving differently under combined charge and mirror symmetries. It is one ingredient needed to explain why the universe holds more matter than antimatter. Flavor-diagonal means the effect appears without particles changing type, which makes it subtle but widely testable.

The review explains why such violation matters for searches beyond the standard model of particle physics. It then surveys progress in quantifying the hadron-level interactions that produce observable effects. Those effects include electric dipole moments of atoms, nuclei, and nucleons, time-violating neutron optics signals, and angular patterns in beta decay. A final section covers one recent attempt on the strong CP problem, a related fine-tuning puzzle, that adds no extra fields or interactions.
arxiv-2606-23780:
Sarin tests how the spread of radioactive nickel inside an exploding star distorts what astronomers infer from its light curve, in a 2026 paper on supernova physics. Standard fits treat the ejecta as one uniform zone powered by radioactive decay. Real explosions mix their nickel 56 outward to varying degrees. Moving nickel outward thins the material above it, so light escapes faster. Sarin models the ejecta as multiple shells instead.

The multi shell calculations show outward mixing produces faster, brighter rises at fixed nickel mass, ejecta mass, and energy. A fast bright rise is therefore not proof of low ejecta mass or of extra engine power, since mixed and engine driven curves overlap heavily. One zone fits to mixed curves look good yet return biased masses. For collapsars enriched with rapid neutron capture material, the signature is not always extra infrared light. It depends on placement and viewing angle.
arxiv-2606-23880:
Fesanghary and Havaldar prune false causal links out of large time series datasets with a gated refinement step, in a 2026 paper on causal discovery. Finding which variables truly drive which others is central to climate science, neuroscience, and gene regulation. Constraint based methods are rigorous but their nonlinear tests become infeasible at scale. Score based methods need arbitrary thresholds to binarize their scores. GRACE starts from a fast linear test skeleton that keeps almost all true edges, false positives included.

Each candidate edge gets its own learnable gate, pushed toward fully open or fully closed by a sparsity penalty. Useful edges survive because they improve prediction. On synthetic networks up to one hundred variables, GRACE sharply improves accuracy over its base method at a fraction of the cost of full nonlinear testing. On Elbe River data it recovered nine of eleven causal edges.
arxiv-2606-24080:
Pulikodan, Desai, and Ghosh look for a cheaper way to adapt speech recognition to languages with little transcribed data. Writing out speech by hand is slow and costly, which leaves thousands of languages poorly served by automatic speech recognition. Their 2026 idea inserts an extra training stage between general pretraining and final fine-tuning, one that needs no transcripts at all and uses pictures instead.

Speech clips from the Vaani dataset were collected using images as prompts, so each recording naturally pairs with a picture. The team aligns sound representations from a pretrained FastConformer audio encoder with image representations from vision encoders, nudging the audio model toward the paired meanings. After this alignment stage, fine-tuned models consistently recognise speech better than models fine-tuned directly. The result suggests audio-image alignment is a practical, transcript-free adaptation step for low-resource languages.
arxiv-2606-24180:
Khaled, Abdulkadir, and Eltahir survey a decade of deep learning for completing three-dimensional medical scenes. Scanners capture only part of an anatomy, and algorithms must infer the rest. Their systematic review spans 2016 to 2026. It begins with voxel-based semantic completion in the SSCNet era. It ends with generative diffusion priors married to real-time Gaussian splatting. Scene completion also serves navigation and augmented reality, but the review centres on medical use.

Representation paradigms structure the story. Voxel grids give way to point-based learning, implicit neural fields, transformer networks, and diffusion models. Rendering-aware Gaussian primitives come last. Khaled's team builds a taxonomy of the decade's contributions, and weighs what each paradigm bought and cost. Open challenges are catalogued alongside the progress. A closing research agenda points to the directions the authors judge most promising for clinical-grade completion: fast, faithful, and honest about uncertainty.
arxiv-2606-24280:
Deng, Pezzi, Lin, and Onorato revisit the famous Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou recurrence, in a chain whose atoms alternate between two masses. In the original single-mass chain, energy placed in one vibration mode returns instead of spreading evenly, defying expectations of quick thermalisation. The diatomic version, studied in 2026 with a cubic anharmonic potential, shows two distinct kinds of recurrence.

One kind is the classic recurrence. Its period scales with nonlinear strength, much as in the monatomic chain. The second kind is new to the diatomic system. Energy recurs through resonant interaction between modes from the acoustic and optical branches. The team proves an optical-acoustical-acoustical three-mode resonance exists. A reduced Fourier-space model reproduces the same behaviour. Numerical checks on the diatomic Toda lattice and a granular chain show the recurrence survives both. In the continuous limit it reduces to a known integrable system.
arxiv-2606-24580:
Vivek, Sinha, and Sinha study quantum droplets, self bound liquid like drops of ultracold atoms, inside an optical lattice wired to a leaky cavity. A dilute Bose gas and its droplet phase sit in a one-dimensional lattice, while a dissipative cavity mode mediates long range interactions. A classical field approach determines the stationary states and collective excitations of this setup in 2026.

Beyond the usual Bogoliubov sound modes, a polariton like gapped excitation appears. Its frequency softens as the density ordering transition approaches. Its relaxation time diverges at the critical point, a fingerprint of the transition's non equilibrium character. Shaking the cavity field probes the mode dynamically, driving spatio temporal oscillations of both condensate and droplet states. The droplet regime hosts bound modes and solitonic states, including kink like condensates and double droplets. Their strength after sudden quenches is tested, finding breakdowns beyond critical interaction strengths.
arxiv-2606-24880:
Lena Becker and Holger Hermanns check stability of Markov jump linear systems through the lens of temporal logic model checking. Such systems switch randomly among linear modes, driven by an underlying Markov chain. Standard stability notions describe the long term behaviour of mean and mean square values. Those averages can mislead when only some starting states matter. Model checking reasons about specified sets of initial states directly. The authors therefore formalise probabilistic computation tree logic, PCTL, over these systems.

On that base they extend the logic to express moment based stability properties relative to a chosen set of initial states. A full decision procedure for the base logic eludes them, and they say so plainly. The extensions, though, can be handled with linear algebraic techniques, modulo some technical subtleties. Its contribution is a specification language for stability questions that classical moment criteria phrase awkwardly.
arxiv-2606-24980:
Michal Podstawski studies whether small language models can execute graph algorithms step by step without drifting off course. The setting is closed loop: the model repeatedly picks each next action from the current graph and its algorithmic state. Each choice changes what it sees next, so small errors can compound. His framework covers several classical graph procedures and multiple synthetic graph families, with disjoint training, validation, and test data. Both local decision quality and global behaviour are measured.

Metrics include exact rollout accuracy, constraint checks, partial credit, prefix survival, and intervention probes. Adaptation produces dependable policies for structural procedures like traversal and colouring. Weighted algorithms behave differently: they stay far more sensitive to error build up. Podstawski's broader point is about method. Strong next step prediction does not guarantee reliable solo running. Models should be judged on complete closed loop rollouts, not isolated decisions.
arxiv-2606-25280:
Simulating flocks, crowds, and traffic means tuning many interacting numbers, and changing one behaviour often disturbs another. Craig Reynolds presents EvoFlock in 2026, an automatic tuning method that flips the task around. Instead of hand adjusting a flocking model, the user states the desired group behaviour as a scoring function. A genetic algorithm then evolves the model's parameters until the simulated flock scores well, rewarding good spacing, a target speed, and obstacle avoidance.

One surprise emerged from the evolved solutions. The striking alignment of real bird flocks, where neighbours match direction, appeared on its own once proper spacing was maintained. Reynolds frames the method as inverse design for multi agent motion generally, covering herds, schools, and vehicle flows as well as birds. Code and data are released openly alongside the work.
arxiv-2606-25380:
Safety tuning for language models is deepest in English, leaving other languages exposed to toxic output and missed abuse. Soham Dan, Himanshu Beniwal, and Thomas Hartvigsen survey the multilingual problem in 2026. They list attack routes that exploit language choice itself, from translation pivots and code switching to spelling variation and later fine tuning. Task forms, detection methods, and fixes are then organised into one map of the field.

Detection options range from cross lingual models and translation pipelines to probes that read the model's inner states. Mitigation spans data filtering, preference tuning, steering during generation, and editing those inner states. Persistent troubles include thin coverage of low resource languages, harm definitions that shift across cultures, and fragmented evaluation. The survey also warns that aggressive detoxification can silence legitimate dialect and identity related speech.
arxiv-2606-25780:
Two fluid streams collide head on in a T shaped channel and must mix in the stem. Chemical engineers love the geometry. Mohammad Mehdi Zamani Asl and Marc Avila, at the University of Bremen, simulate its fully turbulent regime directly in 2026. Reynolds numbers reach two thousand. The mixing scalar diffuses as fast as momentum. The mixer's transitional regime is well mapped. Its turbulence was not. Their analysis follows the flow down the channel. The journey splits into two stages, then relaxes toward ordinary duct flow.

A jet like stream forms near the junction. It behaves almost self similarly, like a transitional planar jet. Downstream a decay region takes over. There, turbulent energy, dissipation, and scalar variance all fall by power laws. The velocity exponents match decaying turbulence in bounded domains. The scalar's exponent matches unbounded turbulence instead. The authors trace that mismatch to mixing spreading outward from the channel centre.
arxiv-2606-25980: This paper builds FoleySet, a multi-level human-annotated Foley sound dataset. The building builds. Their dataset is multi-level human-annotated. The building is Foley sound. It is audio. FoleySet foleys. The FoleySet is human-annotated. The sound dataset is multi-level.
arxiv-2606-26080:
Changdae Oh and colleagues find a free reward signal hiding inside standard agent training. Process reward models grade each step an agent takes. Building them for long, irreversible tasks is brutally hard. Human labels and Monte Carlo estimates both fail at scale. Their insight starts from reinforcement learning post-training itself. A trained policy already differs from its reference policy in informative ways.

Progress advantage names the recovered signal. The log-probability ratio between the trained and reference policies equals the optimal advantage function. That equality holds under a general stochastic decision model. No annotation is needed, and the signal works across domains. Three applications test it: test-time scaling, uncertainty checks, and failure attribution. Five benchmarks and four model families supply the evidence. The byproduct signal beats confidence-based baselines everywhere. It even beats dedicated trained reward models, despite needing no task-specific training at all.
arxiv-2606-26280:
Ahmed Rakin Kamal follows the fate of Ramond-Ramond fluxes as a circle shrinks out of existence in string theory. Type 0A string theory carries a doubled Ramond-Ramond sector, pictured in a proposed M-theory dual as two circles joined at a point. Tachyon condensation shrinks one circle, landing the theory at type IIA. Kamal derives the balance condition a tachyon stationary point must satisfy between the two branches. A branch-odd fluctuation emerges as the tachyon's source near a symmetric background.

Collapsing branches make their fluxes homeless. An unscreened source on the shrinking circle pays a field-energy cost that blows up as the circle vanishes. Infrared screening offers one escape, through a Stückelberg-style mechanism for the relative field. Discharge is another, when a thin wall makes dumping the charge energetically favourable. Standard brane couplings identify the carrier that such a discharge would use.
arxiv-2606-26580:
Yongjun Yoo builds a framework for synthesising electrocardiograms, the electrical traces of heartbeats known as ECGs. Synthetic traces help develop and stress-test heart algorithms. They must preserve believable activation, recovery, and waveform shape. Yoo's framework models the heart as a graph and generates signals with two back ends. One uses a fast wavefront method, the other a richer reaction model.

A certificate guards quality. The activation step is written as a fixed-point problem, and its leftover error measures consistency directly. Candidate traces then pass a two-stage diagnostics pipeline before acceptance. The reaction back end matched the fast back end's activation times to near a millisecond. Recovery tests showed internal gradients set the main T-wave shape. In final curation, the reaction back end accepted more samples and covered more waveform variety than the fast one.
arxiv-2606-26680:
Henning Fernau, Benedek Nagy, R. Jennifer Rose, Robinson Thamburaj, and D. Gnanaraj Thomas introduce two-head returning finite automata for picture languages. A picture language is a set of rectangular symbol arrays, like tiny images. A returning automaton rescans its input repeatedly. This family has two reading heads moving in opposite directions across the array.

The authors map where this family sits among known language classes. Its languages are incomparable with those of context-free matrix grammars, meaning neither family contains the other. They form a proper subset of the languages of returning pushdown automata, which have extra memory. A constrained variant forces both heads to step in synchrony. Its class sits strictly between ordinary returning automata and the two-head family. Closure properties for both families are also established.
arxiv-2606-26880:
Xiao Jia tests whether language model signals predict brain activity during natural story understanding. A model's internal features sum up a text or speech stream in rich detail. Those features can serve as predictors in models of brain responses. Jia analysed data from three public collections covering implanted probes, scalp sensors, and story listening.

Eight frozen language models supplied the features. Careful controls matched timing, nuisance signals, and model capacity. Positive prediction beyond low-level baselines was widespread. A stricter controlled criterion was met by a subset of cases, and removing model features changed scores in most of them. Advantages at the individual participant level were localised, not uniform. The author cautions that full strong claims need joint future data. The features clearly annotate brain activity, with bounded meaning.
arxiv-2606-26980:
Kenrick So, Karim Barigou, and Jens Robben forecast climate-driven deaths with deep learning on top of a classic mortality model. Heat and cold extremes now drive sudden mortality spikes that traditional models miss. Their framework starts with a Lee-Carter baseline, the standard actuarial model capturing long-run trends and seasons by region. Two neural networks then model the excess deaths that weather causes.

One network reads each region alone through convolutional filters. The other treats regions as a graph, letting climate impacts propagate across space. Both extend to quantile forecasts, giving ranges rather than single numbers. French regional data across three decades supplied the test. Both designs beat the baseline and a recent rival across all regions, cutting squared error by roughly a quarter against the rival.
arxiv-2606-27080:
Cui and colleagues present AtgBuilder, a tool that maps how screens connect inside Android apps. Each screen, called an activity, is a visual container where users tap and swipe. An activity transition graph records which screens can lead to which, guiding testing and exploration tools. Static code analysis can invent impossible jumps and miss real ones. AtgBuilder treats map building as seed-supervised link prediction, learning likely links from a few known ones in 2026 tests.

Language models first summarise each screen's layout into a short plain account of its function. Widget triggers, the exact controls causing each jump, are stored as edge attributes rather than blurred into screen features. On a ninety-eight-app benchmark with hand-checked maps, scores beat prior best methods by wide margins. Feeding its maps to three exploration tools also raised screen and transition coverage.
arxiv-2606-27180:
Müller and Kudenko automate a safe form of reward coaching for learning agents. Shaping adds guidance, but naive shaping can teach cheating, called reward hacking. Potential-based shaping is the safe kind, provably keeping the best policies unchanged. It needs a hand-built potential function, a score for how promising each state looks. Their framework learns that function from a vision language model instead, in a method published in 2026.

A small, cheap vision language model ranks pairs of scene images by promise. Preferences train the potential function, which then shapes rewards during learning. Small models label less accurately, yet the noisy guidance still speeds learning in tests. Meta-World and Franka Kitchen robot benchmarks supply the evidence. Learning efficiency improves and resistance to reward hacking holds. Accuracy of the preference labels tracks how large the gains are, giving users a clear quality dial.
arxiv-2606-27280:
Sato presents a patch descriptor search that returns provably exact nearest neighbours while checking only a sliver of the database. Image patches are matched by descriptor vectors, and exhaustive search over every vector is slow. Approximate indexes run faster but can return different answers across runs. Hierarchical Normalization splits each feature vector into a major part and a minor part with prescribed sizes. The minor part's contribution is bounded, giving a safe upper bound on full similarity, in a retrieval paper published in 2026.

Search scans the cheap major part for all entries, then fully scores only entries that cannot be pruned. A layout tuned for processor caches adds practical speed. Speed-ups pass thirteenfold on one benchmark split, with under half a percent of entries needing full scoring in the reported setting. The recommended gentler setting still prunes nearly everything while barely moving error rates.
arxiv-2606-27380:
Liang leads a survey of automated presentation coaching, a field scattered across speech technology subareas. Systems that coach talks draw on pronunciation training, prosody modelling, and speech synthesis, yet no earlier work compared them systematically. The survey sorts systems into speech tutors, fluency and prosody coaches, multimodal trainers, and question-and-answer practice tools. A five-dimensional taxonomy structures the comparison, covering segmental pronunciation, word stress, broader prosody, pacing, and faithfulness of content in this survey paper from 2026.

Mapping each system onto the taxonomy exposes coverage gaps that single-system papers hide. Core methods receive their own review, from text-to-speech exemplars to diagnostics for pronunciation, prosody, and fluency. Three open challenges stand out: too few annotated presentation corpora, feedback that stays fair across speakers' first-language accents, and diagnostics fast enough for live rehearsal.
arxiv-2606-27480:
Dattathri leads a team showing that self-interacting dark matter helps disk galaxies grow stellar bars sooner and stronger. Bars exchange angular momentum with the dark halo around them, so their growth probes dark matter's nature. Idealised high-resolution simulations, backed by kinetic-theory calculations, compare self-interacting halos against standard collisionless ones. In the 2026 astrophysics paper, bars in the self-interacting runs form earlier and reach larger amplitudes, even for modest interaction strengths.

Disks that stay bar-free under standard dark matter, including hot and dark-dominated ones, develop strong bars when self-interaction is on. The cause is broadened bar-halo resonances, which enhance angular momentum transfer from disk to halo, and not the halo core formation once suspected. Late-time core collapse can later weaken or dissolve a bar by raising central density.
arxiv-2606-27580:
Arnav Raj tackles a timing problem in reinforcement learning from human feedback. That method trains chatbots using judgements of answer quality. In production systems, the scores often arrive late. Code checkers may answer several training steps after the text was produced.

Raj proposes Retroactive Advantage Correction, or RAC. Each late result waits in a queue. A weighting curve ages it while it waits. The method then folds it into the next training step as a clipped correction. Raj proves the total correction stays exactly unbiased when the curve returns all of its weight. Otherwise the bias grows in proportion to the missing share. On a small tabular test problem, the best setting cut the bias by a factor of nearly forty-eight. RAC beat a wait-for-the-scores strategy at lower computing cost. It plugs into standard training tools with a two-line change.
arxiv-2606-27780:
World models plan by rolling learned dynamics forward. Many real environments are graphs, not vectors or images. Agents, tools, routes, and dependencies form the nodes and links. Errors may stay local or spread through the graph. Xinyuan Song and Zekun Cai study this long-horizon rollout error in 2026. Their framework covers graph world models with fixed edges and with predicted, dynamic edges.

Graph-valued error bounds are derived. They separate topology-caused amplification from model-caused amplification. A joint node-edge operator handles dynamic-edge rollouts. Guided by the analysis, the authors propose Error-Aware GWM. It combines spectral regularisation, rollout consistency, and critical-node weighting. Across synthetic topologies and agent-graph testbeds, error and planning regret grow as the horizon lengthens. Dynamic-edge training proves necessary when structure evolves. Error-Aware GWM prevents long-horizon divergence while keeping prediction accuracy. Static tasks remain a strength of specialised graph models.
arxiv-2606-28080:
Andrea Lucchini and Nowras Otmen introduce sectionally indecomposable groups in 2026. A finite group is sectionally indecomposable when a simple test holds. If it appears as a section of a direct product, it must already be a section of one factor. Sections are quotients of subgroups, the standard building blocks of finite group theory. The authors study this notion for finite groups.

The study reduces to the monolithic case. The main result completely characterises sectional indecomposability for monolithic primitive groups. One of these groups is indecomposable exactly when its socle is non-abelian, or the socle is a p-group with an extra non-triviality condition. The proof introduces H-Frattini modules and uses the universal p-Frattini cover plus a result of Griess and Schmid. Sectionally indecomposable groups, as a corollary, include every monolithic primitive solvable group. The non-primitive case appears significantly harder.
arxiv-2606-28380:
Mani Hamidi, Sina Khajehabdollahi, Charley M. Wu, and Emmanouil Giannakakis borrow a trick from biology. Brains are born with rich, modular wiring even though the genome that encodes it is tiny; development decodes that compressed blueprint, and experience refines the result. The team mimics the scheme with hypernetworks.

Hamidi and colleagues train a hypernetwork to generate the connections of a modular reservoir, a recurrent network whose internal weights normally stay fixed. Curriculum-based meta-learning shapes the generator so the networks it produces are sparse and structured from birth. Those reservoirs solved difficult temporal tasks with minimal further training and without giving up robustness. Evolution and development, compressed into one learning loop, produced capable networks far cheaper than training each from scratch.
arxiv-2606-28680:
Timothy Blanton, Jesús A. De Loera, and Melissa Sherman-Bennett study permutahedra that survive a change of coordinates. A Coxeter permutahedron is the convex hull of a point's orbit under a finite reflection group, and some choices of the point also make it a Coxeter matroid polytope. As the point moves, triangulations and subdivisions appear and vanish; the persistent ones are the robust features.

The authors show the orbit realization space is contractible, shaped like an open cone. They give a necessary and sufficient condition for a triangulation to persist, sufficient conditions for individual simplices, and asymptotic counts of generic and persistent simplices. Every matroidal subdivision of such a polytope turns out to be persistent, and for flag matroid polytopes the regular subdivisions correspond exactly to cones in the flag Dressian.
arxiv-2606-28980:
Panaccione and colleagues build OvESyn, a system that generates synthetic three-dimensional CT scans of ovarian cancer patients from text descriptions. Ovarian cancer is often found late, so contrast-enhanced CT guides staging and surgery planning. Yet annotated imaging data are scarce, partly due to privacy rules, which limits models that could help. Earlier text-to-scan pipelines needed paired radiology reports and were tested only on chest scans.

OvESyn instead builds standardised Findings and Impression sections from imaging descriptors and routine clinical metadata, never touching original reports. Those texts condition a latent diffusion model adapted to 493 patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer. Ablation tests isolated what matters: adapting the generator to the new body region established the target anatomy, while aligning the vision-language encoder only refined intensity and fine detail. The full model achieved the best fidelity scores, though a generator-only variant covered more variety.
arxiv-2606-29080:
Nguyen and Zhu study a conflict at the heart of protecting cyber-physical systems, such as power grids or vehicles, when the system may secretly be degraded or compromised. A detector watches for hidden bad modes, while a controller tries to keep performance steady. The two have different objectives, and the paper shows why designing them separately, the usual intuition, can fail.

They call the failure resilience-induced blindness. A strong controller with a large resilience margin smooths over the very symptoms that reveal a hidden mode. Belief updates then slow, the detector learns late, and control performance ends up worse. For a two-mode linear Gaussian system, the authors characterise the effect precisely, tying the resilience margin to log-likelihood evidence that detection depends on. Simulations illustrate both the blindness and ways to mitigate it, informing safer joint design.
arxiv-2606-29280:
Atkinson reports a bias in AI advisers for schools, and a fix that removes it. Zero-shot language-model agents, with no task-specific training, systematically recommend acting even when a hindsight-optimal policy says do nothing. He calls this intervention bias. In a six-arm study on a university learning dataset of eight hundred students, the pattern was stark. One leading model recommended action for nearly three quarters of students at a point where the ideal policy intervened for under a third.

Retrieval-based commercial systems were miscalibrated in the same way. Supervised policy learning removed the bias in both tested forms: a Decision Transformer reading student trajectories, and a gradient-boosted classifier on snapshots. Both reached near-zero calibration error, decided in under five milliseconds, and cost nothing per decision. Atkinson stresses the full self-retraining loop he sketches is a design, not a validated claim.
arxiv-2606-29380:
Liu, Liu, and Chen study a hexaquark, a hypothetical particle built from six quarks, in a triquark-antitriquark picture. Their particle mixes charm and bottom quarks and their antimatter partners. They use Regge trajectories, straight line relations that link a particle's spin to its squared mass. Such lines organize families of excited states and let theorists estimate masses that experiments have not yet measured.

The authors build trajectory relations for this hexaquark from known relations for diquarks and triquarks, its smaller building blocks. They examine five series of trajectories, named with the Greek letters lambda, rho, and sigma. A key finding is that most series cannot be copied from meson trajectories, because mesons lack internal substructure. The trajectories instead mirror those of the matching triquark, diquark, and antidiquark parts. Rough mass estimates for the excited states follow from the relations.
arxiv-2606-29480:
Sohn and Nam present DTM-Codec, a neural speech codec that changes its frame rate as speech changes. A codec compresses speech into tokens and rebuilds it later. Variable frame rate coding spends fewer frames on steady sounds and more on rapidly changing ones. Earlier gains often shrank once the extra bits describing which time steps were kept were honestly counted.

Dynamic Token Masking keeps selected encoder tokens and fills the rest with a learned mask embedding. A binary keep-mask travels with the data so the decoder knows each token's position. Their Path Length Equalization selector picks boundaries in linear time and spreads segments evenly. Under a strict matched total bitrate protocol, the codec improves on fixed frame rate baselines broadly, in both reconstruction quality and intelligibility. The gains hold across several operating points. Both authors work at KAIST's Graduate School of Cultural Technology in South Korea.
arxiv-2606-29580:
Yi presents MAM-AI, an assistant that answers medical questions for nurse-midwives in Zanzibar and runs entirely on an ordinary Android phone. Maternal and newborn deaths remain high in sub-Saharan Africa, and many nurses lack full midwifery training. Guidelines are long, and connectivity is intermittent, so consulting them during care is hard.

The system embeds each question with a small model and matches it against eighty-seven guideline documents, split into tens of thousands of passages. A compact generator then answers with citations, fully offline. Layered evaluation of the exact deployed setup delivers a surprise: retrieval works well, and the small embedder ranks near cloud systems. The generator is the weak point, since retrieved context fails to improve its answers and can hurt larger models. Yi deploys the more faithful of two candidate generators, and a redesigned prompt cuts its deflection rate sharply.
arxiv-2606-29780:
Cui and four colleagues compute what an Ellis-Bronnikov wormhole would look like while accreting matter, viewed from both sides of its throat. The Ellis-Bronnikov wormhole is the first proposed traversable example. The authors solve the geodesic equation for photon paths.

When observer and disk sit on opposite sides of the throat, two key quantities differ. Ray tracing produces the far-side image. For optically thick accretion, raising a shape parameter enlarges the wormhole but dims it. For thin accretion, the image resembles an inside-out near-side image. Small-parameter wormholes can mimic black hole images somewhat; large-parameter cases can be ruled out.
arxiv-2606-30280:
Joseph Murtagh and a large team of collaborators track two icy bodies over years of survey photometry, comparing their activity. Comet 103P/Hartley 2 is a Jupiter-family comet returning regularly. Centaur Chiron orbits farther out and erupted in twenty twenty-one. Both objects bridge the path from trans-Neptunian space to the inner system. Long-term behavior of individual objects remains poorly constrained.

Survey data come from ATLAS and the Zwicky Transient Facility. Targeted Las Cumbres Observatory observations fill the gaps. Hartley 2 was followed through its twenty twenty-three to twenty-four apparition. Its activity rises steeply inbound and fades flatter outbound. That asymmetry suggests extra dust contribution after perihelion passage. Brightness sits below prior apparitions, matching reported secular fading. Dust mass loss runs at a few to a dozen kilograms per second. Colors shift blueward near perihelion in the data.
arxiv-2606-30480:
Keith Tran, Colton Harper, and Thomas Price interview programming students about what AI help does to their drive to practice. AI tools can complete introductory assignments in moments. Students then face a plain question: why struggle through them personally? Earlier work studied instructor policies and usage patterns. This study centers the students' own experience instead. Thirteen engineering majors in a MATLAB course were interviewed.

Each student had access to a course-specific AI chatbot. Situated Expectancy-Value Theory framed the analysis of their answers. Students wondered if their programming time was well spent. Some doubted the long-term usefulness of the skill itself. Satisfaction dropped when AI bypassed the productive struggle. Confidence often depended on AI being available nearby. Nearly all preferred learning through effort yet felt shortcut temptation. Some set explicit boundaries and reframed the tension successfully. Others used AI in ways conflicting with their own values.
arxiv-2606-30680:
Xuanyu Liu and four colleagues plan delivery routes for trucks that carry drones and park at smart lockers. In this locker-based system, lockers store parcels and also serve as drone docks for takeoff, landing, handover and battery swaps. A real plan must juggle deliveries, return pickups, battery limits that depend on load, and detours around no-fly zones, all at once.

The team frames route building as a Markov decision process and trains a two-stage deep reinforcement learning heuristic. Stage one solves the truck-only routing with an attention-based encoder and a bidirectional recurrent decoder. Stage two transfers that policy and adds a hybrid dispatch rule to coordinate drones with trucks. Across test instances of different scales, the method beat metaheuristic and neural baselines in most cases. It also kept computation times exceptionally short, which matters for daily fleet planning.
arxiv-2606-30780:
Octavian Pascu, Dan Oneata, Horia Cucu and Nicolas Müller build a deepfake voice detector that runs inside a web browser. Journalists and fact-checkers need to verify audio sources, but cloud-based detectors force them to upload sensitive material, raising privacy risks. The team instead propose an on-device model light enough for a browser plugin, so recordings never leave the user's machine.

Their detector truncates a self-supervised speech backbone, keeping only its early layers, and adds a simple logistic classifier on top. This small model proved both fast and accurate. Against the AASIST baseline it improved accuracy by about ten percent while running inference about forty percent faster. Integrated into a browser plugin, it lets journalists check a clip's authenticity with a click. The authors released the plugin code publicly. They argue the work shows privacy-preserving detection need not sacrifice performance.
arxiv-2606-30980:
He Zhang, Yueyan Liu, Xin Guan, Jie Cai and John M. Carroll study what can go wrong when an AI suggests follow-up questions during research interviews. Interviewing depends on timely, sensitive follow-ups, but workload and unfamiliar topics can limit depth. In a Wizard-of-Oz study, GPT-4o generated follow-ups in real time during live interviews. A human co-interviewer chose which to voice and could edit them first, simulating an assistant while keeping a person in charge. Seventeen interviewers with varied expertise took part.

Five interlocking concerns emerged. Participants worried about harmful or biased wording and harms no one could predict. They worried interviewees would feel disrespected when attention split and body-language cues were missed. They raised unequal access to the technology. They asked who is responsible when harm occurs. And they flagged privacy risks when AI records sensitive talk.
arxiv-2606-31080:
Liu, Shao, and Liao bring counterfactual reasoning into abstract argumentation, a formal way of modeling debates as networks of arguments that attack each other. Explanations there often ask a what-if question. Would an argument still be accepted if some other arguments changed status? Older methods answer with the but-for test: remove the suspected cause and see if the effect vanishes. That test misses refined cases such as preemption and overdetermination, where several causes overlap.

The authors encode each argument's acceptance condition as an equation. An intervention operator can then change sets of arguments at once, or hold witness arguments at their actual labels. The method follows the Halpern-Pearl definition of actual causality. Comparisons show it is more expressive and more reliable than earlier approaches at naming the real causes inside an argumentation framework.
arxiv-2606-31280:
Vlah gives a complete treatment of renormalized galaxy bias at fifth order, the bookkeeping that links galaxy positions to the dark matter field. Next-generation surveys map cosmic structure so precisely that theory must match at the percent level. Bias operators need gradient corrections and their loop terms need counterterms that soak up short-scale unknowns.

The work computes the two-loop power spectrum and the one-loop bispectrum and trispectrum for biased tracers in one framework. Stochastic renormalization of operator products at one point enters through an operator product expansion. All ultraviolet limits of the loop integrals are absorbed by the counterterms, as required. Solving the renormalization group equations shows strong scale dependence in the higher-gradient bias coefficients, a warning for survey analysis that treats them as constants.
arxiv-2606-31580:
