Tang and seven colleagues present LASER, a serving system that trims reasoning length for large models running at the edge. Reasoning models think in long chains of thought, which edge devices struggle to host. Early-exit methods cut chains by confidence, but with one fixed threshold per request they ignore how load swings when many requests compete.

LASER moves the confidence bar with real-time system load, inside a range their tests show is robust. It also pre-allocates a reasoning budget for each request based on difficulty and current capacity. Across two reasoning models, four benchmarks, and varied load, latency falls by 17 to 38 percent and service-level satisfaction rises, at an average accuracy cost of about one percent. Load awareness, not a cleverer threshold alone, does the work.
arxiv-2606-31680:
Xu and Aliaga present ShellMaker, a system that completes the outer build for generated houses and blocks whose interiors already exist. Indoor generators produce floor plans, walls and gaps for doors and windows but stop at a bare shell. Free-form generative models break the fixed footprint or move windows when asked to add facades and roofs. ShellMaker works under those structural constraints as hard rules.

Given a scaffold and a text style prompt, the pipeline builds a complete exterior mesh with physically based materials. It does this through parametric roof generation, language-model refinement of the prompt into part-aware specs, joint wall-roof material retrieval, and geometry-aware assembly. It accepts scaffolds from indoor generators, CityGML and CAD files alike. It beats retrieval and free generative baselines on how well the structure holds together and on design coherence.
arxiv-2606-31880:
Harding and Shapirovsky axiomatize modal logics that can express connectedness in metric spaces. Every metric space yields distance relations: pairs of points closer than a chosen threshold. A space is a-connected when the graph of one such relation links every pair of points by a path. Connectedness in the ordinary topological sense is a second, stronger notion.

Complete axiomatizations are given for both notions. The a-connected case uses a family of distance modalities plus the universal modality. Topological connectedness is captured with the closure modality, the universal modality and a single distance modality. Both logics enjoy the finite model property, and with a finite language they are decidable, the authors show.
arxiv-2606-31980:
Chen and six colleagues introduce DigitalCoach, a dataset for studying whether AI can teach people to use software, not just operate it for them. The dataset holds 72 expert-novice coaching sessions across five applications. It contains 22,752 dialogue turns grounded in 28.1 hours of screen and input recordings, with utterances annotated by dialogue act and coaching method.

State-of-the-art models coach differently from humans in the comparisons. They give more direct instructions, over 45 percent of turns against 30 percent for humans, and fewer explanations, diagnoses and checking questions. Given the coaching method, the best model writes plausible guidance, yet its grounding in the learner's actual screen stays poor. Learners coached by models finished fewer milestones and retained fewer skills in live tests.
arxiv-2608-00380:
Alidadi Shamsabadi, Yadav, and Yanikomeroglu manage interference in a large HAPS network with graph learning. High altitude platform stations can extend terrestrial coverage in vertical networks. They serve ground users and drones with high capacity. Strong line-of-sight links make user channels highly correlated, though. Wide footprints also force many users to share scarce radio blocks.

Their scheme joins user clustering with rate-splitting multiple access. The network is modelled as a heterogeneous graph. A graph neural network allocates common and private RSMA powers. The aim is to maximize the minimum spectral efficiency, fast and at scale. Simulations beat conventional access schemes, they report. Fairness and worst-user results match convex optimization at a fraction of its cost.
aurifontina-chymica-or-a-collection-of-f:
An English alchemy collection of 1680, this book gathers fourteen small treatises on the first matter of the philosophers. The title page states the aim plainly. These tracts will uncover the mercury that many adepts hid with care. They print it openly for the good of mankind in general. A dedication offers the work to Charles II, praised as a patron of learning.

Inside, the stone or elixir ranks as the highest secret in nature, the key to an enchanted castle. Plain recipes follow in the old style. From made mercury come the white and red mercuries. One receipt tells how to grow small seed pearls into great oriental ones, by dissolving them in white water. The hosted scan reads roughly, but the matter is classic seventeenth-century chymistry.
bodin-demonomanie-des-sorciers-french-15:
Jean Bodin, a leading French legal thinker, published De la démonomanie des sorciers in 1580. The four French books form the most learned demonology of their age. Bodin wrote against Jean Weyer's plea for mercy toward accused witches, and his answer is cold juridical rigor from first page to last.

Bodin defines witchcraft, lists its marks, and instructs judges on proof and punishment. He demands severity and distrusts any mercy as weakness. The book became the persecutors' handbook across Europe. Its very learning gave the hunt an intellectual engine. Readers today study it to grasp how a great mind could build a case for the stake.
bracton-de-legibus-twiss-vol3-1880:
Twiss issued the third volume of his Bracton edition in 1880. Bracton's treatise, written in the thirteenth century, was the common law's first full textbook. The Rolls Series edition, with Latin text and English translation on facing pages, was the standard way to read it in the Victorian age.

Volume 3 turns to actions and pleas: the writs by which a medieval Englishman could bring a claim in the king's courts. Bracton explains which writ fit which wrong, and how a case moved from summons to judgment. Procedure was the heart of early common law, since a claim without the right writ simply failed. The volume shows the machinery of royal justice as working lawyers of the 1200s used it every day.
brain-and-mind-1880:
Henry Shipton Drayton and James McNeill wrote Brain and Mind, a manual of mental science on phrenological lines, first copyrighted in 1879. Drayton and McNeill hold that the brain is a bundle of organs, each tied to one faculty. Head shape and size, read with care, show the mind at work.

Early chapters sort the temperaments and set out how organs grow with use. Hope, set near Veneration, joins Acquisitiveness and Cautiousness to make the bold speculator who rebounds from failure. Later parts map single faculties, Agreeableness among them, to spots on the skull. Cases of genius, idiocy, and brain injury fill the proof. The hosted scan is a Google Books copy, wrapper and all. Victorian self-culture in its most confident form stands here.
brett-legends-and-myths-of-the-aborigina:
William Henry Brett was a missionary who spent decades among the native peoples of British Guiana, learning their languages and listening to their stories. In 1880 he published the legends and myths he had gathered, one of the first such collections from the region.

The tales tell of Makonaima, the great spirit, of a world flood, and of the origins of the sun, moon, and animals. Arawak and Carib traditions stand side by side, showing both shared roots and tribal differences. Brett recorded stories that elders feared would die with them. His book remains a basic source for Guiana mythology.
bustan-saadi-1880:
A. Hart Edwards turned Saadi's Bustan from Persian verse into English, in the Wisdom of the East series. John Murray of London put out the book in 1911. L. Cranmer-Byng and Dr. S. A. Kapadia ran the series. A long front part tells who Saadi was and why he wrote.

Chapter one treats just rule, counsel, and the running of a state. Nushiravan's words to his son open its tales. Kings in coarse coats, Darius and a herdsman, and a pearl tale fill the run. Talk of wealth and want sits with the tales. Each short tale bears a point on how men should rule, give, wait, and bear. Kings, devotees, and poor men walk the pages as teachers. The whole book works by tale and turn of speech, not by dry rule lists.
candida-phoenix-philosophica-oder-auffri:
A German alchemy book of 1680 stands here, printed at Frankfurt am Main by Christian Hermsdorff. Full title calls it Candida Phoenix Philosophica, a frank account of the stone's matter and the mercury of the wise. Rainwater gives the key, by the title's own word: its likeness and secret unlock the theme.

True grounds of hermetic thought stand with the theme, set out in clear German, the title vows. Works and steps of the art are shown in full as well. Part one is named here. A motto at the foot sets the path: prayer, reading, deep thought, and work. Arms of the house front the book, with a note on grants from Charles V, Ferdinand I, and Maximilian II in 1570. Scan wear roughs the page, yet title and plan read plain.
cia-0000009880:
Captured American pilots were reportedly used by the Viet Cong for propaganda purposes, an August 1966 report states. Propaganda use meant statements, photographs, or displays aimed at audiences at home and abroad. The heading's reportedly keeps the claim short of proven.

Forced statements hurt twice: they worried families and served the enemy's message war. Officials tracked each use to warn families and judge the pilots' condition. A man reading a statement on film was at least alive on a date. The file thus joins the propaganda watch to the prisoner accounting, where even hostile broadcasts carried evidence.
cia-0000010480:
Prospects for an inclusive Middle East defense organization are weighed in a February 1952 CIA paper. Washington and London hoped to bind the region into an alliance facing the Soviet Union. Egypt's refusal to join on Western terms was the plan's first great obstacle.

The paper tests which states might join, which would not, and what an inclusive pact would require. Alliance building in the region kept failing on the same rocks: nationalism and the Arab-Israeli conflict. Later pacts of the decade inherited every problem named here. This file preserves the design stage, when the map still looked drawable.
cia-0000011780:
Bolivia in August 1967 was the scene of Che Guevara's last campaign, and a CIA paper that month surveys the situation in the country. Guevara's small guerrilla band was being hunted by Bolivian troops trained and advised by the United States. The highland republic, poor and often unstable, had become the test ground for his theory of rural revolt.

The paper covers the government's fight against the guerrillas and the country's wider troubles. It weighs the army, the miners, and the peasants caught between them. Two months later Guevara was captured and killed, so the survey reads as an account written mid-hunt.
cia-0000011980:
Lebanon's politics rested on a delicate balance among its religious groups, and in April 1960 the CIA surveyed the small republic's outlook. Christians and Muslims shared power by a fixed formula, while Nasser's Egypt pressed Arab nationalism on the country from outside. A civil war scare in 1958 had already brought American Marines to Beirut's beaches once.

The paper weighs the sects, the parties, and the foreign pressures pulling at the balance. It treats Lebanon as the region's most fragile piece of political arithmetic. The survey's doubts proved sound: the numbers never quite added up, and the country slid toward worse crises.
cia-0000012280:
Meetings with a Soviet official named Pankovski, of the State Scientific and Technical Committee, are recorded in a CIA paper from January 1961. The near-match of his name with Penkovsky, the colonel then passing secrets, has long made readers look twice at this file. On paper the meetings looked routine, the kind of contact scientific exchanges produced every month.

The notes record what was said across those quiet encounters. Whether by chance or design, they sit at the edge of the era's greatest spy case. For readers, they preserve the ordinary surface under which extraordinary business was being done.
cia-0000012380:
J. Bromley Smith, a White House staff aide, met with intelligence officers in March 1965, and a record of the meeting survives. Smith served the National Security Council staff, the bridge between the agency and the president. Meetings like this one carried intelligence matters to the presidential level, where product met policy in person rather than on paper.

The staff man's notes joined the file alongside the case papers. The White House's interest in the product shows how far good intelligence traveled in those years. For readers, the record is a trace of the spy world briefing power, face to face.
cia-0000013880: An American prisoner was seen near the Vinh Linh Special Zone border, and a CIA note dated September 4, 1967, reports it. The zone sat at the line between north and south, next to Quang Binh Province. A prisoner seen there was likely on the road north. The note adds one more fix on the route into the camps.
cia-0000014780: Activities of the PDP in Panama fill a CIA file dated July 4, 1953. One cell, Cell 6, proposed a clandestine flysheet, per the title. Secret leaflets were the small arms of party warfare in those years. The file preserves a single cell's plan, the finest grain of the party watch abroad. The Panama file now rests in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015280: Fast moving flying objects crossed the sky over Stalingrad in spring 1954, in a CIA report dated July 4, 1956. Speed was the detail that made officers sit up. Slow lights could be balloons or stars; fast ones hinted at craft. The report reached the files two years after the spring it describes.
cia-0000015380: An interview with a deleted name fills a CIA file dated September 4, 1955. The interview takes up an earlier talk of October 27, per the title. The source date is marked unknown. Interviews with names cut out are hard to weigh, yet the file keeps the talk's shape for the record. The interview file now rests in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015480: From June 10 to July 15, 1954, sightings of unidentified flying objects were tallied in a CIA record. Summer's long evenings put more eyes on the sky, and reports often rose. The five week span is set by the title itself. A short, dated tally like this helped staff track whether the wave was growing, holding, or fading that season.
cia-0000028780:
In late 1960, the CIA completed a special estimate on the situation and short-term outlook in Laos, numbered SNIE 68-60. Laos was a small kingdom in Southeast Asia caught in a growing Cold War struggle. Rival factions and outside powers were all pulling at the country, and its near future looked unsure.

The paper weighs where Laos stands and what is likely to happen in the months just ahead. It gives readers a clear view of how American analysts read a fragile state at a tense moment. Papers like this help explain later choices, since they show what officials feared and expected before events unfolded.
cia-0000041180:
American actress Jane Fonda arrived in North Vietnam, in broadcasts preserved in a CIA record dated June 4, 1972. Fonda was a famous critic of the war, and her visit drew worldwide notice. Hanoi's radio made full use of a celebrity guest who opposed her own government.

Inside are the broadcasts as the visit began, reported in Hanoi's own terms. American officials monitored every word, since her trip was a propaganda event. The file opens a famous and bitter episode. Fonda's name became a lasting symbol afterward. It stood in America's long argument over the war and those who opposed it.
cia-0000042780:
Further reportage on the Jesuit assassinations, tied in the title to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front, fills a CIA record dated November 3, 1989. Two files share this catalog date and nearly the same title. Each gathers the wire coverage from its own angle.

Inside, the reports trace how the killings were being told and retold. The FMLN link in the title shows the rebels' place in the coverage. Both sides of the war fought over the story as hard as over ground. The file preserves that contest in print, with the murders still fresh and the blame still unassigned in any court.
cia-0000045180:
Venceremos aired commentary on Ines Duarte, in a CIA record dated October 6, 1985. The rebel station spoke about the captive daughter herself this time. Her case had become the war's most personal story that autumn.

Inside, the guerrilla radio's treatment of her ordeal is preserved. Commentary let the rebels frame her captivity for their listeners. Every word about her was also aimed, over her head, at her father's government and its handling of the whole affair. The file shows the propaganda war running alongside the secret talks, each side telling the country what the other's silence or speech was meant to prove.
cia-0000045980: On June 5, 1991, a CIA item carried word that officials had produced firm proof of an American pilot's death. The word concrete, set in quotes in the headline, shows how hard every claim was pressed that summer. Proof of death was the other side of the missing-men search: it closed a case a family had kept open for years.
cia-0000049380: Dated February 2, 1989, declassified CIA document 0000049380 names the rightist ARENA party as election frontrunner in El Salvador. The item carries a Truth Commission note and focuses on the party's standing before the vote. Readers find a brief political record whose title gives the forecast, preserved in the agency's files on Salvadoran elections that year.
cia-0000096480: British Guiana approaches a critical election, according to declassified CIA document 0000096480, dated October 5, 1964. The heading frames the coming vote as critical for the colony. The brief file is a pre-election agency item, preserved among several Guiana records from that autumn. It is useful as a marker of how the vote was viewed beforehand.
cia-0000097280: Toward a Military Government in Peru is the title of declassified CIA document 0000097280, dated September 6, 1967. The heading reads a direction of travel for Peru's politics. Readers find a short declassified paper on that prospect, its title phrased as a movement toward military rule, filed among the agency's Latin American country studies.
cia-0000107980: Weekly Surveyor Article re Pakistan Negotiating with Niger for Uranium is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000107980, dated January 1, 1977. The title describes an article about Pakistan seeking uranium from Niger. Uranium is named plainly as the material in the heading itself. The brief record is a weekly article item, filed on the first day of 1977.
cia-0000108480: Untitled Cable re Guatemalan Kidnappings is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108480, dated February 1, 1981. The catalog marks the file an untitled cable, then names its subject: kidnappings in Guatemala. No victim or group is named in the heading itself. The brief record is a kidnapping item from the winter of 1981 in the Guatemala files.
cia-0000118680: Dated April 6, 1964, with that date marked as an estimate, declassified CIA document 0000118680 reports that Do Mau would become prime minister. Its untitled heading gives a time phrase that breaks off at the letter N. Within what span is lost where the heading ends in the release. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000119580:
A March 1968 CIA report examines Czechoslovakia's need for Western economic support. Prague's reformers were looking west for the money and trade their program required. The report appeared just as the Prague Spring was taking shape that spring.

Money linked the reform experiment to the outside world. Western loans and markets could keep the new course alive, but they also pulled a Soviet ally toward the West. The report measures that pull in economic terms. It helps explain why the reforms alarmed Moscow: the change in Prague was not only political, it was also about who would finance the country's future.
cia-0000132480: Uruguay reportedly rebuffing the Cuban president fills item 16 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated April 4, 1960. The rebuff was diplomatic rather than dramatic, but its message was plain. Small countries were learning to say no to Castro's embrace that year. The short item reports the refusal and the coolness behind it.
cia-0000132580: Soviet and Czech experts reportedly running building work in Cuba fill item 15 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated September 1, 1960. Its headline breaks off at the word constr, short for construction, and misspells technicians as tecnicians. Bloc experts were helping to build Cuba's new armed strength. The short item reports their presence.
cia-0000132680: Cuba under a Latin America heading fills a CIA item dated March 2, 1961. Six weeks stood between this item and the Bay of Pigs landing. The Cuba file was running at full boil by then. A two-word subject line said all that needed saying about the agency's focus. The short item keeps the entry in the form the series gave it.
cia-0000135880: The record dated about January 1954 is a declassified CIA document about a cassette record, shelved as reel 17 in box 209, folder 011, the shelf mark as its whole heading. The wider file is PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation aimed at the Arbenz government in Guatemala before the June 1954 coup. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136180: The CIA cable from 3 May 1954 deals with immediate delivery to CADICK or ONTRICH on a Calligaris matter, in a file now declassified. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136980: Reports of an aircraft attack on La Mercedes church were false. This June 1954 cable establishes that. A Mexico City report told a dramatic tale. Three anti-communist aircraft took part in an attack, it said. The church stood in the city center. It was built in 1783. It was known for fine altars, costly jewels, and art treasures. It was reported destroyed. A correspondent phoned Chicago on 26 June. He called the story a lie. American eyewitnesses saw no visible damage.
cia-03006380:
A reported attempt on Prime Minister Yoshida's life opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 7 May 1954. His daughter told Ambassador Allison that a rightist tried to kill six people, her father among them, on 4 May. The press played it down as a madman's break-in. Other recent attempts are noted, with police guarding party leaders amid scandal.

A Soviet-trained Korean, Kim Il, takes North Korea's agriculture ministry in the second item. Indochina fills the middle: French doubts of a settlement, Navarre's cease-fire opposed, and Viet Minh forces massing north of the Tonkin delta. The USSR reportedly offers MIG-15 fighters to Finland, priced against a trade credit. Rumania releases political prisoners. Scelba ties Italian EDC ratification to Trieste, and Paraguay's revolt draws a closing comment.
cia-03169380:
Cuba opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 30 August 1957. Leaders of the 26th of July movement plan to step up their campaign against Batista. Assassination of cabinet ministers and police officials is under consideration. Leaked news of police shootings and hanged prisoners fuels the turn. Sabotage, quiet since guarantees were suspended on 1 August, will intensify.

Civic and business opponents claim progress in subverting the armed forces, the regime's traditional bulwark. The USSR reportedly offers Austria a generous cut in reparations deliveries. Britain's gold and dollar reserves have fallen sharply. Speculation against sterling drives the loss, and officials decline for now to draw on fund or American credits. Gomulka is reported in Moscow. A Bulgarian leadership shake-up is indicated. A Watch Report annex closes the issue.
cia-06834380:
Information report distributed 23 November 1993, classed Secret with WNINTEL and NOFORN controls, updates weapons buying in Mogadishu, Somalia. Its subject line names Aideed's weapons and ammunition purchases and the availability of weapons in the city. The report states it is not finally evaluated intelligence.

The report states pro-Aideed buyers were purchasing unusually large amounts of ammunition. They had bought so many mortar rounds, listed as 80 mm (sic) and 120 mm, that no more were available in the market. Since early November the buyers had focused on mortar bombs and RPG-7 rounds, driving a sharp price rise, the report says. Aideed fighters were seen with new RPG-7s in mid-November, and showing off four new weapons at Bar Ubax. Later lines list RPG-7s, RPG-2s, AK-47s, and grenade launchers selling in higher volume than other weapons.
classical-poetry-japanese-chamberlain-18:
Basil Hall Chamberlain studied The Classical Poetry of the Japanese in 1880, the first systematic English treatment of the subject. His pioneering work translates poems from the Manyoshu and the Kokinshu, the great early anthologies. Chamberlain explains forms like the tanka while letting the poems themselves persuade the reader.

Courtly love, war, travel, and the seasons pass in verses of thirty-one syllables. Chamberlain wrote when Japan was just opening to the West, and his sympathy set the tone for later study. The book remains a graceful first door into Japan's classical verse for English readers.
coke-institutes-part3-1680:
The Third Part of Coke's Institutes, printed in 1680, bears the title Pleas of the Crown. Coke wrote it as his account of English criminal law, drawing on his years as attorney general and chief justice. Like the other later parts, it reached print long after his death, when Parliament wanted his learning in public hands.

The volume sets out treason, murder, theft, and the other felonies, with the punishments and procedures that went with them. Coke ranges across statutes and cases to fix the meaning of each offense. His care for exact charges and fair process shaped how criminal law was pleaded. The book is the common law's criminal code as its greatest master left it, stern in penalty yet strict about the forms that protected the accused.
collectanea-medico-physica-oft-hollands-:
Collectanea Medico-Physica, oft Hollands Jaar-Register, by Steven Blankaart, doctor of medicine and practitioner at Amsterdam, was printed at Amsterdam by Johan ten Hoorn in 1680. It opens a Dutch year register of medical and natural observations from all of Europe, beginning with the year 1680. Blankaart built it from his own experience and from reports shared by other gentlemen and amateurs.

His dedication counts four hundred observations already gathered. Yearly continuations were planned, and readers who kept rare observations of their own are invited to share them for the common good. The cases run to anatomy as readily as to cures. One describes a urinary tract with four basins in place of one. Each basin has its own duct, with veins and arteries in due proportion.
count-of-gabalis-1680:
The Count of Gabalis reached English readers in this translation of 1680. The Abbé de Villars had published the French dialogues a decade earlier. In them a German count instructs a young scholar in the secret sciences, above all in the peoples who inhabit the four elements.

Sylphs fill the air, gnomes the earth, undines the water, and salamanders the fire. The count urges marriage with these beings as the sage's true path. Villars writes half in jest, yet his scheme fixed occult elemental lore for good. Later occultists took the dialogues in full earnest. No book did more to populate the invisible world with ordered nations of spirits.
dante-banquet-morley-1880:
Dante called this early work Il Convito, The Banquet, and left it unfinished. An English rendering dated 1880 presents it to modern readers. He offers his own poems as dishes at a feast of thought.

Long comments in prose explain each poem line by line. Love, nobility, and the nature of knowledge fill the learned pages. Dante writes here as a scholar, with the full rigor of his schools. The book shows the workshop where the Divine Comedy was forged. For that reason alone it fascinates: readers watch a great mind stock the tools it would soon use on a masterpiece.
dawkins-early-man-in-britain-1880:
W. Boyd Dawkins published Early Man in Britain in 1880 as the sequel to his Cave Hunting of 1874. Its subtitle places man in the Tertiary period, the deep geological past. The book is a systematic survey of British Pleistocene geology, fauna, and human remains.

Dawkins orders the river gravels and cave deposits into one story of ice ages and shifting animal life. Into that frame he sets the flint tools and bones of Britain's first inhabitants. For decades the book was the standard account of early man in Britain. Its confidence is Victorian; its evidence base was the best then available. Later finds rewrote much, but the frame was his.
dawson-fossil-men-modern-representatives:
J. W. Dawson, a Canadian geologist and college principal, published Fossil Men in 1880. He reviewed the new fossil human finds coming out of Europe. Unlike many peers, he resisted Darwin's account of human descent.

Dawson argued for the recent origin and unity of the human race. He tried to fit caves, skulls, and tools within a biblical frame. His side lost the scientific argument that followed. The book matters now as a clear statement of the anti-Darwinian case by a serious geologist. Dawson wrote from his post at McGill, where he shaped Canadian science education.
discours-admirables-de-la-nature-des-eau:
Waters, springs, metals, and salts are the theme of Bernard Palissy's book, printed at Paris by Martin le Jeune in 1580, with the king's privilege. Palissy styles himself inventor of the rustic figulines of the king and of the queen his mother. He inscribes the work to Antoine de Pons, a knight of the king's orders.

The title promises natural and artificial waters and fountains, stones, earths, fire, and enamels, with other fine secrets of natural things. A treatise on marl for farming is added. Talk between theory and practice carries the book, in the manner of a dialogue. Salt marsh work fills one passage: pools cleaned in May, then sluices opened to let in what water the workers want. The book is a maker's natural philosophy.
eslon-observations-magnetisme-animal-178:
Charles d'Eslon was a Paris doctor and Mesmer's chief disciple. His Observations on animal magnetism appeared in 1780, while the doctrine still rose and before the commissions of 1784 struck it down. D'Eslon pleads the medical case for the magnetic fluid in careful, earnest prose.

He reports cures he witnessed and answers the doctors who scoffed. His standing as a faculty physician made his support hard to dismiss. The book is the key pro-mesmerism tract of the early fight. Readers can hear true belief argued by a trained man of science. It shows how reasonable the fluid seemed before the blindfold tests.
europmc-pmc10212980:
Wu and co-authors review the blood-brain barrier in a 2023 paper, covering its structure, regulation, and role in drug delivery. The barrier is a tight lining in brain blood vessels that keeps toxins and germs out of the brain. That protection also blocks most medicines, which is a central problem in treating brain disease.

The review describes how the barrier is built and how its gates open and close. It surveys tricks to carry drugs across, from tiny carriers to focused ultrasound. The paper maps a key obstacle in brain medicine and the main ways around it.
europmc-pmc10247380:
Depp and a large team report that failing myelin drives amyloid buildup in Alzheimer's disease models, in a 2023 study. Myelin is the fatty coating that insulates nerve fibers and speeds their signals. It frays with age as its maker cells falter, and age is the biggest risk factor for Alzheimer's, for reasons still unclear.

In mouse models, the team found that damaged myelin prompts the deposit of amyloid-beta, the protein that clumps in Alzheimer's brains. Healthy myelin held those deposits back. The work links brain aging in the wiring to the disease's hallmark plaques.
europmc-pmc10365580:
Liu, Wang, and Liu weighed the use of ChatGPT in daily medical care in 2023. ChatGPT is a chat tool that writes text in reply to prompts. Clinics have begun to test it for real tasks. The authors survey what the tool can do and where it may cause harm.

On the plus side, Liu reports help with lists of possible diagnoses for a case. The tool also drafts patient letters, scan reports, notes, and discharge forms. That work can save staff time and cut errors. The authors still call the tool a double-edged sword. They urge care with wrong answers and patient privacy. Future work may add live tracking and care at a distance.
europmc-pmc11049480:
Roshandel, Ghasemi-Kebria, and Malekzadeh review colorectal cancer patterns, risks, and prevention in this 2024 paper. Colorectal cancer grows in the large bowel. In 2020 it caused more than 1.9 million new cases and almost 0.9 million deaths worldwide. It ranks third among cancers for cases and second for deaths.

Rates differ sharply between countries, mainly due to differing risk habits, the authors say. Prevention works on two levels. Primary prevention avoids risks such as alcohol and raises protective habits such as physical activity. Secondary prevention is screening, which finds and removes early growths before they turn cancerous. The review presents the latest evidence on spread, causes, and control programs. Open disputes remain over which factors matter most and which programs work best in each population.
europmc-pmc11186780:
Jin, Li, Jeong, Castro-Martinez, and Zuker map a body-to-brain circuit that reins in inflammation in this 2024 study. The body-brain axis senses organ function, metabolism, and nutrition, and steers them in return. The team asked how this axis answers an immune insult at the body's edge. They tracked signals between the vagus nerve, which links organs to the brain, and the brain itself.

Pro-swelling and anti-swelling cytokines spoke to distinct vagal neuron groups, they found. Silencing the circuit genetically let inflammation run unregulated and out of control. Switching the circuit on instead suppressed the pro-inflammatory response while boosting the anti-inflammatory state. Single-cell gene reads plus functional imaging identified the circuit's parts. The authors say selective control of this circuit could treat disorders from autoimmunity to cytokine storm and shock.
europmc-pmc1140680:
Mair, Piper, and Partridge test whether calories explain why eating less extends life in fruit flies in this 2005 study. Dietary restriction extends lifespan in diverse organisms, including mammals. In rodents it is often called calorie restriction, on the theory that total calories, not specific nutrients, drive the effect. The team asked whether the same holds in Drosophila, the fruit fly.

Cutting either yeast or sugar in the diet reduced mortality and extended life, they found. The gain did not track how many calories the food held. Per calorie, yeast had a much greater effect than sugar. Total calories, they conclude, are not the key factor in this species. The result points to specific nutrients, above all the protein-rich yeast fraction, as the lever. It challenges the assumption that findings from rodents transfer unchanged to other species.
europmc-pmc11415080:
Wang and colleagues review neutrophil extracellular traps in health and disease in this 2024 paper. Neutrophils are frontline white blood cells. They can expel their own loosened DNA, studded with inflammatory proteins, as web-like traps that catch germs. Understanding of these traps in infection, immune regulation, and disease has grown fast in recent years.

Excess traps can block vessels, damage tissue, and prolong inflammation, the review warns. They are implicated in autoimmune disease, metabolic disorders, and cancer. Yet the traps can also help: aggregated traps degrade inflammatory signal proteins, damping the response. Some traps act as autoantigens, targets the immune system wrongly attacks. The authors map the molecules and pathways that control trap formation. They frame that map as the route to therapies that tune traps up or down.
europmc-pmc1226180:
Mager and colleagues tested saliva bacteria as a sign of oral cancer in 2005. The cancer type was oral squamous cell carcinoma. It grows in the lining of the mouth. Early detection still poses a hard problem.

Saliva samples came from 45 patients and 229 cancer-free controls. Counts were taken for 40 common mouth bacteria. Three species stood out with higher counts in patients. Their levels gave useful accuracy for flagging cancer. Mager suggests a spit test could aid screening one day. More work would be needed to confirm the signal. The three species were Capnocytophaga gingivalis, Prevotella melaninogenica, and Streptococcus mitis. They flagged 80 percent of cancer cases.
europmc-pmc1241380:
Zarn, Brüschweiler, and Schlatter examined azole fungicides and hormone making in 2003. Azoles fight fungi on farms and in human medicine. Some also treat breast tumors by lowering estrogen. All work by blocking enzymes that build steroid hormones.

Two blocked enzymes matter most for side effects. One builds sterols that guide germ cell development. The other, aromatase, balances male and female hormones. High azole doses harm fertility and development in several species. Tests confirm many azoles block both enzymes in dishes and animals. Their aim is often poor, hitting mammal enzymes too.
europmc-pmc1241580:
Guvenius and co-authors measured pollutant exposure before and after birth in 2003. Four chemical groups were tracked: flame retardants, PCBs, PCB breakdown products, and pentachlorophenol. Samples covered mother blood, cord blood, and breast milk. Median PCB levels ran about 60 times the flame retardant levels.

Flame retardant patterns differed between mother and cord blood, unlike PCBs. PCB breakdown products made up 53 percent of PCB levels in cord blood. Pentachlorophenol levels were highest in maternal blood at 2,830 picograms per gram. Guvenius shows each chemical crosses to the baby by its own pattern.
europmc-pmc1615880:
Family trees in biology carry more data than the tree alone can show. Chevenet and co-authors built TreeDyn in 2006 to attach that extra data to tree graphics. Taxon facts and gene functions usually sit outside the diagram, forcing tedious manual work.

TreeDyn handles many trees in many windows, with texts and symbols projected onto leaves and nodes from annotation files. Users can query labels, highlight matches, and export graphics in standard formats or save sessions. Scripts automate repeated tasks, and a command line mode builds trees online. Chevenet supplies field-specific packages for common research needs.
europmc-pmc1808080:
Dromer and the French Cryptococcosis Study Group ran CryptoA/D in 2007, a France-wide study of cryptococcosis from 1997 to 2001. The disease is a life-threatening fungal infection caused by Cryptococcus neoformans. Most prior guidance came from trials in HIV patients with brain infection, run before modern HIV therapy.

The prospective study enrolled 230 patients without trial selection bias. Of them, 77 percent were HIV-positive, and 72.5 percent carried fungal serotype A rather than serotype D. Men, HIV-positive patients, and those whose fungus was serotype A all had more severe disease. Failure to clear the fungus by week two was tied to wide initial spread and to high blood antigen levels. Missing the drug flucytosine in early therapy also predicted failure, with odds near four times higher.
europmc-pmc1939880:
Covington and Harmer solved in 2007 a 70-year-old puzzle about why plants answer a growth hormone differently by time of day. The hormone is auxin, which steers plant growth and development in space, much as the circadian clock steers plant life in time. Early researchers noted the time-varying sensitivity but could not explain it.

Genome-wide activity profiling showed many auxin-induced genes are also under clock control. A glowing reporter assay confirmed that the plant's own auxin signaling rises and falls with the clock. Added auxin barely nudged the clock itself, so control runs one way. Both gene responses and growth responses to applied auxin were gated by the clock, meaning the same dose works differently at different hours. Many plant traits may thus hide a circadian layer.
europmc-pmc1942080:
Towner, Leroy and co-authors reported in 2007 the first detection of Marburg virus in a wild bat. Marburg and Ebola viruses cause hemorrhagic fever outbreaks that kill 80 to 90 percent of human patients. Finding their natural animal reservoir is a central open problem, unsolved nearly 40 years after the family was discovered.

In Gabon, the team found Marburg virus RNA and matching antibodies in the Egyptian fruit bat, Rousettus aegyptiacus, a common species. These bats are the first non-primate animals found naturally infected with this virus. The find also extends Marburg's known map into a new part of Africa, meaning more regions face outbreak risk than assumed. It parallels a recent report naming three fruit bat species as likely Ebola reservoirs, strengthening the bat reservoir case.
europmc-pmc1951780:
Stecher, Hardt and co-authors showed in 2007 that Salmonella uses gut inflammation as a weapon against resident microbes. The dense gut community normally shields the host by beating incoming germs, a defense called colonization resistance. How gut germs break that shield was poorly known.

In a mouse colitis model, the response that Salmonella Typhimurium provokes reshaped the gut community and held back its growth. A weakened mutant that cannot trigger gut inflammation was beaten by the resident microbes. Supplying inflammation another way, by adding normal Salmonella at the same time, or using mice prone to bowel inflammation, rescued the mutant's edge. Inflammation was thus both needed and enough to beat colonization resistance. The finding flips the usual framing: here inflammation helps the pathogen, not just the host.
europmc-pmc2125080:
Simon Flexner and Hideyo Noguchi of the Rockefeller Institute reported in 1913 their attempts to cultivate the microorganism of epidemic poliomyelitis. Earlier claims had collapsed: micrococci from spinal fluid and a bacillus from blood were both discredited as the cause. The agent's filterable nature, shown by Flexner and Lewis and by Landsteiner and Levaditi, had discouraged even trying.

False trails had to be cleared first. A clouding of serum broth by filtered nervous tissue, once hopeful, proved to be protein precipitation, not growth. Proescher's stained coccus-like bodies remained of unsettled nature. Against that background the authors set out their culture work, using nervous tissue from infected monkeys and patients. Readers get the cultivation problem of a virus stated honestly, failures included, at the moment it was first taken up in earnest.
europmc-pmc2125180:
Richard M. Pearce and O. H. Perry Pepper published the ninth spleen study in 1914, on what happens to bone marrow after the spleen is removed from dogs. The rule is a transformation. The fatty marrow of the long bones turns into richly cellular red marrow, the blood-making kind.

Timing matters. In the first one to three months the change is slight, in patches or at the edges. After six to twenty months the fat is replaced completely or nearly so. Four animals broke the rule, at eight, nine, ten, and twenty-two months. A third idea, that marrow takes over storing and reworking the iron of old blood pigment, is raised but not fully supported. One dog even fell anemic again while its marrow was busily making sound red cells. Readers get an organ's understudy promoted, for reasons still partly obscure.
europmc-pmc2125280:
G. H. Whipple and J. S. Known liver poisons and circulation disturbances had already been shown to cut the dye's output, validating the test as an index of the liver's working capacity.

Two hours of ether anesthesia usually depresses the excretion curve through the following day. Paraldehyde, in doses giving hours of anesthesia and stupor, produces a definite fall. Chloral and urethane lower output in considerable doses, and alcohol does so in doses large enough to stupefy for hours. A fall to two-thirds or one-half of normal counts, on their scale, as definite liver injury with temporary impairment. One dog given paraldehyde reeled in wild excitement before stupor, a reminder that these were full drug doses, not whiffs. Readers get the anesthetist's hangover measured in the liver, drug by drug.
europmc-pmc2125880:
Herbert D. Taylor and J. Harold Austin ranked the body-wide toxicity of wound antiseptics then in wide use, publishing in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1918. These chemicals were often placed on wounds where the body could absorb them fast. So the pair injected set doses into the bellies of mice and guinea pigs, then ordered the substances by how poisonous each proved.

Eucalyptol and brilliant green topped the list, followed by mercurophen, then mercuric chloride and chloramine-T, with iodine and phenol least toxic of the group. Since a mild solvent called chlorcosane could carry dichloramine-T, they advised dropping the far more toxic eucalyptol for that job. Injecting any listed antiseptic into closed body cavities looked unwise, since all outranked iodine and phenol in toxicity. Skin injection, they add, makes a poor test, because leaking and tissue death distort how much chemical is absorbed.
europmc-pmc2128380:
Christen Lundsgaard and Eggert Möller measured the oxygen in fingertip blood, the so-called capillary blood, and compared it with arterial and venous blood. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1922. They devised a way to draw the skin blood for gas analysis without letting it touch the air.

In a normal resting person, fingertip blood matched arterial blood almost exactly in oxygen content, both near full saturation. Venous blood drawn at the same time stood well below them. Using the known ceiling of the blood's oxygen capacity, the pair showed the same identity without any arterial puncture, in healthy and sick subjects, at rest and after exercise. They argue the identity likely extends to other blood contents, sugar, salt, and uric acid among them. A fingertip sample, on this showing, can stand in for arterial blood.
europmc-pmc2130980:
James B. Murphy and Karl Landsteiner produced sarcomas in chickens by injecting coal tar into induced growths, then transplanted one through eleven generations. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925, from the Rockefeller Institute. Chicken tumors were famous for passing by cell-free filtrates, and the tar tumors were tested against that standard.

Two spindle cell sarcomas arose from the tar injections into induced embryomas. One of them, carried through eleven generations of chickens, proved highly invasive and spread freely to distant parts. Attempts to transmit this tumor by a filtrate or by dried tumor material failed completely. The tar tumor thus breaks the chicken tumor pattern: malignant and transplantable by graft, but not by the cell-free route its cousins use. Tar can start a true malignant growth, the work shows, and that growth then lives by its cells alone.
europmc-pmc2131080:
William A. Perlzweig and Chester S. Keefer purified the water-soluble immunizing antigen of the pneumococcus, in the third paper on that antigen. It appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925, from the Johns Hopkins medical clinic in Baltimore. The antigen was known to dissolve easily in water and salt solutions, which made culture filtrates the place to hunt it.

Massive cultures of Type I pneumococcus were grown and their filtrates worked through a three-step method. Ultrafiltration came first, then precipitation at a definite acidity, then separation of a soluble picrate fraction. The fractions obtained were of protein nature and actively immunizing, able to protect as the whole culture fluid does. The method, the authors conclude, suits the initial purification of this antigen. A protective substance that can be drawn out of broth and handled as a chemical is a step toward a defined vaccine.
europmc-pmc2131180:
Bunting and Eades, in the Pathological Laboratory of the University of Wisconsin, studied healing wounds in a 1926 paper. In a clean skin cut, new fibroblasts line up in a clear pattern as they grow across the wound. What sets that pattern was not plain from sections of healing tissue alone, so the pair varied the pull on rabbit skin wounds.

They cut into the thick skin of the backs of anesthetized rabbits and shifted the direction of tension. Their results support the view that mechanical tension can set the polarity of cell division and the line of growth in forming fibroblasts. A change in tension could also shift the position of fibroblasts already laid down.
europmc-pmc2131580:
Drury and Philip McMaster, at The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, opened a series on the liver and fat metabolism in 1929. Many liver roles in fat handling were agreed, but whether the liver alone breaks fat down was open. Part one compares fat burning, through the respiratory quotient, in normal rabbits and in rabbits deprived of the liver.

Fat burning went on adequately in rabbits with no liver, and even in rabbits with extreme liver failure. A full day after the liver was removed, fat combustion matched that of the normal animal. The liver, the authors conclude, plays no essential part in the breaking down of fat. Other organs must carry that work.
europmc-pmc2140880:
Crozier and Pincus, at Harvard University, tested stereotropism in rats and mice in a 1926 paper. Stereotropism is orientation toward a surface touching the body's side, already known in insects and worms. The question was whether a mammal shows it too. Young rats and mice, and adult mice born blind, were set beside contact surfaces.

The young animals, and the blind adults, turned toward a side contact in the typical way. Cutting off the whiskers or the tail, or both, did not essentially change the response. Equal contact on both sides blocked orientation to either. Unequal contact drew the animal toward the more extensive side. The behavior closely parallels the arthropods, giving a fairly complete instance of a tropism in mammals.
europmc-pmc2140980:
Mice born without rods in their eyes offer Clyde E. Keeler a way to test whether such animals sense light at all. His 1928 study comes from Harvard's Howe Laboratory of Ophthalmology. Rodless mice and normal control mice are placed on an inclined plane, first in darkness and then under light, and their upward orientation against gravity is measured.

In darkness both groups orient in the expected way. Under light the control mice fail to orient, while the rodless mice react almost exactly as they did in the dark. Keeler reads that sameness as no sign of sight in the rodless strain. The paper shows how a gravity-based behavior test can probe vision without training the animals to respond.
europmc-pmc2361680:
Li, Uribe, and Daling compared the clinical features of nine breast cancer types in 2005. Breast cancer is grouped by histologic type, meaning how tumor cells look and arrange under a microscope. Rare types were poorly understood, so the team used a large US registry.

They analysed 135,157 invasive cases diagnosed from 1992 to 2001. Lobular cancers were more likely than ductal cancers to be large, advanced, and spread to lymph nodes at diagnosis. Inflammatory cancers showed the most aggressive profile of all. Mucinous, tubular, and papillary types looked the least aggressive. Hormone receptor patterns also split sharply by type. For example, 68.2% of medullary cancers lacked both estrogen and progesterone receptors, versus 19.3% of ductal cancers, a split pointing to different causes.
europmc-pmc2363380:
Senaratne and co-authors tested bone drugs directly on breast cancer cells in 2000. The drugs, bisphosphonates, are given to stop bone damage when breast cancer spreads to the skeleton. New patient data hinted they might also cut tumor burden in bone, so the team checked for a direct effect.

They exposed three human breast cancer cell lines to four bisphosphonates. All four drugs cut cell survival in all three lines. Zoledronate was strongest, halving growth at doses of 3 to 20 micromolar depending on the line. Pamidronate needed higher doses, and the other two were over a hundred times weaker. Treated cells showed the classic signs of apoptosis, programmed cell death: changed shape, broken DNA, and a cut marker protein called PARP. A protective protein, bcl-2, also fell.
europmc-pmc2568880:
Pruunsild, Kazantseva, Aid, Palm, and Timmusk dissected the human BDNF gene in this 2007 study. BDNF is a growth factor that supports neurons and shapes learning, memory, and pain, and its gene was known to be complicated. The team mapped the gene's full structure. They catalogued its alternative transcripts. They also tested where each version is switched on in adult tissues and brain regions.

They found 11 exons and nine working promoters, each used in specific tissues or brain areas. A partner gene on the opposite strand, called antiBDNF, produces noncoding RNAs with their own complex patterns. In the brain, BDNF and antiBDNF transcripts pair up into double strands. This suggests the antisense partner helps control how much BDNF is made in humans.
europmc-pmc2719080:
Ritchlin and co-authors issued treatment recommendations in 2009 for psoriatic arthritis for the Group for Research and Assessment of Psoriasis and Psoriatic Arthritis (GRAPPA). The disease mixes joint inflammation with skin and nail psoriasis, plus spine disease, swollen whole digits, and sore tendon insertions. Its forms and severity vary widely between patients.

Specialists and patients drafted nineteen recommendations from formal literature reviews for each disease form, covering peripheral joints, spine, skin, nails, and the digit and tendon problems. Members agreed on sixteen of the nineteen at over eighty percent. A grid that factors in severity for each form helps clinicians match treatment to the individual patient in front of them.
europmc-pmc2728480:
Ross and co-authors checked in 2009 how often clinical trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov, the public United States trial registry, later appear in print. Selective publication distorts the evidence doctors rely on, since trials with dull or bad results often stay hidden. Registration was meant to create a public record that makes such hiding harder to sustain.

Looking at completed registered trials, they found low publication rates even after registration, with many trials still unpublished years after ending. Registration alone thus did not ensure that results reach clinicians, reviewers, or patients. The findings support stronger rules that require results, not just trial listings, to be posted and published in a timely way.
europmc-pmc2741580:
Hutton, Draganski, Ashburner, and Weiskopf compared in 2009 two MRI methods for measuring grey matter change in healthy aging: voxel-based cortical thickness and voxel-based morphometry. Both use standard brain scans, but one isolates cortical thickness while the other mixes thickness with surface area and folding. Regions with known age change were their test bed.

Overall the two methods agreed closely on where grey matter declines with age. The thickness method proved the more sensitive of the two, picking up age-linked decline more strongly. Since morphometry blends several anatomical features, using both together can separate true thinning from changes in area or folding. The pairing thus gives a fuller picture of how the aging cortex changes.
europmc-pmc2746580:
Aird and co-authors evaluated in 2002 thirteen novel ruthenium arene compounds as potential ovarian cancer drugs. Ruthenium is a metal, and these compounds may be less toxic than platinum drugs. Platinum drugs are active but suffer resistance and side effects. Ruthenium may act by a different route and keep activity where platinum fails.

Potency in the parent ovarian cancer cell line ranged widely. The best compound matched cisplatin, and two matched carboplatin. Certain ligand features raised activity, including a bidentate chelating group and a more water-averse arene. None of six active compounds was cross-resistant in the cisplatin-resistant line. One compound also worked in mouse tumors, including the resistant model, which merits further work.
europmc-pmc2817680:
Garrick, Taylor, and Fernando set out the correct math in 2009 for feeding breeding value estimates into genomic predictions for livestock. Breeders estimate each animal's genetic merit, its EBV, from records on the animal and its relatives. Those estimates arrive with uneven trust levels, and studies handled them in clashing ways.

The authors show that parent information must first be stripped out, then the estimate must be deregressed, meaning scaled back up by its reliability. They derive the proper weight for each record and prove that two common choices, using reliability itself or error variance as the weight, are both wrong. Mixed data, raw records on some animals and deregressed values on others, can then combine cleanly.
europmc-pmc2892080:
Sibal, Agarwal, Home, and Boger reviewed in 2010 the case against ADMA, a natural blood compound that throttles a vital vessel signal. Healthy vessel linings release nitric oxide to keep blood flow smooth, and low oxide marks failing linings long before heart disease shows. ADMA resembles the oxide's raw material closely enough to block its production, so high ADMA means impaired vessel function.

Levels run high in people with high cholesterol, high blood pressure, heart failure, diabetes, and kidney failure. In patients with coronary artery disease, ADMA predicted heart events and death more strongly than the traditional risk factors did. Early intervention work with the raw material L-arginine tries to outcompete the blocker, though the authors weigh its promise cautiously.
europmc-pmc2893180:
Leung and Wong reviewed in 2010 the pharmacology of ginsenosides, the active compounds behind ginseng's long medicinal reputation. These steroid-like plant molecules come in many variants that the body transforms step by step after swallowing, mainly through gut processing. The review first lays out their structures, how they change in the body, and how much actually reaches the blood.

From there it examines how ginsenosides interact with steroid hormone receptors. Those are the docking sites for cortisol and sex hormones. The contacts explain the wide spread of effects on inflammation, metabolism, and cell growth. That breadth makes them rich raw material for new therapies. One obstacle dominates, though: oral bioavailability is very low, so most of a dose never reaches its targets, and delivery science must fix that first.
europmc-pmc2920080:
Vandenberg and co-authors weighed in 2010 a puzzle about bisphenol A. The chemical is produced in huge volume for plastics and can linings. Blood studies find it everywhere, yet metabolism studies say it should vanish fast. Over eighty biomonitoring studies covering thousands of people in several countries overwhelmingly detected BPA in urine, blood, and tissues of adults and children.

The active, unprocessed form appeared routinely in blood at measurable levels. Two careful toxicokinetic studies, by contrast, predicted swift processing and excretion after oral doses, implying blood levels should be near zero. The review tests explanations for the clash, from non-food exposure routes and skin contact to slow release from body stores, and finds the discrepancy unresolved. Exposure science must settle it before health risk can be judged.
europmc-pmc2965880:
Cronin-Fenton and co-authors tracked hospital stays for blood clots in Danish cancer patients from 1997 to 2006 in a 2010 cohort study. Clots in veins often complicate cancer, yet which tumours carry the worst risk was poorly charted.

Nearly sixty thousand patients were compared with a general population group five times larger. Clot rates ran higher in patients overall and peaked in the first year after diagnosis. Pancreas, brain, and liver tumours, plus a bone marrow cancer, carried the highest rates, as did advanced stage and chemotherapy. Adjusted risks for some tumours rose many times above population levels.
europmc-pmc300680:
Lippman and colleagues dissected how jumping genes, transposons, are silenced and inherited in the weed Arabidopsis in a 2003 genetics study. Barbara McClintock first saw heritable yet reversible changes in transposon activity in maize half a century earlier.

Testing six transposons across mutant plants, they found most silencing lifted. The lift came when DNA methylation was lost. It also came when a chromatin remodeller or a histone editor was lost. Only a few transposons needed one histone methylator in particular. Others needed an RNA interference gene, or a second methylator. Crosses showed active states inherited unevenly by mutant type, and the patterns split the regulators into two interacting groups.
europmc-pmc3034180:
Hafner and coauthors linked in 2010 a longevity related enzyme to protection against age related heart thickening. As hearts age, a pore inside their energy producing mitochondria opens too often, weakening the cells. The enzyme, called SIRT3 in short, removes chemical tags from other proteins. The team found it strips one such tag from the pore's regulator protein.

Mice lacking the enzyme showed more pore opening and swollen mitochondria in heart cells as they aged. By just over a year old, their hearts were thickened and scarred, and they fared worse under added heart stress. A drug that blocks the pore regulator rescued the cell defect. The work points to the tag removal step as a guard against heart aging, and as a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc3052180:
Hoelzer, Moreno Switt, and Wiedmann reviewed in 2011 how people catch Salmonella infections directly from animals, rather than from food. Most cases of this illness are foodborne, but each year many come from contact at home, on farms, in zoos, and in vet clinics. Sick animals shed the germ more often, yet healthy looking animals can shed it for long periods too.

Risk depends on the animal species, its age and care, and on the person's own vulnerability, with young children and those with weak immunity at most risk. Some Salmonella types stick to one host species while others cross easily between hosts. Basic hygiene, such as hand washing after animal contact, cuts much of the risk. The authors note the public often does not know these risks, and they set out practical steps for homes, farms, and public animal displays.
europmc-pmc3106380:
Mohamed Daabiss published a 2011 review in the Indian Journal of Anaesthesia on a grading system used before surgery. The system, set up by a United States society of anaesthesia doctors, sorts patients into five classes by overall health, with an added mark for urgent cases. Daabiss asks how well doctors apply it in practice.

Studies show that grades often differ between doctors judging the same patient, even for common problems. Yet higher grades still track with more complications, longer stays, and higher death rates after many kinds of surgery. The review weighs calls to revise the scale and argues for clearer guidance, so a simple grade stays useful for planning, audits, and research.
europmc-pmc3117980:
Alex Becker and colleagues linked a hallmark Alzheimer protein to brain thinning in healthy older adults in a 2011 paper in Annals of Neurology. The protein builds up years before memory fails, and brain shrinkage follows a known pattern in the disease. The team asked whether build-up already tracks with thinning in people who still think normally.

Brain scans of nearly ninety healthy older adults and a smaller group with mild disease showed that higher protein build-up rose with age. In healthy adults it also matched thinner cortex in rear brain regions, in much the same pattern seen in mild disease. Shrinkage of a deep memory structure linked less steadily. The results suggest disease-like brain change begins well before symptoms.
europmc-pmc3129680:
Alessandro Varani and colleagues built a web pipeline for labelling jumping DNA in bacterial genomes in a 2011 paper in Genome Biology. These small mobile stretches copy themselves around genomes, reshaping them and spreading traits, yet genome reports routinely mislabel or skip them. Manual expert labelling cannot keep pace with sequencing.

Their pipeline combines prediction and labelling tools that follow the main expert database standards, handling one genome or many at once. It shows each element's setting in the genome and draws a map of their spread. Protein and DNA features are both recorded, which correct labelling requires. The authors offer the tool freely online, aiming to lift the quality of bacterial genome annotation overall.
europmc-pmc3149080:
Carol Bennett and colleagues found survey research lacks shared reporting rules in a 2010 paper in PLoS Medicine. Surveys underpin opinion, health, and policy research, yet sloppy reporting hides how a survey was run and blocks fair judgement of its results. Other research fields have adopted minimum reporting checklists; the team asked whether surveys had any.

They searched journal instructions and the published literature for guidance, reviewed evidence on survey reporting quality, and examined recent self-completed surveys against quality criteria. Guidance proved sparse and inconsistent, with no agreement on an optimal standard. Weak reporting of sampling, questions, and response handling was common. The authors lay the groundwork for developing a proper checklist so survey findings can be appraised and compared with confidence.
europmc-pmc3275480:
Jonathan Street and colleagues identified exosomes in human cerebrospinal fluid and profiled their protein cargo, in this 2012 paper in the Journal of Translational Medicine. Exosomes are tiny vesicles cells release, packed with proteins and RNA, already studied in several body fluids as a possible source of disease markers. Whether the fluid bathing the brain and spinal cord carries them had not been established.

Fluid from five surgical patients was concentrated by ultracentrifugation. Marker proteins, density behavior, and electron microscopy all confirmed genuine exosomes. Mass spectrometry detected a modest set of protein signals per person; about a third appeared in every participant, a third in only one, and quantities varied widely between people. The authors call the fluid's exosomes a promising new reservoir for neurological biomarkers, while warning that isolation methods need refinement to tame the variability.
europmc-pmc3280380:
Rebecca Dragovic and colleagues adapted nanoparticle tracking analysis to measure the tiny vesicles cells shed, in this 2011 paper in Nanomedicine. Microvesicles and exosomes carry messages between cells and promise diagnostic value, but measuring them was a bottleneck: electron microscopy is not quantitative and flow cytometry cannot see the smallest vesicles. The tracking method watches individual particles jiggle under a microscope and infers size from their motion.

Working with placental vesicles and human plasma, the team showed the method sizes vesicles down to about fifty nanometers, far below flow cytometry's floor, and counts them directly. Adding fluorescence, with antibody-tagged quantum dots stuck to chosen surface proteins, let them phenotype vesicles as well as size them. The authors offer the approach as a faster, more sensitive standard for a fast-growing field.
europmc-pmc3314680:
Partinen and a large Finnish team charted the same narcolepsy surge from the clinic side, reporting in 2012. Narcolepsy in young children was once very rare in Finland, with only a handful of cases expected each year. In early 2010, sleep clinics suddenly saw dozens of children struck by rapid onset sleepiness, prompting a nationwide count of cases from 2002 onward.

Fifty four children under seventeen were diagnosed in 2010 alone, a rate many times higher than the yearly average of the previous decade. Almost all had received the Pandemrix flu vaccine weeks to months before symptoms began, and all who were gene tested carried a known narcolepsy risk gene. Most also developed sudden muscle weakness, and emotional symptoms were common. Adult rates stayed flat, which the authors say points to the vaccine, likely with other triggers, acting on susceptible children.
europmc-pmc3380580:
Jjingo and colleagues tackled a puzzle in 2012 about DNA methylation, a chemical mark that usually silences genes when it sits at their start. Inside gene bodies the mark is even more common, yet there it tracks with higher activity. The team combined genome-wide data on methylation, gene activity, and chromosome state.

Genes carried more methylation than the stretches between them. The link with activity rose then fell: middling genes were the most methylated, while the quietest and busiest genes carried little. Blocking stray internal start sites explained only a small part of the pattern. The authors propose that access by the marking enzymes shapes most gene-body methylation instead.
europmc-pmc3428680:
Deng and co-authors built a math framework in 2012 for drawing ecological networks inside microbial communities from high-throughput data. Who interacts with whom in a microbe community matters for ecology, but extreme diversity and uncultured members make the structure hard to define. Their method borrows random matrix theory to set network links automatically.

The approach proved robust to noise, a chronic problem in sequencing data. Applied to soil communities under long-term warming, the networks under both warmed and control conditions showed the classic scale-free, small-world, modular shapes. Temperature and soil acidity emerged as key forces shaping the interactions. The whole pipeline was released openly online for other researchers to use.
europmc-pmc3467280:
Uematsu and colleagues charted how two deep brain regions grow from infancy into early adulthood, in a 2012 PLoS ONE study. The amygdala helps process emotion, and the hippocampus supports memory, yet few studies had measured them in babies. The team used MRI scans from more than one hundred healthy people aged one month to twenty-five years.

Both regions grew fast in the first years of life, then leveled off, reaching peak size around the start of the teens. Girls reached peak amygdala size about a year and a half before boys. Both sexes showed a larger hippocampus on the right side, while only males showed that tilt in the amygdala. Uematsu's maps give a healthy baseline for judging development in disorders.
europmc-pmc3493380:
Brucellosis, a bacterial illness caught from livestock, lacks a trustworthy global count, and Anna S. Dean and five colleagues review the frequency evidence for the World Health Organization in 2012. They search 33 databases for studies from 1990 to 2010.

From 2,385 papers, strict screening leaves 60 for quality assessment and only 29 strong enough to analyze. Usable data come from just 15 countries across five broad regions. Incidence swings widely between and even within countries. Half the studies report incidence directly; half report blood-test prevalence, which the team converts. The patchy record itself is a finding: a fair disability estimate for brucellosis must rest on thin ground.
europmc-pmc3532080:
Sequencing reads often carry leftover adapter DNA, and Stinus Lindgreen presents AdapterRemoval in 2012 to clean them. Adapters are the synthetic handles attached for sequencing; reads that run into them corrupt mapping and variant calls downstream.

The tool handles single-end and paired-end data. It finds and strips adapter pieces from either end of a read, merges paired reads that overlap, and can trim low-quality bases on request. Settings tune it to different platforms and experiments, all in the standard FASTQ format. Tests show it trims both data types well. In a field producing floods of reads, this solo-authored note supplies a flexible piece of plumbing.
europmc-pmc3542080:
Gut microbiome types may be an artifact of how you cluster, and Omry Koren leads a nine-author team stress-testing the enterotype idea in 2013. They re-analyze Human Microbiome Project data plus sixteen other studies, varying clustering methods, distance measures, marker picking, sequencing depth, and data type.

At most body sites, key bacterial genera form smooth abundance gradients, not discrete camps. The gut shows a two-humped distribution and the vagina several humps, but not every workflow reveals even those. Enterotype detection, they conclude, depends as much on analytic choices as on biology. The guide warns microbiome researchers against carving continua into types and then believing the carving.
europmc-pmc3572580:
Anita Thapar and colleagues reviewed the causes of ADHD in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry in 2013, focusing on work since 1997. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder still draws argument about its roots: genes, risks before and around birth, family and social conditions, and toxins have all been blamed. Their aim was to weigh which risks are likely causal and which are only fellow travelers.

No single factor explains the disorder, they conclude. It runs in families and is strongly heritable, and its genetic side overlaps with autism and other developmental conditions. Large rare gene variants, some small common ones, extreme early hardship, lead exposure, and low birth weight or early birth carry the most consistent support, yet none is proven fully causal. Many reported environmental links remain mere associations, and newer designs are undercutting some older claims. The review separates firm ground from fashion.
europmc-pmc3591180:
Daria Capece and colleagues reviewed the immune neighborhood of liver cancer in BioMed Research International in 2013. Hepatocellular carcinoma, among the most common and deadly cancers, grows out of long-running inflammation, making it a model case of a tumor fed by its surroundings. Macrophages that settle inside tumors are a chief part of that environment. In the tumor setting they usually take a healing-style form that, perversely, helps the cancer.

In that form they pour out signals that grow new blood vessels, help tumor cells spread, and mute the adaptive immune attack. Patients whose tumors hold many such macrophages fare worse. Three signaling pathways, NF-kappaB, STAT-3, and HIF-1, carry much of the conversation between cancer cells and macrophages. The review gathers what is known about the signals each side sends and weighs where blocking the crosstalk might slow the disease.
europmc-pmc3605280:
Vidisha Tripathi and colleagues pinned a cell-cycle job on a famous noncoding RNA in PLoS Genetics in 2013. MALAT1 is a long RNA that never becomes protein, yet it piles up in cancers and tracks with fast cell growth. In normal human fibroblasts, its level rose and fell with the cell cycle itself. Scanning gene activity after removing MALAT1 showed it steers a battery of division genes and is required to pass two checkpoints, entering DNA copying and completing division.

Removing MALAT1 woke the guardian protein p53 and its target genes, and the division faults rose or fell with p53 levels, marking it as the main go-between. One victim stood out: B-MYB, a cancer-linked switch for late division genes, dropped because splicing factors mishandled its message after MALAT1 loss. The work draws a line from a noncoding RNA to the pace of growth itself.
europmc-pmc3626880:
Souhel Najjar and colleagues reviewed immune activity inside mental illness in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2013. The line between brain disease and mental illness keeps thinning. Autoimmune diseases such as lupus plainly cause mental symptoms. A newer group, synaptic autoimmune encephalitis, can look like pure psychosis and be missed. In parallel, immune problems keep surfacing in depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and obsessive-compulsive disorder, illnesses long blamed on brain chemistry alone.

The chapters assemble human and animal evidence tying immune activity to each condition, from antibody attacks on brain receptors to effects on mood circuits and oxidative stress. The faults in glutamate and monoamine systems may themselves sit downstream of immune triggers in at least some patients. The authors argue that mapping how social stress, genes, immunity, and brain chemistry interact could reveal shared causes. That could open treatments that prevent illness or ease symptoms, aimed at the immune arm.
europmc-pmc3677880:
Spotting where chromatin marks differ between two states gets a dedicated tool from Shen, Shao, Liu, Maze, Feng and Nestler in a 2013 PLoS One article. The data come from ChIP-seq, a method that maps where marked proteins sit on DNA across the genome. Comparing health and disease, or drug and control, calls for software that handles repeat samples well. Their program, diffReps, finds differing sites with or without such repeats and runs from a simple command line.

Two companion tools ship with it, for labelling sites and finding hotspots. Tests covered a human cell line comparison from a public atlas project and mouse brain tissue from cocaine- versus salt-treated animals. In both, the program proved highly sensitive at picking true differences out of noisy data.
europmc-pmc3860380:
Mary Ann C. Stephens and Gary Wand review stress hormones and alcohol in Alcohol Research: Current Reviews, dated 2012 in the record. Stress has long been tied to heavy drinking and relapse. The HPA axis, a hormone chain that runs the stress response, is a prime suspect, with cortisol as its main hormone.

Genes, early life, and current stress all tune the axis. Its control slips in problem drinking, in ways that shift with the stage of dependence. Cortisol can stir the brain's reward system, which may boost alcohol's pull, and it can push habit-based learning, which feeds relapse risk. Cortisol levels during abstinence may even flag who is likely to relapse. The review sorts this mixed picture into a stage-by-stage view.
europmc-pmc3876980:
Iben Lundgaard, with a team of co-authors, studies myelin formation in PLoS Biology in 2013. Myelin is the fatty wrap that speeds signals along nerve fibers, made by cells called oligodendrocytes. What tells a given fiber to get wrapped was not known. Two growth signals get the focus here.

The signals, neuregulin and BDNF, switch the wrapping cells between two modes. In the base mode, wrapping goes on with no need for neuron activity.
