With the signals present, wrapping grows activity-driven: active fibers release glutamate, and a glutamate sensor on the wrapping cell is required. The switch helps explain how busy circuits gain more insulation. It also names targets for diseases where myelin is lost.
europmc-pmc3936280:
Francisco Jose Grajales III and four colleagues guide readers on social media in health care. Their review appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2014. Social media tools are part of daily life in most rich and middle-income lands. Yet many health workers barely know them. Clinicians, managers, colleges, and ministries often miss both the uses and the risks.

The article is a review and a tutorial at once. Case studies show where social media is already at work. Uses include contact with patients and pro-to-pro networking. Education, public health campaigns, and research also appear. The authors set out the risks in plain terms. Privacy breaches are one. Blurred pro boundaries are another. They close with ways to cut those risks. Health groups get a grounded map before they jump in.
europmc-pmc4011680:
Tim M. Blackburn and a large team of co-authors propose one scale for rating the harm done by alien species, in PLoS Biology in 2014. People keep moving species beyond their home ranges, and many such species reshape the places they reach. Harm has been measured in many unlike ways, which blocks fair comparison across species and places.

Their scheme sorts species by the size of their environmental impact, from minor to massive. It can be applied to any group of living things, at any scale, with any sound measure of change. Impact covers harm to native species numbers, gene pools, behaviour, food webs, and the workings of whole ecosystems. A shared scale lets officials rank threats and aim scarce control funds where harm runs largest. It also lets studies in one place inform choices in another. The authors present the scheme as a common language for a global problem.
europmc-pmc4053980:
James R. Wagner and five colleagues untangle how DNA sequence, methylation, and gene activity vary together in human skin cells, in Genome Biology in 2014. The three layers are linked, but which drives which in normal, untransformed cells was murky.

Fibroblasts from over sixty unrelated donors were assayed on all three layers. Only a small share of the most variable methylation sites traced to nearby DNA variants, usually within a short stretch. Thousands of activity-linked regions were mapped the same way. In under a tenth of them, the driving variant also moved methylation. Methylation and activity often rose or fell together with no variant in sight, and not always in the textbook direction. The tie ran strongest in development genes, including all four HOX clusters. Chromatin marks, not position alone, best predicted the sign of the link.
europmc-pmc4080980:
R. M. de Ferrars and colleagues traced what happens in the body after people swallow anthocyanins, the pigments that colour many berries and may protect the heart. Their study appeared in the British Journal of Pharmacology in 2014. These compounds are unstable at neutral acidity, so they were expected to break down heavily.

Eight healthy men took a single labelled dose of one common anthocyanin, and blood, urine, and faeces were collected for forty-eight hours. The team found seventeen labelled compounds, including breakdown products and a chain of further metabolites, with hippuric acid among the main ones. Levels peaked anywhere from two to thirty hours after intake and cleared at very different rates. Knowing these time courses is essential for designing diet studies, the authors say.
europmc-pmc4109880:
Peter J. Hotez, Christopher J. L. Murray, Mohsen Naghavi, and a large team interpreted the Global Burden of Disease Study 2010 for neglected tropical diseases. Their analysis appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2014. The study, published in late 2012, was the broadest attempt yet to measure almost three hundred diseases and risks.

Its yardstick, the disability-adjusted life year, combines early death and years lived with disability. Most neglected tropical diseases disable rather than kill, so this metric is one of the few that captures their chronic toll. Even so, the authors argue, the numbers understate harms such as stigma and lost schooling. They spell out what the estimates mean for funding and control of these long-overlooked infections.
europmc-pmc4127280:
Ravi Kant Upadhyay, in a solo review, took stock of ways to carry drugs past the blood-brain barrier into the brain. His review came out in BioMed Research International in 2014. The barrier is the tight wall of the brain's blood tubes. It guards the brain, but it also blocks most drugs.

The routes he covers span germ drugs, cancer drugs, nerve peptides, and large proteins. Sound waves can help open the wall at a chosen spot. A long list of tiny carriers gets a full airing. It spans fat bubbles, soap-like balls, tree-shaped bits, and carbon tubes. He urges finer tuning of the carriers we have. He also wants new, small ones that do not cut or harm. Then a full dose could reach brain growths, brain germs, and worn brain states.
europmc-pmc4211380:
Tessa Gargett and Michael P. Brown reviewed a safety switch for engineered T cells in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2014. Doctors can fit a patient's T cells with a chimeric antigen receptor that steers them onto cancer cells. The same targeting can strike healthy tissue that shares the marker, a dangerous side effect with no easy brake.

The switch is a gene for inducible caspase-9, an enzyme that triggers cell suicide when a small drug, AP1903, locks two copies together. Cells carrying the switch, above all the most activated ones, die fast after the drug is given. Early trials found the switch reliable. The review covers a third-generation receptor aimed at the GD2 marker on melanoma and related tumours, with the switch built in, then entering phase 1 testing.
europmc-pmc4229780:
Cheau Yih Tan, Han Kiat Ho, and four co-authors tested stem cell exosomes for liver repair in Stem Cell Research and Therapy in 2014. Fluid from mesenchymal stem cells protects injured tissue, and exosomes, the tiny sacs in that fluid, may carry the benefit in a form easier to give as a drug.

In mice poisoned with carbon tetrachloride, exosomes given at the same time lessened liver damage and raised a marker of liver cell division. In dish models of liver injury from paracetamol and from hydrogen peroxide, exosome-treated cells survived better. The treated cells switched on the early genes of liver regeneration and dialed up protective responses. The team presents exosomes as candidates for drug-induced liver injury, a common cause of liver failure.
europmc-pmc4283580:
Jean-Philippe Fortin and seven co-authors present a better way to clean up data from a widely used DNA methylation array. Their study appeared in Genome Biology in 2014. The array measures methylation at hundreds of thousands of sites, but technical noise can swamp real signals, and cancer samples pose a special problem because their methylation shifts across the whole genome.

Their method, functional normalization, uses the array's built in control probes to strip out technical variation while keeping true global change. Tested on cancer atlas data and a large case control study, it beat existing methods at giving results that repeat across experiments. The approach can transfer to other array platforms that carry similar control probes.
europmc-pmc4340880:
Martin H Teicher, Angelika Parigger, and Christian Schmahl built a scale that records not just whether a child was mistreated, but when. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. Childhood abuse and neglect can bend brain development and raise later disease risk, yet older questionnaires lump all years together and miss sensitive periods.

The MACE scale covers ten types of maltreatment, from emotional neglect to sexual abuse and witnessing violence at home, scored year by year through childhood. It was developed and tuned in over a thousand participants using modern test theory. Researchers can now ask which ages carry the deepest risk for each kind of harm, a step toward timing support where it counts most.
europmc-pmc4375780:
Kyung-Ok Cho and co-authors tested whether new neurons born in the adult brain help epilepsy take hold, in Nature Communications in 2015. After a severe brain insult, seizures can become chronic and memory suffers. The hippocampus keeps making new neurons in adulthood, and after an insult that growth goes awry. The team removed adult neurogenesis in mice before triggering acute seizures with a chemical, then watched what followed over months.

Mice without the new neurons developed chronic seizures less often, and the protection lasted nearly a year. Their epilepsy-linked memory problems also returned to normal levels. Unchecked, faulty new neurons thus play a key part in turning a single insult into lasting epilepsy. Targeting that aberrant growth, the authors suggest, could cut repeat seizures and restore thinking after such an insult.
europmc-pmc4383880:
Warren Kibbe and co-authors described the 2015 growth of the Human Disease Ontology in Nucleic Acids Research. The ontology gives diseases standard names and stable identifiers, organized by cause, so that genetic, protein, drug, and trait data can be compared through a shared disease lens. Since 2012 the resource had 192 revisions and added 760 terms, and about a third of all terms now carry written definitions.

Use spread beyond the founding team: the community of contributors grew by more than half in two years, filing hundreds of term requests and guiding curation. Editing was moving to a multi-editor model using shared ontology software. Closer work with the Human Phenotype Ontology and mouse informatics groups was planned. A shared disease vocabulary quietly underpins many cross-database studies.
europmc-pmc4459080:
Antonis Koussounadis, Simon Langdon, In Hwa Um, David Harrison, and V Anne Smith tested a basic assumption of gene studies in Scientific Reports in 2015. Studies routinely flag genes whose message RNA rises or falls with treatment, assuming the matching protein will follow. Across the genome that assumption fares poorly, since message and protein levels often correlate weakly, which has cast doubt on message-only studies.

In an ovarian cancer graft model, the team measured messages and proteins for a set of genes under four drug treatments and in untreated controls, across a time course. Messages that changed with treatment matched their protein products far better than messages that stayed flat. In other words, the very genes a study would single out are the ones whose protein follows. The result restores some confidence in differential expression studies for finding treatment effects.
europmc-pmc4471680:
Kathleen Metzler, Christian Goosmann, Aleksandra Lubojemska, Arturo Zychlinsky, and Venizelos Papayannopoulos uncovered how a neutrophil weapon is released inside the cell, in Cell Reports in 2014. Neutrophils, front-line immune cells, store germ-killing proteins in granules. When they cast out neutrophil extracellular traps, webs of DNA that snare microbes, an enzyme called elastase must travel from granules to the nucleus by an unknown route that needs reactive oxygen.

The team shows reactive oxygen frees elastase from a membrane-bound complex, with a second enzyme, myeloperoxidase, required for the release and for switching elastase on. In the open cell fluid, elastase first chews up the actin skeleton, freezing cell movement, then enters the nucleus to loosen DNA for the traps. Granules, it turns out, hold machinery that moves cargo across membranes without fusing, a new kind of delivery system.
europmc-pmc4543480:
Douglas G. Walker and Lih-Fen Lue review the trouble with labeling microglia states in diseased human brains, in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy in 2015. Microglia, the brain's resident macrophages, change with inflammation, a shared feature of diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. In lab work, macrophage states are sorted into named classes, M1 and several M2 forms, each with its own marker set.

Human brain work lags: the markers on hand are few and tell only part of the story. The most used one, HLA-DR, lights up microglia in many shapes and states, so it cannot pin down a class alone. The authors survey what each available marker can and cannot prove, and warn against importing dish-based labels onto human tissue too confidently.
europmc-pmc4595480:
Joel Pearson and three colleagues published a 2015 review of mental imagery, the act of picturing things without seeing them. Imagery helps people remember, plan, navigate, and decide. The review pulls together work from behaviour studies, brain imaging, and clinical care. It appeared in Trends in Cognitive Sciences.

Brain scans show that imagined and real images share patterns even in the earliest visual area of the brain. Imagery acts like a weak form of seeing, the authors argue. In mental disorders, vivid or unwanted images can drive symptoms. Clinicians can also use imagery as part of treatment. The review gives readers a map of how imagery works and why it matters for both research and therapy.
europmc-pmc4608380:
Shuko Takeda, together with colleagues, released a 2015 study hunting for the form of tau protein that spreads between neurons in Alzheimer's disease. Tau tangles advance through the brain in a set pattern as the disease worsens. The spreading form was unknown. The team tested tau taken from human Alzheimer's brains and from transgenic mice. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

A rare, soluble, high-molecular-weight form of tau carrying phosphate marks stood out. Though scarce, neurons took it up readily, moved it along their fibres, and passed it to connected neurons. Other tau forms did not spread this way. Naming this species gives drug developers a precise target and may lead to a marker that tracks disease spread in patients.
europmc-pmc4700580:
Matteo Lambertini, Lucia Del Mastro, Maria C. Pescio, and a large expert panel issued shared advice on cancer and fertility in BMC Medicine in 2016. Cancer survival has improved, so more young patients face a hard question: treatment may cost them the chance to have children. Guidelines already urge early talks about that risk. In April 2015, specialists from several European countries met in Genova, Italy, to settle ten contested issues in the field.

Their ten recommendations rest on literature reviews plus the panel's own data. Freezing sperm and freezing eggs or embryos stand as standard options; shielding the gonads with drugs and freezing gonadal tissue remain experimental. The panel is frank that most advice rests on weak evidence, with few large trials. Joining registries and ongoing studies, they urge, is how stronger answers will come. The paper helps doctors counsel young patients with one voice.
europmc-pmc4702780:
Manish Sud, Eoin Fahy, Dawn Cotter, and nine colleagues introduced the Metabolomics Workbench in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. Metabolomics measures the small molecules in a sample to read the state of a living system. Studies pile up data in many formats from many species, with no shared home. The Workbench is a public repository built to hold that data and metadata together, spanning more than twenty species from humans to microbes.

Depositors can store mass spectrometry and magnetic resonance data beside study details, protocols, and tutorials. A structure database links the measured metabolites to their chemistry, so studies can be compared across labs and platforms. Analysis tools run on the same site. The project sits inside a national program to coordinate the field's data. Its aim is simple: make metabolomics results findable, reusable, and teachable instead of stranded on single lab computers.
europmc-pmc4733280:
Jasreet Hundal, Beatriz M. Carreno, Allegra A. Petti, and four colleagues presented pVAC-Seq in Genome Medicine in 2016. Cancers carry mutations that create neoantigens, altered protein fragments the immune system can attack as foreign. Finding which mutations yield real targets is the bottleneck for personalized cancer vaccines and cell therapies. pVAC-Seq is a software workflow that joins a tumor's DNA and RNA sequencing data to call candidate neoantigens in one streamlined pass.

The pipeline weighs mutation presence, gene activity, and predicted binding to the patient's immune presentation molecules. It is built to bend to different study designs rather than forcing one recipe. The authors connect the tool to recent checkpoint drug successes, where mutation load predicts response, arguing that naming the exact targets is the next step. The software is freely available, aimed at labs designing patient-specific immunotherapies.
europmc-pmc4762880:
Michael Ramirez leads a large author team in Nature Communications in 2016 on how lung cancer cells escape a targeted drug. Some cells survive drug treatment by going quiet, growing almost not at all. These persister cells were suspected to be a waiting room from which true resistance later steps out, but how wide the escape routes ran was unknown.

Starting from one drug-sensitive lung cancer line, the team grew colonies that beat the drug erlotinib after passing through the quiet state. Screens and gene reads showed the colonies had not found one trick but many, among them the very routes seen in patients. The quiet state, the authors conclude, does not narrow the paths to resistance; it banks cells from which many paths can open.
europmc-pmc4786780:
Elise M. Miner and five co-authors report a new catalyst material in Nature Communications in 2016. Fuel cells need a catalyst to run the oxygen reaction at their cathode, and platinum, the standard, is costly. Cheaper metal-and-nitrogen sites work but are hard to build in exact, repeatable form.

Their material is a metal-organic framework, a crystal sponge of nickel and an organic linker, that conducts electricity on its own. Its nickel sites sit in the flat four-nitrogen grip known to drive the oxygen reaction. In alkaline tests the crystal matched the best non-platinum catalysts and held up under long runs. Because framework chemistry is tunable part by part, the authors present it as a design platform for future fuel cell catalysts.
europmc-pmc4839080:
Claire L. Boulangé, Ana Luisa Neves, Julien Chilloux, Jeremy K. Nicholson, and Marc-Emmanuel Dumas reviewed the gut microbiota in Genome Medicine in 2016. The human gut holds over 100 trillion microbial cells that help set how the body uses energy. Shifts in that community have been tied to obesity and metabolic disease, but the exact links in people stay unclear.

The review pulls together what is known about how gut microbes affect fat storage, energy balance, and the immune system. It weighs animal work, including germ-free rodents, against human data. The authors stress that strong clues exist, yet firm proof of cause in people needs more work before microbe-based treatments can be designed with care.
europmc-pmc4854480:
Nathalie Gideon and co-authors built and tested a 12-item short form of a standard eating disorder questionnaire in 2016. The full form runs 28 items, too long for session-by-session tracking in care. Answers came from 489 people aged 18 to 72 treated at three British specialist services, plus 559 students and charity volunteers for checks.

Careful item analysis and expert review cut the form to 12 items, named the EDE-QS. Scores held together well and stayed steady over time in tests. The short form tracks the full form closely while taking far less time. Clinics gain a quick tool to watch progress and catch slips during treatment.
europmc-pmc4855980:
Surendra K. Sah, K. R. Reddy, and Jiaxu Li reviewed abscisic acid, a plant hormone called ABA, as a route to hardier crops in 2016. Drought, salt, and cold cut yields worldwide, and feeding a growing world population needs tougher plants. ABA helps plants adapt: it steers leaf pore closing, seed storage, and stress defense genes.

The review traces ABA action from signal sensing to gene switches under drought, salt, and cold. Engineering ABA paths is one chosen strategy among several for stress-proof crops. Strengths and risks both get weighed, since the same hormone that guards water also slows growth. The map guides breeders aiming for yield that survives harsh seasons.
europmc-pmc4882480:
Alexandru D. Grigore and co-authors argued in the Journal of Clinical Medicine in 2016 that tumor budding, small cancer cell clusters at a tumor's edge, reflects a partial cell identity switch. Buds appear in many cancers and track with poor outcomes. The switch in question, EMT, turns sheet-bound cells loose. Yet budding lacks one shared definition, one scoring method, and agreed patient splits.

Cells in buds seem stuck halfway: part sheet cell, part rover, a blend that may aid spread while keeping group traits. The review weighs the proof for partial switching and the steps needed before bud counts can guide care as a standard sign. Clear rules come first; the biology is catching up.
europmc-pmc4975080:
Gerjo Kok and eight co-authors present a taxonomy of behavior change methods drawn from Intervention Mapping. Their paper appeared in Health Psychology Review in 2016. Intervention Mapping is a planning system for health programs. Its method list sorts techniques such as feedback, modeling, and goal setting by the theory behind them. Each method works only when set conditions, called parameters, are met. The authors argue the list can double as a coding taxonomy for research.

A shared coding system would let reviewers tag published interventions the same way. That in turn would sharpen meta-analyses that ask which methods work. The authors warn that sloppy translation of a method into practice can make a sound method look weak. They propose a minimal set of traits every intervention report should state. The paper aims at cleaner evidence about what changes behavior.
europmc-pmc4983380:
Ahlke Heydemann, writing alone, argues for standard protocols for the high fat diet mouse model of type 2 diabetes. Her overview appeared in the Journal of Diabetes Research in 2016. Type 2 diabetes is a worldwide epidemic still growing. Mouse models let researchers test causes and treatments, and diet induced obesity mimics how most human cases arise. Genetic models exist, but the high fat diet route matches the human disease's origin, course, and treatment options best, she argues.

The model's weakness is practice, not principle. Feeding takes months to produce the full disease picture, and labs use clashing diets, durations, and measures. Mouse strain differences add more noise. Heydemann proposes a standard set of feeding protocols and analysis steps. Shared standards, she argues, would let studies be compared cleanly and would make preclinical therapy tests, such as those of resveratrol, far more informative.
europmc-pmc5021180:
A. Houlden and seven co-authors report in Brain, Behavior, and Immunity in 2016 that brain injury reshapes gut microbes in mice. The gut community helps guard the body and calm inflammation, and it can affect the brain, but whether the brain talks back was far less clear. The team injured the mouse brain, by blocked blood flow or by trauma, and tracked the microbes of the caecum, a pouch of the large gut.

Both kinds of injury shifted the gut community in set ways. Goblet cells, which make the gut's mucus layer, changed along with levels of noradrenaline, a signal of the automatic nervous system. The results are the first to show that a change in brain state alone can drive specific gut changes, likely through that automatic wiring and the mucus system. The link may matter for the infections and slow recovery that often follow human brain injury.
europmc-pmc5051080:
Yongkun Sun and ten co-authors run a first human trial of the cancer drug anlotinib in the Journal of Hematology & Oncology in 2016. Anlotinib is a pill that blocks several growth switches at once, above all ones tumors use to build blood vessels. The trial enrolled patients with advanced solid tumors that no longer answered standard care, testing dose and schedule for safety, blood levels, and early signs of effect.

A schedule of two weeks on and one week off, at twelve milligrams daily, was chosen to carry forward. The drug lingered long in the body and built up with repeated doses. In the expansion group, three of twenty assessable patients saw tumors shrink partly, and fourteen held stable, most with some shrinkage. The team judges the profile manageable and the early tumor control broad enough to justify larger trials.
europmc-pmc5065680:
Thomas Desautels and eleven co-authors present a machine learning tool for predicting sepsis in JMIR Medical Informatics in 2016. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, kills many hospital patients, and catching it early guides treatment, yet reliable prediction has stayed elusive. Their system, InSight, works from a minimal set of bedside measures: vital signs, blood oxygen, a coma score, and age, with no lab results needed.

Tested on a large public intensive care database under the current Sepsis-3 definitions, InSight outscored five standard bedside and severity scores at forecasting which patients would turn septic hours ahead. It also held up when random readings were deleted to mimic messy real records. The authors show it beating even the complex scores that depend on laboratory values at admission. An editorial masthead in the journal's front matter is sometimes mistaken for this article's authorship; the work is Desautels and colleagues'.
europmc-pmc5076380:
Sandra M. Eldridge and six co-authors, with the PAFS consensus group, extend the CONSORT reporting standard to pilot and feasibility trials in The BMJ in 2016. CONSORT checklists improve how trials are reported. Small randomized studies run before a main trial have different aims, judging whether the big trial can work rather than whether the treatment does, and their reporting had clear weaknesses.

The extension adapts most original items, drops some, and adds others, such as how participants were found and consented, and any preset criteria for proceeding to the main trial. It covers any small-scale randomized forerunner study, whatever its design or the label its authors use. The group built it through a Delphi survey, a consensus meeting, and piloting of the checklist itself. Their hope: reports that state plainly what was tested, what was learned, and how the decision to proceed was made.
europmc-pmc5080780:
Jamie Ross, Fiona Stevenson, Rosa Lau, and Elizabeth Murray update a review of reviews on putting e-health into practice, in Implementation Science in 2016. Governments spend heavily on digital health, yet getting systems into routine care keeps failing. Earlier reviews each covered one technology, setting, or condition, leaving no single map of what helps or hinders. This update searched five databases for systematic reviews from 2009 to 2014.

Forty-four reviews, mostly from North America and Europe, covered records, decision support, and other tools across primary, hospital, and home care. Sorting the findings by an implementation framework, the authors locate success factors at five levels: the technology itself, the wider setting, the organization, the professionals, and the process of change. Fit with inner and outer context deserves special care. They also flag neglected topics, including how systems are sourced, whether staff can trial them, and how patients take part.
europmc-pmc5108580:
Hui Li and a large team of co-authors tested whether MRI scans can reveal breast cancer subtypes, reporting in npj Breast Cancer in 2016. Subtype, set by hormone and growth receptors, guides treatment, but it normally needs tissue tests. The team applied radiomics, computer measures of tumor shape and texture, to scans in a public cancer data set.

They analyzed 91 scans of proven invasive cancers and trained a classifier on the extracted features. Scan features separated estrogen receptor positive from negative tumors quite well, and did moderately for other receptors and for triple-negative tumors. More aggressive cancers tended to be larger and more uneven in how they took up contrast, and texture tracked subtype even within size groups. The authors see a possible non-invasive signature for sorting tumors.
europmc-pmc5115280:
Praveen Thoniyot, Mein Jin Tan, Anis Abdul Karim, David James Young, and Xian Jun Loh reviewed materials that mix nanoparticles into water-rich polymer gels, writing in Advanced Science in 2015. Each part alone has limits: gels are soft and weak, while nanoparticles clump and can raise safety worries.

Combined, the two can cover each other's flaws: the gel gains strength and new functions, and the particles stay spread out and contained. The review covers metals, metal oxides, and polymer particles set in gels. It explains how such composites are made and designed. It also maps where they might serve: speeding chemical reactions, sensing, and drug delivery. Medicine and cleaning polluted water are further uses. It also weighs the safety and design problems that still hold the materials back.
europmc-pmc5123280:
Cynthia Rothblum-Oviatt, Jennifer Wright, Maureen A. Lefton-Greif, Sharon A. McGrath-Morrow, Thomas O. Crawford, and Howard M. Lederman reviewed ataxia telangiectasia in the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases in 2016. The inherited disorder, found in roughly one in 40,000 to 100,000 births, combines worsening balance problems, small dilated blood vessels, weak immunity, cancer risk, and sensitivity to radiation.

The review sets out how the disease varies with age, from toddlers who wobble as they learn to walk to later lung, feeding, skin, and hormone problems. Its cause is faults in the ATM gene, whose protein coordinates the response to broken DNA. The authors explain how doctors suspect and confirm the diagnosis, which look-alike disorders to rule out, and how care is organized.
europmc-pmc5133080:
Nicolai Petry and seven co-authors rechecked how much anemia stems from iron shortage, reporting in Nutrients in 2016. Textbooks long assumed iron deficiency causes half of all anemia, with blood disorders and infections making up most of the rest. The team pooled national surveys from 23 countries across development levels.

For preschool children, iron deficiency accounted for about 25 percent of anemia; for non-pregnant women of childbearing age, about 37 percent. The share fell lower where anemia was very common, especially in rural areas, and where inflammation was high. The authors conclude the true share is well below the assumed half in the countries studied. They urge programs to base anemia strategy on each country's own data, not on a global guess.
europmc-pmc5259880:
Helena Xicoy, Bé Wieringa, and Gerard J. M. Martens systematically reviewed the SH-SY5Y cell line in Parkinson's disease research in Molecular Neurodegeneration in 2017. Parkinson's kills dopamine neurons, which are hard to grow from patients, so most lab work uses this human neuroblastoma cell line, prized for its human origin, nerve-like traits, and easy upkeep. Yet labs handle it in clashing ways.

The review gathers published studies and compares their methods. It covers cell sources, culture media, methods for maturing the cells toward a dopamine-like state, tricks used to mimic Parkinson's, and how often findings were checked in other models. Results varied partly because the cells respond unevenly to the same maturing treatment depending on their source and handling history, and few papers show proper control images. The authors offer the survey as a user's guide, hoping standard practice will make results comparable across labs.
europmc-pmc5309780:
Elisabetta Dejana, Karen K. Hirschi, and Michael Simons reviewed blood vessel cell change in Nature Communications in 2017. Endothelial cells line all blood vessels. In the embryo, plain early cells of this type take on the marks of arteries, veins, or lymph vessels. Some even turn into blood-forming stem cells, and others gain traits needed to build the heart.

In adults, keeping the settled vessel state takes constant signals. When those signals fail, vessel cells can shift toward a scar-like type. That shift helps drive several diseases. The review lays out the signal paths behind these fate changes, the marks that show them, and the open questions. A clearer map of the switches could point to new treatments that hold vessel cells in their proper state.
europmc-pmc5358780:
Pablo Orellano, Nancy Quaranta, Julieta Reynoso, Brenda Balbi, and Julia Vasquez pooled studies of dirty air and asthma flares in PLoS ONE in 2017. Single studies had long hinted that outdoor air pollution can spark or worsen asthma attacks. Their results clashed, though, since many side factors bend the link. The team set out to pool the proof with care for those bends.

They kept studies that tracked same-day or near-day air levels against emergency room visits and hospital stays for asthma. Twenty-two studies passed the bar, from a search of the main databases for the years 2000 to 2016. A pooled method that handles clumping inside studies gave one score per pollutant. Near all main pollutants tied to more flares in both children and adults. Two, sulfur gas and coarse dust, did not reach a firm link.
europmc-pmc5378180:
Duy Tin Truong, Adrian Tett, Edoardo Pasolli, Curtis Huttenhower, and Nicola Segata read strain-level gut microbe maps in Genome Research in 2017. Health ties often rest not on a species as a whole, but on one strain of it. Reading strains from bulk gene data, with no lab culture, had long been a hard nut. Their tool, StrainPhlAn, finds each sample's lead strain from marker genes for each species.

They ran it on more than fifteen hundred gut samples from five world regions, which yielded strain maps for thousands of strains across more than a hundred species. Most strains were personal: a strain marked its host and few others. In some species, set sub-kinds matched set lands. In others, strain change ran smooth across space. Some species proved near clones from gut to gut, while one common kind ranked among the most varied of all.
europmc-pmc5405080:
Marie Strickland and Elizabeth A. Stoll review fuel use in glioma in a 2017 paper in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. Glioma is the most common harmful brain tumor. Cancers were long thought to burn mostly sugar for energy, a pattern called the Warburg effect. Glioma cells also burn amino acids and fats, both for energy and for the raw parts needed to build new cells and skins.

Sugar breakdown feeds both energy and the making of DNA parts, while fats serve as fuel and as membrane stock. Growth signals tie into these fuel paths, and changes in two genes set distinct fuel styles in some tumor groups. Reactive oxygen from the power chain doubles as a signal. The authors gather these paths into one picture of how glioma feeds itself.
europmc-pmc5465380:
Grist and co-authors systematically review mental health mobile apps for preadolescents and adolescents. Their review appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Up to 20 percent of young people have diagnosable problems. Services reach only a fraction of them. Apps promise wider access to help. Stores release them at a rapid pace. Proof of efficacy lagged far behind. The team searched many databases systematically. Coverage ran from 2008 to mid-2016.

Twenty-four publications met the inclusion criteria. They described 15 distinct apps. Only two apps were downloadable by the public. Two small randomized trials tested efficacy. One case study joined them. None showed a significant effect on intended outcomes. Six downloadable apps had content analyses instead. None of those had any research evaluation. Acceptability looked good in feasibility reports. Usage was moderate in those studies. The authors demand robust safety and efficacy trials promptly.
europmc-pmc5540680:
Réu and co-authors present a research article in Cell Reports. Their subject is microglia, the resident immune cells of the human brain. The team asks how fast these cells are replaced. They also ask how long single cells can survive.

The authors used carbon-14 dating on cells from postmortem brain tissue. They report slow renewal, at a median rate near 28 percent per year. Some microglia still lasted more than two decades. They found no large pool of quiet, long-lived cells set apart from turnover. Readers learn that the brain keeps this cell pool through steady, slow replacement across adult life.
europmc-pmc5563280:
Gouin and co-authors review two sensory channels in skin inflammation for Protein & Cell. The channels are TRPV1 and TRPA1. Both sit in sensory nerve endings, where they detect harmful stimuli. Firing them releases neuropeptides that inflame the skin.

That state, cutaneous neurogenic inflammation, shows as itch and redness. The channels also live in skin cells like keratinocytes and mast cells. There they boost the same process. Other inflammation signals can sensitize both channels. That feedback keeps the reaction going on its own. The state feeds lasting disorders like psoriasis and rosacea. The review covers how each channel switches on. It also maps the gene changes they drive. Readers get a full circuit diagram of nerve-driven skin inflammation.
europmc-pmc5596480:
Crous-Bou and co-authors review Alzheimer's prevention in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy. The disease has no cure, and drug trials in clear dementia keep failing. Populations are aging fast. Prevention now draws the field's energy.

Brain changes start about twenty years before symptoms. That long silent stage opens a window for action. Primary prevention targets known risk factors to cut new cases. Secondary prevention finds the disease's early marks in healthy people. Trials then test treatment before neurons are lost. Public-private partnerships are mapping the disease continuum. They also serve as platforms to run those trials. Even a few years' delay in onset would ease the public-health load a lot. Readers get the full prevention landscape in one survey.
europmc-pmc5674680:
Fransen and co-authors test whether aged gut microbes drive the low-grade inflammation of old age. Their research article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Aging brings this slow inflammation, called inflammaging. Older guts also hold a changed set of microbes. The team moved gut microbes between mice. Young germ-free mice got microbes from young or old donors.

Four weeks later, immune cells were checked. Old microbes raised inflammation in the young mice. The small bowel showed clear effects. Bits of bacteria leaked more into the blood. T cells were more active body-wide. Mice with old microbes held less Akkermansia. Two other groups were higher. The authors conclude aged microbes help cause inflammaging. The effect is not just a side result of age.
europmc-pmc5691680:
Schwingshackl and co-authors present an updated meta-analysis in Nutrients. It links Mediterranean diet adherence with cancer risk. The team searched PubMed and Scopus through August 2017. Trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies were eligible. This update adds 27 studies to earlier work. In total, 83 studies covered over two million people. Risk estimates were pooled with a random effects model.

Highest adherence tracked with lower cancer mortality overall. Colorectal cancer risk ran about 18 percent lower. Breast, gastric, and liver cancers also showed lower risk. Head and neck cancer risk was roughly halved. Prostate cancer showed only a slight dip. Among survivors, links with death and recurrence were not significant. Fruit, vegetables, and whole grains drove most benefit.
europmc-pmc5708080:
Rueden and co-authors rebuild a widely used image analysis program for modern science. Their paper describes ImageJ2, a full rewrite of ImageJ. The older program is popular in biology for its ease of use and plugins. Growth, split plugin suites, and technical limits showed the need for a redesign.

The new code splits the data model from the user interface. A fresh plugin system lets the community extend almost every part. That covers file formats, scripting languages, and display tools. The data model now handles very large, many-dimensional datasets. Links with outside programs improve data exchange. Old workflows still run, so users can shift at their own pace.
europmc-pmc5775980:
Sakamoto and co-authors review ELISA tests for plant secondary metabolites. These compounds help plants defend themselves and include many drug and health product ingredients. ELISA uses antibody binding to measure a target with high specificity. The method grew from older radioisotope assays, swapped for safer enzyme labels.

The review explains how the assays are built and read. It covers antibodies and probes, helped by recombinant DNA methods. Worked uses show the tests in quality control of plant products. The authors also note where the tests serve diagnosis and drug monitoring more broadly.
europmc-pmc5785480:
Shinozaki and co-authors map gene activity across tomato fruit tissues as the fruit grows and ripens. Tomato is a model for fruit biology, yet most past work ground up whole fruit walls. That hides the signatures of inner tissues. The team cut tissues by laser or by hand and sequenced their RNA.

Networks of regulators and hormone paths emerge across tissues and stages. Ripening starts in inner tissues and spreads outward in gradients, they find. Marks of epigenetic control vary by place on top of this pattern. The maps reveal control links tied to texture, color, and aroma.
europmc-pmc5792980:
Craigie reports cases of spleen disease in which death followed purulent matter in the blood. He was a senior physician to the Royal Infirmary in Edinburgh. Spleen enlargement was a well recorded topic, he notes. Yet the size the organ can reach, and its inner changes, still drew study.

His account first weighs simple enlargement with little change of structure. He observes that enlarged spleens feel firmer than healthy ones, though many shrink back to normal size. Past writers on the organ are surveyed. The cases then show how spleen disease can seed the blood with pus and kill.
europmc-pmc5824580:
Geerligs and co-authors review what helps or blocks new practices in hospitals. Proven care ideas often stall before they reach patients. Staff who must run them know where the friction sits. The team collects staff reports across many studies.

From 4,239 papers, 43 met their strict rules. Barriers and helpers sorted into three domains. They are the system, the staff, and the intervention itself. Links ran both ways among the domains. The staff-to-intervention link was the strongest of all. Gains in one area could offset gaps in another. Readers get a planning map for making hospital change stick.
europmc-pmc5945880:
Castro and co-authors review interferon-gamma at the crossroads of tumour immune surveillance and evasion. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Interferon-gamma is a cytokine with antiproliferative and pro-apoptotic effects. It is often seen as a major effector of antitumour immunity. Yet therapies based on it have had limited success. Reports now suggest it can also help tumours.

Tumours may stop responding to its signals, the authors note. They may lower their major histocompatibility complexes to hide. They may raise checkpoint molecules such as PD-L1. Still, interferon-gamma responses track with better survival in several cancers. The review argues for finding which patients will respond.
europmc-pmc5976580:
Cristini and co-authors map the proteins that bind RNA/DNA hybrids and single out the helicase DHX9. Their study appeared in Cell Reports. R-loops pair an RNA/DNA hybrid with a loose DNA strand. They serve useful roles but also threaten the genome. Which proteins recognise these structures was largely unknown. The team purified hybrid binders from HeLa cells with the S9.6 antibody. Mass spectrometry then named the partners.

Known R-loop factors appeared beside many new candidates, they report. Helicases, repair factors, and chromatin proteins featured. DHX9 stood out as a top candidate. It curbs R-loops and aids clean transcription ending. With PARP1, it prevents R-loop linked DNA damage.
europmc-pmc6016480:
Robb and co-authors quantify what controls mitochondrial superoxide production by reverse electron transport at complex I. Their study appeared in the Journal of Biological Chemistry. This backward electron flow damages tissue in reperfusion injury. It also feeds signals cells use in normal physiology. The team measured hydrogen peroxide output from heart mitochondria. They varied membrane voltage and the redox states of key pools. An uncoupler let them set those states precisely.

Superoxide output answered to oxygen, voltage, and pool states, they report. Small changes in voltage shifted production sharply. Many drugs act by altering the overall driving forces. Complex I reverse flow emerges as a major signalling mode.
europmc-pmc6052480:
Li and co-authors test a gut molecule's effect on brain aging in mice. Their research article appeared in Aging Cell. The molecule, called TMAO, comes from gut microbe activity. Its blood levels rise with age in humans and mice. It was already tied to heart and vessel disease.

The team gave TMAO to two mouse strains for sixteen weeks. One strain ages fast, the other resists aging. Treated mice showed more senescent cells in the hippocampus. Most of those aged cells were neurons. Mitochondria worked worse and damaging oxygen signals rose. Synapses also suffered visible damage. Proteins tied to learning and memory fell in level. The authors blame a blocked growth signaling pathway. Readers get a gut-brain link worth further study.
europmc-pmc6070480:
Xia and co-authors link dimensions of mental illness to brain connectivity in youth. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Diagnoses map poorly onto brain biology. The team instead let symptoms and scans define dimensions. They studied 663 young people with a sparse correlation method.

Four dimensions emerged from the data. They covered mood, psychosis, fear, and externalizing behavior. Each tied to a distinct connectivity pattern. All four shared weaker separation between two major networks. Mood and psychosis patterns grew clearer with age. Sex differences appeared for mood and fear. Findings mostly repeated in a second sample of 336. Readers get brain-based dimensions that cross diagnosis lines.
europmc-pmc6099580:
Saokham and co-authors review the solubility of cyclodextrins and their drug complexes. Their review appeared in Molecules. Cyclodextrins are rings of glucose units. They trap drug molecules inside their hollow centers. That trapping can fix poor drug properties without changing the drug itself.

Most complexes pair one drug with one ring. Natural rings tend to clump and dissolve poorly. Chemical derivatives dissolve far better. Complex strength depends on the add-ons used. Other ingredients in a formula compete for the rings. Polymers and preservatives shift the balance. The right ring dose maximizes passage through membranes. Readers get formulation guidance for a workhorse excipient.
europmc-pmc6108980:
Yamashita and co-authors wrote a review in Insights into Imaging on convolutional neural networks and their use in radiology. These networks are a class of artificial neural networks that now lead many computer vision tasks. They learn image features on their own through layers of processing.

The review lays out the building blocks, such as convolution, pooling, and fully connected layers. It then shows how the method is applied to scans and other radiology tasks. Two problems get close attention: small datasets and overfitting, where a model fits its training data too well. The authors also cover tricks that cut those risks and look at where the field is heading.
europmc-pmc6216580:
Miguel-Aliaga and co-authors review the gut of the fruit fly Drosophila. The fly gut is a model for gut science. It sends signals that affect feeding and insulin release. It also shapes immunity through its microbes. The review appeared in Genetics.

Adult gut stem cells were found just over a decade ago. Since then, fly work has grown fast. The fly's genes are easy to change. That makes the gut a strong test system. The review covers gut formation and function. It focuses on the midgut, the main digestive part. Topics include stem cells, nerves, microbes, and ageing. Some fly gut mechanisms also apply to humans. They may matter for gut cancer and obesity.
europmc-pmc6233180:
Park and co-authors propose a new body fat index. Obesity raises the risk of heart and metabolic disease. Standard indexes such as BMI have known flaws. The team built a weight-adjusted waist index. The study appeared in Scientific Reports. It used a Korean nationwide cohort.

The index divides waist size by the square root of weight. Data covered more than 465,000 people. The team compared five indexes for disease and death risk. BMI best predicted new diabetes and hypertension. The new index best predicted death from heart disease. Its link to death rose in a straight line. Other indexes showed curved patterns that are harder to read. Pairing the new index with BMI worked best overall.
europmc-pmc6247580:
Csige and co-authors review how obesity affects the heart and blood vessels. Their review appeared in the Journal of Diabetes Research. Obesity raises risk both directly and through linked conditions. Those conditions include high blood pressure, diabetes, and sleep apnoea. Extra weight also reshapes the heart itself. Changes in heart structure and function can lead to heart failure.

Stretched heart tissue raises the chance of rhythm problems and sudden death. The review also covers the obesity paradox, where heavier patients sometimes fare better once heart disease is present. New imaging methods can catch early heart changes before symptoms start. Early care can then aim to prevent attacks and failure. The authors gather the mechanisms behind each link in one place.
europmc-pmc6274980:
Cheng, Ku, and Lin review PGC-1 alpha, a master switch for energy use in the body. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The protein turns on genes for fat burning and energy making. It also guides growth of mitochondria, the cell's power plants. Muscle, liver, fat, heart, and kidney all depend on it.

Newer work links the switch to muscle signals that reach the whole body. It also affects how mitochondria join and split. In kidney injury, its level tracks how well the organ recovers. In cancer its role splits in two. It can suppress some tumours and feed others. The review gathers these roles organ by organ. The picture shows one switch at the centre of body metabolism.
europmc-pmc6280880:
Kowalska and co-authors review pollution indices, the scores used to grade metal contamination in soil. Their review appeared in Environmental Geochemistry and Health. Single scores promise a quick verdict on soil quality. Many such indices exist, each with its own maths. Farm, forest, and city soils all get graded with them. Picking the wrong index can misstate the danger.

Eighteen published indices plus one new one were compared. Data on cadmium, lead, and zinc in three soil types fed all of them. The indices split into single metal and combined families. Further splits follow their purpose and method. Strengths and flaws of each are laid out. Reference background values also draw close review. The authors propose a method for picking the right index. Local background levels anchor their approach.
europmc-pmc6294780:
de Vasconcelos and co-authors film pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death, one cell at a time. Their study appeared in Cell Death and Differentiation. Pyroptosis helps the body fight microbes. It also releases strong immune signals. The trigger is a protein called gasdermin D, cut by inflammatory enzymes. The cut piece punches pores in the cell membrane.

The team used fast live-cell microscopy on mouse macrophages. They set off three types of inflammasome, the sensors that start this death. Small pores opened first and let ions through. The cell then swelled with water. Mitochondria and other inner parts failed next. Only then did the outer membrane burst. The sequence was much the same across all three triggers.
europmc-pmc6318280:
Wu and co-authors identify Prrc2a as a new reader of a common RNA mark. Their study appeared in Cell Research. The mark, called m6A, sits inside messenger RNA. Reader proteins bind it and shape cell fate. The team asked what m6A does in glial cell growth. Those cells build myelin, the sheath around nerve fibers.

Knocking out Prrc2a in mouse brain cells caused thin myelin. The mice also lived shorter lives and moved and learned poorly. Prrc2a helps precursor cells multiply and choose an oligodendrocyte fate. A key target is the gene Olig2, central to that cell line. Prrc2a binds Olig2 RNA and keeps it stable. A second enzyme, Fto, removes the mark and speeds decay. The findings point to new angles on myelin disease.
europmc-pmc6336880:
Johnston and co-authors report final results of the MONARCH 3 breast cancer trial. Their paper appeared in NPJ Breast Cancer. The trial tested abemaciclib as a first treatment. It enrolled postmenopausal women with advanced disease. Their cancers were hormone receptor positive and HER2 negative. None had prior systemic therapy for advanced disease. The drug was paired with a hormone therapy pill.

A total of 493 women joined the randomized study. Half got abemaciclib, half got a placebo, plus hormone therapy. The drug arm lived far longer without cancer growth. Median time was 28.2 months versus 14.8 months. Response rates also favored the drug arm. Side effects stayed within a tolerable range. The authors present the pairing as a strong first option.
europmc-pmc6365380:
Daver and co-authors present a review in Leukemia on FLT3 mutations in acute myeloid leukemia. Mutations in this gene appear in about 30 percent of cases. The most common type, an internal tandem duplication, signals high disease burden and poor outlook.

The review covers how doctors classify risk and why testing matters at diagnosis and again at relapse. It traces progress from broad first-generation FLT3 inhibitors to newer drugs that are more specific and more potent. It also explains how resistance to these drugs arises. The authors argue for combining FLT3 inhibitors with other therapies to produce longer, more durable remissions.
europmc-pmc6383680:
Groeger and Meyle review oral mucosal epithelial cells in Frontiers in Immunology. These cells line the mouth and form a barrier against germs, chemicals, and physical harm. Their layers are held tight by linking proteins and keratin filaments.

Oral bacteria can loosen those links and change how the cells act. Harmful gum bacteria, for example, disturb cell joints and trigger immune signals. Healthy cells also shed and renew in a strict pattern. The review covers cell death, renewal, and defense roles in depth. It shows the mouth lining as an active guard, not a passive wall.
europmc-pmc6439480:
Cieplik and co-authors ask whether mouth germs are learning to resist chlorhexidine, the antiseptic rinse dentists have trusted as their gold standard for more than 40 years. Drug resistance gets watched closely, while resistance to antiseptics stays largely ignored. Worry grew when chlorhexidine use was linked to stable resistance against colistin, a last-resort drug.

Chlorhexidine kills by tearing the germ's outer membrane. Germs answer with pumps that spit the rinse back out, coded by qac genes in staph species, and with rebuilt outer walls in other species. Proof drawn from mouth germs is still thin, and few dentists are watching for it. The authors call for work on biofilms, where weak doses may quietly train germs to shrug off both rinses and drugs.
europmc-pmc6486680:
Liu and co-authors profile gut microbes and blood metabolites across the stages of coronary artery disease, reading bacterial genes and running chemical screens in 161 patients and 40 healthy controls. The mix shifted step by step from health through stable disease to acute coronary syndrome, ruling out a simple sick-versus-well split.

Twenty-nine metabolite modules tracked disease traits, and a bacterial group anchored by Roseburia, Klebsiella, and Ruminococcaceae changed by stage, steering how the body handles taurine, sphingolipids, and ceramides. A classifier built from these measures separated patients from controls with an area under the curve up to 0.955. It could even tell stable disease from acute syndrome.
europmc-pmc6512280:
Reinert and co-authors test blood DNA checks in colorectal cancer care. Their cohort study appeared in JAMA Oncology. It followed Danish patients with stage I to III disease. The team used ultradeep sequencing of cell-free DNA from plasma. Each assay targeted 16 mutations picked from the patient's own tumour.

The study enrolled 130 patients and analysed 795 samples from 125. Before surgery, ctDNA was found in 88.5% of samples. Patients still positive 30 days after surgery relapsed far more often. Seven of ten such patients saw their cancer return. Serial testing after treatment found relapse with 88% sensitivity. Specificity reached 98%. The authors frame ctDNA as a tool for spotting leftover disease.
europmc-pmc6627380:
Pilot and co-authors review surface-enhanced Raman scattering, known as SERS. Their article appears in the journal Biosensors. SERS boosts the weak Raman signal of molecules near metal surfaces. It pairs fingerprint-level identification with very high sensitivity. Cheaper, friendlier instruments have widened its use.

The review first explains the two roots of the boost. Electromagnetic enhancement comes from hot spots in the local field. Chemical enhancement adds a smaller, molecule-specific lift. The authors show how to measure the enhancement factor. They weigh laser wavelength choice, fluorescence, and detector response. Substrate types and fabrication routes get a full survey. A closing set of examples covers biomedical uses, direct and indirect. The prose stays plain for readers outside the specialty.
europmc-pmc6679380:
Lancaster and Huch review disease modelling in human organoids, with a poster alongside. Their article appears in Disease Models and Mechanisms. Organoids are self-organising tissues grown from stem cells. They follow built-in growth programmes in the dish. The result mirrors real organs closely. Human starter cells make human-only processes reachable. Animal models miss many such features entirely. The field exploded after gut organoids arrived in 2009.

The pair survey current methods across organs. Strengths and limits get equal treatment. Scaling up remains a noted weakness. The poster distils the landscape in pictures. Future advances could extend disease modelling further. Regenerative strategies are the longer-term prize. The article serves as a field entry point.
europmc-pmc6691380:
Wang and Li review CD36 signalling pathways and functions in cancer. Their overview appears in Theranostics. CD36 is a scavenger receptor on many cell types. It takes up lipids and recognises dying cells. Thrombospondin-1 and fatty acids are key ligands. In tumours the receptor plays opposing roles. On cancer cells it fuels metastasis. Enhanced lipid uptake and oxidation drive that effect. Therapy resistance follows the same route. On tiny vessel walls it blocks new vessel growth instead. Thrombospondin binding triggers cell death there.

Tumour-linked immune cells add another layer. CD36-driven reprogramming promotes immune tolerance. Expression rises as tumours progress to metastasis. Control networks governing the receptor are mapped. Clinical trials targeting CD36 are surveyed.
europmc-pmc6699480:
Hasan and Yang review what shapes gut microbiota composition and how to shift it. Their review appears in PeerJ. Imbalances in the gut community cause disease. The host fosters favoured microbes. Key factors include secreted microRNAs. Broad defences include mucus and immunoglobulin A. Antimicrobial peptides complete the host toolkit. These factors encourage some bacteria and suppress others. Outside factors reshape the mix too. Diet, antibiotics, and age all shift make-up. Birth mode matters from the very start.

Strategies to shift the gut aim to restore balance. Prebiotics feed favoured bacteria. Probiotics add live microbes. Faecal transplant replaces the whole mix. The review weighs evidence for each approach.
europmc-pmc6728380:
Kim and co-authors grew lung cancer organoids from patient tissue for drug testing. Organoids are miniature organs grown in a dish. Lung cancers differ greatly between patients, so treatment needs to be personal. The team built cancer organoids covering five lung cancer subtypes, plus normal airway organoids.

The organoids kept the shape and gene changes of the original tumors over long growth. They also answered drugs as their genes predicted. A BRCA2-mutant organoid responded to olaparib, and an EGFR-mutant one to erlotinib. A third, with EGFR mutation and MET gain, responded to crizotinib. Fast setup could let doctors test drugs for each patient in time.
europmc-pmc6755980:
Moriguchi and co-authors pooled brain scan studies of glutamate in major depression. Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory signal chemical. Faults in its system are suspected in depression, and it is a drug target. The team meta-analyzed spectroscopy studies that measured glutamate-related levels in patients and healthy controls.

Forty-nine studies qualified, with 1,180 patients and 1,066 controls. Levels of the combined measure Glx were lower in the medial frontal cortex of depressed patients. The drop was clear in medicated patients but not in unmedicated ones. Other brain regions showed no steady difference. The findings narrow where glutamate changes in depression are real. They also flag medication as a factor future studies must handle.
europmc-pmc6769580:
Torres and co-authors review key topics in molecular docking for drug design. Docking uses computers to fit candidate drug molecules into a target's binding pocket. It is fast and cheap, so both universities and industry rely on it. Yet finding true binders, and their exact poses, stays tricky. No straightforward route guarantees the right answer.

The review covers four fronts. Benchmark sets for testing docking tools come first, with their strengths and traps. Consensus methods, which combine several tools, come next. Fragment-based algorithms and machine learning approaches round out the survey. Each advance adds a little accuracy. With growing computer power, the field may one day reach its full potential.
europmc-pmc6806580:
Chen and co-authors present a research article in Microbiome on tiny eukaryotes in a subtropical river. Their team sampled the Tingjiang River in Fujian, in south-east China. They compared wet and dry seasons. The central question was how these communities form. The authors asked whether chance or local conditions matter more.

They used high-throughput sequencing of the 18S rRNA gene and statistical tests. Communities differed by season and thinned with distance. Yet place and water conditions explained only a small share. A neutral model explained about 90 percent of the variation in each season. The authors report that chance processes such as dispersal shaped the communities most.
europmc-pmc6822780:
Choi and co-authors present a computer model in PLOS Computational Biology. Many proteins clump into droplets inside cells through a process like oil separating from water. These proteins carry sticky patches, called stickers, linked by flexible spacers. How that design drives the separation is hard to test by experiment alone.

Their program, LASSI, places such proteins on a lattice and simulates their behaviour. It can compute full phase diagrams, the maps that show when droplets form, for mixtures of several proteins. The tool is open source. The authors aim to help researchers predict how a protein's pattern of stickers and spacers shapes the droplets it forms.
europmc-pmc6844580:
Alexander and co-authors present the G protein-coupled receptor section of the Concise Guide to PHARMACOLOGY 2019/20, in the British Journal of Pharmacology. These receptors sit in cell membranes and pass signals inward. They form one of the largest families of drug targets in medicine. Many common medicines act through them.

Each receptor family gets a compact profile of its key properties and known ligands. The emphasis falls on selective compounds, where they exist. The wider guide covers nearly 1,800 human drug targets in about 400 pages. Entries link to the open Guide to Pharmacology website for fuller detail. This fourth biennial edition fixes a citable record of the field at one point in time.
europmc-pmc6858680:
Chen and co-authors report a study in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer on what controls PD-L1. This protein shields tumours from immune attack, and drugs target it. The interferon signal IFN-gamma was known as its main switch. Which other signals matter, on tumour cells and immune cells alike, was less clear.

The team treated 34 human tumour cell lines and blood monocytes with cytokines found in PD-L1-rich tumours. Beyond IFN-gamma, signals such as IL-27 raised PD-L1 through shared transcription factors. Knocking down STAT proteins cut the response. Some tumours also made PD-L1 without any outside signal. The work maps routes that could be blocked to strip the shield.
europmc-pmc6876280:
Burr and co-authors report a study in Cancer Cell on how tumours hide from T cells. To be attacked, a cancer cell must display fragments of its proteins on a surface platform called MHC class I. Many cancers lose that display and so resist immunotherapy. A genome-wide CRISPR screen hunted for what switches the display off.

The screen named the Polycomb complex PRC2. It silences the whole set of genes that build and load the platform. In low-display cancers those genes carry both activating and repressive marks, a paused state borrowed from embryonic development. Disrupting PRC2 released the brake. The authors say this ancient silencing programme is a drug target for resistant tumours.
europmc-pmc6882880:
Belkina and co-authors present opt-SNE, in Nature Communications. The t-SNE algorithm projects high-dimensional single-cell data into readable maps. Its results hinge on settings chosen by rule of thumb. With millions of cells, poor settings smear real populations together. Their toolkit removes the guesswork by watching the fit as it runs.

Opt-SNE tracks a quality measure, the Kullback-Leibler divergence, in real time. It uses that signal to set the early exaggeration phase and to stop the calculation when more steps stop helping. A tuned learning rate adds further gains. Across test datasets, embeddings came out sharper and computation faster. The authors argue that faithful pictures are a precondition for sound analysis of such data.
europmc-pmc6908580:
Chen and co-authors sort cancers by protein rather than by organ, in Nature Communications. Cancer classification usually follows the tissue where a tumour began. Gene activity studies have added molecular subtypes. Proteins, the molecules that do the work, may draw a sharper map. The team profiled cancers with mass spectrometry, a method that weighs and identifies proteins directly.

Across 532 cancers spanning breast, colon, ovarian, renal, and uterine types, the protein data formed ten pan-cancer subtypes. The groups cut across tissue lineages and appeared again in outside datasets. Two subtypes centred on the immune system, one on adaptive T cell responses and one on antibody-style responses. Pathway signatures separated the groups further.
europmc-pmc6941980:
Martínez-Reyes and Chandel review how mitochondrial metabolites act as signals. Their review appeared in Nature Communications. Mitochondria make energy for the cell, and also shape its fate. They report their own fitness to the rest of the cell through several routes. Intermediates of the TCA cycle, long seen as mere building blocks, join that signalling.

The pair explain how levels of these metabolites steer cell behaviour. They influence chemical marks on chromatin and DNA methylation. They also shape the response to low oxygen, and immune activity. Context matters: the same metabolite can push different outcomes in different tissues. Their summary links this signalling to normal physiology and to disease, and points to where control might be possible.
europmc-pmc6952380:
Shah and co-authors hunt the genes behind heart failure in a huge pooled analysis. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Heart failure is a leading cause of illness and death worldwide. Only a small share of cases come from single-gene heart muscle diseases. Earlier gene studies explained little of its inherited risk.

The analysis covered 47,309 cases and 930,014 controls. Twelve variants at 11 genome sites linked to heart failure. All also tied to coronary disease, atrial fibrillation, or weak heart pumping, pointing to shared roots. Other sites implicated genes for heart development, protein housekeeping, and cell aging. Genetic tests also supported true causal roles for atrial fibrillation, body mass index, and high blood pressure. The findings may guide new treatments.
europmc-pmc6976680:
Lawson and co-authors show how breast milk sugars let infant gut bacteria feed each other. Their study appeared in The ISME Journal. Bifidobacterium bacteria dominate the gut of breast-fed babies. Human milk contains special sugars, called HMOs, that these bacteria can eat and human infants cannot.

The team characterised 19 strains taken from breast-fed infants. Each strain's genome differed, rich in carbohydrate-use genes, yet together they formed a shared pangenome. Abilities to use two test sugars, 2'FL and LNnT, varied by strain. Strains that cracked HMOs leaked by-products: fucose, galactose, acetate, and building blocks that neighbours could grow on. Cross-feeding trials confirmed the sharing. Such cooperation, the authors argue, makes bifidobacteria foundation species in the infant gut, and hints at future diet-based therapies.
europmc-pmc7031380:
Dai and co-authors study soil microbes and phosphorus in The ISME Journal. Microbes drive phosphorus cycling in farm soils and set how much of this nutrient crops can reach. How long-term fertiliser inputs reshape the microbes' phosphorus genes was largely unknown. The team used metagenomics at four long-term test sites with varied nitrogen and phosphorus inputs lasting up to 39 years.

Long-term phosphorus input raised microbial phosphorus lock-up, shifting the balance between starvation-response and transporter genes. That result runs against short-term studies of cultured microbes. Nitrogen told a different story: it lowered soil pH, cut phosphorus-solubilising genes, and loosened links among key genes. The work challenges the idea that nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratios alone control how microbes free up phosphorus in soil.
europmc-pmc7048180:
Tian and co-authors test an old SARS antibody against the new coronavirus in Emerging Microbes and Infections. The 2019 novel coronavirus had already caused more than 11,900 confirmed infections, including 259 deaths, and no vaccine or specific treatment existed. The receptor-binding domain of its spike protein closely resembles that of SARS-CoV. The team asked whether antibodies raised against SARS would cross-react.

One human monoclonal antibody, CR3022, bound the new virus's receptor-binding domain potently, with a dissociation constant of 6.3 nM. Its binding site does not overlap the spot where the domain grips the human ACE2 receptor. Two famous neutralising SARS antibodies that target that ACE2 site failed to bind the new spike at all. The authors propose CR3022 as a candidate therapy, alone or combined with other antibodies, and warn that small differences in this domain decide cross-reactivity.
europmc-pmc7066580:
Newsome and co-authors build a non-invasive score for dangerous fatty liver disease in The Lancet Gastroenterology and Hepatology. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is rising worldwide. The priority is spotting patients whose inflamed form, steatohepatitis, comes with significant activity and scarring, since they progress toward cirrhosis and qualify for trials and new drugs. Biopsy is the usual test, and it is invasive.

The FAST score combines a FibroScan device's liver stiffness and fat measurements with a blood enzyme, aspartate aminotransferase. The team derived it prospectively in patients scheduled for biopsy at seven specialist liver centres in England, then validated it in multiple international cohorts. The score targets patients with an activity score of at least 4 and fibrosis stage 2 or higher. Performance held up across validation groups. A reliable bedside score could reserve biopsies for the patients who truly need them.
europmc-pmc7118080:
Pålsson-McDermott and O'Neill review immunometabolism, the study of how immune cells power themselves, as a route to new anti-inflammatory drugs, in Cell Research. Changing fuel use is not just housekeeping for immune cells: it helps decide whether they attack or calm down. Inflammatory cells switch to fast sugar burning, much like cancer cells.

Four established anti-inflammatory medicines, including metformin and methotrexate, turn out to work partly through metabolism. That proof encourages hunting for specific metabolic steps to block or mimic. The authors focus on sugar burning and the TCA cycle, the cell's central energy loop, as worked examples. Lipid, amino acid, and nucleotide pathways are flagged as further hunting grounds.
europmc-pmc7141480:
Van Lancker and Parolin warn that school closures during COVID-19 could deepen child poverty, in The Lancet Public Health. UNESCO estimated 138 countries had closed schools nationwide, affecting the education of 80% of children worldwide. Whether closures slow the virus was still debated when they wrote.

Two harms stand out for poor children in the United States and Europe. First, food insecurity grows: many children rely on school meals, and 14% of United States households with children faced food insecurity in 2018. Second, learning gaps widen, since out-of-school factors drive much inequality and many low-income homes lack computers, internet, or a quiet place to study.
europmc-pmc7195480:
Calvo-Rodriguez and co-authors measure calcium inside mitochondria of brain cells in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Mitochondria help shape calcium signals inside neurons. Too much calcium taken up can kill the cell. Amyloid beta, the protein that builds plaques, overloads cells with calcium.

Using a targeted calcium sensor and live brain imaging, the team watched mitochondria near plaques. Calcium levels there ran high, and nearby neurons were dying. Applying natural amyloid to healthy brain raised mitochondrial calcium too. Blocking the calcium entry channel reduced the overload in their tests. The findings tie plaque protein to a deadly calcium imbalance. That channel becomes a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc7200080:
Maia and co-authors review structure-based virtual screening, from classical docking to artificial intelligence. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Chemistry. Developing a drug takes years and heavy spending. Computer-aided design narrows experiments to the most promising candidates. Virtual screening predicts how small molecules bind a target protein.

Classical methods score the fit between molecule and binding pocket. Accuracy checks compare predicted poses with known structures. Newer approaches bring in machine learning to improve those scores. The review tracks this shift step by step. It weighs speed and cost against reliability. Readers see why screening has become a standard first pass in drug hunting. The authors expect AI methods to widen its reach.
europmc-pmc7217880:
Seeley and co-authors test how microplastics change microbe communities in salt marsh sediment. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Tiny plastic bits are now common in coastal and deep-sea mud. Their effects on sediment microbes and nutrient cycles were poorly known. The team ran a controlled experiment with four plastic types.

They added polyethylene, PVC, polyurethane foam, or a plant-based plastic to marsh sediment. Each plastic shifted the microbe mix in its own way. Foam and plant-based plastic sped up nitrogen processing steps. PVC slowed those same steps down. Microbes drive the nitrogen cycle that coastal ecosystems depend on. The results show plastic type matters, not just plastic amount. Even the greener plastic altered the sediment community.
europmc-pmc7218780:
Yuyun and co-authors compare cardiovascular disease in sub-Saharan Africa with high-income countries. Their article appeared in Global Heart. Non-communicable diseases now cause about 35 percent of deaths in the region. Heart and vessel diseases lead that group. They account for roughly 13 percent of all deaths there.

The old belief that such diseases were rare in Africa no longer holds. Ischaemic heart disease is now the top cardiovascular killer, followed by stroke. Rheumatic heart disease, driven by untreated infections, still scars many young hearts. Rich countries instead carry far more degenerative valve disease. The authors describe a double burden: infections persist while lifestyle diseases climb. Health systems built for one burden must now fight both.
europmc-pmc7220380:
Zhong and co-authors use single-cell sequencing to find a hidden cell type that manages the bone marrow environment. Their study appeared in eLife. Marrow cells give rise to both bone builders and fat cells. The stem cells behind that split were poorly defined. The team mapped mesenchymal progenitors in young, adult, and aging mice.

They traced two branching paths from progenitors to bone and fat cells. One new subpopulation carries fat cell markers yet holds no fat droplets. These cells appear to regulate the surrounding marrow niche. Their numbers and markers shift with age. The work redefines how marrow fat arises. It may explain links between aging, marrow fat, and bone loss.
europmc-pmc7237880:
Liu and co-authors test whether a simple blood ratio can flag COVID-19 patients heading for critical illness. Their study appeared in the Journal of Translational Medicine. They followed 61 patients as a derivation group and 54 more for validation. Routine lab measures were screened statistically for predictive power. A nomogram, a scoring chart, was built from the winning factors.

The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio came out as an independent risk factor. It compares two white cell types that move in opposite directions during severe infection. Rising ratios marked patients likely to deteriorate early. The chart turns ordinary blood results into a risk estimate. Such a tool costs little and runs anywhere. The authors propose it for early triage of COVID-19 patients. Larger studies would still be needed to confirm it.
europmc-pmc7256180:
