The agency's triggers for judging rivalry did not match building-level facts well. Some areas saw rival presence shrink over time. Prices under flexible rules raised concern for government buyers. GAO urged the agency to define effective competition better. It also urged more data to track the market. The agency disagreed with both calls.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-180:
First responders' tools for chemical and nuclear hazards are tested in GAO report GAO-08-180, dated June 27, 2008. City crews must answer both terror attacks and accidents that release such agents. Two tools guide them. Detectors name the agent in the air. Plume models chart where it will drift and whom it may harm.

GAO found that both tools fall well short in city settings. Detection gear has clear limits, and its testing and standards are thin. Plume models track spread poorly among tall buildings. Data on how exposure harms city crowds are also scarce. The title states the result in plain terms: the ability is significantly limited.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-280:
Computer security at the market watchdog is graded in GAO report GAO-08-280 (February 29, 2008). The Securities and Exchange Commission leans on computer systems to police the markets. Layers of controls must guard its financial and sensitive data. The review grew from GAO's audit of the agency's fiscal year 2007 statements. It checked old flaws and live defenses alike.

GAO tested whether past security weaknesses have been corrected. It also judged how well current controls keep data private, sound, and available. Plans, policies, and hands-on tests inform the findings. The verdict sits in the title: the agency needs to keep improving its program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-380:
School improvement funds under the No Child Left Behind Act are tracked in GAO report GAO-08-380, released February 29, 2008. Over 10,000 schools were flagged for improvement in the 2006-2007 school year. States must set aside 4 percent of their Title I funds to help those schools.

A hold-harmless rule kept 22 states from setting aside the full 4 percent since 2002, since it guards district funding levels first. States still aimed most funds at the lowest-performing schools, though 4 states broke some targeting rules and 4 could not list which schools got funds. The Department of Education had not spotted the targeting issue in its monitoring. GAO recommended tighter monitoring and clear guidance on listing funded schools. The department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-480:
Funding choices for the global AIDS program are studied in GAO report GAO-08-480, dated April 2, 2008. The President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) works in 15 focus countries under a $15 billion law that expires in September 2008. The law sets spending directives for how its funds are split.

Experts told GAO the directives have protected prevention and treatment funds. Many still faulted one directive: 33 percent of prevention money must back abstinence and fidelity messages. Most experts favored a country-based method, where local teams set targets from local data and pick their own tools. Headquarters would still review and approve plans. Most country officials surveyed called the shift workable. GAO urged set guidance on cost data for country teams. The State Department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-680:
Hunger in sub-Saharan Africa has grown, not shrunk, since world leaders pledged in 1996 to halve hunger by 2015. GAO-08-680, dated May 29, 2008, asks why food stays scarce there and how far host governments and donors have gotten toward the goal. Fieldwork covered four African countries.

Hunger persists through low farm yields, weak rural growth, bad policy, and poor health among farm workers. Grain yields run at about 40 percent of those in other developing lands. Rising prices and a shifting climate add pressure. GAO found efforts by hosts and donors short of the need, and urged one joint U.S. strategy with yearly reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-80:
A 48-year embargo bars most trade and travel between the United States and Cuba. Four departments share the job of enforcing it, alongside homeland security work. GAO-08-80, dated November 30, 2007, reviews rule changes from 2001 to 2005 and the strain of policing them.

Looser farm rules lifted exports to Cuba from about $6 million in 2000 to about $350 million in 2006. Tighter rules cut family visits to once every 3 years, but their effect is unknown for lack of data. Heavy checks on Cuba arrivals at Miami airport may crowd out graver threats, GAO warns. It urges two agencies to rethink their effort.
geheimnisse-einiger-philosophen-und-adep:
Printed in 1780, this German volume claims to print secrets of past philosophers and adepts, drawn from the papers an old man left behind. It is the first part of the work. Dense Latin passages sit beside German text, in the mixed style of old alchemical books. The scan is hard to read in places, with old type and worn pages.

What can be made out turns on the tincture, the prized agent that adepts said could heal the sick and change base things. An old adept claims it kept him alive past seventy years, though even it could not hold back the stars. The book is a raw sample of late alchemy in print, valued more as a record of that world than as a clear guide.
grimm-teutonic-mythology-stallybrass-188:
Jacob Grimm, best known for the tales he gathered with his brother, built this vast study of German myth over many years. James Steven Stallybrass turned it into English in four parts from 1880 to 1888. Grimm worked from old poems, laws, and folk speech. He spent years in the work, and the notes grew to a vast heap.

The study traces gods, heroes, beasts, and rites across the old German world. Rune lore runs through it, tied to names, charms, and carved signs. Nearly all later work on German myth starts here, and its notes still guide those who study the north.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol3-1880:
Hering's Guiding Symptoms reached its third volume in 1880, one more shelf of the ten-volume materia medica. The editorial team working from Constantine Hering's notes kept his system intact. Remedies appear in alphabetical order across the set, each with its full train of symptoms.

Mind, head, eyes, and the rest of the body each get their own sections within an entry. Odd and striking signs, the ones homeopaths call characteristic, stand out by their marks. Readers use the set as a court of appeal when smaller remedy books disagree, and Volume III does its share of that settling.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol4-1880:
By its fourth volume, from 1880, Hering's Guiding Symptoms had settled into the shape prescribers relied on. Each remedy entry moves through the body in a fixed order, so a reader always knows where to look. Marks of differing weight point to the signs worth trusting most.

Constantine Hering died the year the volume appeared, leaving his notes to students who kept the work going. What they printed came from provings, tests in which healthy people took a drug and noted each change. Volume IV shows the method at full stretch, a vast card index of symptoms bound as a book.
heroic-romances-of-ireland-translated-in:
Heroic Romances of Ireland in its complete form holds both volumes of A H Leahy's translations of early Irish tales into English prose and verse. Leahy argues in his preface that Ireland's old literature, long hidden, merits a place beside the Greek classics it rivals in age. The set opens with the first volume's romances and runs on through the second volume's shorter cattle raid tales.

Volume 2 gathers five preludes to the great Tain: the raids of Dartada, Flidais, Fraich, Regamon, and Regamna, each with an introduction naming its manuscript source. Leahy prints a verse rendering beside a literal prose translation, so the reader can compare poetry with plain sense. Notes explain names, places, and gaps in the manuscripts, where whole passages are lost. Together the volumes give the heroic age of Ireland, its kings and champions, in one continuous shelf piece.
hershon-talmudic-miscellany-1880:
Paul Isaac Hershon was a Polish Jewish scholar who settled in London and translated rabbinic texts for English readers. His Talmudic Miscellany, published in 1880, gathers a thousand and one extracts from the Talmud, the Midrashim, and the Kabbalah. The book appeared in Trubner's Oriental Series.

Hershon orders his extracts by theme: prayer, ethics, folklore, law, and the sayings of famous rabbis. A gentile reader could browse rabbinic wisdom here without Hebrew or a guide through the vast originals. The miscellany became a classic of its series and a quiet bridge between Jewish and Christian readers.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
Chapter forty-nine of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands reports peace deliberations in Spain. Spinola sends formal notice of the armistice to Madrid, and complaints rise at court. The measure was beneath the king's dignity, courtiers said, and contrary to his interests. Such a truce, they said, was deadlier than open war.

In all that long and dreadful war, Motley writes, no disaster had struck the king like peace. To treat with former subjects as sovereigns undid the monarchy's founding claim. The chapter studies a court that prefers ruin to recognition. Meanwhile the provinces enjoy the breathing space their arms have won. Motley's irony is at its driest here. The whole long history converges on this paradox: Spain must call its rebels a republic, or bleed forever.
hodgkin-italy-invaders-vol-1-1880:
Thomas Hodgkin published Italy and Her Invaders, Volume 1, in 1880. Hodgkin tells the story of the barbarian invasions of Italy from the Italian side. This volume covers the Visigoths, Alaric's sack of Rome in 410, and the Vandals. The fall of the Western Empire unfolds through Italian eyes.

Hodgkin writes with deep learning and humane sympathy for all sides. He studies church, law, and daily life beside battles and kings. The full work grew to eight volumes over many years. It became the English classic of the invasions period. Readers who want the end of Rome told fully and fairly start with Hodgkin. His patience rewards theirs.
how-to-educate-the-feelings-or-affection:
Charles Bray wrote this work on educating the feelings, in an American edition of 1880. Nelson Sizer edited it, with notes, from the third London edition. Bray sorts the mind by the phrenologists' map of feelings. Self-protecting, self-regarding, and social feelings each get trained in turn.

Appetite, combativeness, secretiveness, and love of gain head the lists. Self-esteem and love of praise follow, then the social affections. Each feeling, Bray argues, should be guided by a desire for universal good. He warns that clinging love for persons is not that wider benevolence. Parents and teachers got a system for schooling the heart, organ by organ.
institutes-of-vishnu-jolly-1880:
Julius Jolly translated the Institutes of Vishnu for the Sacred Books of the East in 1880. The text frames its law as the god Vishnu's own teaching. Vishnu instructs the goddess Earth in the duties of humankind.

Civil and criminal justice, penances, and caste duties fill the code. The duties of life's four stages receive systematic treatment. Kingship, ordeals, and inheritance law appear in practical detail. Jolly was a leading authority on Hindu law of his era. His translation presents one of Hinduism's most important legal scriptures. Religion and jurisprudence meet in a single ancient code here. The frame story makes dry law feel like sacred instruction.
james-washington-square-1880:
Henry James published Washington Square in 1880, building it from an anecdote a friend had told him at dinner. James set it in the New York of his childhood, in a house on Washington Square like his grandmother's. He considered it one of his most perfectly made works.

Catherine Sloper is a plain, shy heiress with a large fortune and a brilliant, cold father. When the handsome fortune hunter Morris Townsend courts her, Dr. Sloper forbids the match and threatens to disinherit her. Catherine must choose between obedience and the only love offered her. The tragedy unfolds in drawing rooms, almost in whispers. James called the story's design flawless, and its quiet ending still stings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-natha: Aaron ben Nathan Nata of Trebowla was an author who flourished about the middle of the eighteenth century. At Zolkiev in 1755 he published "Shem Aharon." The book holds halakic novellae on the whole Talmud, plus midrashic readings of the Pentateuch under the sub-title "Netibot la-Shebet." He also published a commentary on Talmudic discussions of the Pentateuch in 1768, titled "Maḳlo shel Aharon."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abigdor-280: Abigdor is both a first name and a family name, the entry explains. It first appeared in the Middle Ages and is still in use. In Russia it is said as Vigder. It is thought to be the Biblical name read as father of Gedor, in First Chronicles, chapter 4. Some scholars have tied it instead to the Latin Victor. The name is used so often, the entry adds, for a set reason. In Chronicles, Abigdor was one of the titles borne by Moses himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-shmoilo:
Lithuanian merchant Abraham Shmoilovich, called the Honorable Sir Abraham, the Jew of Turisk, flourished at the end of the sixteenth century and into the seventeenth. Brest-Litovsk custom books for 1583 list him as an exporter of lumber and cereals.

In May 1595 he took a three year lease on a feudal estate in the Vladimir district, with its people and full manorial rights. Days later he and his wife Rikla Odinna leased the village of Koshar and others nearby. In 1601 still more towns and hamlets were leased to him. The leases made him in effect a lord over the land and its income.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-afia-aaron-880: Aaron Afia was a doctor, thinker, and math man of Salonica. He lived about 1540. He taught Daniel ben Peraḥyah. He helped that pupil turn Abraham Zacuto's "Almanac" from Spanish into Hebrew. He also aided Moses Almosnino in his Hebrew form of a work on the sphere. His own book came out at Venice in 1568. Its title means picked views of the most true and ancient thinkers on the soul, with their word senses. The entry gives those two aids and that one book as his mark.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-albelda-moses-b:
Moses ben Jacob Albelda was a preacher and philosopher in Turkey in the sixteenth century. He preached first at Valona and later at Salonica. After ten years at Valona, a pupil of his asked leave to preach in a synagogue Albelda did not use. Albelda refused, and the flock sent the case to Abraham de Boton at Salonica. De Boton backed the rabbi.

Albelda wrote much, in a long-winded and thoughtful style. His treatises on providence and repentance came out at Venice in 1583 as "Reshit Da'at." His "Sha'are Dim'ah," on the vanity of the world, followed in 1586, with a comment on Lamentations. After his death his sons printed his Pentateuch comment at Venice in 1601. His sermons followed there in 1602, as "Darash Mosheh."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfahan-don-zul: Don Zulema Alfahan, also called Solomon, was a Spanish chief rabbi. His charge covered the communities under the archbishop of Toledo. Archbishop Don Pedro Tonorio removed him from office in 1388. The charge against him was neglect of duty. In his place the archbishop set Hayen, his own private physician. The deed praises the new man as good, prudent, and very learned, and of a good family. The entry records nothing else of Alfahan's life or work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almazan-pedro-d: Pedro de Almazan took part in a plot against an inquisitor. The inquisitor was Pedro d'Arbuez. Pedro got away by flight and lived. His wife Isabella was not so lucky. She was burned at the stake at Saragossa. The date was January 25, 1487. His brothers Pedro and Manuel were burned with her. Pedro himself was burned in effigy in his absence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anatolio-jacob-:
Jacob Anatolio, full name Jacob ben Abba Mari ben Simson Anatoli, was a Hebrew translator of Arabic scientific works. The entry says he flourished about 1194-1256 and came from southern France. Learned kin and friends at Narbonne and Béziers shaped his early studies.

Emperor Frederick II invited Anatolio to Naples. There, under the emperor's support, he turned Arabic science into Hebrew, and Naples became his most fruitful base. Family ties bound him to Samuel ibn Tibbon, the translator of Maimonides. That link drew him into Maimonides' philosophy, and anti-Maimonist opponents later pushed back against that side of his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antigonus-matta:
Antigonus Mattathias was the last Hasmonean king of Judea, and he died in 37 B.C. He was the second son of Aristobulus II. Pompey carried both father and son to Rome as prisoners in 63 B.C., and both escaped in 57 and came home.

Antigonus held back while his older brother Alexander fought for the family rights. After Alexander died, he claimed the crown as sole heir and saw his uncle Hyrcanus as a puppet of Antipater. He first asked Julius Caesar, in Syria in 47, to back his claim. Caesar refused him, despite his family's losses in Caesar's cause. The entry then follows his turn to Rome's enemies and his fight for the throne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arabah-1680:
Arabah is a Hebrew word for desert or steppe. With the article, it names the great sunken valley whose center is the Dead Sea. The entry sorts out its uses passage by passage. Sometimes it means the southern stretch, down to the Gulf of Akabah, sometimes the northern.

The valley's shape is one of the wonders of the earth's surface, the entry says. North of the Sea of Galilee the ground stands 500 feet above the sea. Within 118 miles it falls to 2,600 feet below it, at the Dead Sea bed. Near springs, as at Jericho, rich growth covers it. Elsewhere it is blinding white desert or sand and gravel under fierce heat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ark-of-noah-178:
Noah's vessel during the Deluge fills this entry, starting from Genesis chapters 6 to 8. Built of gopher-wood and sealed with bitumen, it had three stories, a roof, and rooms or cells inside. Genesis gives its size as 300 cubits long, 50 cubits broad, and 30 cubits high. The entry calls it less a ship than a great house set afloat, made to hold Noah, his family, and animals of every kind.

A Babylonian flood story is set beside the Bible account. Both vessels are sealed with bitumen and divided into cells. The Babylonian one rests on Mount Nisir after a week. Noah's rides the waters a year and grounds in the highlands of Ararat. A second part gathers rabbinic lore, from cedars planted 120 years early to claims of hundreds of cells.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-meir-:
Meir ben Moses Cohen Ashkenazi, called Kaz from the initials of Kohen Zedek, was a Polish Talmudist. Born about 1590 at Frankfort-on-the-Main, he died about 1645 at Mohilev on the Dnieper. His father was a judge at Frankfort and later rabbi at Danhausen. As a youth Meir went to Lublin and studied under Meir Lublin, then served as rabbi at Amstebowy and at Mohilev.

Posterity knows him chiefly as the father of Shabbethai Cohen, author of the Sifte Kohen. Nine of Meir's legal answers were printed by a great-grandson as a supplement to his son's work. Most treat marriage questions, and in cases of the agunah, the chained wife, he ruled with notable freedom. The entry calls him the earliest Jewish author in the province of White Russia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-athanasius-2080:
Athanasius was bishop of Alexandria. He was born in 293, probably in Alexandria, and died there on May 2, 373. He became bishop in 326. Twenty of his forty-seven years in office were spent in exile. Enemies he had made drove him out again and again. The entry calls him the greatest fighter of the old Church.

Most of his books are attacks and defenses. His first works struck at heathen worship and argued against Judaism. Then the Arian dispute broke out, and he gave his life to fighting it. That long fight won him the titles the Great and the Father of Orthodoxy. The entry's own stress falls elsewhere. His real weight, it says, was not as a writer or thinker. He made the Nicene faith win, and he shaped the Christian Church for more than a thousand years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avlona-aulona-o:
Avlona, also called Aulona or Valona, is a town and seaport of Albania. It stands on the Gulf of Avlona, on the Adriatic. A flourishing Jewish community stood there from early times. About 1510 the scholar Messer David Leon was called from Salonica to lead its three congregations, at a salary of 70 florins a year.

David preached in the synagogues in turn. Then the town's Jewish groups fell out. Sephardim split from Catalans and set up their own prayer meeting. Soon the Sephardim split in turn, Portuguese against Castilians. The Castilians wanted David to force the Portuguese back under ban. He refused, since the Portuguese were the larger party and had a right to part. A Lisbon doctor tried to make peace with a gift on the eve of the Day of Atonement. His effort failed, and the two sides traded bans, with David heading the Portuguese.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-babenhausen-228: Babenhausen is a city of Hesse, in the district of Starkenburg, Germany. Jews are said to have lived there as early as 1320. In 1337 the Jews suffered cruel attacks in the Armleder raids. At the Black Death in 1349 the community was hit again. From 1643 to 1672 there were never more than six, paying a yearly protection tax of 60 to 70 gulden. The tax later rose to 110 gulden. By 1829 the count stood at 80 Jews. In 1875 it was 92, and about the same when the entry was written.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bakbukiah-2380: Bakbukiah was a Levite who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, as the book of Nehemiah records in its twelfth chapter. The entry about him is a short Bible note built from three verses. One verse calls him second among his brethren. Another places him among the Levites who lived in Jerusalem. A third makes him a porter of the storehouse at the gate. No family line, no dates, and no deeds of his own are given beyond those verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baraffael-baruf: Isaac Baraffael, or Baruffall, was an Italian officer and communal worker who lived in Rome at the end of the eighteenth century and into the next. When the French occupied Rome, he was made major of the national forces on March 18, 1798. After the Neapolitans and their allies retook the city, a heavy tribute was laid on the Jews. Baraffael paid 700 scudi of it, about $700. In 1811 he was elected deputy-representative of the Jewish community of Rome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-leibov-2:
Baruch Leibov was a merchant burned at the stake in St. Petersburg on July 15, 1738. He was one of the Judæo-Polish merchants who, by ability and noble protection, traded profitably in centers where Jews generally might not dwell. In 1722 the merchants of Smolensk complained that he had built a synagogue at Zvyerovichi and thrashed the village priest, who then died. The entry shows the charge was aimed at the Jews as a body, from hatred of them as business competitors.

The synagogue was demolished and its books burned, yet Leibov was allowed to stay at his occupation. Under Catherine I an order expelled him from Russia. Long after, a naval officer named Voznitzyn was accused of having been converted to Judaism and circumcised by Leibov at Dubrovna. Both men were prosecuted together and perished at the stake. The case is called unique in Russian history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bayreuth-2680:
Bayreuth is a principality and city in Oberfranken, Bavaria, where Jews are first named in a record of 1343. A Jew of the town lent money to the burgrave that year. A later grant let the ruler admit Jews to his lands.

The entry tells of suffering in the Black Death years, a chief rabbi set over two districts in 1372, and charters that guarded Jews in court. It counts their yearly payments for protection in florins. Later pages follow court bankers, a palace bought in 1759, and the province's chief rabbis. Yearly payments for that protection ran to many hundreds of florins for the ruling house and its kin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behrmann-lazar-:
Lazar Jakovlevich Behrmann was a Russian teacher and editor born in Friedrichstadt, Courland, on Sept. 26, 1830. He died at St. Petersburg on April 27, 1893. He began as a private teacher in his home town, then opened a school for Jewish boys at Mitau in 1861.

In 1864 St. Petersburg called Behrmann to found its first Jewish school, which he ran until his death. From 1879 he edited a weekly Russo-Hebrew paper there. His manual on the Mosaic law won official backing for use in high schools where Jewish religion was taught. He also taught the Jewish religion at a women's college in the capital for thirteen years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-la-anah-288:
Ben-La'anah is named as the author of an apocryphal book, known from a single mention in the Jerusalem Talmud. That passage groups his works with the book of Ben Sira among books the Mishnah barred from reading. A sixteenth-century writer claimed to have the works before him and called them full of riddles and stupidities.

Much of the entry weighs rival guesses about the name itself. Scholars link it to Ben Tagla, to fox fables, or even to Apollonius of Tyana. The entry presents those ideas as speculation, not settled fact.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berkowitz-henry: Henry Berkowitz, a Russian-born educator in England, was born at Warsaw in 1816. He died at Gravesend on April 5, 1891. He came to London in 1841 and caught the notice of Chief Rabbi Adler, who took him into his household. He then opened a school at Gravesend and built it a strong name by steady effort. Pupils of his rose to leading places in the community. Townspeople of all faiths honored him, and in 1887 he was elected mayor of Gravesend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-besant-sir-walt: Walter Besant was an English novelist. He was born at Portsmouth on August 14, 1836. He died in London on June 11, 1901. He studied at King's College, London, and at Cambridge. The entry notes his help for Russian and Polish Jews. His idea of a Palace of Delight inspired the People's Palace there. From 1868 to 1885 he served the Palestine Exploration Fund. He also co-wrote a history of Jerusalem in 1871. His novel "The Rebel Queen" (1893) had a Jewish heroine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bie-oskar-3280: Oskar Bie was a German archeologist. He was born at Breslau on February 9, 1864. He taught at the Technische Hochschule at Charlottenburg. He also edited the "Neue Deutsche Rundschau." The entry lists four of his books. They treat the Muses in ancient art. They treat ancient combat groups and types. One book is "Das Klavier," from 1898. The entry ends by noting his conversion. Bie had become a Christian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-issachar-: Issachar Baer Bloch was an Austrian rabbi. He lived in the eighteenth century. He was a native of Hamburg. His father wrote the Tosafot Ḥadashim on the Mishnah. Bloch served as rabbi of Eiwanowitz in Moravia. In 1767 Kojetein called him to its rabbinate. He was also at some time rabbi of Dolitschau. His book "Binat Yissakar" collects his sermons. It was published at Prague in 1785.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bolaffio-luigi-:
Luigi Filippo Bolaffio was an Italian journalist and publisher born in Venice in 1846. He died at Milan in 1901. As a youth in Genoa he founded a literary magazine called La Favilla.

Bolaffio wrote for Venetian papers and moved to Milan in 1880. There he edited L'Italia and then founded his own gazette. His sharp politics led to many duels. After a young son died, he left politics and founded a Milan publishing house. With his wife he also wrote sixteen guide-books on Italy, Switzerland, and Paris. Many of those guide-books were rendered into French, English, and German. He also wrote a historical memoir in 1867 and a novel, Augusta, in 1888.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-borodavka-or-br:
Isaac Borodavka was a Lithuanian farmer of taxes and distillery rights in the sixteenth century. He lived at Brest-Litovsk. A royal grant of Jan. 1, 1560, joined him with partners in collecting duties in five towns.

The partners paid 6,808 copes a year for that right. A salt monopoly and brewery rights in three towns followed. Christian rivals envied the Jewish leaseholders, and rivalry fed acts of harm. Servants of the collectors faced false murder charges in several towns. Strict inquiry cleared them, though one accused man died first. A royal decree of 1566 sent such cases to the king himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bryansk-3780: Bryansk appears here as a brief statistical entry on a town in the government of Grodno, Russia. The entry gives figures for 1898 and nothing more. In that year its Jewish population was 2,365, out of a total population of 6,342. Of the Jews, 525 were artisans. Another 85 worked as gardeners and farmers. No history, institutions, or named persons are given in the entry. Its whole content is those counts, which show a large Jewish share of the town and a strong artisan element.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caballeria-bona:
Bonafos de la Caballeria was a fifteenth century writer against the Jews, son of Solomon ibn Labi of Saragossa. On converting to Christianity he took the name Micer Pedro. From youth he studied Hebrew, Arabic, and Latin and gained deep knowledge of civil and canon law. Queen Maria made him a commissioner of the Cortes in 1436 and 1437.

In 1450 he began a work whose title claims zeal for Christ against Jews and Saracens. He spent fourteen years on it, filling it with charges against his former coreligionists. The entry calls the book malevolent and its claims false. Pedro was murdered in 1464, a deed blamed on Marrano instigation. His sons rose high in Aragon, though one fell to the Inquisition in 1504.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantarini-judah: Judah Leon Cantarini, son of Samuel Simon, was an Italian physician and rabbi born about 1650 at Padua. He built a large practice among Christians and Jews in that city. The poor among his patients got four visits a day at no charge. He founded a yeshivah in the Ashkenazic synagogue and taught Talmud there, a field he knew deeply. He also preached. One letter of his survives, on a legal quarrel, written in pure classical Hebrew. He died at Padua on April 28, 1694. His nephew Isaac wrote his obituary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carrion-de-los-:
Carrion de los Condes is an old city of Castile where Jews lived at an early date. Though the Jews outnumbered the Christians and held more property, they submitted in 1126 to King Alphonso VI, who favored them. Many moved to Palencia in 1160. By 1290 the community paid 92,000 maravedis in taxes.

Persecution also marked the town's record. After Christians killed two Jews on a groundless charge, the king ordered an inquiry, hanged ten ringleaders, and jailed other attackers. In the great persecution of 1391 most Carrion Jews were baptized. The town is also noted as the birthplace of Don Santob, the first Spanish-Jewish poet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ceremonies-and-:
Ceremonies are symbolic rites and observances that express certain thoughts or feelings. Every religious system has its own forms, the entry says, just as social life has etiquette. In the Bible, ceremonies may be called testimonies. Other terms cover judgments and statutes, terms applied to both moral and ceremonial laws.

The Rabbis split laws into two kinds. Some rest on reason, such as laws on justice. Others are divine statutes that the evil impulse and the heathen attack, such as the ban on pork. The Prophets stressed moral law and condemned mere ceremonialism. Saadia and Maimonides took up that split. Joseph Albo first divided Bible law into ceremonial, juridical, and moral classes. He admitted he took that scheme from a Christian writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chebar-4280: Chebar is the name of a Babylonian river or canal. By its side Ezekiel saw visions, as Ezekiel i and other chapters report. The Hebrew word nahar, usually rendered river, also served for canal. In Babylonian, Naru Kabaru means great canal. Scholars have often identified Chebar with the Chabor, a stream flowing into the Euphrates at Circesium. The entry calls that a mistake. Ezekiel places the scene in the land of Chaldea. The stream meant is the Kabaru, a large navigable canal near Nippur, named in a Babylonian inscription.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-church-fathers-:
Church Fathers, the early teachers and defenders of Christianity, stand at the center of a very long study. These men worked when Christianity still touched Judaism at many points. Judaism gave them support against paganism, the entry argues, even as they fought it while shaping their own doctrine. They also borrowed the language of Philo, Josephus, and other Hellenistic Jewish writers.

Because fighting paganism required knowing Jewish texts, the Fathers dealt with Jews in person. Through Jewish teachers they absorbed a mass of haggadic material, lore that now forms part of Jewish tradition itself. Jerome gets special notice as the one Father who read Midrashic works himself and used technical Hebrew terms. Only the polemic against Judaism, the entry says, was truly their own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-isaac-448: Isaac Cohen, an English theatrical manager, was born about 1835. Few London managers could match his span, the entry says. He worked first on the Surrey side of the city. Then he spent 34 years in the East End. All told he directed theaters for 44 years. He began at the Victoria in South London as call-boy, then rose to assistant manager. In 1862 he took charge of the East London Theater. In 1872 he moved to the Pavilion Theater, still his post in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-comtino-mordeca:
Mordecai ben Eliezer Comtino, a Turkish Talmudist and scientist, lived at Adrianople and Constantinople. He died at Constantinople between 1485 and 1490, with his earliest dated writing from 1425. Even his family name is in doubt; some manuscripts give other forms, and his biographer used Kumatyano. He studied under Enoch Saporta, a man open to science and tolerant toward Karaites.

He taught Elijah Mizrahi, and two leading Karaites as well, who honored him despite his stand against their teachings. Two of his hymns entered the Karaite prayer book. His Pentateuch commentary ranged over grammar, logic, physics, and stars. In math he pushed the exact sciences in Turkey, with a two-part treatise on arithmetic and geometry and a study of Persian star tables from 1425.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crowns-of-the-r: Crowns of the Righteous draws on a saying of Rab in the Talmud. In the world to come, he teaches, there is no eating, drinking, or marrying. There is no envy, hatred, or quarrel either. Instead the righteous sit with crowns on their heads. They feed on the splendor of the Shekinah. A second saying makes God a crown of glory on each righteous head. The Zohar adds seats ringed with crowns, made ready thirty days before a death. A hymn verse closes the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-daniel-ben-juda: Daniel ben Judah was a liturgical poet who lived at Rome in the middle of the fourteenth century. He was grandfather of Daniel ben Samuel ha-Rofe, a rabbi at Tivoli. According to Luzzatto, he wrote the well-known hymn Yigdal Elohim Ḥai. The hymn sets out the thirteen articles of belief of Maimonides. Ashkenazim sing it in morning prayer. Sephardim sing it on the eve of Sabbaths and holy days. It also stands in the Romania ritual for Saturday evening. Three sources are cited for the credit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-saul-: Saul's son David was a French rabbi who lived in the first half of the thirteenth century. He had been a pupil of Solomon of Montpellier. David was one of the rabbis of Provence who condemned the philosophical works of Maimonides and the study of philosophy itself, during the famous dispute over those books. The entry adds one more trace of him: an anonymous commentary on the tractate Baba Meẓi'a, by a Provençal rabbi, mentions him, and later collections of responsa quote that mention.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-demetrius-i-sot:
Demetrius I Soter was king of Syria from 162 to 150 B.C., a son of Seleucus IV. Sent to Rome as a hostage, he asked the Senate in vain to name him his father's successor. Refused again, he fled with Polybius's help to Tripoli and soon took Antioch. The Romans still opposed him and let a rival hold Babylonia until Demetrius beat him.

For that victory the Babylonians called him Soter, meaning redeemer. In 162 he set Alcimus over the Jews as high priest. His general Bacchides defeated and killed Judas Maccabeus in 160, but Jonathan held out and made peace in 157. Hated for pride and severity, Demetrius fell when Alexander Balas invaded in 153.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dictionaries-he:
Dictionaries, Hebrew traces the making of Hebrew word books across many centuries. The earliest known work of the kind lists the Bible's proper names and is ascribed to Philo of Alexandria. Origen enlarged it in the third century, and Jerome reworked it in Latin in the fourth. No like attempt is traced in Jewish schools before the geonic age.

The first lexicon named in Hebrew literature covers not the Bible but the Talmud. The gaon Ẓemaḥ ben Paltoi wrote it in the ninth century, and only fragments survive. The first known Hebrew lexicon proper is the "Agron." The long article then follows the great medieval word books, Nathan ben Jehiel's "Aruk" among them, and the growth of Hebrew grammar study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-door-and-door-p:
Doors in the ancient Hebrew house hung on wooden pivots set in sockets. They were shut with a lock or a bar and opened with a key, usually of wood. The rich may have used metal keys with ivory handles. A steward carried his key on his shoulder as a sign of office.

Door-posts carried deep religious weight. At Passover, Israelites spread lamb's blood on the lintel and side-posts. Deuteronomy orders God's commands written on the posts of the house. The entry reads these acts as guards against evil spirits and the evil eye. Like customs in Egypt and among Teutonic peoples are set beside them for comparison.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliakim-ben-ash: Eliakim ben Asher Selig was a Polish Talmudic scholar of Yampol. He lived in the eighteenth century. In 1757 the Jews of Poland sent him to Rome. His task was to fight the blood charge against them. He laid a plea before Pope Benedict the Fourteenth. The pope set Cardinal Ganganelli to study the case. The cardinal's report called the charge groundless. The king of Poland then cleared the Jews by decree. An accuser who could not prove the charge now faced death himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliphelet-god-i: Eliphelet is a name borne by five men in the Bible. The name means God is deliverance. The first Eliphelet was a son born to David at Jerusalem. Chronicles lists two sons of that name for David. A second Eliphelet fought among David's thirty warriors. A third came of the line of Jonathan the prince. A fourth came back from the Exile with his clan. A fifth had wed a foreign wife in the days of Ezra. No deeds are told for any of them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-enoch-zundel-be: Enoch Zundel ben Joseph was a Russian Talmudist. He died at Byelostok in the year 1867. His life's work was glossing the Midrash books. He wrote notes on the Midrash of the five scrolls. He glossed the Tanhuma and the Seder Olam as well. More notes treat Midrash Samuel and the Pesikta in turn. The entry is frank on how he built those books. They are mostly gleanings from older gloss writers. His own fresh notes are sown through the mass.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-etam-5880: Etam is a name the entry sorts into four uses. One Etam was a village of Simeon, missing from the parallel list in Joshua. A second, near Bethlehem, was fortified and held by Rehoboam. A third was a rock in Judah where Samson hid after killing Philistines. Near it stood the fountain of Etam, called in the Talmud the highest place in Palestine. Josephus placed that fountain sixty stadia south of Jerusalem. A fourth use in Chronicles may name a person or the Judah place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fairs-5980:
Fairs were set gatherings for buying and selling goods, and the entry traces Jewish dealings with them. Talmudic teachers opposed going, since fairs grew from pagan feasts. The Talmud's word for a fair, yarid, may come from an Arabic term for going down to water. Three Palestinian fair towns are named: Gaza, Tyre, and Bohna. Only buying slaves was allowed there, to lift them out of idolatry.

In the Middle Ages the bar fell away, and Jews became the fairs' chief visitors, even where they could not live. At Leipzig they paid a gate fee of ten thalers and four groschen a head. Town clerks logged every Jewish trader by name. From 1675 to 1700 some 18,182 such traders came, and their fees alone reached 173,000 thalers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ferdinand-ii-60:
Ferdinand II, emperor of Germany, was born July 9, 1578, elected August 28, 1619, and died February 15, 1637. On the whole his reign favored the Jews of the empire, the entry says, despite the Thirty Years' War raging under him. He let Hamburg's Jews build a synagogue in 1627. Vienna's Jews got the same leave in 1624 for 17,000 florins.

He ordered his officers to guard the Jews with special care. Bohemian Jews paid 40,000 gulden a year for that safety, raised to 48,000 in 1628. When Vienna's council sought expulsion, he settled the Jews across the river in fourteen houses instead. He bargained their badge exemption down to 20,000 florins. In 1622 he ennobled Jacob Bassevi of Prague, starting the formal court-Jew system.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fleck-johann-fr:
Johann Friedrich Ferdinand Fleck was a German actor born at Breslau in 1757. He died at Berlin on Dec. 20, 1801. He made his debut in 1777 at Leipsic and stayed there until 1779. He then spent four years at Hamburg. After that he went to Berlin. The entry calls him one of the leading actors of his time.

Esteem for him ran so high that a memorial medallion was struck at his death. Its words praise him as great as an artist and upright as a man. His best roles included Wallenstein, Götz, and Karl Moor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frank-kathi-kat: Kathi Frank, also called Katharina Frankl, was an Austrian actress born at Bösing, near Presburg, on October 11, 1852. She first appeared at the Viktoria Theater in Berlin in 1871. After acting at Potsdam and Bremen, she joined the Vienna Stadttheater in 1872. In 1875 she moved to the imperial court theater, then returned to the Stadttheater in 1876. From 1882 to 1899 she played at Hamburg, Riga, Stuttgart, and Frankfort. In 1900 and 1901 she toured to Moscow, St. Petersburg, and New York. Her chief roles include Maria Stuart, Lady Macbeth, Iphigenie, and Deborah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedlander-mic:
Michael Friedländer was the head of Jews' College, London. He was born at Jutroschin, Prussia, on April 29, 1833. He studied at Berlin and Halle and took his doctor's degree in 1862. He read Talmud as well. Settling in Berlin, he became head of the Talmud school there. In 1865 he gave that up to head Jews' College in London. In 1867 he printed a German commentary on the Song of Songs. He has taken an active part in the schooling of the wider community.

For a Hebrew learned society Friedländer printed Ibn Ezra on Isaiah. He also wrote on the works of Ibn Ezra. He turned Maimonides' great guide from Arabic into English, with notes. He edited a Jewish family Bible in English and Hebrew. He made a handbook of the Jewish religion and a larger book of the same name. Figuring on the Jewish calendar was another of his works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gallah-the-shav: Gallah, the shaved one, was a Hebrew nickname first given to Catholic priests for their tonsure. Later it spread to Greek Orthodox priests as well. The word and its plural turn up often in medieval Hebrew writing. Rabbenu Tam warns against answering in haste like gallahim who argue in tricky ways. Latin script was at times called the writing of gallahim. Folk belief held it unlucky to meet a gallah on the road.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ginsburg-christ:
Christian David Ginsburg, an English Masoretic scholar born at Warsaw on December 25, 1831, was converted in 1846. For a time he worked with the London Society mission to the Jews at Liverpool. He left in 1863 to write full time. His early books covered the Song of Songs, Ecclesiastes, the Karaites, the Essenes, and the Cabala.

He then turned to Masoretic study. In 1867 he gave out Levita Massoret ha-Massoret in English. In 1870 he joined the board revising the Old Testament. He gathered all the remains of the Masorah he could find. Three volumes came out in 1880-86. His new Hebrew Bible text of 1894 drew sharp critique from Blau. He also wrote on the Moabite Stone and helped expose the Shapira forgeries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-golitzyn-count-:
Count Nicholas Golitzyn was a Russian writer born in the second half of the nineteenth century. He became notorious for a history of Russian laws on the Jews. Only its first volume appeared. It covers the years from 1649 to 1825. The entry stresses that the work leans against the Jews. Golitzyn admits in his preface that the subject resists calm study.

He belittles Jewish loyalty during Napoleon's invasion. He blames Senate moves to revise Jewish laws on Jewish intrigue. The entry calls the book a compilation from earlier writers. His own additions, it says, often twist their facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-griliches-abrah: Abraham Avenirovich Griliches was a Russian engraver. He was born at Wilna in 1852. He studied at the Wilna rabbinical school. He finished the Wilna School of Designs in 1869. He then graduated from the St. Petersburg Academy of Fine Arts in 1876. The Imperial Mint took him as engraver that year. He grew noted as a medalist. His medals mark royal deaths, jubilees, and a rail disaster of Oct. 17, 1888. His onyx portraits covered tsars, queens, and Baron Günzburg. Paris gave his work a gold medal in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-habdalah-or-abd:
Habdalah is the rabbinical term for the blessings and prayers that divide holy time from ordinary time. The division can fall between Sabbath and workday, festival and workday, or Sabbath and festival. Law forbids returning to ordinary work after a holy day until the separation has been formally made.

The ceremony centers on a blessing over a cup of wine. At the Sabbath's close, blessings over spices and a fresh light are added. The light must have at least two wicks, and people gaze at their fingernails in its glow. The entry traces the formula's history, debates between the schools of Shammai and Hillel, and legends about the first fire made after the first Sabbath.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halasz-fischer-:
Ignaz Halász, born at Tés in 1855, was a Hungarian philologist who died at Budapest on April 9, 1901. He studied at the gymnasia of Veszprim and Stuhlweissenburg and at the University of Budapest. From 1877 to 1892 he taught at Stuhlweissenburg. In 1893 he became professor of Hungarian philology at the University of Klausenburg.

The Hungarian Academy of Sciences sent him three times, between 1880 and 1890, to the Laplanders of Sweden and Norway. There he gathered much material on folk-poetry and comparative language study. His chief works treat rare word-forming sounds, Hungarian words in North Slavic tongues, the Swedish Lapp language, and the kinship of the Ugro-Samoyed tongues. He also collected Finnish folk-songs and turned Grimm's tales into Hungarian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hananiah-ahunai: Hananiah Aḥunai was exilarch from 761 to 771, by the usual dating, which the entry marks with a question. He was a younger brother of Anan ben David, founder of Karaism. The one source for his election is Karaite. It says Anan, though older and more learned, was passed over for want of religion. Hananiah was chosen in his place after their uncle Solomon ben Ḥasdai died. The exilarch elected in 771 was Zakkai ben Aḥunai. So Grätz takes Hananiah to be that Aḥunai, Zakkai's father.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hart-ernest-abr:
Ernest Abraham Hart, born in London in 1836, was an English physician and medical editor. He trained at St. George's Hospital and joined the Royal College of Surgeons in 1856. He made eye disease his specialty and built a large London practice. He also worked at several hospitals as surgeon and teacher.

From 1866 Hart edited the "British Medical Journal," and its growth owed much to his work. He pushed inquiries into workhouse infirmaries and fought the abuse called baby-farming. Those drives helped shape health law in England. He also wrote against the frauds of hypnotism and mesmerism. He died on Jan. 7, 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hephzi-bah-my-d: Hephzi-bah, glossed in the entry as meaning my delight in her, carries two uses in the Bible as presented here. One is the name to be borne by the restored Jerusalem, given as a sign that God will not abandon it. The other is the name of the queen of King Hezekiah. She was also the mother of Manasseh. The entry is only a short name note. It cites Isaiah and Second Kings for the two uses and gives no further history, dates, or comment.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hibbut-ha-keber:
Ḥibbuṭ ha-Ḳeber, meaning the beating of the grave, is one of seven modes of judgment after death in a named treatise. The entry gives R. Eliezer's account to his pupils. The Angel of Death stands on a grave, strikes the dead person's hand, and asks his name.

For three days the angel beats the body apart with a chain half iron and half fire. Messengers rebuild it so more blows can fall. Eyes, ears, lips, and tongue are punished for their sins. The entry calls this pain worse than hell. Good works, hospitality, true prayer, and humble acceptance of rebuke are named as safeguards.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hiyya-bar-adda-: Ḥiyya, son of Adda, was a Palestinian amora of the first half of the third century. He was nephew of Bar Ḳappara and a pupil of Simeon, son of Laḳish. His name attaches to several laws in the Jerusalem Talmud. He also passed on legal views in the names of three other teachers. He argued with his uncle over one word's meaning in Deuteronomy. He died young. At his funeral his teacher compared him, through a verse in Canticles, to a lily a gardener longs to gather.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horowitz-horwit:
Phinehas Levi Horowitz was a rabbi and Talmudic author born in Poland about 1731. He died at Frankfort-on-the-Main on July 1, 1805. He came from a long line of rabbis and learned mainly from his older brother Schmelke. A bold ruling in a hard divorce case made his name.

In 1771 Horowitz became rabbi of Frankfort. He denounced Mendelssohn's Pentateuch and backed its burning at Wilna in 1782. He also fought secular schooling. His chief book, Hafla'ah, treats the tractate Ketubot. Other works cover Kiddushin, divorce law, responsa, and a cabalistic commentary on the Pentateuch. Near death he lost his sight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-bal-am-abu-:
Abu Zakarya Yahya ibn Bal'am, called Rabbi Judah, was a Hebrew grammarian of Toledo who worked about 1070 to 1090. He came from a respected Toledo family and later settled in Seville. Late in life he turned to law and theology. Moses ibn Ezra praises his quick mind, fine memory, and terse style.

Ibn Bal'am wrote in Arabic, mostly short treatises that boiled down his teachers' larger works. His books treat Hebrew homonyms, particles, and verbs drawn from nouns. A Pentateuch commentary survives in part, as does a short Bible commentary. Two liturgical hymns also carry his name. His sharp tongue spared no rival, and that flaw sits beside his gifts in the portrait.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-vives-vivas: Hayyim ibn Vives, also read Vivas, was a Spanish translator. For David ibn Bilia he turned a farewell letter from Arabic into Hebrew. The letter was written by Ibn al-Sa'igh to his pupil Ali ben Abd al-Aziz of Granada, who gathered his teacher's works. The entry adds a second man of the same name. That Hayyim lived at Xativa when Judah ben Asher was at Toledo. He was then an old man busy with rabbinical study, and Isaac ben Sheshet wrote to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-johann-le:
Isaac Johann Levita was a German professor of Hebrew, born in 1515, who died at Cologne in 1577. He began as a rabbi at Wetzlar. In 1546 he was baptized as a Protestant. When Cologne called him as professor of Hebrew, he took the Roman Catholic faith, and he held that post until his death. In 1556 he wrote a popular Hebrew grammar, whose fifth edition came out at Antwerp in 1570.

He also edited Maimonides' work on astrology and Moses ibn Tibbon's notes on Aristotle's "Physics," both at Cologne in 1555. The entry then follows his son Stephan, born in 1542. Stephan became a Catholic priest and his father's assistant. In 1583 he stunned hearers by denouncing Catholicism as idolatry from his own pulpit. He later wrote an "Apologia" and went over to Calvinism, though reports accused him of returning to Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-jedidiah: Jedidiah Israel was rabbi at Alexandria, Egypt, from 1802 to 1827, the year of his death. His father had held the same rabbinate from 1773 to 1784. Jedidiah studied under Jonathan Galante and presided over an academy named Midrash Rab Yedidyah. He wrote several responsa, some printed inside other rabbis' works. He also annotated the "Kisse Eliyahu" on the Shulhan Aruk. His treatise on divorce, "Mazkeret ha-Gittin," still survives only in manuscript, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jackson-harry-8: Harry Jackson was an English actor born in London in 1836 who died there on Aug. 13, 1885. Young, he left England for Australia and took up the stage. He played at Auckland, in New Zealand, and at San Francisco from 1856 to 1862. About 1870 he returned to England, appearing at the Gaiety and then the Princess', where he became stage-manager. He held that post at Drury Lane too. On stage he played chiefly Jewish parts, or rather caricatures, in melodramas. His Napoleon I drew notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobson-eduard:
Eduard Jacobson, a German dramatist, was born at Gross Strelitz, Silesia, on Nov. 10, 1833. He trained as a physician in Berlin, taking his medical degree there in 1859, but he began writing plays while still a student. His first farce, Faust und Gretchen, appeared in 1856. He died in Berlin on Jan. 29, 1897.

Working alone and with partners, Jacobson wrote burlesques and farces that became stock pieces in almost all German theaters of his day. Named successes include Lady Beefsteak in 1860, Wer Zuletzt Lacht in 1861, and a piece played 300 times in a row in Berlin. Later works include Das Lachende Berlin in 1888 and Goldfuchs in 1890.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jehiel-michael-:
Jehiel Michael ben Judah Löb, also known as Michael Hasid, was a rabbi of Berlin who died in March 1728. After posts in Polish towns he moved to Berlin about 1701 to help run a study house there. A royal edict of 1714 confirmed him as Berlin's rabbi, and in 1721 Frankfort-on-the-Oder was added to his charge.

Learned in Talmud and drawn to Cabala, he at first approved works by a follower of Shabbethai Zevi. He soon owned the error, and at a rabbis' meeting in 1726 he led the call to ban such books. Fearing misuse, he left his own Cabala writings in manuscript, while his Talmud notes were printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ibn-plat: Joseph ibn Plat was a rabbinic authority of the twelfth century, likely born in southern Spain. He settled at Lunel in Provence, though one scholar placed his birth in the Byzantine empire. He spent time in Rome and may have traveled widely. Leading men of Lunel learned from him by word of mouth. He wrote letters to Zerahiah, to Abraham b. David, and to Maimonides. His book on the prayers survives only in part, and his legal works are quoted in later books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-of-corbei: Judah of Corbeil was a tosafist of the thirteenth century. He wrote notes on a great number of Talmud tractates. Later books quote him widely: the Kol Bo, the Tosafot Yeshanim, the notes of Asheri, and the Shittah Mekubbezet of Bezaleel Ashkenazi. His rulings on ritual stand in the Haggahot Maimoniyyot. One ruling of his also appears in the responsa of Meir of Rothenburg. Notes of his on Bible verses are quoted in the tosafot to the Pentateuch. The entry rests on three modern sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-julianus-9080: Julianus led a Samaritan revolt at Nablus in the year 530 against the Romans. He was a son of Samaron, though the entry gives other forms of his father's name as well. Julianus took the title of king or emperor and wore a crown and the other marks of royalty. When the rising was put down, he was executed. His head was sent to Constantinople as a prize. The entry is a few lines long and sends readers to the article on Justinian for the wider tale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kennicott-benja:
Benjamin Kennicott was an English Christian scholar of Hebrew. He was born at Totness on April 4, 1718. He died at Oxford on Aug. 18, 1783. He began as master of a charity school in his home town. Local gentry, struck by his poems, sent him to Oxford. There Hebrew lectures drew him in, and he took his degree in 1747.

In 1751 Dr. Lowth urged Kennicott to gather the variant readings of the Old Testament. Patrons raised nearly £10,000 for the work. Kings of Denmark and Sardinia were among them. He began in earnest in 1758. His two-volume Hebrew Bible came out at Oxford in 1776 and 1780. The entry faults his collations as less than thorough. Still, it calls his work the first broad check of the manuscripts. It showed how close the printed text stood to the old copies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-klein-moritz-93: Moritz Klein was a Hungarian rabbi, born July 7, 1842, at Miskolcz. He studied philosophy at the University of Prague. He also attended Solomon Rapoport's lectures on Jewish theology. In 1863 he took his Ph.D. and his rabbinical diploma. He directed the Jewish communal school in his native city. He preached there at the Great Synagogue. Later he served congregations at Ungvar and at Papa. In 1880 he became chief rabbi of Nagy-Becskerek. His works include a Hungarian translation of Maimonides' "Guide."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ladvocat-jean-b:
Jean-Baptiste Ladvocat, a Christian Hebraist born at Vaucouleurs on Jan. 3, 1709, died at Paris on Dec. 29, 1765. He was a wide-ranging scholar in letters, math, philosophy, history, and classics. In 1742 he became librarian of the Sorbonne. A chair in Bible study followed in 1751. Theses on the Pentateuch, Psalms, and Job won him fame abroad.

Text purity was Ladvocat's crusade. He held that no commentary could stand without a clean Hebrew text. His 1753 Hebrew grammar served the Sorbonne schools for decades. He planned a critical edition set against old versions such as the Hexapla and the Targumim. Even so, he firmly defended the truth and wholeness of the Old Testament in letters dated 1766.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lawson-lionel-9: Lionel Lawson, an English newspaper proprietor born in London in 1823, died there on Sept. 20, 1879. Schooled in Germany, he inherited a fortune from his father. A printing ink factory at St. Ouen in France made him another fortune before he sold it. A like business followed in London. He became one of the main owners of the London Daily Telegraph. He never took an active part in running the paper, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leroy-beaulieu-:
Henri Jean Baptiste Anatole Leroy-Beaulieu, a French historian, was born at Lisieux in 1842. In 1867 he went to Russia to study the Slavic peoples. His findings filled "L'Empire des Tsars et les Russes," three volumes printed from 1882 to 1889. In 1881 he became a professor of modern history in Paris.

For Jewish readers his key work is "Israël chez les Nations" from 1893. It grew from a close study of the Russian Jews. He held that only emancipation could lift them, and that their faults came largely from Christian persecution. He also wrote against anti-Semitism in 1897 and 1902. In 1904 New York Jews honored him during his American lecture tour.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-eleazar-98: Eleazar Levy was a colonial resident of New York city before the Revolution. He fled the city when the British occupied it and settled in Philadelphia. There he went into business. On Aug. 26, 1779, he asked Congress for payment. Forts had been built at West Point on land on which he held a mortgage, and he claimed a loss. In 1783 a committee said no order could be taken on the claim. Levy took the oath of loyalty to Pennsylvania. In 1785 he helped settle the estate of Haym Solomon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lightfoot-john-:
John Lightfoot, an English Christian divine and Talmudist, was born at Stoke-upon-Trent in 1602. He died at Ely in 1675. He studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, and served as curate, rector, and canon. From 1650 he was master of St. Catherine Hall at Cambridge. He sat in the Westminster Assembly.

Sir Rowland Cotton turned Lightfoot to Hebrew study, and he gave his spare hours to it for life. His fame rests on the "Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae," printed from 1658 to 1674. That work sets Talmudic parallels beside the Gospels and other New Testament books. Critics said he knew the Talmud and Midrash better than any non-Jew of his time. He left his library to Harvard College.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-loeb-isidore-10:
Isidore Loeb was a French scholar born at Sulzmatt on Nov. 1, 1839, and he died at Paris on June 3, 1892. He learned Bible and Talmud from his father, a rabbi. He studied at Colmar and at the rabbinical school at Metz, graduating in 1862.

Loeb served briefly as rabbi of St. Etienne, then moved to Paris. From 1869 he was secretary of the Alliance Israélite Universelle and built its library. He taught Jewish history for twelve years and edited a leading journal of Jewish studies from 1880. His books cover Jews in Turkey, Russia, and other lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mantle-of-the-l:
Mantle of the Law, the cover of a Torah scroll, is described in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Its Hebrew name, mappah, comes from a Greek word for a napkin. At first a silk wrapping ran the scroll's full length, guarding the writing from dust. The Talmud already knows it: a scroll without a mantle was turned face down.

The article explains the mantle's later form and care. Shaped like a bag, it slips over the rolled scroll, open below and closed above. Two holes let the scroll's handles pass through. It must be made of new, costly material never used for anything else. Worn-out mantles are not thrown away; they go to the genizah or are sewn into a shroud. Mantles are often embroidered with the Crown of the Law and the Lion of Judah. Women frequently make and present them, sometimes with the donor's name worked in.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matriarchy-1048:
Matriarchy is a social system in which descent and property run through women alone. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs give it a compact treatment in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article asks whether ancient Israel ever lived under such a system. It collects the hints scholars had drawn from the Bible itself.

The evidence offered is suggestive rather than firm. The mothers of kings are named prominently in the Books of Kings, and the wives of the patriarchs hold unusual weight in Genesis. The tribes divide into houses of Rachel and of Leah, whose names were even read as animal names under a theory of totem worship. The article is careful to show that the whole case leans on that totem theory. It points readers to Robertson Smith's “Kinship and Marriage in Early Arabia” for the argument.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-merneptah-greek:
Merneptah, fourth king of Egypt's nineteenth dynasty, stands at the center of the Exodus dating debate, and the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 states the problem plainly in an article by Emil G. Hirsch and W. Max Müller. His father Rameses II built the store cities of Exodus, so Merneptah, the successor, was taken for the Pharaoh of the Exodus itself, fixing the event in the thirteenth century B.C. Then Petrie found the Israel stele: a triumph song of Merneptah's fifth year boasting "Israel is annihilated," named among the settled peoples of Canaan.

The article lets that inscription unsettle the old certainty: Israel sounds already planted in Palestine, though scholars have read it of tribes still wandering or still enslaved. A short coda notes his twenty-five years, the Libyan wars of his first five, and his mummy, newly found at Thebes and lodged at Cairo.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moravia-10980:
Moravia, the Austrian province once part of Bohemia's kingdom, held 44,255 Jews in a population of 2,437,706 in 1900. Gotthard Deutsch writes its long history in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first evidence is the Raffelstetten toll law. It mentions Jews coming from Moravia. The article cautions that this proves traveling merchants, slave-buyers among them, not yet settlement.

Settlement is certain by the eleventh century. Cosmas of Prague mentions Moravian Jews repeatedly. His story for 1096 sets the pattern. As Crusaders approached, the Jews tried to emigrate. Duke Bretislav confiscated their property. His logic was that money made in the country should stay in it. The article follows the province's communities from those beginnings toward the modern census.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-motal-abraham-b:
Abraham ben Jacob Motal was a Turkish rabbi of Salonica, born about 1568 and dead in 1658. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied under Samuel Hayyun and probably under Solomon Kohen. As head of the yeshiva of Salonica's old Lisbon community, he gathered many devoted pupils.

Motal's responsa and decisions were printed inside other men's books, including the Bene Shemuel and Hayyim Shabbethai's collections. Two works stand under his own name. The Torat ha-Nazir, printed in 1821, treats the tractate Nazir and the Nazarite rules. The Magen Abraham deals with divorce bills and the exact writing of names in them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-music-and-music:
Music grew up with poetry among the ancient Israelites, since every poem was also sung. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack survey the subject in this Jewish Encyclopedia article. Music served the Temple, feasts, dances, and harvest festivals. It welcomed generals home, crowned kings, and cheered the shepherd alone with his pipe.

The article follows the rise of professional Temple singers in families, with the crowd answering only Amen or Halleluiah. Choirs sang against each other, as in Nehemiah's two great choruses at Jerusalem's walls. Harmony, the authors argue, was unknown: voices and strings sounded together in unison or octaves. Without fixed strophes, Hebrew melody stayed free, earnest, and close to the speech of the words.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahman-bar-jaco:
Nahman bar Jacob, usually called simply R. Nahman, was a Babylonian amora who died in 320. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. A pupil of Mar Samuel, he was chief justice under the exilarch and head of the school of Nehardea. Marriage into the exilarch's family let him entertain scholars lavishly.

Nahman ruled that a defendant who flatly denies his guilt must take the rabbinical oath. Sure of his own worth, he said any living Messiah would have to resemble him. His sayings run earthy and direct: God let Balaam go to Balak, so shamelessness avails even before Heaven. A visiting Palestinian sage blessed him with the parable of the sheltering tree.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathanson-mende:
Mendel Levin Nathanson was a Danish merchant, editor, and economist. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Altona on Nov. 20, 1780. At eighteen he set himself up in business. He died in Copenhagen on Oct. 6, 1868.

When his banking firm failed in 1831, he turned to economics. His great work traced Danish trade and finance from 1730. He also fought for full rights for Danish Jews. He founded a Jewish boys' school in 1805. A girls' school followed in 1810, kept up by his purse. Full civic rights came by decree in 1814. He later edited the Berlingske Tidende for twenty years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neustadt-phineh:
Phinehas Neustadt was a German rabbi who rose from hardship. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Borek on Sept. 23, 1823. He died at Breslau on Feb. 24, 1902. His father died before he turned two.

His mother apprenticed him to a bookbinder in childhood. Cruel treatment and hunger for study drove him away. He passed a teacher's examination at eighteen years old. Posts in Mecklenburg filled the years to 1855. Arnswalde and Kolberg then took him as rabbi. At Breslau he earned a doctorate from Jena in 1864. His thesis treated immortality in the Talmud. His Hebrew school won state recognition in 1867.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-new-testament-1:
The New Testament is viewed here from a Jewish standpoint. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Kaufmann Kohler for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Church named these books near the second century's close. The name claims a new covenant replaced the old. Its root idea comes from Jeremiah's prophecy.

The entry insists Jeremiah promised renewal, not law's end. Paul's followers, though, read Jesus as that covenant's mediator. Jewish writers use the name only to identify the books. The contents fall in three parts, the entry notes. Gospels and Acts tell the story first. Paul's letters follow, then the Catholic epistles and Revelation. The Gospels arose between 80 and 150 C.E. Mark, the simplest, came first and fed the others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nola-menahem-jo:
Menahem Nola became John Paul Eusthatius at baptism. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was an Italian convert to Christianity. He was born about 1540, it is thought. He died at Rome about the year 1602.

Before baptism he taught Hebrew to Thomas Aldobrandino. That pupil was brother to Pope Clement VIII. The two often debated points of religion together. Aldobrandino likely led him to the Christian faith. He took the name Eusthatius in 1568. His Italian books then defended Christianity in print. One explained the jubilee year's gate ceremony from Scripture. Nine sermons upheld the Trinity and the Messiah's coming. The Vatican keeps his notes on Ruth and Lamentations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orsha-11780:
Orsha is a town in the province of Moghilef, Russia. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Russian tales name the town as far back as the eleventh century. In 1579 a Jew of Brest farmed its customs dues. He farmed the dues of Moghilef and other towns too.

In 1643 a Jew of Orsha helped gather the realm's taxes. By the count of 1897, the town held 13,161 souls. About 7,000 of those souls were Jews of the town. Of them, 950 worked in crafts of the hand. A count in 1880 found 837 houses in Orsha. Jews owned 431 of those houses at that count. The town held one synagogue and ten houses of prayer. Its schools gave lessons to some hundreds of Jewish young.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pamiers-11880:
Pamiers is a chief town of Ariège, in France. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish group lived there in the twelve hundreds. In 1256 the Abbot of St. Antoine gave a grant. It shielded the Jew Bonio, son of Beslinenga, there.

That shield cost Bonio a gold coin in tax each year. In 1279 the Jews of Pamiers made rules for themselves. They curbed the rich gifts they gave at births. They curbed the count of guests at their feasts too. A New Year gift to a child was capped in coin. They barred their folk from the square on the Sabbath. They barred dice and chess games among themselves as well. The abbot passed these rules and showed them good will.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedro-ii-11980:
Pedro the Second ruled Aragon from 1196 to 1213. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1204 he went to Rome for his crown. The pope himself placed it on his head.

At Rome the king swore to guard the Catholic faith. He also swore to hunt down heretics. Jews at home feared they would be driven out. They met him with a Torah scroll and kept a fast. Their fears proved groundless in the end. The king owed Jewish lenders too much to lose them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pfalzburg-12080:
Pfalzburg is a German city in the district of Metz. Gotthard Deutsch and J. Wiener wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish community has lived there since the mid-1700s. In 1770 it counted twelve families. Its cemetery opened in the year 1796.

The town built an old synagogue in 1772. A new one rose on the same site in 1857. The community kept a house with an oratory and bath. Its charity league, founded in 1803, cared for the poor. A Jewish school ran until numbers fell in 1901. One rabbi later led all France.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pipe-12180:
The pipe was a flute-like instrument of the ancient world. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Egypt's monuments show flutes of many shapes. Israel likely played several kinds as well. The Mishnah counts flutes in Temple song.

The Hebrew halil was a bored tube of wood. A cane tongue and few holes made its voice. Each key needed a flute of its own. It sounded at feasts, processions, and pilgrim marches. It also wailed at funerals across the land. Even the poorest mourner would not skip it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poppers-jacob-b:
Jacob Poppers was a German rabbi born at Prague in the mid seventeenth century. The Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father, a noted Talmudist, taught him rabbinic books. Jacob grew very skilled in that learning. He died at Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1740.

Poppers served as rabbi in town after town. He held posts at Coblenz, Treves, and Halberstadt. In 1718 he was called to the rabbinate of Frankfort. He stayed there for the rest of his life. His book Shab Yaakov gathers his rulings in two volumes. It came out at Frankfort in 1742. His Talmud notes were printed inside another man's work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-profiat-12380:
Profiat is a name used by Jews of Provence and northern Spain. Richard Gottheil wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In Hebrew the name is spelled in more than one way. A change of one letter is common in Romance tongues, he notes. In Provençal the name took the forms Prophegue and Profag.

In Latin papers the name shows as Profatius. Jacob ben Makir is one bearer of that form. Copernicus names him in his own work, the article says. In French the name shows as Profait. A record of 1409 names one Isaquetus Profait. The article traces the name through lands and tongues.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-huna-1:
Rabbah bar Huna was a Babylonian teacher of the third set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a son of Huna, head of the school at Sura. He died in the year 322. Men knew him for true piety and deep modesty. Tales of both traits stand in the Talmud.

His father urged him to hear Hisda with great care. Hisda's sharp mind would train him well, his father held. At first Rabbah held back from those talks. The themes raised there did not draw him, it seems. The entry tells how the son grew into a master. It weighs his words beside his father's great name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raschkow-lazar-:
Lazar Raschkow was a German physician and writer born in 1798. Isidore Singer and Moses Löb Bamberger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Raschkow in the province of Posen. He died on August 2, 1870.

The article says his father, the local rabbi, taught him Hebrew. He tutored at Neisse while preparing for higher school. He studied medicine at Budapest and served as an army surgeon. He had to resign over writings for Jewish emancipation. Ill health later ended his medical practice at Mad. He turned to tutoring and writing instead. Near death he wrote his own epitaph. It told the story of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-bonin:
Hugo Rosenthal-Bonin was a German author born at Berlin on October 14, 1840. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied natural science at Berlin and Paris, then traveled widely.

His travels took him through southern Europe, the United States, and Japan. Settling at Stuttgart, he edited the magazine Vom Fels zum Meer from 1889. He wrote steadily, filling book after book with tales and novels. His story collections were translated into many European languages. Titles include Der Diamant-Schleifer, Das Gold des Orion, and Die Tierbändigerin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sachs-wilhelm-1:
Wilhelm Sachs was a German dental surgeon born at Wesenberg on September 22, 1849. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied at Breslau and at the Philadelphia Dental College, graduating in 1872.

Sachs practised dentistry at Vienna and Paris before settling at Breslau. In 1890 he became privat-docent in dental surgery at Breslau's university. He received the title of professor there in 1896, six years later. His book Die Pflege der Zähne, on care of the teeth, appeared in 1887. He also wrote on filling teeth and on pivot teeth for handbooks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-books-of:
Emil G. Hirsch wrote this long Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Books of Samuel. They are two books in the Prophets, the second main part of the Hebrew Bible. They follow Joshua and Judges in the standard order. Samuel and Kings began as single books. The Greek Septuagint joined all four as one history called Books of Kingdoms.

The article first traces how Jerome's Vulgate and later printed Bibles fixed the present split. It then walks through the story chapter by chapter. The first book covers Eli and the young Samuel. It moves to Samuel and Saul, then to Saul and David. Readers get the ark's capture, Saul's rise and fall, and David's victory over Goliath. The survey gives a full map of Israel's first kings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanhedrin-frenc:
Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the French Sanhedrin. Napoleon the First called that Jewish high court into being. It was meant to give legal force to answers given by the Assembly of Notables. The government had put twelve questions to the Notables. They covered marriage, divorce, usury, and Jewish loyalty to France.

Commissioner Molé told the Notables the emperor was pleased. Still, Napoleon wanted a pledge of strict loyalty to those answers. So he resolved to summon a great sanhedrin. It would turn the answers into binding decisions. It would also shape the future status of the Jews. Like the ancient court, it was to hold seventy-one members.
