Their trial model scored consistently and showed signs of real validity. Yet scores differed unfairly across essay topics when human and machine grading were compared. Debelak and Ziegler offer their framework as a shared toolkit for anyone grading by machine.
plos-pone-0354780:
Corrina Moucheraud and colleagues revisit a large phone survey cohort in Kenya two years on, asking who stays reachable in repeated mobile surveys. Phone surveys are booming in lower-income countries, but long-term follow-up by phone was unproven there. From an original group of about fourteen hundred adults first surveyed for a cancer prevention study, the team traced how many were found again and how many completed the new survey.

Retention was high: most of the cohort was found again, and a large majority of those completed the survey. Older adults, men, and higher-income households completed at somewhat higher rates, yet gaps stayed modest. Moucheraud and colleagues conclude that phone panels can hold together well in such settings, and they encourage wider careful use of the method.
plos-pone-0354980:
Atalel Fentahun Awedew led a team of six authors on this 2026 nationwide study of cancer surgery outcomes in Ethiopia. For one week, forty-six hospitals tracked every adult cancer operation nationwide and followed patients for seven days after surgery, recording complications, repeat operations, and deaths.

One in three patients suffered a complication, about one in nine needed another major operation, and roughly one in fifty patients died. Awedew argues the numbers expose weak surgical infrastructure and care routines, and calls for evidence-based strengthening so cancer surgery in Ethiopia becomes safer.
plos-pone-0355280:
Honglei Wei and co-authors built a two-stage statistical framework to turn messy school fitness tests into clear provincial evidence in Sichuan, China. Test batteries differ by grade, so raw scores resist comparison. Their 2026 framework first maps items onto four hidden fitness factors: strength, speed, endurance, and flexibility.

A second stage models those factors across places and years, allowing for leftover geographic clustering. The four factors showed clear, readable spatial patterns across the province. Urbanisation came with higher scores on all four. Other economic, geographic, and environmental factors mattered in domain-specific ways. Wei and colleagues offer the framework for surveillance systems that must compare unlike tests fairly.
plos-pone-0355380:
Martin Ouma and co-authors tested whether extracts of a traditional African plant can protect male fertility against oxidative stress. Carissa spinarum is used traditionally for male infertility, but its chemistry and effects were unproven. Their 2026 study profiled root and leaf extracts, then fed root extract to rats whose fertility was damaged by a stress-inducing drug.

Leaves carried more protective chemicals and stronger antioxidant activity than roots in the test tube. In rats, a mid-level root dose raised sperm count, normal sperm shape, and testis weight. Antioxidant defences in the testes rose while a damage marker fell. Two doses visibly repaired drug-damaged testis tissue. Ouma and colleagues say the results support the traditional use, within animal limits.
plos-pone-0355480:
Fayssal Mekaret and seven colleagues compare ways of modeling a tricky electrical contact in silicon carbide, a material prized for high-power electronics. Where metal meets this semiconductor, the energy barrier that controls current flow is not uniform; it varies from spot to spot. Engineers use different mathematical models to describe that unevenness, and choosing among them is not obvious.

Working with computer simulations across three forms of silicon carbide, the team tested three established approaches. One stresses surface states that pin the energy level, another treats the barrier height as spread out statistically, and the third focuses on small low-barrier patches that carry most of the current. Each revealed a different mechanism, yet all showed current rising with heat in the expected way. The comparison gives device designers clearer guidance for building better contacts.
plos-pone-0355680:
Connor T Panter and colleagues tracked 103 red kites through 180 winters using satellite tags. Red kites are elegant raptors of European farmland. The team asked how much of the birds' winter ground sits inside protected areas. Their 2026 study modeled overlap with Europe's Natura 2000 reserves and other bird areas. It also looked for what predicted a well-protected winter.

Only about a quarter of the kites' core and home ranges overlapped protected land. Birds wintering amid heavy agriculture were worst covered. Birds in Iberia and the Pyrenees fared worse than central European birds. Yet Spain hosts the world's largest wintering population. It also lists the species as endangered nationally. The authors urge new designations aimed at traditional farmland, where legal protection currently thins out.
plos-pone-0355780:
Shaheer Khan, Gautam Talukdar, and Bilal Habib map safe ground for one of the world's rarest large birds in India's Deccan region, in this 2026 conservation study. The Great Indian Bustard, a heavy grassland bird once spread across India and southern Pakistan, now numbers perhaps one hundred to one hundred fifty individuals. Combining landscape surveys with species distribution modeling across an enormous study area, the team estimated where suitable habitat remains.

Only about six to seven percent of the Deccan landscape qualified as suitable. Sixteen critical sites, together about eighteen thousand square kilometers, were named as conservation priorities, forming a mosaic of grassland and farmland. The authors stress that these areas' futures hinge on reviving traditional low-intensity farming and protecting remnant grassland patches. They recommend habitat restoration there as the species' best remaining chance in the south of its range.
plos-pone-0356180:
Koki Nambu and colleagues describe a planned trial of a fibre supplement for a chronic mouth inflammation called oral lichen planus. The condition has no cure, and the team's earlier work found disturbed gut microbes in patients, with too few bacteria that make a calming chemical. Their 2026 protocol sets out a double-blind trial across several centres.

Eighty patients will receive either inulin fibre or a look-alike placebo daily for four weeks, alongside usual care. The main measure is change in the share of the target gut bacteria by week six. Immune markers and wider microbe shifts are secondary measures. No results exist yet; the paper's contribution is a careful, registered test of a gut-directed idea.
plos-pone-0356280:
Ning Shi and three colleagues develop a faster way to judge whether a landslide dam might collapse, in this 2026 study. Such dams form when a slope dumps debris into a river, and their failure can flood downstream towns with little warning. The team used the huge Tangjiashan dam, created by the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake, as their test case, building computer models that treat the debris strength as variable rather than fixed.

Their full model scattered strength values randomly across the dam and ran many simulations to estimate the odds of failure. A leaner local version, which weakens only the most stressed zones, matched the full model's answers while running far more cheaply. The authors offer the method as a practical tool for emergency teams who must judge a new dam's stability within hours, not weeks.
plos-pone-0356380:
Kritika Roka and five colleagues survey mothers in Biratnagar, Nepal, about how they fed their babies, in this 2026 study. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months is among the cheapest ways to protect infant health, yet rates lag in many countries. Interviewers spoke with just over two hundred mothers of children aged six to twenty-three months about feeding since birth and what they knew of the guidance.

Only about thirty-eight percent had breastfed exclusively, for a median of four months, and barely a fifth had adequate knowledge of the recommendation. Many babies received water or formula early, most often because mothers believed their milk was insufficient, or because of work. Mothers in joint families, mothers without schooling, and especially mothers who had no breastfeeding problems were more likely to manage exclusive feeding. The authors call for counseling built into routine mother-and-baby visits.
plos-pone-0356480:
Vera Logan leads a team of seven testing a checklist against the quiet harm of repeat prescriptions, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Older patients on many medicines accumulate side effects nobody is assigned to notice. The intervention is a structured symptom profile patients complete. A practice pharmacist reviews it and acts. Six practices in South West Wales were randomized as clusters. They recruited sixty patients over sixty-five, each on more than four long term medicines, living at home.

The trial paired numbers with a process evaluation. Records before and after were modeled for problems and prescribing changes, adjusting for age, deprivation, and comorbidity. Symptoms on first and second profiles were compared to see what resolved. Patients and staff described the work involved. Harm from unmonitored prescriptions has been documented for decades and prevented by almost nothing. This trial asks whether structured patient reporting can move it.
plos-pone-0356880:
Chia-En Hsieh and colleagues surveyed 345 clinical nurses at a Taiwanese medical center to trace how workplace stress erodes commitment to the profession, and what psychological steps carry the damage. Their 2026 cross-sectional study measured stress, resilience, coping style, and professional commitment, then tested a chain model in which stress works through resilience and then coping.

Stress was indeed linked to weaker commitment, and the chain held: nurses with depleted resilience coped less adaptively, and commitment suffered further, though a direct stress effect remained. Because the design captures one moment, the authors avoid causal claims. Still, the pathway suggests hospitals wanting to keep nurses should invest in resilience training and coping support, not merely exhort loyalty.
plos-pone-0357180:
Bianca Cristina dos Santos led a team of eight researchers studying sickle cell anemia in mice, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. In this disease, misshapen red cells break apart and spill free hemoglobin into the blood, where it does harm. The team tested haptoglobin, a protein the body already uses to mop up that free hemoglobin.

Dos Santos and her colleagues asked whether giving extra haptoglobin could work as a treatment in a mouse model of the disease. Their results point to real promise for that approach. If the effect holds up in later work, boosting a natural cleanup protein could become one way to limit the damage sickle cell disease does to organs over time.
plos-pone-0357380:
Wanjie Kang and Youshun Pan presented a method for hiding messages inside images, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Steganography conceals data within a picture so its very presence stays secret. The hidden data must survive routine handling, such as compression or cropping, or the message is lost or exposed.

Kang and Pan aimed for a method that is both lightweight and robust. Their technique keeps the payload secret and intact even when the image is squeezed or edited along the way. Lightweight design matters for phones and small devices that lack computing power. Secure communication tools benefit when hiding power does not demand heavy software that few people can run.
plos-pone-0357780:
Lingmei Wu and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents an improved detector for weeds in cotton fields, called YOLO-CCG. The setting is complex fields, where weeds hide among crop plants with similar color and shape. The model builds on the YOLO family of fast image detectors.

Reliable weed spotting is the first step toward targeted spraying, which cuts chemical use by treating only where weeds grow. Cotton fields are a hard test because young weeds and cotton seedlings look alike. Agricultural engineers developing spraying robots and drone scouting are the audience for a detector tuned to this crop.
plos-pone-0358080:
Emily R. Spencer and coauthors published a 2026 analysis in PLOS ONE on menopause, human papillomavirus, and cervical disease among middle-aged women in Senegal. Cervical cancer is a leading cancer killer in West Africa, and hormone and immune changes at menopause might affect whether the virus is detected. The team reanalyzed three earlier Dakar studies of women aged forty to sixty, comparing those past menopause with those who were not.

After menopause, women had notably higher odds of a positive HPV test, for both high-risk and low-risk virus types. Odds of cervical cell changes were also higher, though that result was not statistically firm and weakened in checks limited to women with known HIV status. The authors read the pattern as a hint that menopause may help the virus persist or reappear. They argue screening programs in the region should not assume risk ends at midlife.
plos-pone-0358180:
Chunxiao Liu and coauthors published a 2026 gene analysis in PLOS ONE on liposarcoma, a common cancer of fatty soft tissue whose molecular drivers remain unclear. They compared gene activity in tumor and normal fat tissue, mapped how the differing genes interact, and checked key candidates with laboratory tests on real samples. They also estimated which immune cells were present inside the tumors.

Several genes tied to cell division stood out: tumors expressing high levels of a set of seven of them were linked to shorter survival, and a further group predicted earlier relapse. Another ten genes emerged as possible diagnostic markers. The immune analysis found resting mast cells more common in tumor tissue than in normal fat, hinting they may play a role in how the cancer develops. The mast cell finding needs experimental confirmation, but the gene lists give treatment researchers concrete targets.
plos-pone-0358480: Ahmad and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in mathematics on fixed point methods. A fixed point is a value that a function leaves unchanged, and finding one solves many equations. The team built a shared approach for enriched paired mappings. They applied it to Volterra systems, which carry memory of the past, and to chaos in fractional-order systems. One method that covers many cases saves later researchers work.
plos-pone-0358580:
Ruba Malkawi, writing alone in PLOS ONE in 2026, turns fish waste into a drug delivery trick. Baicalein, a plant flavonoid with antioxidant and medicinal promise, barely dissolves in water, which keeps it from being absorbed when swallowed. Malkawi extracted oil from salmon viscera, normally discarded. It became the liquid core of a liquisolid compact. That tablet form spreads a drug through oil on a powder carrier, to speed dissolving.

Laboratory checks found no chemical clash between the drug and its new partners. Heat and X-ray analysis showed the baicalein's stubborn crystal structure largely broken down inside the formulation, the change that lets such drugs dissolve faster. Dissolution tests in a standard apparatus and an antioxidant assay completed the evaluation. The study pairs two sustainability stories: a waste stream becomes a pharmaceutical ingredient, and a hard to deliver natural compound gets a greener vehicle.
plos-pone-0358780:
Jin Chen and three colleagues study why a stubborn breast inflammation returns after treatment, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Granulomatous lobular mastitis mostly strikes young women and often recurs, frustrating patients and doctors. The team reviewed five hundred twenty confirmed cases from a provincial hospital registry spanning 2017 to 2024. They asked whether tiny abscesses seen under the microscope predict relapse. They also asked whether treatment choice changes that risk.

Just over half the patients showed microabscesses in their tissue samples. Statistical models that adjust for other factors singled out microabscess, the side of the affected breast, and white blood cell counts among the independent predictors of recurrence. The authors then compared one year relapse rates across treatment paths, including a class of antibiotics and surgical removal, split by microabscess status. Their stratified results aim at matching treatment intensity to each woman's actual relapse risk.
plos-pone-0358880:
Michelle Beattie, Lesley Campbell, Bev Fraser, and Anna Terje wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on emergency care. It evaluates the Trigger Checklist, a prompt tool, paired with assertive outreach, active follow-up rather than waiting. The aim is to reduce drug-related harm among people arriving at the Emergency Department.

The method is a realist evaluation, which asks what works, for whom, and in what circumstances, instead of chasing one average effect. Emergency departments see drug harm at its sharpest but rarely control what happens after discharge. Hospital teams designing harm reduction links from the emergency door are the readers.
plos-pone-0358980:
Aijie Yu and co-authors investigated in 2026 how the glaciers of the Karakoram have gained or lost mass over the past twenty-five years. The Karakoram range, between Pakistan, India, and China, holds some of the largest glaciers outside the polar regions, and they have behaved unusually compared with shrinking glaciers elsewhere. The team combined observations from several sources to build a fuller picture than any single method allows.

Glacier mass balance decides how much meltwater flows to the rivers that hundreds of millions of people depend on. Tracking it carefully over decades separates real change from year to year weather noise. The study refines the account of a region sometimes called the Karakoram anomaly, where glaciers have resisted the global pattern of loss.
plos-pone-0359280: Lin and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in abstract mathematics. Their topic is bornological stabilization families, a way to describe how sets settle down in spaces with a built-in notion of bounded parts. They also study how sequences of closed sets swing or converge. Such work builds the basic language that other branches of analysis and topology rely on.
plos-pone-0359580:
Bira Belay and Alamiya Abdo published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a cross-sectional study, based in the community, of adolescents in urban Dire Dawa, in eastern Ethiopia. The subject is the daily purchase of unhealthy food by teenagers, and the factors associated with that habit.

Daily buying matters more than occasional treats, because routine purchases of sugary or fatty snacks shape diet and health over years. Surveying a whole community, not just school pupils, catches adolescents who might otherwise be missed. City health officers and school program planners in Ethiopia can use the linked factors to target the shops, prices, and habits behind teen diets.
plos-pone-0360080:
Rodrigo Martinez Alcala and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma, a cancer of the lymph system. The team tested whether staining tumor tissue for three markers, CD68, c-MET, and HLA class II, could help predict how patients would do.

The data come from the H9 trial run jointly by EORTC and GELA, a large randomised treatment study across several countries. As the title states, the marker tests did not show prognostic value in these patients. A clear negative answer like this still helps doctors, because it rules out tests that would add cost and effort without guiding care.
plos-pone-0360380:
Zihan Dong and colleagues unraveled in 2026 how a Burkholderia bacterium frees potassium from biotite, a common mineral in soils. Potassium is one of the three main nutrients crops need, and most of it in soil is locked inside minerals that plants cannot use directly. Certain bacteria can weather those minerals and release the nutrient, acting as living fertilizer.

The authors work out the biochemical steps and the speed of the process, its kinetics, for their strain working on biotite. Knowing the mechanism, rather than only the outcome, helps scientists breed or select better strains and predict how they behave in real fields. The study supports the wider search for biological replacements for mined potash fertilizer.
plos-pone-0360480:
Amanuel Yoseph, Lakew Mussie, Mehretu Belayneh, and Francisco Guillen-Grima wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It reports a trial in Southern Ethiopia on food during pregnancy. The food is amaranth flatbread, made from a grain rich in nutrients, and the outcome measured is maternal anthropometry, body measurements of the mothers.

The trial is cluster-randomized and controlled, meaning whole groups rather than single women were assigned by chance to receive the bread or not. Testing a local, affordable food matters where undernutrition in pregnancy is common. Nutrition programs in similar settings can judge from this design whether amaranth deserves a place in maternal diets.
pmc-10652480:
Wei Xie and co-authors show that a common cholesterol drug can kill colon cancer cells by a fiery form of cell death, in a 2023 study. Outcomes in colon cancer still disappoint, and the drug's anti-cancer paths were unclear. The team treated two colon cancer cell lines and tracked cell survival and death rates. They also measured reactive oxygen, a stress signal, and a chain of proteins tied to this death mode.

Treated cells died in the fiery mode and grew more slowly. Markers of the death chain rose across the board. Blocking either the key cutting enzyme or the oxygen stress blunted the drug's effect, which pins the path down. In mice grafted with the cancer cells, the drug shrank tumors by the same route. The authors present the cholesterol drug as a candidate worth testing for colon cancer care.
pmc-10654680:
Xijing Yan and co-authors test a pair of drugs against liver cancer, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Single-drug care works poorly for this cancer, above all when it is advanced. The pair joins a common pain and fever drug with a targeted cancer drug.

In cell tests and in mice, the pair shrank tumors more than either drug alone. No grave side effects showed in the mouse tests. Gene work found the pair hits many cancer-linked genes and cell pathways at once. The team calls the pair a hopeful option to test further for patients with this cancer.
pmc-10655880:
Kamran Abbasi and a large group of journal editors called on health workers to press for cuts in nuclear war risk, in an editorial published in 2023. The Doomsday Clock stands at ninety seconds to midnight, its worst mark. The UN chief has warned of danger not seen since the height of the Cold War. Arms agreements lag, and the last big review meeting closed with no joint statement.

Even a small war, they write, could kill more than a hundred million at once and starve billions in the cold aftermath. A full war between the United States and Russia could kill billions more and risk the survival of humankind. New fast missiles shrink the time to tell a true strike from a false alarm. The editors urge health voices to push leaders to scrap the bombs.
pmc-10656380:
Hanno Hoppe and co-authors review CT cavernosography for finding and treating venous leak in erectile dysfunction. Their twenty twenty-three paper calls venous leak the most common vessel cause of the condition. Leaking veins drain blood too fast for a firm erection, but the leak can be sealed by embolization.

Older diagnosis used plain cavernosography, a dye study with flat images. CT adds cross-section views that may plan treatment better. The team searched the literature in a systematic way and built a new care path that includes CT. Readers get both the proof base and a step-by-step algorithm for clinics.
pmc-10656480:
Bogdan Obrișcă and colleagues run an open label budesonide study in risky IgA kidney disease, in work from 2023. The steroid acts in the gut, where the faulty antibody response is thought to start. Patients at high risk of decline need options that spare full body steroid harm.

Thirty-two patients took a daily dose for one year, then a tapered dose for another. Urine protein fell by a third at one year and kept falling after. Kidney filter rates held steady across the full three year watch span. Side effects stayed mostly mild and reversible through the treatment course. Protein cuts with stable function mark a favourable risk balance here.
pmc-10656980:
A one-year-old boy in China carried a gene change never reported before, and it reshaped his heart and groin at once. The authors describe a nonsense mutation in ELN, the elastin gene, found by sequencing after the child presented with exercise intolerance, poor weight gain, a heart murmur, and an inguinal hernia. The mutation mildly narrowed the valve above his aorta and severely narrowed his branch pulmonary arteries.

Surgeons rebuilt the narrowed arteries using the child's own pericardium, then repaired the hernia three months later. Six months on, he had recovered well and was gaining weight. The team suggests hernia may belong on the list of signs tied to this gene, pending more cases.
pmc-10659680:
Xianqun Ji, Xiaochen Wang, Liang Shi and Fangtao Tian studied whether an extra day of tranexamic acid after spinal fusion surgery helps patients in 2023. The drug reduces bleeding, and all patients received it during surgery; one group also received it intravenously within 24 hours afterwards.

That group had less drainage, shorter drainage time and a shorter hospital stay, plus fewer blood and albumin transfusions. Blood loss during surgery and operating time were the same in both groups, and complication rates did not differ. No extra clotting events appeared. The authors conclude that short-term use after multi-level fusion is safe and improves early recovery.
pmc-10669580:
Francesca Brutti and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-three comparing two AI approaches for judging skin lesions. Melanoma rates have risen fast, and early diagnosis improves survival. The team asked whether a classic image-analysis pipeline or a deep learning network better separates harmless moles from malignant ones in magnified skin images.

Both models trained on the same large public set of more than twenty-five thousand images. On a separate test set of two hundred images, the deep learning method reached higher accuracy and specificity than the classic ensemble method. The authors note both did well in validation, but the network generalized better to unseen images. They suggest such tools could speed population screening when joined with clinic devices.
pmc-10671580:
Landon Moore and co-authors review, in 2023, the gene variants of a protein kinase that marks cancer stem cells. Cancer survival gains have lagged behind biology gains, so fresh strategies are needed. The kinase comes in several forms, made by alternative promoters and splicing, and those forms are shaped by chemical marks on DNA.

All forms keep the same enzyme core, so their distinct roles must come from other parts of the protein. The review covers what each form does and how the two promoters are controlled. The authors propose pairing drugs that steer which form is made with drugs that target the kinase itself. That pairing, they argue, could beat either alone.
pmc-10675180:
Parts printed by selective laser sintering often contain pores, a weak point of the method, yet no one had lined up the published porosity numbers side by side. Morano and co-authors gather results from many studies on pure and blended polymers, both amorphous and semi-crystalline types. For each material they tabulate the printing settings alongside the measured porosity.

The review gives builders a direct comparison of how much void space each material and setting tends to leave. The authors argue such a table can guide material choice and process tuning. They present the work as a reference for advancing printed polymer quality across labs.
pmc-10675480:
Xiaolong Huang and co-authors pin down what one small auxin-responsive gene does for a rice seedling. The SAUR family answers the growth hormone auxin within minutes, but rice carries so many copies that single functions hide. Their 2023 paper studies OsSAUR10, whose message carries a built-in self-destruct tag that makes it fleeting by design.

The protein sits in the cell membrane, and its gene switches on in specific tissues, stages, and hormone conditions. Knocking the gene out with CRISPR produced dwarf plants with narrow stem segments, fewer tillers, and lower yield, and microscopy showed its cells failing to elongate. Curiously, adding extra copies changed little, as if the plant guards the dose. The gene also steers two gene groups, those making auxin and those pumping it around the plant.
pmc-10687280:
Jiaxiong Tan and co-authors built a risk score in 2023 for neuroblastoma, a childhood cancer of the nerve tissue whose course swings from mild to deadly. They fused genes tied to one famous cancer driver with genes tied to cell aging, hunting a better forecast than either set alone.

Using 498 patient samples and 307 aging related genes, they distilled a six gene signature. The score sorted patients by outcome more sharply than any single gene could. Tumors flagged high risk showed worn out killer T cells bearing both an exhaustion marker and an aging marker, above all when the cancer driver was amplified. The authors offer the score for prognosis and for reading the tumor's immune state.
pmc-10691380:
Shuai Wang and seven co-authors mapped a research field where knee arthritis meets cell aging in a 2023 bibliometric study. Aging cells are thought to drive knee osteoarthritis, and the authors charted who publishes what on the pair. They analyzed 1,074 papers from 1992 to 2023 in a major citation database.

Output grew about 30 percent a year. The United States led in papers and citations, and one journal dominated influence. The most productive author had 31 papers, yet collaboration between authors was weak. Sixty percent of the 1,556 institutions sat in one country group the analysis highlights. The study offers newcomers a map of the field's leaders, journals, and hot topics.
pmc-10691680:
Ibarra-Sanchez, Abelsen, Chen, and Wisløff track in twenty twenty-three how schooling levels pattern weight and health habits over time in northern Norway. Unequal weight, smoking, inactivity, and heavy drinking help explain social gaps in chronic disease, but how they move together across life was unclear. The team used two waves of a big regional survey, nearly nine thousand adults, spaced about eight years apart.

Most people stayed in the same weight and habit groups at follow-up. Healthy patterns, and shifts toward them, clustered among the most educated. Less educated groups more often kept or gained risky patterns. The authors say measuring such uneven exposures can help set policy priorities to close health gaps.
pmc-10692180:
Sadegh Hosseinniaee and four co-authors used plants to pull toxic metals from mine soil in a 2023 study. The soil near a lead zinc mine held lead, cadmium, and zinc at levels that harm health. Three local plant species that hoard metals were grown in pots of the soil, with a helper chemical added at four dose levels.

The helper freed more metal for uptake, and plant tissue levels rose. Stress guard enzymes in the plants also rose with the dose. The top dose cut leaf green and plant bulk, so more was not always better. One species hoarded all three metals well. The team says the helper plus the right plant can clean such soil, with care on dose.
pmc-10692880:
Jinqing Yang, Zhifeng Liu, Qicong Wang, and Na Lu published a 2023 study of what makes a health post on a question-and-answer site attract good answers, and what makes it popular. Such sites are now a first stop for health information. The team collected all health posts from Metafilter, a well-known site of this kind.

Their collection ran to more than eighteen thousand posts. Statistical models then measured what influenced two scores: how many favorite marks a post won, and how many comments it drew. What a post said influenced both, most of all its tone. A warm tone won more favorites but drew fewer comments. How actively and how widely the poster took part on the site also influenced the scores, in opposite ways. The topic area of a post influenced popularity more than answers. The study maps which posts fly and which sink.
pmc-10693080:
Stomach cancer kills often and is usually caught late, so doctors need better ways to forecast its course. Zhang and co-authors mine gene data for a signature tied to fat metabolism, a set of pathways tumors rewire as they grow.

Combining bulk tumor data with single-cell sequencing, they sifted hundreds of lipid-related genes down to two that mattered most, GPX3 and NNMT. A risk score built on the pair split patients cleanly: low-risk patients lived significantly longer in two separate datasets. The score also fed a bedside chart that predicted survival well. Immune profiling showed the high-risk tumors carried a different mix of immune cells, rich in natural killer cells and macrophages. The authors offer the two-gene test as a tool for tailoring treatment to the patient.
pmc-10693480:
Williams and co-authors probe the safety of dry needling deep back muscles near the spine, in a 2023 cadaver study. Physical therapists needle the lumbar multifidi to treat low back pain. Safety work had covered kidneys and lungs in the upper lumbar area, but not whether a needle can slip into the spinal canal. Using ultrasound guidance on a fresh-frozen cadaver lying face down, they followed a documented technique at the junction of chest and low back.

The needle, placed one centimeter off the spine's midline and angled inward, pierced the ligament covering the canal and entered the canal space. The finding does not ban the technique, the authors note. It argues for strong anatomy training and ultrasound use when needling at this level.
pmc-10693580:
Michelle Evans and co-authors fix a blind spot in disease counting in a 2023 paper. Rural clinics see only a slice of illness, since distance and cost keep patients home. Raw clinic counts then mislead maps of where disease truly strikes.

Their estimator, ZERO-G, models how sampling intensity varies with facility traits and corrects for the many zeros. Applied to malaria records from a rural Madagascar district, it cut geographic and money bias by over ninety percent. Agreement with survey-based patterns doubled. The method yields real-time incidence at a grain nearly ten times finer than usual facility reports. Better maps mean fairer targeting of scarce health resources.
pmc-10694280:
Mwesige and co-authors report a newborn repair done with few resources. The baby had esophageal atresia with a fistula to the airway. Such defects block feeding and threaten life without prompt surgery. The term infant weighed 3 kg at birth. Signs included choking, spit-up after feeds, and a swollen belly.

Scans showed the blocked esophagus and the abnormal link. A heart scan found a moderate ductus that had not yet closed. The team did an open repair on day six of life. The repair worked, and the child survived. The authors stress sharp suspicion, teamwork, and skill in low-resource care.
pmc-10694380:
Yakun Luo, Qing Shi, Lu Wang, and two colleagues write a research letter on a transcription factor that helps kidney cancer cells multiply, published in two thousand twenty-three. The cancer is clear cell renal cell carcinoma, whose advanced cases resist surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, and often outlast targeted drugs too.

The factor, TCF19, had already shown prognostic value: its levels predict patient survival. What it actually does in these cells was unstudied. The authors set out to dissect the mechanism behind its effect on proliferation. Their title names the axis they uncover: TCF19 epigenetically regulates FOXM1 and AURKB, two drivers of cell division. Understanding such circuits is how new drug targets and biomarkers are found. The letter reports the analysis of TCF19 expression in tumor tissue and the experiments that follow. It addresses clinicians and researchers hunting better options for a stubborn cancer.
pmc-10694580:
Chen-Chan Hsieh and colleagues give a step-by-step protocol for turning human stem cells into cartilage cells without the usual growth factor, in this methods paper from twenty twenty-three. Mesenchymal stem cells can become cartilage, bone, or fat. The standard cartilage recipe uses TGF-beta, but it can overshoot, pushing cells toward bone-like hypertrophy and other fates.

Their route blocks the Wnt signal instead, which steers the cells to cartilage more cleanly. The protocol details each step: forming the cell pellets, applying the Wnt blockade, and refreshing the medium on schedule. It also details the tests used to prove the cells became cartilage. The authors offer the method to labs building cartilage therapies that need efficient, on-target differentiation, and point to their earlier study for the full evidence behind it.
pmc-10694880:
Jenner and four co-authors review eye-tracking as a way to study social thinking in people with intellectual disability. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-three. Classic tasks lean hard on language and general thinking, which can mask the social skills they aim to measure.

Eye-tracking watches where people look, offering a gentler probe. The team searched four databases and kept forty-nine sound studies across many disability groups. A pooled analysis of twelve studies linked gaze on social parts of images with autism traits on clinical scales. The technology measured several kinds of social attention. The authors judge it a useful tool for this group, including for understanding how autism overlaps with intellectual disability.
pmc-10694980:
Chenxi Liu and eight co-authors traced Chinese pig genes inside Danish breeding pigs, in a 2023 study. Taihu Lake pigs from China are famous for large litters. Their genes entered some European breeds decades ago. Whether Danish Large White pigs carry that heritage was unclear. The team re-sequenced genomes from over three hundred Eurasian pigs.

Shared DNA stretches confirmed Taihu genes inside the Danish breed. Genes in those stretches clustered in nerve development pathways. One stretch on a single chromosome stood out for how widely it was shared. The Taihu version of that stretch improved breeding results across several pig groups. A nearby gene was active in reproductive tissues and differed between high and low fertility sows. The authors name it a candidate cause of the fertility gain.
pmc-10696080:
Ashley Lyons and co-authors time the glow life of dye marks with paired photons in place of fast clocks, in a study from 2023. Glow life tells how a mark sits in its world, yet clock based reads stall at a few tenths of a billionth of a tick. Pair bunch counts have no such wall. Their pace is set by the flash span alone, which can run a tenth of that tick or less.

Dyes with lives from one to seven ticks were read in about a tick each. The same trick read the syrup grade of sweet water blends through a spin mark whose life swings ten fold with syrup grade. That gives touch free reads of flow at tiny scales.
pmc-10696680:
Xuechen Tian and colleagues characterized in 2023 two Actinomyces strains from the human mouth and proposed them as new species. These bacteria live on body surfaces and help form dental plaque, yet the two strains' true classification had stayed unresolved despite years of use in studies. Genome and gene sequencing were used to settle it.

Both draft genomes were about three million bases with high GC content. Many gene checks placed each strain on its own lineage, and whole-genome similarity scores fell below species thresholds against known relatives. Each strain also carried many unique gene clusters and genomic islands. The names Actinomyces acetigenes and Actinomyces stomatis were proposed, with notes on possible virulence traits and defense systems.
pmc-10696780:
María Gallego-García and co-authors review making fuel oil inside yeast, in a 2023 paper. Biodiesel is renewable, but today's supply grows on farmland, tying fuel prices to food crops and sparking a food-versus-fuel fight. Oily yeasts offer an escape: they pack their cells with fat much like vegetable oil, without needing fields.

The catch is cost, so the review focuses on feeding the yeasts cheap, non-synthetic sugars, above all sugars freed from woody plant waste. Within a biorefinery, where every stream earns its keep, yeast oil could finally compete. The authors round up the latest advances and name the hurdles that remain, from feedstock handling to oil recovery at scale.
pmc-10696880:
Zhengbo Wei and Sheng Li pool trials of a two-drug pairing for children's cough-variant asthma in a 2023 meta-analysis. In this asthma form, a stubborn cough is the main symptom, and the question was whether adding montelukast to inhaled fluticasone beats the steroid alone.

Nine studies met the criteria. The combination raised the overall effective rate and cut cough recurrence. Children on both drugs also settled their cough sooner and recovered lung function better, measured by a standard breathing index. Safety outcomes were part of the pooling. The authors conclude the pairing is effective and safe for this condition.
pmc-10697980:
Pamela Soh and eleven co-authors study prostate cancer gene risk in Black South African men in a 2023 paper. African ancestry raises risk of prostate cancer and harsh disease. Most gene studies were done far from Sub-Saharan Africa. Known risk lists may thus miss African-relevant signals.

The team read whole genome data from Black South African men. A broad risk score from past studies failed to sort cases here. They then scanned exome variants in 798 men for finer links. Some genes tied to risk, and others tied to aggressive disease. Two genes stood out for harsh disease in the scan. The authors call for wider African inclusion in gene studies.
pmc-10698880:
Marta Giezek and co-authors studied why many foster grandparents run out of patience, in a 2023 paper. In Poland, grandparents form the largest group of kinship carers, often raising grandchildren into old age. Seventy-five carers aged sixty-one to ninety-seven in the northwest answered surveys in 2018 and 2019, with standard mental health scales.

Nearly half, about forty-seven percent, reported lacking patience with the children. The deficit tracked a weaker sense of coherence, above all feeling life is manageable. Impatient carers also reframed problems positively less, sought emotional support less, and vented more. Fixed traits like personality and general confidence showed no split. The authors point support toward coping skills, not character.
pmc-10698980:
Limin Luo and co-authors test whether ultrasound measures of heart muscle work can forecast trouble for patients whose blood pressure resists treatment, in a study published in 2023. Resistant hypertension affects roughly ten to twenty percent of treated patients and carries high risk of organ damage. Myocardial work combines pressure with strain imaging to judge how efficiently the heart pumps.

The team enrolled 283 patients in 2018 and 2019 and followed them for three years. About 29 percent suffered an adverse event, most often kidney insufficiency or heart attack. Work indices from the baseline scan separated those who later had events from those who did not, offering a noninvasive warning sign. Early identification could focus closer follow-up on the patients most likely to deteriorate.
pmc-10700280:
Soha Elshaer and Mona Shaaban grow silver and copper nanoparticles with the help of a soil microbe in a 2023 study. The goal is a weapon against biofilms, the slimy shields that let bacteria shrug off antibiotics.

Using a Streptomyces strain as the factory, the team made tiny, even particles of both metals. In lab tests the particles stopped bacteria from settling and cut the living cells inside existing films. They also broke down mature films grown by three tough hospital pathogens. Gene activity tied to film building dropped in all three. The authors propose the particles as add-on therapy against resistant infections.
pmc-10701980:
Han, Xie, Shao, Li, and Du study how ventilator use injures lungs in mice in twenty twenty-three. Mechanical ventilation can harm lungs in patients with severe respiratory failure. The injury involves inflammation driven by immune cells and their signals. The team focused on macrophages that live in the air sacs of the lung.

Mice were ventilated with high tidal volumes to model the injury. Removing the macrophages eased the lung injury and lowered levels of an enzyme they release. Blocking that enzyme had a like effect. The enzyme switched on a pathway in airway lining cells that disturbed mitochondria, the energy centres of the cell. Cell experiments matched the animal findings. The authors say the pathway may be a target for prevention or treatment.
pmc-10702780:
Some adults live for years with low blood platelets from an immune fault, and a few also lose red cells the same way. Debbie Jiang and co-authors asked in 2023 how often a born gene fault in the immune system lies behind such cases in adults.

The team screened forty four adults at one US clinic with a gene test that spans more than three hundred and seventy genes. No case of a born immune fault turned up. Eight adults carried one copy of a fault gene, which is not enough to cause the illness. The authors say broad gene screening in adults with these blood faults is apt to find little.
pmc-10703780:
Daiana Rodrigues-de-Souza and co-authors compare pelvic and back muscle traits between men and women in a 2023 study. Muscle tone, stiffness, and elasticity guide rehab, but sex differences in the lumbopelvic zone were unmapped. The study enrolled thirty-five healthy women and thirty-five men, all of childbearing-age range and without children for the women.

A handheld device measured tone, stiffness, elasticity, and slow deformation traits at the pelvic floor and lower back. At the pelvic floor, women showed higher tone and stiffness and lower elasticity than men. At the back, men showed higher tone and stiffness instead. Links to age, body mass, and function appeared mostly in men. The authors stress that sex gaps flip by site.
pmc-10703880:
Siming Zhang and eight co-authors scan a family of growth-slowing genes across many cancers in 2023. The family has six members and sits in cell membranes. Past work links the family to how cancers start and spread, but a full scan across tumor types was lacking.

Using a large public cancer atlas, the team checked gene levels, patient outlook, and links to mutation load and drug response. Most family genes ran low in tumor samples. Their levels tied to how long patients lived and to the mix of immune cells in tumors. The scan marks the family as a possible guide for prognosis and for picking drugs.
pmc-10704280:
Myrian Fan and co-authors gather the evidence on nature as therapy for autistic children in a 2023 review. Gardens, farms, and outdoor programs are widely offered to children on the spectrum, yet the proof behind them was scattered. The team searched ten databases plus grey sources for trials and controlled studies reporting health outcomes.

Twenty-four studies with seven hundred seventeen children qualified, spanning roughly ages five to eighteen. Pooling thirteen studies in a meta-analysis found a significant, moderate-sized benefit in the negative direction the scales reward, pointing to improved functioning. Outcomes covered social, behavioral, emotional, and sensory domains, plus children's own reported wellbeing. Studies that could not be pooled were summarized under standard guidance. The authors call the signal promising but the base thin, and they map exactly which designs future trials should run.
pmc-10707580:
Shiping Wei, Wenxiu Wang, and Feirong Xiao describe a sea fungus that turns dissolved manganese into mineral crusts, in a 2023 study. Manganese oxides are reactive minerals that steer the movement of carbon, nutrients, and metals in nature, and microbes are thought to make most of them. The team isolated a marine fungus strain and watched it work.

Under microscopes, oxide grains formed on the fungal threads and wrapped parts of them in a filament-shaped mat. Tests showed the mineral is poorly crystalline and mostly in a high oxidation state, proof the fungus converted the metal rather than just collecting it. Understanding how fungi build these minerals clarifies how manganese cycles through oceans and soils, and hints at biological routes to useful oxide materials.
pmc-10707780:
Metal-organic frameworks are porous crystals prized for their tunable structure and huge inner surface. A research team built two such frameworks that differ mainly in how much fluorine they hold. They wired the materials into triboelectric nanogenerators, small devices that turn rubbing motion into electric power.

More fluorine meant stronger power output from the generator. The team then used the charged materials to build a self-powered shield against corrosion for metals. Powered by motion alone, the system actively protects metal surfaces from rusting. The 2023 study ties a small change in crystal makeup to both better energy harvesting and a working anti-corrosion device that needs no battery.
pmc-10708080:
Tukhbatullin and co-authors use sound-driven glow in a 2023 study to spot traces of ring-shaped fuel molecules in plain hydrocarbons. Their crystals, salts of two rare earths, glow when shaken by ultrasound in oil. When benzene-like molecules are near, the glow takes on their own light bands.

The glow grew in step with how much of each ring molecule was added. Detection limits reached as low as a tenth of a part per million for one of them. The glow even showed in shop-bought fuels spiked with gasoline. A glow test could screen fuels fast.
pmc-10708280:
Siegfried Reipert and co-authors speed up a preservation method that lets electron microscopes see lichens in near-living detail. Standard chemical fixation is slow and creates artifacts, while freezing methods lock living structure in place but took far too long to adopt. Their automated protocol adds constant agitation to freeze substitution, the step where frozen water is swapped for solvent.

Applied to three lichen species, the method preserved the native state of the algal and fungal partners and their shared outer matrix. The images reveal varied fungal threads, the matrix itself, and crystallized metabolite deposits, plus algal pockets crowded with mitochondria. The authors expect the faster protocol to spread cryo-preparation through lichen research.
pmc-10708680:
Liu and co-authors propose a way to pack more data channels into free-space light links. Light beams that carry orbital angular momentum can multiply channels and raise capacity. In practice, imperfect beam making and sorting limit how many states get used. Their scheme uses a multi-ring perfect vortex beam. A checkerboard method encodes both brightness and phase into a single hologram. The beam's four rings act as separate channels in one spot.

Each ring carries its own angular momentum beam independently. That layout raises both total capacity and capacity per unit of space. The scheme needs only a small range of momentum states. The authors frame it as a path to denser optical links.
pmc-10708780:
Seismic surveys map the deep Earth by listening, and dense listening is dear. Titova and co-authors lay out a sparser net in 2023 that still hears truly, by the maths of compressive sensing. Their design runs in two steps.

First, a random scatter of sources and ears is cast, backed by a known recovery rule. Then extra points are sewn in so no gap between neighbours grows too wide, backed by a second rule. The count of live and skipped points bends to the budget. Shifted points — the field's daily accident — are tested for how much harm they do. A sparse net with proof under it could cut the cost of mapping oil, water, and fault lines.
pmc-10709280:
Istvan Z Kiss, Luc Berthouze, and Wasiur R KhudaBukhsh ask how much of a contact network can be learned back from epidemic data. Their 2023 paper notes that spread over networks breaks with old mass action models, but exact network models are too large to fit to data. A leaner mean field model, the pairwise model, keeps the problem workable.

The team tests that model with a standard spread pattern of susceptible, infected, and recovered people. They fit it two ways: a likelihood method for daily case counts, and a survival based method for person level data like recovery times. On simulated data with no model mismatch, both routes recover disease and network values well, despite tangled links between parameters. Trouble starts when the model and the data diverge.
pmc-10709380:
Five researchers in the Netherlands tested whether mobile phone fields change brain waves, in a study published in 2023. Earlier work on this question often suffered from weak controls, so results were hard to trust. The team built a careful test setup and used a strong form of statistics to weigh what they found. Their work used healthy adult volunteers.

Thirty-two people took part in a blind test with two eighteen-minute sessions each. In one session the phone field was on, and in the other it was a sham, with the order swapped between groups. Sensors at 63 points on the head recorded brain waves while eyes were open or closed. The tests gave signs of a field effect on alpha waves when eyes were open. The setup may help later tests of new phone signals.
pmc-10709880:
Mihyeon Seong, Dajung Ryu, and Sohyune Sok published a 2023 study of nursing students in South Korea. They explored how students view disaster safety. Thirty students sorted statements about disasters into a grid. The method reveals shared viewpoints, not just averages. Better understanding can shape disaster training.

Four viewpoints emerged from the sorting patterns. One stressed national responsibility for safety. Another stressed personal responsibility. A third focused on being prepared in advance. The fourth emphasized education. Each type implies a different teaching strategy. Nursing schools can match lessons to how students actually think.
pmc-10709980:
Yongbing Sun and colleagues ask how social support eases anxiety and depression in people living with HIV, in this study from China, published in twenty twenty-three. Support from family and friends is known to help, but the path from support to calm was unclear. The team proposed that resilience, the skill of bouncing back, carries the effect.

One hundred sixty-one patients at one hospital filled in scales for support, resilience, anxiety, and depression. Both anxiety and depression ran lower where support and resilience ran higher. Statistical tests then showed the chain: support predicted resilience, and resilience predicted lower distress. Once resilience was counted, support's direct link to distress faded away, meaning resilience fully carried it. The authors advise care teams to widen patients' support networks precisely because support builds the inner strength that holds distress down.
pmc-10710780:
Rami Al-Dwairi and co-authors examine what months inside an eye do to the silicone oil surgeons use to hold the retina in place. Their 2023 study analyzes oil removed from four patients after vitrectomy for diabetic eye disease, where membranes and detachment threaten sight. The oil should keep the retina attached, but it tends to emulsify, breaking into droplets that cause complications.

Laboratory tests tracked chemical bonds, thickness, light behavior, and buoyancy in the samples. Bond breaking and thinning lined up with longer implantation, hemorrhages during surgery, lens status, and how fully the eye was filled. Aggressive disease distorted the oil's optical properties most. Implantation averaged about nineteen months. The authors convert these findings into a risk list for surgeons: the longer oil stays and the rougher the eye's state, the faster it degrades. That argues for timely removal once the retina is stable.
pmc-10711980:
Congwei Wang and co-authors cook up an injectable gel that heals its own cuts and dissolves on two different commands: light and peroxide. Self-healing hydrogels serve drug delivery and tissue scaffolds, and polypeptides make them body-friendly. Their 2023 recipe links peptide blocks built from two modified amino acids onto a four-armed polymer hub.

Greasy peptide segments huddle together, which both knits the gel after damage and pockets oily drug cargo. Peroxide flips one segment's sulfur chemistry water-loving; light snaps the other segment into a charged acid. Either trigger loosens the huddle and speeds drug release. The dual response lets clinicians pick their key — a lamp or the chemistry of inflamed tissue. Biomaterials readers get a gel with two off-switches.
pmc-10713580:
Six researchers led by Eli Worth studied how to slow the stiff fiber growth that harms red blood cells in sickle cell disease. The disease stems from a fault in one hemoglobin chain. The fetal form of hemoglobin blocks fiber growth, so most work tries to switch that form back on or mimic it.

The team instead changed a single site on the other chain, the alpha chain. That change slowed fiber growth as well as fetal hemoglobin did. Because it works on its own path, it could pair with other treatments to boost their effect. The authors present it as a new tool in the search for stronger sickle cell therapies.
pmc-10713680:
Emma Parkins and seven co-authors study a tiny RNA that shapes memory circuits in this two thousand twenty-three paper. MicroRNAs fine-tune gene activity after genes are read, and they act fast at synapses. One of them, miR-324-5p, is known to raise seizure risk. The team removed its gene in mice and also blocked it with a drug-like molecule. Both moves thinned the small spines where excitatory synapses sit in the hippocampus.

Knockout mice also shifted spine shapes away from thin, unstable forms. Measures of key proteins and messages changed as well. The electrical strengthening tied to learning was impaired. The work links one small RNA to the physical basis of memory. Neuroscientists studying plasticity are the readers.
pmc-10714480:
Jiayan Chen, Yimeng Chen, Guanghao Qin, and fifteen colleagues lay out a head-to-head eye drop trial in this two thousand twenty-three protocol paper. Diabetes is rising, and about seventy percent of diabetic people have dry eye disease, which damages the corneal surface and nerves while tear production falls. Anti-inflammatory treatments exist, but two drops, three percent diquafosol and zero point one percent hyaluronic acid, had never been rigorously compared in diabetic dry eye.

The planned single-center, triple-blind randomized trial assigns two hundred two patients equally to either drop, one drop six times daily for eight weeks. Outcomes span the tear film, corneal staining and sensitivity, tear inflammation markers, meibomian gland function, corneal nerves, and symptom questionnaires, measured at baseline and weeks four and eight. The protocol promises a standardized verdict on which drop better serves diabetic patients, whose dry eye is common but understudied.
pmc-10714680:
Si Su and co-authors survey microbes living in ticks from Inner Mongolia, in a 2023 study. Ticks carry many germs, and local herding gives them rich habitat. More than nine hundred ticks of two species were gathered from sheep pastures and forest bushes.

Gene sequencing of mixed samples mapped the bacterial mix in each area. One genus dominated, making over half of all reads, and included a newly described species found in one tick type in two areas. Other common groups included organisms tied to animal and human disease. Signs of double infection appeared in one region. The authors warn that sheep at the sites face exposure to several pathogens at once, and urge watchfulness in herding areas.
pmc-10714880:
Opare-Asamoah and co-authors catalog the bacteria behind newborn sepsis at a large hospital in northern Ghana. Sepsis in newborns is an emergency that demands fast, accurate lab work. The team took blood samples from 275 babies judged to have sepsis. Samples came from a single vein draw under sterile care. Lab staff identified each germ and tested which antibiotics still worked. A standard disk method measured drug sensitivity.

Most babies, about 79%, arrived with early-onset illness. The profile of germs and drug responses guides local prescribing. Knowing which drugs fail locally can save lives where time is short. The study gives the unit a current map of its sepsis threat.
pmc-10714980:
Yuanyuan Luo and Xiaojie Ma present a 2023 study on predicting the return of cervical cancer after radiotherapy. They studied patients with intermediate and advanced cancer treated at one hospital between June 2017 and January 2023. The goal was a simple chart, called a nomogram, that estimates each patient's risk of recurrence.

Records for 114 patients were analyzed with regression methods. Two blood markers stood out as independent predictors: an enzyme called thymidine kinase 1 and a standard tumor antigen. The chart built from them scored well on accuracy tests. It beat both stage-based prediction and either marker used alone. Check curves showed the risk estimates matched real outcomes closely, which could help doctors plan follow-up care.
pmc-10715980:
Kyazimzade and co-authors present a case of heart failure shock during pregnancy, a rare but deadly event. Shock in pregnancy threatens both mother and fetus, and fast action matters. Care works best when heart, pregnancy, and critical care teams act together. The case covers shock that arose before delivery in one patient.

Doctors used a mechanical support device to keep blood moving. The device served as a bridge, buying time until the pregnancy could safely continue to viability. The report walks through how the team judged timing and risk. It offers a template for centers that may face the same rare crisis. Early recognition is the central lesson.
pmc-10716080:
Lin Zhu and co-authors study leaf surface bumps in rice in a 2023 paper. Tiny bumps called papillae dot rice leaves and shape how light enters and water leaves. Their effect on photosynthesis was unclear, so the team bred a mutant line that lacks the bumps entirely.

A gene called SPD25 proved to control bump growth on both leaf faces. Mutant leaves held less silicon and wax, lost water faster, and kept less moisture. Their pores closed down to save water, but that also cut the carbon dioxide supply for photosynthesis. Surplus light energy was shed safely as heat, and the light-harvesting system stayed intact. The authors say the bumps strike the balance between food making and water loss.
pmc-10716180:
Kenichi Takahashi and co-authors study a protein called Rab7 in pancreatic acinar cells. The protein is known to work in autophagy and endocytosis, paths cells use to clear waste and take in material. The team had found that it helps protect against acute pancreatitis. What it does in cells that release digestive juices on signal was unclear.

The team used mice bred so that only the pancreas lacked the protein. Tests showed the protein sits on zymogen granules, small sacs that store digestive enzymes before release. Enzyme release after a gut signal was the same in mice with and without the protein. The sacs were smaller and more numerous without it, but counts fell after a day without food in both groups. The authors conclude it helps the sacs mature, but not cleanup or timed release through regulated exocytosis.
pmc-10716280:
Five authors led by Xiaotong Chen review light-linked particles in atom-thin sheets of a class of materials. The sheets are single layers of transition metal compounds, known for strong light output. In such thin sheets, charge pairs bind tightly into excitons, which can then join with other particles. These larger groups can gain new traits and can be tuned in ways a lone exciton cannot.

The review sums up work on these groups in single sheets and in stacked pairs that form moire patterns. It covers how the groups form, how they act, and how labs detect them. Strong spin and valley traits in these sheets hint at uses in new light-based and quantum tools. The authors close by sketching how these groups could help probe deep questions in many-body physics.
pmc-10716680:
Paul Connelly and co-authors report in 2023 the case of a young transgender man who had a heart attack while on testosterone therapy. Hormone receptors sit throughout the heart and blood vessel system, yet how gender-affirming hormone treatment affects heart risk is largely unknown. The authors use the case to raise awareness of care gaps for transgender patients.

The patient was 31, used injected testosterone, and had no history of high blood pressure, cholesterol problems, diabetes, or smoking. Scans showed chest pain came from a severe narrow spot in one heart artery, treated with two stents. Other arteries showed leftover plaque disease, watched under standard drug care, and the hormone therapy went on. The authors argue that missing data on heart outcomes in transgender people feeds unequal care. They call for better training and more research.
pmc-10718280:
Richard Shaw, Alistair Jukes, and Rodney Allan described this 2023 surgical report on two patients with giant aneurysms at the base of the brain. These swollen, stretched arteries can press on the brainstem and grow worse over time. Tube-based treatments often fall short for such lesions. A high-flow bypass, which reroutes blood through a vein graft, offers a last-resort fix.

Both patients had growing aneurysms that squeezed the brainstem. The staged operations linked an artery in the neck to one in the brain, then closed the diseased vessel and eased pressure in the skull. Scans after surgery showed the aneurysms shut out, with no stroke. One patient improved greatly over a year, while the other declined. The authors stress that the approach stays high risk.
pmc-10718480:
Lee and four co-authors scope phone and web tools that aid lung cure stick in this twenty twenty-three review. The lung cure runs months, and missed doses breed drug-proof germs. Tech aids could keep sick folks on plan with less ward strain.

Inside, five years of banks gave the team near thirty fit works. Text pings, dose bells, and web watch care led the aid types found. Most aids sped self-care for sick folks and eased staff work as well. Two-way tools, with pings back and forth, sat rare in the pool. The team backs talk-both-ways builds as the next step for the field.
pmc-10719080:
Christopher Wallick and co-authors measure the payoff of fast antiviral treatment when flu hits lung disease patients, in a 2023 study. The patients have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Flu often triggers dangerous flare-ups in them. The team used insurance claims across five flu seasons. Patients treated within two days of diagnosis were matched to untreated peers. Over four thousand treated patients were included. Care use and costs were tracked for over a year.

Treated patients flared less in the first month. The gap persisted across the following year. Hospital stays for lung and pneumonia causes fell sharply. Emergency and clinic visits also dropped. Costs followed the same pattern, with one small exception. Pneumonia outcomes favored treatment at every window. The authors argue speed matters in this group. Early antivirals, they say, pay for themselves. The study is retrospective, so matching carried the causal weight.
pmc-10719880:
Laymon Ball, Ana Bedoya, Charlotte Taylor, and Laura Lagomarsino build a probe set for tracing family relationships in the coffee plant family, in a 2023 paper. The family is huge and varied, but family trees for it have rested on a handful of genes. Target enrichment can pull hundreds of single-copy genes at once, yet no probe set existed for this family.

Working from public genome resources, the team designed probes for two thousand regions in two branches of the family, then tested them across twenty-seven family members and one outsider. The probes recovered most targeted regions, working best within the subfamily they were designed from. The resulting family tree resolved relationships at several scales with strong support at nearly every node, matching earlier studies while showing gene tree disagreement. The set, named Rubiaceae2270x, also worked outside the family, and the authors offer it for evolutionary studies.
pmc-10722880:
Keogh, Thompson, Crouse, and Narayan test whether moose hooves can record reproductive history, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Hormones stored in keratin tissues like hair and hooves preserve a timeline of stress and reproduction. The team collected hoof tissue from immobilized moose. They validated immunoassays for cortisol and progesterone in hoof and hair.

Both hormones were measurable and varied among samples and animals. Pregnant females showed about twice the progesterone of non-pregnant moose in post-breeding hoof locations. Front hooves grew faster than rear ones, with growth peaking in summer. Adult female hooves held roughly two years of growth, spanning up to two reproductive cycles. The method even detected previous pregnancies in postmortem samples. Hair progesterone, by contrast, did not track reproductive state.
pmc-10725080:
Rodrigo Vilares-Morgado and co-authors reply, in a 2023 letter, to comments on their study of repeated eye injections in patients with glaucoma spectrum diseases. The injections, which block a growth factor, treat serious retinal disease, but doctors worry they might speed optic nerve damage in eyes already at risk.

Past studies on the worry used nerve fiber thickness as the measure and reached mixed results, often with no comparison group. The authors explain their design, which tracked thickness change over time against a proper control. They note that the layer thins with age anyway, so only a well-built comparison can show whether the injections add real harm.
pmc-10725680:
Dirk Deleu and co-authors give hands-on guidance in 2023 on a tablet drug for a relapsing nerve ill. The ill, multiple sclerosis, flares and fades and wears the brain over years. New strong drugs have widened choice but made plans more complex for each patient.

The drug works by resetting the body shields in two short courses a year apart. Most patients then show no clear ill work for years. The Qatar experts weigh when to start, when to watch, and how to treat when ill work returns. Their local view turns broad trial proof into ward steps. Doctors in the region gain a shared playbook for a drug many are new to.
pmc-10729180:
Lin Ang and co-authors lay out a protocol for mapping every systematic review of traditional medicine, a project commissioned by the World Health Organization. Traditional medicine is a mainstay or complement of care worldwide, and thousands of reviews have already synthesized its trials, but no one has charted the whole landscape. The team will search seventeen databases for reviews from 2018 to 2022. Pairs of reviewers will screen, extract data, and grade quality with a standard tool.

Results will be drawn as interactive maps sorted by disease and by type of traditional intervention. The point is to show where evidence piles up and where it is absent, so future trials can be aimed at the gaps. No ethics approval is needed, since only published work is used. The document is a plan, registered in advance, meant to keep the mapping honest and reproducible.
pmc-10730680:
Shining light on chosen cells to switch them on or off has reshaped physiology, and three specialists survey where the craft stands. Sophia Ohnemus, Johannes Vierock, and Franziska Schneider-Warme write the review in 2023. The classic method joins gene tools with optics to steer one cell type inside living tissue. Light-gated channels, the spark of the modern boom, allow millisecond firing of chosen cells.

Today's kit spans pumps, light-driven enzymes, and glow sensors for calcium, voltage, and acidity. Delivery by viruses or cell grafts puts the tools where they are needed. Light gear for stimulation and watching has advanced alongside. The authors trace uses across physiology and name what still limits the method.
pmc-10731280:
Suzheng Zheng and colleagues analyzed five-year survival in cutaneous melanoma in the United States. Their 2023 paper uses national cancer registry data. Melanoma of the skin is aggressive and threatens patient survival. Period analysis tracked relative survival across many years. Data were split by age, sex, race, and subtype.

Five-year relative survival rose for melanoma overall and its subtypes. The biggest gain appeared in amelanotic melanoma cases. That subtype climbed from under seventy to over eighty percent. A statistical model was built on the stratified data. It predicts five-year survival for the years just after the data window. Such forecasts help planners gauge treatment progress. They also highlight groups where survival still lags.
pmc-10735380:
Long-term care for older and disabled people is a giant, quiet industry, and Christine Bishop introduces a 2023 symposium that studies it with the tools of economics. The five papers she surveys ask how such care is produced, what people demand of it, and what it costs. Each paper brings a policy lesson.

Home care works as a production process where family help and paid help each lift different parts of health. When the pandemic cut family visits to nursing homes, deaths rose, which prices the worth of those visits. Other papers track rising nurse wages and contract staffing, measure how German users answer price rises, and compare dementia care spending in Mexico and among Mexican-origin families in the United States. Bishop frames the set as evidence for smarter long-term care policy.
pmc-10735580:
Sarah Neller and co-authors built a model of how caregivers engage with a dementia training program in a 2023 paper. Active engagement is known to make caregiver programs work, yet it is rarely measured well, which blocks comparison and improvement. Their program, EnACT, uses arts-based, multi-sense activities and short caregiver-informed scenes to help carers handle dementia behaviors.

Nine caregivers helped refine the program across six focus groups. The team coded how participants engaged with seventeen activities and drew a diagram for each. Those diagrams merged into a three-step cycle: personal and program starting points feed interaction, and interaction leads to the program's near-term effects. The model gives future programs a shared language for planning and measuring engagement.
pmc-10735680:
Mercedes Bern-Klug and Denise Gammonley give a session talk on the clashes of values that nursing home social workers face. Their 2023 paper starts from the load of need in such homes: stays range from weeks of rehab after a hip fix to the last years of life. Homes run short of trained hands even as residents grow frailer.

When a resident's rights clash with a family's wishes or a staff member's rights, the social worker is the one called in. The talk draws on both talk-based and count-based studies. It sorts the kinds of clash these workers meet, and the training they say they lack. The aim is to equip them as a resource for fair calls.
pmc-10735880:
Chemotherapy can leave breast cancer survivors with foggy thinking, and a mindfulness program may clear some of that fog. Cecile Lengacher and Richie Reich report a large trial in this 2023 paper. Two hundred twelve survivors joined. They were assigned to a six-week mindfulness course, an education support program, or usual care.

Thinking was tested with both lab tasks and self-ratings. Mood and body symptoms were tracked too, at the start and over twenty-six weeks. Everyone improved somewhat across the study. The question was whether mindfulness beat the comparison programs by the predicted pattern. Non-drug options matter for survivors wary of more medication. Trial evidence guides which programs clinics should offer.
pmc-10735980:
Rohit Pradhan and co-authors introduce a symposium on agency nurses in nursing homes in this 2023 summary. Nursing homes care for frail elders, and care quality rides on steady, skilled nursing staff. Homes have long battled turnover and absence, and the pandemic deepened the shortage, pushing many to hire contract nurses.

The gathered studies ask what drives homes to use contract staff and what follows. Talks cover staffing mix and depth, the home and market traits tied to heavy contract use, and the effects on turnover, quality, and finances. Agency staff can cost more and know the home less well, which may hurt teamwork. The editors say the findings should guide managers and policy makers.
pmc-10736080:
Amy Rauer and co-authors track older adults' social leisure during the pandemic in a 2023 study. After long distancing, vaccines raised hopes of meeting again, but new variants clouded the risk. One hundred thirty-six adults in the United States reported their enjoyable activities at three points from mid-2021 to early 2022.

Total leisure held steady across the three waves. Who shared it, though, shifted: partners came first at every wave, then solo time, with friends and family last. Time with partners and family fell in the last wave, when cases peaked. Even solo pastimes such as computer use were shared less. The authors note joy held up, but sharing it with loved ones waned.
pmc-10736280:
Phyllis Cummins and Philip Taylor present a 2023 session summary on how community colleges train health care workers for an aging population in the United States. Older adults need more care at home, in nursing homes, and in labs, and many of these jobs need no four-year degree. Colleges are a main source of that workforce.

Talks in the session covered future demand for care jobs and how the pandemic changed training at one college. Other talks looked at the reading, math, and problem skills students need, drawn from employer views. One case showed a college training lab scientists for local hospitals.
pmc-10736380:
Most older adults want to grow old in their own homes. Jon Pynoos surveys what stands in the way and what has improved. Many homes carry hazards and lack grab bars, ramps, or other supports. Falls and hard daily tasks follow. The people who need modifications most are the least likely to have them. The lecture builds on Powell Lawton's work on person-environment fit.

Pynoos reviews progress in research, services, policy, and consumer education. Housing is now widely seen as a health issue, which opens new doors. He closes with actions for practitioners, researchers, and advocates. The goal is homes that support aging for everyone, not just the well-off.
pmc-10736480:
