Pratima Gangupantula and Alissa Cooney reviewed, in a 2023 chart study, how hospital geriatric teams trim drug lists after older patients fall. A third of older adults fall each year, and taking many drugs at once raises that risk sharply. A hospital stay offers a rare chance to prune the list.

Of 283 patients admitted after falls in early 2023, 84 percent took five or more drugs. Geriatric reviewers advised cuts for 85 percent of that group. Over half had a drug stopped outright, seven in ten had one held, and a quarter had one tapered. Blood pressure drugs, pain pills, acid blockers, and opioids topped the cut list. The study shows deprescribing is already routine in this ward, and names the drug classes to watch first.
pmc-10736580:
Yan-Jhu Su, Janelle Fassi, and Christine Fruhauf introduce a symposium on using technology in education for older adults, from twenty twenty-three. Online learning for life has grown common, but tech changes faster than many older people can follow. That gap between age groups is known as the digital divide.

Five talks make up the session. One covers an online program mixing age groups that tackled age bias. Others cover design rules for tech support for older learners, cases from other countries, and a campus program where students coach seniors. The last talk weighs the gains and strains of tech for older learners in Taiwan. The aim throughout is learning that includes all ages.
pmc-10736680:
Four authors describe a training program in older adult mental health in this 2023 conference abstract. The program builds basic skills for generalist clinicians, who often meet older patients first but may lack training in late life mental health.

A team of geriatric experts reviewed skill lists from several fields and picked fourteen key knowledge areas. Content became a fourteen hour online course with checks and expert videos, plus a three day in-person version with practice on a simulated patient. Early online learners rated the course highly, and in-person learners raised their knowledge scores by fourteen percent. Both formats aim to spread scarce geriatric skill widely.
pmc-10736780:
Shevaun Neupert and Yuval Palgi present a symposium report from 2023 on how aging feels in daily life. How old a person feels can affect mood, memory, health, and even length of life. Most past work drew on rich Western samples, which leaves other cultures out.

A global group was formed to gather daily diary data in five countries. The talks cover the United States, Turkey, Germany, the United Kingdom, and Israel. Daily stress made people feel older in several samples. Good daily events and absorbing tasks made people feel younger. One talk compares Jews and Arabs inside Israel, and Israel with the United States. The group says culture shapes how daily life and felt age connect.
pmc-10736980:
Nicole Richards, Zexi Zhou, and Karen Fingerman study gratitude, close ties, and life satisfaction in late life. Their work from two thousand twenty-three draws on a study of daily life and well-being. More than three hundred adults, from sixty-five to ninety-two years old, took part and named their closest social partners.

Adults with more gratitude felt more satisfied with life, the team found. Warmth from close partners also tracked with higher satisfaction, while conflict alone did not. Gratitude seemed to guard satisfaction when warmth from partners was low. In high conflict ties, though, satisfaction fell for all, gratitude or not. The authors call the links between gratitude and well-being complex.
pmc-10737180:
Jennifer Turner, Jacqueline Mogle, Nikki Hill, and David Almeida asked how everyday memory slips affect how people feel, and through that, their wider well-being. Their study was published in 2023 and draws on a national United States sample of more than two thousand adults. Each day, participants noted memory lapses and their mood.

On days with more lapses, people felt more negative and less positive emotion. In turn, better daily mood went with stronger overall well-being, and worse mood with weaker well-being. The links held as a chain: lapses shaped mood, and mood shaped long-term well-being scores. The authors argue that small daily events matter for health because of the feelings they stir. That insight could guide efforts to soften the sting of normal forgetting.
pmc-10737380:
Yuanjin Zhou, Tatiana Sadak, Nayanika Ghosh, and Elizabeth Phelan study the link between pain and fear of falling in older Americans with dementia, in a 2023 paper. Both pain and fall worry are common in this group, yet both are often missed by clinicians. Data came from the 2015 National Health and Aging Trends Study. The analysis covered one thousand one hundred three community-dwelling people with dementia who answered for themselves, with a mean age of seventy-nine.

A single case cannot prove benefit, they acknowledge, but they argue the cheap adjuncts merit controlled study in sepsis.
pmc-10758680:
Abbas Ghazanfar and colleagues sort kidney transplant patients by who fared worst with COVID-19, to sharpen follow-up care, in this study from twenty twenty-three. Transplant patients take immune-damping drugs, so infection risk runs high. The team reviewed its follow-up program's patients through the pandemic's first year.

Of five hundred five recipients in the program, twenty-nine caught the virus and eight of them died, a death toll of more than a quarter among the infected. Survival fell with age over sixty-eight, male sex, and non-Caucasian background. Diabetes was present in nearly all who died. Routine blood values also warned: low kidney function, low albumin, low hemoglobin, and low calcium each marked higher risk. The authors argue these everyday numbers, already collected at every visit, should trigger earlier, closer care for the patients they flag.
pmc-10762880:
Ahmad Alrasheedi and co-authors test what diabetes patients know about complications in this 2023 study. The survey ran in diabetes clinics at a specialist hospital in Saudi Arabia's Qassim region. Over three hundred sixty patients answered a checked questionnaire.

Three quarters knew diabetes brings complications, and two thirds said a doctor had raised them. Specialists were the top information source, ahead of social media and relatives. Most patients had lived with the disease over a decade, and most had family history. Knowledge levels split by age group. The authors frame the gaps as targets for clinic teaching.
pmc-10764180:
Qingyuan Qian and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-three, how low-pressure, low-oxygen conditions affect blood gases and red blood cells in rats. The team simulated an altitude of six thousand five hundred meters in small and large chambers. Blood from the abdominal aorta was sampled for gas measures, red cell counts, and hemoglobin. They varied exposure length, hypoxia mode, recovery at normal oxygen, and repeat exposure after preconditioning. A drug, acetazolamide, was also tested.

Hypoxia disturbed acid-base balance, worse with longer exposure. Red cell counts and hemoglobin rose with exposure time too. Reoxygenation effects on acid-base balance were stronger for rats in the small chamber. The drug eased reoxygenation effects. Hypoxia mode and the drug had little effect on red cell counts or hemoglobin.
pmc-10787080:
Grant Borne and ten colleagues review Palforzia, the first approved oral immunotherapy for peanut allergy. Peanut allergy can kill, and avoidance was long the only strategy. Palforzia feeds patients carefully escalating peanut protein doses to retrain the immune response. The narrative review summarizes the clinical trials behind approval. It explains the dosing mechanism and how the therapy is used in real practice.

Current research concentrates on age groups that respond best. Other studies pair oral immunotherapy with additional immune modulators to deepen tolerance. Many optimization questions remain open, including who benefits most and how durable protection is. The twenty twenty-three update frames Palforzia as both a treatment and a research platform: proof that food allergy can be modified, not merely managed by vigilance.
pmc-10801080:
Carlo Cappelli, Elisa Gatta, and Salvatore Ippolito ask why thyroid hormone dosing, a century and a half after the treatment began, still misses so often. Levothyroxine cures hypothyroidism in principle, and guidelines dose it by body weight, yet many patients sit on suboptimal therapy. Their review, published in 2023, retraces the drug's road from sheep-thyroid injections to modern formulations built to survive troubled stomachs.

The obstacles to a tailored dose are catalogued: absorption quirks, body composition, interacting drugs and foods, and the bluntness of the blood tests that steer adjustment. The authors then look forward, to digital therapeutics, software that coaches and monitors patients toward their targets, as the missing layer between the right pill and the right patient. Their answer to the title's question is not yet, but the dream now has an engineering plan.
pmc-10801180:
Philip Manfield and four co-authors report early evidence for a rapid trauma therapy technique in a 2024 paper. The flash technique aims to shrink the sting of a disturbing memory with little distress during treatment. Four similar studies, run during trainings in the United States, Australia, and Uganda, each gave volunteers a single fifteen minute group session.

Over six hundred fifty people rated a disturbing memory's intensity before and after. Average disturbance fell by more than two thirds in every study, a large and significant effect. Only two of over eight hundred sessions saw slight increases, and both eased in a repeat session. Follow up at four weeks suggested gains held. The authors call the technique acceptable and safe, pending stronger trials.
pmc-10808380:
Jaimie Shaff, Xinzi Wang, Janel Cubbage, Sachini Bandara, and Holly Wilcox published this study in 2023. It looks at the mental health of adults in the United States who identify with more than one race or ethnic group. This fast-growing group is often left out of standard health research.

The team ran a two-wave online survey with 1,359 adults in 2022, then interviewed seventeen of them. More than half reported at least one mental health concern. Rates of anxiety, depression, trauma symptoms, and suicidal thoughts passed national averages. Trauma, discrimination, and small daily slights played a large role in these outcomes. Strong social support and a firm sense of ethnic identity helped protect people. The authors call for care and research that include this group by design.
pmc-10816580:
Juice color steers buyers before taste gets a say, and Marek Kardas and co-authors asked diet experts which orange juice tint wins, in work from twenty twenty-three. Lab gear first measured the juices' true shades. Experts then ranked tint appeal through glass and bottle, with labels hidden and shown.

The winning juice was fairly dark with a deep orange cast. The loser wore green-blue tints. Labels shifted picks: the labeled favorite read brighter and more yellow than its peers. Experts, the study finds, favor bright, vivid orange. Makers are urged to tune both juice shade and pack design together, since each bends the other's charm.
pmc-10822680:
Xianwu Pang and co-authors map HIV virus types among men who have sex with men in Guangxi, China, in a paper published in 2023. The catalog lists the work under 2024, but the journal record in the text gives 2023. Knowing which virus strains spread, and how fast, guides local prevention work. The team studied people newly diagnosed between 2016 and 2021.

Gene sequences from the virus were linked into a spread network. Sixteen strains appeared, and one strain made up just over half of cases. Two-thirds of people fell into fifty-nine clusters of linked infections. Younger, unmarried men and those with high virus levels clustered more often. One strain formed bigger clusters and grew faster than the others.
pmc-10826880:
Guang-Zhao Cao and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three study of the traditional formula Pien Tze Huang applied to diabetic wounds. Diabetic ulcers heal slowly and cause much disability. Existing treatments fall short, prompting interest in this established remedy.

Diabetic rats with full-thickness wounds received the formula at two doses or a growth-factor drug. Treated wounds closed faster with richer collagen. Gene sequencing and network analysis traced the biological routes involved, backed by protein tests. The work gives a molecular account of how an old formula speeds repair, supporting controlled clinical evaluation.
pmc-10827980:
Sthitaprajna Sahoo, Hak-Kyo Lee, and Donghyun Shin screen natural compounds for inhibitors of a key foot and mouth disease virus protease, in work published in 2023. The disease is highly contagious in cloven hoofed livestock and has no specific antiviral treatment. The 3C protease is essential for viral replication, which makes it a prime drug target.

Structure based virtual screening tests a library of more than 69,000 natural compounds against the protease. Five candidates bind strongly and pass property and quantum chemistry checks. Long molecular dynamics simulations of all five complexes, each 300 nanoseconds, show overall structural stability by several standard measures. The candidates offer starting points for antiviral development in animal health.
pmc-10830380:
Jigna Dharod, Christina Frazier, Jeffery Labban, and Maureen Black study breastfeeding length and baby growth in low-income families, in a study published in 2023. Fast early weight gain raises later health risks, and feeding style may shape it. The team followed 256 mother-baby pairs at a clinic in the southeastern United States, checking feeding at two, four, six, nine, and twelve months.

Most mothers were African American or Latina, and most took part in a food aid program. Babies were breastfed for a median of about 4.75 months, most often mixed with other feeding, and over a quarter of mothers still nursed at one year. Babies nursed past six months gained weight more slowly than those nursed for shorter spans. About a third of babies showed rapid weight gain.
pmc-10844480:
Sulaiman Muhetaer and eight co-authors map how depression intertwines with quality of life in 1,735 Chinese cancer patients. Rather than score each life domain alone, the team built a network linking depression with fifteen domains from a standard cancer questionnaire. Nearly two thirds of the patients carried some degree of depression. In the network, depression sat at the center, alongside nausea, pain, and physical function.

A second analysis traced likely direction: depression seemed to drag down overall quality of life mainly through emotional function, pain, physical function, and sleeplessness. The drag ran strongest in patients with moderate to severe depression, and the pattern hinted the influence may run both ways. The authors urge routine depression screening and early treatment in cancer care. The study appeared in 2023, though the catalog lists 2024.
pmc-10844580:
Chen-Shuan Chung and co-authors show that throat cancer patients live longer when the esophagus is screened in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Head and neck cancers often seed a second cancer in the esophagus. A magnified scope with special light can spot it early.

The team reviewed two hundred sixty-one patients with hypopharyngeal cancer at one hospital. About a quarter grew a second primary tumor, most often in the esophagus. Patients screened within six months of diagnosis and kept on regular watch had markedly better survival in adjusted models. Late stage still worsened odds. The authors back early screening plus steady surveillance for these patients.
pmc-10860680:
Wai Kwong Tang and co-authors set out a trial protocol for treating fatigue after stroke in this study, published in 2023. Post-stroke fatigue is common and blocks recovery, and drugs often fail against it. The trial tests a gentle brain stimulation method that passes a small current through the scalp to shift brain activity, an approach tried for fatigue in other brain diseases.

The double-blind trial will enroll 156 adults with chronic stroke, split evenly between real and sham stimulation. Real treatment gives two twenty-minute sessions a day for five days, with an electrode over the movement area of the injured side. Fatigue scores will be tracked at five points over four weeks. The authors present the design as a proof-of-concept step toward a new option for stroke survivors.
pmc-10909080:
Priyanka Ravi and colleagues interview users of tobacco tooth powder about why they trust a harmful habit, in this qualitative study from twenty twenty-three. The product, a smokeless tobacco rubbed on teeth and gums, comes in forms such as mishri and gul. Smokeless tobacco is tied to cancers of the mouth, throat, and pancreas, yet this form is sold as dental care.

Thirty users at a dental hospital spoke in depth. Family, friends, easy access, and curiosity started most of them. Many believed the powder helps teeth, gums, and even digestion, and most rated it gentler than other tobacco. Some knew the harms and had tried to stop, but none had sought professional help to quit. The authors call for plain awareness drives and stronger health warnings on these products, since myth, not ignorance alone, keeps the habit alive.
pmc-11001280:
Jie Gao, Liming Tao, and Zhengxuan Jiang review treatments for diabetic eye disease in a 2023 paper. Diabetes can damage the retina, the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye, and the disease is a leading cause of vision loss. The review centers on oxidative stress, a buildup of harmful oxygen byproducts, as a driver of that damage.

The authors gathered past work on how this stress harms retinal vessels. They then surveyed antioxidant therapies meant to mop up the harmful byproducts. In animal studies, such treatments slowed the decay of small retinal vessels. Human trial data, though, remain thin. The review closes by calling for more clinical trials before these therapies can be advised with confidence.
pmc-11065180:
K Osungbade and a large team drew lessons in two thousand twenty-four from a top Nigerian hospital's response to the COVID-19 outbreak. Stopping hospital-spread infection is a core duty of health managers. Their qualitative study interviewed leaders of infection control and key units at University College Hospital in Ibadan about how the response was built.

Four themes emerged. A screening protocol and a dedicated triage area came first. Inside clinics, spacing, hand hygiene, protective gear, cleaning, and waste handling formed the second theme. Surveillance links with the disease unit formed the third. Staff training and mental support for infected staff formed the fourth. The authors offer the account as a template for peer hospitals.
pmc-11225480:
Ruth Ketty Kisuza and nine co-authors survey how Ugandan university students suffered and coped during a COVID-19 lockdown. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three, set at Makerere University during the country's second lockdown.

Three hundred and one undergraduates answered a semi-structured questionnaire. The median age was twenty-three, and most were male and single. Nearly half worried about COVID-19. The top harms were disruption of studies, named by over nine in ten, and money problems, named by six in ten. Listening to music led the coping list. The team also hunted factors tied to worry. The portrait can help universities plan support for the next campus closure.
pmc-11271080:
Rupsa Mallik, Eszter Kismodi, and Sundari Ravindran report on a roundtable about the money behind advocacy for sexual and reproductive health and rights, in an article published in 2023. The meeting, held in September 2022, brought funders and advocates together to ask whether current funding helps or hinders the movement. Two groups, a journal and a grant-making fund, hosted the talks.

Participants mapped how grants are given today and how success gets measured, since those measures steer future funding. Many worried that present patterns may blunt the bold advocacy needed to counter rollbacks of rights. The article shares early ideas for a way forward and calls for a shared set of values, principles, and strategies. The aim, the authors say, is not just more funding but better funding, centered on people and movements.
pmc-11390080:
Özge Aydın Güçlü and co-authors build a pocket scoring system to guess which emergency patients actually have COVID-19. When tests are scarce, a quick score helps decide who to swab first. The team reviewed 1,187 people who came to a pandemic clinic in Turkey between April 2020 and March 2021, splitting them into groups to build and then check the score.

Five admission features carried the signal. A typical viral pattern on chest imaging was worth five points and breathlessness two, while cough, fatigue, and muscle pain earned one each. Imaging and breathlessness were by far the strongest predictors. The finished score caught about seventy-one percent of true cases in validation, offering a simple triage aid.
pmc-11489280:
Luis Angel Ortiz-Lango and co-authors reviewed risk factors for a foot fracture in a 2024 paper on sports injuries. The break hits the fifth metatarsal, the long bone on the outer edge of the foot. It has been linked to body traits such as flat or high-arched feet, foot ills, and thin bones, and to sport traits such as moves, surface, and style of play.

The team gathered past studies to weigh which factors matter most. No clear accord had formed on the top risks, so a joined view was overdue. Their summary sorts inner body risks from outer sport risks. Trainers and doctors can use it to spot athletes at risk and shape guards or drills.
pmc-11531880:
Cao and co-authors census large and mid-sized mammals in Xishuangbanna over a decade. Camera traps ran from 2012 to 2022 across nine sites. The team set 784 traps in eight reserves and one state forest farm. Records found 43 species in six orders and 37 genera. Nine species from old records did not appear.

Small, split reserves lacked big predators and big grazers. Most common species also showed lower counts in those sites. The less guarded forest farm held rich mammal diversity. Mix of species varied a lot by site, most for rare species. The authors warn that large, rare mammals face the most risk.
pmc-11532480: Andreas Mischok, a solo author, surveys a display technology in a 2024 commentary. Exciton-polaritons are hybrid particles, part light and part matter excitation, long studied for lasers, chemistry, and quantum optics. Recent work, he reports, shows their striking promise for screens: very efficient, very bright, and with the purest colors in principle. The short piece argues that this fundamental physics topic is ready to move toward future display products, where color purity and efficiency are prized.
pmc-11533180:
Two skull surgeries for blood clots on the brain are weighed by Syed Hasham Ali and co-authors in a 2024 review. Acute clots above the brain demand fast action, and surgeons either lift a bone flap and replace it or leave it off to ease swelling. Which is better has long been disputed.

Fifteen studies from three databases feed a meta-analysis run under standard review rules. Death and recovery scores headline the pooled outcomes. A matched subgroup analysis trims bias from sicker patients landing in one arm. Clearer odds can help surgeons and families choose under the worst time pressure in medicine.
pmc-11534980:
Ana Maria Pandolfo Feoli and co-authors adapt a short eating confidence scale for Brazil in a 2024 study. The scale measures how sure people feel that they can control eating in tough moments, such as stress or social pressure. No checked version existed in Brazilian Portuguese, which left local clinics without the tool.

The team translated the scale back and forth, tested it with expert panels, and ran it with two hundred twenty eight people. All eight items were kept, and scores split into two factors as in the source scale. Scores linked sensibly with binge eating and eating behavior measures. The authors offer the scale as a sound tool for research and care in Brazil.
pmc-11535480:
Syed Ali, Hiba Ali, and Mohd Aziz hunt for blockers of an immune checkpoint protein by computer in a 2024 paper. Immunotherapy boosts the immune response against cancer, and blocking the PD1/PDL1 pathway activates T cells against tumors. New blockers of the ligand PDL1 are actively sought.

The team screened one hundred thousand compounds from the ZINC database plus approved drugs computationally for high-affinity candidates. Selected drugs were conjugated with silver and gold nanoparticles, and the conjugates' cancer-killing activity was tested. Combining virtual screening with nanoparticle delivery aims at cheaper, targeted immunotherapy candidates.
pmc-11536780:
Martine Myhre and three co-authors counted pre-hospital care for young children in central Norway, in a study published in 2024. Calls involving children are rare, so crews get little practice with them. The team read five years of call logs for one county with about 43,000 children under twelve. They added helicopter crew files for the most serious cases.

Of about 109,000 calls, six in a hundred were for young children. Half of those led to a ground or air crew being sent out. Breathing distress, altered awareness, and injury topped the list of causes. Of 309 helicopter cases, more than four in ten received advanced treatment from the flight doctor, with breathing help the most common. The authors say the rarity itself is the risk, and they point training toward the gaps they found.
pmc-11538280:
Xin He and eight co-authors use a genetics method to test whether gut microbes and blood chemicals actually cause acne. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Acne is a common skin disease of the young that carries heavy money, body, and mood costs.

Links between the gut, blood, and skin are often proposed, but plain observation cannot prove cause. The team used gene variants as natural instruments for four hundred and twelve gut microbes and two hundred and forty-nine blood compounds. They ran the test in both directions and added a mediation step to trace chains from microbe to chemical to acne. Some factors looked protective and others harmful. The results give drug and diet research firmer targets than simple association studies.
pmc-11542480:
Iris Xiaoxue Yin and five co-authors engineer a nanomaterial that sticks to teeth, kills cavity bacteria, and rebuilds mineral at the same time. Silver nanoparticles fight Streptococcus mutans but can stain teeth and wander off. Anchoring silver to graphene quantum dots functionalized with alendronate, a bone-seeking drug fragment, aims the particles at tooth mineral.

The composite was characterized by electron microscopy and spectroscopy, then tested for toxicity against gum fibroblasts and tooth stem cells. Binding to hydroxyapatite was measured directly. Antibacterial power against the cavity bacterium was checked by imaging and colony counts. Finally, mineral regrowth on human dentine was assessed by micro-CT and microscopy. The work targets prevention that stays where it is painted.
pmc-11545580:
Jaroń, Grajek, and Kobza survey what drives good doctor patient talks about patient rights during the pandemic in twenty twenty-four. Patients have a right to clear facts about their health and care, and to ask questions. The team surveyed two hundred three adults face to face at a rehab clinic in twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-two. Patients split into active talkers and passive ones.

A third of patients asked questions or had the chance to do so. That active group got far more facts about their state, tests, and outlook. They also rated talks with doctors far higher on trust, clarity, and warmth. The authors say the heart of a good visit is full facts plus room for questions.
pmc-11546080:
Feng Guan and co-authors catalog a defense gene family in bitter gourd and test one member against wilt fungus in a 2024 study. The vegetable doubles as medicine, yet its resistance machinery is little mapped. The SCPL gene family serves growth and defense roles across plants.

Thirty-two family genes were found, sorted into three classes, most carrying light, hormone, and stress response switches. Several switched on strongly after infection, mainly in resistant varieties. One, McSCPL22, sat in vessel tissue exactly where the fungus attacks and peroxide forms. Its behavior ties it to two hormone defense pathways. The authors flag it as a breeding target for wilt resistance.
pmc-11546580:
Pedro Forte and co-authors test a long exercise plan for older adults, in work from 2024. The eight-month plan mixed many forms of training. Twenty-four adults were split into a training group and a control group. Body makeup, fitness tests, and a sleep survey were taken at the start and the end.

The training group curled more, stood from a chair faster, and stepped far more in two minutes. Body fat fell by a tenth, though flexibility dropped. Sleep quality jumped by near half in the training group and fell in controls. Better sleep tied to leaner bodies and stronger fitness after the plan.
pmc-11562280:
Franklin Ly and co-authors test portable biofeedback devices that people with chronic pain can use at home, in a 2023 study. Biofeedback shows users their own body signals so they can learn to calm them.

Across three four-week pilot studies, users held two ten-minute sessions a day. Most sessions ended with lower self-rated pain and anxiety than they began with. Bigger drops in anxiety went with bigger drops in pain. Users also finished the programs with lower overall pain and anxiety than at the start, and reported high satisfaction. The authors argue that home devices could widen access to this kind of pain care.
pmc-11570580:
Jiale Yu, Zhijuan Guo, and Junyi Zhang reviewed in 2024 research on the Schlafen gene family in malignant tumors. These genes take part in cell growth, cell specialization, immune responses, blocking viruses, and copying DNA. They also shape how tumors respond to chemotherapy, which makes them of strong interest for cancer care.

Human Schlafen proteins share three domains, with cutting and unwinding enzyme roles at the ends and a linker in the middle that may bind other proteins. The review covers the family's structure and sequence, its roles across tumor types, and its links to immune cells that enter tumors and to immune checkpoints. The authors assess Schlafen genes as possible drug targets and as partners in combined treatments.
pmc-11570880:
Chris Acquah and eight co-authors study two light-activated compounds that could treat cancer, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. Such drugs, called photosensitizers, wake under light and harm tumor cells. Newer versions swap oxygen atoms for sulfur to avoid heavy atoms, shifting the light they absorb and boosting their active states. How they relax after absorbing light was still murky.

The pair studied were thio-coumarin and thio-acridone. The team fired ultra-short light pulses and tracked changes from trillionths of a second out to millionths. Computer chemistry backed the readings. The path they mapped explains how the compounds settle into long-lived, reactive states. Those states do the work in light therapy, so the map helps design better drugs.
pmc-11570980:
Massuda and co-authors test whether breathing pure oxygen harms the inner ear in newborn rabbits born with a hernia of the diaphragm, a birth defect that can leave babies hard of hearing. They compare fetuses with the defect and healthy ones, with and without ventilation at normal or full oxygen. Bleeding inside the cochlea is scored from none to severe.

Without ventilation, babies with the defect and the controls bleed about the same. With 100 percent oxygen, though, the defect group bleeds far worse, about three times the severity of the controls. The authors argue that oxygen levels during ventilation deserve care, since softer settings might protect hearing in babies born with this hernia.
pmc-11574180:
In some materials, electrons spontaneously bunch into a wave pattern that distorts the crystal with it. Yu-Ting Huang and co-authors predict a rich family of these charge density waves in nine flat materials made of group III and VI elements. Their case rests on first-principles calculations.

The trigger differs from the usual story: broad, flat stretches of unstable vibration span the whole zone of the crystal's momentum map. That breadth lets many wave patterns form, including a chiral Star-of-David design. The materials' electronics are simple, built from few orbital types, yet the transitions can flip a metal into an insulator or widen a gap sharply. The authors say this family opens a new dimension in two-dimensional wave materials and fresh clues to where such waves come from.
pmc-11575780:
Samyah Alanazi and Naif D Alenzi profile a red bee glue from Brazil and test it against a sleeping-sickness parasite. Their 2024 paper analyzes propolis made by a stingless bee species, mapping its chemistry for the first time with chromatography and magnetic resonance methods. Twenty-nine compounds were identified across several families. Most were polyphenols, and two were purified in quantity.

Against the sleeping-sickness parasite, one fraction of the extract was strikingly strong, beating the crude extract roughly eight-fold. The two purified compounds showed moderate activity of a similar order. The same fraction and one compound also killed human leukemia cells in culture, at levels approaching a standard drug. The margin of safety is a question the paper leaves open. The authors conclude the red propolis is a rich polyphenol source worth further study.
pmc-11576880:
Hao Zou and co-authors trace how sleep length bends thinking in older adults through two middle links: daily living ability and depression. Both short and long sleep have been tied to cognitive decline, but the path between them stayed dark. The team draws on a large Chinese aging survey from twenty eighteen.

Their 2024 study runs a chain mediation model on thousands of older adults. Sleep length, daily living skill, mood, and cognition all move together in the data. On both sides of a seven-hour split, weaker daily skills and deeper depression carry the effect of odd sleep onto weaker thought. The authors urge care teams to fix sleep early and treat the two middle links in step.
pmc-11577580:
Lucy Frost and co-authors explore family choices in a teen vaccine trial in Tanzania in 2024. Research with children is needed so they gain from its fruits, but harm must be weighed. Law often demands parent consent up to age eighteen, while teen assent rules stay vague. The team studied a trial of a vaccine against a cancer linked virus.

They spoke with teen girls who joined the trial and with their parents or guardians. Talks probed how families weighed the choice together and who held sway. The findings expose gaps between formal consent rules and family practice. Trial teams can use them to design fairer consent talks.
pmc-11578180:
Hyeongho Min and co-authors build a soft grip bot that apes the velvet worm's slime trick to hold slick flesh sans harm. Far-run small bots must grip creased, wet, soft stuff with low push. Their 2024 build lays a field-tuned stuff in a soft pad: soft to land wide, then stiff on a field call to hold fast. The grip rite runs in three steps: land soft, hold the wide touch, then stiffen.

A frame in the pad backs the rite's grip. Show runs span wet organ hauls, a nut spun off a bolt, and aid in a mouse growth cut. Sure, soft grips could serve flesh work where hard claws can't go.
pmc-11580280:
Mehmet Kaya and co-authors report one center experience with intravenous immunoglobulin for lupus in a 2024 study. Lupus is a long term autoimmune disease that can affect almost any organ. The treatment, given through a vein, has no firm guideline for lupus, yet many clinicians view it as effective.

Records covered thirty one patients, most treated for blood involvement and many for refractory disease. The team tracked side effects, changes in other immune drugs, and clinical and lab measures after treatment. Inflammation values, protein in urine, and immune markers were among the outcomes examined to describe who may suit this therapy.
pmc-11585580:
Norihiro Yamada and co-authors hunt a blood marker for depression in a 2024 study. Diagnosing major depressive disorder still rests on reported symptoms and mood, with no lab test to confirm the state. Tiny parcels called extracellular vesicles ride in the blood, and their sugar coatings might carry a signal.

Plasma vesicles from patients and matched healthy controls were sorted by size and probed with lectins, proteins that bind set sugars. Two sugar signals ran low in patients during a depressive phase, then recovered in remission. Protein analysis pointed to von Willebrand factor as the main carrier of one signal. That sugared form of the factor split patients from controls and split a patient's dark phase from their remission. The authors propose vesicle sugar tests to flag depression risk during treatment.
pmc-11585980:
Tiantian Dai, Yanshuang Jia, and Yi Zhang test if clot parts cause egg-organ cancer in a 2024 study. Past reads tied the two, but a tie can run back or ride a third thing; a gene coin toss can split cause from tale.

Gene marks that stand for each clot part were set by side of cancer counts from two vast gene banks. Four parts told a cause tale: high marks for each tracked high odds of the cancer. Checks for slant and stray paths backed the four. A pool of both banks added a fifth part to the list. The authors say the clot web is no mere mark of the ill: it may be one of its roots, and a new aim for care.
pmc-11586480:
Yang Huang and five co-authors built prediction charts for liver bile duct cancer after surgery, in a 2024 study. Blood levels of liver enzymes before surgery may carry clues to outlook, but their value for this cancer was unclear. The study pooled 605 patients from many centers.

High levels of all four enzymes tested went with worse survival and a higher chance of return. The charts rest on five factors: how many enzymes ran high, a blood marker level, having more than one tumor, spread to lymph nodes, and growth into small vessels. The charts beat the standard staging system in tests, and their forecasts matched real outcomes well. The authors offer them for planning care after surgery.
pmc-11586780:
Jennifer Petkovic and a large team of co-authors review guidance on involving interest-holders in health guideline work in two thousand twenty-four. Guidelines shape care, so the people affected by them should have a voice in their making. Those voices range from patients and payers to policy makers and the public.

A major checklist sorts guideline work into eighteen topics, one of which covers engagement. That topic, though, does not say how to engage, and input could be sought at every stage. The review maps what guidance exists across the full process. It is one of four linked reviews that will feed new guidance on engagement by many groups at once.
pmc-11587780:
Ouyang and six co-authors study citrus canker tolerance at the gene level, in work from twenty twenty-four. Citrus bacterial canker is a major disease that threatens the citrus industry. A resistant bud mutant of a common sweet orange offers a natural comparison.

The team compared leaf traits and gene activity between the susceptible Newhall cultivar and its resistant mutant Longhuitian. Transcript profiling revealed distinct regulatory patterns tied to tolerance. Such gene maps can guide breeding or editing for canker resistant citrus, reducing spray use and crop loss in groves worldwide.
pmc-11590280:
Emergency stenting saves heart attack patients, yet some go on to develop heart failure during the same hospital stay. Hui Song and co-authors mine records of nearly seven hundred such patients in this 2024 study to build a tool that flags who is at risk.

Five factors stood out on their own: older age, two blood markers of damage and clotting, a weaker pumping score, and a heavier burden of artery disease. Combined in a chart-style scoring model, they separated future failure cases from safe ones with good accuracy in both test groups. The authors offer the model for early, tailored watchfulness after surgery.
pmc-11590780:
Inès Elhani and co-authors measured inflammation markers in 2024 to compare disease severity across gene forms of familial Mediterranean fever. The disease brings repeated inflammation attacks. Classic cases carry two faulty gene copies, but one-copy carriers also get sick, in a milder form that seldom scars the organs. Whether those carriers need lifelong colchicine is contested.

The team profiled the biomarkers by genotype, with a close look at carriers, including those who had stopped treatment. If one-copy disease truly runs cooler, its blood markers should say so. The title gives the answer the data supported: severity is reduced in heterozygous patients, in the analysis reported. The byline is long; the work is framed by its lead author. Readers get lab evidence for a dosing debate that affects many carriers' daily pills.
pmc-11591480:
Mai Kadry and Rehab Abdel-Megeed tested whether thioctic acid and two natural products can shield rat brains from inflammation-driven depression, published in 2024. A bacterial toxin, LPS, triggers depression-like states in rats and stresses the protein-folding machinery inside neurons. The team tracked a web of signaling genes tied to mood, growth, and stress responses. Treatments were thioctic acid, burdock, and propolis, a bee product.

The treatments raised protective gene activity, including a brain growth factor and a calming receptor gene. They also cut oxidative damage markers and quieted stress-pathway genes that LPS had switched on. The authors read the pattern as a coordinated reset of the signaling web. They propose the three agents as prospective therapies for inflammation-linked depression. The work is preclinical, in rats, and the authors frame the pathway as a fresh target.
pmc-11591880:
Junbiao Wang and co-authors tested compounds from the chaga mushroom against breast cancer cells in 2024. Chaga, a fungus used in traditional Chinese medicine as a tea, contains triterpenoids with noted anticancer traits. To mimic drinking it, the team digested a chaga water extract in vitro, then identified its parts with high-resolution mass spectrometry. Four triterpenoids, including inotodiol and betulin, stood out as the main active parts.

The extract reduced viability of breast cancer cell lines representing HER2-positive and triple-negative subtypes, and disturbed their cell cycles. A key process emerged: the triterpenoids inhibit dihydrofolate reductase, an enzyme cancer cells need to copy DNA. That is the same target as some established chemotherapy drugs. The title reports the compounds also act synergistically with standard treatments. Mushroom chemistry rarely yields such a certain process, making this a lead worth following.
pmc-11595580:
So Yeon Yoon and co-authors build a rainwater filter from palm waste carbon in a 2024 study. Rainwater can carry heavy metals, organic pollutants, and gut germs, so it needs cleaning before use. Their cartridge stacks three forms of activated carbon made from palm shells: plain carbon, carbon doped with magnesium and silicon, and carbon doped with silver.

The magnesium-silicon layer added surface area and binding sites, which lifted heavy metal capture. In column tests that mimic a working filter, the full cartridge beat plain carbon and a commercial carbon. It removed one and a half to two times more Escherichia coli germs, and more metals and organics as well. The silver layer added disinfection. The authors present the system as a single pass answer for rainwater with mixed pollution.
pmc-11596280:
Petar Kazakov and co-authors test a seaweed-based plant booster on raspberries and strawberries in a 2024 study. The product, SuperFifty, is made from brown algae and had already helped other crops under stress. Berry trials were missing, so the team primed plants and measured fruit size, yield, and nutrition in detail.

Primed plants grew bigger fruit and yielded about forty-two percent more raspberries and thirty-four percent more strawberries. A scan of one hundred fruit compounds showed the good stuff stayed level: antioxidants, key amino acids, sugars, acids, and vitamins matched untreated fruit. Mineral checks agreed. The booster thus raised quantity without diluting quality, a pairing growers rarely get.
pmc-11597380:
Gerloff and three co-authors evaluate proficiency testing in the Global Polio Laboratory Network in a 2024 paper. Labs in the network must pass yearly blind panels to keep their accreditation. Panels use safe RNA samples that mimic real poliovirus targets.

Labs run standard screening tests and report types for each sample. Most labs passed on their first try in both years covered, and most earned perfect scores. The few that failed got help to find the cause and nearly all passed a repeat panel. Results stayed strong despite the Covid-19 pandemic. The authors credit careful adherence to updated test procedures and algorithms.
pmc-11597880:
Methylene blue, a common dye and drug, kills viruses in lab dishes, which raised hopes it might treat COVID-like infections. The authors test it against a pangolin coronavirus closely related to SARS-CoV-2. In dish tests, the dye strongly inactivated virus particles outside cells. Yet it did not stop the virus from copying itself inside infected cells. The comparison drug nirmatrelvir showed the opposite pattern: no direct killing, but strong blocking of replication.

In mice bred to be vulnerable to the virus, methylene blue gave no protection against a lethal infection. Tests in mouse plasma help explain why: plasma raised the dose needed for the dye to work, so blood components weaken it. The authors conclude that direct virus killing in a dish does not guarantee benefit in a living animal. Their findings offer a caution and a guide for future antiviral work.
pmc-11599580:
Andreia Penso Pereira and three colleagues ask whether the social networks of people with diabetes predict who shows up for eye screening. Diabetic retinopathy screening prevents blindness, but attendance varies. Using records of nearly seventy-six thousand patients grouped under twenty Portuguese primary care clusters, they built a social network for each cluster and computed its structure.

Paradoxically, the least connected networks, split into many small communities, had the highest screening adherence. Non-adherence concentrated in a small group of highly connected individuals, and node-level metrics pinpointed where the problem is worst. The authors offer network analysis as a planning tool for targeting screening interventions.
pmc-11599780:
Nine researchers in China rank pollution sources in campus dust for control action in a 2024 paper. Dust that settles and resuspends carries toxic trace elements through the air, and campuses sit in its path. The team sampled surface dust at universities in Xi'an and split the elements by source.

Zinc, lead, and copper stood out at high enrichment, with lead and zinc driving overall pollution. Four sources emerged: traffic exhaust, traffic wear, mixed, and natural, with traffic wear the largest share. Ecological risk ran serious, led by lead from exhaust. Cancer risk to students traced mainly to traffic exhaust as well. The authors name exhaust control as the first priority.
pmc-11600580:
Wei Lu and a large team design soft nanocapsules to improve light-based cancer therapy, in a 2024 paper. Tumors block drug delivery with dense tissue and abnormal blood vessels. Their capsules are soft silica spheres coated with an enzyme that digests part of that dense tissue.

Softness helped the capsules enter tumor cells better than stiff versions, and the enzyme coating helped them push deeper into tumor spheroids. Loaded with a light-activated drug, the capsules strengthened therapy in mice after injection into a vein. Gene analysis showed the treatment changed tumor genes tied to tissue breakdown and energy production. The authors present the dual design as a way past tumor barriers.
pmc-11600680:
Yinghang Wang and co-authors studied how formula milk marketing reaches into the health system in two Chinese cities, in a 2024 paper. Breastmilk is widely seen as the healthiest food for babies and mothers. A World Health Organization code, adopted over forty years ago, limits formula marketing. Yet firms still push their products hard, now also through social media.

The study is qualitative and covers Beijing and Jinan. It asks how marketing shapes parts of the health system built to support breastfeeding. Clinics and staff may be drawn into industry practices without noticing. The authors aim to show where that capture happens. Findings can inform stronger guardrails for mothers and babies.
pmc-11601180: The 2024 digest previews one issue of the Bulletin of the World Health Organization, in short form. The issue's theme is sexual health, opened by editorials on well-being, mpox, and a pathway to cut deaths of mothers and newborns. The digest lists the month's reports by region and topic, from a Tanzanian phone-based trial on HIV prevention for sex workers to a refined world survey of sexual practices. It closes with pieces on sexual exploitation in crisis settings. The item serves as the journal's table of contents in prose.
pmc-11602880:
Care for mothers and newborns in Bamako, the capital of Mali, has shifted a lot over two decades. Mariam Traoré and co-authors chart those shifts in this 2024 study, using national health survey data from 2001 to 2018. City care levels vary with poverty and with the flow of people moving into the capital. The security crisis that began in 2012 added further strain.

Women who were not poor and had not moved got more care than poor or migrant women. The gap tied to how long a woman had lived in Bamako was large, and it tended to grow over time. One clear case was the share of women getting at least four checkups before birth. There, the gap by poverty stood at seven points in 2001 and at 8.3 points in a later survey year.
pmc-11603480:
Andrew Sagalov and seven colleagues compare heart risks in cardiac amyloidosis against other stiff-heart diseases, in a twenty twenty-four study. In amyloidosis, stray proteins clog the heart muscle. Other stiff-heart causes include iron overload and sarcoid. The team drew on a national hospital database for twenty sixteen to twenty nineteen, covering more than thirteen thousand patients.

Amyloidosis patients faced near four times the stroke risk of the other group. They also had double the rate of a dangerous fast heart rhythm. Yet their risk of the common flutter rhythm was lower. Death rates in hospital were alike in both groups. The authors argue screening should weigh these rhythm and stroke gaps.
pmc-11603680:
Aravind Dilli Babu and co-authors review when to start blood thinners after stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation, in work from 2024. Starting too late risks another stroke, while starting too early risks bleeding in the brain.

The pooled analysis covered eleven studies with more than thirteen thousand patients. Early starters began at about three and a half days, late starters at about six days. The early group had lower rates of repeat stroke and of brain bleeding. Other outcomes, such as major bleeding and death, did not differ clearly. The authors note few trials and call for more.
pmc-11603880:
Jayoung Park, Jongho Heo, Woong-Han Kim, and Sugy Choi survey, in a 2024 study, what migrant workers in South Korea knew about Covid care and immigration rules during the pandemic. Migrant numbers there are climbing fast, and undocumented workers were left most exposed, yet research on them is thin. The team used a 2021 survey of 537 international migrant workers.

Workers without documents had lived in the country longer and earned less than those on work visas. None of them could join the national health insurance scheme. Most saw their income fall early in the pandemic. After adjusting for background and language skill, undocumented workers were far less likely to know the treatment and immigration policies that applied to them. The authors call the gap a policy blind spot.
pmc-11603980:
Middle ear infections are common in Ethiopia and can cost children their hearing, yet national numbers on the bacteria involved and drug resistance were scattered. Mihret Tilahun and co-authors pooled the published studies: 70 studies for the broad picture and 14 for a combined statistical analysis covering 3,667 isolates from patients suspected of ear infection.

About 73 percent of suspected cases proved bacterial, though studies varied widely. Resistance to multiple drugs was almost as common, at about 72 percent. Staphylococcus aureus was the most common isolate, followed by Proteus species and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The authors call the mix of high infection rates and high resistance alarming, and they urge stronger treatment guidance and follow-up.
pmc-11604780:
Han and co-authors present a 2024 study on moving assets between blockchains with a math-tuned liquidity model. Chains increasingly need to swap value, yet user-friendly bridges stay scarce. Their design pairs liquidity contracts across chains and picks the pairing by convex optimization. That pairing is provably the single global best match, they argue, which pins down the shortest crossing time.

A uniform method mints matching NFT identities across the whole chain set. Automated market-maker curves supply instant liquidity on arrival. Tests measured crossing time, robustness, and how fast the solver settles. Incentive trials for users rounded out the checks. The authors pitch free, fast asset movement as basic plumbing for the multi-chain era.
pmc-11605080:
Jeffrey Lipton writes alone in a 2024 essay on monitoring a blood cancer. Chronic myeloid leukemia led the targeted therapy era: a gene fault was found, then a pill that blocks it turned a fatal disease into a managed one. Care now rests on molecular monitoring, tracking the fault's signal in blood over time. Lipton frames that watch through an old proverb about missing the forest for the trees.

The risk he names is real: teams can chase tiny signal wiggles and lose the patient's whole picture. His essay weighs when deep response means treatment can pause and when numbers mislead. For a disease held in check for decades, judgment about what to watch becomes the core skill.
pmc-11605880:
Chimezie Nzoputam and co-authors measure what Nigerian women know about preventing malaria, in the country that carries the world's heaviest malaria burden. Nigeria accounts for nearly a third of global malaria deaths, and prevention knowledge is a frontline defense. Their 2024 paper analyzes the 2021 Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey, covering 14,476 women of childbearing age.

Fewer than half, about 43.5 percent, had good knowledge of prevention. Schooling mattered most: women with secondary or higher education had well over twice the odds of good knowledge. Hearing malaria messages more than doubled the odds as well. Women from better-off households knew more, and rural women knew less. The multilevel analysis separated personal, household, and community effects. The authors argue that message campaigns are working where they reach, and that reaching rural and less-schooled women is the clear next job for malaria control.
pmc-11606180:
Alba González-Fernández and co-authors test a pig vaccine given by mouth in a 2024 study. Glässer's disease, caused by a bacterium that steals iron from its host, hits young pigs hard. Current shots target single strains and are often given to sows, whose antibodies can block the piglets' own response.

The vaccine uses one of the bacterium's iron-grabbing proteins, delivered through the mouth's lining to spark local immunity. Challenged with several Spanish field strains of different types, vaccinated animals were protected across types, the cross-coverage farmers need. An oral, broad vaccine would simplify herd protection where injections are costly in labor and stress.
pmc-11606980:
Stack two sheets of a layered material with a slight mismatch and a moiré pattern emerges — a long-period texture that can rewrite the material's behavior. The usual mismatch is a twist. Fengrui Yao and co-authors show in 2024 that uneven strain works too, in multilayers of the magnetic crystal CrBr3.

Tunneling measurements through CrBr3 barriers behaved exactly as they do in small-angle twisted junctions known to host moiré magnetism, with neighboring regions magnetized in opposite senses. Raman measurements and modeling pinned the cause on differential strain inside the stack, which shifts how layers stack and how their spins couple from place to place. Unlike a twist, strain could in principle be tuned in place, even at low temperature. The authors offer the route as a new way to print magnetic superlattices.
pmc-11607080:
Elham Farokh Gisour, Fatemeh Jahanimoghadam, and Pouya Karimipour compare three materials for saving the pulp of baby molars, in a clinical trial from 2024. The procedure, pulpotomy, removes the diseased top of the pulp and seals the rest. The standard agent, formocresol, has long raised safety questions, so rivals are wanted.

Ninety-six children aged three to nine each had one molar treated with formocresol, Portland cement, or NeoMTA Plus. Clinical success at six and twelve months was total in all three groups. X-ray success ran a few points lower, with NeoMTA Plus on top at 96.9 percent at one year. Gaps between groups were too small to count as real. The authors name both rivals as sound stand-ins.
pmc-11607880:
Anne-Violette Bruyneel and co-authors map the web of factors behind musicians' playing injuries in this 2024 paper. Student musicians face high rates of pain tied to practice. Two hundred thirty-five Geneva music students answered surveys on health, habits, and mind. Over a third had suffered a playing-related disorder in the past year.

Network analysis drew the links between all the factors at once. Psychological distress tied most strongly to having a disorder. Among sufferers, how much pain blocked practice linked to distress, performance anxiety, self-rated health, and fatigue. Body factors like posture showed no direct link. The authors say mental health care belongs inside injury prevention for young musicians.
pmc-11607980:
Haidong Gao and co-authors present a 2024 study of blood gene messages as early marks of brain bleeding from high blood pressure. Such bleeds are a dire complication and strike with little warning. Marks that flag them in the first hours could open new care targets.

The team compared blood cells from patients and healthy volunteers and found thousands of genes with split activity. A short list of eight candidate marks was checked in depth. Seven ran high in patients and one ran low. The marks tied to paths for low oxygen response and swelling signals. Some marks also tracked with lung infection, poor nutrition, and other complications after the bleed. Age added risk for lung infection as well.
pmc-11608480:
Pyo and coauthors ask if blood pressure shapes heart valve infection risk in diabetes. The infection is grave and can kill if missed. Diabetes already raises infection risk for many patients. The team used a national health database in Korea.

The full set held more than 2.6 million people. Groups split by normal, raised, and high blood pressure. Low body weight was checked as an added risk too. Follow-up ran for about seven years on average. Just over 1,700 new infections arose in that span. High pressure tracked with the top infection rates.
pmc-11609280:
Behnam Dehdari and three co-authors analyze foam stability for oil recovery using dimensionless numbers in a 2024 paper. Foam pushed into a reservoir can steer fluids toward trapped oil, but heat and salt break foam down. The team mixed one polymer, two surfactants, and six nanoparticle types to stabilize it.

They tracked surface tension, bubble traits, and thickness through scaled ratios borrowed from fluid physics. A new scaled measure for electrical conductivity joined the set. One ratio, which folds in droplet height, described stability better than the other two. Acidic particles carried stronger charge and steadied foam more than the other particle type. Bubble coarsening over time also tracked stability. The authors offer the numbers as benchmarks for comparing foam recipes.
pmc-11610280:
Karin Smit and co-authors describe home monitoring for very ill COVID-19 patients in the Netherlands in this 2024 paper. Remote checks at home promised early warning when a patient began to worsen, so that help could come before severe illness set in.

The team searched academic and grey sources from March 2020 to March 2023 for Dutch programs, leaving out plans for early hospital discharge. Ten programs were found and seven gave their protocols. All served adults at risk of severe disease and used certified medical devices for close follow-up. The paper maps what the programs shared, giving future planners a base model.
pmc-11610380:
Vardhaman Patel and co-authors study treatment switching in psoriasis in a 2024 real-world analysis. Patients on older, non-biologic systemic drugs sometimes move up to biologics, and the team asked whether how burdened patients feel, not just how severe doctors rate their skin, predicts that switch.

The study followed adults in a large American psoriasis registry who had never used biologics. About thirty-eight percent of the more than eight hundred patients started a biologic soon after enrollment. Greater self-reported burden and worse quality of life each raised the odds of switching, even after accounting for physician-rated severity. The findings center the patient's own experience.
pmc-11611080:
Taewook Kim asks in 2024 why knee pain often fails to match knee X-rays. Pain can show up with a clean scan, and worn joints can sit silent. Knowing what drives pain in each case could sharpen early care as lives grow longer.

Kim used a national Korean health survey from 2010 to 2012 with 5,191 people. Two model types linked pain to age, sex, weight, and health traits, split by scan grade. Age, being female, and higher weight tied to pain in both scan groups. For clean scans, lower fat share also mattered; for worn joints, weak bones stood out. A boosting model ranked age and weight at the top.
pmc-11611180:
Soonok An, Jisoo Youn, Qihao Zhan, and Soo-Jung Byoun gauged partner violence among young adults in South Korea. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with intimate partner violence. Such harm peaks in young adults, yet proof on Korean youth and on care fit to their culture is scarce. An online survey of six hundred young adults, drawn by a simple random pick, read both harm done and harm faced.

Life long rates for both sides sat near three in ten. More than a fifth told of each in the past year. Stats models tied a set of traits to each side. Readers who build prevention for Korean youth get base rates and a trait map to aim at.
pmc-11611580:
Szczepan Jakubowski and a large team of co-authors study payment policy for orphan drugs in a 2024 paper. Orphan drugs treat rare diseases, and each European country decides on its own whether public funds will pay for them. The team asked how proof of safety and benefit, and formal value checks, shape those choices.

They built a list of approved orphan drugs from a European registry and sent a survey to experts in twelve countries. Safety checks were required in ten of the twelve, and benefit checks in eleven. The authors then compared country rules with real payment choices. Their study shows how much the process itself, not just the drug, affects patient access.
pmc-11611880:
Sriram Ravichandran and co-authors study what happens when the teacher in active learning is a human with biases, in this 2024 paper. Active learning lets a model pick which examples to ask about, speeding its training. When people supply the labels, quick mental rules can skew their answers, and the team asked whether that skew breaks the method.

They paired two known human rule models with four active learning methods and three classifiers across fifteen data sets from health, marketing, and transport. With biased labels, performance dropped sharply, sometimes below random picking. Their fix, a method that seeks out low-density regions in a psychology-inspired way, beat the best rival by a wide margin overall. The authors urge designers to model the human labeler from the start.
pmc-11612180:
Xinghua Wang studies the image of rural trips in a 2024 paper on smart tech. Rural scenic spots want a strong image that draws guests and keeps their stay green and sound. Sensors can watch air, water, and guest flow in real time, while deep networks can read the landscape on their own.

Wang built a score and fix model on big data, with trips along the Yellow River as the test case. A dense network named and sorted rural scenes with high care. Truth of the scene and its service sites swayed the image most. The model guides spots that wish to lift their draw.
pmc-11612280:
Yong Zheng, Weiheng Zheng and Xia Du present Rice-YOLO, a light model for detecting rice pests, in work from 2024. Fast, accurate pest spotting matters for control, yield and quality. Pests are hard to sort because classes look alike, ages differ within a class and field backgrounds are messy, so standard detectors often struggle.

Built on YOLOv8-N, their model adds an efficient detection head, deep supervision layers and an improved dynamic upsampling module. Tests used a large public pest dataset and a sixteen-class rice pest dataset built for this task. Rice-YOLO beat prior detection methods on mean average precision and F1 score in the reported experiments, while staying light enough for field use.
pmc-11612380:
Gülden Gök, Şevket Tulun, and Hakan Çelebi map, in a 2024 study, heavy metal pollution in the soil of a Turkish university campus, treating it as a miniature city. They sampled nine points across the grounds and measured contamination with standard indices. The soil ran alkaline, which tends to lock metals in place.

Lead stood out. It concentrated where students circulate and gather. By a combined pollution index, three quarters of the campus rated moderately to highly polluted, and the rest clean. Statistical source tracking split the blame: natural background supplied about 57 percent, industry and traffic about 21, farming about 13, and other sources the remainder. Lead tied mainly to the traffic and industry mix. The authors urge continuous soil monitoring to keep the long-term buildup in view.
pmc-11612480:
Toshihiko Matsumoto and co-authors report real-world results for an appetite drug in cancer cachexia, in this 2024 observational study. Cachexia, the wasting syndrome of advanced cancer, resists treatment. Forty-three patients with gastric or colorectal cancer received anamorelin, mostly alongside chemotherapy, and were tracked for appetite and weight.

After three weeks, over half reported better appetite and about half gained weight; gains partly held at twelve weeks. Starting the drug before second-line chemotherapy and having colorectal cancer predicted early improvement. Patients who gained weight by twelve weeks also lived longer. The authors argue for starting anamorelin early rather than as a last resort.
pmc-11612580:
A team of co-authors presents a study from two thousand twenty-four on whether social media buzz tracked with doctors' prescribing during COVID-19. The drug in question is hydroxychloroquine, an old malaria drug promoted early in the pandemic on thin evidence. Social platforms spread health claims fast, with little checking, which can push practice ahead of proof.

The team gathered the drug's use in forty-eight United States hospitals across two thousand twenty. They set that beside posts on X, formerly Twitter, that mentioned the drug or its brand name, sorted by whether the tone was positive, negative, or neutral. The design tests for a population-level link between chatter and prescribing.
pmc-11613380:
Peiyang Lin and five colleagues test whether the available oocytes rate predicts pregnancy in assisted reproduction, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Ovarian stimulation and embryo culture can affect how oocytes mature. The rate summarizes what share of retrieved eggs are usable. The team reviewed nearly eight thousand treatment cycles at a Fujian hospital.

Analysis linked several factors to clinical pregnancy, including hormone levels, endometrial thickness, and follicle counts. The available oocytes rate itself contributed independently. A cutoff near thirty-four percent separated outcome groups in the analysis. Matched comparisons below and above that threshold showed significantly different stimulation drug doses. The authors argue the rate helps evaluate stimulation quality. It may also guide clinicians adjusting protocols for better oocyte development.
pmc-11613780:
Nozomu Motono and co-authors describe a hard case of trauma-induced clotting failure after a fall from a roof. Their case report appeared in 2024. The patient, a 68-year-old man with epilepsy, broke ribs, his collarbone, an elbow, and his pelvis, and bled into his right chest. Emergency surgery five hours after the fall stabilized him. Blood tests, though, showed the trauma itself had wrecked his clotting: hemoglobin and platelets stayed low and clotting time stayed long despite transfusions and clot-protecting medicine.

On the second evening the chest bleeding worsened and surgeons reopened it, finding slow oozing from the many rib fractures. The authors walk through the management choices, arguing the case shows why trauma teams must treat the clotting disorder itself, not just the holes it springs from.
pmc-11614480:
Ryan Antar and co-authors report a rare benign tumor deep in a child's palm, in work from twenty twenty-four. The tumor type, calcifying aponeurotic fibroma, usually sits near tendons in the hand or foot. Deep palm involvement is exceptionally rare and hard to diagnose.

The patient was a nine year old girl with a slowly growing mass on the inner side of her left palm. Scans showed an ill defined growth with fatty streaks across two finger bone spaces, raising fears of an aggressive tumor. Surgeons removed it at the margins while sparing tendons, bone, and nerves. The quiet spot and lack of symptoms had let it grow unusually large. One year on, no return was seen.
pmc-11614880:
Ahmed and co-authors pool the evidence on a timing question after cardiac arrest. When the heart tracing shows a heart attack without ST elevation, does an early look at the coronary arteries help? The team searched for trials and observational studies on this question. They compared early angiography with delayed or no angiography after out-of-hospital arrest. Results from 16 studies covering 4,737 patients were combined using a random-effects model.

Early angiography was linked to lower long-term death rates and better brain outcomes at discharge. The benefit, though, came mostly from observational studies. The randomized trials alone did not show the same clear gains, so the authors advise reading the findings with care. For emergency and cardiology teams, the review maps a contested question: the pooled numbers favor early action, but the strongest study designs are the least certain.
pmc-11615680:
Xiaochao Xia and co-authors study a protein called FAM3C as a driver and marker of glioma, a serious brain tumor. Their 2024 paper combines database analysis with lab tests on tumor tissue, cell lines, and mice. Earlier work had hinted that this protein helps cancers grow.

Higher FAM3C levels tracked with higher tumor grade and worse patient outcomes. Silencing the gene slowed glioma cell growth, movement, and invasion, while boosting it did the reverse. The protein worked through the Notch signaling pathway, and blocking that path blunted its effects. Tumors in mice echoed the cell results. The authors propose FAM3C as both a prognostic marker and a possible drug target.
pmc-11616080:
Blake Dear and co-authors test web-based talk therapy in real student care in a 2024 study. Strain of mind is rife among college students and can sink grades or end a degree. More students now seek help, which has pushed web forms of care to the fore.

Their five-week web course for worry and low mood ran as part of routine care for New Zealand students. The team weighed how well it worked and how well students took to it. Most past proof came from tight trials, not live clinics. Schools gain real-world marks for a cheap way to stretch scarce care staff.
pmc-11616180:
Hiroki Hirano and Keiko Ishii published a 2024 study on childhood hardship and adult well-being. They surveyed adults in the United States and Japan. Participants reported hardships from their childhood homes. They also rated happiness, loneliness, trust, and emotional expression.

The authors asked whether trust and expression explain lasting effects. People who express positive feelings may recover better. People who trust others may feel less lonely. Comparing two cultures tests whether these paths hold broadly. Findings like these can guide support for adults with difficult childhoods. The study treats emotional habits as possible bridges to better health.
pmc-11616780:
A resistance gene that defeats last resort antibiotics travels inside gene swapping machinery, and a 2024 study by William Matlock, Liam Shaw, and Nicole Stoesser maps its world tour. The gene, blaGES-5, was first reported in Greece in 2004 and has since appeared across the globe.

From 104 genome fragments carrying the gene, the team clustered the surrounding integrons, the elements that capture and shuffle such genes. Copies riding plasmids looked different from those settled in chromosomes, which sat almost all in one hospital strain of Pseudomonas with a fixed cassette order. A disruptive insertion may freeze that order in place.
pmc-11616880:
Li, Zhang, Montag, and Hisham link communication overload to information overload and videoconference fatigue, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Videoconferencing surged with remote work and study, bringing fatigue as a side effect. A limited capacity model of message processing frames the investigation. Two studies test the model in education and work contexts.

Study one surveys four hundred eighty-nine students in educational settings. Study two covers professionals in Singapore and Germany with large samples. More frequent meetings consistently predict higher communication overload. Perceived overload in turn predicts information overload and fatigue. Findings hold across students and professionals and across countries. Design and norms should curb verbal overload in meetings.
pmc-11617380:
Put on a pair of artificial ears that reshape how sound arrives, and your sense of up and down in space goes haywire, briefly. Cesare Parise and co-authors measure how fast listeners recover in a 2024 study of new spectral cues for vertical localization.

Participants wore devices that altered the ear's acoustic fingerprint, then trained with feedback linking sound to movement. Within twenty minutes, their localization gain, bias, and precision had fully adapted to the new ears. Removing the devices produced aftereffects in the opposite direction, though precision recovered within a few trials. The speed of the adjustment surprised even the authors. Human spatial hearing, they conclude, rewrites its map far faster than textbooks suggest.
pmc-11619280:
Chenglong Yao and co-authors asked whether a simple blood-based score can flag heart rhythm trouble in patients with acute coronary syndrome. The score, called the TyG index, combines blood fats and sugar and stands in for insulin resistance, a known risk factor for atrial fibrillation. The team reviewed six hundred thirteen patients treated in Tianjin between twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-four.

A feature-picking method narrowed the risk list to heart disease, valve disease, the TyG score, age, and one blood pressure measure. Higher scores tracked a steadily higher risk of the rhythm problem, with no bend in the line. The score alone predicted cases fairly, and a model built from all five factors did better. The authors say the cheap score could help spot patients who need closer watching.
pmc-11619680:
Xiaobing Yang and five co-authors weigh in 2024 whether alcohol use raises or lowers risk of rheumatoid arthritis, a joint-attacking autoimmune disease. Past findings conflict, with genes and lifestyle tangled together. Two data routes are combined to triangulate the answer.

Survey data from a national health study cover 32308 adults across two decades. Regression and subgroup checks probe the drinking-arthritis link there. A Mendelian randomization study then uses gene variants as natural experiments for spirits intake, drawing on large genome data sets. Sensitivity checks test the robustness of the causal read. The paired design aims to separate a true alcohol effect from confounding habits that travel with drinking.
pmc-11620980:
Xiaotong Guo and co-authors present a case where a newer scan tracer may outshine the standard one in a rare cartilage disease. Relapsing polychondritis inflames cartilage across the body, and when it starts in the airways alone, diagnosis drags. Their 2024 paper follows a forty-nine-year-old woman with a year of dry cough and breathlessness on exertion.

Steroids eased her symptoms fast, and the dose was tapered away over weeks, with a second drug beside them. The clinical thread supports the imaging thread: comparing the FAPI tracer against the standard FDG tracer on PET/CT for this disease. Airway-only cases carry poor outlooks, so a sharper scan matters. Rheumatologists and imagers get a rare head-to-head in a disease with no dedicated test.
pmc-11621380:
Zheng-yu Su and seven co-authors compared two exercise prescriptions for teenage boys with obesity in a randomized trial, in this 2024 study. One program was steady moderate cycling; the other was high-intensity interval training, short hard bursts separated by easy pedaling. Both are known to help the heart and blood vessels, but which repairs more in adolescents was untested.

Forty-four boys, about fourteen years old, trained for eight weeks. Fitness was measured as peak oxygen uptake, vessel stiffness by pulse wave speed, artery flexibility by ultrasound, and the balance of the autonomic nervous system by heart rhythm patterns. Nearly all boys finished the program. The head-to-head design matters for schools and clinics: if intervals deliver equal or better gains in less time, they solve the scheduling problem that kills exercise programs for teenagers.
pmc-11621580:
Sridhar Panneerselvam and co-authors build a fire-spotting system that learns across sites without pooling their images. Forest and indoor fires call for fast, sharp detection, yet models trained in one place can stumble in another.
