Their method, IOFireNet, trains a shared model through federated learning, so each site keeps its data and sends only model updates.

Images first pass through a filter that strips noise, then a clustering step splits fire from non-fire zones pixel by pixel. A light mobile network handles the heavy lifting on site, flagging spread, severity, and the area at risk for early warnings. In tests, the system topped ninety-eight percent accuracy at spotting fires and beat four well-known image networks, while its zoning step beat older segmentation tools.
pmc-11622180:
A team of neuroscientists asks what one gene does inside the brain's inhibitory cells. Faults in SYNGAP1 cause intellectual disability with epilepsy and autism traits, but most work had focused on excitatory neurons. The team lowered the gene's dose only in interneurons born in one embryonic zone, then narrowed it further to two cell families, and recorded brain activity and behavior in the mice.

Mice with the early, broad reduction showed abnormal cortical rhythms and an oversized response to a forty-hertz sound. They also could not adapt to repeated sounds, a flaw traced to one cell family but not the other. Social behavior suffered, and the mice could not unlearn a fear memory. Narrower reductions spared those behaviors. The authors infer that timing and cell type decide which symptoms appear, and that early-born interneurons are a likely source of the cortical and social problems.
pmc-11622480:
Wei Zhang and co-authors studied lung spots that touch a lung seam in two thousand twenty-four. Ground glass spots on scans can be early lung cancers. Some sit attached to the seam between lung lobes. A half-moon sign at that seam may hint at invasion. Judging invasion guides how much lung surgeons remove.

The team reviewed scans for more than two hundred spots. All spots were confirmed by surgery and tissue tests. They split into early change, minimal invasion, and full invasion groups. Age and spot size differed clearly across the groups. Scan density measures also separated the groups. Combining factors beat any single clue alone. Such joint reading helps plan smaller, safer operations.
pmc-11623080:
Jingting Zhang and co-authors chart the global burden of lung and airway cancers caused by smoking from 1990 to 2021 in a 2024 analysis. Smoking is the main risk factor for these cancers, and tracking deaths and lost healthy years shows where the harm is moving. Data came from the Global Burden of Disease study for that full span.

Total deaths and lost years rose over the period, yet rates adjusted for age fell, a sign that population growth drove much of the rise. Rates stayed far lower in women than in men. East Asia held the highest death rate in the final year, and Central Europe the highest lost year rate, with Greenland highest among single countries. The authors also link national rates to a social and demographic index, finding unlike trends by development level.
pmc-11623480:
Patricia Gita Naully and a team of co-authors design a vaccine candidate for chronic hepatitis B on the computer, in two thousand twenty-four. Chronic infection persists because the immune system fails to clear a small hidden form of the virus. Two viral proteins help control that hidden form and make good targets.

The team gathered protein data from ten virus types and picked shared pieces that immune cells can recognize. They joined those pieces with helper parts into one candidate design. Computer checks predicted the design would be safe, stable, and able to cover nearly all people worldwide. Simulations showed it binding immune receptors and stirring antibody and cell responses.
pmc-11623780:
Meyer and co-authors lay out a Danish plan to build a health program that ignores the scale entirely. Weight-loss programs rarely keep weight off long term and can feed harmful cycles and stigma. Their 2024 protocol instead co-designs a weight-neutral program with the people it should serve, following a national framework for complex programs.

Four design rounds move from discovery interviews with town officials and experts, through seminars with health workers and people who have lived the existing programs, to content workshops and validation. Themes from all that talk will scaffold the program's activities. The design rests on body acceptance, joyful movement, eating by appetite, and cutting stigma. The project is fully funded and underway.
pmc-11623880:
Wang and seven colleagues assess a temple incision face lift in Chinese patients in twenty twenty-four. The method lifts a deep facial tissue layer called the SMAS. Surgeons anchor that flap high to raise sagging cheek fat. The aim is a younger midface and softer nose to mouth folds.

Ninety-five patients had the operation between twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-three. Sixty-one completed follow up from six months to two years. Most reported satisfaction with the aesthetic results. No lasting facial nerve injury or other major complication occurred. The flap reached from above the eye corner down past the cheek bone. The authors say success demands deep knowledge of facial anatomy. The working space is small, so the technique is demanding.
pmc-11624280:
Bingxin Liu and co-authors present a 2024 study of how a dangerous tick-borne virus uses a host RNA mark to copy itself. The virus causes severe fever with low platelets and kills a high share of patients. A chemical mark on RNA, called m6A, shapes many infections, but its role here was largely unknown.

Mapping the marks on the viral RNA, the team found that a reader protein binds them. In one line of results the binding cut the viral RNA's stability. The virus, though, drives a second change, adding a lactate-based tag to that same reader, which tips the balance back toward copying. The paper traces this tug of war in detail.
pmc-11624680:
Youcef Bagdad and Maria A Miteva review how artificial intelligence is being used to find new antibacterial drugs. Their 2024 review starts from drug resistance, a global threat that weakens standard treatments for many infections. AI has emerged as a tool to speed the hunt for fresh candidates.

The review sums up methods that found small molecules and peptides able to kill bacteria, including strains that resist current drugs. It walks through case studies where AI-guided picks proved active in tests. The authors also weigh the challenges and openings in this use of AI, from data quality to validation. With resistance rising faster than the drug pipeline, they argue AI progress matters for keeping infections treatable.
pmc-11625080:
Qitong Wu, Deeptashree Nandi, and Dipali Sharma present a 2024 review on TRIM29, a protein that acts as a hub in cancer growth. Most of its family helps tag proteins for disposal, but TRIM29 does far more. It boosts several classic cancer pathways at once, pushing growth, spread, and the shift that lets cells wander.

The review maps how the protein is itself controlled: by small RNAs, by chemical marks on DNA, and by tags added after it is made. TRIM29 also blunts how well some cancer drugs work and steers cell metabolism. In a few settings it seems to suppress tumors instead, a context puzzle the authors explore. They close with ideas for drug combinations that route around it. The hub status makes it a tempting target.
pmc-11625680: Qura Tul Ain and co-authors report a tuberculosis patient who developed a rare cluster of chest complications at the same time, in work published in 2024. The complications were pus and air in the chest cavity in many pockets, air under the skin, and air around the heart. Each alone is serious, and together they are rare. Their growth sharply raises the risk of illness and death in such patients. The authors stress that apt and timely care must be ensured for better outcomes in these cases.
pmc-11625980:
Fabian Bäumler and co-authors map the leg muscles of mantises and kin in a 2024 paper. Mantis front legs both walk and snatch prey, a rare two job limb. How muscle layout shifted from plain walk legs to grab legs was unclear.

Fine scans and cuts laid out the muscles in seven far flung mantis kinds. Chest legs in four kinds gave the walk side match. Each muscle was traced from base to tip in three dimensions. Maps show which muscles grew, split, or moved for the grab. The charts give legs a shared name set for cross kind study.
pmc-11626080:
Among teenagers with major depression, thinking about suicide and acting on it may not be the same brain state. Hui Zhong and eight co-authors scanned four groups with resting brain imaging. The groups held 37 patients who had attempted suicide, 34 with suicidal thoughts only, 20 with neither, and 20 healthy controls. They compared a measure of how densely each brain region connects to the rest of the brain.

The groups differed in a few telling spots. The ideation group showed denser connections in a visual region at the back of the brain and in the left precentral gyrus. It showed sparser ones in a right frontal region. Those values tracked the suicide scores on a depression scale. The attempt group sat between, denser than controls in the visual region. The authors read the pattern as a signature that separates thoughts from acts.
pmc-11626180:
Begüm Babür and co-authors pull apart two kinds of learning inside social rejection, in a 2024 study. A snub hurts, yet it also teaches: people track who rewards them with real chances to meet, and who values them, a second signal called relational value. In a matching game, players saw both at once, whether the match landed and how keen the other side was. Brain scans and a Bayesian model read the two lessons apart.

Choices honored both teachers. Players picked partners who paid off in matches and who prized them. The brain split the work: outcome learning lit the classic reward circuits, while value learning lit regions tied to rejection's sting. The authors say the sting is a signal, not just pain: it updates an inner ledger of one's worth to others, steering who we chase and who we drop.
pmc-11626480:
Nevra Keskin Yilmaz and co-authors pull together mouse studies in 2024 to judge how well gene therapy restores hearing. The type of hearing loss they study comes from harm to hair cells in the inner ear or to the nerve that carries sound. Gene therapy has grown as a hopeful route to treat it.

The team searched three large databases for studies with clear designs that measured hearing with a standard brain response test. They used set rules to pull out data and to grade each study's quality. Then they combined the results into one overall view. A pooled result like this shows if the gains seen in single labs hold up across many labs. It can also point to which treatment choices work best before tests move toward people.
pmc-11626980:
Xinyi Ye and ten colleagues race two antidepressants head to head on both mood and thinking in Chinese patients with major depression, in a 2024 trial. Depression dulls cognition as well as mood, and the newer drug vortioxetine markets itself on cognitive benefits. Escitalopram, a standard, was the comparator.

One hundred thirty-one patients were randomized for eight weeks, with seventy healthy controls for baseline contrast. Patients began clearly worse on mood, anxiety, pleasure, and most cognitive domains. Both drugs lifted all three symptom scales similarly, with no significant edge either way. Cognition improved across processing speed, attention, learning, and reasoning in both groups, again without a statistical gap; social cognition alone stayed flat. Side effects were mostly mild, nausea leading. The authors conclude the two drugs performed equivalently here, a useful datum for prescribers weighing the cognition claim.
pmc-11627080:
Jason Dunlop and Russell Garwood reviewed the higher classification of fossil scorpions in 2024. Scorpions have a rich, deep fossil record, and their family tree has been drawn and redrawn for over a century. The review walks through that history in order.

Early schemes split scorpions by leg tips, then by belly plate shapes, then by a disputed first body segment. Later cladistic schemes traced a path from early side branches to modern scorpions, marked by book lungs and jaw parts. Within the modern group, paleosterns and orthosterns split by lung opening placement. The authors weigh the rival schemes and give a summary classification, with family and genus names set in their time line.
pmc-11627180:
Eleven researchers choose a dosing plan for a first human trial of an ovarian cancer antibody in a paper from 2024. The drug, ubamatamab, links T cells to a marker found on ovarian tumors. Lab tests measured cell killing and immune signals. Monkey data scaled into predicted human drug levels. Mouse tumor studies set the concentration range where the drug works.

A starting dose of a tenth of a milligram proved acceptably safe in patients. Step-up dosing tamed the immune reaction syndrome that followed. Clinical activity matched levels predicted from the mouse work. The team settled on target blood levels and two expansion regimens, with or without a second immune drug. The study shows preclinical data guiding trial design.
pmc-11628580:
Peter Briggs, Lawson Trimmell, and Javier Monzón compare two ways to collect lone star ticks, in a 2024 paper. Tick borne disease in the United States has more than doubled since the early 2000s, so efficient tick collection matters for many kinds of study. The team ran dragging and carbon dioxide baited trapping side by side at six sites in two range zones.

Dragging beat trapping for collecting young ticks. For adult males and females the two methods tied. No regional gap in efficiency showed. The authors also weigh material and labor costs of each method. Collectors who need many ticks fast can pick dragging for young stages and either method for adults.
pmc-11628980:
Marlene Martin, Manuel Seraydarian, James Gasper, and Triveni DeFries track what happens after hospitals start a monthly anti-alcohol injection, in work from twenty twenty-four. Very few Americans with alcohol use disorder get medication for it. Hospital stays offer a chance to spot the disorder and start treatment. The long-acting injection cuts drinking days and heavy drinking days. Charts of dozens of started patients are reviewed after discharge.

About a third get at least one dose in the first three months. A near equal share stop the injection in that window. The rest never follow up after leaving the hospital. Most patients do attend some follow-up after discharge overall. Top reasons for stopping include a wish for daily pills instead. Missed doses prompt clinician switches to pills in many cases. Prescribing hurdles and access barriers also drive drop-off.
pmc-11629580:
Jiani Liu and co-authors chart the aroma styles of Ningxia Chardonnay wines in a 2024 study. The wines come from the eastern foothills of the Helan Mountain in China. Twenty-nine wines were tasted and sorted with two sensory methods. Two styles emerged: lively wines with citrus and floral notes from two sub-regions, and implicit wines with truffle and kerosene notes from a third.

Chemical analysis found one hundred ninety-one aroma compounds in the wines. A handful of them formed the likely core of each style. The team also measured twenty-six phenolic compounds, which shape taste and color. The implicit-style region's wines looked more yellow, matching their higher flavanol content. The authors say the maps of aroma and color can guide growers and winemakers. They may also help shoppers pick wines by style.
pmc-11629780:
Hein Rune Skjoldal and colleagues compare two plankton samplers for measuring zooplankton biomass in the Barents Sea. Their 2024 study draws on decades of monitoring from an annual autumn survey.

The dataset covered hundreds of MOCNESS stations and thousands of WP-2 stations with size-fractioned dry-weight biomass. MOCNESS consistently collected more large-fraction biomass and less small-fraction biomass than the WP-2. The authors interpret this as less avoidance by large plankton and more extrusion of small plankton. Three research vessels collected the data, with no clear effect from towing speed differences. The comparison supports consistent calculation methods across the long time series.
pmc-11630980:
Yanan Tuo and co-authors link a belly-fat index to psoriasis in US adults. The index divides waist size by the square root of weight, aiming at central obesity. Skin and weight have long traveled together. Survey data from 2009 to 2014 covered 15,932 adults over age 20.

Each one-unit rise in the index came with 14 percent higher odds of psoriasis. The top quarter of the index carried 38 percent higher odds than the bottom quarter. The link held after wide adjustment and ran stronger in men. The authors suggest this cheap tape-and-scale measure could help flag adults who merit skin checks and weight counseling.
pmc-11631180:
Oyanagi, Horii, Ishikawa, and Takizawa report an odd gut case in a 2024 paper. A 77-year-old woman came in after vomiting blood. Scans showed her small gut hung on the wrong side and bent sharply by the aorta. A scope found a tear at the top of her stomach, the cause of the bleeding.

A week later the gut sat in its normal place on its own. Two months on, the shift and the bleeding both came back. Surgery showed the fixing band was present but the upper gut was loosely held. The team blamed weak fixation, not a birth twist of the gut. The loose gut likely kinked, drove vomiting, and tore the stomach lining.
pmc-11631380:
Kiley Seymour, Jarrod McNicoll, and Roger Koenig-Robert test whether being watched changes basic vision itself. Their 2024 paper looks past choices people control, at an automatic skill: noticing faces. They used a method that hides images from view while flashes reach the other eye. Watched participants broke through to see faces faster than unwatched ones.

A control test ruled out the idea that people just tried to please the experimenters. So surveillance reached below deliberate behavior, into raw visual processing. The effect is hardwired and beyond will, the authors argue. That finding matters for debates on camera spread and public mental health. Being watched, it seems, tunes the brain to spot other people whether we want it to or not.
pmc-11631580:
Xieli Ma and co-authors compare combined Chinese and Western medicine for Sjogren syndrome, in work from 2024. In this illness the immune system harms glands that make tears and saliva. Many drug mixes are used, and a network method can compare them all at once, even without head to head trials for each pair.

The team searched eight databases for randomized trials up to May 2023. Sixty-six trials with over five thousand patients were kept. Four Chinese drugs and three Western drugs were in the mix. The analysis ranks how well each blend worked and how safe it was.
pmc-11631980:
Anna Reuter and co-authors use machine learning to flag diabetes patients in South Asia who may miss heart risk goals, in work from twenty twenty-four. Many at-risk patients fail to control sugar, pressure, and cholesterol together. Clinicians lack a structured way to spot those patients early. Data come from two finished trials in urban India and Pakistan. Over fifteen hundred adults with diabetes feed the models.

Common clinic data predict failure to hit goals a year later. Patients in the top risk quarter are flagged for extra support. Flagging proves sharpest for sugar control and for meaningful gains. Precision for pressure and cholesterol goal failure runs lower. Gains-based flags score high across all three risk factors, though. Such flags could target scarce staff time where it helps most. Routine care in low-resource clinics is the intended home.
pmc-11632380:
Priscila Santos and Karen Kapheim test an idea about why some bees live longer, in this 2024 study. Many bees pass winter in diapause, a paused stage of development, but some lineages have lost that pause. The authors reasoned that losing it might free adults to live longer, a step that could also pave the way toward social living.

They compared twenty-seven bee genomes from species with and without the prepupal pause. Species that lost the pause had also lost a growth hormone and its receptor, and they showed a telling pattern in a known lifespan pathway. There, genes that extend life sat under tighter purifying selection, while genes that shorten life sat under looser selection. The authors argue these shifts could lengthen adult life and change how bees answer nutritional signals, both of which matter for the rise of social colonies.
pmc-11633180:
Lucía Guggeri and co-authors published a 2024 study on a protein that helps fat tissue form, studied in zebrafish. Obesity has tangled causes, and rare genetic diseases can reveal its pathways. One clue came from a syndrome where tiny hair-like sensors on cells, called cilia, fail. Cell studies had linked a protein, Fstl1, to both cilia and fat cell formation. The team tested that link in living fish.

Zebrafish carry two versions of the gene. Knocking down one version reduced cilia in early embryos and slowed fat tissue formation in larvae. The second version partly covered for the loss. A new mutant fish line confirmed the effects. On a high-fat diet, fish lacking the first version showed changed activity in fat cell markers. The results support the protein as a regulator of fat tissue development. The authors say pinning down such proteins helps explain how obesity begins.
pmc-11635280:
Yusheng Wang and co-authors compare two ways of removing a small piece of lung for early cancer, inside a day surgery model where patients aim to go home within forty-eight hours. One group had robot-assisted surgery; the other had camera-guided keyhole surgery. The records covered 204 patients treated in Changzhou between 2021 and 2023.

The robot group fared better on most short-term measures: shorter operations, less blood loss, less drainage, and drains removed sooner. Their pain scores were lower and they needed less pain medicine. Far fewer robot patients missed the forty-eight-hour discharge, eleven against thirty-nine. Complications also ran lower overall. A side analysis tied delayed discharge to pain medicine use in the first day, operation length, bleeding, and a history of tumors. The authors favor the robot route for this setting.
pmc-11635680:
G Plason Zuerkanah Plakar and co-authors model how bacterial glues stick to graphite in this 2024 paper. Microbes coat surfaces with sugary adhesins, a key step in biofilms and in fuel-cell anodes. The team simulated three such molecules on a graphite surface. They used quantum chemistry and molecular dynamics to watch the binding.

All three molecules could attach, and one sugar, N-acetylglucosamine, bound most eagerly. Treated graphite held the molecules better than plain graphite. Warm, basic conditions favored attachment across the board. Hydrogen bonds, electric pulls, and ring stacking drove the grip. The authors say the picture can guide fuel-cell design and anti-fouling work.
pmc-11636080:
Davide Potrich and co-authors published a 2024 study on whether zebrafish can do a simple kind of counting. Zebrafish are small fish often used in brain research. They like to swim with groups of their own kind. The team used that shoaling habit to test whether a male fish tracks how many females he has seen.

In the tests, females were shown one at a time and then hidden behind one of two panels. The male could swim toward either panel. With one female against two, he chose the panel hiding the larger group. With two against three, or two against four, he did not. As long as the total stayed at three or fewer, the fish seemed to handle adding and taking away. They even acted as if they grasped an empty set, the idea of zero. Speed and timing of the display also shaped their choices.
pmc-11637480:
Berner and six colleagues compare drug options for early frozen shoulder in twenty twenty-four. The stiff, sore shoulder eases best when treated in its early pain phase. The team pooled thirty-one studies, most of them trials. A network method ranked injections and pills against physical therapy.

Steroid shots into the joint eased pain and raised function by twelve weeks. Platelet rich plasma shots did the same, and alone improved range of motion. Common pain pills and one gel like shot showed no gain. Bias and mixed study traits temper the verdict. The authors urge early care and cleaner trials.
pmc-11637980:
UBE2C is a small enzyme in the cell's protein-recycling system that also helps drive the cell division cycle, and tumors of many kinds make too much of it. Mengjie Zhao and eight co-authors review its role across cancers in a 2024 paper. High levels show up in common, deadly malignancies of the lung, breast, and food pipe, among others.

The review maps how the enzyme feeds cell growth, invasion, spread, and resistance to drugs. Because of that reach, the authors argue it could serve three jobs at once: a warning marker, a forecast of outcomes, and a drug target. They call for deeper work on how it behaves inside the tumor's surroundings, to carry it from lab finding to clinical use.
pmc-11638480:
Ilaria Arduino and colleagues wrap drug-carrying fat bubbles in tumor membrane so the brain tumor welcomes its own poison, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Glioblastoma hides behind the blood-brain barrier and sheds drugs quickly. Their liposomes wear fragments of glioma cell membrane, a disguise meant to fool guards and to home on the same tumor type.

The hybrids were made in microfluidic chips, themselves simplified by 3D printing, which kept quality high and costs down. Loaded with two standard chemotherapy drugs, the bubbles crossed a model blood-brain barrier, sought out their matching glioma cells, and kept the drugs' killing power. The authors pitch membrane-cloaked liposomes as a practical way to smuggle proven drugs into a cancer that defeats them at the gate.
pmc-11638680:
Quillaia extract, from the bark of a South American tree, makes drinks foam and is approved in the European Union as additive E 999. A panel of the European Food Safety Authority reviewed a request to allow it in food supplements too, in solid and liquid forms, though not for infants and young children. The panel had already set a safe daily intake in an earlier review.

The panel modeled what people would consume if the new uses joined the current ones in flavored drinks and cider. Using typical use levels rather than maximum ones, exposure stayed under the safe limit for every age group. The opinion clears the extension on safety grounds, leaving the final authorization to regulators.
pmc-11639780:
Huseyin Yonder and co-authors propose a new score in a 2024 study to predict death from Fournier's gangrene, a fast and deadly flesh-eating infection of the genital and perineal area. Doctors already use several scores to judge risk in this emergency. The team wanted a tool built for this disease alone.

They looked back at patients treated at three hospitals in one Turkish province between 2014 and 2024. The group covered twenty patients who died and a much larger group who survived. Their new index combines a set of measures taken at intake. They test how well the index splits those who died from those who lived, and compare it with older scores. A surer early warning could speed up surgery and intensive care.
pmc-11639980:
Agnieszka Drab and co-authors pool world data on birth control pills and breast cancer risk in a 2024 review. Risk patterns may differ by region as economies and habits change. The team gathered seventy-four observational studies covering nearly two hundred thousand women and compared risk region by region.

Overall risk with pill use rose clearly in Asia and the Middle East, both at a relative risk near 1.29. Africa and the Americas showed small, uncertain rises, and Europe showed none. Subgroup checks tied the variation to study and population features. The authors present the first region-aware summary of this evidence, while noting that pooled observational data cannot prove cause.
pmc-11640080:
Xinge Jia and co-authors present a 2024 study of maize starch reworked by two enzymes acting together, aiming at better texture and processing behaviour. Single-enzyme tweaks change starch only so much. Pairing beta-amylase with alpha-glucosidase lets the two cut and rebuild chains in synergy, opening properties neither reaches alone.

The team ran the treated starch through a battery of instruments: electron microscopy for shape, X-ray and infrared tools for crystal and chemical order, and calorimetry plus viscosity rigs for cooking behaviour. They tracked how granule structure, chain lengths, and pasting changed with the double treatment. The results guide food makers who need starch that behaves predictably in processing.
pmc-11640380:
Ewa Kowolik and co-authors test light based therapy with tiny particles against a grave brain tumor in 2024. The tumor is the most common aggressive brain cancer in adults. Light therapy uses a drug that wakes under light and kills cells. The particles carry such a drug and also aid imaging. The team targets tumor blood vessels.

Tests ran in cell layers, cell balls, and tumors in eggs and mice. The therapy killed both vessel cells and tumor cells in dishes. It curbed ball growth and wrecked tumor vessels in eggs. In mice, vessels were harmed and oxygen fell a bit. Effect strength in mice hinged on how many vessels the tumor had at the start.
pmc-11640480:
Tamara Muñoz-Caro and co-authors showed in 2024 that webs of DNA thrown out by sheep immune cells, when triggered by a liver fluke's proteins, can kill liver cells in the dish. The fluke burrows through the liver and ruins sheep farming worldwide. Infected tissue runs low on oxygen, so the team worked at low oxygen too.

The fluke proteins boosted web formation under low oxygen, and a drug blocking the cell's oxidant engine cut it back. The webs proved toxic to liver cells on contact. The proteins also raised release of a tissue-cutting enzyme, though a surface marker stayed flat. The authors suspect the webs, meant as defense, help carve the liver damage of the disease when uncontrolled.
pmc-11640780:
Consolación Lima-De-La-Iglesia and co-authors review, in 2024, complementary therapies used around pregnancy, birth, and the weeks after. Care is trending toward more natural, less medicalized options, and interest in these therapies is rising. The review included only randomized trials, checked for bias with a standard tool.

Seventeen trials were selected from a large search. Water therapy, exercise balls, pressure point work, virtual reality, and foot reflex work eased labor pain. Scent therapy, a form of acupuncture with mild current, and massage helped pain after cesarean birth. Yoga lowered anxiety and low mood in pregnancy and after birth. The authors conclude these options help across all three phases.
pmc-11640980:
Texas has hundreds of counties and a lopsided map of medical specialists. Syed Jafri, Subi Gandhi, and Edward Osei mapped in 2024 where cardiologists, lung doctors, and hormone specialists are missing across the state's 254 counties.

They geocoded practice locations and weighed them against local disease burden and population, allowing a fifty-mile travel limit. Heart doctors fell short in one hundred ninety-six counties. Lung and hormone specialists showed similar gaps, concentrated in the rural west. The authors call the pattern a clear rural-urban divide. Their remedies include incentives for rural practice, wider telemedicine, and help with transport.
pmc-11641180:
Ling Li and co-authors study how a hormone controls the summer reproductive pause of a grassland beetle, in a 2024 paper. The beetle, a new pest in Inner Mongolia, spends summer in an obligatory break from breeding. The hormone, called 20E, is best known for steering insect growth and molting, but its hand in this pause was unclear.

The team cloned the gene for the hormone’s receptor from the beetle. Dosing females with the hormone switched on that receptor, a second hormone receptor, and an egg-yolk gene, while cutting a fat-making gene and body lipid. The treated females entered the pause later. The chain shows the hormone working through both receptors to time the beetle’s summer rest.
pmc-11641280:
A protein from a pig virus does something remarkable in the nervous system: parked in mitochondria, it blocks cell death and shields neurons. Jeflie Tournezy and co-authors asked in 2024 whether that viral X protein could help in ALS, where motor neurons die early as their mitochondria fail. They tested a peptide slice of the protein and two delivery routes in the standard ALS mouse model.

In cultured motor neurons the peptide restored energy levels. In living mice, treated animals moved better, kept more working motor units, and retained more motor neurons, though survival did not lengthen in this severe model. The authors call the protection clear and the delivery the next problem to solve.
pmc-11641680:
Alessandro Bertoldo and co-authors review what a grape compound may do for women's fertility, in a 2024 paper. The compound, resveratrol in full once here, is praised for anti-ageing and heart effects. Hints that it aids fertility have grown, yet the proof was scattered.

The team searched four databases to May 2024 and kept twenty-four studies. Nine covered women who sought natural or aided conception. Fifteen tested human cells and tissues in the lab. The sum suggests gains in egg and ovary function, though the base is thin. Dose and timing remain unsettled, and effects on implantation need care. The authors call for stronger trials.
pmc-11642080:
Claudio Monselli and co-authors review rehab after hip surgery in a 2024 paper. A hip socket problem called femoroacetabular impingement causes pain in athletes and active people. Keyhole surgery can fix the joint shape, but results hinge on a structured rehab program afterward.

Three databases were searched to April 2024 under standard review rules. Studies had to detail rehab after keyhole surgery for this hip problem. Fourteen studies with 1,105 patients made the final cut. The review sums up what the best programs share, from early motion work to return to sport tests, giving clinics a current state of the art to copy.
pmc-11642280:
Hyunsue Do and co-authors compare gout in Korean men and women in a 2024 national cohort study. Gout patients often carry other illnesses that shape their risk of death. Records covered adults who took urate-lowering therapy between 2002 and 2019. The team compared symptoms, other illnesses, and causes of death by sex.

Women started treatment older and carried more other illnesses than men. Kidney disease was the top cause of death overall and for women. For men, lung cancer led instead. Age, smoking, low weight, diabetes, and low blood counts all raised death risk. Sex-aware follow-up, the study suggests, should weigh kidneys for women and cancer screening for men.
pmc-11642680:
Doina-Antonia Mercan and co-authors build a slow release carrier for an antifungal drug in a 2024 study. The drug, micafungin, fights serious fungal infections and sits on a global priority list, yet dosing it well is hard.

Their carrier starts with tiny iron oxide cores, five to seven nanometers wide, spun in a vortex mixing device. A salicylic acid shell steadies the cores, and a porous silica shell grows over them in a magnetic field. The drug loads into that shell. A battery of imaging and chemical tests confirmed the structure. Flow tests showed a slow release, with about half the drug out after two hours, and a fine mass analysis verified the cargo at the molecular level.
pmc-11643080:
Xiang Li and co-authors design a tiny heat engine from polar molecules in a 2024 paper. Quantum heat engines use quantum effects in small systems, and this one runs the Otto cycle, a four-step loop of heating, expansion, cooling, and compression.

The working material is a set of polar molecules held in a lattice of light and an electric field. The molecules interact through their electric poles. The team computes how work and efficiency change with field strength, interaction strength, and bath temperatures. Tuning those knobs improves the engine's output. They also test how entanglement and quantum coherence in the molecules affect performance. The study shows polar molecules as a workable base for such engines.
pmc-11643280:
Leclercq reviewed colloidal tectonics in this paper from twenty twenty-four. The concept treats small building blocks, called tectons, that assemble themselves into particles and larger structures. Living systems inspired the idea, and chemists now design their own versions. Each assembled system shows traits such as two-sided solubility, predictability, or reversibility.

The review walks from natural examples to lab-made systems. Uses include stabilizing emulsions for catalysis and carrying drugs. Precise control of each block's traits lets new behaviors emerge at the assembled scale. Theory for designing fresh systems closes the survey. Leclercq frames the field as engineering at the nano and micro scales with bioinspired rules.
pmc-11643380:
Hye Jin Lee and co-authors build a light sensitive memory device in a 2024 paper for brain like computing. The part, made with a gallium oxide film between platinum contacts, can act as both a resistor style and capacitor style memory cell. Such dual parts could sense and compute in one place, saving energy in smart devices.

Light color sets the memory's mood. Ultraviolet light locks in long term memory, while red light gives short term traces that fade. Paired pulse tests show the capacitive mode holds its state longer than the resistive current mode. Learning trials improved with repeated light pulses, and a small pixel array stored gray levels by light strength. The results suit vision sensors with built in memory.
pmc-11643580:
Ashley Donato and co-authors check how heat sterilizing changes tiny cellulose crystals coated for medical use. Their 2024 study coats the crystals with a charged polymer in two chain lengths, long and short. Such crystals began in drug delivery and now draw wider medical interest. Once in body fluids, they pick up a coat of proteins that can shift their size, charge, and action. The team tested both coats after autoclave treatment.

Heat changed the coated crystals a lot, most of all with the short coat. The long coat hit cell life and blood fit harder than the short one. Cell immune replies also shifted with whether serum was present, a sign that the protein coat steers how cells read the material.
pmc-11643680:
Maria Carrupt and co-authors wrote this 2024 study on how silver content shapes the aging of copper thin films. Such films serve in smart windows, batteries, and solar panels, and rust is their slow enemy. The team sprayed pure and silver-doped copper coatings, then aged them two ways: a year in room air, and a bake at two hundred degrees.

Pure copper films grew in a clean crystal form with a strong favored grain direction. Silver made the films shed water more and blurred that favored grain, above all after baking. Heat grew oxides of both metals, dropping surface energy and wetting further. The authors say the results help gauge how long coated devices will last in service.
pmc-11643780:
Marcin Mikulewicz and co-authors measure metal release from braces wires in 2024. Wires are made from several alloys, and ions that leak in the mouth may trigger allergies. Nickel is a prime concern for sensitive patients.

Each wire type sat in fake saliva at body heat for four weeks. Two alloy types released far more nickel and chromium than stainless steel wires. The authors stress that material choice matters for patient safety, above all for those with metal allergies. Their data aim to guide choices that lower the risk of adverse reactions in orthodontic care.
pmc-11643880:
Zixuan Wang and co-authors grow faceted gold crystals with no seeds or soaps for a flour safety sensor, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. A charged form of hydrazine both shrinks the gold and caps its growth. The crystals come out even, with rare high-index faces.

Those faces shrug off alcohol yet attack peroxides with vigor. A coated electrode then sniffed out a banned flour whitener by its current. The test proved keen and picky in the team's hands. Wider use in catalysis and light tools is forecast. Readers get a simpler path to fancy gold shapes, plus a food guard.
pmc-11643980:
Broccoli's healthiest compounds are locked in its cells, and Ivona Karaula and co-authors dissolve them out with designer solvents in a 2024 study. Their solvents are natural deep eutectic mixtures, syrupy blends of betaine with sugars, glycerol, or malic acid, meant to replace harsher chemistry.

Software first predicted which blends would dissolve polyphenols and glucosinolates best. Five betaine blends went to the bench, and their extracts beat the standard ethanol extract on polyphenol content and antioxidant strength. One sugar blend led overall. The malic acid blend pulled out nearly six times the glucosinolates of ethanol. The compounds also kept better in the new solvents. Because the extracts need no purification, the authors pitch them as ready-to-use ingredients for foods and supplements.
pmc-11644080:
Amina Bramki and co-authors study the leaves of a bramble plant gathered in Algeria in a 2024 paper. The plant, Rubus ulmifolius, is a wild blackberry relative. The team made an extract from its leaves with a solvent and tested what the extract contains and what it can do in lab tests and computer models.

Screening found the leaves rich in plant compounds such as flavonoids and tannins, and measures of key groups ran high. A gas-based analysis named the main small compounds, among them gallic acid and caffeic acid. Tests showed a strong power to block oxygen-driven damage, a trait tied to many health claims for plant extracts. The computer work adds guesses about how the compounds might act in the body.
pmc-11644180:
Epoxy is strong but brittle, and plant fibers offer a greener way to toughen it. The authors test what happens when microcrystalline cellulose, a powder made from plant fiber, is mixed into epoxy at levels from half a percent up to two percent by mass. They bend the samples at several speeds, strike them in impact tests, and probe how the material stores and sheds energy across vibration frequencies.

Adding the cellulose raised bending strength, stiffness, and stretch before breaking, and the gains grew with the amount added. Impact tests showed better energy absorption, and the dynamic tests showed a stiffer response with improved damping. The team concludes that this cheap bio-based filler meaningfully strengthens and toughens epoxy, a useful step toward sustainable materials for demanding engineering uses.
pmc-11644280:
Zhaneta Georgieva and co-authors test how light color changes the powers of a green microalga in a 2024 study. The alga, a Bulgarian strain of Coelastrella, is rich in compounds prized for health products. Light is its food, and the color of that light may steer what it makes.

Cultures grew under red-blue light, pure blue light, or white light. Extracts were then checked for antioxidant content, for killing power against ten microbes, and for effects on two cancer cell lines versus normal cells. Blue light strengthened several of the desired actions. Tuning light recipes could turn algal farms into more potent sources of natural compounds.
pmc-11644980:
The authors present an acoustic camera simulator for robotic use in a 2024 paper. Forward looking imaging sonar has become a key sensor for marine robots, since it sees where cameras fail. Testing robot perception needs simulated sonar images that are fast and realistic.

Their simulator builds acoustic images from scene depth alone. It treats the sonar beam as a set of rays from the camera center and applies a simplified sonar model plus error models for environmental effects. Built inside a standard robot simulator, it needs no extra components. Tank tests compared simulated and real images, both visually and by measures.
pmc-11645080:
Valentin Iordache and colleagues compared low-power long-range radios for connected vehicles. Their 2024 study tests five communication technologies in the field. Vehicles joining Internet of Things networks need cheap, frugal links. Candidates included two Bluetooth forms, ZigBee, nRF24, and LoRa. Tests ran between a roadside unit and a moving car.

Three settings hosted the trials: open road, forest road, and city road. Range, message rate, and error rate were measured for each module. Satellite positioning data anchored the distance calculations. Vehicle-to-infrastructure and vehicle-to-IoT uses frame the work. Results show which radios hold up at speed and range. The study guides smart transport builders on link choice.
pmc-11646380:
Ahmad Yani Noor and co-authors respond to a study on geographic atrophy costs and falls in a 2024 letter. The study tallied care use, spending, and injurious falls in older patients with the blinding retinal disease. Medicare Advantage records supplied its data. The letter writers praise and probe it.

They recap the burden: more hospital stays and clinic visits than peers without the disease. Fall risk, especially head injury, rose as vision worsened. Added yearly costs passed a thousand dollars per patient. The findings fit earlier work, they note. The letter adds context for readers weighing how much advancing eye disease costs patients and health systems.
pmc-11646980:
Eleonora Sosa Cuevas and co-authors map blood immune traits in melanoma patients on anti-PD1 therapy in a 2024 study. Checkpoint drugs bring big wins, yet many patients fail to respond or suffer immune side effects.

The team tracked blood immune cells before and during first-line treatment with deep flow methods. Responders began with more of certain dendritic cells, killer T cells, and memory gamma delta T cells. Treatment reshaped checkpoint marks, activation states, and killing receptor patterns across cell types. Dendritic cell function shifted, and T cell orientation changed deeply. The patterns link the starting immune landscape to outcome. Doctors may one day read blood to forecast who will gain.
pmc-11647180:
Flóra Vajna and co-authors compare plants, bees, hoverflies, and spiders across habitats in a Central European agricultural landscape. Their 2024 study deals with the rapid decline of semi-natural grasslands, a key part of farmland biodiversity.

Restoring grassland by sowing wildflower fields is one response, but how arthropod groups react was little known in the Pannonian region. The team compared three habitats: sown wildflower fields, semi-natural road verges, and adjacent crop fields. Species counts, individual numbers, and assemblage composition were recorded for producers and pollinators, plus spiders. Contrasting patterns among groups show that one habitat does not serve all taxa alike.
pmc-11647280:
Marit van Stigt and co-authors lay out a trial plan, called PORTRAIT, in a 2024 paper. Babies born with a blocked food pipe often also have a soft windpipe that can collapse. That collapse brings repeated chest symptoms and, in bad cases, blue spells or stopped breathing. A later operation can fix the windpipe to the spine, but it means a second surgery.

The trial asks whether doing that fix at the first surgery prevents collapse and later illness. Seventy eight babies with the common type will be split by chance across centers in several countries, with neither families nor assessors told the group. Windpipe state is checked during care, and effects are tracked over time.
pmc-11647580:
Fabela-Hardy, Moreno-Ruiz, Necoechea-Osuna, and Conde-García present a case in twenty twenty-four of back pain caused by a rare birth defect of the aorta, the main artery. A man in his fifties had six months of back pain that common pain drugs did not ease. His heart tests were mostly normal, but a chest X-ray showed a widened central chest area.

Detailed scans found a pouch on the aorta pressing on his windpipe, plus an artery branch in the wrong place. Surgeons removed the pouch and rebuilt the branch, and after rehab he had no symptoms. The authors stress that lasting back pain can hide a vessel defect. Good scans can reveal it before the pouch tears, a far more deadly event.
pmc-11647880:
Jonathan Raybin and co-authors show that an electron beam can push tiny particles around on a liquid surface, and pull them back. Their twenty twenty-four article studies silica nanoparticles pinned to the surface of ionic liquid droplets. Beam-driven assembly could shape materials at scales where other fields lose their grip, but its mechanisms were murky.

A scanning electron microscope both watched and drove the particles. By tuning the beam voltage, the team flipped the force: low voltage repelled particles, high voltage drew them in. Patterns formed and dissolved on command. Tracking single particles showed the cause is a flow in the liquid, born from trace chemical damage by the beam. Uses in photonics and catalysis are proposed.
pmc-11648080:
Taber Yim and co-authors report a 2024 study on a common kitchen chemical, caffeine, inside lithium-sulfur batteries. Such batteries hold much charge, but sulfur compounds drift from one side to the other as they run. That drift, called shuttling, wastes active material and harms the lithium side. Additives can slow the drift, yet how they work is often unclear.

The team shows for the first time that caffeine cuts the drift current and slows the loss of charge over many cycles. A light-based test run while the battery worked showed shifts in caffeine's own signals. Those shifts rose and fell with the birth of the drifting compounds. The pattern fits a mild pull between caffeine and the compounds, which holds them back.
pmc-11648180:
Gabriela Elbert and co-authors recount closing a measles outbreak in Buenos Aires in a 2024 study. The outbreak ran from late 2019 into early 2020 across the metro area, just as COVID-19 hit. The team logs the response and how standard Pan American Health Organization closure rules were applied.

Control leaned on stepped up vaccination and tighter case watch. Records from national surveillance, the federal shot registry, and outbreak files fed the check. Viral spread met the set criteria for interruption on spread, shot cover, and lab grounds. The case shows closure proof can hold even in a strained setting.
pmc-11649580:
Helal and colleagues studied how gut germs change in people with anorexia nervosa after hospital care. Their work mixed a broad review of past studies with close tracking of a few patients. A short correction notice from twenty twenty-four fixes part of that work.

The notice says three chart notes were placed under the wrong charts, so each note must move. It then prints the notes in the right places. Those notes describe charts for three patients at set time points. They cover germ groups, how mixed the germs were, and a ratio of two large germ groups. Readers get the right labels, so the charts can be read as meant.
pmc-11649980:
Zixuan Fan and six co-authors measure the burden of vaginitis across five Chinese provinces in 2023. The condition is common and treatable, yet it raises the risk of poor pregnancy outcomes and of catching other infections. The survey covered women aged eighteen to seventy-four. Risk ran highest in women aged thirty-five to fifty-four, in those with three or more pregnancies, and in women who smoke or drink.

Two provinces, Hubei and Yunnan, showed clearly higher rates than the rest. One protective factor stood out: women who knew about cervical cancer screening fared better, which the authors read as screening visits catching vaginal infections early. They urge health programs to aim at the high-risk groups first. Widening screening awareness and access, they argue, would shrink the gaps in women's reproductive health.
pmc-11650080:
Krista Oei and colleagues piloted a food photo app for teenagers in two thousand twenty-four. The app estimates meal nutrition from pictures. Teenagers with obesity often avoid written food logging. Photo logging feels easier and faster. The app also supports personal nutrition goals. Clinicians view the data through a separate portal. Displays for teens minimize calorie counting focus.

Usability testing ran through several improvement cycles. Teen clinic patients tried tasks and gave interviews. A randomized pilot phase followed the refinement. Feasibility in a real obesity clinic was the core question. Digital tools must fit teen habits to work. This phased approach models careful health app testing.
pmc-11651080:
Nao Yamamoto Nishimura and co-authors present a 2024 case report on a jaw joint cyst that slowly blocked a man's ear canal. The case links the cyst to wear-and-tear arthritis of the jaw joint.

The man, aged 62, came in with swelling of the front wall of his left ear canal. Surgeons removed the lump, and lab checks showed a fluid-filled ganglion cyst. The swelling returned within three months, and scans showed an enlarged jaw joint head. As the canal closed fully, the team reshaped both the jaw joint and the ear canal. The patient healed well with no return of swelling. The authors note that ear canal lumps of this kind may hide jaw joint disease.
pmc-11651180:
Kourosh Eftekharian and co-authors run, in a 2024 randomized trial, a head-to-head test of two steroid injections for sudden hearing loss with no clear cause. Both drugs are shot through the eardrum as an add-on to standard oral steroids, but which one restores hearing better was unsettled.

Seventy-five patients were assigned at random to methylprednisolone or dexamethasone injections, twice a week for two weeks, alongside oral treatment. Sixty-nine finished the study. Hearing was compared tone by tone, by word recognition, and by recovery class at three months. Trials like this help ear specialists pick the add-on drug with the best odds of saving a patient's hearing window.
pmc-11652180:
Chan Wang and co-authors study why city shoppers in China buy quinoa foods in a 2024 paper. Quinoa is sold as a health food, and buyers with more income now care more about what food does for the body. The team asked how trust in health claims and the views of people around a shopper shape buys.

Their data came from a survey of 1,078 people across 16 districts of Shanghai. About 38 percent had bought quinoa goods. Trust and peer views both raised the chance of a buy and the price people would pay. The strength of each force shifted with what a shopper liked, so the authors urge clear labels and honest health claims.
pmc-11652380:
Ababye Wmeskel and co-authors measure how many toddlers in Merhabete Woreda, Ethiopia, received the second dose of measles vaccine, and what made the difference. Two doses guard children best, yet coverage in the country sits below the global target for wiping out the disease. The team surveyed families of 732 children aged 24 to 35 months in June 2022, using staged random sampling and a guided questionnaire.

Just over 63 percent of the children had received the second dose, far under the 95 percent goal. Children were more likely to be covered when their mothers knew the dose schedule, gave birth in a health facility, attended more than four pregnancy checkups, and kept the child's immunization card. Mothers aged 25 to 34 also had higher uptake.
pmc-11653580:
Nine researchers in the Netherlands asked whether fats in the blood can show how far a common liver disease has gone, in work published in 2024. The disease builds fat in the liver and can worsen into swelling, scarring, and cancer. A biopsy is still the main way to grade it, since stage-sorting blood tests are lacking. The team read the full fat profile of blood from patients at known stages.

The study covered seven people without the disease and thirty-two with it, eleven of whom had the swollen form. People with the disease carried more of several fat classes in their blood than healthy peers. Only a few single fats set the swollen form apart, and most were too scarce to serve as tests. One fat stood out as a possible marker, with higher levels in patients whose disease had not yet turned swollen.
pmc-11653880:
An extra bone beside the foot's navicular is common and usually silent, but in athletes it can turn training into injury. Bin Liu and eight co-authors compare the proteins of that extra bone with normal bone in 2024, from five injured patients after three months of training. They count both the proteins present and the chemical tags that switch them.

One hundred forty-seven proteins differed, pointing at cell adhesion and the scaffolding between cells, with two collagen genes as the busiest hubs. Five tagged proteins differed too, tied to fat handling in fat cells. Inflammation, bone repair, and bone balance proteins all appear in the pattern. The authors offer the map as a first molecular account of the injury and a guide for treatment.
pmc-11653980:
Kate Odgers-Jewell and co-authors study student placements in an urban Indigenous health service in a 2024 paper. Culturally safe care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people needs a workforce trained by immersion, not lectures alone. One community-controlled organization hosted 938 students from 32 fields over two and a half years.

Surveys before and after placement measured knowledge, skills, awareness, and self-development. Agreement rose across the board on matched answers, and written reflections were read with an Indigenous analysis method. Students called the stay a key step toward working with respect in such health care. The authors present the model as a template for building a culturally responsive workforce.
pmc-11654080:
Xiaojiang Zhao and co-authors built a scan model in a 2024 study to spot immune clusters in early lung tumors. Tertiary lymphoid structures are small immune hubs that form inside tumors and can signal a better outlook. Finding them now takes tissue checks after surgery, so a scan-based read before surgery would aid planning.

The team gathered chest scans and tissue slides from patients with stage I lung adenocarcinoma at more than one center. A program cut out each tumor and pulled fine texture traits from the scan. Their combined system, RAITS, uses those traits to call whether the hubs are present. It may also sort patients by outlook for tailored care.
pmc-11654180:
Melanie Trimmel and co-authors explore shared research roles in a 2024 study on psychosis risk. People with lived experience of mental health states now join study teams more often, and that shift is seen as a gain for the field. Less is known about how the work feels from inside for both sides.

The study sits inside a joint project on high risk states for psychosis. Professional researchers and co-researchers with lived experience took part. Through a qualitative approach, the team gathered how each group saw the shared work, its rewards, and its strains. The account can guide future projects that want true partnership rather than token input.
pmc-11654280:
Osama Mohamed Elsayed Ramadan and four co-authors published a 2024 qualitative study on what helps and hinders nurses in Saudi Arabia when adopting artificial intelligence tools. AI promises better decisions and patient care, but frontline nurses decide whether it actually enters practice. Their perspective was little studied in the region.

Forty eight registered nurses from four facilities took part in focus groups. Analysis followed a technology acceptance framework, sorting comments into perceived usefulness, ease, support, and resistance. Perceived benefit to patient care was the strongest driver, named by most participants, with organizational support close behind. The authors propose an extended acceptance model tailored to nursing. Their findings give managers a checklist for rollouts that nurses will actually use.
pmc-11654380:
Rachael Kendrew and co-authors interview patients about wearable activity tracking in severe pulmonary hypertension, in this 2024 qualitative study. Breathlessness and fatigue limit daily life in pulmonary arterial hypertension and its thromboembolic cousin. The six-minute walk test measures capacity in clinic, but wrist actigraphy could show real-world performance at home.

Adults from the United Kingdom and United States joined one-on-one online interviews mixing open concept discussion with structured debriefing. The aim was to learn which aspects of physical functioning matter most to patients, which actigraphy measures capture them, and over what timeframes. Patient views are needed to prove the measures valid before trials adopt them as endpoints.
pmc-11654980:
Smaragdi Marinaki and co-authors follow adults in Greece with a kidney disease that scars the filters inside the kidney, in work published in 2024. The disease is a common cause of heavy protein loss in urine. The team used a national registry to track who reached kidney failure and what shaped that risk.

The study covered 579 patients seen over nearly four decades, with a mean age of 46 years. Two factors stood out in the analysis. Higher kidney function at the start meant better survival of the kidneys. Patients whose disease went into full or partial remission fared far better than those with no remission. Patients who got immune-suppressing drugs reached full remission more often, but also relapsed more. The work guides how doctors weigh treatment for this disease.
pmc-11655180:
Margo Goldfarb and co-authors present a 2024 study on how plants make beta-alanine, a small building block with many jobs. In plants it helps answer stresses such as drought, heat, and flooding. It also feeds into making vitamin B5 and coenzyme A, two vital molecules.

Plants can build beta-alanine from several starting materials, unlike bacteria, which use one route. Working with a model plant, the team fed labeled forms of isoleucine and propionate to cells. Tracking the labels showed both feed into beta-alanine through a shared middle step. They then found three enzymes, all aminotransferases, that can run the final step of that route. The work links amino acid breakdown to a wider stress and vitamin network.
pmc-11655280:
Giulia Ciminelli, Claire Witham, and Melissa Bateson study how captive rhesus monkeys use enrichment items, in a paper from 2024. Enrichment is meant to improve welfare, but staff need to know if animals keep using the items or lose interest over time. Checking that by hand takes a lot of staff hours.

The team built two camera based tools that watch the monkeys on their own. One tracks a white drum that holds raisins, in nine groups, both full and empty. The other counts monkeys using a puzzle in twelve groups. The monkeys kept showing interest in the food drum even months later. The authors argue that such tools can make welfare checks faster and more steady, so staff time can go where it helps most.
pmc-11655480:
Valerie Glutsch and co-authors report in 2024 on giving a paired immune drug set a second run in a rare, fast skin cancer that had spread. The pair had lifted response rates in patients who failed a first immune drug, but what to do when the pair itself stops working was unknown.

Three patients who had gained from the pair, then worsened, got the pair again. Two in three responded, the same rate as their first run. Gains held across months of follow up with no new loss of control yet seen. The small set hints that a second run can work, the authors note with care.
pmc-11655580:
Yan Li and Lili Liang study why some breast cancers resist radiotherapy, in a 2024 paper on two proteins locked in a regulator-and-target relation. One, a zinc finger protein called ZBTB14, was picked out by data analysis as a hub tied to resistance. The team found it scarce in tumors and cells that failed to respond to radiation. Its target, a membrane protein called TMEM208, showed the opposite pattern and ran high in the same samples.

Lab tests showed the first protein binds and switches down the gene for the second, cutting its output. Raising the first protein in cancer cells slowed their growth and shrank tumors in animals, and it made resistant cells answer to radiation again. Forcing the second protein back up undid those gains. The authors read the pair as a switch for resistance: when the regulator fades, the target rises and treatment fails.
pmc-11655880:
Yang Liu and co-authors assemble the full genome of a tropical purple sea urchin at chromosome level. Their 2024 paper presents the first such reference for Heliocidaris crassispina, a species valued ecologically and commercially and used as a lab animal. Long-read sequencing supplied the raw text; chromosome-contact data ordered it into scaffolds.

The genome spans about 710 million bases, with ninety-eight percent anchored onto twenty-one pseudo-chromosomes. The team cataloged 18,665 protein-coding genes and the major families of non-coding RNA. A standard completeness check scored ninety-seven percent. The reference should support resource surveys, genomic breeding programs, and marine ranch management for this urchin, and it enriches the thin genomic library for sea urchins generally.
pmc-11656380:
Ryota Uchimura and co-authors build a cell-entering peptide that kills blood cancer cells without the usual death pathway. Many leukemias resist treatment by blocking apoptosis, the tidy cell death route. Their peptide joins a NOTCH1 fragment to a viral entry tag. It slips into leukemia cells through a gulping route called macropinocytosis.

Inside, NOTCH target genes switch down, and death follows fast. Membranes burst, spilling cell contents, with no caspase alarm fired. Normal blood cells and solid tumor lines stayed unharmed in the tests. Four greasy building blocks in the fragment proved vital to the kill. The agent offers a spare route against stubborn leukemias and lymphomas.
pmc-11656580:
Ping Du and co-authors study how a blood-based feed changes human stem cells in a 2024 paper. The feed, made from platelets, can stand in for serum and help the cells renew. Two stem cell kinds, from marrow and from fat, were grown in the feed and checked in depth.

Cells in the feed grew smaller, spread less, and formed many small fat drops. Those drops set them apart from true fat cells grown the same way. Gene reads flagged growth paths at work, and blocking one key path cut fat build-up, which pins its role in the shift.
pmc-11657180:
Yueh-Lin Lee and co-authors measure in this 2024 study how burned out Taiwan's critical care staff remain after the pandemic. A survey of 254 doctors and nurses in one large hospital system, paired with a review of twenty Asian studies, used the standard Maslach inventory. Overall burnout hit about thirty-five percent, while emotional exhaustion ran far higher at seventy-one percent.

The young, the unmarried, and the less experienced suffered most, alongside staff pulling long hours and night shifts. Heavy workload, paperwork, and scarce leave topped the stressor list. Asian studies varied widely, sixteen to eighty-two percent. The authors say pandemic strain itself has faded from the drivers.
pmc-11657580:
Julius Mayer, Daniel Baum, Felix Ambellan, and Christoph von Tycowicz grade Alzheimer's disease from the shapes of brain structures, working with the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, in a 2024 paper. Shape analysis reads anatomy from medical images, but classic shape spaces demand complete, topologically uniform shapes, which real scans rarely provide. The team adapts functional maps, a correspondence technique from geometry processing, to relax those demands.

On top of the maps they build new shape descriptors and feed them to a graph convolutional network that classifies disease state. Tested on the open ADNI database, the classifier separated healthy controls from Alzheimer's patients and improved on state-of-the-art geometric deep learning results. The authors argue that functional maps make shape-based grading robust to the messy, incomplete shapes of clinical data. They present the pipeline as a general route for morphometric classification beyond this one disease.
pmc-11657880:
Jamal Ataya and co-authors link confidence to diabetes control and mood in a 2024 survey study. Self-efficacy, the belief that one can manage one's own health, shapes daily diabetes care. The study asks how that belief tracks emotional distress and well-being.

Hundreds of patients in Damascus answered standard scales in face-to-face interviews. Tools measured management confidence, diabetes problem areas, and general well-being. Traits like sex and age entered the analysis of who fares best. Care that builds confidence may lift mood as well as blood sugar. The study gives local clinics a lever beyond drug doses.
pmc-11658080:
Na Zhang and co-authors report two pregnancies carrying a tiny missing piece at the tip of chromosome 10, in work from 2024. Deletions in the 10p15.3 region are rarely described, so each new case sharpens the picture of what the missing genes do.

Among 5,258 amniocentesis cases, two fetuses carried a pure deletion of about 556,000 DNA letters spanning two known genes. One showed a thickened neck fold and inherited the deletion from a father whose only sign was mild language trouble. The other had unusual vertebrae and mild spinal curvature, and at twenty months showed speech and motor delays. The authors offer the pair as a guide for prenatal counseling.
pmc-11658680:
Shaftoe and Gillis issued a correction in twenty twenty-four to their review of how load reshapes the heart in fish and mammals. The review compared hearts across species to learn how hearts adapt. The correction fixes how one older study on a turtle heart was read.

The older study showed more collagen, a tough fibre, in one heart layer after cold exposure. It did not show that the layer grew thicker, as the review first said. So a line in one figure and one cell in a table were removed. Both the web text and the PDF were updated, and the authors say sorry for the errors.
pmc-11659880:
Sun and five co-authors test if a twin gene's loss deepens a worm nerve fault in this twenty twenty-four study. The main gene guides link growth and wire ends in worm nerves. Its near twin sits close by and shares most of its code.

Inside, gene cuts made worms that lacked both genes at once. Their link and wire faults matched the main-gene lone loss band. A tagged prey protein rose by the same span in both bands. Past plant-in tests also failed to save the main loss with the twin. The team reads the twin as a by-stand gene in this work.
pmc-11660380:
Youzhao Ma and co-authors link metabolic syndrome to worse breast cancer outcomes in a 2024 study. The syndrome bundles belly fat, blood pressure, sugar, and lipid problems. Among 910 patients treated with chemotherapy before surgery at one center, eighteen percent had the syndrome. Most tumors were stage two or three.

Patients with the syndrome reached complete tumor disappearance less often. Five-year disease-free survival ran about seventy-three percent for them, against eighty-four percent without the syndrome. Overall survival showed the same gap. The disadvantage held among premenopausal women as well. Links with menopause status and stage were also found. The authors argue metabolic health belongs in treatment planning, not just in long-term prevention talk.
pmc-11661880:
Saskia Locke, James Doonan, and Bryn Jones survey recent advances in caring for fragility fractures, the breaks that occur when osteoporotic bone meets minor trauma. British guidance stresses prompt, coordinated multidisciplinary care and early mobilization. Medical therapy now includes the bone-building drug romosozumab for patients at imminent fracture risk.

Regional nerve blocks are replacing opioids for many, with less delirium. Surgeons have gained polyaxial and far cortical locking systems that let osteoporotic bone heal by controlled motion, plus cement-augmented screws for grip in weak bone. Minimally invasive approaches preserve blood supply and shorten recovery. The authors expect future gains in vertebral and pelvic fracture care aimed at independence.
pmc-11662180:
Pooja Khakhar and co-authors compare three ways of shaping root canals in baby molars and the cracks each leaves behind, in a lab study from 2024. Cleaning and shaping the canal is a core step in saving a decayed baby tooth. Rotary files speed the work, but they can start tiny cracks in the root that shorten the tooth's life.

Eighty canals from pulled baby molars were split into four groups of twenty. One group was shaped by hand files, one by an older rotary system, and one by a newer rotary system, with a control set for comparison. The roots were then checked for microcracks. The study weighs speed and ease against root damage, a trade off that guides tool choice in children's dentistry.
pmc-11662680:
Chelsea Blankenchip and Kevin Corbett show how a bacterial repressor senses loose DNA strands to switch on immune defenses, in a study from 2024. Bacteria carry immune systems against the viruses that hunt them. Those systems must stay off until truly needed, or they harm their host. The repressor, CapW, holds one such system quiet by gripping double-stranded DNA.

When damage frees single strands, CapW grabs them with a special domain. That grab changes its shape and frees the genes it guards. In a test bacterium, this switch proved key to fighting off a dormant virus. The authors map the full chain from sensing to gene release. Their work explains a whole family of like repressors. It also shows how bacteria balance defense against self-harm.
pmc-11662980:
Murdoch Leeies and co-authors examine organ donation after death in one Canadian province in a 2024 study. They ask whether donors flagged as higher risk for infection are treated fairly by the system. Such flags have been criticized as unfair to sexual and gender minority donors.

The team reviewed all referrals to the provincial donation body from 2015 to 2021. They compared how often families were approached and how often they agreed, for higher-risk donors versus standard donors. Higher-risk status did not clearly change the chance of being approached. The study also weighs other equity-linked traits, aiming to show where the donation path may treat groups unevenly.
pmc-11663380:
Zhu Zhu, Chun Yang, Mengsu Zeng, and Changwu Zhou study how the mix of two cancer types in one liver tumor shapes outlook. Their 2024 study splits combined tumors by how much of the second, bile-duct type they hold. Cases are set against pure bile-duct cancers after surgery.

More than three hundred patients took part across both tumor kinds. Combined tumors with a small bile-duct share fared better than pure bile-duct cancers. Those with a large share fared worse on both return of disease and survival. Scan traits also split by share, and one rating class predicted a large share on its own. The authors suggest care for the large-share group follow the pure bile-duct plan.
pmc-11663480:
Sinian Li and co-authors report a case where tuberculosis passed from mother to fetus before birth, in work from two thousand twenty-four. The mother conceived through lab-assisted fertilization, a path that raises tuberculosis risk. Both mother and her three-month-old baby were found with spread tuberculosis, including a brain lesion in the baby.

Gene sequencing proved the same drug-resistant strain in both. Drug care began fast and worked well for both patients. The baby's plan had to change several times due to liver harm and acid buildup from the drugs. The authors urge vigilance in such pregnancies.
pmc-11663580:
Marcus McHale and Ronan Sulpice present AlGrow, a graphical interface for measuring area and growth of targets with varied colors. Their 2025 paper grows out of work on macroalgal growth, where image segmentation was a bottleneck.

An earlier platform captured and analyzed arrays of sea lettuce discs to assess growth diversity. Extending it to other algae, such as dulse, ran into poor color boundaries and wider color ranges. AlGrow lets users define a target color volume as a hull in color space. Images are then segmented by color distance to that hull, and growth rates are computed across a series. The tool aims to be easy, fast, and accurate.
pmc-11663880:
Keigo Onda and five co-authors test whether two quiet signs of spontaneous theory of mind agree in the same adults. Theory of mind here means the fast, untaught sense of what a person with a false belief will do next. One sign is anticipatory gaze, where the eyes look ahead. The other is reaction time, how fast a person responds to an object's place. Their 2024 study blends both tests into a single task so the two signs can be compared head to head.

Both signs appeared in healthy adults, and they moved together: strong gaze bias went with strong reaction bias. In adults with autism, both signs differed from the norm. A model using both signs separated autism from healthy adults best of all. The team concludes that the pair taps one shared skill. The combined task may help clinics judge social difficulty in adults with autism.
pmc-11664080:
Mohammed Almutairi and co-authors review links between cell powerhouses and ADHD in a 2024 article. Mitochondria make energy for cells, and their cleanup system, called mitophagy, removes worn units. Past work ties disturbed balance in these systems to ADHD, a disorder marked by poor focus and impulsive acts. Causes named range from pollution and stress chemistry to inflammation and gene faults.

The review gathers cell and molecular studies on these faults in ADHD. Gene links include variants in systems for dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, the brain's signal carriers. The authors argue the interplay between energy balance and cleanup is a rich area for new work. Grasping it could point to fresh treatments for the disorder.
pmc-11664280:
Mohammad Keshavarzi, Moein Ghasemi, Mohammad Amin Manavi, Ahmad Reza Dehpour, and Hamed Shafaroodi test how a common drug calms seizures in mice, and whether nitric oxide carries the effect. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. A third of epilepsy patients still seize despite modern drugs, so fresh angles are needed.

Seizures were triggered three ways: a slow vein infusion, a belly injection of a convulsant, and a maximal electric shock. The drug, pentoxifylline, was dosed alone and with a nitric oxide building block or with blockers of its making enzymes. Thresholds, delays, and deaths were scored. The design separates which enzyme branch, if any, the drug leans on. The work probes a cheap, approved drug as a possible seizure add-on.
pmc-11664580:
The authors trace the atomic shifts behind a crystal that flips between insulator and metal, a switch that could serve as an artificial neuron. Their 2024 study uses a copper vanadium oxide crystal grown whole, millimeters across. Brain-inspired computing needs such sharp, programmable switches, but the atomic moves behind them stayed obscure.

Whole-crystal oscillators let the team watch the structure change as the switch flipped, using single-crystal X-ray diffraction.
