The flip runs from a magnetically ordered insulator to an unordered metal. Copper ions were seen ordering into a superlattice between the crystal's layers as the state changed. The paper ties that atomic ordering to the change in conductance.
pmc-11665180:
Masoomeh Latifi and co-authors review how outdoor air pollution affects women's fertility in a paper published in 2024. The review searched major databases for studies from 2013 to mid-2023 that linked air pollutants with fertility outcomes. Eligible designs included trials, case-control studies, and cohort studies.

Across the evidence, dirtier air went with lower fertility, fewer live births, poorer embryo quality, lower implantation rates, and more miscarriages. Four parts of traffic pollution stood out: fine particles, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur compounds, and carbon monoxide. The authors describe effects on egg quality at the gene level and on fetal growth. They urge greater public and official awareness to cut exposure, since pollution is hard for individuals to escape.
pmc-11665480:
Hanchao Cheng and co-authors test whether health literacy drives hepatitis B treatment in China in a 2024 study. China carries a heavy hepatitis B burden, yet few patients get antiviral drugs. Low health literacy may keep people from knowing the disease, its cure path, and where to seek care.

An instrumental variable design helps separate true cause from mere correlation in survey data. The authors trace how literacy feeds awareness, knowledge, and active care seeking. Findings can steer where health teaching funds do the most good. Wider treatment is also a step toward the global goal of ending viral hepatitis. Literacy, in this frame, is a medical tool in its own right.
pmc-11666280:
Claudia Schulz and co-authors test whether scent dogs can smell COVID-19 in animal samples, in a 2024 pilot study. Dogs already detect infected people quickly by scent. After the pandemic peak, infected human samples for dog training grew scarce. Lab animals like ferrets and hamsters could supply controlled samples instead.

Respiratory samples came from infected humans, hamsters, and ferrets, plus ferrets with a flu virus. An automated device presented samples blind, with no trainer cues. Dogs scored much the same on animal samples as on human ones. Both hit rates and correct rejections stayed high across the tested scenes. Animal models may keep scent dog training supplied for future outbreaks.
pmc-11667180:
Ritam Naha and co-authors show how two proteins jointly coordinate the assembly of the MICOS complex that shapes the inner folds of mitochondria, published in 2024. That complex, built from two subcomplexes, organizes the cristae where energy production happens. Losing one subunit, MIC13, causes severe disease with liver and brain involvement and crista defects.

The team found that removing a mitochondrial protease in cells lacking MIC13 rescued the other subcomplex and the junctions between folds. A partner protein, SLP2, turned out to anchor many complex parts and shield one subunit from destruction by that protease. Removing both proteins broke assembly of the second subcomplex too. Restoring the first subcomplex fixed the rest. The authors propose the pair acts as a controlled seeder for the whole assembly.
pmc-11667280:
Neumann, Subah, and van der Westhuizen study how Liberia made community health workers into paid professionals. These workers are central to fair care, yet few nations formally employ or pay them. Health policy forms inside power struggles among funders and governments.

The case follows Liberia's Community Health Assistant program at national scale. Using Lukes' theory of power, the authors credit strong government will for the win. Liberia pushed back on funder resistance to paying workers and reclaimed decision control. Agreement across ministries strengthened that hand. Local proof framed around workers' rights helped proactive talks with funders.
pmc-11668580:
Yao Jiang and Shan He report two children healed from deep chest wound infections after heart surgery with a homemade suction drainage method in a 2024 case report. Such infections are rare but can be devastating after the breastbone is opened.

Their do-it-yourself negative pressure setup holds steady suction and flushes small fluid volumes at intervals. The suction draws out infected fluid, while flushing stirs fresh granulation tissue to grow. Both children formed healthy new tissue over the wound bed. Systemic infection came under control during treatment. Both wounds closed fully, and both patients left the hospital in good condition. The simple build offers a low-cost option where commercial devices are scarce.
pmc-11668780:
Hongdong Sun and co-authors linked hand grip strength to death risk in a 2024 health study. Grip strength is a simple gauge of muscle health and has been tied to bone loss in past work. What it means for long-term death risk in people whose bones are already thin was less clear.

The team drew 1,343 adults with low bone mass from a large United States health survey from 2013 to 2014. Death records were checked through the end of 2015. With a stats model that weighs many traits at once, they tested whether weaker grips went with higher death risk. The study hints that a quick grip test may help flag patients who need closer care.
pmc-11668980:
Klemens Höfer and co-authors present a 2024 protocol for a study of health apps in German mental health care. Mental illness touches about 28 percent of German adults each year. Since 2020, some apps can be prescribed and paid for by public insurance, and many target mental health. Yet doctors prescribe them with clear reluctance, a sign that fit problems persist.

The project will map current app use, weigh ways to weave apps into talk therapy, and name the blocks. Methods mix a scoping review, focus groups, expert talks, and insurance claims data. The end goal is policy advice for smoother use of the apps in outpatient care. Funded by a federal innovation fund, the work speaks to payers, doctors, and patients alike.
pmc-11669180:
Diana Guimaraes and co-authors report a spinal epidural abscess in a young man with none of the usual risk factors, in a 2024 case paper. Such abscesses are a rare complication of epidural pain catheters, and a missed one can leave lasting nerve damage. Prevention rests on spotting high-risk patients and strict sterile technique, and outcomes hinge on fast recognition and treatment.

The patient was healthy, with no medical history of note, and had an epidural catheter placed to fix a broken shin bone plateau. Two attempts at placing the catheter were the only flag in his story. He still developed the abscess. The authors stress close watching after the procedure for new signs, quick lab tests and MRI when suspicion rises. Treatment means early antibiotics tuned by culture results, plus surgery to drain the collection when needed. The case shows how unpredictable this infection can be.
pmc-11669680:
Erdenebat and co-authors report a mouse study, published in 2024, on which brain cells prion diseases attack first. Prions are misfolded proteins that spread through the brain and kill neurons, but the damage is patchy, not even. Why some cells fall and others resist was unknown. The team infected mice with one prion strain and tracked where the bad protein built up. They compared two broad cell classes: those that excite their neighbors and those that calm them.

The prion strain spread far more readily in the excitatory cells. Those cells also died off in greater numbers. The pattern helps explain the patchy maps seen in patients. It suggests that cell identity, not just location, sets vulnerability. Future work can ask what makes excitatory cells so welcoming to prions. That answer might point to ways of slowing a disease group that is now untreatable.
pmc-11669880:
Emilie Bryne, Kathrine Høyvik Bergum, and William Gilje Gjedrem set out a trial protocol for improving prisoners' oral health, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Prisoners suffer poor oral health from limited care access, poverty, and low prioritization. A pilot using motivational interviewing showed promise.

Four prisons in Norway's Rogaland County recruited toward three hundred twenty inmates. Participants are randomized to oral hygiene packages with or without motivational interviewing, a thirty-minute counseling session among the intervention components. The trial is multicenter and double-blinded by design. Protocols published in advance lock methods before results arrive. If counseling plus supplies beat supplies alone, prison health services gain an inexpensive, scalable intervention.
pmc-11669980:
Ling-Yu Bai, Ming Zhao, and Kui-Ying Ma report a heart rhythm case and review the drug behind it, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. A seventy-five-year-old woman came in with chest tightness, breath loss, and one faint. Her dangerous ventricular rhythm kept returning in hospital.

Standard drugs and electric shocks failed to settle it. Once nicorandil was added, the rhythm stopped. The drug opens potassium channels, which steadies the heart's electrical timing. The authors pair the case with a literature review and pitch nicorandil as a strong option when usual care fails.
pmc-11671980:
Frank Larkin's 'At a glance' column sums up the highlights of an ophthalmology journal issue for busy readers. Each short entry distills one article's question and answer. The topics span the modern eye clinic, from corneal transplantation to contact-lens infections and inflammatory eye disease.

One entry reports that surgeons' growing experience lengthened graft survival across more than eleven thousand corneal transplants in a national registry. Another finds an added eye-drop drug no better than standard care in a severe allergic eye emergency. A twenty-year update keeps contact lenses as the top risk for infected corneas. Further entries cover grading systems that save clinic visits, registry data on immune-suppressing treatment, and a head-to-head of drugs for a sarcoid-related eye inflammation. The column serves as a map to the issue.
pmc-11672480:
Villata leads a team building a 3D skin model for testing antibacterial therapies in a 2024 paper. Resistant bacteria are making skin infections harder to treat. Flat cell cultures cannot mimic the tangle of a real infection, so better lab models are needed.

Their model joins an outer and inner skin layer and forms a real barrier. The team wounded, infected, and treated the model with antibiotics. The unwounded barrier slowed bacterial growth on its own. Wounds and infections triggered matrix building, inflammation signals, and defense peptides. Cell types shifted roles as in healing skin. One bacterium's death released substances that flipped the inflammation pattern. The authors offer the model as a screening platform.
pmc-11672580:
Nan Li and co-authors compare bypass surgery against stenting for the toughest coronary disease in a 2024 study. Patients with left main or triple-vessel disease can get off-pump bypass grafts or modern drug-eluting stents. Records from one Chinese heart hospital over eight years supplied the contest.

After matching, three hundred sixteen pairs were compared over about four years. Deaths, major events, and heart attacks did not differ between groups. Stent patients more often needed repeat procedures and saw chest pain return. Bypass patients, though, suffered more strokes. The authors read bypass as a favorable strategy for this disease pattern, with the stroke trade-off kept in view.
pmc-11672680:
Van Leuven and co-authors ask whether antibiotic use in hospital wards feeds drug resistance in the slimy biofilms inside sink drains. Such films can shelter dangerous bacteria. The team sampled drains in four wards of a German hospital and matched the findings to each ward's prescribing records.

Every ward's drains held medically relevant species. A resistance marker gene grew more common as ward antibiotic use rose. Visible drug resistance in the bacteria, though, showed no matching trend. Lab-grown films shifted their makeup depending on the starting community and the drug added. The authors conclude there is no single general effect of low-dose antibiotics on drain films.
pmc-11672780:
Rhianna Vergeer and co-authors examine what happened to drinking when the pandemic blocked alcohol treatment, in a 2024 study. Lockdowns and strained services cut many people off from help for alcohol use disorder. Whether that interference worsened problem drinking was undocumented. The team surveyed close to three hundred adults in a national pandemic study during 2020 and 2021.

People who reported blocked treatment scored clearly higher on a standard problem-drinking screen. Stress levels and personal resilience were tested as buffers or amplifiers of that link. The survey design adjusted for background traits and prior drinking history. The findings argue that keeping treatment reachable during crises is itself a drinking intervention. Future emergency plans should protect addiction care access.
pmc-11672880:
Dildar Hussain and co-authors review five years of progress in PET-CT imaging in this 2024 paper. The method fuses two scans: one traces body processes with a mild radioactive marker, and the other maps anatomy. Together they show both where tissue sits and how it behaves.

The review covers sharper image reconstruction, motion correction driven by data, and timing methods that pin down where signals arise. Case studies show the gains in finding lesions, sorting out what a disease is, and judging whether treatment works in practice. The authors also look ahead at coming tools and hurdles, urging careful testing of new methods so the gains reach patients in daily care.
pmc-11673080:
Ilaria Roato and co-authors review aging in mesenchymal stromal cells in a 2024 paper. These cells help maintain and repair many tissues and can turn into several cell types, which has drawn many clinical trials. Few protocols, though, have won approval, and one barrier is cell aging, called senescence.

Aging cells show changes in shape and gene control, DNA damage, shorter telomeres, and a distinct pattern of secreted signals. They also lose protein quality control and suffer mitochondrial problems. The review collects what is known about the causes of this aging. It then surveys current and future strategies to delay or reverse it and to extend the working life of the cells for therapy. The authors ask whether the field is ready for clinical use.
pmc-11673280:
The authors examine family incivility and adolescent depression in a 2024 paper. Rude, disrespectful treatment inside families can harm teenage mental health. The study tests whether self compassion carries that effect, and whether the pathway differs for boys and girls.

Two waves of data came from nearly one thousand Chinese high school students. Family incivility at the first wave predicted depression later. For girls, the link ran indirectly through lowered self compassion. For boys, the effect was direct, with no mediation. The authors argue interventions should account for these different pathways by sex.
pmc-11673380:
Ana Isabel Sanchez and colleagues assessed a program for perpetrators of gender-based violence. Their 2024 paper evaluates the reGENER@r program in Spain. The two-month program uses psychoeducational and cognitive-behavioral methods. It runs as an alternative measure to prison sentences. The study tracked change across many psychological measures.

Thirty-seven convicted men completed self-report checks before and after the program. Measures covered emotional intelligence, empathy, and coping responses. Emotional dependency, gender role conflict, and sexist beliefs were also tracked. The team tested change for both statistical and clinical weight. Marked improvements appeared in the reported results. Such programs aim to cut repeat violence by shifting beliefs and skills. Evidence on what changes inside them guides future design.
pmc-11673680:
Vsevolod Filonov and a large team synthesize a phosphorus analogue of a key metabolic compound, in a 2024 chemistry paper. The analogue swaps a carboxyl group for an H-phosphinic group, which mimics its shape. Such analogues can pass through normal enzyme steps and form new active products inside cells.

Earlier work showed the analogue and its glutamate form both kill bacteria, with partly different targets. Here the team shows the glutamate form serves as a substrate for a major metabolic enzyme, with a best working range shifted toward alkaline conditions. They also made the target compound enzymatically in a stereospecific way and tracked its forms by NMR.
pmc-11673880:
Paula Antelo-Pais and co-authors present a 2024 Spanish study on uric acid levels and heart risk factors. High uric acid is a known risk marker, but harm may start below the classic cutoff. The team used entry data from a national primary care cohort. Patients were split into quarters by uric acid level, separately by sex, and classic risk factors were compared across quarters.

Risk factors grew steadily from the lowest to the highest quarter in both sexes. Body mass, waist size, blood pressure, and LDL cholesterol all climbed in step. A standard risk score rose across quarters in women. The pattern held after adjustment for other traits. The authors say even normal-range uric acid tracks a heavier risk load. Cutoffs for concern may need a second look.
pmc-11673980:
Yao-Kuang Wu and co-authors link a hemoglobin fragment to sepsis severity in intensive care patients in this 2024 study. Sepsis kills more ICU patients than almost any other condition. During sepsis, free hemoglobin spills from broken red cells into the blood.

Neutrophil enzymes then chew that hemoglobin into fragments like hemorphin-7. The team measure the fragment and two of those enzymes in a Taiwan ICU cohort. Levels are set against sepsis and shock status over the hospital stay. A fragment that tracks shock could warn teams hours earlier. The study also maps how hemoglobin breakdown feeds the crisis. Prospective sampling gives the timeline a firmer footing than chart reviews.
pmc-11674280:
Biye Wang, Lu Wang, Tao Tao, and Wei Guo add brain wave evidence on response response binding, in a 2024 paper. The effect is the linking of two responses planned and made apart from each other, a fresh angle on action control. Behavioral proof was rich, but electrical proof from the brain was scarce.

Thirty six people did a prime and probe task where the needed responses could repeat or change between phases. Repeated responses were faster, as past work found. Brain waves also differed: one component was larger and two peaked sooner in the repeat case. The study bridges behavior and brain signals for this binding effect.
pmc-11674480:
William Middlezong and co-authors speed up the diagnosis of a leukemia where hours decide survival, in a 2024 paper. Acute promyelocytic leukemia brings dangerous bleeding, but a targeted drug reverses the clotting failure if started at once. Treatment hinges on spotting the PML::RARA gene fusion, and standard tests are slow. The team built a nanopore sequencing method that uses CRISPR guides and adaptive sampling to enrich the fusion region without amplification.

The approach promises low cost, simple setup, and fast turnaround. They tested it against the diagnostic need: a same-day answer a hospital lab can actually run. Faster fusion detection translates directly into earlier treatment and fewer early deaths from bleeding in this leukemia.
pmc-11674780:
Isabel Rodenas Quinonero and co-authors weighed three ways to check bone marrow spread in a type of lymphoma, in work published in 2024. The study covered one hundred forty eight patients across Spain. Marrow spread is part of first staging for this cancer, but its value in risk scores was unclear.

Biopsy was far more sensitive than imaging scans at finding marrow spread. Imaging, though, carried stronger power to predict how patients would fare. Joining both gave independent value for survival in patients treated intensively. The authors propose a new risk index that adds the imaging result, and it split patients into three groups with clearly different outcomes. They say biopsy stays essential for staging.
pmc-11674880:
Anna Gimenez-Palomo and a large team of co-authors present a 2024 review of mitochondria, the cell's power units, as markers of illness state in bipolar disorder. Faulty power units may explain swings in energy across mood phases. The review weighs evidence for a two phase pattern of energy supply.

Studies report power faults in bipolar disorder, with signs that shift between manic, low, and calm phases. Oxidative stress also runs high. If confirmed, such markers could guide care fitted to each patient's phase and flag those at risk of a poor course. The authors are frank about limits: the review was not systematic, designs vary, and modulator drugs lack firm backing.
pmc-11674980:
Katia Rupel and co-authors present a 2024 study of smart nanocarriers for a cancer drug. The carriers are tiny self-assembling spheres built on cellulose, a plant polymer. A fluorescent unit is attached so the spheres can be tracked by their glow. Doxorubicin, a standard cancer drug, rides inside. The link holding it breaks in acid, and tumors are more acidic than healthy tissue. Unloaded spheres measure about sixty nanometers across.

Loaded spheres measure about eighty-six nanometers, with most of the drug packed inside. Dialysis tests show the release responding to acidity as designed. Drug delivery teams get a carrier that is visible, plant-based, and acid-triggered. Tracking matters because a carrier that cannot be followed cannot be dosed wisely. Cellulose also eases safety worries that synthetic carriers raise. The work sits at the bench stage, proving build and behavior before any animal step.
pmc-11675080:
Liping Wang, Xuming Hu, Chenyue Tao, Jacob Xiang, and Hengmi Cui identified a natural antisense RNA that appears to restrain liver cancer, in this 2024 study. The RNA, called NRAS-AS, is the mirror-strand partner of a known cancer gene, NRAS. The team found it by sequencing liver cancer cells and then tested what it does.

Raising the antisense RNA in two liver cancer cell lines slowed their growth and spread, pushed them toward cell death, and reshaped their division cycle. Silencing it did the opposite. Mice given cells with extra antisense RNA grew smaller tumors. In patient samples, the antisense ran low where the cancer gene ran high, and its protein fell when the antisense rose. The authors propose it as a possible drug target and test marker.
pmc-11675180:
Rong Huang, Rachel Chazan-Cohen, and Delaina Carlson trace, in a 2024 study, how early family conflict reaches children's behavior years later in low-income homes. Conflict at home is a known risk for children's mental health. The paths it travels were unclear.

The team followed 1,622 children from toddlerhood into early adolescence. Conflict predicted more maternal depression at age three and more detached parenting at age five. Depression, in turn, linked to more behavior problems in children, both inward and outward kinds. Detached parenting showed a differing, milder pattern. Pinpointing the middle steps tells support programs where to intervene: easing a mother's depression may matter as much as calming the home.
pmc-11675380:
Angelo Sanfelice and co-authors pair in 2024 lab runs with a chance model of a shake fed power tap that drinks wide band trem ors. Such taps can milk power from the wild shakes of roads and gear. A fair model must span both the tap and its drain wire load.

A soft spring chance form with white noise drives the sim. Two loads face off: a plain block and a diode bridge with a charge store. Draw curves by load size peak at a best load in both. Sim and bench marks match well. High tie reads bare the off rest marks of the tap.
pmc-11675480:
Dejun Xiong and co-authors study a gene called ISCA1 across many cancers in a 2024 paper. The gene helps build iron-sulfur clusters, small parts that many proteins need to move energy and do their work. The team asks how the gene links to a form of cell death driven by iron, and to the immune cells around a tumor.

Using large cancer data sets, the authors track the gene's level, its changes, and patient outcomes in many tumor types. They also test drug ideas with computer docking models. The gene stands out most in thyroid cancer, where it may serve as a marker for outlook and for response to immune therapy. It also works with distinct partner genes in distinct cell types. The team sees it as a lead for new drugs.
pmc-11675880:
The authors reviewed voluntary blood donation in a 2024 paper on modern health care. Given blood keeps surgery, trauma care, and long-term disease care running, and a steady pool of keen donors keeps the supply safe. Donors who give by choice tend to be in good health, which lifts the safety of each unit.

pmc-11675980:
Alba González Moreno and co-authors link creative confidence and social skill in Portuguese students in a 2024 study. pmc-11676180:
Maitane Serrano and nine co-authors feed male mice an omega-3-rich diet and trace changes in the brain's cannabinoid system and behavior, in a study from twenty twenty-four. pmc-11676380:
Frank Strnad and co-authors read how growth curb in the womb shapes mouse brain cells and guard cells past birth. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. pmc-11676480:

Hasan Turut and co-authors test chest drainage fluid for virus traces in 2024. COVID patients with fluid or air around the lungs often need a chest tube. Tube placement can spray fine droplets, which puts staff at risk. The team asked whether the drained fluid itself carries the virus.

pmc-11676880:

pmc-11676980:
Xun Pan and co-authors tune a solar cell plastic by changing its mix in a 2024 study. The base plastic pairs thiophene and quinoxaline units and is cheap to make in few steps, a plus for large scale solar films. pmc-11677080:
Bin Tang and nine co-authors offer a narrative review from two thousand twenty-four on psoriasis and extracellular vesicles. Psoriasis is a long-term skin disease that also harms joints and raises care costs. Vesicles are tiny sacs with a lipid skin that cells release into the body.

The review explains how these vesicles help cells talk to each other and carry cargo such as miRNA. Through that cargo they can shape immune response, cell growth, and cell change, and thus help drive the disease. The authors also weigh vesicles as treatment tools in their own right. They discuss using them to carry drugs straight to target tissue.
pmc-11677180:
Giuseppe Dell'Anna and co-authors review a hard cancer problem in a 2024 article with clinical scenarios. Some advanced cancers block both the bile duct and the gastric outlet at once. Endoscopic ultrasound guided methods now offer a less invasive way to open both routes.

The review covers biliary drainage routes such as hepaticogastrostomy and choledochoduodenostomy, plus antegrade stenting. These methods report high technical and clinical success in the cited work. They cut the need for high-risk surgery or drainage through the skin. For patients in palliative care, that means food and bile flow can be restored with less burden. Scenarios show how teams pick among the options.
pmc-11677280:
Emma Fernández-Llamazares and co-authors build and test new membranes for proton exchange membrane fuel cells, devices that turn hydrogen into power with low emissions. They start with polysulfone, a sturdy plastic, and blend in an ionic liquid plus silica particles coated to repel water. pmc-11677380:
Boyne and co-authors study whether sitting time links to prescription drug use in adults. Past work tied physical activity to lower medication use, but sedentary time itself was rarely tested. Sitting is linked to chronic disease and death risk even after activity levels are counted, so its own role matters.

The pilot study measured sedentary time with devices rather than self-reports, which are often inaccurate. Adults also reported their own prescription medication use for comparison. The team examined total sitting and sitting patterns apart from exercise. Results may show if cutting sitting could ease medication burden.
pmc-11677580:
Konrad Kaminiów and co-authors review how the cellular immune system fights syphilis in a 2024 paper. The bacterium Treponema pallidum is a master invader that can linger for decades, and roughly eight million adults caught syphilis in 2022 alone, with rates climbing on several continents. Antibodies get the headlines, but cells do much of the fighting.

The review explains how T lymphocytes switch on, how signal proteins rally the attack, and how macrophages and dendritic cells spot and swallow the pathogen. It also catalogues the bacterium's evasions: its surface barely provokes immunity, and it can dampen the very activation meant to kill it. When cellular defense falters, late damage to brain and heart follows. Understanding this duel informs vaccine hopes for one of humanity's oldest scourges.
pmc-11677780:
Breathing fine dust is linked to depression in people, and Hi-Ju Kim and six co-authors build a rat model to find out how. Male rats inhaled PM2.5 particles through the nose daily for four weeks, with behavior tests run weekly. The exposed rats gave up sooner in a swim test, a standard sign of depressive-like behavior, showing lost motivation.

Stress markers in the cells' protein-folding machinery rose there, along with an oxidant-producing enzyme, while other regions were much less affected. A marker of dopamine production fell in the same region, pointing to faltering dopamine signaling. The authors propose that pollution-driven stress in the hypothalamus drives the behavior, and that easing that stress could treat pollution-linked depression.
pmc-11677880:
Zhuolu Zhang and co-authors tested whether spraying a plant hormone helps tea plants withstand salty soil in a 2024 study. Salt stress cuts crop quality and yield worldwide. Brassinosteroids, a family of plant steroid hormones, are known to help plants cope with stress, but their action in tea was unproven.

The hormone eased several stress signs, with strength varying by variety. Tea regions face growing soil salinity from irrigation and climate shifts, so a spray that buys tolerance has direct value for growers.
pmc-11678280:
Plant cellulose, the fiber in every stem and husk, can soak pollutants out of dirty water once it is chemically dressed. They sort the dressing methods: adding acid groups, nitrogen groups, oxidation, graphene coats, plasma treatment, and mixes of these.

Each treatment shifts pore structure, shape, and chemical toughness in its own way. Case studies show the dressed fibers pulling heavy metals and organic pollutants from wastewater. Combined methods give the toughest, best-performing materials. The authors weigh the green appeal against scale-up cost and flag where proof is thin. Their verdict: cellulose sorbents are close, but need cheaper production to win.
pmc-11678380:
Junhan Li and co-authors make a slippery fiber mat to stop internal scarring after surgery in a 2024 study. Abdominal adhesions follow most operations and can cause pain and blockages. Drug-loaded films risk side effects. A drug-free route uses water itself as the lubricant.

Friction fell to a low point at the best loading, and bound water rose with lecithin share. The mats stayed strong and cell-friendly. In rats, adhesion scores dropped to near the floor. Lubrication, not medication, does the work.
pmc-11678480:
Wenyun Li and eight co-authors sequence in 2024 the genome of an edible mushroom prized for a calming compound. The mushroom, a widely farmed enoki relative, is rich in GABA, a natural chemical that eases nerve activity. Knowing its genome should expose the genes that build the compound.

The assembly spans about forty-one million bases across one hundred forty scaffolds and holds over fourteen thousand genes. Family trees place the mushroom near honey fungus and shiitake. Two candidate genes for the key GABA-making enzyme were found, and shape modeling hints the second is the stronger catalyst. The genome also maps hundreds of enzymes for chewing through plant matter.
pmc-11678680:
Suseela Raj and co-authors link low vitamin D after kidney transplant to a virus-driven kidney disease, in a 2024 study. The BK polyomavirus can inflame the transplanted kidney, and vitamin D supports immune defense, yet deficiency is common in recipients. Records of 3,308 recipients tied vitamin D levels measured in the first two years to later virus problems.

Blood virus levels alone showed no tie to vitamin D. The kidney disease itself, though, struck far more often in the deficient group, with risk roughly quadrupled after adjustments, and insufficiency doubled it. The authors suggest keeping vitamin D replete may help protect the graft, a cheap lever worth testing in trials.
pmc-11678880:
Daniella Da Silva and co-authors coax fat stem cells toward bone in this 2024 study. Weak bones in osteoporosis break easily, and standard drugs fall short. Fat-derived stem cells could rebuild bone, but left alone they prefer to become fat instead.

The authors offer the recipe as a frame for bone repair, pending animal tests.
pmc-11678980:
Bendejacq-Seychelles and co-authors hunt in 2024 for fungal toxins that harm branched broomrape, a parasitic weed with a wide host range. The weed devastates many crops worldwide. pmc-11679080:
Henrik Nost and co-authors review polarized training for endurance athletes in a 2024 paper. High effort work is known to raise max oxygen uptake and work economy, but the best mix of effort was still open.

The team searched two databases and kept fourteen studies after screening a far larger pool. Polarized plans seemed to raise max and peak oxygen uptake and work economy over short spans. The best mix paired a moderate share of hard work with a large share of easy work. The authors note that most proof covers short periods, so longer tests are still needed.
pmc-11679380:

pmc-11679680:

pmc-11682880:

pmc-11688180:

pmc-11688380:

pmc-11688480:

pmc-11688880:

pmc-11689880:

pmc-11690180:

Another finds that feeling older brings more stressors yet warmer lifts from good events. A third shows good mood bridges social time to feeling younger. The last splits emotion beliefs by age. pmc-11690380:
Patricia Opresko wrote a 2024 study of how oxidative damage at telomeres, the caps on chromosome ends, pushes cells into early retirement. pmc-11690580:

pmc-11690780:

A second shared barriers, facilitators, and solutions raised by frontline providers, health care leaders, and policy makers. pmc-11690880:

pmc-11691080:

pmc-11691380:

Having a child was associated with more hospitalizations in urban homes, but not in rural ones. The study aims to sharpen understanding of the family role at the end of life.
pmc-11691580:
Complaints about nursing homes in Ohio jumped sharply in five years, and Robert Applebaum and co-authors asked what homes do with that flood, in work from twenty twenty-four. A state survey of all licensed homes in twenty twenty-three fed the study. Complaints strain both families and the inspection corps, which now lags its own timetable.

Homes were asked whether a set staff member owns complaints, and whether complaint reviews feed their quality work. Talks with state survey teams fill out the picture. A long lag sits between a complaint visit and its ruling, the data show. The authors close with steps for homes and states to cut both complaints and the harm they signal.
pmc-11691680:
David Rehkopf, Frank Furstenberg, Christian Jackson, and John Rowe report a national health study from 2024. Using survey data on more than seven million people, they ask how health and daily function changed for adults near the age when they stop work.

The authors find wide gaps by income, with the poorest groups having many more days of poor health in a month. Health got worse over time for low and middle income groups, most of all for people in their fifties. If the trend holds, that group will reach later life in worse shape than those before them, with costs for work and care.
pmc-11691780:
Kayla Garner and four co-authors published a 2024 coordinated analysis of whether how healthy people feel predicts how well they think later in life. Seventeen longitudinal studies, seven from a global aging network, ran identical models on harmonized data. The question: does self-rated health in early and middle adulthood track cognitive function now and years later, and does it flag dementia risk?

Early results say yes. People with better subjective health beliefs showed better thinking at the same age and at follow-ups stretching 4 to 27 years. Gender and baseline age moderated the links, which survived adding objective health measures, at least in part. The authors discuss the findings through lifespan and health-behavior theory. They propose self-rated health as a cheap early warning sign for cognitive decline.
pmc-11691880:
Diane Zheng and seven co-authors link vision to performance on a cognitive challenge test in older adults in this 2024 paper. The test probes semantic interference, a subtle memory failure that predicts early Alzheimer's disease. Vision loss is itself a risk factor for decline. The study covered 133 adults aged sixty-one to eighty-eight with normal cognition or early impairment. About sixty percent identified as Hispanic or Latino. Vision checks measured sharpness and contrast sensitivity.

Only contrast sensitivity mattered. Better contrast reading tracked with stronger storage capacity and with recovery from interference. It also tracked with fewer interference intrusions. Sharpness showed no link at all. Contrast sensitivity is the skill of telling apart shades close in brightness, used in every daily task from faces to steps. The authors suggest vision changes travel with the earliest cognitive ones.
pmc-11691980:
Shiyu Lu examines what volunteering does for midlife and older adults in a 2024 study. Past research counted volunteer hours and stopped there. Lu argues that depth of engagement in the role may matter as much as time spent.

The study covered 665 Hong Kong residents aged fifty-five and over. People were sorted by hours, by engagement level, and by profiles that mix the two. Volunteering over fifty hours a year tracked with better well-being and self-rated health than not volunteering. Medium and high engagement showed the same pattern. Thinking skills benefited across all volunteer groups, with active and dedicated volunteers gaining most. Lu suggests weaving volunteering into social prescribing for healthy aging.
pmc-11692080:
Rinanda Shaleha, Nelson Roque, and Erin Harrell study what keeps older adults using brain training technology in a 2024 paper. One hundred eighteen adults aged sixty five and over took part in a tech based cognitive training program. Prior work found that how the program was framed mattered little, so the authors tested personal motivation instead.

Motivation was measured from game performance, with steady success and low failure marking high motivation. Statistical models showed a strong link: each step up in motivation came with a clear rise in how faithfully participants stuck with training. Model comparisons confirmed motivation improved prediction a lot. The authors suggest game design that feeds motivation can raise adherence in such programs.
pmc-11692180:
Alex Speers and Amala Soumyanath lay out a stepwise plan for testing herbal supplements properly in older adults. Their overview appeared in twenty twenty-four. Supplement use is rising among seniors, yet good proof of benefit is scarce, product quality varies, and mixing herbs with many medicines adds risk.

Their center in Oregon studies two herbs tied to brain and body resilience in aging: gotu kola and ashwagandha. The pipeline starts with checking what is actually in each product. It then tests how the herbs act in cells and animals, and how to measure their compounds in blood. Human safety and dosing studies follow. The aim is the solid groundwork that fair, optimized trials in older adults require.
pmc-11692380:
Brain dopamine signals and walking quality in older adults are linked by Mauricio Gil-Silva and co-authors in work dated 2024. Walking worth is more than pace; smooth, steady steps count too. The team scanned a dopamine-linked site in 199 adults near seventy-five years old, none with Parkinson disease. Back sensors worn on a short walk scored step traits in three planes.

Lower signal-site counts in one brain zone tied to more jagged vertical and side step patterns. Some trend links also ran the other way for rate traits. On the whole, richer dopamine marks sat with steadier, less wild gait. The zone may help hold walk control with age.
pmc-11692480:
Eduardo Silveyra and Soham Al Snih wrote a study in two thousand twenty-four on multiple chronic conditions and disability in older Mexican American adults. Longer lives mean more people live with several diseases at once. The authors asked whether the link between disease count and trouble with daily tasks differs for women and men.

They followed nearly one thousand adults aged seventy-five and older who began the study without disability, over twelve years. Women with three conditions had higher odds of later disability than women with at most one. Both sexes with four or more conditions faced higher odds, but the pattern was clear and significant only in women. The authors call for programs that account for these sex differences.
pmc-11692580:
Siting Chen and co-authors link longevity genes to aging paths in older adults in a 2024 study. Aging unfolds across body, mind, and mood at once, not in single tracks. The team used a national retirement study spanning 1998 to 2016.

Over seven thousand adults aged sixty-five and up were sorted into four joint aging trajectories. Two groups kept low impairment, split by disease load, while two carried broad impairment. Long-lived adults clustered most in the healthiest group for both Black and White participants. Gene risk scores for longevity patterned differently by race within those groups. The authors urge joint study of genes and social factors.
pmc-11692780:
Okyere Kontor, Veneranda Nyarko and Paul Botwe wrote a 2024 study on what sets the age of natural menopause in Ghanaian women. That age links to later chronic disease risk. Data on it in Ghana are scarce, the team notes. Just under three hundred postmenopausal women at one hospital clinic answered a structured survey.

Under half showed solid knowledge of menopause. The average age at natural menopause came out just under fifty. Most women fell in the expected mid-forties to mid-fifties band. Age at first period, age at first pregnancy and past contraceptive use tied to timing. The authors urge better menopause education.
pmc-11692880:
Jasmin Tahmaseb examines how age and immigration are framed for older immigrant women in the United States, in a study from 2024. Older immigrants make up a real share of the older population, yet media often picture both groups with bias. Such framing can deepen isolation and distress in later life.

Life history interviews with eighteen women over seventy explored goals, concerns, and supports. The women said hostile campaign talk on immigration worsened their daily lives as they faced late-life challenges. A check of ten news articles over two months showed discriminatory framing of age and immigration together. The study also records resilience and coping among participants.
pmc-11692980:
Jaime Perales-Puchalt and co-authors validate dementia care scales for Latino family carers in a 2024 study. Care questionnaires must measure truly in the groups they serve. Latino families carry a large share of dementia care. Trial baseline data offered a test bed.

One hundred carers answered scales about themselves; slightly fewer covered the person they aid. Symptom, burden, mood, and life quality tools were included, in English and Spanish. Links between scales ran the expected ways, nearly all significant. Each scale also held together well on its own. The battery measures reliably here, clearing the way for support trials that include Latino families fairly.
pmc-11693080:
Zambrano Garza and co-authors present a 2024 study on what gets stroke survivors moving in daily life. Exercise cuts the risk of a second stroke, and partners may be an untapped engine. Eighty-eight Canadian survivors wore activity monitors for up to two weeks. Morning and evening surveys captured solo and shared plans and confidence.

Solo morning intentions predicted both reported and measured activity that day. Solo confidence did not. Shared intentions and shared confidence with a spouse both tracked with more self-reported movement. The results argue for treating the couple, not just the patient, in rehab plans. Daily-life sampling caught links that one-off surveys would miss.
pmc-11693180:
Madeline Nichols and John Geldhof tested in 2024 how the widely used PANAS mood questionnaire is structured in mid- and late-life adults. The scale's factor layout has long been debated. Their data came from 1,176 people who rated daily emotions over eight days. The analysis separated within-person day-to-day patterns from between-person habits, and sorted emotion words by pleasantness and activation level.

A five-factor model fit well at both levels. The factors split high-energy negative feelings from quieter negative ones, and positive feelings into high-energy, plain and low-energy groups. Factors stayed distinct, with moderate correlations between them. The authors urge researchers to weigh both pleasantness and activation when linking mood to health. A two-score reading of the scale may blur real differences. Daily emotion studies especially should use the finer structure.
pmc-11693280:
Xiangyu Zhai and co-authors test in 2024 if the wealth of a home area links to muscle loss in older adults who live at home. Loss of muscle mass and strength, called sarcopenia, can leave older people frail. A person's own income and schooling were known cues, but area traits got less study.

Nine hundred forty three adults past age sixty in Hong Kong took part. Muscle mass, grip, and walk scores set who had the loss. The worst off third of areas showed far higher odds than the best third, even after own traits were weighed. Area wealth counts on its own.
pmc-11693380:
Shuna Khoo, Zhihao Ma, and Lile Jia map how well-being hangs together for adults with different schooling in Singapore in a 2024 study. Singapore's older adults today had far less schooling than the cohort now aging, so support programs must serve both profiles. The team surveyed a representative community sample of more than five thousand adults.

Using network analysis, they mapped links among the elements of well-being for each education group. The patterns differed sharply. For residents with less schooling, well-being centered on present conditions such as illness, eating habits, and quality of life. For the highly schooled, it centered on balance, harmony, and expected quality of life ten years ahead. The authors say programs can be judged by whether they move the central factors for each group.
pmc-11695880: Ranajit Chatterjee and Lalit Gupta published a short editorial in 2024 in a critical care journal. It weighs a urine test proposed for spotting kidneys about to fail in very ill patients. The test builds on a drug challenge: a dose of a water pill, then a salt check on one urine sample. Supporters say the salt reading can flag which patients will worsen. A cheap bedside flag would matter, since failing kidneys in the unit often turn grave fast.
pmc-11696380:
Chengfang Liu and three colleagues capture carbon dioxide with a three-part deep eutectic solvent in a 2024 study. Such solvents are cheap, low-hazard liquids that can soak up the gas, but older versions regenerated poorly and drank in water.

Adding a promoter compound to a betaine and glycol base lifted performance. At the best mix, the solvent held about a fifth of its weight in carbon dioxide at thirty degrees. Added water weakened uptake, a caution for damp gas streams. After five capture-and-release cycles the capacity stayed strong. The authors present the blend as a workable step toward greener capture liquids.
pmc-11696780:
Hao Zhu, Xuan Yin, and six co-authors study brain bleeds found in unborn babies by MRI scans. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, reviews cases from two large hospitals over near ten years. The bleeds were first spotted on ultrasound. MRI then gave a clearer look before birth.

The set holds one hundred twenty-six cases, most of them single babies. The most common added problem was swelling of the brain's fluid spaces. About a third of cases showed that trait. Other cases showed missing or extra fluid pockets in the head. The size of the bleed did not match the count of added problems. The team links scan traits to how the babies fared at birth.
pmc-11698480:
Abdelfatah Elsenosy and co-authors compare surgery with gentler care for a leg pressure syndrome in a 2024 review. Chronic exertional compartment syndrome squeezes leg muscles during exercise, causing pain that fades with rest. Cutting the fascia, called fasciotomy, is the classic fix, while rest and therapy offer a non-surgical path.

Four cohort studies met the bar for pooling under standard review rules. Pain scores, return to activity, and quality-of-life scales formed the main measures. Satisfaction and complications were tracked as secondary outcomes. Athletes and soldiers, who meet this syndrome often, need a fair verdict. Pooled data can show whether the knife truly beats patience.
pmc-11699280:
Justin Bradfield, Ian Dubery, and Paul Steenkamp report chemical tests on a very old hunting tool kit from South Africa, in a 2024 paper. A bone from a large grazing animal, about seven thousand years old, came from Kruger Cave. The hollow bone held three bone arrowheads packed in an unknown substance, marking it as a quiver.

Lab analysis found two heart-active poisons in the filling, digitoxin and strophanthidin. The two poisons come from different plants, so the mix was a true recipe, not a single plant sap. A third fat-linked compound hints at one more toxin in the blend. The find is the oldest firm proof of a mixed hunting poison. It also supports an older claim about a similar compound found on a much older wooden tool.
pmc-11699580:
Jayshree Dawane and co-authors test a standardized ashwagandha root extract against anxiety and depression in stressed rats. The herb is a staple of Indian traditional medicine. Rats under chronic varied stress got one of three extract doses, a standard drug, or nothing, over 36 days, then faced maze and swim tests.

Treated rats behaved less anxiously and less hopelessly, in line with dose. Blood and brain chemistry shifted too: serotonin and a growth factor rose, stress hormones fell, and inflammation markers dropped. The authors see the extract as a candidate for both prevention and care.
pmc-11701480:
An editorial in a 2024 issue of eClinicalMedicine surveys diabetes drugs that have outgrown their first job. The drugs mimic a gut hormone, GLP-1, that boosts insulin, slows digestion, and curbs appetite. The first of the class reached patients in 2005, modeled on a hormone from a lizard's saliva.

Since then the family has grown to include several weekly injections, and landmark trials have shown some of them cut heart risk as well. Weight loss has become a major use in its own right. The editorial takes stock of the class's widening reach and the questions that trail it, from cost to long-term safety.
pmc-11702980:
Jian Wu and eleven co-authors published a 2024 paper on making oilseed rape fragrant using gene editing. Oilseed rape is a major oil crop, and scent strongly affects the value of farm products. In rice, fragrance comes from a broken gene that lets a scent compound build up.

The team asked whether the same trick works in rape, which carries several copies of the related gene. Using CRISPR editing, they knocked out two copies of one gene that do the same job. Edited plants accumulated 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the compound behind the scent in fragrant rice. The result opens a path to fragrant rape lines with added market value. It also shows a known fragrance pathway can transfer across crops.
pmc-11704880:
Rachel Jimenez, the journal's editor, introduces in 2024 the annual print issue of Advances in Radiation Oncology, a journal devoted to radiation treatment research shared freely online. Each year the editors pick a few of the most striking articles from the past year's online run and gather them into print.

The editorial explains the journal's open access mission: removing paywalls and geography from who can read and join the field. The print collection offers readers another way to meet the work, whether discovering a study or revisiting one. Jimenez frames the selection as a snapshot of where radiation oncology moved this year.
pmc-11704980:
Fahad Butt and four co-authors report a quality project that raised the standard of daily notes in a newborn intensive care unit, in a 2024 paper. Patchy notes can hurt care for fragile infants. The team first picked seven key points that each note should cover, then audited thirty notes from early 2022. They built a standard note template around those points and trained staff in its use.

Audits then ran every three months for a year, with forty-five notes checked per round. Staff heard feedback each round, and the template was reshaped to fit their needs. By the final round, notes covered eighty-one percent of the key points, well past the sixty percent goal. The authors credit the loop of template, audit, and feedback for the steady gain.
pmc-11705380:
Michael Straughn and Teresa Boitano survey blood clot prevention for ovarian cancer patients in this 2024 editorial. Clots strike up to a quarter of gynecologic cancer patients. They delay treatment and can kill, so prevention choices matter.

The piece introduces three studies in the same journal issue on clot prevention in these cancers. One maps silent clots after major debulking surgery and their risk factors. The editorial weighs when and which preventive anticoagulation to use, with direct oral drugs in focus. Care spans chemotherapy before surgery and recovery after it. The authors frame prevention as a way to keep cancer treatment on schedule.
pmc-11706680:
Kenneth Davis and Christian Montag link core feelings to how people judge their lives, in a 2024 paper. One famous scale asks people to rate life as a whole and is said to tap thought, not feeling. A second scale taps six deep emotion systems first mapped in animal brains, such as fear, play, and seeking. The team gave both scales to two groups of English speakers and checked if the scores moved together.

They did, and strongly, in both groups. Happier life ratings went with lower fear and lower sadness tied to parting from loved ones. They also went with higher play and seeking, though less strongly. The authors say the life scale is far from pure thought. They add that calm at the low end of the sadness system may sit at the heart of feeling that life is good.
pmc-11709080:
Devendra Bhardwaj, Rajesh Kumar, and Yogesh Bahurupi surveyed impostor feelings among nursing students in India, in a 2024 study. Such feelings make capable people feel like frauds in new roles. They are tied to low self-esteem and anxiety in trainees. Just over three hundred students from six nursing schools took part.

Frequent to intense impostor feelings appeared in over four in ten students. At least moderate feelings appeared in over half. Second-year students scored worse than third-year students on all three measures. Impostor scores rose with anxiety scores and fell as self-esteem rose. Low self-esteem proved a strong predictor of impostor feelings in their model. The authors recommend mentorship programs and supervised training. Early screening for psychological strain is also advised for nursing schools.
pmc-11709380:
Yu Chen and co-authors test social inference in early Alzheimer's disease and ask which brain regions support it, in a research paper from 2025. Reading emotions and intentions is often assumed to survive early disease, yet lab work shows slippage. Everyday conversation loads the mind heavily, which may expose the weakness.

Fifty-two patients and fifty-two healthy peers watched video conversations and judged feelings and intentions. Brain scans measured tissue integrity in the cerebrum and the cerebellum, a region often overlooked in social research. Both areas predicted test performance. The study argues the cerebellum deserves a place in accounts of social decline in Alzheimer's disease.
pmc-11709480:
Lise Colmant and eight co-authors report a study of wayfinding in older adults, published in twenty twenty-five. The work asks if errors in tracking one's own path link to early signs of Alzheimer's disease. The team used a game where people moved in a virtual space and then tried to return to the start point.

Ninety adults took part, some with mild memory loss and some with none. Brain scans checked for amyloid and tau, two proteins tied to the disease. People with early disease signs but no symptoms did worse when no landmark was present. Turn errors linked most to tau in key brain areas. The authors say such tests may spot change before memory fails.
pmc-11709580:
Omar Garcia Rodriguez and co-authors pool Alzheimer's data to test how a famous risk gene behaves across groups in a 2025 analysis. One gene variant raises Alzheimer's risk strongly, and earlier work hinted its effect differs by sex and ancestry. The evidence on interactions, though, was thin.

The team combined fifty data sets with over thirty thousand people aged fifty-five and up. Statistical models weighed disease status against age, sex, ancestry, and gene type, with special models for the ancestry of the gene's own neighborhood in mixed-ancestry groups. Carrying one or two copies of the risk variant raised risk in both sexes without a clear sex gap, whichever ancestry group was examined. The analysis continues into comparisons by the variant's local ancestry background. Big pooled studies like this keep single-center quirks from steering the field's beliefs.
pmc-11709680:
Laynie Dratch and co-authors revisit a ten-year-old rule book for sorting the family trees of patients with frontotemporal degeneration by their chance of a gene cause. Their 2025 study comes from the Penn center that built the rule book. The rules sort each tree into five bands, from high risk to likely sporadic.

The team first re-sorted the first group of 306 trees with fresh family facts. They then asked whether wider gene tests, past the three classic genes, lift the hit rate. Last, they ran the rules on a fresh group of 400 trees from patients with the wider set of related ills. The aim is a rule book that still earns its keep as gene knowledge grows.
pmc-11709780:
Bonnie Scott, Amtul-Noor Rana, and Robin Hilsabeck present a 2025 study testing a hands-on measure of fading motivation in older adults. Loss of motivation often warns of coming dementia, yet clinics lack objective tests for it. The team built two versions of an effort-for-rewards task: one using finger tapping for physical effort, one using working memory for mental effort. Five younger and six older adults played both, choosing when to work harder for gains or to avoid losses.

Both age groups weighed risk and reward when choosing effort. Younger adults pushed harder for gains than to dodge losses. Older adults matched that pattern on the physical task but not on the mental one. In older adults, more fatigue and apathy went with less effort of both kinds. The authors call the results early evidence for the measure.
pmc-11709880:
Catherine Munro studies whether early amyloid patterns predict later apathy in older adults in a 2025 paper. Apathy is a common symptom in Alzheimer's disease and has been linked to amyloid and tau load. Whether amyloid in specific regions tied to apathy forecasts it was unclear.

Two hundred cognitively healthy, non-depressed adults from a Harvard aging cohort had brain scans at baseline. Apathy was rated years later by both the adults and people who know them. The study asks if the two rating sources tell different stories against the same brain data. Such work may sharpen early signs of decline.
pmc-11709980:
Genes that load the body with iron may also raise the risk of dementia, human data hints. Adrienne Milward and co-authors build a mouse that carries both iron-load gene faults and Alzheimer's amyloid, in a 2025 study. They cross two known mouse lines to make the new one.

By six months, the new mice showed heavy damage to brain blood vessels. Vessel walls thickened, narrowed, burst, and leaked, and iron sat inside many walls next to amyloid. Plain amyloid mice showed far less of this harm. The team says iron plus amyloid may starve brain cells of blood early in disease. The model could help split dementia into truer subtypes.
pmc-11710180:
Marjorie Metzger shares a 2025 conference abstract on brain rhythms in ALS, a disease best known for muscle weakness. Up to half of patients also develop thinking or behavior changes. Metzger recorded dense scalp EEG at rest in 99 patients and 78 healthy controls, then sorted the signals into brief, repeating brain states.

A hidden Markov model found twelve states with distinct patterns of power and coordination. Time spent in four states tracked with worse behavior scores from caregivers. Another state tracked with weaker verbal fluency. Several of these states centered on the frontal lobes. The work links fleeting brain states to the non-motor side of ALS.
pmc-11710280:
Chunyu Wang, Jian Liu, Lianchun Wang, Dylan Mah, and Fuming Zhang review evidence, published in 2025, that a rare sugar coating on cell surfaces may matter in Alzheimer disease. The coating is heparan sulfate, and it binds many proteins. A rare form of it, marked by a chemical change called 3-O sulfation, has been tied to disease risk by large gene studies. The gene behind it is named Hs3st1.

Using lab methods that track how molecules bind, the team showed that tau sticks to this rare form. Tau is the protein that builds the tangles seen in Alzheimer brains. ApoE, a protein whose forms strongly change disease risk, also binds it, and the riskiest form binds tightest. A new test found much more of this sugar form in Alzheimer brains than in healthy ones. They argue it could serve both as a drug target and as a sign of disease.
pmc-11710380:
Samantha L Strickland and co-authors hunt, in a 2025 study, for immune gene networks shared across Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Body-wide inflammation threads through many chronic diseases. Gene activity maps may show which immune paths stay switched on in the sick brain and blood alike.

The team pooled public RNA data from six brain regions and blood in Alzheimer's and mild cognitive cases, plus blood in Parkinson's cases. Large consortia supplied the samples, from brain banks and aging cohorts. After cleaning and adjusting the data, they built co-expression networks and looked for modules that survive across tissues. Kept modules tied to immune signaling would mark shared drivers of chronic disease. Such shared paths could guide precision care across diagnoses.
pmc-11710480:
Vindhya Vishwanath and co-authors profile vision linked thinking skills in older adults in India in a 2025 study. Such skills blend sight and thought and can flag early dementia, yet few data exist for aging Indian groups. The team measured several vision based tasks and linked scores to age, sex, and schooling.

The sample held one thousand two hundred seventy one urban adults aged forty five and older in a Bangalore aging study. Older age tied to slower copying and weaker scores on most vision tasks. Women scored better on visual attention, quick recall, and one broad vision measure. Schooling data are reported by sex as well. The profile gives clinics local norms for judging early decline.
pmc-11710580:
Wilson Peng and co-authors report a 2025 mouse study of how extra iron in food affects the brain. Iron is needed for brain work, yet people with Alzheimer disease often show high brain iron. The team asked if high iron changes cell energy use or plaque size, and if effects differ by sex.

Young male and female mice, both normal and disease model mice, ate plain food or iron rich food for eight weeks. Iron raised top energy use in male model mice but not in females. It also hurt energy control in both sexes. Plaque size grew in female model mice only, while plaque count stayed the same. The authors plan work on why the sexes differ.
pmc-11710680:
Ipsita Mohanty and co-authors looked for new bile acids in stool samples and linked them to food and to signs of Alzheimer disease, in work from 2025. Bile acids help the body take in fat and send signals between the gut and brain. The team used a large new library of spectra to spot far more of these compounds than before.

They found more than a hundred bile acids, most of them new finds. Some rose or fell with meat, fish, fruit, and greens in the diet, and some tracked with memory scores and a brain marker of disease. The study shows that wider lab matching can reveal links that older lists missed.
pmc-11711980:
Ula Hwang writes in 2025 about finding dementia and thinking problems in the emergency department. Older adults make many visits to these departments each year. People who live with dementia visit more often and face more risk of a visit that could have been avoided.

Hwang notes that three decades of work show dementia is often missed in this fast setting. Missed cases can lead to longer stays, lower satisfaction, and faster loss of thinking skills. Short screening tools exist, yet their use is uneven. The piece sets out why better checks in emergency care matter for patients and families.
pmc-11712080:
Stephanie Ruth Young and seven co-authors published this study in 2025. It tests two app-based tools that screen older adults for thinking problems during primary care. One app runs on a tablet in the clinic waiting room. The other runs on the patient's own phone before the visit.

In the first study, ten clinics offered the tablet tool during yearly wellness visits for adults over sixty-five. About a third of eligible patients finished it, with wide gaps between clinics. Patients and staff named fixable problems, such as unclear progress and no Spanish version. In the second study, fifty-one adults used the phone app twice at home. Scores were steady across the two tries, and users rated the app easy to use. The authors see both tools as workable.
pmc-11712180:
Emily Beswick and co-authors ask whether people accept digital tools for spotting dementia early in this 2025 study. Phones, wrist monitors, and headbands can catch faint signs of decline. Whether users welcome such watching decides if the tools help in practice.

Participants came from a Boston University Alzheimer's research center. Over a year, they used up to nine devices in two-week rounds every three months. The kit spanned active and passive phone apps, activity bands, a brainwave headband, and an oxygen ring. Interviews probed what felt acceptable and what grated. The study gives designers the user's terms for early detection tech.
pmc-11712380:
Charlotte Teunissen and co-authors model the long-term blood effects of an Alzheimer's drug in a 2025 paper. The drug, lecanemab, targets toxic protein clumps tied to the disease. Past trials showed marker gains and slower decline in early disease.

The team pooled data from two large trials and built exposure models for four blood markers. Runs then tested four years of steady dosing, a stop at eighteen months, and shifts to rarer dosing at set points. Marker data ran up to four years in the main trial. The models help planners weigh how long gains last if dosing thins or stops.
pmc-11712480:
Anna Dewenter and a large team of co-authors ask what drives memory loss in clinic patients in this 2025 study. Patients at memory clinics often have two problems at once: Alzheimer's disease and damage to the brain's small blood vessels. The team tested whether blood markers and advanced brain scans could tell the two apart.

They studied seventy-six patients with blood tests, thinking tests, and detailed scans. A blood marker tied to Alzheimer's, along with thinning in a known brain region, tracked closely with poor memory for past events. Markers of vessel damage tracked with other kinds of thinking problems instead. The authors argue that pairing blood tests with the right scans can point each patient toward care aimed at the true cause of the decline.
pmc-11712580:
Sonja Soskic and five co-workers wrote a 2025 study on how harmful proteins spread in the brain in Alzheimer's disease. Amyloid and tau build up in set patterns as the disease grows. Brain cell receptors may help or hinder that spread. The team added maps of receptor density to models of spread through brain links.

They split patients with amyloid into early and late groups based on tau in one brain area. Then they checked if receptor-weighted models matched real scans better than plain models. Receptors that seemed to guard an area were used to slow the model there. The work tests a new layer for these spread models.
pmc-11712780:
Mahsa Dolatshahi and a large team used a special brain imaging method in two thousand twenty-five to link belly fat in midlife to signs of brain inflammation. Midlife obesity raises Alzheimer's risk, but whether it ties to brain inflammation was unclear. Fifty-four cognitively normal middle-aged adults had brain and belly scans at a strong field strength.

The imaging method splits water motion in tissue into parts that hint at cell swelling, fibre loss, and fluid build-up. Belly fat depots, both deep and under the skin, were measured by hand-checked software. Comparing obese and non-obese adults, and high versus low belly fat, tests whether fat tracks with brain tissue changes tied to inflammation.
pmc-11712880:
Spotting amyloid in the brain early usually takes a costly scan or a spinal tap. Zhibo Wang and six co-authors built a prediction model in 2025 from ordinary blood tests and cognitive scores, across five hospitals in China, to flag amyloid pathology in early Alzheimer's disease.

The team studied 278 people with mild impairment or dementia. All were checked with amyloid scans or spinal fluid, plus blood measures like amyloid ratios, tau, and a nerve damage marker, and the APOE gene. Random forest methods picked the strongest signals and built models trained on 223 patients and tested on 55. The authors evaluate how well the integrated model separates amyloid-positive from negative cases, aiming at cheaper triage in varied clinics.
pmc-11712980:
Deborah Alawode, Amanda Heslegrave, and Henrik Zetterberg build two supersensitive assays for rare forms of amyloid-beta, the plaque protein in Alzheimer's disease. The standard blood marker shifts too little between patients and controls to trust, so new forms are being hunted. Their 2025 assays use a single-molecule counting platform with a fresh boost in sensitivity. One hunts amyloid-beta 43, a long form. The other hunts a shortened form with a pyroglutamate cap.

Eight cerebrospinal fluid samples — one Alzheimer's case, four mixed, and three controls — ran at four dilution levels each. The long form was measurable in about 69 percent of readings, and the shortened form in about 94 percent. Most readings fell below the platform's low calibration mark. The shortened form's dilution line ran poor in five of six complete sets. A boosted reader is needed to grade both forms firmly, and blood testing comes next.
pmc-11713080:
Annie Dang and co-authors map in this 2025 meta-analysis where Alzheimer's disease shrinks the brain versus where it starves it, and find the two maps barely touch. Standard biomarker schemes lump atrophy and low metabolism together as one degeneration sign. Pooling hundreds of published contrasts from imaging databases, the team charted each pattern across Alzheimer's and mild impairment.

Shrinkage clustered in memory's core, the hippocampus and temporal lobes. Low metabolism clustered at the back, in parietal lobes and the posterior cingulate. Overlap covered only about a tenth of either map. The authors suggest the split reflects two different pathologies that staging schemes should separate. Two signs, two maps: the split may steer which drug suits which stage of the disease in a given patient.
pmc-11713180:
Kavita Singh and co-authors present a 2025 brain imaging study of healthy aging and hidden thinking decline. Many older people lose ground long before daily life shows it, and standard scans miss early change. The team uses a rich diffusion scan method on hundreds of adults from a public aging data set.

People were split by test scores into lower and higher thinking groups. Fine measures of tissue structure differed between groups in areas for memory, speed, and spatial thought. Sound and sense areas differed too. Simple displacement measures proved most sensitive. The authors say such scans could flag early decline in people who still look healthy on the surface.
pmc-11713280:
Family caregivers carry much of the care for people with illness or disability, often at a cost to their own health. Anderson explores whether a caregiver's beliefs about the role can soften or sharpen that cost. Caregivers did a word task that quietly exposed them to positive or negative words tied to caregiving, such as wisdom or guilt. The study then measured how burdened they felt, their confidence, and their view of their quality of life.

Early results suggest that even a brief wash of negative words made caregivers feel their burden more heavily than those given positive words. The work follows earlier findings that beliefs about aging can shift health and memory in older adults. Anderson plans a follow-up study on how feelings of support and confidence shape a caregiver's outlook. The study treats mindset as a small lever with real weight.
pmc-11713380:
Rotem Paz and fourteen co-authors scan young carriers of an Alzheimer's gene change in a 2025 paper. The change duplicates the APP gene and causes early disease. One family pedigree carries this novel rearrangement. Brain scans began before symptoms for many carriers.

Fourteen carriers and nine non-carrier kin joined the study. Deep brain nuclei showed the earliest oddities on scans. Amyloid deposits ran very high in those nuclei. A key brain network showed fraying links after age thirty. Tiny bleeds and white matter spots appeared from the late twenties. The amygdala ran slightly larger in carriers. The basal ganglia may host the first pathology, they suggest.
pmc-11713580:
Siva Manohar Reddy Kesu, Neelam Sinha, and Hariharan Ramasangu build a computer tool in 2025 that sorts dementia stages from a standard rating scale. Doctors rate thinking problems with a score that covers memory and daily skills. Sorting patients early helps families plan and start care. The team turns each patient's scores into a grid image using a rule system borrowed from simple computing models.

In their method, score values spread across the grid cells like drops of dye in water. A deep learning network then reads the spread pattern in each image. It sorts patients into stage groups based on the patterns. Tools like this one could give small clinics a cheap second opinion from data they already collect.
pmc-11713680:
Marissa Todd and co-authors measure the burden that swallowing problems place on caregivers of people with early dementia, in a study from 2025. Caregiver burden is widely noted in dementia, but past work had not weighed the part played by dysphagia, or trouble swallowing. Diet level and disease stage might both shape that burden.

The team studied 29 patient-caregiver pairs at the first visit of a swallowing trial. Caregivers filled in a general burden scale and one built for swallowing problems. Scores on the swallowing scale were low on average, and worry about the future and fear of choking ranked highest. Scores did not vary by dementia stage. Wider diet limits, though, tracked with higher swallowing burden.
pmc-11713880:
James Galske and co-authors present a 2025 study on how much daily care older emergency patients need at home. Over 15 million informal caregivers help people living with dementia in the United States. How much help emergency patients need, by thinking level, was little known, so the team surveyed their caregivers.

Patients fell into three groups: diagnosed dementia, hidden cognitive impairment found by a caregiver screening test, and intact thinking. Caregivers reported the hours of care they give each day. The study compares those hours across the groups to size the hidden workload. Results can help emergency departments plan support and referrals for families. Care hours are a real cost that charts rarely record. This work puts numbers on it.
pmc-11714080:
Standard Alzheimer's drugs aim at amyloid and tau, with modest success, so other pathways deserve a look. Meher Garg and Inhan Lee mine a public dataset of gene activity in a memory-related brain region from 46 patients and 32 controls. They search for pathways that run hot in the disease and might explain synaptic failure and cell damage.

Three pathways stood out: Rap1 signaling, focal adhesion, and, unexpectedly, the shigellosis pathway named for a gut infection. Five genes sat in both the Rap1 and shigellosis sets, and five others linked Rap1 to focal adhesion. The authors propose these shared genes and pathways as candidate markers and drug targets. They stress the findings need direct testing in future work. The analysis appears in 2025.
pmc-11714280:
Payton White and co-authors studied sleep waves in older African Americans carrying a gene risk for Alzheimer disease, in a 2025 paper. The ABCA7-80 variant raises late-life disease risk. Slow waves in deep sleep help clear waste and lock in memory. The team asked whether carriers show weaker slow waves.

Participants came from a long-running Rutgers aging study. All were cognitively unimpaired at testing. Sleep recordings measured slow oscillation power in non-REM sleep. Carriers showed diminished power beside non-carriers. Weak sleep waves may be an early sign worth tracking in memory clinic visits.
pmc-11714480:
Theresa Harrison, Susan Landau, Suzanne Baker, Martin Boswell, and William Jagust describe a pipeline that harmonizes Alzheimer PET scans across studies. Their 2025 paper builds the Berkeley pipeline because multi-site scans vary by scanner and protocol. Shared tools let the field pool costly imaging data.

Tracer-specific rules and smoothing align resolution across sites first. Processing then runs with or without an MRI, defining regions, normalizing intensity, and computing uptake ratios. Tau scans also get partial volume correction. Automated quality images let staff check alignment and region outlines. Formatting tools then curate the numbers for release. Public release lets outside groups test Alzheimer biomarkers on a common scale, widening use of each scan.
pmc-11714580:
