Anum Saeed and co-authors examine a 2025 registry study of heart patients and later dementia. The records came from more than forty-seven thousand adults aged fifty or more with known heart and vessel disease. All had care that cleared or bypassed blocked heart vessels. The team looked at levels of the so-called good cholesterol in the blood. They then tracked who was later recorded as having dementia.

Over about five years, close to four percent of the patients had a new dementia record. Women faced a higher risk than men, though their good cholesterol levels were also higher on average. Low levels of that fat were linked to higher dementia risk in men. In women, the link did not hold in the same way. The authors say sex must be kept in mind when such blood fats are read as a risk sign.
pmc-11714680:
Nicole Grant and Natalie Phillips link hearing loss to brain network patterns in a 2025 study. Hearing loss raises dementia risk, and the brain's default mode network shifts in hearing loss, in subjective decline, and in mild impairment alike. Those shifts track worse test scores and, in impairment, the march toward dementia. The team study the network in elders who carry both hearing loss and early cognitive complaints.

Data came from a national dementia assessment study. If altered connectivity is the bridge between deafness and decline, it becomes a treatment target: hearing care might protect the network. The study sharpens that hypothesis in the exact group where prevention could start earliest.
pmc-11714780:
Clémence Cavaillès and four co-authors linked measured sleep to thinking skills across race and ethnic groups in a 2025 study. Most past work used self reported sleep and drew mostly on white groups. Their team used a week of wrist motion records to score sleep in a mixed group of older adults.

Eight hundred fifty five people took part. Mexican American and Black members slept less, woke more, and slept less soundly than white members on every measure. The study then tied each sleep trait to four thinking scores, for planning, focus, language, and memory. Group splits were checked where the link seemed to shift by background. The authors say fair sleep research must measure sleep, not just ask about it.
pmc-11714880:
Adriana Perez, Elena Portacolone, and Maria Aranda evaluate a national push to enroll more Latino and Hispanic participants in dementia trials. Their 2025 study uses the network of a consortium between a Hispanic nurses group and the Alzheimer's Association. Low enrollment limits how far trial results can be trusted for this population.

The team ran a randomized trial of recruitment strategies in four cities with large Latino populations. Referral counts were compared between sites that got the program and sites that used usual outreach. Focus groups and interviews gathered views from staff, partner officers, and people who chose to enroll. One hundred forty-five potential participants were referred across the intervention sites, yet the head reports further steps were still hard.
pmc-11714980:
Marcia Regina Cominetti and ten colleagues test a blood protein as an Alzheimer's marker in a group most biomarker studies skip: older Brazilians with little schooling. The protein, ADAM10, has shown promise elsewhere, but rich-country cohorts are usually highly educated, and schooling itself bends test scores. The study asks whether age still drags cognition once education is counted.

Eighty-one elders split between healthy controls and patients. Patients were older, had fewer school years, scored worse on a standard mental test, and differed in blood ADAM10. Education mediated part of the age effect even at low levels. The authors argue biomarker cutoffs must respect schooling.
pmc-11715280:
Jingkai Wei and five co-authors asked how a person's view of self and traits shape the risk of dementia. Views and traits can steer habits, social life, and mood, which all touch brain health. Past proof on which ones matter has been thin and mixed. The team used a big US aging survey that ran from 2010 to 2020.

The survey held fourteen thousand ninety-nine adults aged fifty and up. Over about seven years, five hundred ninety new cases of dementia were logged. High worry, held-in and shown anger, gloom, a sense of being boxed in, and lone states all raised the risk. So did a bleak view of what lies ahead and ill will toward others. Care with tasks and an open mind leaned the other way, toward lower risk.
pmc-11715380:
Sadaf Arefi Milani and co-authors study overlapping symptoms in older Mexican Americans in a 2025 paper. Low mood, pain, and poor sleep often arrive together in old age, and dementia may change the pattern. Data came from a long-running survey of Mexican Americans aged seventy-five and up in the Southwest. Probable dementia was judged by a standard test score plus a daily-living limit.

Pain meant pain while bearing weight. Low mood and sleep trouble were defined by standard symptom scales with fixed cutoffs. The team compared how the three symptoms overlap in people with and without probable dementia, and how that differs between men and women. Such maps help clinics screen for the whole cluster rather than one complaint at a time.
pmc-11715480:
Jessie Yan and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on how often United States doctors used tests to diagnose memory loss and dementia. Scans, spinal fluid tests, and blood tests can make an Alzheimer's diagnosis earlier and more exact.

The team used full Medicare records for more than six hundred fifty thousand people aged sixty-seven or older, newly diagnosed between twenty fifteen and twenty twenty. In the year before diagnosis, most had a blood test and about half had a brain scan. CT scans were common, while PET scans and spinal fluid tests were rare. Test use crept up a bit across the six years. The authors say the sharp tests needed for new disease-changing drugs were barely used in that span.
pmc-11715680:
Michelle Coleman and co-authors study in 2025 whether a deep brain area tied to feeling helps predict memory scores in Alzheimer's disease. Known waste linked areas shrink in the illness, but recent work hints this area, the insula, also plays a part in memory.

The team looked back at scans and memory tests for one hundred sixty one patients with mild loss or full illness, plus forty one healthy peers. They split patients by whether the waste marker was present or absent. Shape measures of the insula and known areas were then matched to word list recall, to test if the insula adds news the known areas miss.
pmc-11715780:
Ping Wang, Yeunjoo E Song, and a large team of co-authors sorted Amish adults over sixty into subgroups by blood markers of Alzheimer's disease. Their 2025 study uses two plasma measures: the amyloid beta ratio and a phosphorylated tau marker. These markers sit closer to the disease's core lesions, plaques and tangles, than symptom based labels do.

Blood tests ran on sensitive commercial assay kits. Age, sex, and study center effects were removed from the marker values first. Clustering on the cleaned markers sought groups that share disease machinery and, perhaps, treatment responses. An Amish cohort offers a distinct genetic and lifestyle setting for such grouping. The approach aims at trial designs that match patients to therapies by biology rather than by symptoms alone.
pmc-11715880:
Theresa Harrison and co-authors ask whether the rules linking amyloid to tau in the aging brain hold across the very different cohorts science now pools. Over twenty-one hundred cognitively normal older adults from four studies had amyloid and tau PET scans harmonized onto common scales, alongside sex, race and ethnicity, and APOE genotype.

In pooled models, women accumulated disproportionately more tau in the entorhinal cortex as amyloid rose, an interaction not seen in the wider temporal region. Non-Hispanic White participants gained more tau per unit of amyloid than Black participants. Carrying the APOE4 variant steepened the amyloid-to-tau slope as well. The authors argue these interactions mostly generalize, which is what makes pooling honest, but they must be modeled rather than averaged away.
pmc-11715980:
Hilal Salim Al Shamsi and five co-authors ask whether diet changes the link between depression and blood markers of Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 study. Depression and poor diet each raise disease risk, but their joint effect on early markers is less clear. The data come from an Australian study of aging, imaging, and lifestyle.

Eighty-nine adults aged sixty and older with normal thinking gave diet records, mood scores, and blood samples. Among men who ate less of a Mediterranean style diet, depression went with higher levels of a nerve damage marker. A similar pattern held for non-carriers of the main risk gene, for both that marker and one amyloid protein. A Western diet showed no such effect. The authors suggest diet may buffer some harm from low mood.
pmc-11716080:
Robb and co-authors examine in 2025 whether slow blood arrival to the brain helps explain the link between widened brain arteries and small vessel disease. Widening of arteries is tied to higher Alzheimer risk and to more white matter spots on scans, a sign of that disease. The team studied 249 adults in a memory and aging project who began free of dementia or stroke.

Brain scans measured the inner width of two main arteries, the timing of blood arrival, and white matter burden. Arrival timing was higher, meaning slower, in connection with wider arteries. Statistical tests then ask how far slow arrival carries the effect of widening on white matter burden, in line with the study title.
pmc-11716180:
Ravneet Dhaliwal and co-authors ask why older adults who notice memory slips so rarely see a doctor about them, in a 2025 survey study. Health programs assume that feeling at risk pushes people to seek care. The team tested that idea with a standard model of health behaviour. They surveyed community adults who had no diagnosis of a thinking disorder.

The survey covered 279 adults in the United States, aged sixty to ninety-six. About a third said they had noticed trouble with memory or thinking. Many rated their risk of dementia above average, and a quarter said they worried about it. Yet of the 101 people who noticed problems, only three had seen a doctor about them. The authors say worry and risk alone do not move people to act, so programs need stronger prompts.
pmc-11716280:
Yara Yakoub and co-authors report a 2025 study on a rare scan pattern in people at risk for Alzheimer's disease. The pattern is a brain scan with no plaque signal but a clear tau signal, in people with no symptoms yet. Past reports found such people, but how they fare over time was not clear.

The team studied 252 adults with no symptoms who had a parent or kin with the disease. Only three people, just over 1 in 100, showed the rare pattern. Blood and spine fluid tests called all three plaque positive, though their scans did not. One went on to mild loss and one to dementia in the years that followed.
pmc-11716380:
Gu and co-authors test whether brain network connectivity can buffer thinking against small-vessel damage in older adults, in this 2025 study. The condition studied is the commonest form of vascular cognitive impairment. Its hallmark, bright spots of white matter damage on scans, tracks with weaker executive function.

The team studied thirty-eight community-dwelling older adults with the condition. They measured damage volume from structural scans and resting connectivity inside three candidate networks. Executive function came from a timed trail-making test. The analysis asks whether stronger connectivity softens the damage-to-thinking link, as a neural sign of cognitive reserve would. The study design targets a gap in explaining why similar damage hits people unevenly.
pmc-11716480:
Shuqi Wang and co-authors test whether heart and lung fitness guards against dementia even in people born with high genetic risk, in work from 2025. Fitness reflects how well the heart and lungs supply the body. Its tie to thinking and dementia was unclear.

Over sixty-one thousand dementia free adults in the UK Biobank were followed for up to sixteen years. Fitness was estimated from a six minute bike test and split into low, middle, and high thirds. Thinking tests covered memory of several kinds and speed. The team then asked whether high fitness softened the risk carried by dementia linked genes. A modifiable shield would matter most for those at highest inherited risk.
pmc-11716580:
Cecilia Anza-Ramirez and co-authors, with the IMPACT Dementia Study Group, design a phone-based system to find dementia in Peru and weigh its cost. Dementia is under-diagnosed in lower-income countries, where specialists are scarce and awareness low. Their 2025 paper describes a project with phases: first build a mobile screening and diagnosis system with local partners, then test it, then judge cost-effectiveness at population scale. Carers are part of the design, since families carry most dementia care.

A screening tool only helps if the system behind it can act on a positive result. The economic arm asks whether population screening pays for itself in a stretched budget. The authors set out the plan and its early steps. Their work targets a real diagnostic gap in a specific country, not a demo market.
pmc-11716680:
Sarah Ackley and co-authors ask whether the link between tau buildup and thinking ability changes with age, in a study published in 2025. Tau tangles are a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, and PET scans can now measure tau in living brains. Data came from the ADNI cohort, aged fifty-five to ninety, and from a study of people over ninety.

The team related region-by-region tau levels, grouped by Braak stage, to mental status and dementia rating scores within age bands. From sixty to eighty, more tau consistently meant worse cognition. The pattern at the oldest ages was less settled in the truncated report, and the team adjusted for education, sex, and genetic risk. Knowing whether the tau-cognition link holds into the nineties matters for trials that enroll the oldest patients.
pmc-11716780:
Julie Midroni and co-authors predict Alzheimer disease years ahead from wrist motion data plus simple personal facts, in work from twenty twenty-five. Drugs work best before symptoms, but brain scans cost too much for mass screening. A wrist sensor worn ten days records daily activity rhythms. A neural network fuses those rhythms with easy clinical facts. Cohort elders without dementia at recording form the study base.

The fused model catches most future cases in the test group. Its balance of misses and false alarms beats single-source models. Motion-only and facts-only networks both trail the combination clearly. Accuracy holds for those with and without mild impairment. Survival analysis confirms the output tracks disease-free years. Cheap wrist screening could triage who needs costly scans.
pmc-11716880:
Huitong Ding and co-authors link ring-measured sleep to thinking scores in older adults. Their 2025 study enrolls seventy-five people from a Boston aging research cohort, who wore a sleep ring at home over many nights across two-week spans each quarter.

The ring logged measures such as unstable light sleep and the share of the night spent with very low blood oxygen. Eleven sleep measures tied to at least one part of a standard thinking test. The low-oxygen share stood out: it tracked with a lower total score and with weaker naming, recall, and abstraction. The authors read sleep as a changeable lever for brain health, while calling for larger studies to confirm the links.
pmc-11726880:
José Castro-Martínez and co-authors apply a game-theory tool to gene data from brain disorders in this 2024 study. The disorders covered are autism, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression, which together affect millions. Their molecular roots stay poorly mapped, and standard gene hunting can miss faint patterns.

Their method, CASh, scores each gene by its contribution across the whole data set, resampling many times for stability. Applied to nine data sets, it found differing genes that older methods overlook. The authors say the sharper gene lists could ground better diagnostic tests. They also see the lists as firmer starting points for targeted treatments. The study positions the method as a robust option for faint-signal data.
pmc-11727080:
Anna Santarsiero and co-authors review how immune cells and cancer cells trade fuel in liver cancer, in a 2024 paper. Macrophages are immune cells that can take two broad states: one attacks tumours, the other helps them grow. Cancer cells can push macrophages toward the helpful state, and those macrophages in turn keep cancer cells alive.

The review focuses on the metabolic features of each macrophage state and of liver cancer cells. Signals released into the tumour surroundings, including from mitochondria, trigger the switch in macrophage state. Liver cancer cells are notably flexible in how they use fuel, which helps them adapt to changing conditions. By mapping this crossroad, the authors aim to point to fuel-based ways to weaken tumours and support anti-tumour immune cells.
pmc-11727180:
Erick de la Barra and co-authors model earthquake patterns that arise from more than one source at once, in a 2024 paper. Some regions mix volcanic quakes with tectonic ones. Others mix shallow and deep events. Their combined size statistics form multi-peaked patterns that single models fit poorly.

Case studies cover two Alaskan volcanic regions and the Kii Peninsula in Japan. The team analyzed quakes across space, time, and magnitude. A non-extensive statistical framework fit the mixed patterns far better than single-source models. Time gaps and distances between events also showed multi-part structure. Better fits sharpen hazard estimates in mixed-source regions. Seismologists gain tools to unmix overlapping earthquake families.
pmc-11727280:
Ulrich Kemmo Tsafack and co-authors present a 2024 method for picking out the genes that matter in very large multi-omics datasets. In such data, each gene comes with several kinds of molecular readings, and genes can be strongly linked to each other. That three level structure makes the search for real signals hard, since most variables must be cut first.

Their method groups linked genes, then screens within each group to drop the unimportant ones. Once the list is small enough, a penalized model picks the key genes and readings. The authors prove a guarantee that true signals survive the screen. In tests, it beat rival methods. They also used it on breast cancer data to find genes and readings tied to the disease, as a real world check.
pmc-11727680:
Cervical cancer hits Central and Eastern Europe harder than the rest of the continent, and local factors may drive that gap. Vladimir Vuković and co-authors mapped the disease across Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina in a 2024 study. Data ran from 2016 to 2020 and were grouped by local government areas. The team linked case and death rates to population density and to how many women's health services each area had.

Serbia and the Republic of Srpska showed higher case rates than the Federation area. Death rates, though, ran highest in Serbia and lowest in the Republic of Srpska. Rates were adjusted to a world standard so areas could be compared fairly. Areas were also split into thirds by rate to compare social and care factors. The study gives planners a map of where need is greatest.
pmc-11728280:
Tatsuki Isogai, Koichiro Hirosawa, and Kenichi Suzuki review imaging methods for single extracellular vesicles in a 2024 article. Cells release these tiny membrane packets, thirty to one thousand nanometers wide, carrying proteins and nucleic acids. They help cells communicate and can prepare sites for cancer spread, but they vary widely from one particle to the next.

Bulk methods average away that variety. The review covers tracking of fluorescent, metal tagged, and unlabeled single particles, plus super resolution and atomic force imaging. These tools measure size, content, and physical traits particle by particle. Remaining challenges are outlined.
pmc-11730080:
Hailee M Morrison and Arpita Bose review a family of purple bacteria as tiny factories for a circular economy, in a 2024 paper. Purple non-sulfur bacteria eat waste and sunlight and pay out useful goods. The review tours their trades: making bioenergy, cleaning wastewater, fertilizing fields, and forming bioplastics inside their own cells.

They can also serve as protein feed and as platforms for fine chemicals brewed from refuse. Frontier uses pair them with electrodes or partner microbes. The authors argue these versatile metabolisms could help cut emissions and loop resources over the next two decades, if engineering keeps pace with the biology. The cells ask for little: light, waste streams, and room to grow.
pmc-11736380:
Parasites of the gut and blood sap horses of health and their owners of income, yet data for southern Thailand were missing. Tanakorn Phetkarl and three co-authors fill that gap in a 2024 survey of horses in one province. They took dung and blood from seventy-nine horses on eleven farms.

Dung was checked three ways, from a float test to a count of eggs per gram. Blood and worm types were named by a gene-copy test. The team also weighs how sex, age, and body state track with gut parasite rates. Such a first map for the province tells vets where deworming and checks should focus. It also sets a base line against which later shifts can be read.
pmc-11770680:
Eike Buhr and Mark Schweda ask what privacy means for people with dementia, a theme care ethics has largely skipped, in a paper from 2024. Privacy draws wide care in nurse ethics as a whole, yet for dementia it draws near none, as if a private sphere had lapsed with memory. The authors call that lapse a fault that clashes with the felt needs of those who live with the state.

Stock tales of privacy lean on free self rule, which fades as dementia deepens. The authors trace where that lean breaks and build a wider tale. Early on, self rule counts still hold. Later, heed for a person own tastes, plus firm marks of worth and well being, take the lead. Privacy keeps weight even past the reach of choice.
pmc-11771280:
Binsheng Fu and co-authors present Chinese clinical practice guidelines for split liver transplantation in children, issued in 2024. A liver transplant can cure end-stage liver disease in a child. Splitting one donor liver between recipients stretches a scarce supply. Children's cases have their own rules and risks, though, so adult habits cannot simply carry over.

The guidelines were built by national transplant and surgery societies. They cover how to judge donors and donor livers. Matching donors to children gets its own section. So do the cutting planes and the rebuilding of ducts and vessels. Standard steps should cut complications and spread good results beyond a few expert centers.
pmc-11772480:
Marina Zaychikova and a large team of co-authors report the isolation of a new bacteria-infecting virus in Russia, in this study published in 2024. The virus, named Vic9, attacks Mycobacterium species, the group that includes the tuberculosis germ. Such viruses are studied both for what they show about virus diversity and as possible tools against drug-resistant infections.

The team grew Vic9 on a harmless host species and placed it in the B2 subcluster of its virus family, the first of that group found in Russia. They measured how fast it sticks to cells, how long it hides inside them, and how many copies burst out. Its genome holds eighty-nine genes, with one odd stretch in a gene cluster that stands out even among close relatives. Vic9 could also kill the tuberculosis strain, though weakly.
pmc-11783280:
Mark Edward Gonzales and three co-authors built a tool to guess which host a phage infects from its protein shapes. Their paper deals with phage-host interaction calls. Past tools lean on gene text reads from language models. Those reads miss shape facts, though shape sets whom a phage can dock. Their tool, PHIStruct, feeds shape aware protein codes into a small neural net.

The codes come from a shape tuned protein model, run on the phage's dock proteins. It calls the host genus from a set of hard to treat kinds. Next to fresh tools it held the best blend of precision and recall, with the top F1 across trust marks. Readers get host calls that hold even when gene texts drift far apart.
pmc-11788080:
The fungus Candida albicans lives quietly in healthy mouths but turns dangerous when immunity is suppressed. Raja Veerapandian and four co-authors built a mouse model of that state, using cortisone injections and fungus laced drinking water, to watch oral infection unfold. Under suppression, the fungus formed thick biofilms on the tongue, its filaments damaging the surface layers and invading tissue, while resident mouth bacteria also bloomed and gut microbes shifted out of balance.

Spores and cells shed from the mouth colonized the gut, harmed its lining, and spread onward. The fungus turned up in liver samples, and a bacterial partner, Enterococcus faecalis, appeared in tongue, liver, and stool. Sequencing of stool microbes confirmed the imbalance and showed helpful species declining. The authors argue the model captures how oral fungal infection in suppressed hosts damages local tissue and seeds wider disease.
pmc-11788380:
Zhong-jiao Xu and co-authors report a genetic syndrome case with heart valve faults in a 2025 paper. A 13-year-old child showed overgrowth, distinct facial traits, and learning disability. Heart scans found fluid around the heart, a swollen left ventricle, and a leaking, prolapsed mitral valve. The pattern pointed to a genetic cause.

Gene sequencing found a new mutation site in the DNMT3A gene. That gene fault causes Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome. Care combined medical treatment with psychological and social support. The child improved under a precise diagnosis. Regular follow-up, the authors stress, guards against sudden death risk and keeps care tuned to the child state.
pmc-11788580:
Liwen Guo and co-authors report a cervical cancer case whose skin spread vanished under tailored therapy, in work from 2024. Skin spread from this cancer is rare, seen in about one percent of patients. Such lesions are often mistaken for infection or rash, delaying the right response.

A drug marker test showed a high score for a key immune target. Treatment paired two cycles of chemotherapy with a vessel-blocking drug. Four further cycles added an immune drug matched to that marker. Scans then showed a complete response that held steady for over eight months. The authors offer the regimen as a guide where no standard exists.
pmc-11789180:
Eder and Weil report two new cadmium tellurium oxide crystals. Both crystals grew as single forms in hot water under pressure. One form stacks in flat layers like sheets. The next form builds a full three-axis frame.

The first form holds five cadmium atoms per unit set. Its cadmium centers bind six or seven oxygen atoms each. Bond lengths span a narrow range in that form. The second form holds four cadmium and five tellurium atoms. Both forms share one growth bath yet take distinct shapes. Full bond maps are given for each crystal type.
pmc-11799280:
Juan Liu and colleagues test how negative feedback shrinks self deception, in work from 2025. Mild self deception can help people, but long running self deception brings heavy losses. Feedback that contradicts rosy self views may wear the habit down over time.

A forward looking test setup ran under no, vague, and real negative feedback arms. Early tests showed the answer holding group cheating more with rosier self beliefs. Both feedback types cut self deception across later repeated test rounds. Real feedback cut deeper than vague feedback, and gains grew with repetition. Falling rosy beliefs drove the drop, with money rewards also in play.
pmc-11801780:
A large team of authors reply in 2025 to a letter about their study of drug prescribing. Yashashri Shetty and co-authors had checked if prescriptions in India followed standard care guides. Their work was based in centers for the wise use of drugs.

The reply says the study found clear gaps from the guides. Heartburn drugs, used alone or with other drugs, drove much of that gap. The team warns of higher cost and more side effects. They note that new training for medical students now treats prescription writing as a skill to practice early.
pmc-11805080:
Rakesh Jha and co-authors screen newborns for genetic disorders in tribal regions of central India in a 2024 study. Sickle cell disease, thalassemia, and a red cell enzyme deficiency are common challenges in these communities. Early screening in newborns allows care to start before symptoms cause harm.

The team screened 382 newborns with a liquid based laboratory method for the two blood disorders and a color test for the enzyme deficiency. They found twenty-eight cases of sickle cell disease, thirty-five of thalassemia, and thirty-four of the enzyme deficiency. Maternal education was significantly linked to how common these disorders were. The authors call for broad newborn screening programs in tribal populations to improve early detection and care.
pmc-11809680:
Rubber trees earn their keep in the tropics, but dry seasons kill young plantations, so breeders want clones that shrug off drought. Syarifah Aini Pasaribu, Mohammad Basyuni, Edison Purba, and Yaya Hasanah grew seven clones at three water levels in a 2023 trial to find which traits mark a tolerant plant.

Three Indonesian IRR 400 clones stood in the trial beside two standards. As water fell, total sugar and proline piled up in the leaves, and those two measures best separated tolerant from tender clones. Chlorophyll and a battery of protective enzymes were also tracked. Screening seedlings by sugar and proline, the authors suggest, could pick drought-ready clones years before field trials would.
pmc-11813880:
Ayman Salah and co-authors test whether a seaweed supplement shields broiler chickens from a feed toxin, in a study the head dates to 2024. The toxin, ochratoxin A, contaminates grain and harms organs. One hundred sixty day-old chicks were split into four groups. One ate plain feed. One ate toxin-laced feed. One ate feed with the supplement, a Spirulina algae. The last group got both. The trial ran six weeks.

Toxin feed raised harmful blood fats and a damage marker. It lowered antioxidant defenses and immune response. The supplement improved growth and feed efficiency. Blood fats fell with supplementation. In toxin-exposed birds, the supplement restored antioxidant enzymes. It also softened damage in organs. Carcass traits were tracked as well. The authors conclude the algae blunts the toxin's harm. Poultry producers in contaminated regions could benefit. Dose and cost questions remain for farm use.
pmc-11841080:
Amir Mohareb, Patrick Miailhes, and co-authors track liver germ odds in folks with two germs who stop a key drug, in a 2024 study. New HIV drug plans drop the drug that also held liver germ down. What that drop does to liver germ hold was not yet known in full.

A French pool splits folks to stay, stop, or never start sets. Most stay set folks keep liver germ low at near all trips. Stop set folks keep full low marks while off the drug in trips. High liver germ ties to wild HIV, low guard cells, and set blood marks. Picked folks may hold sans the drug, the team says.
pmc-11843280:
Wenjing Zhang and co-authors survey sonopharmacology, the control of drug activity through ultrasound rather than light. Light-switchable drugs inspired the field first. Light, though, harms tissue and barely penetrates it.

Ultrasound reaches deep into the body safely. Clinics already use it for imaging and focused therapy. Strong low tones can damage normal cells nearby. Higher tones are safer but need clever chemistry to work. Mechanochemistry now lets sound flip drug states on demand. The review traces methods for triggering release and activation. Spatial and timing control are the field's promise. Safer sound settings remain the key challenge ahead. The field is young and growing fast in labs and clinics.
pmc-11843580:
Edwin Ardiansyah and co-authors read whole gene sets in work whose head dates it to 2024, from West Java in Indonesia. Labs guess unread gene spots from read ones, but their maps rest on European reads. Those maps run weak for the rest of the world.

The team read full genes of more than two hundred West Javanese and joined them with East Asian reads from a world trove. Three guess maps came out: one Asian, one local, and one joined. Near two million fresh gene marks turned up in the local set. Gene teams in the world fourth-biggest land gain maps that fit their own folk.
pmc-11855080:
Gijae Seo examines health-themed fairs held in Korea under Japanese rule, in a 2024 history study. The catalog title is in Korean, while the text itself studies how Japan used hygiene exhibitions as a tool of rule. Such fairs mixed fairground appeal with lessons about disease and the body.

Seo traces how Japan took fair culture from the West and reshaped it in its own style. Health fairs then spread to colonial Korea from about 1920, growing into contests that toured small districts. Posters, models, and photos taught hygiene while also stirring fear of disease. Drawing on newspapers of the time, the study shows how these shows tied health teaching to colonial control.
pmc-11864880:
Yayong Chen and co-authors present a self-training method for deep networks that spot plants in drone photos, in work from 2024. The setting is a dry, hot valley, where rough ground makes hand tuning slow and costly. Their method joins a transfer learning score with a sampling method that learns from rewards.

The transfer score finds fast start settings, so later rounds need only a small share of the data and time. The sampling method then grows the data set on its own and trims human error. Four network types were trained with the full method. The best one reached high scores on two accuracy measures. The authors offer the method as a way to cut hand work in field data tasks.
pmc-11871880:
Morris Muriuki, Sherry Oluchina, and Bernard Mbithi study strain on family caregivers of cancer patients in a 2024 study at a national referral hospital in Kenya. Cancer care runs over a long course, much of it as outpatient visits. Around the world, families carry most of that daily care, yet little was known about their strain in Africa.

The team surveyed two hundred fifty-five family caregivers at the hospital's outpatient cancer clinic in early 2020. They gathered both counted answers and open accounts. They looked for caregiver traits, such as age, income, and relation to the patient, that line up with strain in the role. Naming those factors is a first step toward support plans that ease the load on families who hold up long-term care.
pmc-11879980:
Ling Xiao and five co-authors explore a new infection signal in blood in a study whose text is dated 2024. Red blood cells carry a sensor on their surface that can bind loose DNA. That DNA often comes from the cell's own power units when tissue is stressed. The team asked whether this pair could help track infections.

They measured the sensor on red cells from healthy people and from patients with bacterial infections. The sensor level ran lower in patients than in healthy controls. DNA pulled from the cell surface was counted with a precise lab method. The team checked how those counts lined up with a common swelling marker. Their early results suggest the pair shifts in a steady way during infection. More work is needed before clinics could use it as a test.
pmc-11888680:
Aparna Sudhan and eight colleagues chemically fingerprint a traditional Ayurvedic oil used for weakness and joint pain, in a 2024 paper. Balaswagandhadi tailam is prescribed for fever, muscle wasting, nerve pain, and paralysis in that practice. Modern evaluation of such remedies needs hard lab evidence of what they contain.

Gas chromatography with mass spectrometry separated and identified the oil's components. The list runs to about twenty bioactive compounds, including fatty acid esters, sterols such as campesterol and sitosterol, and vitamin E. Several entries are known healing agents in the literature. The authors argue the mixture plausibly underlies the oil's traditional effects. They stop short of clinical claims, calling for further research on how the components act. The study is offered as a template for vetting classical formulations with modern instruments.
pmc-11948580:
Hart leads a team mapping gene activity and chromatin access in lupus T cells in a 2024 paper. In lupus, helper T cells aid harmful immune attacks. Patients' cells show changed chemical marks on DNA and packaging proteins.

Most patients, whatever their disease activity, had more open chromatin carrying signs of inflammatory signals. The changes reached even naive T cells. Data pointed to a family of signals, including TNF, as drivers of the altered state. One patient subgroup stood out: those taking blood pressure drugs called ARBs lacked the TNF-linked pattern. The authors ask whether these drugs can calm disease-driven states.
pmc-11970180:
A blood test could help sort harmless ovarian growths from cancer before surgery, sparing women needless risk. Mini Sharma and co-authors compared four tests and scores for that task in a 2024 study. One hundred women before menopause with an ovarian mass took part, and all went on to surgery. Tissue results after surgery gave the true answer for each case. Thirty of the women had cancer.

A combined score that joins two blood markers with menopause status scored best overall. One newer marker, HE4, came next, ahead of the older marker and an older index. The authors say HE4 alone does not beat the older marker. Used in sequence or inside the combined score, though, it lifts accuracy.
pmc-11976080:
Abdulmajeed Alotaibi, Ahmad Alghamdi, Hatem Alshammari, Christel Larsson, and Evaggelia Papia present a 2024 lab study of how to prepare ceramic tooth repairs before gluing them in. The bond between a glass ceramic piece and the tooth's inner layer decides how long the repair lasts. Cleaning and pretreating the surface in the right way can raise that bond.

The team mounted twenty five human back teeth and flattened them to bare the middle dentin layer. Five groups got different pretreatments and cleaning steps before cementing. The teeth were then cut into tiny test sticks, aged with heat cycles, and pulled until the bond broke. A control group and one fluoride treated group bonded best.
pmc-12006980:
Chunyu Wang and seventeen co-authors find strong activators of an understudied pain receptor. Their 2024 paper targets MRGPRD, a sensor for pain, itch, and inflammation. Few activators were known, and the best, beta-alanine, binds weakly. Weak tools kept the receptor's biology in the dark.

Two new compounds bind about one hundred times more tightly. Structures of the receptor with each compound were solved. The two sit in the pocket in distinct poses. The pocket itself flexes widely to host them. Those poses reveal the recognition motifs the receptor reads. Drug designers now have firm ground for building on this target.
pmc-12016980:
Josué Veiga and co-authors map which animals sandflies feed on near bird nests in a dry part of Spain, in work from 2024. Sandflies spread a parasite and several viruses, yet most feeding studies focus on homes and farms. Wildlife roles are thus often missed.

Over three years, the team trapped flies by two methods and named the blood source in each fed fly. Six fly species and thirteen host species turned up. Humans were the top source, then a bright bird called the European roller, then wild boar. Most fly species fed mainly on wild mammals, though some also fed on birds, and one fed only on birds. The web was dense and loose, which the authors say will complicate control of the diseases.
pmc-12080080:
Alyson Campbell and Christine Cassidy wrote a discussion paper in 2024 on a new kind of nursing role. Nurse scientists who study how to put research into daily care are the focus. The authors ask how such nurses can help change health systems in Atlantic Canada and in places like it.

Prince Edward Island and its health plan serve as the main case. The authors map the plan's top goals and show, with clear examples, where these nurses could lead each one. They argue that the work needs fair pay, real support, and buy-in from system leaders. Rural areas, where such examples are rare, may gain the most.
pmc-12082680:
Okon and co-authors probe drug-proof germs in lung illness among people with HIV in Uyo, Nigeria, in work from 2024. They took sputum from sixty-one people with signs of chest infection who were on standard HIV therapy. Lab tools named the germs grown, and gene tests searched the germs for traits that block drugs.

Germs grew in about four in ten samples. One staph type was most common, and proof was strong against two common drugs. Four proof genes turned up, and one of them sat in every germ that blocked many drugs. The team urges close watch and firm action in this at-risk group.
pmc-12110480:
Kierian Uzochukwu, Anthony Ugbenyen, and Olulope Ajayi present a 2024 study on metabolic syndrome in pregnant women in Auchi, Nigeria. Data on this cluster of risks in pregnancy are scarce in developing countries, yet the syndrome flags women at risk of poor outcomes. The team recruited 223 pregnant women from local hospitals, gathered lifestyle and background details, and measured body size and blood markers.

About eleven percent met the syndrome definition. Low protective cholesterol was the commonest single problem, affecting over a third. Obesity touched about fourteen percent, high blood sugar about twenty-two percent, and high blood pressure under five percent. No social or lifestyle factor linked significantly to the syndrome. The authors urge vigilant monitoring of pregnant women to catch the condition early. They frame the numbers as a baseline for a neglected topic.
pmc-12118280:
Yang and co-authors review single glowing probes that watch two cell organelles at once in two thousand twenty-four. Organelles are the cell's work zones, and they trade signals to keep the cell running. Faults in their network feed many diseases, yet their fast interplay is hard to see.

Glow imaging suits the task since it is gentle and can track change live. The review sorts probes that target two organelles and shine in two colors, by how they aim and how they glow. Uses in biology and medicine are covered for each class. The authors close with current limits and where probe design should go next, to guide fresh work in the field.
pmc-12259280:
Birhan Assega and co-authors hunted soda lakes in Ethiopia for bacteria that make the enzyme L-arginase, a candidate cancer drug. The enzyme starves cancer cells by breaking down an amino acid they need. From thirty-one water samples the team grew 102 colonies and screened them for enzyme output. The best producer, a strain of Alcaligenes aquatilis from Lake Chitu, was identified by gene sequencing. Tuning eight growth conditions nearly doubled its output.

The work, published in 2024, shows that extreme soda-lake microbes can supply a medically interesting enzyme at useful levels. Bacterial production matters because the enzyme must be made cheaply and in bulk to be a practical therapy. The authors present the strain and its tuned recipe as a starting point for development. Further steps would test the enzyme's purity, safety, and real anticancer effect, none of which this screening study attempts.
pmc-12329380:
Heydar Ali Balou and co-authors compared stool test results with colon findings in older adults from a large Iranian cohort. The fecal immunochemical test, or FIT, flags hidden blood in stool and is a common first screen for bowel cancer. The team enrolled 1,158 volunteers over fifty and sent 172 of them, half with positive tests and half with negative ones, for colonoscopy.

About a third of those scoped had colon lesions. People with a positive FIT carried lesions far more often than those with a negative one. Lesion location did not split by test result or by patient traits. Lab findings on the tissue samples did differ between the groups. The study supports FIT as a useful sorting step, while showing that a negative result does not clear the colon on its own.
pmc-12400380:
Xiang-Yi Hou and co-authors review night urination in a 2025 paper. Waking to urinate at night is common and cuts deep into life quality. It links to low mood, fogged thought, and fall injuries.

Causes span high total urine output, night-heavy output, a small bladder hold, and sleep faults. Charts of void times and amounts now help sort which cause rules in a given patient. First care is habit change, from fluid timing to sleep hygiene. Drugs from several classes have gained support in trials, each with its own cautions. The review gathers current checks and care into one guide for clinic use.
pmc-12490480:
Mild thyroid underactivity and selenium levels in Iranian women are surveyed by Hadavi and co-authors in a 2024 study. The condition, where one hormone runs high while others stay normal, raises the risk of full thyroid failure. The thyroid also holds the body's richest selenium store, and the mineral steers thyroid hormone use.

Five hundred fifty women aged twenty to fifty-five in North Khorasan province gave blood samples. Hormone tests split out the mild cases, whose selenium was then compared with matched healthy women. Rates for the province were not well known before. If low selenium tracks the condition, diet or supplement steps could be tested as cheap prevention in the region.
pmc-12660980:
Wan-Feng Zhang and his eight co-authors, publishing in 2025, untangle a dating problem in a common volcanic rock. The argon-argon method dates basic rocks by measuring argon trapped in minerals. Stray extra argon hides in some samples and scrambles the ages. The team studied a diabase whose whole-rock ages formed a telltale saddle shape, a classic sign of contamination.

Their feldspar, measured separately, gave one clean age: about 48.7 million years. Chemical and mineral mapping then fingered the culprit. Altered amphibole, a mineral reshaped by later heating, held most of the stray argon. The authors advise dating teams to avoid separates containing that mineral in basic rocks. Their combined approach, chemistry plus imaging plus the dating itself, offers a template for spotting the same trap elsewhere.
pmc-12661680:
Maria Amalia Pesantes and co-authors listen to users of health services in rural northern Peru on what they expect from local primary care. Care that meets users' expectations is a mark of a responsive health system, yet rural expectations in low- and middle-income countries are rarely studied. Their 2025 study rests on interviews with 15 patients with chronic conditions, 7 local leaders, and focus groups with 109 clinic users.

Users felt abandoned, like orphans, in their own words. Their concerns ran beyond the usual lacks of medicines and staff. They felt disrespected, with their health needs ranked below those of people with money or who live in the city. The state sends young, inexperienced doctors to rural communities and stocks ineffective medications, they said. Fixes must fit each place, the team argues, and young doctors need steady guidance, not lone posts.
pmc-12661780:
Family-based treatment is a leading therapy for young people with restrictive eating disorders, but specialists are scarce in rural areas. Jocelyn Lebow and nine co-authors adapt the therapy for delivery by primary care teams and try the adapted version in small-town and rural clinics. They describe the changes they made and follow six children and teenagers through treatment.

Three patients completed the program and one stepped up to standard specialist treatment, matching the design's intent as a lower first step. The authors call this proof of concept for rural delivery, not proof of effectiveness. A pilot trial of feasibility and acceptability comes next, with clinical outcomes still to be measured. The case series appears in 2025.
pmc-12662880:
Yang Zhang, Yanyan Jiang, and Zeng Xu test refined intensive care nursing for severe pancreas swelling in a trial of eighty-four patients, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. The refined plan adds a trained team, custom care plans, tight organ watch, teaching media, mind support, and staged feeding. Usual care alone formed the control.

Refined care cleared symptoms faster and cut hospital stays. Harm events ran near seven percent versus about twenty-four with usual care. Mood scores eased and life quality rose across all domains. Satisfaction topped ninety-five percent in the refined group. Readmission rates did not differ. Readers get a care bundle with broad gains for a deadly illness.
pmc-12663280:
Pickled greens from Vietnam yielded a germ that may earn a place in health foods. Minh Tan Pham and four co-authors pulled a Bacillus strain from the pickles in 2025 and ran the gauntlet a would-be probiotic must pass. The strain stood up to stomach-level acid and to bile salts at gut strength. Two common drugs could still kill it, a safety point in its favor.

Fed sugar, the strain joined in crowd work against four gut foes, slowing each in the dish. It also made more of two short fats that gut walls like. The team are plain that dish proof is a first gate, not a health claim. Beast and human trials would have to carry the strain the rest of the way.
pmc-12663580:
Maryna Zhylina and co-authors trace how the structure of biochar develops when barley waste pellets are slowly heated without oxygen. Their 2025 study joins a push to turn farm waste into useful products instead of burning it. Biochar can serve as a sorbent that soaks up pollutants.

The team first found a durable pellet mix of mostly barley straw with some bran. Pellets were heated at three temperatures and held for one to three hours. The resulting chars were compared on yield, carbon and nitrogen content, surface area, and pore spread. Higher temperature and longer holding raised surface area and widened the pores. Those traits decide how well a char can adsorb, so the recipe map helps producers tune char for water or soil uses.
pmc-12664180:
Keyong Zhang and four co-authors present a 2025 gene study of Astragalus membranaceus, a valued medicinal plant that suffers in cold weather. They mapped its full set of WRKY genes, a family of switches that help plants grow and face stress. The team also asked how these genes steer the making of flavonoids, plant compounds tied to both drug quality and cold defense.

The scan found 94 WRKY genes spread on eight chromosomes, sorted into six groups. Sixteen of the genes changed activity in the cold, and four stayed switched on. Two of them tracked with higher flavonoid output and with the build-up of nine cold-linked flavonoids. The authors propose a path from those two genes to flavonoids to cold defense.
pmc-12664280:
Liu and seven co-authors mapped skin peptides in twenty twenty-five in a frog whose skin makes many guard compounds. Finding those peptides is hard in kinds with no genome map. Their pipe joins gene reads with mass reads of the skin wash to catch more of them.

A fix for start-site slips lifted find rates by more than three fifths. They found more than one hundred such peptides, most of them new for this frog. One family held the bulk, with wide spread between frogs of one group. Most of the peptides tie to defense work, the gene maps show.
pmc-12666080:
Prabhdeep Kaur and a team of co-authors report treatment outcomes from a hypertension control program scaled across fifteen Indian states, in two thousand twenty-five. More than a million people with high blood pressure were enrolled at public facilities in eighty-nine districts. Records covered care from two thousand eighteen into two thousand twenty-two.

About forty-four percent of those still in care had their pressure controlled. Control ranged widely, from top states above half to others below a quarter. It also fell when two readings, rather than one, defined control. Younger patients, men, and people with diabetes faced a higher risk of uncontrolled pressure. Higher-level facilities also lagged. The authors call for focused strategies for those groups.
pmc-12666180:
Murad-Kassam and co-authors set out a plan to map research on how racialised older adults with dementia experience hospital stays, and how their caregivers fare. Such patients can face stigma, bias, and care that ignores their culture. Their 2025 protocol follows a standard scoping method and a reporting checklist, with the review registered in a public registry.

Searches will span six databases plus grey sources such as Alzheimer society sites. Two reviewers will screen papers on their own before comparing notes. Findings will be laid out in tables and prose, with gaps and advice for future work drawn out. Results will go to journals, conferences, and community groups. No ethics approval is needed since all sources are public.
pmc-12679080:
Shuang Xu and co-authors report a trial from 2025 on liver cancer care. The study covers people with small liver tumors who also had anxiety or low mood. Ninety patients were split into two groups of equal size. One group had ultrasound guided treatment, and the other had standard keyhole liver surgery.

The team tracked stress scores, blood markers, liver tests, and problems after surgery. They also checked how fast patients got better and whether the cancer came back within six months. Stress scores fell more in the ultrasound group after surgery. The paper compares both paths so doctors can weigh calmer care against standard surgery.
pmc-12692280:
Bartosz Jaroszewski and co-authors tune a fiber mat that leaks a cancer drug on a set clock in a 2025 study. A mat laid in the flesh can dose the spot for weeks, where a flood dose harms the whole.

The mat is spun from a blend that rots in the flesh. Three blends, split by their mix share, leaked at three paces. A splash of a water-kind part sped the leak more. Form, rot, and leak were read in dish, and the freed drug still killed growth cells in dish and in mice. The authors say the mix share is a true dial: pick it and the mat keeps its clock. Such mats could let a ward dose each sick by their own need.
pmc-12693180:
Evelyn Granizo and five co-authors sharpen porous silicon microcavities that trap light. Their 2025 paper blends simulation with bench work to tune the structures. These sponges of silicon are cheap to make and rich in surface area. Their light-trapping quality, though, rarely passes a factor of one hundred.

Room-temperature recipes were redesigned with theory as the guide. Built cavities then checked the predictions directly. The quality factor roughly doubled in the new structures. Models say further gains remain available. Stronger trapping boosts sensors and light-driven devices alike. The work shows simulation-led fabrication beating trial and error.
pmc-12693980:
Laure Migayron and a large team study immune memory cells in pale skin in a 2025 paper. In vitiligo, the immune system kills the cells that give skin its color, leaving pale patches. Self-hunting memory cells may lurk in skin that still looks sound, well past the patch edge, yet what holds them in check was not known.

Cell and gene-read tools showed the same memory cell groups in sound and near-patch skin. Near patches, attack paths ran hot, while sound skin kept the cells quiet. The study names the brakes that guard sound skin, a lead for creams that hold them.
pmc-12696080:
Perrine Lardellier and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five comparison of lab methods for checking messenger RNA quality. Products built on messenger RNA power new vaccines and medicines, but the molecules break down easily. Broken strands cannot make the right protein, so makers must measure damage reliably.

Three methods were tested on raw and finished material. Two used gel separation in fine tubes with different light detection. The third used a pairing chromatography method. All three tracked integrity and purity, while chromatography separated stray forms more sharply. The study also flagged functional joined molecules that routine methods might miss or misread.
pmc-12698480:
Li Tang and co-authors survey fast-moving tools for screening bowel cancer, the world's second deadliest cancer. Early screening cuts both new cases and deaths. The classic tools, scope exams and stool blood tests, are now joined by molecular rivals.

The review covers tests that read DNA, RNA, proteins, and metabolites in stool or blood. It also covers combined multi-omics designs and AI help in reading images. Guidelines from major countries are compared, including where they disagree. The authors close with tailored strategies that fit screening to each person's risk. No single test wins everywhere. The field's task is matching test, person, and setting with better evidence.
pmc-12700880:
Lili Zhao, Jizi Li, and Xiuli Bao model pricing and green work in the electric car supply chain. State rules give car makers credits for clean cars, which they can trade for cash. The maker sets green effort and wholesale price, while the shop sets the sale price in their two-tier chain. The team built a game model that tracks how those picks play out over time, alone or as one firm.

Joint play beat split play on profit, energy marks, and green effort in every run. A share pact that splits both gains and green costs can thus tempt both sides to join. Terms for when each side signs are worked out in full. Number runs then weigh how credit price and the credit rate per car sway the pact. The dual credit rule earns a pass mark.
pmc-12701080:
Tian Li and co-authors proposed in 2025 a gentler way to launch drones with compressed air. Air launch is fast, but the sudden push loads the drone heavily, which forces stronger, costlier frames. Their plan uses several air chambers that fire in a timed sequence.

A model that treats air as a real gas was built and checked against tests. Runs compared one chamber with two or three chambers, matched or varied in size. All multi-chamber runs reached the same exit speed with lower peak load. The best case, three varied chambers, cut peak load by about a third. The trade is a more complex launcher for a lighter drone.
pmc-12702780:
Beilei Ye and co-authors sort thinking profiles in older adults with type two diabetes, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Over five hundred patients at a large hospital took a standard thinking test. The team grouped scores into hidden profiles and weighed factors tied to each group.

Three profiles emerged: full, partial, and at-risk thinking loss. The partial group held over half the patients. Sex, schooling, years with diabetes, and blood sugar control each shaped profile membership. D varied mental activity and good nutrition also mattered. The authors urge early steps on sugar control, mental variety, and social support.
pmc-12705980:
Shengtao Huang and co-authors map in 2025 RNA methylation patterns cell by cell in breast cancer, comparing first tumors with matched spread to lymph nodes. Methylation marks on RNA help steer cell behavior, but their pattern across cell types was unclear. Data from five patients fed scores for each cell, with cell types named by standard tools, and groups of high and low marking compared in depth.

Spread nodes scored lower than first tumors, most sharply in immune cells. Low marking tied to more mature states, more malignant traits in surface cells, and weaker immune talk. Gene groups split a large public cancer cohort into two clusters with distinct survival and immune profiles. The authors link falling methylation to cancer spread.
pmc-12706480:
Krismer and co-authors hunt for a rare delayed harm after brain aneurysm bleeding in this 2025 case study. Fluid-filled cysts can form along the spinal cord months later and injure it. Reviewing 19 years of admissions at their center, the team looked for who developed these cysts and what set them apart.

Five of about 1,100 survivors developed cysts, and every case followed a burst aneurysm at the back of the brain with heavy blood pooling around the trunk vessels. In that subgroup the rate topped 11 percent. None of the five had received active blood washing, a therapy started midway through the period. Surgery left most patients still needing walking help.
pmc-12706880:
Pratheepa Kumari Rasiah and co-authors tested a stem cell treatment for eye damage after head injury, in this 2025 study. A gene called COL4A1 builds part of the basement membrane, the thin sheet that supports blood vessels. Faults in it weaken vessels throughout the body, and case reports hint that trauma then harms vision more easily. No lab evidence for that link existed.

In mice, the team lowered the gene's activity in the retina, then delivered a mild air-blast brain injury. They tracked vision, retinal tissue, and gene activity for four weeks. A treatment made from the liquid that fat-derived stem cells grow in, rich in the missing protein, was injected into the eye after injury. The title reports the outcome: the treatment restored the membrane defects. The work links a genetic weakness to trauma risk and tests a cell-free repair approach.
pmc-12706980:
Valter Cordeiro Barbosa Filho and colleagues describe how stakeholders co-created the logic model for a health-promoting school program in socially vulnerable areas of a Brazilian capital. The World Health Organization backs health-promoting schools as a core strategy. Yet school programs based on implementation science are still rare, above all in vulnerable areas. Building it with others should help it win support and last.

The co-creation went in three stages: planning, doing and checking, and final check. The logic model was built on a framework for such research, with determinants, strategies, mechanisms, and outcomes. Planning drew on facts from theory, evidence, and practice, through five strategies. Stakeholders were researchers, teachers, managers, health workers, students, and recent school graduates.
pmc-12707780:
Volkan Selmi and five co-authors test two simple ways to ease prostate biopsy in a 2025 trial. The biopsy, guided by ultrasound through the rectum, is the standard check for prostate cancer, but it can hurt and cause strong anxiety. The team compared music, conversation, and no extra support during the procedure.

Ninety patients at a university hospital in Türkiye were split evenly into the three groups. Pain and anxiety were scored before and after. Talk with the staff cut both pain and anxiety by clear margins. Music, by contrast, scored about the same as the control group. The authors suggest that engaging the patient in conversation is a cheap, drug-free way to make the test easier.
pmc-12708680:
Guosong Wang and co-authors report an antibody that disarms a whole family of herpesviruses in this 2025 study. The family includes the human cold sore and chickenpox viruses and several animal viruses that plague farms and pets. No broad shield against the group existed, because each virus was fought one at a time.

The antibody, named 16F9, latches onto a shared weak spot on a surface protein the viruses use to fuse with cells. By jamming that fusion step, it blocked infection in lab tests. In female mice it treated a wide range of diseases, from brain and eye infections to skin and newborn herpes, across several virus species. Crystal-clear microscope structures showed exactly where it binds. The authors present the protein it targets as a foundation for broad anti-herpes drugs and vaccines.
pmc-12708880:
Sirine Mabrouk and Hatem Dhaouadi turn grape seed waste into activated carbon and test it as a sponge for removing an antibiotic from water, in this 2025 study. The drug, ceftriaxone, is an emerging pollutant that passes into waterways. Activated carbon is a proven cleaner, and making it from farm waste adds a second benefit.

Lab tests showed the carbon is richly porous with a large working surface. Uptake of the drug followed a standard speed model, and the soaking pattern fit a layered picture. Computer modeling of the molecules pointed to strong hydrogen bonds as the grip holding the drug on the carbon. The drug also resisted washing back off, which supports a chemical bond rather than a loose hold. The authors rate the material a strong, low cost option for water cleanup.
pmc-12708980:
Daniel Arauco-Lázaro and four co-authors report in 2025 a Peruvian patient with a rare syndrome linking heart defects and skeletal malformations to the ABL1 gene. The 20-year-old man had suffered five episodes of collapsed lung. His hands showed skeletal malformations, and his joints were unusually loose.

A gene panel for connective tissue disorders found a single altered copy of ABL1, a variant classed as probably disease-causing. That finding confirmed the syndrome diagnosis. Reports from new regions widen the known reach of rare genetic conditions and sharpen the clues that should prompt testing. For this patient, a molecular answer ties together lung, heart, and skeletal signs that might otherwise seem unrelated.
pmc-12709080:
Miho Kikuta and co-authors tested fillers for a dental resin used to repair decay at the root of a tooth, in a 2025 study. The base resin is a known glue-like mix used in dentistry. The team added three kinds of filler at a low share: a plant-free glass that can feed mineral growth, a second glass, and a carbon-based filler. A store-bought version with the carbon-based filler served as the yardstick.

The mineral glass slowed setting and weakened bending strength, though it did prompt slight mineral growth in a body-like fluid. The carbon-based filler cut setting time and raised the bond strength to root dentin. After heat-and-cold cycles, groups with that filler kept stronger bonds than the rest. The authors conclude that this filler suits repair work, above all in wet spots where bonding is hard to keep.
pmc-12709680:
Feng-Juan Gao and nine co-authors widen the known mutation spectrum of gyrate atrophy, a rare inherited eye disease, in patients from Yunnan province. The condition, caused by faults in the OAT gene, progressively destroys the choroid and retina. Multi-ethnic Chinese populations had been little studied.

Eight patients from five families shared high myopia, early vision loss, and raised blood ornithine. Atrophy around the optic disc appeared in most eyes and tracked with worse vision and longer eyes. Four mutations were new to science, including the first pathogenic variant found in the gene's five-prime untranslated region. A minigene test proved that variant disrupts splicing. The authors stress population-specific profiles for diagnosis.
pmc-12710880:
Knowing what shields a person from a virus is key to judging vaccines, yet the shield has two arms that work as one. Cody Meissner and three co-authors survey that problem in 2025. One arm makes antibodies that block the virus, and blood levels of those are easy to read.

The other arm runs through T cells, whose work is far harder to assay. So most of what is known about protection rests on antibody counts, which leaves the cell arm in shadow. The right shield also shifts by virus and by the door it uses to enter the body. The authors list the many factors that muddy the cell side of the story. Their aim is a fuller account of who is safe, and why, after illness or a shot.
pmc-12711080:
John Paul Byagamy and co-authors survey worm infections in school children in northern Uganda in this 2025 study. These infections can cause anemia, poor nutrition, and slower learning. Data for the Lango area were scarce, so the team tested 802 primary school children from January to March 2023.

Stool and urine tests looked for a water-linked worm disease and other gut parasites. About one child in three had the main worm disease, and one in five had other gut parasites, most often roundworm and hookworm. Older primary classes had higher odds of infection. The authors use the risk patterns to guide where control work should focus first.
pmc-12711880:
Aurelien Bustin and co-authors pair a new heart scan with AI reading in a 2025 paper. Finding scars in heart muscle guides treatment after heart attacks, but the standard MRI view washes out exactly where scar meets blood, hiding damage along the inner wall. Expert hand analysis is also slow and variable.

Their sequence, called SPOT, blends bright-blood and black-blood views to give sharp scar-to-blood contrast in one acquisition. An AI framework then finds and measures the injured tissue automatically, with no operator in the loop. The platform was validated in simulations, animal infarct models, and patients with heart disease. The authors pitch it for earlier, more consistent diagnosis of ischemic injury. Automated quantification also promises fairer comparisons across hospitals, where reader experience currently varies. The paper is a platform report as much as a results paper.
pmc-12714080:
Carlos Valladares and four co-authors sum what is known on droxidopa, a blood-press drug, used off-label in intensive care. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-five. Long drip drugs to hold blood press bring harm, and droxidopa is cleared for a nerve-based press drop on standing. The team swept four bases through April twenty twenty-five for real patient data on its ICU use to wean drips.

Seven small past-look works held one hundred sixty-one patients in all. Time to drip stop ran from one day to five. ICU stay ran long where told. The team call the proof thin and mixed, and urge more and stricter work.
pmc-12715080:
Yi Zhou and co-authors investigated in 2025 how an immune drug called pomalidomide makes built T cell treatment work better against blood cancers. CAR-T treatment, where a patient's own T cells are fitted with a synthetic receptor, makes high remission rates in lymphoid malignancies. But too many responses fade as the cells exhaust and disappear. Clinicians had noticed pomalidomide synergizing with the treatment without knowing why, so the team attacked the process from three directions.

In lab assays, pomalidomide boosted CAR-T cell proliferation and killing in a manner that depended on the cells being activated. Raised their output of key effector molecules and cell-recruiting chemokines, favored long-lived central memory cells. And reprogrammed their metabolism. Mouse xenograft models tested the mix in a living system, and single-cell sequencing of blood from a lymphoma patient treated with both mapped how the wider immune setting was remodeled.
pmc-12716580:
Ying Wu and co-authors report keyhole surgery repairs for newborns born with a hole in the stomach wall. Their 2025 case series covers four baby boys treated at a children's hospital in Shanxi between 2022 and 2024. The defect leaves part of the stomach muscle missing, and the stomach can tear open soon after birth.

All four babies showed vomiting, feeding trouble, and swollen bellies, with scans confirming free air. Laparoscopic repair finished in every case without switching to open surgery, taking about one hundred minutes on median. No leaks or bleeding followed, though one baby later struggled with feeding. At six months, three babies grew well and one lagged mildly. The authors favor the keyhole route for skilled teams.
pmc-12718280:
Jeesun Chun, Yo-Han Ko, and Dae-Hyuk Kim describe a new virus found inside a helpful fungus in this 2025 paper. Trichoderma harzianum is a fungus farmers use to fight plant diseases. Fungi host viruses of their own, called mycoviruses, which can change how the host behaves.

The team screened the fungus's double-stranded RNA and found an unknown virus in one strain. Deep sequencing read its full genome: four segments, each carrying a single gene. The largest segment codes for the virus's copying enzyme. The others code for a chemical tagging enzyme, a coat protein, and a protein of unknown role. Family trees place the virus as a new member of the Alternaviridae. Cataloging such viruses matters, since they can weaken or strengthen the fungus farmers rely on.
pmc-12718580:
Astrid Dauchez and ten co-authors test whether bone health can be screened from scans that prostate cancer patients already receive. Their study came out in 2025. Hormone therapy for this cancer thins bones and raises fracture risk, yet bone density is rarely checked at baseline.

The team measured bone attenuation, a density signal, in the lower spine on both a combined PET and CT scan and a stand-alone CT scan. The two methods agreed well at all three vertebrae measured. Longer hormone therapy went with lower attenuation values. About one in five patients had a spinal fracture, and those patients had clearly lower attenuation. The authors conclude that routine scans can flag osteoporosis risk without extra appointments or radiation.
pmc-12719880:
Svetlana O Kushch and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five chemistry study of competing ring-forming reactions that build fused drug-like scaffolds. A two-headed starting alcohol can react through nitrogen or oxygen first. That choice decides which ring system forms.

Three ingredients combined in one pot: the diamine alcohol, a fluorinated building block, and varied methyl ketones. The ketone's tail steered which product dominated. Dual acid-base catalysis sharpened selectivity for simple ketones. Products carried up to three handed centers, giving several mirror forms. Structures were proven with magnetic resonance and X-ray methods.
pmc-12722280:
Monira Aldhahi and six co-authors grade, in 2025 work, four Arabic sleep questionnaires against each other. Patients fill these forms to report sleep depth, daytime dozing, and the toll poor sleep takes. A form can be famed yet still fit a new tongue or a mild case poorly, so the team used a strict item test on all four.

More than three hundred healthy Arabic-speaking adults with mild sleep signs filled all four forms. Three of the forms showed weak trust scores and poor aim at mild cases, with one item even misfitting its scale. The fourth, trimmed from sixteen items to thirteen, passed each check: clean order, good fit, and high trust. The team names it the soundest of the four for Arabic speakers.
pmc-12722780:
Hansoo Song and co-authors published a study in 2025 on how to judge workplace health systems in large firms. A good system protects worker health, but firms need fair rules to rate how well their system works. The team set out to build such a set of rules.

The team first drafted rules from past writing on the topic. Then twenty experts in work medicine and hygiene rated the rules in two survey rounds. Rules that scored too low on expert agreement were cut or revised. Talks with firm health managers also shaped the final list. The end result was twenty-eight rules in four areas. The authors say firm health chiefs can use the list to track and improve their systems over time.
pmc-12723080:
Five authors report a hospital study from two thousand twenty-five on a blood disease in which the body attacks its own red blood cells. The disease is primary warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. They ask what a positive indirect antiglobulin test, a lab screen for antibodies in the blood, means when a patient is first diagnosed.

The team looked back at records for eighty adults treated at one Jordanian hospital. About two thirds had a positive test at the start. Those patients had higher levels of a marker of cell damage and more relapses after steroid doses were lowered. Response to steroids was also lower in that group.
pmc-12723180:
Emi Watanabe and co-authors study in 2025 how a year-long online training changed the work ties of mental health staff in Japan. The course taught both core knowledge and team care across trades. Most such courses serve students, not staff already in jobs, so effects on real teams were little known.

Surveys before and after drew maps of who works with whom for fifty-three staff in twelve trades. Well-linked trades lost a bit of their central place, while less-linked ones gained. The web as a whole grew more centered on a few hubs. Training may thus rebalance who turns to whom at work.
pmc-12723880:
Ali Alsharif and four co-authors test how well dentures made by digital methods keep their color against staining drinks. Their 2025 study compares three ways of making full dentures: molded, milled from one block, and a two-piece mix of printing and milling. Color matters because stained dentures look old fast.

Forty-five samples were soaked for a week in water, coffee, or red wine. Coffee stained more than wine. Milled samples resisted wine stains better than molded ones. A standard cleaning routine then restored the original colors, and the pattern held through a second staining round. The authors stress that material choice and daily cleaning decide how long dentures keep their looks.
pmc-12727580:
Long Chen, Jiuhe Wang, and Jinglian Qu chart, in a 2025 study, the burden of two lung diseases among people aged fifteen to thirty-nine in China, set against the other G20 nations. Scarred-lung disease with sarcoidosis, plus lung cancer, threaten the young more than public discussion admits.

Using the Global Burden of Disease 2021 data, the team tracked cases, deaths, and lost healthy years from 1990 to 2021. China's age-standardized rates fell steadily over that span. The analysis split the change into drivers like population growth and ageing, compared each G20 country, and projected China's rates forward to 2050 with a time-series model.
pmc-12727780:
Guy Ron and co-authors ask, in a 2025 study, whether pairing focused radiation with targeted drugs beats pairing it with standard chemotherapy for lung cancer that has spread to the brain. The radiation method, stereotactic radiosurgery, may also help drugs reach the brain and stir the immune system.

The team reviewed ten years of records for sixty-one patients with brain spread from non-small cell lung cancer. All had the radiation, plus either mutation-matched targeted therapy or standard chemotherapy. The targeted group went much longer before the brain disease grew again. Five-year survival was forty percent against nineteen percent, a gap that fell just short of firm statistical proof.
pmc-12727880:
Yangxiu Wu and a large team of co-authors built a resource on how cancer cells keep their chromosome ends alive in a 2025 paper. Immortal growth is a hallmark of cancer, granted by telomere maintenance, yet drugs barely exploit it. The team measured telomere biology across 976 cancer cell lines.

They added fresh protein data for most lines and merged it with gene, drug response, and gene-knockout data. Telomere states proved far more varied than the classic two-mechanism picture. The team derived protein and gene-activity signatures that predict which mechanism a line uses. They also found weak points tied to the alternative lengthening route and drug sensitivities tied to telomerase levels. The resource aims to speed telomere-directed drugs and matching tests.
pmc-12728180:
