Mukesh Maheshwari and colleagues released in 2025 a dataset on heavy 5G demand in the Liverpool City Region of the United Kingdom. Real network data from providers are rarely public, which makes it hard to study how crowds use mobile networks at big events. The project covered two event venues in Liverpool.

A digital twin fed a system level simulator to build the data. It covers three thousand users at one venue and twelve thousand at the other, with ten thousand samples in all. Each record gives user position, traffic type, which radio unit served them, signal quality, throughput, and error rate. The dataset was checked against real measurements and shared in a simple format.
pmc-12728580:
Ting Zhang and five co-authors traced how brain structure before COVID predicted fear during the pandemic and strain a year later, in a study published in 2025. A total of 115 students in Chengdu had brain scans before the outbreak. At its peak they scored their fear. A year later the team scored stress and broad distress markers.

Two deep zones, the insulae, stood out: more volume there meant more fear at the peak. The link held with sex, age, and whole brain size held constant. Fear then carried the brain link onward: it bridged the insula tie to later stress and distress scores. The authors say such scans could flag who needs early help in the next outbreak. Fear is the path to treat.
pmc-12729080:
Mozhgan Derakhshan-sefidi and co-authors pool a quarter century of Campylobacter data in Iran in a 2025 review. This bacterium is a leading cause of gut infection worldwide. Iran lacked a national picture of its spread and drug resistance.

Seven databases were searched for studies from 2000 to 2025, following standard review practice. Forty-six studies qualified for pooling. Quality was graded with a standard checklist, and a random-effects model produced the national estimate. Trend lines over two decades and resistance patterns across strains were the twin goals. The synthesis gives health planners a baseline for food safety and antibiotic policy. Full pooled figures sit in the paper's results.
pmc-12729180:
Huashuang Ou and eight co-authors pin a protein called TRIM3 as a driver of cartilage cell death in osteoarthritis, in a 2025 study. The disease wears down joint cartilage and disables millions. Its inner drivers stay partly unclear, which blocks drugs that change its course. The team tracked the protein in diseased and healthy cartilage.

Diseased cartilage held far more of the protein. Cutting it in cells lifted a guard protein and lowered a death protein. A growth signal path also woke up when the protein fell. Blocking that path erased the guard effect. Cell death after an inflammatory trigger fell by two fifths, and a key cartilage protein held up far better.
pmc-12729680:
Subarna Barua and co-authors published this methods study in 2025. Bats make up nearly a fifth of all mammal species and matter for pollination, pest control, and disease tracking. Naming a species correctly is harder than it looks. Looks and calls overlap between species, and the standard DNA barcode gene varies too much in places. The team built a simpler test around a short stretch of another gene, the mitochondrial 12S rRNA.

Using sequences from 232 species, they designed one primer pair that copies a fragment of about two hundred letters. That fragment separated every species analyzed. The test worked on all 241 real samples tried. Its identifications agreed with expert naming in 97.2 percent of cases. Two samples hinted at an undescribed species. Ten species from six genera turned up in the set. The authors offer the assay as a sturdy tool for conservation work.
pmc-12729880:
Anxin Li, Yanan Meng, and Martin Drapeau test group therapy for students in psychological subhealth. Their exploratory study from twenty twenty-five sorts students by core predicament. Subhealth means struggling without a formal diagnosis. Trauma, study pressure, and family dysfunction form separate groups.

Sixty students split evenly across the three predicament types. Half received eight weeks of group intervention. The programme blends thinking skills with social support ideas. Overall mental health and depression improved with treatment. Trauma students gained most on sensitivity and anxiety measures. Different struggles responded differently to the same programme. Matching support to predicament type may raise student wellbeing faster.
pmc-12730080:
Gao and co-authors present a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis on movement after limb-saving surgery for bone tumors near the knee. Surgeons replace the diseased thigh or shin bone end with a metal implant. Young patients need the joint to work well for decades. The review asks how gait and strength compare with healthy peers.

Four databases yielded twenty-three studies with 692 people in total. Patients walked slower, with shorter steps and lower pace than controls. Knee bending and straightening strength both fell markedly. Forces and joint power during walking also shifted. The authors say rehab plans should target these lasting gaps in gait and strength.
pmc-12730180:
Neža Repar and co-authors test whether iron oxide nanoparticles kill healthy vessel-lining cells the same way they kill tumors. The particles, coated in silica, can trigger ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death that cancer therapy hopes to exploit. What they do to non-cancerous cells was unclear. Their 2025 study treats human vein endothelial cells with the particles and watches the chemistry.

At the tested doses, fat oxidation and reactive oxygen species climbed steeply, up to about five- and four-fold, and the cells died by ferroptosis, not apoptosis. Two known ferroptosis blockers blunted the harm, confirming the route. Oleic acid, the fat in olive oil, also protected the cells, cutting death from fifty-eight to twenty-six percent. A side finding warns microscopists: under the electron microscope, the two death types look too alike to tell apart.
pmc-12730280:
Yongkang Shi and co-authors review how chemical tags added to proteins after they are built help drive pancreatic cancer. Their 2025 paper covers a cancer known for fast spread and poor response to treatment. These tags, called post-translational modifications, can switch proteins on or off and move them within the cell.

The review walks through six kinds of tags, from phosphate and ubiquitin to newer ones like lactyl groups. Each tag is tied to steps in tumor growth inside the cancer's dense local setting. The authors then sum up drugs and trial ideas that aim at these tag systems. They hope blocking the right tags could open new treatment paths for a cancer that badly needs them.
pmc-12730380:
Sofia Kasradze and co-authors locate where seizures start in the brain using scalp recordings in a 2025 study. Finding the seizure onset zone guides surgery for patients whose epilepsy resists drugs. The usual method needs electrodes placed inside the skull. The team instead tracked information flow in scalp signals with a causality method built on a new factorization algorithm.

They studied six patients who were being assessed for surgery, across pairs of brain regions and short time windows. The method found the start zones and the paths seizures took from them. Its answers matched the good surgical outcomes seen in all six cases, each reaching the best outcome class. The authors see promise for safer planning and for wider studies of brain information flow.
pmc-12730480:
Solafah Abdalla and colleagues review preclinical gene therapy for Crohn's disease and its path toward patients, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Progress has been constrained by several challenges. Optimal gene targets are hard to identify. Therapy-resistant cells in chronically inflamed tissue, especially the gut's nervous system, are hard to reach. Animal models mostly rely on toxin-induced colitis, unlike human disease.

The review synthesizes major preclinical studies in Crohn's and related bowel diseases. Vector platforms are compared by type, promoter, and administration route. Biodistribution data from rodent and primate gut tissue are critically assessed. Strategies targeting the enteric nervous system get special attention. Possible aims include calming intestinal inflammation directly. Local gene delivery during surgery might also prevent postoperative recurrence. The authors frame the field's foundations for translational research.
pmc-12730580:
Li and colleagues sequence the full mitochondrial genome of a small fish found only in southwest China in twenty twenty-five. The fish belongs to a carp subfamily whose family tree is unsettled. Its full ring of mitochondrial DNA was read and charted gene by gene. The team then rebuilt the subfamily tree from thirteen protein coding genes.

The genome held the usual fish gene set plus a control region. One transfer RNA broke the classic cloverleaf shape. The tree split the subfamily into two big limbs, not one clean branch. The study fish landed in the more derived limb, apart from its named kin. The genome adds a firm data point for carp taxonomy.
pmc-12730680:
Malysko-Ptasinske and co-authors boost gene delivery into cells in 2025 using gold specks plus ultra-short electric pulses. Electric pulses can open cell walls to let genes in without viruses, but the shortest pulses were once thought too weak. Gold specks near the wall can sharpen the field right where it counts.

Mouse cancer cells got a glow gene in bursts of pulses as short as a ten-millionth of a second in span. Even the shortest bursts moved the gene into over a tenth of cells, the team reports. Adding gold specks lifted success several-fold for short and longer pulse plans alike. A stronger, virus-free way to load cells could help lab gene work and future cell therapies alike.
pmc-12730780:
Auliya Akbar and co-authors test a joint injection for worn knees in sheep, in a 2025 study of osteoarthritis. The disease damages cartilage, which heals poorly on its own. Tiny packets released by fat stem cells, called exosomes, have shown promise in small animals.

Eighteen sheep with induced knee damage were split into three groups. One got exosomes plus a gel like acid found in joints, one got exosomes alone, and one got the acid alone. After six weeks, the combined group showed the largest area of smooth hyaline cartilage. Microscope and surface checks supported the gain.
pmc-12730880:
Nobukazu Hokamura and co-authors check whether chest radiation adds risk to immune drug care in a 2025 study. The drugs free the immune system to fight cancer of the food pipe and the joint to the stomach. Some feared that radiation plus these drugs would spark more immune side effects. The team read records for 58 patients treated from 2021 to 2024.

Side effects hit 28.6 percent of patients who had chest radiation and 39.1 percent of those who did not. Hard side effects were rare in both groups. The order of the two treatments and the gap between them did not shift the rates. A paired immune drug plan did show far more side effects than single drugs. The authors read chest radiation as no added risk here, while they warn the group was small.
pmc-12731380:
Daniel Ibanez and co-authors present a 2025 survey of how child joint specialists across North America treat Kawasaki disease, an illness that inflames blood vessels in children. When a first dose of the standard antibody treatment fails, the best next step is unknown. The survey asked doctors what they actually do in that spot and in related hard cases.

Of 102 alliance members invited, most replied, and just over half were child rheumatologists. For failed first treatment without artery damage, a second dose was the most common choice. Choices spread much wider once artery swelling appeared, mixing steroids, repeat doses, and a biologic drug. The authors say the wide spread shows a clear need for shared guidance.
pmc-12732080:
Bypass surgery can restore blood flow to a struggling heart, but grafts can fail and disease can march on. Lucia La Mura and co-authors review in 2025 how the full range of heart imaging can guide care after such surgery. Each tool answers a different question about grafts, muscle, and flow.

Ultrasound scans come first, giving quick reads on pumping strength and valve action. CT scans check whether grafts stay open, while magnetic scans measure scar and living tissue. Nuclear scans trace blood flow in fine detail. The authors match the choice of test to the patient: quiet checks for those without symptoms, and deeper hunts for those whose symptoms return.
pmc-12732380:
Yan Liang and colleagues published a 2025 food study comparing ways to dry orange slices. The oranges came from Gannan, a major growing region. Fresh fruit processing options there are limited. Two drying methods were tested side by side. Freeze-drying used vacuum and cold. Hot-air drying used heated airflow.

Freeze-dried slices looked whiter and brighter. They kept more vitamin C as well. Hot-air slices held more protective plant compounds. Aroma chemicals shifted under both methods. Tasters scored the sensory qualities of each batch. Neither method won on every measure. Producers can choose based on cost and target quality.
pmc-12732480:
Johal, Dunne, Bolooki, and Sandler review in 2025 how adult orthodontic options differ in quality of life, pain, and side effects. The options span removable aligners and fixed braces on the outer or inner tooth side. Their search had no language or date limits and was registered in advance.

Data from 35 studies covered 2,611 participants, most with fixed outer braces. Nine studies fed a pooled analysis. Pain score gaps between aligners and outer braces across the first week are reported with care. Bias was scored with three standard tools by study type. The review helps adults weigh comfort against other treatment traits.
pmc-12732580:
Chunjie Liu and co-authors study a gene switch in sheep egg-nest cells in a 2025 paper. The gene makes the first enzyme in the chain that builds a key breeding hormone. Its activity helps nest cells grow and sort, which backs egg ripening in the Qira Black sheep breed.

Tests showed the gene's activity tracks with how well the nests grow. Marks laid on its start zone, called methylation, set how strong that activity runs. Those marks shift as nest cells pass through growth stages. The team maps the best window in which the gene steers cell growth. Breeders gain a gene mark for picking top sheep lines.
pmc-12732680:
Mirela Sarbu and co-authors studied fat-like molecules called gangliosides in lung cancer that had spread to the brain. Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common form of lung cancer of its class and often spreads to the brain in late stages. Those spreads are a leading cause of illness and death, so early detection matters.

Using a method that sorts molecules by shape as well as mass, the team mapped how these fats change in tumor tissue from the brain. One type, GM3, appeared at higher levels, and the wider pattern of the fats shifted as well. Such changes could point to markers for finding brain spread sooner. The work also hints at targets that future treatments might aim at.
pmc-12732780:
Sarah Moncado and co-authors check how often inherited variants spotted in tumor testing are confirmed by true germline testing. Their 2025 study covers adults with solid tumors at two United States community cancer centers. Tumor profiling often turns up variants that may be inherited, with implications for the patient and their family.

The team reviewed patients who had both tumor profiling and dedicated germline sequencing. They measured the agreement rate between the two, checked whether confirmed variants matched the patient's tumor type, and analyzed how strongly each variant appeared in the tumor data. Community centers handle most cancer care, so rates measured there matter more than academic-center figures. Confirming a variant can change treatment and trigger screening for relatives.
pmc-12732880:
Jayson Forbes and Alejandro Arrieta ask in a 2025 study whether wider health coverage strained safety culture inside United States hospitals. Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act brought a surge of new patients. That surge may have stretched staff and chipped at the habits that keep patients safe.

Panel data with hospital fixed effects compared safety culture scores in expansion and non-expansion states. In small hospitals, expansion linked to a small but real drop in teamwork within units. Medium and large hospitals showed weaker openness about errors, with staff less sure that mistakes would not be held against them. The authors urge planners to pair access gains with added staff and support, sized to each hospital, so safety culture does not pay the price.
pmc-12732980:
Meizhu Dang and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-five, a natural antifreeze peptide from grass carp on wet gluten protein. Gluten is the elastic protein network in wheat dough. Freeze-thaw cycles damage it in frozen foods. The peptide, GCAFP, may serve as a natural cryoprotectant. The team measured freezing behavior, water states, flow traits, and microstructure with calorimetry, magnetic resonance, rheology, and electron microscopy. Adding half a percent of the peptide lowered the freezing point clearly.

It also widened the melting range, a sign of better freezing stability. After five weeks frozen, ice crystal growth in the treated gluten was less than in controls. After five freeze-thaw cycles, freezable water fell. The peptide curbed water migration and ice recrystallization.
pmc-12733080:
Guy Hutton and Sue Coates review the toolkits used to judge how strong a country's sanitation economy is and how ready it looks for investment. Toilets and waste systems in poorer nations face a vast funding gap. Sound gauges of markets and ground rules could pull in the money to close it.

The pair hunt frameworks through web search and talks with sector bodies and universities. Thirty-nine toolkits turn up, in wide variety: focus, indicator counts, country reach, and data style all scatter. Use has been patchy, with few kits picked up by second groups, though some results get cited far and wide. The review weighs what each kit truly measures and where they overlap or clash. Future sanitation gauges, the authors argue, should rest on proof and shared terms.
pmc-12733180:
Weirong Yang, Ning Han, and Xiangnan Zhang test a tea fungus on obese mice in this 2025 paper. The fungus, Eurotium cristatum, comes from Fu brick tea and has shown anti-obesity promise. The team asked whether it works by changing gut germs and by switching on sugar making in the gut wall, a pathway that can calm blood sugar.

Mice on a high-fat diet got the fungus at three doses for eight weeks. Treated mice gained less weight and showed better blood fat, blood sugar control, and liver health, with stronger effects at higher doses. Their guts held more helpful germs, and the gut made more of the short fatty acids that feed the sugar pathway. Key enzymes of that pathway rose as well. Chemical scans showed shifts in fat-related compounds. The authors present the fungus as a diet aid worth further study.
pmc-12733380:
Edward Itelman and co-authors check whether CT scan dye harms kidneys in patients awaiting a valve procedure, in a 2025 study. Planning a transcatheter aortic valve implant needs a detailed contrast scan. Doctors worry the dye may injure kidneys, above all in patients with chronic kidney disease. That fear can delay needed imaging.

The study measured kidney injury after scans using standard global criteria. All scans used a modern, gentler class of contrast agent. Injury rates were tracked in the days after imaging. Results show how often harm truly follows the scan. Heart teams can then weigh the small risk against clear planning gains. Patients with weak kidneys are the group most affected by the answer.
pmc-12733480:
Elena Mikhaylova and co-authors review gene editing in farm pigs in a 2025 paper. Traditional breeding struggles with traits shaped by many genes, and the pig gene pool is narrow. Gene editing can add helpful changes directly, even ones first found in other species.

The review reports strong progress on pigs that resist viral disease and on pigs with better meat yield and quality. Harder problems remain, such as lameness and harmful behaviours like tail biting, which the authors say may need editing to solve. Wider farm use is held back by the need for large tissue samples, surgery, and cell culture work. The field also leans toward medical research. The authors weigh these gains and limits for future pig farming.
pmc-12734180:
Flora Kafunda and co-authors test whether chlorination can kill insects in wastewater in work from 2025. Chlorine is still used to treat water from insect facilities, despite harm from its byproducts and thin proof that it works on arthropods.

The team soaked Mediterranean fruit fly eggs in ten chlorine strengths for up to forty-eight hours. Survival fell as strength and time rose, but deaths never reached one hundred percent even at the highest strength. Weak solutions had little effect. The authors conclude chlorination cannot ensure eradication and favor heat treatment instead.
pmc-12735780:
Jamir Pitton Rissardo and Ana Leticia Fornari Caprara review the role of vitamin D in Parkinson's disease in a 2025 paper. The vitamin is thought to protect nerve cells, but its link to this disease has stayed murky. The review joins blood level studies, supplement trials, and gene studies in one synthesis.

Across sixty-three studies with roughly ten thousand people, patients had clearly lower vitamin D levels than healthy adults. Lack of the vitamin was more common among patients, and ample levels linked to a modestly lower risk of the disease. Supplements gave small, non-significant gains in movement scores. One variant in the vitamin's receptor gene linked to the disease most steadily. The authors call for care in judging cause and effect.
pmc-12735980:
Marta Hoelm, Zdzisław Kinart, and Stanisław Porwański study how a sugar-based carrier molecule grabs an anticancer drug. The drug, dacarbazine, is light-sensitive and unstable, so a host that shelters it could help. The carrier is a hybrid ring stitched from sugar units, urea bridges, and a crown ether loop. Computer modeling said the drug does not slip inside the ring's cavity. Instead it clings to the outside, hydrogen-bonding with the sugars, the bridges, and the crown.

Magnetic resonance tests in heavy water matched that picture, with the sugar signals shifting most. Electrical measurements across a temperature range showed the pairing forms on its own, releases heat, and is driven by that heat release while the system grows more ordered. The carrier bound the drug more strongly than the standard cyclodextrin hosts. The authors propose it as a delivery platform.
pmc-12736380:
Neeltje Rosenberg and co-authors test a new compound against a rare disease in which bone grows inside muscle and tendon. The disease locks joints over time and leaves patients immobile. A faulty gene leaves a growth receptor switched on, driving the stray bone.

The compound blocks that receptor's signaling in lab tests. The team profiled how strongly and how cleanly it acts. Blocking the altered receptor is a leading strategy in this disease, with several trials under way. A new entrant matters because current options are few and the disease starts in childhood. The lab profile decides whether the compound deserves animal and human tests. The report lays out that first evidence in full.
pmc-12736480:
Arelmys Bustamante Miranda and co-authors grade a cleaner PVC process on paper in a 2025 study. PVC is cheap, strong, and everywhere, but making it drinks water and energy and leaves residues such as the monomer, a carcinogen, and the alcohol used in the process. The improved design links mass and energy flows and recycles its water with a no-discharge system of paired treatment reactors.

Savings in one place can push burdens elsewhere, so the team scored the design with a waste reduction algorithm across four operating scenarios. The aim was to find which stages and flows carry the biggest environmental load. Cases combining integration with full water recycling in PVC are rare in the literature, which makes the comparison a useful design reference.
pmc-12736580:
Lila Rana, Aayush Dulal, Xin Chen, and Xinhua Tang propose a graph temporal convolutional network for indoor positioning with WiFi signals. Their 2025 paper deals with locating people inside buildings, where satellite signals fail.

Commodity WiFi positioning struggles with multipath fading and blocked paths, so sub-meter accuracy is hard. Their hybrid model uses graph convolutions to encode access point geometry, and temporal convolutions to capture signal dynamics. Both signal strength and round-trip time features are used, with a gating mechanism that weighs each access point. Tests ran in four areas, from a lecture theatre to a full building floor. Sensitivity to access point density was also analyzed.
pmc-12736780:
Mattias Drake and co-authors measure chronic subdural hematomas in a cohort of 257 patients in this 2025 paper. A hematoma of this kind is a slow blood collection under the skull's lining, common in older adults. Its volume and density shape treatment choices, yet hand measurement is slow and often skipped. The team studied scans taken before first time surgery, covering 339 hematomas in all.

Raters measured volume by outlining the blood on every second scan slice. They compared those values with the quick ABC/2 formula used at the bedside. The two methods agreed strongly, and raters agreed with each other almost perfectly on volume. Agreement stayed strong for width and midline shift, but fell for fine density patterns. The authors offer the data set as a reference standard for testing automatic measurement tools. They back routine volume checks in trials and care.
pmc-12736880:
Graham Finlayson, Yi-Tun Lin, and Abdullah Kucuk present a fix-it step that sharpens any method for recovering full color spectra from plain camera images. Their 2025 paper covers algorithms that guess the light spectrum behind each pixel, plus methods that use a color photo to sharpen a blurry spectral scan.

Any spectrum, their theory says, splits into two parts: one the camera can see and one it cannot. A recovery method often gets the visible part wrong. Their step swaps in the correct visible part, computed straight from the photo. They prove the swap always cuts error and can never add any. Tests across many methods confirm the gain. A shortcut for scenes that follow simple color models adds a further boost.
pmc-12737280:
Hospitals now gather patient data from bedside sensors and wearables, and that data must move between systems without leaking. Norjihan Abdul Ghani and four co-authors propose a security framework for that traffic in a 2025 paper. Their design does the locking and checking at the network edge, near the devices, rather than in a distant cloud.

The framework mixes three tools: elliptic curve cryptography for key exchange, AES for fast scrambling, and a hash-based code that proves data was not altered. The authors say it is the first side-by-side comparison of such hybrid setups for edge health exchange. Their tests measured processor load, memory use, and growth with data size. The full mix gave strong protection with light processing, which suits small edge hardware and keeps delays low.
pmc-12737380:
Shato Chow and co-authors measure how fake astigmatism dulls sight in young adults. Their 2025 study fits 45 healthy volunteers, aged 18 to 35, with lenses that mimic the blur. Three lens strengths and three tilt axes were tested on each person.

Sharpness at near and far range fell across most lens mixes. Depth sense suffered most with a strong lens set at a slanted axis. Reading speed also dropped once slanted lenses passed a set strength. The strongest lenses, above all on slanted axes, caused the worst loss of function. The work gives a clean gauge of how much each kind of blur costs the eye.
pmc-12737580:
Mojca Dobaja Borak and five co-authors report the case of a man bitten by a nose-horned viper in two thousand twenty-five. The bite caused his platelet count to crash three times within one day. Platelets are the small blood cells that help form clots. Each crash put him at risk, yet tests told a surprising story about his blood.

Each time, doctors gave him antivenom made from antibody fragments, and his count bounced back. Tests run after each dose showed his platelets still worked well. They formed clots at a normal pace and did not switch on when they should not. So the venom seems to remove platelets from the blood without damaging the ones that remain. The case offers a clean model of this rare effect.
pmc-12738580:
Lithium metal batteries promise more stored energy, but a fragile surface film makes them fail early. Aoyuan Chen and co-authors report a 2025 additive that helps a tougher film form on the metal.

The additive is a cesium salt with a strongly donating partner ion. As the film first forms, cesium ions shed their solvent shells and shape the film's growth. The partner ion breaks down early and enriches the film with a sturdy fluoride compound. Test cells kept nearly all their charge per cycle, and full cells held most of their capacity over hundreds of cycles. The same additive also steadied cells built with a common high-energy cathode.
pmc-12738680:
Yu, Hou, and Lin (2025) built a recommender system that draws on both tangled relationship graphs and a user's past behavior. Recommenders fight information overload, but sparse data holds them back. Graph models handle rich, mixed-type relationships well, while other tools remember long user histories; few do both at once. The team's design, the Heterogeneous Graph Memory Transformer, pairs a graph transformer with memory modules that keep long-range context from past interactions.

Tested on three public datasets from shopping and review platforms, the model beat strong baselines on standard ranking scores, posting the best results on each set. Extra analyses showed it held up under uneven data and added noise. The authors present the design as a step toward recommenders that cope better with the messy, shifting nature of real user-item data.
pmc-12738780:
Korea's top baseball league became the first to let a machine call balls and strikes, in twenty twenty-four. Kichang Lee, Kyungsik Han, and JeongGil Ko studied what changed. They used pitch data from two thousand five hundred fifteen games across several seasons. Math models compared human and machine calls in the gray zone at the edge of the strike zone. Four questions guided the work, covering fairness, consistency, player adjustment, and strategy.

Robot calls follow the rule book zone more evenly than human calls. Players adjusted their swings and takes to the new standard. The authors draw lessons for leagues weighing the same move. Their case study shows how a sport can absorb automated judgment without losing its shape.
pmc-12740880:
Mingkang Zhang and five co-authors build a screening tool for fatty liver in people with diabetes. Their 2025 paper targets metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. The condition rides along with type 2 diabetes yet often hides early. A tailored prediction model for this group was missing.

Records of over four thousand seven hundred patients fed the search. A shrinkage method picked eight predictors, from body mass to blood fats. The team shaped them into a nomogram with online and spreadsheet calculators. Accuracy held up in training, internal, and outside American data. The tool beat four older fatty liver models. Subgroup checks supported wide use. Clinics gain a cheap first screen for a silent disease.
pmc-12742080:
Xiaoyi Ji and a large team published a study protocol in twenty twenty-five for putting a prostate biopsy AI through unusually strict validation. Grading prostate biopsies is subjective, and pathologists disagree enough to sway treatment. AI systems can match experts in their home laboratory yet stumble elsewhere, a generalizability problem recent reviews keep flagging.

The protocol pre-registers a retrospective test on an independent cohort, scoring the system on grade, cancer volume, and pattern detection against independent pathologists. Bias risks that plagued earlier studies are designed against from the start. Publishing the protocol before results exist is itself part of the rigor. The study aims to produce the kind of external evidence regulators and clinics actually need.
pmc-12742180:
Farhad Pirouzmand and co-authors set out the protocol for a trial on blood clot prevention after traumatic brain injury. Clots in the veins are a common harm after such injuries, yet the standard preventive drug may raise the risk that bleeding inside the skull grows worse. When to start the drug is thus an open question.

Their 2025 protocol describes a randomized trial with a Bayesian adaptive design. Patients with moderate to severe injury get the heparin drug dalteparin either early, within three days, or late, after day seven. All patients also receive standard pressure-based prevention. The trial aims to give clinicians firm ground for a choice they now make with thin proof.
pmc-12742580:
Frailty stalks older patients whose diabetes has damaged their nerves, and seven authors built a tool to spot it early. They recruited 400 such patients at a Guangdong hospital and recorded which ones were frail, about 28 percent, then searched for the factors that best separated the groups.

Six factors made the final model: age, marital status, regular exercise, sleep quality, nutrition score, and depression score. The team turned them into a nomogram, a chart that converts a patient's answers into a frailty risk. Internal checks with a thousand resamples showed the chart separates frail from non-frail patients well and that its risks line up with reality. Decision analysis said using it would help in practice. The authors note the model still needs testing in other hospitals and regions before wide use.
pmc-12743480:
Joanna Koort and three co-authors surveyed online case tools for veterinary students in a 2025 paper. The University of Helsinki built two web tools: one with interactive cases in animal disease patterns, the other in bacteriology. The team asked whether working through the cases measurably improved students' skills.

Students filled in tests before and after the cases across several school years, 104 for the disease tool and 191 for the bacteriology one. Both tools raised thinking skills and broader academic skills by a small but firm margin. Reasoning tests and graded written answers both improved. The authors present the cases as a working model for digital teaching in veterinary schools.
pmc-12743680:
Jérémy Mercier and co-authors review in 2025 how to watch for prostate cancer return after a focused ultrasound treatment. The treatment, called HIFU, blasts the tumor with sound waves while sparing healthy tissue. Afterward, standard blood tests and scans can miss a return, since treatment changes the gland's shape.

The review gathered eight studies from major databases. Standard MRI scans remain the norm but read the treated zone poorly. A newer scan, PSMA-PET, hunts a marker found on prostate cancer cells. It caught hidden returns with high accuracy, even when blood tests were low and other scans had failed. The authors call it a strong partner to standard checks, pending larger trials.
pmc-12744580:
Repeated head impacts in contact sports can harm the visual system, and little is known about how to protect it. Jon Kelly and co-authors followed thirty-one college rugby players through a season. Half were randomly given a supplement of macular pigment carotenoids plus omega-3 fats, and half a placebo. Before and after the season the team measured eye structure thickness with a scanning method. They also tested contrast sensitivity and flicker perception, and checked blood markers linked to brain injury.

Skin tests confirmed the players absorbed the supplement. One eye measurement thinned slightly over the season in both groups. A blood marker of nerve damage rose after the season in the placebo group but not in the supplement group, and flicker perception trended better with the supplement. The authors read the results as early, mixed evidence that the supplement may help protect vision.
pmc-12745280:
Simone Göppert, Sebastian Springer, and Martin Zacharias probe how helper proteins load cargo onto immune display proteins in a 2025 study. The display must hold its cargo firmly for immune cells to read it well. Two helpers pry the display cleft open in much the same way, but the full role of that shift was not clear.

The team ran long computer models of the display with and without each helper. The shift shook loose weak cargo and could partly free mid-grade cargo. Only strong cargo pulled the cleft shut and shed the helper, which points to a built-in grade check in the load step.
pmc-12746580:
Arjun Singh and Rajvir Singh review the gut hormone system built around endothelin in a 2025 paper. The system helps run gut motion, fluid release, feeling, and swelling. One signal, endothelin-1, acts through two kinds of locks on many gut cells, and faults in the system show up in gut ills.

Too much of the signal and too much action at one lock can drive swelling, pain, weak gut lining, and stiff muscle. Drugs that block the locks may ease such ills, the authors note. Gaps remain on which cells send which signals, so the review maps what is known and what still needs work.
pmc-12748180:
Terkawi, Kadoya, and Endo wrote a 2025 editorial on immune cells called macrophages in muscle, bone, and joint disease. These diseases, from worn joints to bone loss, limit movement and quality of life. Current drugs often fail to rebuild tissue, so the editors argue research must learn how the body keeps and repairs its own tissues.

Macrophages can help repair or drive harm, shifting states with local cues. The old two-state model now looks too simple, the editors note, since single-cell scans show a smooth range of states. Their special issue gathers four reviews and one research paper on these cells in health, repair, and disease.
pmc-12748680:
Jakub Gazda and co-authors test whether the voice can betray a hidden brain disorder of liver disease. Covert hepatic encephalopathy clouds thinking in many patients with liver failure, yet standard tests are slow or complex, so clinics rarely use them. The team recorded patients holding a steady vowel sound and mined the recordings for telling traits.

A machine learning model, XGBoost, sorted patients with the best accuracy of the tools tried. Its strongest clues were in how the voice held its volume and tone. Patients with the disorder kept a flatter volume and a harsher vocal quality than others. The model's stated risks also matched real outcomes well across the range. A short voice recording may one day screen for the condition in minutes.
pmc-12748780:
Naihui Chu and a large team test a new tuberculosis drug in a phase 2a trial, in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. The drug, JDB0131, is a third-generation nitroimidazole, a family that already produced two approved TB medicines. Fifty-two newly diagnosed patients were randomized across three dose levels of the new drug, with the older drug delamanid and standard combination therapy as controls.

Over fourteen days, the new drug killed bacteria in sputum faster than delamanid at the highest dose, and all dose levels beat it on time-to-positivity measures. Side effects were frequent but none serious. The authors call the compound a promising new antituberculosis agent.
pmc-12748980:
Ting Zeng and co-authors test lawn grass under dry soil in a 2025 study. The grass is Axonopus compressus, a common turf type, plus six new variants of it. Dry spells driven by climate change put turf under strain, so tough types are in demand.

Seven variants grew for eight weeks in a glasshouse under full, mid, and low water. Drought cut leaf size and shoot mass, while roots grew more. Three variants kept finer leaves under all water levels. One variant raised its green pigment under drought while most lost it. Stress chemicals rose in all plants. The work flags which variants cope best with dry soil.
pmc-12749080:
Wu and seven colleagues coax a ring shaped molecule out of naphthalene by breaking its aromatic calm in twenty twenty-five. Naphthalene is a fused double ring that resists change. Adding an oxygen bridge across one ring makes a useful but fragile epoxide. A manganese catalyst modeled on enzymes did the job with a mild oxidant.

Electron poor rings gave epoxides where rich ones gave hydroxyl products instead. The swap hinged on the ring's substitution pattern. Math modeling traced the split to two distinct paths. One runs through a radical route, the other through a charged one. Such epoxides are rare catches, the team notes.
pmc-12749280:
Diwei Shi, Donghwan Ji and Jinhye Bae build hydrogels with ligament-like strength in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. Synthetic hydrogels are usually far weaker than ligaments, among the strongest natural gels in the body. Their design borrows the ligament's trick: fiber-shaped elements bundled in parallel.

The fibers mix polymer-particle clusters inside a continuous polymer network. Strong particle interactions and tight confinement spread load efficiently and dissipate energy, breaking the usual trade-off between stiffness and stretch. The gels reached high tensile strength and toughness while stretching over four times their length. Bundled to millimeter scale, they held tens of kilograms and worked as strain sensors.
pmc-12749480:
Pooria Kabiri and Amir Saman Nooramin propose a new structure for a graphene metamaterial filter for terahertz waves in a 2025 paper. The device can act as a band pass filter, which lets a set band of waves through, or as a band stop filter, which blocks that band.

Layers of graphene form the core, and its chemical potential sets the type, the working frequency, and the width of the band. Stacking units gives higher-order filters. A circuit model guides the design and tests. The response holds steady across wave angles and across a wide tilt of the beam, which suits spectroscopy and light control.
pmc-12749780:
Atefeh Tahmasebzadeh leads a team that teaches a net to read eye tumor response. Their study from twenty twenty-five deals with uveal melanoma after plaque therapy. Response falls into shrink, grow, stable, or other types.

Sound images from diagnosis were labeled by eye doctors. Labels used the response seen after the plaque care. Two deep nets were trained and scored on the task. One net beat the other on a mean score across classes. It also led on each response class in the checks. Early response guesses could shape follow up care.
pmc-12749980:
Gebremedhin Gebreegziabiher, Tefera Belachew, and Dessalegn Tamiru run a randomized trial of lifestyle therapy for metabolic syndrome in adults, in a 2025 paper. The syndrome bundles belly fat, high blood sugar, high blood pressure, and abnormal blood fats. Lifestyle change is the recommended first treatment.

One hundred fifty adults were split evenly between a three-month program of diet, exercise, and behavior counseling and a control group. The program group improved on nearly every measure, from weight and waist size to blood sugar and pressure. Their count of syndrome components fell more, and their odds of recovery were about four times the control group's. Syndrome rates fell in both groups, but far more with therapy.
pmc-12750380:
Praveen Singh and co-authors test a yeast-made biosurfactant for squeezing more oil from rock while storing carbon dioxide, in a 2025 study. The sophorolipid soap, brewed by Candida bombicola, was checked for structure, then pushed through carbonated water flooding tests. It proved strongly surface-active at just 250 parts per million.

The soap cut water's surface tension from 72 to 31 units and nearly erased the oil-water boundary tension, an 85 percent drop. It also flipped rock surfaces from oil-loving to water-loving, freeing trapped oil. Mixed with a polymer, it absorbed 77 percent more carbon dioxide than water alone, and stayed stable under pressurized gas. The authors pitch biosurfactants as a greener engine for oil recovery with a storage bonus.
pmc-12750580:
Catherine Giroux and co-authors validate a questionnaire on learning health systems in a study from two thousand twenty-five. A learning health system joins care, data, and research so practice improves continuously. Organizations need a way to judge their readiness before adopting the approach.

Experts from Canada and abroad rated draft items over three Delphi rounds, checking importance, relevance, and clarity. The final tool holds sixty-eight items in four domains, covering the path from performance data to knowledge and back to performance, plus core values. Many items were revised or dropped along the way. The authors say the measure can gauge readiness, and they call for tests of its measurement quality.
pmc-12750880:
Nila Norouzi and co-authors describe a 2025 study of nursing and midwifery students and their skill at spiritual care. Care for the spirit is part of whole person care, yet students vary in how ready they feel. The team asked if self belief and sense of trade identity predict that readiness.

More than two hundred students who had begun ward work filled three scales. One scale rated spiritual care skill, one rated trade self belief, and one rated trade identity. Both self belief and identity tracked with higher skill scores. A model test found self belief was the strongest of the predictors, with prior training also helping. The authors urge schools to add full spiritual care training to their plans.
pmc-12751180:
Xi Luo and Weiwei Jin link antioxidant-rich diets to lower odds of sarcopenic obesity, in work from 2025. The condition pairs muscle loss with excess fat, a double burden in aging. A composite index scores total dietary antioxidant intake across foods.

Two cohorts fed the analysis, one American with 4,388 people and one Chinese with 276. Higher energy-adjusted index scores tracked lower odds of the condition in both. The top fifth of scorers showed markedly lower odds than the bottom fifth. Blood markers of inflammation and nutrition partly carried the link. Diet quality may thus guard muscle while limiting fat gain.
pmc-12751480:
Jun Jie Lim and co-authors explore how medical students feel about a two-stage clinical exam in a 2025 paper. In the sequential format, all students first sit a shorter screening exam. Only those below the pass line sit a second, confirming exam. The design saves resources and sorts borderline cases well, but how students experience it was little known.

The team interviewed twenty-two students after two full exam rounds. Students drew confidence from practice chances, watching peers and seniors, kind words, clear communication, and well-spaced tests. Doubt about the format, unclear pass marks, slow feedback, and thin support dragged confidence down. Those who saw the exam as a growth chance stayed motivated, while those who saw it as punishment grew anxious. The authors note a paradox: high pass rates beside lasting stress.
pmc-12751580:
Lakshanee Dahanayaka and co-authors ask whether the chemistry of Basella alba, a leafy green eaten across Sri Lanka, rides on its genes. Earlier work found the plant's nutrients and antioxidants shifting by agro-climatic zone. If genes drive the shift, growers can breed or source for the richest leaves.

Their 2025 study fingerprints plants from fifteen locations with random DNA markers and sets the pattern against the known chemistry. A handful of primers gave clear, repeatable bands, and nearly every band varied across sites, proof of wide diversity. Similarity scores sorted the sites into kin groups, with some pairs near twins and others distant. The genetic map now stands beside the chemistry map, ready for the correlation test.
pmc-12751980:
Vincent Tardy, Emilie Lyautey, and Victor Frossard watched lakebed microbes change over five months, sampling every two days or so. Shoreline sediments in Lake Bourget host dense microbe communities that power much of the lake's chemistry. The team asked whether change there runs on rules, driven by the environment, or on chance. They studied the whole community and then split it into smaller co-moving groups.

Viewed whole, the community shifted little, and chance processes like drift did most of the work. Measured conditions explained only seventeen percent of the change. The group view told a richer story. Six modules emerged, each with its own rhythm, and the two largest answered to the environment in opposite ways. For one module, conditions explained over half its change. The authors argue that whole-community averages can hide the real dynamics living one level down.
pmc-12752080:
Olga Zayts-Spence, Pauline Luk and David Edmonds interviewed in 2025 eighteen Hong Kong medical students who trained during the COVID-19 pandemic, asking how it shaped their mental health. Student distress matters because it shadows later patient care and staff retention. Earlier local work was mostly surveys, which miss lived detail. The team recorded and transcribed the talks, then coded them for themes about stress and coping.

Stressors fell into physical, social and educational groups, from isolation to disrupted clerkships. Coping leaned on support from others, and in harder cases on thoughts of leaving medicine entirely. The authors call for universities and hospitals to align policies that protect student well-being. They argue the lessons still apply after the emergency years. Training systems should plan for the mental strain of disrupted cohorts.
pmc-12752180:
Yisi Liu and co-authors chart blood fat disorders on one of the world's highest plateaus, in a 2025 study. The Pamirs Plateau rises over four thousand meters. No survey of this kind had been done there. The team used yearly health exam data from 2021 to 2024. Adults living in the county for at least a year were included. The sample covered about a quarter of the local population.

Blood fat disorder was the commonest condition found. High blood pressure, slow heart rhythm, and fatty liver followed. Prevalence ranged from about twenty-five to thirty-eight percent. A key cholesterol measure ran lower than in lowland groups. The local Tajik majority kept steady, favorable profiles with age. Others showed stronger age swings. Risk factors included being male, older age, and diabetes. Frequent drinking and higher schooling also linked to the disorder.
pmc-12752880:
Jian Ding and co-authors hunted in 2025 for genes that link diabetes to joint wear, a pairing often seen in clinics but not explained. Finding the shared machinery could point to treatments for patients who carry both diseases.

The team combined several routes: a gene based causal test, scans of gene activity in two data sets, network maps, and lab checks. They found 142 genes changed in both diseases, with two standing out as strong markers. Computer docking suggested one compound could hit both marker proteins at once. A lab test confirmed both genes are active as predicted. The authors offer the pair as leads for drugs and diagnosis.
pmc-12753680:
Yi-Jun Wang, Bhargav Patel, and co-authors stand as the named team on a formal pull back note from the journal side, in a 2025 note. The note ends a past work that claimed a blend blocks drug pump out in cancer cells. Such pull backs mark the work as no longer sound to cite or build on.

Shot overlap claims drive the pull back in full. Slice shots in the past work seem to match shots in a kin work by the same team. More than a score of shot pairs are named in the note list. Pump and death mark shots join the stain shots in the claims. The journal side made the call to retract.
pmc-12753780:
Qingshan Li and four co-authors screen for key genes tied to a fresh cell death form in psoriasis. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Psoriasis drives skin cell overgrowth, and the death form, called disulfidptosis, may play a part. Gene web tools sifted a past data set for gene groups tied to the ill.

One gene group tied to the ill most, and six hub genes were named. Three of them ran high in sick skin and stood as driver genes. One, SLC7A11, steered free sulfur marks and a flare path in lab tests. Skin stain, blot, and gene checks backed the finds. The team flags the three as marks for tests and cures.
pmc-12753880:
Hua Mao and co-authors review live monitoring of gases dissolved in transformer oil, in a 2025 paper. A transformer's oil betrays its health: stray sparks, hot spots, and arcs each brew telltale gases. Reading them early warns of failure and grades the gear's aging. The old way, lab tests on drawn oil, is slow, and the gases themselves can burn or blow, a risk to crews on site.

The review sorts the live tools built in the last six years. One line runs a mini gas chromatograph at the tank. Another reads light spectra from the oil. A third sniffs with gas sensors. Each is scored on how little it can detect, how fast it answers, and what it costs to keep. The authors see the field moving toward smart, sharp, always-on watch, feeding a grid that guards itself.
pmc-12754380:
Yao Peng and co-authors argue that bone and joint research worldwide needs outcome questionnaires reshaped for each culture. Their 2025 article deals with patient reported outcome measures, the forms patients fill in about pain and function. Such forms only stay valid abroad if they are translated, adapted, and retested with care. The authors highlight a study that validated an Arabic foot and ankle questionnaire. It proved reliable for Arabic speaking patients with injuries.

The authors call for smoother ways to fold adapted forms into daily practice. They also want studies of how the forms change treatment choices. Large multi center trials using them are a further goal. The piece is a commentary urging the field to invest in adaptation.
pmc-12754880:
Ashleigh Johnson and co-authors explored in 2025 what helps or hinders sports play for Hispanic girls in a rural border county. Fewer than a third of American children meet activity goals, and rural Hispanic girls join sports late and in low numbers. The team interviewed girls, parents, coaches, and program staff in a mostly Hispanic county in Southern California. Two frameworks guided their reading of the talks.

Factors showed up at every level, from role models and hot weather to program cost and family time. Good coaches, parent support, and a shared community value for youth helped. The authors urge programs shaped to local needs. Wider access could narrow health gaps tied to gender, income, and place.
pmc-12756780:
John Fredy Ricardo Marroquin and co-authors study a thin film material called InSb in a 2025 paper that mixes lab tests with theory. The material moves electric charge very fast, which makes it of use for heat sensing and other fine tools. Films of it are grown on a base that does not quite match, and that growth can leave flaws in the film.

The team grew films by two methods and then hit them with gamma rays. They tracked how flaws in the films changed after that dose. The aim is to learn if the films can hold up in harsh places, such as space, where rays are common. By comparing the two growth methods side by side, the study shows which route leaves a film that stands up better to harm.
pmc-12764780:
Shalini Singh and fourteen co-authors uncover a sugar-coated disguise HIV uses to dodge immune killing. Their 2025 paper shows that infected helper T cells remodel their surface sugars, raising the ligands for a family of checkpoint receptors on myeloid immune cells. When those receptors engage, the myeloid cells' killing is damped, much as a brake pedal slows a car.

The team then built a countermeasure: an HIV-targeting antibody fused to an enzyme that strips the sugars off. In dishes, the construct sharply improved killing of infected cells by both monocytes and neutrophils from the same donors. In humanized mice, it lowered viral load and calmed inflammation. The authors frame the sugar shield as an evasion mechanism worth drugging, and the antibody-enzyme as a template for clearing infected cells that the immune system currently overlooks.
pmc-12764880:
Salniccia and five co-authors test nerve gliding therapy after brain injury, in work from twenty twenty-five. Acquired brain injury can stiffen and weaken an arm, limiting daily tasks. Neurodynamics, gentle nerve movement methods, help muscles and nerves in other groups, so benefit was plausible here.

Twenty-four patients were split evenly in a blinded randomized trial. One group got one session of median nerve neurodynamics. The other got a placebo session. Tests right after measured grip strength, spasticity, pain, joint range, and muscle electrical activity. A single session design shows instant effects only, a first step before longer programs are tested.
pmc-12764980:
Tso and co-authors show that a living breakwater gets better at its job as oysters move in. Engineers increasingly seed reef builders on coastal defenses, hoping nature will share the work, but proof that growth changes performance was missing. The team measured waves and oyster growth at two sites across two recruitment seasons.

A standard engineering model, refitted with ecological measures, found oyster length a good predictor of the structure's effective thickness. The authors argue defenses should be designed to improve with age, not just decay.
pmc-12766680:
Zahraa Abou Khalil and a large team watch copper atoms reshape themselves inside a metal-organic framework while it works as a photocatalyst. The frameworks, built on the UiO-66 design with extra acid groups on their links, split formic acid under light. Live infrared and X-ray probes tracked the surface and the copper during the reaction.

More acid groups meant more internal anhydride formation, which tracked efficiency one to one. Light also rebuilt the copper from mixed higher states into a paired low-state system that does the work. Charge flowed from the zirconium clusters to the copper under light. Calculations backed the picture and give design rules for light-driven catalysts.
pmc-12767380:
Tianyue Zhang and co-authors probe how failing cell power plants and immune cells drive diabetic kidney disease. The disease is a grave side effect of diabetes, shaped by many forces. Which forces cause it, rather than just track it, was unclear. The team used a gene-based method that mimics a trial, plus single-cell gene reads from kidney tissue. They also checked blood cells from patients for changed genes.

In sick kidneys, key genes fell in filter and tube cells, and immune cells moved in. Blood cells showed raised genes tied to swelling. The named genes and cell paths offer new drug targets.
pmc-12767480:
Yucheng Gao and co-authors test which style of exercise best guards bones after ovary loss in mice. Their 2025 study matches two training styles for total distance: short hard bursts and steady mid-pace runs. Both ran for twelve weeks in mice whose ovaries were removed, a model of bone loss after menopause. Scans then measured bone loss and inner bone wear.

Steady mid-pace runs, but not hard bursts, curbed bone loss. That style also calmed the cells that eat bone and cut swelling signals in bone, blood, and gut. It restored gut germ mix and sealed the gut wall, while hard bursts did neither. The authors tie the bone gain to this gut-bone path.
pmc-12767580:
Awad Khalifa, Hassan Adam, and Faisal Musa study how climate variation is reshaping land use in Kassala State, Sudan, in a 2025 paper. Land cover shifts matter because farming and grazing depend directly on them, and the area suffers wind and sandstorms. The team combined satellite images from 2002 and 2023, weather station records, and interviews and group talks with local stakeholders.

Rainfall fluctuated, temperatures crept up, and wind speeds rose over the period. Forest cover shrank from about seventeen percent of the area to about thirteen percent, while bare land and shrubland spread. Image classification and change detection mapped the pattern, and field data grounded it. The authors recommend agroforestry measures, above all windbreaks and shelterbelts of hardy acacia trees, to blunt sandstorms and slow land degradation. They frame the work as both a record of two decades of change and a practical plan for limiting further loss.
pmc-12767980:
Radiation for left breast cancer grazes the heart, and Budhi Singh Yadav and co-authors check the damage decades later in this 2025 study. Eighty-seven women treated with shorter, stronger radiation courses at least ten years earlier got heart scans and stress imaging. The team looked for patches of heart muscle starved of blood flow.

Such patches showed in 36 percent of patients, but nearly all were mild and sat at the heart's tip, nearest the old treatment field. Pump function had slipped in only two patients, and four had suffered heart events. A lung-distance measure over 2.5 centimeters marked those with bigger patches. The authors read the record as mostly mild late harm, tied to how much heart sat in the beam.
pmc-12768680:
Aléxia Vieira and four co-authors report a study coded OP66, published in twenty twenty-five. They looked at how well reports in Brazil say that patients and the public took part. The reports came from CONITEC, the national group that decides which new health tools public care will pay for. The years covered were twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four.

The team read the reports again and checked them with a short guide called GRIPP2-SF. That guide has five items and is meant to lift the quality of such reporting. Patient input is valued more and more around the world, but it stays hard to do well in Brazil. Readers learn how the reports were sorted and what the checks can show.
pmc-12768780:
Vanessa Pirolo surveys barriers that people with diabetes face in Brazil after new tools enter the public health system. Brazil counts about 16 million adults with the condition. Her 2025 study ran online interviews with 1,843 adults who have diabetes. The talks took place over about seven weeks in mid 2024.

Most of those asked were over 60, and most had type 2 diabetes. Large shares also had high blood pressure or high cholesterol. Most took oral drugs, and most got tests and free drugs through the public system. Six in ten named steady access to medication as the top factor in keeping on top of the disease. The survey maps where access still snags after new tools are approved.
pmc-12770480:
Sayantan Mondal, Agustín Mangiarotti, Rumiana Dimova, and Qiang Cui study how protein droplets reshape cell-like membranes in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Disordered proteins can condense into droplets that stick to membranes and bend them. The details of that touching interface were incomplete.

Using microscopy, light-based chemistry probes, and two simulation styles, the team watched a simple droplet pair meet artificial membranes. Stickiness could be tuned by the membrane's charged lipid share, and a contact angle measured it in both lab and computer. The membrane under the droplet flowed about half as fast, because lipids crowded there and packed tighter. Local lipid sorting also appeared where droplet met membrane. The framework joins experiment and simulation cleanly.
pmc-12771880:
Ana Moreira, Nazaré Rego, and José Crispim build in 2025 a framework for judging the value of a health service, and try it in a radiology department. Past value programs often never defined value plainly. They also tended to be complex, hard to repeat, and deaf to what patients and staff care about.

Their four step frame uses multi criteria decision methods to weigh many aims at once. The trial site was the radiology unit of Portugal's second largest general hospital. Managers, doctors, radiographers, and patients all took part. The team built a set of 160 indicators to score the service. A frame that admits local weights could travel to other services without losing what value means locally.
pmc-12772580:
William Bello and co-authors tested how long a cancer drug stays stable in prefilled eye syringes in 2025. Topotecan is injected into the eye to treat a childhood eye tumor. It holds up better at room heat and harms the eye less than the older drug, which makes prefilled syringes attractive.

Two strengths of the drug were stored in syringes under three conditions: warm, chilled, and frozen. Tests ran for twelve months and checked appearance, acidity, and drug level. Both strengths stayed stable for a full year when chilled or frozen, with no solid particles and no real change in acidity or strength. A breakdown product appeared only in warm storage after three months.
pmc-12776180:
Amanda Herrmann, Christopher Grant, and Lyudmila Bazhenova review targeted treatment for a lung cancer gene pathway in a 2025 article. Changes in the MET gene can drive non small cell lung cancer on their own or help it resist other drugs. The review covers the last decade of work on this pathway.

Four kinds of MET change are covered: a skipped gene segment, extra gene copies, excess protein, and gene fusions. For each, the authors sum up how it is detected and classified. Treatment options include blocking drugs, antibodies, dual target antibodies, and drug carrying antibodies. Approved options remain limited, and the authors map key challenges and future directions for the field.
pmc-12776980: Scorza, Scorza, and Finsterer write a short 2025 letter on how to spot delirium in children in intensive care. The text supplied here gives the title and citation only, with no body. Its stance is plain from that title. A bedside score called CAPD flags too many children who do not have the state. A full psychiatric exam should thus be the preferred route.
pmc-12777880:
Jian Hou and co-authors review how to combine continuous kidney replacement therapy with extracorporeal life support. These machines take over heart or lung work in critically ill patients. Kidney injury is very common in this group and marks a worse outlook. When and how to start kidney support alongside these machines remains unsettled.

Trials of early kidney support in general intensive care patients have not shown a clear survival gain and hint at harms. Yet they barely included heart and life-support patients, whose fluid and pressure problems differ. The authors argue for tailored thresholds, such as diuretic resistance and venous congestion in heart shock, and call for pragmatic trials that account for how devices and organs interact.
pmc-12780080:
Cristina Cerrillo and co-authors studied early design of battery cell machines in a 2025 paper. Makers of lithium-ion cells must build lines that are safe for workers and light on the planet. Yet they have little guidance on how to fold safety and green goals into the first design steps for the machines themselves.

The team checked European rules for battery making and past work on safe and green design. They then gathered facts from two machine makers on the main steps of cell making, from mixing to drying and pressing. Their map shows where rules bite and where design can improve. It gives makers a start point for cleaner, safer lines.
pmc-12780380:
Luciano Bulgarelli Maqueda and co-authors test a new robot route for lung surgery that keeps tools out of the rib cage. In standard robot lung work, tools pass between the ribs, which can hurt nerves and cause pain that lasts. The new route slips under the ribs from below. Their 2025 report covers a first-phase trial of the method in people set for lung cancer surgery.

Twenty cases are in the final count. No case had to switch to a standard route, and no patient died in the first month. Most blood loss was small, stays in hospital ran to two days at the mid point, and chest tubes came out fast. A quarter of patients had some snag, most often a long air leak. Most rated their recovery as fair to top grade two days on.
pmc-12780680:
Xia Weng, Jiyun Zhu, and Xiaoshuai Zhou search for a gene based marker that predicts who benefits from a common antibody drug in colon cancer, in work published in 2025. The drug blocks blood vessel growth, but no reliable marker foretells response. Data came from six hundred twenty cancer cases with varied drug exposure.

One gene stood out as the top predictor. High levels of it went with far better response rates and longer survival in the main set and in two check sets. Lab work showed the gene slows a fat based signal that drives cell movement, by acting on two partner genes. A three gene model predicted drug failure with good accuracy. The authors propose the panel for sorting patients.
pmc-12784580:
Lujain Alchalabi and co-authors study why asylum seekers and refugees in Switzerland struggle to get dental care, in a 2025 paper. Care is often limited to urgent work like pulling teeth. Coverage depends on legal status, canton, and time in the country. Many people affected do not know what is covered.

The team held sixteen interviews with Arabic-speaking newcomers in two cantons. They also watched care inside three clinics. Money limits, permit rules, language gaps, and low control led people to delay care. Delay made their oral health worse. A known access framework explained part of the picture, but missed how the system shapes people's own sense of need.
pmc-12784880:
Emmanuel Irimaso and a large team hunt for drug-resistant bacteria in pigs and pig farms in Rwanda, in a 2025 pilot study. They swabbed noses, rectum samples, manure, and dust on 29 farms across four districts, 114 samples in all. The targets were staph bacteria resistant to methicillin and gut bacteria that shrug off a key class of antibiotics.

They found 32 resistant gut isolates, mostly Escherichia coli carrying extended-spectrum beta-lactamase genes, plus four livestock-type MRSA isolates. Many strains resisted several drug classes at once. The authors warn that pigs and farm environments act as reservoirs of priority pathogens and call for joined-up surveillance of animals, people, and surroundings.
pmc-12785080:
Deo Ruhagazi and eight co-authors track cranes returned to the wild in Rwanda, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Few left the release area, and those that did left much later. Their home ranges and longest trips were far smaller. The authors link this to feeding by keepers and long years in cages. Staying put may aid short-term survival, but the team urges long-term checks on survival and breeding.
pmc-12785180:
Mengyi Jiang and Meixiang Zhou build a simple model to forecast survival for patients with pancreatic cancer. They tested cutoffs two ways, then screened the strongest factors into a final model.

Several blood values and ratios carried independent weight, including neutrophils, lymphocytes, two tumor markers, and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, alongside cancer stage. The final model combines sex, age, treatment, stage, tumor grade, two markers, and that ratio. Its discrimination score, a C-index of 0.73, shows fair predictive power. pmc-12785580:
Anna Dębińska, Hanna Danielewicz, Anna Drabik-Chamerska, and Barbara Sozańska studied how genes and smoke together shape childhood allergy disease in this 2025 paper. Asthma and eczema often arrive as a pair, a combined pattern thought to grow from shared genes plus early-life surroundings.

The team followed 188 children from before age two to age six. All had doctor-confirmed eczema or asthma status, and parents reported tobacco smoke exposure at home in the early years. DNA tests read two genes flagged by an earlier genome-wide study of gene-environment interplay. The question was whether those gene variants raise the risk of eczema or the combined pattern, and whether smoke exposure bends that risk. Such interplay studies point to which children most need smoke-free homes.
pmc-12785680:
Sergey Sypalov and eight co-authors present a lab method for finding brominated by-products in drinking water. Their 2025 paper notes that disinfection keeps water safe but leaves chemical traces, and the bromine-bearing ones are hard to catch. Standard tests need a separate reference sample for each target compound, which slows broad screening.

Their setup pairs two detectors after a liquid separation step. One detector spots any compound that carries bromine. The other reads fine mass data to guess each compound's structure. Together they can both find and measure these by-products without a reference sample for each one. Tests on real drinking water worked as hoped. pmc-12785780:
Zhenghai Liu and co-authors test ways to cut sulfur dioxide use in semi sweet wine in a 2025 study. The gas guards wine against spoilage, but makers want to use less of it without losing quality.

One common treatment deepened the wine color, which suits sweet white wine poorly. Two treatments, a yeast product and glutathione, kept color bright and phenols stable. pmc-12786280:

The joint picture points to hormone disruption, oxidative stress, inflammation, and metabolic systems out of balance acting together. The authors offer the joint approach as a template for judging risks from chemicals around us to breeding health.
pmc-12787780:

Their fix borrows spectral unmixing: the stain absorbs light in a narrow, known pattern, while refraction smears evenly across wavelengths, so the two can be separated pixel by pixel.

pmc-12787880:
Fanlei Lu and co-authors present a 2025 paper on predicting ore quality in a foam-based mineral process. Air flow, slurry level, ore traits, and chemicals all shift the foam, so reading it is hard.

A fusion module blends the two views deeply. The design also states how unsure each prediction is, which helps plant staff trust the output.
pmc-12788080:

pmc-12788280:

pmc-12788480:

pmc-12788580:

Blood tests found about sixty-two percent of the women in the insufficient range, with average levels well below the healthy mark. Only about a quarter sat at or above twenty units. Deliveries were mostly vaginal, with about a quarter by cesarean. Awareness of the vitamin's importance was low and tracked with the deficiency. pmc-12795280:

Their tests point to gut microbes as a middle step between habits and health. Microbe richness in the gut explained over a quarter of the score's link to a marker of insulin resistance. pmc-12795680:

pmc-12796080:

Factor analysis and structural modeling tested the pathways. The model allows influence to run in both directions. Results show where interventions could bite. Counselors gain a named mechanism rather than vague screen-time worry. The study grounds a global debate in Indian campus data.
pmc-12796880:

The planned trial tests home-based treatment and asks whether it protects the heart and brain, and whether effects depend on the exact points used. A large author team from Chinese medicine centers designed the study. Results, when they come, will test both the therapy and its point rules.
pmc-12800180:
Yadeta Bedasa, Adeba Gemechu, and Amsalu Bedemo study climate-smart farming in Ethiopia in a 2025 paper. Using survey data from several hundred households and a model that accounts for farmers choosing their own practices, they found clear gains. The authors urge policy that builds farmer skill first, since the practices pay off most in skilled hands.
pmc-12801780:
Myrrah Kamwiyo and co-authors interview the staff who folded depression care into chronic-disease clinics in rural Malawi. They praised the therapy guide, the group format, and steady mentoring. Their complaints were practical: travel costs for patients, heavier workloads, and missed visits. pmc-12804780:

Tested on the Osong railroad test track in Korea, the method located rail alignments with an average error of about three point six millimeters. The authors say the automation cuts the time needed to build digital railroad models and makes maintenance planning faster and more consistent.
pmc-12804980:

They suggest polyamine support as a route to guard patients during radiation therapy.
pmc-12807980:

The aim was a clear toxicity ranking, so doctors can weigh gains in survival against the harm each plan is most likely to cause.
pmc-12808180:

Working network activity, though, needed a third factor that the others could not replace. One broth matched the other when fed the right blend. pmc-12808680:

Past tools read whole cells or whole crowds, not one array at a time. The team joined a live-cell kinase read with new optics to watch single arrays answer scent shifts. The arrays turned out uneven, like a mosaic, not the uniform sheet many models presumed. That patchwork helps explain the keen sense bacteria show with so few parts.
pmc-12812980:

The team tracked phytoplankton and bacterial communities along eutrophication gradients. These tiny organisms form the base of the river food web and signal water quality early. Their responses show which species thrive or fade as nutrients climb. The findings guide protection of a river that supplies drinking water far beyond its banks.
pmc-12813080:

Stops near the city center worked better as a pair, while outer stops lagged on access. The authors say the city still has time to plan ahead. pmc-12814580:
