Blood tests dominate heart risk screening, so a non-invasive stool marker would be welcome. The team compared 593 heart disease patients, split into heart attack, unstable angina, and stable angina groups, with 200 healthy adults. Fecal sulfatide was measured in every participant.

Sulfatide ran notably higher in patients than in controls. The heart attack group topped both angina groups. In adjusted models the marker stood as an independent risk factor, and its accuracy curve reached 0.893, a strong showing. The authors propose stool sulfatide for early prediction and risk sorting, pending checks in wider populations.
pmc-12815280:
Alessandro Godono and co-authors combine trials of workplace health programs in a 2025 meta-analysis. Heart and metabolic risk factors, such as weight and blood pressure, are common in working adults. Employers run promotion programs against them, but the overall payoff across studies needed a pooled check.

The review kept 44 studies with nearly 50,000 workers. Nine of twelve outcomes improved in a meaningful way. Body weight, waist size, body fat, and blood pressure all fell, and good cholesterol rose. Total cholesterol, triglycerides, and fasting glucose did not change clearly. Programs worked best for high-risk groups, when led by health professionals, and over shorter spans. Most findings carried moderate to high certainty, the authors report.
pmc-12815780:
Kaichao Shao, Huijuan Ren, and Peizhe Xu ask whether shifting views on gender roles push rural mothers in China into business ownership, in a 2026 study. Using national social survey data, they tracked how a more equal gender role attitude relates to mothers starting ventures. The setting matters because rural women's economic potential often goes untapped.

A better gender attitude raised the entrepreneurship rate of rural mothers by 4.89 percent. The lift was stronger for necessity-driven ventures than for opportunity-driven ones, and it helped mothers without higher education while showing the opposite pattern for graduates. Family support and access to information shaped the effect. The authors also found spillovers: these mothers created jobs for other women.
pmc-12816180:
Zhao and Huang asked whether regular exercise goes along with less smoking, using a large national survey of China, in work published in twenty twenty-five. Knowing why the two habits might link could help public health programs do double duty.

The study drew on the twenty twenty-one China General Social Survey and kept two thousand three hundred seventy-three valid cases. People who exercised more tended to smoke less, and the link survived several different statistical checks. It was strongest for middle-aged adults and somewhat larger for men than for women. Better mental health and stronger social support each explained part of the connection. Higher income made the link stronger still. Because the data capture one moment in time, the authors are careful to call the pattern a correlation, not proof of cause.
pmc-12816280:
Granzyme B is a weapon that killer immune cells use against cancer, and high levels of it have long been read as a good sign. Yubi Zhang and four co-authors review the darker side in 2025. Work from recent years shows the same molecule can also help tumors grow and spread.

Cells beyond the classic killers, including tumor cells themselves, can release granzyme B into the tissue around a tumor. There it can reshape the scaffolding between cells, push cells toward a more mobile state, and help new blood vessels form. The review gathers these sources and paths into one account. The authors say future cancer drugs should weigh both faces of the molecule.
pmc-12816380:
Yanbing Li and Refath Farzana review how movable bits of DNA have turned a gut germ into a grave global threat. Their paper deals with Klebsiella pneumoniae, once a germ that struck mainly the weak. New strains now cause harsh illness in healthy people, and drug-proof strains kill at high rates. Movable DNA parts, such as plasmids and jumping genes, drive much of this change.

These parts ferry strength and drug-proof traits between germs. Some merged parts carry both kinds of trait at once. The authors argue that drugs and tests that jam the movement of these parts could slow the merge of strength and resistance in this top-priority germ.
pmc-12816580:
Kristoffer Walsh and co-authors map, in a 2025 study, a web that sets how fruit fly cells wake a stress lead, ATF4. Cells meet strain by kinases that lift ATF4's build from its RNA. Its lead-in holds the rules, yet more hands were thought to help. A screen found one: the cap-bind protein 4EHP, needed for ATF4 calls in the fly's fat body and in ill models. A fish-for-mates screen named its top mate: NELF-E, a brake on gene read speed. Protein counts then tied both to the small ribosome half and to start parts eIF3.

Cut any of the set, and ATF4 and its gene brood fall. The web thus guards cell stock in growth and in ill states alike.
pmc-12816680:
Mei Shang and Pyeoungkee Kim propose a lightweight attention model for segmenting medical images, in a 2025 paper. Segmentation outlines lesions and organs so doctors can measure them. Convolutional networks do this well but see only small patches at a time. Transformer designs see the whole image yet cost too much for clinics with modest hardware.

Their model adds attention across several dimensions while staying light. It aims to capture long-range links without heavy computation. That balance targets real hospital and edge settings. Tests on medical data sets judge both accuracy and speed. A model that runs on small machines widens access to AI image tools. Rural and low-resource clinics stand to gain most.
pmc-12817680:
Gamil Taher Abdulmughni and six co-authors examine stomach cancer patients in Yemen in this 2025 case control study. They ask whether infection with the stomach bacterium Helicobacter pylori goes along with the levels of two tumor markers, called CEA and CA19-9, in the blood.

The team measured both markers in eighty-five patients with the infection and eighty-five without it. Median levels of the two markers were nearly the same in both groups, and no real link appeared between the infection and either marker. One link did stand out: infection was tied to cancers located in the cardia and fundus, the upper parts of the stomach. The authors say that pattern needs more study to uncover the reasons behind it.
pmc-12817780:
Ilario Ferrocino and a large Italian team test whether shared lab procedures can make microbiome research more reliable, in a 2025 paper. Labs often prepare samples and extract DNA in their own ways, which makes studies hard to compare. The SUS-MIRRI.IT project wrote standard operating procedures for samples from fermented foods, soils, and waters, then put them to an interlaboratory trial.

Fifteen research units worked on 120 shared samples and sequenced the same genetic marker. Results matched well across labs, with no real differences in microbial diversity or composition between replicates or sites. The authors say the validated procedures give future studies a common base and make large meta-analyses more feasible.
pmc-12818380:
Joana Rodrigues Ferreira and co-authors report a rare case of bowel blockage caused by a gallstone in a 2025 article. The stone slips from the gallbladder into the gut through an abnormal channel and lodges in the narrow small bowel. The condition mostly strikes older women with other illnesses, and its vague symptoms often delay diagnosis.

The patient was an eighty-four-year-old man with four days of vomiting, stomach pain, and inability to eat. Scans guided by suspicion confirmed the blockage, and he was stabilized in intensive care. When drug treatment failed, surgeons cut the bowel and removed the stone, and a scope later broke up remaining material. He recovered well, with no new episodes over six months. The case favors gentler approaches for frail patients.
pmc-12821180:
Zhoumeng Ying and a large team predict which children with mycoplasma pneumonia gain from bronchoscopy. Their two-centre study from twenty twenty-five uses causal machine learning. The scope procedure helps some children with stubborn lung collapse. Others recover without it, so selection matters greatly.

Scan scores were measured by an AI system automatically. Clinical and lab data joined the scan features. A causal forest estimated each child benefit from the procedure. One cohort built the model and another validated it. Benefit varied substantially between children with similar illness labels. Feature rankings show what drives the predicted benefit. Doctors could aim an invasive procedure at likely responders.
pmc-12821280:
Maria-Tzousi Papavergi and co-authors review the complement cascade as an old immune arm turned foe in Alzheimer's disease. Their 2025 paper traces how this blood-born defense, vital for pruning synapses as the brain grows, can reignite in aging and eat synapses instead. In Alzheimer's and its vessel cousin, stray complement feeds plaque growth, synapse loss, swelling, and barrier leaks.

The review runs from human finds to animal models and stem-cell-grown brain cells. Genes, gene switches, and gut signals tune the cascade. Blood marks of its firing and drugs that block its parts close the tour.
pmc-12821580:
Kieran Sandhu and co-authors chart 24 years of kidney biopsy trends in Australia. Small kidney masses turn up more and more often, and many prove benign or slow-growing. A needle biopsy can clarify the diagnosis before major surgery, yet it was long reserved for other uses. The team extracts billing data for percutaneous renal biopsies from 2000 to 2024, excluding children, and adjusts counts by population.

About 31,870 biopsies take place over the period. Rates climb steadily, adding about 4.9 procedures per 100,000 people overall. Men receive biopsies more often than women. New South Wales posts the largest rise, while South Australia, Tasmania, and the capital territory fall. Rates peak in the 55 to 74 and over-75 age groups. The ratio of biopsies to kidney removals also grows, matching the consensus that biopsy should guide care of small masses.
pmc-12822080:
Jonah Amponsah, Jeffrey Thompson, and Shellie Ellis map how the drivers of obesity change from place to place across the United States. A single national model can miss local drivers, and rates are known to run higher outside big cities.

The team linked county obesity rates for more than three thousand counties to income, schooling, and habits. A model that lets each driver act at its own scale fit the data far better than one global model. City status mostly guarded against obesity, but that shield faded or flipped in parts of the West. Income and schooling linked to lower rates in most places.
pmc-12822180:
High blood pressure runs in families, but its genetics are spread across hundreds of small effects. Abdullah Aldhufairi and four co-authors review the field in 2025, tracing the hunt from single candidate genes to giant biobank scans and full sequencing. They gather which genes and pathways the evidence keeps naming.

Calcium handling in vessel walls, salt transport in the kidney, adrenal hormone making, and immune tone emerge as the four actionable systems. Some signals act only in one sex or one ancestry, and rare large effect variants surfaced in Middle Eastern groups. The authors sketch risk scores and drug choices fitted to a person's genetic subtype. They frame precision care as the field's next step.
pmc-12822280:
A sprained ankle often tears the ligament that steadies its outer side, and other parts may be hurt at the same time. Qirui Yu and six co-authors reviewed scans from 1,005 patients with such injuries in 2025, all read with high frequency ultrasound at one hospital over four years. They measured ligament thickness and mapped which companion parts were damaged.

The neighboring calf ligament grew thicker when the main tear was complete than when it was partial. Tears of that ligament and of a strap across the front of the ankle often came with the main injury. Right ankles showed a slightly thicker calf ligament, which the authors link, with caution, to right side dominance. They urge sonographers to check the companion parts every time.
pmc-12824180:
Servert Lerdo De Tejada and co-authors combine light fingerprinting with machine learning to detect hydrocephalus quickly, in a 2025 diagnostic study. Hydrocephalus is a buildup of spinal fluid in the brain that raises pressure and harms nerves, and early signs in babies often appear late. The team read the fluid's molecular fingerprint with surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy on silver-coated paper strips. Samples came from 117 patients, 47 with the condition.

A random forest model read the fingerprints and, in blind testing, reached 97 percent accuracy within five minutes per sample. It caught 95 percent of true cases and cleared every control. The gear is portable, a plus for clinics with few resources. The authors also built checks that flag overfitting and show which spectral features drive each call.
pmc-12824380:
The vagus nerve links the brain to organs and helps control blood sugar, energy use, and inflammation. Yu Zhe Li and a large team of co-authors traced a signaling chain inside that nerve in mice in 2025. Removing a brake protein called PTEN from vagus nerve cells raised the nerve's output. The mice resisted obesity, insulin resistance, and body-wide inflammation on a high-fat diet.

Removing the insulin receptor from the same cells did the opposite, worsening metabolic health. Removing both proteins at once rescued the harm, proving the two act in one pathway. The authors say this insulin signaling axis in the vagus tunes the balance between the body's two autonomic branches.
pmc-12824980:
Alex Harker and Suhail Tarafdar review how medical education adapts teaching for autistic students in this 2025 paper. They searched medical education databases for studies on autistic medical students and junior doctors. Seven articles passed the screen, three with high risk of bias. Four themes emerged. Training that raises staff awareness helps, as do careful language choices and individual practical adjustments. Autistic clinicians as role models gave students insight into their own strengths and gaps.

One proposal stood out: rethinking how empathy is taught, with sessions co-created by faculty and autistic students. That change could help all students, not only autistic ones. Other proposals face cost and feasibility limits in the United Kingdom for now. The evidence base is thin, the authors stress. They call for more research, and for judging each strategy in wider settings before adoption.
pmc-12825280:
Jia Zou and four co-authors train community doctors in a structured communication method and measure whether their patient conversations improve, in this 2025 study. One hundred and twenty-eight general practitioners from ten primary hospitals in Chongqing took three months of training. The course mixed lectures, case studies, and interactive practice, built on the five step SEGUE framework.

Observed and scored before and after, the doctors' total communication score rose by a full point, a statistically strong gain. Opening the encounter, drawing out information, and giving information improved most. Understanding the patient's view and closing lagged behind. Senior doctors gained the most, juniors the least, though all groups improved. The authors conclude targeted training works, and they point to the two stubborn steps as the next teaching frontier.
pmc-12827180:
Nancy Uriegas and three co-authors ask women athletes at historically Black colleges about food access, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Campus food settings can be thin, and athletes need fuel to train. The team explored how these students eat, shop, and cope.

Ten athletes living in dorms took part in long interviews, after a survey on energy needs. Half were food secure and half were not. Four themes emerged: dorm life, personal factors, convenience, and nutrition awareness. Students described few ways to cook, cafeteria food that varied in quality, and tight schedules that drove quick choices. Food existed on and off campus, yet many felt the options fell short for sport. The study gives schools a view from the athletes' side.
pmc-12827280:
Eleven researchers tested a modified amino acid as a treatment for a severe childhood brain disease in mice, in a 2025 paper. CLN1 disease, a form of Batten disease, destroys nerve cells fast and kills early. The drug, N-acetyl-L-leucine, has helped patients with a related storage disorder, raising hopes it might help here too.

Mice lacking the disease gene received the drug in food from weaning or from four months of age. Treatment did not extend survival. Walking and balance tests showed no real gains, apart from tiny shifts in a few step measures for early-treated mice. Brain tissue showed no drop in immune cell activation or stored waste. The authors conclude the drug alone has limited value for this disease. Its action may simply miss the core fault driving CLN1.
pmc-12827980:
Nan Cai, Minghui Zhao, Yantong Ke, and Xin Liu published a 2025 study on a quantum enhanced learning system for volleyball tactics. Calls in volleyball come fast. Many players move at once, and the state of play can take a huge number of forms. A learning system that trains by trial and reward strains under that load.

Their hybrid design adds quantum circuits to a classical network. Quantum state encoding packs rich features into a compact form. Quantum steps run in parallel and speed up training. In simulated tests, the system chose tactics more accurately than classical rivals. It also settled in far fewer training rounds. Its answers came within tens of milliseconds. The work is a simulation study, not a court side tool. Still, it sketches a path for quantum assisted coaching.
pmc-12828680:
Yipu Li and colleagues compare a radioactive brachytherapy stent with conventional plastic stents for malignant blockage of the ureter. Their 2026 initial experience report covers patients treated over five years.

Thirty patients received the new stent loaded with radioactive seeds, while forty-one received standard stents. Technical success was complete in both groups, and complication rates did not differ significantly. Local disease response at eight weeks was far higher with the brachytherapy stent. Control of visible blood in urine was also much better in that group. Overall survival was longer with the new stent. The authors call it safe and effective while noting longer follow-up is needed.
pmc-12828980:
Yeganeh Khazrai and co-authors test a strict ketogenic therapy in adults with excess weight, in work from 2025. Diet reshapes gut microbes, which in turn affect weight and metabolism. Very low energy keto plans promise fast loss, but gut effects need tracking.

Forty-one adults began a twenty-eight day plan using meal replacements. Thirty-one finished and were measured at the end. Weight, body mass index, and fat mass all fell clearly. Gut profiles shifted, with two major groups falling and two rising. Genera tied to gut health rose, while several sugar-linked genera fell. Stool chemicals were profiled as well. The single-arm design limits causal claims.
pmc-12829180:
Ola Saraya and five co-authors wrote this 2025 study on a meaning-centered teaching program for people with schizophrenia. Drugs ease symptoms but often leave the search for purpose untouched. Logotherapy, a therapy built around finding meaning, was shaped into a seven-week course of thirteen sessions for forty-five stable patients.

Before and after measures used Arabic versions of standard scales. Resilience rose clearly after the course, and belief in one's own ability rose even more. Guilt toward others, though, barely moved. Resilience and self-belief also rose together, closely linked. The authors say meaning-focused teaching can rebuild inner resources alongside drug care. Guilt, they suggest, may need a different therapy aimed at how patients think about others' minds. Longer follow-up would test whether the gains last.
pmc-12829280:
Shaon Das and M D Ray report a rare spread of ovarian cancer to an armpit lymph node, with no breast involvement. Their 2025 case concerns a fifty-four-year-old woman treated three years earlier for stage IV high-grade serous ovarian cancer. She had received chemotherapy and major surgery. On follow-up, a blood marker rose and scans showed a persistent right armpit node plus deep belly nodes.

A biopsy proved the node was ovarian cancer, while breast imaging stayed clean. She got more chemotherapy, then repeat debulking surgery with heated chemotherapy in the abdomen and node removal. The single node measured three centimeters. The authors urge checking the armpit in ovarian cancer follow-up.
pmc-12829480:
Soybeans carry a protein, soybean agglutinin, that lowers how well farm animals digest the feed. Kafer and eight co-authors switch off the gene behind it, Le1, using CRISPR gene editing in a Brazilian soybean variety. Plants were screened with gene tests, protein gels, and clumping assays, and later generations were checked for edited plants free of the editing machinery.

Of twenty edited events, one carried a small deletion that wrecked the protein. Its seeds showed no trace of the agglutinin band and no clumping activity. Field traits, including yield and seed weight, matched the unedited variety. The authors present the low-lectin lines as a route to better feed for pigs and poultry. The catalog lists the paper under 2026, but the journal head records it as published in 2025.
pmc-12830380:
Mohsen Zarei and colleagues built a light cipher to keep photos safe as they cross networks of tiny sensors. Sensor nodes have little power and sit in open places, so heavy encryption drains them. Their scheme mixes elliptic curve math with a fuzzy logic system tuned by an optimization algorithm.

A hash-based key generates shifting substitution boxes, while fuzzy rules scramble pixel order and values. Tests on standard images showed near-perfect randomness and strong resistance to statistical and noise attacks. A 256 by 256 image encrypted in under a second. The balance of speed and strength suits battery-powered sensor networks.
pmc-12830580:
Jieyu Chen and six co-authors build a computer model of a complex hip socket fracture to test which fixing method holds best. They mapped fracture lines from scans of seventy real cases, then built a detailed model from one healthy volunteer's scans, adding ligaments and cartilage. Into that model they placed the fracture and tested three screw setups, plus no fixing at all, under five body positions.

Breaks that crossed both columns and breaks of the front wall were the most common types. The setup combining two kinds of screws moved least under load and spread stress best in most positions. The unfixed model moved most, as expected. The authors suggest the combined setup may give the steadiest hold, while noting that patient trials must confirm it. They also advise care with early weight bearing after surgery.
pmc-12830880:
Hyesoo Wang and co-authors examine, in a 2025 study, tiny parcels released by a friendly gut bacterium and put to work outside the cell. The parcels, called extracellular vesicles, came from Lactobacillus rhamnosus, a well-known probiotic strain. The team compared natural vesicles with vesicles squeezed from broken cells, a lab-made stand-in.

Both types looked round under the microscope, but their protein cargo differed. A heat-shock protein marked only the natural set. Across more than thirteen hundred proteins found, the natural vesicles leaned toward signaling and transport roles, while the cell-made ones leaned toward growth machinery. In lab assays the natural vesicles also fought oxidation and calmed inflammation more strongly. The authors back them as the better base for probiotic products, with skin health named as one aim.
pmc-12830980:
Haruna Takami and co-authors grow lab models of chondrosarcoma, a bone cancer that resists standard chemo and radiation. Their study, published in 2025, builds organoids, small tumor copies grown from patient tissue. Such models are scarce for this cancer, which limits drug testing.

Two organoid lines grew well and, when placed in mice, kept the look and gene pattern of the source tumors. Gene checks found broken copies of PTCH1 and BCOR, pointing to an active growth signal path. A drug that blocks that path, vismodegib, hit the organoids hard in tests. The team offers these first models as a platform for hunting new treatments.
pmc-12831280:
Hanife Altınışık and four co-authors test a dental filling cement strengthened with fluoride-loaded nanoparticles. Their 2025 study works with glass ionomer cement, a common filling material, and dentin, the tooth layer under enamel. The question is how well the cement grips dentin that decay has already softened, where bonds often fail.

Sixty human molars were split between sound dentin and dentin softened by an acid bath to fake decay. Three cements were compared: the plain one, one with chitosan, and one with chitosan particles carrying fluoride. On sound dentin all three gripped about equally. On softened dentin the fluoride-particle cement gripped far better than the plain one. The plain cement also lost grip on softened dentin, while both modified cements held steady. The authors back the particle version for decayed teeth.
pmc-12831380:
Yao Qin, Yuanyuan Chen, and Qingshan Cai gave an early report in 2025 on a drug plan for hard-to-treat tuberculosis. Some forms of the lung disease no longer respond to the main drugs. The plan adds a drug called delamanid. The team ran a single-group study at one hospital in Hangzhou, China. Patients were treated for twenty-four weeks and then checked.

Twenty-nine patients began, and twenty-six finished the first phase. All who had live germs in their spit at the start were clear by the end of the phase. Lung scans showed clear gains for most. Side effects were common but mostly mild, led by liver test changes and low blood counts. No one died, and most patients had good outcomes at this early check.
pmc-12834180:
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors have changed cancer care, but they are often taken alongside many other drugs, and the combinations can backfire. The authors review how these interactions happen, drawing on a drug interaction database, official drug labels, and the published literature. They separate two families of interaction. One family changes how a drug is absorbed, spread, broken down, and cleared. In the other, two drugs' effects add up, clash, or multiply at the same target.

Interactions of the first kind can arise through direct blocking, chemical modification of enzymes, or changes in gene activity. Either family can push a patient toward toxicity or leave the cancer drug too weak to work. The authors argue that knowing the mechanism behind an interaction helps clinicians adjust doses in advance rather than react to harm. They frame the review as groundwork for safer dosing strategies in patients on these therapies.
pmc-12834880:
Ron Hays and co-authors gather expert views on updating the CAHPS patient experience surveys in a 2025 paper. These surveys are the standard United States tool for rating care, but users question their length, content, and score spread. The team ran a structured Delphi process with twenty panelists, from survey sponsors to patient advocates and federal staff.

Panelists rated forty-six current topic areas as required, optional, or cut, in two rounds with a group discussion between. Agreement tightened across rounds, with rating reliability rising clearly. Comments explained the reasoning behind contested items. The findings give the survey program a grounded agenda for its next revision, balancing what patients must be asked against survey fatigue.
pmc-12835080:
Oh and Heo trace how sleep, smartphone overuse, and depression influence each other over time in Korean teenagers, in a 2025 study. They followed 2,052 adolescents through three yearly waves of a national panel survey, using a statistical model that lets each factor predict the others later.

Poor perceived sleep consistently came first, forecasting later smartphone overdependence and more depressive symptoms. Depression also fed back, predicting worse sleep afterward, while the smartphone link ran mainly through sleep. The authors argue sleep is the central lever: improving it could interrupt the cycle, and they suggest the findings should shape youth mental health policy.
pmc-12835180:
Oya Kahvecioğlu and thirteen co-authors compare kneecaps across hoofed animals in a 2025 study. The kneecap acts as a lever when an animal walks or runs. The team asked whether its shape mirrors how each species moves. Five species took part, from cattle and bison to sheep, goats, and roe deer.

They scanned more than three hundred fifty kneecaps into 3D models. Shape software then charted how the bones differ in form. Cattle stood apart with a distinct shape cluster. Bison overlapped heavily with sheep in shape space. Hooved plant eaters from one family showed wider side growth of the bone. That pattern fits animals that carry heavy loads on their legs. The authors frame shape as a useful clue to movement style.
pmc-12835280:
Khaled Allemailem, Faris Alrumaihi, and Ahmad Almatroudi designed in 2025 a candidate vaccine, on the computer only, against a bacterium that causes bloody diarrhea in poor regions. No strain-specific targets had been well mapped for this germ. Their method sifted the full protein set to find surface proteins that are both harmful and likely to draw an immune reply.

Two proteins passed the screen. Short pieces from them were picked by many immune rules, then joined with a booster piece and linkers into one construct. Modeling gave the construct a sound shape and strong contact with a human immune receptor. Code checks suggested it could be made well in a common lab bacterium.
pmc-12836980:
Zexiong Gong and eight co-authors review how gut microbes may drive nerve pain through the immune system, in a 2025 paper. Neuropathic pain follows nerve damage and resists standard treatment, and its burden grows as chronic diseases spread. The microbes in the gut release small products, including fatty acids, bile acids, and compounds from tryptophan. These products can calm or stir immune activity far beyond the gut.

The review follows how those signals reach immune cells such as macrophages, microglia, and T cells. Several pathways are traced, including ones that switch inflammation on or damp it down. By linking gut chemistry to pain signaling, the authors highlight new treatment ideas that target microbes or their products rather than nerves alone.
pmc-12837080:
Yulong Li, Zhongbao Zhou, Yong Zhang, and Huantao Zong pool trial results on a kidney stone tool in a 2025 paper. Surgeons reach stones through a small back opening and wash the fragments out. A suction sheath pulls the wash out faster, which keeps pressure inside the kidney low. High pressure can drive infection, so the tool may make the surgery safer.

The review gathers ten strict trials with 1,540 patients in total. Suction sheaths were compared with standard sheaths on success and harm. The team split results by the stone-breaking tool used and by stone shape. Pooled proof like this helps surgeons choose gear based on many patients, not one hospital's habit.
pmc-12837180:
Measuring how a child with Guillain-Barré syndrome walks usually takes a motion lab the clinic does not have. Yu-Sun Min tested a pocket alternative in 2025: two smartphones filming the child, with software that turns video into three-dimensional joint angles, no markers on the body. Two cases carry the proof of concept.

One boy's swing and push-off faults, tied to a treatment-related relapse, visibly eased alongside strength and balance gains over six weeks of rehab. A girl with normal strength still showed stiff hip and knee motion the angles caught, matching her balance disorder. Every session fit inside routine clinic time. Min proposes the setup as a low-cost digital biomarker for recovery.
pmc-12842180:
Clara Barragán-Avilez and co-authors study in 2025 whether extracts from avocado plants can kill the young of a mosquito that spreads dengue. The mosquito breeds in the Americas, and the disease it carries has no strong drug treatment and patchy vaccine cover. The insects also grow resistant to common sprays, so new control tools are needed.

The team profiled the plant chemicals in extracts from one avocado type and tested them on mosquito larvae. Plant based killers could offer a greener path than harsh chemicals if they work well. The study checks both what is in the extracts and how strong the killing effect is. Results like these help judge whether a common farm plant could join the fight against a disease that harms many people each year.
pmc-12842680:
Yunchen Yan and co-authors mine a deep sea bacterium in 2025 for new antimicrobial compounds. The strain came from a cold seep, where communities thrive without sunlight, and such places are rich sources of fresh drug leads.

Three known indole compounds were first taken from the strain. Feeding it indole as a building block then yielded two new indole dimers and nine more known compounds. Their structures were solved with spectroscopic tools and light based measures. Some of the compounds strongly blocked a crop fungus at very low doses. One blocked a common hospital germ at an even lower dose, which marks it as a strong lead.
pmc-12843280:
Itaconic acid, a building block for plastics and resins, is brewed by a fungus fed on sugars, and the broth's phosphate level may steer the brew. Ákos Molnár and co-authors test nine phosphate levels in 2025, from near none to plenty, in controlled fermenters. Three levels got a close reading of growth, yield, and gene activity.

Phosphate shaped mainly how much fungus grew, and through that, how much acid each batch yielded. Both too little and too much cut the yield; a middle level gave the best output. A stress gene's activity rose as phosphate fell, hinting at a coping role. The authors conclude phosphate tunes the brew from the side, while deeper limits rule the acid itself.
pmc-12843780:
Virjinia Doltchinkova and co-authors probe bee venom peptide effects on cell membranes in 2025. Melittin, the main peptide in honey bee venom, is a model for how such peptides meet cell surfaces. Red blood cells and liver energy-center membranes are prime early targets.

Charge tracking, bursting tests, transport measures, and microscopy mapped the peptide's action. At low doses it latched onto red cell surfaces by charge and altered proton flow through a key channel protein. Cell shape and a damage marker shifted as well. Energy-center vesicles clumped together under treatment. The authors sketch a charge-based mechanism tied to membrane stability.
pmc-12843980:
Jie Yu and co-authors published a 2025 study of dihydromyricetin, a compound from a vine, fed to dairy cows, and what it did to their gut microbes and metabolite profiles. High-yielding cows carry a heavy metabolic load. It wears down their defenses and sets them up for farm diseases. The compound is known to fight oxidative damage and inflammation in the body, but its use in ruminants was little studied.

The team fed the compound to half of fourteen mid-lactation cows for sixty days, at a small share of the diet. Blood tests showed a rise in one antioxidant defense score. Gut microbe readings showed more of the beneficial kinds: fiber digesters and friendly commensals rose. Metabolite readings in feces and blood shifted too, with a set of named compounds on the rise. The team reads the compound as a support for the health of the cows.
pmc-12844080:
Mengyu Yuan and a large team of co-authors isolated in 2025 a compost bacterium that kills root-knot nematodes and boosts tomato growth. These worms are among the worst crop pests worldwide, and chemical killers face growing limits. The strain came from fermenting mushroom waste. Its broth was tested on worm juveniles and eggs in the lab, then on tomato plants in pots.

The broth killed nearly all juveniles within two days and blocked almost all egg hatching. The strain also makes a growth hormone, iron-scavenging compounds, and frees phosphate for plants. Tomatoes dosed with broth grew far heavier shoots and roots and formed far fewer root galls than water-treated plants. The active compounds survived heat, light, and storage, aiding field use.
pmc-12844280:
Miguel Suárez and co-authors published a 2025 study on death risk in liver cancer tied to alcohol and fatty liver disease. Both causes are now leading sources of this cancer in rich countries. The team wanted to find which facts at diagnosis best predict death, using machine learning tools.

They studied 91 patients from many centers who were diagnosed between 2008 and 2023. Five machine methods were tested, and a random forest model did best by a wide margin. Blood albumin, a ratio that mixes inflammation and albumin, cancer stage, and a liver score were the top factors. A newer liver score beat older forms, while a common tumor marker had little value. The authors say liver health and body inflammation beat tumor markers for early risk calls.
pmc-12845180:
Aşkın Evren Güler, Mehmet Cudi Tuncer, and İlhan Özdemir published a 2025 lab study on pairing a diabetes drug with a standard cancer drug against cervical cancer cells. The diabetes drug, sitagliptin, had shown hints of anticancer action. The team grew HeLa cells, a standard cervical cancer line, and treated them with each drug alone and with both together for 48 hours.

The pair killed far more cells than either drug alone, and math checks confirmed the two drugs amplified each other. The combined treatment raised reactive oxygen levels and pushed more cells into programmed death. It also slowed the cells' movement and spread, and turned down two growth pathways. The authors present the pairing as a candidate for further study, not yet a treatment.
pmc-12846580:
Kuczaj and co-authors check whether one class of immune suppressing drugs changed COVID-19 outcomes for heart transplant patients. Such patients face high infection risk, and this drug class, mTOR inhibitors, might also slow the virus. Their 2025 study follows 556 recipients at one center from 2020 to 2024, matching the drug's users against similar non users.

Infection rates were alike, about a third in each group, and hospital stays did not differ clearly. Overall deaths ran higher among the drug's users, driven by those also on a second drug family. Strikingly, no COVID-19 death occurred in the subgroup on the drug without that partner family. The authors judge the regimen no worse for COVID-19 and flag the subgroup result for more study.
pmc-12847780:
Kevin Albert Kasper and co-authors build a wearable that judges frailty on the device itself, with no cloud and no wearer effort. Constant health tracking makes data floods that clinics cannot digest, and sending data out drains batteries. Their frame pairs clinical-grade signal capture with on-device AI.

The system reads gait, a strong frailty sign, and condenses weeks of signals into clean trends. Trials with sixteen, then fourteen, wearers matched gold-standard tools. Ten-day wear tests ran without any wearer interaction. The authors argue that edge AI of this kind can make long, quiet monitoring practical in real care.
pmc-12847880:
Smith and co-authors explain in 2025 why a NASA alloy, GRX-810, performs so well at extreme heat. Demand is rising for alloys that work past 1100 degrees Celsius yet stay printable. The alloy is strengthened by fine oxide particles and built by additive manufacturing.

Pull and creep tests ran up to about 1316 degrees, in both build directions. Heat cycling and oxidation were compared with top nickel alloys. Atomic scale imaging and modeling trace the edge to unusually fine yttrium oxides formed during printing. Those particles hold strength and slow creep where most alloys fail.
pmc-12849180:
Zareen Kiran and five colleagues compared two diabetes drugs for safety during Ramadan fasting at a single center. Fasting from dawn to dusk destabilizes blood sugar, and sulfonylurea drugs are notorious for causing dangerous lows. The prospective cohort ran from March to June twenty twenty-two. Patients on stable empagliflozin or sulfonylurea regimens, alongside other standard drugs, were followed through the fast. Hospital admissions for hypoglycemia and blood sugar control were the outcomes.

The empagliflozin group reported slightly fewer hypoglycemic episodes, about twenty-seven versus thirty-one percent. Both groups improved their long-term glucose marker significantly and similarly. Women made up sixty percent of the empagliflozin group. For the hundreds of millions who fast with diabetes, even small safety margins matter. This twenty twenty-five study supports preferring the newer drug class when lows are the chief fear.
pmc-12849380:
Cheikh Yebouk and co-authors compile Mauritania's traditional plant medicine into a first pharmacopoeia, in this 2025 review. The desert country sits where sub-Saharan and Arabo-Berber healing cultures meet, yet its plant lore was scattered and under-recorded. The team mined seven decades of studies, theses, books, and folklore.

They catalogued one hundred thirty-three medicinal plants used against seventeen disease groups, led by digestive and skin troubles. Moorish healers hold the deepest documented knowledge, while three other peoples keep distinct, barely studied traditions. The authors call for field work to capture that diversity before it fades.
pmc-12849480:
Laetitia Waast and co-authors set strand-true tests for both read ways of the weak-immune germ's code in sick folks' cells. The study appeared in 2025. Trials watch cell germ code levels to track rest and wake of the germ. The germ also writes in the flip way, goods that can spur or hush its growth.

Two test kits read each way on its own, for main and side germ kinds. Checks proved each kit sees its own way and not the twin. A drop-count form cut spread next to the stock form. Spleen and blood cells from sick folks fed the proof runs.
pmc-12849580:
Aytül Eynur and co-authors measured how much energy women burn during Kangoo Jumps exercise sessions, in a 2025 study. The workout uses springy rebound boots and is done to music in recreational sport settings. Thirteen women took part on a voluntary basis.

A portable gas analyzer tracked oxygen use, heart rate, breathing, and fat burn while the women exercised. Music pace was fixed at two speeds, a slower aerobic phase and a faster anaerobic one. Every measure differed clearly between the phases, from energy rate to carbon dioxide output. The authors judge the workout as a strong energy burner whose load rises steeply with music pace.
pmc-12849680:
The authors compare the fat-carrying particles in the blood of healthy people and of people with type 2 diabetes, with and without heart disease riding along. Diabetes raises heart risk largely through these lipoproteins, and the team asked whether blood pressure trouble or heart disease itself deepens the distortion. Using magnetic resonance profiling, they measured 65 traits of the particles in 393 healthy controls and 390 patients.

Diabetes alone shifted the picture: fats rose inside every major particle class, and the counts of the two lightest particle types climbed. The low-density particles, by contrast, thinned out in number. The design lets the authors separate what diabetes itself does from what its companions add. They frame the particle fingerprint as a finer gauge of heart risk than standard cholesterol numbers.
pmc-12852680:
Maryam Mirarzgar and co-authors study in 2025 how cold and swinging temperatures harm kiwifruit buds and flowers. Their subject is the Hayward type, grown in an orchard near Rasht, Iran. Dormant canes were cut, chilled for a long set period, then exposed to hard cold or to a warm then freezing swing at three growth stages.

Buds were classed as normal, aborted, or misshapen, and tissue slices were checked under a microscope. Cold at later stages caused severe harm, with undone flower parts, cell shrinkage, and dead tissue in food transport strands. Bud loss rose as growth advanced, and swinging heat and cold caused even higher loss at the last stage. Buds kept at steady growth room warmth formed organs normally, marking late stages as the most fragile.
pmc-12853980:
Ahmed Alhadithi and Mohammed Almansour scope the world's literature on teaching medical students to lead and manage. Tomorrow's doctors will run teams, budgets, and systems, yet undergraduate programs teach leadership in wildly different ways. A global map of the frameworks in use was missing.

Searching three databases and gray sources to early 2025, two reviewers screened more than fifteen hundred records. They chart which competency domains the frameworks name, how schools teach them, and how students are assessed. The spread itself is the finding: no shared standard yet. Their synthesis hands curriculum designers the menu of proven approaches, and the case for converging on one.
pmc-12854880:
Wei Li Neo leads a team of seven authors in 2025 in measuring the spray thrown off by ear surgery, and testing a dome that traps it. Drilling the mastoid bone behind the ear, a routine step in ear operations, flings droplets from the surgical field, a contamination route for the whole theater team.

On cadaver specimens, the team drilled under three setups: no microscope, microscope alone, and microscope fitted with their Otodome barrier drape. Fluorescent fluid revealed where the spray landed. Comparing the maps shows how much protection a simple physical barrier buys during high-speed drilling.
pmc-12855980:
Jianghao Pang and co-authors read the full genome in 2025 of a rare tree of China. The tree, Berchemiella wilsonii, is on the national guard list and counts among the land's plants with the tiniest wild stands. Three read methods were joined: long exact reads, short reads, and a map of how the genome folds. The result is a near gap-free set for both copies of the genome.

Each copy spans about twenty-two dozen million letters across twenty-four chromosomes, capped at both ends by the marks of true ends. Checks found near all of a standard gene set in place. More than twenty-two thousand coding genes were named, and near all got a known role. The team says the genome is a first for the species and a base for its guard work.
pmc-12858980:
Yonggan Zhang, Liyong Ge, and Yong Wu tackle false signals in a 2025 radar paper. Passive radar listens with signals from radio or phone towers, which makes it cheap and hard to jam. It needs a clean copy of the source signal, but echoes from targets can leak into that copy.

The leak creates ghost peaks that share a target's speed shift but sit at the wrong range, hiding real targets. The authors trace how the ghosts form and then propose a fix. Their fix checks patterns across many frames and masks suspect spots around strong anchors, avoiding the heavy rebuild steps of older methods.
pmc-12859380:
Harpreet Kaur Mohel and co-authors review the nerve supply of the triceps in a 2025 anatomy paper. Textbooks say the triceps brachii, the big muscle at the back of the upper arm, is fed only by the radial nerve, but dissection and clinical reports keep finding exceptions.

Searching three databases, the team screened hundreds of records and kept twenty-seven studies with human data. The axillary nerve often helps supply the long head, in some populations in over a third of cases. The ulnar nerve sometimes feeds the medial head. Such variation matters when surgeons plan operations or read nerve injuries.
pmc-12859880:
Nirmala Priyadarshani and co-authors adapted a survey on attitudes toward aging into Sinhala in 2025 and checked that it works well. Attitudes to aging shape health, but they vary with culture, so tools must be tested in each setting. The team gave the survey to 185 older adults living in care homes near Colombo, Sri Lanka. They also gave a standard quality-of-life survey for comparison.

The three parts of the survey — loss, growth, and body change — each held together well. Scores lined up with quality-of-life scores as expected. Married people and those with chronic disease scored higher on all three parts. The authors judge the Sinhala version sound for use with older adults in care homes.
pmc-12866580:
Maliheh Alimardani and colleagues measured cancer testis antigens in gastric cancer tissue in a 2025 study. These antigens are normally found only in germ-line cells, the placenta, and cancer cells. That pattern makes them possible targets for cancer vaccines. The team checked three of them: MAGE-A4, LAGE-1, and NY-ESO.

RNA came from fresh tissue samples from 76 patients before any treatment. About one in five tumors showed raised levels of each antigen. Raised NY-ESO was linked to tumor site, depth, and stage. It was also linked to overall survival. The authors say these antigens may help predict outcomes. They may also serve as targets for a gastric cancer vaccine.
pmc-12874680:
Jodi Holtrop, Brooke Dorsey-Holliman, and Alison Hamilton guide researchers through choosing interview-style methods for implementation studies, in a 2025 paper. Their field studies how proven health practices spread into real clinics. Qualitative methods reveal the processes, relationships, and settings that shape that spread. With so many methods on offer, teams often default to a few familiar ones, and guidance for choosing is thin.

The paper starts from the research goal and question type, then lays out method options by their key traits. Decision paths and practical trade-offs are spelled out, with short accounts of the main methods and teaching examples. The authors hope to widen the field's toolkit, matching each study to methods that fit its purpose and budget rather than habit.
pmc-12877180:
Wanghong Shi and a team of co-authors show how lost DNA methylation wakes silent RNAs in a model plant, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Long non-coding RNAs from between genes stir when the methylation guard drops. The team used nanopore reads of both RNA and DNA in mutant Arabidopsis.

They found 340 lincRNAs switched on and 209 held steady against methylation loss. The same patterns appeared in wild plant populations. Fifty data features trained six machine learning models to sort the woken RNAs. The best model scored near-perfect precision, with methylation and jumping genes as top clues.
pmc-12883980:
Bianco and co-authors test plant compounds from the ayahuasca vine against inflammation in nerve cells, with an eye on the brain effects of COVID-19. The vine's beta-carboline alkaloids, harmine and harmaline, are known to calm immune activity. The team inflamed a human nerve cell line with a bacterial toxin, then added the two compounds or a whole vine extract. They also compared cytokine levels in blood from intensive care and ward patients with COVID-19.

The toxin raised two inflammatory signals, IL-6 and TNF-alpha, and both alkaloids cut them back sharply. The extract lowered TNF-alpha and a master inflammatory switch, but not IL-6. The treatments also shifted the expression of virus-entry genes in the cells, in mixed directions the authors report carefully. Blood from intensive care patients showed high IL-6. The authors conclude the compounds show anti-inflammatory promise in this cell model.
pmc-12888680:
Yasmine Khan and co-authors model what delayed breast cancer diagnosis in the first COVID wave may cost Belgium over five years, split by tumor subtype. Screening was halted from March to June 2020, and fear of infection kept women away. In all, 135 invasive cancers went undiagnosed in that window. No stage shift showed in 2020 itself, but missed cancers tend to surface later, at worse stages, with higher costs and worse quality of life.

A Markov model compared two cohorts of 10,147 women: one with the disrupted care of 2020, one following the trends of 2017 to 2019. It projected quality-adjusted life years, direct medical costs, and deaths over five years, from the payer's view. The split by subtype matters, because delay hits fast, aggressive triple-negative cancers harder than slow luminal ones. The study turns a four-month pause into numbers planners can use.
pmc-12903280:
Samuel Azupio and co-authors review calcium-sensing kinases as hubs of plant stress defense in a paper whose head dates it 2025. Plants read drought, salt, and heat partly through calcium pulses in their cells. A family of kinases, the CDPKs, decodes those pulses and answers with phosphorylation.

The kinases close leaf pores, balance ions, and switch on defense genes. They also steer antioxidant systems and cross-talk with other signals. Gene family members split the work, some redundant, some stress-specific. That precision suits crop engineering: tune one kinase, harden one trait. The review weighs prospects for breeding tougher crops as climates swing. Stress-proof harvests start with signals like these.
pmc-12907180:

Subi Gandhi and three co-authors surveyed college students in the summer of 2021, during the early pandemic, about non-prescription drug use. Screening tools measured depression and substance use alongside background questions.

Use was reported more often by male students than female students, at 20.81 against 13.11 percent. Drinking alcohol two to four times a month more than tripled the odds, and being twenty-two or twenty-three nearly quadrupled them against age twenty. Gender, infection history, and housing showed no link. The authors urge targeted support on campuses during crises.
pmc-12913580:
Hadida Yasmin and co-authors studied a complement protein at the meeting point of mother and fetus in preeclampsia, in work published in twenty twenty-five. The protein, properdin, is the only known booster of one arm of the complement immune system. Too much complement activity at that interface can harm the placenta. The team gauged properdin in placenta tissue, blood, and placenta-derived vesicles from affected and healthy mothers.

Affected placentae carried far more properdin, at both gene and protein level, along with two partner complement factors. In blood and vesicles, though, properdin ran lower than in healthy pregnancies. Staining showed it spread through the affected placenta, pooled near knots of dying nuclei. The authors say properdin may help drive complement damage in the placenta and could be part of how this severe condition takes hold.
pmc-12923180:
Amelie Endres and four co-authors set out the plan for a trial that adds memory rework therapy to standard talk therapy for depression, in a protocol from 2025. Many patients carry harsh past memories, often from childhood, that feed their low mood and self views.

In imagery rescripting, a patient recalls a hard memory with a therapist and reshapes it in the mind so its feel and sense change. Sixty six patients in ongoing therapy will get three such sessions or a calm imagery control. Mood scores will be checked at the start, after care, and at two later visits.
pmc-12934280:
Edina Mendelné Pászti and co-authors test which apricot roots and tops survive Hungarian weather in a study of new orchards. Climate shifts threaten apricot profits. Pairing the right rootstock with the right scion may steady yields. A randomized block trial plants the combinations.

Five rootstocks and sixteen scions make nine hundred sixty trees. Spacing is wide, and survival is counted against the starting number for each pairing. Vigorous rootstocks clearly suited the lowland soil and climate better than moderate ones. Their strong root growth kept plantations in condition. Slower roots lagged behind. The trial guides growers choosing pairs for a warming future.
pmc-12935880:
Zheng Yang, Weihong Huang, and Heng Zhang present a study of an explainable deep learning system for reading biosensor data in health checks. Their network reasons over a graph of sensors through time, guided by how the body works, and gives probability based answers. A second mechanism adjusts how fine the diagnosis is, by uncertainty and signal disorder.

On four data sets it beat transformer rivals on accuracy and ranking scores. It also reports how unsure it is, plainly. The authors aim at clinic and wearable use, where a black box verdict is not enough: doctors need to see why, and how much to trust it.
pmc-13064780:
Jacob Appel writes alone in a 2024 essay on advance directives in schizophrenia. People with the illness can state care wishes ahead of crisis through psychiatric advance directives. Unlike medical directives, these remain little used in the United States, and state law caps their force. Appel weighs the evidence for them and the legal and ethical knots they raise.

He argues that fears of patients opting out of care wholesale are likely unfounded. Used well, the documents give weight to a patient's own values at the moment they are least able to speak. The essay speaks to clinicians who balance autonomy against protection daily. It makes a case for wider, careful use of the tool.
pmc-13075380:
Deardorff and nine co-authors build, in 2025 work, a death-risk model for adults in prison, to flag who may need end-of-life care. Locked wards hold many ageing, sick people, yet staff lack a fair way to spot who nears death. A sound model could steer kind care and mercy release calls.

Near ninety thousand adults held a year or more in California prisons fed the build. Facts used spanned age, housing tier, movement limits, hospital use, and long-term ills. Half a percent died of natural causes in two years. The model sorted risk with high skill and matched counts well. At a five percent risk line it caught near half of deaths while wrongly flagging few. The team offers it for care talks.
pmc-13085680:
Satoshi Yamada and co-authors forge a joint score to forecast relapse in a wart-like airway disease, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Records of one hundred twenty-five patients from sixteen Japanese centers split into check and test sets. Virus stains on tissue fed a new tissue score.

Three stain marks, each worth one point, formed the tissue score. Both it and the older clinic score forecast return on their own. Joined, they sorted patients into mild, middle, and severe bands with clear gaps in relapse-free time. Mild cases rarely came back, and severity eased with repeat surgery. Virus grains were seen where one stain lit up. Readers get a sharper forecast for an unruly disease.
pmc-13085980:
Xueying Wang and three co-authors pooled in 2026 the evidence on deep learning for spotting breast cancer spread to armpit lymph nodes. Knowing whether cancer has reached those nodes shapes treatment, yet checking without surgery is hard. The team searched four databases and graded twenty-eight studies covering 20,811 patients. Across all imaging types, the models caught about eighty percent of spread cases and cleared about eighty-five percent of clean ones. CT-based models scored highest, with ultrasound and MRI close behind. Scores for telling the two groups apart were strong throughout. The authors say the tools are ready to support, though not replace, clinical judgment before surgery.
pmc-13086580:
Everyone pictures rushing water when they hear the word flood, yet Mason Majszak, Abdallah Zaki, and Omar Wani argue in this 2026 paper that the term has no settled formal meaning. The authors work at the border of philosophy and water science. They ask what parts of the idea are physical and what parts rest on shared judgments about how things ought to be.

Their answer splits the idea into layers. A physical flood is water pooled or flowing past a set rarity limit, where the limit itself rests on human judgment. Such a flood then counts as welcome or harmful only once people judge the water good or bad. That split, they argue, explains why towns can agree on the water yet disagree on whether to build defenses.
pmc-13089380:
China's elder care talk is being rebuilt around joined-up care, and Yue Zheng and Min Liu map the logic, the blocks, and the paths in work from twenty twenty-six. National policy sets the frame from above, while local pilots tune the service models. The pair call this a two-track drive: policy down, practice up.

Four blocks stand out. Health and elder systems stay split; providers hold uneven power; plans prize buildings over human ties; and users' own voices sit at the edge. The fix, they argue, is to center the elder: give users a formal seat in policy, build knowledge from their side, and judge care by ties as much as by beds.
pmc-13113080:
Irmak Fatoş Korkmaz and four co-authors test whether the anesthetic ketamine can also kill colon cancer cells in a dish. Their 2026 study treats HT-29, a human colorectal cancer cell line, with ketamine for twenty-four hours. A standard viability test measures how many cells live, and flow cytometry counts those entering programmed death.

The title states the outcome: ketamine drove death and slowed growth in these cells. Lab-dish results are a long way from patient benefit, but they flag drugs worth a second look. Anesthetics are given during cancer surgery anyway, so any anti-cancer side effect would be free. The authors frame the work as an early in vitro probe. It joins a wider rethink of what surgical drugs do beyond sleep.
pmc-13117380:
Ana Roque and co-authors test two ways to check children's eyes, with no drops to widen the pupils, in a 2026 study. Good checks help doctors choose care. They used plots of how far apart the two ways fall, plus tests of error size. Next to the first way, the handheld tool gave a clear shift toward short sight for sphere. The team also checked if the match held or changed by type of eye fault. The results help clinics judge which way to trust.
pmc-13118080:
Lingang Yang and co-authors design a shared-aperture antenna array for 5G base stations that spans a very wide frequency range, published in 2026. The low-frequency module uses a two-layer parasitic coupling design, while the high-frequency module uses a slotted patch. Metal baffles around the elements reshape the boundary conditions and block coupling paths between them. In tests, the built prototype covered an even wider range than targeted, with steady gain in both bands and a good match across the whole span. The baffles fixed distortion in the high-frequency radiation pattern, keeping radiation stable and directional.
pmc-13126580:
Seven researchers measure mumps immunity in Kenyan hospital patients in a 2025 paper. Mumps spreads easily and can cause serious illness, despite an effective vaccine. The team tested blood from 451 volunteers at county hospitals in the Coast and Central regions between late 2020 and late 2021.

pmc-13128380:

pmc-13130180:

pmc-13132980:

pmc-13133380:

The authors present 6g as a promising candidate for further work.
pmc-13135580:

The authors call the drug's long-term performance strong against older therapy. They ask for work on predicting who responds best. Protocol tuning is the other open task.
pmc-13137480:
Simon Flügel and co-authors present, in a 2026 paper, a sharper set of definitions for peptides inside a large chemistry database called ChEBI. The database sorts chemical knowledge, but hand sorting cannot keep pace with new findings. Peptides form a huge branch of the database, with nearly fifteen thousand entries.

The team built sixty-seven classes for peptides, with plain-language definitions made more precise than the old ones. Each definition also has a formal logic form that a computer can check. A method turns those forms into an automatic sorter for new compounds. Tests against the current sorting exposed clashes and gaps, and experts rated the new wording in a survey.
pmc-13138080:
Kelly Kan and ten co-authors show that a probiotic yeast can wake a protective gut pathway in celiac disease by teaming with resident microbes, in this 2026 study. Celiac guts mishandle a chemical family from tryptophan that should switch on the AhR defense pathway. In gluten-sensitized mice carrying the human risk gene, the yeast switched that pathway on and eased gluten damage.

The trick needed partners. Patient microbes boosted the pathway only when indole-making bacteria, such as one Lactobacillus species, were present to supply raw material. The authors frame the yeast as fixing a known microbial shortfall in celiac disease. They call for clinical trials, above all for patients who stay ill on a gluten-free diet.
pmc-13139280:
Sahra Kabiri and co-authors test how blood from patients with a rare autoimmune disease attacks the retina's support cells. The team bathed human Müller cells, which manage water and ions in the retina, in serum from three patient groups and from healthy donors. They then measured the cells' key channel and signalling proteins.

pmc-13180880:

Kuan-Jung Lin and co-authors test a compound against stubborn prostate cancer cells in a 2026 laboratory paper. pmc-13184180:

pmc-13185680:

Wen-Xuan Lei and co-authors review brain scans in people with weak muscles and weak thinking, in a 2026 article. Sarcopenia means steady loss of muscle strength, mass, and function with age. Mikaela Bloomberg and co-authors ask whether long-term paths of memory and word skill shape how older adults spend their day. pmc-13188180:
Wenjing Han and co-authors build a model to predict a serious complication after brain tumor surgery in a study published in 2026. pmc-13189080:
Fanjing Wang and co-authors review targets for therapy, how drugs work, and ways to bring drugs to the body, for diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Their 2026 review covers a state that is common in diabetes, and that leaves people weak and in pain.

Brown, McGovern, Schickle, Sharp, and Apprill studied coral microbes in this paper from twenty twenty-six. A temperate coral off the United States East Coast sleeps through winter each year. pmc-13190780:
Alexandra Kautzky-Willer and co-authors present updated guidelines on high blood sugar in pregnancy in this 2026 paper, written in German with an English summary. pmc-13191780:
Mustafa Al Jaafar and Alyaa Aljafr report a case of Klippel-Feil syndrome, the rare condition where neck vertebrae fuse from birth. pmc-13207080:

pmc-13207580:
