pmc-13212680:
Andrew P. Loehrer and a large team map in 2026 where new cancer cases and late-stage diagnoses cluster across Indiana. Knowing whether hotspots for different cancers overlap would help planners aim screening and outreach money.

The study placed more than 130,000 patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2019 onto fine-grained maps for breast, colorectal, and lung cancers. Hotspots for new cases barely overlapped with hotspots for late diagnosis within each cancer type. Late-stage hotspots overlapped somewhat more across cancer types, and incidence hotspots for breast and colorectal cancer overlapped most. The patchwork pattern argues for place-based strategies tailored to each cancer and outcome.
pmc-13213080:
Samhitha Munugoti and co-authors recount in 2026 an extreme case of autoimmune insulin resistance in a 24-year-old man. Antibodies attacked his insulin receptors, and at the peak he needed staggering daily insulin doses while also developing newly discovered lupus.

Standard immune treatments followed one after another, including steroids, several antibody drugs, blood plasma exchange, and immune globulin, yet resistance persisted because long-lived plasma cells kept making the harmful antibodies. A drug aimed at those plasma cells finally turned the course. Insulin needs fell steadily, and seventeen months after he arrived he stopped insulin altogether with normal blood sugar control. The case argues for plasma-cell targeting when usual therapy fails.
pmc-13213280:
Syed Muhammad Raza Abidi and co-authors ask whether brain waves during a long seizure can predict how bad a mouse's later epilepsy will be, in a study from 2026. In this mouse model, a drug shot into the amygdala triggers a long seizure, and repeat seizures follow weeks later. The later burden varies a lot between animals, which hampers drug trials.

The team drew spectral and statistical features from about 40 minutes of brain wave data in 19 mice. Several classifiers trained on those features, checked by cross-validation. A support vector machine did best, with a weighted score of 0.74. It sorted the middle-burden group with care. On a fresh group of 11 mice, though, the forecasts weakened, so wider tests are still needed.
pmc-13213580:
Syeda Sumayya Tariq, Muhammad Salman Haleem, and Reaz Uddin use in 2026 a type of AI that writes new drug shapes the way chat tools write text. Their foe is a germ enzyme that breaks carbapenem drugs, among the last strong antibiotics doctors hold in reserve.

They trained the tool on millions of known compounds. All of the shapes it wrote were sound, most passed the usual rules for drug-like traits, and few raised harm flags. The team then docked the best shapes into the enzyme on a computer and ran long motion sims. Four shapes held firm and gripped the enzyme about as well as a drug now in use. The same path could hunt drugs for other germ enzymes.
pmc-13213780:
Zeaxanthin, a pigment with health value, sits in the skin of chili peppers, but measuring it usually means slow lab chemistry. Liang and co-authors build a camera-based method: multispectral imaging reads the light bouncing off the pepper skin, and a small neural network turns that signal into a pigment estimate. Among four learning methods, the network did best alone.

Adding two lab measures, capsanthin and total carotenoid content, pushed accuracy much higher, with fit values above 0.92. A stripped-down version using a simple red index instead of one lab measure still scored well. The authors offer the method for fast, high-volume screening of pepper quality.
pmc-13215180:
Congcong Gai and colleagues reconstruct in 2026 how the Southern Hemisphere's great westerly winds have shifted their balance over twenty million years. These winds steer moisture, temperature, and ocean circulation, and past warm periods may preview their future behaviour.

Chemical and magnetic fingerprints in South Pacific seafloor sediment reveal where wind-blown dust came from. Until about eight million years ago the dust flew mainly from central South America, helped by a strong subtropical jet in the middle Miocene. Afterwards Australia took over as the dominant source. Climate simulations support the shift. In warm states, the authors suggest, the westerlies grow more lopsided between ocean basins, a feature future projections should capture.
pmc-13215380:
Headlines about trace lead in tampons raised a fair question: how much lead could actually reach the body? Corie Ellison and co-authors answer with lab work plus a mathematical model. They first measured where lead sits in menstrual fluid, finding most of it rides with red blood cells and the rest largely bound to proteins in plasma.

The model then tracked lead through four hours of tampon use: release, spreading in fluid, soak-back into the tampon, and passage through vaginal tissue. Most released lead ended up reabsorbed by the tampon. Under a third of one percent, under a nanogram, could reach tissue. The 2026 study argues context matters more than presence.
pmc-13215880:
Ignas Juodžbalis and co-authors report a 2026 astronomy study that weighs a black hole directly in a distant 'little red dot' galaxy. Such compact red objects are common among early galaxies, and their black hole masses were previously estimated only by indirect formulas.

Gravitational lensing magnified the galaxy, which sits at redshift 7.04, and deep spectroscopy from the James Webb Space Telescope mapped gas motion around its centre. The rotation pattern fits a point mass of about fifty million suns and rules out a dense star cluster as the explanation. Almost no room remains for stars in the host, which suggests a massive black hole seed caught near the start of its growth.
pmc-13216280:
Sandip Mallikarjun Kale and a large team present a 2026 genomics study of hop, the plant that gives beer its bitterness. Most modern cultivars mix European and North American ancestry, yet how each lineage contributes the prized bitter acids was unclear.

The team built chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assemblies of the hybrid cultivar Apollo and painted European or North American ancestry along each chromosome. Some chromosomes showed suppressed mixing between the two origins. Comparing chemistry and genes exposed diversity in the bittering pathways of the two lineages, and beneficial alleles from both sides added up to raise bitter acid content. The authors offer the reference as groundwork for genome-guided hop breeding.
pmc-13217080:
Luke Wilson and co-authors study, in 2026, how tobacco makers in the United Kingdom passed tax rises to shoppers in small stores. Tax works only if prices actually rise, and earlier work on supermarkets found uneven passing. The team used sales data from small retailers over nearly five years, matched with tax rates and area deprivation scores.

For both factory cigarettes and roll-your-own tobacco, prices rose by more than the tax across the whole price range. The extra rise grew with product price in England, Scotland, and Wales. In Scotland, stores in better-off areas passed on more. The results show tax pricing varies by price, place, and neighborhood.
pmc-13217180:
Pongsakornkullachart and colleagues present two case reports where Duchenne muscular dystrophy appeared together with a chromosomal condition. Duchenne dystrophy is an X-linked muscle disease caused by faults in the dystrophin gene. Down syndrome and Turner syndrome are far better known, and each rarely coincides with a single-gene disorder of this kind.

The two cases show how one diagnosis can hide or mimic parts of another. Muscle weakness, growth, and development must be read against both conditions at once. For clinicians, the reports argue for full genetic workups when a child's picture does not fit one label. For families, they show why care plans need both lenses.
pmc-13217880:
Tobit Steinmetz and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, a universal index for how mature antibody-making cells are. The maturity of these plasma cells shapes vaccine success and autoimmune disease. Judging it today is patchy and lab-bound.

The team pooled public human cell-sorting data from vaccination and infection samples. Harmonized marker readings trained a random forest model, which scored strongly in training and held up in testing. The finished index was then applied to bone marrow and gut, where long-lived cells reside. A single ruler for maturity could standardize vaccine studies across labs. It also gives disease researchers a shared yardstick for the cells that keep immunity alive.
pmc-13218980:
Felipe Hernández, André Rubio, and Andrés López-Pérez wrote a 2026 editorial on how invading animals spread germs. Invasive species that adapt well, move far, and breed fast can carry multi-host germs into new ecosystems. That spread, sometimes called pathogen pollution, threatens wild animals, farm animals, and people alike.

The editorial opens a set of four studies on the theme, from different places and settings. One study looks at city rodents as a quiet route for spread. The editors argue for joined watch efforts that treat human, animal, and ecosystem health as one. The set shows why invaders deserve a place in disease planning.
pmc-13219380:
Mesut Aydemir studies exam mode and stress in distance learners in a 2026 paper. Open distance learning widens reach, yet test fear can still bar the way. Fear feeds delay, and delay drags grades. Aydemir asks if online exams soften that chain for learners with disabilities. Data came from 667 undergraduates in a large distance system. Of them, 118 held formal disability notes. Grades came from school records.

The chain held for all: fear fed delay, and delay cut grades. For disabled learners the mode bent the last link. The harm of delay ran strong in room exams and weak in online ones. Gains did not prove cause, since folk chose their mode. Still, the read backs online tests as a kind space that cuts snags. Fair test design, Aydemir says, is part of fair school reach.
pmc-13220080:
Peiran Liao and co-authors introduce a set of studies on new natural products and what those products do. Natural products from plants, microbes, and sea life have long been a rich source of drugs. Much of that chemical space is still unexplored, despite centuries of study.

The set holds five pieces, with two reviews and three research reports. The reviews cover products drawn from classic medicinal herbs. The research pieces report new compounds, their structures, and their effects in tests. Themes run from swelling and oxidation to tumors and metabolic disease. The editors frame the set as a push for clean supply and clear proof of how these compounds work.
pmc-13220380:
Hui Yan and Jia-hong Gao compared two ways to fix a hormone-releasing device inside the womb in 2026. The device treats adenomyosis, a condition where womb lining grows into the muscle wall. If the device slips, treatment fails, so fixation matters.

Forty-two patients at one hospital were split evenly between an anchoring method and a stitching method. The anchoring surgery took about thirteen minutes, less than half the time of stitching. After placement, pain scores and bleeding scores fell in both groups, and blood hemoglobin rose. Womb size also shrank by six months in both groups. Other outcomes are compared across visits at one, three, and six months.
pmc-13220580:
Marcus F. Johansson and colleagues interview Swedish spouses who care for partners with dementia about life and unmet needs in a 2026 study. Most people with dementia live at home, and a spouse is the one holding their life together, at a cost to the carer's well-being. Services built without hearing carers risk missing what would help.

Twenty-four spouses took part in interviews, analyzed thematically. Two themes organize the findings. The first, being consumed by caring, describes the slide from partner to carer and the feeling of confinement. The second, longing to be seen and feel supported, captures what carers ask for: acknowledgment of their situation as people in their own right, and care good enough for their partner. The couple's needs are inseparably tangled. The authors recommend professionals protect the spouse's sense of self and treat the couple, not the patient alone, as the unit of care.
pmc-13221880:
Pamela Lutsey and co-authors present a 2026 study on blood thinners for cancer patients with venous clots. Cancer raises clot risk, and the choice among oral anticoagulants can change the odds of bleeding or death. The team compared apixaban, rivaroxaban, and warfarin in older Americans on Medicare.

They identified over 30,000 patients aged 65 and up who filled a prescription between 2011 and 2019. Within six months, 634 suffered a hospital-level bleed and nearly 6,000 died. Apixaban carried a lower bleeding risk than rivaroxaban overall, with a hazard ratio of 0.68. The pattern held across most cancer sites. Warfarin users formed the largest group, a legacy of older practice. The results can steer first-choice prescribing.
pmc-13221980:
Rida Assaf, Basel Fakhri, and co-authors predict bacterial operons, groups of genes switched on together, by turning gene data into text for a language model, in a 2026 paper. Knowing operons helps researchers reconstruct pathways and guess gene functions. Older tools lean on rigid hand-built features or curated networks, which fail on poorly annotated genomes.

Their method writes each pair of neighboring genes as a short natural-language description covering orientation, gap length, base composition, annotations, protein families, and conservation. A RoBERTa model then judges whether the pair belongs to one operon. The model held up across six bacterial genomes, including tests that leave one species out entirely, and stayed stable when some features were removed at test time.
pmc-13222580:
Cheng-Wei Lu and Kuo-Chen Chang write a 2026 letter raising unaddressed biases in a study of anticoagulant prevention in trauma patients. Their central concern is uneven imaging: patients given anticoagulation received far more leg ultrasounds and chest CT rechecks than the comparison group. Finding more clots in the more-scanned group may reflect looking harder, not treatment failure.

Selection bias compounds the problem, since clinicians gave the drug to older, longer-staying, higher-risk patients by judgment rather than chance. Standard regression cannot fully undo that sorting, Lu and Chang argue, suggesting matching or weighting methods instead. Blinded outcome checks and complete-imaging subgroups would also help. The letter urges readers to discount the reported event gap accordingly.
pmc-13222780:
Selene Cipri and co-authors present a 2026 case report of a child carrying a newly found harmful variant in the POT1 gene. The gene guards telomeres, the caps on chromosome ends, and inherited faults in it cause a rare syndrome that predisposes families to tumours. The young patient developed two cancers early: a high-grade brain tumour and a kidney cancer.

The team characterized the case in molecular detail and placed the variant within the known syndrome. Early onset of several primary tumours is the syndrome's hallmark, and this variant had not been reported before. Documenting it widens the map of the condition and sharpens screening advice for families who carry such faults.
pmc-13222980:
Fabian M. Wedmann and colleagues studied heat and mental health care in Bolzano, Italy, in 2026. Heatwaves are growing more frequent and intense across Europe. Long heat exposure may worsen psychiatric symptoms. It may also raise demand for urgent mental health care. The team gathered daily emergency psychiatric consultations for three separate years. They added daily admissions to acute psychiatric wards. Weather records came from the provincial environment agency. Time-series models tested several heat measures.

Models with weekday patterns fit the data best. Adding a cumulative heatwave measure improved fit in every year. Single-day high or low temperatures did not help. Heatwave duration beat isolated heat peaks as a predictor. No yearly seasonal pattern explained the effect. The authors read heat as an independent driver of demand. They urge mental health services to plan for climate change. Early warning systems should trigger extra readiness, they say.
pmc-13224680:
Rodrigues and co-authors test in 2026 whether a bedside chest imaging method can spot lung clots fast, without a risky trip to the scanner. The method maps air and blood flow from skin electrodes, and the team added a wasted ventilation index that flags air reaching lung zones with no blood. Piglets with blocked lung arteries served as the test bed, checked against contrast scans.

The index was tuned on over a hundred animal cases, then tried in patients with acute breathing failure and in a chronic clot group. Accuracy in both settings is the paper's core report. The target users are intensive care teams who must rule clots in or out quickly.
pmc-13226780:
Prabha M. Kumarage, Sachini Gunasekara, and Mirka Saarela describe a 2026 dataset of Reddit discussions about generative AI in education, gathered between September 2022 and October 2025. The window brackets the public launch of ChatGPT, letting researchers watch debate evolve. Posts came from 320 education-related communities, then were cleaned to strip names and details.

The release holds 984 original posts and 8,346 comments, each labelled by stakeholder group: students, educators, or parents. Each item carries details of community, time, and response counts. Because the material is openly shared with privacy care, other teams can reproduce or extend studies of how teaching, learning, and assessment are being renegotiated in public conversation.
pmc-13226880:
Thandazile Sibindi, Jennifer-Anne Chipps, and Talitha Crowley survey a 2026 study of primary-care nurses in South Africa's Western Cape on climate change and health. Nurses stand on the front line for heat, drought, and storm-related illness, yet evidence from lower-income settings is scarce. About three quarters knew about climate change, mainly through television and social media. Two thirds had personally lived through extreme weather, and three quarters had treated climate-sensitive illness, especially respiratory problems. Concern and motivation ran high, but climate-friendly habits were far commoner at home than at work, and very few nurses spoke with policy makers. The authors call for stronger institutional backing.
pmc-13227080:
Israa A Serhal, Reem Al Makari, Ali Kallas, and Ghenwa K El Dakdoukii describe a two thousand twenty-six case report of a toe cancer disguised as infection. A seventy-eight-year-old farmer had a persistent sore between her toes. Imaging suggested deep infection and possible bone involvement.

Virus typing detected human papillomavirus type six, usually classed low-risk. Stubborn toe lesions in older patients deserve biopsy before assumptions harden, the authors warn.
pmc-13227280:
Akram Khezri and colleagues test a 2026 plant-based stand-in for gelatin in dairy desserts, made by treating potato starch with ozone. Ozone is a clean oxidising agent, and the team combined it with preheating and tuned starch levels to minimise weeping and maximise firmness. The optimised starch then fully replaced gelatin alongside carrageenan in a semi-solid dessert at several ratios.

The best blend used the highest starch level with the lower carrageenan level. Its hardness and gel strength closely matched the gelatin control, and weeping fell to control-like levels as starch rose. Tasters rated flavour on par with the original, with only small texture and colour differences. Firmness measurements showed a slightly stronger, still elastic gel, supporting the swap.
pmc-13228080:
Haruka Nakagawa Kamura and co-authors build a steady plasmid tool for fair tests of antibiotic resistance enzymes. Their twenty twenty-six paper tackles beta-lactamases, enzymes that break key antibiotics. Past tests cloned the gene into random carriers, so enzyme levels varied and studies clashed.

Their mini F plasmid sits at one to two copies per cell, a fixed low dose. A tac promoter, a ribosome start site, and terminators were added for controlled output. With the dose held steady, drug tests read the enzyme true reach rather than the carrier noise. Labs gain a shared bench tool for comparing new resistance enzymes as they emerge.
pmc-13229280:
Daniel P. In lung cancer, excess tagging by this enzyme marks immune cells for death, helping tumours evade attack. Knowing the fleeting shape the enzyme and its target adopt mid-reaction is the key to designing blockers.

The team combined kinetic isotope effects, which track atomic motion during the reaction, with computational chemistry to reconstruct that transition state. The resulting structure explains the enzyme's chemistry step by step. It also supplies the blueprint for transition-state analogues, molecules shaped like the fleeting form that should bind tightly and shut the enzyme down.
pmc-13229380:

One, called m54.5, sits inside the gene for the virus's DNA-copying enzyme, a stretch few expected to hold a second gene. Its protein moves to the cell nucleus. There it binds the cell's own protein-disposal machine and a partner enzyme.

Adding the protein on its own froze cells at the first growth stage and piled up the disposal machine's targets. A virus stripped of the gene grew at normal speed in dishes, but fared a bit worse in mouse lungs two weeks after infection. The twenty twenty-six study shows that even a virus's most basic gene can hide a second tool, one that bends the host cell cycle to the virus's ends.
pmc-13229780:
Yanan Deng and co-authors pool the trials on exercise for postmenopausal women losing muscle in this 2026 review. Sarcopenia, the age-linked drain of muscle and strength, hits women harder after menopause as hormones fall. Exercise is the standing prescription, but its true yield in this group was unsettled.

Seventeen randomized trials with 744 women made the cut. Pooled results showed real gains in the muscle mass index, in grip and knee extension strength, and in walking speed, a timed stand-and-go test, and one-leg balance. Body mass index did not move, a reminder that the change is in muscle, not weight. The authors back structured exercise as standard care for these women, woven into clinic routines rather than left as advice.
pmc-13230280:
Pedro Henrique Furst Leite and colleagues test in 2026 whether one hormone injection can replace two before radioiodine treatment for thyroid cancer. The standard plan gives two daily shots of lab-made thyroid stimulating hormone so leftover thyroid tissue absorbs the treatment. Because the drug is costly, the team tried a single shot in eighty-eight patients.

Every patient reached the target hormone level needed for treatment after the single dose. Age and body weight each helped predict how high the level rose the next day. Patients could keep taking their usual thyroid hormone pills, avoiding the strain of stopping them. Trials that follow cancer outcomes over time are still needed before the cheaper plan becomes routine.
pmc-13231280:
Cheng Zhang and colleagues build in 2026 a gene control network in blood that may help explain rheumatoid arthritis. Circular RNAs, micro RNAs, control factors, and standard genes can sponge and tune each other, shaping immune activity. Public datasets for each layer were pulled together and filtered for changes seen in patients.

Hundreds of changed molecules in each layer narrowed to a small starting network after cross-checking several databases. Lab tests in arthritic rats checked the shortlisted parts in blood, and most matched the dataset patterns. One micro RNA did not hold up and its branch was cut, leaving a tighter final network. The map nominates a focused biomarker set for follow-up, without proving that the sponge effects cause disease.
pmc-13232280:
Yiming Wang and colleagues test in 2026 how the brain keeps vision steady across the quick eye jumps called saccades. Before each jump, some vision cells shift their sensing zones toward where the eyes will land. Uneven zone sizes across the visual field raised a puzzle about how updating stays uniform everywhere.

Their circuit model predicted that true uniform updating in visual space would leave zone sizes unchanged during the shift. Updating measured in brain space instead would stretch or shrink the zones. Recordings from two brain areas matched the first pattern, with shift sizes alike for cells at varied positions. Checks confirmed zone sizes held steady during remapping, supporting a circuit that protects stable sight across every jump.
pmc-13232780:
Dimitrios Zikos and colleagues comment in 2026 on a hybrid method for mapping huge, messy literatures such as social media health studies. Classic mapping tools match exact keywords, which splits one idea across many synonyms and leans on hand-set cutoffs. The study under discussion replaces word matching with meaning vectors from biomedical language models.

Citation-aware and medical text models place papers in a meaning space, then clustering groups true neighbors without forced borders. Statistical checks come first, with large language models used later for reading and synthesis. Time patterns in the map could help judge public health campaigns after the fact. The price is a computing skill bar that many health teams do not yet clear.
pmc-13233380:
Shuo Ma, Zhiqing Zhang, and Qi Yuan study why retired Chinese professors volunteer to teach in a 2026 paper. Silver-age teachers bring deep experience to regions short on staff. Policy makers puzzle over why some stay on after their terms while others leave.

Blending two behavior theories, the team surveyed program teachers through chain referral sampling. Personal norms sat at the center, carrying the effect of other factors into teaching intent. Seeing the problem, believing the work helps, and feeling peer approval all strengthened those norms. Belief in impact also lifted peer approval itself. The findings map a path from outside views to inner duty to action.
pmc-13233580:
Bjørnar Berg and colleagues published a 2026 prediction study on recovery after surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis, a narrowing of the spinal canal that is a leading reason for spine operations. Results vary widely between patients, so the team built models forecasting disability and pain twelve months after surgery. Development used Norway's spine registry, with more than thirty thousand patients.

The finished models were then tested in Swedish and Danish registries covering tens of thousands more patients. Simple linear regression predicted the main disability score with average errors around twelve to thirteen points, and fancier machine learning brought no clear gain. Because the models held up across three countries, the authors offer them for shared decision-making conversations before surgery.
pmc-13233980:
Jared D W Price and colleagues published a 2026 cancer study hunting for weaknesses that appear only when a cancer switches its telomerase enzyme back on. Nearly all cancers reactivate telomerase to keep their chromosome ends intact, yet blocking the enzyme itself has disappointed. The team used a dosage-lethality screen with CRISPR and gene silencing across matched cell pairs that differed only in telomerase expression, then checked the hits in animals and patient-derived mini-organs.

One gene, FTSJ3, stood out. It chemically decorates the telomeric RNA called TERRA, keeping that RNA stable. Removing FTSJ3 unraveled the protective wrapping at chromosome ends, causing genome instability and death in telomerase-positive cancer cells while sparing normal ones. The authors nominate this RNA-editing step as a drug target.
pmc-13234080:
Danielle R Lavage and colleagues published a 2026 letter reporting a study of simpler machine learning for sepsis, the life-threatening reaction to infection. Clinicians increasingly use complex models to sort sepsis patients into subtypes, yet black-box tools sit awkwardly at the bedside. The team asked whether regression models built on Boolean logic, simple and/or combinations of yes-no conditions, could match heavier machine learning.

Their target was the delta subtype, the SENECA grouping tied to the worst outcomes and distinct treatment responses. Models trained on more than twenty thousand health records from twelve Pittsburgh hospitals. They then faced a later test set of over forty-three thousand records, plus an outside cohort of about a thousand patients. The letter frames parsimony as the prize: a subtype rule a clinician can actually hold in mind.
pmc-13234680:
Hot acid water, like that in power plants, eats most lab electrodes before a test can finish. Muna Abdulaziz and co-authors test a platinum film built for that harsh bath in a 2026 study. The film sits on sapphire, with a tantalum layer below and a sealed edge cap.

Samples sat in sulfuric acid at 200 degrees under their own steam pressure. Both plain and heat-treated films kept over 80 percent of their active area after stress cycles. Surface scans tracked small shifts in chemistry and shape. Past work on such films stayed at far milder heat. The result is a first step toward reusable sensors for hot water systems.
pmc-13234980:
Zhuangyue Lu and co-authors grew in 2026 pine seedlings in soils representing worsening rocky desertification of karst land in southwest China. Such land has shallow, nutrient-poor soil that limits plant recovery. Yunnan pine is a native tree widely planted to restore these sites. One-year-old seedlings spent sixty days in control soil or in soil from lightly, moderately, or severely degraded sites.

Growth held up under light degradation but fell progressively as conditions worsened. Under light stress, seedlings stored more soluble sugar relative to starch, a shift that may aid flexibility. Nutrient ratios differed sharply between roots, stems, and needles, pointing to nitrogen shortage overall. Severe stress lowered potassium and sodium while some other minerals accumulated in stems and needles. The authors describe a coordinated carbon, nutrient, and ion response that fails as degradation deepens.
pmc-13235380:
Jahidul Haque Chaudhuri and Dhiman Chatterjee studied in 2026 a water treatment reactor that uses collapsing bubbles to break down pollutants. Hydrodynamic cavitation forces water through a shaped opening, creating vapour bubbles whose collapse releases intense local energy. Computer simulations first optimized the opening shape for strong collapse at low energy cost. Experiments then filmed bubble behaviour and tracked removal of a blue dye.

A cloud cavitation pattern, with bubbles shedding and collapsing in cycles, gave the greatest treatment potential. Pressure swings in the flow matched closely with how much dye lost its colour. That link offers a cheap, fast way to predict reactor performance without chemical sampling every time. Energy use per litre compared favourably with published reactors at similar dye removal. The authors present the design as a strong candidate for scaling up wastewater treatment.
pmc-13235480:
Seddio and co-authors studied surgery outcomes, published in 2026, for back patients with a history of incarceration. Each year, nearly 700,000 people leave United States correctional facilities. They carry heavier disease burdens and face thinner access to care than most. Whether that history worsens results after common back surgery was unknown. The team used a large national insurance claims database to find patients who had a single-level disc operation between 2016 and 2023.

Patients with an incarceration history used more opioid pain relief after surgery. They also visited emergency departments more often and suffered more adverse events. The authors frame the history as a marker of unmet need rather than a personal failing. Knowing the risk lets surgical teams plan stronger follow-up and support for this group. The study adds spine care to the list of fields where reentry health gaps show up.
pmc-13235580:
Seven researchers test orchid stem residue as a chicken feed additive in a paper from 2026. The residue comes from a Dendrobium orchid used in traditional products. Sixty-three broilers ate a plain diet or one with raw or fermented residue for forty-five days. Early growth slowed on both residue diets, though the gap vanished later. Roasted breast meat was then tested for texture, oxidation, and flavor chemistry.

Both residue diets cut a key oxidation marker in the roasted meat. The fermented form shifted flavor the most, raising aldehyde share sharply. Chemical profiling found fifty-two differing metabolites. Docking tests suggested aroma compounds fit smell receptors well. The authors see value in a waste stream, with flavor gains.
pmc-13236680:
Donghai Wang and co-authors studied in 2026 children in southwest China with a long-lasting bacterial chest disease that causes chronic wet cough. The rule combined pneumococcal disease, a very high share of one white cell type in lung fluid, and prior inhaled steroid use. The authors call for more research in lower-income settings.
pmc-13237380:

That is a distinct lesson from safety that merely happens. Knowing its wiring helps explain how animals learn to repeat what protected them, a core of adaptive behaviour.
pmc-13239280:

Reports from 2016 to mid-2024 covered people aged six to twenty-nine. He counted eleven serious cases among more than fourteen thousand adverse event reports for this vaccine and compared reporting proportions against all other vaccines.

Most cases occurred ten to thirty days after vaccination, more in females, and none died. pmc-13239480:
Silvia Turco and colleagues compare DNA barcoding choices for mapping fungi living on potato plants in a 2026 methods study. Researchers read a gene region called ITS to name fungi, but they can target its first part, second part, or full length, and the choice shapes what they find.

Using two sequencing technologies on leaf and root samples, the team saw clear differences between markers. The second segment gave the richest, most even picture in leaves, while full-length reads suited roots better. The first segment recovered many reads yet skewed heavily toward the host plant itself. Combining markers, they conclude, captures the community most completely.
pmc-13239680:
Patel and co-authors weave a blood pressure skills module into health courses in a 2026 study. High blood pressure drives deaths worldwide, yet trainees often measure it sloppily for lack of standard teaching and practice.

Medical and assistant students took an association e learning module beside normal coursework. Pre and post surveys plus observed exams show knowledge and confidence rose sharply in both groups. Skill at spotting accuracy pitfalls and at the technique itself improved, and live exams confirmed cleaner technique and patient talk. The authors back structured practice as part of core training.
pmc-13239880:
Xiaoxiao Wang and co-authors review how to manage low blood cell counts in people with chronic liver disease, in a 2026 paper. Low platelets and low white cells are common once scarring of the liver advances. They raise the risks of bleeding and infection and can delay other treatments. Several causes stack up: a swollen spleen traps cells, the liver makes less of the growth signals, the bone marrow is suppressed, and the immune system destroys cells.

Treatments range from platelet transfusion and spleen procedures to drugs that mimic or trigger the body's own growth signals. Each carries trade-offs, including a risk of blood clots with some newer drugs. The authors argue care should be tailored to the patient's stage, cause, main driver, clot risk, and the urgency of planned procedures. They call for studies on risk-based treatment plans and the long-term safety of new agents.
pmc-13239980:
Hiroko Hasegawa and colleagues revisit a stomach sarcoma case with deeper genetic testing in a 2026 report. The tumour belonged to a recently recognised subtype where the CIC gene fuses with DUX4, a rearrangement that makes the cancer aggressive and easy to confuse with Ewing sarcoma under the microscope.

Broad genomic profiling of the removed tumour confirmed the fusion and pinned down the diagnosis. Treatment followed Ewing-style chemotherapy regimens and produced brief responses, yet the cancer quickly became resistant and progressed. The authors argue that early comprehensive gene testing is essential for such rare tumours, and that new treatment approaches are badly needed.
pmc-13240080:
Sam Pepper and co-authors compare who gets CAR-T cell therapy in Kansas through trials versus standard care. Their 2026 study covers patients treated for blood cancers at the University of Kansas cancer center and health system. CAR-T is a costly, complex treatment made from a patient's own immune cells, and reaching the center can be hard for rural families.

Records show about eight in ten patients came from urban areas, and just over half lived within fifty miles of the center. Rural patients made up one fifth of both groups. The team checked gaps by race, sex, age, and local doctor shortages. Their aim is a clear map of where access to this advanced care falls short.
pmc-13240380:
Juuso Rissanen and co-authors test whether insulin resistance changes how hard exercise feels or how well the brain is supplied with oxygen in a 2026 study. Forty-eight healthy premenopausal women completed a full cycling fitness test while researchers tracked heart function and oxygen levels in the front of the brain.

Women with higher insulin resistance reported the same effort levels and showed the same brain oxygen responses as women with lower resistance. Brain oxygen readings also failed to track either insulin measures or how steeply effort rose. What did predict a faster rise in perceived effort was a higher body mass index and poorer lung function. The authors conclude insulin resistance itself leaves these responses untouched.
pmc-13240580:
Dat Tran and co-authors review dose math for brachytherapy past the long standard water based rule. Their review from 2026 notes that the TG-43 rule treats tissue as plain water, missing scatter limits and tissue variety. Model based methods and Monte Carlo simulation count real tissue, scatter, and shield loss instead.

A guided search of one database found 284 records, and forty two full studies fit the rules. Each compared at least two of the three routes in pelvis, breast, or head and neck care. Gaps between the old rule and the tissue aware routes swung with tissue type, scatter, and source shape, with no steady tilt. In near uniform soft tissue the old rule mostly over read target dose.
pmc-13240780:
Song Zhu and colleagues offer a 2026 review of CRISPR tools for studying RNA control networks in prostate cancer. RNA molecules help drive this cancer, yet their roles are tangled and hard to map. Gene editing systems now let researchers switch RNA-related genes on, off, or edit the RNA itself.

The review covers several RNA classes, including messenger RNA, small regulatory RNAs, circular RNAs, and long non-coding RNAs. It links these molecules to cancer growth, spread, and drug resistance. Newer strategies include RNA editing with Cas13, targeted delivery systems, and vaccines built from messenger RNA. Remaining hurdles involve safe delivery and personal fit. The authors frame CRISPR-RNA work as a foundation for precision treatment.
pmc-13240880:
Shou's team at Huanghuai University examined how adding yttrium changes the ratcheting behavior of magnesium under uneven cyclic loads. Ratcheting, a creeping strain buildup, shortens the life of loaded parts. Pure magnesium proved stronger in a single static pull. The alloy behaved very differently once loading repeated.

The magnesium-yttrium alloy accumulated ratcheting strain far more slowly and grew harder as cycles mounted. Its fatigue life grew much longer as a result. Electron microscopy showed dense tangles of unusual dislocations spreading deformation evenly. The authors present yttrium alloying as a route to fatigue-resistant magnesium parts.
pmc-13240980:
Rozenblit, Labkoff, and Safran argue that health data governance must stretch from data stewardship to model stewardship. Their commentary answers recent warnings about AI built on electronic health records. Rules written for secondary data use assume data stays put. Trained models instead travel, carrying local clinical habits as portable artifacts.

That portability, the authors contend, breaks the old governance frame categorically. A model can outlive its dataset and spread one hospital's patterns everywhere. Drawing on two decades of stewardship design, they propose governing the model itself. Oversight should follow the artifact, not just the records behind it.
pmc-13241480:
Draganov and colleagues reported in 2021 that ivermectin could turn cold breast tumors hot. Their npj Breast Cancer paper claimed synergy with immune checkpoint blockade. The journal's editors have now pinned an Editorial Expression of Concern to that article. The notice signals unresolved questions about the paper's reliability.

Expressions of concern alert readers while editors weigh evidence and possible further action. The paper put forward combining ivermectin with checkpoint immunotherapy for breast cancer. No verdict on the findings accompanies this notice. Readers are directed to treat the original results with caution pending resolution.
pmc-13241580: Kinjo's team at Tokyo Women's Medical report a case of adenosine-sensitive focal atrial racing arising years after a Fontan operation. Catheter mapping placed the focus on the crista terminalis, close to the sinus node. Heat ablation ended the racing. The authors caution that later Fontan rework or a Maze operation could miss this focus. They urge ablation for such rhythm faults before any rework is tried.
pmc-13242180:
Malek Baroudi and others put out a 2026 study testing software pipelines for gene activity data. RNA reading produces huge data sets for study. Many pipeline mixes exist for handling them. Weak living signals are easy to lose. The team studied faint effects like low-dose radiation.

Ninety pipelines were tested on rat, zebrafish, and mouse data. One ranking method set results against a trusted lab test. Another used machine learning to split dose groups. Joining both gave a fuller picture of results. The best pipeline recovered key workings of living cells. The study guides teams facing faint signals.
pmc-13242380:
Faraj and McCutcheon at MD Anderson review how radiosurgery for pituitary adenomas quietly erodes hormone function. Focused beams control leftover or returning tumors well. Hormone calm in secreting tumors, though, can lag years behind surgery. The review weighs how often it strikes, who is at risk, and shielding plans.

Gland failure strikes between a fifth and a half of treated patients. Damage lands on the hypothalamus, gland, or stalk, with axes failing in shifting order. Shortfalls may surface years later, so hormone checks must last for life. Sharper imaging cuts, careful dose tuning, and gland shifting reduce stray exposure.
pmc-13242780:
Henning Schäffler and co-authors publish a 2026 national survey of training and confidence in reading fetal heart monitoring traces in Germany. Cardiotocography guides labor care, yet interpretation varies between clinicians. The survey asked midwives, doctors, and trainees about scoring systems, teaching, and self-rated confidence.

Over a thousand professionals responded, and nearly all used the monitoring routinely. One global scoring system dominated. Formal training coverage split sharply by profession: most midwives had it during training, while very few junior doctors did, leaving them to learn from colleagues. Fewer than half of junior doctors reported a structured start in the delivery room. Confidence was only moderate across groups, and nearly everyone wanted structured repeat training.
pmc-13243980:
Lisa Connery and co-authors report glycemic control by final dose in a trial of weekly insulin efsitora for insulin-naïve type 2 diabetes. Their 2026 paper analyzes a phase 3 trial that used a fixed-dose titration scheme.

The weekly insulin had matched daily insulin glargine on blood sugar reduction over fifty-two weeks. Doses came in fixed steps, adjusted every four weeks toward a fasting glucose target. About three hundred treated participants were grouped by their dose at the final week. Baseline traits and outcomes were compared across those groups. The question is practical: who ends up needing the top dose, and how well does each dose level control sugar.
pmc-13245680:
A nerve-sheath tumor in the rectum usually announces a genetic syndrome, which makes a lone one, in a patient with no syndrome, a diagnostic puzzle. Karam Karam and six co-authors report such a case in 2026: a twenty-six-year-old man with vague abdominal pain and a small growth under the rectal lining.

Scope-guided removal and lab work confirmed an isolated rectal neurofibroma, a benign tangle of nerve cells and fibers. Gut neurofibromas almost always ride with neurofibromatosis type 1, and the mimic list includes stromal tumors and schwannomas, so tissue proof mattered. The authors review what is known about these rare loners, including their molecular roots and the open question of malignant potential.
pmc-13247580:
Md Robiul Awoal and co-authors published a 2026 dataset of mango leaf photographs for use in classifying leaf diseases by machine. Mango farms in Bangladesh lose yield and fruit quality to leaf diseases. Spotting a disease early can stop its spread and save the crop.

The leaves were collected in Naogaon District, a major mango-growing area in the north of the country. Photographs were taken in natural daylight, so the true appearance of each leaf is preserved. The set holds close to five thousand raw photographs in five groups. One group is healthy leaves. The other four are diseases: anthracnose, powdery mildew, leaves that turn brown, and gall midge, a pest that swells the leaf. The team offers the set as a foundation for systems that can flag leaf diseases in the field.
pmc-13247680:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes issued this 2026 safety opinion in the EFSA Journal on extending the approved uses of a food enzyme. The enzyme, beta-galactosidase, breaks down lactose and is produced by a genetically modified Bacillus licheniformis strain for the company Novozymes. It had already passed safety evaluation for one manufacturing process, and the applicant wanted two more processes covered.

The panel recalculated how much of the enzyme Europeans would eat under all three processes, estimating worst-case exposure in milligrams of total organic solids per kilogram of body weight per day. Combining that exposure estimate with the earlier toxicology evaluation, the panel concluded the enzyme raises no safety concern under the revised conditions of use. Such opinions are the scientific basis on which European regulators approve food enzymes.
pmc-13248380:
Wanghong Su and co-authors present a study dated 2026 on mouth health and muscle loss in rural western China. Sarcopenia, the age-linked loss of muscle and strength, drives decline in older adults. Whether poor oral health feeds into it was unclear.

The team surveyed adults aged forty-four to ninety in poor villages between December 2024 and January 2025. In all, 263 people took part, with a mean age near sixty-four. Oral frailty and sarcopenia risk were scored with standard short scales. Body composition, grip strength, and walking speed were measured directly. Statistical models then linked mouth health to muscle risk. A mediation analysis tested whether muscle mass, physical performance, or diet carried the effect.
pmc-13248780:
Tiglao and Adao hunted for free-living amoebae in tap water in Quezon City, Philippines, reported in 2026. These microbes live widely in water and soil, and some can infect people or shelter harmful bacteria. The pair sampled twenty-six faucets in homes, laboratories, restrooms, and public parks, then identified what grew using shape and DNA sequencing.

Sixteen faucets, about three in five, carried amoebae. Twenty-one isolates were named, most often Vermamoeba vermiformis, with several other genera appearing once each. Two isolates defied identification. Given the high hit rate, the authors urge routine monitoring of city water systems to protect public health.
pmc-13248980:
Hadžić and colleagues reviewed how obesity changes asthma and its newest treatments, in a 2026 narrative review. Fat tissue presses on the lungs mechanically and stirs body-wide inflammation and metabolic trouble, creating a distinct obese asthma pattern. That pattern often responds unevenly to standard care, so the team examined how biologic drugs perform in heavier patients.

Obese patients more often show a neutrophil-heavy inflammation type that many biologics do not target. Results vary by drug, with tezepelumab showing the broadest benefit so far. The authors also note promise in diabetes drugs that aid weight loss, and they call for trials designed around obese patients, including better dosing and marker studies.
pmc-13249780:
Treittinger and co-authors probe how fast mental control adapts when task rules flip, in a 2026 psychology study. In Stroop tasks, where a color word must be named by its ink, interference shrinks when clashes are frequent. Earlier work found adaptation lands quickly in one direction and sluggishly in the other, an asymmetry the team tested with every participant experiencing both switches across four experiments.

Practice effects, from simple speeding to item-specific learning, repeatedly masked or mimicked the asymmetry in the color-word version. A cleaner face-name version, with fresh stimuli for the second switch, showed the lopsided adaptation clearly and in either order. The authors discuss what this stiffness means for theories of mental flexibility.
pmc-13249880:
Zhu and a Chinese team built an artificial eye material that adapts to light like a real retina, in a 2026 Nature Communications study. Their device pairs titanium dioxide with a conductive polymer whose electrical behavior shifts as it absorbs or releases water. Heat from incoming light tips that water balance, dimming the device's sensitivity in bright scenes and boosting it in dark ones, with no control circuitry needed.

Arrays of the devices fed a neural network that recognized images under mixed lighting, bright and shadowed in the same frame, with accuracy above ninety-one percent. The authors propose the self-adjusting sensor for self-driving cars and humanoid robots that must see across harsh, uneven light.
pmc-13250380:
Yılmaz and colleagues test whether blood group predicts survival after surgery for early-stage colon cancer. Their 2026 Cancer Management and Research study reviews one hundred fifty-eight patients with stage two or three tumors treated at one center between 2016 and 2024. Blood group antigens can affect cell sticking and inflammation, which motivated the question.

Patients were followed for a median of about two and a half years, and just under one fifth of them died. Those with blood group B lived shorter lives than those with group O, and group B stayed an independent warning sign after other factors were weighed. Other blood groups showed no clear survival difference. The authors propose blood typing as a cheap extra prognostic marker, pending larger prospective checks.
pmc-13250880:
Lewis and co-authors evaluate a guided online therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder inside routine British health care. Their 2026 European Journal of Psychotraumatology study covers Spring PTSD, a digital trauma-focused cognitive behavioral program with brief therapist support. Four hundred sixty adults with a primary PTSD diagnosis supplied outcome data.

Symptoms of PTSD, general distress, daily functioning problems, and subjective distress all fell from start to finish of treatment. Patients who finished rated the program highly, most calling it excellent or good. Large amounts of missing data, gathered through busy therapists, limited how firmly engagement could be judged. The authors back guided digital therapy as workable and scalable, while urging better data routines in real services.
pmc-13251080:
L Skipper and colleagues make the case for patient involvement in Long COVID research in this 2026 paper. Involving patients and the public can make research safer and fairer, yet it often stays tokenistic or missing altogether.

Drawing on their network's reflections and one running trial, the authors show patients acting as collaborators at every stage, from shaping questions to study design and delivery. That input changed how the team handled outreach, access, and participant safety. Flexible and accessible ways of working were key. Although built around Long COVID, the authors say the approach fits other long-term conditions and wider clinical research.
pmc-13251280:
Getachew Mihiret and a large team pool pregnancy weight data in Ethiopia in this 2026 review. How much weight a mother gains in pregnancy shapes her own and her baby's health, but Ethiopian figures had never been combined.

Thirteen studies with 6,099 women gave an average gain of just under ten kilograms. Only about four in ten women gained within the healthy range, while over half gained too little and about eight percent too much. Eating three or more meals a day, animal-source foods, and three or more clinic visits supported healthy gain. Being underweight before pregnancy raised the risk of gaining too little.
pmc-13252480:
Sotirios Nedios and co-authors published a 2026 study that sets a standard way to examine hearts removed after radiotherapy beam treatment for a wild heartbeat. The treatment fires beams at the heart scar that drives the abnormal beat. It is a new, non-surgical path for beats that resist drugs. What it does to human heart tissue was unclear.

The standard way sorts tissue into three zones: healthy tissue away from the beams, irradiated tissue with thin scarring, and irradiated tissue with thick scarring. Maps of the electrical activity of the heart and of the beam dose steer the cuts. Analyses span beam scans, stained sections, cell markers, molecular panels, and live cell tests. Two removed hearts bore the protocol well, three to five months after their beams. Irradiated zones showed stress markers up, and set electrical channel proteins shifted.
pmc-13253480:
Xuebi Wu and colleagues review the intertwined biology of fatty liver disease and a stiff-heart form of heart failure in a 2026 article. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction increasingly occur in the same patients. The authors frame the pairing through a heart-liver metabolic axis, a two-way conversation between the organs.

Shared drivers fill the review: insulin resistance, fat toxicity in tissues, chronic low-grade inflammation, hormonal activation, small-vessel dysfunction, and scarring in both organs, with gut signals feeding the loop. Clinically, heavier liver scarring flags a subgroup of heart failure patients whose whole metabolic system is more deranged and whose organs remodel further. Treatments now span lifestyle programs, SGLT2 inhibitor drugs, incretin-based therapies, and liver-directed approaches. The authors argue this overlap group deserves dedicated trials and joint clinic pathways.
pmc-13253580:
Azam and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on a purified botulinum toxin for upper face lines. Frown lines, forehead lines, and crow's feet are often treated together. The drug, incobotulinumtoxinA, is a clean form of the standard toxin. Proof for treating all three areas at once was scattered, so the team pooled the trials.

Searches across five sources found three randomized trials with 704 adults in total. The pooled result showed clear gains in line scores one month after treatment versus placebo. Reviewers graded the proof quality with a standard system. Side effects such as headache were tracked as well. The authors say the drug works for combined treatment.
pmc-13253980:
Rayan Khalid and Imad Fadl-Elmula report a rare chromosome disorder in a 2026 case report from Sudan. A five-month-old girl had slow growth, unusual facial features, a cataract present at birth, and a hole between the heart's lower chambers. Notably, she lacked the iris defect that gives Cat Eye Syndrome its name.

Gene tests confirmed an extra marker chromosome from chromosome 22, written as 47,XX,+idic(22)(q11.2). The authors call hers the first documented case from Sudan. They say the case widens knowledge of how the syndrome can look and shows the need for gene testing access in African populations.
pmc-13254080:
Yanbo Wang and colleagues compare two blood pressure drugs as initial treatment after a major heart attack in a 2026 matched analysis. The patients had STEMI, a fully blocked coronary artery, treated successfully with reperfusion, and their heart pumping fraction sat in the mid-range between forty and forty-nine percent. One group started on sacubitril/valsartan, a combination drug, and the other on benazepril, a standard agent.

From 134 eligible patients at a Hebei hospital, propensity matching built two balanced groups of thirty-five. After one month, the sacubitril/valsartan group showed a greater shrinkage of the heart's end-systolic volume, the leftover blood after each beat. Their ejection fraction and a sensitive strain measure of muscle shortening also improved more than the comparison group's. Rates of major adverse cardiac events and safety problems did not differ between groups, and the authors call the short-term functional advantage preliminary.
pmc-13254180:
Xuejing Liu, Junling Ma, and Fangrui Ding examine red blood cell transfusion in the smallest preterm infants in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. These babies, born before twenty-eight weeks, frequently need transfusions, yet the balance of benefit and harm by transfusion threshold remains debated. The study covered 545 such infants admitted between 2012 and 2024.

About sixty-three percent received at least one transfusion. Adjustment for illness severity and treatment era produced a split picture. Each additional transfusion was linked with higher odds of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, a chronic lung condition, and lower odds of surviving free of severe complications. Yet higher transfusion counts also tracked with lower risks of severe brain injury and death. Transfusion count showed no independent link with severe eye disease or necrotizing enterocolitis. The authors present the findings as input to threshold policy rather than a verdict.
pmc-13254380:
Samie Asghar Dogar and co-authors audit what drives anaesthetic gas emissions at a large hospital in Pakistan in a 2026 study. Surgery gases punch far above their weight in warming, and a dosing gadget sold as a saver may matter less than daily choices.

Six months of machine data cover more than seven thousand cases. Nitrous oxide use proved the strongest emission driver, with gas choice and fresh gas flow next. The gadget's effect flipped sign by gas and vanished for nitrous oxide. Case length did not matter. The audit says habits, not hardware, hold the big lever.
pmc-13254880:
Netanel Kramer, Steven L Jacques, and Daniel Wangpraseurt present a protocol for measuring how coral skeletons scatter light in 2026. A coral's stony skeleton is not just scaffolding. Its optical properties govern how much light reaches the algae living in its tissue. That light supply shapes how well the coral photosynthesizes and thrives.

The workflow begins with optical coherence tomography scans of skeleton cross-sections. These yield attenuation and reflectance values. Theory then converts them into scattering coefficients and a measure of scattering direction. Those inherent optical properties feed Monte Carlo simulations. The simulations fire millions of virtual photons through three-dimensional skeleton geometries reconstructed from imaging. The output is a map of light fluence across skeleton and surrounding water at high resolution. The approach is non-invasive, leaving samples intact for further study. The authors intend the protocol to serve reef research on light environments.
pmc-13254980:
Ghazaleh Soleimani and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on a weak spot in brain stimulation research: the fake treatment used for comparison. Their focus is transcranial magnetic stimulation trials for addiction. A convincing sham matters because any real benefit must beat the placebo response.

Surveying 140 addiction trials run through 2024, the authors found wide variety in control designs, and only 94 used a sham at all. Half of those relied on tilting the coil away, a trick that can still deliver a meaningful electric field to the brain. Simulations they cite show even weak fields can shift cell signaling. The authors warn that sloppy shams blur trial results and call for stricter, better-reported control conditions.
pmc-13255280:
Risly Nmm and four co-authors report a near-fatal case of leptospirosis stacked with rare complications, in a two thousand twenty-six case report and literature review. The patient was a previously healthy forty-four-year-old Sri Lankan man.

He arrived with high fever, deep jaundice, and kidney failure from Weil's disease, the severe form of this water-borne bacterial infection. Despite early antibiotics and steroids he developed atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, heart muscle inflammation, lung injury, and liver damage, needing sustained dialysis. Antibody testing confirmed leptospira. Therapeutic plasma exchange joined the multidisciplinary effort and he gradually improved, though still dialysis-dependent at discharge. The authors flag plasma exchange as a possible rescue therapy.
pmc-13255580:
Sigmar Stelzner and colleagues followed rectal cancer patients for ten years in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Some patients still had cancer in nearby lymph nodes after combined radiation and drug treatment before surgery, a sign of poor response. The team compared their long-term outlook with similar patients who went straight to surgery.

Hospital records spanning decades supplied cases with proven node spread and no distant spread. Return of cancer nearby, cancer-specific survival, and overall survival were charted over time. Baseline traits were mostly similar between groups. Oncologists gain long-horizon evidence for counseling patients whose nodes stay positive after pre-surgery treatment.
pmc-13255980:
Dokyeong Kim and colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study of sFRP1, a signaling modulator, in metastatic melanoma. The protein is often described as a tumor suppressor silenced in other cancers, so its role here needed clarifying. The team measured sFRP1 in melanoma samples and tested a blocking compound, WAY-316606, in cells.

Metastatic melanomas carried higher sFRP1 levels, and higher levels tracked with worse patient outcomes. The inhibitor slowed melanoma cell growth, migration, and invasion in culture. Normal cells were largely spared at the same doses. The authors conclude that, in this cancer, sFRP1 supports spread rather than suppressing it. They propose its pathway as a candidate target for drugs aimed at metastatic disease, pending animal and clinical testing.
pmc-13256780:
Mahdi Alayyafi and colleagues test in a 2026 exploratory study whether combining two imaging-based scores predicts surgical outcomes after radical nephrectomy, the removal of a cancerous kidney. The RENAL score grades tumor complexity, while the MAP score estimates sticky fat around the kidney; both were designed mainly for partial nephrectomy planning.

The retrospective analysis covered 52 patients treated at a Saudi tertiary hospital between January 2024 and June 2025, with scores read from preoperative CT scans. Neither score, alone or combined, significantly predicted complications, blood loss, or operating time. The RENAL score correlated modestly with hospital stay length. The authors treat the null result as exploratory, given the small cohort and few events.
pmc-13257080:
Ahmed, Getting, Ashioti, and Lange tested whether blocking peptidylarginine deiminase enzymes helps brain cells recover from ischemia-like injury. These enzymes alter proteins and are blamed in central nervous system damage. Human neuron-like and astrocyte cell cultures went through oxygen-glucose deprivation, scratch injury, and bacterial toxin exposure, with pan-enzyme and isozyme-specific blockers applied at several time windows.

The pan-blocker Cl-amidine sped wound closure in both cell types and reduced histone citrullination. It also shifted structural markers and lowered an inflammatory cytokine in astrocytes after deprivation plus toxin. The two cell types carried different main isozymes. The authors argue several family members add to acute injury, making broad blocking appealing.
pmc-13257380:
Joshua Yang leads a 2026 study of arctigenin, a plant lignan from burdock, against three breast cancer subtypes. Breast cancers differ by hormone and growth receptors, and each type needs its own testing. Cell lines for estrogen-positive, HER2-positive, and triple-negative disease were treated in dishes and in mouse tumors.

Growth slowed in all three subtypes as dose rose, though gene targets shifted by subtype. Cell cycle arrest landed at different checkpoints in different lines, and programmed death increased. Treated cells also closed wounds more slowly, signaling weaker migration. Daily oral dosing shrank mouse tumors over eight weeks without obvious toxicity, and a proliferation marker fell. Cancer researchers gain a multi-target candidate for deeper preclinical work. Human dosing, safety, and benefit remain entirely untested at this stage.
pmc-13257480:
Mohammed Hammamy and colleagues measure how printer choice and build angle affect dental splint accuracy in a 2026 study. A digital splint design from a scanned model jaw served as the reference. Ten splints per group were printed on two LCD machines and one DLP machine at three tilt angles.

Both printer type and angle significantly changed trueness, with error growing as tilt increased. LCD systems produced lower error than the DLP system at every angle. No interaction appeared between the two factors, which simplifies guidance. All systems still landed within clinically acceptable bounds. Dental labs gain a cost argument: cheaper LCD printing matched or beat the pricier option here. Standard post-processing in the protocol keeps the comparison fair for practices weighing equipment purchases.
pmc-13257780:
Wang and a team of colleagues tested nutrition therapy delivered by WeChat for gestational diabetes in twenty twenty-six. This diabetes appears in pregnancy, and diet therapy is its foundation. Yet many patients struggle to keep up complex diet plans without steady support, so a phone-based program may help.

The trial enrolled ninety-four women at a university hospital clinic, half getting the WeChat program and half standard care. Three mini-programs delivered coaching built on a behavior change framework. About sixty-eight percent of the program group stuck to their diet plan on most days. Their pregnancy weight gain fell more over time than controls. Blood sugar after meals and long-term sugar markers also improved, though fasting sugar did not. Eighty-eight women finished the study.
pmc-13258380:
Resül Çolak and colleagues compare gum thickness traits between orthodontically treated adults and untreated peers in a 2026 study. One hundred eighty people aged eighteen to thirty-five were split evenly by treatment history. Gum phenotype was judged by probe visibility at a lower front tooth, beside plaque, gum, and pocket measures plus hygiene habits.

Treatment history showed no link to gum phenotype, and periodontal measures matched between groups. Treated patients reported better oral hygiene habits, the one clear behavioral gap. Male sex and wider keratinized gum each independently predicted a thick phenotype by strong margins. Orthodontists gain a planning point: phenotype looks inborn more than treatment-made. Checking gum thickness before moving teeth still matters for recession risk, regardless of a patient's treatment past.
pmc-13258480:
Fareeha Arshad and colleagues offer a 2026 review of how food compounds may help prevent or treat liver cancer. Hepatocellular carcinoma usually grows out of long term liver injury, and survival stays poor despite newer immune drugs. The authors gather laboratory, animal, and clinical reports on plant polyphenols and related food supplements.

Several compounds act on growth and inflammation pathways inside liver cells. Some may also help standard drugs work better in early tests. Poor absorption, uneven product quality, and few strong human trials limit clinical use today. The review closes with priorities for safer trials that match compounds to tumor cause and patient markers.
pmc-13258580:
Boran Cui and colleagues review flow driven corrosion inside multi product pipelines in a 2026 article. Such lines face mixed fluids, high heat, and high pressure that speed metal loss. The authors explain how water wetting, mass transfer, and shear stress from flow drive the damage.

Three inspection methods receive close attention for finding corrosion without cutting pipe open. Guided wave ultrasound, magnetic leakage tools, and eddy current tools each carry strengths and limits. Future sections point to machine learning and digital twin models for smarter monitoring. Pipeline operators gain a compact guide to matching inspection tools with corrosion risk over a line lifetime.
pmc-13259280:
Martin Xu and co-authors give drone pilots a guide rail instead of taking the controls. Fully automatic inspection flights face rules and risks, while hand flying makes photo coverage patchy. Their 2026 platform overlays planned paths in augmented reality while a pilot keeps manual command.

A second module grades coverage live, flagging redundant views and shaky triangulation geometry. In a building facade trial, guided pilots held planned spacing and stand-off distances far more evenly. The resulting photo sets sampled the surface uniformly, which improves three-dimensional reconstruction quality. Human judgment plus computation, they argue, beats either alone.
pmc-13259580:
Robert Campbell, Devin Sydor, and Chaim Bell comment on where Canada's scarce anesthesiologists should stand during cataract surgery. Their 2026 CMAJ commentary responds to new Ontario research on care models for the operation. A workforce crisis in anesthesiology frames every line.

The study they discuss found modestly fewer emergency visits and complications when an anesthesiologist took part. Yet surgical risk scores were never built for cataract work, the authors note. pmc-13261980:

pmc-13262580:

pmc-13263380:
Nan-Nan Wang and four colleagues review the brain's waste-clearing system and its failure in brain diseases, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. The system, called glymphatic, washes the brain by moving fluid along vessels with help from support cells. A water channel on those cells drives the flow. When the wash fails, toxic waste builds up and diseases speed ahead.

pmc-13263480:
Sarah Sintzel, Kelly Dilworth, and Jean-Noël Evain reviewed in 2026 how bedside stomach ultrasound can tell whether a child about to undergo anesthesia has a full stomach. pmc-13264180:
Grace Getman and colleagues report a dangerous skin infection during cancer treatment in a 2026 case report. Ecthyma gangrenosum causes dark, dead-looking plaques with a red rim and usually strikes people with weakened immunity. The patient had metastatic leiomyosarcoma, a soft tissue cancer that had spread, and was receiving chemotherapy that lowered blood cell counts, a known setup for this infection.

Immediate anti-pseudomonal antibiotics are the first response while cultures return. The authors stress early recognition, since delay raises the risk of sepsis, severe complications and death in an already fragile patient.
pmc-13264280:
Mike Groenhof and colleagues published a 2026 study of mating contact shapes in Choleva beetles. Male genitals often differ fast between close species, and the team asked whether a non-genital contact part follows the same pattern. They studied a small leg joint, the metatrochanter, in males.

pmc-13264580:

Headache was the top sign in both groups. Rates rose sharply over the period, from under one case per 100,000 people a year to over six. The rise was steepest in women aged 18 to 39. The authors urge ongoing tracking.
pmc-13264780:
Five doctors report a hard liver abscess case in a 2026 paper. A 70 year old man came in with two weeks of worsening pain under the right ribs. Scans showed an 11 centimeter pocket of pus in the right liver, split into many chambers, and cultures named a Klebsiella germ.

Antibiotics and a drain through the skin failed to settle his pain or his blood counts. Surgeons then used keyhole surgery to cut part of the liver and open the abscess cavity. Scans after surgery showed marked clearing, and his symptoms and blood counts settled. The team backs early keyhole drainage when skin drainage fails on such cases.
pmc-13264880:
Minmin Leng and colleagues published a 2026 study building a scale for nurses to judge how well they manage limb position in stroke patients with one-sided weakness. Statistical checks split the items into four clean factors and confirmed the structure. The scale scored high on consistency and stayed steady on repeat testing. The authors say it gives clinics a valid way to spot weak practice and target training.
pmc-13264980:
Nora Boldermo Rian and co-authors wrote a 2026 Norwegian study on long-term prescriptions of Z-hypnotics, a common class of sleeping pills, in people with chronic muscle and joint pain plus insomnia. The authors note age and sex gaps dwarf the pain effect in most groups.
pmc-13265180:
James C L Chow reviews artificial intelligence in radiation treatment planning, in a 2026 narrative review. Planning radiotherapy is complex and labour intensive. The review covers contour drawing, dose prediction, automated plan creation, and plan checking. Automated contouring and knowledge-based planning are the most mature uses. Newer tools benchmark plans and explore trade-offs across planners. Problems with data quality, general use, and interpretability still limit adoption. The author argues these systems work best as support for human judgement, with careful validation.
pmc-13265680:
Haoyu Su and colleagues relate a composite sugar and fat index to gum disease in United States survey data, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The link looked roughly linear and was clearer in people without hypertension. The authors suggest the cheap composite could help flag people more likely to have gum disease.
pmc-13265880:
Hao Jiang and colleagues test a garlic residue and jujube mixture as feed for meat ducks, in a 2026 study. The byproduct mix was first profiled chemically. Computer network analysis predicted antioxidant and gut benefits. Feeding trials at an Anhui farm checked those predictions.

pmc-13266880:
Eric K Singhi and co-authors survey in 2026 how people use social media to learn about lung cancer, running polls through Instagram stories over three weeks. pmc-13267380:
Khaled Awawdi and colleagues wrote a 2026 interview study on hospital quality scores in Israel. National indicators rank hospitals, but set measures can miss the facts of single cases. pmc-13268280:
Hyemin Kim and Seunghye Choi survey what shapes nurses' attitudes toward end-of-life care in Korea. pmc-13268880:
Meshal Alfarhood and co-authors build in 2026 a deep learning system that classifies liver tumors on CT scans and explains its decisions. pmc-13269480:

Reporting gaps limit firm conclusions.
pmc-13269580:

pmc-13270080:

pmc-13270180:

pmc-13270480:

pmc-13271080:

pmc-13271480:

pmc-13271880:

pmc-13272180:

pmc-13272480:

pmc-13272580:

pmc-13272880:

pmc-13272980:

pmc-13273180:

pmc-13273380:

pmc-13273680:

pmc-13273780:

pmc-13273980:

pmc-13274880:

pmc-13275580:

pmc-13275680:

pmc-13275880:

pmc-13276080:

pmc-13276280:

pmc-13276580:
