The team removed the tag's three writer enzymes from the embryonic mouse skin layer. Skin cells then failed to mature, the barrier never formed, and hair follicles and touch cells did not appear. Single-cell data showed mixed-up cell identities and stray gene programs. The tag works mainly by holding back the start of gene reading at key control sites. All three enzymes were needed together, marking the tag as a core driver of skin development.
pmc-13377480:
H. Mark Kenney and Francisco Tausk tell of skin ills that share one map in a 2026 case report and review. The two ills, scaly red plaques and white skin loss, are known mates since 1890. Most tales mix split and shared spots on the body.

The new case is rare: fresh plaques grew just in old white-loss zones, and in no next spot. That strict share has a name in skin craft and is a rare bird. The review gathers past such cases and weighs why one ill would pick the next ill's ground. Shared turf may point to shared roots in the skin's immune life.
pmc-13377580:
Athina Tousia and co-authors summed up deaths on bikes and e-scooters in a 2026 review. Two-wheel deaths take a large share of road deaths, most of all in poor and mid lands. The search spanned three data banks from 2014 to April 2026.

Watch work of three types was pooled: group, match, and snapshot. Logs held hat use, drink and drug use, wound maps, and folk facts. Finds split too much for one pooled sum, so the team laid them in tale form. Hat laws and drink laws exist, yet deaths stay high, which makes the driver list of use to road leads.
pmc-13377880:
Benhui Pang and co-authors dress glass strands to firm cold-land clay in a 2026 study. Freeze and thaw rounds crack and sap clay beds under roads in cold zones. Glass strands were coated in two steps, the next with a dust of white paint ore, to grip the clay more hard.

Clay bound with cement kin and the dressed strands beat plain bound clay by up to half in crush strength at top dose. Past 20 freeze rounds it held more strength and let less water in. Fine scans showed tight grips and fine pores. Such beds could hold roads in cold zones for more years.
pmc-13378380:
Kayhan Alvandipour and co-authors describe a 2026 method for mapping the many shapes and states of human microglia, the immune cells of the brain. Microglia shift between states that affect brain health, but capturing that variety across many cells is hard. The team grew microglia from human stem cells in the lab.

They photographed the cells with two staining methods and measured each cell in two ways, by hand-designed features and by features learned by a computer. A grouping method then assigned each cell a probability of belonging to each state, which captures cells in transition. The learned features from one staining method proved most informative and matched well with signs of inflammation inside the cells.
pmc-13379680:
Arantxa A Corona Bacelis and co-authors describe a 2026 case of bowel cancer that first showed up as swollen glands in the neck. Bowel cancer usually spreads to the liver or lungs, so glands in the neck as the first sign is extremely rare. Their patient was a 68-year-old woman with no other major illness.

She had lost weight, and a blood marker for bowel cancer was markedly raised. Tissue from a neck gland confirmed cancer that had spread, and a camera examination of the bowel found the source in the transverse colon. Chemotherapy combined with a drug that blocks blood vessel growth shrank the disease steadily. Over follow-up she reached a complete clinical response.
pmc-13382180:
Zhiyang Xie and colleagues wrote a 2026 narrative review of jaw angle surgery in Asian patients who seek a slimmer lower face. Many designs for cutting the jaw angle exist, plus newer supporting technologies. Practical guidance on matching technique to each patient's jaw shape and goals has been limited.

The review, based on literature searched to the end of 2025, explains how techniques differ in where the cut starts, ends, and runs. A long curved cut remains common for prominent angles, while other designs suit different bone and soft-tissue features. The authors stress that endpoints should include appearance and function, not bone removal alone, and they discuss complications and long-term bone remodelling.
pmc-13382580:
Kalvis Brangulis published a 2026 study of the machinery that builds the outer membrane of the Lyme disease bacterium. Gram-negative bacteria insert barrel-shaped proteins into their outer membrane using an assembly machine. In the well-studied gut bacterium that machine has five parts, but in this spirochete it is simpler, with only three.

Modelling predicted how the three parts fit together into a closed ring shape unlike the arrangement in other bacteria, and measurements confirmed which parts bind and where. Crystal structures of pieces of the main component showed its flexibility. A partner system appears fused with the main machine here. The map helps explain how this pathogen builds its surface.
pmc-13383080:
Gutierrez and colleagues study how Lake Baikal's sculpin fishes lightened their skeletons to leave the floor for water, in 2026 evolutionary morphology research. Sculpins lack swim bladders, so buoyancy must come from the body. Two Baikal genera independently became mid-water swimmers. Using micro-CT scanning and shape analysis across ten species, six bottom-dwelling, two intermediate, and two pelagic, the team measured bone mineral density, porosity, and thickness. They compared body shapes between habitat groups.

Reductions in skeletal density evolved independently in the pelagic and intermediate lineages, with mineral density showing the most consistent drops. Reductions spread through the skull, and the jaws, though the densest bones, showed the greatest change: a 56.86 percent decrease in mineral percentage and a 21.39 percent increase in porosity in pelagic species. Bodies shifted toward elongation, smaller eyes, and higher fin placement. Gutierrez reads the pattern as predictable evolution under the physics of floating.
pmc-13383480:
Jingyu Yan's team built a cell-powerhouse-targeted gel to regrow bone in diabetes-linked gum disease, in a 2026 study. Diabetes-linked gum disease mixes metabolic disorder with chronic swelling, failing mitochondria, excess reactive oxygen species, and weak bone metabolism. The team combined antioxidant, mitochondria-targeting, and regenerative functions in one injectable system.

A manganese-zinc-tannic acid enzyme mimic carrying the SS31 peptide was set in a heat-sensitive PLGA-PEG-PLGA gel. The mimic acts like superoxide dismutase and catalase to clear reactive oxygen, while SS31 guides it into mitochondria to restore energy production. In animals, the gel curbed jaw bone loss, grew new bone, and shifted immune cells toward repair.
pmc-13384880:
Haiyang Sun and six co-authors build a sepsis warning model for stroke units in this study. The head of the text dates the work to 2025. Sepsis is a leading killer of patients with severe brain vessel disease in intensive care. Early prediction could buy time for antibiotics and support.

The model rests on 157 patients admitted over nearly three years with major stroke or brain bleeding. Blood samples within two days of onset measured a panel of inflammation and injury markers. Clinical traits joined the lab values in the analysis. Adjusted regression selected the signals that best foretold sepsis. The unit-specific tool aims to flag high-risk patients before infection declares itself.
pmc-13385880:
Rui Yan and co-authors build a chart that predicts heart-related death in young Hodgkin lymphoma patients. As cure rates rise, heart disease has become a top cause of later death in this group. Data came from a national cancer registry, split into training and check sets. A competing risk model weighed heart death against death from the cancer itself.

Risk rose with Black race, male sex, older age, early diagnosis years, and radiation care. The chart scores fifteen and twenty-five year risk from six inputs, adding stage to that list. Checks showed strong sorting power and sound calibration of the scores. Use tests backed its worth for clinic choices. The authors offer it as a guide for long-term heart watch.
pmc-13386880:
Sreyashi Ghosh, Jenet Narzary, and Mehmet Orman study UV damage repair in bacteria in 2026. Sunlight's UV-B band harms DNA and drives mutation, a force in evolution. What long exposure does to the cell's repair response was less clear.

Long UV-B exposure disrupted reading and protein building and blunted the SOS alarm, without much membrane or oxygen-radical change. Mutation fell and cells lost the power to form colonies early. Gene knockouts showed which repair paths matter most: some were vital, others minor. One deletion worsened colony loss alone, exposing a layered repair network.
pmc-13389880:
Mao and colleagues test whether the ITIH cluster, a schizophrenia-associated region on chromosome 3, also confers risk in Japanese patients, in 2026 genetics research. Schizophrenia affects 1 percent of people, with heritability estimated at 60 to 85 percent. Genome-wide studies in Europeans implicate these inter-alpha-trypsin inhibitor genes, which surface in bipolar illness. The team ran a case-control study and haplotype analysis of variants, then resequenced the ITIH1 gene hunting damaging changes and modeled their effects on the protein.

A difference in frequencies appeared for a window combining rs2710322 and rs1042779. Resequencing found 4 harmful variants in ITIH1 whose predicted effects could destabilize the protein. Effects were modest, as expected, and the authors frame the result as supportive rather than decisive. Mao suggests ITIH1 may contribute in Japanese patients, extending a European signal across groups, and nominates the gene for functional follow-up.
pmc-13390080:
Yuval Tamir and co-authors link the shape of single cells to the proteins they carry and to the state of the tissue around them. Cell shape guides what tissue can do, but imaging limits and averaging across cells hid the shape-protein link. The team used multiplexed imaging, which maps many proteins in place, together with machine learning.

Across cell types, diseases, and disease states, they found a two-way link: shape predicts protein levels, and protein levels predict shape, with the link strongest for markers of cell state. Shape cues also hinted at what some proteins do. One screen found a group of large tumor cells carrying the p53 marker in two cancers. Adding shape data also sharpened a neural network's reading of disease state in tissue.
pmc-13391480:
Zhilin Zhang and a large team build, in 2026, a tough hydrogel that can both move heavy loads and sense its own motion. Soft gels usually force a trade-off between strength and response speed, limiting their use as artificial muscles.

A cascade polymerisation strategy toughens the multiphase gel so it can bear loads while still actuating quickly. The team also derived a coding law linking mass and deformation. The gel can thus encode binary information through its movement. They built logic-gate units too. Those units close a loop from light trigger to signal, processing, and robotic action. Soft robotics engineers gain a material that unites muscle, sensor, and simple logic in one body.
pmc-13391780:
Jiawei Shen and co-authors build TrAcE, a deep learning model that predicts when removing a breathing tube will fail in intensive care patients. Published in 2026, the model answers a gap in older tools, which use one time snapshots and miss how a patient's state shifts. TrAcE fuses steady data with time series data in a transformer network.

Trained on about 5,900 patients from a large care database, it was tested on a separate local set of about 6,800. Scores beat rival models in both checks. An explainability method shows which features drive each call. Against the standard breathing test, the model flagged ready patients about a day earlier on average, in real time.
pmc-13392180:
Edel Ryan's team used a three-round Delphi study with twenty-two global experts to create best-practice guidance for including children with autism in local body play sessions. Children with autism are less active than peers, and barriers are well shown, but methods to overcome them needed a shared view.

Sixteen shared-view statements, agreed at sixty-seven percent or higher, formed the STARTS guidance covering skill growth, coach and volunteer training, session aims, resources, bridging-to-mainstream moves, and welcome supports. Clubs can use STARTS when setting up or adapting sessions so children with autism join in fully.
pmc-13393480:
Muayad Saud Albadrani reviews research on climate change and women's reproductive and sexual health in a 2026 systematic review. Rising heat, disasters, and shifting environments have been linked in prior studies to fertility, ovarian reserve, menopause timing, and mother and child health, and reproductive choices.

Following PRISMA guidance and a registered PROSPERO protocol, the review gathers and weighs studies across those outcomes. It pulls the scattered literature into one framework for researchers, clinicians, and educators. Policy readers can use it to see where the findings are firm, where it is thin, and what health planning should watch next.
pmc-13393780:
Gong and colleagues report a 2026 randomized controlled trial on preventing perioperative hypothermia, a dangerous drop in body temperature during surgery under general anesthesia. At a single hospital, 206 patients scheduled for operations lasting four to eight hours received either passive insulation with cotton quilts or a multimodal strategy. The strategy combined pre-warming, forced-air blankets, warmed fluids, a warmer room, and medication. Core temperature was tracked throughout surgery and afterward.

By the end of surgery, hypothermia struck 69.2 percent of the passive group but only 27.5 percent of the multimodal group, a wide gap. At discharge from the operating room, the rates were 72 percent against 28 percent in favor of active warming. Postoperative cardiac adverse events occurred in 3.85 percent of control patients and none of the warmed patients. The authors urge hospitals to make proactive, layered warming standard care for long operations.
pmc-13393880:
Seda Serhatlioğlu and others record breast feeding under war among Palestinian women in a 2026 interview study. War writing has stressed feeding rates and food value, while mothers' own lived tales went largely unheard.

Lack of food, forced flight, unsafe shelter, and deep trauma wore feeding down at a structural level, yet mothers still used feeding for food, calm, closeness, mood steadiness, and mother-baby bond. The writers hold that guarding breast feeding in war is a duty no aid plan may skip, not an optional extra. Aid chiefs gain a stark, human brief on feeding under siege.
pmc-13394080:
Hong Zhang and others review paper-strip gene tests for bedside diagnosis in a 2026 paper. Fast, true gene reads are key to early care, yet lab gene tests are slow, dear, and fiddly.

Paper strips offer a cheap swap, but gene spotting and signal boost inside paper strands have been hard. New strips build 3D nooks from porous strands and treated mats, lifting base reads and ease of use. The review maps signal boost and noise hush tricks from sample in to read out. Field clinics gain a guide to gene tests that fit in a pocket, not a lab.
pmc-13394480:
Yangsong Wang and colleagues describe, in 2026, how tumours borrow the thymus to shield themselves. The thymus trains T cells and deletes those that attack the body. Two kinds of plasmacytoid dendritic cells gather there in mice with tumours, the team found. One kind carries tumour parts into the thymus and prompts deletion of tumour-fighting T cells.

The second kind slows the making of fresh T cells and releases type I interferon. A signal named CCR9 guides both kinds into the thymus. Mice that lacked CCR9 kept stronger anti-tumour defence and grew smaller tumours. The authors call this a hidden route to immune tolerance.
pmc-13395980:
Manoj Kumar and colleagues review brown algae as a farm input that can lift crop growth and help plants withstand stress, in a 2026 article. Extracts of these seaweeds are rich in natural sugars such as alginates, fucoidans, and laminarins, plus vitamins, minerals, and polyphenols.

With climate pressure and heavy chemical use straining food production, interest in gentler inputs has grown. The review pulls together earlier work on how seaweed extracts act on plants, from growth signals to stronger defenses against disease, drought, and salt. The authors present brown algae as a practical, lower-impact tool for modern farming, while sorting proven effects from claims that still rest on thin proof.
pmc-13396080:
Lingzhi Luo and co-authors built a light-based processor that can update its own settings while it works, and describe it in a 2026 paper. Most computer chips, including earlier light-based ones, run with fixed settings, so they cope poorly when incoming data changes character mid-task.

Their temporally plastic photonic processor pairs two kinds of light circuits. A slow, reconfigurable part holds stable long-term processing, while a fast part adjusts on the fly, and a loop of optical delay acts as short-term memory. The design targets real-time jobs such as signal handling and control, where retraining a fixed chip is too slow and electronic memory limits bite.
pmc-13396180:
Min Wu and others test whether brain waves for known names foretell coma fate in a 2026 forward group study. Coma fate in intensive care steers weighty choices yet stays hard to guess, and task brain wave tests may bare hidden awareness.

Across five intensive care wards, 461 acute brain harm patients were screened and 81 made the final set, with one ward's patients kept for outside check. Brain waves for known versus strange names were weighed as fate signs. Doctors gain a bedside wave sign that may sharpen coma fate calls without new invasive tests.
pmc-13396280:
Hong Seok Oh and co-authors revisit a 17th-century writer's idea of melancholy in a 2026 study of how depressive symptoms hang together in Asian patients. Richard Baxter, an English churchman, treated guilt as central to melancholy, and the authors test whether guilt still shapes the pattern of modern depression.

Data came from a prescription-pattern study spanning 11 Asian countries. Patients were split by whether strong guilt appeared among their symptoms, based on one survey item about feeling bad about oneself. Network analysis mapped which symptoms link most tightly in each group and which sit at the center, showing whether guilt-rich depression forms a distinct web.
pmc-13396380:
Bhattacharjee and co-authors present, in 2026, FORGE, a framework that predicts which cancer patients will benefit from targeted drugs, grounded in gene essentiality. Targeted inhibitors work by blocking proteins a cancer cell cannot live without, yet most sensitivity models ignore that mechanism. FORGE jointly factorizes two data types, drug response measured by IC50, the dose halving cell growth, and gene dependency scores from knockout screens, learning shared embeddings for both.

From those embeddings the team derived a Benefit Score, an index for predicting prognosis under targeted therapies. The design contrasts with expression-only predictors such as DeepHE and XGEP, which report 94 to 96 percent accuracy at the narrower task of calling gene essentiality. By forcing drug response and gene dependency into one model, FORGE ties its predictions to the drug's actual target biology. The authors offer the score as a stratification tool for matching patients to targeted treatments.
pmc-13396480:
Maria Zimmermann and others use signed tales to test brain tale ladders shared by all tongues in a 2026 brain-scan study. Spoken tales engage a brain time ladder from words to plots, but whether signs share that ladder was untested.

Twenty born signers watched a Polish Sign tale from Poe plus scrambled cuts during brain scans. Signed tales synced layered brain nets, with front-temple zones tracking sentence build and the default net tracking plot, as in speech. Top-side wall zones showed a sign-only long-time mark. The paper proves tale shape in the brain crosses tongue mode.
pmc-13396680:
Jiang and colleagues improve, in 2026, thermal de-icing by engineering the type of ice that forms against a surface under airflow. Ice on aircraft wings costs lift and safety, and electric heating is the incumbent fix. Wisdom held that flow conditions alone dictate ice type, but their non-wetting microstructured surfaces grow a porous rime layer under flow, changing how the ice lets go when heated.

The microstructures fragment pre-frozen droplets with help from the airflow, shrinking the ice crystals. Smaller crystals block heat pathways differently, thickening the rime layer, which melts free as direct solid-ice contact rather than through an energy-wasting water film. The effect cut thermal de-icing energy consumption by roughly 56 percent without extra energy input in their experiments. Earlier work shows porous rime alone can trim melting time by 27.2 percent, context the authors build into a surface-design strategy.
pmc-13396880:
Ali Gohar and co-authors present a patient in whom two autoimmune diseases overlap, a combination called Reynolds syndrome, in a 2026 case report. One disease, primary biliary cholangitis, slowly destroys the liver's small bile ducts; the other, systemic sclerosis, hardens skin and organs and appears here in its limited CREST form.

The authors' warning is practical: in a CREST patient whose liver enzymes stay cholestatic, meaning bile flow is blocked, doctors should suspect this overlap rather than blame the skin disease alone. A blood test for anti-mitochondrial antibodies and early treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid improve the outlook. Delay lets portal pressure rise toward dangerous bleeding.
pmc-13397380:
Mark Rodgers and co-authors gather, in a 2026 umbrella review, what is known about keeping children out of state care. Reviews upon reviews exist on why children enter care, but the help that prevents entry got less joint attention. The team pulled together thirty-three systematic reviews from rich countries since 2013, half on risk and protective factors and half on interventions. Quality was scored with a standard tool.

Risks and shields sorted into layers: the child's and mother's health and habits, social support and maltreatment, and living and working conditions such as poverty and services. Many factors are changeable, and the team matched interventions to the factors they could move. The map shows policy makers where a push could keep families together, from mental health care for mothers to income support.
pmc-13397680:
Mohammad Mehdi Rajabi and others probe generational gaps in ageism among Iranian nurses in a 2026 study. Ageism in health care can thin care quality and worsen outcomes for older patients, and generational upbringing may shape nurses' views.

Two hundred and ten nurses from two Tehran referral hospitals, picked by stratified random sampling, were grouped as Generation X, Y, and Z and scored with a proven ageism scale. The study compares views across cohorts shaped by different lives and cultural settings. Nurse educators gain proof for generation-aware anti-ageism training.
pmc-13397780:
Vitaliy Voznyy and a large team reviewed trials of a nerve block used after lung surgery to see if it eases pain and cuts opioid use. Their 2026 review covers the erector spinae plane block, an injection near the spine that numbs chest wall nerves, compared with usual care without the block. Lung surgery often brings strong pain, heavy opioid use, and nausea, so safer pain control is a pressing clinical goal.

The review pooled 20 randomized trials with 1,391 patients and tracked pain at rest and on movement at 6, 12, and 24 hours. Patients given the block reported lower pain at each time point and used less opioid in the first day, with fewer cases of nausea and vomiting. The authors present the block as a useful addition to lung surgery pain plans. Readers should note that trial methods and block techniques varied, so the size of benefit may differ by setting.
pmc-13399280:
Christopher David Chapman, Myles Hyla Edward Dakin, and Richard Aspinall investigated a defined hypochlorite solution in 2026, asking whether the antiseptic does more than kill germs. Hypochlorite is a long-used disinfectant. Its use on severe burns improved survival after infections in ways germ killing alone seemed unable to explain. The team suspected the solution also reshapes the wound's inflammatory signals.

Lab tests confirmed that a concentration of 7 millimoles per liter wiped out both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. The same strength attacked two signaling proteins unevenly. IL-6, which drives inflammation, lost its function about three times faster than IL-10, which calms inflammation, after only five minutes of exposure. Tests on skin cells checked how much direct exposure the tissue could tolerate. The authors argue that trimming IL-6 while sparing IL-10 could quiet wound inflammation, reduce scarring, and help explain the survival benefit seen in burn care.
pmc-13399380:
Marcia Maria Gimenez and team tested ankle nerve stimulation for overactive bladder after ischemic stroke in women. Their 2026 prospective case series addresses neurogenic overactive bladder, where stroke damage disrupts bladder control and harms quality of life. Transcutaneous tibial nerve stimulation sends mild pulses through skin near the ankle to calm bladder nerves.

Thirty-one women completed twice-weekly, 30-minute sessions for six weeks, with follow-up at six months. Daytime voiding fell from about 12 to 7 times per day. Urgency episodes dropped from about 13 to 1, urge incontinence fell sharply, and nighttime voiding also improved, with gains largely holding at follow-up. The work supports the therapy as a noninvasive option, while its small, uncontrolled design calls for randomized trials.
pmc-13399480:
Junhui Wu, Zerui Dai, and Dawit Dibekulu revisit how the English future expression be going to became grammar, in a 2026 corpus linguistics study. The phrase began as literal motion toward a place. It was then reanalyzed so that to marked intention and future time instead of direction. The authors test a middle idea, critical frequency: a threshold of use, in ambiguity-rich contexts, at which the shift ignites.

Drawing on three large text collections, EEBO, Google Books, and the modern COCA corpus, they measured the expression's frequency across centuries. They date the critical window to 110 years, from 1580 to 1690, with a synchronic intensity of 0.81 occurrences per million words at the threshold, as their calculations report. The authors present the case as confirmation that a measurable threshold exists. They offer it as a template for quantifying other grammaticalization stories.
pmc-13399580:
A Tuscan study group asks whether steroid nasal sprays still matter beside a biologic drug in a 2025 paper. Severe sinus disease with polyps now often gets dupilumab, an antibody that blocks a key allergy signal. Sprays are traditionally paired with it, but their added value was unproven.

Seven centers followed 123 patients on the drug for a year. Symptom scores, polyp grades, smell tests, and scan scores all improved clearly. About a quarter of patients used their spray loosely. Early on, loose users felt better faster by symptom score, while steady users gained more on polyp and smell measures. By twelve months the groups converged, raising fair questions about blanket spray advice.
pmc-13400580:
Ken Watanabe and colleagues analyze, in 2026, which patients with thyroid cancer spread to the lungs respond to radioactive iodine therapy. The treatment is a mainstay for differentiated thyroid cancer, yet results vary widely once lung spread occurs. Predicting response could spare futile treatment.

The team reviewed 186 patients treated between 2010 and 2024, grading response by scans, imaging of iodine uptake and a blood marker. Overall disease control, counting complete, partial and stable outcomes, was under a quarter of cases. Patients younger than 55 and those whose lung spread was found at the time of thyroid surgery fared better. A lung uptake score also tracked outcome strongly, while the starting dose made no clear difference.
pmc-13400680:
Jingcheng Zhang and colleagues examine, in 2026, pancreatic cancer surgery where a major vein must be removed along with the tumor. In borderline or locally advanced cases after drug therapy, cutting out part of the portal vein system is often needed for a complete operation. Whether that step itself worsens outlook was unclear.

Among 117 patients operated on after initial therapy, 65 had vein resection and 52 did not. Complications and deaths around surgery were similar, as were overall and disease-free survival times. Within the resection group, however, finding true cancer invasion in the removed vein wall under the microscope marked much shorter survival. The vein invasion, not the resection, carried the grim signal.
pmc-13401380:
Lili Shao, Ruyi Zhang, Yinqing Huang, and Xiaochun Dai published a 2026 study building a prediction model for mild cognitive impairment in older adults who live with several chronic conditions at once. Early screening matters because impairment can hide inside multimorbidity.

The cross-sectional study enrolled 238 older inpatients at a Wenzhou Medical University hospital between April 2022 and February 2025, testing cognition with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment Basic scale. About 27 percent had mild cognitive impairment. Risk rose with age at or above 80 years, hearing impairment, and emotional disorders, each roughly tripling or quadrupling the odds. Higher education, frequent exercise, and frequent social activity were protective. The authors turned these factors into a nomogram chart and validated it in a separate group of 68 patients.
pmc-13401580:
Hirakawa and colleagues test, in 2026, whether blood levels of VEGF-A isoforms predict how EGFR-mutated lung cancer responds to targeted inhibitor drugs. They studied 64 patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer treated with EGFR-TKI monotherapy at Hiroshima University Hospital between 2009 and 2023. Before treatment they measured serum total VEGF-A and the isoforms VEGF121 and VEGF165 by immunoassay.

Overall response rate was 78.1 percent, with median progression-free survival of 7.5 months and overall survival of 31.8 months in the cohort. Only VEGF121 separated responders from non-responders, running higher in non-responders at a median of 446.6 versus 322.1 picograms per milliliter in responders. Above a cutoff of 339.3 picograms per milliliter, response rate dropped to 64.9 percent from 96.3 percent below it, and progression-free survival shortened to 6.2 months from 14.4 months in the comparison. The authors propose serum VEGF121 as a pre-treatment stratification marker.
pmc-13401680:
Setayesh Sindarreh and co-authors conducted a 2026 observational study of influenza in patients with blood cancers, hunting for factors tied to death. People with hematologic malignancies are among the most vulnerable to severe flu results, yet risk details are sparse.

The cross-sectional study included 90 patients with confirmed influenza and a blood cancer. It collected demographics, cancer type and status, flu type, symptoms, and lab and imaging findings. Hospital stay length, intensive care admissions, and deaths were also recorded. The mean age was about 34 years, with patients ranging from toddlers to a 91-year-old. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia was most common at about 46 percent, followed by acute myeloid leukemia at about 22 percent, lymphomas, myeloma, and rarer types. Analysis focused on which features, from cancer type to intensive care need, separated survivors from those who died.
pmc-13401880:
Meng Chen and Chengcheng Che developed a machine learning model to sort clinical nurses in China by their risk of compassion fatigue, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The exhaustion that comes from sustained caring work harms both the nursing workforce and patient care, and spotting high-risk nurses early could target support.

A survey of 969 nurses in Liaoning Province classified fatigue using the established Professional Quality of Life Scale cutoffs. About 56 percent met criteria for elevated symptoms. Feature selection combined the Boruta algorithm with LASSO regression, and eight machine learning algorithms were trained and compared on discrimination, accuracy, recall, and F1 score. The winning model was interpreted with SHAP analysis, which shows how much each factor pushes a prediction up or down, keeping the tool explainable rather than a black box.
pmc-13402580:
Donglin Fu and six co-authors trace how sepsis drives skeletal muscle atrophy through three signaling pathways: FoxO1/3a, NF-κB, and mTOR. Sepsis frequently leads to muscle wasting and functional decline, but its molecular mechanisms remained unclear. Their 2026 study pairs a mouse model of sepsis with cultured muscle cells dosed with a bacterial toxin. They track three protein-degrading systems: autophagy, the ubiquitin-proteasome system, and calpain pathways.

All three degradation systems ran hot in sepsis, and muscle function fell. Two signaling pathways that spur the breakdown were upregulated, while mTOR, a growth pathway, was suppressed. Drugs or genetic deletion that blocked key components of these pathways, especially one ubiquitin ligase, mitigated the atrophy and preserved function. The team maps a coordinated drive behind the wasting and names therapeutic targets within it. Human tests would be the next step.
pmc-13402680:
Tyler D Dexter and a large team show that prefrontal parvalbumin neurons, fast inhibitory cells that pace local brain chatter, join working memory work only when the job gets hard. Past rodent studies disagreed on whether these cells matter for holding information in mind. Using fiber photometry to watch the cells and optogenetics to steer them, the team ran mice through a touchscreen working memory test at varied difficulty.

The cells raised their activity, and proved necessary, only under high-demand conditions; easy versions of the task ran fine without their extra push. That demand split, the authors suggest, explains the clash in earlier literature: studies using light tasks would miss the cells role entirely, while heavy tasks expose it. The result frames working memory support as a reserve system the prefrontal cortex calls in when load climbs.
pmc-13402880:
Deepak Kumar Singhal leads a team surveying dental students on tobacco habits, a pointed choice since dentists are often the first to spot tobacco damage in the mouth. Tobacco kills more than 8 million people a year worldwide, most in poorer countries, and India ranks among the largest producers and consumers, with cheap products everywhere. Use typically starts between ages 14 and 25, making campuses prime ground for prevention.

Their cross-sectional questionnaire maps how common smoking and smokeless habits are among future dentists, and in what patterns. The stakes are double: students own health, and their credibility as counselors, since health workers are urged under the WHO tobacco framework to advise quitting at every chance. Findings on stains, halitosis, and precancerous lesions tie the survey back to the clinic, where dental teams can catch early harm.
pmc-13403280:
Alexandre Lahens and team pinned down medical factors that skew kidney function guesses in a large French group. Their 2026 cross-sectional work weighs kidney filtration rate formulas, based on creatinine, cystatin C, or both, against true filtration gauged with a radio-isotopic tracer in 3,838 patients. Formulas use age and sex, but medical states can skew results and mislead dosing.

For creatinine formulas, HIV infection, high body mass, loop diuretics, and cotrimoxazole tracked with underguessing, while younger age, female sex, lower body mass, transplant past, and cirrhosis tracked with overguessing. Cystatin C formulas showed a distinct skew pattern, with older age, HIV, steroids, and transplant past underguessing. The work urges doctors to spot formula-bound skews before trusting a single guess.
pmc-13403380:
Yinuo Wen and many co-authors tested in 2026 whether tiny twisted particles could help a weak eye lens stay in place. In this illness, the fibers that hold the lens wear down over time. The team coated small plastic particles with a natural amino acid that gave them a left-handed twist.

In lab dishes, the particles calmed angry immune cells and slowed the breakdown of support tissue. In rats, they drew in a calmer type of immune cell instead. Two key fiber proteins came back, and the lens fibers rebuilt. The approach may one day offer a low-surgery option for this and similar tissue-loss diseases.
pmc-13403580:
Suleiman Ameir Idrissa headed a 2026 review of vaginal yeast infections caused by species other than the usual one in sub-Saharan Africa. Such species answer drugs in mixed ways, which makes care harder. The team pooled 14 studies from nine countries, covering 3,587 women of childbearing age.

About one woman in eight carried one of these less common species. They made up about 35 percent of all confirmed yeast finds. One species, Candida glabrata, led the list at near 16 percent of isolates. Wide gaps between studies call for caution. Still, clinics need species-level tests to pick drugs well.
pmc-13404580:
Ezequiel Monferrer and team mapped sex-bound behavioral and brain effects of teen social stress in mice. Their 2026 work puts 264 mice through social defeat, direct in males and vicarious in females, between postnatal days 26 and 35. It then tracks anxiety, depression-like behavior, movement, stress hormones, and tryptophan metabolites into adulthood. Teen years are a tender window, yet sex-bound long-term patterns had been unclear.

Both stress forms raised corticosterone in both sexes, and females showed a lower share of susceptibility than males on social interaction testing. Short-term effects differed by sex and resilience, with movement rises in defeated males and less back grooming in defeated females. Long-term shifts were few, mainly lasting anxiety in resilient females. The work shows that resilience status and sex shape stress outcomes, muddying one-size-fits-all models.
pmc-13406280:
Sunanda Yogi and Amit Singh review how brain cells break down in a 2026 article on diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. Each disease has its own signs, yet they share deep faults: proteins fold wrong, cell power units fail, rust-like damage builds and swelling flares. Each one adds its own twist on top.

A layered marker scheme pulls the strands together for earlier spotting of disease and risk. Shared paths across diseases hint that drug mixes hitting more than one target could help more. The pair argue that reading the diseases side by side, not one by one, sharpens both tests and cures. Signals that pass between paths get close attention as a shield for nerve cells.
pmc-13407580:
Xingze Li and co-authors profile, in 2026, the bacteria living around macadamia tree roots, asking whether nut cultivar or tree age shapes that hidden community. Soil came from five major cultivars at five and eight years old, and gene sequencing charted which bacteria lived there and what they likely do.

Two bacterial phyla dominated, Actinobacteria and Chloroflexi, with Rhodoplanes the leading genus. Cultivar proved the strongest driver of group differences, while age mattered in ways that depended on the cultivar. Likely functions centred on processing amino acids, carbohydrates, and lipids, matching host needs. Bacteria mostly co-occurred positively in tidy modules, hinting at cooperation. The authors suggest cultivar-aware microbial starters could support yield and quality in macadamia orchards.
pmc-13407880:
Fei Wu and co-authors studied a protein channel that helps colon cancer spread, in work published in 2026. The channel is often found at high levels in these tumors, and high levels went with worse survival. The team asked how the channel holds cancer cells in a mixed state between two cell forms.

When the channel was turned down, cancer cells grew, moved, and invaded less, and more cells died early. The mixed cell group shrank, and two growth signal paths became less active. Blocking either path had the same effect as turning the channel down. The authors name the channel as a possible drug target to slow spread.
pmc-13408580:
Takako Eguchi Nakajima and co-authors survey doctors and patients in 2026 about side effects of a drug pair used for late bowel and stomach cancers. Hard data on how the pair feels in daily care, beyond blood effects, has been thin.

Web surveys reached doctors who prescribe the pair and patients who take it. Patients reported tiredness, appetite loss, and nausea more often and sooner than doctors expected. Tiredness and appetite loss hurt patients most and were hardest for doctors to ease. Patients also prized clear word on dosing, side effects, and cost more than doctors grasped. The gap points to better talks and care plans.
pmc-13408680:
Benedikt Kuhn, Peter Kovermann, and colleagues resolve in 2026 a long argument about a membrane protein that seemed to break the rules dividing transporters from channels. The protein, SLC26A11, is abundant in the brain and had been described both ways. Structural imaging, biochemistry, and simulations together settled the question: it truly does both jobs.

By every structural hallmark the protein is a working transporter, and the team identifies it as the long-sought exporter that moves sulfate out of lysosomes, the cell's recycling units. Its transport cycle also opens an uncoupled chloride conductance, switched by the very sulfate transport it accompanies. That dual nature suggests routes toward treating brain swelling, where chloride movement matters, and toward probing lysosomal storage diseases, where sulfate handling goes wrong.
pmc-13409080:
Sumathy Ravi and co-authors build a questionnaire in 2026 with, rather than for, people living with type 2 diabetes in Western Sydney. Clinic visits are short and clinician-led, so patients' own priorities often surface too late or never. Ten patients and eight health professionals, from specialists to pharmacists, shaped the Diabetes Priorities Questionnaire through hybrid focus groups at a hospital service in a disadvantaged, culturally diverse district.

Four conversations structured the design work: what the tool is for, whether it is usable, what good completing it does, and whether it asks the right questions. Draft items went back to participants repeatedly, and their recorded feedback drove successive revisions. The finished tool is meant to be completed before appointments so consultations start from the patient's agenda. The report documents the codesign process other services would need to repeat locally.
pmc-13410580:
Yewon Han and Lee Sael present in 2026 a faster way to spot gene networks that change in colon cancer. Cancer cells rewire how genes act together, not just how much each gene is used. Older network methods capture that rewiring slowly and often miss the full picture.

Their method, shortened to EDLNA, splits gene activity data into hidden patterns for healthy and cancer samples separately. Comparing the two networks flags which gene links changed. Extra checks against protein networks and gene switches then find working modules. On test data the method ran much faster than rivals at similar accuracy. On real colon cancer data it found stage-linked gene groups that simple gene-by-gene scans missed.
pmc-13411280:
Safia Ansari and colleagues review in 2026 cases of a runaway inflammation syndrome, HLH, at an urban hospital serving a vulnerable population. The syndrome mimics sepsis and cancer, which delays its recognition, and adult data from underserved groups are thin. Records spanned 2019 to 2025 at one tertiary center.

Screening 273 flagged patients yielded 68 likely cases, narrowed to 25 after careful review. Seventeen were recognized during their hospital stay, while eight met criteria only in hindsight. Recognized patients were younger and mostly Black or Hispanic, often uninsured. Death struck about half the recognized group and nearly nine in ten unrecognized patients. Specialist consultation reached every recognized case, which hints recognition itself saves lives.
pmc-13411580:
Jie Zhou and colleagues surveyed 319 older cancer patients in five Guangdong hospitals in 2026 to untangle why digital health tools can feel daunting. Tech anxiety can shut patients out of online care, and the team tested whether skill with digital health explains part of the link between feeling isolated and feeling anxious about technology.

Isolated patients tended to score lower on digital health literacy and higher on tech anxiety, and literacy carried part of that link in the model. The paper points hospitals toward pairing companionship and plain digital coaching, rather than simply rolling out more apps.
pmc-13411880:
Zenia Taluja leads a team in 2026 stress-testing draft survey questions about phone and internet access with villagers in Uttar Pradesh, India. Measuring the digital gender gap demands questions people actually understand. One hundred one cognitive interviews, more with women than men, walked through 118 Hindi-translated draft items.

Seven problem families surfaced, from wrong word choices and tangled phrasing to alien ideas like online privacy or hacking. Questions about permission to use a phone tangled with ideas of help, since phones get shared. Rating scales and vague time frames confused many respondents. Nearly every question needed revision despite careful translation, which proves the worth of this slow checking step.
pmc-13412480:
Shiho Ohnishi, Keiichi Hiramoto, Nobuji Yoshikawa, and Shosuke Kawanishi test a licorice compound against aging in a 2026 mouse study. The compound is glycyrrhizin, drawn from licorice root. It calms swelling by blocking a protein that fans it. The team asked if it also keeps up Klotho, a protein tied to slow aging, which falls as animals grow old.

Old mice got the compound by mouth three times a week for twelve months. Treated mice gained less fat and showed less liver fat and kidney aging. They stayed active and kept their balance skills. Blood tests showed higher Klotho and its partner IGF-1, lower kidney strain marks, and lower swelling signals. A guard enzyme in liver and kidney rose as well.
pmc-13415880:
Assem F. Alabu-Husain and co-authors introduce a Pray Optimization Algorithm for hard engineering search problems, in 2026. The method mimics steps of Islamic prayer gatherings in three phases: finding a suitable mosque, aligning the congregation, and accumulating a score that drives convergence toward the best solution.

Standard benchmark problems from the CEC2017 suite tested the algorithm against six strong rivals, with statistical tests confirming its edge. Three classic engineering problems followed. Finally the method planned trajectories for a six joint industrial robot arm, beating five current methods there. Ritual inspired search joins the long list of human inspired optimizers.
pmc-13415980:
Shun Aoki and colleagues report a bladder cancer case with an unusually good outcome after surgery alone, in 2026. A woman aged seventy-six came with visible blood in her urine for a month. Scans and cystoscopy found a three centimeter tumor on the bladder's left wall, with no spread to nodes or distant sites.

Tissue examination after initial resection identified primary large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, a bladder cancer type reported fewer than fifty times. This cancer is aggressive and usually treated with surgery plus chemotherapy. Radical bladder removal alone was used here. Long term freedom from recurrence followed, which the authors present as evidence that early curative surgery can sometimes suffice.
pmc-13417980:
Cynthia Schneider and colleagues map what helps or hinders lung cancer screening uptake, in a 2026 scoping review. Low dose scans cut deaths in high risk smokers, yet participation stays low. Studies from 2013 to mid 2025 were sorted with a behaviour framework covering capability, opportunity, and motivation. Thirty nine studies met the criteria.

Awareness of personal risk, belief in screening benefits, and clinician recommendation most often lifted uptake. Misconceptions, competing life priorities, and fear of results most often held people back. Knowing screening helps did not always translate into attending. Programmes should pair clear communication with easier access and support around fear, stigma, and trust.
pmc-13418380:
Elia Tamagnini and colleagues engineer a coronavirus spike protein that can no longer grip its human receptor yet still trains immunity, in a 2026 mouse study. Vaccines use spike to raise antibodies, but spike's grip on the ACE2 receptor has been proposed as a factor in rare side effects. Point changes were designed to break that grip while keeping the protein's shape.

Mutant spikes bound ACE2 poorly in lab tests. In mice they raised immune responses equal to or better than the natural spike and protected animals on challenge. The design offers a template for vaccine antigens stripped of unwanted host interactions.
pmc-13418480:
Huihui Xu and colleagues model whether a new liver cancer drug pairing is worth its cost in China, in a 2026 economic analysis. Finotonlimab plus bevacizumab beat the older drug sorafenib on survival in trials for inoperable liver cancer. Their model extrapolated survival and tallied costs and quality adjusted life years from the health system view.

The pairing added about 1.27 life years and 0.93 quality adjusted years, yet cost about 48,000 dollars more. Cost per quality year came to roughly 52,000 dollars, well above the stated willingness to pay line. Every sensitivity check kept it above the line, with zero chance of cost effectiveness at that threshold.
pmc-13418780:
Pulcherie Pelembi and colleagues sequenced coronavirus variants in Bangui, Central African Republic, from January to August 2022 in a 2026 study. Variant data from the country were scarce even as Omicron spread worldwide, leaving local planners blind to which lineages circulated.

The team retested 102 positive nose swabs from the Pasteur Institute biobank with confirmatory testing and nanopore sequencing in Paris, building a local variant picture for surveillance. Public health teams gain a baseline for spotting new lineages early and tuning prevention for future waves for Bangui clinics and national planners alike in future outbreak planning.
pmc-13419180:
Robi Cynthia Chacha and Ermias Mergia Terefe audit how medicines are used at a referral hospital in Kenya, scoring practice against World Health Organization yardsticks. Poor medicine use raises costs and feeds drug resistance, a burden felt hardest in lower-income health systems. Their study ran in the outpatient department of Thika Level 5 Hospital.

The team reviewed 600 prescriptions and watched 100 patient visits, then checked the facility itself for readiness. Standard WHO tools covered prescribing habits, the care patients actually received, and the stock and systems behind both. Yardstick scores like these show managers exactly where habits drift from safe practice. The audit gives the hospital a baseline for targeted fixes rather than broad guesses.
pmc-13419280:
Yong and colleagues piloted in 2026 a national digital programme for type 2 diabetes in Brunei Darussalam. Type 2 diabetes needs steady self-management, and hybrid care mixes app-based support with clinician contact. The sixteen-week programme combined remote health coaching, digital lessons, self-monitoring, and messaging, plus scheduled video visits.

Among those with full data, average blood sugar control improved markedly over the sixteen weeks. About two in three participants hit the preset target for lowering HbA1c, a long-term blood sugar measure, and about six in seven lowered it at all. Fasting glucose, body mass index, waist size, cholesterol, and triglycerides all improved significantly. Quality of life scores rose as well. Completion and video visit attendance were high, and most respondents reported satisfaction with the programme.
pmc-13420280:
Charity Kakuru and colleagues measure how often adults with hypertension in central Uganda treat themselves without a prescription, and what drives the habit. Self-medication here meant taking blood pressure drugs in the last 90 days without formal guidance, by the study's own definition. Their survey ran at Masaka Regional Referral Hospital during August and September 2024.

The study enrolled 192 clinic patients with a mean age of 58 years in the reported group, and 143 of them, some 75 percent of the total, were women. A structured questionnaire captured background and clinical traits, and a modified regression method sorted the linked factors. Unsupervised pressure treatment can mask poor control and clash with prescribed plans. Local rates give the clinic a factual base for counseling and refill policies.
pmc-13420480:
Allison Perko and colleagues recount a neck stabbing case where surgeons, exploring the wound of a 23-year-old man bleeding heavily, found no internal carotid artery on the injured side. Being born without that artery is an extremely rare vessel variant. The right common and external carotid branches were found and named during the dissection, yet the internal branch simply was not there.

The left side, checked by imaging, showed the full normal set of carotid branches. Blood had clearly found other routes to the brain across his life, which is why the variant stayed hidden until trauma forced the question. Bleeding control and repair had to proceed without the expected anatomy as a guide. Trauma teams gain a reminder that a missing vessel on exploration may be a birth variant, not an injury effect.
pmc-13420780:
Aoibheann Power and co-authors survey registered dietitians in Ireland about simulation-based education, training that uses role-play or simulated patients to build clinical skills. Their 2026 mixed-methods study combines a questionnaire with interviews to map knowledge, attitudes, and actual use.

The study included 114 dietitians, fifteen of whom were interviewed. Although 78 percent had encountered simulation activities and 85 percent wanted more training, only 14 percent actually used simulation-based education. Greater familiarity went with more positive attitudes, greater motivation, and fewer worries about resources and cost. Years of experience was the only significant predictor of use. Interviews revealed confusion about what counts as simulation, with many using role-play without naming it as such. Barriers included time, educator training, resources, and institutional support, and the authors call for clearer definitions and coordinated training.
pmc-13421080: Lin Meng and colleagues are named in a correction for their study of a grape gene tied to cold tolerance. The notice is a correction only and alters one time point. In the section on a partner gene, the peak in gene activity was first given as one day of cold. The fixed line gives two days instead. The error is logged in the notice alone to guard the version of record, and no other results change.
pmc-13421380:
Ignacio Fuentes leads a thirteen-author team evaluating, in a 2026 paper, two ruthenium-based glowing compounds as stains for lignified plant cell walls under the confocal microscope. Seeing lignin-rich walls matters for plant anatomy, yet a stain must work inside tissue that glows on its own and must coexist with other labels.

Applied to fixed stems of the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, both compounds lit up secondary walls, concentrated in water-conducting vessels and supportive fibres. Their pattern matched established lignin staining methods. Pairing with a second stain separated general wall structure from the ruthenium-marked zones, and the team identified a far-red third label that interferes least. Computer modelling of the compounds' structures rounds out the comparison.
pmc-13421480:
Mohan Gupta and colleagues tested in 2026 whether spacing practice and brief rests truly improve motor sequence learning, challenging popular memory findings. Two experiments varied correct sequences per trial and break lengths while holding total practice constant on a standard motor task.

Spaced groups performed better by the end of training, yet on a later test with conditions equalized, group scores were statistically indistinguishable, and more breaks did not raise learning. The paper argues that learning happens during performance itself, with rest effects reflecting temporary fatigue rather than lasting gain in motor learning.
pmc-13421780:
Luis Jesús Garza, José Rodrigo Alcántara Dzib and Luis Raúl Miramontes present, in a 2026 case report, a 66-year-old woman whose scans showed two tumours side by side. She had been treated for breast cancer in 2023, so a new adrenal lump beside a kidney mass raised the obvious fear of spread.

Surgeons removed the right kidney. Under the microscope the kidney tumour proved to be a high-grade clear cell renal cancer with sarcomatoid features, small and confined. The adrenal lump, full of fat on imaging, was a pure lipoma — a rare benign fatty tumour — and not metastasis or the more common myelolipoma. The authors use the case to argue for careful imaging-pathology correlation before assuming the worst.
pmc-13422280:
Martin Ågren leads a seven-author team investigating, in a 2026 Swedish study, what wears adult teeth down. Tooth wear blends grinding, scrubbing and acid erosion, and single-factor studies had blamed everything from age and saliva to jaw clenching without settling their relative weight.

Residents of Jönköping aged twenty to eighty received standardised dental examinations and questionnaires covering health, habits and social background. Examiners scored erosive and physical wear separately and combined, while participants reported their own teeth grinding and jaw dysfunction was assessed clinically; saliva flow and buffering were measured too. Multivariate models then weighed each factor's contribution at once. The authors single out self-reported grinding for special attention in the analysis.
pmc-13423080:
Venerito and colleagues pair a weight-loss drug with biologic therapy in this 2026 matched study of obese patients with psoriatic arthritis, a joint-and-skin disease where obesity blunts biologic response. Thirty-one patients starting tirzepatide, a dual-action metabolic drug, alongside a biologic were matched to 62 similar patients starting biologics alone, and outcomes were compared at six months.

The combination group lost body mass index while controls gained slightly, a gap of minus 2.9 versus plus 0.4 points on the index, and their inflammation marker CRP ended significantly lower. Patient-acceptable symptom state on a disease-impact questionnaire was reached by 48 percent of the tirzepatide group against 21 percent of controls, an odds ratio of 3.44 in the matched analysis, and near-clear skin was also more common. Physician-scored joint targets did not separate significantly, a subthreshold pattern the authors read as real but partial benefit.
pmc-13423180:
Vundamati and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the wider health effects of alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to a sugar found in mammal products. The allergy starts with a lone star tick bite, which primes the immune system against the sugar alpha-gal. The review looked past food reactions to surgery and hospital care, screening 729 records and keeping 14 studies.

Kept studies reported severe allergic reactions not only to foods but also to medical products from mammals. Gelatin, some antibodies, and other surgical ingredients triggered anaphylaxis, a dangerous whole-body reaction, in some patients. Blood transfusions also posed a risk in reported cases. Most evidence came from observational studies in the United States, which limits how far results apply elsewhere. The authors urge surgical and emergency teams to ask about tick-related meat allergy before using mammal-based products.
pmc-13423480:
Yu, Lee, and Kim combine generative AI with mechanics in this 2026 study. They design functionally graded metamaterials. These engineered frames change stiffness smoothly from place to place. Interpolation between known designs often breaks connectivity. It strands struts midair. So the team built a latent diffusion process that respects topology from the start. The process adapts the image-generation technique to three-dimensional graph shapes.

Unit cells are encoded as distinct tokens in a squeezed latent space. They are then diffused and decoded. A mechanistic guidance signal steers generation toward asked-for elastic properties. The framework made everything from repeating frames to graded architectures. The graded forms kept smooth mechanical transitions and intact connectivity throughout. The authors present the method as a scalable alternative. It beats both hand interpolation and purely data-driven generators for inverse design. In inverse design, engineers specify targets and receive a printable structure.
pmc-13423880:
Wittrock and a multi-institute team present magnon momentum microscopy. It is a soft X-ray method that directly images magnons. Magnons are the quantized waves of aligned spins in magnetic materials. The method maps them across a two-dimensional momentum map. Short-wavelength magnons matter for future wave-based computing. Yet detecting them has been a long-standing experimental obstacle.

The team applied the method to yttrium iron garnet, a standard magnonic material. They revealed a rich variety of nonlinear magnon interactions, not seen before. The method is sensitive enough to capture these interactions across wide stretches of the dispersion plane at once. It works at nanometer wavelengths with no frequency ceiling. It also adds element specificity plus bulk sensitivity. The authors present it as a versatile platform for studying short-wavelength and nonlinear magnonics.
pmc-13424580:
Sraya Greenberger leads an eleven-author review of fifteen years of childhood eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic allergic inflammation of the gullet, at their centre. Charts covered 138 children diagnosed between 2009 and 2023, tracking how the disease was found, how patchy it is along the gullet, and how treatment evolved.

The average age at diagnosis was about eight years, and three quarters of patients were boys. Vomiting led the symptoms at 39%, then swallowing trouble and food sticking. Visible changes clustered in the lower gullet, yet biopsies told a patchier story. Some segments cleared the diagnostic threshold while others fell below it. Inflamed tissue sometimes hid under a normal-looking surface, especially high in the gullet. The authors draw sampling lessons for diagnosis.
pmc-13424680:
Boyle and colleagues argue that early drug trials in severe lung failure need better yardsticks for success. The syndrome, called ARDS, fills the lungs with fluid and has no proven drug cure. Many past trials may have missed real gains by use of blunt end measures.

Death alone hides gains that fall short of saving life yet still help patients. The team backs a running scale that tracks each patient's state day by day. Such a scale can spot shifts in health path that one fixed date would miss. It can also weigh death and time on life support in one fair frame. Better yardsticks could help small early trials pick drugs worth large tests.
pmc-13424880: Mohammed Shanshal and Muna Abuayyash present a short image case from 2026 about a small skin growth on the shoulder of a 69-year-old man living with HIV. The spot was a tiny, shiny pink bump, and its pattern under a scope gave no clear answer. Tissue study showed a poroid hidradenoma, described as the rarest growth in its family of sweat gland tumors. The authors stress that changing bumps in patients with weak immune systems need tissue checks and full removal, since looks alone can mislead.
pmc-13426080:
Carlos Diaz-Salazar and colleagues show that human-specific gene copies slow microglial maturation to match drawn-out human brain development in a 2026 study. Human cortical microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, mature structurally and transcriptionally more slowly than mouse microglia. The duplicated genes SRGAP2B and SRGAP2C are the only human-specific duplications expressed in human microglia, and they lower abundance of the ancestral SRGAP2A protein.

Transplanting human stem-cell-derived microglia and using mouse genetic models showed these copies are both necessary and sufficient for the slow maturation pattern. Delayed microglial timing in turn shifts when synapses develop, linking one gene family to human brain neoteny. Brain growth in man runs on a slow clock, and this work ties that slow pace to a gene set found in no beast but man.
pmc-13426380:
Maria Epifania V. Collantes and Mykha Marie B. Tabuzo systematically reviewed stroke linked with methamphetamine use in a 2026 article following PRISMA guidance. Searches covered studies from 2020 to March 2026, with bias judged by the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and eight studies, mostly retrospective cohorts, qualified. The review separated ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke and gathered related vessel and heart pathology.

Affected patients were mostly men, younger than non-users, with fewer traditional vascular risk factors and other illnesses. Mapping mechanisms and subtypes helps emergency teams suspect stimulant involvement in strokes occurring at unusually young ages. Eight sets of data is a thin base, yet the same theme runs through all of them, which lends the shared claim some real weight.
pmc-13426480:
Inumaru and colleagues published a 2026 study mapping two breeding forms of a disease-carrying tick. The Asian longhorned tick spreads fevers in Japan and nearby lands. Some of its populations breed with males, while others clone themselves without males. The team checked 1,750 ticks gathered across 23 Japanese prefectures.

The cloning form turned up in every region the team sampled nationwide. The mating form stayed limited to central and western parts of Japan. Neighboring spots sometimes held one form while the next held both together. The team also built a fast DNA test that sorted every tick correctly. Finer local mapping is their next step for fever risk control. The two forms may differ in how they spread fevers to people.
pmc-13426980:
Zewudu Mulatie and colleagues pooled studies on whether warning flags from automated blood analysers can spot blood cancers early. These machines scan blood samples and raise flags when cell patterns look abnormal, hinting at leukaemia, lymphoma, or related marrow diseases.

Across 28 studies, the flags caught about 91 percent of true cancer cases and correctly cleared about 89 percent of healthy samples. Results varied a lot between studies, driven by which flag type and machine brand each lab used. Flags for abnormal lymphocytes or young blast cells performed especially well in the analysis. Mulatie backs the flags as a cheap first screen, above all where lab resources are scarce.
pmc-13427580:
Josephine S. F. Chow leads a very large team behind a 2026 trial on training for home peritoneal dialysis in Australia and New Zealand. In that treatment, patients clean their blood through the belly lining, and infections at the catheter site or inside the belly remain a frequent problem. Whole dialysis centers, rather than single patients, were assigned by chance to a standard teaching program or to usual local training. The program followed international guidelines for both nurse trainers and new patients.

National registries supplied the outcome data, with time to a first dialysis-related infection as the main measure. Researchers also tracked catheter removal, switches to hospital dialysis, deaths, and quality of life. Pragmatic trials run inside routine care are rare in dialysis, so the design itself offers lessons for testing education at scale.
pmc-13427780:
Bakbak and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on surgery for pouches that bulge from the bladder. Such pouches form when urine pressure stays high, often from prostate blockage. The team gathered 44 studies covering 458 men treated since 1975. Approaches ranged from scope work to open, keyhole, and robot surgery.

Three in four men had prostate surgery at the same time as pouch repair. Major complications stayed rare, at about two in a hundred cases overall. Open surgery tended to bring more blood loss and longer hospital stays. Scope repair showed the shortest operating times in the gathered reports. Every approach improved urine flow, so choice should fit each case. Patient fit, pouch size, and surgeon skill should drive the final choice.
pmc-13427980:
Ziqi Liu and colleagues track, in a 2026 study, thinking problems after removal of tumors on the brain's language-dominant side. Meningiomas at the skull base near the temple can be reached by a route under the temporal lobe. The team enrolled 23 right-handed patients with tumors in the petroclival area during mid to late 2024. Thinking tests and resting brain scans ran the day before surgery, one week after, and three months after.

Patients operated on the dominant side, usually the left, dropped sharply on several test scores at one week. Six of ten in that group showed clear decline, while the non-dominant group held steady. Brain scans pointed to a disturbed network involving the cerebellum, the structure at the back of the brain. The title frames the disruption as temporary, an idea the three-month scans were designed to check.
pmc-13428480:
Havva Terzioglu, Phillip McMullen, and Guliz Barkan report a 2026 case of a rare and aggressive tumor found in the lung. The tumor is a variant of a growth called inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, marked by round cells, odd features, and changes in a gene named ALK. Finding it first in the lung is very uncommon, and naming it from needle samples is hard.

The patient was a woman in her late fifties who came in with cough and short breath and was found to have a mass in her right lung. A needle sample showed spindle cells with many immune cells, and stains pointed toward this tumor family. After the lobe was removed, the tissue showed the round cell form with strong abnormal marks. Gene tests found the tumor's ALK gene joined to a partner gene, which can guide drug choice.
pmc-13429580:
Mingliang Cheng and co-authors show, in a 2026 study, that blasting a magnetic metal with oxygen plasma turns it into a light-powered semiconductor. Bulk photovoltaic materials generate current from light without the layered junctions of normal solar cells, yet they rarely coexist with magnetism. Their starting material, an iron-gallium-tellurium compound, conducted like a metal and ordered magnetically. Oxygen treatment localized its electrons and flipped it to a p-type semiconductor while keeping magnetism above room temperature.

Devices built from the treated material produced strong currents with no applied voltage, across a broad light range. A small magnetic field could tune the output in a straight-line fashion. Using the measured response, the team demonstrated image cleanup and feature separation with about 92 percent recognition accuracy. Self-powered, magnetically rewritable light sensors are the platform promised.
pmc-13429880:
Thomas Wainwright asks whether research on shoe inserts for big toe joint arthritis is asking the wrong question. Reviews show average benefits too small to matter for the typical patient. Wainwright argues that averaging hides the real story: inserts reshape load at one specific joint, so effects should vary by person.

Some patients may gain a lot even when the average gain is near zero. He also notes a mismatch in guidelines, which stress exercise, though exercise can barely change load at this far joint. Drawing on hip arthritis work, he contrasts capacity building with load changing care. The commentary urges treatment matched to mechanism and to the individual.
pmc-13430780:

pmc-13438880:

pmc-13439180:

pmc-13439380:

pmc-13440180:

pmc-13441780:
