Sequencing nearly one hundred fifty new AML patients found the intronic variant often, above all in core binding factor leukemias.

Carriers had worse overall survival. Lab work showed the variant makes cells keep an intron that should be spliced out, cutting correctly spliced transcripts and likely producing truncated proteins or triggering decay of the message. The unstable protein may help explain the worse clinical outcomes.
pmc-13570780:
Wang and co-authors flag a lung guard clan that drives grave breath ill. Grave breath ill is a long flare ill with stiff drug hold. Steroid drugs oft fail to tame it in grave hosts. Guard cells in the lung steer much of that flare. One clan, the gap guards, had stayed dim in past reads. The team read lone-cell genes and flow counts in a mouse set.

Two hits set off the grave state in the mice. Lung bits from a house dust mite and a salt mix did it. Grave care wiped the home sac guards from the lungs. New sac guards tied to weave fix took their place. A gap clan with low Lyve1 and high MHCII rose to lead. That clan bore high CCR2 and CCR5 marks in its reads. A dual block drug then tests that clan's worth.
pmc-13570880:
Bo Chen and Xiangyi Li combine, in a 2026 cohort study of a Chinese aging survey, a blood-fat marker of artery disease and a frailty index into one combined score. The index counts health deficits. They then ask whether the score predicts new arthritis. More than four thousand adults aged forty-five and older without arthritis at entry were followed from 2011 to 2020.

About a third developed arthritis over ten years. Each step up in the combined score raised risk slightly. The highest third of scores carried about fifty-five percent more risk than the lowest third, in a curved rather than straight-line pattern. Blending metabolic and frailty information may flag older adults who deserve earlier joint monitoring, pending outside confirmation.
pmc-13571280:
Masafumi Tsurutani and co-authors map gene activity in microglia in mouse models of social problems. Their paper follows earlier work on oxytocin neurons in the paraventricular hypothalamus, a brain area tied to social behavior.

Valproic acid before birth, a teratogen, causes social harm and hurts those neurons. What it does to non-neuronal cells was less clear. The team found changes in microglia from that area, and spatial methods showed shifts in subtypes. Turning on oxytocin neurons early, which rescued the animals in past work, also changed these cells. The study broadens the search for causes of odd sociability.
pmc-13571480:
Jessica Shen Tsy Wu Kim and co-authors run a small blind trial in 2026 of toxin shots for a painful armpit skin disease. The disease brings sore lumps, pus pockets, and tunnels under the skin, and pain is the top drag on life quality. The toxin calms sweat glands and may cut the bursts that feed the disease for three to six months.

Each patient had both armpits in play for at least a year, with flares at least once a month. One side got the toxin in 25 small skin shots, and the other side got plain salt water, with no one told which was which. Checks ran at weeks 2, 12, and 24, with no other care in between. The design tests the shot as a low-harm choice for this hard disease.
pmc-13571680:
Shuo Qiang and co-authors pinpoint a fibrotic cell subpopulation in degenerating spinal discs in a 2026 study. Disc degeneration brings pain and disability, and one cell subtype drives its scarring, yet that subtype's markers were unmapped. Two genes kept surfacing in bulk studies without a known home.

Machine learning over eighty-one bulk profiles nominated the pair, and single-cell data from two cohorts located them in the fibrotic subpopulation. The two programs they mark, integrin signaling and protein glycosylation, run coupled in those cells. Immune crosstalk and drug predictions were explored too. Naming the culprit cells gives disc research a target finer than the whole tissue.
pmc-13572280:
Yunnan Hu and co-authors mapped world research on a deadly tear in the body's main artery, in a 2026 study. The tear, called aortic dissection, is a sudden emergency with high death rates. The team joined two views: a wide count of published work, and a close look at the gene signals inside torn tissue.

They gathered 5,170 papers from the year 2000 to 2025 and tracked who wrote them and which themes grew hot. Output sped up after 2010. Gene data from single cells then split well-known genes from little-studied ones. The paired view gives future teams both a map of the field and fresh leads to test.
pmc-13572380:
Sanika Kulkarni, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 review of whether blood pressure drugs that act on the renin-angiotensin system relate to depression. Two drug classes are in focus: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers. Lab work hints these drugs might lift mood, but human data have been mixed.

The team searched five databases for studies of adults, up to November 2024, and kept 15 studies with more than 7 million people in all. Eight studies linked the drugs to lower rates of depression, six found no clear link, and one found a small rise in major depression. Gains showed most in large registry studies that used doctor-coded diagnoses. The authors say varied methods and leftover bias bar firm claims, and they call for cleaner future studies.
pmc-13572480:
Isabel Pinheiro and colleagues released a multi-modal dataset for mapping kiwifruit growth stages automatically, publishing the data paper in 2026. Hand counting of buds, flowers, and fruit takes about ten minutes per square metre, making orchard-wide monitoring impractical and yield forecasts imprecise. The dataset pairs 1,665 annotated images from bud to fruit set with georeferenced videos carrying manual ground-truth counts.

An adapted 17-class growth-stage system merges visually similar stages, drops troublesome categories, and adds structural classes, organised across plant parts, genders, and stages. The images train computer-vision models while the videos validate automated counting at plant level. The resource should advance precision kiwifruit farming, from pollination timing to yield prediction.
pmc-13572580:
Taguchi and co-authors test preventive coiling of side branches during aneurysm repair in this 2026 study. Endovascular repair seals a weak aortic bulge from inside, but blood leaking back through branches can regrow the sac. Their low-volume center applied a fixed anatomy-based rule for who gets preventive embolization.

Of 132 elective patients, 30 received coils and 102 did not. The coiled group actually started with riskier anatomy, including wider feeder arteries. Yet at 24 months none of the coiled patients showed sac growth. Five-year re-intervention was 0 percent with coils against 10.8 percent without. The authors say a standardized rule makes results reproducible even at small centers.
pmc-13573180:
Veronika Farková and co-authors track fatty acids in transition milk from robot-milked cows in a 2026 study. The milk a cow gives just after calving shapes calf health, and its fat profile is part of the benefit. Automatic milking systems can collect it separately, but the profile shifts fast.

Eighteen Czech Fleckvieh cows were sampled at every milking over four days. Short and long chain fats rose as milking number grew, while medium chains fell, and unsaturated fats gained on saturated ones. The cow's parity history swayed a handful of individual acids. Gaps between milkings barely mattered. Milking count and parity, the authors conclude, drive the profile.
pmc-13573380:
Xianyao Li, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 investigation of microbes that live on tea tree bark and in the soil below. Tea is a major crop in Yunnan, China, and its microbes shape plant health. The team asked where bark microbes come from and what steers their mix across regions.

Samples came from Pu'er, Lincang, and Xishuangbanna, the main tea zones. Source tracking showed soil acts as the reservoir for bark: in Pu'er it held all bark bacteria and about two thirds of bark fungi, with little flow back. Soil held wider variety, while bark picked a narrower set. Plant type shaped bark bacteria most, and place shaped soil mixes. Nitrogen and organic matter in soil drove change in both niches. Soil microbes leaned to nutrient cycling, bark microbes to carbon fixing and stress defence.
pmc-13573480:
Mingkun Yang and co-authors link blood sugar paths to death risk after brain bleeding in a 2026 study. Erratic glucose is common in intensive care patients with non traumatic intracranial hemorrhage, but single readings may miss the story. The team mined a large United States hospital database for two thousand two hundred sixty such patients.

Grouping the first seventy two hours of readings produced four paths: steady low, moderate stable, falling, and rising. Every non low path carried clearly higher death risk at twenty eight days, and the pattern held at six months and one year. The rising path fared worst. The authors suggest the path itself, not just the starting level, should guide early risk sorting.
pmc-13573680:
Tang and seven co-authors show the enzyme USP10 restrains esophageal cancer by stabilizing a NOTCH pathway fragment, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Oxidative stress imbalance is a major factor in this cancer. USP10 removes ubiquitin tags from the NICD1 protein fragment. That stabilization shapes antioxidant gene activity.

Losing USP10 destabilizes NICD1 and speeds cancer development in models. Extra USP10 gene therapy slows tumor formation in animals. Low USP10 levels link to worse patient prognosis. The enzyme responds to oxidative stress by protecting NICD1. USP10 emerges as a candidate therapeutic target.
pmc-13573980:
Jethwa and colleagues examined in 2026 what happens after new mothers screen positive for depression at the six-week checkup. They followed records from more than eight thousand patients at one center. Screening with a standard questionnaire is routine, but whether a positive screen turns into care was poorly charted. The team tracked referrals to social work and psychiatry for a year after birth.

About one patient in eight received a new mental health referral after the screening visit. Positive screens drew far more referrals than negative ones, roughly thirty-seven versus five in a hundred for social work. Still, most positive-screen patients were never referred, a gap the authors call critical. Referrals after positive screens also came faster, mostly within two months. The authors back screening across the whole perinatal period, not once.
pmc-13574280:
Wang and co-authors present a 2026 study on a drug candidate for an ultra-rare bone disease, fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva. In this disease, a mutant receptor makes soft tissue turn to bone after injury or even on its own. The drug, BCX9250, is a small pill that blocks that receptor, called ALK2. The team tested it in binding assays, cells, and mouse models.

The drug bound strongly to both normal and mutant forms of the receptor. In cells carrying the disease mutation, it shut down the false signal that activin A wrongly triggers. Mouse tests covered both new bone growth and its return after removal. BioCryst developed the compound as an oral option for patients.
pmc-13574680:
Xinang Xiao and seven colleagues built a diagnostic model for risky neck artery plaque that mixes tongue photos with blood tests, in a 2026 study. The patients all had coronary heart disease. Soft, unstable plaque in the carotid artery raises stroke risk, and the team wanted a cheap, non-invasive way to flag it.

They gathered records from 523 patients and split them by ultrasound into vulnerable and stable plaque groups. Tongue color values from several tongue regions differed clearly between the groups. Tongue measures also tracked with some blood markers, though weakly. Four machine learning models were trained on the data, and the best, a gradient boosting model, separated the groups fairly in validation. The authors present tongue imaging as an early exploratory aid for risk sorting. They stress that larger prospective studies must confirm any clinical use.
pmc-13574780:
Yunchong Guo, with six colleagues, carried out a 2026 study of gene-mark shifts in men whose low testosterone stems from severe obesity. This hormone drop is common in very heavy men and can persist after surgery. The team asked whether the weight-loss drug semaglutide leaves marks on gene control tags.

Samples came from two healthy controls, seven men with the condition, and four men checked again after drug use. The team read chemical tags on DNA and small RNA switches that tune genes. Six RNA switches differed, and eighty genes carried altered DNA tags, most on the X chromosome. One switch governed many of the tagged genes. Four well-linked hub genes surfaced, all tied to fat and sugar handling. The authors stress the read is early and needs larger checks.
pmc-13574880:
Guangzhi Wan, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 study of frailty before cancer and survival after it in older adults. Frailty, a worn-down state of low reserve, is known to worsen odds once cancer is present. Its weight when measured years before any diagnosis was far less clear.

The team drew on a large United States ageing survey, taking its 2006 wave as the start line. Adults aged fifty-two and up who were free of cancer at entry had their frailty scored then. Records ran through the end of 2020, so later cancers and deaths could be tracked against that early score. A long view like this separates frailty's own drag from the shock of diagnosis. The authors aim to show whether an early frailty check can flag patients who will need extra support.
pmc-13575180:
A Benmakhlouf leads a 2026 computing study of two rare-earth gold compounds under pressure. The compounds, ErAu and TmAu, mix a rare earth metal with gold in a simple cubic form. Such materials blend traits of metals and ceramics, and pressure can stiffen or destabilise them.

Calculations from first principles tracked structure, stiffness, sound speeds, and electronic states up to 20 gigapascals of pressure. Both compounds stayed mechanically stable across most of that range and behaved as ductile metals. Pressure generally raised stiffness and the Debye temperature, a marker of lattice vibration. Extra calculations showed localised electron states respond to correction terms without changing the metallic nature. The authors offer the values as reference data for later experiments.
pmc-13575480:
Reem Ahmad and co-authors lay out a roadmap for bringing particle minibeam therapy into clinics in a 2026 review. The technique splits radiation into narrow beams of protons, ions, or electrons, sparing healthy tissue while keeping dose shape at depths ordinary X-rays cannot reach. Like any new radiotherapy, it needs solid proof of safety, efficacy, and feasibility before routine use.

The review maps the linked challenges across physics, biology, and engineering, and names priority research areas and steps toward clinical adoption. Most steps apply across particle types, with type-specific notes where they matter. The authors present the roadmap as a coordinated guide from experimental concept to safe clinical practice.
pmc-13575680:
Quntai Qiu and co-authors report a case from 2026 of a valve swap through the neck vein in a man with an extreme heart shape. His right-side valve leaked in a torrent, and his right upper heart chamber had grown giant. He had already had one valve swapped by open surgery and one by tube, so a fresh open run was ruled too risky.

Scans showed the valve ring stretched to an oval far past the norm. The team picked a valve that grips leaflets and anchors to the wall sheet, so it needs no outward push to hold. A long bend path forced a slanted neck entry and hard depth calls. One month on, his breath grade had eased two steps with no real leak.
pmc-13575780:
Radha Gopalaswamy and Selvakumar Subbian published a review in twenty twenty-six on post-tuberculosis lung disease, the lasting damage TB leaves after the infection itself is cured. Survivors increasingly carry chronic breathing disability that health systems barely count. The review places the condition inside the full arc of TB biology.

The authors cover definitions, global burden, and the inflammatory, fibrotic, and vascular pathways that keep injuring the lung. Clinical forms range from blocked airways and bronchiectasis to fungal complications. Diagnosis, risk sorting, and management are discussed for rich and poor settings alike, with a section on children. They close on the field's gaps: naming, biomarkers, and trials that treat survivorship as part of TB care.
pmc-13575880:
Kangju Son and four colleagues study whether chemotherapy helps older patients with pancreatic cancer that has spread, in a 2026 Korean population study. Trial data for the oldest patients are thin, so the team turned to national insurance and cancer registry records from 2012 to 2019.

Among 20,549 patients, 8,652 received chemotherapy. Median survival fell gently with age in treated groups, from nine months in the youngest band to six months at age 81 and above. Untreated patients lived a median of two months at every age. Matched comparisons in patients aged 76 and older favoured treatment strongly. Two modern drug combinations still gave clear gains at ages 76 to 80. The authors conclude age alone should not rule out chemotherapy.
pmc-13576080:
Alexandre Casadei-Ferreira and co-authors peer inside the ant stinger in a 2026 study of the genus Diacamma. The stinger is a famed venom tool, but some of its inner parts are barely understood. Among them are the valvilli, two small flaps in the valve chamber that help pump venom through the sting.

Using four kinds of advanced imaging, from X-ray micro-tomography to electron microscopy, the team mapped the flaps in fine detail. The flaps turned out to be patchworks, not uniform sheets: zones of hard and springy material sit side by side, and only parts of the flap can bend. That build, the authors argue, suits a flap that must flex in one place and hold firm in another as venom is pumped. The work redraws a part that textbooks had sketched too simply.
pmc-13576280:
Wang and colleagues investigate in 2026 how inflamed blood vessel cells talk to astrocytes through extracellular vesicles, tiny parcels cells release. Astrocytes are the star-shaped support cells of the brain. Together these cell types form much of the blood-brain barrier, and inflammation disrupts it.

Treating vessel cells with the inflammatory signal TNF-alpha changed their parcels' cargo wholesale: hundreds of messenger RNAs rose or fell, alongside many regulatory RNAs of two other classes. Feeding those parcels to astrocytes shifted the astrocytes toward inflammation, movement, and RNA processing programs, and away from supporting neurons and calcium balance. One cargo change mattered most: less of the RNA for a brake protein let the master inflammatory switch NF-kappaB fire more freely, raising cytokine release. Restoring the brake protein inside astrocytes blunted that response.
pmc-13577180:
Xueqi Li and six co-authors set out a trial protocol in two thousand twenty-six for a needle-knife treatment for neck pain from cervical spondylosis. This wear of the neck spine is a common pain source, and standard care such as drugs and therapy often works slowly or weakly. Acupotomy joins acupuncture ideas with soft-tissue release to free adhesions and ease muscle tension.

Their trial will assign patients at random to ultrasound-guided acupotomy or standard medication. Assessors and statisticians stay blind to group, and the sample size was set by power analysis. Care runs three weeks, with twelve weeks of follow-up. Pain intensity is the main outcome they will judge.
pmc-13577280:
Qian Mi and co-authors survey dialysis staff in China about preventing vein clots, in this 2026 paper. Blood clots in veins are a serious risk for patients on dialysis. Staff knowledge and habits decide how well prevention happens at the bedside.

More than five hundred questionnaires went out across centers, and most came back valid. Overall scores for knowledge, attitude, and practice sat at a moderately high level, and the three moved together. Training frequency, use of risk checks, and knowing the guidelines each predicted stronger scores. The authors point to regular training and routine risk assessment as levers for safer care.
pmc-13577880:
Pierre Rosenbaum and co-authors profiled antibodies against the coronavirus in two thousand twenty-six. They targeted the spike's receptor-binding domain. Those antibodies can block infection outright. They also recruit other immune attacks on infected cells. The team studied memory antibodies from early infections. Binding sites on the domain split them into classes.

Strong neutralizers often lost grip on Omicron variants. Non-neutralizers binding conserved spots stayed broadly reactive. Neutralizers still performed other antiviral functions well. They tagged cells for killing and debris clearance. Complement deposition added a third weapon. Function thus splits by the exact binding site. Vaccine design may chase breadth across all functions.
pmc-13578080:
Michael Griessmair leads a team on new catheters for distal stroke clots. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with small vessel blockages. Such far out clots are hard to clear by machine means.

Past work showed promise for Q aspiration catheters nearby. Records from one center's stroke data base were reviewed. Blockages treated with the new catheters were included. Success scores and first pass effects were tracked. Function at ninety days was the clinic outcome. Harms during the procedure were logged and weighed. Results split by clot type and technique used.
pmc-13578180:
Jianye Yuan and co-authors present a 2026 study of how uneven gene activity is inside lung tumors. Working with non-small cell lung cancer, the most common form of the disease, they ask whether genes that stay steady across a tumor can help predict who gains from immune therapy.

The team mapped that unevenness with single-cell data from many tumor regions, then used six machine learning methods to build a six-gene score. Tumors with low scores held more immune cells and more active immune pathways. Two score genes get close study in lab tests, one linked to weaker anti-tumor defense and one to scar-like tissue around tumors. The score may help doctors pick patients for immune drugs.
pmc-13578280:
Galal Sherif and co-authors blend plant nanofibers into gear oil and measure gains in friction, wear, and noise, in a 2026 study. The fibers, drawn from lignin and cellulose, were mixed at four loadings from 0.25 to 1 percent. Microscopy and diffraction checks confirmed the fibers' shape and structure before testing began.

Half a percent proved the sweet spot: friction fell by up to 42 percent and wear by about a quarter. Vibration and sound levels dropped 18 to 25 percent at low and best loadings. Worn surfaces showed a protective fiber film at the best mix, while heavier loadings clumped and scratched. The authors pitch the fibers as a green route to quieter, longer-lived gear oils.
pmc-13578680:
Xiaolong Qu and co-authors built an AI system that reasons over time to predict chronic stomach inflammation care in a 2026 study. Chronic gastritis unfolds through linked events over months and years. Standard prediction tools flatten that history and lose the order in which symptoms, tests, and treatments occurred.

Their system stores medical events in a temporal knowledge graph and lets a reinforcement learning agent walk its paths to forecast diagnosis and treatment steps. Walking the graph keeps the reasoning trace visible, unlike a black-box score. The team developed and validated the system on clinical data. Such tools could help doctors anticipate which gastritis patients will worsen and which treatment sequence fits their history.
pmc-13579380:
Lin Li, Xiu-Li Yan, and Cheng-Feng Qin set out in 2026 how a virus's own cutter can be turned into a drug trigger. Most virus drugs block a step the virus needs: entry, copying, or protein cutting. Their path flips that logic. The cutter's work becomes the signal that marks a cell as infected.

Their tool parks a pore-making protein in cells, muzzled by a tail the virus cutter can snip. When the cutter snips, the pore is freed and the cell bursts, which also sounds a local immune alert. Sent as mRNA in fat drops, it curbed hepatitis A in mice and eased liver harm. The same build was stretched to Zika and to the COVID virus. The pair maps the road to trials.
pmc-13579680:
Bhanu Prasad and co-authors (2026) search the genomes of patients with loin pain hematuria syndrome for a genetic explanation. The syndrome combines chronic flank pain with blood in the urine, yet shows no urological cause. It can disable the people it affects. The authors reason that rare variants might be to blame. The suspect genes are ones that maintain the kidney's filtration barrier: in the vessel lining, the basement membrane, or the podocyte cells.

They performed exome sequencing in 29 consecutive patients. Seventeen had the syndrome, and twelve had persistent painless blood in the urine alone. Analysis first checked a curated panel of 130 genes linked to blood in the urine. It then widened to the whole exome, with variants judged by clinical criteria. Among the syndrome group, most had visible blood and all had chronic pain. Many reported kidney stones, and several had family histories of stones.
pmc-13579880:
Hongzi Zhu and colleagues report a rare yeast infection that took hold in a leg wound of a healthy 67 year old woman, in a 2026 case report. The yeast, Trichosporon asahii, usually strikes people with weak immune defenses, yet her system was sound. After surgery to clean and stitch a lower leg injury, her skin died back in patches, oozed pus, and tunneled into pockets, while blood inflammation signs stayed oddly normal.

Three lab methods agreed on the yeast's identity, and drug tests showed it yielded to voriconazole. Three weeks of repeat cleaning surgery, vacuum drainage, and the drug brought the wound under control and started healing, after which the drug was stopped. The authors flag the mismatch between fierce local damage and quiet blood tests as the tell for this invader.
pmc-13580080:
Ce Dong, Junbin Zheng, and Yucheng Jiang reviewed trials of saw palmetto extract and sexual function in men in 2026. The extract comes from the Serenoa repens plant and is a common herb choice for an enlarged prostate gland. Some men prefer it to drugs that can harm sexual function, yet trial results have been mixed.

The team pooled six trials that compared the extract with a placebo pill. The pooled result showed no clear gain or loss in sexual function from the extract. Quality of life also showed no clear gain. Results varied widely across trials, though the spread shrank in the subgroup that used one shared score scale.
pmc-13580180:
Josie Rojo and co-authors report a chemistry caution in a 2026 flash communication. A past paper described a route to a nickel fluoride complex with two phosphine arms. Such complexes matter for catalysis and bond-making work. The new team tried the route and hit snags worth sharing.

Their route gave a distinct nickel salt in solid form. With a close cousin phosphine, the target formed only in fully dried solvent. In the mixed solvent from the old report, a chloride cousin formed instead. The fluoride bridges also proved short-lived in solution, reacting with the medium. The note helps labs avoid silent traps.
pmc-13580380:
Hong-Yu Long and co-authors build a model to flag severe gallbladder attacks before surgery, in a 2026 study. Acute cholecystitis is a painful gallbladder inflammation that can turn severe. Spotting severe cases early guides safer care. The team used patient data from two large hospitals, with one site held back as an outside test.

Their model stacks two learners in layers. One reads image features from CT scans using an attention-based network. The other reads clinical and imaging traits with a boosting method. A simple final layer merges both forecasts. An explanation tool shows which inputs mattered most. The stacked model beat each single learner at both sites. Doctors get a tool that is both sharper and open to inspection.
pmc-13580580:
Manuel Bibes and six co-authors review applied spintronics, the field that uses electron spin as well as charge. Their twenty twenty-six review traces the arc from giant magnetoresistance to today's wider toolkit: spin-orbit coupling, collective spin waves, and electric control of magnetism. Spin can carry signals that charge alone cannot.

The review centers on how spin and charge convert into each other, and on effects that read or move magnetic states with current and voltage. These mechanisms power magnetic sensors and magnetic memory chips. They also feed newer ideas: racetrack memory, spin logic, and odd computing schemes. The authors map shared principles across materials and sketch where spin devices may go.
pmc-13581480:
Gahana Kataria and Vaishali Dhawan present the case of a three-year-old girl born with a shortened, bowed right leg and fewer, smaller toes on that side. X-rays showed the fibula bone completely absent, the tibia curved forward, and a reduced toe count. The left leg was normal.

Together, these features fit the rare FATCO spectrum, a congenital condition of faulty lower-limb development whose genetic basis remains unknown. Orthopedic plans centered on gradual limb lengthening, with amputation and a prosthesis considered as a way to improve function and mobility. The report offers clinicians a clear picture of a seldom-seen limb pattern.
pmc-13581580:
Wu and co-authors build a tool to flag very preterm babies at risk of poor growth after birth in this 2026 study. Growth faltering often strikes during the switch from tube feeding to milk feeding. The team reviewed 260 infants born at 28 to 31 weeks and screened their early records for warning signs.

Six factors mattered most: birth timing, sex, days to regain birth weight, mother's diabetes, mother's blood pressure disorder, and a kidney marker in blood. A classic statistical model beat four machine learning rivals, and a chart built from it predicted risk strongly. The authors offer the chart for spotting babies who need personal feeding support early.
pmc-13581680:
Wanyan Zhou and others put out a 2026 clinical trial report from the Shanghai Mental Health Centre on treating the negative symptoms of schizophrenia. Negative symptoms, such as flat emotion and low motivation, drive much of the hardship from schizophrenia and respond poorly to current drugs. The trial added the antidepressant agomelatine to patients' current antipsychotic drugs.

Outpatients with prominent negative symptoms were assigned at random to the combined treatment or comparison care, with raters scoring symptom scales during the study. Brain-wave recordings were also collected to build a model predicting who responds. Work of this kind searches for both better drug combinations and early signals of benefit.
pmc-13581880:
Naif AlJohani and five co-authors review how to revive donor immune attack when acute myeloid leukemia comes back after a stem cell transplant. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. Comeback hits near half of transplant patients and is the top cause of death in this group. Old rescue steps, like more chemo or donor cell drips, help just a few.

The review sorts comeback into three kinds of immune escape, like lost markers or raised shields. Each kind is matched to cell cures built for it, such as armed T cells and NK cells. A four-path plan keys care to clone tests done first. Gaps that block standard use are laid out at the end.
pmc-13582380:
Kim B Kuchemüller and colleagues build a math model of virus making in human kidney cells and plug it into a live monitoring frame, in a 2026 study. The model tracks living, dead, and burst cells against food use, waste buildup, and virus specific harm. First tuned on adenovirus cultures, it was then refitted to two other gene therapy virus types with only small parameter changes.

A sensor layer reading the broth's electric behavior fed live cell counts into the model as it ran, a setup the team calls a digital shadow. In perfusion runs the shadow tracked real cell counts closely and called growth and infection timing on the fly. The authors pitch the pairing as a step toward a full digital twin that can steer virus factories.
pmc-13582580:
Pravalika, Afthab, and Rajamani build a compact neural network for reading coronary angiograms on an FPGA chip in a 2026 paper. Heart artery disease is a top global killer, and plaque findings guide care. Large diagnostic models are too heavy for small devices.

Knowledge from a big teacher network was distilled into a small student network shaped for hardware. The student scored very high accuracy and related measures on held-out images, and held up under cross-checks. Placed on the chip, it answered in microseconds with high throughput and low power use. The authors present the system as real-time support for plaque assessment. Tests used a standard train and test split.
pmc-13582980:
Cells that divide too many times retire permanently, and their retirement reshapes the whole body. Nadia Da Silva Fernandes and co-authors track that process at the level of proteins. Using mass spectrometry, they measured how the full protein set of a cell changes as replicative senescence sets in. The changes unfold in stages, and they move together rather than at random.

Proteins drain away from the chromatin, the cell's packed DNA. The machinery that builds new proteins thins out. Mitochondrial proteins grow strangely insoluble. Cleanup systems, both autophagy and the proteasome, lose their edge. The team compares this pattern with other stressed cell states and finds a distinct signature. Their dataset is a resource for anyone studying how aging cells reorganize themselves.
pmc-13583180:
Parviz Marouzi and co-authors built machine learning models that predict, separately for each fracture type, whether an orthopedic trauma patient will stay in hospital a long or short time. Stay length drives bed planning and discharge work, yet broken hip, wrist, and ankle patients follow very different courses. One shared model blurs those differences.

Records from three trauma centers were cleaned from over 300,000 diagnosis entries into visit-level groups for four fracture sites, each with thousands of admissions. Models were trained and checked within each fracture group. Fracture-specific prediction respects how unlike these injuries are. Hospitals could plan beds and staffing with fewer surprises.
pmc-13583280:
Miguel Victor Bringel Sales and co-authors presented a 2026 study of sepsis, a severe response to infection. They focused on ferroptosis, a form of cell death that depends on iron. This process is linked to organ harm and death in sepsis, but its gene control in humans was not well mapped.

The team joined data from seventeen past studies of blood from sepsis patients and healthy people. The data came from three kinds of gene tests, some at the level of single cells. Signs of this cell death grew stronger as illness got worse and were stronger in adults. Cells called monocytes were the main source in blood, and eleven genes were raised across the data sets.
pmc-13583680:
Wenpeng Li leads a team on breaking down tetracycline with cavitation and UV. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with an antibiotic pollutant. Two oxidants are compared in the joined system.

Rising inlet pressure grew cavities and cloud shed in tests. Cavitation alone removed most drug at a mid pressure. One oxidant responded more to the joined process than the other. Best removal rates neared full clean in one hour. Acid settings suited one system, with lower energy cost. Dose and pH were tuned for best results.  Two oxidants were tested side by side in the platform.
pmc-13583780:
Maryam Razaghi, Sharon Unger, and eight co-authors set out a trial of donor milk for newborns in Canada. Their protocol, from twenty twenty-six, runs at Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto. Mother's own milk is the best food for babies, yet top-up feeds are common in well-baby units. When a top-up is needed, staff must choose formula or pasteurized donor milk with little trial evidence.

The trial will enroll one hundred twelve babies at higher risk of needing a top-up. That group covers babies of diabetic mothers, small babies, and late preterm babies. Each baby is assigned by chance to donor milk or formula top-ups. Feeding and health outcomes will be compared during the hospital stay.
pmc-13583880:
Biji and co-authors explore what spiritual wellbeing means to people with advanced cancer receiving palliative care in northern Kerala, India. Spiritual health is a core part of end-of-life care, yet patients' own accounts of it are rarely recorded in low- and middle-income settings.

The team interviewed twenty patients in depth and grouped their accounts into four themes. Suffering was physical, emotional, social, and financial at once; family, community, and staff support brought healing; acceptance and inner strength helped people cope; and faith, prayer, and ritual gave meaning. The authors argue that palliative care should treat spirituality as woven through all of these, not as religion alone.
pmc-13583980:
Kimiya Karimi, Sahebali Manafi, and Fatemeh Mirjalili cook up a wound dressing that fights germs, supports tissue, and releases medicine slowly, in a 2026 study. Complex infected wounds need all three jobs at once, and no single dressing did them well.

Their gel blends seaweed and shell-derived polymers with mineral nanoparticles and thyme extract. The final recipe was porous and uniform, far tougher than plain gel, and swelled strongly without falling apart. Cells thrived on it, reaching high viability after three days. It killed over ninety-eight percent of a common bacterium and a mold, at tiny doses. Medicine leaked out in two phases over time. Animal testing still lies ahead.
pmc-13584280:
Daan Langeveld and colleagues put a whole body of trial reports under a microscope in this 2026 integrity study. The reports are 223 randomized controlled trials, the gold standard design for testing treatments, all tied to groups built around one researcher. The team suspected that the numbers in those trials looked too tidy, with too little of the random scatter that real sampling should leave behind.

Their checks compared starting traits and dropout counts in those trials against 103 trials from other groups on like topics. Dropout numbers came out even far more often than chance allows, and equal dropout across trial arms was three to four times more likely than in the comparison set. The pattern was strongest when the key researcher led the author list. The team questions the worth of those trials.
pmc-13584480:
Nassirou Ibrahim and a large team audit teen health services in Niger in this 2026 study. Teenagers need care for sexual and reproductive health and for mental health, yet in poor settings both can be patchy and wasteful. The team surveyed 160 public health sites in the capital region of Niamey and in Maradi, checking what was on offer and how well each site used its resources.

Nine in ten sites offered sexual and reproductive care to teens, but only one in ten offered any mental health support. On a standard efficiency scale, sites averaged a score near 45 percent, which leaves wide room to do better with the same inputs. The authors call for training staff to handle teen mental illness and for stocked pharmacies that carry the products teens need.
pmc-13584680:
Yasmin Padoin and co-authors study root canal rinses in a 2026 lab paper. During root canal treatment, the canal is washed with disinfecting fluids, sometimes across two visits. Those fluids can change the root's dentin, the hard tissue under enamel, in ways that may weaken the tooth.

Bovine roots were treated with salt water, bleach solution, or chlorhexidine, in one or two simulated visits. Breaking strength did not differ between groups. Roughness was highest when bleach was used over two visits, matching erosion seen under the microscope. Chlorhexidine lowered dentin hardness, while visit count did not. The authors conclude that rinses alter dentin's surface traits without changing its fracture resistance in this model.
pmc-13584780:
Malik Raihan Ahmad, Riyazuddeen and Mohammad Jane Alam dissect an ionic liquid mixed with two alcohol solvents, in work published in 2026. Density, sound speed and viscosity were measured for the pure liquids and their blends across temperatures, then turned into excess and deviation values that expose how the molecules interact.

Infrared spectra, quantum chemistry and molecular dynamics simulations all probed the same mixtures from different angles. Fitted curves matched the measurements closely, and the theory layers agreed on the interaction picture. The combined frame is offered as a template for predicting how such designer solvents behave before anyone mixes them in a plant.
pmc-13585080:
Sayali Athawale, Nikita Mohelay, Puneet Batra, Aditya Talwar, and Ashish Kumar Singh compared clear aligners with standard expanders for narrow upper jaws in children in 2026. Mixed dentition, when baby and adult teeth share the mouth, is a common window for widening. Aligners offer a discreet rival to fixed expanders.

Searches to August 2025 found eight studies with four hundred twelve children, average age about eight. Pooled results favored expanders for widening between both the canine teeth and the molars; the molar gap was the clearer one. Widths, arch size, molar tilt, and palate depth were all tracked. Bias checks used standard tools for trials and other designs. The review gives orthodontists a pooled view of the trade-off.
pmc-13585280:
Luciano Dyballa and co-authors draw maps of how mouse visual areas encode the world. Their 2026 study builds encoding manifolds, layouts that place neurons by what stimuli they prefer and how their responses unfold. It uses a large public data set spanning the primary visual area and five higher ones.

Each area's manifold formed a smooth, continuous sheet where selectivity and timing vary in orderly ways, with layer and cell-type patterns woven in. One surprise recurred everywhere: neurons that love natural scenes prefer either very coarse or very fine gratings, never the middle. Layer patterns split too, with grating taste concentrated deep and scene taste higher up. The authors present the manifolds as a way to see sensory coding whole.
pmc-13585480:
Plants build many key compounds from one shared pathway, and two branch chemicals sit near its end. Anya Franks and six co-authors tracked how fast those two chemicals, chorismate and isochorismate, turn over in Arabidopsis leaves in a 2026 study.

Using labeled carbon dioxide, the team watched fresh carbon move through leaf pools over minutes. Chorismate stayed mostly inside chloroplasts and renewed very fast, while isochorismate sat outside them in far larger amounts and renewed more slowly. A mutant plant that cannot export isochorismate lost most of its pool, which backs the picture. About a third of the chorismate pool, they calculate, flows on into isochorismate and toward salicylic acid, a defense signal.
pmc-13585580:
Rashid Mir and a large team use whole-exome sequencing to find genetic variants in coronary artery disease patients, in work published in 2026. The disease reflects genes, environment and lifestyle together. Sequencing covered 28 patients, many of whom also had hypertension, high lipids, obesity or type 2 diabetes.

The study found many thousands of variants across 108 genes in the group. Genes tied to heart muscle structure, such as TTN, were hit most often. A focused set held 21 variants classed as pathogenic or likely pathogenic, eight of them new. The authors present these variants as candidates that may shape risk, severity and outcomes, and that merit follow-up in larger groups.
pmc-13585980:
Derya Okuyan and colleagues untangle two signals that switch on an invasion gene in prostate cancer cells. The gene, MMP14, makes the only membrane-bound collagen cutter in its family, a tool tumors use to chew through tissue. Working with PC3 prostate cancer cells, the team varied two inputs: a growth signal called TGF-beta and low oxygen, mimicked with a chemical stand-in.

Low oxygen proved the stronger driver, lifting the gene's output and protein levels on its own and with the growth signal added. Tests with trimmed copies of the gene's control region showed the full-length version answered every treatment, while short versions fell quiet under the growth signal alone. A partner collagen gene moved the opposite way. The picture is of oxygen stress running the show, with TGF-beta playing a tangled supporting part.
pmc-13586580:
Donghua Xuan and co-authors review how deep learning now watches rare wildlife automatically, in a review from 2026. Camera traps, drones, and video feeds generate more footage than people can scan. The team analyzed 159 studies from 2014 to 2026 across four tasks: naming the species, re-identifying individuals, estimating age and sex, and reading behavior and pose.

They trace three waves of models, from convolutional networks to attention designs to large foundation models. Case studies span giant pandas, Amur tigers, great apes, and marine mammals. Stubborn problems include weather interference, scarce training data, habitat shift, and weak field hardware. Fixes range from data augmentation to model compression. The authors flag gaps in multi-sense learning and on-device deployment.
pmc-13586680:
Riccardo Castagnoli, Luca Pecoraro, and Elio Novembre reply in 2026 to a letter on their review of high IgE in children. IgE is a blood protein tied to allergy, and very high levels call for a careful search for the cause. Their review dealt with high levels that are not part of a known gene syndrome.

The reply sorts out the terms they used. Plain high IgE means any value above the range for a child's age, they say. Their stricter term means a level above a set high mark, used to flag cases that need a full work-up. They also explain why their charts mix both terms and how the age ranges in their table were built. They thank the letter writer and accept his other term as a fair choice.
pmc-13586780:
Lanjie Chen and co-authors argue that glioblastoma care should look past the tumor's own turf to the brain's borderlands for immune help. This brain cancer shrugs off immune therapy that works in lung or skin tumors. Its home ground lacks normal lymph drainage and hides behind the blood-brain barrier.

The review maps the border stations: the meninges, the choroid plexus, skull bone marrow, and the sleeves around vessels. Immune cells gather and take orders at these gates, even when the tumor core stays cold. Fresh work on brain immunity shows these borders steer what reaches the tumor. Therapy that trains or recruits at the borders might sneak help past the barrier. The authors chart which border routes look most ready for trials.
pmc-13586880:
Xianlin Zeng and co-authors show that a stiffened liver can push immune cells into a harmful state, in a 2026 paper. Liver scarring, called fibrosis, makes the tissue around cells harder. Dendritic cells, which train the immune system, work poorly as therapy in such livers. The team asked whether the stiffness itself miseducates these cells, and through what chemistry.

In lab tests, stiff surroundings made dendritic cells mature in the wrong way: they waved more alarm signals, ate less debris, and calmed fewer regulator cells. Tracing the cause, the authors found the stiffness shut down a control protein, which cut cholesterol export and let cholesterol pile up inside the cells. Removing cholesterol or switching the control back on fixed the behaviour. In mice, pairing two drugs softened the liver and restored immune balance.
pmc-13586980:
Fons van der Plas and co-authors run a grassland experiment in 2026 on what happens when plant communities grow more alike across patches. Local loss of species is known to cut plant growth, but loss of variety between patches had not been tested in this way.

Fifty six plots were each split into four subplots on two soil types. The team sowed the same, partly overlapping, or fully distinct species mixes across the subplots. After four years, high variety between subplots raised total plant growth. The gain ran in part through higher local variety over time, not just through a larger total species pool. The study is the first of its kind to vary both scales at once.
pmc-13587380:
Bol Puoch Deng and co-authors survey African buffalo in Gambella National Park in Ethiopia, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Field teams walked set lines across four habitat types in wet and dry seasons. They counted herds, read droppings for diet, and watched daytime behavior at set moments.

Counts pointed to a few thousand buffalo, with more females than males among adults. In dry months, herds crowded into wetlands and forest. Being near water and tree cover raised the chance of finding buffalo, while homes nearby lowered it. Grass formed the diet, led by one common species. The authors urge guarding wetlands and travel routes.
pmc-13587580:
Josef Klhůfek and five co-authors present a 2026 hospital study on the blood chemistry pattern of patients with low sodium who take spironolactone, a diuretic also used for heart failure. The drug is linked to low sodium, but its full biochemical signature, especially alongside a second diuretic, was underdescribed. The team compared over five hundred admitted patients with the condition, sorting them by which diuretics they took.

After adjusting for kidney function, spironolactone users showed higher potassium, urea, and uric acid in blood. The pattern held in careful subgroup comparisons and in adjusted models, with the drug independently tied to higher potassium and about a quarter higher urea. Surprisingly, urine tests did not show the kidneys holding back potassium. Adding the second diuretic did not clearly change the pattern. The authors map a signature clinicians can recognize when this drug is in play.
pmc-13588180:
Simon Berger and six co-authors unveil an automated screening rig for a tiny roundworm used worldwide in biology labs, in this 2026 paper. The rig images living worms in microfluidic chips at fine detail without the fiddly handling that has held back such screens. They prove it on a study of one cell that must break through a membrane, a process much like cancer cells invading tissue.

Over forty thousand animals were imaged and scored by a custom neural network with accuracy above ninety-two percent. Silencing 193 candidate genes one by one, the screen recovered forty-one of fifty-two known invasion genes. It also flagged fifty-one new candidate regulators. The authors say the system opens fast, sharp screening to ordinary labs, for gene hunts and drug tests alike.
pmc-13588580:
Lederman Bookobza and co-authors compare hospital stay after weight loss surgery in a 2026 study from Brazil. The Roux-en-Y bypass is the most common such surgery in the country and can be done through one big cut or small cuts with a camera. Stay length matters for cost and for patient recovery.

Charts for 64 patients with like health profiles feed the check, 31 with small cuts and 33 with a big cut. Most patients were women, at 84.4% of the group, with a mean age near 44. Of the traits checked, only stay length split clearly by surgery type. The small cut group stayed a mean of 2.45 days, less than the big cut group.
pmc-13589080:
Livia Bresciani and a large team compared the severity of two malaria species in hospital patients in the Peruvian Amazon, in a study from twenty twenty-six. One species has long been viewed as the dangerous one, while the other was seen as mild. Growing reports challenge that view, above all where transmission is low.

Records covered three years at a regional hospital. Most admitted malaria patients carried the supposedly mild species. Just over half of all admissions met world criteria for severe disease. That share was nearly identical for the two species. The authors argue the mild reputation is undeserved in this setting, and severe cases of the second species are likely undercounted.
pmc-13589380:
Xinbing Hu and co-authors mapped in 2026 three new target sites on a virus protein that could anchor diagnostic tests. The virus causes hemorrhagic disease in deer and other ruminants and spreads by biting midges. Its VP7 protein is shared across virus types, making it a prime target for blood tests.

The team made the protein in bacteria, immunized mice, and created four antibody-producing cell lines. Cutting the protein into pieces pinned down three short stretches that the antibodies recognize. Those stretches are conserved across virus types, sit on the surface of the protein, and do not cross-react with two related viruses. The work lays groundwork for specific diagnostic kits.
pmc-13589580:
Shuangfeng Xu and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how engineered bubble-like carriers might help the brain heal after a stroke. Recovery of movement and thought after ischemic stroke stays poor with current care. Cells naturally release tiny bubbles called exosomes, which ferry small RNA messages between them. Loading those bubbles with chosen messages offers a cell-free way to nudge repair.

The review explains how such messages act on the whole neurovascular unit, the team of vessels and brain cells that must recover together. It then covers ways to aim the bubbles and pack them with cargo, building a guided delivery system. Matching treatment to the stage of stroke damage gets special attention. The authors close with the factory-level hurdles, from standard production to potency testing, that block clinical use.
pmc-13589980:
Nouf Ahmed Banakhar and co-authors review in a 2026 study why Saudi health workers underreport safety incidents and how to fix it. Fifteen studies from 2020 to 2025 met their bar. Underreporting was stark: about half of workers in many studies had filed no report at all, and in basic clinics the share reached nine in ten.

Drug errors and near misses were the most filed types. Barriers grouped into four kinds: a blame culture, heavy workloads with weak feedback, clumsy reporting systems, and personal fears. The authors align fixes with the national Vision 2030 plan, urging habits and systems that make reporting safe and worthwhile.
pmc-13590080:
Young-Shin Lee and five colleagues present a 2026 study mapping dementia's uneven burden across older Americans. Drawing on a national aging survey of over seven thousand five hundred adults, they classified cognitive status as probable, possible, or no dementia, then weighed risk factors by race and ethnicity.

Age, low education, stroke, falls, and depression raised the odds of dementia, while being female and using vision or hearing aids lowered them. The disparities were stark. Hispanic adults over eighty-five faced a sixty percent predicted probability of probable dementia, against thirty-five percent for White peers. Low education hit Hispanic adults hardest. The authors call for culturally tailored care and for insurance that covers hearing and dental services.
pmc-13590280:
Lori Boies compares AI, peer, and teacher feedback on student science writing in a study from 2026. Generative AI can now comment on drafts, but how its comments stack up against human ones is unclear. The study ran inside real undergraduate biology classes.

Students wrote two kinds of pieces: infographics and explanatory articles. Feedback came from ChatGPT-5, classmates, and instructors. Agreement between sources was scored with a standard statistic. Students rated each source for usefulness, trust, and effort sparked. Agreement varied with the kind of assignment and class. The results help teachers decide where AI comments help and where human eyes remain key.
pmc-13591180:
Kalyn C Jannace and colleagues tested a service-dog training program for military-connected people living with posttraumatic stress. The nonrandomized pre-post trial ran from 2019 to 2022 at two major military hospitals in the National Capital Region. One hundred eighteen participants, averaging 37.8 years of age, attended twice-weekly training sessions for six weeks after four weeks of baseline assessment.

Scores fell significantly on all three outcome scales: posttraumatic stress dropped by 5.8 points, anxiety by 1.5 points, and depression by 1.2 points. Training a dog for placement with another veteran may therefore work as an engaging adjunct to standard care. The absence of a control group means the gains cannot be credited to training alone.
pmc-13591280:
Roberto Montorsi and co-authors pool randomized trials on ways to prevent pancreatic fistula after pancreas surgery. A fistula, a leak from the pancreas, causes most illness and death after partial pancreas removal. Many preventive steps have been tested, yet experts still disagree on which ones work.

The team searched a large database of pancreatic surgery trials spanning two decades. They used both older and newer standard definitions of serious fistula. They flagged steps that cut fistula rates in at least one trial. Then they combined trial results for those steps in meta-analyses. The work is the first review of its kind across all partial pancreas operations. It gives surgeons a ranked view of the proof.
pmc-13591480:
Jolie Demchur and co-authors report a 2026 study on clinic signs that may split two gut diseases in horses before tissue results return. One is a swelling disease of the bowel and the other is a cancer of the same tract. Both can look alike at first, yet their outlooks differ a lot, so early hints help owners plan.

The team read records for 46 adult horses with a final tissue diagnosis: 28 with the swelling disease and 18 with the cancer. Sharp belly pain and repeat belly pain were far more common in the swelling group. Enlarged belly lymph nodes on ultrasound showed in the cancer group alone, in 60 in 100 of them. Blood and lab values barely split the two groups at all. The team says the two stay hard to tell apart on clinic signs alone.
pmc-13591580:
Emmanuel Nageeb, Sare Demirtas, and John Felder describe a surgical method for rebuilding arms and legs with very thin skin flaps taken from the belly, in this 2026 article. Rebuilding a limb needs soft, flexible tissue that restores shape and lets the limb move early. In heavier patients, the usual donor sites stay too bulky even when thinned, and extra trimming operations delay recovery.

The belly offers the body's largest skin reserve and can usually be closed directly, yet surgeons rarely use it for limbs, fearing it is too thick. The authors set out a systematic harvest at two depths, skimming above or below the fatty layer, using two known blood vessel routes of the lower abdomen. Their approach shows the overlooked donor site can supply large, thin, well-fed flaps. For patients facing limb repair, that widens the options beyond the usual thigh and groin sources.
pmc-13593780:
Maximiliano Correa Lara, Jaime Garcia Chavez, and Erika Martinez Hernandez link immune genes to stem cell behavior in aplastic anemia in this 2026 study. In this disease, the immune system destroys the marrow's stem and progenitor cells. Certain class II immune genes track strongly with who gets it. Which self-peptides those genes present was largely unknown. The team compared thirty-five patients with hundreds of healthy controls. Gene activity data from untreated stem cells added a second layer.

Genes that stood out in patients were cross-checked in a single-cell data set. That filter kept genes most active in the stem cells themselves. The aim is a short list of candidate self-targets for the immune attack. Such targets could explain why only some gene carriers fall ill. They might also guide gentler, targeted treatments in future. The work combines genetics with gene activity in one design.
pmc-13593880:
Yinan Zhang, Dinuo Li, and Xin Zhang test a rosemary compound against stomach cancer that has learned to resist a standard drug, in a study from 2026. The drug, called 5-FU, is a mainstay of stomach cancer care, but tumors often stop answering it over time. The compound, carnosic acid, was known to fight tumors and tune immunity, yet its role in resistant disease was unclear.

The team worked with cancer cells that answer the drug and cells that resist it, plus mouse models of both kinds. Adding the compound made cells easier to kill, slowed their growth and movement, and curbed a shift linked to spread. It also boosted the killing power of immune T cells. The effects ran through a signal pair the authors name, which they probed with gene and protein tests.
pmc-13594480:
Abdallah El Bizri and co-authors weighed stroke risk in kidney disease in two thousand twenty-six. They studied patients with an irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation. Such patients face clot risk, but kidney failure adds bleeding risk. That clash makes blood-thinning choices hard for doctors. The team used a huge national hospital database to compare groups.

Records covered two recent years of admissions across the country. Patients with failed kidneys were matched to similar patients without it. The team compared clot strokes, brain bleeds, and mini-strokes. Death during the hospital stay was also tracked. Matched groups numbered in the tens of thousands of pairs. The findings help doctors judge thinning drugs in this frail group.
pmc-13594880:
Eleven researchers mapped the genes that control iron levels in the heart, in work published in 2026. The heart needs iron for energy and steady beating, but too much or too little can harm it. The team used a family of lab mice called BXD, whose genes vary in known ways. They combined gene maps with measures of heart iron across many strains.

Heart iron ranged widely across the mouse strains, and much of that gap was passed down through genes. High iron linked to smaller heart mass, extra beats, and slower signals between heart chambers. A group of genes that rose and fell together tracked iron levels in both young and old mice. The team named three genes that may act as upstream switches, moving iron through heart cells in steps.
pmc-13594980:
Sacco, Li, Smyth, Sanguinetti, and Bussi present a model for RNA structure, in work from twenty twenty-six. RNA molecules fold into shapes that decide their function. In real life they flicker among many shapes, not one fixed form.

Most tools give one shape or an average map. Chemical probing gives signals from the whole mix, but reading them is hard. Their model, MERGE-RNA, builds the physics of the probing test into the fit. It learns a small set of shared parameters across molecules and repeats. The output is a weighted set of shapes that fits the data with the least forced change.
pmc-13595080:
Takuma Yamashita and co-authors present software that finds off-target cuts in genome editing with fewer false alarms. Their 2026 paper addresses a safety risk: editing tools can cut DNA at unintended sites, which could cause harm, including cancer risk. Lab assays that scan the whole genome for such cuts tend to over-report them.

Their tool scores each candidate cut site with a statistical method, then applies added filters. Compared with the current standard tool, it found more true off-target sites with fewer obvious false ones. The assay it serves is the simplest of its cell-free kind, which makes the software widely usable. Better off-target maps matter before editing therapies reach patients, the authors argue.
pmc-13595180:
Ahmad Subahi and colleagues surveyed radiography interns and recent graduates from two Saudi universities about how well their training built the skills needed for safe practice. Sixty-one respondents came from the 2020 to 2023 cohorts. They rated their perceived growth, course coverage, and confidence. They also rated the value of clinical placements across seven areas of professional competence.

Ratings ran positive for communication, procedural and technical knowledge, patient care, and teamwork, and respondents saw those areas as important for their future work. Two areas lagged on every measure: medico-legal and ethical knowledge, and spotting significant findings on images, arguably the two where mistakes carry the heaviest consequences. The authors offer the pattern as a map for curriculum repair, noting the study rests on self-perception from a small group rather than tested ability.
pmc-13595480:
Anouk E C Bruijnzeels and colleagues followed colorectal cancer survivors for two years to test whether inflammation tracks the many faces of cancer fatigue. Within a population-based Dutch study, 411 newly diagnosed patients gave blood and answered fatigue questionnaires at diagnosis, one year, and two years, alongside a matched comparison group without cancer.

Eleven inflammation markers were measured. The soluble TNF receptors related most consistently to nearly every fatigue dimension. Those receptors are signals tied to a master inflammatory switch. The dimensions covered general, physical, and mental fatigue, plus reduced activity and motivation. Other markers joined in for specific dimensions, and mental fatigue showed the steadiest pattern. Survivors displayed a broader inflammation-fatigue web than the comparison group. The authors see inflammation as a plausible lever for easing survivorship fatigue, with the TNF pathway first in line.
pmc-13595580:
Wangyouyi Chen, Yiwen Bai, and Liuling Song pool trial results on whether gentle mind-body exercise improves balance in older adults who are frail or close to it, in a 2026 review. Poor balance drives falls, a major risk at that stage of life. Tai chi, baduanjin, and yoga are widely advised, but their effects on each side of balance were unclear.

Searching seven databases, the team found ten randomized trials with twelve comparisons. Mind-body exercise improved overall balance by a moderate margin. It also improved moving balance, the kind used while walking and turning, and standing balance by larger margins. Subgroup checks hinted that two to four sessions a week, of about half an hour to an hour, worked well. The authors weigh how frailty stage and exercise dose shape the gains.
pmc-13597180:
Vanessa De Rubeis and co-authors build a measure of intrinsic capacity, the sum of a person's body and mind reserves, for Canadian adults. The idea captures how aging unfolds unevenly, yet studies have measured it in clashing ways. A shared yardstick built on national data can steady the field.

They draw on a national aging study with just over thirty thousand adults. Experts and records point to eighteen candidate measures across movement, vitality, mood, senses, and thought. Factor tests find a seven-part shape under one general score. The general score proves steady and tracks healthy aging and frailty as expected. Sub-scores run less steady and should stay exploratory for now. Clinics and planners gain a tested way to sum reserve in older adults.
pmc-13597680:
When a spine level next to a past fusion wears out, surgeons must fuse again, and two routes compete for the job. Kaiqiang Zhang, Li Xia, and Zhenbin Wang compared them in a 2026 study of 107 revision patients. One group got an oblique side approach, the other a back approach, for single-level adjacent segment disease.

The side approach took longer in the operating room, about 309 minutes against 271, but lost far less blood, about 362 milliliters against 609. Pain, disability, and quality-of-life scores ended equal at every check. The side route restored disc height and spinal curve angles more strongly. Follow-up ran at least a year, with fusion and complication rates tracked for both. The authors present the trade as time and blood against alignment gains.
pmc-13597780:
Yongsheng Fu, Jian Wang, and Weiguo Wang reviewed coumarins in two thousand twenty-six. Coumarins are natural plant compounds with many actions. They calm inflammation and fight oxidation. Muscle and bone diseases were the review's focus. Covered conditions include osteoporosis, arthritis, and bone cancer. Degeneration and abnormal growth drive these diseases.

Coumarins act on several major signaling pathways. They can raise bone density in studies. Cartilage breakdown slows under their influence. Joint membrane overgrowth also eases. Some compounds block bone cancer cell spread. Clinical translation still needs much more work. The review maps promise alongside clear gaps.
pmc-13597880:
Losa and co-authors test a genome editing method designed to cut DNA with fewer off-target errors. Their guides mix RNA and DNA parts, a design called chRDNA, and pair with the Cas12a enzyme. Prior lab work showed the hybrid guides raised accuracy for both Cas9 and Cas12a. Here the team moved the method into living animals. They aimed it at three genes tied to known diseases: Pcsk9, Angptl3, and Ttr.

The editors were packed into lipid nanoparticles and given as a single vein dose. The target genes relate to high cholesterol and to transthyretin amyloidosis. The study checks whether precise gene disruption can work in the body. Results bear on future one-dose treatments for inherited disease.
pmc-13598580:
Zhang and four co-authors tested low doses of l-carnitine in mice in twenty twenty-six. L-carnitine helps move fatty acids into cell furnaces for burning. Most past work studied deficiency or fatty diets, leaving its everyday nutrition effects under normal chow unclear.

Healthy mice on standard chow got low oral doses for thirty-five days. Their livers grew lighter with less stored fat as dose rose, and liver cells shrank with fewer fatty droplets. Deep molecular profiling pointed not to stronger fat burning but to weaker fat making. Several pathways for amino acids, sugars, and cell building blocks also shifted. The authors recast l-carnitine as a network-level regulator of liver fat balance, not just a transport helper.
pmc-13598680:
Jeremy B Ducharme and co-authors asked whether pancreatic cancer scrambles the daily clocks of the breathing muscles and heart, extending the known circadian damage of cancer wasting beyond the limb muscles. Using a mouse model that grows pancreatic tumors in place, the team collected diaphragm and heart tissue every four hours across a full day at the onset of wasting.

Roughly sixty percent of rhythmic genes lost their rhythm in both tissues. In the diaphragm, core clock components faded and metabolic programs broke down in step with rest-phase timing, while inflammatory networks gained rhythm and peaked during rest. Heart disruption centered on networks for cardiac signaling, insulin response, and nerve-related genes, with a smaller inflammatory gain. The authors argue that clock collapse in the muscles that breathe and pump may help explain why cachexia kills, and they map the damage tissue by tissue.
pmc-13599880:
Floriane Le Vilain-Abraham and co-authors publish the protocol for THINK, a large French trial on blood pressure in kidney disease. High blood pressure drives the heart and kidney damage of chronic kidney disease, yet after the standard first drugs, no evidence favours one next step over another. The authors' hunch is that these patients carry too much fluid, so a water-expelling diuretic should be the second move.

The trial randomises whole centres, forty of them, to either a diuretic-based intensification algorithm or usual care, enrolling 720 patients with moderate to severe kidney disease and uncontrolled pressure. The main endpoint bundles kidney failure, steep kidney decline, cardiovascular events, and death. Blood pressure control, quality of life, and safety are tracked for two years. As a protocol paper, it sets out the design before results exist.
pmc-13600080:
Aging is a loss of the body's power to correct itself, David Bar-Or, Jason Williams, and Daniel Paredes propose in a 2026 paper. Longevity science now prizes healthy years and bounce-back power over raw lifespan. Classic hallmarks list what breaks with age, but not how those breaks add up to lost adaptability.

Their frame names five steps of self-correction: sense a disturbance, scale a response, repair damage, stop the response, and reset for the next test. Each step can be scored from stress-response curves, apart from hallmark counts. Chronic low-grade inflammation fits as a response that fails to switch off. The frame aims to guide drugs that restore correction, not just patch single defects.
pmc-13600280:
Mychal Beebe and Ankur Tayal report a 2026 case of chiropractic care for a man whose neck artery had been partly torn in a car crash. The 54-year-old arrived with severe neck pain, headaches, and a stiff neck, eight months after the crash damaged his left internal carotid artery. Because hands-on neck treatment after an artery injury raises safety questions, the clinicians first reviewed his history, examination, and imaging to judge the risk acceptable.

Over six months he received five adjustments with the Blair upper cervical method, aimed at the top neck vertebra, whose alignment with the skull looked altered. Pain ratings, a neck disability questionnaire, and a general health survey all improved over the treatment period. Beebe and Tayal stop short of firm claims from a single case. They call for more research on whether this care is safe and useful after traumatic artery injury.
pmc-13600380:
Sara Falck-Jones and co-authors compare ways of harvesting immune cells from the upper airways during respiratory infections, in a 2026 study. The nose and throat are where viruses land first, and the immune cells gathered there decide how illness unfolds. Yet researchers lack agreed methods for collecting those cells, unlike the easy chemistry of fluid samples. Patients with flu-like illness and healthy controls gave matched samples four ways.

The methods were deep nasal aspirate, nostril swabs, nasal scrapes, and blood. The aspirate won: it yielded the most living immune cells, including the monocytes and dendritic cells that raise the alarm, with no extra discomfort or blood contamination. The authors recommend it for studies that follow airway immunity over time, where cell quality decides what can be learned.
pmc-13600980:
Satı Coşkun Yazgan and co-authors argue, in a 2026 commentary, that a major lung cancer trial deserves a second look beyond its negative headline. The phase 3 trial added an immune drug after surgery for early lung cancer lacking two gene changes. It found no gain in time without disease return.

Mixed results across related trials raise questions about timing, leftover disease, and patient selection. The authors propose a framework crossing treatment timing with molecular leftover disease. They caution that comparing across trials cannot prove either factor causes success. The piece is openly hypothesis-generating. Its value lies in organizing the next round of trial design rather than rescuing a failed drug.
pmc-13601280:
Na Wang and co-authors (2026) traced how a dangerous bacterium picked up extra virulence. The ST11 line of Klebsiella pneumoniae resists last-line antibiotics, and some members have turned hypervirulent. The textbook route is a fused plasmid carrying virulence genes. Sequencing 112 local resistant isolates and comparing thousands of public genomes, the team found something different in the dominant local lineage.

In most of the hypervirulent local isolates, the virulence region for aerobactin, an iron-gathering system, sat in the chromosome itself. Insertion sequences marked the break points. Those isolates also killed wax moth larvae faster than comparable strains without the arrangement. Global family trees grouped similar strains into one lineage found mostly in China so far. The authors warn that surveillance focused only on plasmids will miss this chromosomal route.
pmc-13601580:
Jialong Wang and co-authors report a 2026 method to grow wafer scale single crystals of atom thin semiconductors on sapphire. Such crystals could serve as channel material in future chips pushed to the atomic limit. Growing them as one clean crystal across a whole wafer has been hard to do in a robust, simple way.

The team treated the sapphire surface with metals that match the crystal and the base, forming a low symmetry layer. That layer guided the growth of two inch monolayer wafers by a standard gas method. No foreign elements were added, and the crystals showed high quality. Test transistors built from them switched well, with strong on off ratios and good charge speed.
pmc-13601880:
Ivan Norscia, Edoardo Collarini, and Giada Cordoni study how play spreads in ape groups and toddler classes in a 2026 paper. Observers logged play across two chimpanzee groups, bonobos, gorillas, and two classes of children under three, checking whether bystanders joined within three minutes of a play burst.

Joining spiked after play began nearby, confirming contagion. Males, youngsters, and those close to the action caught the fever most. Groups with more young members and friendlier relations showed stronger spread. Because the pattern spans all living hominids, it likely predates their common ancestor. Readers get an evolutionary window on shared joy.
pmc-13602280:
Farrah Bakr and co-authors report brain tumors in people with a rare sun-sensitivity disorder in a 2026 paper. Xeroderma pigmentosum cripples DNA repair, so sunlight brings extreme burns and skin cancers, and about a third of patients develop nerve degeneration. Internal cancers are a newer worry. The United Kingdom's national service for the disorder followed five patients who developed primary brain or spine tumors.

The five, aged twenty to seventy-nine, carried two genetic subtypes of the disorder. Their tumors ranged from gliomas and meningiomas to a rare slow-growing type. Younger patients with one subtype developed the aggressive tumors, while milder cases grew slow meningiomas late. One patient died of glioblastoma. The authors urge routine neurological checks and targeted brain imaging for this group.
pmc-13602780:
Gülçin Cagay Sevencan and Sevcan Akça compare tools for washing a medicine paste out of the hidden corners of root canals. The paste, calcium hydroxide, disinfects between visits but must come out before filling, and it clings in the thin bridges between curved canals. Using 3D-printed resin molars with standardized bridges, they tested five rinsing methods, from a plain needle to sound, ultrasound, and two laser-driven streaming systems.

None of the methods cleaned the bridges fully. The strongest laser system, SWEEPS, cleared about forty-eight percent of the area, ahead of its sister laser method. Sound and ultrasound sat in the middle. The plain needle lagged far behind, at about eleven percent. Position mattered too: bridges near the crown cleaned best and those near the tip worst. The authors say laser help is real but partial.
pmc-13603180:
