Daniel Amoako reviews how drug resistance spreads through nature in this 2026 paper. Antibiotics are given to single patients or animals, yet their effects reach whole ecosystems. Bacteria trade resistance traits as drugs seep into soil and water.

The review follows that spread beyond farms and clinics into the wider environment. It sets out why resistance in nature matters for human and animal health alike. Readers get a plain map of a problem that crosses borders and species. The piece argues that control efforts must look past the point of use.
pmc-13603280:
Amalys Sanchez Garcia and colleagues expose adult zebrafish to cold water for three weeks. Their behaviour study from twenty twenty-six compares chilled and normal tanks. Temperature strongly shapes fish physiology and behaviour. Lab zebrafish underpin many drug and brain studies worldwide.

Four tests measured diving, light preference, social choice, and mirror response. Cold fish moved less and explored less overall. They stayed near the tank bottom more often. Mirror engagement dropped under chronic cold conditions. Social preference for other fish stayed largely intact. Effects persisted beyond short exposures reported before. Housing temperature is therefore a real variable in zebrafish experiments.
pmc-13603480:
Omer Unal and co-authors test whether a red-wine compound protects the retina in epileptic rats, in a 2026 study. Epilepsy damages the nervous system through cell stress and death, and the eye's retina suffers too. The compound, resveratrol, is known for calming such stress. The team traced the pathways behind any protection.

Thirty-two male rats were split into four groups. One got the seizure drug alone, one the compound alone, one both, and one neither. Brain-wave recordings graded seizure severity. Retinal tissue was checked for a signaling protein, cell-death markers, scarring signs, and stress chemicals. Results of this kind may point to add-on therapies that spare vision in epilepsy.
pmc-13603980:
Min Ook Kim reviews a class of tiny materials built to fight oxidative damage. Such damage drives disease, spoils food, and wears out farm crops and goods. Older antioxidants fade fast or reach their targets poorly. The review sorts the new nano-scale options into four kinds: materials that are antioxidants by nature, ones that mimic enzymes, coated particles, and carriers that deliver classic antioxidants.

Kim weighs how size, shape, surface, and dose set the strength of each kind, and how a protector can flip into a harm-doer. Proof from lab dishes, animals, and trials is kept apart, since a dish result is not a cure. Safety and fate in the body and the wild get close attention. The review maps uses from medicine to food keeping.
pmc-13604080:
Haifeng Li, Xueying Zhang, Guijun Chen, Yaru Zhou, Ying Sun, and Lixia Huang build a neural network that reads emotion from brain waves and blood flow signals together. Their paper was published in twenty twenty-six. Pairing the two signals is a growing route toward machines that sense feeling.

Older methods slice signals into fixed frequency bands and link channels only in pairs. Both choices miss how bands shift between people and how whole channel groups fire together. The new design adapts band splitting to each signal, then builds a hypergraph where one link can join many channels at once. Spatial and frequency views merge in one model. The framework targets finer emotion reading for brain-computer interfaces.
pmc-13604180:
Daniela Segala, Bianca Interlenghi, and Rosario Cultrera weigh, in a 2026 study, cancer load and body swelling in people who live with HIV in Ferrara, Italy. Drugs now control the virus well, yet cancer stays a real burden for this group. Cancers not tied to AIDS now make up most cases. The team read records of 566 people and built a score from four routine blood marks of swelling, such as IL-6 and CRP.

Sixty-four people, 11.3 percent, had a past cancer, with 79 diagnoses in all. About 71 percent of those were cancers not tied to AIDS. Most cases sat in the low swelling band, with scores of 0 or 1. High scores linked to low counts of CD4 cells, a key immune cell. One mark, D-dimer, rose more in the non-AIDS cancer group. The score gives clinics a cheap gauge from tests they already run.
pmc-13604280:
Yunyun Xiao and co-authors compare repair protein loss patterns in womb lining cancer in a 2026 study. Some tumors lose DNA mismatch repair, and the exact proteins lost vary. The team asked whether those patterns track with clinical traits and with a marker that guides immune therapy.

Records covered 675 patients treated from 2017 to 2025. Of these, 502 tumors kept repair and 173 lost it, split into three loss pattern groups. Repair lost tumors showed lower body mass, higher grade, and more spread into vessel spaces, plus higher marker levels. A newer staging system caught their local aggression better than the older one. Marker scores also differed within the loss groups.
pmc-13604380:
Ran Zhao, Xiuli Gong, Na Dong, and Xiaoyan Dong test, in a 2026 study, if a mother's mild germ exposure in pregnancy shifts sugar tags on her pups' antibodies. A long-held claim says early germ contact guards against allergy. Past work shows a low dose of a germ wall part, LPS, in pregnancy eases airway allergy in mouse pups. The tags in view, N-glycans, sit on IgG antibodies and steer what those antibodies do. Their role in this passed-down guard was not known.

Pregnant mice got a low LPS dose or salt water on day 15. Pups were met with house dust mite, a common allergen, at six weeks. The team pulled IgG from pup blood and read its sugar tags by a liquid method. Twelve tag peaks and five tag traits were counted for each pup.
pmc-13604480:
Ricardo Villa-Bellosta argues that the first energy currency of life was not ATP, in this 2026 paper. His candidate is a simpler compound, inorganic pyrophosphate. Cells run on ATP, but ATP needs nucleotides, selective catalysts, and membranes to be remade. That makes it a poor fit for life's start. A simpler way had to link outside energy to chemical change.

It can form under volcanic heat, with minerals, and in wet-dry cycles. It holds enough energy to drive steps such as adding phosphate groups and moving ions. If the supply kept coming, he argues, it could have fostered phosphorylated sugars. Those sugars could tie early carbon chemistry to networks like those in cells today. Later compounds could then remake the supply, in part closing the loop. On this view, ATP took over jobs once spread across simpler phosphates, and traces of that setup persist today.
pmc-13604580:
Weiao Kong and co-authors present a 2026 review on the two-way traffic between gut microbes and the brain in autism. Autism often comes with gut problems, and rising rates have not been matched by treatments for its core traits. Past work mostly studied how gut microbes affect the brain in one direction.

The review builds a fuller picture in which immune, hormone, and metabolic signals run both ways between gut and brain. Evidence from microbe sequencing, animal studies, and other recent work is gathered into one network view. The authors argue that this two-way framing can point to new treatment targets. They also note where the evidence is still thin or mixed.
pmc-13604780:
Laura Serrano-Aguilar and co-authors hunt for blood markers that separate autoimmune epilepsy from other epilepsy, in a 2026 exploratory study. Autoimmune cases are driven by chronic brain inflammation and may respond to immune therapy, but no blood test flags them. The team measured twenty-three inflammatory proteins in eighteen autoimmune patients, thirty-three other epilepsy patients, and sixteen healthy controls.

One marker, IL-12, ran lower in the autoimmune group, yet the difference faded once multiple-testing corrections were applied. A model adding drug resistance and EEG pattern separated the groups better, but the authors stress the small, single-center sample. They present the IL-12 signal as a hypothesis for larger prospective studies, not a ready test.
pmc-13605580:
Rafik El-Mernissi and Naoual El Menyiy lead a large team profiling hemp essential oil and testing whether it blocks the enzymes that drive blood sugar spikes. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Slowing starch and fat digestion is a known route to blunting glucose rises. Plant oils are candidate sources for such blockers.

Chemical analysis found a complex terpene mix led by one dominant compound. In glassware the oil inhibited starch-splitting and sugar-splitting enzymes, plus the fat enzyme lipase. It also slowed the formation of harmful sugar-protein products at several stages. Docking simulations placed the main terpenes inside the enzymes' active pockets. Drug-likeness predictions for those molecules were computed as well. The authors present the oil as a multi-target candidate. Living-system tests remain the obvious next step.
pmc-13606080:
Tang and co-authors compare two Chinese meat pigeon breeds at the level of ovaries, genes, and small molecules, in a 2026 study. Shiqi and Dabao pigeons differ in breeding history, but whether their reproductive machinery differs was unknown. The team recorded laying across hundreds of pairs per breed and profiled hormones, follicles, gene activity, and metabolites in smaller groups.

Dabao females carried far more progesterone and much larger mature follicles, though follicle counts and flock-level laying records looked similar. Hundreds of genes differed, clustering in matrix, cholesterol, and hormone pathways, while metabolite differences narrowed to a few bile-acid compounds. The authors call the molecular picture exploratory.
pmc-13606180:
Diejun Jia and colleagues frost crayfish tails with a cocktail of natural gels and antifreeze proteins, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Freezing freshwater crayfish wrecks texture as ice crystals tear muscle and water escapes on thawing. Chitosan and carrageenan sugars form hydrogel moisture barriers; antifreeze proteins restrain the ice itself.

A response surface design tuned the blend, with water-holding capacity as the score. The optimum landed at zero point eight one percent carrageenan oligosaccharide, zero point six one percent chitosan, and zero point one seven percent antifreeze protein, holding seventy-two percent of the tissue's water. Spoilage and oxidation measures guided the single-factor groundwork. The authors offer the recipe as a basis for frozen crayfish products that thaw like fresh, and for polysaccharide gels in seafood preservation generally.
pmc-13606280:
Bikash Kumar Pati and co-authors asked whether a plant compound can firm up a fish paste gel used in Asian cooking, in a 2026 study. The paste, surimi, was enriched with a shell-derived sugar known to aid health. The plant compound, quercetin, is a yellow pigment found in onions and apples. The team stirred in five small doses and ran a battery of lab tests on the set gels.

Up to the second-highest dose, the gels grew stronger, harder, and better at holding water. Doses made the gel's protein web denser and more heat-stable by encouraging cross-links. The gels also fought free radicals and two kinds of bacteria more strongly as the dose rose. The cost was color: the gels lost some whiteness to the pigment. The authors name the near-top dose as the best trade.
pmc-13606480:
Enas Mohamed Lotfy and seven co-authors published a study in twenty twenty-six on burnout among nurses, weighing three forces at once: the shift roster, home-life balance, and long-term illness. One hundred nurses at two army hospitals in Egypt filled in a twenty-item burnout scale in the spring of twenty twenty-five.

Seven in ten nurses landed in the mid range of burnout, and about one in eight scored severe. In the final model, which explained near half the spread in scores, joy with work-life balance was the strongest shield by far: the happier the balance, the lower the burnout. Shift traits and chronic illness played their own parts once balance was held still. The authors say rosters that guard home life may do more for nurse health than most wellness add-ons.
pmc-13606580:
Yilong Lu and co-authors catalog a calcium sensing gene family in sour jujube, a tough fruit tree, in work from twenty twenty-six. The genes, called CBL, help plants adapt to salt, alkali, and drought stress. Sour jujube endures such stress well, yet its CBL family had not been mapped.

Ten CBL genes were found and sorted into three family branches. All carry the classic hand shaped motifs of calcium sensors and sit mostly at the cell membrane. Four genes were active across many tissues. One gene rose steadily under long salt alkali stress and binds two partner proteins in yeast tests. The map gives breeders candidate genes for hardier fruit crops.
pmc-13606780:
Mohammed Moghadasian and Hibah Khawar read three-day food records of 68 college students against an old national food guide. Past large studies showed most young and old Canadians fall short on fruit and vegetables. Their 2026 analysis, drawn from a 2018 thesis dataset, grades four food groups plus energy, nutrients, fiber, and water under the superseded 2011 Canada's Food Guide. Sex differences ran through all groups.

Fruit, vegetables, and milk groups split most by sex. Plant foods sat below the guide's recommended amounts in most records. Energy, protein, fats, cholesterol, vitamins A, C, and D, sodium, and fiber also differed firmly by sex. The vegetable shortfall is the through line from teen to older datasets. Larger sets must test whether the map holds beyond this campus, they say.
pmc-13607180:
Dental work can injure the nerves that serve the jaw and tongue, and late spotting of the damage can cost a patient their best chance to heal. Alfonso Acerra, Francesco Giordano, Massimo Amato, Iman Rizki, and Alessandro Santurro review how these injuries are found today. They weigh the bedside touch tests dentists rely on against newer tools that measure nerve signals or image the nerve itself.

The bedside tests are common but give a weak grip on how bad the damage is. Signal-based tests add hard numbers, and a special scan can show the injured nerve directly. Used together early, the review argues, the tools sort patients by outlook and guide care, and they also matter in court.
pmc-13608480:
Hari Pankaj Vanam leads a six-author team through two puzzling fungus cases from car crash wounds in the Emirates. Crash wounds often carry soil fungi, and a fungus in a culture dish does not prove infection. Worse, some isolates refuse to form spores, defeating shape-based identification and routine mass spectrometry. Reference laboratory sequencing rescued both identifications.

The first patient, a 55-year-old man with a crushed, degloved hand, grew a sterile mold that sequencing named Subramaniula asteroides. No invasion test was done, no antifungal given, and the wound healed with surgery and antibiotics. The second, a 40-year-old man with severe arm trauma, grew Aspergillus quadrilineatus, identified across three gene regions. Doctors started voriconazole, then stopped after fifteen days, judging colonization likelier than infection. The authors argue for molecular identification of stubborn molds, and for restraint in treating what may only be passing contamination.
pmc-13608880:
Yanlong Gao and co-authors sprinkle nickel over a strontium titanate powder to make a better light-driven cleaner for textile wastewater. Dyes such as methylene blue resist breakdown and stain water far downstream. Sunlight-powered catalysts could destroy them, but common ones waste much of the light.

The nickel was spread finely by heating in ammonia gas from a decomposing salt. Loading was dialed by the strength of the nickel soak. At half a percent nickel, the powder destroyed the dye fully in seventy-five minutes under a lab lamp. Its rate ran over three times the plain powder's. Charge separation likely explains the gain. Cheap boosts to known catalysts matter at plant scale.
pmc-13608980:
Levent Deniz leads an eight-author team checking whether white blood cell mix mirrors neck artery narrowing. Monocytes come in classical, intermediate, and non-classical flavors, each playing a part in plaque growth. The team studied 73 adults who had carotid ultrasound, splitting them at 50 percent narrowing of the internal carotid artery. Monocyte subsets were profiled by flow cytometry with inflammation markers and artery wall thickness.

Patients with significant narrowing carried more classical monocytes and fewer non-classical ones, plus higher white cell and neutrophil counts, fibrinogen, and HbA1c. Non-classical share also fell as artery wall thickness rose. Adjusted for age, sex, and blood pressure, a lower non-classical percentage still tracked narrowing. Adding fibrinogen, neutrophils, and HbA1c erased that link, while fibrinogen stayed significant. The monocyte pattern is part of the broader inflammatory state accompanying advanced carotid disease, the authors conclude, not a standalone signal.
pmc-13609080:
Guole Qin, Daizu Xie, Changqin Zhou, Delong Guan, and Jing Song present a 2026 study mapping the chemistry of a medicinal fern, organ by organ. Only the fern's rhizome, its thick underground stem, counts as the official drug part. Roots, stems, leaves, and young shoots are thrown away as farm waste.

The team profiled all five organs with a high end chemical scan, naming 2,765 compounds. Organ identity ruled the chemical pattern: leaf and root sat at opposed extremes, while stem, shoot, and rhizome formed a linked group. The rhizome held unique ring compounds, and the discarded organs proved rich in other useful chemicals, the authors report.
pmc-13609180:
Danaja Plevel and co-authors test whether a blood protein can warn of harm after surgery to remove part of the pancreas, in a 2026 study. Problems after this surgery are common and can be grave. A blood sign that shows early could let teams act in time. The protein they track is best known from heart work, where it rises when tissue is hurt.

Blood levels were taken before surgery and on days two, four, and six after it. The final group held fifty-three patients, most of them women. Those with cancer had far higher levels before surgery than those without. Patients in a worse health class also started higher. The team test how levels link with severe problems and with pancreas-specific harm after the operation.
pmc-13609480:
Gavrila Timis and co-authors review virus testing as a test of cure after cervical treatment in a 2026 systematic review. Removing high-grade precancerous tissue works well, yet some women still face residual or returning disease, and follow-up needs a reliable check that the treatment truly cleared the risk.

Fifteen studies covering nearly twenty-two thousand treated women were synthesized. Event rates for returning high-grade disease sat in the low single digits in most studies. Where accuracy could be compared directly, testing for high-risk human papillomavirus generally beat cytology on sensitivity, and a negative result was reassuring almost every time.
pmc-13609580:
Pagtalunan, Zhang, and Liu review a new class of molecules tied to a common herpesvirus. Human cytomegalovirus can be life-threatening for people with weak immunity and is the leading viral cause of birth-related infection, linked to small head size, hearing loss, and developmental delay. The virus hides in the body for life, switching between quiet and active phases.

Recent work shows the virus also produces circular RNAs, ring-shaped transcripts that interact with both viral and host messages. The review gathers what these rings do during infection, how they are found and studied, and how they might shape disease. The authors float them as candidates for future markers or treatments.
pmc-13609680:
Almeria, Rogers, and Mullins test a food safety method across many labs in work from twenty twenty-six. The target is a parasite that causes diarrhea outbreaks. It has been linked to Mexican style dishes that hold raw cilantro, such as fresh salsa.

The standard manual method was proven for cilantro alone, not for mixed foods. A prior study tuned it for salsa. Six food agency labs then each tested blind coded salsa samples with the updated gene based method. They also checked how long the parasite can be found in stored salsa. Shared proof across labs is key before a method becomes routine.
pmc-13609780:

pmc-13610680:

The cavities pack tightly and run deeper than they are wide. The hybrid route is fast and could scale to factory output. The team sees uses in optics where low reflection counts. Burst mode beam shaping aids the patterning step.
pmc-13611080:
Khalid Ahmed and co-authors wrote a case series from 2026 on severe injuries to the pancreas. The pancreas sits deep in the belly, so bad injuries to it are rare but hard to treat. pmc-13611380:
Bhishma Oli and co-authors review how the size of ground tire rubber affects asphalt in a 2026 paper. Rubber from waste tires can make road binder tougher, but studies disagree on how much it helps. The team gathered work from three databases and sorted it by theme. Themes covered how the rubber is made, how it swells in hot asphalt, flow and fatigue behavior, and storage.

Bigger rubber grains, swollen with asphalt oils, give strong physical support and hold up well at high heat. Finer grains mix in faster, thanks to their larger surface, and keep the binder stable in storage. Sizes that studies liked most clustered in a mid range, though the best size shifts with binder type, rubber source, and recipe. The authors treat that cluster as a hint, not a design rule.
pmc-13611480:
Caterina Rizzo and co-authors draw lessons from a restaurant food poisoning outbreak in southern Italy that involved several germs at once. Foodborne outbreaks hit immunocompromised people hardest, and this one included a cancer patient among the exposed diners. The team combined a retrospective cohort study with an environmental investigation of the restaurant.

Four of six exposed people fell ill within one to two days of the shared meal, a food-specific attack rate of one hundred percent. Three previously healthy adults stayed sick for fifteen to twenty-one days and later developed post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome. Stool tests used multiplex PCR, and kitchen water was sampled during the official inspection. Beyond tracing the source, the authors argue that vulnerability patterns from such outbreaks can point to who would gain most from future gut vaccines.
pmc-13611980:
Damian Stodulski and co-authors review the largest recorded outbreak of Bundibugyo virus, a cousin of Ebola now spreading in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. The event already ranks as the second-largest Ebola-family outbreak in history. It has crossed borders, killed many of its victims, sickened health workers, and met a world with no approved vaccine or specific drug for this virus.

The review explains what makes the outbreak significant for virology and public health, and where readiness falls short beyond the better-known Ebola virus. Diagnostics are thin, treatments are unproven, and surveillance leans on systems built for one virus rather than the whole family. The authors urge broader planning across the filovirus family: better tests, genomic tracking, vaccine candidates, antiviral platforms, and stronger local health systems. Their warning is plain: preparation aimed at a single virus leaves dangerous gaps when its relatives strike.
pmc-13612180:
Maylis Douine leads a sixteen-author team surveying people who mine gold illegally in French Guiana's Amazon forests. It asked about work, health, violence, food, safety, and care access, then clustered answers into profiles.

Hardship was layered. Over half, 55.7 percent, rated their health medium or poor, and 43.9 percent lived over a day's travel from the nearest health facility. About 44 percent felt unsafe, 29.8 percent had faced violence, and 16.7 percent had no social support. One in five experienced moderate hunger, and 21.9 percent screened at elevated mental-health vulnerability. Food insecurity tied to isolation and money trouble; mental vulnerability to being female, isolated, or feeling unsafe. The authors call for harm-reduction work and cross-border public health for this hidden population.
pmc-13612480:

Two germ kinds let the foe in fast yet starved its growth past entry. Fat reads show those germs cut slick fats in the host, and one fat fed back won the foe its growth. Two more germ kinds shed goods that kill foe spores in the gut. Most kin strains tried also cut the foe.
pmc-13613580:
Dequan Zhu and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a 73-year-old woman with two rare problems at once. She arrived with burning pain in her throat and upper chest, and doctors first suspected a heart attack.

Scans showed the double arch and how her neck and arm arteries branched from each side. Surgeons opened her chest in an emergency operation and found a tear about two centimetres long. The team reflects on how they planned the repair around the unusual anatomy, since no agreed playbook exists for this pairing. The case may guide other surgeons who meet the same rare mix.
pmc-13613680:
Sumaya Mehelay leads a large team presenting a 2026 framework meant to help health care groups build real equity into their daily work, not just state it as a goal. Recent pushes for equity, diversity, and inclusion grew after the pandemic laid bare deep unfairness and racism in health systems. The authors asked whether such efforts reach the roots of the problem, and set out to build guidance that does.

Their group mixed people with lived experience of structural unfairness with clinicians, scholars, and health leaders, and they drew on a rapid scan of earlier frameworks. The result is a practical frame for shifting power: changing who decides, whose voice counts, and how policies are written. Health groups can use it to test whether their equity work changes systems or only adds surface programs.
pmc-13613980:
Zhao and co-authors build a scoring chart that predicts dangerous belly pressure after surgery in patients with severe belly infection. Raised pressure inside the abdomen can harm organs and lengthen intensive care stays. Their 2026 study reviews 116 adults who had surgery and then received opioid pain relief in intensive care, of whom 49 developed the pressure problem within two days.

Older age, higher body mass, and higher blood lactate each raised the risk. Higher albumin levels and use of one pain drug, oxycodone, each came with lower risk. The team folded those five factors into a chart that sorted patients fairly well and matched real outcomes closely. They say the chart could flag high-risk patients early and guide care choices around surgery.
pmc-13614180:
Ana González-Ruiz leads a team testing whether human hair can track long-term contact with endocrine-disrupting chemicals, substances that interfere with hormones and are tied to chronic disease. Blood and urine are the usual test materials, yet both capture only recent contact because the body clears these chemicals fast. Hair grows slowly and may hold a longer record. The team built a method covering 44 such chemicals from five families.

Their lab routine combined exact measurement with a wider screen for related breakdown products, checked in paired hair, blood, and urine samples from 20 people after menopause. Comparing the three materials shows what hair adds and where it falls short. A hair-based record could help health studies link years of low-level contact with later illness, rather than relying on a single day's urine test.
pmc-13614480:
Nicole Baughman and Annmarie MacNamara tested in 2026 how letting a bad feeling stay, without fighting it, works over time. Seventy-nine people viewed upsetting pictures that were mild or strong, and either accepted their feelings or just viewed the pictures. Brain waves and personal ratings were tracked during the task.

Accepting helped lower a brain signal for mild pictures early on, but not for strong ones. It lowered felt arousal for both kinds, though. Later, pictures that had been accepted drew a smaller brain signal than pictures that had only been viewed. The benefit for strong pictures came later rather than at once. The authors place acceptance among effortful ways to handle feelings, with both strengths and limits.
pmc-13614680:
Aishwarya, Puthalath, and Kim present a small device meant to make eye measurements steadier, in this 2026 letter. The standard handheld gauge is easy to tilt, and light, alignment, and patient movement all shift the reading from one examiner to the next.

It was drawn on a computer and made with a three-dimensional printer, with a bracket, an arm, and a base that slots into the lamp. The lamp gives steady light and support, so exams can be done hands-free. The authors offer the design as a cheap way to make readings agree between visits and between doctors.
pmc-13614980:
Agnieszka Sabiniewicz, Nadine Brühl, Antje Haehner, and Thomas Hummel present a 2026 update of the labels used in the Sniffin' Sticks smell test. They swapped unfamiliar labels for familiar ones and balanced how often each answer appears, changing 31 percent of the labels in the set. Forty more volunteers then retook the new version after a gap of days to check its stability. Fairer labels mean a low score is more likely to reflect a weak nose, not a dated word list.
pmc-13615080:

Eight patients with long-term sinus inflammation and nasal polyps received dupilumab, 300 milligrams every two weeks, for six months. Nose swabs from the middle passage were taken before treatment and at the end.

pmc-13615480:
J. Kurwinkel and colleagues describe four dogs with unexplained lumpy inflammation around the eye, a condition with no found cause and no germs in the tissue. pmc-13615580:
Timothy Khumpan and a large team of co-authors published this 2026 study on telling apart two kinds of neuroendocrine tumors. Gene markers tied to the cell cycle and to rapid cell division marked the aggressive group. The work points toward molecularly informed diagnosis for these rare cancers.
pmc-13615680:
Fredrik A F Markussen and four co-authors build a way to sip brain fluid continuously from a hibernating hamster. Catching those shifts needs sampling that does not wreck the hibernation itself.

An analysis pipeline flags which ones build up or drain away during torpor. The proof of concept opens future studies.
pmc-13615980:

pmc-13616480:
Alia Djekidel and co-authors compare plant extracts picked in different seasons from a desert herb used in folk care. Their 2026 study covers both the scented oil and the soaked extracts of Artemisia herba-alba. The team wanted to know how the time of picking changes the plant's active mix.

The results suggest harvest timing matters for any future product.
pmc-13617080:
Grazia Pastorino and co-authors compared thinking and social skills in children with autism, children with attention deficit disorder, and typically developing peers, in work published in 2026. The autism group struggled more with understanding minds, shifting rules, and flexible design tasks. In the attention group, social scores leaned heavily on executive skills. In the autism group they did not. The authors argue screening and support should be tailored to each profile.
pmc-13617180:

pmc-13617580:

pmc-13617980:

pmc-13618180:

pmc-13618380:

pmc-13619380:

pmc-13620280:

Each link was classed as a smooth downhill run or one with a small bump below the hill. The tool gives chemists a firm check beside live motion tests.
pmc-13621480:

pmc-13623280:

pmc-13623380:

pmc-13623480:

pmc-13623580:

The team checked for uneven results across studies and for small-study bias with set tools. Planned subgroup and sensitivity runs tested how sturdy the pooled answer was. The authors aim to give clinicians and families a firmer read on a daily habit that is easy to change.
pmc-13623780:

pmc-13623980:

pmc-13624480:

pmc-13625280:

pmc-13625680:

pmc-13625880:

pmc-13626480:

pmc-13626880:

pmc-13626980:

pmc-13627280:

pmc-13627380:
