pmc-13652080:
Na You and nine colleagues test whether a gene called ARHGAP40 can slow clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most common form of kidney cancer. Drawing on large cancer datasets, the team found the gene switched down in tumors, partly through added methylation on its promoter. Laboratory experiments then raised or lowered its activity in cancer cells, and a mouse model checked the effect on tumor growth.

Restoring ARHGAP40 curbed malignant behavior, and the gene physically interacted with RhoA, a known driver of cell movement. Its presence also shifted signals through the PI3K and AKT pathway and changed how cells handled glutamine and oxidative stress, measured through glutathione and reactive oxygen levels. Rescue experiments confirmed the chain of effects, marking ARHGAP40 as a candidate brake on this cancer and a possible guide for new treatment ideas.
pmc-13653180:
Ke Xu and co-authors compare two valve diseases after the same rhythm surgery. Their 2026 study asks how often atrial fibrillation returns after a modified Cox-Maze IV procedure. It compares two groups: patients whose mitral leak stems from a stretched atrium, and those whose valve was scarred by rheumatic fever.

From two hundred twenty-one patients they matched thirty-two pairs with like backgrounds. The atrial-cause group relapsed more: before discharge their recurrence risk ran over three times higher, and by one year roughly thirty-one percent had relapsed against six percent. Death rates matched at every check. The authors advise tighter rhythm monitoring after surgery for the atrial-cause group, whose fibrillation seems harder to keep away.
pmc-13654480:
Arthur Chow and co-authors published this cell therapy study in 2026. AI protein design can now generate new binding proteins against cancer targets within weeks. Whether those binders work inside living therapies is another question. The team built 1,758 designed binders against three blood cancer targets, BCMA, CD19, and CD22. They slotted the binders into chimeric antigen receptors, the steering parts of engineered T cells, and screened them at scale.

The screens covered binding strength, T-cell activation, and killing of tumors in living animals. Three problems kept appearing. Some receptors signaled without any target present, some could not reach their target properly, and some hit the wrong tissues. The team developed practical screens and variant tricks to fix each flaw while keeping on-target power. Their framework offers a route from computer-designed proteins to safer candidate cell therapies.
pmc-13654680:
Komatineni Ravikumar, Rajat Naik, Sarbari Swaika, and Mohammed Abdul Salam wrote this 2026 letter on measuring blood pressure by ultrasound when cuffs fail. In shock, with wild rhythms, large arms, or after revival, cuff machines often return no reading at all, leaving emergency teams to guess at a number that drives fluids and drugs.

The writers review a bedside ultrasound route to the number. Doppler work began in niche settings, but handy techniques have spread since 2017, with firm validation only after 2024. The proof so far is promising yet thin. They call for larger prospective trials before the method can stand as a valid stand-in for the cuff in emergency and critical care.
pmc-13657880:
Chengcheng Yang and co-authors build a gene score for lung cancer immune care in a 2026 study. Lung adenocarcinoma is a leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Immune drugs help only a share of patients, and good forecast markers are lacking. Tired T cells, worn out from long tumor fights, may hold clues to who benefits.

The team screened factors tied to T cell tiredness in tumor gene data. Four factors linked to survival and split patients into high and low risk groups. A six gene score was then built from genes that differed between groups. Lab tests confirmed the six genes' levels in tumor and normal tissue pairs from their hospital.
pmc-13659380:
Aakriti Aggarwal led a 2026 survey of sentinel lymph node sampling in early-stage cervical cancer in the United Kingdom, a technique that spares lymph node removal while preserving cancer safety. Evidence and guidance support the approach for small tumors, yet how far it had entered UK practice was unclear. The team, with review from the British Gynaecological Cancer Society, sent a survey to 460 members over six weeks in 2024.

Only thirty-two replies arrived, a 7.0 percent response rate, mostly from gynecological oncologists. Two-thirds of respondents used sentinel sampling for at least one gynecological cancer, but only fourteen used it for early cervical cancer. Barriers cited often were weak evidence, missing national guidance, limited access to ultra-staging pathology, and restriction to trials. Every non-user said they would adopt the technique. Readers should weigh the small, self-selected sample against its signal: enthusiasm exists, but guidance and pathology capacity lag.
pmc-13659480:
Two skin diseases that should not be treated the same way sometimes arrive together, and Rachel Daher and co-authors report a drug that calmed both, in a 2026 case study. Their patient, a seventy-five-year-old woman with long-standing plaque psoriasis, developed bullous pemphigoid, a blistering disease driven by antibodies against the skin's basement anchors.

The trap is therapeutic: a treatment for one disease can flare the other. The team chose deucravacitinib, a pill that blocks the TYK2 signaling enzyme and so damps the interleukin pathways feeding psoriasis. Under it, both the plaques and the blistering improved and stayed controlled. The authors note the drug's role in blistering disease was unproven, and present the case as a reason to study TYK2 blockade where psoriasis and pemphigoid collide.
pmc-13660180:
Steven Liu, Ravi Malpani, Sophia Lubrin, and Vatche Israbian report a case of primary mediastinal synovial sarcoma, a rare and aggressive cancer in the center of the chest. Their 2026 report shows how the disease can hide at first.

A 45-year-old woman had a growing cough, fatigue, and chest discomfort, yet her first chest X-ray looked normal. Six weeks later, worse breathlessness and trouble swallowing led to new scans. They showed a large infiltrative mass pressing on the main airways, lung vessels, and left atrium. A bronchoscopic biopsy confirmed biphasic synovial sarcoma with an SS18 rearrangement. The tumor could not be removed, and the course turned fatal.
pmc-13661880:
Rama Maganti and co-authors reply to critics of their sleep study in a 2026 letter. The study used brain wave records to track deep sleep in people with sleep apnea. Critics warned that one brain wave measure may not show cell level sleep pressure alone. They also raised worries about a floor effect and a math flaw in the slope measure.

The authors agree the brain wave sign is not a pure marker and note missing brain scans as a limit. They reject the floor effect claim with group data that sit far above zero. They also explain how the slope was built hour by hour for each person. Their view is that the flat overnight pattern still points to weak sleep pressure build up.
pmc-13662280:
Alina Krasilia and co-authors study one part of a DNA copying machine across cancers in a 2026 paper. The machine copies DNA with high accuracy before cells divide. One small part helps the machine assemble and link to other parts. Yeast work showed faults in its twin gene cause unstable DNA and slow cell cycles.

Across tumor types, high levels of the part linked to shorter survival in some cancers only. Gene levels predicted outlook better than extra gene copies did. High gene levels often did not yield high protein levels, a gap the team traces to non coding gene forms. Linked gene patterns tied the part to cell growth control paths.
pmc-13665380:
Nikoleta Koliou and co-authors review AI help in surgical consent in a 2026 paper. Language models can make surgical facts easier to reach and grasp. Yet the authors stress that tools cannot take over the clinician's role in shared choices or the legal needs of valid consent. Their review walks the patient path from diagnosis and explanation through option weighing to the consent itself.

Along the way it weighs plain digital tools, model aided talk, tailored risk forecasts, and direct consent studies. Views of patients and professionals enter too, as do legal and ethical guardrails. The takeaway steers hospitals toward help that informs patients better while keeping human judgment and consent law firmly in charge.
pmc-13668680:
Claudia Hanson and co-authors reported this trial in 2026 on births in sub-Saharan Africa. About three million babies each year are stillborn or die soon after birth. The ALERT program aimed to cut that toll in hospitals with a bundle: staff helped design the changes, then got training, quality checks, and coaching for ward leaders.

Sixteen hospitals in Benin, Malawi, Tanzania, and Uganda took turns starting the program, so wards could be compared fairly. More than 134,000 women gave birth during the trial. Early deaths around birth fell by about a fifth in program periods. Stillbirths alone did not fall by a clear margin. The team says the mix of steps, fitted to each site, can save newborns even with few hospitals in the test.
pmc-13668980:
Flávia Oliveira Brito and co-authors present a 2026 study of how grinding and sprouting change what the body can take from chia seeds. Chia is rich in plant compounds and healthy fats, but a whole seed may pass through the gut only partly used. The team asked which treatment frees more of these nutrients during digestion.

They ran lab digestion on whole and ground seeds and sprouts, then measured plant compounds, antioxidant strength, and fats. Ground samples released far more of all three than whole ones, and one prized compound appeared only in ground samples. Sprouting alone helped less. The authors conclude grinding matters more than sprouting for nutrient access.
pmc-13669680:
Kristine Hole, Birgit Wollmann, Julia Stingl, and Espen Molden re-read old lab spectra to spot a class of stomach drugs in patients on a common mood drug. Their study is from two thousand twenty-six.

The mood drug's fate in the body rests in large part on one gene. Yet in real life, the gene and the true rate often do not match. The stomach drugs are a prime suspect, since they block the same path. The team went back to the high-grade spectra kept from past drug checks. By exact mass and shard marks, they could see if such a drug was there. That lets them gauge how much the mismatch is the drug's work.
pmc-13669880:
Andreas Winkler and co-authors describe a single heart case in a 2026 report. A seventy-nine-year-old woman had a leaking tricuspid valve, the valve between the right chambers of the heart. A clip device placed through a catheter had fixed the leak at first, a method often used when open surgery is too risky.

The leak later returned in severe form, and her symptoms grew worse despite drug treatment. A second clip procedure was not possible, so the surgeons removed the clips with care and repaired the valve in open surgery. Seven months later, scans showed only a mild leak, and the patient felt much better. The authors note that open repair stays a sound backup as clip treatments spread.
pmc-13670880:
The pulse that each heartbeat sends through brain arteries is tracked by a measure called the pulsatility index. High values are linked to disease of the brain's small vessels. In a 2026 study, Webb and co-authors ask a simple question: does raising heart rate lower that pulse measure?

They studied twenty people receiving pacemakers for a slow heart rate. As the paced rate rose from 50 toward 100 beats per minute, ultrasound readings from a main brain artery fell steadily. Each ten-beat rise cut the index by about 0.07, through lower peak flow speed and higher flow between beats. Because the change was caused by pacing, the authors suggest heart rate itself could become a way to ease pressure pulses in the brain.
pmc-13671680:
Paul Macharia and co-authors published this study protocol in 2026. It lays out the building and testing of a digital mental wellness platform for Kenyan adolescents and young adults. Mental illness is a leading cause of disability in this age group, while trained professionals are scarce and stigma runs high.

The platform, delivered through social media with an AI chatbot, is being co-designed with young people from three settings: an urban settlement, a peri-urban town, and a rural area. The plan runs in three phases: interviews to shape the design, building with repeated refinement, then a two-month trial with screening questionnaires and usage data. Early fieldwork began in January 2026, with usability testing to follow by mid-year. The authors aim to learn whether such a tool is feasible, usable, and welcome in daily life. Full findings will appear in later papers.
pmc-13672280:
Shajar Abbas and co-authors model heat and mass flow in a thick nanofluid in a 2026 paper, with a neural network as the solver. The fluid carries two sizes of carbon nanotubes in a glycol base. It flows over a plate with magnets and electrodes that push the flow, a setup called a Riga plate.

The plate sits in a porous layer whose density varies. Heat radiation adds to the mix. The team first rewrote the flow laws in a simpler form and solved them with a grid method. Those answers trained a neural network using a fast learning rule. Such trained nets can then predict flow behavior in seconds, a help for engineers who design cooling and coating systems.
pmc-13672680:
Drugs that block HDAC enzymes loosen DNA packaging and can slow cancer, but their effect in solid tumors is uneven. Jintian Song and co-authors hunt for the backup system that lets gastric cancer cells keep their genes running under such treatment, in a 2026 study. Their screens point to COMPASS, a protein complex that licenses gene promoters for activity.

A part of that complex, WDR5, proved to be the weak joint. Cancer cells with more WDR5 and more of its promoter mark were more sensitive when both the drug and a WDR5 blocker were applied. Breaking the WDR5 pocket thinned the promoter mark at growth genes and held transcription down even after the drug washed out. The authors propose pairing the two treatments to make suppression last.
pmc-13672780:
Muhammad Zafar and co-authors show in a 2026 study that human land use has raised the tsunami risk in large lakes. Around the world, erosion from farming and building sends extra sediment to lake deltas. That load steepens the delta front until it can collapse under water and push up a wave. The team studies Lake Iseo in northern Italy as their main case.

Two thousand years of heavier land use tripled the sediment flow to the lake. Geological records and simulations show that two medieval earthquakes set off major delta collapses. The waves ran up to great heights on the shores. Old accounts and archaeology back the reconstructions. Since then, erosion has rebuilt the delta, leaving today's shore towns exposed to the same kind of failure.
pmc-13673680:
A plant embryo must switch genes on and off in the right pattern as it forms. Janik Scotton and co-authors study one part of that control system in a 2026 paper on Arabidopsis, a small plant widely used in research. They focus on ALFIN-LIKE proteins, which read a chemical mark on the packaging of DNA that signals active genes.

That mark, called H3K4me3, sits on histone proteins around which DNA is wound. Reader proteins interpret the mark and help turn it into decisions about which genes run. The team's findings show that reading this mark is essential for the embryo to set up its body pattern correctly. The work connects a molecular reading step to the earliest choices that shape a plant.
pmc-13673780:
Yajie Zhuang and Ying Shen challenge the subgroup design of a real-world study of fatty liver disease, in this 2026 letter to the editor. The study under discussion measured quality of life and healthcare use in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, a serious liver condition. Its subgroups split patients by whether they had extra heart and metabolic risk conditions.

The letter argues the split is circular: current guidelines require at least one such risk factor to diagnose the disease at all. So the group labeled as having no additional comorbidities is restricted by construction, and headline comparisons between subgroups are undermined. The issue, they note, went unaddressed in the original discussion.
pmc-13674480:
Sathyanarayana Paladugu and co-authors show that a flash of light can steer the molecules of a ferroelectric liquid crystal, no wires needed, in a 2026 paper. Screen pixels today use a mild liquid crystal realigned by voltage on glass electrodes. Swap in the ferroelectric kind, whose molecules carry a shared electric lean, and the whole game softens: far weaker fields can swing it. The team shone low-power light on such a cell.

The light wakes a weak field inside the clear electrode itself, tens of volts per meter. That whisper proved strong enough to realign the ferroelectric lean, yet too weak to move the old crystal. The authors call the pairing extraordinarily light-sensitive. They pitch it for light-run photonics, sensors, and smart windows, where the picture is written by light alone. The effect also widens the known playbook of this young material class.
pmc-13674680:
Charlene Duchanois and co-authors present a 2026 study of unplanned births outside hospital in France, drawn from a registry over thirteen years. More than three thousand such births were logged by mobile intensive care units. Most mothers had low risk pregnancies, and most homes sat within about twenty minutes of a hospital.

Complications hit about one in twelve mothers and one in twenty-three babies. Early birth was by far the strongest risk factor for trouble. Cold newborns were the other big flag, affecting most babies checked. Travel time to hospital, long suspected, showed no link to complications. The authors argue for universal readiness of first responders, above all for warmth and early birth care.
pmc-13676080:
Moore and colleagues tested in 2026 whether repeated R2 star scans can track prostate changes during radiotherapy on an MRI-linac. R2 star is sensitive to deoxyhaemoglobin, so it may mark tumor hypoxia. Fifteen patients had five-fraction ablative treatment. Scans were taken before treatment, during it, and at follow-up for some.

After two fractions, R2 star fell in both the whole prostate and the tumor, while prostate volume rose. By follow-up, values were back near baseline. Patients on hormone therapy started with higher R2 star and smaller glands. The team says the changes are measurable, but the mechanism behind them needs more work.
pmc-13676380:
Spine surgery after a fracture carries extra risk when the patient also lives with a mental disorder. Kenta Takakura and co-authors check that risk in a 2026 study of Japanese hospital records. They sort 23,148 emergency fixation patients into groups with schizophrenia, mood disorders, or neither.

Death rates in hospital did not differ across the groups. Complications after surgery, though, ran higher in both disorder groups than in controls. About one in five patients with schizophrenia had a complication. Return to hospital within thirty days also stayed alike across groups. The authors urge extra care around surgery for patients with mental disorders.
pmc-13676780:
Agustina Mazzoni leads a large international team laying out the protocol for a living systematic review of the RSV vaccine given in pregnancy. Respiratory syncytial virus is a leading cause of severe lung disease in infants, worst in the first six months. The bivalent prefusion F vaccine was licensed for pregnancy in twenty twenty-three on the strength of one pivotal trial.

Real-world evidence on effectiveness across settings and seasons, and on antibody transfer to the baby, remains thin and scattered. The review will continuously synthesize new post-licensure data on efficacy, effectiveness, and immune response rather than freezing the evidence once. Living reviews suit fast-moving vaccine policy, where guidance must update as studies land.
pmc-13676980:
Xinyu Yang and colleagues studied antibody-making centers in the immune system in two thousand twenty-six. These centers form inside lymph tissue after infection or vaccination. B cells there refine antibodies over time. The cells need steady gene control to keep their identity. The team asked whether cell metabolism supports that control.

Boosting one mitochondrial enzyme raised a key fuel molecule. That molecule loosened a repressive mark on a master gene. The master gene stayed active, and B cells kept dividing. Antibody quality improved in their tests. Blocking the fuel pathway weakened the effect. The same axis also worsened a lupus-like illness in mice.
pmc-13677080:
Mikayla Spinler, Jason Woodworth, Mike Tokach, and four colleagues link sow appetite to piglet growth in this two thousand twenty-six animal science paper. How much a nursing sow eats shapes both her litters and her body condition. The authors pooled data from eight studies covering nearly one thousand first-litter gilts and thirty-four hundred older sows. Lactation feed intake was sorted into quintiles, and regression models were fitted for litter gain and sow weight change.

Higher intake raised litter daily gain and litter size at weaning in groups, linearly. Young gilts lost less weight as intake rose, with the biggest improvement at the low end of intake. Older sows shifted from losing to gaining weight as intake increased, and over half of them gained weight. Feed intake and litter gain explained over half the variation in sow weight change, and the fitted equations give producers prediction tools.
pmc-13677280:
Delip K Das and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six field study of what black-tailed godwits eat at a key stopover in the Bengal delta. The delta hosts two great migration flyways at once. Knowing the menu explains why birds return and how many the site can support.

Mud samples from many foraging spots tracked bottom-dwelling prey through the season. Droppings and pellets from roosting birds revealed actual diet. Birds ate both animal prey and plant material. Comparing diet with availability shows how selective the godwits are. Such knowledge guides protection of feeding grounds under pressure.
pmc-13677980:
Empey and co-authors report a 2026 pilot trial on returning gene test results to adults with high blood pressure and African ancestry. Near half of people with this condition miss their blood pressure goals, and gene-drug interplay may blunt drug effects. The trial enrolled 1,874 people and split them between fast return of gene results and return at trial end.

Advice tools matched two genes to drug choice and dose. Fast return did not lower top-number blood pressure at three months across the whole group. The report then turns to subgroups with lax control or gene types that call for action.
pmc-13678280:
Mohsen Naraghi and co-authors chart fifteen years of a rare nose tumor at one referral center, in a 2026 case series. Olfactory neuroblastoma grows in the upper nasal cavity and behaves unpredictably, sometimes returning years after treatment. Because it is so rare, the traits that forecast its course remain fuzzy.

The team reviewed nine confirmed cases treated between 2007 and 2022. Records covered symptoms, imaging, tumor grade under the Hyams scale, treatments given, and how and when recurrences appeared. Paired with a literature review, the series adds careful detail to a thin evidence base. Even small series matter here: pooled, they are how doctors learn which patients need the closest watching.
pmc-13678680:
Reyhaneh Arefimehr and co-authors report a 2026 study on tiny carriers that deliver a plant extract and a cancer drug together against breast cancer. Breast cancer stays a top cause of cancer death, so gentler and stronger therapies are in demand. Pairing a plant extract with a standard drug inside one carrier could hit the tumour from two sides at once.

The carriers rest on a shell polymer from crustacean shells, loaded with both agents. They came out round and small, held most of their cargo, and freed the drug slowly over three days, unlike the fast burst of the free drug. In two breast cancer cell lines, the loaded carriers killed far more cells than either agent alone. They pushed cells into a death program, stalled their cycle, and lifted a stress-response gene.
pmc-13678880:
Getting healing genes into the cell nucleus is the main block for gene therapy that avoids viruses. Lee and co-authors review two ways past that block in a 2026 paper. In cells that rarely divide, the nuclear wall stays shut, so DNA left outside it cannot work.

One way tags DNA with small signals that hitch a ride on the cell's own import system. The other way uses DNA stretches that borrow import help from the cell's own switch proteins. The review weighs when each way works or fails, and what new facts about the nuclear gate change the odds. Carrier design tips close the paper, aimed at safer future treatments.
pmc-13679680:
Schöll, Mair, and Litz report a case, published in 2026, in which ultrasound found a deep spinal infection. Infection of a small joint at the back of the spine is uncommon and easy to miss. It can look like ordinary back pain at first. Scans by magnetic resonance are the standard way to find it, along with any nearby pus pockets. In the reported case, an ultrasound scan spotted the problem first.

The infection sat in a joint of the lower back and had spread toward the space around the spinal cord. Finding it early matters, because spread can threaten the cord itself. The authors note that sound-based scans can reveal such pockets beside the spine. Their case argues for keeping ultrasound in mind when back pain has no clear cause. It also reminds doctors that this rare infection is more common than once thought.
pmc-13680780:
Zihou Liu and co-authors prove that a heart hormone talks straight to the adrenal gland in living animals. Atrial natriuretic peptide, ANP, keeps blood volume in balance, and dish studies hinted it also throttles aldosterone, the salt hormone. The team bred mice whose zona glomerulosa, the adrenal layer that makes aldosterone, lacks the ANP receptor GC-A.

Without the receptor, that layer grew thicker, held more aldosterone-making cells, and poured more hormone into the blood. A salty diet, which normally trims the layer, failed to do so, and the mice slid into volume-loaded high blood pressure. Human adrenal cells told the same story in reverse. Tumors that overmake aldosterone showed far less of the receptor, hinting the brake is lost in disease.
pmc-13681080:
Mohamed Badr asks why diabetic foot ulcers stall after blood flow is restored in a 2026 review. Opening the artery is central to saving the limb. Yet many wounds still refuse to close afterward. The review names this the patency-to-healing gap.

Healing needs more than an open vessel, the review argues. Local perfusion, infection control, and pressure relief all matter. Viable tissue and the patient's reserves count as well. Two landmark trials showed results hinge on who is studied. A checklist named PIPPP bundles the checks for clinicians. It is offered as a hypothesis, not a proven rule. Slow area shrinkage should trigger a plan rethink.
pmc-13682480:
William Mouton and co-authors trace a vicious cycle in severe COVID-19 in this 2026 study. Virus protein in the blood, called antigenemia, marks the worst cases, but what drives the virus into the bloodstream was unclear. The team profiled patients across three hospital cohorts, with mild COVID and severe flu patients as comparisons.

Blood and nose samples were checked against forty-five host and viral measures. Sustained activity of type I interferon, a front-line antiviral signal, paired with the viral protein in a self-feeding loop. Single-cell data and airway models helped pin down drivers of the spread. The analysis also weighed the pattern against the risk of dying in hospital.
pmc-13682580:
Andrew Kirkpatrick and co-authors tell, in twenty twenty-six, the story of a pioneering trauma room in Calgary, Canada, and the lessons of its decline. The room, called RAPTOR, merged imaging scans with surgery in one space. Bleeding patients could get scans and operations without moving. It opened in twenty thirteen as the first such room designed by a trauma program. At the time, it was seen as a shift in care. Since then, the space has grown outdated and fallen out of favor with key users.

The authors weigh the room's physical, operational, and admin parts against past literature. The concept has great merit for saving lives, they say. But such costly rooms must be future-proofed, or they fade fast.
pmc-13684580:
Jariel Ramírez-Virella and eight co-authors test a brain-targeted compound that curbs eating in obese mice without the side effects of its drug family. Activating the neurotensin receptor suppresses feeding, but one signaling route causes problems. A modulator called SBI-553 favors a gentler route.

Lean mice on normal food ate no less under either dose tested. Obese mice on a high-fat diet ate less right away at both doses. The higher dose also cut refeeding after hunger in both diet groups and reduced weight regain in obese mice. Movement and wheel running stayed normal throughout. The team presents the compound as a candidate obesity strategy.
pmc-13684780:
Yu Zhang and co-authors present PRS-CARV, a frame that improves genetic risk scores by adding rare variants, in a 2026 paper. Standard scores rely on common variants because rare effects are hard to estimate without huge sequencing cohorts. Their method uses summary data plus notes on what variants do.

The frame merges rare variant burden scores with common-variant scores. In simulations it beat common-variant scores throughout. In a real pregnancy and heart health cohort with whole-genome data, adding rare variants improved prediction of lipid traits by a few to eleven percent. The authors argue the method makes rare data usable without new large cohorts, aiding precision medicine.
pmc-13687180:
Hao Tang, Helene Fachim, Michael Harte, and Gavin Reynolds test whether a growth factor's link to an inflammation pathway breaks down in Alzheimer's disease, in a study from 2026. The growth factor, BDNF, supports brain cells. The pathway, the NLRP3 inflammasome, drives inflammation. Both are tied to the disease, but their tie to each other in human brain tissue was untested.

The team used post-mortem temporal cortex from patients and controls. In controls, BDNF gene activity and its chemical tagging tracked levels of several inflammation genes in a tidy way. In Alzheimer's brains, those links were lost. A potassium channel gene instead tracked BDNF in the disease group alone. The authors read this as a rewired relation that may shape the disease.
pmc-13688780:
Yunbin Fan and co-authors link cadmium, a toxic metal in the environment, to osteoarthritis through a gene better known from brain disease. Mining health survey data, they found higher blood cadmium tracked with more arthritis in a dose-wise pattern. Network and machine learning tools then singled out the gene APP as a hub.

Cell maps placed APP mostly in fibrocartilage cells, turned up across arthritis cartilage. Genetic evidence hinted APP normally protects joints, but cadmium-driven inflammation may flip its processing toward harm. Patient blood checks backed the immune angle. The authors propose APP as a screening and treatment lead.
pmc-13689380: The authors sequence four full genomes of a cattle virus found in farmed white-tailed deer in Florida. Bovine viral diarrhea virus type 2 had never had a complete coding genome published from Florida deer. The four isolates came from deer found dead in 2018, and all belonged to sub-genotype a of the virus's second type. The sequences give veterinarians and wildlife researchers a reference for spotting this virus in deer herds and for comparing deer strains with cattle strains.
pmc-13689880:
Alina Murji and co-authors described a case in 2026 of a heart tumor that blocked blood flow and caused fainting in rural Tanzania. A woman aged 20 years came to a local health center after repeated fainting spells. A bedside ultrasound scan at the point of care showed a mass inside her heart.

She was sent to a regional hospital, where a fuller team workup found a myxoma in the left lower chamber. The growth blocked the outlet at times, which fit her fainting. She was cleared for surgery and had the mass removed at the national hospital. The authors stress bedside scans, heart imaging, and clear referral steps. Their case shows how linked local and national care can bring heart surgery within reach in places with few resources.
pmc-13693080:
Dhananjay Alagundagi and co-authors published a study in 2026 on the gene-control messages breast cancer cells ship out in tiny vesicles under nutrient stress. Such vesicles ferry proteins and RNA between cells. Mining patient vesicle data and two cell lines, the team hunted small RNAs changed by starvation and mapped their target genes. Network tools picked out hub genes for lab checks.

Twenty-five small RNAs shifted, with thousands of predicted targets. Two hub genes stood out, though neither tracked patient survival. One small RNA and one hub transcript rode abundantly in vesicles from both cell lines. Another RNA stayed mostly inside cells. The authors name these as candidate parts of a stress communication network.
pmc-3428680:
Deng, Jiang, Yang, and co-authors present network methods for studying microbial communities. Learning how species in a community interact, and how they respond to change in nature, is a central goal in ecology. Defining network structure in a microbe community is very hard, though.

Microbial diversity is extremely high, and most interactions cannot be observed directly. Their analysis builds networks from survey data, linking species that rise and fall together. Such maps help predict how groups react to pollution, warming, or drugs, and which members hold a community together.
pmc-5076380:
Eldridge, Chan, Campbell, and their co-authors extended the CONSORT statement in 2016 to pilot and feasibility trials. CONSORT is a guideline that improves the transparency and quality of reporting for randomized controlled trials. Pilot and feasibility trials, which test whether a full trial can be run, were often reported poorly.

The extension adapts CONSORT items to these smaller, preparatory studies. It stresses aims such as testing recruitment and procedures, rather than judging treatment effects early. Clear reporting helps funders decide whether a full trial is worth its cost. It also stops weak pilot results from being oversold as evidence of benefit.
pmc-5708080:
Curtis Rueden, Johannes Schindelin, Mark Hiner, and many others described ImageJ2 in 2017. ImageJ is a long-running image analysis program used across biology and beyond. It is loved for its simple macros and the many plug-ins users share.

ImageJ2 rebuilds that base to handle modern image data, which can be huge and have many dimensions. It keeps the old interface and plug-ins working while adding a cleaner core for developers. Labs can keep trusted workflows and still handle new kinds of images. The paper explains the design choices that let old and new parts work together.
pmc-6941980:
Inmaculada Martínez-Reyes and Navdeep Chandel reviewed mitochondrial metabolites in health and disease in 2020. Mitochondria are signaling hubs that help set cell fate, not mere power plants. Their inner cycle, the TCA cycle, sits at the center of that signaling.

Metabolites from the cycle leak signals that steer gene activity, immune behavior, and growth. Broken cycle enzymes cause cancers and metabolic disease through those signals. The review connects classic biochemistry to new findings on cell communication. It reframes a textbook pathway as a control board for physiology. Worked disease examples include cancer, diabetes, and immune disorders driven by faulty cycle signals.
pmc-7299280:
Thomas Rogers and colleagues reported in 2020 that they had isolated powerful antibodies able to block SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. They reasoned that people who had recovered from the infection would carry antibodies shaped by real encounters with the virus. Finding the strongest of those antibodies was the first step toward turning them into a treatment.

The team screened blood from survivors, picked out the antibodies that stopped the virus most completely, and tested the best candidates in a small animal model. The leading antibodies protected the animals from disease. Published during the first year of the pandemic, the study showed that a survivor's own defenses could be copied into a drug, a path several treatments later followed.
pmc-8352980:
Sandra Lopez-Leon and colleagues pooled the evidence in 2021 on the lasting effects of COVID-19, counting more than fifty of them. Their systematic review and meta-analysis gathered studies that followed patients for weeks to months after they had supposedly recovered. They searched major medical literature collections to find every relevant follow up study available at the time.

Combining the results, the authors estimate how common each lingering problem was, from fatigue and breathlessness to hair loss and trouble concentrating. The sheer range of affected organs surprised many readers. The review gave clinicians and health systems an early map of the long tail of the disease, and it underlined the need for dedicated follow up care.
podcast-dannyjones-AziCjLnp780:
Dennis McKenna is a pharmacologist who has studied psychedelic plants for half a century, and the brother of the famed psychonaut Terence McKenna. With Danny Jones, he discusses the beings users of DMT report meeting in that drug's brief, intense state, and the ancient roots he traces for such encounters.

McKenna approaches the entities question as a scientist who has also had the experiences, which makes him an unusual witness. He separates what the chemistry does from what the visions mean, and refuses easy answers in both directions. Jones presses him on whether the beings are real. The episode preserves a serious researcher's fullest public thinking on a subject science mostly avoids, delivered with more honesty about uncertainty than either believers or skeptics usually allow.
podcast-dannyjones-EpW2lFqxx80:
Robert Salas was an Air Force officer stationed at a nuclear missile base in 1967 when, by his account, a glowing object hovered over the gate and his missiles went offline. On Danny Jones's podcast, the former nuclear warfare officer argues that something disturbing is still interfering with America's nuclear arsenal.

Salas has told his story to Congress and journalists for decades, and other veterans have reported similar shutdowns. The military's explanations differ, and no physical proof has settled the matter. What the episode offers is a trained officer's testimony, consistent over a lifetime, about the most sensitive weapons on earth. Jones questions him closely. Listeners must decide what such testimony is worth, which is exactly the problem the disclosure debate keeps circling.
podcast-dannyjones-LQZtTgA1N80:
Physicist Matthew Szydagis works on dark matter detection deep underground. He joins Danny Jones to discuss a startling extension of his field. It is evidence, as he presents it, that UFOs have been present on earth for a million years. His path runs from particle physics to the fossil and historical record of strange objects.

Szydagis applies a detector scientist's habits to fringe material, asking what would count as data and what is only story. Jones follows him from laboratory practice to ancient reports. The million-year claim is Szydagis's own reading, not his field's consensus, and the episode labels it by its framing. Listeners get something rare in this series: a working experimentalist explaining, carefully and on the record, why he thinks the UFO evidence deserves laboratory-grade attention.
podcast-joerogan-LeCpHugyI80:
Biogerontologist Aubrey de Grey joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 638, an early entry in the show's science run. De Grey argues that aging is a kind of damage the body can, in time, be repaired against. When this aired, the idea still sounded like science fiction to most ears.

He lays out the seven kinds of damage he wants medicine to fix, and his guess at the timeline. Rogan asks what a world without aging would do to work, family, and meaning. The episode preserves a bold claim at an early stage, from the man who made ending aging a public cause.
podcast-joerogan-RD-9Ghvt480:
Duncan Trussell's episode 1313 of the Joe Rogan Experience is another entry in the show's longest friendship. Trussell, comedian and host of a family-hour podcast of his own, treats Rogan's studio like a second home. Their talks need no news hook to get going.

The conversation drifts across psychedelic tales, the puzzle of the self, and the jokes Trussell builds from both. Rogan keeps one foot on the ground, telling his own stories between the flights. The episode is a pure example of the pair's chemistry, the blend of stand-up and soul talk that made Trussell a signature guest.
rochester-poems-1680:
The Works of the Right Honourable John, Earl of Rochester, are printed here for the booksellers of London and Westminster, in an edition dated 1718 and priced at one shilling. Its title page promises satires, songs, translations, and other occasional poems. A Satire against Mankind leads the contents, at page three.

Tunbridge-Wells, a satire, follows, with an imitation of Horace and A Satire against Marriage. A Letter from Artemisa in the Town to Cloe in the Country and The Maim'd Debauchee stand in the list. Upon Nothing, The Advice, The Discovery, and an elegy from Ovid's Amours show the range of Rochester's wit, grave and wild by turns.
scheele-air-and-fire-1780:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele was a Swedish apothecary who built a great lab life on a small wage. His work on air and fire came out in German in 1777, then in English in 1780. He did his best work in small towns, far from the great schools.

Scheele found the gas we now call oxygen on his own, and named it fire air. He printed his claim late, so the fame went to men who spoke first in public. The book is his own record, and it shows a fine hand at trials.
shabistari-gulshan-i-raz-whinfield-1880:
Mahmud Shabistari was a Persian poet of Tabriz. In 1317 he answered seventeen questions on Sufi doctrine in verse, and he called the poem Gulshan-i Raz, the Rose Garden of Mystery. E. H. Whinfield published his English version in 1880, with an introduction and notes drawn from the great commentary of Lahiji. The Persian text pages are left out of this copy; the English matter is complete.

Question by question, Shabistari treats the self, the heart, the beloved, wine, and the tavern of ruin as signs of the soul's road to God. His answers became the pocket summa of Persian Sufism. Students memorized the couplets for six centuries. Whinfield's version was the first door into the garden for English readers.
sixth-and-seventh-books-of-moses-1880:
The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses, in this 1880 English edition prepared under Johann Scheibel's name, is a German folk grimoire ascribed to Moses. A grimoire is a handbook of spells, seals, and conjurations for practical use. No book of spells traveled further in American folk practice.

Its pages give seals, psalms, and formulas for healing, finding treasure, binding enemies, and turning luck. German settlers carried it into Pennsylvania Dutch country, and from there it passed into African-American hoodoo practice. Conjure workers treated the book itself as a power object, kept wrapped and hidden like a weapon.
sixth-seventh-books-moses-1880:
The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses claim to print the lost magic books of Moses himself. This English edition of 1880 carried the German folk text to American readers. Packed with Solomonic seals, psalm charms, and conjurations, it became the most famous American grimoire of its kind.

In Pennsylvania Dutch country, the book became the backbone of pow-wow magic. Healers used its seals and words for cures, protection, and treasure. Copies passed through farm families as working tools, sometimes feared as much as valued. The 1880 printing fixed the text that spread through German America. Charms and cures from that world are still whispered where the book is kept.
the-afghan-wars-1839-42-and-1878-80: Archibald Forbes wrote The Afghan Wars 1839-42 and 1878-80. Portraits and plans support the text. A front plate shows Sir Frederick Roberts. Part one lists the first war's chapters. The March to Cabul comes first. Two years of occupation follow. The Road to Ruin and The Catastrophe come next. The siege and defence of Jellalabad follows. Retribution and Rescue closes that part. Part two opens the second war. Two campaigns and a lull before the storm start it.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Old Age and Death, the closing part of Spanish Passions in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, is not Casanova's own narrative but an editorial appendix and supplement. It follows the 1894 London edition in Arthur Machen's translation, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. The editors admit uncertainty: the author may have died before finishing, or the concluding volumes were destroyed, or the manuscript fell into bad hands. Materials for continuing the story are extremely fragmentary.

What can be told comes largely from the Prince de Ligne's memoirs. Pardoned at last, Casanova returned to Venice as a secret agent of the State Inquisitors, in plain language a spy, and made an indifferent one. Later he became librarian to Count Waldstein at the Castle of Dux, near Teplitz. There he spent fourteen years, resenting bad coffee, ill-cooked macaroni, barking dogs, and small tables.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-30:
Headed volume thirty-two in its own pages, though the record calls it volume thirty, this portion covers 1579 and 1580 in chapter two. Parma feints at Antwerp, invests Maastricht, and negotiates with Walloon envoys in his camp amid festivities that produce a treaty of reconciliation.

Religious tumults shake Antwerp and Utrecht while Orange enforces religious peace. At Maastricht mining and countermining, attacks on two gates, and gradual encroachment end with the town taken and a horrible massacre, followed by solemn thanksgiving. Negotiation and patient siege-craft advance together steadily under Parma's guiding hand.
tob-0144-56880:
After the sweeping systems of the first two volumes, volume three of The Secret Doctrine gathers looser material. Blavatsky left essays, fragments, and notes on occult history and symbolism, much of it unfinished at her death in 1891. Editors shaped the mass into a third volume.

Readers find teachings on hidden adepts, the inner meaning of symbols, and the secret history of religions. The tone shifts from chapter to chapter, since the pieces were written for different purposes. Fans prize the volume for hints dropped nowhere else. Newcomers fare better starting with volume one, then returning here.
tob-0180:
Cairo, 1904: Crowley said a voice named Aiwass dictated the Book of the Law to him over three days. The short, fierce text became the central scripture of Thelema, his new religion. Its best-known line lays down the law of the new age: do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law.

Three chapters speak in the voices of Egyptian gods, mixing command, prophecy, and riddling verse. Followers treat each line as charged with meaning; critics see a curiosity of occult history. Either way, few short texts have founded so much. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-9480:
Pindar, the leading lyric poet of ancient Greece, wrote odes to honor men who won at the Olympic Games. The Olympian Odes praise victors in running, wrestling, boxing, and chariot racing. Morice's English translation is the version named for this entry.

Each ode mixes praise of the winner with myths of gods and heroes linked to his city or family. Pindar warns winners to stay humble, since gods give success and can take it away. His grand, dense verse set the pattern for praise poetry in the West, and later poets from Horace onward studied him closely.
un-ga-res-a-69-80:
Peace around the Mediterranean Sea is the broad theme of Resolution A/69/80, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The lands that ring the sea, the text holds, bear the chief duty for its peace, safety, and joint work. It welcomes the steps of Euro-Mediterranean states to deepen their ties, above all in the fight against terror, through the joint code agreed at Barcelona in 2005.

Past pledges and meetings of the shore states are recalled in force. A fresh push came in 2008, when the Paris summit launched a stronger pact, the Union for the Mediterranean. The vote keeps the sea's peace framed as a shared task, from Gibraltar to the Levant.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Hosted under the Resolution 180 label, the text here is the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women. The General Assembly adopted the treaty on 18 December 1979, through resolution 34/180. An opening note explains the convention's background. It turns the earlier declaration against discrimination against women into a binding treaty. An expert committee watches over it.

The articles define discrimination against women. They then require states to ban it in law and in daily life. They cover voting and public office, nationality, and schooling. They also cover jobs and equal pay, and health care. They cover equality in marriage and family life. They call for an end to traffic in women.

Resolution 69/80 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns security and cooperation in the Mediterranean region. It treats Mediterranean security as closely tied to European and international security. It calls on states of the region to join disarmament and non-proliferation instruments. It calls on them to report military spending openly. It encourages joint action against terrorism, organized crime and drug trafficking. A further report is requested from the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-1380:
Western Sahara's referendum mission received a three-month renewal in late 2001. On 27 November 2001 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 28 February 2002. The Secretary-General had written to the Council that month. The Council recalled its backing of his envoy's search for a settlement. The dispute between Morocco and the Polisario Front remained unresolved.

The Secretary-General owed an interim report by 15 January 2002. A fuller assessment had to arrive by 18 February. The Council stayed seized of the matter. Short renewals like this one kept the ceasefire under watch. They also reflected how far the parties were from agreeing on a vote.
un-sc-res-1480:
Timor-Leste's support mission gained a final full year in May 2003. On 19 May 2003 the Security Council extended UNMISET until 20 May 2004. The Council praised the Timorese people and government. Their young state was building its institutions on democratic values. It also praised the mission's work under the Secretary-General's special representative. UNMISET was helping to train the national administration and police.

The extension kept United Nations backing in place for a second year of independence. The mission's name recalled its task, support for East Timor. Its staff worked beside Timorese officials rather than ruling directly. That marked a change from the earlier transitional administration. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter.
un-sc-res-1580: From 2004 comes Resolution 1580, a Security Council act preserved through an English Wikisource transcription of the official record. The document's authority rests on its form as much as its content: a single agreed text, voted once, binding in effect. The entry keeps that text complete, including the closing calls for follow-up reports.
un-sc-res-1680:
Lebanon's sovereignty resolution gained a progress check on 17 May 2006. The Secretary-General's third report on resolution 1559 (2004), dated 18 April 2006, noted real gains through the Lebanese national dialogue. Other parts lagged. Militias were not broken up or disarmed. State control did not run over all territory, and arms had moved into Lebanon for militias in the past six months. Beirut's prime minister had addressed the Council in April.

The Council repeated its call to apply resolution 1559 in full. All states and parties named in the report were told to cooperate at once. Syria was strongly encouraged to answer Lebanon's request for border talks and diplomatic ties. The Council praised Lebanon's steps against arms smuggling and welcomed the national dialogue's decision to disarm Palestinian militias outside the camps. It backed the Secretary-General and his envoy in their work.
un-sc-res-1780: In 2007 the Council voted Resolution 1780 into the record, and the text is preserved here via English Wikisource. The fifteen members' product is a single document with two voices: the preamble's measured assessment and the operative part's direct instructions. Readers who need to know what the Council required can go straight to those numbered lines.
un-sc-res-180:
African states brought a complaint to the Council. Thirty-two of them raised the case of lands under Portuguese rule. Resolution 180 was adopted on 31 July 1963. It recalls Assembly texts on those lands. The Assembly had called them Non-Self-Governing Territories. That status comes from the UN Charter. It points toward full freedom in time.

The Council confirms Assembly Resolution 1514. That text dates from 1960. It called for quick steps to hand power to local peoples. Their freely stated wishes were to guide the change. Race, creed, and colour were not to bar anyone. The Council also rejects Portugal's stance. Portugal called its colonies overseas parts of itself. The Council says that stance clashes with these principles.
un-sc-res-1880:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1880, adopted on 30 July 2009. A presidential election was set for 29 November 2009 under the Ouagadougou peace deal. Key reunification steps had to finish by September, two months before the vote. The peacekeeping mission and the French force backing it were near the end of their terms.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends both mandates until 31 January 2010. The mission must help the parties finish the remaining peace tasks. Disarmament of militias and former fighters continues. The electoral commission gets technical and logistical support for a safe vote. The mission also guards human rights work and helps restore police and courts across the country.
un-sc-res-280:
Lebanon brought the Council to Resolution 280, adopted on 19 May 1970 by eleven votes to none, with four abstentions. Israeli forces had struck deep into Lebanon on 12 May. The Council had already demanded a full pullout that same day. Earlier warnings after past raids had gone unheeded.

The Council calls the attack planned ahead and large in scale. It condemns Israel for breaking its duties under the Charter. It deplores Israel's failure to obey the earlier texts on Lebanon. Such armed attacks, the Council declares, can no longer be stood for. If they recur, the Council warns, it will weigh firm steps under the Charter to enforce its word.
un-sc-res-380:
Morocco's Green March entered Western Sahara in November 1975. Hundreds of thousands of civilians walked into the territory. The Council had twice told Morocco to call the march off. Its president had appealed directly to the king. The march went ahead anyway. On 6 November 1975 the Council deplored that it had taken place. The situation, it said, had seriously deteriorated.

Morocco had to withdraw all the marchers from the territory at once. All parties had to avoid acts that could raise tension further. They also had to cooperate with the Secretary-General. The Assembly's own review of the territory's status ran in parallel. Spain left within months, and Morocco took control of most of the territory.
un-sc-res-580:
South Africa's deadly raid into Lesotho was condemned on 30 December 1985. Lesotho's letter of 23 December told of unprovoked and premeditated killings. Six South African refugees and three Lesotho nationals lay dead in Maseru. The Council recalled resolution 527 (1982), passed after an earlier South African raid on the same city.

The Council strongly condemned the killings and the violence done against Lesotho, in flagrant breach of its sovereignty. South Africa had to pay full and adequate compensation for the loss of life and damage. Lesotho's right to give sanctuary to the victims of apartheid was reaffirmed. Member states were asked to give Lesotho urgent economic help to strengthen its power to receive and keep refugees. South Africa was called to settle its disputes by peaceful means. It also had to honor its pledge not to destabilize its neighbors or let its soil serve attacks on them.
un-sc-res-80:
Kashmir's demilitarization was pressed by the Security Council on 14 March 1950. The United Nations Commission for India and Pakistan had won agreement on a cease-fire, a cease-fire line from July 1949, and a plebiscite plan for the state's future. A Canadian general's talks on troop withdrawals had been reported to the Council. Both governments won praise for their statesmanlike steps so far.

The Council called on India and Pakistan to prepare and carry out a demilitarization programme within five months. It decided to appoint a United Nations Representative to push the process and help settle remaining disputes. The two governments were told to keep the cease-fire faithfully and guard law and order. The Council thanked the commission and the general for their work. It agreed the commission would be wound up one month after both sides reported the representative's appointment accepted.
un-sc-res-980: Judge Sir Robert Yewdall Jennings resigned from the International Court of Justice in 1995. His departure took effect on 10 July that year. On 22 March 1995 the Security Council set the date to fill the vacancy. The election would be held on 12 July 1995. It would take place at a Council meeting and at a General Assembly meeting. The Assembly was in its forty-ninth session. The short text performs only that scheduling task.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The Sahara envoy's compromise talks frame this extension of 2001. On 27 November, the Council adopted Resolution 1380 without dissent. It took note of the Secretary-General's letter of 12 November. The vote mission, MINURSO, was marking time that year. The envoy was testing if Morocco and the Polisario Front could take a deal instead of the stalled vote.

The text extends MINURSO's mandate to 28 February 2002. An interim report is due by 15 January. A full assessment must follow by 18 February. The Council stays seized of the matter in the meantime. Those February reports listed four paths for the territory. They set the agenda for debate through 2002 and 2003.

One year after Timor-Leste's independence, the Council kept its support mission there running. Resolution 1480 passed unanimously on 19 May 2003. The mission was called UNMISET. It was helping the young state build courts and police. It also supported administration and defense forces. Slowly, it was handing power to local officials.

The mandate now ran to 20 May 2004, the planned finish date. The text underlines police training as a top priority. It welcomes better ties between Timor-Leste and Indonesia. It also presses for border agreements. And it demands justice for serious crimes committed during the violence of 1999.

A military mutiny on 6 October 2004, in which senior officers were assassinated, shook Guinea-Bissau's fragile transition, and on 22 December 2004 its United Nations office is extended and reshaped. UNOGBIS, the Peace-Building Support Office, had watched over the transition. Legislative elections had been held that March, but the new institutions remained weak.

UNOGBIS is renewed as a special political mission with a revised mandate. The office is to help strengthen state institutions, support the rule of law and the fight against impunity, and assist the transition toward planned presidential elections. The Secretary-General is asked to review the office's work, and the National Assembly is urged to act on reforms, including in the security sector.

Resolution 1680, passed on 17 May 2006, pushes Lebanon and Syria on the loose ends of a 2004 text. That text, 1559, had told all armed groups in Lebanon to lay down their arms. It had told all foreign troops to leave. Talks among Lebanon's own leaders had moved some points on. But armed groups still held their guns. Fresh arms had crossed into Lebanon in the past six months.

The Council urged Syria to say yes to Lebanon's wish for two things. One was a clear line for their shared border. The other was full, normal ties, with envoys in each other's capitals. It also told all sides to carry out 1559 in full, and asked for fresh news on progress.

Haiti's stabilization mission, MINUSTAH, is extended until 15 October 2008 on 15 October 2007. Haiti had completed its local and municipal elections in April 2007, the final round of a long electoral cycle. Progress on security, the rule of law, and development are linked as gains that reinforce each other.

The Secretary-General's plan to reconfigure the mission, trimming its military side and strengthening its police, is endorsed. MINUSTAH is to keep backing the Haitian National Police, help reform the justice and prison systems, and support border management. It is also asked to give technical expertise to the government and to work with the United Nations country team on aid and recovery across the country.

Portugal's African territories are taken up on 31 July 1963, in a case brought by thirty-two African member states. The General Assembly had declared the territories Non-Self-Governing and had called for power to pass to their peoples at once. The Council's own Angola resolution of 1961 had gone unheeded by Lisbon.

The Assembly's declaration on ending colonial rule is confirmed, and Portugal's policies are affirmed to run against the Charter. Lisbon is called on to grant the territories' peoples their rights, including self-determination leading to independence. All states are asked to stop giving Portugal any help that lets it continue repression, and to block arms sales for that purpose. The Secretary-General is to report by 31 October 1963.

Côte d'Ivoire's election date is locked in as UNOCI is renewed in Resolution 1880, adopted on 30 July 2009. Under the Ouagadougou Political Agreement the first round of the presidential election was set for 29 November 2009. Voter registration was complete. But the provisional voters list was still unpublished. Human rights violations, including sexual violence, persisted.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews UNOCI's mandate until 31 January 2010, centred on supporting free, open, fair, and transparent elections. It insists the Ivorian actors respect the 29 November date. It says any postponement would break faith with the Ouagadougou Agreement. It demands the provisional voters list be published before the end of August 2009. The Secretary-General's Special Representative must certify the voters list and every electoral stage under the five-criteria framework. The Council warns it is ready to impose targeted sanctions on anyone threatening the electoral process.

Resolution 2580, adopted on 8 June 2021, is a single operative sentence from the Security Council. It decides who should lead the United Nations next. Having considered the question, the Council recommends to the General Assembly that António Guterres be appointed Secretary-General of the United Nations for a second term. The term runs from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2026. Under the UN Charter, the General Assembly makes the appointment on the Council's recommendation, so this brief text carries the full weight of the choice.

Israeli forces had struck deep into Lebanon in May 1970. Resolution 280, adopted on 19 May 1970, was the Council's angry response. Eleven members backed it. Colombia, Nicaragua, Sierra Leone, and the United States abstained. Both Lebanon and Israel had presented their cases.

The Council judged the attack planned and large in scale. It condemned Israel for striking in breach of the Charter. It repeated a solemn warning: further attacks would not be tolerated. If they came, members would consider firm steps to enforce their decisions. The text also mourns the deaths and damage caused by the fighting.

A vast march of Moroccan crowds crossed into Western Sahara in November 1975. King Hassan II had called the Green March to claim the land. Spain was set to quit the colony. The Council had begged the king to call the march off. He did not. Resolution 380 passed by common consent on 6 November 1975, the day the march crossed the line.

The Council voiced its grief that the march had gone ahead. Morocco had to pull all marchers out of the land at once. All sides had to work with the UN chief. His task came from two texts passed that fall. The vote did no good in the short run. Morocco held the land. A war with the Polisario Front ran for years. The file marks the start of a long, stuck fight.

Resolution 580, adopted on 30 December 1985, condemns a South African raid into Lesotho. The Council heard Lesotho's foreign minister describe unplanned, deliberate killings blamed on South Africa. Six South African refugees and three Lesotho nationals had been killed. Members said the attack broke Lesotho's sovereignty and was meant to punish the small kingdom for sheltering people fleeing apartheid.

The Council strongly condemns the killings and demands that South Africa pay full compensation for the lives lost and the damage done. It backs Lesotho's right to give shelter to victims of apartheid and asks member states to send urgent economic help so Lesotho can care for refugees. It demands steps to tear down apartheid and asks for a small UN presence in Maseru to watch the situation.

Resolution 80, adopted on 14 March 1950 by eight votes to none with two abstentions, restarts the UN effort on Kashmir. A UN commission for India and Pakistan had produced ceasefire and plebiscite agreements, and a Canadian general, A. G. L. McNaughton, had explored the remaining gaps in talks with both governments. Hostilities had stopped in January 1949 and a ceasefire line was drawn that July.

The Council praised both governments for the steps already taken, including agreeing that Fleet Admiral Chester Nimitz would serve as plebiscite administrator. It then moved to replace the commission with a single United Nations representative, who would press ahead with demilitarizing the state so the promised vote on Kashmir's future could be held.

Judge Sir Robert Yewdall Jennings, a British jurist on the International Court of Justice, resigned his seat effective 10 July 1995. Resolution 980, adopted on 22 March 1995, exists for one narrow reason: fixing the date on which his replacement on the world court would be elected.

The members chose 12 July 1995, two days after the resignation took hold. Voting would take place in parallel, at a Security Council meeting and during the General Assembly's forty-ninth session, because judges of the Court must be elected by both bodies. The text also records, in formal language, that Jennings's departure left a gap covering only the remainder of his original term.
uslaw-usc-t2-s180:
Section 180 of Title 2 of the United States Code orders a single legislative information system for Congress. In the age of the text, several systems gave Congress electronic access to its own documents. Duplication among them wasted money, and this section says so.

The stated purpose is to cut the cost of information support for Congress. The saving comes from ending duplication among the rival systems. A definition then fixes what counts as legislative information. It is information prepared within the legislative branch itself. The list begins with the text of publicly available bills and amendments. Committee hearings and committee reports are included. So is the text of the Congressional Record and data on the status of bills. The section builds one doorway to the working papers of Congress.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1980: Section 1980 of Title 2 of the United States Code bars the Capitol Police from running a mounted horse unit. It sits in Chapter 29 of Title 2, on the Capitol Police, in the subchapter on powers and duties, current through Public Law 119-134. The bar covers fiscal year 2006 and every fiscal year after it. Within sixty days of the Act's passage, the Chief of the Capitol Police had to transfer the unit's horses, equipment, and supplies then in hand to the Chief of the Park Police.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4580:
Section 4580 of Title 2 of the United States Code allows a lump sum payment for accrued yearly leave of Senate employees. It sits in Chapter 45 of Title 2, on congressional pay and benefits, in the Senate part. The version here is current through Public Law 119-134.

When a Senate employee's service ends, the head of the employing office may authorize payment for the leave built up. Two things must hold first. The office head must have approved a written leave policy that lets staff build up leave and sets when it may be paid. The head must also certify in writing to the Financial Clerk how many days are due. There must also be funds enough to cover the payment. The sum is capped at the lesser of twice the monthly rate of pay, or the daily rate times the days of leave due.
wallace-island-life-1880:
In Island Life, published in 1880, Wallace asks why islands hold such strange mixes of plants and animals. He draws on his years in Malaysia and on reports from sailors and collectors worldwide. Islands, he argues, are natural test cases for how life spreads and changes. The book grew from the same travels as his Malay Archipelago.

Wallace weighs two answers: creatures rafted or flew across seas, or old land bridges once joined now-split lands. He uses ice ages, sea depth, and fossils to test each island case by case. His work founded island biogeography and still guides the study of island species.
willis-improved-chart-for-recording-a-de: The scan pages here show the title pages, partly garbled, of a character chart by Professor A. B. Willis, and nothing else is present. The chart was made to record a reading of character by phrenology, physiognomy, and physiology. Those three arts judged a person by head shape, face, and body. Cameron, Amberg and Company printed it in Chicago in 1880. A Library of Congress stamp marks the copy. The full title repeats on a second page, calling the chart improved. No filled-in reading appears in these pages.
wood-order-zeuglodontia-nature-1880:
Searles Wood makes a bold claim for the sea serpent in his Nature note of 1880. Wood was a sage of old life forms. Ships oft told of a great long necked beast in far seas. He holds the beast could be a zeuglodon. Such whales of old ages had snake like frames. Thought long dead, one may yet live in deep seas men can't sweep.

His note is brief, grave, and writ for sages, not crowds. It gave the serpent a place in the tree of life. The row it sparked ran for years. It is a key text of that row.
yeates-affidavit-nsa-1980:
The National Security Agency fought in court to keep 156 UFO reports sealed, and its sworn word is this file. The in camera affidavit of Eugene Yeates, dated October 9, 1980, was sworn in the case of CAUS against the NSA. Yeates was chief of the agency's Office of Policy.

He tells the judge, in a closed filing, why each of the reports must stay dark. The papers were communications intelligence tied to foreign air and spy craft. Freed at last in 2009, with black bars still in place, the affidavit is the core file of NSA UFO secrecy. It shows the agency guarding its silence by law.
zola-attack-on-mill-1880:
Edmund Gosse translated The Attack on the Mill and its companion war sketches. Zola wrote the title tale in 1880, a decade after the Franco-Prussian War. The setting is a village mill on the day of a wedding feast.

Soldiers seize the mill in the midst of the joy, and the feast turns to slaughter. Few war stories in any language match its force and pity. The sketches around it extend the same bleak view of war's waste. Anger burns through every page at lives thrown away for pride and flags. Readers who know Zola only from the long novels will find his power in brief form here.
zollner-transcendental-physics-1880:
Johann Zollner claimed a fourth span of space in Transcendental Physics, his book in English from 1880. Zollner was a chief of star lore at Leipzig. He sat with Slade, a famed seer, and saw knots tied in sealed cords, rings passed through wood, and goods moved in ways no hand in our space could work, he swore.

A fourth span, with souls in it, is his bold key. Peers cried fraud and shame. Fans hailed a new age of science. The book is the row's most famed flash point. Its claims still spark heat.
